## The Complete Course of Patrology

Or the universal, complete, uniform, convenient, economical library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived from the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, carefully corrected through comparison with one another and with numerous manuscript codices; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of every page and indicating its subject matter; augmented with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is easy for the reader to discover which Fathers commented on the individual books of Scripture and in what places in their works they did so.

An edition of unsurpassed accuracy, and easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the very convenient form of the volumes and its consistent similarity throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection itself—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and little works previously scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works concerning every age, place, language, and literary form.

## Second Series

In which are published the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J. P. Migne, publisher of the universal library of the clergy, or of the complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology was printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition is sold for 1,200 French francs; the Greek-Latin for 1,300. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

## Historical Notice

(From Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*)

[Col. 0009A]

Smaragdus, abbot of Saint Michael on the Meuse in the diocese of Verdun, of the Order of Saint Benedict, was also previously a teacher who instructed the brothers of the monastery in grammar. In the year 810 he was at Rome at the conference between the pope and the legates of Charlemagne concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit. In 824, together with Frotharius, bishop of Toul, he was appointed judge by the emperor Louis the Pious in the dispute between Ismundus, abbot of Milan, and his monks. He left the following monuments of his talent:

1. A Commentary on the Gospels and Epistles to be read in the divine offices throughout the year. Strasbourg, 1536, folio. Trithemius calls it a *Postilla*. Possevinus, in volume II of his *Apparatus*, p. 418, and Wion, in *Lignum vitae*, II, 77, state that these sermons were translated into German by Caspar Hedio.

2. *The Diadem of Monks*, or concerning the virtues especially of clerics and monks, compiled from the sayings of the Fathers. Paris, 1532, octavo; 1640, duodecimo; Antwerp, 1540, octavo; and in the *Maxima Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XVI, p. 1305.

3. A Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict. Cologne, [Col. 0009B] 1575, folio. It was published after the Synod of Aachen held in 817, since it repeats certain of its statutes. It was wrongly published among the works of Rabanus Maurus, because various passages occur in this commentary that Smaragdus repeated from *The Diadem of Monks* and *The Royal Way*. John a Bosco published the verses prefixed to this commentary in the *Bibliotheca Floriacensis*, vol. I, p. 290.

4. *The Royal Way*, of the same character as *The Diadem of Monks*, is found in Dacherius, *Spicilegium*, vol. V, p. 1, earlier edition, and vol. I, p. 238, later edition.

5. *Acts of the Roman Conference*, in the year 810, in Sirmond, [Col. 0009C] *Councils of Gaul*, vol. II, p. 256; Labbe, [Col. 0010A] vol. VII, p. 1194; Hardouin, V, p. 969. In the Heilsbrunn Library there is a parchment codex whose title presents it as Book II of the *Conferences*, containing sixteen chapters. Whether it should be referred to this work or is instead a separate work, I cannot say. See Hocker’s Catalogue, p. 11.

6. The letter of Charlemagne to Pope Leo concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit is also attributed to our author, in the same place, p. 1199; Hardouin, p. 973.

7. A letter to Louis Augustus, written jointly in the name of Frotharius, bishop of Toul, and Smaragdus the abbot, is found as the third among Frotharius’s letters, in André Duchesne, *Writers of the History of the Franks*, vol. II, p. 71.

8. *The Greater Grammar*, or Commentary on Donatus. Mabillon saw a manuscript copy in the monastery of Corbie, from which he published the preface and several specimens of the book in his *Analecta*, p. 358. The work is divided into fourteen books; in another codex a fifteenth book, on Orthography, is appended. In it he produced examples chiefly from sacred rather than profane authors, and sometimes introduced the etymologies of Gothic and Frankish words.

9. A Commentary on the Prophets; and

10. A History of the Monastery of Saint Michael remain unpublished. You may read various matters concerning this Smaragdus in the *Chronicle of the Monastery of Saint Michael*, presented in Mabillon’s *Analecta*, pp. 350 ff., and in Mabillon’s note, p. 357; in the *Literary History of France*, vol. IV, p. 439; Bulaeus, *History of the University of Paris*, vol. I, p. 641; and Leyser, *History of the Poets of the Middle Ages*, p. 284.

[Col. 0009D] [Note: [Col. 0009D] We reprint this according to the extremely rare edition of Georg Ulrich, the printer Andlaw, issued at Strasbourg in March 1536, which the most learned D. Jung, director of the Strasbourg library, kindly supplied to us. The chronological notice given on the title page is demonstrably false from many monuments. Fabricius in his *Bibliotheca*, Dacherius in his *Spicilegium*, and the authors of the *Literary History of France* judge that our Smaragdus was 150 years younger and should be assigned to the time of Louis the Pious; we follow them. EDITOR.]

## Of Smaragdus the Abbot, a Man Most Distinguished for Holiness and Learning

He lived in the year of Our Lord 970.

A learned and devout exposition of the Gospels and Epistles read in churches throughout the cycle of the year, gathered with remarkable yet lucid brevity from the principal Doctors of the Church—Origen, Jerome, Chrysostom, Ambrose, Augustine, Cyprian, Cyril, Gregory, Victor, Fulgentius, Cassiodorus, Eucherius, Tychonius, Figulus, Bede, Primasius, and others—extremely useful and necessary for all ministers of the Church who are prevented by limited means from obtaining each of these authors individually.

Recently discovered, revised, and published for the advancement of the Christian Church.

[Col. 0009]

## The Printer Sends Greetings to the Pious Reader

[Col. 0009D]

What Pliny writes in his *Natural History* about gems—that the majesty of nature is compressed within them, and that no part of nature is more marvelous—this, I may say without injustice, applies to Smaragdus, the author of this book. Whatever the Catholic Fathers—Origen, Hilary, Jerome, Augustine, Cyprian, Cyril, Gregory, Victor, Fulgentius, John Chrysostom, Cassiodorus, Eucherius, Tychonius, [Col. 0011A] Isidore, Figulus, Bede, and others—possess, he has gathered in these Collections like a jewel, with marvelous yet lucid brevity.

And since, as the authorities on rhetoric say, it is the same art to be able to discuss a subject at great length and to report it in few words, Smaragdus has sufficiently demonstrated through this labor how great his ability in expression is, although he is an abridger and a transmitter. For so he calls himself in the preface to his Collections: a transmitter, who, as it were, has diverted little streams from great rivers and the whirlpools of the sea; an abridger, who has compressed into a narrow compass and made an epitome of what others wrote at length.

I am not unaware, however, that a prodigious corruption of Latin and Greek books alike has resulted from epitomes. To this cause they attribute the loss of Livy, Florus, Theopompus, Trogus, Justinian’s imperial law, and the theological master of the *Sentences*. Not to mention how many of the best Greek authors we owe to these abridgers as losses. For what else do we possess of Stephen of Byzantium’s *On Cities* or of Hesychius except the mutilated epitome of each? [Col. 0011B]

Yet since in those times a rich supply of books was not available to everyone—and that outstanding gift of God, by which books are made known throughout the Christian world through the art of printing, had not yet been bestowed upon Germany eighty years ago through God’s indescribable benevolence—many good and Christian men wished, out of brotherly charity, to care for the things of others through this abbreviated path and through epitomes, for the public benefit of the churches.

Among these, therefore, our Smaragdus stands out. I would not doubt that if the holy Fathers themselves—Origen, Chrysostom, Augustine, and the others—were alive, they would by no means disapprove of their most sacred labors being distributed for the benefit of the churches, whether in whole or in part, through this Collection of his.

Alexander the Great wished to have himself engraved on an emerald, but by no one other than Pyrgoteles, unquestionably most distinguished in that art. In the same way, the Fathers could hardly have been displeased to have themselves engraved and, as it were, compressed by this Smaragdus of ours. For what he diligently gathered from every side, like a bee, from these excellent authors—whatever might shed light on the readings of the Epistles and Gospels, so that he might bring greater edification to the churches—he certainly did not do so in order that anyone, satisfied with this work, should read less attentively, much less reject altogether, those divine monuments of the Fathers from which he drew his material.

Rather, through this transmission he sought—and undoubtedly achieved—the result that many people, after tasting these little streams, would become more eager to drink from the springs, and, as the proverb says, would follow these rivers as guides to the sea. For what our transmitter here offers for tasting from the holy Fathers is of such a kind that it cannot fail to awaken a greater thirst for itself.

Those, however, who could not reach that vast sea of the most sacred labors which the holy Fathers left to the churches could at least enjoy through these little streams that heavenly water which the Lord, through the channels constituted by the works of the divine Fathers, has granted to us. He did this lest the less learned—those who have not been given the ability to draw better things from Scripture themselves—should pour upon Christ’s sheep water from their own or others’ stagnant pools, water which, even if not wholly harmful, would nevertheless contaminate and make less pure, less pleasing, and less wholesome the waters of salvation flowing from the fountain of Scripture. [Col. 0011D]

The word of God is indeed a lamp to our feet and a light to our paths. The word of Christ is truth, and the simple discourse of truth; and the best interpreter of all is Christ himself, the only-begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father, who also *ἐξηγήσατο*—that is, explained to us—all the things pleasing to the Father, John, chapter 1.

Nevertheless, since the holy Fathers, sharing in the Spirit of Christ, from whose fullness they received, have left us their holy thoughts and interpretations of Scripture, and since they do not wish these to be read otherwise than as attendants assigned to the queen, Holy Scripture, it would surely be the mark of an ungrateful heart to disdain these gifts of God—just as no queen is so exalted that she refuses the service of her attendants.

Formerly a single monastery might possess perhaps one book, and everyone would read it. Such was the heat and ardor for reading sacred things, and for handling them day and night. Later, as winter came on and reading grew cold, it happened that people possessed many books and no one read, while others were admitted to read only with reluctance, behaving as in the saying about the dog lying in the manger.

That monasteries and colleges were schools is clearer than anyone could deny—not only in the time of Smaragdus or in the preceding century, but even in the times of the apostles and apostolic men, as may be seen from Philo’s book *On the Contemplative Life of the Suppliants* (*περὶ βίου θεωρητικοῦ ἱκετῶν*). He calls them by the Greek word *σεμνεῖα*, that is, places of honorable people. Those who withdrew into them celebrated the mysteries of an honorable and chaste life; they read the books of the Law and the volumes of the Prophets, as well as hymns to God and other similar writings. Trained in these disciplines and exercises, they grew toward a perfect and blessed life through continual study.

From sunrise until evening, all their time was spent in exercises of study, by which they were imbued through the sacred writings with divine philosophy, bringing the teachings of the Fathers into allegorical [Col. 0012B] understanding, and so forth.

And John the Evangelist—although Amelius the Platonist calls him a barbarian, he nevertheless speaks things that learned Plato did not know and eloquent Demosthenes did not understand—when, after Domitian had been killed and Nerva had permitted him to return from exile to Ephesus, is said to have returned as though to his own school.

The best and most learned men were placed in charge of these schools, such as Pantaenus, Origen, Clement, Demetrius, Dionysius, Heraclas, and others. From these schools men who had advanced to that point were chosen as presbyters and bishops.

And what were the monasteries in Jerome’s time except schools in which there were men and women devoted to God, who devoted the whole time of their lives to learning and explaining the divine books, or to the sacred psalms and prayers?

With the passage of time—since nothing in human affairs is stable and every thing has its own old age—the condition of colleges and monasteries grew worse from day to day, and the praise of ancient times was overthrown, so that this song, wisely used among the ancients, could be applied to those times:

> The age of our fathers, worse than that of our grandfathers,  
> Brought forth us, more depraved,  
> Soon to give birth to an even more vicious offspring.

But this is not the place to lament such matters. Would that most monasteries today were what they were six hundred years ago, if they were not granted the opportunity to go farther—although every good person desires that they be directed and reformed toward the apostolic Pole Star—so that, if they were unwilling to read Holy Scripture itself, divinely inspired and useful for teaching, and the authors who interpret a purer theology, they might at least use these Collections and cultivate their own assigned portion.

And since everything is flourishing again in this age—piety, learning, honorable disciplines, and the study of languages—many people could be educated from the revenues of monasteries for this purpose, so that in time they might be useful and productive for the Christian commonwealth.

Cicero, though a secular man, was no less concerned with what the republic would be after his death than with what it was in his own time. Much greater concern rests upon spiritual men, and upon those for whom such generous provision has been made, that they may devote themselves so that many may eventually become fully qualified to teach.

Indeed, in order to bear witness to my earlier diligence and life as a *κοινοβίτης*—a member of a religious community—when this Smaragdus, which I had not previously seen in print, came into my hands in a copy that was neither complete nor well written, yet the abbot pleased me as a man learned in sacred literature, not ignorant of secular letters, sharp in intellect, composed in speech, and distinguished for the holiness of his life—for John of Spanheim writes of him in this way—I began to consider whether I might perhaps find something of Smaragdus somewhere among the useful books in our libraries, by which the stains of the copy that had been brought to me could be wiped away, its gaps joined, its confusions arranged, and its lacunae repaired.

For just as nature has hidden gems in the deepest places, while worthless things are readily found everywhere, [Col. 0013A] so this Smaragdus, too, was hitherto known to very few, so that not even his name was established with certainty.

And behold, as the saying goes, *ἀπὸ μηχανῆς*—“from the machine,” or by an unexpected intervention—I came upon two volumes of Smaragdus, skillfully written on parchment in ancient characters. With their help, and especially with the help of the *αὐτόγραφα*, and, so to speak, originals of the Catholic Fathers, with no small care, labor, and diligence I undertook to restore this author and, like a gem long hidden, bring him out of the darkness.

The Greek and Hebrew passages which the learned man cites several times—thereby giving us reason to suppose that he was by no means without knowledge of languages—were so mutilated and corrupted that scarcely anyone, however keen-sighted, could make out even the ashes and shadows of the letters.

As for the poems which he cites from Christian poets—Sedulius, Prudentius, and others—with which he sometimes makes his discourse shine like little stars and gleam with gems of thought, I took care that they might be read more easily and more clearly.

Therefore, excellent reader, judge kindly of this labor of mine, devoted to restoring and stripping clean this Smaragdus. [Col. 0014A]

Certainly, whatever judgment may be formed of this author, he composed this commentary from the most approved Fathers of the Church—Origen, Augustine, Chrysostom, and others—with such skill that anyone who reads it with a thirsting mind for truth will certainly experience what is attributed to gems: that they not only delight but also aid through definite remedies.

Such readers will receive from it not merely the benefits of learning and the pleasure of devout reading, but effective remedies against every disease of the soul. They will also be able to supply these remedies to others and will be equipped to devote faithful service to the Church of Christ, now—alas!—scattered and severely afflicted by no few dangers both to doctrine and to life.

Through this service, may the elect of Christ everywhere be joined together, advance, and grow daily more and more in the pure faith of Christ, in the knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness, and in the hope of eternal life, so that through many people the glory of God, the public good, and public integrity may be advanced. May Christ bring this to pass. Amen.

[Col. 0013]

# Life of Smaragdus

By Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim

Smaragdus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael in Saxony, of the Order of the holy Father Benedict, was a man highly learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, sharp in intellect, polished in speech, devout in life and conduct, and a celebrated regulator of monastic discipline.

In explaining the Holy Scriptures he made his name widely known and gained a great reputation for learning. For he wrote many distinguished volumes, of which the following survive:

One book on the Rule of our most holy Father Benedict.

One book on the entire Psalter.

Eleven books on the Epistles and Gospels throughout the cycle of the year.

One book of sermons to the brothers and to others.

Also a notable work on the virtues, which he entitled *The Diadem of Monks*.

He is also said to have written many other volumes on both divine and secular writings, which have not come into our hands.

He flourished during the times of the illustrious emperors Otto I and Otto II.

[Note: [Col. 0013B] Certainly an anachronism, as we have already said above. EDITOR.]

[Col. 0013]

# The Preface of the Lord Smaragdus to the Collections of Epistles and Gospels for the Seasons and Saints’ Days

[Col. 0013C]

Seeing that many people in the Church diligently seek the mystical meanings of the divine Scriptures and prefer to gather their typological fruits, I undertook to collect this one book, filled with the flowers of allegory, from many sources.

From the treatises and published sermons of the great Fathers—Hilary, Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, Cyprian, Cyril, Gregory, Victor, Fulgentius, John Chrysostom, Cassiodorus, Eucherius, Tychonius, Isidore, Figulus, Bede, Primasius, and from the writings of Pelagius and Origen, which must be read cautiously—I have acted both as a transmitter and as an abridger, as it were from great rivers and the whirlpools of the sea into little streams.

Thus, if someone lives under such pressure from natural sloth that he cannot seek much in the sacred writings through his own exertion, he will at least not cease to ruminate on these excerpts gathered and joined together by us, though they be but small.

For knowledge of sacred reading supplies a staff to the weak and weapons to the strong. It crushes the crafty ambushes of enemies with strength and happily promises eternal crowns to victors.

Therefore, like a dish filled with various delicacies, we place this little book before the diligent reader, so that when he has tasted its ambrosial flavor with the palate of his mind, he may exercise himself in the broadest field of the divine Scriptures and diligently seek the Lord’s word in abundance. May he embrace it as food that gives the soul divine life.

Strengthened by it through constant application, may he live more wisely in the present age and more happily in the age to come.

This too should be noted: just as the seasons and days correspond, so in this *Book of the Count* [Note: [Col. 0013D] Observe that Smaragdus calls this book the *Book of the Count*, although the reason cannot easily be determined. Some think that, since the Order of Saint Benedict has had many men born of illustrious ancestry, such as Ulrich, Conrad, and others, either Smaragdus was a count or he inscribed these Collections to a count. Or perhaps, because this compilation of Catholic teachers is like a handbook, so that it is always at hand like an inseparable companion. Yet when the bear is present, there is no need to search for its tracks. See Sigebert in his *Chronicles*.], readings from the Apostles or Prophets that correspond to the Gospels have been usefully placed according to words or actions.

With the help of divine grace, wherever I see an appropriate place to join their harmonies at the end of the exposition of the Gospel, I shall join them. Thus, by carefully observing how the readings answer one another with a harmonious voice and correspond in seasons, days, and actions, the diligent reader will find them without delay.

[Col. 0015]

# Verses of Smaragdus, Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Michael the Archangel

[Col. 0015A]

Whoever loves to know the typological meanings of the Law  
And desires to gather the life-giving fruits of the teachers,  
Seek the pen of this excellent little book;  
Examine its pages diligently and with discerning mind;  
Learn what typology it contains beneath its lifted veil.

It bears food for the soul, seasoned with the word of salvation;  
It is powerful in sacred and profoundly typological figures;  
It shines with meanings and gleams in joyful speech;  
It marks out bright fields of silver with a distinct boundary,  
And contains within its bosom, in a many-worded order,  
All the richly burdened gifts of God,  
Scattered with the seed of the prophets.

From their own labor the Fathers cut  
Golden metals from the earth, with God’s favor, [Col. 0015B]  
And from them, filled with polished speech, [Col. 0016A]  
I have striven, in my own modest measure, to compose these books.

From these I wished to join together this little book,  
Filled with sacred grace,  
With God inspiring me.

May it clearly unfold for me the Dindyma—the heights—of the Law,  
And show what it contains in sacred figures laid bare;  
May it disclose hidden things and reveal mysteries too.

It brings into the midst of sacred doctrine everything  
That long lay hidden, enclosed beneath a blind covering.  
May it, radiant, drive harmful lurking places from the mind,  
Break its bonds, remove the darkness from the heart,  
And illumine the fibers of the mind with sacred breath,

So that, drenched with heaven’s dew,  
Your heart’s rich field may be able,  
Through the cultivation of the teachers’ plough  
And the divine seed cast upon it,  
To yield a hundredfold harvest.

[Col. 0015]

# The Collections Begin

## On the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord

### Epistle of the Blessed Apostle Paul to the Romans, Chapter I

> “Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the Holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh; who was predestined to be the Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord, through whom we have received grace and apostleship, for the obedience of faith among all the nations, for his name, among whom you also are called by Jesus Christ our Lord.”

The word *epistle* is Greek and is said to derive from *ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐπιστέλλειν*, which means “to send,” because it is sent to those who are absent. Epistles were invented for this reason: so that we might inform absent persons if there is anything they ought to know. They are also called *apostles* from *ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐπιστέλλειν*, which, as I said, means “to send.”

[Col. 0015D]

### Paul

Victor, bishop of Capua, says:

> “He who was formerly called Saul the persecutor, after hearing a voice from heaven, ceased from his intention of persecution and was thereafter called Paul, from *ἀπὸ τῆς παύλης*, which means ‘from cessation.’”

(From Origen.)

Our first question seems to arise concerning Paul’s name: why is he who is called Saul in the Acts of the Apostles now called Paul?

We find in the divine Scriptures that certain names were changed—for example, Abram into Abraham, Sarai into Sarah, Jacob into Israel, and Simon into Peter. Some, however, used two names, such as Solomon, who was also called Jedidiah; Zedekiah, who was also called Jehoiachin; and Uzziah, who was also called Azariah.

Matthew is also Levi, and the one whom Matthew writes as Lebbaeus Mark records as Thaddaeus. In accordance with this custom, therefore, it seems to us that Paul also used two names. As long as he ministered to his own people, he was called Saul, a name that seemed more native to his ancestral designation. He was called Paul, however, when he wrote laws and commandments for the Greeks and the Gentiles.

For the statement of Scripture itself, “Saul, who is also Paul” (Acts 13), clearly does not indicate that Paul’s name was imposed upon him for the first time then, but shows that it was already an older designation.

### Servant of Jesus Christ

(From Origen.)

Let us ask why he who writes elsewhere, “You have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8), here declares himself a servant.

Whether we understand this according to the humility that the Lord taught when he said, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew 11), or as referring to him as an imitator of the one who “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2), we have not gone astray.

For the servitude of Christ is nobler than every freedom. What, then, is it to be Christ’s servant except to be a servant of the word of God, of wisdom, justice, truth, and all the virtues—which is Christ?

### Called to Be an Apostle, Set Apart

The name “called,” because it pertains to all who believe in Christ, may appear to be general, since each person is called according to what God foresees and chooses in him: one as an apostle, another as a prophet, another as a teacher (Ephesians 4).

In Paul, however, not merely a general calling to apostleship is designated, but also an election that followed according to the foreknowledge of God (Romans 8), in that he is said to have been set apart for the Gospel of God. Elsewhere he says of himself:

> “When it pleased God, who set me apart from my mother’s womb, to reveal his Son in me” (Galatians 1).

And in the Acts of the Apostles the Holy Spirit says:

> “Set apart for me Saul and Barnabas for the work to which I have chosen them” (Acts 13).

He who is not ignorant of the mind foresaw that Paul would labor more abundantly than all the others in the Gospel; that he would preach the Gospel of Christ in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness, and amid other dangers. Therefore he set him apart from his mother’s womb.

### For the Gospel of God

The Gospel, *Εὐαγγέλιον*, means “good announcement,” namely, of Christ’s birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven.

[Col. 0017B]

In other places it is called the Gospel of Christ. For Mark says, “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ.”

But because Christ is the Word, and “in the beginning was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1), one and the same thing is called the Gospel of God and the Gospel of Christ.

For the Lord himself says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10), and the Father speaks, saying, “All that is mine is yours, and yours is mine”; therefore the Gospel of the Father is the Gospel of the Son (John 17).

### Which He Promised Beforehand Through His Prophets in the Holy Scriptures

What was foretold concerning Christ through the prophets should also be understood as having been foretold concerning the Gospel. For example:

> “The Lord will give the word to those who evangelize with great power” (Psalm 67);

and:

> “How beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize good things” (Isaiah 52);

and many other passages.

At the same time, he shows that he preaches no other Christ than the one whose Gospel the prophets promised would come. He asserts that those prophets are God’s prophets, since they previously sang of Christ in the Holy Scriptures.

### Concerning His Son

Much of the Son’s grace is noted here, whose birth in the flesh is also found to be unlike that of others, since he was born of a virgin.

### Who Was Made for Him from the Seed of David According to the Flesh

He was made through the Spirit. For if he was made according to the flesh, then he was certainly not made according to the substance of the Word.

### Who Was Predestined to Be the Son of God in Power

This, then, is the predestination of the saints, which shone forth most clearly in the Holy of holies. No one who rightly understands the utterances of Truth can deny it.

For we say that the very Lord of glory, insofar as he was made human, was predestined to be the Son of God. The teacher of the Gentiles cries out at the beginning of his Epistles concerning the Son of God:

> “Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh; who was predestined to be the Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection of the dead.”

Therefore, just as that one was predestined to be our head, so we were predestined in great numbers to be his members. For God calls many people his predestined sons, so that he may make them members of his one predestined Son.

### According to the Spirit of Sanctification

(From Origen.)

He is called the Spirit of sanctification because he grants holiness to all, as it is also written elsewhere concerning him:

> “He became for us wisdom from God and sanctification” (1 Corinthians 1).

### By the Resurrection of the Dead of Jesus Christ Our Lord

Not of all who rise, but of those who belong to Christ.

In Christ himself the pattern of resurrection is displayed, so that the Son of God, first of all, might open the way of resurrection to his sons. Concerning them he himself said:

> “Because they are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection” (Luke 20).

Through whom we received grace and apostleship. He says that he received grace and apostleship through Christ, as mediator between God and humanity. “Grace” is to be referred to endurance in labors, as he himself says: “I worked harder than all of them—not I, but the grace of God with me” (Rom. XV); “apostleship,” to authority in preaching. Or else, he received grace in baptism and apostleship when he was directed by the Holy Spirit.

For obedience to the faith among all the nations, for his name’s sake, among whom you also are called to belong to Jesus Christ our Lord. He shows that the grace of the Gospel is to be preached to those who obey. By “among all the nations” he shows that he received apostleship so that they might obey faith, not the law. “For his name’s sake,” that is, we act in place of his name, as he himself says: “As the Father sent me, so I send you; and whoever receives you receives me” (John XX).

Among whom you also are. That is, “among you Romans also I received the apostleship of preaching.”

## READING FROM THE PROPHET ISAIAH, CHAPTER LXII

[Col. 0018C]

> “Thus says the Lord: For Zion’s sake I will not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest, until her righteous one goes forth like brightness, and her savior is kindled like a lamp. And the nations shall see your righteous one, and all kings your illustrious one. And you shall be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord has named. And you shall be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord, and a diadem of royalty in the hand of your God. You shall no longer be called Forsaken, and your land shall no longer be called Desolate, but you shall be called My Will Is in Her, and your land shall be inhabited, because the Lord has been pleased with you.”

For Zion’s sake I will not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest, until her righteous one goes forth like brightness. (From Jerome.) Here the prophet’s person is introduced as speaking: “For Zion’s sake I will not be silent,” but I shall cry out for a very long time and join prayer to prayer, until the one who was promised comes forth, “like brightness,” as her righteous one, and illumines the whole world with his splendor.

And her savior, so that he may be kindled like a lamp. He is the one who said in the Gospel, “I am the light of the world” (John VIII), and of whom John said, “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being,” and so forth (John I).

And the nations shall see your righteous one, and so forth. That is, they shall see the righteousness by which the Creator of all has shown mercy to the nations.

And you shall be called by a new name, and so forth. That is, she shall no longer be called Jerusalem and Zion, but shall receive a new name, namely, “Christian.”

And you shall be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord, and so forth. The Church shall be like a crown of beauty in the hand of the Lord and like a royal diadem in the hand of her God: a crown when the multitude of believers has crowned her, and a diadem of sovereignty when the martyrs have adorned her with the variety of their jewels. The Church, which had previously been possessed by idols and abandoned by God, shall dwell joyfully with Christ, and Christ shall rejoice with her, just as a bridegroom rejoices in his bride.

## GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER I

> “Now the generation of Christ was as follows. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. But Joseph her husband, being righteous and unwilling to expose her, resolved to dismiss her secretly. While he was considering these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying: ‘Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife. For that which has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit. She shall give birth to a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he himself will save his people from their sins.’”

Now the generation of Christ was as follows. (From Jerome.) Why did he not say “the generation of Jesus Christ,” but only “of Christ”—that is, why did he give not both names but one? As this has been handed down by our predecessors, he reserved it for the future narrative, where the angel immediately adds: “And you shall call his name Jesus” (Matt. I), and so forth. Since the evangelist foresaw that he would shortly write how he was called, he ought not to anticipate and preempt it. “Generation” may mean Christ himself, generated in the flesh, so that “the generation of Christ” means the same as if one said, “the generation that is Christ.” Or, as some read it, the order of the words may be: “Thus was the generation of Christ,” that is, “thus this genealogy pertains to Christ.” It continues:

When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph. (From Jerome.) It is asked why the Lord was born not from an unmarried virgin but from one who had been betrothed. First, so that through Joseph’s genealogy Mary’s origin might be shown, since it is the custom of the divine Scriptures to construct genealogies not through women but through men. Second, so that she would not be stoned by the Jews as an adulteress. Third, so that, when fleeing into Egypt, she would have the comfort of a husband. Ignatius added a fourth reason: so that the birth might be concealed from the devil, while he thought that Christ had been born not from a virgin but from a wife.

Before they came together. She was discovered by no one other than Joseph, who, with marital privilege, already knew nearly everything about his future wife. What is said—“before they came together”—does not imply that they came together afterward, as the deceitful Helvidius wishes, but Scripture indicates what did not happen. It should be noted that when it says “before they came together,” the verb “to come together” signifies not sexual intercourse itself but the time of the marriage rites, which ordinarily precede intercourse, when the woman who had previously been betrothed begins to be a wife. (From Bede.) Therefore, “before they came together” means “before they properly celebrated the solemnities of marriage.”

She was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. Certainly, according to the order just mentioned, they came together afterward, when Joseph took his wife in obedience to the angel’s command; but they did not have intercourse, since it follows: “And he did not know her.”

She was found to be with child. By no one other than Joseph, who, with marital privilege, already knew nearly everything about his future wife. Thus he soon perceived, with a curious gaze, that her womb was swelling. Elsewhere also we find it written: “With child,” it says, not “receiving into the womb,” because it declares that the conception was not received from elsewhere but was formed within, when the Holy Spirit came upon her, enclosed within the integrity of the virginal womb. It continues.

But Joseph her husband. It is the custom of the Scriptures to call betrothed women wives and betrothed men their husbands.

[Col. 0020B]

Being righteous. A righteous man would by no means violate the temple of righteousness, which she had conceived before they came together. The evangelist rightly calls Joseph righteous, so as to commend him as a suitable witness to her. (Vulgate.) Joseph is called righteous so that, through the prerogative conferred by righteousness, he may be shown to have deserved to know the grace that had been bestowed upon blessed Mary, and therefore he could neither accuse her nor presume to abandon her. Rather, suspended in astonishment before the novelty of the miracle, he was considering abandoning his betrothed—not because of the recklessness of the conception, but out of reverence for the new fertility. Hence the angel also warns him as though he were in doubt.

And unwilling to expose her. That is, to defame her. The word “expose” is often found in a bad sense; the Greek expression does not inappropriately signify this as well: παραδειγματίσαι, that is, “to make public,” or “to expose openly.” He did not wish to make the conception of his betrothed known to everyone.

He resolved to dismiss her secretly. “To dismiss,” as many maintain, is used for “not to take her as his wife.” Or certainly, he wished to dismiss her—that is, to free her from the penalty of adultery, as though she were innocent. He did not wish to hand her over to punishment as an adulteress, since he knew that she was free from every charge of defilement. “Secretly,” he says, lest, by dismissing his wife, he should bring upon her the charge of sexual misconduct, or, by freeing her, make himself appear guilty of adultery.

While he was considering these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream, and so forth. Many agree that this angel of the Lord was Gabriel. To a good and righteous man thinking good and righteous thoughts, a good and righteous messenger appropriately appeared. For such things are often found in the holy Scriptures: when people are attentively thinking about God, timely consolation is supplied. Thus, while two were walking along the road and speaking about him, the Lord appeared to them (Luke XXIV). Again, while the eleven apostles were speaking about him, he was present among them, although the doors were closed (John XX). (From John Chrysostom.) Why in a dream and not rather openly? Clearly because he was a thoroughly faithful man and did not need a more manifest revelation. The shepherds, by contrast, were given a more manifest revelation because they were further removed from such instruction by their rustic way of life. It continues.

[Col. 0021A]

Joseph, son of David. In saying “Joseph, son of David,” he addresses him with the affection of one who encourages, so that he would not terrify him as though he were unknown, since he was known both by name and by lineage. It is an indication of familiarity to call someone by his proper name. At the same time, it should be noted that Joseph is said to be the son of David, so that Mary might be shown to have come from David’s stock. For the Lord says to Moses: “No one shall enter into marriage except from his own tribe” (Num. XXXVI). (Vulgate.) Why is he not instead called the son of Jacob, but is said to be the son of David, with so many progenitors omitted in between? It is so that the royal origin might be declared, from which the birth of Christ was foretold as destined to come.

Do not fear to take Mary as your wife. For he was afraid to acknowledge as his wife the woman whose conception he had discovered to be spiritual. (From Bede.) “To take” does not mean to join her in marital intercourse but to receive her into an inseparable fellowship of spiritual companionship. The angel also calls Mary by her own name, so that the names of both might be shown to have been written in heaven, since the angel named them on earth. It continues:

For that which has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit. “Born in her,” he says, not “seeded from outside.”

She shall give birth to a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he himself will save his people from their sins. The etymology of the name Jesus follows when he says, “He will save his people.” The people saved from their sins through him is truly his own people.

## READING FROM THE PROPHET ISAIAH, CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0021C]

> “The people of the nations who walked in darkness have seen a great light; light has risen upon those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death. For a child has been born for us, and a son has been given to us. And his rule has been made upon his shoulder. And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end to his peace. He shall sit upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish and strengthen it in judgment and righteousness, from now and forever. The zeal of the Lord will do this.”

The people of the nations who walked in darkness have seen a great light. (From Jerome.) When this passage is explained in this way, at Christ’s coming and as his preaching shone forth, first the land of Zebulun and Naphtali was freed from the errors of the scribes and Pharisees and shook off the very heavy yoke of Jewish traditions from its neck. Later, through the Gospel of the apostle Paul, who was the last of all the apostles, preaching was increased—that is, multiplied—and the Gospel of Christ shone to the boundaries of the nations and across the way of the whole sea. Finally, the entire world, which had previously walked or sat in darkness and was held in the bonds of idolatry and death, saw the bright light of the Gospel.

Light has risen upon those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death. I think the distinction between death and the shadow of death is this: death belongs to those who went down to hell with dead works. “The soul that sins shall itself die.” The shadow of death belongs to those who sin but have not yet departed from life; for, if they wish, they can still do penance.

For a child has been born for us, and a son has been given to us. This child, therefore, who was born from a virgin, is called Emmanuel, that is, “God with us.” He has rule upon his shoulder, either because he himself carried his cross, or because it is written of him: “The Lord God has revealed his holy arm to all the nations.” And again: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII). After the first two names, therefore, he shall be called by six other names: Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. For, as many think, the names are not to be joined together so that we read “Wonderful Counselor” and again “Mighty God.” Rather, “Wonderful” is to be read separately—the Hebrew term is [Hebrew term missing or illegible]—and “Counselor” separately, which in their language is called [Hebrew term missing or illegible]. “God” is likewise separate; “Mighty” is called [Hebrew term missing or illegible] in Hebrew. “Father of the age to come” refers to what is fulfilled in our calling; and “Prince of Peace” refers to the one who said to the apostles: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XX). No one who has read, according to the Apostle, that the Lord Savior is our peace will doubt this.

His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end to his peace. Nor can anyone doubt the Savior’s manifold dominion or his peace, which has no end, if he has read in the Psalms: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. II). And again: “And an abundance of peace until the moon is taken away” (Ps. LXXII), that is, until the consummation of the age.

He shall sit upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish and strengthen it, and so forth. His rule and dominion will be over the throne and kingdom of David, which had been dispersed after the Babylonian captivity, so that he might establish and strengthen it and show it to be perpetual. Thus God’s promise will not be judged empty from the time of the incarnation to eternity.

The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this. “Zeal,” that is, the Lord’s emulation, did this, because they provoked him to emulation by following those who were not gods, and he provoked them to emulate a nation that was not a nation (Rom. XI).

## GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER II

> “Now it happened in those days that a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be registered. This registration was the first made when Quirinius was governor of Syria. And all went to be registered, each to his own city. Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, into Judea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David, to be registered with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant. And it happened that, while they were there, the days were fulfilled for her to give birth. And she gave birth to her firstborn son, wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for him in the inn. And shepherds were in that region, keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock. And behold, an angel of the Lord stood beside them, and the glory of God shone around them. And they were afraid with great fear, and the angel said to them: ‘Do not fear. For behold, I announce to you good news of great joy, which will be for all the people, because today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David. And this will be a sign for you: You will find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger.’ And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.’”

[Col. 0023B]

A decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be registered. (From Bede.) This new registration of the world bore witness not only to the coming of that supreme King, who would enroll his elect, gathered from every region of the world, in the register of eternal blessedness; it also assisted the leaders of that same kingdom with the peaceful calm of its rule. For, since all nations had been subdued by the storm of wars, the terrifying shadow of the Roman name, so to speak, protected Christ’s disciples, who were going to preach throughout the world wherever they wished to go for the sake of the word, from the heat of the rebellions then threatening them.

Thus a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should declare its census, because the decree of the King Christ was imminent, through which the whole world would attain salvation. He, most perfectly fulfilling the name “Augustus,” as one who both desired his own people to increase and was himself sufficient to increase them, commanded that those subject to the registration of his profession should be marked not by the taking of money but by the offering of faith: “Go,” he says, “into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark XVI).

This registration was the first made. This indicates either that it was the first of those registrations that encompassed the whole world, since many regions of the earth are already frequently said to have been registered, or else that it then first began, when Quirinius, a single man appointed by Caesar with the consent of the Roman senate to exercise authority over the nations, was sent to Syria. Just as then, under Augustus’s rule and Quirinius’s governorship, everyone went to declare the census, each to his own city, so now, with Christ ruling through the leaders of the Church—that is, its teachers—or rather with Christ urging us on and promising rewards, let us all go; let no one be excluded from the census of righteousness. Let us come to him who says, “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.” Let us take his yoke upon us and learn from him, because he is gentle and humble in heart, and we shall find rest for our souls.

For this is our city and homeland: namely, the blessed and heavenly rest of souls. To go to that city of peace and rest and devoutly return a treasure to our King is to contemplate the joys of eternal light through daily growth in virtue and faith, and, in order to acquire them, to despise both the prosperity and adversity of the world. Once they have been acquired, it is to offer God a gift more precious than gold: ourselves, cleansed from every defilement of flesh and spirit. It continues.

Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, into Judea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, and so forth. (From Bede.) Joseph is interpreted as “increased” or “increase.” Galilee means “transmigration,” “revolving movement,” “wheel,” or “confession”; Nazareth means “flower,” “shoot,” or “purity”; Judea means “confession” or “glorifying”; Bethlehem means “house of bread”; David means “strong of hand” or “desirable.” He received this name because he had bravely struck down the giant and had been handsome in appearance and beautiful in face. This prefigured the one who was to be born from his house and family, who alone would conquer the prince of the world, “beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XLV). He too was born in Bethlehem so that he might be the shepherd of rational sheep, that is, the ruler of simple souls.

And it happened that, while they were there, the days were fulfilled for her to give birth, and she gave birth to her firstborn son. The Lord is rightly born in Bethlehem, not only because of the indication of his royal lineage but also because of the mystery of the name. (From Gregory.) Bethlehem is interpreted as “house of bread,” for he himself is the one who says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John VI). The place where the Lord was to be born was therefore previously called “house of bread,” because it was destined that he should appear through the substance of flesh, the one who would refresh the minds of the elect with inward nourishment.

(From Bede.) Even to this day, and until the consummation of the age, the Lord does not cease to be conceived in Nazareth and born in Bethlehem, whenever any hearer, having received the flower of the word, makes himself a house of eternal bread. Each day he is conceived through faith in the virginal womb—that is, in the mind of believers—and is brought forth through Baptism. Each day the Church, the mother of God, accompanying her author, ascends from the wheel of worldly conduct, which is what Galilee signifies, into the city of Judah, namely, confession and praise, and pays the tribute of her devotion to the eternal King.

Following the example of the blessed ever-virgin Mary, the Church, at once married and immaculate, conceives us as a virgin from the Spirit, gives birth to us as a virgin without pain, and, although betrothed to one, yet made fertile by another, is visibly joined in each of her parts—which together make one Catholic Church—to the bishop appointed over her, while she is filled by the invisible power of the Holy Spirit.

Hence Joseph is rightly interpreted as “increased,” indicating by this name that the teacher’s diligence in speaking accomplishes nothing unless it receives an increase of heavenly assistance so that it may be heard. As for the statement that Mary gave birth to her firstborn son, it should not be understood, against the Helvidians, to mean that she also produced other children, as though “firstborn” could be said only of one who has brothers, just as “only-begotten” is ordinarily said only of one who lacks brothers. Both the testimony of the Law and manifest reason show that all only-begotten children can also be called firstborn, but that not all firstborn children can be called only-begotten. That is, “firstborn” does not mean only one after whom others came, but anyone before whom no one had emerged from the womb.

Christ Jesus is therefore only-begotten in the substance of his divinity, firstborn in the assumption of humanity; firstborn in grace, only-begotten in nature.

And she wrapped him in swaddling clothes and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for him in the inn. (From Bede.) “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” He who clothes the whole world in splendor is wrapped in poor rags, so that we may be able to receive the first robe. Through whom all things were made, his hands and feet are bound in swaddling clothes, so that our hands may be extended toward good works and our feet directed along the way of peace. He whose seat is heaven is confined within the narrowness of a hard manger, so that he may enlarge us through the joys of the heavenly kingdom. He who is the bread of angels is laid in a manger, so that he may refresh us, like holy animals, with the grain of his flesh. He who sits at the right hand of the Father lacks a place in an inn, so that he might prepare many dwelling places for us in his Father’s house.

Although the fact that he was born not in his parents’ house but in an inn and on the road can be understood more profoundly through its symbolism. For he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). Therefore, although through the essence of divinity he remains truth and life, through the mystery of the incarnation he became the way by which he might lead us to our homeland, where we would enjoy truth and life.

And shepherds were in that region, keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock. The fact that shepherds kept watch over their flocks of sheep when the Lord was born signifies that, in the manifest administration of the Church, shepherds of chaste souls would keep watch, to whom it is said: “Feed the flock of God that is among you” (1 Pet. V).

And behold, an angel of the Lord stood beside them, and the glory of God shone around them. (From Gregory.) The angel rightly appears to shepherds who are keeping watch, and the glory of God shines around them, because those who diligently know how to preside over faithful flocks deserve, more than others, to see sublime things. While they themselves piously keep watch over the flock, divine grace shines more abundantly upon them.

(From Ambrose.) Observe the beginning of the rising Church: Christ is born, and the shepherds begin to keep watch. The shepherds rightly keep watch whom the good Shepherd instructs. The flock, therefore, is the people; the night is the age. The shepherds are priests—or perhaps it is that shepherd to whom it is said: “Be watchful and strengthen the others,” since he appointed not only bishops but also angels. An angel instructs Mary, an angel Joseph, and an angel the shepherds; the citizens of heaven bear witness that God is to be conceived, has been conceived, and has been born, so that they may sufficiently instruct mortals and ceaselessly render service to their Creator. For in what follows they are also said to be present at his temptation, suffering, rising, and ascension into heaven.

And they were afraid with great fear, and the angel said to them: Do not fear; for behold, I announce to you good news of great joy, which will be for all the people. (From Bede.) Not for all the Jewish people, most of whom proved rebellious, but eternal and great joy is announced to the whole people of the faithful, gathered from every tribe, nation, and language into the one Church of Christ.

Because today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David. Here it should be noted that the angel, speaking to shepherds during the watches of the night, does not say, “Tonight,” but “Today a Savior has been born for you.” This is for no other reason than that he had come to announce great joy. For where sorrow is signified, night is often added or mentioned, as in: “You will all be scandalized because of me on this night” (Matt. XXVI).

Nor did the angel, surrounded by such great light, appear without purpose, so that the glory of God is said to have shone around the shepherds—that is, to have scattered rays of light upon them from every side. Such a detail is never added in the entire sequence of the Old Testament, despite the many appearances of angels. Rather, he mystically foretold what the Apostle later expressly taught: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near. Therefore let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light; let us walk honorably as in the day.”

And this will be a sign for you: You will find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes, and so forth. (From Bede.) It should be carefully noted that the sign given of the Savior’s birth is an infant not covered in Tyrian purple but wrapped in filthy rags; not to be found on couches ornamented with gold but in a manger. This means that he assumed for our sake not only the condition of humility and mortality but also that of poverty: “Although he was rich, he became poor for us, so that by his poverty we might become rich” (2 Cor. VIII). Though he was Lord of heaven, he became poor on earth to teach earth-dwellers that the kingdom of heaven can be acquired through poverty of spirit.

And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will. As one messenger announces that God has been born in the flesh, a multitude of the heavenly host immediately flies in and bursts forth with harmonious voice in praise of the Creator, both offering Christ the devotion of their service, as always, and instructing us by their example. Whenever one of the brethren resounds with words of sacred instruction, or whenever we recall to mind what is godly that we have read or heard, we ought immediately to render praises to God with mouth, heart, and deed.

The arriving choir of angels is rightly given the name “heavenly host.” It humbly serves that powerful leader in battle who appeared to overthrow the powers of the air, and it vigorously troubles those same opposing powers with heavenly weapons, so that they may not be able to tempt mortals as much as they wish.

Because the true God is born as a human being, peace is rightly sung to humanity and glory to the Lord. The angels glorify God incarnate for our redemption because, when they see us received, they rejoice that their own number is being filled. They request peace for human beings because those whom they had previously regarded as weak and rejected now, with the Lord born in the flesh, they venerate as companions.

When they ask peace for humanity, they explain for whom it is intended: for people of good will, that is, for those who receive the Christ who has been born—not for Herod, the chief priests, and the Pharisees, or the other Antichrists, who, after hearing of his birth, were troubled and pursued him with swords as far as they were able. “There is no peace for the wicked,” says the Lord (Isa. XLVIII); but “great peace belongs to those who love your name, O Lord, and there is no stumbling-block for them” (Ps. CXVIII).

## EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE HEBREWS, CHAPTER I

> “In many parts and in many ways, long ago God spoke to the fathers through the prophets. But in these last days he has spoken to us in his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages. He is the radiance of his glory and the imprint of his substance, sustaining all things by the word of his power, and, having made purification for sins, he sits at the right hand of Majesty in the highest places. Having become so much superior to the angels as he has inherited a name more distinguished than theirs. For to which of the angels did he ever say: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’? And again: ‘I will be his Father, and he will be my Son’? And again, when he brings the firstborn into the inhabited world, he says: ‘And let all his angels worship him.’ To the angels he indeed says: ‘He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flame of fire.’ But to the Son: ‘Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the scepter of righteousness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.’ And: ‘You, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you will remain. And they will all grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will change them, and they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will not fail.’”

In many parts and in many ways, long ago God spoke to the fathers through the prophets. (From John Chrysostom.) By saying, “In many parts and in many ways, long ago God spoke to our fathers through the prophets,” he signifies what is said elsewhere: “For I multiplied visions, and I was represented in the hands of the prophets” (Hos. XII). But when what follows says, “In these last days he has spoken to us in his Son,” it is as though he were saying: “What is so great if he sent prophets to our fathers? To us he sent his own only-begotten Son.”

Whom he appointed heir of all things. When he says, “Whom he appointed heir,” he signifies the humanity to whom it was said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. II). Therefore, it is no longer Jacob alone who is the Lord’s portion, nor Israel alone his lot; rather, the blood of Christ embraces as an inheritance all the nations, divided throughout the whole world, each distinctly.

(From Cassiodorus.) “Inheritance” is derived from *hero*, that is, “lord,” because the lord rules over it with free authority.

(From John Chrysostom.) Here he uses the name “heir” to establish and demonstrate two things: that he is the proper Son, and that no loss of dominion can befall him. When, therefore, he says, “Whom he appointed heir of all things,” the whole world is understood.

Through whom, he says, he also made the ages. Where are those who say, “There was a time when he was not”? For just as the Father is said not to judge anyone but to judge through the Son, because he begot him as judge, so also he is said to work through the Son, because it is clear that he begot him as the maker (John V).

Who is the radiance of his glory and the imprint of his substance. The Apostle was not speaking these things from his own understanding, nor did he discover this dispensation through human ingenuity; rather, the administration of the Holy Spirit suggested these things to him. We must receive this with reverence, because he was born impassibly from the Father himself, neither diminished nor in any way reduced, but true God from true God, almighty from almighty, light from light, from whom all things exist, through whom all things exist, and in whom all things exist.

Sustaining all things by the word of his power. The Arians are accustomed to argue: When God said, “Let there be light” (Gen. I), the Father commanded and the Son obeyed. But behold, we show that he perfected all things by his own word: “Sustaining all things,” he says—that is, governing them—for he holds together things that are falling and tending toward nothing. It is no less to hold the world together than to have made it. But if one must speak somewhat more boldly, it is even greater. In making, the essences of things were produced from things that did not exist; in sustaining, what has been made is held together so that it does not return to nothing. Thus, while they are governed and things opposed to one another are fitted together, a great and exceedingly wondrous sign of immense power is revealed.

[Col. 0028C]

Having made purification for sins. After saying those great and exceedingly wondrous things above, he now speaks also of his care for us and of the purification of sins that he accomplished for us. Peter likewise says of him: “He himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree, so that, having been freed from sins, we might live for righteousness” (1 Pet. II). John says: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood, and made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father.”

He sat at the right hand of Majesty in the highest places. By saying “in the highest places,” he does not confine him to a location but shows him to be higher than all, even to the throne of the Father’s glory. Therefore, just as the Father is in the highest places, so also is the Son. Their sitting together demonstrates nothing other than equality of honor.

[Col. 0028D]

Having become so much superior to the angels as he has inherited a name more distinguished than theirs. In the statement “having become,” understand “having been received,” as though he were saying, “he was received as superior by the angels.”

For to which of the angels did he ever say: You are my Son? (From Cassiodorus.) Let us attend to what he says: “He said to me, ‘You are my Son,’” which he was also going to say to him after his baptism: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” And so that you might understand Christ as one person—that is, the Word made flesh—he added: “Today I have begotten you.”

By saying “today,” he shows the co-eternity of his majesty. For “today” in God begins with no beginning and is enclosed by no end. There is no “was” there, nor “will be”; rather, it always remains and always is, and whatever you say of him is “today.” When he says, “I have begotten you,” he signifies that birth of which Isaiah says: “Who shall recount his generation?” (Isa. LIII).

And again: I will be his Father, and he will be my Son. In these two verses the wickedness of the Jews is utterly overthrown. For what is clearer, what is plainer, than that the one who invokes the Father should be believed to be the Son, and again that the one who calls someone his Son should be believed to be the Father?

And when again he brings the Firstborn into the world, he says. (From John Chrysostom.) He therefore calls the entrance the assumption of flesh; for we were outside God, like those who are bound in chains outside royal courts. Christ likewise brought this about: coming forth to us—that is, taking flesh—and being placed among us, he made the King’s commandments known; and thus, cleansing us from sins and turning us toward God, he introduced us into the royal court, as the best mediator. Therefore he calls the advent of his incarnation an “exit.” For he possessed the whole world when he was acknowledged by all, just as if someone introduced a person into a certain house and immediately ordered all the leaders of that household to adore him together, bowing down. So he also commanded all the angels to adore Christ according to the flesh, saying: “And let all the angels of God adore him.”

And to the angels he says: “Who makes his angels spirits.” (From Cassiodorus.) “Who makes his angels spirits.” “Spirit” is a general name for an incorporeal and powerful substance, operating visibly or invisibly according to what is divinely inspired in it. The name “angels” does not signify nature but obedience: ἄγγελος, in Greek, means what is translated in Latin as “messenger.” For when they are sent, they become angels, although they are known by nature to be spirits. He added “his” in order to show that they are those who obey the Lord’s commands with an upright mind.

“And his ministers a flame of fire.” (From Jerome.) He calls it burning fire, so that in some it may pour in the light of truth, while in others it may consume sins. This fire purifies the holy and consumes sinners. Let the one who is holy not fear this fire; let the one who is a sinner fear it. I think these fires are his angels. Whom, then, do these angels consume? Whoever is wood, hay, or straw; but whoever is gold, silver, or precious stones will indeed be cast into the fire, but will be found purer.

But to the Son: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever.” (From John Chrysostom.) Behold the great difference: they were created, but he is uncreated. Do you see how he distinguishes them, and with what clarity he separates creatures from the Creator, calling them ministers and him Lord; servants and heir? To his own Son he says: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever.” Here you have the insignia of the kingdom: “And the rod of equity,” he says, “the rod of your kingdom.” Here you have another insignia as well. (From Cassiodorus.) This rod signifies the rule of divine equity, which is truly called straight because it is bent by no crookedness. This rod governs the righteous and strikes the impious; it truly sustains those who plead. But this rod does not grow from the turf of a tree; rather, it proceeds from the justice of divinity itself: unconquered strength, the straightest equity, inflexible discipline.

“You have loved justice and hated iniquity.” This is the straight rod: to love equity and hate wickedness. No one perfectly loves justice unless he also detests evil deeds, since things of different qualities cannot occupy one place at the same time. Nor can black be seen at that moment in the place where brightness has settled, because the presence of light is the absence of night.

“Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.” (From Jerome.) Other kings, who prefigured him and were called his companions in ruling, were anointed with corruptible oil. But here the Son of God was anointed by God the Father with the oil of gladness—that is, of resurrection, ascension, and dominion—for Christ is anointed by nature, while we are anointed by grace.

“And you, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands; they will perish, but you will remain.” (From Cassiodorus.) When he says, “In the beginning you founded the earth, Lord,” he shows what cannot be denied by sound minds: that the Creator is known to have existed before his creatures, without any beginning. And observe this: here he destroyed, with marvelous brevity, the opinions of the philosophers. The first is that the world was created by no one; the second, that it will remain without end. But when it is said, “In the beginning you founded the earth, Lord, and the heavens are the works of your hands,” that first wicked persuasion is refuted. When it is declared, “They will perish,” he revealed that they will have an end, so that no one, in pagan error, might place confidence in the stars, since he understood that they would be changed. But when he says, “You will remain,” just as he shows the Lord’s eternity while he created all things, so he says that, after the heavens have been changed, he himself will remain in the glory of his majesty.

“And all things will grow old like a garment.” By saying “all things,” I think he does not designate angels or spiritual creatures, which will remain in their dignity, but those things that are shown to be subject to change. When he says, “They will grow old like a garment,” this seems to be applied to the fragility of flesh; for that grows old which, in the manner of clothing, is consumed by death.

“And like a cloak you will change them, and they will be changed.” By “cloak,” that is, covering, we should perhaps understand the heavens, which cover the earth like a veil and, like other things, will likewise be changed. And to show that the works of the Lord will now remain under eternity, he says: “You will change them, and they will be changed,” because they will never return to this corruptible state. For if they were afterward subject to corruption, they would not be said to have been changed. As the prophet Daniel testifies, saying: “For wisdom and strength and understanding are his, and he changes times and ages” (Dan. II), he added this.

“But you are the same, and your years will not fail.” This is set in opposition to what was said: while those things are changeable, the Lord always remains immutable. It indicates his omnipotence, because he truly is himself when he continually performs works worthy of him. It subsequently declares his nature, because he alone knows how to exist through himself; in order to exist, he needs no other helper. Thus, in these three verses, both the change of creatures and the Lord’s eternity have been described with marvelous brevity.

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER I

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of human beings. And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it. There was a man sent by God, whose name was John. He came for testimony, to bear testimony to the light, so that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but he came to bear testimony to the light. He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. He came into what was his own, and his own did not receive him. But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God—to those who believe in his name, who were born not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of a man, but from God. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.”

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word,” and so forth. (From Augustine.) “In the beginning was the Word.” In what beginning? “And the Word was with God. And God was the Word.” The names of words must be said repeatedly, as though words had become cheap. Behold, I say “word” when I say “God”; how brief is what I have said—four letters and two syllables. Is this whole thing, “God,” merely four letters and two syllables? Rather, as cheap as this is, so precious is what is understood by it. What has happened in your heart when I said “God”? Some great and supreme substance is conceived: living, perpetual, almighty, infinite, present everywhere, wholly present everywhere, excluded nowhere. When you think these things, this is the word concerning God in your heart.

(From Bede.) The other evangelists describe Christ as born in time, but John testifies that he was in the beginning, saying: “In the beginning was the Word.” The others mention that he suddenly appeared among human beings; he declares that he was always with God, saying: “And the Word was with God.” The others confirm him as a true human being; he confirms him as truly God, saying: “And God was the Word.” The others speak of him as a human being who dwelt among human beings in time; he shows him as God remaining with God in the beginning, saying: “He was in the beginning with God.” The others testify to the great deeds he performed as a human being; he teaches that God the Father made every visible and invisible creature through him, saying: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” There were heretics who said: “If he was born, then Christ existed at a time when he did not exist.” The evangelist refuted them in his first statement when he said: “In the beginning was the Word.” There were others who believed Christ to be human only and not God; he crushes them in what follows when he says: “And God was the Word.”
