“All things were made through him.” (From Augustine.) Every creature was made through him—greater, lesser, heavenly, infernal, spiritual, bodily. For no form, no structure, no harmony of parts, no substance of any kind that can possess weight, number, or measure can exist except through that Word and from that creative Word to whom it was said: “You have ordered all things in measure, number, and weight.”

“And without him nothing was made.” Sin was not made through him, and an idol was not made through the Word.

(From Jerome.) Idols are excluded by this statement. Therefore the Apostle says: “We know that an idol is nothing” (1 Cor. VIII).

(Vulgate.) All things created or made through the Word are good and subsist in their own manner. Therefore everything created subsists in its own manner; everything that subsists has a nature; nothing lacks a nature; therefore nothing fails to subsist. Evil was made without the Word; without the Word nothing was made; therefore evil is nothing. But nothing does not subsist; therefore evil does not subsist. No evil subsists; every creature subsists. Therefore no evil is a creature. Consequently, evil is neither any good, nor does it subsist in any way, nor is it any creature; and everything that exists in any manner is good and exists only through the Word.

“What was made: in him was life.” (From Augustine.) This should be punctuated as follows: “What was made”—pause here—and then continue: “In him was life.” The earth was made, but life is not in the earth itself. Yet wisdom is in it: a certain special reason by which the earth was made. This is life. You see the earth; in the art there is earth. You see the heaven; in the art there is heaven. You see the sun and moon; these exist in the art, but outside it they are bodies, while in the art they are life.

“And the life was the light of human beings.” Therefore that life through which all things were made is itself light—not the light of just any animals, but the light of human beings, because human beings are enlightened by it, whereas cattle are not enlightened. For the human being was made in the image of God and possesses a rational mind through which he can perceive wisdom.

“And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.” Unbelieving, unjust, wicked, rapacious, greedy people, lovers of the world—these are the darkness that does not comprehend the Lord, that is, does not understand him. Purge from your eye whatever is evil, and you will see wisdom, which is God: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V).

There was a man sent by God, whose name was John. Since the Lord Jesus Christ was human in such a way that God was hidden in him, a great man was sent before him, through whose testimony the one who was more than human might be discovered. And who is this? “There was a man.” And how can this man speak the word concerning God? “Sent by God.” What was he called? “Whose name was John.” Why did he come? Listen.

“He came for testimony, to bear testimony to the light, so that all might believe through him. He was not the light,” and so forth. What sort of person was this who bore testimony to the light? John was something great: immense merit, great grace, and great exaltation. Why, then, did he come? To bear testimony to the light. For what purpose? So that all might believe through him. And concerning what light was he to bear testimony? “He was the true light.” Why was “true” added? Because an enlightened human being is also called “light,” as the Lord Jesus says to his disciples: “You are the light of the world,” and the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord.” Our eyes, too, are called lights; but unless a lamp is lit during the night or the sun rises during the day, those lights are open in vain. So John was light, but not the true light, because he became light through illumination.

“He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world.” (From Bede.) Every person, that is, who is enlightened either by natural intelligence or by divine wisdom. For just as no one can exist from himself, so no one can be wise from himself; rather, this comes from the one who illuminates, concerning whom it is written: “All wisdom is from the Lord God.” The Evangelist subsequently describes both of his natures—his divine nature, by which he always remains wholly everywhere, and his human nature, through which he was born in time, appeared enclosed in a place—saying:

“He was in the world.” (From Augustine.) Do not think that he was in the world in the same way as the earth, heaven, moon, stars, trees, animals, and human beings are in the world. God was not in the world in that way, but as an artist governing what he made. God, infused throughout the world and present everywhere, by the presence of his majesty makes and governs what he made.

“And the world was made through him, and the world did not know him.” What does “the world was made through him” mean? Heaven, earth, sea, and everything in them are called the world. Did the heavens not know him, when they sent the star (Matt. II)? Or did the angels not know him, when they approached and ministered to him (Matt. IV)? Or did the stars not know their Savior? Everything everywhere bore testimony. Who, then, did not know him? The lovers of the world, who, by loving the world, were called “the world.” They deserved to be called what the place was where they dwelt. Those who do not love the world live bodily in the world, but in heart they inhabit heaven.

“He came into what was his own.” (From Bede.) He came into what was his own because he appeared, through his humanity, in the world that he had made through his divinity. Thus he was in the world through his divinity; he came into the world through his incarnation. To come or depart belongs to humanity; to remain and to be belongs to divinity.

“And his own did not receive him.” Human beings, that is: the Jews whom he had chosen for himself as a special people, to whom he had revealed the mystery of his knowledge, whom he had glorified through the marvelous deeds of their ancestors, to whom he had given the teaching of his law, from whom he had promised that he would become incarnate, and among whom he showed himself incarnate as he had promised. They, for the most part, refused to receive him. Many from both peoples rejected him, and many received him; concerning these the Evangelist proceeds to say:

“But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God,” and so forth. (From Augustine.) Great benevolence, great mercy! The Only-Begotten was born, and he did not wish to remain alone. God sent into this world the one and same Only-Begotten whom he had begotten and through whom he had created all things, so that he might not be alone but might have adopted brothers. We were not born from God as he, the Only-Begotten, was, but were adopted through his grace. Therefore the power to become children of God is given to those who believe in him, while they are also given the very power to believe in him. Our Lord has only a mother on earth, while we have only a father in heaven. For when he had received mortal Adam, he gave human beings his immortal Father, God.

(From the Vulgate.) Having first received the power of adoption as a divine gift, they afterward attained the merit of being children of God.

“Who were born not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of a man, but from God.” (From Augustine.) What he says—“from bloods”—is not Latin but is expressed in Greek in the plural, αἱμάτων. Among Latins, “blood” is always said in the singular; but the translator preferred, according to the grammarians, to speak somewhat less correctly in Latin, while nevertheless explaining the truth to weak hearers. If he had said “from blood” in the singular, he would not have expressed what he intended. Human beings are born from the bloods of male and female. What does he add: “Nor from the will of the flesh”? He used “flesh” for the woman, because when she had been made from Adam’s rib, Adam said: “This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh.” And the Apostle says: “No one ever hated his own flesh,” that is, his wife. Our carnal generation takes its origin from bloods—that is, from the nature of male and female. Spiritual generation, however, is supplied by the grace of the Holy Spirit. Distinguishing it from carnal generation, the Lord says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. What is born from flesh is flesh, and what is born from Spirit is spirit.”

“And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” (From Jerome.) The Word became flesh so that we might pass from flesh into the Word, while the Word did not cease to be what it had been. Nor did the human being lose what he was born as; his glory was increased, not his nature changed.

(From Augustine.) Therefore this physician came in such a way as to extinguish the vices of the flesh from the flesh and, by death, to kill death. For this reason the Word became flesh, so that we might be able to say: “We saw his glory.” What sort of glory? The glory that the Son of Man became.

(From Bede.) “And the Word became flesh.” Nothing else should be understood than if it were said: “And God became human,” by putting on flesh and a soul. Thus, just as each one of us is one human being consisting of flesh and soul, so from the time of the incarnation the one Christ consists of divinity, flesh, and soul.

“And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father.” Human beings could not see Christ’s glory before the incarnation; after the incarnation they saw it, observing his humanity shining with miracles and understanding that divinity lay hidden within. This was especially true of those who merited contemplating his glory when he was transfigured before his passion on the holy mountain, when a voice descended to him from magnificent glory: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (2 Pet. I). After his passion, having seen the glory of his resurrection and ascension, they were marvelously renewed by the gift of his Spirit. Through all these things they clearly understood that such glory belonged not to any ordinary saint but only to that human being who, in divinity, was the Only-Begotten from the Father.

“Full of grace and truth.” (From Fulgentius.) He is full in his divine nature, because God is truth, and full in his human nature, in which he became truly human through grace. In that fullness he is God in the form of God, equal to God; in this fullness he is a servant in the form of a servant, because he was made in the likeness of human beings and was found in appearance as a human being (Phil. II).

(From Bede.) Christ Jesus was and is a human being full of grace. By a singular gift, above other mortals, he was granted to be truly God immediately from the moment he was conceived in the Virgin’s womb and began to become human.

## HARMONY

The readings of these two passages agree in many respects. The Gospel says: “In the beginning was the Word.” The Apostle says: “You, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth.” The Gospel says: “All things were made through him, and the world was made through him.” The Apostle says: “Through whom he also made the ages.” It should be noted that both called the Lord Jesus Christ God: the Gospel when it says, “And God was the Word”; the Apostle when he says, “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever” (Ps. XLV).

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT STEPHEN

### READING FROM THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, CHAPTER V

“Stephen, full of grace and fortitude, performed wonders and great signs among the people. But some members of the synagogue arose, which was called that of the Libertines, Cyrenians, and Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, disputing with Stephen; and they could not resist the wisdom and the Spirit who spoke. When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart and gnashed their teeth against him. But Stephen, being full of the Holy Spirit and gazing into heaven, saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. And he said: ‘Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the power of God.’ But crying out with a loud voice, they stopped their ears and rushed upon him with one accord. And having driven him outside the city, they stoned him; and the witnesses laid aside their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. And they stoned Stephen, calling upon the Lord and saying: ‘Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.’ Then, kneeling down, he cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘Lord, do not hold this sin against them.’ And when he had said this, he fell asleep in the Lord.”

“Stephen, full of grace and fortitude.” (From Jerome.) Stephen, Στέφανος in Greek, is called “crowned” in Latin. In a beautiful manner, what he was going to receive in reality was anticipated by a kind of presage in his name: stoned humbly, but crowned sublimely. In Hebrew, however, it is interpreted as “your standard”—whose, if not that of the martyrs who would follow, for whom he became the first model by suffering and dying for Christ?

“He performed signs and wonders.” Wonders are so called as things that speak beforehand, that is, as things proclaiming something new and far in the future. Signs are indications, named from the fact that they signify something.

“But some members arose from the synagogue called that of the Libertines, Cyrenians, and Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, disputing with Stephen.” “Synagogue” is Greek; in Latin it means “assembly.” The Libertines were those freed from slavery and granted liberty. It is established that those who first resisted the faith of Christ came from a servile stock; although emancipated by human beings, they were nevertheless slaves of sin. Cilicia is interpreted as “assembly,” “mourning,” or “vomit.” Alexander is interpreted as “removing the constrictions of darkness.” Asia is interpreted as “raised” or “exaltation.”

“And they could not resist the wisdom and the Spirit who spoke.” This is what the Lord himself says to his martyrs: “For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries will not be able to resist or contradict” (Luke XXI).

“When they heard this, they were cut to the heart and gnashed their teeth.” When conscience is reproved, it is impatient, and they could not endure the truth of Christ. Their ears displayed the fury of their minds in their faces. They gnashed their teeth against him, wishing to tear his flesh and showing themselves to be beasts. They threatened from the very place where they appeared only as beasts, and this was fulfilled in them: “When a human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. XLIX).

“But Stephen, being full of the Holy Spirit and gazing into heaven, saw the glory of God.” Because he was full of the Holy Spirit, he gazed into heaven. For the fullness of the Holy Spirit did not permit him to look upon earthly things. Moses, too, is said to have seen the glory of God, and the people, at the consecration of the Lord’s house, are said to have seen the glory of the God of Israel (Exod. XXXIV). The Apostle John likewise says in the Gospel: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father” (John I).

“And Jesus standing at the right hand of God.” He said “standing,” not “sitting.” He stood with his martyr and fought as though positioned in battle. Stephen was being stoned, and Jesus was receiving the blows.

“Behold, I see the heavens opened.” The way is already open to me. I am still on earth, yet I gaze even upon the kingdom of heaven. Your stones have opened these heavens to me; through your persecution you have opened heaven to me. Until now I had not seen the heavens opened. My blood is the key to heaven. It is as though he said: “Lay down your stones, confess Jesus, and you too will see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.” But they, holding the stones, could not hear the truth of persecution.

“And the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the power of God.” Since the Lord Jesus Christ is the perfect Son of God and of man, why did the blessed martyr prefer to call him the Son of Man rather than the Son of God? He would seem to have brought greater glory to both if he had wished to call him the Son of God rather than the Son of Man. He did this, surely, so that by this testimony the unbelief of the Jews might be confounded—those who remembered that they had crucified a human being and refused to believe him God. To strengthen the wisdom of the blessed martyr, therefore, the gate of the heavenly kingdom is opened; and lest an innocent human being, stoned, should falter on earth, the crucified God-man appears crowned in heaven. Why? Because standing belongs to one who fights or gives assistance. He rightly saw standing at the right hand of God the one whom, among persecuting human beings, he had as his helper.

“But crying out with a loud voice, they stopped their ears.” (From Jerome.) O depraved minds! They close their ears lest, when opened, truth should enter through them. They close their ears because they also had their eyes closed and did not see the heavens opened.

“And they rushed upon him with one accord.” One impiety, one assault: they showed greater agreement in wickedness than in religion.

“And having driven him outside the city, they stoned him.” (From Bede.) The Lord also suffered outside the gate; he chose us from the world for his heavenly kingdom and glory. Stephen, as a stranger to the world, is stoned outside the city. For he had no abiding city here but sought the future one with his whole mind. In accordance with the transformation of circumstances, the martyr of a pure heart directs his gaze toward heaven, while the stiff-necked persecutor stretches out his hands toward the stones.

“And the witnesses laid aside their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.” Why did the false witnesses first stone him? Because the law had commanded that whoever gave testimony against someone in a capital case should himself cast the first stone at the one whom he had first killed with his mouth (Deut. XVII).

(From Jerome.) They lay aside their garments because they had already cast away God’s help. Saul is interpreted as “temptation” or “hell.” Rightly, therefore, those who were stoning the martyr left their garments beside hell.

“And they stoned Stephen, calling upon the Lord and saying: ‘Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.’” Observe his confession: he sees a man standing, yet confesses him as Lord. It is as though he said: “Lord Jesus, you stand as a human being, but you help as God. You stand; you have risen so that you might receive and embrace me as I come. The son calls upon the father; the martyr calls upon the director of the contest (agonothete). Lord Jesus, receive my spirit, which is driven from my flesh because of its confession of you. It is right that the spirit poured out for you should be received by you.”

“Then, kneeling down, he cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘Lord, do not hold this sin against them.’ And when he had said this, he fell asleep.” (From Bede.) He prayed standing for himself, but bent his knee for his enemies, because their greater wickedness required a greater remedy of supplication. Wonderful was the virtue of the blessed martyr: he burned with zeal, so that he openly reproached those who held him with the faults of their faithlessness; yet he burned with love, so that even in death he prayed for those by whom he was being killed.

## THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER XXIII

“Jesus said to the crowds of the Jews and to the chief priests: ‘Behold, I send to you prophets and wise men and scribes; and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues; and you will persecute them from city to city, so that all the righteous blood poured out upon the earth may come upon you, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar. Amen I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation. Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to you, how often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling! Behold, your house will be left to you desolate. For I say to you, you will not see me from now on until you say: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’”

“Jesus said to the crowds of the Jews: ‘Behold, I send to you prophets and wise men and scribes, and some of them you will kill and crucify and scourge in your synagogues, and you will persecute them from city to city, so that you may fill up the measure of your fathers.’” (From Jerome.) That is: complete what was lacking in them. They killed servants; you crucify the Lord. They killed prophets; you kill the one who was proclaimed through the prophets. This can also be referred to his disciples, concerning whom he now says: “Behold, I send to you prophets,” and so forth. At the same time, observe, in accordance with the Apostle’s writing to the Corinthians, that the disciples of Christ possess various gifts (1 Cor. XII): some are prophets, who proclaim future things; others are wise, who know when they ought to deliver a discourse; others are scribes, thoroughly learned in the law, who write upon the tablets of their hearts. From their number Stephen was stoned, Paul was killed, Peter was crucified, and the disciples were scourged in the Acts of the Apostles; they persecuted them from city to city, driving them out of Judaea so that they might pass over to the people of the nations.

“So that all the righteous blood poured out upon the earth may come upon you.” (From Bede.) It is asked how the blood of all the prophets and righteous can be required from one Jewish generation, since many saints, whether before the incarnation or after the death and resurrection of the Savior, were killed by other nations, and the Lord himself, although the Jews shouted for it, was nevertheless crucified by a Roman governor and Roman soldiers. But it is customary for the Scriptures often to count two generations of human beings, namely, the good and the wicked: those who are born not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of a man, but from God; and those to whom it is said: “You are from your father the devil,” and elsewhere: “Serpents, brood of vipers.”

(Jerome.) Let us briefly explain why the blood of righteous Abel up to Zechariah, son of Barachiah, is required from that generation, although it killed neither of them. It is a rule of Scripture to recognize two generations, of the good and of the wicked. The generation of the good is the one of which it is written: “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob” (Ps. XXIV); and elsewhere concerning all the saints: “The generation of the upright will be blessed” (Ps. CXII). But concerning the wicked: “Brood of vipers,” and: “All these things will be required from this generation.” And also: “O crooked and perverse generation, is this how you repay the Lord, foolish and senseless people?” (Deut. XXXII, 6); and: “A nation without counsel and without understanding.” Therefore these people, who acted against the Apostles in the manner of Cain and Joash, are said to belong to one generation; and all the saints who are alike in virtues appear to constitute one generation.

“From the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah.” (From Bede.) It is asked why he specifically named these two, Abel and Zechariah, since neither was present at that time and many saints were killed by them afterward—surely on account of the equality of their crime. Cain killed his brother Abel when there was no just cause. Likewise King Joash killed the son of the priest who had raised him, rescued him from death, and hidden him for seven years in the temple when Athaliah, his grandmother, had killed all the royal offspring out of desire for the kingdom, especially his foster brother. Forgetting all these benefits, he killed him. It is also asked: If the blood of those who were killed after him comes upon them, does Zechariah signify the saints who will suffer at the end of the world, whose blood altogether will come upon the evil generation whose wickedness is united? For this reason it is not surprising that it begins with the blood of Abel, who was the first to suffer martyrdom. But why should it be required up to the blood of Zechariah, since many were killed after him before the birth of Christ, and immediately after his birth the innocent children of Bethlehem were slain by this generation (Matt. II)? Unless perhaps the reason is that Abel was a shepherd of sheep, while Zechariah was a priest; one was killed in the field, the other in the temple court. By their names he wished to indicate martyrs of both orders: laypeople, certainly, and those devoted to the service of the altar.

“Whom you killed between the temple and the altar.” (From Jerome.) Between the wall of the temple and the inner altar of incense—or, as others say, between the ruins of the temple and the outer altar of sacrifices. It is asked who this Zechariah, son of Barachiah, was who was killed between the temple and the altar, since we read of many Zechariahs. But, lest unrestricted opportunity for error be granted us, what is added clearly indicates whom he means: “Whom you killed between the temple and the altar.” He wishes to signify the Zechariah who was killed by Joash, king of Judah, as the history in Kings relates. Yet it should be observed that this Zechariah was not the son of Barachiah but the son of Jehoiada the priest. Hence Scripture reports: “Joash did not remember the kindness that Jehoiada his father had done for him” (2 Chron. XXIV). Since we identify the Zechariah and the place agrees with the killing, we ask why he is called the son of Barachiah and not of Jehoiada. Barachiah in our language means “blessed by the Lord,” while Jehoiada is interpreted as “justice”; therefore a man full of justice is rightly called blessed by the Lord.

Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you. [Col. 0040B] (From Jerome.) He calls “Jerusalem” not the stones and buildings of the city, but its inhabitants, whom he mourns with a father’s affection, just as we read elsewhere that, when he saw it, he wept (Luke 19).

How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling. In saying, “How often I wanted to gather your children,” he testifies that all the prophets sent before him had been sent by him. We also read in the Song of Deuteronomy of a bird gathering its nest beneath its wings: “As an eagle protects its nest and hovers over its young, spreading its wings, it took them up and carried them upon its feathers” (Deut. 32). And appropriately, since he had called Herod, who was plotting his death, a fox (Luke 13), he compares himself to a bird. [Col. 0040C] For the treacherous fox never ceases to lay ambushes for birds. What he says, “those who were sent to you,” means “those who had been sent for your benefit.” “How often I wanted”—as if he were saying: “You return evil to me, though I wanted to gather from Egypt and Babylon the chicks beneath my wings.” The two wings of the Lord are Moses and Aaron, who led the people out of Egypt; or Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, together with Joshua son of Jehozadak, the leaders who led the people of Israel out of Babylon. It is asked how he can say, “How often I wanted,” when the Prophet says, “The Lord has done everything that he desired”—that is, “I did not will this from my side, but you willed it from yours.”

Behold, your house will be left desolate. (From Jerome.) He had already said this same thing through Jeremiah’s person: “I have abandoned my house; I have forsaken my inheritance; my inheritance has become for me like a hyena’s den” (Jer. 12). We plainly see that the desolate house of the Jews is that same temple which formerly shone most magnificently in men’s eyes: it lost Christ, its inhabitant, and, eager to seize the inheritance, killed the heir. Alternatively: “Behold, your house will be left desolate”—that is, “now it is yours, not mine, though formerly it was called my house.” It will be left desolate in punishment for the cross; or the Jewish temple will be abandoned by the Lord, its inhabitant, and he will pass over to the Church of the nations.

(From Bede.) He now calls the very city that he had called his nest the house of the Jews. Not unjustly deprived of the Lord’s help, it is left to its own control, because it not only scorned being protected by the wings of that omnipotent bird whom Matthew calls a hen, [Col. 0041A] but also handed over to the foxes for devouring the same bird who wished to protect it—that is, it handed Christ over to Herod and Pilate to be crucified. Nor was it long before it was given as prey to those same foxes, that is, to the kings of the earth. For after the Lord had been killed, the Romans came and, as though plundering an empty nest, took away their place, nation, and kingdom.

(From Jerome.) It should be known that the hyena, which was mentioned above in the testimony of Jeremiah, is an animal that lives at night on the corpses of the dead and is accustomed to dig bodies out of tombs; there is no impurity on which it does not feed. Such is Israel: it offended its Lord and was handed over to the bites of every beast, since it has indeed been abandoned by the Lord.

For I tell you: You will not see me from now on until you say, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” [Col. 0041B] (From Augustine.) The crowds certainly said these words to the Lord when he was coming to Jerusalem. But since Luke does not say where the Lord went away from here, so that he would not come except at the time when this would already be said—for he continues on his journey until he comes to Jerusalem—this must plainly be understood mystically of that coming of his in which he will come in glory, especially since Matthew testifies that the Lord spoke of the praises previously uttered to him by the crowd.

(From Jerome.) By the same words, “until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,’” he means this: “Unless you repent and confess that I am the one of whom the prophets sang, the Son of the almighty Father, you will not see my face.” The Jews have been given a time for repentance. Let them confess, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” and they will behold the face of Christ.

## AGREEMENT

The agreement of these two readings lies in the fact that both mention the stoning of the righteous, and together make one reference to it. The reading from the Acts of the Apostles speaks plainly and specifically of the already accomplished stoning of blessed Stephen. The Gospel reading, however, speaks generally, not specifically, of the stoning of some prophet or other.

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT JOHN THE EVANGELIST

### READING FROM THE LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE EPHESIANS, CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0041D]

“Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ: just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, so that we might be holy and blameless in his sight in love. He predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ unto himself, according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace, with which he favored us in his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which has abounded toward us.”

Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who blessed us with every spiritual blessing [Col. 0042A] in the heavenly places in Christ. (From Jerome.) Just as God, good according to his substance, makes us good through participation in himself, so, being himself blessed, he grants that we be blessed. He blessed us not with one blessing only, but with all blessings—not in the sense that each of us receives everything, but that, while individuals possess one, several, or many blessings, all of us possess individual blessings from the whole—and not with earthly blessings, but spiritual ones. It is asked how, while we are still placed on earth, he has blessed us with a heavenly blessing. Either because our manner of life is in heaven, and we are not of this world, but, having laid aside the image of τὸ χοϊκόν, “the earthly,” we bear the image of the heavenly, and do not live in the flesh but in the spirit; or because every spiritual blessing, although it is on earth in Christ, is nevertheless reckoned among heavenly things. “He blessed us,” he says, “with every spiritual blessing”—that is, in the word of God, wisdom, virtue, and the other virtues.

The passage may be read in two ways: “Blessed is God, and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” so that “blessed” modifies God, who is the creator of all things, and then the distinction is made that he is also the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ; or so that “God and Father” jointly refer to our Lord: blessed is the God of the man who was assumed, and his Father, who in the beginning was with God, the Word who was God. This does not mean that the man who was assumed is one person and the Word who assumed him another, but that one and the same person is proclaimed now in exalted terms and now in humble terms, according to the different circumstances.

Just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world. [Col. 0042C] Wishing, therefore, to show that God chose us so that we might be holy and blameless before him—that is, before the Lord—before the world was made, in the presence of God, for whom all future things are already accomplished and all things are known before they come to be, Paul used this expression, saying, “before the foundation of the world.” But when he says, “so that we might be holy and blameless,” the difference between holy and blameless is this: one who is holy can also be understood to be blameless, but one who is blameless is not thereby immediately holy. Little children are blameless, since with an uncorrupted body they have not committed sin; yet they are not holy, because holiness is acquired through the will and through devotion.

In love he predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, and so forth. This too may be read in two ways, so that “in love” is joined either with what precedes or with what follows. With what precedes: “so that we might be holy and blameless before him in love.” With what follows: “in love he predestined us,” and so forth. It should also be understood that, although he predestines us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, we cannot become sons beforehand unless we receive faith in and understanding of the Son of God, Jesus Christ. He is Son by nature, whereas we are sons by adoption. He was never not the Son; we were predestined before we existed. We received the spirit of adoption when we believed in the Son of God.

According to the good pleasure of his will. (From Jerome.) The word εὐδοκία, which the Latin translator rendered as *placitum*, “good pleasure,” is formed in Greek from two complete words, ἀπὸ τοῦ εὖ καὶ τοῦ δοκεῖν—that is, from *eu*, “well,” and *dokein*, “to seem” or “to please.” We can therefore render it *beneplacitum*, “good pleasure,” because not everything that pleases immediately can be said to please well; rather, “good pleasure” is used where what has pleased is shown to have pleased rightly.

To the praise of the glory of his grace, with which he favored us in the beloved. Therefore, all the grace that we attain is completed for the glory and praise of the one who favored us in the beloved—that is, in the Lord Jesus Christ the Savior—because apart from wisdom, truth, justice, peace, and redemption, all of which are understood in Christ, there can be no good. Nor should it be thought that the Latin manuscripts read “in his beloved Son,” but simply and absolutely, “in the beloved.” This seems to me to be understood as if “by all” were supplied. [Col. 0043B] For if Christ, as we have often said, is wisdom, justice, peace, joy, and so forth, even those who cannot follow these virtues love their names; no one is so openly wicked that he does not say that he loves wisdom and justice. This is the beloved whom I think is signified in Isaiah: “I will sing for my beloved, and a vineyard was made for my beloved” (Isa. 5), and in the Psalm: “And the beloved, like the son of unicorns” (Ps. 29).

In whom we have redemption. The person redeemed is one who is captive and, having fallen into the power of enemies, has ceased to be free. Thus some say that we too are captives in this world, held under rulers and powers by the yoke of slavery, and that we cannot unfold hands bound in chains or lift our eyes upward before Jesus Christ, the Redeemer and Son of God, arrives—he who [Col. 0043C] gave his own blood, rescued us from slavery, and bestowed freedom upon us.

Through his blood. The blood and flesh of Christ are understood in two ways: either that spiritual and divine flesh and blood of which he himself says, “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6), and, “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have eternal life” (John 6); or the flesh that was crucified and the blood that was poured out by the soldier’s spear.

The forgiveness of sins. Consequently, after the redemption through Christ’s blood, we are said to have received forgiveness of sins, because unless we have been redeemed, our sins are forgiven in vain; nor can we receive pardon before the victorious one, once bloodied, has accepted the price on our behalf. [Col. 0043D]

According to the riches of his grace, which abounded toward us. Whoever understands the statement, “You have been saved by grace and not by works” (Eph. 2), knows that, according to his riches, God’s grace abounds toward us, especially in the Church gathered from the nations. Is there not a greatness of graces in Paul and in the other saints, of whom it is said, “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6). The person who does not make these riches of grace empty in himself is the one who, as far as human frailty permits, labors and strives and says with Paul, “His grace toward me was not empty” (1 Cor. 15). But whoever slips into worse things will be impoverished by the wealth of God’s grace within him.

[Col. 0044A]

## GOSPEL OF JOHN, LAST CHAPTER

“Jesus said to Peter, ‘Follow me.’ Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following—the one who had reclined at supper upon his breast and had said, ‘Lord, who is the one who will betray you?’ When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, ‘Lord, but what about this man?’ Jesus said to him, ‘If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me.’ Therefore this saying went out among the brothers, that that disciple would not die. Yet Jesus did not say to him that he would not die, but, ‘If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?’ This is the disciple who testifies concerning these things and wrote them, and we know that his testimony is true.”

Jesus said to Peter, “Follow me.” (From Bede.) After the Lord Jesus had signified by what death he would glorify God, he immediately added, “Follow me,” as though he were plainly saying: “Since I did not fear first to undergo the punishment of the cross for your redemption, why do you fear suffering the cross for confessing my name? You will be glorified by the more glorious crown of martyrdom the more closely you follow your master’s path in earning it.”

Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following. From this it is evident that, when Jesus had said to Peter, “Follow me,” he rose from the place of the meal and began to leave. Peter followed him, and so did the disciple whom Jesus loved, namely John, the very one who wrote this Gospel. Jesus loved him—not to the exclusion of the others, but more familiarly than the rest, for the special privilege of chastity had made him worthy of a greater love. He loves all, since he says to all, “As the Father loved me, I also loved you; remain in my love” (John 15). But he loves this man above all because, chosen by him as a virgin, he remained a virgin forever. Histories report that Jesus called him from his wedding, when he wished to marry, and that he bestowed a greater sweetness of his love upon the one whom he had withdrawn from carnal pleasure.

The one who reclined at supper upon his breast. When that disciple reclined upon his master’s breast, this signified not only the love present at that moment but also a mystery concerning the future. For it already indicated that the Gospel which the same disciple would write would contain, more abundantly and more deeply than the other pages of sacred Scripture, the secrets of the divine majesty. Since all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Jesus’ breast, he deservedly reclines upon his breast—the one to whom he grants, more than to the others, the singular gift of wisdom and knowledge. We know that the other Evangelists spoke more about the miracles of our Savior and less about his divinity. John, however, writing very little about his human actions, devoted himself rather to explaining the mysteries of the divine nature, plainly suggesting how great were the streams of heavenly teaching that he drew from Jesus’ breast and poured forth for us. The text continues: “When Peter saw him, Jesus said”:

“Lord, but what about this man?” Blessed Peter had heard that he would glorify God through the passion of the cross, and he also wished to know by what death his brother and fellow disciple would pass over into eternal life.

Jesus said to him, “If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me.” He says, “I do not want him to be perfected through the passion of martyrdom, but to await the last day without the violence of a persecutor, when I myself come and receive him into the dwelling of eternal blessedness.” What is that to you? You must remember only that you are to follow my footsteps by undergoing the gallows of the cross.”

This does not mean that John did not previously endure many labors and afflictions for the Lord. In the Acts of the Apostles he is found scourged with the other apostles, when they went away rejoicing [Col. 0045B] from the presence of the council because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus (Acts 5). Ecclesiastical history also relates that Domitian Caesar placed him in a cauldron of boiling oil; yet, protected by divine grace, he emerged as unharmed as he had been removed from the corruption of carnal desire. Not long afterward, because of his unconquerable steadfastness in preaching the Gospel, the same ruler banished him into exile on the island of Patmos. There, although deprived of human consolation, he deserved to be lifted up by frequent consolation through divine vision and address. Finally, there he wrote with his own hand the Apocalypse, which the Lord revealed to him concerning the present or future state of the Church.

Thus it is clear that the promise that he would remain until the Lord came did not mean that he would live in the world without the labor of struggle, but rather that he would leave the world without the pain of passion. For we find it recorded in the writings of the Fathers that, when he was worn out by old age and knew that the day of his departure was near, he summoned his disciples, gave them exhortations, celebrated Mass, and bade them a final farewell. Then, descending into the place dug for his burial and having prayed, he was laid with his fathers, already free from the pain of death and, as we find, untouched by corruption of the flesh.

(From Augustine.) Who would not also be moved to inquire about these two apostles, Peter and John? Why did the Lord love John more, when Peter loved the Lord more? Wherever John mentions himself, so that he may be understood without naming himself, he adds that he was the one whom Jesus loved. Many proofs can be offered that the apostle Peter loved Christ more than the others. But, without going farther afield, this appears sufficiently clearly in the Lord’s third manifestation, in the reading immediately preceding this one, where he asked Peter, “Do you love me more than these?” He certainly knew the answer, yet he asked so that we, who read the Gospel, might recognize Peter’s love for the Lord both in the one who asked and in the one who answered.

When Peter replied, “I love you,” he did not add, “more than these,” because he answered according to what he knew about himself. He could not know how much he was loved by another, since he could not see another person’s heart. Yet by saying in the earlier words, “Yes, Lord, you know,” he himself sufficiently declared that the Lord, who knew, had asked what he asked. The Lord therefore knew not only that Peter loved him, but also that Peter loved him more than the others.

If, then, we ask which of two people is better: the one who loves Christ more, or the one who loves him less, who would hesitate to answer that the one who loves more is better? Likewise, if we ask which of two people is better: the one whom Christ loves less, or the one whom he loves more, we shall undoubtedly answer that the one who is loved more by Christ is better.

I shall therefore attempt, in the manifest mercy of the one whose justice is hidden, to discuss, according to the strength he himself grants, the resolution of so great a question. “If I want him,” he says, “to remain”—that is, to await the end of his own condition, not the end of the world. What he adds, “until I come,” can be understood not only of that general coming by which the world will be dissolved, but also of the coming by which he deigns daily to visit his saints.

When he says, “Do you love me more than these?” this can be understood to mean that John, who was loved more particularly, is distinguished from the others. But according to the mystical meaning, active life is signified in Peter and contemplative life in John. Both the present and the future are represented in each.

The Church, whose figure Peter bore because of the primacy of the apostleship, received from Christ the keys of the kingdom of heaven. In the rock—that is, in the power of loosing and binding sins—what the Church is properly in Christ, Peter is symbolically in the rock: by this symbolism Christ is understood as the rock and Peter as the Church. This Church, which Peter signified, remains amid evils for as long as it loves and follows Christ, and is freed from evils. It follows Christ more fully in those who struggle for the truth even unto death, to whom Peter himself says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2). This is why he was told, “Follow me.”

There is another immortal life, which is not amid evils, where we shall see face to face what is now seen through a mirror and in a riddle (1 Cor. 13). The Church therefore knows that two lives have been divinely proclaimed and commended to her: one in faith, the other in sight; one in pilgrimage, the other in eternity; one in labor, the other in rest; one on the way, the other in the homeland; one fighting with an enemy, the other reigning without an enemy. One is good but still wretched; the other is better and blessed. The former is signified by the apostle Peter, the latter by John.

Therefore it is said to the one, “Follow me,” but of the other, “If I want him to remain until I come.” It is as though he were saying: “You follow me by imitating me in enduring temporal evils. Let him remain until I come to give eternal blessings.” “I want him to remain”—that is, to await me—because what is signified through him will not be fulfilled now, but when Christ comes.

This is the disciple who testifies concerning these things and wrote them. Here blessed John plainly identifies his own person by his office, while avoiding identifying it by name. He testified to the Word of God by preaching; he testified by writing; he testified again by teaching; and he testifies even now by revealing these things.

From the time of the Lord’s passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven until the final years of Domitian’s reign, for approximately sixty-five years, he preached the word without any written aid. But when he was sent into exile by Domitian, who became the second persecutor of Christians after Nero, heretics burst into the Church like wolves into sheepfolds abandoned by their shepherd: Marcion, Cerinthus, Ebion, and the other Antichrists, who denied that Christ existed before Mary, stained the simplicity of evangelical faith with perverse teaching.

After Domitian’s death, however, when the pious ruler Nerva permitted John to return to Ephesus, nearly all the bishops of Asia at that time, together with delegations from many churches, compelled him to speak more profoundly about the coeternal divinity of the Father and of Christ, since they believed that the writings of the other three evangelists contained sufficient testimony concerning Christ’s humanity.

John replied that he would not do so unless, after a fast had been proclaimed, everyone together prayed to the Lord that he might be able to write what was worthy of him. When this had been done, instructed by revelation and filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, he exposed all the darkness of the heretics and scattered it by the sudden light of truth, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

Making the entire course of his discourse correspond to this opening, he taught with the clearest assertion that our Lord Jesus Christ was truly human, truly made from a human being in time, and also truly God, truly born eternally from God the Father, and truly always existing with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Indeed, he disclosed all the mysteries of divine truth and true divinity as fully as no other mortal was permitted to do.

This privilege was rightly preserved for a virgin: in order to investigate the mysteries of the incorruptible Word, he himself proceeded incorrupt not only in heart but also in body. To show that no one should doubt the truth of his words, John himself took care to demonstrate it. After saying, “This is the disciple who testifies concerning these things and wrote them,” he immediately added, “And we know that his testimony is true.”

Since, therefore, together with all the faithful, we know that his testimony is true, let us take care in every respect to attain the eternal gifts promised through our Lord Jesus Christ: by understanding what he taught with right faith and practicing it through right action. He lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## AGREEMENT

The agreement of these two readings lies in the fact that one makes reasonable mention of John’s human activity and name, while the other mentions only his activity. The Lord guarded him from every stain from infancy and made him holy; therefore the apostolic reading aptly applies to him, especially where it says, “Blessed is the God who chose us,” and so forth.

## ON THE FEAST OF THE HOLY INNOCENTS

### READING FROM THE BOOK OF THE APOCALYPSE OF JOHN THE APOSTLE, CHAPTER FOURTEEN

“I saw a Lamb standing upon Mount Zion, and with him one hundred forty-four thousand, having his name and the name of his Father written on their foreheads. And I heard a voice from heaven, like the voice of many waters and like the voice of a great thunder; and the voice that I heard was like that of harpists playing their harps. And they were singing as though a new song before the throne of God and before the four living creatures and the elders; and no one could sing the song except the one hundred forty-four thousand who had been purchased from the earth. These are the ones who were not defiled with women, for they are virgins. These follow the Lamb wherever he goes. These were purchased from humanity as first fruits for God and for the Lamb, and no lie was found in their mouth. They are without blemish before the throne of God.”

I saw a Lamb standing upon Mount Zion. The Lamb is Christ, of whom John says, “Behold, the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world.” Mount Zion, which is interpreted as “watchtower” or “vision,” signifies the Church in this passage. The Lord Jesus Christ is said to stand upon it, granting it the help and protection of his power.

Notice that earlier the beast was said to stand upon the sand of the sea, while the Lamb is said to stand upon Mount Zion, and with him are one hundred forty-four thousand. This is the number of God’s people. A finite number is placed here for an infinite one, and a sacred number is used to signify a hidden mystery. For three multiplied three times makes nine, and four multiplied by four makes sixteen. But nine times ten times six hundred make forty-four [the printed computation is corrupt]. By this number the fullness of the virgin host is mystically indicated, so that, when such a numerous multitude is spoken of, there may be no doubt concerning the remaining members of the Church.

Having his name and the name of his Father, and so forth. Earlier he had said of the beast rising from the earth that it caused all—the small and the great, the rich and the poor, the free and the slaves—to have a mark on their right hand and on their foreheads. Here, by contrast, concerning the servants of God, lest a weak spirit should suppose that anyone had either succumbed or perished under the violent force of the persecution, he adds: “Having his name and the name of his Father written on their foreheads.” By “his name” the Lamb’s name is understood, and by “the name of his Father,” the name of God the Father.

And I heard a voice from heaven. That is, the Church, which is frequently called “heaven” in the divine Scriptures. For it is written concerning the Church, “Heaven is my throne.” And concerning the preachers of that same Church it is written, “The heavens declare the glory of God.” The great voice of the saints is the great devotion of love, which he says he heard from heaven, when he had declared that those who uttered the voice stood on Mount Zion. Thus he shows that by Mount Zion he meant nothing other than the Church, which, raised up by sublime contemplation into joy, celebrates the struggles of its king with both praise and imitation, in order to overcome the burdens of affliction. This is truly to sing psalms to the Lamb who stands.

Like the voice of many waters and like the voice of a great thunder. What is meant by “the voice of many waters” except the voice of preachers? What is meant by “the voice of a great thunder” except the voice of the Gospel? Hence certain apostles are also called sons of thunder. The Gospels are thunders when, threatening, they say: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.”

And the voice that I heard was like that of harpists playing their harps. What is signified by the voice of harpists except the harmonious voice of all the preachers and their single concord, which resounds as a song of love in pure hearts? All the saints are God’s fellow-harpists, crucifying their flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5), and praising him with psaltery and harp. How much more do those do so who, by the privilege of angelic chastity, make themselves wholly and uniquely a sacrifice to the Lord, denying themselves, taking up their cross, and following the Lamb wherever he goes.

And they were singing as though a new song. What is signified by the new song except the New Testament and the confession of the faithful: “I believe in God the Father almighty, and in Jesus Christ his Son, our Lord, and in the Holy Spirit”? The person who sings this new song is happily renewed, having laid aside the old human being through the grace of baptism. This song consoles the purest mind and delights it to the marrow. The new person must sing the new song, not the old person who has not yet laid aside Adam’s sins. It is truly a new song because the world had never before heard such a song.

New. It is not stained by any oldness, but always perseveres in the grace of its own dignity.

Before the throne. The throne is the perfect Church, which deserved to be heaven because it is the dwelling place of God. The thrones are those of the Lord Savior, which he already possesses in his majesty, as it is written: “The soul of the righteous is the throne of wisdom” (Wis. 7).

And before the four living creatures. The four living creatures signify the four Gospels, which elsewhere are described as full of eyes before and behind. “Before,” because they preach concerning the future judgment.

Behind. Because they give testimony from the Old Testament. What follows is:

And the elders. He signifies those of whom he had said above:

“And around the throne were twenty-four seats, and upon the thrones twenty-four elders, seated and clothed in white garments.” These signify either the doubled Decalogue together with the four Gospels, or the twelve apostles and the twelve patriarchs: Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Joshua, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and David.

And no one could sing the song except the one hundred forty-five thousand who had been purchased from the earth. To sing the song of the Lamb uniquely means to rejoice with him forever, above all the faithful, even in the incorruption of the flesh. Yet the other elect can hear the song, although they cannot sing it, because through love they rejoice in the exalted state of those singers, even though they do not rise to their rewards.

For they are virgins—those who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. Blessed Augustine beautifully explained this when he exhorted virgins:

“Go forward,” he says, “holy people of God, boys and girls, males and females, celibates and unmarried women; go forward by persevering to the end. Praise the Lord more sweetly, whom you contemplate more abundantly. Hope more happily in him whom you serve more earnestly. Love more ardently him whom you please more attentively. With your loins girded and your lamps burning, await the Lord when he comes from the wedding (Luke 13). You bring to the wedding of the Lamb the new song that you will sing on your harps—such a song, certainly, that no one will be able to sing except you.

“For one who was more beloved by the Lamb than the others saw you in the Apocalypse—the one who was accustomed to recline upon his breast. He saw you as twelve times twelve thousand holy harpists, with undefiled virginity in the body and inviolate truth in the heart. Follow the Lamb, because the Lamb’s flesh too is virginal. Follow him in virginity of heart and flesh wherever he goes. For what is it to follow except to imitate? Because Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example so that you might follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2).

These are the ones who were not defiled with women, for they are virgins. He calls them virgins because of the integrity of faith. Thus the Apostle speaks of the universal Church: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present a pure virgin to Christ.” Tichonius also interprets this vision not only specifically of virgins, but generally of the whole Church.

These were purchased from humanity as first fruits for God and for the Lamb, redeemed by Christ’s precious blood, as the Apostle says: “You were bought with a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6). These first fruits are chosen by the Holy Spirit from that holy and blameless flock of the Church as more holy and more excellent offerings, according to the merits of their will.

And no lie was found in their mouth. He did not say, “There was no lie in their mouth,” but “no lie was found.” As the Apostle says: “And such were some of you, but you were washed” (1 Cor. 6). And: “The injustice of the unjust will not harm him on the day when he turns from his injustice”; he can be a virgin, and deceit will not be found in his mouth. By virgins he means the chaste and modest.

They are without blemish before the throne of God. “Without blemish” means without sin. The righteous are then without blemish when they receive the gifts of pardon, as the Prophet says: “You will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Ps. 51). Blessed, therefore, are the blameless who deserve to enter eternal life.

## GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER TWO
«Behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph, [Col. 0051A] saying: “Rise and take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell you; for Herod is going to seek the child in order to destroy him.” And rising, he took the child and his mother by night and withdrew into Egypt, and was there until Herod’s death, so that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: “Out of Egypt I called my son.” Then Herod, seeing that he had been mocked by the magi, became very angry. And he sent and killed all the children who were in Bethlehem and in all its borders, from two years old and under, according to the time that he had ascertained from the magi. Then what had been spoken through the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled, saying: “A voice was heard in Rama, weeping and loud lamentation; [Col. 0051B] Rachel weeping for her children, and she refused to be comforted, because they are not.” But when Herod had died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying: “Rise and take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel. For those who sought the child’s life have died.” And rising, he took the child and his mother and came into the land of Israel. But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning in Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there. And being warned in a dream, he withdrew into the regions of Galilee. And coming, he dwelt in a city called Nazareth, so that what had been spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: “For he shall be called a Nazarene.”»

“Behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph,” [Col. 0051C] saying: “Rise and take the child and his mother.” He does not say “your child,” nor “the child of the woman,” but by a special privilege the child alone is named. It follows:

“And his mother.” For he does not say, “Take your wife,” or “your spouse,” but “his mother,” for his true Father is in heaven. Because Babylon and Egypt, more than all other lands, showed what was at the beginning, namely that he would reform both of them and set them ablaze with the fire of faith, we also learn that from the very beginnings of life one must be prepared for temptations and snares. For as soon as he was born, a tyrant rages against him; he flees into Egypt, and his mother is driven into a barbarous and hostile region. For it is not said, “Take your spouse,” but “his mother,” because, once the birth had been established by the sign, every suspicion was dismissed.

“And flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell you; for Herod is going to seek the child in order to destroy him.” We may also understand Herod’s hatred, by which he wished to destroy Jesus, specifically as referring to the persecutions inflicted in Judea during the time of the apostles: when envy grew strong, nearly all the preachers of the word were expelled from the province and, in order to preach among the Gentiles, were scattered far and wide. Thus it happened that the Gentile world, figured by Egypt, previously darkened by sins, received the light of the word. For this is what it means that the child Jesus and his mother were transferred through Joseph into Egypt: that the faith of the Lord’s [Col. 0052A] incarnation and fellowship with the Church were entrusted through holy teachers to the Gentiles.

“And rising, he took the child and his mother by night and withdrew into Egypt.” Egypt is interpreted as “darkness” and “sorrow.” Therefore Joseph’s flight with Mary and the child into Egypt signifies that the teachers, together with the law and the preaching of Christ’s name, would pass over to the Gentiles who were in the darkness and night of unbelief.

“And he was there until Herod’s death.” What he says—“and he was there until Herod’s death”—whether the time is calculated as four years, as some think, or merely two years, as others hold, indicates figuratively that faith in Christ will remain among the Gentiles until their fullness enters and thus all Israel is saved. Herod’s death signifies the end of the evil purpose by which Judea now rages against the Church.

“So that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled.” We say that this is written in the prophet Hosea (Hos. XI). We may also bring forward a testimony from Numbers, where Balaam says: “God called him out of Egypt. His glory is like that of a unicorn” (Num. XXIII).

“Out of Egypt I called my son.” The fact that Jesus is again called from Egypt signifies that the Jews will believe at the end of the world, in accordance with the saying: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI). Yet it can also be understood allegorically. After he came into the Egypt of this world, the Father led him out and took him to himself, so that he might prepare the way for those who were to ascend from the Egypt of this world [Col. 0052C] to the Lord.

“Then Herod, seeing that he had been mocked by the magi, became very angry.” The phrase “then Herod” is joined to the statement that the magi had returned by another way. “He became angry,” with the disturbance mentioned above still remaining. “Very” is added because he had been mocked by the magi.

“And he sent and killed all the children.” In the death of the innocents, the precious death of all Christ’s martyrs was prefigured. The fact that the little children were killed signifies that one must attain the glory of martyrdom through the merit of humility. For unless someone is converted and becomes like a little child, he cannot give his life for Christ. “Who were in Bethlehem and in all its borders.” The fact that they were killed in Bethlehem and throughout all its borders shows that persecution by the faithless will rage not only in Judea, from which the Church began, but also throughout the whole Church, wherever it has been spread across the world; and that the patience of the godly will be crowned.

“From two years old and under, according to the time that he had ascertained from the magi.” That is, from a child of two years down to a child of one night old. According to the anagogical sense, those who were killed signify people perfect in doctrine and conduct. Those who were under that age signify simple or uneducated people, yet equally strong through the steadfastness of an unfeigned faith. The fact that they were killed, while Christ, whom they sought, escaped alive, indicates that the bodies of the martyrs can indeed be killed by the ungodly, but Christ, for whose sake the entire persecution rages, cannot in any way be taken from them, whether living or [Col. 0053A] dead. They truly testify: “Whether we live, we live to the Lord; whether we die, we die to the Lord” (II Cor. V).

“Then what had been spoken through the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled.” Here Jeremiah, recalling an ancient history, speaks of the lamentation of the survivors and the slain. Because of a Levite’s wife, who had been forced into prostitution and consequently killed, and who was divided by her husband into twelve parts, corresponding to the twelve tribes, all Israel rose up and destroyed the entire tribe, with only three hundred men remaining.

“A voice was heard in Rama,” and so forth. As for the statement “in Rama,” we should not suppose that it refers to the name of the place near Gabaa; rather, Rama is interpreted as “high,” so that the meaning is: “A voice was heard on high,” that is, scattered far and wide. For what does Rama have to do with Rachel? Rachel was the mother of Benjamin, and after her death she was buried in the hippodrome near Bethel. Since the tomb was nearby and the field had fallen by lot to Benjamin, Rama also belonged to the same tribe; and consequently, both on account of its rulers and of the very place of the slaughter, he called those who had been killed her children.

Spiritually, “a voice in Rama,” that is, “on high,” together with “great weeping and lamentation,” clearly announces the mourning of the holy Church, which groans over the unjust killing of its members. This mourning does not, as the enemies chatter, fall into emptiness, but rises all the way to the throne of the heavenly Judge; and, like the blood of Abel the first martyr, the blood of the other martyrs also cries out to the Lord.

[Col. 0053C]

“Rachel weeping for her children.” Benjamin was born from Rachel, and Bethlehem is now in his tribe. The question therefore arises: how can Rachel weep for the children of Judah—that is, for Bethlehem—as though they were her own? We shall answer briefly: because she was buried near Bethlehem in Ephrata and, from the eternal lodging of her little body, received the name of mother. Or because Judah and Benjamin were two joined tribes, and Herod had ordered that the children be killed not only in Bethlehem but also throughout all the regions around it, we understand, through the mention of Bethlehem, that many from Benjamin also were slain.

Figuratively, however, Rachel—whose name is said to mean either “ewe” or “one seeing the Lord”—represents the Church, whose entire attention is devoted to watching so that it may be worthy to see the Lord. She is also the one hundredth sheep whom the Good Shepherd, leaving the ninety-nine sheep of the angelic powers in heaven, went to seek on earth; and when he found her, he placed her on his shoulders and thus carried her back to the flock.

“And she refused to be comforted, because they are not.” She weeps for her children and did not accept consolation. This may be understood in two ways: either because she considered them eternally dead, or because she did not wish to be consoled concerning those whom she knew would live. Spiritually, Rachel signifies the Church, which mourns the removal of the saints from this world, but does not wish to be comforted in such a way that those who conquered the world by death should return with her to endure again the struggles of the world. For they are not to be recalled into the world, from whose hardships they have escaped once for all, to be crowned with Christ.

[Col. 0054A]

“But when Herod had died.” Herod’s death signifies the end of the evil purpose by which Judea now rages against the Church.

“Behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying: ‘Rise and take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel.’” The phrase “in a dream” always signifies that, once they are dead to the world, angels are present. The fact that, after Herod’s death, Jesus returns to the land of Israel announces the end of the world, when, with Enoch and Elijah preaching, the Jews will receive the faith of the truth after the flame of their present-day envy has been put to sleep. And rightly, when he leaves Judea, he is said to flee, and this is said to occur by night; but when he returns, there is no mention either of flight or even of night. For those whom he once left as persecutors in the darkness of sins, he will revisit when, because of the light of faith, they finally seek him.

“For those who sought the child’s life have died.” (From Jerome.) From this passage we understand that not only Herod but also the priests and scribes were plotting the Lord’s death at that time.

“And rising, he took the child and his mother,” and so forth. He did not say, “He took his son and his wife,” but “the child and his mother,” as though he were a foster-father, not a husband.

“But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning in Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there.” Archelaus is interpreted as “recognizing lion”; Herod as “leathery” or “skin of glory” (Josephus, *Antiquities*, book XVII, chapter 10). That Herod who later made an alliance with Pilate was this Herod’s son and Archelaus’s brother. Tiberius Caesar also banished Archelaus himself to Lugdunum, a city of Gaul, and made his brother Herod successor to the kingdom.

(From Bede.) When Joseph, after the birth of Christ, feared to go into Judea because of Archelaus and, at the angel’s warning, withdrew into Nazareth of Galilee, this signifies the final times of the present Church. At that time, because of the blindness of mind that now afflicts Judea, it does not cease persecuting Christians as far as it can, but the persecution of Antichrist will rise up more fiercely against them. The part of Judea, therefore, in which Archelaus reigned—whose name is interpreted as “recognizing lion,” concerning whom the Apostle says, “Your adversary goes about seeking whom he may devour”—represents the faithless followers of Antichrist.

“And being warned in a dream, he withdrew into the regions of Galilee, [Col. 0054D] and coming, he dwelt in a city called Nazareth.” Galilee, where the Lord is transferred, signifies that part of the same nation which at that time will receive the faith of Christ. Hence Galilee is appropriately understood as “transmigration.” Nazareth, however, is interpreted as “flower” or “shoot.” For the more the holy Church, with ardent desire, migrates from those whom it has seen on earth toward the attainment of heavenly things, the more abundantly it flourishes and puts forth the shoots of spiritual virtues.

“So that what had been spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: ‘For he shall be called a Nazarene.’” (From Jerome.) If he had set down a fixed example from Scripture, he would never have said “through the prophets,” but simply “through the prophet.” By now calling them prophets in the plural, he shows that he did not take the words from Scripture, but the meaning. For *Nazaraeus* is interpreted as “holy.” Every Scripture bears witness that the Lord would be holy. We may also say otherwise: that in the same words, according to the Hebrew truth and according to the idiom of that language, it is written in Isaiah: “[Hebrew text unclear in the supplied source]. A branch shall go out from the root of Jesse, and a Nazarene shall rise or grow from his root.”

## HARMONY

The harmony of these two readings is especially pleasing here, because John saw in heaven the firstfruits of the earth with the Lamb. Concerning them he says that they are without falsehood, without blemish, and virgins. For the little children who were killed for the Lord’s sake are also the firstfruits of the earth, because they were the first to merit the palms of martyrdom for the Lord; and they are virgins, without falsehood, and without blemish.

## ON THE OCTAVE OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

### READING FROM THE LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO TITUS, CHAPTER II

«The grace of God our Savior has appeared to all people, instructing us that, denying impiety and worldly desires, we should live soberly, justly, and godly in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, so that he might redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself a people acceptable to him, zealous for good works. Speak these things and exhort.»

“The grace of God our Savior has appeared to all people.” Here he speaks of the grace of the Gospel, concerning which we read in Zechariah: “He has made grace equal to grace” (Zech. IV). And John says: “We have all received from his fullness, grace for grace” (John I), that is, in place of the grace of the law, the grace of the Gospel. “To all people,” that is, to those to whom he appeared. For he himself is the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world—that is, everyone who is enlightened. He is the one who wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. He is the one who says to his apostles: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them”; and, “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved.” Behold how the grace of God the Savior appeared to all people.

“Instructing us.” (From Cassiodorus.) To instruct is to teach, for the word itself signifies knowledge that has been apprehended. The uneducated person is called *rudis*, “new” or “unformed.” An instructed person is, as it were, raised from the countryside—that is, separated from ignorance and established within the boundaries of learning.

(From Jerome.) The Lord also says to Jerusalem through Jeremiah: “Instruct Jerusalem, lest perhaps my soul depart from you” (Jer. VI). Jerusalem is instructed so that it may be corrected, so that God’s soul may not depart from it and reduce it to solitude, but so that, once instructed, it may always have the Lord as its inhabitant.

“That we should deny impiety.” Here he means that impiety which Zechariah saw sitting upon a leaden vessel or mass. We may call it by another name, idolatry, and the denial of Christ. In Greek, they call it **τὴν ἀσέβειαν** (*tēn asebeian*, “impiety”).

[Col. 0056A]

“And worldly desires.” Everything carnal that is desired, and every worldly ambition, is worldly. Shameful desires, the will or craving of the body—all desires are carnal. Peter urges us to abstain from all of them, saying: “I beseech you, as strangers and sojourners, to abstain from carnal desires, which wage war against the soul” (I Pet. II). As though he said: “Do not desire carnal desires, but desire heavenly and eternal things, because the desires of the flesh wage war against holy conduct and against the soul itself.”

“Soberly.” He says “soberly,” that is, cautiously, wisely, thoughtfully, and temperately, setting before our eyes what the Lord says: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with debauchery, drunkenness, and the cares of this world” [Col. 0056B] (Luke XXI).

“And justly.” Justly, that is, rightly and equitably. Hence John says: “You know that God is just, and everyone who practices righteousness has been born from him” (I John III). *Justice* is so called as though it were “the standing of right” (*juris status*). Its parts are to fear God, to venerate religion, and to possess humanity and devotion. Hence it follows:

“And godly in this age.” Justice must be joined with devotion lest it become immoderate. Devotion is a part of justice, understood properly, as Augustine says, as the worship of God. Justice is equity or uprightness, which gives each person what belongs to that person.

“Awaiting the blessed hope.” (From Cassiodorus.) Hope is the expectation of future goods. It expresses an attitude of humility and the obedience of diligent service. Hope is called **ἐλπίς** (*elpis*) in Greek, and it is an expectation concerning the future. Its opposite is despair, when a person is entirely without hope and has no possibility of progressing, because, while someone loves sin, he does not hope for future glory. The person who faithfully keeps God’s commandments is the one who waits with confidence.
