Hope is rightly called blessed where we shall be worthy to be sons of God and heirs—indeed, heirs of God and coheirs with Christ. There, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. There our sins will be forgiven and eternal life will be granted. There we shall possess the splendor of the sun and fellowship with the angels.

“And the coming of the glory of the great God.” It should be noted that in this brief Epistle he calls the Lord Jesus “Lord” twice. The same Apostle also says in the Letter to the Hebrews: “But to the Son: ‘Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever’; and, ‘God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness’” (Heb. I). And John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I). You will find many other testimonies concerning this most holy name. We await the coming of his glory according to the angelic promise, which says to the disciples: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I).

(From Origen.) But it is that glory which is awaited of which the Savior himself says: “When the Son of Man comes in the glory of his Father and of the holy angels” (Matt. XXV). This does not mean that the glory of God and of the angels is one and the same, but that the glory of the Father will be so great when the Son of Man comes to judgment that it can be apprehended only by the angels or by those saints of whom it is said: “They will be like the angels of God.” Of this coming of the glory of God the Apostle Peter also says: “He may be found to the praise and glory and revelation of Jesus Christ” (I Pet. I). To praise, when he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom.” To glory, because then the righteous will shine like the sun in the revelation of Jesus Christ—that is, in the future judgment.

“And of our Savior Jesus Christ.” Jesus is the proper name of the Son of God according to the flesh, as the angel Gabriel said to the blessed Mary: “You shall call his name Jesus” (Luke I). In Latin this means “Savior,” because he saves his people from their sins [Col. 0057B]. Christ received his name from anointing, for *chrisma* means “anointing,” and *Christus* means “anointed.” Spiritually, the Psalmist says concerning him: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness” (Ps. XLV).

“Who gave himself for us.” As the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Walk in love, as Christ also loved us and gave himself for us” (Eph. V).

“So that he might redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse us,” and so forth. (From Cassiodorus.) He redeemed us and freed us from every bond of iniquity by which we were held captive, and from unbelief; and he cleansed us through baptism, in which all original sins and committed offenses are washed away, so completely that nothing unclean can remain in us.

[Col. 0057C]

“Zealous for good works.” The same Apostle admonishes us to pursue good works, saying: “We exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain, so that our ministry may not be blamed, but that in everything we may present ourselves as God’s ministers: in great patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distresses, in blows, in prisons, in disturbances, in labors, in vigils, in fastings, in purity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in gentleness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God, with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left” (II Cor. VI), and other things of the same kind. Hence it appropriately follows:

“Speak these things and exhort.” As though he said: “Let all your speech consist in this exhortation and persevere in it.”

## GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER II

«After eight days had been completed for the circumcision of the child, his name was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb. And when the days of Mary’s purification according to the law of Moses had been fulfilled, they brought Jesus to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord: “Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord”; and to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the law of the Lord: a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons. And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon. [Col. 0058A] This man was righteous and devout, awaiting the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was in him. And he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ. And he came in the Spirit into the temple. And when the parents of the child Jesus brought him in, to do for him according to the custom of the law, he himself took him into his arms, blessed him, and said: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace; for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you prepared before the face of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles and the glory of your people Israel.”»

“After eight days had been completed for the circumcision of the child.” (From Ambrose.) The child is therefore circumcised. Who is that child, if not the one of whom it was said: “A child is born for us, a son is given to us” (Isa. IX)? For he was made under the law so that he might gain those who were under the law (Gal. IV). You see that the entire sequence of the old law was a type of what was to come. The infant was not commanded to be circumcised on the eighth day without reason, since the rock by which we are circumcised was Christ. The people were circumcised with knives of stone, but the rock was Christ. Why on the eighth day? Because in the sequence of weeks the first day is also the eighth. When the seven days are completed, one returns to the first. The seventh having ended, the Lord was buried; the return to the first occurred when the Lord was raised. The Lord’s resurrection promised us an eternal day and consecrated for us the Lord’s day, which is called *Dominicus* and is seen properly to belong to the Lord because on that day the Lord rose again.

(From Bede.) He who appeared in the flesh without any stain of corruption accepted in the flesh the circumcision decreed by the law; he who came in the likeness of sinful flesh, but not in sinful flesh, did not reject the remedy by which sinful flesh was accustomed to be cleansed. Likewise, he did not reject the water of baptism, by which he wished the people of the new grace to be washed from the filth of sins. He underwent circumcision not from necessity but as an example. Your brotherhood should know that the same aid of saving treatment which circumcision under the law provided against the wound of original sin is now customarily provided by baptism in the time of revealed grace. The difference is that they could not yet enter the gate of the heavenly kingdom until the one who gave the law came and bestowed the blessing, so that the God of gods might be seen in Zion. After death, they were comforted in blessed rest in Abraham’s bosom and, happy in hope, awaited entry into the peace above.

For the one who now cries out solemnly and beneficially through his Gospel, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III), then cried out through his law: “The male whose flesh of his foreskin has not been circumcised, that soul shall perish from his people, because he has broken my covenant” (Exod. XIII; Lev. XII)—that is, because the covenant of life, given by me to human beings in paradise, was transgressed when Adam sinned, and in that sin all sinned, he shall perish from the assembly of the saints unless he is helped by a saving remedy.

“His name was called Jesus,” and so forth. (From Bede.) In receiving the name Jesus on the day of his circumcision, he acted in imitation of the ancients, like the patriarch Abraham, who first received the sacrament of circumcision and the testimony of the promise. On that same day, together with his wife, he also received an enlargement of his name: he who had previously been called Abram, that is, “exalted father,” was thereafter called Abraham, that is, “father of many nations.”

(From Jerome.) “Your wife Sarai,” the Lord says to Abraham, “shall not be called Sarai, but Sarah.” Those who think that Sarah was first written with one *r* and that another *r* was later added are mistaken. Sarai was first called by [an unclear Hebrew form in the supplied source]. After the [unclear letter], that is, the element *i*, was removed, a letter was added, read as *a*, and she was called [an unclear Hebrew form in the supplied source], *Saraa*. The reason for the change of the name is that previously she was called “my princess,” that is, the mistress of one household only; afterward she was called simply “princess,” that is, **ἄρχουσα** (*archousa*).

“And when the days of her purification according to the law of Moses had been fulfilled, they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord.” (From Bede.) The law decreed that a little child should be brought to the temple of the Lord on the thirty-third day after circumcision and that an offering should be given for him. It also mystically signified, as we have said, that no one is worthy of the Lord’s sight unless circumcised from vices, and that no one can perfectly enter the joys of the heavenly city unless freed from the bonds of mortality.

But if you examine the words of the law itself more carefully, you will certainly find that not only was the incarnate Lord free from the contagion of sin and from the condition of the law, which he nevertheless deigned to undertake all the more so that he might prove it holy, just, and good and free us from its servitude and fear through the grace of faith; even the mother of God herself, just as she was free from intercourse with a man, was also exempt from legal obligation.

For Moses says: “If a woman, having received seed, gives birth to a male, she shall be unclean for seven days, as during the days of the separation of her menstruation, and on the eighth day the infant shall be circumcised. She herself shall remain thirty-three days in the blood of her purification” (Lev. XII). Note, therefore, that it is not every woman who gives birth who is designated unclean and taught to be cleansed according to the rite of the law, but the woman who has conceived from received seed—clearly distinguishing her from the one who conceived as a virgin and gave birth to a son.

“And he called his name [an unclear form in the supplied source], which is interpreted ‘God with us.’” Therefore neither the son who is God with man nor the mother who gave birth through the working of the Holy Spirit needed victims and sacrifices by which she might be purified. Yet, so that we might be freed from the bond of the law, the blessed and ever-virgin Mary voluntarily submitted to the law, just as the Lord Christ did.

“As it is written in the law of the Lord: ‘Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord.’” [Col. 0060A] The phrase “every male opening the womb” signifies the firstborn of both human beings and animals. It was commanded that both be called holy to the Lord and therefore belong to the priest. The provision was that he should receive a price for the human firstborn and cause every unclean animal to be redeemed. “Its redemption,” he says, “shall be after one month, for five shekels of silver.”

Without entering into a more subtle treatment, it should briefly be stated that all those firstborn were either figures of the one who, although he was the only-begotten Son of God, deigned to become the firstborn of every creature and truly and uniquely holy to the Lord, because he committed no sin and no deceit was found in his mouth; or they were an indication of our devotion, since we ought to attribute to the Lord’s grace every beginning of a good action that we, as it were, conceive in the heart, and redeem evil deeds by offering worthy fruits of repentance for each of the five senses of body or soul.

Thus, when he says “opening the womb,” he speaks according to the customary manner of describing birth. It is not to be understood, as the heretics claim, that our Lord should be thought to have profaned by his exit the sacred lodging of the womb which he sanctified by entering it—that the blessed Mary was a virgin until the birth but not a virgin after the birth. Rather, according to the Catholic faith, with the virgin’s womb closed, he came forth from it like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber. Concerning this the Prophet beautifully says: “He turned me toward the way of the gate of the sanctuary on the outside, which faced east; and it was closed. And the Lord said to me: ‘This gate shall be closed; it shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it. For the Lord God of Israel entered through it, and it shall be closed. The prince shall sit in it, to eat bread before the Lord’” (Ezek. XLIV).

It may also be understood mystically: no one except the Lord can open the womb of the virgin Church through water and the Holy Spirit in order to regenerate children for God. For this reason this male child is called holy to the Lord with incomparable dignity.

“And to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the law of the Lord: a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.” (From Bede.) It was said in the law that for a child, if male, on the fortieth day, and if female, on the eightieth day after birth, a spotless lamb was to be offered as a burnt offering, and a turtledove or young pigeon as a sin offering. “But if her hand does not find the means,” it says, “and she cannot offer a lamb, she shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one as a burnt offering and the other as a sin offering.”

Although the Lord Jesus Christ was rich, he became poor for us and wished a poor offering to be given for him, so that by his one poverty he might make us rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom that God promised to those who love him.

Morally, whether someone produces strong works or weak works—distinguished by the terms “male” and “female”—if these are to be lawfully consecrated to the Lord, he must offer both a sheep of innocence and a turtledove or dove of compunction. Since these birds have groans instead of song, they appropriately signify the tears of the humble.

And it is fitting that there were two: one for sin and the other as a burnt offering. A burnt offering is so called because it is entirely consumed by fire. There are, in fact, two kinds of compunction: the soul thirsting for God is first pierced by fear, and afterward by love. Thus the person who first wept lest he be led to punishment offered the turtledove for sin; from the second he makes a burnt offering when afterward he begins to weep most bitterly because he is delayed from entering the kingdom.

There is this difference between turtledoves and doves: the dove, which is accustomed to live, fly, and mourn in a flock, signifies the activity of the communal life, of which it is said: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV). The turtledove, however, which delights in solitude to such an extent that if it should accidentally lose its mate it remains alone thereafter, signifies the heights of the contemplative life, because this virtue belongs to few and is assigned to them individually.

Again, when I enter my room, close the door, and pray to the Father in secret, I offer the turtledove. But when I seek companions in the same work, singing with the Prophet, “Come, let us worship and fall down before God; let us weep before the Lord who made us,” I carry doves to the altar.

“And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon.” The Lord’s generation received testimony not only from angels and prophets but also from elders and the remaining righteous. Every age and both sexes support faith in the miracles of these events: a virgin gives birth, a barren woman bears, a mute man speaks, Elizabeth prophesies, a magus worships, an unborn child leaps while still in the closed womb, a widow confesses, and a righteous man waits.

“And this man was righteous and devout, awaiting the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was in him.” (From Bede.) He is rightly called righteous and devout, because righteousness is difficult to preserve without fear. He is rightly called righteous because he sought not his own grace but that of the people. He desired to be freed in body from the bonds of frailty, but he waited to see the promised one. For he knew that blessed were the eyes that would see him, but until he came he did not wish to depart.

“And he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ.” Observe the expressions of Scripture. He says that he would “see death.” How do those eyes see, and with what eyes, when death closes the very eyes by coming? But “to see death” means to experience it. We too, by living in the heavenly Jerusalem, frequenting the thresholds of the Lord’s temple—that is, following the devout examples of the saints in whom he dwells—shall merit to receive the word of the Lord in our hands and to embrace it with the arms of faith and love.

“And he came in the Spirit into the temple.” When he says, “He came in the Spirit,” he signifies that by the same grace of the Spirit through which he had previously foreknown that the Savior would come, he now recognized him as already coming and as about to be seen by him.

And when his parents brought in the child Jesus, to perform according to the custom of the law, he himself took him in his arms. [Col. 0062A] Figuratively, Simeon receives Christ: an old man receives an infant, to teach us to put off the old man, who is corrupted together with his deeds, and, renewed in the spirit of our mind, to put on him who was created according to the Lord in righteousness, holiness, and truth. The elder receives the infant Christ to suggest that this world, as though already worn out by old age and a long lifetime, would return to the innocence and, so to speak, infancy of Christian conduct, and that its youth would be renewed like that of an eagle.

And he blessed the Lord and said: “Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word in peace.” The old man’s desire was fulfilled: as the world itself declined into old age, he came to the old man who found the world old. Let the world hear: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth.” Let the old be set aside; let newness arise.

Because my eyes have seen your salvation, which you prepared before the face of all peoples. Blessed are the eyes that see what Simeon saw; blessed are those who did not see and believed. “That very thing,” he says, “which you prepared for nearly all peoples, nations, and languages to behold in mind and faith, and which you foresaw as something to be sought with hope and love—that salvation of yours, long desired, I now contemplate with the eyes both of flesh and of the heart.”

A light for the revelation of the Gentiles and the glory of your people Israel. He calls it a saving light for both peoples: Christ, prepared by God the Father. Yet he comes especially as the glory of Israel, for whom he had long been hoped and from whom he had been foretold. He is called the revelation of the Gentiles because he himself deigned to visit, reveal, and enlighten the eyes of their minds, already plunged into profound blindness and lifted up by no hope of the Lord’s coming. And rightly the revelation of the Gentiles is placed before the glory of Israel, because, “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved.”

## CONCORDANCE

The readings of these two passages agree in this respect: both speak of the Lord’s manifestation, which first took place in the temple.

## SUNDAY AFTER THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

### THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE GALATIANS, CHAPTER IV

“While the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a servant, although he is lord of all; but he is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by his father. So we also, when we were children, were serving under the elements of the world. But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made subject to the law, so that he might redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons of God. And because you are sons of God, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying: ‘Abba, Father.’ Therefore he is no longer a servant but a son; and if a son, also an heir through God.”

While the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a servant, although he is lord of all; but he is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by his father. [Col. 0063A] In accordance with the comparison adopted in the argument, the discourse develops its exposition. Here he calls the Jewish people a servant: it served under the letter of the law with carnal observance, a child in faith and alien to the understanding of spiritual teaching, although the Lord had bestowed the treasures and riches of divine knowledge upon the Gentiles, who were subject to the service of demons. For the Gentiles, who by nature had squandered the substance of their unbelief, were needy and poor. Here he calls the rulers and priests “guardians” and “stewards,” since they appeared to exercise authority over the people. But when he says:

Until the time appointed by the father. Understand this as the time when a father, departing from this life, entrusts his son to guardians and stewards by careful arrangement. In accordance with this comparison, the Father of the Only-Begotten appointed a time for the law lasting until the coming of the Son. [Col. 0063B]

So we also, when we were children, were serving under the elements of the world. That is, the observances of days and seasons, which we received for this reason: so that, through idleness, we would not wander off to idols. For if the Jews too were serving the elements, in what did they differ from the pagans? It is well known that pagans worship the elements; the Jews, however, served the Lord not the elements but under the elements, because of new moons, Sabbaths, circumcisions, and other such things. These are carnal. For whatever is visible is carnal and belongs to the elements. Thus, in the respect we mentioned above, the Jews served under the elements. In another respect they possessed a spiritual law, which both forbids sin and exhorts them to love the Lord God, who had been promised to come to them in order to forgive sins. [Col. 0063C]

But when the fullness of time had come, the Lord sent his Son. That is, when, through the habitual practice of transgressions, scarcely anyone could keep the law. Or certainly the fullness of time should be understood as the time when, with the world flourishing in its peoples, it seemed opportune and salutary to the Lord to offer the remedies of salvation to the Gentiles, for whom the age of the sixth world-period could by nature now suitably receive them. The fullness of time can therefore be understood as the age of the aging world, receiving pardon. In that age the knowledge of truth was entrusted and imparted to it just as, quite properly, the instruction of profound matters is entrusted to a son in his mature years. And indeed, the ages past, which in our first parent were guilty and held under the infernal prison, required a long delay, so that after many ages they might be freed by the coming of Christ’s expiation. [Col. 0063D]

Made of a woman. “Woman” signifies not corruption but sex. Indeed, as soon as Eve was made, she was called “woman” (Gen. III). The Lord himself also said to his mother: “Woman, what is this to me and to you?” (John II). In saying “of a woman,” he shows that Christ assumed human incarnation not in the customary manner, from the union of man and woman, but through the Holy Spirit from the mother alone. For the same Apostle says to the Corinthians: “Just as woman is from man, so also man is through woman” (I Cor. XV). Thus, just as at the beginning of creation woman was taken from man, so Christ according to the flesh is from the mother alone.

The first condition of humanity: the first man was not born but made. The second, from the side of a man. The third, from man and woman. The fourth, from God and a woman without a man. There had already been one without man and woman; another from man without woman; a third from man and woman. The fourth, from a woman without man, remained. But this fourth liberated the three: made subject to the law, so that he might redeem those who were under the law. He himself remained under the law until, after he was baptized, he began to preach the Gospel of the New Testament. If he had not been made subject to the law, he could not easily have summoned the Jews to obedience. They seemed more readily able to listen to a teacher who was the champion of their own law and of their own race, just as the Apostle says of himself: “To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews; to those under the law, as though I were under the law, in order to win those under the law.” [Col. 0064B] But he could save the Gentiles, who were alien to the law, even if he had not been placed under the law.

So that we might receive adoption as sons. That is, we Jews by nature would not readily have received his calling if he had not been made subject to the law. It was more readily possible for the upholder of the law to invite the sons of the law to life.

And because you are sons of God, God sent his Son into your hearts. The Father proves us to be sons adopted by him when he mercifully pours out upon us the Spirit of his Son, and graciously does so, so that the very sharing of the Paraclete, who proceeds from both, might declare us heirs of the Father and fellow-heirs of the Son. In this statement he has clearly explained the Trinity. [Col. 0064C]

Crying, “Abba, Father.” That is, he cries out within our hearts, by hidden inspiration, that God is our Father.

Therefore he is no longer a servant but a son. That is, why do you wish to become a servant, when, having received the Spirit of the Son, you have become a son and heir? By this he proves that we are all one Son of God in one Spirit. For the whole Christian people, believing in the one Son of God and becoming one body of Christ, is rightly called one son.

And if a son, also an heir through God. Not through merit or nature, but through the Spirit of grace, concerning which he says in the Epistle to the Romans: “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are sons of God; and if sons, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, but fellow-heirs with Christ” (Rom. VIII).

## THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER II

“Joseph and Mary, the mother of Jesus, were marveling at what was being said about him. And Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother: ‘Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and as a sign that will be opposed; and a sword will pierce your own soul, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.’ And there was Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She had advanced in many days and had lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity. She was a widow until the age of eighty-four; she did not depart from the temple, serving with fastings and prayers night and day. And coming at that very hour, she gave thanks to the Lord and spoke of him to all who were awaiting the redemption of Israel. [Col. 0065A] And when they had completed everything according to the law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own city, Nazareth. The child grew and became strong, being filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was with him.”

Joseph and Mary, the mother of Jesus, were marveling at what was being said about him. (From Bede.) Here Mary represents the synagogue, while Joseph represents the law. He calls Joseph the Savior’s father—not because, according to the Photinians, he was truly his father, but because, for the preservation of Mary’s reputation, he was regarded by everyone as his father. Yet he can also rightly be called his father in the sense in which he is rightly understood to be Mary’s husband: without bodily intercourse, their union binds them together, much more closely, indeed, than if he had been adopted from elsewhere.

And he said to Mary his mother: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall.” How is he for the fall, unless because he is also a stone of offense and a rock of stumbling—that is, a fall for those who stumble at the word and do not believe? Of them he himself says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin.” Otherwise:

(From Jerome.) Let something in me that was standing wrongly fall and suffer ruin, so that it may rise to something better. The pride of sin had raised itself up; let it fall. Before I believed, the good in me lay prostrate while the evil stood. After he came, whatever evil was in me collapsed: fornication, uncleanness, lust, idolatry, and the other plagues experienced a beneficial ruin. This is the ruin for which Jesus first came: to destroy it, so that when those things have been destroyed and put to death, all good things may rise and be built up in me. Therefore it must be considered lest perhaps our Savior came for some people as a fall and for others as a resurrection, rather than coming for the same people as both fall and resurrection.

I must first fall, and when I have fallen, rise afterward to what is good, lest the Savior be the cause of an evil fall for me; rather, he made me fall for this reason, so that I might rise. My fall will be much more beneficial to me than the time when I seemed to stand. For I stood in sin, and because I stood in sin, my first benefit was to fall and die to sin. You were unrighteous: let the unrighteous person fall in you. You first loved prostitutes: let the fornicator perish in you. You were a sinner: let the sinner fall in you, so that afterward you may be able to rise and say: “If we have died with him, we shall also live with him; and if we have been conformed to his death, we shall also be conformed to his resurrection” (II Tim. II; Rom. V). [Col. 0065D]

And for the resurrection of many in Israel. (From Bede.) “For the resurrection” is fitting, because he is light, because he is the glory of the people of Israel, because he says: “I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live” (John II).

(From Ambrose.) There are two resurrections. One is the first, which exists now and belongs to souls; it does not allow them to enter into death. The second is that of which the Lord says: “The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (John V). He said “those who hear,” meaning those who obey, who believe, and who persevere to the end. There is another second resurrection, which is not now but will take place at the end of the age. It belongs not to souls but to bodies. Through the final judgment, some will be sent into the second death and others into that life which has no death. [Col. 0066A]

And as a sign that will be opposed. (From Jerome.) By scribes and Pharisees, heretics and pagans, of course. By “the sign that will be opposed,” understand the faith of the Lord’s cross. Concerning it the Jews say to the Apostle Paul: “For concerning this sect it is known to us that everywhere it is opposed” (Acts XXVIII). We all know that what has been written about the Savior is true; but among unbelievers and heretics everything written about him is a sign that is opposed. The virgin mother is a sign opposed by the Marcionites. He had a human body, and this is a sign that is opposed. He rose from the dead, and this is a sign that is opposed. And why pursue many examples? Everything written about him is a sign opposed by unbelievers and heretics. [Col. 0066B]

And a sword will pierce your own soul. (From Ambrose.) Neither the letter nor the history teaches that Mary departed this life through the suffering of bodily death. For it is not the soul but the body that is pierced by a material sword. Therefore he displays a prudence not ignorant of the heavenly mystery. For the word of God is living, powerful, and sharper than every two-edged sword; it penetrates to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and searches the thoughts of the heart and the secrets of souls.

Otherwise. (From Augustine.) It is credible that the tribulation and grief of the Lord’s passion are signified by the name of the sword. By it the mother’s soul was wounded through the experience of grief; and to this day, and until the consummation of the age, the sword of the most severe tribulation does not cease to pierce the soul of the present Church, as she groaningly experiences that the sign of faith is opposed by the wicked, that many rise with Christ when they hear the word of God, but that more fall away from belief.

And so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed. (From Augustine.) When he says, “so that the thoughts of many hearts may be laid bare,” I think this should be understood to mean that through the Lord’s passion both the plots of the Jews and the weakness of the disciples were made evident.

(From Bede.) It was once uncertain which of the Jews would prefer to receive Christ’s favor, which they certainly knew was to come. When this birth was heard of, the thoughts of their hearts were immediately revealed: King Herod was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him; the shepherds, with fear and joy, sounded forth praise to God and announced peace to human beings. Once his teaching and power had been widely proclaimed, some flocked to him as a teacher of truth, while others fled from him as a deceiver. When the sign of his cross was raised, some, blaspheming and mocking as though he had been delivered over to a just death, ridiculed it; others grieved bitterly that the author of life should die. [Col. 0066D]

And there was Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. (From Bede.) It accords with the mysteries of the Church that Anna is interpreted as “his grace” and is the daughter of Phanuel, whose name means “the face of God.” Thus she sings with the Psalmist: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. IV). And she descended from the tribe of Asher—that is, “blessed.” Among the twelve patriarchs, Asher is eighth in order of birth; it has often been emphasized that this number is sacred in the New Testament. [Col. 0067A]

(From Ambrose.) For Anna is interpreted as “his grace,” and she represents the prophets. Her father Phanuel is likewise interpreted as “the face of God.” Asher means “blessed.” Asher, the blessed one, represents the people of believers; alternatively, it is interpreted as “the richness of bread,” which descended from heaven.

She had advanced in many days and had lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity. Seven years: that is, the synagogue with the heptad, or afterward through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. “From her virginity,” because she was with her husband for seven years.

[Col. 0067B]

And she was a widow until the age of eighty-four. (From Bede.) According to the mystical interpretation, because she signifies the Church, which in the present is widowed, as it were, by the death of her Bridegroom and Lord. The number of years of her widowhood also signifies the time of the Church. For seven times twelve makes eighty-four. Seven refers to the course of this world, which revolves through seven days, while twelve refers to the perfection of apostolic teaching. Therefore, whether it is the universal Church or any faithful soul that strives to devote the whole time of its life to apostolic institutions, it is praised as though multiplying seven by twelve and serving the Lord for the symbolic eighty-four years.

Likewise, the period of seven years during which she had remained with her husband corresponds most appropriately to the time of the Lord’s incarnation. As I said, the number seven generally indicates the perfection of a period; but there the number seven years is expressed because of the privilege of the Lord’s majesty, in whose flesh I taught the simple. Here, because of the height of apostolic dignity, seven years are multiplied by twelve. [Col. 0067C]

She did not depart from the temple, serving with fastings and prayers night and day. (From Ambrose.) For she had been a widow for many years, and such a widow as the Apostle describes: “Not living in luxury, lest, while alive, she should die,” but persisting in prayers night and day. Thus, by praying and humbly entreating for many years, she was worthy to see the humble one whom she worshiped as exalted.

And coming at that very hour, she gave thanks to the Lord and spoke of him to all who were awaiting the redemption of Israel. Simeon prophesied; she had prophesied while joined in marriage; a virgin had prophesied; a widow also had to do so, lest any condition or sex be lacking. Therefore Anna is introduced as one who, both by the services of widowhood and by her character, was plainly worthy to be believed to announce that the Redeemer of all had come. [Col. 0067D]

And when they had completed everything according to the law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own city, Nazareth. (From Bede.) At this point Luke omitted what he knew Matthew had sufficiently explained: namely, that after these events the Lord was carried by his parents into Egypt so that he would not be found and killed by Herod, and that, after Herod’s death, he finally returned to Galilee and began to inhabit his own city, Nazareth. [Col. 0068A]

The child grew and became strong, being filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was with him. The distinction of the words must be noted. Insofar as the Lord Jesus Christ was a child—that is, had assumed the condition of human weakness—he had to grow and become strong. But insofar as he was also the Word of God and eternal God, he neither needed to become strong nor could he increase. Hence he is most rightly said to be full of wisdom and grace: of wisdom, because in him all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily; of grace, because great grace was given to that mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, so that from the moment he began to become human he was perfect both as man and as God.

Human nature does not receive this, that wisdom should be complete before twelve years of age. Just as everything in him was wondrous, so his childhood was wondrous, so that he might be filled with the wisdom of God. [Col. 0068B]

## CONCORDANCE

The readings of these two passages agree both in the mother and in the law. They agree in the mother because the Apostle says: “Born of a woman,” while the Gospel says: “He said to Mary his mother.” They agree in the law because the Apostle says: “Made subject to the law,” while the Gospel says: “And when they had completed everything according to the law of the Lord.” For the legal ceremonies were offered for him in accordance with the law.

## ON THE DAY OF THE THEOPHANY

### READING FROM THE PROPHET ISAIAH, CHAPTER LX

“Arise, shine, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you. For behold, darkness will cover the earth, and gloom the peoples; but the Lord will rise upon you, and his glory will be seen in you. And nations will walk in your light, and kings in the splendor of your rising. Lift up your eyes round about and see: all these have been gathered together; they have come to you. Your sons will come from afar, and your daughters will rise at your side. Then you will see and overflow with abundance; your heart will wonder and be enlarged, when the multitude of the sea has been turned toward you and the strength of the nations has come to you. An inundation of camels will cover you, the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah. All those from Sheba will come, bearing gold and frankincense and proclaiming praise to the Lord. Every flock of Kedar will be gathered to you; the rams of Nebaioth will minister to you.”

Arise, shine, Jerusalem, for your light has come. (From Jerome.) This is said to the Church, which was first gathered from the Jewish people and transmitted to the Gentiles through the apostles the light that had risen upon her. She is told, “Arise, shine,” so that she who fell among unbelievers may rise among the faithful, and she who fell in the synagogues may rise in the Churches. For your light has come—the light promised to you by all the prophets, which you continually awaited.

And the glory of the Lord has risen upon you. Therefore the glory of the Lord, which once was over his tabernacle and temple, has risen over you. Of this it is said: “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. LXXXIX).

For behold, darkness will cover the earth. That is, those who set their minds on earthly things.

And gloom the peoples. Or, as it is read in Hebrew, “tribes,” which properly refers to the Jews. [Col. 0069A]

But the Lord will rise upon you. That is, Christ, the sun of righteousness.

And his glory will be seen in you. Of this it is written: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John I).

And nations will walk in your light. We all walk in the light of the apostles, which shines in the world, and the darkness did not comprehend it.

And kings in the splendor of your rising. This refers to the time when you were first born in Christ, a matter fulfilled both spiritually and carnally: kings, whose heart is in the hand of the Lord and over whose mortal body sin does not reign, walk in the splendor of the rising Church, or in him who arose within the Church, and submit their necks in faith to the true King, Christ. We see this fulfilled every day, when, after the error of idolatry has been removed, Roman rulers pass over to the faith of Christ. [Col. 0069B]

Lift up your eyes round about and see: all these have been gathered together; they have come to you. This is said to the Church, which was first gathered to the apostles in Zion. Concerning them we also read in the Acts of the Apostles that devout men from the whole world were in Jerusalem to receive the word of God; in the languages of their own and foreign peoples they either heard others speaking or themselves spoke to the rest.

Your sons will come from afar. Let us be sons, then, we who came to the Lord from afar, once strangers to God’s covenant and his promises. But what does the Apostle say? “You who were once far away have been brought near” (I Pet. II). [Col. 0069C]

And your daughters will suck milk. When he says, “Your daughters will suck milk,” he signifies that souls nursing in Christ and in the baptism of little ones—for Peter also speaks of them: “Like newborn infants, desire rational and guileless milk” (I Pet. II)—suck the milk of the apostles. To these little ones and nursing infants Paul also spoke: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV).

Then you will see and overflow with abundance; your heart will wonder and be enlarged, when the multitude of the sea has been turned toward you and the strength of the nations has come to you. When you lift up your eyes and see your sons coming, then you will rejoice and be flooded like rivers by sudden waters; your heart will wonder and be astonished—indeed, it will be enlarged. Hearing the Apostle say, “Be enlarged yourselves” (II Cor. VI), do not, through narrowness of heart, become unable to have Christ as an inhabitant, for he says in the Gospel: “I and the Father will come, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John XIV). [Col. 0069D]

An inundation of camels will cover you, the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah. All those from Sheba will come, bearing gold and frankincense and proclaiming praise to the Lord. After the riches of the sea and the strength of the nations, flocks of camels and the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah are promised to Jerusalem. All these come from Sheba, bearing gold and frankincense and, greater than these, proclaiming the Lord’s salvation (Matt. XII). Midian and Ephah are regions beyond Arabia, rich in camels, and the whole province is called Sheba. The queen of Sheba also came from there to hear Solomon’s wisdom, herself bearing gold and frankincense. [Col. 0070A]

Every flock of Kedar will be gathered to you; the rams of Nebaioth will minister to you. Kedar is a region of the Saracens; Nebaioth is one of the sons of Ishmael. From their names the wilderness is called, a land lacking crops but full of flocks. Thus, through the familiar names of barbarian peoples who are near Israel, the conversion of the whole world is proclaimed.

In this passage Midian is interpreted as “iniquity”; Ephah as “loosed” or “pouring out”; Sheba as “conversion” or “captivity”; Kedar as “darkness” or “mourning”; Nebaioth as “prophecy.” Therefore flocks of camels, loosed from the bonds of iniquity and pouring out their souls to God, will cover Jerusalem with gifts. All will come from captivity, bringing conversions along the paths of faith and the frankincense of sacrifice. Through these gifts, not content merely with their own salvation, they will advance so far as to proclaim God’s salvation also to others.

Their gifts contain the chief things: gold, understanding (sic), and frankincense of the finest fragrance, as in the words: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL), and “We are the good fragrance of Christ” (II Cor. II), in every place; and the rams are the prophets. Of them the twenty-eighth Psalm sings: “Bring to the Lord, you sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams.” They will come and offer themselves as a sacrifice to the Lord, and become acceptable offerings, so that the Church of Christ may be glorified.

Concerning such sheep the Savior spoke to his disciples: “Go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. X). This is properly understood of those chosen from the Gentiles to serve as priests and ministers of the Savior. [Col. 0070C]

## THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW, CHAPTER II

“When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: ‘Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East and have come to worship him.’ But when King Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. And gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where Christ was to be born. They said to him: ‘In Bethlehem of Judea. For thus it is written through the prophet: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you will come forth a leader who will rule my people Israel.”’ Then Herod secretly summoned the Magi and carefully learned from them the time when the star had appeared to them. And sending them to Bethlehem, he said: ‘Go and inquire carefully about the child; and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and worship him.’ When they had heard the king, they went away. And behold, the star that they had seen in the East went before them until, coming to the place where the child was, it stood above it. When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. And entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother. And falling down, they worshiped him. And opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. And having received an answer in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back to their own country by another way.”

When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judea. It is appropriately called Bethlehem of Judea to distinguish it from the Bethlehem situated in Galilee, as can be found in the Book of Joshua (Josh. XIX). It is the city of David, which gave birth to the Savior of the world. It was formerly called Ephrata; afterward Jacob, when he pastured his flocks there, gave it the name Bethlehem through a prophecy of the future. The name is interpreted as “house of bread,” because of the bread that descended there from heaven.

In the days of King Herod. This Herod was the son of Antipater of Ascalon and of Cypris, an Arabian woman. He died in the thirty-seventh year of his reign from dropsy, with worms swarming throughout his body. Under his son Herod Christ suffered. For this reason the kings and rulers of Judah at that time are said to have been foreigners, because it had been foretold: “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thigh, until he comes to whom it has been promised; and he will be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX). [Col. 0071B]

Behold, Magi came from the East. Since the one who is sought is the East, he is indicated as coming from the East because he himself leads us to himself.

To Jerusalem, saying. They came to Jerusalem because “the law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. II). Or else, so that the Jews might be condemned for remaining ignorant of Christ’s birth, which was near to them, while Magi came from afar. The purpose was also that, when the priests were asked by the Magi where Christ would be born, they might be left without excuse concerning his coming.

The Jews assert that Shem, the son of Noah, whom they call Melchizedek, founded the city of Salem in Syria after the Flood; the kingdom of that same Melchizedek was there. Later the Jebusites occupied it, and from them it received the name Jebus. Thus, by joining the two names Jebus and Salem, it was called Jerusalem. Later, under Solomon, it was called Hierosolyma, as though “Hierosolomonia.” In former times it was also corruptedly named by poets, and afterward was called Aelia by Hadrian. Zion is also located there; in Hebrew its name is interpreted as “watchtower,” because it was built on high and looks out upon things coming from afar. [Col. 0071D]

Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? That is, king of confessions, the king who was born and came to enlighten all nations. Of him Isaiah says: “A child has been born for us” (Isa. IX). They give the reason when asked, “Who told you?”

We saw his star in the East, and we have come to worship him. They say that they saw the Lord’s star either through knowledge of their art or through Balaam’s prophecy, which says: “A star will rise from Jacob, and a staff will arise from Israel, and will strike the rulers of Moab” (Num. XXIV). They report that this star, like a dove, was seen neither before nor afterward, because neither before nor afterward was one like the person whom it revealed born. “We saw his star”—not ours, not a star of heaven, but the star of the King who was born. [Col. 0072A]

(From Augustine.) We do not place the birth of any human being under the destiny of the stars; how much less should we believe that the temporal birth of the one who is the eternal Creator and Lord of all was made subject to the conditions of the stars. Therefore the star that the Magi had seen, when Christ was born in the flesh, did not exercise dominion according to a decree but served as a witness. It was not subject to his command but indicated him through its service. Accordingly, it was not one of those stars that, from the beginning of creation, maintain their course and order under the law of the Creator. Rather, with the new birth of the Virgin, a new star appeared. As it went before the Magi who were seeking Christ, it displayed the mystery of its service until, by going before them, it led them to the very place where the infant Word of God was. [Col. 0072B]

(Vulgate tradition.) Some think that the Magi who went to worship the Lord were descendants of Balaam, learned in the discipline of astronomy, and that the star was not among the known constellations, since it did not move in the same celestial order as the others. It was carried by its own distinctive motion, indicating the place where the Lord had been born.

Others say that they were the descendants of Balaam son of Beor, because they followed his sect. Others say that they were Persians, as Canorius says in verse:

“Then the Persian orders them also to hasten their swift step.”

Jerome says: The Chaldeans affirmed that the stars were gods; hence the name of their god indicates the true Lord. For this reason they are thought to have been Chaldeans, since he says: “We saw his star in the East”—that is, either, being positioned in the East, we saw a star rise, or we saw it rise from east to west. [Col. 0072C]

Having laid the foundations of the historical account, let us contemplate the spiritual meaning. Bethlehem, interpreted as “house of bread,” signifies the Church or the human heart, in which Christ, who said, “I am the living bread” (John VI), is born. Herod, interpreted as “leathern” or “skin of glory,” signifies the devil reigning in the world.

The three Magi signify the human race together with physics, ethics, and logic. Physics—that is, natural philosophy. Ethics—that is, moral philosophy; for among the Greeks customs are called ἦθεα (*ēthea*). Logic—that is, rational philosophy; for “reason” is called λόγος (*logos*) in Greek. The Magi who question the priests signify the Church of the Gentiles; the priests signify the law or the synagogue. [Col. 0072D]

(From Gregory.) We must ask why, when the Redeemer was born, an angel appeared to the shepherds, while a star—not an angel—led the Magi to worship him. Clearly, because the Jews, who used reason, ought to have been taught by a rational creature, that is, an angel. Since the Gentiles did not know how to use reason, they were led to know the Lord not by a voice but by signs. Prophecy was given to the Jews as believers; signs were given to the Gentiles as unbelievers.

(From Bede.) It is clear that the Magi understood Christ as a man, which is why they say, “Where is he who has been born?”; as a king, since they say, “King of the Jews”; and as Lord, since they say, “We have come to adore him.” They also formed this very exalted understanding of him: since he was King of the Jews, he was also capable of saving the nations that wished to believe in him and come to him. They proved this especially by their arrival and their deed.

As for the star that appeared to them, some say that it served as their guide from the East as far as the vicinity of Bethlehem. But an examination of the Gospel’s own truth shows that this was by no means so. Rather, they saw the star only in the East and immediately understood that it signified the rising of the King born in Judaea; therefore they came to Judaea. Once they had learned from the prophetic testimonies that he had been born in Bethlehem, they set out there and were granted as their guide the star they had seen in the East. It appeared to them not in the highest part of the sky among the other stars, but near the earth.  
[Col. 0073A]

“Hearing this, King Herod was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.” (From Gregory.) When the King of heaven was born, the king of earth was troubled, because earthly exaltation is thrown into confusion when heavenly majesty is revealed. Others hold that Herod resented the title “king” being applied to Christ because Augustus had decreed that no one should be called king or god without his approval. He says that all Jerusalem was troubled with him because the king’s disturbance is the people’s disturbance.

“And gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where Christ was to be born.” The Magi announce only a king; Herod seeks Christ. Thus he confesses the very king about whom he inquires. Then the place of his birth is sought, and once he has been announced, it is disclosed. For one who had not been announced could not have been sought. Why, then, did God wish this to be inquired of the Jews? So that, while they point out the one in whom they do not believe, they might be condemned by their own testimony. For the Magi went on and adored him; the Jews remained behind, though they had identified him.  
[Col. 0073C]

“But they said to him: ‘In Bethlehem of Judaea; for so it is written through the prophet: And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah, for from you will come forth a Ruler who will govern my people Israel’” (Micah 6). It is as though he said: “You are one among the chief cities exercising rule, because from you two rulers will be born, namely David and Christ.”  
[Col. 0073D]

“Then Herod secretly summoned the Magi and carefully learned from them the time when the star had appeared to them.” He feared that the Magi would not return to him for some reason, as in fact happened; therefore, having secretly summoned them, he learned from them the time of the star’s appearance. Hence the narrative here also breaks off when they privately disclose the time of the star.

“And sending them to Bethlehem, he said: ‘Go and inquire carefully about the child; and when you have found him, report back to me, so that I too may come and adore him.’ When they had heard the king, they departed.” Once he had learned of the birth of our King, Herod turned to crafty devices lest he be deprived of his earthly kingdom. He asks that he be told where the child could be found. He pretends that he wishes to adore him, so that, if he could find him, he might destroy him; but because he sought him deceitfully, he was not worthy to find him.  
[Col. 0074A]

“And behold, the star that they had seen in the East went before them until it came and stood over where the child was.” Where Herod is, the star is not seen; where Christ is, it is seen, and it shows the way to those journeying toward Christ, because he himself, according to the mystery of the incarnation, is both star and way, and through himself he leads us to himself.

“When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy; and entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother.” They rejoiced with exceedingly great joy because greater joy comes from things found than from things possessed. That child is found with his mother of whom Isaiah says: “A child is born for us, a son is given to us” (Isaiah 9).

[Col. 0074B]

“And falling down, they adored him; and opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.” It was the tradition of the ancients that no one should enter before a king or lord to make a request empty-handed.

(From Gregory.) The Magi proclaim him whom they adore through mystical gifts: by gold, the King; by frankincense, God; by myrrh, a mortal. So too there are heretics who believe that he is God but do not believe that he reigns everywhere: they offer him frankincense, but not gold. There are others who consider him a king but deny that he is God: they offer him gold, but not frankincense. There are others who confess that he is both God and King but deny that he assumed mortal flesh: they offer him gold and frankincense, but not myrrh.

Let us offer him gold, so that we may believe that he reigns everywhere. Let us offer frankincense, so that we may believe that the one who appeared in time existed as God before time. Let us offer myrrh, so that, while we believe him to be impassible in his divinity, we may also believe that in our flesh he was mortal.

Yet gold, frankincense, and myrrh may also be understood in another way. Gold signifies wisdom, as Solomon testifies when he says: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Proverbs 21). By frankincense, which is burned for God, the power of prayer is expressed, as the Psalmist testifies: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Psalm 140). By myrrh, the mortification of our flesh is signified. Hence the holy Church also says: “My hands dripped with myrrh” (Song of Songs 5).

Therefore, we offer gold to the newborn King if we shine before him with the splendor of heavenly wisdom. We offer frankincense if we burn the thoughts of the flesh through holy devotion to prayer upon the altar of the heart. We offer myrrh if we mortify the vices of the flesh through abstinence.  
[Col. 0074D]

“And having received an answer in a dream not to return to Herod,” and so forth. The Magi indicate something of great importance to us by returning to their own country by another road. Our country, in truth, is paradise. We departed from our country by becoming proud, disobeying, pursuing visible things, and tasting the forbidden food. But we must return to it by weeping, obeying, despising visible things, and restraining the appetite of the flesh. We return to our country by another road, because we departed from the joy of paradise through pleasures and are recalled to it through lamentation.  
[Col. 0075A]

## HARMONY

The clear and most pleasing harmony of these two readings is evident: both speak mercifully of the calling of the nations, and both speak concordantly and mystically of the gifts offered to the Lord.

## FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THE EPIPHANY

### READING FROM THE LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER 12

> “I appeal to you by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your reasonable service. And do not conform yourselves to this age, but be transformed in the renewal of your understanding, so that you may prove what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God. For I say, through the grace that has been given to me, to everyone who is among you: not to be wiser than one ought to be wise, but to be wise unto sobriety. And to each one God has apportioned a measure of faith. For just as in one body we have many members, though all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another.”

(From Origen.) After the Apostle had taught above how the substance of religion was transferred from the Jews to the nations and from carnal observance to spiritual observance, he proceeds to sanctify the conduct and institutions of this spiritual observance, and says:

“Therefore I appeal to you, brothers, by the mercy of God.” Because all had been confined under sin, human salvation now rests not upon merits but upon the mercy of God. Therefore, as one who has undertaken the office of reconciling you to God, I appeal to you not by his power but by the mercy of God. What do I appeal to you for?

“That you present your bodies as a living sacrifice.” He calls that sacrifice living which bears life—that is, Christ—within itself. And he says: “We always carry in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus Christ may also be manifested in our body.”

“Holy.” He calls that sacrifice holy in which the Holy Spirit dwells, as in the statement: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3).

“Pleasing to God.” He calls that pleasing to God which has been separated from sins and vices. For those who mortify their members, restraining the acts of their body from the incitement of lust and anger, offer to the Lord acts that are pleasing to him. They rationally offer a living, holy sacrifice pleasing to the Lord.

“Your reasonable service.” Here he calls service worship, which formerly consisted in the bodies of mute animals. “Now,” he says, “let it be offered in the body of a rational human being.” Let your bodies become a sacrifice to God rather than the bodies of animals, because it is fitting to offer such sacrifices to the Lord; but no sound and honorable reason accepts the offering of rams, goats, and calves to an immortal and incorporeal Lord.

“And do not conform yourselves to this age.” He shows that there is one form of this age and another of the age to come. Those who love the present age and the things of the age are adapted according to the form of the present age. But those who do not regard the things that are seen, which are temporal, but the things that are not seen, which are eternal, are transformed and renewed according to the form of the age to come.

See, then, lest anger come into your heart, together with evil desire, greed, and the other things in which the present age delights, and impose upon you the form of the present age. But if, on the contrary, gentleness, patience, meekness, self-restraint, faith, truth, and the other virtues dwell in your heart, they make you conform to the age to come, and make your soul so beautiful that the Word of God says to it: “You are altogether beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song of Songs 4).  
[Col. 0076A]

“But be transformed in the renewal of your understanding.” Our understanding is renewed through exercises in wisdom, meditation on the word of God, and understanding of his law. The more one progresses daily through reading the Scriptures, and the higher one’s understanding ascends, the more one becomes always new and new each day. Understanding may also be renewed for righteousness and self-restraint, for faith and patience, and so forth.

“So that you may prove what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.” Many things are thought to be the will of God when they are not; in this a person whose understanding has been renewed may nevertheless err and be deceived. It belongs not to every kind of understanding, but to one that has been thoroughly renewed, to test in each thing we do, say, or think whether it is the will of God, and to do, say, or think absolutely nothing that one does not perceive to accord with the will of God, because whatever is good, pleasing, and perfect is the will of God.  
[Col. 0076C]

“For I say, through the grace that has been given to me.” Paul, as he says elsewhere, speaks not in persuasive words of carnal wisdom, but through the grace given to him (2 Corinthians 1). There is a great difference between one who speaks through grace and one who speaks through human wisdom. Indeed, some eloquent and educated men, though they say many things in a polished and learned manner, nevertheless, because they do not speak through grace, cannot move any of their hearers either to faith, to fear of God, or to compunction of heart. Others, speaking simply and without great eloquence, convert many unbelievers. This is what it means to speak through the grace given to Paul.

“To everyone who is among you, not to be wiser than one ought to be wise.” What he says, “to everyone who is among you,” is similar to saying: “To everyone who is in God,” whose being is always being. When he says, “not to be wiser,” he seems to apply this statement to those who are proud branches of the wild olive and insult the branches broken from the good olive, saying that they must not be wiser than they ought to be—that is, wiser than one ought to be wise.

I, however, say that heretics are wiser about Christ than they ought to be wise, since they deny that he is the Son of the God who created them, and invent many other things about him beyond what they ought to know.  
[Col. 0076D]

“But to be wise unto sobriety.” (From Gregory.) Since, through heavenly grace, we are led to understand higher things, the more subtly we are lifted up, the more we must always press ourselves down in humility within our understanding. Let us not attempt to be wiser than one ought to be wise, but let us be wise unto sobriety, lest, while examining invisible things too deeply, we go astray.

What is called *sōphrosynē* (σωφροσύνη) in Greek was translated by our elders in our books—that is, in the divine Scriptures—as “sobriety”; by other learned men it is rendered “temperance.” This temperance is considered one of the four principal virtues. Therefore, to be wise unto sobriety means to be wise temperately—that is, to preserve temperance in everything we do, say, or perceive.

“And to each one, just as God has apportioned a measure of faith.” This means that each person should know and understand what measure of God’s grace is within him, which he has deserved to attain through faith. Sometimes a person receives from God the ability to be wise in the work of charity, or in mercy toward the poor, or in caring for the weak, or in defending widows and orphans, or in the exercise of hospitality. God has therefore apportioned these individual gifts to each person according to the measure of faith.

But if the person who has received grace to be wise in one of these matters does not understand the measure of grace given to him, and wishes to be wise in a matter for which he has not received grace; if he does not wish to learn but to teach what he does not know, then, though he has less wisdom, he wishes to be wiser than he ought. To make this still clearer, the Apostle introduces an example and says:

“For just as in one body we have many members, though all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another.” He most orderly constructs through these words the whole body of the Church. Just as the individual members of the body each have their own functions, yet by mutual agreement yield to one another, so, he says, in the Church, which is the body of Christ, each of us has different functions. For example, one is an eye through wisdom, another is a hand through works, another is an ear through listening. Yet from all the members there is one body in Christ Jesus our Lord.

How, then, is this body in Christ? It is the same in truth, wisdom, righteousness, and sanctification, all of which Christ is, as we have often said.

## THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER 2

> “And when Jesus was twelve years old, they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast day. When the days had been completed and they were returning, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it. Thinking that he was in the company, they came a day’s journey and sought him among their relatives and acquaintances. Not finding him, they returned to Jerusalem in search of him. And it came to pass that after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. All who heard him were astonished at his understanding and his answers. And seeing him, they were amazed. His mother said to him: ‘Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I, sorrowing, were seeking you.’ And he said to them: ‘Why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?’ And they did not understand the word that he spoke to them. And he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and he was subject to them. And his mother kept all these words in her heart. And Jesus advanced in wisdom, age, and grace before God and human beings.”

“And when Jesus was twelve years old, they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast day; and when the days had been completed and they were returning, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem.” (From Bede.) He had been shown from his birth—or rather, from his human conception—by clear signs of miracles to be God. When the appropriate time of life arrived, he also began reverently to disclose and reveal both his substances: what he owed to the Father according to the truth of divine majesty, and what he owed to his mother according to the frailty of the humanity he had assumed.

Not without providence did he reveal the first beginnings of his faith at the age of twelve, for these were to be revealed and made clear throughout the whole world through the ministry of the twelve apostles. We may also say that, just as by the number seven, so by the number twelve—which is composed by multiplying the parts of seven among themselves—the universality and perfection of things or times is signified. Therefore, since all places and times ought fittingly to be occupied, it is rightly from the number twelve that the radiance takes its beginning.  
[Col. 0078B]

“And his parents did not know it. Thinking that he was in the company, they came a day’s journey and sought him among their relatives and acquaintances; and not finding him, they returned to Jerusalem in search of him.” Someone may ask how the Son of God, raised with such care by his parents, could have been left behind through forgetfulness when they departed. The answer is that it was customary among the children of Israel, when they gathered in Jerusalem for feast days or returned to their homes, for the men and women to travel separately in processions. Infants and children could go indifferently with either parent. Therefore, blessed Mary and Joseph may each have supposed that the boy Jesus, whom they did not see accompanying them, had returned with the other parent.

“And it came to pass that after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions.” He sits in the midst of the teachers as a fountain of wisdom, but as an example of humility he first seeks to listen and question the teachers rather than instruct them. So that little children might not be ashamed to learn from their elders, God himself was not ashamed, in keeping with the condition of human age, to listen to human beings. So that no weak person might presume to teach, that child wished to be taught by asking questions—he who, through the power of his divinity, supplied the word of knowledge to those very teachers of his.  
[Col. 0078D]

“All who heard him were astonished at his teaching and his answers, and seeing him, they were amazed.” Those who heard him were astonished, and those who saw him were amazed. They were all the more astonished at the wisdom of his answers because, seeing how few his years were, they looked down on him. But we know that he is the one of whom the prophet once rejoiced and exulted: “A child is born for us, a son is given to us, and his name will be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God” (Isaiah 9). Therefore, let us not wonder at him who became a human child in such a way that he nevertheless remained what he had always been: God and Mighty.  
[Col. 0079A]

“And his mother said to him: ‘Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I, sorrowing, were seeking you.’ And he said to them: ‘Why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?’” He does not rebuke them for seeking him as a son. Rather, he compels them to raise the eyes of their minds to consider what he owes to the one whose Son he is eternally, because he is both God and man.

At one moment he displays the exalted things of divinity; at another, the lowly things of human frailty. As a human being, he questions his elders; as God, he answers what astonishes the elders and learned men. As the Son of God, he remains in the temple of God; as the son of man, he returns with his parents wherever they command.  
[Col. 0079B]

“And they did not understand the word that he spoke to them. And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them.” What else should the teacher of virtue do but fulfill the duty of piety? What else should he do among us except what he wished to be done by us? He showed deference to his father; he showed deference to the handmaid. For she herself says: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord.” He showed deference to his putative father, and he showed deference to the true Father and Lord. Born of a mother, he preserved her virgin and chaste.

Certainly he was not separated from the Father by will, action, or time, so that, instructed by his example, we might recognize what we owe to parents who endure so much for us.  
[Col. 0079C]

“And his mother kept all these words in her heart.” Whether she understood them or was not yet able to understand the words of the Gospel, she stored them all together in her heart, as though to ruminate upon them and examine them more carefully. Let us therefore learn chastity in all things. She preserved the testimonies of faith in her heart no less with a modest mouth than with her body. And if she remains silent before the apostolic commandments, why do you, after the apostolic commandments, desire more to teach than to learn?

“And Jesus advanced in wisdom and age,” and so forth. This passage refutes both the Manichaeans and the Apollinarians, showing that the Lord possessed true flesh and a true soul. For just as age belongs to the flesh, so advancement in wisdom belongs to the soul, as does grace. Yet he could not advance in wisdom at all if he did not possess the natural understanding granted to human beings for the sake of reason.

A few things should be said here about his name. Jesus is interpreted as “Savior.” Not only the etymology of this sacred name but also the number of its letters gives off the fragrance of the mysteries of our perpetual salvation. In Greek it is written with six letters: Ἰήσους, namely ι, η, σ, ο, υ, σ. Their numerical values are 10, 8, 200, 70, 400, and 200, which together make 888, a number that enlarges the figure of the resurrection.

For what 8 signifies simply, 10 and 100 signify in multiplication. We may also say that 8, taken absolutely, presents the example of the resurrection in the name of the Savior to mortals; and that through 10, the Lord has instructed and assisted us by figures to understand how the Decalogue of the law ought to be fulfilled in our resurrection, so that, just as he rose from the dead, we too, with his help, may be able to rise. The 100 indicates the glory that will follow us in the future. For the number one hundred, which passes from the left hand to the right, prefigures the happiness of that time of which the Lord says: “Again I will see you, and your heart will rejoice” (John 16).  
[Col. 0080A]

## HARMONY

Although not in words, a harmony of these two readings is found in their action. The parents, ascending to Jerusalem with the sacrifice, entered the Lord’s temple, which the Apostle urges us spiritually to do when he says: “I appeal to you by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to the Lord,” and so forth.

## SECOND SUNDAY AFTER THE EPIPHANY

### READING FROM THE LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER 12

> “Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us: whether prophecy, according to the proportion of faith; or ministry, in ministering; or the one who teaches, in teaching; the one who exhorts, in exhortation; the one who gives, in simplicity; the one who presides, in diligence; the one who shows mercy, in cheerfulness. Love without pretense: hating evil, clinging to good; loving one another with brotherly affection, anticipating one another in honor; not sluggish in diligence, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord; rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation; persevering in prayer, sharing in the needs of the saints, pursuing hospitality. Bless those who persecute you; bless, and do not curse. Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep. Being of the same mind toward one another; not setting your mind on high things, but associating with the humble.”

“Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us.” (From Primasius.) A gift depends not on our own judgment but on the will of the giver. Glory is promised in the future to all believers, but in the present the grace of virtues is granted to one whose heart is so pure that he is deemed worthy to receive it.
