“Whether prophecy, according to the proportion of faith.” He said “of faith,” not “of the law,” either because that faith deserved it, or because each person receives only as much as he believes.  
[Col. 0080D]

“Or ministry, in ministering.” (From Origen.) We can bring all these things back to the rule stated above: not to be wiser than one ought to be wise. For example, the one who ministers must not, in ministering, be wiser than he ought; nor must the one who teaches, in teaching, or the one who exhorts, in exhortation, be wiser than he ought. Many, after receiving ministry or teaching, became wiser than they ought to have been. Inflated with arrogance or dissolved in luxury, they fell headlong.

(From Primasius.) He is speaking of priestly ministry or the diaconate.

“Or the one who teaches, in teaching.” The one who teaches is greater than the one who exhorts.

[Col. 0081A]

“The one who exhorts, in exhortation.” (From Origen.) Exhortation is a form of teaching and of speech by which afflicted souls are lifted up through wisely adapted passages from the divine Scriptures and words gathered together into a unified discourse. But if speech possessing the power of God’s grace is applied to a despairing soul, it penetrates its heart, provides consolation, and restores hope once despair has been removed.

“The one who gives, in simplicity.” He says that one ought to do this in simplicity of heart—that is, not even to appear to be doing good to those in need while inwardly seeking praise from human beings. It is not simplicity if one thing appears to be done by the hands while another is sought in the heart.

“The one who presides, in diligence.” Whoever presides over the brothers or over the Church must be diligent—not with regard to human causes or worldly affairs, for such concern ought to be foreign to those who preside over the Church, but with the concern of which the Apostle says: “There is the daily pressure upon me, the concern for all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?” (2 Corinthians 11).  
[Col. 0081B]

“The one who shows mercy, in cheerfulness.” (From Primasius.) Mercy should be shown especially toward the sick. The title of mercy is universal and should be offered toward all with a peaceful spirit. “God loves a cheerful giver,” and without doubt he hates a sorrowful one (2 Corinthians 9).

(From Origen.) Whoever gives away his money, if he is an unbeliever and despairs of receiving it back, is necessarily saddened as one who has lost it. But whoever does this with faith and hope acts with cheerfulness and joy, certain that these small things which he spends at God’s command will bring him immense riches of heavenly wealth and, moreover, eternal life.  
[Col. 0081C]

“Love without pretense.” There must be complete purity in a Christian, just as God is pure light. To pretend belongs to servants. Let us love not only with the tongue but in deed and truth. Thus, if necessary, let us also die for one another.

(From Origen.) I think that every love which is not according to God is pretended and not genuine. For God, the creator of the soul, has implanted in it, along with the other virtues, the affection of love, so that it may love God and the things God wills. Therefore, whoever loves anything other than God and the things pleasing to God must be said to possess a false and pretended love. Likewise, if someone sees his neighbor in error and does not correct him, his love must be called pretended. Love should contain nothing flattering and nothing artificial.

“Hating evil.” It may perhaps seem strange that, among the other goods of the virtues, hatred is also introduced and set forth by the Apostle as necessary. Hence it is certain that the affection of hatred is also present in the soul. It is praiseworthy to hate vices and sins; for unless a person hates vices, he cannot love or preserve virtues.

“Clinging to good.” Let us cling to the good. We should also observe that, just as he says elsewhere, “the one who clings to the Lord is one spirit,” so here too he says: “Let us cling to the good,” undoubtedly so that it may happen to us to be one with the good.  
[Col. 0082A]

“Loving one another with brotherly affection.” It is as though he said: “Love one another as brothers, as though born from one mother.” We have received this commandment: that we love one another, just as God also loved us.

(From Origen.) We are therefore commanded to love our brothers, not to judge them. If you think that someone is ungodly and therefore do not consider him worthy of love, listen: Christ died for the ungodly. Or if, because your brother is a sinner, you therefore do not think he should be loved, listen: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners. But if he is righteous, he is all the more worthy of love, for the Lord loves the righteous.  
[Col. 0082B]

“Anticipating one another in honor.” (From Primasius.) If we always observed this and maintained love and patience—if we judged ourselves lesser than everyone else—we would neither willingly injure anyone nor grieve deeply over an injury inflicted upon us.

(From Origen.) This is what the Lord also taught when he reproved the scribes and Pharisees for claiming the first places at banquets. He teaches that when you are invited to a dinner, you should recline in the last place (Luke 14).

“Not sluggish in diligence.” (From Primasius.) Do not become sluggish and inactive in God’s work through concern for the world. Above, he admonished the one who presides to be diligent; now he gives this common command to everyone, lest any of us hear the Lord say: “Wicked and lazy servant.”  
[Col. 0082C]

“Fervent in spirit.” The Lord does not love those who are cold, and he is nauseated by those who are lukewarm. We are truly fervent in spirit if we are cold toward the world.

(From Origen.) He wishes us, who live under the law of the Spirit, to have nothing slack and nothing lukewarm within us, but to accomplish everything with spiritual fervor and the warmth of faith.

“Serving the Lord.” The one who serves the Lord is the one who can say to us: “One Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him.” Neither lust, greed, nor empty glory will any longer rule over him.

“Rejoicing in hope.” The one rejoices in hope who does not regard the things that are seen but awaits the things that are not seen, and who knows that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8).  
[Col. 0082D]

“Patient in tribulation.” (From Primasius.) Endure everything for the joy of future hope, as it is written: “Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various trials” (James 1), and because “tribulation produces patience, patience proven character, and proven character hope” (Romans 5).

“Persevering in prayer.” Perseverance in prayer provides us assistance in adversity. Where human weakness is insufficient, God’s help must be sought through prayers.

“Sharing in the needs of the saints.” It is as though he said: “Minister to those who, for Christ’s sake, have despised all their possessions and for a time require the ministrations of others.”  
[Col. 0083A]

(From Origen.) Do this honorably and decently: do not provide assistance to the needy saints as though giving alms, but in a certain sense hold our resources in common with them, and remember the saints either in solemn collections or so that we may advance through remembering them.

“Pursuing hospitality.” In one statement he embraces the full magnificence of hospitality. By saying that hospitality must be pursued, he shows not only that we should receive the guest who comes to us, but also that we should seek guests, be solicitous, pursue them, and search for them everywhere, so that they do not perhaps sit in the streets or lie outside under the open sky. Recall Lot, and you will find that he did not wait for guests; he himself sought them (Genesis 19). This was to pursue hospitality.  
[Col. 0083B]

“Bless those who persecute you.” Expounding the moral teaching more fully, the Apostle orders the actions, mind, intention, and even the mouth and tongue of the disciples. He does not want those who believe in Christ to utter a curse from their mouths, but to speak well, bless, and proclaim what is good, so that by this they may be recognized both as servants of a good Lord and as disciples of a good teacher.

It should nevertheless be understood that the language of blessing is used in different ways in the Scriptures. God is said to bless, and human beings or the other creatures are commanded to bless God. But God’s blessing always bestows some gift upon those whom he blesses; human beings, on the other hand, are said to bless God when they praise him and give thanks.  
[Col. 0083C]

“Bless, and do not curse.” The Apostle exhorts us that when we are provoked by enemies, we should not return curses for curses, but do what he writes about himself when he says: “We are cursed, and we bless” (1 Corinthians 4).

“Rejoice with those who rejoice.” Here too a suitable and appropriate distinction must be made. We should not share in just any kind of rejoicing as Christians. If I see someone rejoicing over the gain of money or the prominence of worldly honor, I ought not to congratulate those whose joys I know will be followed by mourning and tears. But because the Lord says to the apostles: “Rejoice because your names are written in heaven,” if we see someone performing an action worthy of being written in heaven—whether an act of righteousness, charity, peace, or mercy—and performed in such a way that it deserves to be recorded in the book of life, we ought to rejoice with such people.

Likewise, if we see someone turned away from error and, having abandoned the darkness of ignorance, come to the light of truth, attaining forgiveness of sins and the grace of the Holy Spirit, we ought to rejoice with such people.

Weep with those who weep. We are not commanded to weep with those who weep for their dead, or with those who mourn worldly losses, since we know that the sorrow of this world produces death. Therefore tears are not to be joined with such people. Rather, one must weep with those of whom the Lord says: “Blessed are those who weep, for they shall be comforted.” If someone weeps for his sins, if someone turns to repentance after his transgressions and washes away his error with tears; if someone, placed in this dwelling, also groans and longs to return to Christ, and through holy desire is cleansed by an outpouring of tears—we should join our tears to those people and associate our groans with theirs. For the sorrow that is according to God produces enduring salvation through repentance.

### Having the same mind toward one another

This sentence has been made more obscure, not by its nature, but by its interpretation. This is what it says: that we should think about a brother as we think about ourselves, and wish for our neighbor what we wish for ourselves, just as the Lord also said in the Gospel: “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do the same for them.”

### Not aspiring to high things, but associating with the humble

He teaches that pride must be avoided in every way. For this is what “to think highly” means; and rightly, pride must be avoided, since Scripture says: “For pride is the beginning of departure from the Lord.” He aptly explained the instruction in humility in a single statement: to associate with the humble, love the humble, and bend oneself toward them means to become accustomed to imitating him who, although he was in the form of God, assumed the form of a servant and humbled himself unto death (Phil. II).

*(From Primasius.)* This man savors pride who desires to avenge his own injury by himself and does not consent to humble things—that is, to humility.

## THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN, CHAPTER II

> “A wedding took place at Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. Jesus and his disciples were also invited to the wedding. When the wine failed, the mother of Jesus said to him: ‘They have no wine.’ And Jesus said to her: ‘What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.’ His mother said to the servants: ‘Whatever he tells you, do it.’ Now six stone water-jars had been placed there, according to the purification of the Jews, each holding two or three measures. Jesus said to them: ‘Fill the jars with water.’ And they filled them to the brim. Jesus said to them: ‘Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast.’ And they took it. When the master of the feast tasted the water that had become wine, and did not know where it came from—though the servants who had drawn the water knew—he called the bridegroom and said to him: ‘Every man first sets out the good wine, and when they have become drunk, then the inferior wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.’ Jesus performed this beginning of signs at Cana of Galilee and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him.”

### A wedding took place at Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there

*(From Bede.)* It is not without a mystery that a wedding is reported to have taken place on the third day after the events described in the preceding passage of the Gospel. It signifies that, in the third age of the world, the Lord came to unite the Church to himself. The first age of the world, before the law, shone through the examples of the patriarchs. The second, under the law, shone through the writings of the prophets. The third, under grace, shone through the proclamations of the Evangelists, like the third light of day. In this age our Lord and Savior appeared incarnate for the redemption of the human race. Moreover, the fact that the wedding is said to have taken place at Cana of Galilee—that is, in the zeal of an accomplished migration—typologically announces that those are especially worthy of Christ’s grace who, through the zeal and fervor of pious devotion, by striving for the better spiritual gifts, and by good works, know how to migrate from vices to virtues and from earthly things to eternal things, through hope and love.

### A wedding took place at Cana of Galilee

*(From Jerome.)* The Lord came into this world to a wedding because he joined the holy Church to himself. Concerning her the Apostle says: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (II Cor. XI). He therefore has the Church as his bride: he redeemed her with his blood, gave her the Holy Spirit as a pledge, and joined her to himself in the womb of the Virgin. The bridegroom is the Word, the bride is human flesh; and the two together are one Son of God and the same Son of Man. He became the head of the Church and came forth from the bridal chamber like a bridegroom. His bridal chamber was the Virgin’s womb. He came to a wedding at Cana of Galilee, a sign of a certain sacrament: for *Cana* is interpreted as “zeal,” and *Galilee* as “migration accomplished.”

### And the mother of Jesus was there

The mother of Jesus is shown at the wedding as the synagogue, because she prompts Christ to perform the miracle.

### Jesus and his disciples were invited to the wedding

By coming to a wedding, the Lord—apart from the mystical meaning—wished to confirm what he himself had made. For elsewhere he says: “What God has joined together, let no man separate” (Matt. XIX).

*(From Bede.)* The first setting of the wedding was Judea, in which the Son of God deigned to become man, consecrate the Church through participation in his body and blood, and strengthen her in faith through the pledge of his Spirit. But when the nations were called to faith, the desired joys of that same wedding reached to the ends of the earth.

### And when the wine failed

As the Lord reclined at the wedding, the wine failed, so that, through the better wine miraculously produced by him, the glory of the God hidden in the man might be revealed and the faith of believers in him might be strengthened. If we seek the mystery, then, when the Lord appeared in the flesh, that pure sweetness of the legal meaning had gradually begun to fail because of the Pharisees’ carnal interpretation. He soon converted what appeared to be carnal commandments into spiritual teaching, and transformed the entire surface of the legal letter into the power of heavenly grace in the Gospel. This is what it means to make wine from water.

### His mother says to Jesus, “They have no wine,” and Jesus says to her, “What is there between me and you, woman?”

*(From Augustine.)* He did not dishonor his mother, since he commands us to honor our parents; nor did he deny that she was his mother, since he received flesh from her. But when he says, “What is there between me and you, woman?”, he signifies that, in his divinity—the power by which the miracle was to be performed—he had not temporally received his beginning from his mother, but had always possessed eternity from the Father.

### My hour has not yet come

“My hour has not yet come”—the hour when I shall demonstrate, by dying, the frailty of the humanity taken from you. The hour, therefore, namely the hour of the Passion, had not yet come, because miracles had to be performed, the Lord’s divinity had to be commended, and the Lord’s humanity had to be commended in the very sharing of mortality. But the hour came when he showed what he and his mother had in common, when, as he was dying on the cross, he entrusted the Virgin to the virgin disciple. Recalling this hour while hanging on the cross, the Lord said to his mother: “Woman, behold your son,” as though he had said: “Behold: what I took from you is now shown by dying; yet this nature will afterward be glorified in the glory of the resurrection.”

### His mother says to the servants, “Whatever he tells you, do it”

His mother knew the humanity of her Son. Although he appeared to deny what she was asking, the mother nevertheless knew the goodness of her Son, who did not wish to deny what was requested. She confidently instructed the servants to fulfill the commands of the Son who was giving orders.

### Now six stone water-jars had been placed there

Water-jars are vessels for water; in Greek, water is called ὕδωρ (*hydōr*). Water signifies knowledge of Sacred Scripture, which habitually both washes its hearers from the filth of sins and gives them drink from the fountain of divine knowledge. The six vessels containing it are the devoted hearts of the saints, whose perfection of life has been set before right-believing people as an example through the six ages of the world, up to the Lord’s coming. The vessels are rightly made of stone, because the hearts of the righteous are strong, being made firm by love of that stone of which the Apostle Peter said: “Coming to him, a living stone, you yourselves are built up like living stones” (I Pet. II).

### According to the purification of the Jews

The water-jars were rightly placed according to the purification of the Jews, because the law was given through Moses only to the Jewish people, whereas the grace and truth of the Gospel came through Jesus Christ both to the Gentiles and to believing Jews (John I).

### Each holding two or three measures

*(From Augustine.)* What does “holding two or three measures” mean? This expression especially commends a mystery to us. The word *measure* derives its name from measurement, just as do urns, amphorae, and other measures. The Greeks call measures μέτρα (*metra*). It does not say that some held two measures and others three; rather, the six water-jars themselves held two or three measures. If it had said only “three,” our mind would be directed solely toward the mystery of the Trinity. But when the Father and the Son are understood, there are, as it were, two measures; when the Holy Spirit is also understood, there are three measures.

Another interpretation: the two measures are circumcision and uncircumcision. In these two names you have all the nations: they are the two measures. From these two walls Christ was made the cornerstone. Let us also show three measures among the nations themselves. There were three sons of Noah, through whom the human race was restored. To them the Apostle says: “We received a measure reaching even to you.” Here, then, you have three measures among the Gentiles.

*(From Bede.)* Each holds two or three measures because the authors of Sacred Scripture sometimes speak only of the Father and the Son, and sometimes also mention the Holy Spirit. In the two or three, understand the Trinity, while the whole is one God. But as much as water differs from wine, so much does that meaning differ by which the Scriptures were understood before the Savior’s coming from the meaning that he himself revealed when he came.

### Jesus says to them, “Fill the water-jars with water”

What else is signified by the servants who did these things than the disciples of Christ? They filled the water-jars with water—not by themselves filling the legal and prophetic Scriptures, but by understanding them wisely and opening them faithfully.

### They filled them to the brim

Because they understood correctly that there was no age of the world devoid of holy teachers who, whether by words, examples, or writings, opened the way of life to mortals. God could have filled empty jars with wine, since at the beginning of the world he created all things from nothing; but he preferred to make wine from water, teaching typologically that he had not come to abolish or condemn the law and the Prophets, but rather to fulfill them.

Let us therefore look at the six water-jars filled with the saving water of Scripture. Let us also see that same water changed into the sweetest fragrance and taste of wine.

In the first age of the world, a brother killed the righteous Abel. For this he was crowned with martyrdom; in the Gospels and Epistles he is written of as righteous, while the impious murderer is named. Whoever, hearing these things, fears being condemned with the impious and desires to be blessed with the righteous, therefore casts away every source of hatred and envy and strives to please God through the sacrifice of righteousness. He finds in Scripture a vessel from which he may rejoice, having been healthfully washed and given drink.

But if he understands that Cain the murderer signifies the perfidy of the Jews, that Abel’s killing signifies the Passion of the Lord Savior, and that the earth which received his blood is the Church, which received Christ’s blood as the mystery of her renewal, then he certainly finds water changed into wine, because he has understood the sayings of the law in a more sacred way.

In the second age of the world, the world was destroyed because of human sins by the waters of the Flood, from which Noah alone, with a few others, deserved to be saved on account of his righteousness. Whoever, hearing of this devastation, begins to live more correctly, desiring to be saved with the few and fearing to be destroyed with the many, has found a water-jar by which he may be cleansed. But if he understands the ark as the Church, Noah as Christ, the water as baptism, and the dove as the anointing of the Holy Spirit with which the baptized are imbued, he marvels that wine has been made from water, because he recognizes that his cleansing was prophesied in the ancient history.

In the third age, God tested Abraham when he commanded him to offer his son as a burnt offering. Abraham does not delay in doing what is commanded, but a ram is sacrificed in place of the son, while Abraham himself is blessed for his obedience. Hearing this, you too strive to be obedient and have found a water-jar in which you may be cleansed. But if, through the offering of the only Son, you understand the Passion of Christ—who suffered in his humanity but remained impassible in his divinity, since the Son is offered but a ram is slaughtered—and if you understand that Abraham’s blessing has been fulfilled in you, who believe from among the Gentiles, then he has certainly made wine from water for you, because he has given you spiritual understanding.

In the fourth age, David, humble, innocent, and gentle, receives the kingdom after the proud Saul has been rejected. Hearing this, if you begin to devote yourself to humility and innocence and to drive pride from your heart, you have found a draught of the clearest water with which to refresh yourself, in the fourth water-jar filled with a saving fountain. For if you understand Saul as the Jews, David as Christ, the carnal destruction of the kingdom of the Jews, and Christ’s kingdom as everlasting, you perceive wine made from water, by drinking which you rejoice forever.

In the fifth age, the sinful people are led into Babylon, but after seventy years, having repented and been corrected, they are brought back to their homeland through Jesus the great priest. If, hearing this, you flee through fear of sin to the remedy of repentance, you have been washed by the water of the fifth jar. But if you understand Babylon as the confusion of sins, Nebuchadnezzar as the devil, Jesus the priest as the high priest Jesus Christ, and the seventy years as the fullness of good works bestowed through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, you have wine made from water, because you understand that what has been written pertains to you.

In the sixth age, the Lord appeared in the flesh. On the eighth day of his birth he was circumcised, and on the thirty-third day he was brought to the Temple, where offerings were made for him. By observing these things according to the letter, we plainly learn with what diligence we must undertake the mysteries of the Gospel faith, since he himself, bringing the blessing of grace, first fulfilled the ceremonies of the elders and thus took care both to receive and to hand on the new sacraments.

Behold, you have the sixth water-jar for washing away sins and drinking the joys of life, bringing water purer than the others. But if in the circumcision on the eighth day you understand baptism, and in the bringing into the Temple and the offering of the victim you recognize a figure of the faithful entering from the baptistery into the holy altar and being consecrated through communion in the Lord’s body and blood, then you have indeed been endowed with the purest, unmixed wine made from water.

But if, further, you interpret the day of circumcision as the general resurrection, and understand the circumcised being brought into the Temple with offerings to signify the saints, now incorruptible, entering with the gifts of good works to behold the appearance of the divine majesty, then you will see wine made from water to such an extent that, in wonder, you will say to the Creator: “How splendid is your intoxicating cup!”

### Jesus says to them, “Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast,” and they took it

When the master of the feast tasted the water that had become wine—though he did not know where it came from, while the servants who had drawn the water knew—wine made from water was served to the master of the feast in the house of the wedding, which is the Church of Christ. A dining hall is described as being there because there are plainly three orders of the faithful in the Church: the married, the continent, and the teachers.

### The master of the feast calls the bridegroom and says to him, “Every man first sets out the good wine…”

It belongs to teachers to recognize the difference between the law and the Gospel, between truth and shadow, and to set forth the new grace of evangelical faith and the gifts of the perpetual heavenly homeland.

### “This was the beginning of signs that Jesus performed at Cana of Galilee…”

By this sign he manifested that he was the King of glory, and therefore the Bridegroom of the Church: he came to the wedding as an ordinary man, but as God he changed the elements of heaven and earth as he wished.

Thus the Lord did not wish to make the wine for the wedding feast out of nothing. Rather, he commanded six water-jars to be filled with water and miraculously changed it into wine. For he bestowed the six ages of the world with the abundance of saving wisdom, which, when he came, he enriched with the power of a higher meaning. Carnal people understood carnal things only in a carnal way; he reserved spiritual things to be understood spiritually.

### Then Augustine

“And on the third day a wedding took place at Cana of Galilee.” Therefore, when Christ shone upon the world darkened by obscure sins, he came to the wedding on the day of the Trinity. He was the true cluster of grapes containing within himself the wine of life, but the battle of the cross had not yet arrived.

### His mother says to him, “They have no wine”

For a little while, O most flourishing Virgin; for a little while, let the Jew prepare the wood, and then the wine will be able to come forth. Why do you run before the time to the vat, when Judas has not yet set his heel upon one [reading uncertain]?  You have only just deserved to produce a jeweled offspring, and already you are trying to press your cluster? But he who plucked punishment from the wood must await the remedy on the wood. And he who gathered fruit from the illustrious tree must await the harvest at the cross.

### Jesus says to her, “What is there between me and you, woman?”

Here Christ exalted his divinity above his mother; he did not deny his mother. Nor did he deny that he was born from flesh, but he subjected his mother to his own majesty.

### My hour has not yet come

The hour was not the hour of what had been done, but of what had been willed; not of necessity, but of willingness; not the hour in which he would be forced to die, but the hour in which he would deign to be slain for the world.

Meanwhile Christ makes tasteless draughts miraculous. Insipid liquid was poured into the jar, and intoxicating streams were drawn out. No grape was pressed, yet wines boiled without a vine. Christ did in the liquid what, at the appointed time, he does in the vine.

The wedding passes over to Christ, and the Church changes her bridegroom. At one time Judea also had no wine, because she did not receive the gift of consecrated blood; and while she was married to the Law, she found nothing to drink. Christ came, changed the Law into grace, poured out the cup of blood, and by dying made a banquet.

Those six water-jars whose water was changed into wine signified the six ages of the world. In those six ages, as in six water-jars, prophecy was not absent. But when Christ was not understood in them, water rather than wine was drunk from them.

The first jar was filled in Adam, when Eve was fashioned from his side while he slept. Christ slept on the cross, and from his side the Church was formed. But because the Jewish people did not understand that this was fulfilled in Christ, it savored not of wine but of water.

The second jar was filled in Noah. Thus, through the mystery of the ark or of the Flood, the human race was saved, just as through the sacrament of the cross or of baptism the whole world is rescued from death.

The third jar was filled in Abraham. For just as Isaac himself carried the wood to the place of the burnt offering, so Christ himself carried the cross, the instrument of his Passion, to the place of suffering.

The fourth jar was filled in David, who, both in humility and through many tribulations, prefigured Christ the Lord.

The fifth jar was filled in the time of Daniel. For he saw a stone cut without hands—that is, Christ born from the mountain, namely from the kingdom of the Jews, cut without hands because without the work of marriage—and this stone filled the whole world by his grace.

The sixth jar was filled in John the Baptist, who preached to the Jews: “Bear fruits worthy of repentance; for God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.”

These six ages of the world, therefore, were filled like six water-jars by the servants—that is, by the patriarchs and prophets.

### Each holding two or three measures

Why three? Because of the mystery of the Trinity. Why two? Because of the two commandments, love of God and love of neighbor. And in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one.” Behold the two. “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” Behold, you have the three.

The master of the feast tasted the water that had become wine—that is, the Lord of the world—and said: “Every man first sets out the good wine, and when people have become drunk, then the inferior wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.” For the law too is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good. But the Law and the Prophets prophesied until John; therefore, when the Lord came, the Mosaic wines failed, and the wines of blood flowed forth. The former reached their termination; the latter took their beginning.

Finally, this was the beginning of the signs Jesus performed: when, having been slain, he fed the nations, and, having been wounded, made a banquet from the wine of his blood.

## HARMONY

In accordance with the Apostle’s distinction of gifts, a harmony of readings is formed through the difference among these water-jars. The hearts of the saints are water-jars, filled from the fountain of gifts. The servants who drew the water, and to whom the mother said, “Whatever he tells you, do it,” are the servants of Christ, to whom, according to the Apostle (I Cor. XII), ministry is given for ministering.

## THIRD SUNDAY AFTER THE EPIPHANY

### EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER XII

> “Do not be wise in your own eyes, repaying no one evil for evil. Provide what is good, not only before God but also before all people. If it is possible, insofar as it depends on you, live at peace with all people. Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath. For it is written: ‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay,’ says the Lord. But if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink. For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head. Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.”

### Do not be wise in your own eyes

Whoever seems wise to himself is, with arrogance, a fool. Nor can one know the true wisdom of God who honors his own foolishness as though it were wisdom. Indeed, in the preceding discussion Paul himself taught that this had been the cause of the Jews’ unbelief, saying of them: “For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to the righteousness of God.” Thus whoever is wise in his own eyes cannot be wise before God.

*(From Primasius.)* Do not glory in human wisdom, but be fools to the world so that you may be wise before the Lord, as it is written: “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach from your law” (Ps. XCIII).

### Repaying no one evil for evil

If inflicting evil is to sin, repaying evil is not righteousness, but a similar sin—or, as I judge, an even graver one. For the person who first inflicted evil may perhaps not have recognized that what he was doing was evil. But the one who repays evil, by the very fact that he is moved to take revenge, confesses that he recognized the evil of what he repays. Therefore one must always look to him who said: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deut. XXXII).

*(From Primasius.)* It is human wisdom to seek to repay enemies in kind; it is folly in this world if we offer the other cheek to one who strikes us. If we possess such great patience and humility, we shall be able to appear approved not only before God but also before human beings.

### Providing what is good, not only before God but also before human beings

*(From Origen.)* A person provides what is good before all people, not in order to please the vices or customs of each individual. Otherwise what the same Apostle said would be contradicted: “If I were still trying to please people, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. I). Rather, the person who so maintains the balance of his life, conduct, and actions that he cannot be reproached by anyone provides what is good before all people. For the Apostle did not say that we should please everyone, but that we should provide what is good before all: that is, that we should do what is good before everyone, whether what is good pleases them or does not please them.

### If it is possible, insofar as it depends on you, live at peace with all people

The Apostle, lest another person’s disposition—if it should happen to be hostile—seem to hinder us from the good of peace, gave a very moderate command: our own disposition should always be ready for peace, and the blame for discord should rest not with us but with the other person. Therefore he rightly adds: “Insofar as it depends on you”—that is, insofar as it accords with your purpose and your faith.

*(From Primasius.)* Let what belongs to you be this: keep peace with everyone, and say: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceful.”

### Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath

*(From Origen.)* How those who do not avenge themselves are to give place to wrath seems to me capable of a twofold interpretation. First, by the very fact that they do not return hand for hand, so to speak, or insult for insult, they give the anger of the person who inflicted the injury room to pass away and vanish. No one is so enraged that, if he receives no retaliation, he will rage again; rather, as his fury is poured out and dissipated, he grows calm.

There is also another way of giving place to wrath. Those who sin store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath, when God will repay each person according to his works. If, then, we avenge ourselves, it is no great matter, for example, whether we return a slap for a slap or a stone for a stone. But if we reserve these matters for God’s vengeance, we give place to wrath, because in judgment God will exact punishments far more severe than we can inflict.

*(From Primasius.)* We either give place to wrath by fleeing from it or by allowing it to do harm.

### For it is written: “Vengeance is mine”

“I will avenge it as though it were my own injury,” says the Lord, “not as though it were your injury.” For the prophet says: “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zech. II).

### “I will repay,” says the Lord

He promises that he will repay those who do good.

### But if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head

The purpose is that, when he understands that coals have been heaped upon him through your undeserved mercy, he may shake them off—that is, be converted and love you, whom he had once hated. Otherwise this is not mercy but cruelty: if you do it so that something worse may happen to him, although the Lord commanded you to pray for him, saying: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you.” By feeding and giving drink to your enemy, we reconcile him to peace with us. But if he persists in wickedness, he himself heaps the fire upon his own head.

*(From Origen.)* Let us see whether this command may perhaps contain a more worthy meaning. Jeremiah says to the sinful daughter of Babylon: “You have coals of fire; sit upon them; they will be a help to you.” Perhaps, then, these coals of fire that are heaped upon the enemy’s head are heaped for his help. It can happen that a mad, savage, and barbarous enemy, if he experiences our kindness, if he sees our humanity, affection, and piety, may be seized by compunction of heart and feel repentance for his offense. From this a kind of fire may be kindled in him, which may torment and burn him through the consciousness of his offense. These are the coals of fire that are heaped upon his head through our work of mercy and piety.

The head is called the chief part of the heart, and it is rightly called the head, since all the members are governed by its understanding and prudence.

### Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good

The person who, provoked by evils, returns evil is overcome by evil. But the person who, having received evils, gives back good conquers evil with good. One is said to have conquered another when he brings him over to his own side, as in the case of a heretic or pagan. If, therefore, he makes you repay him in kind, he has conquered you by making you like himself. But if, through your patience, you make him cease from his injury, you have conquered him.

## THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER VIII

> “When Jesus had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. And behold, a leper came and worshiped him, saying: ‘Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me.’ Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying: ‘I will; be cleansed.’ And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. And Jesus said to him: ‘See that you tell no one, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift that Moses commanded as a testimony to them.’ When he had entered Capernaum, a centurion approached him, asking him and saying: ‘Lord, my servant lies at home paralyzed and is suffering terribly.’ And Jesus said to him: ‘I will come and heal him.’ The centurion answered and said: ‘Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant will be healed. For I too am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, “Go,” and he goes; and to another, “Come,” and he comes; and to my servant, “Do this,” and he does it.’ When Jesus heard this, he marveled and said to those who followed him: ‘Amen, I say to you, I have not found such faith in Israel. I say to you that many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. But the children of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’ And Jesus said to the centurion: ‘Go; let it be done for you as you have believed.’ And the servant was healed in that hour.”

### When Jesus had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him

When the Lord descended from the mountain—that is, from heaven into the world—great crowds of the human race followed him through faith. For unless he had descended, no human being would have ascended to heaven.

### And behold, a leper came and worshiped him, saying: “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me”

He attributed the power to the Lord’s will, but he did not doubt the Lord’s will. Yet, as one conscious of his own condition, he did not presume. This leper signified the people of the Gentiles, who, having been pierced with compunction, came to the Lord’s mercy.

### Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying: “I will; be cleansed”

*(From Jerome.)* Consider how humble the response is. The leper had said, “If you will.” The Lord answered, “I will.” The leper said, “You can cleanse me.” The Lord says, καθαρίσθητι (*katharisthēti*), “Be cleansed.” Therefore, contrary to what most Latins think, it should not be joined and read as “I will, be cleansed,” but separately, so that he first says, “I will,” and then commands, “Be cleansed.”

### And immediately his leprosy was cleansed

*(From Bede.)* There is nothing intermediate between God’s work and his command, because the work is present in the command. Hence it says: “He spoke, and they were made,” because God’s will is power. The Law indeed prohibits touching lepers, but he who is Lord of the Law does not submit to the law; rather, he makes the law. He did not touch the leper because he was unable to cleanse him without touching him, but to show that he was not subject to the law and did not fear contagion as human beings do. He could not be contaminated, for he was the one who freed others.

### And Jesus said to him: “See that you tell no one”

Why is he commanded to tell no one, except to teach that our good deeds are not to be publicized but concealed, so that we may abstain not only from monetary reward but also from the reward of gratitude?

### But go, show yourself to the priest

He is commanded to show himself to the priest so that the priest might understand that he had been healed not by the order of the law but by the grace of God, which is above the law.

*(From Jerome.)* He sends him to the priests for various reasons. First, because of humility, so that he might appear to show deference to the priests. For the Law had commanded that those who had been cleansed from leprosy should offer gifts to the priests. Secondly, so that, when they saw the leper cleansed, they might either believe and be saved, or, if they did not believe, become without excuse; and also so that he would not appear to violate the Law, as they so frequently accused him of doing.

*(From Bede.)* “And offer the gift that Moses commanded as a testimony to them.” He commands him to offer sacrifice in order to show them that he was not abolishing the Law but fulfilling it. Walking according to the Law yet standing above the Law, he healed those whom the remedies of the Law had not healed. And rightly it is added: “As a testimony to them”—that is, if they believe in the Lord, if they depart from the leprosy of impiety.

Since this man typologically signifies the human race weakened by sins, he is rightly described not merely as a leper but as full of leprosy. For all have sinned and lack the glory of God. They are to be cleansed by the outstretched hand of the Savior—that is, by the incarnate Word of God touching human nature—and may be able to hear with the Apostles: “Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John XV). Those who had long been detestable and were kept apart from the people of God in the camps may now at last be restored to the Temple and offered to the priest, namely to the one of whom it is said: “You are a priest forever” (Ps. CX). Hearing from the Apostle that “the temple of God is holy, which temple you are,” let them offer for their cleansing what Moses commanded: that is, let them present their bodies as a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to God (Rom. XII).

When they had entered Capernaum, a centurion approached him, beseeching him and saying. It is asked how this agrees with the fact that Luke says the centurion sent messengers, whereas Matthew relates that he himself approached the Lord. The answer is readily apparent: Matthew, for the sake of brevity, said that he himself approached, since his desire and will were truly presented before the Lord. Mystically, he also commends to us what is written: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Psalm 34). [Col. 0095A] Luke, moreover, disclosed the whole manner in which the event took place.

“Lord, my servant lies at home paralyzed and is grievously tormented.” And Jesus said to him: “I will come and heal him.” Seeing the centurion’s faith, humility, and prudence, he immediately promises that he will go and heal him. His faith consisted in this: although he was from the Gentiles, he believed that the servant could be saved by the Savior. His humility consisted in judging himself unworthy that the Lord should enter beneath his roof. His prudence consisted in seeing, beyond the bodily covering, the divinity concealed within; he knew that what was visible even to unbelievers would not profit him, but that which lay hidden inwardly would. Allegorically, however, Capernaum—which is interpreted as “field of consolation” or “most beautiful village”—signifies the Church. The centurion, because of the perfection indicated by the number in his name, signifies the firstfruits of the Gentiles, such as Cornelius or the eunuch baptized by Philip (Acts 8). The servant who lies paralyzed in the house and is grievously tormented by the demon signified the people of the Gentiles, who, in the house—that is, in this world—lay unbelieving, worshiping idols and serving demons.

(From Bede.) “And in reply he said: ‘Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter beneath my roof.’” Because of the consciousness of his Gentile life, he considered himself more burdened by the Lord’s gracious condescension than helped by it. Nor did he think that he could have Christ as a guest, since, although he possessed faith, he had not yet been instructed in the sacraments. But because divine grace knows how to grant what our weakness does not presume to request: another centurion also, who, like this one, prefigured the believing people from the Gentiles, received the gift of the Holy Spirit before he was baptized because of his great faith and righteousness [Col. 0095C]; and this man, though not yet catechized, deserved both to have his faith praised by the Lord and his servant saved.

“But only say the word, and my servant will be healed.” Great was the centurion’s faith, because he confessed the power of the word in Christ and adapted his words to the mysteries of our healing: “Although we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Corinthians 5).

“For I too am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me.” He says that he is a man subject to authority, whether of a tribune or of a governor, yet able to command those beneath him; so that it may be understood that he who is much more God and all-powerful possesses an innumerable army of angelic power [Col. 0095D], obedient to his commands.

“And I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” He wishes to show that the Lord also can accomplish what he wills not only through the bodily arrival of his presence but through the ministry of angels. For bodily illnesses or opposing powers had to be driven away—those by which a human being is often reduced to weakness—and this occurs both by the word of the Lord and through the ministry of angels.

Alternatively. The soldiers and servants who obey the centurion are natural powers, a considerable number of which many people who come to the Lord bring with them. Concerning these, in the praise of Cornelius and the centurion, it is said that he was “a just man and one who feared God, with all his household, giving many alms to the people and always praying to God” (Acts 10) [Col. 0096A].

When Jesus heard this, he marveled. He marveled because he saw that the centurion understood his majesty. But who had produced that faith or understanding in him, except the very one who marveled at it? And if someone else had produced it, what would he marvel at, since he knew it beforehand? It must therefore be noted that when the Lord marvels at something, he indicates that it ought to be marveled at by us, who still need to be instructed in this way. For all such emotions, when they are attributed to God, are not signs of a disturbed mind but of a teaching master.

And turning to the crowds that followed him, he said: “Amen, I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel.” He is not speaking of all the patriarchs and prophets of former times, but of the people of the present age, to whom the centurion’s faith is therefore preferred [Col. 0096B]. They had been instructed by the Law and the admonitions of the Prophets; this man, however, believed spontaneously, with no one teaching him.

“But I say to you that many will come from the east and the west and will recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.” For the God of Abraham, the creator of heaven, is the Father of Christ. Therefore Abraham is in the kingdom of heaven, and with him the nations that have believed in Christ, the Son of the Creator, will recline. This also fulfills the meaning of which we spoke above in connection with the centurion’s faith: the privilege of the Gentiles is demonstrated when peoples who will believe from the east and the west are mentioned in relation to his faith.

“But the sons of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” By the sons of the kingdom he signifies the Jews, over whom God formerly reigned; they will be cast into the outer darkness. Darkness is always within, not outside; but because one who drives the Lord away from himself abandons the light, those darknesses are called “outer.” “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth”: if weeping belongs to the eyes and gnashing of teeth displays the bones, then the resurrection of bodies and of those same members that had fallen is real.

The centurion’s humility agrees with this, since he said: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter beneath my roof,” as does the Apostle’s word, where he says: “Do not be wise in your own sight.” But the works of mercy that the Savior performed toward the leper and the centurion’s servant agree with the Apostle’s exhortation, in which he says: “Providing what is good not only before God but before all people” [Col. 0096D].

# THE FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER THEOPHANY

## READING FROM THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER 13

“Do not owe anyone anything, except to love one another. For whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. For: ‘You shall not commit adultery; you shall not kill; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not covet your neighbor’s property.’ And if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this word: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ Love of one’s neighbor does no evil. Therefore love is the fullness of the law.”

[Col. 0097A]

(From Origen.) When he says, “Do not owe anyone anything,” it is certain that he is referring to sin. We have often and repeatedly shown that sin is a debt. Paul therefore wants every debt of sin to be paid, so that no debt of sin remains with us at all. Nevertheless, he wants the debt of love to remain and never cease from us; for this is beneficial both to pay daily and always to owe. Finally, he explains in what follows how great a virtue love is.

“For whoever,” he says, “loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. For: ‘You shall not commit adultery. You shall not kill. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness. You shall not covet’; and if there is any other commandment, it is restored in this word: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’” And, briefly gathering the final reasoning for so great a good, he says:

[Col. 0097B]

“Love of one’s neighbor does no evil. Therefore love is the fullness of the law.” Above he had said that whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. Since it seemed difficult to understand how anyone could fulfill the whole law in a single statement, he gives the fullest explanation by saying: “Love of one’s neighbor does no evil,” and therefore “love is the fullness of the law.”

Apply love to each individual commandment of the law and see how easily everything is fulfilled. Can one who loves his neighbor kill him? It is certain that no one kills the person whom he loves. Love, then, is what fulfills the commandment that says, “You shall not kill.”

And again: Does one who loves his neighbor commit adultery with his wife? Certainly never. If, therefore, you love your neighbor, you do not commit adultery; likewise, one who loves his neighbor does not steal what belongs to him. One who loves his neighbor does not bear false witness against him. Similarly, all the other commandments of the law are kept without any labor if there is love toward one’s neighbor.

Yet I think that in this passage the Apostle wished to say something more concise. For if you inquire more carefully who our neighbor is, you will learn from the Gospel that our neighbor is the one who came, placed us—wounded by robbers and stripped by demons—upon the beast of his body, carried us to the inn of the Church, and gave two denarii for our care and attention to the innkeeper, whether to Paul himself or to everyone who presides over the Church. He granted the expenses for our care from the New and Old Testaments. If, therefore, we love this neighbor, we fulfill the whole law and all the commandments in his love [Col. 0097D].

“For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.” It cannot happen in any way that one who loves Christ with all his heart and with all his strength should do anything displeasing to Christ. One who loves him not only does not kill him—something the law prohibits—but does not even become angry with his brother, because he delights so greatly in the one whom he loves. He not only does not commit adultery, but does not even look upon a woman with lust; rather, he says to him—or perhaps to himself—“My soul longs for the living God” (Psalm 42).

When would one who loves Christ think about theft, since he has even abandoned all his possessions, whatever he had, in order to follow Christ? When would one who loves Christ bear false witness, knowing that the one he loves was betrayed by false testimony? Necessarily, then, one who loves Christ also loves his neighbor. For by this one sign a person is shown to be Christ’s disciple: if he has love toward his neighbors. It is certain that one who does not love his neighbor does not know Christ [Col. 0098A].

# GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER 8

“When Jesus had embarked in the boat, his disciples followed him. And behold, a great disturbance arose on the sea, so that the boat was covered by the waves. But he was sleeping. They came and woke him, saying: ‘Lord, save us; we are perishing.’ And he said to them: ‘Why are you afraid, you of little faith?’ Then he rose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and a great calm arose. The men marveled, saying: ‘What sort of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?’”

When Jesus had embarked in the boat, his disciples followed him. (From Bede.) In this voyage the Lord deigns to show both natures of his one and same person: he who sleeps in the boat as a human being restrains the fury of the sea as God by his word.

According to the allegory, however, the sea or lake that he wishes to cross with his own is understood as the dark and bitter turmoil of the present age. The boat into which they embark is understood better than anything else as the tree of the Lord’s Passion. By its benefit, the faithful, having crossed the waves of the world, obtain the dwelling of the heavenly homeland, as though the security of a stable shore [Col. 0098C].

That the Savior himself embarked in one boat with his disciples he explains elsewhere, when, after announcing the mystery of his Passion and resurrection, he immediately said to all: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.”

And behold, a great disturbance arose on the sea, so that the boat was covered by the waves. For no one could sail across this world without Christ, since even those with whom the Lord is present are often shaken by the storm of worldly temptations. And the οἰκονομία—the divine dispensation—is preserved in the Apostles, so that you may understand that no one can depart from the course of this life without temptation, because temptation is the exercise of faith. Let us therefore, as though keeping watch through the night, awaken the true God, the helmsman [Col. 0098D].

Now there was a contrary wind for them. The contrary wind signifies the devil; the disturbance and waves signify the blasphemy of persecutors, aroused by demonic storms. Christ himself is not troubled by these; rather, the weakness of the disciples is shaken.

But he was sleeping. While the disciples were sailing, Christ fell asleep, because, when the faithful were trampling upon the world and meditating in their hearts upon the rest of the future kingdom, while they were casting behind them the faithless arrogance of the world through the favorable breath of the Holy Spirit or the rowing of their own effort, the hour of the Lord’s Passion suddenly arrived. Hence Mark rightly reports that this took place as night was approaching, so that the setting of the true Sun might be signified not only by the Lord’s sleep but also by the hour when the light was departing [Col. 0099A].

They came and woke him, saying: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.” The disciples wake the Lord so that, while he sleeps, they may not perish through the violence of the waves, because, having seen his death, they sought his resurrection with the greatest prayers. They feared that if he remained asleep too long in the death of the flesh, their own mind would perish forever in spiritual death.

And he said to them: “Why are you afraid, you of little faith?” (From Jerome.) They are rightly rebuked because they were afraid while Christ was present, since whoever clings to him cannot perish. Therefore he strengthened their faith, restored tranquility, and commanded the wind to cease—not the north wind, nor the southwest wind, but precisely that wind to whom the angel Michael said in the Epistle of Jude: “May the Lord rebuke you” (Jude 1) [Col. 0099B].

Then he rose and rebuked the winds and the sea. From this passage we understand that all creatures perceive their Creator. For those creatures to whom he rebukes and gives commands perceive the one commanding them—not according to the error of heretics, who think that all living things are insensible, but by the majesty of the Creator, to whom things that are insensible among us are sensible.

Then he rose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and a great calm arose on the sea. Rising, he rebuked the wind because, when the resurrection had been celebrated, he overthrew the devil’s pride, destroying through death the one who held the power of death. Rising, he caused the storm of the water to cease because, by rising from the tomb, he weakened the mad rage of the Jews, who, shaking their heads, had cried: “If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him” [Col. 0099C].

The men, however, marveled, saying: “What sort of man is this, that the winds and the sea obey him?” It was not the disciples but the sailors and the others who were in the boat who marveled. But if someone contentiously wishes to say that those who marveled were the disciples, we will answer that they were rightly called “men,” since they did not yet know the Savior’s power.

## Morally

(From Bede.) When each of us, marked with the sign of the Lord’s cross, determines to leave the world, we certainly embark in a boat with Jesus and attempt to cross the lake. Yet he who neither slept nor will sleep, always guarding Israel, nevertheless often seems to fall asleep while we are sailing, as though amid the roar of the sea. This happens when, as the assaults of unclean spirits, wicked people, or our own thoughts increase amid our efforts toward virtue, the brightness of faith is darkened, the height of hope withers, and the flame of love grows cold.

In such storms we must run to that helmsman; we must diligently awaken him who does not serve the winds but commands them. He will at once restrain the storms, restore tranquility, and grant us the harbor of salvation [Col. 0099D].

## Allegorically

(From Jerome.) The boat is the Catholic Church; the disturbance on the sea is the persecution of Christians, which first arose in the world. The contrary wind was the devil [Col. 0100A]. The Lord slept when he allowed persecutions to occur. He is awakened by that cry of the Church of which the Psalmist says: “From the ends of the earth I cried to you, when my heart was in anguish.” He rebuked the winds and the sea when, in his mercy, he commanded the persecutions stirred up by the devil through human beings to cease. A great calm arose when peace was restored to the universal Church.

# HARMONY

The Apostle exhorts us not to owe anyone anything but to love one another. Although fear is not in love, it is present in debt. The Lord rebukes the frightened Apostles, saying: “Why are you afraid, you of little faith?”—as if he were saying: Let those who are held liable as debtors to the devil be afraid; you, who are with the liberator, have nothing more to fear [Col. 0100B].

# THE SUNDAY OF SEPTUAGESIMA

## READING FROM THE FIRST EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER 9

“Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize? Run in such a way that you may obtain it. Everyone who competes in the contest exercises self-control in all things. They do this to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one. I therefore run in this way, not as though toward uncertainty. I fight in this way, not as one beating the air; but I discipline my body and bring it into servitude, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified.

“For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea. And all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ.”

You do not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize. Here he compared the race in the stadium with righteousness or faith. For just as there, although all run within the stadium, only the one who has run well is judged worthy of the prize, so here, although all believers are contained within the boundaries of faith, only those who have lived righteously receive the heavenly prize, which in Greek is called βραβεῖον, “prize.” And because among those who run in the stadium he signifies one receiving the palm—that is, the one who has held the right faith [Col. 0100D] and kept the commandments—he exhorts us to run in such a way that we may deserve to obtain the heavenly rewards.

Everyone who competes in the contest exercises self-control in all things. Ἀγών in Greek means “contest” in Latin. Therefore every ἀγωνιστής, that is, “contestant,” who strives to obtain the prize, exercises self-control in all things—that is, from all foods that customarily impede his running.

They do this to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one. The crown of which the Psalmist says: “You have crowned us with the shield of your good will” (Psalm 4). For “crown” is interpreted as victory. Let us give thanks to God and beseech him that, in his good will, he himself may be the shield, the crown, and the prize of our victory [Col. 0101A].

I therefore run in this way, not as though toward uncertainty; I fight in this way, not as one beating the air; but I discipline my body and bring it into servitude, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified, and so forth. I do not run in vain or beat the air in uncertainty or pretend to be engaged in a contest; rather, through abstinence, affliction, and labors, I discipline my body and bring it into servitude, as he says elsewhere: “In many fasts, in vigils, in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness, in labors, in prisons,” and so forth. “Lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified,” by failing to do what I say (2 Corinthians 6).

Alternatively. “I run in this way, not as though toward uncertainty.” In a worldly race, if one person arrives first, those who follow come in vain [Col. 0101B]. In the spiritual race, however, we are certain that all receive the prize who preserve to the end the gifts bestowed by God; but one who preaches for the sake of human approval cannot be certain of his reward.

“Not as one beating the air,” and so forth. That is: I do not do anything out of a desire for vanity, but serve Christ with the intention of my heart and the mortification of my body.

“Lest I myself should be disqualified.” A person is disqualified when he teaches only by word and not by example, making his teaching itself disqualified.

For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud. He speaks of the cloud that preceded them as a pillar and that figuratively signified Christ. For Christ is a pillar to us because he is upright and firm, supporting our weakness; he shines by night and does not shine by day, so that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind (John 6) [Col. 0101C].

And all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea. This means the Red Sea. Baptism, certainly consecrated by Christ’s blood: the enemies who follow from behind die, and past sins are marked. Moses, who liberated God’s people from Egypt, bore the figure of Christ.

And all ate the same spiritual food. By food he means the spiritual manna that the people ate in the desert. Manna is a type of spiritual food that became reality in the Lord’s resurrection, in the mystery of the Eucharist. This is also the bread of angels: Christ, whom human beings ate, because through him both angels and human beings live [Col. 0101D].

And all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ. The Apostle shows that, as long as the people of Israel were in the desert, a rock followed them throughout their entire journey, so that streams might suffice for the people and all their possessions, until they came to the land of Moab and dug a well for themselves.

What he says in what follows—“But God was not well pleased with most of them”—has this meaning: no one should place confidence merely in baptism or in spiritual food or spiritual drink. If someone violates baptism or, after receiving heavenly food, lives wickedly, he will suffer more severely in the future, because he neglected greater benefits, than the afflictions that the children of Israel endured in the present [Col. 0102A]. Why did he say that they drank water from the rock following them? Because Christ, whom these things prefigured, was to come afterward.

# GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW, CHAPTER 20

“The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. After agreeing with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard. Going out around the third hour, he saw others standing idle in the marketplace and said to them: ‘Go, you too, into my vineyard, and whatever is just I will give you.’ They went. Again he went out around the sixth and ninth hours and did likewise. Around the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing there, and he said to them: ‘Why are you standing here idle all day?’ They said to him: ‘Because no one has hired us.’ He said to them: ‘Go, you too, into my vineyard.’

“When evening came, the lord of the vineyard said to his steward: ‘Call the laborers and give them their wages, beginning with the last and going on to the first.’ Therefore when those who had come around the eleventh hour arrived, they received one denarius each. When the first also came, they thought that they would receive more. But they too received one denarius each. On receiving it, they murmured against the householder, saying: ‘These last worked for one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who bore the burden of the day and the heat.’ But he answered one of them: ‘Friend, I do you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for one denarius? Take what is yours and go. I wish to give to this last one the same as to you. Or am I not permitted to do what I wish? Or is your eye evil because I am good?’ Thus the last will be first, and the first last. For many are called, but few are chosen.”

The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. (From Gregory.) Who more fittingly bears the likeness of the householder than our Creator, who rules those whom he created and possesses his elect in this world as a lord has subjects in his house? He has a universal vineyard, namely, the Church, which has produced holy branches from righteous Abel to the last elect who will be born at the end of the world.

This householder hires laborers to cultivate his vineyard in the morning, at the third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours, because from the beginning of this world to its end he never ceases to gather preachers to instruct the people of the faithful. The morning of the world was from Adam to Noah; the third hour from Noah to Abraham; the sixth from Abraham to Moses; the ninth from Moses to the coming of the Lord; and the eleventh from the coming of the Lord to the end of the world. In this last period the holy Apostles were sent as preachers, and they received the full reward even though they came late.

Therefore, to instruct his people, the Lord never ceased to send laborers [Col. 0103A]: first through the patriarchs, then through the teachers of the Law and the prophets, and finally through the Apostles. While he cultivated the conduct of his people, he worked through laborers in the cultivation of the vineyard, although anyone who, in any period or measure, lived with right faith and good action was a laborer in this vineyard.

The laborer of the morning, the third, sixth, and ninth hours signifies that ancient Hebrew people who, through their elect, from the very beginning of the world, while striving to worship God rightly, never ceased to labor in the cultivation of the vineyard. At the eleventh hour the Gentiles are called. To them it is said: “Why are you standing here idle all day?” For, after such a long period of the world had passed, they had neglected to labor for their life and therefore stood idle all day.

Consider, brothers, what they answer when questioned [Col. 0103B]. They say: “Because no one has hired us.” No patriarch had come to them, no prophet. What does “No one has hired us to work” mean except that no one preached to us the ways of life?

What, then, will we say in our defense, while ceasing from good works, when we have come to faith almost from our mother’s womb, when we have heard the words of life from our very cradles, and when, from the breasts of the holy Church, we have received the drink of heavenly preaching together with the milk of the flesh?

We can also distinguish these same differences of hours in each individual according to the stages of life. The morning is the childhood of our understanding. The third hour may be understood as adolescence, because the sun seems already to rise high as the heat of youth increases. The sixth is youth, because the sun appears fixed at the center, while the fullness of strength is given to the sun [Col. 0103C]. The ninth is understood as old age, in which the sun seems to descend from its high axis, because age declines from the heat of youth. The eleventh hour is the age called decrepit or veteran. Hence the Greeks call the very old not γερώντας but πρεσβυτέρους, “elders,” indicating that they are more than merely old; they call them more advanced in age.

Therefore, because one person is brought to a good life in childhood, another in adolescence, another in youth, another in old age, and another in decrepitude, laborers are called to the vineyard at different hours.

# HARMONY

The agreement between these two readings consists in this: just as the Apostle grants the prize to the runner, so the Gospel grants a denarius to those who persevere in labor [Col. 0103D]. And what the Gospel says—“Many are called”—the Apostle expresses by saying: “All indeed run.” What the Gospel calls “few chosen,” the Apostle identifies by saying that, because of the unity of Christ’s body, one receives the prize.

# THE SUNDAY OF SEXAGESIMA

## READING FROM THE SECOND EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER 11

“You gladly tolerate fools, although you yourselves are wise. For you tolerate it if someone brings you into slavery, if someone devours you, if someone takes from you, if someone exalts himself, if someone strikes you in the face. I speak according to dishonor, as though we had been weak in this respect. But in whatever someone dares—I speak in foolishness—I too dare. They are Hebrews? I too. They are Israelites? I too. They are the seed of Abraham? I too. They are ministers of Christ? I speak as one less wise: I more so. In many labors, in more abundant imprisonments, in blows beyond measure, frequently in deaths. From the Jews five times I received forty less one. Three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; three times I suffered shipwreck; I spent a night and a day in the deep sea; often on journeys; in dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own people, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers; in labor and hardship, in many vigils, in hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold and nakedness.

“Besides those things that are external, there is my daily pressure: concern for all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire? If it is necessary to boast, I will boast of what concerns my weakness. The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying. In Damascus, the governor under King Aretas guarded the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me; but I was let down through a window in a basket through the wall, and so I escaped his hands.

“And if it is necessary to boast, it is not profitable. But I will come to visions and revelations of the Lord. I know a man in Christ fourteen years ago—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know; God knows—who was caught up to the third heaven. And I know such a man—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know; God knows—who was caught up into paradise and heard secret words that it is not lawful for a human being to speak.

“On behalf of such a one I will boast; but on my own behalf I will boast of nothing except my weaknesses. For even if I should wish to boast, I would not be foolish. I will speak the truth. But I refrain, lest anyone think of me more highly than what he sees in me or hears from me. And lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to strike me with blows. Because of this I three times besought the Lord that it might depart from me. And he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.’ I will therefore gladly boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me.”

[Col. 0104D]

For you gladly tolerate fools, although you yourselves are wise. This means: I am astonished that, although you are wise, you have so easily agreed with fools. If you willingly listened to those preaching perversely, you ought much more to listen to me, who speak useful things. He briefly reproves the manner in which they obey unskilled teachers, saying:

“For you tolerate it if someone brings you into slavery.” That is, you listen to and obey those who wish to subject you to the slavery of the Law, or to the pride of the priests who appeared to exercise authority among the Jewish people.

“If someone devours you.” That is, if some exhaust you either through banquets or gifts [Col. 0105A].

“If someone takes from you.” That is, if someone ensnares you with words of flattery. For “to take” means “to regard as pleasing.” We call those things “acceptable” that are shown to be pleasing to us. Or certainly, he takes from you what his greed has demanded, as was said above: “He devours you at banquets; he takes from you in gifts.” Or “he takes” means “he snatches,” and therefore those birds that snatch are called accipitres, “hawks.”
