“If someone exalts himself.” That is, you tolerate someone who is puffed up by Jewish pride, whether through presumed knowledge or through confidence in his ancestry.

“If someone strikes you in the face.” That is, if someone rebukes you even when you are present.

“I speak according to dishonor.” As if he were saying: I do something dishonorable by claiming something for myself from the nobility of my ancestry. It is a great dishonor if someone who has become a son of God through regeneration boasts of earthly and carnal nobility [Col. 0105B].

“As though we had been weak in this respect.” That is, as though in this matter we possessed less than they did, and did not preach to you things more true and powerful.

“In whatever someone dares—I speak in foolishness—I too dare.” I can dare to do this, if I wish. Here he compares himself with the Apostles in consideration of his labors.

“They are Hebrews, and I too; they are Israelites, and I too; they are the seed of Abraham, and I too.” That is, if they boast that they are Hebrews, Israelites, or the seed of Abraham, I too can boast, because I belong to this race.

“They are ministers of Christ, and I too.” It must be noted that if someone boasts even of Christ’s ministry, he does not boast wisely.

“I speak as one less wise: I more so—in many labors, in more abundant imprisonments, in blows beyond measure,” and so forth. (From John Chrysostom.) He did not say, “I have preached as much as they have”; rather, setting aside all splendid deeds, he enumerates the evils he endured, either as a sequence of sufferings or as occasions of glory [Col. 0105C].

“From the Jews five times I received forty less one.” Five times thirty-nine, as though he had received the punishment of a transgressor of the Law.

(From Bede.) What he says, “From the Jews five times I received forty lashes less one,” means that he was scourged by the Jews five times, yet in such a way that he was never struck forty times, but one less. For the law had commanded (Deut. 25) that those who flogged an offender should temper the measure of punishment so that the number of blows did not exceed forty. That this was understood in this way by the ancients is also attested by a painting in the same book, which the most reverend and most learned man Cuduinus, bishop of the East Angles, brought with him to Britain when he returned from Rome. In that book, nearly all the sufferings or labors of the apostle himself were depicted in their appropriate places. This passage was painted as though the Apostle were lying naked, torn by scourges and covered with tears, while a torturer stood over him, holding in his hand a four-thonged whip, but retaining one of the thongs in his hand and extending only the other three for striking. The painter’s meaning is very clear: he made him beaten with three thongs so that, by this means, he might complete the number of forty blows. For if he struck with four thongs, striking ten times he would inflict forty blows; but if with three thongs, striking thirty times, he would thereby complete forty blows [the transmitted wording is arithmetically uncertain].

“Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned,” and so forth. It is possible that he endured these things at the hands of the Gentiles, but not all of them are found in the Acts of the Apostles, since the Epistles, too, do not contain everything that is found written in that history.

When he says, “Once I was stoned,” you have this in the Acts of the Apostles: “Certain Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and, having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, supposing him to be dead” (Acts 14).

When he says that he was beaten with rods, you have this there in the Acts of the Apostles: when they were in the region of Macedonia, in a city that was a colony, because of a certain girl who had a spirit of Python and whom Paul had healed, the crowd and the magistrates rose up against them; they tore their garments and ordered them to be beaten with rods (Acts 16). And after they had inflicted many blows upon him, they sent him to prison. Elsewhere, the tribune ordered him to be brought into the fortress, scourged, tortured, and bound with straps. With reference to these and similar things he says: “In prisons more abundantly, in blows beyond measure” (2 Cor. 11).

Three times I suffered shipwreck; a night and a day I was in the depths of the sea; often on journeys; in dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own people, dangers from the Gentiles. By “my own people” and “the Gentiles” he refers to the time when the Jewish crowd gathered, seized Paul, and dragged him outside the temple, or when the high priest Ananias ordered those standing by to strike him on the mouth (Acts 23). For his own people, the Jews, were also seeking to kill him.

Dangers at sea. This refers to the time when, while they were sailing, they were endangered and ran the ship aground. The prow remained fixed and immovable, while the stern was being broken apart by the force of the sea; some reached the shore by swimming, while others were carried there on planks (Acts 27).

Dangers from false brothers. These are the people of whom he says elsewhere that “they slipped in to spy out our freedom” (Gal. 2).

In labor and hardship, in many watchings, in hunger and thirst, in many fasts, and so forth. Of these we may give one testimony from the Acts of the Apostles. “When there had been much fasting,” he says, “and day was beginning to dawn, Paul urged everyone to take food, saying: ‘Today is the fourteenth day that you have been waiting and remaining fasting, taking nothing. Therefore I urge you to take food for your health, because not a hair of any of your heads will perish.’ And when he had said this, he took bread, gave thanks to God, broke it, and began to eat” (Acts 28).

Besides those things that are external, my daily pressure, the care of all the churches. As though he were saying: besides those things that are already customary and are thought lighter because of their familiarity, he shows what that care is by what follows, saying: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11).

(From John Chrysostom.) Then he introduces another distinguished achievement, and here again we find something more of suffering, since he speaks magnificently of his own fate: “My daily concourse,” and the frequent disturbances that came upon him. “The care of all the churches.” He did not say “correction,” because this contains more of suffering than of virtue. “Who is weak, and I am not?” He did not say “I correct,” but “I am weak.” “Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” That is, I become a participant in his grief. If, then, great sufferings have great rewards, among all sufferings nothing is worse or more destructive than weariness and sadness of spirit.

If it is necessary to boast. If they wish to boast, let them boast in the things in which I boast, although compelled to do so; but because they do not possess these things, they boast in carnal matters.

I will boast of the things that concern my weakness. He designated by the name of weakness the things he mentioned above, because they surpass human weakness.

The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying. Since he is about to say something difficult—that the Jews had stirred up even the rulers of the Gentiles against him—he first invokes God’s testimony, lest it be thought that he was engaging in genuine boasting that kingdoms had risen against him and had been unable to prevail. He enumerates these things in order to show the difference between true and false apostles.

The governor of Damascus, under King Aretas, was guarding the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me; and I was let down through a window in a basket by the wall, and so escaped his hands. He was the governor of that people over which Aretas reigned. Shall we now say that Paul feared death, when he testifies that he sought it for love of Jesus? But when he saw that, in that place, there was less fruit for him and great labor, he preserved himself for labor elsewhere, where there would be fruit. For the courageous soldier of God did not wish to be held within an enclosure; he sought the field of battle.

And if it is necessary to boast, it is not expedient. It is not expedient for me, certainly, according to humility; but I am compelled by the necessity already mentioned to say something about myself.

But I will come to visions and revelations of the Lord. As though he were saying: my weaknesses are mine, but the visions are not mine; they are the Lord’s.

I know a man in Christ, fourteen years ago—whether in the body, I do not know; God knows—caught up in this way to the third heaven. Whether he is speaking of himself and, for the sake of humility, speaking of another, or of someone else, either interpretation can stand.

Saint Ambrose says in his book *Hexameron*: “Whether there is one heaven or several is a matter of dispute. Some assert that there are many, while others deny that there are any besides one. Yet in the ecclesiastical books we read of ‘heaven of heavens,’ and the Apostle understands himself to have been caught up to the third heaven. But human rashness should presume nothing concerning their number. God made them neither shapeless nor confused, but distinct according to a certain rational order of their own.”

Fourteen years ago. Observe how great the necessity of speaking presses upon him, since he is compelled afterward to disclose what he had concealed for fourteen years. When he repeats, “And I know such a man, whether outside the body I do not know; God knows, for he was caught up into paradise,” he shows that this was another vision, which also appeared clearly, and that he believed he had been transported with his body.

And he heard secret words that it is not lawful for a human being to speak. “Secret,” that is, hidden, which no one is permitted to utter; or words that it is impossible for human nature to recount.

On behalf of such a man I will boast, but on my own behalf I will boast of nothing except my weaknesses. Either, “on behalf of such a vision, but on my own behalf nothing”; or, “on behalf of my virtue,” because it is not mine but a revelation of the Lord. Therefore I will give glory not to myself but to God, in my weaknesses—that is, in the tribulations that I endure for Christ. Consequently, labor, which is full of afflictions, can have consolation and cannot have vanity.

For even if I should wish to boast, I would not be foolish. A person is found foolish when, setting aside humility of heart, he flatters himself either with false praise or even with true praise.

For I will speak the truth, but I will spare, lest anyone think of me above what he sees in me. There are also hidden things that I could truthfully bring forth, but I spare them—that is, I do not do so. The manifest things are sufficient, even if the hidden matters remain concealed. Let each person judge me only by what he sees in me or has heard from me.

And lest the greatness of the revelations exalt me, a thorn of my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan. I conceal the revelations, but lest they exalt me even in the secrecy of my heart, I need chastisements that remind me that I am human.

To buffet me. Satan buffeted him by raising up tribulations and dangers or by inflicting bodily ailments. Some say that he suffered from a headache.

Because of this I besought the Lord three times that it might depart from me, and he said to me: “My grace is sufficient for you.” We observe that even holy people sometimes asked for something contrary to what they received. We also learn that an importunate request may deserve a response even when it does not obtain its desired effect, and that the Lord’s dispensation is understood to have granted precisely what at times it does not grant. “My grace is sufficient for you”—that is, whether the grace you possess or the grace that I daily furnish and supply to you.

For virtue is perfected in weakness. As in the holy Job or Eleazar. In enduring bodily weakness, the strength of the soul is revealed; it proves the one who is tested and commends the one who has been proved.

I will gladly boast in my weaknesses. Gladly, certainly, after he learned that what he had thought harmful was beneficial.

So that the power of Christ may dwell in me. When, through the afflictions of the saints’ labors, humility of heart grows and hope of future reward strengthens the spirit, then the power of Christ dwells in the soul.

## THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER 8

“When a very large crowd was gathering, and people were hurrying to him from the cities, he said by way of a parable: ‘The sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell beside the road, and it was trampled, and the birds of the sky devoured it. And some fell upon the rock, and when it had grown up it withered, because it had no moisture. And some fell among thorns, and the thorns that sprang up with it choked it. And some fell on good soil, and when it had grown it produced fruit a hundredfold.’ Saying this, he cried out: ‘Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.’ His disciples asked him what this parable meant. He said to them: ‘To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to the others in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand. Now this is the parable: The seed is the word of God. Those beside the road are the ones who hear; then the devil comes and takes the word from their heart, lest they believe and be saved. Those upon the rock are the ones who, when they hear, receive the word with joy, but they have no roots; they believe for a time, and in the time of temptation they fall away. The seed that fell among thorns refers to those who have heard and, as they go on their way, are choked by the cares, riches, and pleasures of life, and produce no fruit. The seed in good soil refers to those who, hearing the word in a good and excellent heart, hold fast to it and bear fruit with perseverance.’”

When a very large crowd was gathering, and people were hurrying to him from the cities, he spoke a parable: “The sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell beside the road, and it was trampled, and the birds of the sky devoured it.” The Lord deigned to explain this parable himself in order to make known that he was speaking figuratively and to teach that the meanings of things should also be sought in those matters that he did not wish to explain himself. But since the Lord himself disclosed that the seed is the word of God and that the various soils signify the different hearts of hearers, we must understand no one better than the Son of God as the Savior whom he left us to seek. He went out to sow his seed because, coming forth from the bosom of the Father, to which created things had no access, he came into the world for this purpose: to bear witness to the truth. Hence, according to the other Evangelists, when he was about to speak this parable, he is said to have gone out from the house, approached the sea, and boarded a boat—clearly indicating by the position of his body what he conveyed through the course of his speech.

The things that the Lord explained are to be received with devout faith; what he left to our silent understanding should be touched upon briefly. The seed that fell beside the road perished through a double injury: it was trampled by passersby and carried off by birds. The road, therefore, is the heart worn down and dried out by the constant passage of evil thoughts, so that it cannot receive the seed of the word or bring it to germination. Thus whatever good seed falls upon such a road is trampled by the course of evil thought and snatched away by demons, who are called “birds of the sky” either because they are heavenly and spiritual in nature or because they fly through the air.

And some fell upon the rock and, when it had grown, withered, because it had no moisture. By “rock” he means a hard and untamed heart, penetrated by no plow of true faith. The moisture at the root of the seed is, according to another parable, like the oil that nourishes the virgins’ lamps—that is, love and perseverance in virtue.

And some fell on good soil and, when it had grown, produced fruit a hundredfold. By “a hundredfold fruit” he means perfect fruit, for the number ten is always understood as signifying perfection, because the keeping of the law is contained in the Ten Commandments. The active and contemplative life are joined together in the commands of the Decalogue, because in them both love of God and love of neighbor are commanded. Love of God belongs to the contemplative life, while love of neighbor belongs to the active life. The number ten, multiplied by itself, rises to one hundred. Thus one hundred rightly signifies great perfection, as it is said of the person who left earthly things for the Lord: “He will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. 19). For whoever despises temporal and earthly things for God’s name also receives perfection of mind, so that he no longer desires what he has despised, and in the age to come reaches the glory of eternal life. Good soil, therefore, is made fertile with a hundredfold fruit when a teachable heart is endowed with the perfection of spiritual virtues.

Saying this, he cried out: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.” Whenever this little admonition is inserted either in the Gospel or in the Apocalypse of John, it shows that what is being said is mystical and that we should seek it with greater attentiveness.

His disciples asked him what this parable meant. No one should suppose that the disciples immediately questioned the Savior after the parable had ended. Rather, as Mark says: “When he was alone, those who were with him, along with the Twelve, questioned him about the parable,” and he said to them: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God,” and so forth (Mark 4).

But to the others in parables, so that seeing they may not see and hearing they may not understand. Mark says: “But for those who are outside, everything is done in parables.” Therefore let us enter with Christ’s disciples into God’s sanctuary, so that we may understand the final things of the mysteries of the kingdom of God. Those who draw near to his feet will receive his teaching, saying with the Psalmist: “Open our eyes, and we shall consider the wonders of your law.” Rightly do those hear in parables and in riddles who, with the senses of their hearts closed, neither wish to enter nor care to know the truth, having forgotten the Lord’s command: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.”

Those beside the road are the ones who hear; then the devil comes and takes the word from their heart, lest they believe and be saved. Mark writes of this seed: “These are the ones beside the road, where the word is sown; and when they hear, Satan immediately takes it away” (Mark 4). Matthew says: “Everyone who hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches it away” (Matt. 13). From this it is clearly taught that those sown beside the road are people who do not deign to receive the word they hear with any faith, any understanding, or even any opportunity for usefulness, however slight.

Those sown upon rocky ground and among thorns, as the Lord explains, are people who indeed approve the word they have heard and taste its usefulness and desire, but are prevented from reaching what they approve: the adversities of this life frighten them, while its prosperity flatters them. Against both kinds of harm, the one who said, “By the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute, as deceivers and yet truthful” (2 Cor. 6), took care to protect the seed he had received. Know, therefore, that these three kinds of soil designate all those who fail to put into practice the word they have heard. The good soil is the one that preserves the seed it has received from all these things. Jews and Gentiles, who are not even deemed worthy to hear, are excepted.

The seed that fell among thorns refers to those who have heard and, as they go on their way, are choked by cares, riches, and the pleasures of life, and produce no fruit. It is remarkable that the Lord interpreted the thorns as riches, since thorns prick, while riches delight.

(From Gregory.) Yet they are thorns, because by the prickings of their thoughts they lacerate the mind; and when they drag it as far as sin, they make it bleed as though from an inflicted wound. In this passage, as another Evangelist bears witness, the Lord rightly calls them not simply riches but deceitful riches. They are deceitful because they cannot remain with us for long; they are deceitful because they do not remove the poverty of our mind. Only those riches are true that make us rich in virtues.

It should also be noted that, when explaining the passage, the Lord says: “Cares, pleasures, and riches choke.” They choke because by their importunate thoughts they strangle the throat of the mind; and, by not allowing good desire to enter the heart, they kill, as it were, the passage of vital breath. It should further be noted that he joins two things to riches: cares and pleasures. For they oppress the mind through anxiety and dissolve it through abundance. Contrary things make their possessors both afflicted and unstable. But because pleasure cannot coexist with affliction, at one time they afflict them through the anxiety of guarding their possessions, and at another they soften them through abundance into pleasures.

The seed in good soil refers to those who, hearing the word in a good and excellent heart, hold fast to it and bear fruit with perseverance. Good soil, as we said above, is not opposed to the three varieties of soil in every respect. It willingly receives the seed of the word and, preserving what it receives amid adversity and prosperity until the time of fruit, brings forth fruit. Good soil bears fruit through perseverance because none of the good things we do is truly good if we do not also endure the evils of our neighbors with equanimity. For the higher anyone advances, the harsher is what he finds in this world to bear. As the love of the present age diminishes in our mind, the adversity of that same age increases. Hence we see many people doing good and yet laboring beneath a heavy burden of tribulations. But, in accordance with the Lord’s word, they bear fruit through perseverance, because when they humbly receive the scourges, after the scourges they are raised up sublimely to rest.

What is said according to Matthew—that one bears fruit and produces in one case a hundredfold, in another sixtyfold, and in another thirtyfold—refers the thirtyfold to marriage. The joining of the fingers itself, as though embracing and binding together with a tender kiss, depicts husband and wife. The sixtyfold refers to widows, because they are placed in hardship and tribulation. Hence they are also pressed down upon the higher finger; and the greater the difficulty of abstaining in part from the enticements of the will, the greater the reward.

But, reader, attend carefully to the number one hundred. They are transferred from the left hand to the right, with the same fingers but not the same hand by which married women are signified on the left. The widow, making a circle, expresses the crown of virginity.

Alternatively, the thirtyfold fruit refers to the word that builds faith in the holy Trinity. The sixtyfold refers to the perfection of works, because there are six days in which one ought to work. The hundredfold refers to the eternal life of the kingdom at the right hand.

## CONCORD

The Corinthians had received the word of truth from the apostles, but by consenting to false teachers they had lost it. The Apostle rebukes them, saying: “I marvel that, although you are wise, you willingly consent to fools.” The Gospel statement agrees well with this, where it says: “The devil comes and takes the word from their heart” (Luke 8).

## IN QUINQUAGESIMA

## THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER 13

“Though I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have love, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. And though I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and though I have all faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. And though I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and though I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing. Love is patient; love is kind. Love does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own interests, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never fails. Whether prophecies will be brought to an end, or tongues will cease, or knowledge will be destroyed. For we know in part and we prophesy in part. But when the perfect comes, what is in part will be brought to an end. When I was a child, I spoke as a child, understood as a child, and reasoned as a child. But when I became a man, I put away childish things. Now we see through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I shall know just as I am known. But now these three remain: faith, hope, and love; and the greatest of these is love.”

Though I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels. In these passages the Apostle is concerned to show that, since certain people sought the gift of tongues with great desire, he should place the kindness of love before it, by which they might advance in love of neighbor. Signs are given for unbelievers, but love imitates the angels.

I have become like sounding bronze. That is, something that contributes nothing to the benefit of the soul but merely produces a clang without usefulness.

And though I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge. Prophecy, which declares the future, and knowledge of mysteries, which discloses the hidden things of Scripture, are great in themselves. But when compared with love, they are placed behind it in merit, so that without love they cannot be possessed for long. Thus they are found to be of little use without love. Love, however, embraces even these things within itself. It is not surprising that it is preferred to the various gifts, since it is the perfection of virtues and the fullness of the law. As we read: “Love is the fullness of the law”; and again: “Love of neighbor works no evil.” Without love, no faith can persevere; and because it does not contain the end of good things within itself, it will fail at the end.

And though I have all faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. Here “all faith” is understood as the great faith that in the Gospel is compared with a mustard seed—not because of its smallness, but because of its completeness or vigor. It should be noted that among the other things mentioned, even all faith that moves mountains is of no benefit without love.

And though I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and though I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing. The distribution of possessions, contempt for possessions, and contempt for present things are also found among the philosophers of the Gentiles, and some pagans handed their bodies over to the flames for the sake of human glory. Therefore, if anger against one’s neighbor or malice is held in the heart, the glory of martyrdom may be approached but cannot be completed. As we read in the Gospel: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I shall say to them, ‘Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity’” (Matt. 7). These people therefore lost their labors, either by neglecting love, undertaking them out of vanity, or afterward committing iniquity in their deeds.

Love is patient. He now describes, one by one, the members and forms of love. Just as those who love their children patiently bear all their injuries, so the one who loves either neighbor or God is overcome by no one’s injuries.

Love does not envy. “Envy” may be understood as emulation, imitation, or jealousy. It means imitation where he says: “Be zealous for the better gifts.” Here, however, he uses it for jealousy: “Love does not envy,” that is, it envies no one. No one envies the person whom he truly loves, whatever glory or honor he sees that person possessing; rather, he gladly embraces all that person’s happiness as though it were his own.

Does not act perversely. Things that are not right but perverse are called “perverse.” Love does not act in this way, because it does everything in proper order and completely excludes every vice.

Is not puffed up. That is, it is not lifted up into pride, which is the mother of vices, because it strives to possess the fullness of virtues.

(Vulgate.) This manner of expression must be considered carefully. For love itself cannot, in its own right, either envy or be puffed up; rather, every person who becomes a participant in that love is neither puffed up nor envious, truly because he has been enriched by the gift of love. The Apostle uses this manner of expression elsewhere when he says: “He who knew no sin, for our sake he made sin, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him.” We do not become righteousness by believing, but become participants in righteousness; that is, we are found righteous through faith in Christ. When he says “sin,” he means a sacrifice for sin, as Isaiah says: “They shall eat the sins of my people”—that is, offerings made as a sacrifice for sin.

Is not ambitious. An ambitious person is called proud because he seeks honors. Love is not like this, because it does not seek to be greater than others; it establishes its highest degree in humility.

Does not seek its own interests. That is, it does not think only about what is useful to itself, but about how it may minister by serving others beneficially.

Is not provoked. That is, it is not provoked by the injuries of others, because it cannot be provoked by the one whom it loves, nor moved to any passion.

Does not think evil. It not only does not do evil; it does not even think it. Great is the virtue of love, which excludes evil even from the sense of thought.

Does not rejoice over iniquity. That is, it is saddened if it sees that someone has either committed iniquity or endured it.

But rejoices with the truth. That is, it rejoices either over good works or over faith and truth when it sees that its neighbor possesses such goodness.

It bears all things, and so forth. It considers the fault of its neighbor light because it either awaits that person’s correction or promises itself a reward for long-suffering.

Love never fails. “Does not fail” means that it does not slip away or go beyond its proper bounds. It alone endures into the future; or, certainly, because it is true, it will neither change nor come to an end.

Whether prophecies will be brought to an end, and so forth. Those things that pertain to human beings will be completed; those things that advance love of neighbor and love of God will remain.

For we know in part and prophesy in part. Now we do not know all things, nor do we prophesy all things. These things are destroyed in such a way that they advance us, for through them we shall come to those things; and thus they will be brought to an end when truth removes the shadow and reality removes the hope.

But when the perfect comes, what is in part will be brought to an end. What is in part is what is sought in a mirror and in a riddle by the desire of one who longs. The perfect is present when what is promised in expectation is granted to the saints as their possession.

(From John Chrysostom.) What the old law has endured from the new does not immediately speak against the dignity of the new law. Yet when we possess the kingdom of heaven, we say that even the new law will cease. Although greater things succeed it, we nevertheless confess it, because, since the rewards are greater and the grace of the Holy Spirit more eminent, greater contests will consequently also be required.

When I was a child, I spoke as a child.

(From Primasius.) By the example of physical growth, he wishes to show spiritual progress.

(From Ambrose.) Thus the prophecy of remarkable human beings in this life must be compared with the life to come as a child is compared with a young man. Yet Elisha saw his servant receiving gifts while he himself was not present. So, when the perfect comes and the corruptible body no longer weighs down the soul, bodily eyes will not impede those holy people from seeing the things that are to be seen.

When I became a man, I put away the things that belonged to a child.

(From Primasius.) He shows how the things he mentioned above are brought to an end, like children who are unable, with the serene vision of the heart, to perceive the light of perfect truth.

Now we see through a mirror. That is, we see in figure, through the mirror of faith and through the understanding of the law, as an image of realities.

In a riddle.

(From Ambrose.) A riddle is an obscure parable that is difficult to understand. Just as by the name “mirror” he wished an image to be understood, so by the name “riddle” he wished a likeness—yet an obscure and difficult one to perceive—to be understood. Indeed, it would not be called a riddle if vision were easy.

But then face to face. That is, when the things hoped for have been placed before our eyes.

But then I shall know just as I am known. Just as God knows me perfectly, so then I shall know the things of God according to the capacity of my mind.

But now these three remain: faith, hope, and love. Faith advances toward hope, and hope toward love. In the present there are three; in the future there will be only the love of the saints, angels, and God. Whatever faith and hope promised, love will bring to completion. Therefore what will always remain is greater than what at some point ceased.

## THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER 18

“Jesus took the Twelve and said to them: ‘Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that has been written by the prophets concerning the Son of Man will be fulfilled. For he will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, and spat upon. And after they have scourged him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.’ And they understood none of these things; this saying was hidden from them, and they did not understand what was being said.

Now, when he was approaching Jericho, a certain blind man was sitting beside the road begging. When he heard the crowd passing by, he asked what this was. They told him that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by. And he cried out, saying: ‘Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me.’ Those who went before rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more: ‘Son of David, have mercy on me.’ Jesus stopped and ordered him to be brought to him. When he had drawn near, he asked him, saying: ‘What do you want me to do for you?’ He said: ‘Lord, that I may see.’ And Jesus said to him: ‘Look up; your faith has saved you.’ Immediately he saw and followed him, glorifying God. And when all the people saw it, they gave praise to God.”

Jesus took the Twelve and said to them: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that has been written by the prophets concerning the Son of Man will be fulfilled. For he will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, and spat upon; and after they have scourged him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.”

(From Gregory.) Foreseeing that his disciples’ minds would be disturbed by his passion, the Savior foretells to them long beforehand both the punishment of that passion and the glory of his resurrection, so that when they saw him dying, just as it had been foretold, they would not doubt that he would also rise.

(From Bede.) Foreseeing also that certain heretics would arise in the Church who would say that Christ had taught things contrary to the law and the prophets, and that a different God was to be believed in the Old Testament and in the New, he shows that the prophecies of the prophets were directed toward no mystery more than that of his own dispensation, which he temporarily assumed for our sake. Thus the fulfillment of his prophecy is celebrated in his passion, and the perfection of his later glory. He also most clearly refutes the madness of the pagans, who mock his cross, when, as one foreknowing the future, he reveals the time of his approaching passion and, as one fearless of death, goes to the place of his death.

And they understood none of these things, and this saying was hidden from them, and they did not understand what was being said. We read in the Gospel according to John that, when the Lord said, “If I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself,” the crowd replied: “We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever; and how can you say, ‘The Son of Man must be lifted up’?” (John XII). What, then, is the reason that the disciples could not understand the mystery of the Lord’s Passion, repeated to them so many times, while the Jews understood at once a single saying, and one expressed so obscurely that the evangelist considered it worthy of explanation—“Now he said this,” he says, “signifying by what death he was going to die”—and immediately understood that the lifting up of the cross was meant? It is because the disciples could not bear to hear of the death of the one whose life they most desired to see. They knew him not only as an innocent man but also as the true God, and therefore thought that he could in no way die. Moreover, because they were accustomed to hear him often speaking in parables, whenever he said anything about his Passion they believed that it was not to be understood as it sounded, but, prompted by love, was to be referred allegorically to something else. The Jews, however, because they had conspired to kill him, understood whatever he said about his Passion or cross. For he was speaking of what they greatly desired to happen and were striving to accomplish. Thus, in a wondrous and unusual manner, the same mystery of undergoing the cross—which love concealed from believers—was revealed to unbelievers by envy.

[Col. 0117A]

Now it happened that, as he approached Jericho, a certain blind man was sitting beside the road, begging; and when he heard the crowd passing by, etc.

(From Gregory.) This blind man signifies allegorically the human race, which, expelled in its first parent from the joys of paradise and ignorant of the brightness of the heavenly light, suffers the darkness of its condemnation. But when Jesus is said to be approaching Jericho, the blind man is illuminated. For Jericho is interpreted as “Moon.” In sacred language, however, the moon signifies the weakness of the flesh, because, diminishing at monthly intervals, it represents the decline of our mortality. Thus, when our Creator approaches Jericho, the blind man returns to the light: when the divinity assumed the weakness of our flesh, the human race received back the light it had lost.

This blind man is rightly described as sitting beside the road and begging. For Truth itself said: “I am the way.” Therefore, one who does not know the brightness of eternal light is blind. But if he already believes in the Redeemer, he sits beside the way. If he believes but neglects to ask in order to receive eternal light, and ceases from prayer, the blind man indeed sits beside the way, but does not beg. If he truly believes and entreats, the blind man sits beside the way and begs.

And he cried out, saying: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me.” [Col. 0117D] Those who went before rebuked him, telling him to be silent; but he cried out all the more: “Son of David, have mercy on me.” What do those who precede the coming Jesus signify except the crowds of carnal desires and the throngs of vices? Before Jesus comes to our heart, these disperse our thoughts by their temptations and disturb the voices of our heart in prayer. Often, when we wish to turn to God after committing sins and strive to plead against those very vices that we have committed, the phantoms of the sins we have committed come upon our heart, strike against the sight of our mind, confuse our spirit, and suppress the voice of our supplication. But the more the crowd rebukes him and tells him to be silent, the more loudly he cries out. For the more violently we are pressed by the tumult of carnal thoughts, the more fervently we must persist in prayer.

[Col. 0118A]

But Jesus, standing still, ordered him to be brought to him. Behold, he stands who had been passing by before. For while we still suffer the crowds of phantasms in prayer, we sense Jesus passing by us to some extent. But when we persist intensely in prayer, Jesus stands and restores the light, because God is fixed in the heart and the lost light is restored.

And when he had drawn near, he asked him, saying: “What do you want me to do for you?” But he said: “Lord, that I may see.” Did the one who could restore light not know what the blind man wanted? Rather, he wants the blind man to ask for what he already knows both that we will ask and that he will grant. For he insistently urges us to prayer, yet says: “Your Father knows what you need before you ask him.” [Col. 0118B] He asks, therefore, in order that the request may be made; he asks in order to stir us to prayer. Hence the blind man immediately adds: “Lord, that I may see.”

Behold, the blind man asks the Lord not for gold but for light. He considers it of little value to seek anything outside the light, because even if a blind man can possess something or other, without light he cannot see what he possesses. Let us therefore imitate the one whom we have heard to have been saved both in body and in mind. Let us seek from the Lord not false riches, not earthly gifts, not fleeting honors, but light. And let us not seek the light that is confined to a place, ends with time, varies with the interruption of nights, and is seen by us in common with the animals. Let us seek the light that we can see with the angels alone, because neither does it have a beginning to initiate it nor an end to confine it.

Faith is certainly the way to this light. Hence the blind man is rightly answered immediately as he is illuminated: [Col. 0118C] “See; your faith has saved you.” Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, if we already recognize the blindness of our pilgrimage; if, believing in the mystery of our Redeemer, we sit beside the way; if, by entreating, we ask our Creator daily for light; if, now seeing that same light through understanding, we have been illuminated after blindness, let us follow in action the Jesus whom we see in our mind, and let us hold fast by imitating his footsteps.

For the one who imitates Jesus follows him. He says: “Follow me, and let the dead bury their dead.” “Follow,” that is, imitate. Again he urges us, saying: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (Matt. VIII). If, then, we seek the joy of reward at our destination, let us maintain the bitterness of repentance on the way. Thus it comes about that not only does our life advance toward God, but our very manner of life also inflames others to the praise of God. Hence it is added there: “And when all the people saw it, they gave praise to God.”

CONCORDANCE

The agreement of these two readings consists in this: both mention illumination—one concerning the blind man’s bodily eyes, the other concerning the spiritual eyes of the mind—saying: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face.”

AT THE BEGINNING OF LENT

THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS, II, CHAPTER VI

“We urge you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For he says: ‘At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.’ Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. Giving no one any cause for offense, so that our ministry may not be blamed. But in everything let us present ourselves as God’s ministers: in great patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distresses, in blows, in prisons, in seditions, in labors, in vigils, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in gentleness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left; through glory and dishonor, through evil report and good report; as deceivers and yet truthful; as unknown and yet known; as dying, and behold, we live; as chastened and not killed; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as needy, yet enriching many; as having nothing, yet possessing all things.”

We urge you not to receive the grace of God in vain.

(From Primasius.) He receives the grace of God in vain who, having been called in Christ, still follows the old institutions of the Law.

For he says: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.” The acceptable time and the day of salvation are this life, as the Savior says: “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you,” because in that age there can be no correction, as we read: “For in death there is no one who remembers you” (Ps. VI).

(From Jerome.) Only now can we find salvation, because, according to the testimony of the Prophet, “in hell no one will confess.”

Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.

(From Primasius.) As elsewhere: “Therefore, while we have time, let us do what is good.” This life is called a day because it is suitable for working, and it is enclosed by the night of judgment, which is darkness in which no one will be able to work. This life is also called summer, in comparison with which ants are said to labor for the present and await the coming winter.

Giving no one any cause for offense.

(From Jerome.) Let no one be offended by our example, lest what is thought to be our fault be attributed instead to the Law.

(From Primasius.) That is, lest perhaps through our negligence we destroy unbelievers, and lest, in what has displeased them, they judge the fault to belong rather to our religion and Law; and lest those who are hostile should, because of a man’s sin, revile our rule and holy institution.

So that our ministry may not be blamed.

That is, so that it may not be displeasing in certain respects, and so that even the good may appear to incur offense because of the fault of a few.

But in everything let us present ourselves.

The one who provokes the desire for virtue himself mercifully ministers virtue to us; and if we desire it from him who commands it to be cultivated, we are helped.

As God’s ministers.

God’s ministers ought to serve God in everything, to be recognized by their works as worshipers of the true God; and just as he allows himself to be blasphemed by the wicked and, in the present life, does not deny his benefits even to the ungrateful, so we must not be overcome by evil but overcome the wicked with good.

In great patience.

(From Jerome.) Not in small or moderate patience, but in great patience.

In tribulations.

Every injury is called a tribulation.

In necessities.

That is, let us endure everything that is necessary in the manner in which it must be endured.

In distresses.

Every deprivation is a distress.

In blows, in prisons.

He urges us to suffer for Christ, if necessary, what Christ himself suffered, when the people and the magistrates joined together against him and, after inflicting many blows with rods, sent him into prison.

In seditions, in labors, in vigils.

Here he describes not insignificant members of patience; for in exercises of labor there must be no less vigilance of mind than of body.

In fastings.

(From Ambrose.) Fasts are necessary for our soul, as medicine is for wounds. They bring healing to eternal life, provided that they are commended by the testimony of two things: prayer and mercy.

In chastity, in knowledge.

(From Jerome.) Just as bodily chastity is necessary for us, so is chastity of mind. That is true chastity which is defiled neither in mind nor in deed, and which also grants us knowledge in proportion to our purity. It should be noted that knowledge is a form of virtue if a person is instructed by it and not puffed up.

In long-suffering.

That is, in prolonged endurance. Long-suffering is the fortitude of spirit in enduring adversities.

In gentleness.

Gentleness exists when we produce bitterness in no one through our words and fulfill what the same Apostle says: “Let all bitterness, and wrath, and shouting, and blasphemy be taken away from you, with all malice”; and when we say the testimony of Wisdom: “His jaws are sweetness, and he is the object of every desire.”

In the Holy Spirit.

That is, possessing these things, let us make ourselves worthy of his dwelling through the sincerity of our hearts.

In unfeigned love.

Love is unfeigned when we do for others everything that we wish to be done for us. As the Apostle John says: “Let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth.” Love is also unfeigned when, with kindly affection, we correct the sins and faults of our brothers.

[Col. 0120D]

(From Ambrose.) Love securely possesses the whole greatness and height of the divine utterances. By it we love God and our neighbor; it endures in adversities, exercises moderation in prosperity, is strong in harsh sufferings, cheerful in good works, most secure in temptation, broadest among true brothers, and most patient among false ones.

In the word of truth.

The Word and the Truth is Christ, whom we ought to bring forth aptly and suitably from the Law, in whose mysteries he is hidden.

In the power of God.

That is, in the power of Christ, let us fight against the devil, whom Christ overcame by the weapons of righteousness and the Law.

With the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left.

(From Gregory.) All who strive toward the entrance of life must have weapons on both the right and the left. He has weapons on the right whom prosperity does not exalt; on the left, he whom adversity does not cast down. Paul carried weapons on both sides when he said: “With the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor.” Adversity did not break him, nor did prosperity lift him up into mental swelling. He bore weapons on the right and on the left: he remained strong in adversity and humble in prosperity.

Therefore, in order that weapons may be borne on the right and on the left, confidence in adversity and fear in prosperity must always be present to our minds, lest adversity drag us into despair or prosperity lift our spirit into reliance upon itself.

[Col. 0121B]

Through glory and dishonor.

(From Primasius.) That is, through the glory of virtues and the dishonor of blows, contempt, and prisons.

Through evil report and good report.

Let us receive all these things equally with patience. Let those who praise us not exalt us, and let those who slander us not cast us down, because it is sometimes necessary that both groups lie. Looking instead to our conscience, we ought not to believe others more than ourselves concerning our own good deeds.

As deceivers and yet truthful.

Why “deceivers”? Because they teach a person to despise what he has and hope for what he does not have; to pass by what is placed before the eyes with the senses turned away and closed; and to unfold with insatiable desires what is removed from the eyes. By saying “deceivers and truthful,” he explained “evil report and good report,” because some called them deceivers, while others called them not only truthful but, on account of their virtuous works, gods. It is therefore no wonder that the apostles were called deceivers, since concerning the Lord himself some said, “He is good,” while others said, “No, but he deceives the crowds” (John VII).

As unknown and yet known.

Unknown to the faithless and ungrateful; known to the faithful and just.

As dying, and behold, we live.

This refers to reaching the point of despair concerning life, as when Paul was thought to have died after being stoned, yet rose and taught at Lystra (Acts XIII).

As chastened and not killed.

As we read: “The Lord chastening has chastened me, but he has not delivered me to death” (Ps. CXVII). We speak of chastening both by words and by blows, as Pilate said concerning the Lord: “Having chastened him, I will release him,” that is, having scourged him with blows.

As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing.

Sorrowful in the severity of outward appearance, but rejoicing in heart even amid tribulations in expectation of the reward; for it is written: “Your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John XVI).

(From Ambrose.) Whoever tells a dream adds the word “as if”: “As if I were speaking,” “as if I were riding”—everything is “as if.” When he wakes, he finds nothing of what he had seen. Thus, those who now open their eyes to the joys of the world pass through the “as if” of those things and come to their reality. The happiness of the world is their “as if”; their punishment is their reality. Our sorrow is an “as if,” but our joy is not an “as if.” The Apostle did not say, “as if rejoicing.”

As needy, yet enriching many.

In the very fact that we are needy, we abound in others, when alms are given through us. Or, being needy in earthly things, we make others rich in heavenly things. He says “as sorrowful” and “as needy” to show that these are not true evils, but as if shadows and images of sufferings in comparison with the eternal reward.

As having nothing.

As Solomon says: “The whole world is the wealth of the faithful person.” No one possesses more than the one who needs nothing. He needs nothing who seeks nothing beyond what is necessary.

THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0122B]

“Jesus was led by the Spirit into the desert to be tempted by the devil. And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry. And the tempter approached and said to him: ‘If you are the Son of God, say that these stones should become loaves of bread.’ But he answered and said: ‘It is written: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.’ Then the devil took him into the holy city and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him: ‘If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down. For it is written: He has commanded his angels concerning you, and they will lift you up in their hands, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone.’ Jesus said to him: ‘Again it is written: You shall not tempt the Lord your God.’ Again the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and said to him: ‘All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.’ Then Jesus said to him: ‘Go away, Satan. For it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’ Then the devil left him, and behold, angels approached and ministered to him.”

Jesus was led by the Spirit into the desert to be tempted by the devil.

(From Gregory.) Some commonly wonder by what spirit Jesus was led into the desert, because what follows says: “The devil took him into the holy city,” and again: “He took him to a very high mountain.” But it is truly and without any doubt suitably understood that he was led into the desert by the Holy Spirit, so that his own Spirit might lead him there where the evil spirit would find him for temptation.

But behold, when it is said that God the man was taken by the devil either onto a high mountain or into the holy city, the human mind recoils and the ears tremble at hearing it. Yet we recognize that these things are not incredible if we consider other things that happened in him. Certainly the devil is the head of all the wicked, and all the wicked are members of this head. Was Pilate not a member of the devil? Were the persecuting Jews and the soldiers who crucified him not members of the devil? What, then, is surprising if he allowed himself to be led by that one onto a mountain, when he also endured being crucified by his members?

It was therefore not unworthy of our Redeemer that he wished to be tempted, since he had come to be killed. For it was right that he should overcome our temptations by his own temptations, just as he had come to overcome our death by his death.

But we must know that temptation occurs in three ways: suggestion, pleasure, and consent. When we are tempted, we often fall either into pleasure or even into consent, because, having been propagated from the sin of the flesh, we carry within ourselves the source of the struggles we endure. God, however, who was incarnate in the Virgin’s womb and came into the world without sin, endured no opposition within himself. He could therefore be tempted through suggestion, but the pleasure of sin did not wound his mind.

And therefore all that devilish temptation was external, not inward. But if we consider the order of his temptation, let us ponder how greatly we are freed from temptation. The ancient enemy rose against the first man, our parent, with three temptations: he tempted him through gluttony, vainglory, and avarice, and by tempting him overcame him, subjecting him to himself through consent.

He tempted him through gluttony when he showed him the forbidden fruit of the tree and persuaded him to eat. He tempted him through vainglory when he said: “You will be like gods.” And he tempted him through avarice when he said: “Knowing good and evil.” For avarice concerns not only money but also exaltation. It is rightly called avarice when elevation is sought beyond measure. If the seizure of honor did not belong to avarice, Paul would never have said concerning the only-begotten Son that he “did not regard equality with God as something to be seized.” Thus the devil drew our parent into pride by stirring him to avarice for exaltation.

But by the same methods by which he laid the first man low, he himself fell before the second man when he tempted him. He tempted him through gluttony when he said: “Say that these stones should become loaves of bread.” He tempted him through vainglory when he said: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.” He tempted him through avarice for exaltation when he showed him all the kingdoms of the world and said: “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.”

But he was overcome by the second man by those same methods by which he boasts of having conquered the first, so that he might leave our hearts captured at the very entrance through which he had held us captive.

There is another matter, dearly beloved brothers, that we must consider in this temptation of the Lord. When tempted by the devil, the Lord answered with the precepts of sacred Scripture. Though by the word that he was he could have plunged his tempter into the abyss, he did not display the power of his might. He gave only the precepts of divine Scripture, so that he might offer us an example of his patience, in order that whenever we suffer anything from wicked people, we may be stirred toward instruction rather than vengeance.

Consider how great is God’s patience and how great our impatience. If we are provoked by insults or any injury, moved by fury we either avenge ourselves as much as we can or threaten to do what we cannot. Behold, the Lord endured the devil’s adversity and answered him with nothing but a word of gentleness. He bore one whom he could have punished, so that his praise might increase all the more if he overcame his enemy not by destroying him but by enduring him for a time.

It should also be noted that what follows says: “When the devil had departed, angels ministered to him.” By this, what else is shown than the two natures of one person? He is man, whom the devil tempts, and he is the same Lord, to whom angels minister. Let us therefore recognize our nature in him, because unless the devil had seen him as a man, he would not have tempted him. Let us venerate his divinity in him, because unless he existed as God above all, angels would in no way minister to him.

And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights.

Because the reading of these days is appropriate to Lent—for we have heard of the forty-day abstinence of our Redeemer, and we are beginning the season of Lent—we must examine why this very abstinence is observed for the number of forty days.

Moses fasted forty days in order to receive the Law a second time. Elijah abstained for forty days in the desert. The author of humanity himself, coming to human beings, took no food at all for forty days. We too, insofar as we can, endeavor during the annual season of Lent to afflict our flesh through abstinence.

Why, then, is the number forty observed in abstinence? Is it not because the power of the Decalogue is fulfilled through the four books of the holy Gospel? Ten multiplied by four rises to forty, because we fulfill the commandments of the Decalogue when we carefully observe the four books of the holy Gospel.

From this another meaning may also be discerned. In this mortal body we subsist from four elements, and through the pleasures of that same body we transgress the Lord’s commandments. The Lord’s commandments, however, were given through the Decalogue. Therefore, since through the desires of the flesh we have despised the commandments of the Decalogue, it is fitting that we afflict that same flesh forty times.

There is, however, another possible understanding of this season of Lent. From the present day until the joys of the Paschal solemnity there are six weeks. Their days amount to forty-two. When the six Sundays are subtracted from these as days of abstinence, no more than thirty-six days remain in the abstinence. Since the year consists of three hundred and sixty days, while we afflict ourselves for thirty-six, we give God, as it were, the tithes of our year. We who have lived for ourselves throughout the year we have received are mortified through abstinence for our Creator in the form of its tithes.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, just as you are commanded in the Law to offer tithes of your possessions, so strive to offer him tithes of your days. Let each person, insofar as his strength permits, mortify his flesh, afflict its desires, and put to death shameful lusts, so that, in accordance with Paul’s word, he may become a living sacrifice. A sacrifice is both offered and alive when a person does not depart from this life and yet kills himself with respect to carnal desires.

The flesh drew us joyfully into guilt; when afflicted, let it lead us back to pardon. For the author of our death transgressed the commandments of life through the fruit of the forbidden tree. Therefore, since we fell from the joys of paradise through food, let us rise again to them, insofar as we can, through abstinence.

[Col. 0125A]

(From Bede.) The forty days and nights during which he is tempted signify the whole period of this age, during which he never ceases to tempt his members, namely, the holy Church. For the world in which we serve the Lord is fourfold. There are ten commandments, and by observing them we who serve the Lord struggle against the tireless army of the enemy. Ten multiplied by four makes forty; therefore the whole period of our warfare is suitably included in the number forty, both days and nights.

After he had been baptized, the Lord was driven by the Spirit into the desert and tempted by Satan, so that he might offer an example of life to his faithful, who, after receiving the remission of sins in baptism, must gird themselves not only to practice works of virtue but also to endure persecution for righteousness.

He withdraws into the desert to teach us that, having abandoned the world’s attractions and the company of the wicked, we must serve the divine commandments in everything. He is tempted alone by the devil to show us that all who wish to live piously in him suffer persecution, and that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.

He is tempted for forty days and forty nights to indicate that, as long as we live here and serve the Lord—whether prosperity flatters us, which pertains to the days, or adversity strikes us, which corresponds to the figure of night—the adversary is always present throughout the world for those who walk in the Law of the Lord, and he never ceases to hinder our journey by tempting us.

(From Ambrose.) The Lord fasted when he was tempted before his death, while still needing food. But he ate and drank when he was glorified after the resurrection, no longer needing food. In the former case he displayed our labor in himself; in the latter, he displayed his consolation in us, defining both by forty days.

By this number the forty-day course of this age appears to be signified, in those who are called by grace to him who did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it. The Law has ten commandments. Now the grace of Christ has been spread throughout the world, and the world is divided into four parts; ten multiplied by four makes forty. For the Lord gathered those whom he redeemed from the regions—from the east and the west, from the north and the sea.

Fasting, therefore, for forty days before the death of the flesh, he seems to cry out: “Abstain from the desires of this age.” Eating and drinking for forty days after the resurrection of the flesh, he seemed to cry out: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt., last chapter).

Fasting belongs to the tribulation of struggle, because one who is in the contest abstains from everything. Food belongs to the hope of peace, which will not be perfected until our body—whose redemption we await—has put on immortality. We do not yet glory in having attained it, but we are already nourished by hope. The Apostle shows that we carry out both at once when he says: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation.”

It is as though one thing belongs to food and another to fasting. For while we travel along the Lord’s way, we fast from the vanity of the present age and are refreshed by the promise of the future: here we do not set our heart upon it; there we feed our heart again.

Augustine likewise says: Just as one, two, three, and four together make ten, so one, two, three, and four multiplied by four make forty. The number four rightly signifies the body, because of the four well-known natures from which it consists: dry, moist, cold, and hot.

And because progression extends from the point to length, from length to breadth, and from height to the solidity of the body, which are likewise contained in the number four, the number forty is not incongruously understood to signify the temporal dispensation accomplished for our salvation, when the Lord assumed a body and deigned to appear visibly to human beings.

Thus one, two, three, and four—which signify the Creator through three and the creature through seven, the number of the week by which the movement of the world revolves—multiplied by four, that is, demonstrated temporally through the body, make forty. For there is this difference between “four” and “four times”: four is in a state, while four times is in motion.

Therefore, just as four refers to the body, so four times refers to time; and the mystery enacted bodily is indicated on account of those who were entangled in love of bodies and subject to times. Thus the number forty, as has been said, is suitably believed to signify the temporal dispensation itself. Perhaps this is why the Lord fasted for forty days: to show the poverty of this age, which is governed by the movement of bodies and by time.

[Col. 0126C]

Afterward he was hungry.

(From Bede.) The Lord’s hunger after completing the days of his fast, whereas nothing of the kind is written about Moses or Elijah when they fasted, occurred so that the terrified enemy would not flee from him. The enemy had seen him proclaimed by so many heavenly signs and, in abstinence, made equal to the most excellent men. He hungers as the humble God-man, so that the exalted man-God might not be revealed to the enemy. For just as he showed himself to be truly God in the forty-day fast, so in hunger he must be believed to be truly man.

And the tempter approached and said to him: “If you are the Son of God.”

It is asked for what reason he had judged him to be the Son of God. No doubt, by God’s permission, he had heard the Father saying: “This is my beloved Son,” or because he knew that he had been foretold by the prophets.

(From the Vulgate.) [Col. 0126D] The tempter asks what he was not worthy to recognize. His venerable birth was scarcely known at that time to a few, to whom he himself had nevertheless deigned to reveal it. But three mysteries were hidden from the prince of this age: virginity, birth, and Passion.

(From Bede.) The ancient enemy recognized that the Redeemer and conqueror of the human race had come into the world. Hence, through a possessed man, he said: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?” Yet earlier, when he saw him subject to suffering, when his humanity seemed capable of enduring mortal things, whatever he had suspected concerning his divinity was thrown into doubt by the arrogance of his pride.

For, knowing nothing except what is proud, when he saw him humble he doubted that he was God. Thus he turned to the devices of temptation.

Say that these stones—

(From Jerome.) It is suitably said to one who is hungry: “Say that these stones should become loaves of bread.” But, devil, you are held by two opposing considerations. If stones can become loaves at his command, then you tempt one who possesses such great power in vain. But if he cannot do it, you suspect the Son of God in vain.

But he answered and said: “It is written: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.”

The testimony is taken from Deuteronomy. The Lord answered in this way because he had undertaken to overcome the devil by humility, not by power. At the same time, we should observe that unless the Lord had begun to fast, the devil would not have had an occasion for tempting him, in accordance with the saying: “My son, when you approach the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation.”

The Savior’s response itself also indicates that the one who was tempted was man. Therefore, if someone does not feed upon the word of God, that person does not live.

(From Ambrose.) Thus he taught that the appetite for pleasure must be so subdued that one must not yield even to hunger. Therefore, whoever is nourished inwardly by the word of God does not seek pleasure in this wilderness.

Then the devil took him into the holy city and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.”

The devil’s voice always wishes everyone to fall downward.

(From Fulgentius.) He means Jerusalem by “the holy city.” The pinnacle of the temple was therefore a seat of teachers, a platform in the middle of the temple; and from this it is evident that the devil lies in wait even in holy places.

But a question arises: how are the temptations said to have taken place in the desert, when this one is testified to have occurred both in the holy city and upon the pinnacle of the temple? Some say that the other temptations took place in the wilderness and this one in Jerusalem; others say that this one too took place in the wilderness, but was shown only in the mind.

For it is written: “He has commanded his angels concerning you, and they will lift you up in their hands.”

(From Jerome.) This is not a prophecy about Christ but about another holy man. The devil therefore interprets the Scriptures wrongly. Certainly, when he speaks as though to a weak person about the aid of angels, he keeps silent, as a deceiver, about his own trampling, because he knows that it is written concerning himself: “You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample upon the lion and the dragon.”

(From Cassiodorus.) All these names are appropriately applied to the devil. He is an asp when he strikes secretly; a basilisk when he openly spreads poison; a lion when he persecutes the innocent; a dragon when, with impious ferocity, he devours the negligent. Yet all these things lay prostrate and subdued beneath the feet of the Lord at his glorious coming.

“Lest you strike your foot against a stone.” That is, lest he should stumble against the Law, which seemed to be written on stone tablets, whose fullness he had come to confirm with saving integrity.

Then Jesus said to him: “Again, it is written: You shall not tempt the Lord your God.” [Col. 0128A] (From Jerome.) He breaks the devil’s false arrows drawn from Scripture with the true shields of Scripture. It should also be noted that he brought forward testimonies only from Deuteronomy, in order to display the mysteries of the second Law.

(From Augustine.) “You shall not tempt,” he says, “the Lord your God.” For he was being suggested to—as though he were merely a man—that he should test by some sign how great he was, that is, how much power he possessed with God. This is done wrongly when it is done; for it belongs to sound doctrine, whenever a person has something that he ought to do, not to tempt the Lord his God.

Again the devil took him to a very high mountain. The mountain is called high because the devil is defeated there, and his pride is there trampled down and laid subject. Alternatively, the high mountain signifies the devil’s pride. The devil hastens to lead him to the mountains, so that those by which he himself had fallen might also bring down the others. The Lord descended to lowly things so that he might overcome the devil by humility. [Col. 0128B]

And he showed him all the kingdoms of the world, and so forth. That is, all desirable things contained in gold and silver, precious stones, and costly garments; or this may simply be understood to mean that the whole world was shown to him in an instant.

And their glory. The glory of the world—which will pass away together with the world—is displayed on the mountain and upon its summit.

And he said to him: “I will give you all these things, if you will fall down and worship me.” (From Jerome.) The arrogant and proud man speaks even this boastfully—not because he has power over the whole world or is able to give all its kingdoms, but because he speaks these words in persuasion and arrogance. Here it is shown that every ambitious person, by falling, worships the devil. It is asked why Matthew and Luke disagree in the order of the temptations. Without doubt, Matthew followed the order of Adam’s temptation, whereas Luke followed the order of the events.

Then Jesus says to him: “Go, Satan.” It is not the case, as many suppose, that Satan and the apostle Peter are condemned by the same sentence. To Peter he says, “Go behind me, Satan,” that is, “Follow me, you who are contrary to my will”; but here he hears, “Go, Satan,” and “behind me” is not added, so that eternal fire is to be understood.

For it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve.” When the devil says to the Savior, “If you will fall down and worship me,” he hears in reply that he himself ought rather to worship him as his Lord and God. Someone might perhaps ask how this agrees with the command that the Lord alone is to be served, and with the Apostle’s words, “But through charity serve one another.” The origin of the language in which Scripture was written readily resolves this difficulty. In Greek, service is customarily designated in two ways and with different meanings. One term is λατρεία (*latreia*), and another is δουλεία (*douleia*). *Douleia* means common service, that is, service rendered either to God, to a human being, or to any part of nature; from it the Greek name for a servant, δοῦλος (*doulos*), is also derived. *Latreia*, however, denotes that service which is owed solely to the worship of the divinity and which must not be shared with any creature. Hence those who devote to idols the life, prayers, and sacrifices that they ought to have offered to the one God are called idolaters.

We are therefore commanded to serve one another through charity, which in Greek is δουλεύειν (*douleuein*). We are commanded to serve the one God, which in Greek is λατρεύειν (*latreuein*); hence the phrase “and him alone you shall serve,” which in Greek is λατρεύσεις (*latreuseis*). Again: “For we are the circumcision, serving God in spirit” (Phil. III), which in Greek is λατρεύοντες (*latreuontes*). [Col. 0129A]

Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and ministered to him. (From Jerome.) Temptation comes first, so that victory may follow. The angels minister in order to confirm the dignity of the victor.

## AGREEMENT

The agreement of these readings is made clear and evident in a manner appropriate both to the practice of fasting and to the season of Lent. [Col. 0129B]

## FIRST SUNDAY IN THE FIRST MONTH

### THE FIRST EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE THESSALONIANS, CHAPTER IV

“We ask and exhort you in the Lord Jesus that, just as you received from us how you ought to walk and please God, so you should walk, that you may abound more and more. For you know what instructions I gave you through the Lord Jesus. For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication; that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire, as the Gentiles do, who do not know God. And that no one should overstep or defraud his brother in business, because the Lord is the avenger of all these things, as we told you beforehand and testified. For God did not call us to uncleanness, but to sanctification.” [Col. 0129C]

“We ask and exhort you in the Lord Jesus that, just as you received from us how you ought to walk, so you should walk.” (From Primasius.) After praise and consolation, exhortation begins, as though he were saying: “You for whom Christ is the way, follow him by walking in worthy steps,” that is, in gentleness, charity, humility, obedience, peace, and every virtue.

That you may abound more and more. For as faith grows with age, so the progress of virtue ought to increase, just as food and appetite increase with the growth of the body. [Col. 0129D]

For you know what instructions I gave you through the Lord Jesus. That is, I exhorted you to serve the living and true God and to await his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus, who rescued us from the coming wrath, and so forth.

For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication. Sanctification withdraws the Christian from every form of incontinence. Incontinence is not fitting for one who is holy to approach the body of Christ, especially since Moses too, wishing to sanctify the Jews, commanded the whole people to abstain from every woman.
