For whoever abstains from fornication, with God’s help withdraws from many vices. From fornication arise obscene speech, vulgarity, frivolity, and much foolish talk. [Col. 0130A]

(From Cassiodorus.) There is also another, exceedingly wicked fornication, from which we ought to abstain in every way. It is the fornication of which the Psalmist says: “You destroyed all who fornicate away from you” (Ps. LXXIII). To fornicate away from the Lord is to stray from his chaste love through adulterous thoughts; to prefer the world’s luxury and refuse the discipline of heavenly commandments; and, finally, to commit fornication in polluted understanding by believing anything contrary to the Catholic faith.

That each of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor. Let each person sanctify and honor his own vessel—that is, his own body—by keeping it chaste for God. For without chastity no one will see God.

[Col. 0130B]

Not in the passion of desire, as the Gentiles do, who did not know God. As though he were saying: “Take care that, by serving excessive and immoderate lust, you do not become like the Gentiles, who do not know the God who loves chastity.”

And that no one should overstep or defraud his brother in business. As though he were saying: “Let none of you, after devoutly agreeing to abstinence with his partner, attempt by any deception to do him violence; nor let anyone defraud another in any kind of transaction.”

Because the Lord is the avenger of all these things, as we told you beforehand and testified. God is the avenger not only of fornication and public disgrace, but also of every transgression against any good thing that has been prescribed. For it is better not to make a vow than, after making one, not to fulfill what was promised. [Col. 0130C]

For God did not call us to uncleanness, but to sanctification. Even excessive incontinence can be counted as uncleanness, since it does not permit a person to receive the body of Christ boldly. When he says, “but to sanctification in Christ Jesus,” it is as though he were saying: “You were called to live according to the example of Christ; for whoever has this hope sanctifies himself, just as he is holy. Therefore be holy, because I too am holy, says the Lord.”

## THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER XV

“Jesus went out and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a Canaanite woman came out from those districts and cried out to him, saying: ‘Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David; my daughter is grievously tormented by a demon.’ But he did not answer her a word. And his disciples came and asked him, saying: ‘Send her away, because she is crying out after us.’ But he answered and said: ‘I was not sent except to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel.’ But she came and worshiped him, saying: ‘Lord, help me.’ He answered and said: ‘It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs.’ But she said: ‘Yes, Lord, for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.’ Then Jesus answered and said to her: ‘O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you wish.’ And her daughter was healed from that hour.” [Col. 0130D]

Jesus went out from there and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon. (From Jerome.) Leaving behind the scribes and Pharisees, his accusers, he crosses over into the region of Tyre and Sidon in order to heal the Tyrians and Sidonians.

[Col. 0131A]

The Canaanite woman comes out from her former districts, crying out in order to obtain health for her daughter. Observe that, in the fifteenth place, the Canaanite daughter is healed.

“Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David; my daughter is grievously tormented by a demon.” She who had already come out from her own districts now knows to call him the Son of David, having abandoned the error of the Tyrians and Sidonians through a change of place and faith. “My daughter is grievously tormented by a demon.” I think that by the daughter of the Church he means the souls of believers, who were grievously tormented by a demon while they were ignorant of the Creator and worshiped a stone.

But he did not answer her a word. This was not because of Pharisaic pride or the arrogance of the scribes, but lest he should appear contrary to his own command, by which he had ordered: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans” (Matt. X). For he did not wish to give the accusers an opportunity, and reserved the perfect salvation of the Gentiles for the time of his passion and resurrection. [Col. 0131B]

And his disciples came and asked him, saying: “Send her away, because she is crying out after us.” At that time the disciples still did not know the Lord’s mysteries, or, moved by mercy, they asked on behalf of the Canaanite woman, whom another Evangelist calls a Syrophoenician; or, wishing to be rid of her persistence, they asked because she called out repeatedly, not to a compassionate but to a stern physician.

But he answered and said: “I was not sent except to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel.” This does not mean that he was not also sent to the Gentiles, but that he was sent first to Israel, so that, when they did not receive the Gospel, the transfer to the Gentiles might justly take place. [Col. 0131C]

But she came and worshiped him, saying: “Lord, help me.” Under the person of the Canaanite woman, the faith, patience, and humility of the Church are wondrously proclaimed. Faith, by which she believed that her daughter could be healed; patience, by which, though so often rejected, she persevered in prayer; humility, by which she compared herself to little dogs. O wondrous reversal of circumstances! Israel was once the son, while we are dogs; according to the difference of faith, the order of names is changed. Of them it is later said: “Many dogs have surrounded me” (Ps. XXI), and: “Beware of dogs; beware of evil workers” (Phil. III). But of us, converted to the grace of mercy, he says: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice” (John X). And concerning the daughters: “Your faith has saved you.”

He answered and said: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs.” But she said: “Yes, Lord, for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.” It should certainly be noted that the woman, believing as one of the Gentiles, speaks mystically. Which little dogs eat beneath the table from the children’s crumbs? The table is Holy Scripture, which supplies us with the bread of life. Hence the Church says: “You have prepared a table before me in the presence of those who trouble me” (Ps. XXII). The children’s crumbs are the inner mysteries of Scripture, by which the hearts of the humble are accustomed to be refreshed. Therefore the little dogs do not eat crusts but crumbs from the children’s bread, because the Gentiles converted to the faith seek in the Scriptures not the surface of the letter but the marrow of spiritual meanings, which they see advancing through good works. And they eat beneath the table of their masters when, humbly subject to the words of sacred discourse, they place all the duties of their heart and body beneath the fulfillment of what has been commanded, so that they may rightly raise themselves, through the merit of due humility, toward the rewards promised by the Lord in heaven. [Col. 0132A]

Then Jesus answered and said to her: “O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you wish.” And her daughter was healed from that hour. Because of the mother’s great faith, the demon departed from the daughter. Here an example is given of the instruction of infants, since through the faith and confession of their parents in baptism, children who are not yet able by themselves either to understand or to do anything good or evil are freed from the devil. [Col. 0132B]

(From Bede.) Typically, this Gentile woman, coming to the Lord with faith, signifies the Church gathered from the Gentiles. She is called a Canaanite because, moved by the zeal of faith, she came to the Lord and abandoned idols. *Canaan* is interpreted as “zeal.” She prays to the Lord for her demon-possessed daughter, just as she pleads with heavenly mercy on behalf of her peoples, who do not yet believe, so that they too may be freed from the devil’s deceptions. The fact that the Lord first did not answer her signifies that, while he was present in the flesh, the Gentiles did not hear the word from his mouth. The fact that the apostles say to the Lord, “Send her away”—that is, “Receive her prayers”—because “she is crying out after us,” signifies that after the Lord’s resurrection and ascension, hearing the apostles’ preaching, she cried out in order to be heard. The fact that Matthew says she came out from her districts signifies that they alone approach faithfully and rightly in prayer who leave behind the former dwellings of their unbelief and, with devout dedication, transfer themselves into the house of the Lord, namely, the Church. [Col. 0132C]

## THIRTIETH SUNDAY

### READING FROM THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE EPHESIANS, CHAPTER V

“Be imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave himself for us, an offering and sacrifice to God for a pleasing fragrance. But let fornication and every uncleanness or greed not even be named among you, as is fitting for God’s holy people; nor obscenity, foolish talk, or vulgar joking, which is improper, but rather thanksgiving. For know this and understand that every fornicator, or unclean person, or greedy person—which is the service of idols—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. Let no one deceive you with empty words; for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief. Therefore do not become partners with them. For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light. For the fruit of light consists in all goodness, righteousness, and truth.” [Col. 0132D]

[Col. 0133A]

Be imitators of God, as beloved children. (From Jerome.) I do not think that in all the other things God has done a human being could imitate him as well; but, for example, just as he is merciful and sends rain upon the good and the evil, so let us also pour out our goodness upon all people. When we have done this, we shall be beloved children, whether of Paul himself or, as I think more rightly, of God.

(From Primasius.) We are children of God by imitation, not by nature, as the Savior says: “So that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. VI).

And walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave himself for us, an offering and sacrifice to God, for a pleasing fragrance. (From Jerome.) Whoever fights against sin for the salvation of others even unto blood, so that he gives his own life for them, walks in charity, imitating Christ, who loved us so greatly that he endured the cross for the salvation of humanity. For just as Christ gave himself for us, so such a person, willingly dying for those whom he can help, will imitate him who gave himself to the Father as an offering and sacrifice for a pleasing fragrance; he too will become an offering and sacrifice of God for a pleasing fragrance. [Col. 0133B]

But let fornication, every uncleanness, or greed not even be named among you, as is fitting for the holy. If a certain Cynic philosopher had not existed who taught that every bodily titillation and emission of semen should not be avoided, the holy Apostle, writing to the Ephesians, would never have joined every uncleanness to fornication and connected greed with uncleanness. He does not mean the greed by which we desire to accumulate money, but that of which we spoke above: “Let no greedy person overstep his brother in business” (I Thess. IV), that is, in the business of adultery, which is an insatiable wandering through every kind of disgrace and lust, and which appropriately receives the general name of obscenity. [Col. 0133C]

Foolish talk or vulgar joking, which is improper. I think foolish talk belongs not only to those who tell obscene stories in order to provoke laughter and, by feigned stupidity, mock even more those whom they desire to please, but also to those who are considered wise in the world and, arguing about physical matters, say that they have clearly comprehended the sands of the shores, the drops of the ocean, the expanse of the heavens, and the point of the earth. The difference between foolish talk and vulgar joking is this: foolish talk contains nothing wise in itself, whereas vulgar joking descends from a prudent mind and deliberately seeks certain words—polished, rustic, or witty—which we may call playfulness by another name, in order to provoke laughter in those listening. Yet these things must be entirely driven away by holy men, for whom mourning is more fitting: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” [Col. 0133D]

But rather thanksgiving. Someone might ask: What does thanksgiving have to do here after the prohibition of fornication, uncleanness, and the other vices? In this passage, it is not named in the sense in which we give thanks to God, but in the sense in which we are called gracious or witty among human beings. Christian speech ought to be seasoned with salt, so that it may possess grace before those who hear it. [Col. 0134A]

But know this and understand that every fornicator, or unclean person, or greedy person—which is the service of idols—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. It should be noted that, of the six vices prohibited above— fornication, uncleanness, greed, obscenity, foolish talk, and vulgar joking—he has now mentioned only three: fornication, uncleanness, and greed. Whoever is subject to these cannot possess an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. For if a foolish talker and a vulgar joker were excluded from the kingdom of God, would not the judgment concerning the three whom we have specifically distinguished appear harsh, in refusing to pardon the weakness of human frailty, since even words spoken in jest would condemn us? “Whoever does not stumble in speech is a perfect man.” Although someone may be free from fornication, uncleanness, and lust, if he is nevertheless a foolish talker and vulgar joker, he will not retain the place he would have possessed had he not had these vices.

Someone may reply: Granted that foolish talk and vulgar joking do not incur the same guilt as fornication, uncleanness, and greed; should he not nevertheless have mentioned obscenity together with the three? To this it must be said that here obscenity signifies hidden thoughts, when our senses are inflamed toward lust, the soul is kindled and set ablaze by the titillation of the flesh, and yet is restrained by the fear of God and the judgment of the mind. Finally, above he named three together without obscenity, saying: “Let fornication, every uncleanness, and greed not even be named among you”; afterward obscenity was numbered together with foolish talk and vulgar joking. Just as foolish talk and vulgar joking do not destroy or forever exclude a person from the kingdom, so neither does this obscenity.

In many passages of the prophets we find idolatry called fornication: “They fornicated after their idols,” he says, “and were led astray by the spirit of fornication” (Hosea IV). Fornication can therefore also be understood of idolatry. If the greedy person is understood as one who acquires money by any means and desires to possess coins by right or wrong, he is an idolater in this respect, because he worships the image of the coin and venerates the idols engraved upon it. Just as the belly is the god of the gluttonous, so money can most rightly be called the god of the covetous. Especially since in another place the Apostle calls greed idolatry.

In addition, we must consider what he intended by saying “in the kingdom of Christ and of God”: whether the kingdom of Christ is one thing and the kingdom of God another, or whether the Father and the Son possess the same kingdom. If he had said, “in the kingdom of the Son and of the Father,” we would come through the Son to the Father; and although there would be a distinction of persons, there would nevertheless be one majesty of those who reign. But since he has said, “in the kingdom of Christ and of God,” let us understand the Lord himself as Christ, because even when he delivers the kingdom to God and the Father, the Father will not be all things in all, but God will be all things in all. Wherever God is, both the Father and the Son may be understood. Moreover, what we say concerning the Father and the Son, let us understand likewise concerning the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0134D]

[Col. 0135A]

Let no one deceive you with empty words. Words that deceive and overthrow are empty and void; but those that edify their hearers are full, abundant, and richly supplied.

For because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief. The children of unbelief are called this in the same way as the children of perdition and fornication, the children of death, and the children of Gehenna, along with many similar expressions that are very easy to find in various passages of Scripture.

Therefore do not become partners with them. A person becomes a partner or fellow-partner of the children of unbelief when he is found in fornication, uncleanness, or greed, because of which the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief. He is called a partner because he participates in and shares in evil works; a fellow-partner is one who is a partner together with others. [Col. 0135B]

For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. When they were called darkness because of their wickedness, they were converted to better things and are now called light in the Lord. Everyone who does evil hates the light; concerning the righteous it is said: “But now you are light in the Lord.” The person who does evil is dark, and is a child of night and darkness; but whoever does truth and comes into the light is light, a child of light and of day.

Walk as children of light. If God is light and there is no darkness in him, they are children of light. Likewise, if Christ is the true light, his children too are those to whom he says: “My little children, I am with you only a little longer” (John XIII). The children of light are therefore also the children of God the Father, as is gathered from the fact that they are children of Christ Jesus. [Col. 0135C]

For the fruit of light consists in this, and so forth. The fruit of light is not only in goodness but also in righteousness and truth. Where goodness is, there is righteousness also; where righteousness is, there consequently is truth. Therefore, according to the good Father of Christ—as they themselves also confess—there are both goodness and truth. Where goodness and truth are found with him, and not with another, there is righteousness, as the Apostle now teaches. Let Marcion also understand that Christ himself is called goodness, truth, and righteousness: goodness, because he gives grace to those who believe in him not according to their works but according to his mercy; righteousness, because he repays each person according to what he deserves; and truth, because he alone knows the causes of all creatures and of all things. [Col. 0135D]

## THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER XI

“Jesus was casting out a demon, and it was mute. When he had cast out the demon, the mute man spoke, and the crowds marveled. But some of them said: ‘He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons.’ Others, testing him, were seeking from him a sign from heaven. But when he saw their thoughts, he said to them: ‘Every kingdom divided against itself will be desolated, and house will fall upon house. If Satan too is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebub. But if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they themselves will be your judges. But if I cast out demons by the finger of God, surely the kingdom of God has come upon you. When a strong, armed man guards his courtyard, all that he possesses is in peace. But if one stronger than he comes upon him and defeats him, he will take away all his weapons in which he trusted and distribute his spoils. Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. When an unclean spirit has gone out from a man, it travels through waterless places, seeking rest and not finding it. It says: ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds it swept clean. Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself. They enter and dwell there, and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first. It happened that, while he was saying these things, a certain woman from the crowd raised her voice and said to him: ‘Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you.’ But he said: ‘Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.’” [Col. 0136A]

Jesus was casting out a demon, and it was mute; when he had cast out the demon, the mute man spoke, and the crowds marveled. (From Bede.) According to Matthew, this demoniac was not only mute but also blind. He is said to have been healed by the Lord so that he both spoke and saw. Thus three signs were performed together in one man: the blind sees, the mute speaks, and the demon-possessed is freed. This happened then in a bodily sense, but it is also fulfilled daily in the conversion of believers: when the demon is first expelled, they behold the light of faith; then mouths that had previously been silent are opened to the praises of God. [Col. 0136C]

But some of them said: “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons.” (From Jerome.) These were not some ordinary people in the crowd making the accusation, but the Pharisees and scribes, as the other Evangelists testify. The crowds, who seemed less educated, always marveled at God’s works; but the others either tried to deny them or, when they could not deny them, to distort them by a sinister interpretation, as though these works were not acts of divinity but of an unclean spirit.

Therefore, “by Beelzebub,” who was the god of Ekron. For *Beel* itself is *Baal*, while *Zebub* means “fly.” According to certain corrupt copies, the name should not be read with an *l* or a *d* at the end, but with a *b*. Thus *Beelzebub* is interpreted as “Baal of flies,” that is, “man of flies,” or “one who has flies.” They gave the prince of demons this name because of the filth of sacrificial blood, from whose most impure ritual or name they called him prince of demons. [Col. 0136D]

And others, testing him, were seeking from him a sign from heaven. (From Bede.) Either they desired fire to come from above, as in the manner of Elijah, or, in the likeness of Samuel, thunder to roar in summer, lightning to flash, and rains to pour down—as though they could not also slander these things and say that they had happened through hidden and various disturbances of the air. But you who slander what you see with your eyes, hold in your hand, and experience through its usefulness, what will you do about things that come from heaven? You will surely reply that the magicians in Egypt also performed many signs from heaven (Exod. VII, VIII).

But when he saw their thoughts, he said to them: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be desolated, and house will fall upon house.” He answered not their words but their thoughts, so that they might in this way be compelled to believe in the power of one who saw the hidden things of the heart. But if every kingdom divided against itself will be desolated, then the kingdom of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is not divided. Without any contradiction, it will not be desolated by some assault but will remain in eternal stability. [Col. 0137A]

But if Satan too is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebub. By saying this, he wished it to be understood from their own confession that, by refusing to believe in him, they had chosen to be in the devil’s kingdom—which, being divided against itself, could not stand. Let the Pharisees choose whichever alternative they wish. If Satan cannot cast out Satan, they could find nothing against the Lord to say; but if he can, they should take much greater care for themselves and depart from his kingdom, which, divided against itself, cannot stand. But in what power the Lord Christ casts out demons, so that they may not think him the prince of demons, let them attend to what follows:

But if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they themselves will be your judges. He said this concerning his disciples, the sons of that people, who were certainly well aware that they had learned no evil arts from the good Master by which to cast out demons in the name of the prince of demons. “Therefore,” he says, “they themselves will be your judges.” That is: these lowly and despised things of the world, in which not artful wickedness but my holy simplicity appears, will themselves be my witnesses and your judges.

Alternatively, he means the sons of the Jews, the exorcists of that people, who according to custom cast out demons by invocation; and by a prudent question he constrains them to confess that this was the work of the Holy Spirit. If the expulsion of demons among your sons, he says, is attributed to God and not to demons, why does the same work in me not have the same cause? Therefore they themselves will be your judges—not by power but by comparison: they attribute the expulsion of demons to God, while you attribute it to Beelzebub, the prince of demons. [Col. 0137C]

But if I cast out demons by the finger of God, surely the kingdom of God has come upon you. This is the finger whom the magicians also confess when they performed signs against Moses and Aaron, saying: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. VIII). By this finger the stone tablets were also written on Mount Sinai. Therefore the hand and arm of God are the Son of God, while his finger is the Holy Spirit. The substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one. Let not the inequality of the members trouble you, since the unity of the body builds up.

Alternatively, the Holy Spirit is called the finger of God because of the distribution of gifts that are given through him individually, whether to human beings or to angels; for in none of our members is division more apparent than in the fingers. When he says, “the kingdom of God has come upon you,” he now calls the kingdom of God that by which the impious are condemned and separated from the faithful who are now doing penance for their sins.

Alternatively, the kingdom of God is Christ, concerning whom it is said elsewhere: “The kingdom of God is within you”; or, “The kingdom of God will come upon you,” that sublime throne from which John said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is drawing near.” [Col. 0138A]

When a strong, armed man guards his courtyard, all that he possesses is in peace. He calls the devil strong, and his courtyard the world, which lies in wickedness. Until the Savior’s coming, the devil possessed it as an ill-ordered empire, because he rested without opposition in the hearts of unbelievers. Hence elsewhere he is also called the prince of the world, as the Lord says: “For the prince of the world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV); and again: “Now the prince of the world will be cast out,” concerning which expulsion what follows here is added.

But if one stronger than he comes upon him and defeats him, he will take away all his weapons in which he trusted and distribute his spoils. He is speaking about himself: not by a deceitful operation acting in agreement with the devil, as they accused him, but by stronger power he conquers and frees human beings from the demon. What are the weapons in which that wicked strong man trusted? Spiritual wickedness. His spoils are the very human beings deceived by him. Christ the victor distributes them; this is the mark of a triumphant conqueror, for, leading captivity captive, he gave gifts to human beings, appointing some as apostles, others as evangelists, some as prophets, and others as pastors and teachers. [Col. 0138B]

(From Bede.) He therefore enters the house of the strong man—that is, this world of mortals, established under the devil’s power insofar as death itself is concerned. For it is written concerning him that he has the power of death. He enters, therefore, the house of the strong man, that is, the human race under his dominion, and first binds him—that is, restrains and curbs his power—with stronger bonds of his own power. Thus he seizes his vessels, whatever he has predestined to seize, freeing them from the devil’s power so that, without the devil’s interference, they may believe in Christ by free will. [Col. 0138C]

Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. (From Jerome.) Let no one think that this concerns heretics and schismatics, although that meaning could also be understood incidentally; from what follows and from the tenor of the discourse, it refers to the devil. The devil’s works cannot be compared with those of the Savior: the devil desires to hold human souls captive, while the Lord frees them; the devil preaches idols, while the Lord recalls them to the knowledge of the one God; the devil draws them toward vices, while the Lord calls them back to virtues.

When the unclean spirit had gone out of a man, it wandered through waterless places. Although this may be understood simply as the Lord’s having added these words to distinguish his works from Satan’s, namely, that he himself always hastens to cleanse what is polluted, whereas Satan hastens to contaminate what has been cleansed with worse filth, nevertheless it may also appropriately be understood of any heretic, schismatic, or even wicked Catholic. At the time of baptism, the unclean spirit that had previously dwelt in such a person is cast out through the confession of the Catholic faith and renunciation of his former way of life; and it traverses waterless places—that is, it searches out the hearts of the faithful, cleansed of the flowing softness of fickle thought—to see whether it might perhaps establish there some foothold of its wickedness. But it is rightly said:

“Seeking rest, and finding none.” For, fleeing chaste minds, the devil can find for himself a place of rest only in the heart of the wicked. Hence the Lord says of him: “He sleeps under the shadow, in the secret places of the reed, and in moist places” (Job 40). “Under the shadow,” namely, darkened consciences; “in the reed,” which is bright on the outside but empty within, hypocrites; “in moist places,” insinuating himself into wanton and soft minds.

He says: “I will return to my house from which I came.” This verse is to be feared, not explained, lest the fault we had believed extinguished in us should, when we are negligent and unoccupied, overwhelm us again.

[Col. 0139B]

“And when he has come, he finds it swept clean.” That is, cleansed by baptismal grace from the stain of sins, but not enriched by any diligence in good works. Hence Matthew rightly says that this house was found empty, swept clean, and adorned: cleansed, namely, from former vices through baptism; empty of good deeds through negligence; and adorned with counterfeit virtues through hypocrisy.

“And then he goes and takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter and dwell there.” By the seven evil spirits he designates all vices. Whoever after baptism is seized either by heretical depravity or by worldly desire is immediately cast down into the depths of every vice. Hence those spirits are rightly called “more wicked” when they enter, because such a person will have not only the seven vices opposed to the seven spiritual virtues, but will also pretend, through hypocrisy, to possess the virtues themselves.

“And the last state of that man is worse than the first.” For it was a lesser evil for him not to know the way of truth than, after having recognized it, to turn backward. We read that this was fulfilled particularly in Judas the traitor, Simon Magus, and others of the same kind. But the Savior himself, according to Matthew, explained the general direction of this parable: after concluding it, he immediately added, “So will it also be with this most wicked generation.” That is, what I have recounted as customarily happening in the case of one individual does not cease to happen generally in the whole nation of this people.

For the unclean spirit went out from the Jews when they received the law, and wandered through dry places, seeking rest for himself. Expelled, that is, from the Jews, he wandered through the solitudes of the nations. When these nations afterward believed in the Lord, and he found no place among them, he said: “I will return to my former house, from which I came. I have the Jews, whom I had previously abandoned.” And when he came, he found it empty and swept clean. The temple of the Jews was empty, for it did not have Christ as its guest, who says: “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 21). Since, therefore, they did not have the protection of God and the angels, but were adorned with the superfluous observances of the Pharisees, the devil returned to them; and, adding to himself a sevenfold number of demons, he dwelt in his former house. Thus the latter state of that people became worse than the former.

For they are now possessed by a far greater number of demons, blaspheming Christ Jesus in their synagogues, than they had been possessed in Egypt before receiving knowledge of the law. For it is one thing not to believe that he is to come, and another not to receive him who has come. Understand the number seven added to the devil either with reference to the Sabbath or with reference to the number of the Holy Spirit: just as in Isaiah seven spirits of the virtues are said to have descended upon the branch from the root of Jesse and upon the flower that rises from his root, so conversely the number of vices may have been consecrated in the devil.

And it happened that, while he was saying these things, a certain woman from the crowd raised her voice and said to him: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that nursed you.” This woman is shown to possess great devotion and faith. While the scribes and Pharisees were both tempting and blaspheming the Lord, she recognized his incarnation before all others with such sincerity and confessed it with such confidence that she confounded both the slander of the leaders present and the faithlessness of future heretics.

For just as the Jews then, by blaspheming the works of the Holy Spirit, denied the true and consubstantial Son of God the Father, so later heretics, by denying that Mary ever-virgin, through the working power of the Holy Spirit, supplied material from her human members to the only-begotten God who was to be born, said that one ought not to confess him as the true and consubstantial Son of his mother according to his humanity. But if the flesh of the Word of God, born according to the flesh, is declared foreign to the flesh of his virgin mother, then the womb that bore him and the breasts that nursed him are blessed without reason.

For by what logic can he be believed to have been nourished by her milk if he is denied to have been conceived from her seed, when, according to the natural philosophers, both fluids are shown to flow from the origin of one and the same source? Unless, perhaps, one should think that the virgin could provide the seminal material of her own flesh by nursing the Son of God in the flesh, but could not provide it by giving birth to him—an act supposedly involving a greater and unprecedented miracle. Yet the Apostle opposes this opinion, saying: “God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4).

Nor should we heed those who think that the text ought to be read, “Born of a woman, made under the law,” but rather, “made of a woman,” because, conceived in the virginal womb, he drew flesh not from nothing, nor from elsewhere, but from his mother’s flesh. Otherwise he would not truly be called the Son of Man, since he would have no origin from man.

Therefore, in opposition to Eutyches, let us also raise our voice with the Catholic Church, whose type this woman represented. Let us raise our minds above the midst of the crowds, and say to the Savior: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that nursed you.” Truly blessed is the mother who, as someone says (Sedulius),

> Gave birth as a mother to the King,  
> Embracing the Godhead that encompasses all things in an eternal circuit,  
> Possessing a mother’s joys together with the honor of virginity;  
> He who holds heaven and earth throughout the ages, whose  
> Dominion remains without end—she who, with blessed womb,  
> Was never seen to have a first equal to her, nor to have a successor.

But he said: “Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.” The Savior appropriately affirmed the woman’s testimony. He declared blessed not only her who had deserved to give bodily birth to the Word of God, but also all who should strive to conceive the Word spiritually through the hearing of faith, and to give birth to it through the keeping of good works, whether in their own heart or in that of their neighbors, and, as it were, to nourish it.

For the same mother of God was blessed in one respect because she became the temporal minister of the Word’s incarnation, but much more blessed in another because she remained eternally the guardian of that same Word, whom she was always to love. By this saying he secretly strikes the learned men of the Jews, who sought not to hear and keep the word of God but to deny and blaspheme it.

## FRIDAY OF THE SECOND WEEK OF LENT

[Col. 0141B]

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER 4

> “Jesus, therefore, wearied from his journey, was sitting thus beside the well; and it was about the sixth hour. A woman came from Samaria to draw water. Jesus said to her: Give me a drink. For his disciples had gone into the city to buy food. Therefore that Samaritan woman said to him: How is it that you, though you are a Jew, ask me for a drink, since I am a Samaritan woman? For Jews do not associate with Samaritans. Jesus answered and said to her: If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that says to you, Give me a drink, you perhaps would have asked him, and he would have given you living water. The woman said to him: Lord, you have nothing with which to draw, and the well is deep. From where, then, do you have living water? Surely you are not greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well, and he himself drank from it, and his sons and his cattle? Jesus answered and said to her: Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again. But whoever drinks from the water that I shall give him will never thirst. Rather, the water that I shall give him will become in him a spring of water welling up into eternal life. The woman said to him: Lord, give me this water, so that I may not thirst, nor come here to draw. Jesus said to her: Go, call your husband, and come here. The woman answered and said: I have no husband. Jesus said to her: You have spoken well, I have no husband. For you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband; you have spoken the truth in this. The woman said to him: Lord, I see that you are a prophet. Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, and you say that the place where one ought to worship is in Jerusalem. Jesus said to her: Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, because salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming—and now is—when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For the Father also seeks such people to worship him. God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth. The woman said to him: I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ; therefore, when he has come, he will announce all things to us. Jesus said to her: I am he who speaks with you. And immediately his disciples came, and they marveled that he was speaking with a woman; yet no one said: What are you seeking? or: Why are you speaking with her? Therefore the woman left her water jar and went into the city, and said to those men: Come and see a man who told me everything I have done. Surely he is the Christ? Therefore they went out of the city and were coming to him. In the meantime the disciples were asking him, saying: Rabbi, eat. But he said to them: I have food to eat that you do not know. Therefore the disciples said to one another: Has someone brought him something to eat? Jesus said to them: My food is to do the will of him who sent me, so that I may accomplish his work. Do you not say that there are still four months, and then the harvest comes? Behold, I say to you: Lift up your eyes and see the regions, for they are already white for the harvest. And he who reaps receives a reward and gathers fruit for eternal life, so that both he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together. For in this the saying is true: One is he who sows, and another he who reaps. I sent you to reap what you did not labor for; others labored, and you have entered into their labor. From that city many of the Samaritans believed in him because of the word of the woman, who testified: He told me everything I have done. Therefore, when the Samaritans had come to him, they asked him to remain there; and he stayed there two days. And many more believed because of his words. And they said to the woman: We no longer believe because of your speech. For we ourselves have heard, and we know that this man is truly the Savior of the world.”

“Jesus, wearied from his journey, was sitting thus beside the well; it was about the sixth hour.” What else, then, is meant by “Jesus, wearied from his journey,” except that Jesus was wearied in the flesh, weak in the flesh? His journey is the flesh assumed for our sake, because he would not come to us unless he assumed the form of visible flesh. Since, therefore, he deigned to come to us in such a way that he appeared in the form of a servant, having assumed flesh, that assumption of flesh is his journey.

Why, then, at the sixth hour? Because it was the sixth age of the world. He came to the well wearied, because he bore weak flesh. He came to the well because he came to the depth of this dwelling-place of ours, concerning which it is said: “From the depths I have cried to you, Lord” (Ps. 130). He sat because he was humbled.

And a woman came from Samaria to draw water. This woman represented the Church. For the Church was to come from the Gentiles, alien to the race of the Jews. Let us therefore listen to her, recognize ourselves in her, and in her give thanks to God on our behalf. That water which she had come to draw from the well is the pleasure of the world, deep and dark; here men draw it with the water jar of desire, for the water jar also signifies desire.

Jesus said to her: “Give me a drink.” He who was asking for a drink thirsted for the woman’s faith. He asks for a drink and promises a drink. He is in need, as though he were about to receive, and he overflows, as though he were about to satisfy.

“If you knew,” Jesus said to her, “the gift of God, and who it is that says to you, Give me a drink, you perhaps would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.” The gift of God is the Holy Spirit. The water that the Lord promised to give her, so that she would not thirst forever, is that of which it is said: “With you is the fountain of life, Lord.” And again: “We shall be satisfied with the good things of your house.” For how shall those thirst who will be intoxicated with the abundance of your house? He was promising, therefore, a kind of richness and satisfaction, and she, not yet understanding, said to him:

“Lord, give me this water, so that I may not thirst, nor come here to draw.” Jesus said to her: “Go, call your husband, and come here.” What does this mean? “Call your husband”—that is, apply your understanding. Seeing, therefore, that the woman did not understand, and wishing her to understand, Jesus said: “Call your husband. This is why you do not know what I am saying: your understanding is not present. Call your husband; present your understanding, by which you may be taught and corrected.”

Apply understanding as a husband, and understand what I am saying. These things do not pertain to the will of the ears, nor to the eyes, nor to the sense of smell, nor to taste, nor to touch; they are grasped by the mind alone and drawn up by understanding alone. But she had not yet called her husband—that is, she had not yet applied her understanding.

She answered and said: “I have no husband.” Jesus said to her: “You have spoken well, I have no husband. For you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband; you have spoken the truth in this.”

Many have understood the woman’s five husbands as the five books of Moses. The Samaritans used them and were under the same law. For this reason they also possessed circumcision. I have another interpretation: it seems to me that the woman’s five husbands are the five bodily senses of the soul. Why are they called husbands? Because they are legitimate, made by God and given by God to the soul.

The soul is still weak when it is governed by these five senses and acts under these five husbands. But when understanding, imbued with wisdom, begins to govern the soul, and, having become discerning, begins to separate just from unjust, good from evil, useful from useless, chastity from impurity—so that it may love the one and avoid the other—and charity from hatred, so that it may be in the one and not in the other, this husband had not yet succeeded the other five husbands in this woman.

Where understanding does not succeed, error rules. Concerning this the Lord said to her: “The one whom you now have is not your husband.” This error was not a legitimate husband but an adulterer. “Call,” therefore, the Lord says, “not the adulterer but your husband, understanding, so that you may grasp me and not, through error, form some false opinion about me.”

The woman said: “Lord, I see that you are a prophet.” Then the husband began to come, though he had not yet come fully. She thought the Lord was a prophet. Indeed, he was also a prophet, for he said of himself: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (Luke 4). It was also said of him to Moses: “I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, like you” (Deut. 18)—like you, namely, in the form of flesh, not in the eminence of majesty.

[Col. 0144A]

“Our fathers worshiped on this mountain.” Jesus said to her: “Woman, believe me.” For there was already in you one who could believe, because your husband is present; you began to be present through understanding when you called me a prophet. Therefore, woman, believe me, because the hour is coming, and now is. What hour? The hour when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.

“We worship what we know; you worship what you do not know, because salvation is from the Jews.” He gave much from the Jews, but do not take these to mean the reprobate. It was indeed said in the person of the Jews, but not of all Jews—not of the reprobate, but of those such as the apostles were, such as the prophets were, such as all those holy men were who sold all their possessions and placed the proceeds of their goods at the apostles’ feet. For God did not reject his people whom he foreknew.

This woman heard this and added:

“I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ. Therefore, when he has come, he will announce all things to us.” She was now worthy that he should be revealed to her. Messiah means “anointed.” In Greek, χριστός (*Christos*) means “anointed”; in Hebrew, [the source breaks off here].

Christ says to her: “I am he who speaks with you,” and so forth. Therefore the woman left her water jar when she heard, “I am he who speaks with you.” Having received Christ the Lord into her heart, what could she do except immediately abandon her water jar and run to evangelize?

“Water jar” is called by a Greek name. In Greek, ὕδωρ (*hydōr*) means “water,” as though one were to say “water-vessel.” Here it signifies desire: she cast away desire and hurried to announce the truth. Let those who do not wish to evangelize learn from this: let them cast away the water jar at the well and then run to announce Christ, just as she, having thrown off her burden, ran to the city and said to those men: “Come and see a man who told me everything I have done. Surely he is the Christ?” and so forth.

“Do you not say that there are still four months, and then the harvest comes?” and so forth. This woman was already ripe fruit, and the harvests were white and seeking the sickle. For what had previously been sown through the prophets had become ripe and desired the sickle and the threshing floor. Only the reapers remained to be sent, and therefore the Lord also said to them:

“I sent you to reap what you did not sow; others sowed, and you entered into their labors.” Who labored? Abraham himself, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, the other patriarchs, and all the prophets. Read their labors: in all their labors there is prophecy of Christ, and therefore they are sowers.

The harvest was therefore already prepared in Judea. What happened to it? A few grains were taken from that harvest and sown throughout the world, and another harvest arose, which is to be reaped at the end of the age. Thus the harvest grows amid the weeds, whose reapers are not the apostles but the angels.

Observe what is said: “Let him who sows and him who reaps rejoice together.” The apostles and the prophets had labors belonging to different times, but they will enjoy the same joy and receive their reward together: eternal life.

“They asked him to remain there, and he stayed there two days,” and so forth. Christ is announced through Christian friends. As through the woman—that is, through the Church—announcing him, those who are outside and are not yet Christians come to Christ. They believe through this report. He remains with them for two days; that is, he gives them the two commandments of charity: love of God and love of neighbor. And many more, and more firmly, believe that he is truly the Savior of the world.

## SATURDAY OF THE SECOND WEEK OF LENT

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER 8

> “Jesus went to the Mount of Olives, and at dawn he came again into the temple, and all the people came to him; and sitting, he taught them. Now the scribes and Pharisees brought a woman caught in adultery and set her in the middle, and said to him: Teacher, this woman has just been caught in adultery. In the law Moses commanded us to stone such women. What, then, do you say? They said this to test him, so that they might accuse him. But Jesus, bending down, wrote with his finger on the ground. When they persisted in questioning him, he straightened up and said to them: Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her. And again bending down, he wrote on the ground. When they heard this, they went out one by one, beginning with the elders. And Jesus remained alone, with the woman standing in the middle. Straightening up, Jesus said to her: Woman, where are they who accused you? Has no one condemned you? She said: No one, Lord. And Jesus said to her: Neither will I condemn you. Go, and from now on sin no more.”

Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. The Mount of Olives signifies the sublimity of the Lord’s kindness and mercy. In Greek, ἔλεος and ἤλεος mean “mercy”; *Olivetum* is called from *oleum*, “oil,” and the anointing of oil itself ordinarily brings relief to the weary. This oil also surpasses other oil in virtue and purity, and whatever liquid one wishes to pour over it, it immediately rises above and floats upon it. Thus it appropriately signifies the grace of heavenly mercy, concerning which it is written: “The Lord is gentle toward all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144).

“And at dawn he came again into the temple.” The time of dawn also demonstrates the rising of that same grace, by which, once the shadow of the law had been removed, the light of evangelical truth was to be revealed. Jesus therefore goes to the Mount of Olives to declare that the fortress of mercy resides in him. He comes again at dawn into the temple to signify that, with the light of the New Testament beginning, he was to disclose and offer that same mercy to the faithful, who are his temple.

“And all the people came to him, and sitting, he taught them.” The Lord’s sitting suggests the humility of his incarnation, through which he deigned to have mercy on us. It is rightly said that when Jesus was sitting and teaching, all the people came to him, because after he had become near to human beings through the humility of his flesh, his word was more readily received by many. For by arrogant impiety he was despised by many; yet “the meek heard and rejoiced.”

“Now the scribes and Pharisees brought a woman caught in adultery, and set her in the middle, and said to him: Teacher, this woman has just been caught in adultery; in the law Moses commanded us to stone such women,” and so forth. If he decided that she should be stoned, they would mock him as though he had forgotten the mercy he always taught. If he forbade her to be stoned, they would gnash their teeth against him and condemn him, seemingly with justification, as a supporter of crimes and an opponent of the law.

“But Jesus, bending down, wrote with his finger on the ground.” Through Jesus’ bending, humility is expressed; through the finger, which is flexible in the articulation of the joints, the subtlety of discernment is expressed. Through the earth, moreover, the human heart is shown, which habitually produces either good or evil fruits.

When the Lord was asked to judge the sinful woman, he did not immediately give judgment. First he bent down and wrote on the ground, and only then, when he was insistently questioned, did he judge. He was teaching us figuratively that whenever we see the faults of our neighbors, we should not judge them by reproving them before we have humbly returned to our own conscience and carefully examined it with the finger of discernment. We must diligently distinguish what pleases or displeases its Creator, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Brothers, if a person is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. 6).

“When they persisted in questioning him, he straightened up and said to them: Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her.” The scribes and Pharisees were setting traps for the Lord on every side, thinking that he would either be merciless in judgment or unjust. But, foreseeing their plots, he passed through them like a thread through a spider’s web, displaying in every respect both the judgment of justice and the gentleness of mercy.

Behold the restraint of mercy: “Let him who is without sin among you.” Behold again the justice of judgment: “Let him be the first to throw a stone at her.” As if he had said: If Moses commanded you to stone such a woman, see that he did not command sinners but righteous men to do this. First fulfill the justice of the law yourselves, and then, with innocent hands and a pure heart, hasten to stone the guilty woman. First fulfill the spiritual decrees of the law—faith, mercy, and charity—and then turn to judging carnal matters.

“And again bending down, he wrote on the ground.” In accordance with ordinary human custom, it may be understood that the Lord wished to bend down and write on the ground before his wicked testers in order to direct his face elsewhere and give them the opportunity to leave. He foresaw that, struck by his answer, they would depart more quickly than they would ask further questions.

“When they heard this, they went out one by one, beginning with the elders, and he remained alone, with the woman standing in the middle.” But this figuratively admonishes us in that, both before and after giving judgment, he bent down and wrote on the ground. We are thereby taught that both before reproving a sinful neighbor and after carrying out the ministry of the correction owed to him, we should examine ourselves with a suitable investigation of humility, lest we be entangled either in the same offenses that we rebuke in them or in any others.

It could happen, for example, that the very person who has judged a murderer deserving of death is found, through hatred of his brother, to be guilty of death in himself before the eyes of the Creator. Similarly, one who accuses a brother of the crime of fornication may fail to see in himself the offense of pride. Therefore the judge of another’s crime is commanded to write it in his own heart with the finger of discernment, lest he be found guilty in himself.

What remedy, then, what means of salvation, remains for us amid such dangers? Nothing except that, whenever we see another sinning, we should immediately bend down—that is, recognize how cast down we are by the condition of our weakness, unless divine mercy sustains us—and look upon ourselves humbly. Let us write with the finger upon the earth; that is, let us weigh the matter with careful discernment and consider whether we can say with blessed Job: “Our heart has not reproached us throughout our whole life.”

He rightly wrote upon the earth while bent down, and when he stood upright he brought forth words of mercy. For what he promised through fellowship with human weakness, he bestowed upon all as a gift of mercy through the power of divine might.

“Straightening up, Jesus said to her: Woman, where are they who accused you? Has no one condemned you?” She said: “No one, Lord.” And Jesus said to her: “Neither will I condemn you. Go, and from now on sin no more.”

No one dared to condemn the sinful woman, because each had begun to perceive in himself something that he recognized as more deserving of condemnation. But let us see with what gift of mercy he who drove away the crowds of accusers by bringing forth the weight of justice lifts up the woman who was accused. The text continues:

“Jesus said: Neither will I condemn you. Go, and from now on sin no more.” For he is merciful and compassionate and releases past sins. Because he is just and loves justice, he forbids her to sin any more.

*(From Augustine.)* They were saying among themselves: “Either he will order her to be stoned, and he will lose the gentleness by which he pleases people; or he will order her released, and we will hold him as a transgressor of the law.” What, then, did the Lord answer? He ordered her to be stoned, saying: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her.” For the law wished to have such ministers as would first avoid what they blamed in others.

What does “He bent down and wrote on the ground” mean? Eternal Majesty descended to us, and, clothed in mortal flesh, descended to this dwelling-place of ours, where we live mortally; and he wrote on the ground with his finger. To write is to make a sign, and letters are signs of sounds. When I say “God,” these two syllables and four letters are signs of the great reality called God, at whose sound every human conscience trembles.

Therefore, what else does “he wrote on the ground” mean except that he made signs on the ground? Everything the Lord did here—whether he raised the dead or gave sight to the blind—he was writing on the ground. All such things are signs of realities, expressed in the body and signified in the soul. For what he wished to do in the soul, he prefigured in the body.

Lazarus did not rise in such a way that he would not die again; nor, when he healed the eyes of the blind, did he prevent them from being closed in death. What benefit, then, did it have that he made signs—that is, wrote on the ground with his finger? Bodily deeds directed wonder; wonder suspended judgment; and this caused people to seek the power of visible realities and to be invisibly healed so as to contemplate invisible things.

## HARMONY

Although these two readings agree with one another extensively in a figurative sense, historically their harmony is found in the very name of the mountain.

[Col. 0148B]

## THE TWENTIETH SUNDAY

## THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE GALATIANS, CHAPTER 4

> “It is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But the son of the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman was born through the promise. These things are spoken allegorically. For these are the two covenants: one indeed from Mount Sinai, generating unto slavery, which is Hagar. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, joined to the Jerusalem that now is, and it is in slavery with its children. But the Jerusalem that is above is free, which is our mother. For it is written: Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because many are the children of the deserted woman, more than of her who has a husband. But we, brothers, are children of promise according to Isaac. But just as then he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the spirit, so also now. But what does Scripture say? Cast out the slave woman and her son. For the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman. Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman, by the freedom with which Christ has freed us.”

“It is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman.” *(From Augustine.)* Both indeed came from Abraham’s seed. But in the case of the one, the custom of nature displays his lineage; in the case of the other, the promise gave him birth, signifying grace. There human practice is shown; here divine beneficence is commended.

“But the son of the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman was born through the promise.” *(From Primasius.)* Ishmael was the son of the flesh; Isaac was the son of faith. Abraham begot the former from a slave woman according to carnal custom; he received the latter contrary to nature by believing the promise.

“These things are spoken allegorically.” That is, one thing is figured from another. The Apostle gave a rule for how we ought to allegorize: namely, that while the truth of the history remains, we should understand the figures. For after saying that Abraham truly had two wives, he subsequently indicated in a mystical sense what those very women prefigured. This is directed against those who wish everything to be understood according to the letter and do not accept an allegorical meaning.

“For these are the two covenants, one indeed from Mount Sinai.” The teaching of the Old and New Testaments is like two mothers, but the Old Testament was given through Moses on Mount Sinai.

*(From Ambrose.)* The Old Testament, which generates unto slavery from Mount Sinai, profits nothing except insofar as it bears witness to the New Testament. Otherwise, as long as Moses is read, a veil lies over their hearts. But when someone passes from there to Christ, the veil of those who pass over is removed, since the very direction of attention is changed—from the Old to the New—so that each person may put on the New.

“Generating unto slavery, which is Hagar.” He said “generating unto slavery” because the Jews, through fear of present punishment and danger, were compelled as slaves to observe the commandments. Christians, however, are invited to the easy yoke and light burden by rewards, as free persons. Those others, as slaves, are occupied even with various works because of moral precepts. For us, as sons, all servile burdens are removed once the moral precepts have been fulfilled; while they, serving the priests under obligation, were also compelled to pay tribute. We, however, owing nothing except charity, voluntarily honor our bishops.

“Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, joined to the one that is now Jerusalem, and it is in slavery with its children.” From the qualities of the places he demonstrates the difference between the covenants. He therefore wishes Hagar to be understood as the synagogue, and the earthly Jerusalem, to which Mount Sinai, where the law was written, is joined. Its children therefore serve under the burdens of legal commandments.

“But the Jerusalem that is above is free.” In the person of Sarah he signifies either the Church or the heavenly Jerusalem. Therefore the mediator and high priest of the New Testament came from heaven, and the Gospel was preached not in one place of Judea but throughout the whole world.

“Which is our mother.” From the children of the Church, which is free, the Jerusalem above is built; therefore the Galatians, as free children, ought not to be slaves.

“For it is written: Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail.” He proves that we have another mother, better than the Jerusalem of the Jews. The Church, the mother of the Gentiles, had long been deserted by the Holy Spirit. Before the grace of regeneration she had no two sons, but afterward she gave birth to the nations and peoples, with God working within her.

How numerous are the children of the deserted woman—that is, of the Church, whom Anna prefigured when she said prophetically: “For the barren woman has borne seven, and she who had many children has grown weak,” that is, the Synagogue through the transgression of her unbelieving children. In the seven, the sevenfold grace of the Spirit is indicated. It should be noted that when he says, “The children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who had a husband,” the Synagogue is not entirely excluded from bearing children; rather, the multitude of the Gentiles is preferred to it. For she too, in the apostles and through the apostles, first bore the people who came from the [Col. 0150A] Jews. Hence the two chief apostles divided among themselves the hosts of those who believed in Christ, of the circumcision and of the Gentiles, so that from both peoples they might build up Jerusalem, previously deserted and poor.

“More than she who has a husband.” Here understand the Synagogue, which was oppressed as though by the yoke of a husband, that is, by the burden of the law; or certainly this should be referred to the fact that, before she was cast out, she believed that she had a husband.

But we, brothers, are children of the promise according to Isaac. That is, not according to Ishmael; just as it was promised to Abraham concerning Isaac, so concerning us it was promised that all nations would be blessed in him.

“But just as then he who was born according to the flesh...” Those who are carnal always persecute those who are spiritual. Therefore we should not be surprised, [Col. 0150B] but should recognize from this that we are spiritual if such people persecute us—something the Apostle indicated elsewhere under another mystery: “The flesh resists the spirit, and the spirit resists the flesh.”

Those who can understand should recognize that the Catholic Church suffers persecution from the pride and impiety of carnal people. For whatever the true and legitimate mother Church does—even if it is felt to be harsh and bitter—she does not repay evil with evil, but opposes the evil of iniquity with the good of discipline by expelling it.

“He was persecuting him who was according to the spirit.” It is written in Genesis: “Because Ishmael was playing with Isaac” (Gen. XXI). But here it is shown that it was not a simple game, since he calls it persecution. Hence it is understood that he wished to make the play clownish and frivolous, as he himself was, [Col. 0150C] so that he might not be preferred to Isaac in the inheritance. Therefore Abraham was commanded, by casting Ishmael out, to heed Sarah’s voice.

“So also now.” That is, these people similarly seek to make you slaves of the law.

“But what does Scripture say? Cast out the slave woman and her son.” However greatly iniquity may exalt itself, it is still a slave woman and must be subjected to the holy. Likewise the Jews, however much they boast that they are Abraham’s children, so long as they remain children of the slave woman and live carnally under the yoke of the law, will not be able to share the inheritance with us.

“For the son of the slave woman will not be heir with the son of the free woman.” Now, therefore, we must ask why Sarah previously wished her husband to receive a son from the slave woman, or why she now commands that he be expelled from the house along with his mother—not because she was inflamed by jealousy, [Col. 0150D] but because she was compelled by the mystery of prophecy. For Hagar, as the Apostle says, bore a carnal people into slavery. Sarah, however, bore a free people, who were called not according to the flesh but in freedom—the freedom with which Christ freed them. By this mystery, therefore, it was prefigured that the earlier people, generated in the house of Rachel—that is, of the Church—for slavery to sins, would not remain forever, nor be heirs or companions of the worshipers of Christ, nor possess the kingdom of heavenly glory with the noble son, that is, with the faithful people. The fact that Hagar, when she departed, placed the child upon her shoulders signifies that the sinful and foolish people of the Jews weighed down the neck of their mother, the Synagogue, when they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII). The fact that Hagar wandered in the wilderness with her son signifies that the Synagogue, expelled from its land together with its people, is without priesthood and sacrifice throughout the whole world and is utterly ignorant of the way, which is Christ.

Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman, by the freedom with which Christ freed us. We must not, then, abandon our mother and follow the slave woman. For although she was the wife of the same husband, she was so only for a time, because Sarah could not yet give birth—that is, because the Church had not yet been made fertile by the Spirit as her husband.

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0151A]

“Jesus went across the Sea of Galilee, which is that of Tiberias. And a great multitude followed him, because they saw the signs [Col. 0151B] that he performed upon those who were ill. Jesus therefore went up onto the mountain, and there he sat with his disciples. Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was near. When Jesus had therefore raised his eyes and had seen that a very great multitude was coming to him, he said to Philip: ‘Where shall we buy bread, so that these people may eat?’ But he said this to test him, for he himself knew what he was going to do. Philip answered him: ‘Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for them, so that each might receive even a little.’ One of his disciples, Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, said to him: ‘There is one boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are these among so many?’ Jesus therefore said: ‘Make the people sit down.’ [Col. 0151C] Now there was much grass in the place. The men therefore sat down, about five thousand in number. Jesus then took the loaves and, after giving thanks, distributed them to those who were seated; likewise also as much of the fish as they wished. When they had been filled, he said to his disciples: ‘Gather up the fragments that remain, so that they may not be lost.’ They therefore gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves and the two fish that remained after those who had eaten. When those people had seen the sign that he had performed, they said: ‘This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world.’”

[Col. 0151D]

“Jesus went across the Sea of Galilee, which is that of Tiberias, and a great multitude followed him,” and so forth. (From Bede.) First, according to the historical sense, it should be said that the Sea of Galilee, which is distinguished by many names according to the diversity of the surrounding regions, is called the Sea of Tiberias only in those places where it displays Tiberias, a city which, as they say, offers a healthy habitation because of its warm waters. For, with the Jordan flowing through it, it extends eighteen thousand paces in length and five in width. Mystically, however, the sea signifies the turbid and swelling waves of this world, in which all wicked people, delighting unjustly, like fish given over to the depths, do not direct their minds toward heavenly joys. Hence that same sea is aptly called Galilee, that is, “wheel,” because the love of the passing world, as though into a whirlpool, casts down hearts and does not permit them to rise toward the desires of eternal life. Concerning such people the Psalmist says: “The wicked walk in a circle” (Ps. XII). [Col. 0152A]

But as Jesus departed across the Sea of Galilee, a very great multitude followed him, so that it might receive from him the highest gifts of the teaching, healing, and heavenly nourishment of salvation. Before the Lord appeared in the flesh, only the Jewish nation followed him by believing. But after, through the dispensation of his incarnation, he approached, trod upon, and crossed the waves of corruptible life, a very great multitude of believing nations immediately followed him, desiring to be spiritually instructed, healed, and satisfied.

Jesus therefore went up onto the mountain, and there he sat with his disciples. We should not believe that it happened without reason that Jesus, going up onto the mountain, sat there with his disciples, but, when the multitude came to him, descended and refreshed it in the higher places, whom shortly before he had healed in the lower places. [Col. 0152B] Rather, this was mystically to signify that the Lord distributes his teaching and charisms according to the capacity of those receiving them: to minds still weak and spiritually childlike he entrusts simpler instructions and reveals the more obvious mysteries; but to those of higher and more perfect understanding he discloses the more hidden secrets of his majesty, suggests the loftier paths of devoted conduct, and promises the higher gifts of heavenly rewards.

“Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was near.” The fact that, as the Passover approached, the Lord taught, healed, and refreshed the crowds can be interpreted mystically in this way: Passover is called a “passing over,” and all whom the Lord restores through the inward sweetness of his gifts he prepares for a salutary passage, so that they may transcend carnal desires through the elevation of the mind and likewise trample underfoot the weak desires and adversities of the world through heavenly hope and love. [Col. 0152C]

“When Jesus had therefore raised his eyes and had seen that a very great multitude was coming to him, he said to Philip: ‘Where shall we buy bread, so that these people may eat?’” The fact that Jesus is said to have raised his eyes and seen the multitude coming to him is an indication of divine compassion, since heavenly mercy is accustomed to meet all who seek to come to him. And so that they may not go astray while seeking, he does not cease to open the light of his Spirit to those who hasten toward him. That the eyes of Jesus mystically signify the gifts of his Spirit is testified by John in the Apocalypse. Speaking figuratively of him, he says: “And I saw a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth” (Rev. V). [Col. 0152D]

“But he said this to test him, for he himself knew what he was going to do. Philip answered him: ‘Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for them, so that each might receive even a little.’” When the Lord tested Philip and said, “Where,” he said, “shall we buy bread so that these people may eat?” he acted according to a provident dispensation—not so that he himself might learn something he did not know, but so that Philip, when tested, might recognize the slowness of his faith, which he himself did not know, though the Teacher did, and might correct it through the miracle. For he ought not to have doubted in the presence of the Creator of all things, who brings bread forth from the earth and gladdens the human heart with wine, that bread purchased for a few denarii could suffice for thousands of crowds—not merely so that each might receive enough, but even so that each might depart satisfied. [Col. 0153A]

“One of his disciples, Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, said to him: ‘There is one boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are these among so many?’” The five loaves with which he satisfied the multitude of the people are the five books of Moses. Once these have been disclosed through spiritual understanding and multiplied through a now more abundant sense, they daily refresh the hearts of faithful hearers. They are rightly reported to have been barley loaves, because of the harsher decrees of the law and the coarser coverings of the letter, which concealed the marrow, as it were, of the inner spiritual meaning. [Col. 0153B]

The two fish that he added signify, not inappropriately, the writings of the psalmists and the prophets. One by singing and the other by speaking, they related to their hearers the mysteries of Christ and the Church that were to come. And the heralds of that age are rightly figured by aquatic creatures, since the people of the faithful could in no way live without the waters of baptism.

Some think that the two fish, which gave a pleasant taste to the bread, signify those two persons by whom that people was governed, so that through them it might receive the direction of counsel—namely, the royal and the priestly persons. To these also that sacred anointing pertained. Their duty was never to be broken or corrupted by the storms and waves of the people, and to break through the violent contradictions of the crowds like opposing waves, while at times yielding to them without abandoning their integrity. [Col. 0153C] They were, in short, to live like fish amid a stormy sea, so to speak, in the turbulent administration of the people. These two persons, however, were merely prefigured; Christ alone bore both offices, and fulfilled them alone not figuratively but literally.

“There is one boy here,” and so forth. The boy who had the five loaves and two fish, yet did not distribute them to the hungry crowds but offered them to the Lord to distribute, is the Jewish people, childish in its literal understanding; or it is the people that kept within itself the sayings of Scripture in a closed form.
