When the Lord appeared in the flesh, he received these sayings and showed what usefulness and sweetness they contained. He disclosed how, through the manifold grace of the Spirit, what had seemed scanty and contemptible overflowed, and he extended these things to be administered to all nations through his apostles and their successors. [Col. 0153D]

Hence other evangelists rightly report that the Lord gave the loaves and fish to the disciples, while the disciples ministered them to the crowds. For when the mystery of human salvation had begun to be proclaimed by the Lord, it was confirmed for us by those who heard it. He broke and distributed the five loaves and the two fish to the disciples when he opened their understanding, so that they might understand everything written about him in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms. The disciples set them before the crowds when, going forth, they preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed. [Col. 0154A]

“Jesus therefore said, ‘Make the people sit down’; now there was grass,” and so forth. The grass upon which the crowd sits while being refreshed signifies carnal desire, which everyone who wishes to be satisfied with spiritual nourishment ought to trample and suppress. For “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. XI). Let him therefore sit upon the grass and crush the flower of the grass—that is, let him discipline his body and subject it to servitude, tame the pleasures of the flesh, and restrain the passing indulgences of luxury—whoever desires to be refreshed by the sweetness of the living bread.

“The men therefore sat down, about five thousand in number.” The five thousand men who ate signify the perfection of the life of those who are refreshed by the word, to whom the Apostle says: “Act manfully and be strengthened” (1 Cor. XVI). [Col. 0154B] The number one thousand, beyond which no human reckoning increases, commonly signifies the fullness of the matters under discussion. By the number five, however, the five well-known senses of our body are expressed: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. All who strive to act manfully and be strengthened in each of these, living soberly, justly, and devoutly and being renewed by the sweetness of heavenly wisdom, are represented by the five thousand men whom the Lord satisfied with mystical food.

(From Origen.) They rightly sat down, according to Mark, by fifties and hundreds. The fiftieth psalm is the psalm of repentance; it signifies those who, still engaged in repentance for their sins, come to God’s banquet and receive the hearing of the word. Those counted by hundreds are those who, already relying upon the hope of forgiveness, sigh only for the desire of eternal life. [Col. 0154C] Alternatively, the groups of fifty signify those who cease from evil deeds, while the groups of one hundred signify those who cease even from evil thoughts.

“Jesus therefore took the loaves and, after giving thanks, distributed them to those who were seated, and likewise of the fish as much as they wished.” The Savior does not create new kinds of food, but, taking what the disciples had, he blesses it. Coming in the flesh, he preached nothing other than what had been foretold. But he demonstrates how full of the mysteries of grace are the writings of the law and the prophets. He gave thanks so that he might teach us always to give thanks for gifts received from heaven, and also to indicate how much he rejoices in our progress. [Col. 0154D] He broke the loaves and, through the apostles, distributed them to those who were seated, because through holy teachers, who preached these things throughout the world, he distributed the mysteries of prophecy.

“When they had been filled, he said to his disciples: ‘Gather up the fragments that remain, so that they may not be lost.’” What remains from the crowds is gathered up by the disciples, because the more sacred and hidden mysteries of the divine utterances, which cannot be grasped by the untrained, must not be carelessly neglected but sought out by the mature.

“They therefore gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five loaves that remained.” The number twelve ordinarily signifies perfection. The twelve baskets rightly express the twelve apostles, and through the apostles the whole chorus of spiritual teachers—despised by people outwardly, but inwardly filled with saving food. [Col. 0155A] For it is well known that baskets are ordinarily used for servile work. Yet he filled baskets with fragments of bread who chose the weak things of the world in order to confound the strong.

“When those people had seen the sign that he had performed, they said: ‘This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world.’” They rightly called the Lord a great prophet, a herald of great salvation, who was already to come into the world. He himself also deigned to call himself a prophet when he said: “It is not possible for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem.” But they had not yet advanced to complete faith, because they did not know how to call him God as well. [Col. 0155B]

We, with a more certain knowledge of truth and faith, seeing the world that Jesus made and the signs with which he filled it, should say: “This is truly the mediator between God and human beings, who would fill the world with divinity; and the world was made through him.” He came in the humanity that was his own, to seek and save what had perished and to restore the world that he had made.

## MONDAY AFTER THE TWENTIETH

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER II

[Col. 0155C]

“The Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. And he found in the temple those selling sheep and oxen and doves, and the money-changers sitting there. And after making something like a whip from cords, he drove them all out of the temple, the sheep and the oxen as well; he poured out the money of the money-changers and overturned their tables. And to those who were selling doves he said: ‘Take these things away from here, and do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.’ His disciples remembered that it was written: ‘Zeal for your house has consumed me.’ The Jews therefore answered and said to him: ‘What sign do you show us, since you do these things?’ Jesus answered and said to them: ‘Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.’ The Jews therefore said: ‘This temple was built in forty-six years, and you will raise it up in three days?’ But he was speaking about the temple of his body. When therefore he had risen from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken. When he was in Jerusalem at Passover, on the feast day, many believed in his name, seeing the signs that he performed. But Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them, because he knew them all, and because he had no need for anyone to testify concerning a human being. For he himself knew what was in a human being.”

“The Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.” The fact that, as the Passover approached, Jesus went up to Jerusalem gives us a clear example of how vigilantly we must submit to the Lord’s commands, since he himself, appearing in human weakness, observed the decrees that he established by the authority of his divinity. [Col. 0155D] For lest servants should think that, without the frequent sacrifices of prayers and good works, they could either escape punishments or receive rewards, the Son of God himself went up among those who serve, to be worshiped and offered as a sacrifice. Let us see what he found them doing in Jerusalem and what he himself did there.

“And he found in the temple those selling oxen and sheep and doves, and the money-changers sitting there.” The money-changers sat at tables so that payment might readily be assessed between the buyers and sellers of sacrifices. Thus the things being sold in the temple appeared to be sold lawfully, since they were bought for the purpose of being offered to the Lord in that same temple. But the Lord himself did not wish anything belonging to earthly commerce—even commerce thought honest—to be displayed in his house. He drove out the unjust traders and expelled them all together with the things in which they traded. [Col. 0156A]

What, then, my brothers, do we think the Lord would do if he found people entangled in quarrels, occupied with frivolous talk, or caught up in any other crime—he who saw people buying sacrifices to be offered to him in the temple and took care to drive them out?

“And after making something like a whip from cords, he drove them all out of the temple, the sheep and the oxen as well; he poured out the money of the money-changers and overturned their tables, and said to those who were selling doves: ‘Take these things away from here, and do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.’” We should greatly fear that he may find and condemn us in the temple as money-changers or sellers of oxen, sheep, and doves.

Oxen signify the teaching of heavenly life. Sheep signify works of purity and devotion. Doves signify the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Those sell oxen who offer the word of the Gospel to their hearers not out of divine love but with an eye to earthly profit—people whom the Apostle condemns because they announce Christ “not sincerely.” [Col. 0156B] Those sell sheep who perform works of devotion for the sake of human praise; concerning them the Lord says: “They have received their reward.” Those sell doves who give the grace of the Spirit that they have received not freely, as commanded, but for a reward. They confer the laying on of hands, by which the Spirit is received, not necessarily for monetary gain but for the favor of the crowd; they grant sacred orders not for the merit of life but for favor.

They lend money in the temple who serve earthly things openly in the Church rather than heavenly things in sincerity, seeking their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ.

“His disciples remembered that it was written: ‘Zeal for your house has consumed me.’” (From Augustine.) Let zeal for the house of God consume every Christian. You are a member of God’s house; if you happen to see anything perverse, strive to correct it and do not cease from amending it. For example, if you see a brother running to the theater, forbid him, warn him, admonish him, if zeal for the house of God consumes you. If you see others running off and wanting to get drunk, forbid those whom you can, restrain those whom you can, frighten those whom you can, speak gently to those whom you can; nevertheless, do not cease. [Col. 0156C]

He is a friend: let him be gently admonished. She is a wife: let her be restrained with the greatest severity. She is a maidservant: let her even be checked by blows. Do whatever you can according to the person whose role you bear. Do not cease to win Christ, because you were won by Christ, and fulfill in yourself: “Zeal for your house has consumed me.”

But if you are cold and sluggish, waiting only upon yourself, as though you were sufficient for yourself, and saying in your heart, “Why should I concern myself with another’s sins? My soul is enough for me; let me preserve it whole for God,” does there not come to your mind that servant who hid his talent and refused to distribute it? [Col. 0157A]

It should also be noted that not only are those sellers of doves who make God’s house a house of trade by seeking payment in money, praise, or even honor through conferring sacred orders. So too are those who exercise a spiritual rank or grace in the Church, which they received through the Lord’s generosity, not with a simple intention but for the sake of some human return, contrary to the words of the Apostle Peter: “Whoever speaks, as the words of God; whoever serves, as from the strength that God supplies, so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ” (1 Pet. IV).

The cords with which he scourged and drove the wicked from the temple are the growths of evil deeds, from which material for condemning the reprobate is supplied to the strict Judge. [Col. 0157B] Hence Isaiah says: “Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity” (Isa. V). And Solomon says in Proverbs: “His own iniquities capture the wicked, and he is bound with the cords of his sins” (Prov. V). For whoever heaps sins upon sins, for which he will be condemned more severely, gradually increases and lengthens the cords by which he will be bound and scourged.

He also poured out the money of the money-changers whom he had expelled and overturned their tables, because at the end, when the reprobate are condemned, he will remove even the appearance of the very things they loved, according to what is written: “The world will pass away, and its desire.” And to those who sold doves he said: “Take these things away from here, and do not make my Father’s house a house of trade” (1 John II). [Col. 0157C] He commanded the sale of doves to be removed from the temple because whoever has freely received the grace of the Spirit ought freely to give it. Hence that magician Simon, who wished to purchase it with money so that he might sell it at a higher price, heard: “May your money be with you for destruction; you have neither part nor share in this word” (Acts V).

The Jews therefore answered and said to him: “What sign do you show us, since you do these things?” Jesus answered and said to them: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” The evangelist later made clear which temple he meant: namely, the temple of his body, which they would destroy through the Passion and which he himself would raise from death after three days.

Since they were asking the Lord for a sign—why should he have driven the customary commerce from the temple?—he answered that he was entirely justified in expelling the wicked from the temple because that temple signified the temple of his body, in which there could be absolutely no stain of sin. [Col. 0157D] Nor was it without reason that he cleansed the figurative temple of crimes, since he who could raise the true temple of God, destroyed by human beings through death, from the dead by the power of divine majesty, also cleansed the figure.

The Jews therefore said: “This temple was built in forty-six years, and you will raise it up in three days?” They understood it one way and answered accordingly. But lest we also understand the Lord’s spiritual word carnally, the evangelist subsequently explained which temple was meant.

When they speak of a temple built in forty-six years, they do not signify its first construction but its second. Solomon completed the first temple in the greatest peace of his reign through a very splendid labor of seven years. After it had been destroyed by the Chaldeans, it began to be rebuilt seventy years later, at the command of Cyrus the Persian, when the captivity had been released. But the children of the exile, because of the opposition of neighboring nations, could not complete the work that Zerubbabel and Joshua were carrying out until forty-six years had passed. [Col. 0158A] This number of years also corresponds most suitably to the perfection of the Lord’s body.

For writers on natural matters report that the human body is perfected over this many days. During the first six days after conception it has the appearance of milk; during the following nine it is changed into blood; then over twelve days it is solidified; during the remaining eighteen it is strengthened until the complete formation of all the limbs; and from that point onward, until the time of birth, it increases in size. Six, nine, twelve, and eighteen make forty-five. [Col. 0158B] If we add one—the very day on which the body, differentiated into its members, begins to grow—we arrive at the same number of days in the building of the Lord’s body as we find years in the construction of the temple.

And that temple made by human hands prefigured the Lord’s most holy flesh, which he took from the Virgin, as we learn from this passage; the following transmitted clause is textually corrupt: “quae quia ea quod corpus ejus, quod est Ecclesia, quia unusquisque fidelium corpus animamque designabat”; it appears to say that it signified his body, which is the Church, and the body and soul of each believer, as we find in many places of Scripture.

The first Adam, after sin, heard: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III). [Col. 0158C] But the second Adam said of himself: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II).

The first Adam was scattered throughout the whole world; in the second he was gathered together. This is signified by the name Adam, which is written with four letters, α, δ, α, and μ. These four letters signify the four parts of the world into which Adam was scattered in his children. Therefore these four letters are found at the beginnings of the names of the parts of the world. For ἄρκτος, which means “north,” begins with α; and δύσις, which means “west,” begins with δ; and ἀνατολή, which means “east,” begins with α; and μεσημβρία, which means “south,” begins with μ. These are the four parts of the world. [Col. 0158D]

Beginning with these four letters, which, when considered according to Greek reckoning, make forty-six—α being one, δ four, α again one, and μ forty—their total is forty-six. This mystically signifies the forty-six years during which the temple of Christ’s body was built in the Virgin’s womb, as we said above.

The flesh of Christ, which was taken from Adam, was destroyed by the Jews and built again by him, according to the writings of the prophets. Therefore the evangelist says: “For he was speaking about the temple of his body.”

“When he had risen from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture”—that is, the prophets, who foretold that Christ would rise on the third day—“and the word that Jesus had spoken,” namely: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”; that is, “On the third day I will raise up what you will destroy on the cross.” [Col. 0159A]

“When he was in Jerusalem at Passover, on the feast day, many believed in his name, seeing his signs that he performed. But Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them, because he knew them all, and because he had no need for anyone to testify concerning a human being, for he himself knew what was in a human being.” They did not believe in him in such a way as to be worthy for Christ to dwell in them. Their faith may be compared with that of catechumens: they believe in Christ, but Christ does not entrust himself to them, because unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. Christ entrusts himself to no one except one who is worthy to enter the kingdom of God; and no one is worthy to enter the kingdom of God unless he has been born of water and the Spirit. [Col. 0159B]

## WEDNESDAY AFTER THE TWENTIETH

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER IX

“Passing by, Jesus saw a man blind from birth, and his disciples asked him: ‘Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he should be born blind?’ Jesus answered: ‘Neither this man sinned nor his parents, but so that the works of God might be manifested in him. I must perform the works of him who sent me while it is day. Night is coming, when no one can work. As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.’ When he had said this, he spat on the ground, made clay from the spittle, and spread the clay upon his eyes. And he said to him: ‘Go and wash in the pool of Siloam,’ which is interpreted as ‘Sent.’ [Col. 0159C] He therefore went and washed, and came back seeing.

“Then the neighbors and those who had previously seen him, because he was a beggar, said: ‘Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?’ Some said: ‘It is he.’ Others said: ‘No, but he is like him.’ But he said: ‘I am he.’ They therefore said to him: ‘How were your eyes opened?’ He answered: ‘The man who is called Jesus made clay and anointed my eyes, and said to me: “Go to the pool of Siloam and wash.” I went, washed, and I see.’ And they said to him: ‘Where is he?’ He said: ‘I do not know.’

“They brought him to the Pharisees, the man who had been blind. Now it was the Sabbath when Jesus made the clay and opened his eyes. Again the Pharisees asked him how he had come to see. But he said to them: ‘He put clay upon my eyes, and I washed, and I see.’ Some of the Pharisees therefore said: ‘This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath.’ [Col. 0159D] Others said: ‘How can a sinful man perform such signs?’ And there was division among them.

“They said again to the blind man: ‘What do you say about him who opened your eyes?’ But he said: ‘He is a prophet.’ The Jews therefore did not believe concerning him that he had been blind and had come to see, until they called his parents, of the man who now saw, and questioned them, saying: ‘Is this your son, whom you say was born blind? How then does he now see?’

“His parents answered them and said: ‘We know that this is our son and that he was born blind. But how he now sees, we do not know; nor do we know who opened his eyes. Ask him; he is of age. Let him speak for himself.’ [Col. 0160A] His parents said these things because they feared the Jews. For the Jews had already conspired that if anyone confessed Christ, he should be expelled from the synagogue. Therefore his parents said: ‘He is of age; ask him.’

“They therefore called again the man who had been blind and said to him: ‘Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner.’ He therefore said: ‘Whether he is a sinner, I do not know. One thing I know: though I was blind, now I see.’ They therefore said to him: ‘What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?’ He answered them: ‘I told you already, and you heard. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?’ [Col. 0160B]

“They reviled him and said: ‘You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses. We know that God spoke to Moses; but as for this man, we do not know where he is from.’ The man answered and said to them: ‘Why, this is remarkable: you do not know where he is from, and yet he opened my eyes. We know that God does not hear sinners; but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God hears him. From the beginning of the world it has not been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a person born blind. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.’

“They answered and said to him: ‘You were born entirely in sins, and are you teaching us?’ And they cast him out.

“Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and when he had found him, he said to him: ‘Do you believe in the Son of God?’ He answered and said: ‘Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?’ [Col. 0160C] Jesus said to him: ‘You have seen him, and the one speaking with you is he.’ He said: ‘I believe, Lord,’ and falling down, he worshiped him.”

Jesus, passing by, saw a man blind from birth, etc. This blind man signifies the human race. This blindness befell the first man through sin, from whom we all derived our origin—not only of death but also of iniquity. The Lord came, spat on the ground, and made clay from his saliva, because the Word became flesh; he anointed the man’s eyes and sent him to the pool of Siloam, which is interpreted as “Sent.” The Lord Jesus Christ, indeed, was sent; for unless he had been sent, none of us would have been released from iniquity. He therefore washed his eyes in that pool, was baptized in Christ, and was enlightened. Blindness is unbelief, and enlightenment [Col. 0160D] is faith.

For they put a question to the Lord: “Who sinned, this man or his parents, that he should be born blind?” Jesus answered: “Neither did this man sin, nor his parents, that he should be born blind.” His parents did have sin, but it was not because of that sin that he was born blind; rather, it was so that the works of God might be manifested in him. When he says, “I must work the works of him who sent me, while it is day,” he evidently wished himself to be understood as the day in this passage; for he himself says, “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” But when he says, “The night is coming, when no one can work,” he speaks of that eternal and dark night in which the reprobate will be tormented without end, to whom it will be said: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” [Col. 0161A]. That is, into the outer darkness, where the wicked servant will be cast with hands and feet bound. Therefore, while it is day for us—he who said, “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age”—let us do good to everyone, so that that night may not overtake us, in which no one can work, but can only receive what he has done.

*(From Jerome.)* Siloa is a spring at the foot of Mount Zion. It does not bubble forth with continuous waters, but at uncertain hours through the hollows of the earth. There the blind man washes with the mud (*luto*); his blindness wiped away, he received the clear light of his eyes. This indicates that the blindness of the Jews, or of all unbelievers, cannot be healed in any other way than through the teaching of Christ’s waters, which flow gently, without the noise and clamor of words. For in Isaiah we read of the waters of Siloë, which [Col. 0161B] “go with silence.”

## Friday after the Twentieth

### The Gospel of John, Chapter XI

“There was a certain man sick, Lazarus of Bethany, from the village of Mary and Martha her sister. Now Mary was the woman who anointed the Lord with perfume and wiped his feet with her hair; her brother Lazarus was sick. Therefore his sisters sent to him, saying: ‘Lord, behold, the one whom you love is sick.’

“When Jesus heard this, he said to them: ‘This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.’ Jesus loved Martha and her sister Mary and Lazarus. When he heard, therefore, that he was sick, he then remained two [Col. 0161C] days in the same place. After this he said to his disciples: ‘Let us go again into Judea.’ The disciples said to him: ‘Rabbi, just now the Jews were seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?’

“Jesus answered: ‘Are there not twelve hours of the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if he walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.’ He said these things. And after this he said to them: ‘Lazarus our friend sleeps, but I am going to awaken him from sleep.’

“Therefore his disciples said: ‘Lord, if he sleeps, he will be safe.’ But Jesus had spoken about his death, whereas they thought that he was speaking about ordinary sleep. Then Jesus said to them openly: ‘Lazarus has died, and I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe, because I was not there; but let us go to him’ [Col. 0161D].

“Then Thomas, who is called Didymus, said to his fellow disciples: ‘Let us also go, so that we may die with him.’ Jesus therefore came and found that he had already been four days in the tomb. Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away. Many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother.

“When Martha heard that Jesus had come, she went to meet him; but Mary was sitting at home. Martha therefore said to Jesus: ‘Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.’

“Jesus said to her: ‘Your brother will rise again.’ Martha said to him: ‘I know that he will rise in the resurrection on the last [Col. 0162A] day.’ Jesus said to her: ‘I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live. And everyone who lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?’

“She said to him: ‘Yes, Lord; I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, who has come into this world.’ When she had said this, she went away and secretly called her sister Mary, saying: ‘The Teacher is here and is calling for you.’ As soon as she heard this, she rose quickly and came to him. For Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him.

“The Jews who were with her in the house and were consoling her, when they saw Mary rise quickly and go out, followed her, saying: ‘She is going to the tomb to weep there.’ When Mary came to where Jesus was, she saw him and fell at his feet, saying to him: ‘Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.’

“Jesus, therefore, when Mary came [Col. 0162B] to where he was and he saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, groaned in spirit and troubled himself. And he said: ‘Where have you laid him?’ They said to him: ‘Lord, come and see.’ And Jesus wept.

“Then the Jews said: ‘See how he loved him.’ But some of them said: ‘Could not he who opened the eyes of the man born blind have caused this man also not to die?’

“Jesus therefore, groaning again within himself, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone had been placed over it. Jesus said: ‘Take away the stone.’ Martha, the sister of the one who had died, said to him: ‘Lord, by now there is an odor, for he has been dead four days.’

“Jesus said to her: ‘Did I not tell you that if you believe, you will see the glory of God?’ [Col. 0162C] Therefore they took away the stone. Jesus, lifting his eyes upward, said: ‘Father, I give you thanks because you have heard me. I knew, indeed, that you always hear me; but because of the people standing around I said this, so that they may believe that you sent me.’

“When he had said these things, he cried out in a loud voice: ‘Lazarus, come forth!’ Immediately the man who had died came out, bound hand and foot with strips of cloth. His face was wrapped in a cloth. Jesus said to them: ‘Unbind him and let him go.’ Therefore many of the Jews who had come to Mary and had seen what he did believed in him.”

“There was a certain man sick, Lazarus of Bethany, from the village of Mary and Martha his sister, etc.” [Col. 0162D] Among all the miracles performed by our Lord Jesus Christ, the resurrection of Lazarus is especially proclaimed. Yet in the Gospel we read that the Lord raised three dead persons. He raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, still lying in the house; he raised the young man, the son of a widow, carried outside the city gate; and he raised Lazarus, buried and four days dead. These three dead persons signify three resurrections of souls.

Let each person look upon his own soul: if it sins, it dies, for sin is the death of the soul. The first death is consent to sin. This death was signified by that girl, who had not yet been carried outside but lay dead in the house, as though the sin were still hidden within. The second death is not merely to consent to sin but also to commit it. This was signified by the young man, whom the Lord raises and restores repentant to his mother, that is, to the Church [Col. 0163A]. The third kind of death is terrible: an evil habit, signified by Lazarus. Hence it is rightly said of him that he “stinks.” He begins to have a very bad reputation. Yet the sinner must not despair, because the Lord mercifully raised them all.

When it is added, “This sickness is not unto death,” he consequently continued: “but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.” There are heretics who deny that the Son of God is God. Let them hear: “This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God”—that is, of the Son of God.

“Jesus answered: Are there not twelve hours of the day?” etc. What does this answer mean? As far as I can see, he wished to rebuke their doubt [Col. 0163B] and unbelief. They wanted to advise the Lord not to die, although he had come to die. He rebuked them and said: “Are there not twelve hours of the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble.”

He showed himself to be the day, because spiritually he is the true day; the twelve hours are the twelve apostles. To show himself to be the day, he chose twelve disciples. “If I am the day,” he says, “and you are the hours, follow me, because the hours follow the day, not the day the hours.” Let the hours, then, follow the day; let the hours proclaim the day. Let the hours be illumined by the day, let the hours be enlightened by the day, and through the preaching of the hours let the world believe in the day. In brief, this is what he said: “Follow me, if you do not wish to stumble.”

When he said, “Lazarus our friend sleeps,” he spoke truly. To his sisters he was dead, since they could not raise him [Col. 0163C]; to the Lord he was sleeping, for he raised him from the tomb with as much ease as you now awaken a sleeper from his bed.

Many things can be said about the four days, according to the obscure passages of Scripture, which produce many meanings in accordance with the diversity of those who understand them. Let us also say what it seems to us that the four-day dead man signifies. Just as in the case of the blind man we understand, in a certain way, the human race, so perhaps in this dead man we shall understand many things. For one reality can be signified in different ways.

When a human being is born, he is already born with death, because he carries sin from Adam. Behold one day of death, which a human being derives from the propagation of death. Then he grows and begins to approach the rational years, so that he may understand the natural law, which [Col. 0163D] everyone has fixed in the heart: “What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another.” People transgress this law; behold a second day of death.

Moreover, the divine law, through God’s servant Moses, says to him: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not bear false witness; honor your father and your mother,” etc. Behold, the written law is given, and it too is despised. Behold the third day of death. What remains? The Gospel comes. Therefore the letter without grace made those who transgressed it guilty, while grace freed those who confessed.

Christ is preached everywhere; Gehenna is threatened; eternal life is promised—and this too is despised. People transgress the Gospel. Behold the fourth day of death; rightly, he already stinks. Is mercy to be denied even to such people? Certainly not. The Lord does not disdain to approach even such persons in order to raise them [Col. 0164A].

Then Martha said to Jesus: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.” Jesus said to her: “Your brother will rise again.” Because I am the resurrection and the life, whoever believes in me, even if he has died in the flesh, will live in the soul until he rises, and the flesh will never afterward die. And everyone who lives in the flesh and believes in me—even if he dies for a time because of the death of the flesh—will not die forever, because of the life of the spirit and the immortality of the resurrection. Do you believe this?

She said to him: “Yes, Lord; I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who has come into this world.” When I believed this, I believed that you are the resurrection and the life, and that whoever believes in you, even if he has died, will live.

“Jesus, therefore, when he saw her weeping, groaned in spirit,” [Col. 0164B] etc. What does it mean that Christ troubles himself, except that he shows you how you ought to be troubled when you are weighed down and oppressed by such a mass of sin? You examine yourself, see yourself guilty, and reckon: “I did that, and God spared me; I committed that, and he delayed punishment; I heard the Gospel, and despised it; I was baptized, and returned again to the same things.” What shall I do? Where shall I escape?

When you say these things, Christ already groans in your heart, because faith groans. If faith is in us, Christ is in us. Therefore your faith concerning Christ is Christ in your heart. In the voice of the one who groans, the hope of the one who will rise appears. Let Christ groan; let the human being rebuke himself. Christ wept; let the human being weep. Why did Christ weep, except to teach the human being to weep?

The human being ought, in a certain way, [Col. 0164C] to groan while accusing his evil deeds, so that the habit of sinning may yield to the force of repentance. He said: “Where have you laid him?” Do you know that he is dead, and do you not know where he is buried? This too is a sign, because God acts as though he does not know the human being who has been lost. Such is God’s voice in Paradise, after the human being sinned: “Adam, where are you?”

They say to him: “Lord, come and see.” What does “See” mean? Have mercy. For the Lord sees when he shows mercy.

Then the Jews said: “See how he loved him,” and so forth. What does “he loved him” mean? “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” The dead man is under the stone; the guilty man is under the law. The law given to the Jews was written on stone. All, however, are guilty under the law; those who live rightly live together with the law. What, then, does it mean to remove the stone? To preach grace [Col. 0164D].

What does it mean that he cried out in a loud voice: “Lazarus, come forth”? How difficult it is for one to rise whom the weight of an evil habit oppresses. Yet he rises; by hidden grace he is given life within. He rises after the loud voice, still bound hand and foot. “His face was wrapped in a cloth.” Yet he had already come forth. What does this signify?

When you show contempt, you lie dead; and if you show contempt for as many things as I have mentioned, you lie buried. When you confess, you come forth. But God brings it about that you confess: he cries out through a human voice, that is, he calls with great grace. But so that his sins might be loosed, the Lord said to his ministers: “Unbind him and let him go.” This means: “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.”

[Col. 0165A]

## Fifth Sunday in Lent

### The Epistle of Blessed Paul the Apostle to the Hebrews, Chapter IX

“Christ, appearing as High Priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made with hands—that is, not of this creation—and not through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood, entered once for all into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption.

“For if the blood of goats or bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled upon the defiled, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself unblemished to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God?

“And therefore he is the mediator of the New Testament, so that, with death having intervened for the redemption [Col. 0165B] of the transgressions committed under the former Testament, those who have been called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

“Christ, appearing as High Priest.” *(From Origen.)* There is indeed one great High Priest, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is not merely the priest of priests but the High Priest of high priests; not only the chief of priests but the chief of the chief priests, just as he is King of kings and Lord of lords. He is the one who, penetrating the veil (which the Apostle interpreted as heaven), now stands before the face of God for us, always living to intercede.

“Of the good things to come.” Either of the various spiritual gifts that were given to believers [Col. 0165C] through the Holy Spirit at the first coming, or of all the good things to come, concerning which the Psalmist confidently said: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm XXVII).

“Through the greater and more perfect tabernacle.” *(From John Chrysostom.)* Here the Apostle calls Christ’s flesh a tabernacle. For Christ’s flesh is called a tabernacle, possessing divinity within itself. In him, the Apostle says, “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily.” And rightly he called Christ’s flesh a greater and more perfect tabernacle, since both God the Word and the whole operation of the Spirit dwell in it.

“Not made with hands.” That is, not formed from human seed, but born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary. Daniel saw that very stone—that is, Christ—cut from the mountain, that is, from the kingdom of the Jews, without hands (Daniel II), because he was born without marital intercourse and filled the whole world by his grace [Col. 0165D].

“Not of this creation.” That is, he did not construct it without the Spirit, nor is it from this creation; that is, he is not from these created things but is spiritual, from the Holy Spirit.

“Not through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood he entered once for all into the holy places,” etc. Christ changed everything. He entered the holy places—that is, heaven—not through another’s blood but through his own, once for all, and by one entrance obtained eternal redemption.

“For if the blood of goats or bulls and the ashes of a heifer [Col. 0166A] sprinkled upon the defiled sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more the blood of Christ.” *(From Origen.)* If, he says, the blood of bulls can cleanse the flesh, much more has the blood of Christ wiped away the stain of the soul. In this very diversity of sacrifices, a shadow was given to them, but the truth has been reserved for us through Jesus Christ.

For them, oxen and goats were slaughtered; birds were offered, and fine flour was sprinkled. For us, however, the Son of God was sacrificed. The various types of sacrifices bore beforehand the image of Christ’s passion. After he himself had been offered, all those sacrifices ceased which had preceded him as his type or shadow, prefiguring that sacrifice which the one true priest offered, the mediator between God and human beings.

The promised figures of that sacrifice had first to be celebrated through animal victims [Col. 0166B], for the future cleansing of flesh and blood, which shall not possess the kingdom of God. Through that one victim there would be forgiveness of sins contracted through flesh and blood, and that same bodily substance would be changed into a heavenly quality.

He was offered in the calf because of the power of the cross; in the lamb because of innocence; in the ram because of leadership; in the goat because of the likeness of sinful flesh, so that he might condemn sin from sin. In the turtledove and the dove, because of God and the human being, since he was shown to be the mediator of God and humanity in the union of two substances.

Moreover, in the mingling of fine flour was clearly represented the Church gathered from believers through the water of baptism, which is the body of Christ.

Morally, we offer a calf as a gift to God when we overcome the pride of the flesh; a lamb when we correct irrational impulses and foolish behavior; a kid when we conquer wantonness; a dove when we display simplicity of mind; a turtledove when we preserve chastity of the flesh; unleavened loaves when we walk in the way of sincerity and truth [Col. 0166C].

“Who through the Holy Spirit offered himself unblemished to God.” That is, he offered an unblemished sacrifice. He was free from sins. This was accomplished through the Holy Spirit, not through fire and not through anything belonging to another.

“And cleansed our conscience from dead works, to serve the living God.” Here he makes clear that those who possess dead works—that is, sins [Col. 0166D]—cannot serve the true and living God. Just as one who touched a dead person was made unclean, so one who commits sin is even more defiled. To touch a dead person is, as it were, to follow or imitate someone who is dead in sins, or oneself.

“And therefore he is the mediator of the New Testament, so that, with death having intervened for the redemption of the transgressions committed under the former Testament, those who have been called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance.” This mediator became the Son of the Father and our mediator. He carried words and brought them to us from the Father through those who conveyed them. He died for us and made us worthy of the testament. In this way the testament was made firm.

[Col. 0167A]

### The Gospel of John, Chapter VIII

“Jesus was saying to the crowds of Jews and to the chief priests: ‘Which of you will convict me of sin? If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me? Whoever is from God hears the words of God. For this reason you do not hear them, because you are not from God.’

“Then the Jews answered and said to him: ‘Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?’

“Jesus answered: ‘I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you have dishonored me. I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges.

“‘Amen, amen, I say to you, if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.’

“Then the Jews said: ‘Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham died, and the prophets [Col. 0167B] died, and you say: “If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death.” Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets died. Whom do you make yourself?’

“Jesus answered: ‘If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say that he is our God, and you do not know him. But I know him. And if I were to say that I did not know him, I would be like you, a liar. But I know him, and I keep his word.

“‘Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and rejoiced.’

“Then the Jews said to him: ‘You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?’

“Jesus said to them: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, before Abraham came to be, I am.’

“Therefore they took up stones to throw at him. But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.”

“Jesus was saying to the crowds of Jews and to the chief priests: ‘Which of you will convict me of sin?’” *(From Gregory.)* Consider the gentleness of God. He had come to forgive sins, and he said: “Which of you will convict me of sin?” He does not disdain to demonstrate through reason that he is not a sinner, although by the power of his divinity he could justify sinners.

“If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me?” Why, except because you are children of the devil and not of truth? Children not by nature but by imitation. They were creatures of God, for he is the creator of flesh and soul; but through vice they were imitators of the devil.

“Whoever is from God hears the words of God. For this reason you do not hear them, because you are not from God.” If the one who is from God hears God’s words, and whoever is not from him cannot hear his words, let each person ask himself whether he perceives God’s words in the ear of his heart and understands from whom he comes.

Truth commands us to desire the heavenly homeland, to crush the desires of the flesh, to avoid the glory of the world, not to seize what belongs to others, and to give away what is our own. Let each of you consider whether this voice of God has grown strong in the ear of his heart and recognize that he is now from God [Col. 0167D].

Then the Jews said: “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” Having received such an insult, let us hear what the Lord replies.

[Col. 0168A]

“I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you have dishonored me.” Since “Samaritan” is interpreted as “guardian,” and he is truly the guardian of whom the Psalmist says, “Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain,” and to whom Isaiah says, “Guardian, what of the night? Guardian, what of the night?” (Isaiah XXI), the Lord did not wish to answer, “I am not a Samaritan,” but said, “I do not have a demon.”

Two accusations had been brought against him. He denied one and, by remaining silent, consented to the other. He had come as the guardian of the human race, and if he had said that he was not a Samaritan, he would have denied that he was its guardian. But he remained silent about what he recognized and patiently rejected what he had heard falsely said, declaring: “I do not have a demon.”

Here the Lord gave us in himself an example of patience [Col. 0168B]. If he had wished to answer the Jews, “You have a demon,” he would certainly have spoken the truth, for unless they had been filled with a demon, they could not have spoken so perversely about God. But after receiving the insult, Truth did not wish to say even what was true, lest he appear not to have spoken the truth but to have returned an insult because he had been provoked.

What does this teach us except that when we receive insults from those close to us through falsehood, we should also keep silent about their true faults, lest the ministry of rightful correction be turned into weapons of anger?

“But I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges.” It is written: “The Father has given all judgment to the Son” (John V). Behold, the same Son, when he receives insults, reserves the insults inflicted upon him for the Father’s judgment, thereby showing us how patient we ought to be [Col. 0168C] while he does not yet wish to avenge himself—even he who judges.

Whom does he wish to be understood when he says, “There is one who seeks it and judges,” except the Father? What does “judges” mean? He distinguishes. How is there one who seeks and judges? The Father distinguishes and separates my glory from your glory. For according to the form of a servant, there is a great difference between Christ’s glory and that of other human beings.

“Amen, amen, I say to you, if anyone keeps my word,” etc. He speaks of the second death, of eternal death, of the death of condemnation with the devil and his angels. That is the true death. The death of the body, however, is a kind of departure for the saints to a better life, but for the impious it is a departure to perpetual punishment. It is this death that Truth wished to indicate when he says: “He will never see death” [Col. 0168D].

Then the Jews said: “Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham died, and the prophets,” etc. They were angry because they were already dead with the death that had to be avoided. They could not avoid the death by which Abraham and the prophets died—that is, the death of the flesh. For Abraham and the prophets lived in the spirit, concerning whom Truth himself says: “He is not the God of the dead but of the living” (Matthew II).

Jesus answered: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing; it is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say that he is our God, and you have not known him. But I know him. And if I were to say that I did not know him, I would be like you, a liar. But I know him, and I keep his word.”

[Col. 0169A]

The Lord Jesus Christ refers his glory to the Father, from whom he is God. He calls him his Father, though they said that he was their God, whom they did not know. For if they had known the Father, they would have received his Son. He spoke as the Son, keeping the Father’s word; yet he himself was the Word, the Father’s Word, who spoke to human beings.

It should be noted that the Lord saw them resisting him with open hostility, yet he did not cease to proclaim himself to them repeatedly, saying:

“Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and rejoiced.” Abraham saw the Lord’s day when, as a figure of the supreme Trinity, he received three angels as guests. After receiving them, he spoke to the three as though to one. For although there is a plurality of persons in the Trinity, there is unity of divinity in nature [Col. 0169B].

But the carnal minds of his hearers do not lift their eyes above the flesh. They consider only the age of his flesh, saying:

“You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” Our kind Redeemer drew them away from contemplating his flesh and led them toward contemplation of his divinity, saying:

“Amen, amen, I say to you, before Abraham came to be, I am.” “Before” belongs to past time; “I am” to the present. Because divinity does not have past or future time but always possesses being, he did not say, “Before Abraham, I was,” but “Before Abraham, I am.”

Hence it is also said to Moses: “I am who I am” (Exodus III). And: “You shall say to the children of Israel, ‘He who is has sent me to you.’”

[Col. 0169C]

Abraham had a before and an after, since he could approach through the manifestation of his presence and depart through the course of life. Truth, however, always possesses being, because nothing begins for him in an earlier time, nor is anything brought to an end in a later one.

But the minds of unbelievers were unable to endure these words of eternity, and they ran to the stones. They sought to overwhelm with stones the one whom they could not understand. What the Lord did in response to the fury of those throwing stones is shown when the text immediately adds:

“But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.” It is very remarkable, dearest brothers, that the Lord avoided his persecutors by hiding himself, since, if he had wished to exercise the power of his divinity, he could have bound them in their own blows by the silent command of his will or overwhelmed them with the punishment of sudden death [Col. 0169D]. But because he had come to suffer, he did not wish to exercise judgment.

Why did he hide himself, except because our Redeemer, having become human among human beings, speaks one thing to us by word and another by example? What does he say to us by this example except that, even when we are able to resist, we should humbly avoid the anger of the proud?

## The Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ Begins

*(Matthew, chapter XXVI; Mark, chapter XIV; Luke, chapter XXII.)*
“‘You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.’ Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the courtyard of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas. [Col. 0170A] And they took counsel to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him. But they said: ‘Not on the feast day, lest perhaps a disturbance arise among the people.’

When Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, a woman approached him carrying an alabaster flask of expensive ointment, and she poured it over his head as he reclined. Seeing this, the disciples were indignant and said: ‘Why this waste? For this could have been sold for much and given to the poor.’ But Jesus, knowing this, said to them: ‘Why do you trouble this woman? For she has performed a good work for me. For you always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me. For by pouring this ointment on my body, she did it for my burial. Truly I tell you, wherever this gospel is preached [Col. 0170B] in the whole world, what she has done will also be told in remembrance of her.’

Then one of the Twelve, who was called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said to them: ‘What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?’ And they fixed for him thirty pieces of silver. And from then on he sought an opportunity to hand him over.

On the first day of Unleavened Bread, the disciples approached Jesus, saying: ‘Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?’ But Jesus said: ‘Go into the city to a certain man and say to him: “The Teacher says: My time is near; I will keep the Passover with you, together with my disciples.”’ And the disciples did as Jesus had directed them, and they prepared the Passover.

When evening came, he reclined with his twelve disciples. And while they were eating, he said: ‘Truly I tell you, one of you [Col. 0170C] will hand me over.’ And being greatly grieved, they began, each one, to say: ‘Surely it is not I, Lord?’ But he answered and said: ‘The one who dips his hand with me into the dish—he will hand me over. Indeed, the Son of Man goes as it is written concerning him. But woe to that man through whom the Son of Man will be handed over. It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.’

Then Judas, who handed him over, answered and said: ‘Surely it is not I, Rabbi?’ He said to him: ‘You have said so.’

While they were dining, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat; this is my body.’ And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: ‘Drink from it, all of you. For this is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness [Col. 0170D] of sins. But I tell you: from now on I will not drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I shall drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom.’

And after singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. Then Jesus said to them: ‘You will all be scandalized because of me on this night. For it is written: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.” But after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee.’

Peter answered and said to him: ‘Even if all are scandalized because of you, I will never be scandalized.’ Jesus said to him: ‘Truly I tell you: on this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.’ Peter said to him: ‘Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.’ Likewise [Col. 0171A] all the disciples said.

Then Jesus came with them to a village called Gethsemane and said to his disciples: ‘Sit here while I go over there and pray.’ And taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and distressed. Then he said to them: ‘My soul is sorrowful even unto death. Remain here and keep watch with me.’ And going forward a little, he fell on his face, praying and saying: ‘My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.’

And he came to his disciples and found them sleeping. And he said to Peter: ‘So, were you all unable to keep watch with me for one hour? Keep watch and pray, so that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.’

Again, for the second time he went away [Col. 0171B] and prayed, saying: ‘My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done.’ And he came again and found them sleeping, for their eyes were weighed down. And leaving them, he went away again and prayed a third time, saying the same words.

Then he came to his disciples and said to them: ‘Sleep now and rest. Behold, the hour is near, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us go. Behold, the one who will hand me over is near.’

While he was still speaking, behold, Judas, one of the Twelve, came, and with him a large crowd sent by the chief priests and the elders of the people, with swords and clubs. Now the one who handed him over had given them a sign, saying: ‘The one whom I kiss is the man; seize him.’ And immediately approaching Jesus, he said: ‘Hail, Rabbi!’ and kissed him. And Jesus said to him: ‘Friend, why have you come?’ Then they approached, laid hands on Jesus, and seized him.

And behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand, drew his sword, and striking the servant of the high priest, cut off his ear. Then Jesus said to him: ‘Put your sword back in its place, for all who take up the sword will perish by the sword. Or do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will at once provide me with more than twelve legions of angels? How then would the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen in this way?’

At that hour Jesus said to the crowds: ‘Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs, to seize me? Every day I sat among you teaching in the temple, and you did not seize me. But all this has happened so that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled.’ Then all the disciples, abandoning him, fled.

But those who had seized Jesus led him to Caiaphas, the high priest, where the scribes and elders had gathered. Peter followed him from a distance, as far as the courtyard of the high priest. And entering inside, he sat with the attendants to see the outcome.

Now the chief priests and the whole council sought false testimony against Jesus, so that they might put him to death. And they found none, although many false witnesses came forward. Finally, two false witnesses came forward and said: ‘This man said: “I can destroy the temple of God and rebuild it after three days.”’

And the high priest rose and said to him: ‘Do you answer nothing to what these men testify against you?’ But Jesus was silent. And the high priest said to him: ‘I adjure you by the living God: tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God.’ Jesus said to him: ‘You have said so. Nevertheless, I tell you: from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power of God and coming on the clouds of heaven.’

Then the high priest tore his garments, saying: ‘He has blasphemed! Why do we still need witnesses? Behold, now you have heard the blasphemy. What do you think?’ And they answered, saying: ‘He is liable to death.’

Then they spat in his face and struck him with blows; others slapped his face, saying: ‘Prophesy to us, Christ: who is it that struck you?’ [Col. 0172B]

Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard. And one servant girl approached him, saying: ‘You also were with Jesus the Galilean.’ But he denied it before everyone, saying: ‘I do not know what you are saying.’

As he went out through the doorway, another servant girl saw him and said to those who were there: ‘This man also was with Jesus the Nazarene.’ And again he denied it with an oath: ‘I do not know the man.’

After a little while, those standing nearby approached and said to Peter: ‘Truly, you also are one of them, for even your speech makes you known.’ Then he began to curse and swear that he did not know the man. And immediately the cock crowed. And Peter remembered Jesus’ word, which he had said: ‘Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.’ And going outside, he wept bitterly.

When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders took counsel against Jesus, so that they might put him to death. And binding him, they led him away and handed him over to Pontius Pilate the governor.

Then Judas, who handed him over, seeing that he had been condemned, was moved to repentance and returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and the elders, saying: ‘I have sinned by handing over innocent blood.’ But they said: ‘What is that to us? You see to it.’

And throwing the silver pieces into the temple, he withdrew; and going away, he hanged himself with a noose. But the chief priests, taking the silver pieces, said: ‘It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, since it is the price of blood.’ After taking counsel, they bought with them the potter’s field as a burial place for foreigners.

For this reason that field has been called Acheldemach—that is, Field of Blood—to this day. Then what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled, saying: ‘And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of the one whose value was assessed, whom they assessed from the sons of Israel, and they gave them for the potter’s field, just as the Lord directed me.’

Jesus, however, stood before the governor. And the governor questioned him, saying: ‘Are you the king of the Jews?’ Jesus said to him: ‘You say so.’ And when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing. Then Pilate said to him: ‘Do you not hear how many things they testify against you?’ And he did not answer him a single word, so that the governor marveled greatly.

Now on the solemn day the governor was accustomed to release to the people one prisoner whom they wished. [Col. 0173A] At that time they had a notorious prisoner called Barabbas, who had been sent to prison because of a rebellion.

When they had gathered, Pilate said to them: ‘Whom do you want me to release to you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?’ For he knew that they had handed him over out of envy.

While he was sitting on the tribunal, his wife sent to him, saying: ‘Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered many things today in a dream because of him.’

But the chief priests and elders persuaded the people to ask for Barabbas and to destroy Jesus. The governor answered and said to them: ‘Which of the two do you want released to you?’ And they said: ‘Barabbas.’ Pilate said to them: ‘What then shall I do with Jesus, who is called Christ?’ They all said: ‘Let him be crucified.’ He said [Col. 0173B] to them: ‘Why, what evil has he done?’ But they cried out even more, saying: ‘Let him be crucified.’

Now Pilate, seeing that he was accomplishing nothing, but rather that a disturbance was arising, took water and washed his hands before the people, saying: ‘I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man; you see to it.’ And the whole people answered and said: ‘His blood be upon us and upon our children.’

Then he released Barabbas to them, but Jesus, after scourging him, he handed over to them to be crucified.

Then the governor’s soldiers took Jesus into the praetorium and gathered the whole cohort around him. And stripping him, they put a scarlet cloak around him. And weaving a crown of thorns, they placed it on his head, and a reed in his right hand; and kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying: ‘Hail, king of the Jews!’ [Col. 0173C]

And spitting on him, they took the reed and struck his head. And after they had mocked him, they stripped him of the cloak and dressed him in his own garments, and led him away to crucify him.

As they went out, they found a Cyrenian man coming toward them, named Simon; they compelled him to carry his cross. And they came to a place called Golgotha, which is called the Place of the Skull. And they gave him wine to drink mixed with gall. And when he had tasted it, he refused to drink.

After they had crucified him, they divided his garments among themselves, casting lots, so that what had been spoken through the Prophet might be fulfilled: ‘They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast a lot.’

And sitting down, they kept watch over him. And above his head they placed the written charge against him: ‘This is Jesus the Nazarene, the King of the Jews.’ Then two robbers were crucified with him, one on the right and one on the left.

Those passing by blasphemed him, shaking their heads and saying: ‘Ah, you who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.’

Likewise the chief priests, mocking him with the scribes and elders, said: ‘He saved others; he cannot save himself? If he is the king of Israel, let him come down from the cross now, and we will believe in him. He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he wills. For he said: “I am the Son of God.”’ The robbers who had been crucified with him also reproached him in the same way. [Col. 0174A]

From the sixth hour, darkness came over the whole earth until the ninth hour. And around the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani’—that is, ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’

But some of those standing there and hearing this said: ‘This man is calling Elijah.’ And immediately one of them ran, took a sponge, filled it with vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave him a drink. But the others said: ‘Let him be; let us see whether Elijah will come to save him.’

But Jesus, crying out again with a loud voice, gave up his spirit. And behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom. And the earth was shaken, and the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened. And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep [Col. 0174B] rose. And coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they came into the holy city and appeared to many.

Now the centurion and those who were with him keeping watch over Jesus, seeing the earthquake and the things that were happening, were greatly afraid, saying: ‘Truly, this was the Son of God.’

There were also many women there at a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him. Among them was Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee.

When evening had come, a certain rich man from Arimathea arrived, named Joseph, who himself was also a disciple of Jesus. He approached Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered that the body be given up. And Joseph, taking the body, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth and placed it [Col. 0174C] in his own new tomb, which he had cut out in the rock. And he rolled a large stone against the entrance of the tomb and went away.

Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb.

The next day, which is Preparation, the chief priests and Pharisees gathered before Pilate, saying: ‘Lord, we remember that while that deceiver was still alive he said: “After three days I will rise again.” Therefore command that the tomb be guarded until the third day, lest perhaps his disciples come and steal him and say to the people: “He has risen from the dead”; and the last deception will be worse than the first.’

Pilate said to them: ‘You have a guard; go and secure it as you know how.’ But they went and secured the tomb, sealing the stone together with the guard.’”

[Col. 0174D]

You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified, etc. After two days of the most glorious light, that of the Old and New Testament, the true Passover is celebrated for the world.

Passover, which in Hebrew is called [the Hebrew term is absent in the supplied text], is named not from suffering but from passing over, because when the destroyer saw the blood on the doorposts of the Israelites, he passed over and did not strike them.

Morally, however, our own passing over—that is, our Phase—is celebrated in this way: if, leaving earthly things and Egypt behind, we hasten toward heavenly things.

According to the text of the Old Testament, there is this distinction between Passover and Unleavened Bread: Passover was the name given solely to the day on which the lamb was killed in the evening—that is, on the fourteenth day of the first month. But on the fifteenth day, when they went out from Egypt, the feast of Unleavened Bread followed; this solemnity was established for seven days, that is, until the evening of the twenty-first day of the same month. Yet the evangelists customarily use the terms indiscriminately, calling the day of Unleavened Bread Passover, and calling the days of Unleavened Bread Passover.

Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the courtyard of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas, and took counsel to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him. But they said: ‘Not on the feast day, lest perhaps a disturbance arise among the people.’

They gathered and took counsel about how to kill the Lord, not fearing a disturbance, as the simple wording demonstrates, but taking precautions lest he be taken from their hands through the assistance of the people.

[Col. 0175B]

When Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper. Not because he remained a leper at that time, but because he had formerly been a leper and was afterward cleansed by the Savior, while his former name remained.

Simon himself is also said to mean “obedient”; according to another interpretation, his name can be rendered “clean,” and it was in his house that the Church was healed.

A woman approached him carrying an alabaster flask of expensive ointment, and she poured it over his head as he reclined. This woman was Mary Magdalene, the sister of Lazarus, whom Jesus raised from the dead, as John explicitly records (John 11). He also testifies that this event took place six days before Passover, before Jesus came to Jerusalem seated on a donkey, with palms and the praise of the crowds.

She is the same woman—not another—who, as Luke writes, once, while still a sinner, came and washed the Lord’s feet with tears of repentance [Col. 0175C] and anointed them with the ointment of devout confession. And because she loved greatly, she earned forgiveness for many sins from the merciful Judge (Luke 7).

Now justified and having become intimate with the Lord, she poured holy oil not only on his feet, as that same John relates (John 12), but also on his head, as Matthew and Mark testify.

Alabaster is a kind of white marble marked with various colors, which is commonly hollowed out for ointment vessels, because it is said to preserve their contents especially well without corruption. It is found around Egyptian Thebes and Damascus in Syria, whiter than elsewhere; the finest, however, is found in India.

Nard is an aromatic shrub with, as they say, a strong and thick root, but short, black, and brittle, although fragrant because of its rich growth. It resembles cypress in its harsh taste and has a small, dense leaf, whose tips spread into spikes. Hence learned perfumers praise the twin products of nard: its spikes and its leaves.

This is what Mark says: “spikenard ointment” (Mark 14), namely, expensive ointment. For the ointment that Mary brought to the Lord was made not only from the root of nard, but—what made it more precious—from the addition of its spikes and leaves; thus the grace of its fragrance and efficacy was increased.

Natural philosophers report of nard that it is principal among ointments; therefore it was rightly offered for anointing the Lord’s head and feet. There are many kinds of it, but all are herbaceous except the Indian variety, which is more precious.

Mystically, this devotion of Mary ministering to the Lord [Col. 0176A] signifies the faith and piety of the holy Church, which speaks in the Song of Songs, saying: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance.” When the Church confesses with worthy reverence the power of Christ’s divine nature, which he possesses in unity with the Father, it truly anoints his head with precious ointment.

But when it receives with worthy reverence the mysteries of the humanity he assumed, it pours on the Lord’s feet the ointment of genuine nard—that is, faithful and true nard.

Seeing this, the disciples were indignant and said: ‘Why this waste? For this could have been sold for much and given to the poor.’

Mark, like Matthew, speaks here by synecdoche, using the plural number for the singular. For John, speaking more distinctly, testifies that Judas said this, and that he said it out of greed, because he was a thief and, having the money box, carried away what was put into it (John 13).

It may also be understood that the other disciples either felt this way or said this, or were persuaded by Judas when he said it; and that Matthew and Mark expressed the will of all even in their words. But Judas said it for the reason that he was a thief, while the others said it out of concern for the poor.

Jesus, knowing this, said to them: ‘Why do you trouble this woman? She has performed a good work for me, for you will always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me.’ (From Jerome.)

It seems to me that in this passage he is speaking of bodily presence, since after the resurrection he would by no means be with them in the same way as he was then, in all their companionship and intimacy. Remembering this, the Apostle says: ‘And if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer in that way’ (2 Cor. 5).

For by pouring this ointment on my body, she did it for my burial. What you think is the wasting of the ointment is the service of burial. Nor is it surprising that she gave me the good fragrance of her faith, since I am about to pour out my blood for her.

Truly I tell you, wherever this gospel is preached in the whole world, what she has done will also be told in remembrance of her. Throughout the whole world it is not so much this woman as the Church that is preached: the Church that buried the Savior and anointed his head.

Then one of the Twelve, who is called Judas [Col. 0176D] Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said to them: ‘What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?’ etc.

Many people today detest Judas’s crime—his selling of the Lord, his Teacher and his God, for money—as monstrous and wicked, yet they do not guard against committing the same crime. For when, in exchange for gifts, they give false testimony against anyone, they plainly deny the truth for money and sell God for money. For he himself said: ‘I am the truth’ (John 14).

When they defile the fellowship of brotherhood with some plague of discord, they betray the Lord, because God is love. Therefore those who despise the commands of love and truth betray God, who is love and truth.

John writes in his Gospel that when the Lord had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas the son of Simon Iscariot; and after the morsel Satan then entered into him (John 13). This is not contrary to Luke, who records that he had already been invaded by Satan before the morsel (Luke 22), because the one whom Satan now entered in order to deceive, he entered afterward so that, once handed over to him, he might possess him completely.

On the first day of Unleavened Bread, the disciples approached Jesus, saying: ‘Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?’

He calls the first day of Unleavened Bread the fourteenth day of the first month, when, having cast away leaven, they used to make sacrifice—that is, kill the lamb—in the evening. Explaining this, the Apostle says: ‘For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed’ (1 Cor. 5). Although he was crucified on the following day, that is, on the fifteenth day of the moon, nevertheless on this night, when the lamb was sacrificed, he both entrusted to his disciples the mysteries of his flesh and blood to be celebrated, and, being seized and bound by the Jews, consecrated the beginning of his own sacrifice—that is, of his Passion.

But Jesus said to them: ‘Go into the city to a certain man and say to him: “The Teacher says: My time is near; I will keep the Passover with you, together with my disciples,”’ etc.

Mark says: ‘Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you’ (Mark 14). The jar signifies the weakness of the apostles, through whom the same grace was to be ministered to the world. Hence they say: ‘But we have this treasure in earthen vessels.’

Luke, however, says: ‘When you enter the city, a man carrying a pitcher of water will meet you,’ etc.

A man carrying a pitcher of water runs to prepare the Passover for the disciples, so that it may be shown that the mystery of this Passover is to be celebrated for the complete cleansing of the whole world. Water signifies the laver of grace, while the pitcher signifies a complete measure.

Therefore they prepare the Passover where a pitcher of water is brought, because the time has come when, for the true worshipers of the Passover, the typical blood is removed from the threshold and the baptism of the life-giving fountain is consecrated for the removal of sins.

In another evangelist it is written that they found a large upper room furnished and cleansed, and there they prepared it for him. The large upper room is the spiritual law, which, emerging from the narrowness of the letter, receives the Savior in a lofty place.
