For whoever still observes the letter that kills, whoever understands nothing else in the lamb than an animal, certainly celebrates Passover in the depths, because he has not yet learned to comprehend the majesty of the Spirit.

But whoever follows the bearer of water—that is, the herald of grace—into the house of the Church, transcends the roof of the letter through the life-giving Spirit and prepares a dwelling for Christ in the lofty lodging-place of the mind, because he understands that all the mysteries of the Passover and all the other decrees of the law were written with reference to this.

When evening had come, he reclined with the twelve disciples. And while they were eating, he said: ‘Truly I tell you, one of you will hand me over,’ etc.

At this point Luke introduces the Lord as saying: ‘With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.’ First he desires to eat the typical Passover with his disciples and thus reveal to the world the mysteries of his Passion, so that he might both prove himself the fulfiller of the ancient and legal Passover and, by teaching that this belonged to the figure of his dispensation, forbid it henceforth to be observed in a merely carnal manner. Rather, with the shadow having passed away, he demonstrates that the light of the true Passover has already arrived.

The Son of Man indeed goes, as it is written concerning him. But woe to that man through whom the Son of Man will be handed over. (From Jerome.)

He foretells the punishment, so that the man whom shame had not overcome might be corrected by the punishments announced. But even today and forever, woe to that man who approaches the Lord’s table in wickedness, whose mind is defiled by treachery, and whose inner being is polluted by some crime, so that he is not worthy to participate in the holy offerings of Christ’s mysteries.

It would have been better for that man if he had not been born. [Col. 0178B] (From Jerome.)

He should not therefore be thought to have existed before he was born, since no one can be well off unless he exists. Rather, it is simply said that it is much better not to exist than to exist wickedly.

Judas answered and said: ‘Surely it is not I, Rabbi?’ Jesus said to him: ‘You have said so.’

He joined the manner of a flatterer with a sign of unbelief. For the others, who were not going to betray him, say: ‘Surely it is not I, Lord?’ But this man, who was going to betray him, does not call him Lord but Teacher, as though he might have an excuse if, after denying the Lord, he had at least betrayed his Teacher.

While they were dining, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, gave it to his disciples, and said: ‘Take and eat; this is my body.’

After the typical Passover had been completed and he had eaten the flesh of the lamb with the apostles, he took bread, which strengthens the human heart, and passed over to the sacrament of the true Passover. Just as, in its prefiguration, Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God, had offered bread and wine, so he too might represent it in the truth of his body and blood.

And in Luke we read of two cups with which he gave drink to the disciples: one of the first month and another of the second, so that whoever could not eat the lamb among the holy in the first month might eat the kid among penitents in the second month.

He himself breaks the bread that he gives to the disciples, to show that the breaking of his body would not come without his own will and arrangement, but, as he says elsewhere, that he has authority to lay down his life and authority to take it up again.

Which bread, indeed? For the sake of the certainty of the sacrament, before breaking it he also blessed it. For the human nature that he assumed and was about to suffer, he himself, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, filled with the grace of divine power.

He blessed the bread and broke it because he deigned to subject the assumed human being to death in such a way as to demonstrate that the power of divine immortality truly existed in him. Thus he taught that he would be raised from death all the more swiftly.

And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: ‘Drink from it, all of you; for this is my blood of the New Testament,’ etc.

Because bread strengthens the body, while wine produces blood in the flesh, the former is mystically referred to the body of Christ and the latter to his blood. But because we too must remain in Christ, and Christ in us, water is mixed with the wine of the Lord’s cup.

For, as John testifies, the waters are the peoples (Rev. 17). And no one may offer either water alone or wine alone, just as one may not offer a grain of wheat alone without the addition and preparation of water in bread, lest such an offering signify that the head should be separated from the members, and lest it falsely suggest either that Christ could suffer without love for our redemption, or that we could be saved and offered to the Father without his Passion.

When he says: ‘This is my blood of the New Testament,’ he refers to the distinction from the Old Testament, which was consecrated by the blood of goats and calves (Exod. 24).

[Col. 0179B]

But I tell you: from now on I will not drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I shall drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom.

This verse can indeed be understood simply, as meaning that from this hour of the supper until the time of the resurrection, when he was to come in the kingdom of God, he would not drink wine. For afterward the Apostle Peter testifies that he took food and drink, saying: ‘We who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.’

But it is much more fitting to understand that, just as above he denies that he will again eat the typical lamb, so also he denies that he will again taste the typical drink of the Passover, until, after the glory of his resurrection has been shown and manifested, faith in the kingdom of God comes to the world.

And after singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. This is what we read in the Psalm: ‘The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord who seek him’ (Ps. 21).

The hymn may also be understood as that hymn which, according to John, the Lord sang while giving thanks to the Father. In it, lifting his eyes upward, he prayed for himself, for the disciples, and for those who were to believe through their word.

And beautifully, after imbuing the disciples with the sacrament of his body and blood and commending them to the Father through the hymn of devout intercession, he leads them up to the Mount of Olives, to signify typologically that through receiving his sacraments—and through them the help of his intercession—we ought to ascend toward higher gifts of virtue and the charisms of the Holy Spirit, with which we may be anointed in our hearts.

If anyone is troubled by the question why, after the apostles had eaten, the Savior gave them his body and blood, whereas by the universal custom of the Church we are taught to receive the same sacraments while fasting, let him hear briefly: the apostles then communicated after eating because it was necessary first to complete that typical Passover and then to pass over to the sacraments of the true Passover.

Now, in honor of so great and so fearful a sacrament, the teachers of the Church have judged it fitting that we should first be fortified by participation in the Lord’s Passion, first consecrated inwardly and outwardly by spiritual food, and afterward have our bodies restored by earthly nourishment and humble foods.

Then Jesus said to them: ‘You will all be scandalized because of me on this night.’ (From Jerome.)

He foretells what they are going to suffer, so that when they have suffered it they may not despair of salvation, but may be freed through repentance. And he significantly adds, ‘on this night,’ because just as those who become drunk become drunk at night, so those who are scandalized endure their scandal at night and in darkness.

Luke says that the Lord said to Simon: ‘Behold, Satan has asked for you, to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail’ (Luke 22).

When Satan seeks to tempt them and, as one who cleanses wheat, to shake them by winnowing, he teaches that no one’s faith can be tested by the devil unless God permits it.

For Satan’s seeking to sift the good means that he pants with the fires of his malice for their affliction. For insofar as he enviously desires their temptation, he asks for it as though seeking their testing.

‘And you, when once you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.’ Just as, he says, I protected your faith by praying so that it would not fail when Satan tempted you, so you too must remember to raise up and strengthen the weaker brothers by the example of your repentance, lest they perhaps despair of forgiveness.

For it is written: ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’ (From Jerome.)

The good shepherd is struck so that he may lay down his life for his sheep, and so that from many flocks of error there may come to be one flock and one shepherd (Zech. 13).

Truly I tell you: on this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times. (From Jerome.)

Peter was making his promise out of the fervor of faith, while the Savior, as God, knew what was to come. And note that Peter denied him three times during the night. After the cock had crowed and, as the darkness diminished, the approaching light had been announced, he turned and wept bitterly, washing away the stains of his threefold denial with tears.

Then Jesus came with them to a village called Gethsemane, etc.

The place of Gethsemane, where the Lord prayed, is still shown today at the foot of the Mount of Olives. A church has now been built above it. Gethsemane is interpreted as “valley of the rich” or “valley of abundance.”

The words and deeds of our Savior, as has often been said, are not the only things filled with mystical figures; the places and times in which he acts and speaks are also filled with them.

When the Lord prays on the mountain, he silently admonishes us that we ought to seek only lofty things in prayer and to petition for heavenly goods. But when he prays in the valley—and in the valley of the rich or of abundance—he likewise indicates to us that humility must always be preserved in our prayers, together with the inward richness of love.

Then Jesus said to them: ‘My soul is sorrowful even unto death,’ etc.

The Lord is not sorrowful because of death, for bodily condition—not fear of death—moved him. Since he assumed a body, he had to undergo everything belonging to the body: to hunger and thirst, to be touched, and to be sorrowful. But the divinity does not know alteration through such affections.

And going forward a little, he fell upon his face and prayed. Luke, however, says: “He was withdrawn from them about a stone’s throw,” as though this had symbolically admonished them to direct the stone against him—that is, to carry to him the intent of the Law that had been written on stone. For that stone can reach as far as he does, since “Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X).

And saying: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me,” etc. In invoking the Father, he says according to Mark, using the twofold name, “Abba, Father,” and thereby shows that he is God and Savior of both peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles. For *Abba* signifies the same as *Father*. But the former is Hebrew, while πατήρ (*patēr*) is Greek and *pater* is Latin. Thus, to teach that both peoples would believe in him and that he would be invoked by both, he himself first invokes him in both languages.

“The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak,” etc. This is directed against the rash, who think that they can attain whatever they have believed. Therefore, let us fear the frailty of the flesh as much as we trust in the ardor of the mind.

“My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done,” etc. He does not say, “Let what I am expressing in human feeling happen,” but rather, “Let what I descended to earth by your will be accomplished.” Thus, he says: “If it can happen that the multitude of the Gentiles believes without the destruction of the Jews, I decline the Passion. But if they must be blinded so that all the Gentiles may see, let not my will, Father, but yours be done.”

Again he went away and prayed, saying the same words for the third time, etc. Luke, however, says: “An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him.” Elsewhere we read: “Angels came and ministered to him” (Matt. IV). Thus, as evidence of both natures, he is described both as having angels minister to him and as being strengthened by an angel, since he who existed as God before the ages became human at the end of the ages. And Luke adds: “Being in agony, he prayed more earnestly.” *Agony* is understood as eagerness or confidence. What follows, according to the same evangelist, is this:

“And his sweat became like drops of blood.” He does not attribute this to the sweat of weakness—for sweating blood is also contrary to nature—but rather wishes it to be understood that the earth was watered and sanctified by his blood. This was openly declared not for his sake, since he already knew it, but for ours: that he had already obtained the effect of his prayer, namely, that by his blood he would cleanse the faith of the disciples, which earthly frailty still exposed, and that whatever scandal his death had caused them, he would wholly erase by dying. Indeed, by his innocent death he would raise the entire world, dead through sins, to heavenly life.

Then he came to his disciples and said to them: “Sleep now and rest,” etc. After saying, “Sleep now and rest,” and adding, “It is enough,” and then continuing, “The hour has come; behold, the Son of Man will be handed over,” it is certainly understood that after saying to them, “Sleep and rest,” the Lord remained silent for a while, so that what he had promised might take place, and then added, “Behold, the hour is near,” or, “The hour has come.” Therefore, the word “enough” was placed after those words: that is, “It is enough that you have rested now.”

[Col. 0182A]

“Rise, let us go; behold, he is near who will betray me,” etc. It is as though he were saying: “Let them not find us as if we were afraid and hesitating; let us go voluntarily to death, so that they may see the confidence and joy of those who are about to suffer.”

Judas came to Jesus and said: “Hail, Rabbi,” and kissed him. It was an impudent and criminal presumption to call him “Master” and to impose a kiss upon the one whom he was betraying.

Jesus said to him: “Friend, for what have you come?” This is to be understood in two ways. “For what have you come?”—that is, “To what crime have you fallen, that as a disciple you should betray your Master, and, though you were an apostle, should become a traitor?” Or “For what have you come?” may be understood with the following implied: “Do this; leave the kiss and fulfill the traitor’s office.”

And behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand, drew his sword, struck the servant of the high priest, and cut off his ear. In another Gospel we read that Peter did this with the same ardor of mind with which he did everything else. The servant of the high priest, whose name was Malchus—that is, “king”—is the Jewish people, which through unbelief became a servant of wickedness. He lost his right ear so that he might hear the entire usefulness of the letter with the left. But the Lord Jesus, among those Jews who wished to believe, restores the right ear and makes the servant a royal and priestly people. In another sense, the ear cut off for the Lord and healed by the Lord signifies hearing renewed after the old condition has been removed, so that it may exist in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter. Whoever receives this from Christ will also be granted to reign with Christ.

Then Jesus said to him: “Put your sword back into its place,” etc. Since the sword signifies vengeance—as the Apostle says concerning the judge, “For he does not bear the sword without reason” (Rom. XIII)—the sword here is rightly understood as vengeance. “Put away the sword,” as though he were saying: “Let vengeance cease.”

In another sense: “Put the sword into its place,” that is, “Turn the word of preaching toward the Gentiles, where, according to Paul, it may find an open and great door.” In yet another sense: After the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, he says to Peter, through whom the entire order of preachers is signified: “Turn the sword of the word of preaching toward Israel.” For “all who take up the sword will perish by the sword” (Gen. III). By what sword? By that, certainly, which turns like fire before paradise, and by the sword of the Spirit, which is described as part of the armor of God (Eph. VI).

“Or do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he would presently provide me with more than twelve legions of angels? How then would the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen in this way?” I do not need the help of twelve apostles, even if all of them should defend me, since I could have twelve legions of angels. Among the ancients, one legion consisted of six thousand men. Because of the brevity of the present time, we do not undertake to explain the number; it is enough merely to state the figure: seventy-two thousand angels, corresponding to the nations and languages into which the human race is divided, are represented by the twelve legions.

Now all this happened so that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled, etc. What are the Scriptures of the prophets? “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. XXI); and elsewhere: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter” (Isa. LIII). And in another place: “Because of the iniquities of my people I was led to death.”

Then all the disciples, leaving him, fled. Among them, as Mark says, a certain young man followed the Lord, clothed in a linen garment over his naked body.

When the garment was thrown off, he fled away naked. We understand that this young man was John. But his fleeing naked from the wicked signifies both the action and the soul of those who, to become safer from the attacks of enemies, cast away whatever they seem to possess in this world, and have learned to serve the Lord naked rather than, by clinging to worldly possessions, to give adversaries an opportunity to tempt them and turn them away from God. This follows the example of blessed Joseph, who, leaving his cloak in the adulteress’s hands, sprang outside, preferring to serve God naked rather than, clothed in worldly desires, serve the prostitute (Gen. XXXIX).

But they seized Jesus and led him to Caiaphas the high priest, etc. Josephus reports (*Jewish Antiquities*, Book XVIII, chapter 8) that this Caiaphas had purchased the high-priesthood from Herod for only one year. It is therefore no wonder if an unjust high priest judges unjustly.

Peter followed Jesus from a distance, etc. He rightly followed from a distance, because he was shortly to deny him; for he could not have denied him if he had clung closely to Christ. Mark, however, says: “He was sitting with the servants and warming himself at the fire.” There is a fire of love, and there is also a fire of desire. Of the former it is said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it should burn?” (Luke XII). Of the latter: “Behold, all of you who kindle a fire, girded with flames, walk in the light of your fire and of the flames that you have kindled.” The former, descending from heaven upon the believers in the upper room of Zion, taught them to praise God in various tongues; the latter, the earthly fire of Caiaphas’s hearth in the courtyard, kindled crowds with the flames of denying God. For the apostle Peter desired to be warmed by the coals of these persecutors, because he was seeking the comfort of temporal advantage through the company of the faithless. But immediately afterward, when the Lord looked upon him, he abandoned both their bodily fire and their unbelief in his heart.

Finally, two false witnesses came and said: “This man said, ‘I can destroy the temple of God and rebuild it after three days.’” How are they false witnesses if they say what we read above that the Lord said? A false witness is one who does not understand words in the same sense in which they are spoken. The Lord had spoken of the temple of his body, but they also slander him in the very words, adding or changing a few things, as though they were making a just accusation. The Savior had said: “Destroy this temple”; they change it and say: “I can destroy the temple of God.” “You,” he says, “destroy it, not I,” because it is unlawful for us to lay hands upon ourselves. Then they alter the words and say, “and rebuild it after three days,” so that he might appear to have spoken specifically about the Jewish temple. But to show that it was a living and breathing temple, the Lord had said: “And I will raise it up in three days.” To build is one thing; to raise up is another.

Then the high priest said to him: “I adjure you by the living God to tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God.” Jesus said to him: “You have said it.” Then the high priest tore his garments.

*(From Jerome.)* The one whom fury had hurled from the priestly throne, rage now provokes to tear his garments. He tore his garments to show that the Jews had lost the glory of the priesthood and that the high priest’s seat was empty. It is also a custom among the Jews, when they hear something blasphemous and apparently directed against God, to tear their garments. We read that Paul and Barnabas did the same when they were honored with the worship of gods in Lycaonia (Acts XIV). Herod, however, because he did not give glory to God but yielded to the people’s excessive praise, was immediately struck by an angel.

In a deeper mystery, it happened that during the Lord’s Passion the Jewish high priest himself tore his garments, while the Lord’s tunic could not be torn even by the soldiers who crucified him. This signified that the Jewish priesthood would be torn apart because of the crimes of its priests. But the solidity of the holy universal Church, which is accustomed to be called the garment of its Redeemer, can never be torn apart. Rather, even if Jews, Gentiles, heretics, or wicked Catholics despise the humility of the Lord and Savior, its purity will remain inviolate until the consummation of the age among those whom the lot of election has found worthy.

“Nevertheless I tell you: From now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power of God and coming on the clouds.” If, therefore, O Jew, pagan, and heretic, contempt, weakness, and the cross are for you a disgrace in Christ, see that through these things the Son of Man, born human from the Virgin’s womb, will sit at the right hand of God the Father and come in his majesty on the clouds of heaven.

Then they spat in his face, and, according to Mark, “they covered his face.” This fulfilled what is written: “I gave my cheeks to blows, and I did not turn my face away from the disgrace of spitting” (Lam. III).

They covered his face, not so that he would not see their crimes, but so that they might hide from themselves, as they once did to Moses, the grace of knowing him. For if they believed Moses, they would perhaps also believe the Lord (John V). That veil remains over their heart to this day, unrevealed. But for us who believe in Christ it has been removed. For it was not without reason that, when he died, the veil of the temple was torn in two. The mysteries of the Holy of Holies, which had remained hidden throughout the entire time of the Law and concealed from carnal Israel, were thereby disclosed to the worshipers of the New Testament.

And one maidservant approached him, saying: “You also were with Jesus the Galilean.” Why was he first exposed by a maidservant, when men could certainly have recognized him more readily? Was it not so that this sex might appear to have sinned in the killing of the Lord, and that this sex might be redeemed through the Lord’s Passion? Therefore a woman was the first to receive the mysteries of the Resurrection and was entrusted with its commands, so that she might abolish the ancient terror of transgression.

After a little while, those who were standing there approached and said to Peter: “Surely you also are one of them, for your speech makes it evident.” This was not because Peter’s speech belonged to another language or because he was of a foreign nation—for both those who accused and those who were accused were Hebrews—but because every province and region has its own peculiarities and cannot avoid its native manner of speaking. Thus the Ephraimites, in the Book of Judges, could not say σύνθημα (*synthema*, the password or signal-word) (Judg. XIII).

And immediately the cock crowed, and Peter remembered the word of the Lord; or, according to Luke: “The Lord looked at Peter.” When the Lord looked upon him, Peter returned to his heart and wiped away the stain of his denial with tears of repentance. For not only when repentance is performed, but also so that it may be performed, the mercy of God is necessary. For his looking upon someone means that he takes pity on him.

When morning came, the chief priests took counsel and handed Jesus over, bound, to Pontius Pilate. [Col. 0185B] He was led not only to Pilate but also to Herod, so that both might mock the Lord. And observe the priests’ diligence: they stayed awake throughout the whole night in their wickedness, so that they might commit murder and hand him over to Pilate bound. They had this custom: whoever they had sentenced to death, they handed over bound to the judge.

Then Judas, who betrayed him, seeing that he had been condemned, threw the silver pieces into the temple, departed, and hanged himself with a noose. The weight of his wickedness expelled the greatness of his greed. Seeing that the Lord had been sentenced to death, Judas returned the price to the priests, as though it were in his power to change the persecutors’ sentence. Thus, although he changed his mind, he did not change the outcome of his original intention. It did him no good to repent, since through repentance he could not correct his crime.

But the chief priests, having taken the silver pieces, said: “It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood.”

*(From Jerome.)* Truly they strain out a gnat and swallow a camel. If they do not put the money into the treasury—that is, into the storehouse and gifts of God—because it is the price of blood, why is the blood itself shed?

After taking counsel, they bought with it the potter’s field as a burial place for foreigners. They did this with one intention, so that through the purchase of the field they might leave an everlasting memorial of their wickedness. But we, who were foreigners to the Law and the Prophets, turned their wicked purpose toward salvation and rest in the price of his blood. It is called the potter’s field because our potter is Christ.

Then what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled [Note: [Col. 0185D] These words are not found in Jeremiah, according to Jerome]: “And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of the one who was appraised, whom they appraised from the sons of Israel, and they gave them for the potter’s field, just as the Lord appointed for me.”

And when he was accused by the chief priests, he answered nothing. Hence Luke says that Pilate told the chief priests: “I find no charge in this man.” This is what he himself had said to his disciples on the day before he suffered, among other things: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV). But because the ruler of the world—that is, Pilate—absolved him in whom he found nothing worthy of condemnation, he did not answer the chief priests. He was thereby compared to a lamb, so that in his silence he might be regarded not as guilty but as innocent. When he was silent, like a lamb about to be sacrificed for the whole flock, he displayed patience; but when he answered, like a good shepherd, he fought on behalf of the sheep entrusted to him against the snares of wolves and robbers.

When they had assembled, Pilate said to them: “Whom do you want me to release to you, Barabbas or Jesus who is called Christ?” The seditious robber and author of murders was released to the Jewish people—that is, the devil, who long ago, because of the fault of pride, had been driven from the light of his homeland and cast into the prison of darkness. For this reason the Jews cannot have peace, because they preferred to choose the leader of seditions rather than the Lord.

But since Barabbas is interpreted as “son of the father,” or “son of their teacher,” he can bear the type of Antichrist, whom those to whom he says, “You are of your father the devil,” will prefer to the true Son of God. The son of the devil is called Antichrist not because he is born from him, but because he imitates him.

While he was sitting on the tribunal, his wife sent to him, saying: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered many things today in a dream because of him.” Observe that dreams are often revealed by God to Gentiles, and that in Pilate and his wife, who confessed the Lord’s righteousness, there was testimony from the Gentile people.

Pilate said to them again: “What shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” They all said: “Let him be crucified.” This fulfilled what is said in the Psalm: “Many dogs have surrounded me” (Ps. XXI), and what is said by Jeremiah: “My inheritance has become for me like a lion in the forest; they raised their voice against me” (Jer. XII).

But Pilate, seeing that he was accomplishing nothing, took water and washed his hands before the people, saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man,” etc. Pilate took water in accordance with the prophetic saying: “I will wash my hands among the innocent” (Ps. LXXII), so that through the washing of his hands the works of the Gentiles might be cleansed, and so that he might in a certain manner separate us from the wickedness of the Jews who cried out, “Crucify him.” He thereby testified, saying: “I wished to release an innocent man, but because a riot is arising and I am being accused of the crime of rebellion against Caesar, I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man” (John XIX).

The whole people answered, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” This imprecation remains upon the Jews to the present day, and the Lord’s blood is not removed from them. Thus Isaiah says: “If you stretch out your hands toward me, I will not hear you; your hands are full of blood.”

Then the soldiers stripped Jesus and wrapped him in a scarlet cloak. Or, according to Mark, they clothed him in purple. That scarlet cloak was put upon him by the mockers in place of royal purple; it was a kind of red purple very similar to scarlet. It may also be that Mark mentioned the purple that the cloak contained, although the cloak itself was scarlet.

Mystically, therefore, in the purple with which the Lord was clothed, his flesh, which he subjected to sufferings, is signified. Concerning it the Prophet had previously said: “Why then is your garment red, and your clothing like that of those who tread the winepress?” In the crown that he wore, the assumption of our sins, for which he deigned to become mortal, is revealed. In accordance with this, his forerunner bore witness to him, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I). For the Lord himself testifies that thorns are customarily placed as a sign of sins, when he said to the first-created man after his fall into sin: “Your land will bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. III). This plainly means: “Your conscience will not cease to produce for you the pricks and barbs of vices.”

But since, according to Luke’s Gospel, the Lord was clothed in a white garment before Herod, while according to the other Evangelists he was mocked by Pilate’s soldiers in scarlet or purple clothing, the two accounts, taken together, express in one case the innocence and purity of the humanity he assumed, and in the other the reality of his Passion, through which he was to attain the glory of the immortal kingdom. Just as purple imitates the color of the blood poured out for us, so the garment signifies the kingdom into which he entered after his Passion and which he opened for us to enter.

But since the Apostle said: “As many as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ,” and Isaiah said to the Lord concerning all the elect: “You will clothe yourself with them as with an ornament” (Isa. XLIX), the entire multitude of his elect, divided into venerable martyrs and the rest of the faithful people, may most appropriately be signified in these two garments of the Lord. He is clothed in white when he is surrounded by the pure confession of the righteous. He is clothed in purple or scarlet when he rejoices in the triumph of victorious martyrs.

And plaiting a crown of thorns, they placed it on his head, and a reed in his right hand, and the rest. In the scarlet cloak he supports the bloodstained works of the Gentiles; in the crown of thorns he dissolves the ancient curse; in the reed he kills poisonous creatures. Or, he held the reed in his hand so that he might write the sacrilege of the Jews.

As they went out, they found a Cyrenian man coming toward them; or, according to Mark, “coming from the countryside, named Simon.” They compelled him to carry his cross.

*(From Jerome.)* Care must be taken lest what John writes appear contradictory, namely, that the Lord himself carried his cross. This is to be understood as follows: when Jesus went out from the praetorium, he carried the cross himself, according to John; afterward they imposed it upon Simon to carry. This order is entirely fitting, because he himself suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps (1 Pet. III).

And because this Simon is said to have been not a Jerusalemite but a Cyrenian—and Cyrene is a city of Libya, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts II)—the peoples of the Gentiles are rightly signified through him. Once foreigners and strangers to the covenants, they are now, through obedience, citizens and members of God’s household. As it is said elsewhere: “Heirs indeed of God, but co-heirs of Christ” (Rom. VIII). Hence Simon is appropriately interpreted as “obedient,” and Cyrene as “heir.”

Nor should it be passed over that this same Simon is said to have come from the countryside. A countryside is called a *pagus*, from the Greek word πηγὴ (*pēgē*), which signifies “spring.” Thus several rural houses together are called a *pagus*, because such settlements are accustomed to be founded around springs. Hence *pagani* are called so as if they were “country-dwellers.” We therefore call pagans those whom we see alienated from the city of God and, as it were, lacking the manner of urban life.

But when Simon comes out from the *pagus* and carries the cross behind Jesus, this signifies the people of the nations, who, having abandoned pagan rites, obediently embrace the footsteps of the Lord’s Passion.

According to Luke, the Lord said to the women who followed him at this point: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me, but over yourselves and over your children,” and he adds: “For if they do these things in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?” (Luke XXIII).

*(From Bede.)* The green wood signifies himself and his elect, while the dry wood signifies the wicked and sinners. “If I,” he says, “who committed no sin, who am rightly called the tree of life, and who bring forth twelve fruits of grace in each month, do not leave the world without the fire of suffering, what torment do you think awaits those who are empty of fruits and, moreover, are not afraid to consign the tree of life to the flames?”

And they came to the place called Golgotha, which is the place of the Skull. Outside the city of Jerusalem and beyond the gate were places where the heads of condemned persons were cut off; these places received the name *calvariae*, that is, “of the decapitated.” For this reason the Lord was crucified there, so that where formerly there had been a place of the condemned, there the standards of martyrdom might be raised. And just as, for the salvation of all, he became the curse of the cross, was scourged, and was crucified, so he was crucified as though guilty among the guilty, so that where sin abounded, grace might abound all the more (Rom. V).

How, then, the Lord, placed upon the cross, was positioned, and what royal figure the same placement of his most sacred body contains in itself, Sedulius beautifully described in verse in his *Paschal Poem* (Book V):

> At once, suspended upon the summit of the outspread wood,  
>   
> In holy devotion changing the wrath of judgment,  
>   
> He himself was the peace of the cross, and, illuminating  
>   
> The violent timber with his own limbs, clothed punishment with honor,  
>   
> And granted that the penalty should rather be a sign of salvation,  
>   
> Sanctifying the torments themselves in himself and making them blessed.  
>   
> And lest anyone fail to know that the form of the cross is to be venerated,  
>   
> Which, triumphantly bearing the Lord, by powerful reason  
>   
> Gathers together the four quarters of the squared world:  
>   
> From the head of the author the brilliant East shines forth;  
>   
> The sacred feet are touched by the setting star;  
>   
> The right hand holds the North, the left raises the central axis,  
>   
> And all nature lives from the limbs of its Creator,  
>   
> While Christ governs the whole world, embraced by the cross.

The Apostle also describes the moral figure of the most holy cross when he says: “Rooted and grounded in love, so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth” (Eph. III), and “to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge.”

In breadth he signifies the good works of love; in length, perseverance in holy conduct unto the end; in height, hope of heavenly rewards; in depth, the inscrutable judgments of God, from which this grace comes to human beings.

These correspond to the mystery of the cross as follows. The transverse wood, on which the hands are stretched, is understood as breadth, because of the significance of works. Length extends from the transverse beam itself down to the earth, where the entire crucified body appears to stand; this signifies persistence, that is, enduring patiently. Height extends upward from the transverse wood to the part that rises above it toward the head, signifying expectation of heavenly things. Thus good works and perseverance in them are not to be thought of as undertaken for earthly and temporal benefits, but rather for that eternal reality above which faith, working through love, hopes to attain.

Depth is that part of the wood which lies hidden, fixed beneath the earth; from it all that rises above is brought forth. So, from the hidden will of God, one person is called to participation in so great a grace in one way, another in another. But the surpassing knowledge of the love of Christ is that love where the peace exists which surpasses all understanding (Phil. IV).

And they gave him wine mixed with myrrh to drink, and he did not accept it.

*(From Jerome.)* God speaks to Jerusalem: “I planted you as my true vineyard; how have you become a bitter vine of another kind?” (Jer. II). A bitter vine produces bitter wine, which it offers to the Lord Jesus Christ, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. LXXXVI).

When it is said, “and he did not accept it,” or, according to Matthew, “when he had tasted it, he would not drink,” this indicates that he indeed tasted the bitterness of death for us, but rose again on the third day. When Mark says, “He did not accept it,” this is understood to mean, “He did not accept it in order to drink.” He tasted it, as Matthew testifies. Thus what Matthew says, “He would not drink,” Mark expressed by saying, “He did not accept it,” while omitting the fact that he had tasted it.

But when Mark says that it was wine mixed with myrrh, this is to be understood as what Matthew called “mixed with gall.” He used gall to signify bitterness, for wine mixed with myrrh is also extremely bitter. It is possible, however, that both gall and myrrh were added to make the wine exceedingly bitter.

After they had crucified him, they divided his garments, casting lots. The evangelist John explained this more fully: the soldiers divided the other garments into four parts, according to their number, but cast lots for the tunic, which was seamless and woven from above throughout.

*(From Augustine.)* The Lord’s four-part garment signified his four-part Church, spread throughout the entire world, which consists of four regions, and distributed equally—that is, harmoniously—to all those regions. The tunic for which they cast lots signifies the unity of all the parts, which is held together by the bond of love.

For if love, according to the Apostle, is the more excellent way, surpasses knowledge, and is above all commandments, the garment that signifies it is rightly said to be woven from above throughout. And what is commended by the casting of lots except the grace of God? Thus it reaches all through one person, when the lot pleases everyone, because the grace of God also reaches all in unity. When the lot is cast, the matter is entrusted not to any person’s status or merits but to the hidden judgment of God.

And they placed above his head the charge against him, written: “This is Jesus, King of the Jews.” Beautifully, the inscription that testifies that Christ is King is placed not beneath but above the cross. Although on the cross he suffered in the weakness of his humanity for our sake, above the cross he shone with the majesty of a king. Fittingly, because he is both king and priest, when he offered the outstanding sacrifice of his flesh to the Father on the altar of the cross, he also displayed the dignity of the kingship indicated by the inscription. Thus it might become known to all who wished to read—that is, to hear and believe—that through the cross he had not lost his empire, but rather confirmed and strengthened it.

For the fact that this name was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—Ἰησοῦς ὁ Βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων, “Jesus, King of the Jews,” and *Jesus Nazarenus rex Judaeorum*, “Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews”—expresses what the same Apostle subsequently adds: “And every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II).

As far as the literal meaning is concerned, these three languages stood out there above the others: Hebrew, because of the Jews who gloried in the Law; Greek, because of the wise among the nations; and Latin, because of the Romans, who at that time ruled many, almost all, nations. Whether they wished it or not, therefore, the whole kingdom of the world, all worldly wisdom, and all the mysteries of divine Law testified that Jesus is King of the Jews—that is, the ruler of those who believe and confess the Lord.

Then two robbers were crucified with him, one on the right and one on the left, etc. The robbers who were crucified on either side of the Lord signify those who, under the faith and confession of Christ, undertake either the struggle of martyrdom or the discipline of stricter continence.

All who undertake these things solely for eternal and heavenly glory are surely designated by the merit and faith of the robber on the right. But those who renounce the world either for the sake of human praise or with any less worthy intention rightly imitate the mind and actions of the blaspheming robber on the left. Concerning such people the Apostle says: “If I deliver my body so that I may burn, if I give all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I do many other things, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. XIII). But blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matt. V).

Those passing by blasphemed him, shaking their heads, etc. They blasphemed because they were passing by the way and did not wish to walk in the true path of Scripture. They shook their heads because they had already moved their feet and were not standing upon the rock.

Likewise the chief priests and scribes said, etc. Even unwillingly, the scribes and Pharisees confess that he saved others; therefore your own judgment condemns you. For the one who saved others could, if he had wished, also have saved himself.

“Let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him.”

*(From Jerome.)* A deceitful promise! What is greater: to come down from the cross, or to rise from the tomb after death? He rose, and you do not believe him. Even if he had come down from the cross, you likewise would not have believed him. But it seems to me that the demons inspired this utterance. As soon as the Lord was crucified, they sensed the power of the cross and understood that their strength had been broken. Therefore they sought to make him come down from the cross. But the Lord, knowing the adversaries’ snares, remained on the gibbet in order to destroy the devil.

And the robbers who had been crucified with him reproached him. Here, by the figure called σύλληψις (*sýllēpsis*, collective attribution), both robbers are said to have blasphemed on account of one robber. Luke, however, asserts that while one blasphemed, the other rebuked the blasphemer and confessed, saying:

[Col. 0191B]

“Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” The Apostle testifies that three virtues above all remain in the hearts of the faithful when he says: “Now these three remain: faith, hope, and love” (1 Cor. XIII). The robber, suddenly filled with grace, received and preserved all three on the cross.

He had faith, for he believed that the Lord would reign, although he saw him dying alongside himself. He had hope, for he requested access to his kingdom. He also vigorously retained love in his death, for he both rebuked his fellow robber, who was dying for a similar crime, on account of his wickedness and proclaimed to him the life that he himself had come to know.

Jesus said to him: “Amen I say to you, today you will be with me,” etc. (From Bede.) For the Lord always grants more than is asked. The thief had asked that the Lord remember him [Col. 0191C] when he came into his kingdom. But the Lord said: “Amen I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.” For to be with Christ is life, because where Christ is, there is the kingdom.

Some relate the two thieves crucified with the Lord to the two classes of the baptized: “For all of you who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death.” Both were crucified alike, but one became worse through blasphemy on the cross, while the other became a martyr through his confession, because through baptism we are washed when we are sinners. Some, while praising in faith, hope, and charity the God who suffered in the flesh, are crowned. Others, while refusing to possess either faith or the works of baptism, are deprived of the gift they received. (From Jerome.) In the two thieves, the two peoples—the Gentiles and the Jews—are represented. Both first blasphemed the Lord; afterward one, terrified by the greatness of the signs, repented, and to this day rebukes the blaspheming Jews.

“From the sixth hour darkness came,” etc. (From Jerome.) I think this happened so that the prophecy might be fulfilled: “The sun shall set at noon” (Amos 8). And elsewhere: “The sun went down while it was still midday” (Jeremiah 13). As though it could not bear to see the impious crime, the sun withdrew its rays; and the earth itself trembled in the presence of the deed being perpetrated.

(From the Vulgate.) The veil of the Temple is torn, so that the things which had been honorably concealed might, because of such a crime, be exposed and dishonored. As Josephus relates, voices of the heavenly powers, wishing to depart from the Temple, were also heard. [Col. 0192A]

At the Lord’s resurrection, however, no signs of terror appear to the faithful, but everything is seen as an indication of joy. Angels flash in white garments; people run with joy to the tomb, where the dead one is not found, but where death is recognized as conquered. The women are addressed with a peaceful voice; and, to say more, all the mysteries of eternal salvation are revealed.

It should also be noted that the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour—that is, when the sun was about to withdraw from the center of the world—and at that time he said to the thief: “Today you will be with me in paradise.” For it is written concerning Adam when he sinned that he heard the voice of the Lord God in the afternoon (Genesis 2). Therefore the order both of reason and, indeed, of divine mercy required that, at the same hour when the Lord had then closed the gate against Adam in his transgression, he should now open the gate of paradise to the repentant thief. [Col. 0192B] And at the hour when the first Adam, by sinning, brought death into this world, at that same hour the second Adam, by dying, should destroy death.

“And around the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘Heli, Heli, lama sabachthani,’ that is, ‘My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?’” (From Augustine.) Just as hunger, thirst, and weariness belonged not to divinity but to the body, so also what he says, “Why have you abandoned me?” is the voice of the body. As a human being, therefore, he speaks; as a human being, he is troubled; as a human being, he weeps; as a human being, he is crucified.

(From Ambrose.) What he cries out is yours; he received this from you. For your liberation he put on flesh.

“But some of those standing there, when they heard this, said: ‘This man is calling Elijah.’” (From Jerome.) Not all of them, but some—whom I suppose were Roman soldiers—did not understand the peculiarities of the Hebrew language. From his saying “Eli, Eli,” they thought that Elijah had been invoked by him. But if you wish to understand that it was Jews who said this, they are also acting according to their usual practice: they slander the Lord as weak because he is supposed to be imploring Elijah’s help.

“And immediately one of them ran, took a sponge, filled it with vinegar,” etc. These things happened so that the prophecy might be fulfilled: “In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psalm 68). The Jews themselves were the vinegar, having degenerated from the wine of the patriarchs and prophets. As though from a full vessel, they were filled with the iniquity of this world, possessing a heart like a sponge, fraudulent through its cavernous and twisted hiding places. Since hyssop is a lowly herb that cleanses the breast, we appropriately understand the hyssop around which they placed the sponge full of vinegar as signifying Christ’s humility, which they surrounded and which they thought they had encompassed. Hence the words in the Psalm: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed.” We are cleansed by Christ’s humility, because unless he had humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father even unto death on a cross, his blood would certainly not have been poured out for the remission of sins—that is, for our cleansing.

By the reed on which the sponge was placed, Scripture is signified, since Scripture was fulfilled by this deed. Just as a tongue may be called Greek, Latin, or any other language, signifying the sound expressed by the tongue, so a reed may be called a letter, because writing is done with a reed.

“Jesus, crying out again with a loud voice, gave up his spirit.” (From Bede.) To give up the spirit is an indication of divine power, as he himself had also said: “No one can take my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord, so that I may take it up again” (John 10).

Wood against wood; hands are openly extended against hands that were continually extended, and are offered, nailed with the nails, in place of those that cast Adam out. In place of the hands that expelled him, hands are offered that would embrace and recall the whole earth. In place of humiliation, exaltation; in place of the pleasant and deadly taste, the taste of gall is received; death is exchanged for death, darkness for darkness, burial for burial, resurrection for resurrection. All these things are a kind of care that God exercises toward us, and medicine for our weakness.

“And behold, the veil of the Temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.” (From Bede.) The veil of the Temple is torn so that the Ark of the Covenant and all the mysteries of the Law that had been concealed might appear and pass over to the people of the nations. For it had previously been said: “God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel” (Psalm 57). But now: “Be exalted, O God, above the heavens, and your glory,” he says, “over all the earth.” And earlier in the Gospel he said: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matthew 10). But after his Passion: “Go,” he says, “and teach all nations” (Matthew, last chapter). The veil of the Temple was torn, and all the mysteries of the Law that had previously been concealed were disclosed and passed over to the people of the Gentiles.

(From Jerome.) In the Gospel, which we often mention, we read that the veil of immeasurable size above the threshold of the Temple was broken and divided. Josephus also relates (Book 7 of The Jewish War, chapter 12) that the angelic powers who had formerly been guardians of the Temple then cried out together: “Let us depart from these dwellings.”

It must be asked whether the veil of the Temple was torn on the outside or within. It seems to me that, at the Lord’s Passion, the veil torn was the one placed outside in the Temple and called the outer veil, to signify that now we see in part and know in part. When perfection comes, the inner veil will also be torn apart, so that we may see all the mysteries of the house of God that are now hidden from us. [Col. 0193D] What do the two cherubim signify? What the oracle? What the golden vessel in which the manna was stored? For now we see through a mirror, in an image; and although the veil of history has been torn for us and we enter the court of God, we cannot know his secrets and all the mysteries that are kept closed in the heavenly Jerusalem.

“And the earth was shaken.” This accords with what is written in Haggai: “Yet once more I will shake the heaven and the earth, and the one desired by all the nations will come,” so that they may come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Haggai 2).

“And the rocks were split.” This signifies the future resurrection, or the hard hearts of the Gentiles, or all the prophecies of the prophets. They too received from Christ, the Rock, together with the Apostles, the name “rocks,” so that whatever had been enclosed within them by the hard veil of the Law might be split open and made visible to the Gentiles.

“And the tombs were opened.” Concerning these it is written: “You are whitewashed tombs outwardly” (Matthew 23), which within are full of the bones of the dead. Therefore they were opened so that those who had previously died in unbelief might come out of them and live with the risen and living Christ, and enter the heavenly Jerusalem.

According to the literal sense, no one should think it unreasonable to call Jerusalem the holy city after the Savior’s death, since the Apostles continued to enter the Temple until its destruction and, for the sake of those who had believed from among the Jews, continued to practice the ceremonies of the Law. A period of forty-two years from the Lord’s Passion was granted to them for repentance. But they persisted in blasphemy. Two bears came out of the forests of the Roman nations, tore them apart, and killed them. From that time Jerusalem was called not holy, but spiritually Egypt and Sodom.

“And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose,” etc. (From Bede.) Those who rose from the dead when the Lord rose must also be believed to have ascended with him when he ascended into heaven. Nor should faith be given in any way to the rash opinion of those who think that they later returned to ashes and were again shut up in the tombs that had previously been opened, by the same people to whom they had appeared alive a short time before, as is customary with the dead.

(From Jerome.) Just as Lazarus, who had died, rose again, so many bodies of the saints rose, in order to show that the Lord had risen. Yet although the tombs had been opened, they did not rise before the Lord rose, so that he might be the firstborn from the dead. When it is said, “They appeared to many,” it is shown that this was not a general resurrection visible to everyone, but a particular one shown to many, so that those who deserved to see might behold them.

It is asked why Mark says: “It was the third hour, and they crucified him,” while John says: “It was the preparation of Passover, about the sixth hour.”

(From the Vulgate.) Some say that this occurred through an error of the writers. But it does not seem to me that any interpolation should be admitted into the divine Scripture, which is received by the Church spread throughout the whole world through an inviolable tradition. Nor should an opportunity thereby be given to heretics to reject those passages in which they claim that the divine decrees have been violated. Could such a major reading have remained hidden for so many centuries? Or could an introduced falsehood have failed to be corrected?

What, then, shall we say, except that, according to Mark, either he intended to say that Christ was crucified at the third hour in accordance with the words of the Jews when they cried, “Crucify him,” or that he wished to designate him as already crucified because at that hour he had been sentenced and handed over to death? According to John, how could he have been suspended on the cross at the sixth hour? I think this is better explained by the marvels that occurred: from that very moment the sun concealed the rays of its light, lest it should see the injury inflicted upon its Creator.

Or, if he was crucified at the third hour, this does not conflict with John, who says: “It was the preparation, about the sixth hour” (John 19). For *parasceve* means “preparation,” and the Passion of Christ, which is truly the Passover, was prepared before daylight, while he was being led to Annas the high priest, while it was still night. Nor is it without reason that John records six hours from the hour of the night when Jesus was led into Annas’s house until the third hour. Three night hours could indeed have elapsed, followed by the time from the preparation of the Lord’s Passion until the third hour of the day.

According to John, the six hours are most correctly understood. He did not add the words without reason: “It was the preparation, about the sixth hour,” that is, the hour of preparation. For the Savior’s Passion began from the time when he was led to judgment for the salvation of the world.

[Col. 0195B]

“Now when the centurion and those who were with him guarding Jesus saw the earthquake and the things that were happening, they were greatly afraid, saying: ‘Truly this was the Son of God.’” (From Bede.) It was not the centurion alone who glorified God, but also the soldiers who were with him guarding Jesus. As Matthew writes, when they saw the earthquake and the things that were happening, they were greatly afraid, saying: “Truly this was the Son of God.”

How great, therefore, was the blindness of the Jews, who, although so many mighty works had been performed by the Lord and so many signs had appeared at his death, refused to believe and, more insensitive than the Gentiles, scorned both to glorify God and to fear him. Therefore the faith of the Church is rightly represented by the centurion. When the veil of the heavenly mysteries had been opened through the Lord’s death, the Church immediately affirmed, while the synagogue was silent, that the Lord Jesus was both truly a righteous man and truly the Son of God.

The very sum of one hundred, which, through the bending of the fingers, passes from the left hand to the right—as was mentioned above—also corresponds most appropriately to the mysteries and faith of the Church. In place of the Law, the Gospel has been entrusted to it; in place of the riches of the earth, the heavenly kingdom has been promised.

“There were many women there, watching from a distance,” etc. This is what the Lord himself, in the Psalm, complains to the Father in an explicit account of his Passion, saying: “You have put far from me friend and neighbor and my acquaintances because of misery” (Psalm 87).

“Who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him.” (From Jerome.) It was a custom among the Jews, and was not considered blameworthy according to the ancient practice of the nation, for women to provide food and clothing from their own means for their teachers. Because this could cause scandal among the nations, Paul records that he had renounced it: “Do we not have the right to lead about believing women, as the other Apostles also do?” (1 Corinthians 9).

They ministered to the Lord from their possessions, so that they might reap the material things of those whose spiritual things he reaped. The Lord, the Creator, did not need food; rather, he wished to present a model for teachers, namely, that disciples should be content with food and clothing.

But let us see what sort of companions he had: Mary Magdalene, from whom he had expelled seven demons; Mary the mother of James and Joseph, his maternal aunt, the sister of Mary the mother of the Lord; and the mother of the sons of Zebedee, who shortly before had asked that the kingdom be granted to her sons; along with the other women whom we read about in the other Gospels.

“When evening had come, a certain rich man from Arimathea, named Joseph, arrived,” etc. He is called a *decurion* because he belonged to the order and office of the curia and was an administrator of the curia; he is also commonly called a *curialis* because he administered civic duties. He was from Arimathea, a city of Judea, and he too was awaiting the kingdom of God. Arimathea itself is Ramah, the city of Elkanah and Samuel, in the region of Jamnia near Diospolis.

“He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.” Joseph is praised as having possessed great dignity in worldly affairs, but greater merit before God, so that by the justice of his merits he might be worthy to bury the Lord’s body, and by the nobility of his secular power might be able to obtain that body. For not just any unknown person could approach the governor and secure the body of a crucified man.

“After receiving the body, Joseph wrapped it in a clean linen cloth.” The Lord’s simple burial condemns the extravagance of the rich, who cannot do without riches even in their tombs. According to the spiritual understanding, we can also perceive that the one who wraps Jesus in a clean linen cloth is the one who receives him with a pure mind.

“And he placed it in his own new tomb.” He was placed in a new tomb so that no one could later claim that he had risen from among the other bodies. It is fittingly recorded that the tomb had been hewn from rock. If it had been constructed from many stones, people might have said that it was removed by theft after the foundations of the tomb had been undermined.

Alternatively, the Lord alone is enclosed in the tomb so that the uniqueness of his burial—different from ours—might signify the uniqueness of his resurrection, just as the other mysteries of his dispensation differed from the weakness of our nature. He appeared as a true human being, but he was conceived and born of a virgin mother. He was tempted in every respect according to likeness, without sin. He died, but in the manner he himself willed; he was buried, but for as long as he willed; and he was raised, but when he willed.

This is what he says: “I am solitary until I pass over” (Psalm 140); and elsewhere, concerning his unique burial: “In peace, in the same place, I shall sleep and rest. For you, Lord, have established me uniquely in hope.” That is: while the resurrection of other mortals is reserved for the end, you promised that by a unique gift I would rise from the dead on the third day.

Concerning the Lord’s tomb, those who in our own time have come from Jerusalem to Britain report that it was a round chamber cut out of the underlying rock, of such height that a person standing inside could scarcely touch its roof with an outstretched hand. It had an entrance on the east, toward which the great stone was rolled and set. On the northern side of the tomb was the burial place itself—that is, the place of the Lord’s body—made from the same rock. It was seven feet long and three palms in measure, rising higher than the rest of the floor. This place was open not from above but completely from the southern side, through which the body was brought in. The color of the tomb and burial chamber is said to have been a mixture of red and white.

That venerable tomb also possessed the form of the Lord’s altar, on which the mysteries of his flesh and blood are customarily celebrated. Hence ecclesiastical practice holds that these same mysteries should be consecrated not on silk or dyed cloth, but on linen resembling the shroud in which Joseph wrapped him, in a pure cloth. Just as he offered the true substance of an earthly and mortal nature to death for us, so we too, in remembrance of that awesome and venerable sacrament, should place upon the altar linen that is pure, white, born from the earth, and chastened in many ways as though by a form of mortification.

When it says, “He rolled a large stone to the entrance of the tomb,” the veil signifies what remains in the reading of the Old Testament. For the Law was written on stone; when its covering is removed, the hidden mysteries are revealed.

“Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb.” While the others abandoned the Lord, the women persisted in their service, awaiting what Jesus had promised. Therefore they deserved to be the first to see him risen, because “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.”

“On the next day, which is after the preparation,” etc. *Parasceve* means “preparation.” The Jews who lived among the Greeks called the sixth day of the week by this name; we now call it Friday. On that day they prepared what would be necessary for the Sabbath, according to the command once given concerning the manna (Exodus 16): “On the sixth day you shall gather twice as much,” etc. Jews who live among the Romans more commonly call it in Latin *cena pura*, “the pure meal.”

Since the human being was created on the sixth day and the whole creation of the world was completed, while on the seventh day the Creator rested from his work, he also commanded this day to be called the Sabbath, that is, “rest.” Therefore, rightly crucified on that same sixth day, the Lord fulfilled the mystery of human restoration. When he had received the vinegar, he said: “It is finished”—that is, the entire work of the sixth day, which he undertook for the restoration of the world, was completed.

On the Sabbath, resting in the tomb, he awaited the outcome of the resurrection that was to come on the eighth day. Here an example of our devotion also shines forth: in this sixth age of the world, we must suffer for the Lord and be crucified, as it were, to the world. In the seventh age, that is, when each person joyfully pays the debt owed, the bodies will remain in tombs, while the souls will remain with the Lord in hidden peace. After good works, it is necessary to rest, until, at last, with the coming of the eighth age, the bodies themselves, glorified by the resurrection, receive incorruption together with the souls as an eternal inheritance.

Therefore, beautifully, the seventh day is not said in Genesis to have had an evening, because the rest of souls that now exists in that age is not to be consumed by any sorrow, but is to be increased by the fuller joy of the future resurrection.

In Luke we read: “All his acquaintances stood at a distance, and the women who had followed him.” After these acquaintances of Jesus had returned to their homes once his body had been laid aside, the women alone, who loved him more closely, followed the funeral. They took care to observe how he was placed, so that at the appropriate time they might offer him the service of their devotion.

Even to this day the holy women act in this way on the day of the preparation. Humble souls, the more conscious they are of their own weakness, the more fervently they burn with love for the Savior’s Passion, diligently following his footsteps in this age, in which the future rest must be prepared. If perhaps they are able, through pious attentiveness, to imitate him, they consider carefully in what order his Passion was completed.

In the Gospel of Mark it is written: [Col. 0198B]

“And when they returned, they prepared spices and ointments; and on the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.” The commandment required that the Sabbath rest be observed from evening until evening. Therefore the devout women, after the Lord had been buried, were occupied in preparing the ointments for as long as work was permitted—that is, until sunset. They had done this not only on the day of preparation; after the Sabbath had passed, that is, after the sun had set, as soon as permission to work returned, they bought spices so that they might come in the morning and anoint his body, as the evangelist Mark testifies. For on the evening of the Sabbath, when night had already begun, they were unable to go to the tomb.

After inspecting the Lord’s burial, they returned and prepared spices and ointments. Having read, heard, and remembered the Lord’s Passion, they immediately turned to performing works of virtue that would please Christ. On the Sabbath, having prepared the spices, they remained silent, awaiting the time after the Sabbath when they would come to the Lord with their gifts. When the preparation of this present life was finished, they joyfully awaited the blessed rest, so that, when the time of resurrection appeared, they might meet Christ with the fragrant spiritual acts that are like spices.

Most interpret Mary Magdalene as “illuminating me” or “illuminatrix.” *Magdalus* means “tower.” This Mary signifies the holy Church gathered from the Gentiles. The other Mary signifies the primitive Church chosen from the Jewish people.

“The chief priests and Pharisees gathered before Pilate, saying: ‘Sir, we remember that while he was still alive that deceiver said, “After three days I will rise again.” Therefore command the tomb to be guarded,’” etc.

It was not enough for the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees to have crucified the Lord and Savior unless they also guarded the tomb, obtained a cohort, sealed the stone, and, insofar as they could, opposed their hand to the one who was rising, so that their vigilance might serve our faith. For the more carefully the tomb is guarded, the more clearly the power of the resurrection is shown.

Therefore he was buried in a new tomb that had been hewn from rock, so that, if it had been built from many stones, people might say that he had been removed by theft after the foundations of the tomb had been undermined. That he was to be placed in a tomb is testified by the Prophet, who says: “He shall dwell in a lofty cavern of the strongest rock” (Isaiah 33); and immediately, two verses later, it follows: “You shall see the King in his glory.”

Let us briefly consider what happened to the ministers of Christ’s persecution. First, Herod, under whom the infants suffered, met this end. He was burned externally by a slow fire, while inwardly he was consumed by a vast conflagration. His entire body was putrid and corrupted; he suffered a severe fever, intolerable itching, immense pain in his neck, extensive swelling of his feet, and putrid genitals. He also suffered from a foul swelling. After he had been rubbed with oil, his eyes became dislocated. In despair, he ordered all the leading and noble men of the people to be gathered to him, confined in one place, and said to his sister: “I know that the Jews will rejoice at my death; but so that I may have mourners when I breathe my last, kill them all.”

After having six of his sons killed, he asked for a knife to peel an apple, as was his custom. He raised his right hand against himself and thus died.

After him, his son Herod, under whom the Lord suffered, was struck suddenly by an angel of the Lord because he had not given glory to God. He was distended by an extraordinary swelling of the belly and died after five continuous days, in the fifty-fourth year of his life and the seventh year of his reign.

Pilate was tormented by such calamities that he pierced himself with his own hand.

It would take far too long to enumerate all the disasters that befell the Jews during the forty years leading up to vengeance for the crucifixion. An image of Caesar was placed by night in the Temple by Pilate; when disturbance arose during the solemnity of Passover, thirty thousand of them were killed. When famine broke out, a woman ate her only son. Many other signs were also displayed against them.

For an entire year a star resembling a sword shone over Jerusalem. On one day a heifer brought to the sacrifices gave birth to a lamb. On one night the door of the sanctuary, secured with iron bars and barely closed by twenty men, opened of its own accord. On one day chariots and horsemen were seen being carried through the air. On one day at Pentecost the priests heard movements in the Temple and voices saying: “Let us depart from these dwellings.” On one day of a festival, a certain son of Hananiah, driven out of his mind, cried: “A voice from the east, a voice from the west, a voice from the four winds.” Though beaten, he cried out more and more loudly.

During the Roman siege, 1,100,000 people are reported to have been killed. One hundred thousand are said to have been handed over for sale. It was therefore just that those who had despised the Father and the Son should be destroyed by the Son and the Father—that is, by Titus and Vespasian—and that those who had crucified the Lord during the solemnity of Passover should perish, enclosed by their enemies during that same solemnity.

# PALM SUNDAY

## THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE PHILIPPIANS, CHAPTER 2

“Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus. Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death, and death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, in the glory of God the Father.”

“Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus.” In this passage the Apostle teaches us to maintain humility. He sets before us the example of our Lord Jesus Christ, who, although he exists in one and the same substance of divinity, one with the Father, received, while the power and majesty of his own strength remained hidden, the form of a servant—that is, he assumed a human being. If that Lord and Master ministered to servants and disciples, how much more ought we to serve those who are our equals and our superiors.

“Although he was in the form of God.” (From John Chrysostom.) By saying, “Although he was in the form of God,” he showed that the substance of the Word exists in the nature of God. By saying, “He took the form of a servant,” he signified that the nature of a human being, and not his own substance or person, was united to the one Word. For he did not say that he took one who was already in the form of a servant, lest he suggest that a pre-formed human being was united to the one God the Word.

“He did not consider equality with God something to be seized.” (From Augustine.) He did not seize by robbery what he possessed naturally.

Since the Apostle was speaking of the only-begotten Son of God, insofar as concerns his divinity, according to the fact that he is truly God, he said that he was equal to the Father. This was not for him like robbery—that is, like desiring something alien—but like possessing what was his own.

“But he emptied himself.” (From Chrysostom.) The emptying refers to the God Word’s assumption of human things, or to the union with flesh, which was brought about according to the divine dispensation.

(From Augustine.) He emptied himself not by changing his own form, but by taking the form of a servant. He was not converted or transformed into a human being, abandoning his unchangeable stability; rather, by assuming a true human being, he himself was the one who assumed him. He was made in the likeness of human beings, not for his own sake, but for the sake of those to whom he appeared in human form.

The Son of God was equal by nature to God the Father, but lesser in appearance. In the form of a servant that he took, he is less than the Father; in the form of God, in which he existed even before he received the form of a servant, he is equal to the Father. Therefore, because the form of God took the form of a servant, he is both God and human being. He is wholly God because of the one who assumed, and wholly human because of the human being assumed. Neither of the two was converted or changed into the other by that assumption: divinity was not changed into a creature so as to cease to be divinity, nor was the creature changed into divinity so as to cease to be a creature.

“And being found in appearance as a human being.” The word “appearance” (*habitus*) is derived from the verb “to have.” Therefore appearance is spoken of in relation to something that comes to us so that it may be possessed. We speak of appearance in many ways: of the mind, as in the acquisition of discipline strengthened through practice; of the body, as when one person is more well-nourished than another; or in relation to the limbs, as when we speak of being clothed, shod, armed, and so forth.

There is, however, this distinction: some things that come to us and create an appearance are not changed by us, but change us into themselves. Wisdom, for example, when it comes to a human being, is not itself changed; rather, it changes the person, making the foolish wise. Other things come to us in such a way that they both change and are changed, as food does: it loses its own form, is changed into our body, and we, being nourished, are changed into strength.
