There is a third kind, in which the things that come to us are themselves changed so as to create an appearance, and are in a certain way formed by those in whom they produce that appearance. Clothing is an example: when it is cast aside, it does not have the form it has when worn; when put on, it receives a form that it did not have when removed.

What, then, does “being found in appearance as a human being” mean except that, by possessing a human being, he was found to be a human being? He could not be found to be a human being by those whose hearts were impure and who could not see the Word with the Father, unless he assumed what they could see and through which they might be led to that inner light.

This appearance does not belong to the first kind described above, for the nature of a human being, remaining in itself, did not change the nature of God. Nor does it belong to the second kind, for a human being did not change God and was not changed by him. Rather, it belongs to the third kind. He was assumed in such a way that he was changed ineffably, more excellently and more closely than clothing is changed by a human being when he puts it on.

By this word “appearance,” therefore, the Apostle sufficiently indicated how he said that Christ was made in the likeness of human beings: not by a transformation into a human being, but by being made in appearance when he was clothed with a human being, whom he united to himself in a certain way and joined to immortality and eternity.

“He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death,” etc. Here he gives us an example of perfect obedience, for no death could be worse than death on a cross.

“Therefore God also exalted him.” This passage should be understood with reference to his human nature rather than his divine nature. Human nature could be humbled and exalted; divine nature could not. Therefore, if we too wish to be exalted, we must obey God and his saints even unto death.

Let us not follow a proud disciple who has a humble Teacher; let us not, ungrateful servants, despise a gentle Lord; nor should we consider it beneath us to minister to our equals, since that Lord ministered to servants.

“And he gave him the name,” etc. How did he receive the name so that he might be worshiped—the giver of all heavenly gifts, whom we know from divine testimonies to have been worshiped not only by patriarchs and prophets but also by angels, powers, cherubim, and seraphim? Or how is he said to have been exalted, when he is said to have been humbled more by the flesh he assumed?

But if you consider that the Word became flesh, you will not be surprised that he is said to have been exalted or to have received a name worthy of proclamation. In him the human nature is understood to have been exalted. You, O human being, obtained the dignity of the name through his assumption of flesh.

These things are said of him from the time when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

(From Augustine.) In addition to the fact that the fullness of divinity dwells in that body as in a temple, there is another distinction between that Head and the excellence of any member. It is this: by a uniquely singular assumption of that human being, one person was made with the Word.

Of no saint could it be said, can it be said, or will it be said: “The Word became flesh.” No saint, whatever his excellence in grace, received the name of the only-begotten Son of God, so that what the Word of God was before the ages might be said simultaneously with reference to the human being assumed. That assumption is unique; it cannot in any way be shared with any holy human beings, however outstanding they may be in the holiness of their wisdom.

“So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth,” etc. He suffered and died for all so that every creature might pour out prayer in his name: those in heaven who dwell in heaven, those on earth who live on earth, and those under the earth—whether dead human beings or, as some wish, the guardians of the underworld.

“And every tongue should confess,” etc. That is, the tongues of all the various nations, confessing that he is Lord in the nature and glory of divinity, since he possesses the same glory as the Father.

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER 13

[Col.

[Column 0202C]

“Before the feast of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end. And when supper had been served, the devil having already put into the heart of Judas son of Simon Iscariot that he should betray him, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come forth from God and was going to God, he rose from supper and laid aside his garments; and when he had taken a towel, he girded himself. Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded.

“He came therefore to Simon Peter, and Peter said to him: ‘Lord, are you washing my feet?’ Jesus answered and said to him: ‘What I am doing you do not know now, but afterward you will understand.’ Peter said to him: ‘You shall never wash my feet.’ Jesus answered him: ‘If I do not wash you, you will have no part with me.’ Simon Peter said to him: ‘Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and my head.’ Jesus said to him: ‘He who has been washed has no need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean. And you are clean, but not all.’ For he knew who it was that would betray him. Therefore he said: ‘You are not all clean.’

“After he had washed their feet, he took his garments and, when he had reclined again, said to them: ‘Do you know what I have done to you? You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am. If therefore I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, so that just as I have done to you, you also should do.’”

## Sayings of Saint Augustine on the Lord’s Supper

Passover is a Hebrew name, not a Greek one. Nevertheless, in this name there most aptly appears a certain correspondence between the two languages. For what in Greek is πάσχω (*paschō*) is called in Latin *patior*, “I suffer.” Therefore *Pascha* has been understood as “suffering,” as though the name had been derived from suffering. In its own language, however—that is, in Hebrew—*Pascha* means “passing over.” Thus, interpreting this name for us, the blessed Evangelist says: “Before the feast of Passover, Jesus, knowing that the hour had come for him to pass from this world to the Father.” Behold the Passover; behold the passing over. From where, and to where? Clearly from this world to the Father. Hope was given to the members in the Head, that when he passed over they would certainly follow.

“Having loved his own who were in the world,” and so forth. What does “he loved them to the end” mean except “in Christ”? For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. Alternatively, “he loved them to the end” means “he loved them unto death”: that love led him all the way to death, because he loved his own so greatly that he died for them.

“And when supper had been served, when the devil had put [this] into [Judas’s heart].” The words “when supper had been served,” therefore, mean that it had already been prepared and brought to the table and use of those dining—not that it had been completed or finished. If you ask what the devil put into Judas’s heart, it was certainly this: that he should betray him. This putting does not take place through the ear, but through thought. Such a man had already come to the meal: a spy upon the shepherd, an ambusher of the Savior, a seller of the Redeemer.

[Col. 0203C]

“Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come forth from God and was going to God,” and so forth. If the Father had given all things into his hands, then he had also given the betrayer himself. For if he did not hold him in his hands, he certainly could not use him as he wished. Thus the betrayer had been handed over to the one whom he desired to betray. And so he was doing evil by betraying, while from the one betrayed a good would come, of which he was unaware. For the Lord knew what he was doing for his friends; and thus the Father had given all things into his hands—both the evil in its use and the good in its outcome.

“He rises from supper and lays aside his garments,” and so forth. Although God the Father had given all things into his hands, he washed not the disciples’ hands but their feet. And although he knew that he had come forth from God and was proceeding to God, he fulfilled not the office of God the Lord but that of a human servant; nor did he disdain to wash the feet of the one whose hands he already foresaw would crucify him in his crime. He was stripped of his garments and, when dead, was wrapped in linen cloths. He was stripped, and that whole passion of his is our cleansing. So great is humility for the benefit of humanity that even the sublimity of divinity commended it by his example.

What does “he came therefore to Simon Peter” mean? It should not be understood as though he had already washed some and then came to him, but that he began with him.

“He who has been washed has no need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean,” and so forth. Clearly, he is wholly clean except for his feet. In holy baptism a human being is washed entirely—not excepting the feet, but altogether. Nevertheless, when one afterward lives amid human affairs, one inevitably treads the earth. The human affections, therefore, without which one cannot live in this mortality, are like feet, since through human affairs we are affected. The Evangelist himself made this clear when he said: “For he knew who it was that would betray him.” And: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am.” Therefore you speak rightly because I am.

“If I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet,” and so forth. We learn, brothers, humility from the exalted one. Let us make one another humble, as the exalted one humbly did. Let a Christian not disdain to do what Christ did. For when he says, “I have given you an example, so that just as I have done to you, you also should do,” he shows us that if anyone has a complaint against another, then, just as the Lord forgave us, so we too should forgive one another. Let us therefore forgive one another’s offenses and pray for one another’s offenses. In this way, as it were, let us wash one another’s feet. It is ours, with his granting it, to provide the ministry of love and humility; it is his to hear us and cleanse us from every stain of sin through Christ and in Christ, so that what we forgive others—that is, what we loose on earth—may be loosed in heaven.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: A servant is not greater than his lord,” and so forth. He said this because the Teacher of humility had washed the disciples’ feet, both in word and in example.

*(Smaragdus has here more than the Gospel itself contains concerning the Lord’s Supper. For he appends the golden and most delightful discourse of Christ, which the Evangelist John gives in chapters XIII, XIV, XV, XVI, and XVII, like a swan song with which Christ bids farewell to his own; and he expounds it with marvelous yet lucid brevity from the orthodox Fathers.)*

“I do not speak concerning all of you; I know whom I have chosen.” Whom, except those who will be blessed by doing what he commanded? This man is not among them who ate his bread in such a way as to lift up his heel against him. They were eating the Lord’s bread; he was eating the Lord’s bread against the Lord. They were eating life; he, punishment.

“From now on I tell you, before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe that I am” (John XIII). That is: I am the one of whom Scripture spoke beforehand, where it says: “He who eats my bread will lift up his heel against me.” Then it follows and says:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: Whoever receives anyone whom I send receives me.” That is, according to his humanity. “But whoever receives me receives him who sent me”; that is, whoever receives me according to my divinity receives him who sent me. Thus each person should receive the one who has been sent in such a way that in him he perceives the one who sent him. For if you perceive Christ in Peter, you will find the disciple’s Teacher. But if you perceive the Father in the Son, you will find the Begetter of the Only-Begotten. And thus, in the one who has been sent, we receive the sender without any error.

“When Jesus had said these things, he was troubled in spirit.” What does it mean that he was troubled, except that he consoled the weak in his body—that is, in his Church—by the voluntary likeness of his own weakness? When one who would not be troubled unless he willed it is troubled, he consoles the one who is troubled unwillingly.

The disciples therefore looked at one another, uncertain about whom he was speaking, and so forth. Such devout love did they have for their Teacher, yet human weakness still stirred them against one another. Each person’s conscience was known to himself; nevertheless, because his neighbor’s conscience was unknown, each was so certain of himself that they were uncertain both about one another individually and about themselves in relation to the others.

One of his disciples was reclining at Jesus’ breast. The text first says “at his breast,” and shortly afterward “upon his chest”; it is the same John, whose Gospel this is. When he had reclined upon Jesus’ chest, this was certainly the bosom of the breast, the secret place of wisdom. He says to him: “Lord, who is it?” Jesus answered: “It is the one to whom I shall give the morsel after dipping it.” And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas. After the morsel, Satan entered into him. The betrayer was exposed; the hiding places of darkness were laid bare. What he received was good, but he received it to his own harm, because an evil man received a good thing evilly. What was the bread given to the betrayer except a demonstration of the grace to which he had proved ungrateful? The bread therefore entered the belly of the ungrateful man, and the enemy entered his mind.

And Jesus said to him: “What you are doing, do quickly.” He did not command the crime, but foretold Judas’s evil—for us, good—not so much rushing fiercely toward the destruction of the traitor as hastening toward the salvation of the faithful. The one was conducting the business of his betrayal; the other, that of our redemption.

[Col. 0205C]

“None of those reclining at table knew why he had said this to him; for some thought, because he had the money box,” and so forth. The Lord therefore also had a money box, preserving what the faithful offered and distributing it both for the needs of his own followers and to other needy people. At that time the first form of ecclesiastical money was established. From this we understand that the command not to think about tomorrow was not given so that the saints should preserve no money at all, but so that they should not serve God for the sake of it, nor abandon justice through fear of poverty.

“When he had received the morsel, he went out immediately; and it was night.” When he had gone out, Jesus immediately said:

“Now the Son of Man has been glorified.” Thus day poured forth its word to day—that is, Christ to the faithful disciples, so that they might hear him and love him by following him. And night announced knowledge to night—that is, Judas to the unbelieving Jews, so that they might come to him and seize him in persecution.

“Now,” he says, “the Son of Man has been glorified.” Here I see something that prefigures a great reality. Judas went out, and Jesus was glorified; the son of perdition went out, and the Son of Man was glorified. For Judas was the one on account of whom it had been said to them: “You are clean, but not all.” When the unclean man went out, all the others remained clean and remained with their cleanser. Something similar will happen when this world, conquered by Christ, has passed away, and no unclean person remains among Christ’s people; instead, “they will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.”

[Col. 0206A]

“And God,” he says, “has been glorified in him.” For the glorification of the Son of Man is precisely this: that God is glorified in him. “And immediately,” he says, “he glorified him”—namely, by predicting his resurrection, which was to take place immediately, not like ours at the end of the age.

“Little children, I am with you only a little longer.” They might otherwise have thought that God would glorify him in such a way that he would no longer be joined to them in the fellowship by which he had lived with them on earth. “I am with you only a little longer,” he says—as though he were saying: “I shall indeed be glorified immediately by the resurrection, but I shall not immediately ascend into heaven. I am still with you for a little while.” For, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter I), after the resurrection he spent forty days with them, entering and departing, eating and drinking—not because he had any need to hunger or thirst, but in order to show the reality of the flesh, which no longer had the necessity of eating and drinking, but had the power to do so.

Did he signify those forty days when he said, “I am with you only a little longer,” or does it mean something else? It can also be understood in this way: “I am still with you for a little while; I am still, like you, in this weakness of the flesh”—that is, until he died and rose again. For after he rose again, he was indeed with them for forty days, as has been said, by the manifestation of bodily presence, but he was no longer with them in the fellowship of human weakness.

“You will seek me, and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going you cannot come,’ so I say to you now.” This means: You cannot come now. They could not then come where he was going, but they could come afterward. They were not therefore still too unfit to follow the Lord. He was teaching them how they could become fit to proceed where he was going before them: “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another, just as I have loved you.” These are the steps by which Christ must be followed. This love renews us, so that we may be new human beings, heirs of the new covenant, singers of the new song.

Simon Peter said to him: “Lord, where are you going?” and so forth. The disciple said this to his Teacher, the servant to his Lord, as one ready to follow. Therefore the Lord, who saw his intention and why he had asked, answered him: “Where I am going, you cannot follow me now.” Why are you hurrying, Peter? The rock has not yet strengthened you by its spirit. Do not be exalted through presumption: you cannot now. Do not be cast down through despair: you will follow afterward.

And Peter said: “Why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.” And the Lord said: “Amen, amen, I say to you: the cock will not crow until you have denied me three times.” Behold how quickly you will reveal yourself to be small, though you speak great things; you do not know yourself as little, yet you promise me your death—you will deny your life three times.

“Let not your heart be troubled; believe in God,” and so forth. So that they would not fear death as human beings and therefore be troubled, he consoles them, also bearing witness that he himself is God. You feared death in this form of a servant; let not your heart be troubled—the form of God will raise it up.

But what is meant by what follows: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places”? They were also afraid for themselves, as though they would perish apart from him; and rightly they were troubled. But when they hear: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places; if it were not so, I would have told you, because I am going to prepare a place for you,” they are restored from their disturbance, made certain and confident that, after the dangers of temptation, they will remain with God in Christ. For even if one is stronger than another, or wiser than another, or more righteous than another, or holier than another, “in my Father’s house are many dwelling places.”

There each person will receive a dwelling place according to his merit. Thus God will be all in all, because, since God is love, love will make what each possesses common to all. For each person also possesses what another has when he loves in the other what he himself does not have. There will therefore be no envy arising from unequal brightness, because the unity of love will reign in all.

How does he go and prepare a place if there are already many dwelling places? Are these dwelling places both existing and still to be prepared? He now prepares dwelling places for the dwelling places by preparing those who will dwell in them. He prepared them by predestining them, and he prepares them by working; he does not prepare different ones, but those whom he prepared, those he prepares.

But because they do not yet exist in the completed work, he says: “And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself.” What should we understand the house of God to be except the temple of God? “The temple of God is holy,” says the Apostle, “which you are.”

What does “Where are you going, Lord?” mean? What does “Where are you coming?” mean? If I understand you rightly, you depart neither from where you go nor from where you come. You go by concealing yourself; you come by appearing; yet you remain by governing, so that we may advance by living well.

How will the place be prepared where we can remain in enjoyment? For when he says: “You know where I am going, and you know the way,” he explains it later when he says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.”

“No one comes to the Father,” and so forth. He was going to himself through himself, and we go to him through him—indeed, to the Father also. The Word of God is one thing, and the human being another; but “the Word became flesh,” that is, became human. Therefore the person of the Word is not one person and the person of the human being another, since Christ is one person in both.

Accordingly, just as the flesh died, Christ died, and when the flesh was buried, Christ was buried. Thus we believe with the heart unto righteousness, and thus we confess with the mouth unto salvation. So too, when the flesh came from death to life, Christ came to life. And because Christ is the Word of God, Christ is life. In a wondrous and ineffable manner, therefore, he who never abandoned or lost himself came to himself.

“If you had known me,” and so forth. This is what he said: “No one comes to the Father except through me.” An utter likeness was spoken, the likeness that he has with the Father, so that they would now be said to know the Father because they knew the Son who was like him.

Thus it was said to Philip: “Whoever sees me sees the Father”—not because he himself is the Father who is the Son, but because the Son differs in no respect from the Father’s likeness. It is as though he had said: “If you have seen me, who am altogether like him, you have seen the one whose likeness I am.” It follows:

[Col. 0208A]

“Amen, amen, I say to you: Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do,” and so forth. He said that they would do greater works than he himself did—but he would be doing them in them or through them, in them as though they came from themselves.

What, then, are these greater works? Perhaps the fact that even the shadow of the apostles, as they passed by, healed the sick. For it is greater that a shadow should heal than a fringe: the former through himself, the latter through them. Yet he himself did both. Nevertheless, when he said these things, he was commending the works of his words. They heard him and believed, and the fruit of those same words was their faith. Yet when the disciples preached, the nations also believed. These are unquestionably the greater works.

He did not say, however, “You will do greater works than these,” so that we might think only the apostles would do them. Rather, he says: “Whoever believes in me.” Does everyone who believes in Christ therefore do what Christ did? Among the other good things, he also deigned to grant them this: that he would do greater works through them than apart from them.

Did not that rich man depart sadly from his presence when he sought counsel about eternal life? Yet afterward, what one man did not do after hearing from him, many did when the good Teacher spoke through the disciples. Behold, he did greater works when preached by believers than when he spoke to hearers. At that time his words were his works. And certainly it is less to preach words of righteousness—which he did for our sake—than to justify the ungodly, which he did in us so that we too might do it.

“And whatever you ask in my name, I will do,” and so forth. The Lord promised great hope to his praying followers, saying: “Whatever you ask in my name, I will do.” He did not say merely, “Whatever you ask in any manner,” but “in my name.” For Jesus is interpreted as “Savior.” Therefore, when we wish him to do whatever we ask, let us ask not in any manner but in the name of the Savior. Let us not ask for anything contrary to our salvation. Thus he went to the Father in such a way that he would not leave the needy, but would hear those who asked.

“If you love me, keep my commandments, and I will ask the Father,” and so forth. Here we have, in the Trinity, the Holy Spirit, whom the Catholic faith confesses to be consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Son.

The disciples already had the Spirit whom the Lord promised, yet they did not possess him in the manner in which the Lord promised him; to the extent that he was to be possessed, they did not yet possess him. They therefore possessed less, and more was to be given them. They possessed him secretly; they were going to receive him manifestly. For this too belonged to the greater gift of the Holy Spirit: that what they possessed should become known to them.

When he says, “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate,” he shows that he himself is also an Advocate. For *paraklētos* (παράκλητος) is said in Greek, and in Latin is called *advocatus*, “advocate”; and it is said of Christ: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John II).

“But you,” he says, “will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.” So that they would not think he was with them as a guest, he explained what he meant by “with you” when he added: “and will be in you.” He is given so that he may also be in you. But he cannot be seen and known by us as he ought to be seen and known unless he is in us.

“I will not leave you orphans,” and so forth. After the promise of the Holy Spirit, lest anyone think that the Lord would give him in such a way as to take his own place, so that he himself would no longer be with them, he added: “I will not leave you orphans.”

Although the Son of God has adopted us as sons for his Father and has willed us to have as Father by grace the one who is his Father by nature, he nevertheless himself also displays toward us something like a father’s affection when he says: “I will not leave you orphans.”

Then it follows: “Yet a little while and the world will see me no more, but you will see me; because I live, you also will live.” Why did he say that he lives in the present, while they would live in the future? Because he also promised them the life of the flesh—the life of resurrection—which was already going before them in him and would follow in them.

Thus, in two words, elegantly and briefly, by the present and future tenses, he promised two resurrections: his own, which was soon to occur, and ours, which will come at the end of the age.

But because after the resurrection he also wished to show his own flesh to his followers—not merely to be seen but also to be touched—and did not wish to remove it from them, perhaps this too is meant by: “Yet a little while and the world will see me no more, but you will see me.”

“On that day,” he says, “you will know that I am in my Father,” and so forth. On what day, except the day of which he says: “And you will live”? Then we will be able to see what we believe. For even now he is in us, and we are in him.

“He who has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me”: the one who has them in memory and keeps them in life; who has them in words and keeps them in conduct; who has them by hearing and keeps them by doing. “He,” he says, “is the one who loves me; and I will love him and manifest myself to him.”

“I will love him and manifest myself” means: I will love him for the purpose of manifesting myself. What does “I will love” mean? As though he would love him only then and does not love him now? Far from it. Now he loves him so that we may believe and hold fast to the commandment of faith; then he will love him so that we may see and receive the vision itself as the reward of faith.

Jesus answered and said to them: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him,” and so forth. Thus the Father and the Son work inseparably, and thus they also love inseparably. Behold, with the Father and the Son, the Holy Spirit also makes his dwelling in the saints—within them, certainly, as God in his temple.

God the Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—comes to us when we come to them. They come by helping; we come by obeying. They come by enlightening; we come by contemplating. They come by filling; we come by receiving. Thus their vision for us is not external but internal, and their dwelling in us is not transitory but eternal.

It follows: “And the word that you heard is not mine, but the Father’s.” Rightly, therefore, he attributes to the author whatever the equal one does, since from him he has precisely this: that he is equally equal to him in every respect. Let us not be astonished or afraid. He is not less than the Father, but he is not from anyone except the Father. The word is not his but the Father’s—just as he is not his own image but the Father’s, nor is he, as Son, his own son, but the Father’s.

“I have spoken these things to you while remaining with you,” and so forth. He remained with them by bodily presence, by which he spoke visibly with them. “But the Advocate,” he says, “the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything.”

Whenever, and whoever, the Holy Spirit teaches, the Trinity itself teaches. But since it is the Trinity, it was necessary to make known its individual Persons. Thus the Trinity both speaks and teaches in its entirety; yet unless each Person were also commended separately, human weakness could in no way grasp it, however imperfectly.

“Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you.” This is what we read in the prophet: “Peace upon peace.” He leaves us peace as he goes away; he will give us his peace when he comes at the end. He leaves us peace in this age; he will give us his peace in the age to come. He leaves us peace in which, while remaining, we conquer the enemy; he will give us his peace when we reign without an enemy.

He left us peace so that even here we might love one another. Yet in him and from him we have peace. He himself is our peace, who made the two one (Ephesians II). He is therefore peace for us both when we believe that he is and when we shall see him as he is.

When he added, “Not as the world gives do I give to you,” what else does this mean except that he does not give as human beings give—those who give one another peace for the sake of enjoying without disturbance, not God, but their friend, the world?

“Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it be afraid. You have heard that I said to you,” and so forth. Their hearts could therefore be troubled and afraid because he was going away from them, although he would come to them, lest perhaps the wolf should attack the flock during the shepherd’s absence.

But from those whom the human being was leaving, God was not departing; and the same Christ was both human and God. Therefore he was going away insofar as he was human, and remaining insofar as he was God. He was going away insofar as he was in one place, and remaining insofar as he was everywhere.

“If you loved me, you would surely rejoice because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I.” Insofar as the Son is not equal to the Father, he was going to the Father; but insofar as the Only-Begotten is equal to the one who begets him, he never departs from the Father.

The form of a servant was added; the form of God did not depart. The former was assumed; the latter was not destroyed. On account of the former he says: “The Father is greater than I”; on account of the latter: “I and the Father are one.”

Let us acknowledge the twofold substance of Christ: divine, by which he is equal to the Father; human, by which the Father is greater than he. Yet both together are not two but one Christ, lest God be a quaternity rather than a Trinity.

For just as a human being is one person composed of a rational soul and flesh, so Christ is one person, God and human being. Accordingly, Christ is God, rational soul, and flesh; we confess Christ in all these elements and Christ in each of them.

Who is the one through whom the world was made? Christ Jesus, but in the form of God. Who was crucified under Pontius Pilate? Christ Jesus, but in the form of a servant.

“And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe,” and so forth. What does this mean? Should it not rather have been said: “And now I have told you before it happens, so that you may believe, and when it has happened, you may see”?

He means that when it has happened, they will see him alive after his death and ascending to the Father. Once they have seen this, they will believe that he is the Son of God, who was able to do this because he had foretold and proclaimed it before he did it.

Then what does he say? “I will no longer speak much with you, for the ruler of the world is coming.” Who except the devil? “And he has nothing in me”—that is, absolutely no sin. Thus he shows that the devil is not the ruler of creatures but the ruler of sinners.

What does he say to those reclining at table? “Rise; let us go from here.” Where, except to the place from which he was to be handed over to death?

“I am the true vine, and my Father is the gardener,” and so forth. This Gospel passage, brothers, in which the Lord calls himself the vine and his disciples branches, is spoken according to the fact that he is the Head of the Church and we are his members.

The vine and the branches are of one nature. The mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, although he was God—and we are not of that nature—became human so that in him there might be a vine of the same nature of which we human beings can also be branches.

“And my Father,” he says, “is the gardener.” According to this, therefore, Christ is the vine, in accordance with what he says: “The Father is greater than I.” According to what he says, “I and the Father are one,” he himself is also the gardener.

“Now you are clean,” he says—clean, that is, and destined to be cleansed. For unless they were clean, they could not bear fruit; yet the gardener cleanses everyone who bears fruit, so that he may bear more fruit. Who in this life is so clean that he does not need to be cleansed more and more?

Why did he not say, “You are clean through the baptism with which you were washed,” but instead said, “Because of the word that I have spoken to you”? Is it not because the word also cleanses in water? Remove the word, and what is water except water? The word comes to the element, and it becomes a sacrament, itself also something like a visible word.

That is, we preach the word of faith, of which the Apostle says: “For if you confess with your mouth,” and so forth. This word of faith has such power in the Church of God that through it, by the believer’s believing, offering, blessing, and baptizing, it cleanses even a tiny infant, although the child is not yet able to believe with the heart unto righteousness or confess with the mouth unto salvation.

All this takes place through the word of which the Lord says: “Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you.”

“Remain in me,” he says, “and I in you.” A branch must belong to one of two things: the vine or the fire. If it is not in the vine, it will be in the fire. Therefore, if it is not to be in the fire, let it be in the vine.

His words are then said to remain in us when we do what he commanded and love what he promised.

“In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit,” and so forth. Let us not attribute this to our own glory, as though we possessed it from ourselves. This grace is his, and therefore the glory is not ours but his: that we are made disciples of Christ, because his mercy went before us.

When he says: “As the Father loved me, so I have loved you,” he does not show an equality of nature between ours and his, as there is between the Father’s nature and his, but the grace by which he is the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus.

What then does “Remain in my love” mean except “Remain in my grace”? What does he mean when he says: “As the Father loved me, so I have loved you”? Is grace to be understood here too, by which the Father loves the Son? Just as it is grace by which the Son loves us, since we are sons by grace, not by nature, whereas the Only-Begotten is Son by nature, not by grace?

Or is this also to be referred in the Son himself to his humanity? Certainly. For by saying: “As the Father loved me, so I have loved you,” he shows the grace of the mediator. The mediator between God and human beings is Christ Jesus not insofar as he is God, but insofar as he is human.

The Word was God, the Only-Begotten coeternal with the one who begets him. But so that he might be given to us as mediator through ineffable grace, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

“I have spoken these things to you so that my joy may be in you,” and so forth. What is Christ’s joy in us except that he deigns to rejoice over us? And what is our joy, which he says will be fulfilled, except our participation in him?

Let us therefore love one another as he loved us and handed himself over for us. For no one has greater love than this: that someone should lay down his life for his friends.

Let us imitate him in devout obedience, yet presume in no way to compare ourselves with him. “You are my friends,” he says—a great condescension. We do not deserve to be servants, yet we are called friends.

“Now I will not call you servants, because a servant does not know what his lord is doing.” Since he gave us the power to become children of God (John I), we are not servants but sons.

But whoever does some good and becomes exalted, as though he himself were doing it and not his lord—that servant does not know what his lord is doing. We, however, if we are to be able to be the Lord’s friends, must know whatever our Lord does.

Not only human beings, but even the righteous, are made by him; they do not make themselves. Everything good is given by him, so that in all good things whoever glories may glory in the Lord.

“I have called you friends because everything that I have heard from my Father,” and so forth. How, then, should this be understood? Who would dare to affirm—or believe—that any human being knows everything that the Only-Begotten Son has heard from the Father?

For just as we await the future immortality of the flesh and the salvation of souls, although, having already received the pledge, we are said to have been saved, so we ought to hope for the future knowledge of everything that the Only-Begotten has heard from the Father.

Although Christ said that he had already done this, he said that he had done what he will do, because he has done the things that are to come.

“You did not choose me,” he says, “but I chose you.” This is that ineffable grace; this is the election of God’s grace, of which the Apostle says: “So also at the present time there is a remnant saved according to the election of grace.”

What, then, shall we say when we hear: “You did not choose me,” except that we were evil and were chosen so that, through the grace of the one choosing us, we might become good?

And observe how he does not choose those who are good, but makes good those whom he chooses: “I chose you,” he says, “and appointed you to go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain.”

We therefore had no fruit from which he might choose us. “That you may go,” he says. We go in order to bear fruit, and he himself is the way by which we go; in that way he appointed us to go.

Accordingly, in everything his mercy goes before us: “And that your fruit,” he says, “should remain.” Let love itself, therefore, remain as our fruit.

Remember my word, which I said to you, and the rest. In urging his servants to endure the world’s hatred patiently, the Lord offers them no example more fitting or better than his own. For what else does this mean: “A servant is not greater than his master. If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you”? But, he says, “they will do all these things to you because of my name.” What “all these things,” unless those he has mentioned—namely, that they will hate and persecute the word which they will despise? “If I had not come,” he says, “and spoken to them, they would not have sin.” For he speaks of those about whom he had said: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you.” [Col. 0213C]

The Jews, therefore, persecuted Christ. Were the Jews without sin before Christ came to them in the flesh? Who, even the most foolish, would say so? But there was one great sin—not every sin—which he wishes to be understood under a general name. For this is the sin that encompasses all sins: if anyone does not have it, all his sins are forgiven. This sin was that they did not believe in Christ, who came precisely so that people might believe in him. If he had not come, they would certainly not have had this sin: “Whoever hates me,” he says, “hates my Father.” For how could they love the Father of truth when they hated the truth?

“If I had not done among them works such as no one else has done,” and the rest. Those works, clearly, are the miracles of healing that he displayed in their illnesses, miracles as great as no one had previously granted them. For it is written of him: “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who alone does wonders” (Ps. 71). No one else, therefore, performed whatever works he performed among them. For whenever any human being did something of this kind, he did it through Christ, who was acting; but Christ himself did these things without their doing them.

“When the Paraclete comes, he will bear witness,” and so forth. It is as though he were saying: “They hated me and killed me while seeing me. But the Paraclete will bear such witness about me that he will make them believe in me without seeing me. And you,” he says, “will also bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.” The Holy Spirit will bear witness, and you will also bear witness. For the love poured into your hearts through the Holy Spirit, who will be given to you, will give you confidence to bear witness. By bearing witness and making you most courageous witnesses, he removed from Christ’s friends their fear and changed the hatred of their enemies into love.

“These things,” he says, “I have spoken to you so that you may not be scandalized.” For when love is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, “there is great peace for those who love your law” (Ps. 118), so that there is no occasion of stumbling for them.

Then, indicating what they would have to suffer, he says: “They will expel you from the synagogues.” But what evil was it for the apostles to be expelled from the Jewish synagogues, as though they would not have separated themselves from them even if no one expelled them? Surely he wished to announce that the Jews would not receive Christ, while these men would not depart from him. Therefore they would be cast out, since those who did not wish to be in Christ would cast out those who could not exist without Christ. [Col. 0214B]

“But the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service,” and so forth. This means that they did not know God or his Son. What, then, does “They will expel you from the synagogues” mean? “But the hour is coming”—as though he were saying: “They will indeed separate you, but I will gather you; or they will separate you, but the hour of our joy is coming.” Every Jew who killed Christ’s preachers thought that he was offering service to God, believing that those who turned to Christ were abandoning the God of Israel. O execrable blindness! They thought they were offering service to God by killing God’s servants.

[Col. 0214C]

“But these things,” he says, “I have spoken to you so that, when their hour comes,” and so forth. I have spoken these things to you not merely because you are going to suffer them, but because, when the Paraclete comes, he will bear witness about me, so that you will not keep silent out of fear of these things. “These things I did not tell you from the beginning, because I was with you,” and by my bodily presence I consoled you. “But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’” The cloud received him as he went into heaven (Acts 1). They did not question him in words, but escorted him with their eyes.

“But because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.” Human affection was saddened because the bodily presence, which was carnal, was being taken away.

“But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go away; for if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come,” and so forth. It is as though he were saying: It is expedient for you that this form of a servant be taken away from you. The Word, having become flesh, dwells among you, but I do not yet wish you to love me carnally. Hence what follows: “If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you,” as though he were saying: You cannot receive the Spirit as long as you persist in knowing us according to the flesh. “But if I go away,” he says, “I will send him to you.”

When Christ departed bodily, not only the Holy Spirit but also the Father and the Son were spiritually present with them. For since they were to become spiritual from being carnal, they would certainly possess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit more fully.

“And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, and concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment: concerning sin, indeed, because they did not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will no longer see me.” [Col. 0215A]

The world is therefore convicted of the sin of unbelief, and it is also convicted by the righteousness of those who believe. The comparison itself of the faithful is the condemnation of the unfaithful. Thus the world is convicted of its own sin, but of another’s righteousness, just as darkness is convicted by light.

He will also convict the unbelieving world concerning judgment, because “the prince of this world has been judged”—that is, he has been irrevocably destined for the judgment of eternal fire. The world is therefore convicted by the Holy Spirit concerning this judgment by which the prince of the world has been judged, since the world is judged along with its prince, whom the proud and impious imitate.

What, then, does he mean when he says, “You will no longer see me,” except that they would no longer see him as he was while he was with them? At that time he was still mortal, in the likeness of sinful flesh, able to hunger and thirst, grow weary, and sleep. After this Christ—that is, Christ in this condition—had passed from this world to the Father, they would no longer see him: “You will no longer see me,” as though he were saying: You will no longer see me humble, but exalted; no longer mortal, but everlasting; no longer subject to judgment, but judging.

If that inner Teacher, who spoke outwardly with the disciples, wished to tell us inwardly something about the incorporeal nature of God, as he speaks to the holy angels who always see the face of the Father, we could not yet bear it. Therefore, when he says, “He will teach you all truth,” I do not think that this can now be fulfilled in anyone’s mind, but only then, when we shall see face to face.

Because he is not from himself but from him from whom he proceeds, “he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak.” He will hear from him from whom he proceeds; from him by whom he is, he is; from him from whom he proceeds, he proceeds.

But what follows—“He will glorify me”—may be understood to mean that, by pouring love into the hearts of believers, he made clear to them how the Son was coequal with the Father. Or it may mean that, filled with confidence through that same love and with fear driven away, they would announce Christ to human beings.

Thus his fame spread throughout the whole world. Hence he said, “He has glorified me,” as though he were saying: He will take fear away from you and give you love, so that, preaching me more ardently, you will spread the fragrance of my glory throughout the world and proclaim my honor.

For what they were going to do in the Holy Spirit, he said that the same Spirit would do: “All things,” he says, “whatever the Father has are mine. Therefore I said to you that he will take from what is mine,” and he immediately explains this: The Holy Spirit receives from the Father that from which the Son receives, because in this Trinity the Son is born from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. The Father alone is one who is born from no one and proceeds from no one.

“A little while, and you will no longer see me,” and so forth. For shortly afterward he suffered, and they did not see him. Again, shortly afterward he rose, and they saw him. Hence the Lord’s disciples were saddened by his death and immediately rejoiced at his resurrection. Thus it follows: “Your sorrow will be turned into joy.” Their sorrow will also then be turned into joy when he manifests himself to his own as he is.

When he says, “The world will rejoice,” this may be understood as referring to the wickedness of this world, which rejoiced when Christ was killed. But when he says, “No one will take your joy from you,” because their joy is Jesus himself, he indicates what the Apostle says: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more,” and so forth (2 Pet. 3).

What does he mean by: “On that day you will ask nothing”? The verb used here, “to ask,” means not only to request but also to inquire. When he says, “The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will speak openly,” this must be understood as referring to the future, when “we shall see face to face.” “I will announce to you” means that the Father is seen through the Son. For who knows the Father except the one to whom the Son chooses to reveal him?

“And I do not say to you that I will ask the Father,” and so forth. Insofar as he is human, he intercedes for us with the Father; insofar as he is God, he hears us together with the Father. “For the Father himself,” he says, “loves you, because you have loved me.” Thus it came about that we should be loved: because we have been loved. It is wholly God’s gift to love God. He himself gave love so that he might be loved—he who loved without first being loved.

It follows: “I came forth from the Father and came into this world.” He came forth from the Father because he is from the Father. He came into the world because he displayed to the world his body, which he assumed from the Virgin. He left the world by his bodily departure; he went to the Father by the ascent of the human being; nor did he abandon the world, since he governs it by his presence.

“These things I have spoken to you so that you may have peace in me,” and so forth. After that holy meal, from which the one who was going to betray him departed, he commended this as the purpose of his discourse: that they should have peace in him. For everything we do as Christians is directed toward this. This peace will have no end in time, and every action of our pious intention, which itself was directed toward that end, is undertaken for its sake.

For its sake we are instructed by his sacraments; for its sake we are taught by his wonderful works and words; for its sake we have received the pledge of his Spirit; for its sake we believe in and hope in him, and are kindled with love for him insofar as he grants it. By this peace we are consoled in all afflictions; by it we are freed from all afflictions. For its sake we endure every tribulation courageously, so that in it we may reign happily without any tribulation.

(Cap. XVII.) “Jesus spoke these things, and, lifting his eyes to heaven,” and so forth. Some understand the Son to have been glorified by the Father in that the Father did not spare him but delivered him up for us all. If he is said to have been glorified by his passion, how much more by his resurrection!

His humility therefore begins at the point in the Apostle’s discourse where he says: “He emptied himself even unto the death of the cross” (Phil. 2). His glory begins where he says: “Therefore God also exalted him,” and reaches the point where he is in the glory of God the Father. Humility is the merit of glory; glory is the reward of humility.

But this occurred in the form of a servant. In the form of God, however, he always possesses glory. What, then, does the following mean—“that your Son may glorify you”—since the Father’s eternal glory was neither diminished in the human form nor capable of increase in its divine perfection?

Among human beings, however, he was undoubtedly less known when God was known only in Judea. The children did not yet praise the Lord’s name from the rising of the sun to its setting. But because the Gospel of Christ brought it about that the Father became known to the nations through the Son, the Son certainly glorified the Father.

If the Son had merely died and had not risen, he would certainly neither have been glorified by the Father nor have glorified the Father. But now, having been glorified by the Father through his resurrection, he glorifies the Father by proclaiming his resurrection.

The very order of the words makes this clear: “Glorify,” he says, “your Son, so that your Son may glorify you,” as though he were saying: Raise me up, so that you may become known throughout the whole world. The Son glorified the Father on earth by preaching to the nations; the Father glorified the Son by placing him at his own right hand.

“Every flesh” means every human being; he wishes the whole to be understood from a part.

“And now glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory,” and so forth. Here we should understand the predestination of the glory of the human nature that was in him: the mortal nature was destined to become immortal with the Father. This had already been accomplished by predestination before the world existed, although it would take place in the world at its appointed time.

“And now glorify me”—that is, just as it was then accomplished by predestination, so now accomplish it in reality. Do in the world what had already existed with you before the world; accomplish in its proper time what you established before all times. Grant me the glory that I had with you before the world existed—that is, the glory I possessed with you in your predestination. It is time that, now living, I should possess it with you at your right hand.

“I have manifested your name to the human beings whom you gave me out of the world.” Your name means not the name by which you are called God, which was known in Judea, great in Israel, and widely known to every creature, but the name by which you are called “my Father.” This could not be manifested at all without the manifestation of the Son himself.

For this reason he says that he has done what he would unquestionably do, but it is clear that he speaks of those who were already his disciples, not of all who would believe in him. This is shown by what follows: “While I was with them, I kept them in your name, and none of them perished except the son of perdition,” signifying Judas, who betrayed him. Of that group of twelve apostles, he alone perished.

What follows—“They were yours, and you gave them to me”—shows that, as a human being, he had received the authority to possess them, since the one who was always omnipotent was not always human. Therefore it seems more properly attributed to the Father that he received them from him, since whatever he is is from him, and he himself is also from him. He gave them to himself—that is, Christ God, together with the Father, gave them to Christ as human.

“I gave them the words that you gave me, and they received them.” That is, they understood, retained, and truly knew them—firmly, steadfastly, and without wavering.

“I do not pray for the world.” By “the world” he wishes those who live according to the world’s desire and do not belong to the portion of grace to be understood.

When he says, “I am no longer in the world,” he shows that he would soon depart from the world in bodily presence. But since they would remain longer, he said that he was no longer here while they were still here. He therefore commends to the Father those whom he was about to leave through his bodily absence, saying: “Holy Father, keep in your name those whom you have given me, so that they may be one, as we are.”

He does not say, “so that they may be one with us,” as though we and they were one group, nor does he say, “so that we may be one, they and we.” Rather, he says: “So that they may be one, as we are.” Let them be one in their own nature, as we are one in ours.

“Holy Father, sanctify them in the truth.” What else, then, is “sanctify them in the truth” than “sanctify them in me”? He himself says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” The Father therefore sanctifies in the truth—that is, in his Word, in his only-begotten Son.

What does he mean by “For them I sanctify myself,” except “I sanctify them in myself”? They too are “I,” since those of whom he speaks are his members, and Christ is one—head and body.

It follows: “So that they too may be sanctified in the truth.” What else is this than “in me,” according to the fact that he is the truth? Thus he sanctified himself in himself—that is, the human being in the Word, because Christ is one, Word and human being. He sanctifies the human being in the Word for the sake of his members. “For them,” he says, “I”—that is, for their benefit also, because they too are I, just as it benefited me that I am human without them.

“And I sanctify myself”—that is, I sanctify them in myself as myself, because in me they too are I—“so that they too may be sanctified in the truth.” What does “they too” mean except that, just as I am in the truth, so they may be what I am?

“But I pray not only for these,” that is, for the disciples who were then with him, “but also for those who will believe in me through their word.” Here he wishes all his own to be understood—not only those who were then present in the flesh, but also all who afterward believed and all who would believe until his coming through the apostles’ word.

“And the glory that you gave me I have given them.” What glory, except immortality, which human nature was destined to receive in him? For he himself had not yet received it, but according to his customary manner he uses a past-tense verb for something future because of the predestination of immortality.

“And you loved them as you loved me,” and so forth. The Father loves us in the Son, because he chose us in him before the foundation of the world. Whoever loves the only-begotten Son surely also loves his members, whom he adopted in and through him.

We are not therefore equal to the only-begotten Son, through whom we were created and recreated, merely because it was said: “You loved them as me.” For one who says, “as that is, so is this,” does not always signify equality; sometimes he means only that one thing exists because another exists, or that one thing exists so that another may exist.

“Father,” he says, “those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they too may be with me.” Who are those whom he says were given to him by the Father? Are they not those about whom he says elsewhere: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him”?

He said of himself that he was already there; concerning us, he said that he wished us to be there with him—not vainly, but faithfully considering as accomplished what he does not doubt will come to pass.

[Col. 0219A]

It was not enough for him to say, “I desire that where I am, they too may be.” He added “with me.” To be with him is a great good. The wretched may be where he is, since he is present wherever anyone may be; but only the blessed are with him, because they cannot be blessed except through him.

What he added—“so that they may see my glory, which you gave me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world”—he said “so that they may see,” not “so that they may believe.” This is the reward of faith, not faith itself. What glory of the Lord can this be except the glory by which he is God? “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5).

The Son, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the one true God—for the Trinity is the one true God—is to be known by the pure in heart.

“And I have made your name known to them, and I will make it known.” That is, I have made it known through faith; I will make it known through sight. I have made it known to those journeying in faith; I will make it known to those reigning without end.

“So that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.” How, then, is the love with which the Father loved the Son also in us, except because we are his members? We are loved in him when he is loved in his entirety—that is, head and body.

Therefore he added: “And I in them,” as though he were saying: Because I am also they. In one way he is in us as in his temple; in another way, we ourselves are he, insofar as we are his body, according to that by which he became human in order to be our head.

After Jesus had spoken these things, he went out with his disciples across the torrent of Kidron, up to the passage: “Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear. The servant’s name was Malchus.”

Malchus is interpreted as “the one who will reign.” What, then, does the ear cut off for the Lord and healed by the Lord signify except hearing renewed after the old condition has been cut away, so that it may exist in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter?

Whoever has received this from Christ would doubtless reign with Christ. The fact that he was found to be a servant also belongs to that old condition which generates slavery; this is Hagar. But when healing is added, the figure is one of freedom.

What does Jesus mean when he says: “My kingdom is not of this world”? His kingdom indeed exists here until the end of the age, but it is not from here, because it is a pilgrim in the world. To his kingdom he said: “You are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world.” They were therefore of the world when they were not yet his kingdom, but belonged to the ruler of the world.

But God rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his brightness. It is of this kingdom that he says: “My kingdom is not of this world.”

What does the evangelist Mark mean when he says that the Lord was crucified at the third hour, while John places it at about the sixth hour? It means that the Lord was crucified at the third hour by the tongues of the Jews, but at the sixth hour by the hands of the soldiers.

When he says, “They took his garments and made four parts,” the fourfold division of the garments of our Lord Jesus Christ signified his fourfold Church, spread throughout the four regions of the world. But that tunic, which was cast by lot and not divided, signified the unity of all these parts, held together by the bond of love.

What is commended by the lot except the grace of God?

What shall we say about the cross itself? The Apostle’s words are rightly understood in it: “What is the breadth, and length, and height, and depth.” It is broad in the transverse beam, on which the hands of the one hanging are stretched out; this signifies good works in the breadth of love.

It is long from the transverse beam down to the ground, where the back and feet are fastened; this signifies perseverance throughout the length of time, even to the end.

It is high at the top, where the transverse beam rises above the upright beam; this signifies the heavenly end toward which all works are directed, since everything done well and perseveringly in breadth and length must be done for the sake of the height of divine rewards.

It is deep in the part fixed in the earth. There it is hidden and cannot be seen, but all its visible appearance and prominence rise from it. So, too, our good works proceed entirely from the depth of God’s grace, which cannot be comprehended or judged.

When Jesus therefore saw his mother and the disciple standing, and so forth, this was surely that hour about which Jesus had said to his mother, when he was going to turn water into wine: “Woman, what is that to me and to you? My hour has not yet come.”

Thus the disciple and servant received the mother of his Teacher and Lord into his own household, so that, when what was necessary was distributed to each according to his need, it should be understood that what was necessary was distributed to this disciple in such a way that the portion of the blessed Mary, as his mother, was also placed there, and whatever she needed was entrusted to his care.

What does it mean that they offered vinegar, and so forth? The Jews themselves were vinegar, degenerating from the wine of the patriarchs and prophets. Their hearts, as though taken from a full vessel, were filled with the iniquity of this world, like a sponge made deceitful by its cavernous and winding hiding places.

The hyssop around which they placed the sponge full of vinegar—because it is a lowly herb but cleanses the chest—signifies the humility of Christ, which they surrounded and thought they had outwitted. Hence it is written: “You will sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed.” We are cleansed by Christ’s humility.

The reed signifies the Scriptures, which were fulfilled by this event. When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said: “It is finished.” What else could this mean than what prophecy had foretold so long beforehand? For earlier he had said: “I thirst.” It was as though he were saying: You have done this one thing lacking; give what you are—and it has been fulfilled: “In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68).

What does it signify that one of the soldiers opened the Lord’s side with a spear? It was so that the door of life might in some way be opened there, from which the sacraments of the Church flowed.

Jesus was also placed in a new tomb, in which no one had yet been laid. Just as no one was conceived before or after him in the womb of the Virgin Mary, so no one was buried before or after him in this tomb.

HOLY SATURDAY

THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE COLOSSIANS, CHAPTER III

“If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on those that are upon the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with Christ in glory.”

The Colossians, like the Laodiceans, are Asians. They too had been misled by false apostles, and the Apostle himself did not visit them, but corrected them through a letter. For they had heard the word from Archippus, who had received ministry among them.

Thus the Apostle, already bound, wrote to them from Ephesus through Tychicus the deacon and Onesimus the acolyte; the letter was written from the city of Rome.

“If you have risen with Christ.” Earlier he had said: “If you have died with Christ to the elements of the world.” By “the elements of the world” he intended avarice, luxury, and other similar things. Then, following the mortification of vices, he says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above.” That is, do not merely die to earthly vices; live also for heaven. Desire nothing earthly, seek nothing mortal, pursue your heavenly homeland, and so forth.

[Col. 0221C]

“Where Christ is seated at the right hand of God.” After the victorious Son, who through holy incarnation triumphed over the whole world, had received the glory of the resurrection, an honored seat was given him at the right hand of God the Father.

This sitting signifies nothing other than equality of honor. The expression means that our head was recognized as placed at the Father’s right hand. Those belong there who through faith are not separated from the gift of divinity, in accordance with: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me.”

For if you conceive of the nature of divinity, what place can the Father’s left or right hand have? His full majesty embraces everything everywhere.

“For you have died, and your life is hidden,” and so forth. It may be asked how people who are alive and still situated in this life can be told, “You have died with Christ.”

But elsewhere he says: “All of you who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death.” And because “our old self was crucified together with him,” it is clear that, just as Christ was crucified, died, and was buried for us, and rose again, so we too must crucify our pleasures and desires in imitation of his passion, and in baptism imitate the mystery of his death, burial, and the glory of his resurrection.

Thus, if we have shared in his sufferings, we shall also share in the glory of his resurrection. For if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him now.

We must therefore labor so that nothing belonging to the filth of the old self may be recognized in us. Christ, however, was crucified not partially but wholly, so that we might die entirely to sin and live for God. He lives for God who follows Christ’s footsteps in humility, sanctification, and devotion.

“When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear,” and so forth. Christ is called our life, as he himself said: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14).

And since we are children of God, what we shall be has not yet appeared. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him. Here we must not seek our glory, lest it be said of us: “They have received their reward” (Matt. 6).

THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER XXVIII

[Col. 0222B]

“Now late on the Sabbath, as it was dawning toward the first day of the Sabbath, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb. And behold, there was a great earthquake. For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, approached, rolled away the stone, and sat upon it. His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow. Because of fear of him the guards were terrified and became like dead men. But the angel answered and said to the women: ‘Do not be afraid. For I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come and see the place where the Lord was laid. And go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen, and behold, he goes before you into Galilee. There you will see him, as he told you.’”

“Now late on the Sabbath, as it was dawning toward the first day of the Sabbath, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb.”

(From Augustine.) The fact that different times are described for the women in the Gospels is not a sign of falsehood but of their diligent duty of visitation.

“Which dawns toward the first day of the Sabbath”: by the first part of the night, which is evening, he wished the night itself to be signified; at the end of that night the women came.

But why does he call the night “evening”? Because it was permitted to bring spices in the evening, once the Sabbath had passed. Thus he says “in the evening of the Sabbath,” as though he were saying: They came during the night that follows the Sabbath, at a time when they were free to come whenever they wished.

Or “in the evening of the Sabbath” means not when the day was becoming evening, but when the night was becoming evening—that is, they came at the end of the night.

From the beginning of the world, day preceded night, up to the passion of Christ. From Christ’s resurrection onward, night precedes day.

Or it should be read this way: “In the evening of the Sabbath,” that is, at the dawn which shines at the beginning of the night, while the same light remains throughout the night and brightens toward morning. Therefore perhaps these women remained there from the beginning of the night until morning.

But Mark says: “And very early” (Mark, final chapter), and so forth.

It appears at what hour the Lord rose—namely, in the morning—when, according to Augustine, he is described as having been in the tomb for forty hours: four hours remaining of the day on which he was crucified, twelve hours of the Sabbath night, twelve hours of the Sabbath day, and twelve hours of the night of the Lord’s day—thirty-three hours in the tomb. For this reason, for forty days after his resurrection he often manifested himself to his apostles.

Many have different opinions about the word “evening.” In the Greek Gospel it is written:

**ὀψὲ δὲ σαββάτων τῇ ἐπιφωσκούσῃ εἰς μίαν σαββάτων**

—that is, “late on the Sabbath, as it dawns toward the first of the Sabbaths.” Here it appears that **ὀψὲ**, a feminine noun, is accompanied by **τῇ**, a feminine pronoun. Hence some maintain that *vespere*—“in the evening”—is a common noun, that is, belonging to both masculine and feminine gender, whose ablative is *vespere*. Others maintain that one should say *vespera*, not *vespere*, making it feminine.

Some read the passage more subtly in this way: “Mary came on the first day of the Sabbath, which dawns in the evening of the Sabbath.”

Others understand “Sabbath” to mean “rest”: “In the evening of rest, which dawns toward the first day,” and so forth.

“Toward the first”: the first day is called the Lord’s Day. It was worthy to see the Lord rise and the world be born and restored through Christ.

(From Augustine.) The evening cannot be said to dawn toward the first day of the Sabbath unless by the name “evening” the night itself is understood, which the light brings to an end. It is a customary manner of speaking in divine Scripture to signify the whole by a part.

Thus by “evening” he signified the night, whose end is dawn. At dawn those women came to the tomb; and therefore they came during the night signified by the name “evening.” The whole night was signified by that name, as I have said. Consequently, at whatever point of that night they came, they came during that night.

Since they came at the final part of that night, they unquestionably came during that night. “In the evening, which dawns toward the first day of the Sabbath” can therefore mean only the whole night itself. They came in the evening because they came during that night; and they came during that night because they came during its final part.

(From the Vulgate.) John’s account, which reports that Mary Magdalene came to the tomb at dawn, is not contrary to Matthew, who says that Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to the Lord’s tomb in the evening of the Sabbath. Matthew uses “evening” to mean lateness and delay, as though he were saying “at a late hour of the night.”

We say that something happens late whenever many hours of the appointed time have passed. Since a large part of the night had already elapsed when the Lord rose, Matthew says “evening,” that is, late or belated, which John signifies by “at dawn.” It was nevertheless still dark, so that the hour can be understood as near morning.

“But because of fear of him the guards were terrified and became like dead men. And the angel answered and said to the women: ‘Do not be afraid. For I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified.’”

(From Jerome.) The guards, terrified by fear, lie stunned like dead men. Yet the angel consoles not them but the women: “Do not be afraid.” Let those men fear, he says; let terror remain in those in whom unbelief remains.

But you, because you seek Jesus who was crucified, hear that he has risen and fulfilled his promises: “Come and see where the Lord was laid.” If you do not believe my words, believe the empty tomb.

And go quickly, hasten your steps, and tell his disciples that he has risen and will go before you into Galilee—that is, into the rolling place of the nations, where previously there was error and slipperiness, and where they did not set their footprint with a firm and steady step.

And they went out quickly from the tomb, with fear and great joy, running to announce it to his disciples. A twofold emotion held the women’s minds: fear and joy. The one arose from the greatness of the miracle, the other from their desire for the risen Lord; yet each alike quickened their feminine steps. They went to the apostles so that through them the seed of faith might be scattered.

# HOLY SUNDAY OF EASTER

## EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER 5

> “Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new dough, just as you are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed; therefore let us keep the feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.”

**Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new dough.** That is: let nothing remain in you from the corruption of your former nature; rather, be sincere, with the brightness of grace and the radiance of righteousness.

**Just as you are unleavened.** That is, made unleavened through baptism, which Christ has granted us through his passion [Col. 0224C], being sacrificed not now in the likeness of a lamb but in the reality of his body. Therefore leave in yourselves nothing of your former way of life that could corrupt the sincerity of your nature.

**For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed.** It is as though he said: Christ is not sacrificed by us in figure, as the lamb was by the Jews, but in reality; and we celebrate Passover daily if we do not possess the leaven of malice and wickedness. The Jews, indeed, ate unleavened bread for seven days, and the world was made in seven days, continually turning through its ordered course. We celebrate Passover simply if we live purely and sincerely during these days.
