For what else is leaven but corruption of nature—a corruption that, withdrawing from its natural [Col. 0224D] sweetness, has itself been spoiled by an adulterous sourness?

**Therefore let us keep the feast.** That is: let us who continually abstain from the leaven of malice and wickedness celebrate the solemnities of saving salvation through acts of salvation, and let us be filled inwardly with the unleavened bread of simplicity and truth.

## THE GOSPEL OF MARK, THE LAST CHAPTER

> “Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices so that they might come and anoint Jesus. And very early on the first day of the week they came to the tomb, when the sun had risen. And they said to one another, ‘Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?’ And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away. For it was very large. And entering the tomb [Col. 0225A], they saw a young man sitting on the right, clothed in a white robe, and they were astonished. He said to them, ‘Do not be afraid. You are seeking Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. Behold the place where they laid him. But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you into Galilee; there you will see him, just as he told you.’”

**Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices so that they might come and anoint Jesus.** In the Gospel of Luke it is written that, returning from the tomb, they prepared spices and ointments, and on the Sabbath they kept silence because of the commandment (Luke 24). The commandment of the law, therefore, was that the Sabbath rest should be observed from evening until evening. Accordingly, the devout women, after the Lord had been buried, were occupied in preparing the ointments for as long as work was permitted—that is, until sunset—as Luke writes [Col. 0225B]. What they were unable to complete then because of the pressure of time, they hastened immediately after the Sabbath had passed—that is, after the sun had set, when permission to work had returned—to buy spices, as Mark reports, so that they might come in the morning to anoint his body. For on the evening of the Sabbath, with night already approaching, they did not wish to go to the tomb.

**And very early on the first day of the week they came to the tomb, when the sun had risen.** The first day of the week is the first day after the Sabbath, that is, after the day of rest, which ecclesiastical custom now calls the Lord’s Day because of the resurrection of the Lord and Savior [Col. 0225C]. The same is meant when we read “the first of the week” or “the first day after the Sabbath”: it is the first day after the Sabbath, that is, after the days of rest observed on the Sabbaths. The holy women who had followed the Lord came to the tomb with spices and rendered the service of human devotion even to him whom they had loved while he was alive, though he was now dead. Let us, therefore, who believe in him who died, come with spices to his tomb if, filled with the fragrance of virtues, we seek the Lord with the expectation of good works.

That the women came to the tomb very early, when the sun had risen—that is, when the sky was already growing pale in the eastern quarter, which certainly happens only when the rising sun is near—shows, according to the historical meaning, the great fervor of their charity in seeking [Col. 0225D] and finding the Lord. According to the mystical meaning, it gives us an example: with our faces illumined and the darkness of vices cast away, we should offer the Lord the fragrance of good works and the sweetness of prayers.

**And they said to one another, “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?” And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away, for it was very large.** Matthew sufficiently explains how the stone was rolled away by the angel. Mystically, however, the rolling away of the stone signifies the opening of Christ’s mysteries, which had been held beneath the veil of the letter of the law. The law was written on stone; when its covering was removed, the glory of the resurrection was revealed, the abolition of ancient death appeared, [Col. 0226A] and the hope of everlasting life began to be preached throughout the world.

**And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right, clothed in a white robe, and they were astonished.** Entering from the east into that round chamber cut out in the rock, they saw an angel sitting on the southern side of the place where Jesus’ body had been laid. This was “on the right,” because the body, lying on its back with its head toward the west, necessarily had its right side toward the south. Matthew writes that the angel who rolled away the stone from the entrance of the tomb was first seen sitting upon the stone and then ordered them to enter the place where the Lord had been laid and see that he had already risen [Col. 0226B] from the dead. Luke writes that, entering the tomb, they found two angels standing there in white garments.

Those women, therefore, see angels who came with spices, because those minds look upon the citizens above us who advance toward the Lord through holy desires and with virtues. We should note what it means that the angel is seen sitting on the right. For what is signified by the left except the present life? And what by the right except everlasting life? Hence it is written: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me.” The Church of God has placed the left hand—namely, the prosperity of the present life—under its head, pressing it down with the intensity of supreme love. The right hand of God embraces it, because [Col. 0226C] it is held entirely within his eternal blessedness.

Since our Redeemer had already passed beyond the corruption of the present life, rightly did the angel who came to announce his enduring glory sit on the right. He appeared clothed in a white robe because he announced the joys of our festival. The whiteness of the garment proclaims the splendor of our solemnity. Shall we say “ours,” or his? To speak more truly, let us say both his and ours: the resurrection of our Redeemer was our festival, because it restored us to immortality, and it was the festival of the angels, because by recalling us to heavenly things it filled their number. Thus, at his festival and ours, the angel appeared in white garments, because when we are restored through the Lord’s resurrection to the things above, the losses of our heavenly homeland are repaired [Col. 0226D]. But now let us hear what he says to the women who are coming.

**“Do not be afraid. You are seeking Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. Behold the place where they laid him.”** “Do not be afraid,” he says, as though he were openly saying: Let those who do not love the coming of the citizens above be afraid; let those who, weighed down by carnal desires, despair of being able to attain their society be terrified. But why are you afraid, since you see your fellow citizens?

Thus Matthew, describing the angel’s appearance, says: “His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow.” In the lightning there is the terror of fear; in the snow [Col. 0227A] there is the soothing quality of whiteness. Since almighty God is terrifying to sinners and gentle to the righteous, rightly is the angel, the witness of his resurrection, shown both with a face like lightning and with clothing white as snow: by his appearance he terrifies the reprobate and comforts the devout.

**“You are seeking Jesus of Nazareth.”** In Latin speech, Jesus is interpreted as “saving,” that is, “Savior.” At that time many could have been called by this name, though not substantially but merely by designation. Therefore the place is added, so that it might be made clear of which Jesus it was said: “of Nazareth.” Then the cause is stated more particularly: “who was crucified.” And he adds: “He has risen; he is not here.” “He is not here” is said with reference to the presence of the flesh, although he was nowhere absent with respect to the presence of his majesty.

[Col. 0227B]

**“But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you into Galilee.”** We should ask why Peter is identified by name among the disciples. If the angel had not expressly named him, he who had denied his Master would not have dared to come among the disciples. He is therefore called by name so that he would not despair because of his denial.

Here we should consider why almighty God permitted the man whom he had determined to set over the whole Church to fear a servant girl’s voice and deny himself. We understand that this was done through a great dispensation of mercy, so that the one who was to be the Church’s shepherd might learn through his own fault how he ought to show mercy toward others. He first showed him his own weakness and then set him over the others, so that from his own infirmity he might learn how mercifully to bear with the infirmities of others [Col. 0227C].

Well is it said of our Redeemer:

**“He is going before you into Galilee; there you will see him, just as he told you.”** Galilee is interpreted as “a migration that has taken place.” Our Redeemer had already migrated from suffering to resurrection, from death to life, from punishment to glory, and from corruption to incorruption. He is first seen by the disciples after the resurrection in Galilee because we shall see the glory of his resurrection joyfully after we have migrated from vices to the heights of virtue. Thus, he who is announced in the tomb is shown in the migration of the flesh, because the one recognized in the mortification of the flesh is seen in the migration of the mind.

[Col. 0227D]

# EASTER MONDAY

## READING FROM THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, CHAPTER 10

> “Peter, standing in the midst of the people, said: ‘Men, brothers, God sent the word to the children of Israel, announcing peace through Jesus Christ—he is Lord of all. You know what took place throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism which John preached: Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him. And we are witnesses of all that he did in the region of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They killed him by hanging him on a tree. But God raised him up on the third day [Col. 0228A] and granted that he be made manifest, not to all the people but to witnesses appointed beforehand by God—to us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead. To him all the prophets bear witness, that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.’”

**God sent the word to the children of Israel, announcing peace through Jesus Christ.** The word sent here means the Gospel, or the Lord Jesus Christ himself, because he says to the apostles: “I give you my peace; I commend my peace to you.” That he is Lord of all appears, he says, in the fact that God is not a respecter of persons: he sent his only-begotten Son, who is Lord and Creator of all, to make peace with the human race [Col. 0228B].

**You know what took place throughout all Judea.** Since the Word of God became flesh, “the word” means that human nature, without any preceding merits of good works, was joined to the Word of God in the Virgin’s womb, so that with him it became one person. For this reason we confess that he was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

**Beginning from Galilee after the baptism.** Since it is the rule of the Church that the faithful be baptized in the name of the holy Trinity, it is asked how Luke throughout the entire text of this little book testifies that baptism was given only in the name of Jesus Christ. The blessed Ambrose resolves this as follows [Col. 0228C]:

**(From Ambrose.)** The mystery is fulfilled through the unity of the name. For whether you say “Christ,” you have indicated both God the Father, by whom the Son was anointed, and the Son himself, who was anointed, and the Spirit with whom he was anointed. For it is written: “Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit.” Or whether you say “the Father,” you have likewise indicated his Son and the Spirit of both, provided that you comprehend this also in your heart. Or whether you say “the Spirit,” you have named God the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds, and the Son, because the Spirit also belongs to the Son. Therefore, so that authority may be joined to prayer, Scripture also rightly indicates that we can be baptized in the Spirit, when the Lord says: “You will be baptized in the Holy Spirit,” and the Apostle says [Col. 0228D]: “For in one body we were all baptized in one Spirit.” In another respect, it is especially fitting that we be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, because, as the Apostle says: “All who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death.”

**What John preached: Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him, and so forth.** John therefore preached Jesus as God anointed him with the Holy Spirit, namely when he said: “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit” (Mark 1). And again: “I saw the Spirit descending like a dove upon him” (John 1). Jesus was therefore anointed not with visible oil but with the gift of grace, which is signified by the visible ointment with which the Church anoints the baptized.

Yet he was not then anointed with the Holy Spirit because the Spirit descended upon him after he had been baptized in the form of a dove [Col. 0229A]. At that time he deigned to prefigure his body, that is, his Church, in which the baptized especially receive the Holy Spirit—but through this mystical and invisible anointing.

**He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, and so forth.** That is: the Father was with the Son. It is better to understand it in this way than to suppose that the divinity of the Son is signified as dwelling together with the man whom he assumed; otherwise we might appear to divide Christ into two persons and fall into the doctrine of Nestorius.

**Whom they killed by hanging him on a tree.** Christ suffered; let us die to sin. Christ rose; let us live for God. Christ passed from this world to the Father; let our heart not remain here, but let it follow our head to the things above. He hung upon a tree; let us crucify the desire of the flesh [Col. 0229B].

**God raised him up on the third day.** Who raised him except the invisible God? He slept, began his sleep, and rose again, because the Lord received him, to whom he had said: “Raise me up, and I will repay them” (Psalm 4). He was handed over because of our offenses and rose again for our justification (Romans 5). For in the night of this age there will also be a resurrection of the flesh transferred to the kingdom, whose example has gone before us in our Head.

He rose and flew upward, and on our behalf the One intercedes alone in heaven. He does with the Father what he had asked from the Father, because he is both mediator and creator: mediator in order to ask, creator in order to grant. Therefore, with the most faithful and sincere devotion, let us offer him the prayer he taught us, so that, with his help [Col. 0229C], we may do what he commanded us to do, and, with him giving it, receive what he promised must be received.

**And he granted that he be made manifest, not to all the people, and so forth.** We find, therefore, in the four Evangelists that the Lord is recorded as having been seen by human beings ten times after the resurrection.

First, at the tomb, by the women. Second, by the same women as they returned from the tomb along the road. Third, by Peter. Fourth, by the two going to the village. Fifth, by several in Jerusalem, where Thomas was not present. Sixth, where Thomas saw him. Seventh, at the Sea of Tiberias. Eighth, on the mountain in Galilee, according to Matthew. Ninth, as Mark says, finally, by those reclining at table, since they were no longer going to remain on earth to eat with him. Tenth, on that very day, no longer on earth but lifted up in a cloud.

He had frequent converse with them for forty days before he ascended into heaven [Col. 0229D]. Yet he did not appear to them throughout all forty successive days. During those forty days he appeared whenever he wished, to whom he wished, and in whatever manner he wished.

**To us, who ate and drank with him, and so forth.** Here the blessed Peter explains what is related in the Gospel: namely, that after the resurrection he drank with the Lord—unless perhaps we understand it to be indicated where he says: “Until I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father” (Matthew 26).

**And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is, and so forth.** For he himself says in the Gospel: “The Father judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son” [Col. 0230A] (John 5). Again, he himself “gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.” Who gave it? The Father. To whom did he give it? To the Son. The one to whom he gave life in himself—this Christ—is both the Son of God and the Son of Man. Therefore, because he is the Son of Man, he received the authority to execute judgment; and that judgment will take place at the end of the age. For he ascended into heaven and sat at the right hand of the Father; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead.

**To him all the prophets bear witness.** Whatever was done temporally in order to establish faith either bore witness to this mission or proclaimed the mission itself of the Son of God.

**To receive forgiveness of sins.** David himself, exhorting him, says: “Wash me more and more from my iniquity [Col. 0230B], and cleanse me from my sin. Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities” (Psalm 50). And in the Gospel he himself authoritatively said to whomever he wished: “Your sins are forgiven you.”

**Through his name, everyone who believes in him.** His name was called Jesus by the angel before he was born; the same angel also explained its etymology, adding: “For he will save his people from their sins.” With the prophets bearing witness in his name to the forgiveness of sins, not only Jews but all who believe receive it.

# THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, THE LAST CHAPTER

> “Two of Jesus’ disciples were going that same day to a village sixty stadia from Jerusalem, named Emmaus. And they were speaking with one another [Col. 0230C] about all these things that had happened. And it came to pass, while they were talking and questioning one another, that Jesus himself drew near and went with them. But their eyes were held, so that they did not recognize him. And he said to them: ‘What are these words that you are exchanging with one another as you walk, and why are you sad?’ And one of them, whose name was Cleopas, answering, said to him: ‘Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem, and have you not known what has happened there in these days?’ He said to them: ‘What things?’ And they said: ‘Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who was a man, a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people; and how our chief priests and rulers handed him over to condemnation to death and crucified him. But we were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel. And now, besides all these things, today is the third day since these things happened. Moreover, some women from among us terrified us: they were at the tomb before dawn, and, not finding his body, they came saying that they had also seen a vision of angels who say that he is alive. And some of our men went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not find.’ And he said to them: ‘O foolish men, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and so enter into his glory?’ And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. And they drew near [Col. 0231A] to the village to which they were going, and he pretended that he was going farther. And they urged him, saying: ‘Stay with us, because it is toward evening, and the day is already declining.’ And he entered with them. And it came to pass, while he reclined with them, that he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and handed it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him; and he vanished from their sight. And they said to one another: ‘Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?’ And rising at that same hour, they returned to Jerusalem and found the eleven gathered together and those who were with them, saying: ‘The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon.’ And they themselves related what had happened on the road and how they had recognized him in the breaking of the bread.”

**Two of Jesus’ disciples were going that same day to a village sixty stadia from Jerusalem, named Emmaus, and they were speaking with one another about all these things that had happened.** *(From Bede.)* A stadium, by which the Greeks, as they say under the authority of Hercules, measure distances along roads, is an eighth of a mile. Therefore sixty stadia signify seven thousand five hundred paces, a distance that appropriately suits those who, certain of the Savior’s death and burial but uncertain about his resurrection, were walking.

For who would doubt that the resurrection, which took place after the seventh day of the week, is contained in the number eight? The disciples, therefore, who were walking and speaking about the Lord completed the sixth [Col. 0231C] mile of their journey, because they grieved that he whom they had seen living without complaint had reached death, which he suffered on the sixth day of the week. They also completed the seventh, because they did not doubt that he had rested in the tomb. But they traveled only half of the eighth, because they did not yet fully believe in the glory of the resurrection that had already taken place.

Emmaus itself is Nicopolis, a distinguished city of Palestine which, after the conquest of Judea, was restored under the emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and, when its status changed, also changed its name.

**And it came to pass, while they were talking and questioning one another, that Jesus himself drew near and went with them.** The Lord draws near and accompanies them as they speak about him, both to kindle faith in his resurrection in their minds [Col. 0231D] and secretly to indicate by the presence of his majesty that he would always fulfill what he had promised: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matthew 18).

**But their eyes were held, so that they did not recognize him, and he said to them: “What are these words that you are exchanging with one another as you walk, and why are you sad?”** The Lord appeared to the disciples but did not show them the form by which they would recognize him. Thus the Lord outwardly did in the eyes of their bodies what was taking place inwardly in the eyes of their hearts. Within themselves they both loved and doubted. Outwardly the Lord was present to them, but he did not show who he was. To those speaking about him he displayed his presence [Col. 0232A], but to those doubting about him he concealed the appearance by which they would recognize him.

**One of them, whose name was Cleopas, answering, said to him: “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem, and have you not known what has happened there in these days?”** They thought him a stranger because they did not recognize his face. But in truth he was a stranger to them, since, having already received the glory of the resurrection, he was far removed from the fragility of their nature. He was a stranger to them because he remained outside their faith, since they were still unaware of his resurrection.

**He said to them: “What things?” And they said: “Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who was a man, a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people.”** They confess him to be a prophet and a great one, but remain silent about the Son of God. Thus, since they did not yet believe perfectly—or were concerned lest they fall into the hands of the persecuting Jews, because they did not know who it was with whom they were speaking—they concealed what they had believed to be true [Col. 0232B].

**And how our chief priests and rulers handed him over to condemnation to death and crucified him. But we were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel.** They were walking sadly with good reason, because they were in a way accusing themselves: they had hoped for redemption from the one whom they now saw dead and did not believe would rise. Above all, they grieved that he had been killed without fault, because they knew him to be innocent.

**And now, besides all these things, today is the third day since these things happened. Moreover, some women from among us terrified us, who were at the tomb before dawn and, not finding his body, came saying that they had also seen a vision of angels who say that he is alive.** They are said rightly to have terrified those whose minds were able to perceive more sorrow from the Lord’s body not being found—for they grieved that this should be added—than joy from the resurrection announced by the angels, by which they might have been restored.

**And some of our men went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not find.** Since Luke said above that Peter ran to the tomb, and now Cleopas says that some of them went to the tomb, he mentioned Peter alone at first because Mary had first announced it to him.

[Col. 0232D]

**And he said to them: “O foolish men, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and so enter into his glory?” And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.** At this point, the necessity laid upon us is not to interpret Scripture but is twofold: to humble ourselves. we have neither been instructed in the Scriptures as much as we ought nor devoted ourselves as much as is fitting to fulfilling what we may perhaps have learned.

For if Moses and all the prophets spoke of Christ and of his entering into glory through the narrow way of suffering, by what reasoning do those glory in calling themselves Christians who, according to the measure of their strength [Col. 0233A], neither desire to investigate how the Scriptures pertain to Christ nor long to reach, through the sufferings of tribulations, the glory they desire to possess with Christ?

**And they drew near to the village to which they were going, and he pretended that he was going farther, and they urged him, saying: “Stay with us,” and so forth.** The simple truth did nothing through deceit. Rather, when it is said, “He pretended that he was going farther,” he showed himself to the disciples bodily as he was present to them inwardly. They were being tested, to see whether, even if they did not yet love him as God, they could at least love him as a stranger. But because they could not be strangers to charity, they—those with whom the Truth was walking—invited him to their lodging as though he were a stranger.

Why do we say that they invited him, when it is written there that “they urged him”? From this example it is gathered that strangers should not merely be invited to lodging but even drawn into it [Col. 0233B].

**And it came to pass, while he reclined with them, that he took bread and blessed it, and so forth.** The one whom they did not recognize in the exposition of sacred Scripture they recognize in the breaking of bread. They were not illumined by hearing God’s commandments but by doing them. For it is written: “It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified” (Romans 2). Therefore, whoever wishes to understand what he has heard should hasten to fulfill in action what he has already been able to understand.

**And he vanished from their sight, and they said: “Was not our heart burning within us?”** “I have come,” he says, “to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” [Col. 0233C] (Luke 12). The Lord cast fire upon the earth when, through the breath of the Holy Spirit, he kindled the hearts of carnal people. The earth burns when the heart of the carnal person, previously cold in its own pleasures, abandons the desires of the present age and is kindled with love for God.

“Was not our heart,” they say, “burning within us while he spoke to us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” When the speech has been heard, the soul of the body grows hot; coldness departs; the mind becomes anxious with heavenly desire and alien to earthly cravings. True love, when it has filled the soul, torments it with tears. Yet while it is tormented by such ardor, it is nourished by those very torments; it delights to hear heavenly commandments. And when it is instructed by the commandments, it is set aflame as though by so many torches.

**And rising at that same hour, they returned to Jerusalem [Col. 0233D], and so forth.** It was already known, through the report made by the women and by Simon Peter, to whom the Lord had already appeared, that Jesus had risen. These two found the others speaking of this when they came to Jerusalem. It is therefore possible that, out of fear, they had earlier been unwilling on the road to say that they had heard he had risen, since they had said only that angels had appeared to the women. Not knowing with whom they were speaking, they could reasonably have been anxious lest, by spreading the report of Christ’s resurrection indiscriminately, they should fall into the hands of the Jews.

Thus the Lord is recorded as having appeared first of all the men—to Peter, that is, among all those whom the four Evangelists and the Apostle Paul mention. Paul speaks of the Lord to the Corinthians: [Col. 0234A] “That he was buried, and that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas and afterward to the eleven.”

**And they themselves related what had happened on the road and how they had recognized him, and so forth.** Besides the fact that, because of the condition of their minds, their eyes suffered something similar while they were still unaware that Christ had to die and rise again—not because the Truth deceived them but because they were unable to perceive the truth and imagined something other than reality—this also happened for the sake of a certain mystery: another likeness was shown to them in him, and they recognized him only in the breaking of bread.

Let no one think that he has recognized Christ if he is not a participant in his body, that is, the Church, whose unity the Apostle commends in the sacrament of the bread, saying: “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body.” Thus, when he handed them the blessed bread, their eyes were opened and they recognized him [Col. 0234B]. They were indeed opened to the recognition of him when the impediment that held them back from recognizing him was removed.

It is not inappropriate to understand this impediment in their eyes as having come from Satan, so that Jesus would not be recognized. Nevertheless, Christ permitted it to remain until the sacrament of the bread, so that, once participation in his body’s unity had taken place, the enemy’s impediment might be understood to have been removed and Christ might be recognized. Amen.

# EASTER TUESDAY

## READING FROM THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES

> “Paul rose and, imposing silence with his hand, said [Col. 0234C]: ‘Men, brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to you the word of this salvation has been sent. For those who lived in Jerusalem and their rulers, not recognizing Jesus or the voices of the prophets that are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by judging him. And finding no cause for death in him, they asked Pilate that he should be killed. And when they had completed everything that had been written about him, taking him down from the tree, they placed him in a tomb. But God raised him from the dead. He was seen for many days by those who had gone up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people. And we announce to you the promise made to our fathers, that God has fulfilled this for your children [Col. 0234D] by raising Jesus Christ our Lord.’”

**Paul rose and, imposing silence with his hand, said: “Men, brothers, sons of the family of Abraham,” and so forth.** All to whom the Apostle was speaking were sons of Abraham according to the flesh, just as they themselves said of themselves in this passage: “We are Abraham’s offspring, and we have never been slaves to anyone,” and again: “Our father is Abraham.” The Lord also said to them: “I know that you are Abraham’s children.”

But they were not children of Abraham by imitation, to whom the Lord was speaking when he said: “You are from your father the devil.” How, then, were the Jews children of the devil? Not by birth, but by imitation: “You are from your father the devil,” the Lord says, “and you wish to do your father’s desires.” Behold, then, how they are children of the devil. What are his desires? “He was a murderer from the beginning, and you are seeking to kill me.” Behold how they are children of the devil by imitation.

Those to whom the Apostle was speaking were both children of Abraham because of the origin of their flesh and children by imitation because of the purity of their fear. It was to these in particular that he said: “and those among you who fear God” [Col. 0235A].

**The word of this salvation has been sent.** *(From Jerome.)* This is the word of which Isaiah says: “The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel” (Isaiah 9): that is, God sent his Son, of whom John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word.” He sent him to Jacob, that is, to the Jews, and he came to Israel, that is, to the people of the nations.

The Word of God is himself the Son of God. Therefore, when the Father sent him as the Word from the Father, it was in his Word that he was sent. Thus the same Son was sent by the Father and by the Son, because the Son himself is the Word of the Father. In that Word of God which was in the beginning with God and was God—in that very wisdom of God—the Word was present when he was to become flesh and dwell among us.

When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman, so that the incarnate Word might appear to human beings.

Whoever lived in Jerusalem and its rulers, etc. (From Bede.) Hence it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “For Moses from ancient times has in every city those who proclaim him in the synagogues.” These words plainly show that the reading of the Law or the Prophets was always read by the Jews in the synagogues on the Sabbath.

And when they had completed everything that had been written about him. (From Augustine.) John also relates these words in this way, saying: “Afterward, Jesus, knowing that all things had been accomplished, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said: I thirst,” etc. (John 19). When Jesus had completed everything that had to be accomplished before his death, he handed over his spirit when he wished and as he wished.

Taking him down from the tree. In the wilderness, a bronze serpent was hung upon a tree by Moses, so that the Lord might be signified both as dead in the serpent (John 3; Numbers 21) and as eternal in the bronze—that is, so that it might be shown that he died according to his humanity, yet was, as it were, bronze according to his divinity.

(From Eucherius.) What should be answered to the Jews when they object that testimony: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree”? They say that the man who hangs on a tree is cursed, but that this applies to the guilty, not to the innocent. For the punishment of sin cannot be a curse upon innocence. Indeed, if Mordecai, after the gallows had been prepared, had been hanged to fulfill the sentence of royal cruelty, would they have judged him worthy of this curse? Certainly not. Therefore our Lord hung upon the tree so that, by being hung upon the tree, he might absolve us from the offense committed through the tree of perdition.

They placed him in a tomb. (From Augustine.) Jesus was placed in a new tomb, in which no one had yet been placed. Just as no one before him and no one after him was conceived in the virgin’s womb, so no one before him and no one after him was buried in this tomb.

But God raised him from the dead. The bitter root of the cross vanished; the flower of life rose with its fruits in glory. This is Aaron’s staff, which blossomed after its drying. For the staff that becomes green after being dry is Christ rising after death: he is the flower of virgins, the crown of martyrs, and the grace of the continent.

Who was seen for many days. That is, for forty days. Yet he did not appear continuously to them throughout all those forty days; he appeared whenever he wished, to whom he wished, and in whatever manner he wished.

To those who went up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, etc. Preserving the historical sense, let us consider the spiritual meaning. Galilee is interpreted as “transmigration,” and Jerusalem as “vision of peace.” Those went up with the Lord from Galilee to Jerusalem who, first rejecting here the fuel of vices, migrate to the heights of virtues. They, with our Redeemer, migrated from passion to resurrection, from death to life, from punishment to glory, and from corruption to incorruption. One day they will joyfully see God in the heavenly Jerusalem, if here they abandon their vices and pass over to the heights of virtues.

And we proclaim to you the promise made to our fathers, etc. For it was said to Abraham: “In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.” To Jacob, however: “And in you and in your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed.” Explaining this, the Apostle says: “He did not say ‘in seeds,’ but ‘in your seed,’ which is Christ.” Christ is indeed the seed of Abraham; through faith in this name, blessing was promised to all the families of the earth, namely, to Jews and Gentiles. This means: “I will give you the holy things of David, the faithful things”—that is, whatever I promised David, I, the faithful guarantor, will fulfill for you: namely, that Christ would be born from his lineage.

## THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER 24

> “Jesus stood in the midst of his disciples and said to them: Peace be with you; it is I; do not be afraid. But they were troubled and terrified and thought that they were seeing a spirit. And he said to them: Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself; touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have. And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and feet. But while they still did not believe and were marveling for joy, he said: Do you have anything here to eat? And they offered him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb. And when he had eaten before them, taking what remained, he gave it to them, and said to them: These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, because it was necessary that everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms should be fulfilled. Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures. And he said to them: For thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name to all nations.”

Jesus stood in the midst of his disciples and said to them: Peace be with you; it is I; do not be afraid. John also recalls this appearance of the Lord after the resurrection, saying: “When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were shut where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews, Jesus came, stood in the midst, and said to them: Peace be with you” (John, final chapter). What is surprising if, after his resurrection, he entered through closed doors, destined now to live forever, when, coming to die, he emerged without the virgin’s womb being opened? As for John’s statement that the apostle Thomas was not then with them, whereas according to Luke the two disciples, one of whom was Cleopas, returned to Jerusalem and found the Eleven gathered together with those who were with them, it must undoubtedly be understood that Thomas had gone out from there before the Lord appeared and spoke these words to them.

But they were troubled and terrified and thought that they were seeing a spirit. This was the first thought that arose in the apostles’ hearts—the very belief that the heretics called Manichaeans hold and profess concerning Christ: that he did not possess true flesh, but was a spirit. The Manichaeans never believe that Jesus was a human being, whereas the disciples knew him as a man, with whom they had lived in such close association. But after he died, why should they believe that what they knew could die could be raised? He appeared to their eyes as they had known him, and, not believing that true flesh could rise from the tomb on the third day, they thought that they were seeing a spirit. This error of the apostles is the sect of the Manichaeans.

When these things are brought against them, they usually answer in this way: “What evil do we believe, since we believe Christ to be God? We believe that he was a spirit; we do not believe that he was flesh. Spirit is better than flesh: we believe what is better, and we refuse to believe what is worse.” If there is nothing evil in this statement, let Jesus leave his disciples in this error. What did the disciples believe? They believed Christ to be a spirit. They did not think that he was nothing, but that he was a spirit. Do you think that you are in danger from only a slight illness? Hear the physician’s diagnosis.

[Col. 0237D]

And he said to them: Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? What sort of thoughts, if not false, diseased, and destructive ones? Christ would have lost the fruit of his passion if the resurrection had not been true: “Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts?” It was as if a good farmer were saying: “What I planted there, I shall find there—not thorns, which I did not plant, in your hearts.” Faith descended, because it is from above. These thoughts, however, did not descend from above; they rose in the heart itself like bad grass.

See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself, etc. By many and varied proofs he establishes that his resurrection was certain and real, removing every faithlessness and every doubt concerning it. It would have been little for him to offer himself to the eyes to be seen, if he had not also offered himself to the hands to be touched. By showing his bones and flesh for the disciples to touch, he openly signifies the condition of the true resurrection, which has now occurred in him and will occur in us. This is not as Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, wrote:

> “Our body in the glory of that resurrection will be intangible, subtler than winds and air. For in that glory of the resurrection our body will indeed be subtle through the effect of spiritual power, but tangible through the truth of its nature.”

Nor should the Apostle’s statement be thought to contradict this assertion: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 15). In this passage the Apostle signifies by the name “flesh and blood” not the substance of the true body, but the corruption of mortality. He himself explained this immediately afterward, saying: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption.”

For Scripture speaks of flesh in different ways: according to nature, according to guilt, and according to the corruption of mortality that arose from guilt. It speaks according to nature when it says: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2), and: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). It speaks according to guilt when it says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.” It speaks according to corruptibility when it says: “And they remembered that they were flesh,” that is, fragile and mortal. The Psalmist himself makes clear that this is what he indicated by the term “flesh,” for he immediately adds: “A spirit that goes and does not return” (Psalm 77).

Therefore flesh will not possess the kingdom of God—that is, flesh according to guilt or mortality—yet flesh will possess the kingdom of God: flesh according to nature, which the Lord after his resurrection presented to the disciples to see and touch. Concerning this flesh blessed Job, describing the glory of the resurrection, says: “And again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God” (Job 19). Read the letter of Saint Augustine to Consentius concerning the Lord’s body after the resurrection.

And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and feet. He showed not only his hands and feet, on which the marks left by the nails shone forth, but also, as John testifies, his side, which had been pierced by the lance. By displaying the scar of his wounds, he healed the wound of their doubt and unbelief.

Just as after the resurrection he deigned to strengthen the disciples’ faith and hope by displaying the places of the nails and the lance, so on the day of judgment he will come displaying both these signs of his passion and the cross itself, in order to confound the impiety and unbelief of the proud. He will openly show to all angels and human beings that he is the one who died by the hands of the impious and for the sake of the impious, so that they may see, as it is written: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced, and all the tribes of the earth shall mourn over him.”

It should be noted that pagans commonly construct a charge at this point and mock, with foolish chatter, our faith in the resurrection that we hope for:

> “If your God,” they say, “was unable to heal even the wounds inflicted upon him by the Jews, but carried the marks of his scars into heaven with him, as you claim, with what audacity do you think that he will restore your members from the dust to wholeness?”

They should be answered as follows. Our God, who, when he wished and as he wished, was able to raise from the tomb the flesh that he had already glorified with perpetual immortality, was also able to raise it in whatever condition he wished. It does not follow that he who is shown to have done greater things was unable to do lesser ones. Rather, through the grace of his dispensation, he who did the greater refrained from doing away with the lesser: he who destroyed the dominion of death did not wish to erase the signs of death.

First, he did this in order through these signs to establish the disciples’ faith in his resurrection. Second, so that, interceding for us with the Father, he might show above all what kind of death he had endured for the life of mortals. Third, so that he might continually renew for those redeemed by his death the signs of how mercifully they had been helped, by setting those signs before them. Therefore they should never cease to sing the mercies of the Lord, but should say, as those redeemed by the Lord: “For he is good, for his mercy endures forever” (Psalms 127, 155).

Finally, he did this so that at the judgment he might announce to the faithless, among their other crimes, how justly they are condemned, by displaying even the scars of the wounds that he received from them. It is as if a very brave soldier, at the command of his king, had fought a single combat for the safety of his entire nation, received many wounds, yet killed the enemy, seized his spoils, and brought victory to his people. If, when entrusted to a physician for treatment, he were asked whether he wished to be healed so that no trace of his wounds remained, or rather so that the scars remained while all disfigurement and ugliness disappeared, he would answer that he preferred to be healed in such a way that, with his entire former health and beauty restored, he might forever carry with him the signs of so great a triumph.

Thus the Lord, for the perpetual sign of victory, preferred to carry with him into heaven not the wounds of his passion inflicted for us, but their scars, rather than erase them; yet none of this prejudices the faith of our resurrection. Concerning that resurrection, the true promise declares: “Not a hair of your head shall perish” (Luke 21).

But while they still did not believe and were marveling for joy, he said: Do you have anything here to eat? To make the truth of his resurrection known, he deigned not only to be touched by the disciples but also to eat with them—not as though he needed food after the resurrection, nor as though he were indicating that we will need food in the resurrection for which we hope, but in order by this means to establish the nature of the risen body, lest they think that it was not a body but a spirit, and that he had appeared to them not solidly but merely as an image. He ate by power, not by necessity. Thirsty earth absorbs water in one way, and a burning sunbeam in another: the former through need, the latter through power.

And they offered him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb, and when he had eaten before them, taking what remained, he gave it to them. What are we to believe that the broiled fish signifies, if not the mediator between God and human beings, who suffered? He deigned to lie hidden in the waters of the human race; he wished to be caught in the snare of our death, and, as it were, was broiled in tribulation at the time of his passion.

But he who deigned to become a broiled fish in his passion became a honeycomb for us in his resurrection. By wishing to be represented in the broiled fish as suffering the tribulation of his passion, he wished in the honeycomb to express the two natures of his person. A honeycomb is honey in wax; honey in wax is divinity in humanity.

The Redeemer indicates these things in such a way as to lay out for us who follow him the path of imitation. For behold, he wished to join a honeycomb to the broiled fish in his food, because he receives into his body for eternal rest those who, while they experience tribulations for God here, do not withdraw from the love of inward sweetness. The honeycomb is taken together with the broiled fish because those who here undergo affliction for the sake of truth will there be satisfied with true sweetness.

And he said to them: These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you. That is, while I was still in mortal flesh, in which you also are. At that time he was in the same flesh, but he was not with them in the same mortality. After he rose, he was with them for forty days, as we read, through the presentation of his bodily presence, but he was not with them as a sharer in human weakness.

For it was necessary that everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms should be fulfilled. (From Bede.) See how he removed every ambiguity: he was seen, he was touched, he ate; he was certainly the same person. Yet, lest he appear to have deceived the human senses in any respect, he referred them to the Scriptures. Let the pagans say whatever they wish: “He was a magician; he was able to display himself in this way.” Could a magician, before he was born, have prophesied himself in this way? Bring forth the Scriptures, because what you see was foreseen, and what you behold was foretold. “Hear, O daughter, and see”: hear what was foretold; see what has been fulfilled.

Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures. And he said to them: For thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day. He offers himself to the eyes to be seen and to the hands to be touched. Is the Law insufficient? He recalls the Scriptures. Is that still insufficient? He opens their understanding, so that you may understand what you read. Then, through the established truth of his body, he commends the unity of the Church.

[Col. 0240D]

And that repentance should be preached in his name, etc. Let the perversity of the heretics not bark: throughout the whole world the Church has been spread; all nations have the Church. Let no one deceive us: it is the true Church, it is the catholic Church. It began at Jerusalem and reached us; it is there, and it is here. It did not leave there in order to come here; it grew, it did not migrate.

And rightly it is written, among the other mysteries of the Lord’s mercy, that “it was necessary” that the ministers of the word, who were going to preach repentance and forgiveness of sins in the name of Christ crucified and raised from the dead to all nations, should begin from Jerusalem. This was not only because the oracles of God had been entrusted to them, because their adoption as sons, glory, covenants, legislation, worship, and promises belonged to them, because their fathers were theirs, and from them came Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever (Romans 3). It was also so that the nations, entangled in various errors and crimes, might be summoned by this greatest sign of divine mercy to hope for the obtaining of pardon: they would see that even those who crucified the Son of God had been granted not only forgiveness of guilt by the Father but also the joy of eternal life.

## WEDNESDAY OF EASTER

## ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, CHAPTER 3

> “Peter opened his mouth and said: Men of Israel, and those who fear God, listen. The God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his Son Jesus, whom you indeed handed over and denied before Pilate’s face, when he was judging that he should be released. But you denied the Holy and Just One and asked that a murderer be granted to you; you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead, of which we are witnesses. And now, brothers, I know that you acted through ignorance, as did your rulers. But God, who foretold through the mouth of all the prophets that his Christ would suffer, has fulfilled it in this way. Repent, therefore, and be converted, so that your sins may be blotted out.”

Peter opened his mouth and said. It should be noted that he calls men of the race of Israel and those who fear God to hear the word of the Lord. They are called “men” from their strength: they know neither how to fail through endurance nor to boast with some elation in prosperity, but, fixed in a steadfast spirit and strengthened by contemplation of heavenly things, they remain always fearless.

“Those who fear the Lord,” he says, “listen”—that is, those who have reverence for his name, because no one deserves to hear his words unless he is known also to fear him. The fear of the Lord is just and upright. It renews hearing, grants love, and kindles the ardor of chastity.

The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers. He could have said, “the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,” but he names God three times—God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob—so that you may understand the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. And lest the threefold naming of God produce scandal for you, he adds: “the God of our fathers.” Wisely, therefore, he distinguished the persons and united the nature.

He glorified his Son Jesus. He glorified his Son when, after the exceedingly wondrous resurrection, God granted him to possess the belief of the whole world in that which he had become as a human being. He glorified him with the glory of the resurrection, glorified him with the glory of the ascension, and glorified him by his sitting at the right hand.

Whom you indeed handed over. For this reason Pilate answered the Lord, saying: “Am I a Jew? Your nation and the chief priests handed you over to me; what have you done?” (John 18)—that is, so that you might be handed over to me.

The priests handed over the Lord through envy; Judas handed him over through greed; the Father handed him over for our liberation; the Son handed himself over because of his love for us. Concerning the Father, the Apostle says: “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all.” Concerning the Son: “He loved us and handed himself over for us.”

And you denied him before Pilate’s face. Saying: “Crucify him, crucify him. We have no king but Caesar. We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.”

When he was judging that he should be released. For, as the Gospel says, Pilate was seeking an opportunity to release Jesus, saying: “I find no cause in him,” and neither did Herod. Pilate sent him to Herod, and Herod sent him back to Pilate. Between two acts of impiety, piety moved back and forth, yet impiety could not condemn piety.

The accused is present, and no guilt is found. “You handed this man over to me,” he says, “as one who was turning the people away; and behold, after questioning him before you, I find no cause in him concerning the matters of which you accuse him. You say that he orders tribute not to be paid to Caesar: I have proved that what you allege is false. You say that he teaches against the Law: I have proved that he does not destroy the Law but fulfills it. Everything you have alleged has been found to be the opposite.”

And you asked that a murderer be given to you. There was, as the Gospel says, one called Barabbas, imprisoned because he had committed murder during a rebellion. Barabbas is interpreted as “son of the father.” He signifies the devil, who stirs up many rebellions throughout the whole world—murders, adulteries, and every crime. As soon as Jesus was crucified, this Barabbas was released and strangles the Jewish people.

But you killed the Author of life, etc. You killed him who fashioned the human being from the clay of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul. You killed him who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14), and concerning whom John says: “This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John, final chapter).

And now, brothers, I know that you acted through ignorance. For, as the Apostle says: “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.”

But God, who foretold through the mouth of all the prophets that his Christ would suffer, has fulfilled it in this way. Hence the Lord himself said to Cleopas and the other disciple: “O foolish ones and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that Christ should suffer these things and so enter into his glory?” And beginning from Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them all the Scriptures concerning himself (Luke, final chapter).

If Moses and all the prophets spoke of Christ, and of his entering into his glory through the narrow passage of suffering, how do those who, according to the measure of their strength, neither investigate how the Scriptures pertain to Christ nor desire to reach the glory they wish to possess with Christ through the sufferings of tribulation boast that they are Christians?

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, FINAL CHAPTER

> “Jesus revealed himself again to his disciples beside the Sea of Tiberias. He revealed himself in this way: Simon Peter and Thomas, who is called Didymus, and Nathanael, who was from Cana of Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two other of his disciples were together. Simon Peter said to them: I am going fishing. They said to him: We are coming with you. And they went out and got into the boat, and that night they caught nothing. When morning had come, Jesus stood on the shore, but they did not know that it was Jesus. Jesus therefore said to them: Children, do you have anything to eat? They answered him: No. He said to them: Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find something. So they cast it, and now they were unable to haul it in because of the abundance of fish. Therefore that disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter: It is the Lord. When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he wrapped his tunic around himself, for he was naked, and threw himself into the sea. But the other disciples came in the boat—for they were not far from land, about two hundred cubits—dragging the net of fish. When they came down onto the land, they saw burning coals laid out, and fish placed upon them, and bread. Jesus said to them: Bring some of the fish that you have now caught. Simon Peter therefore went up and dragged the net onto the land, full of large fish, one hundred and fifty-three. And although there were so many, the net was not torn. Jesus said to them: Come, eat. And none of those reclining dared to ask him: Who are you? knowing that it was the Lord. Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and the fish likewise. This was now the third time that Jesus was revealed to his disciples after he had risen from the dead.”

[Col. 0243C]

Jesus revealed himself beside the Sea of Tiberias; he revealed himself in this way. Simon Peter and Thomas, who is called Didymus, and Nathanael, who was from Cana of Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two other of his disciples were together. Simon Peter said to them: I am going fishing. They said to him: We are coming with you. And they went out and got into the boat, and that night they caught nothing.

It may be asked why Peter, who had been a fisherman before his conversion, returned to fishing after his conversion. Since the truth says: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9), why did he take up again what he had abandoned?

But if the virtue of discernment is applied, the answer becomes clear. The occupation that had existed without sin before his conversion could also be resumed without guilt after his conversion. For we know that Peter was a fisherman, but Matthew a tax collector. After his conversion Peter returned to fishing, but Matthew did not return to the business of the tax office. For it is one thing to seek one’s livelihood through fishing, and another to increase one’s money through the profits of tax collection.

There are many occupations that can be practiced without sin only with difficulty, or not at all. To occupations that entangle a person in sin, therefore, the mind must not return after conversion.

When morning had now come, Jesus stood on the shore, but the disciples did not know that it was Jesus. Jesus therefore said to them: Children, do you have anything to eat? They answered him: No.

It may be asked why, after the resurrection, the Lord stood on the shore while the disciples were laboring at sea, when before his resurrection he walked upon the waves of the sea before the disciples. The reason is quickly understood if we consider the circumstance that was then present.

What does the sea signify, if not the present age, which is battered by the tumult of causes and by the waves of corruptible life? What is signified by the firmness of the shore, if not that permanence of eternal rest? Since the disciples were still amid the waves of mortal life, they labored at sea. But because our Redeemer had already passed beyond the corruption of the flesh, after his resurrection he stood on the shore, as though speaking to the disciples in reality of the mystery of his resurrection:

“I no longer appear to you at sea, because I am no longer with you amid the waves of disturbance.”

A great difficulty in fishing was therefore imposed upon the disciples, so that, when the Teacher came, a great elevation of wonder might arise.

He said to them: Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find something. Twice in the holy Gospel it is read that the Lord commanded nets to be cast for fishing: before the passion and after the passion.

Before our Redeemer suffered and rose, he commanded that a net be cast for fishing, but he did not command whether it should be cast on the right or the left. After the resurrection, however, appearing to the disciples, he commanded that the net be cast on the right.

In that fishing so many were caught that the nets were torn; in this one, many were caught, but the nets were not torn. Who does not know that the good are represented by the right and the wicked by the left?

That fishing, therefore, in which it was not specified to which side the net should be cast signified the present Church, which gathers good and wicked together and does not select those whom it draws in, because it does not know which of them it may select. But this fishing, which took place after the Lord’s resurrection, was cast only on the right, because only the Church of the elect will attain the vision of his glory, and it will possess nothing belonging to left-hand works.

In that fishing the net is torn because now, together with the elect, so many reprobates enter the confession of the faith that they even rend the Church itself through heresies. In this fishing, however, many fish, and large ones, are caught, and the net is not torn, because the holy Church of the elect, resting in the continual peace of its Author, is no longer torn apart by dissensions.

They cast the nets, and now they were unable to haul it in because of the abundance of fish. Therefore that disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter: It is the Lord. When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he wrapped his tunic around himself—for he was naked—and threw himself into the sea. But the other disciples came in the boat, for they were not far from land, about two hundred cubits, dragging the net of fish.

When they came down onto the land, they saw burning coals laid out, and fish placed upon them, and bread. This should not be understood to mean that the bread too had been placed upon the coals; rather, the verb “saw” must be supplied separately: They saw burning coals laid out, they saw fish placed upon them, and they saw bread. Or, better: They saw burning coals laid out and fish placed upon them; they also saw bread.

[Col. 0245A]

Bring some of the fish that you have now caught; Simon Peter went up and dragged the net onto the land. (From Gregory.) After such large fish had been caught, Simon Peter went up and dragged the net onto the land.

I believe that your charity already perceives what it means that Peter drags the net to land. The holy Church has been entrusted to him; specifically it is said to him: “Simon, son of John, do you love me? Feed my sheep.” What is later revealed in speech is now signified in action.

Since the preacher of the Church separates us from the waves of this world’s life, it is clearly necessary that Peter should draw the net full of fish to land. He draws the fish to the solidity of the shore who, through the voice of holy preaching, displays to the faithful the stability of the eternal homeland.

He accomplished this through words, through letters, and he accomplishes it daily through signs of miracles. Whenever through him we are converted to the love of eternal rest, whenever we are separated from the tumult of earthly things, what else do we do but draw fish caught within the net of faith to the shore?

Full of large fish, one hundred and fifty-three. This number is not without a great mystery, but the depth of so great a mystery awaits your attention. For the Evangelist would not have carefully expressed the total unless he had judged it to be full of sacramental meaning.

You know that in the Old Testament every activity is prescribed through the commandments of the Decalogue. In the New, however, the power of that same activity is given to the faithful in multiplied form through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. The prophet announces this when he says: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety,” and “the spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him” (Isaiah 11).

But a person perceives activity in this Spirit only if he acknowledges faith in the Trinity, believing the Father, Son, and the same Holy Spirit to be of one power and confessing them to be of one substance.

Since the seven things mentioned above have been more broadly given through the New Testament, while the ten commandments belong to the Old, all our power and activity can be fully contained in the number seventeen, ten plus seven.

Let us therefore multiply seventeen by three, and the result is fifty-one. This number too is not without a great mystery, because in the Old Testament we read that the fiftieth year was commanded to be called the Jubilee, in which the whole people would rest from every labor.

But true rest is found in unity. For one cannot be divided; wherever there is the rift of division, there is no true rest.

Let us multiply fifty-one by three, and the result is one hundred and fifty-three. Since all our activity and power, displayed in faith in the Trinity, tends toward rest, we multiply seventeen three times so that we arrive at fifty-one. Our true rest comes when we already recognize that very glory of the Trinity, which we firmly hold to exist in the unity of divinity.

We multiply fifty-one three times, and we possess the number of the elect in the heavenly homeland, as though the number of the fish were one hundred and fifty-four [sic]. After the Lord’s resurrection, therefore, it was fitting that the net cast should catch as many fish as would signify only the elect of the heavenly homeland.

(From Augustine.) There is also another computation of this number composed of seven and ten. If you count all the numbers from one through seventeen, in this way—one, two, three; add three and you have six; add four to these and you have ten; add five and you will have fifteen—and so, as the numbers increase and are added together through seventeen, the sum of all the numbers multiplied from one through seventeen is one hundred and fifty-three. This computation agrees quite appropriately with the preceding interpretation: the Law in the number ten and grace in the number seven.

Many other things worthy of admiration could also be considered from this, but the narrowness of the present time prevents us from saying them all.

And although they were so large, the net was not torn. The evangelist added an essential detail, saying: “And although they were so many,” or “so large,” as he says above, “full of large fish,” the net was not torn—that is, they were great, but there was no heresy among them; and therefore there were all the more no heresies, because they were great.

Jesus said to them, “Come, have breakfast,” and no one of those reclining at table dared to ask him, “Who are you?” The meaning, then, is this: the evidence of the truth was so overwhelming, since Jesus appeared to those disciples, that none of them dared either to deny it or even to doubt it. For if anyone had doubted, he would certainly have had to ask. Thus it is said: “No one dared to ask him, ‘Who are you?’”—as though it were said, “No one dared to doubt that it was he.”

And Jesus came, took the bread, and gave it to them, and likewise the fish. It should also be noted that the Lord is described as having his final meal with seven disciples: Peter and Thomas, Nathanael and the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples are said to have been present. Why does he celebrate his final meal with seven disciples? Surely because he announces that only those who are filled with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit will be with him in the eternal refreshment. The whole of this age, too, unfolds over seven days, and perfection is often signified by the number seven.

Those, therefore, feast at that final meal on the presence of the truth who now transcend earthly things through their zeal for perfection. The love of this world does not bind them; and even if, through temptations, it makes some sort of disturbance against them, it nevertheless does not blunt their desires once begun. Of this final meal it is said elsewhere through John: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Rev. 19). For this reason he says that they are invited not to breakfast but to supper, since, plainly, at the end of the day the meal is supper.

Those, therefore, who, when the time of the present life has ended, come to the refreshment of heavenly contemplation are invited not to the Lamb’s breakfast but to supper. This supper is expressed by that final meal at which the seven disciples are remembered as being present. For, as we have said, he will then receive into eternal refreshment those who now, filled with the sevenfold grace, long for the love of the Spirit.

[Col. 0247A]

What does it mean that our Redeemer ate a roasted fish after his resurrection, while in another Gospel he is said to have eaten a honeycomb with a roasted fish, whereas here he eats bread with the fish? What does the roasted fish signify, if not Christ who suffered? And what does the honeycomb signify, if not the sweetness of his divinity?

He is a fish because he deigned to lie hidden in the waters of the human race and wished to be caught in the snare of our death; and, as though roasted by affliction, he was roasted at the time of his passion. But he who deigned to become a roasted fish in his passion became a honeycomb for us in his resurrection.

Or perhaps, in the roasted fish, he wished to signify the tribulation of his passion, while in the honeycomb he wished to express both natures of his person. For a honeycomb is honey in wax; and honey in wax is divinity in humanity. This also agrees with the present reading, for he ate fish and bread: the one who, in his humanity, could be roasted like a fish refreshes us with bread through his divinity, for he said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6).

He ate roasted fish and bread, therefore, so that by this food he might show us that he endured suffering through our humanity and brought about our resurrection through his divinity.

“This is now the third time that Jesus manifested himself to his disciples after he had risen,” and so forth. We must refer this not to the manifestations themselves but to the days—that is, to the first day, when he rose; then after eight days, when the disciple Thomas saw and believed; and then to this day, when he did this concerning the fish. How many days later he did this is not stated here. For on that very first day he was seen more than once, as the combined testimony of all the evangelists demonstrates. But, as has been said, his manifestations must be counted according to the days, so that this may be the third.

## AUGUSTINE, ALSO, IN HIS HOMILY FOR EASTER

The preaching of our Liberator is our liberation. We observe two catches of fish in the holy Gospel: one, when the nets were cast at his word, took place earlier, when he chose the disciples; the other took place when he rose from the dead. That first catch signified the Church as she is now; this one, after the Lord’s resurrection, signified the Church as she will be at the end of the age.

In the first catch, finally, he ordered the nets to be cast, but did not say into which part; he did not say to the right or to the left. The fish signified human beings. If he had said “to the right,” only the good would have been intended; if he had said “to the left,” only the wicked. But because good and wicked were going to be mixed together in the Church, the nets were cast without distinction, so that fish might be caught, signifying the mixture of the good and the wicked.

Three things, then, were signified in that first catch: the mixture of good and wicked, the pressure of the crowds, and the separation of heretics. The mixture of good and wicked was signified because the nets were cast neither to the right nor to the left. The pressure of the crowds was signified because so much was caught that they weighed down the little boat. Then the separation of heretics was signified because the multitude was so great that the nets were torn.

Now consider this catch, which has been read today. It took place after the Lord’s resurrection, so that it might signify what the Church will be like after our resurrection: “Cast the net,” he says, “on the right side.” The number of those who stood on the right was therefore distinguished. For he will place the sheep on the right and the goats on the left. “Cast it,” he says, “on the right,” as though he were saying: “I have already risen, and I wish to signify the Church as she will be in the resurrection of the dead.”

In the first catch a multitude was mentioned, but no definite number. In the second, both multitude and size were mentioned, and a definite number was given. Now, before the resurrection comes and the good are separated from the wicked, what the prophet says is fulfilled: “I proclaimed and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number” (Ps. 39). What does “I proclaimed” mean? “I cast the nets.” And what does “they were multiplied beyond number” mean? The number pertains to the saints who will reign with Christ. For now, people may enter the Church beyond the number; they cannot enter the kingdom of heaven beyond it.

Peter drew the nets to shore. A moment ago, when the Gospel was read, you heard this. When you hear “shore,” understand the end of the sea; when you hear “the end of the sea,” understand the end of the age.

In that first catch the nets were not drawn to shore; rather, the fish that had been caught were poured into the boats. Here, however, they drew the nets to shore. Hope for the end of the age: the end will come, for the good of those on the right and the evil of those on the left.

What is this? “They drew in the nets,” he says, “containing one hundred and fifty-three fish.” And the evangelist added an essential detail: “And although they were so large, the net was not torn.” They will be large, but there will be no heresies; and therefore there will be all the more no heresies, because they will be large.

What does “large” mean? Read the words of the Lord himself in the Gospel, and you will find the meaning. In one passage he says: “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it. Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever dissolves one of these least commandments and teaches others to do so”—that is, dissolves them by living badly and teaches them by teaching good things—“will be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5), that is, in the Church, which exists now.

For the Church herself is also called the kingdom of heaven. She has fish swimming together, both good and wicked. In this kingdom of heaven—that is, in the Church of the present age—the one who teaches good things and does evil is called least, because he is there as well. Such a person is not there in the kingdom of heaven—that is, in the Church—as he will be in that future age.
