He teaches good things and does evil; he is necessary there, and he is a hired servant. “Amen, I say to you,” the Lord says, “they have received their reward.”

But “whoever does and teaches” will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. These are the large fish caught on the right: the one who does and thus teaches, who teaches good things and does not contradict his own speech by living badly, even though he has a good tongue as a witness to an evil life. Therefore, the one who does and thus teaches will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.

“But I say to you: unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter,” and so forth. How do you understand the kingdom of heaven now? Is it that of which it is said to those on the right: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom”? Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees.

What does “more than that of the scribes and Pharisees” mean? Consider those scribes and Pharisees who sit on Moses’ seat (Matt. 23). Of them it is said: “Do whatever they say, but do not do what they do. For they say and do not do.” The righteousness of the Pharisees, then, is to say and not to do. Let your righteousness exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees, so that you both speak good things and live well.

As for the number of the one hundred and fifty-three fish, why should we weave the same thing again? You know it. The growing number arises from seventeen. Begin with one and reach seventeen, adding them all: add one and two, and they make three; add three, and they make six; add four, and they make ten. Continue adding them all up to seventeen, and you arrive at one hundred and fifty-three.

Our whole concern, therefore, must be to understand what the seventeen signify, for there is the foundation of the one hundred and fifty-three. What do the seventeen signify? Recognize ten in the Law: ten commandments were given. First, it is called the Decalogue, written on tablets by the finger of God. Recognize the Law in ten; recognize the Holy Spirit in seven. For the Holy Spirit is commended by the number seven.

Therefore he is named in the Law in connection with sanctification. “On the seventh day God made the light”—it is not said that he sanctified it. He made the firmament—it is not said that he sanctified the firmament. He separated the sea from the land and commanded the land to sprout vegetation—it is not said that he sanctified it. He made the moon and the stars—it is not said that he sanctified them. He commanded the animals to come forth from the waters, those that swim and those that fly—it is not said that he sanctified them. He commanded the animals to come forth from the earth, the four-footed creatures and all creeping things—it is not said that he sanctified them. He made the human being himself—it is not said that he sanctified him.

He came to the seventh day, where he rested, and he sanctified it. Through his rest God signified our rest. There, then, our sanctification will be complete, when we rest with him without end. For why would God rest? He was not wearied by working. If you make something by a word, you are not wearied; if you command and it immediately comes to be, you stand and remain whole. He spoke a few words by which he made everything, and suddenly he became tired?

Recognize the Law in ten; recognize the Holy Spirit in seven. Let the Spirit be joined to the Law. For if you receive the Law and the Spirit’s help is lacking, you do not fulfill what you read; you do not fulfill what is commanded you. But a human being under the Law is moreover held liable as a transgressor.

Let the Spirit come and help, and what is commanded is accomplished. If the Spirit is absent, the letter kills you. Why does the letter kill you? Because it will make you a transgressor. You cannot be excused on the grounds of ignorance, because you have received the Law; you have learned what you should do. Ignorance does not excuse you, and the Spirit does not help you—therefore you have perished.

But what does the apostle Paul say? “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3). How does the Spirit give life? Because he causes the letter to be fulfilled, so that it may not kill.

These are the saints who fulfill God’s Law by God’s gift. The Law can command; it cannot help. The Spirit, the helper, comes, and God’s command is fulfilled with joy and love.

For many obey through fear; but those who fulfill the Law out of fear of punishment would rather that what they feared did not exist. Those, however, who fulfill the Law because they love righteousness rejoice even there, since they do not have an enemy.

Therefore the Lord says: “Be reconciled with your adversary quickly, while you are with him on the way” (Matt. 5). Who is your adversary? The word of the Law. What is the way? This life. How is it your adversary? It says, “You shall not commit adultery,” and you want to commit adultery. It says, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property,” and you want to seize what belongs to others. It says, “Honor your father and mother,” and you are insulting toward your parents. The Law says, “Do not love false testimony,” but you do not withdraw from lying.

When you see that this word commands one thing while you do another, is it not your adversary? You have evil as your adversary; do not let it enter the inner chamber with you. Make peace while you are with him on the way. The Lord is present to reconcile you both.

How does the Lord reconcile you? By forgiving sins and inspiring righteousness, so that good works may be done. When, therefore, you have been reconciled with your adversary—that is, with the Decalogue of the Law—through the Holy Spirit you will belong to the seventeen. From that point the number will grow to one hundred and fifty-three. You will be crowned on the right, so that you do not remain to be condemned on the left.

## THURSDAY

## READING FROM THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, CHAPTER 8

[Col. 0250C]

> “An angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying: ‘Rise and go toward the south, to the road that descends from Jerusalem to Gaza; this is deserted.’ And he rose and went. And behold, an Ethiopian man, a eunuch, a powerful official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was over all her treasuries, had come to Jerusalem to worship; and he was returning, seated on his chariot and reading the prophet Isaiah.
>
> “The Spirit said to Philip: ‘Approach and join yourself to this chariot.’ Philip ran up and heard him reading the prophet Isaiah, and he said: ‘Do you think you understand what you are reading?’ He said: ‘And how can I understand unless someone shows me?’ And he asked Philip to come up and sit with him.
>
> “Now the passage of Scripture that he was reading was this: ‘Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth. In his humiliation judgment was taken away from him. Who will declare his generation? For his life will be taken from the earth.’
>
> “The eunuch answered Philip and said: ‘I beg you, of whom does the prophet say this—of himself or of someone else?’ Philip opened his mouth and, beginning from this Scripture, evangelized Jesus to him.
>
> “As they went along the road, they came to a certain water. And the eunuch said: ‘Behold, here is water; what prevents me from being baptized?’ Philip said: ‘If you believe with your whole heart, it is permitted.’ He answered: ‘I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.’ And he ordered the chariot to stop, and both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him.
>
> “When they had come up from the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more. He went on his way rejoicing. Philip, however, was found at Azotus, and, passing through, he evangelized all the cities until he came to Caesarea, preaching the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

An angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, “Rise and go,” and so forth. *(From Bede.)* He is rightly sought, found, and washed at midday who, burning with devotion of heart, deserved to be consecrated to God as a kind of firstfruits of the nations. In him that saying of the Psalmist was spiritually fulfilled: “Ethiopia will stretch out her hands to God” (Ps. 67).

“To the road that descends from Jerusalem to Gaza; this is deserted,” and so forth. It is not the road but Gaza that is said to be deserted. For that ancient Gaza, which was once the boundary of the Canaanites near Egypt, was destroyed down to its foundations, and another was built elsewhere in its place. Allegorically, this signifies the people of the nations, once deserted by the worship of God and cultivated by the preaching of none of the prophets.

The road that descends from Jerusalem to that same place and opens the fountain of salvation is the Lord Jesus Christ, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14), because the heavenly Jerusalem descended to our lowliness.

“And behold, an Ethiopian man, a powerful eunuch.” Because of the strength and integrity of his mind he is called a man. Nor is this undeserved, since he had such devotion to the Scriptures that he did not cease reading them even on the road. He also possessed such great love for religion that, leaving behind the royal court, he came from the farthest parts of the world to the Lord’s temple.

Therefore, with just reward, while he sought Christ as the interpreter of what he was reading, he found the one whom he sought. And, as Jerome says, he found more in the desert fountain of the Church than in the gilded temple of the synagogue. There what Jeremiah declares in wonder was fulfilled: “The Ethiopian has changed his skin” (Jer. 13)—that is, washed clean of the filth of sins, he came up whitened from the washing of Jesus.

“Of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians.” In the Book of Kings we also read that the queen of the South came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon. It was indeed customary among that nation always to be ruled by women, who were called Candaces.

“Who was over all her treasuries,” and so forth. The queen of the Ethiopians, sending her treasurer ahead to Jerusalem, designates the Church of the nations, which would bring to the Lord the gifts of virtues and faith. The etymology of the name also agrees. For Candace can be interpreted from the Hebrew as “changed.” She is the one to whom, in the Psalm, concerning those who will be changed, it is said: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house.”

“The Spirit said to Philip: ‘Approach and join yourself to this chariot,’” and so forth. The Spirit was speaking to Philip in his heart. For the Spirit of God speaks words to us, as it were, through a hidden force, and makes known what must be done.

“Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter.” Just as a sheep, when led to sacrifice, does not resist, so he suffered by his own will. Or, in a deeper interpretation, just as a lamb was accustomed to be sacrificed at Passover, so Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed.

“And like a lamb before its shearer is silent.” For he redeemed us not only with his blood but also covered us with his wool, so that he might warm us, chilled by unbelief, with his garment, and so that we might hear the Apostle speaking to us: “As many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Rom. 6).

“So he did not open his mouth.” During his passion he wished to answer Pilate and the chief priests only briefly, and Herod not at all.

“In his humiliation judgment was taken away from him.” For the judge of all found no truth in the judgment; rather, without any guilt, he was condemned by the riot of the Jews and the voice of Pilate.

“Who will declare his generation?” *(From Bede.)* This may be understood either of his divinity: that it is impossible for us to know the mysteries of his divine birth, of which the Father speaks, “Before the morning star I begot you”; or of the virgin birth, which can scarcely be explained. When Mary asked its manner, she was told through the angel: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you,” so that the mysteries of his birth are spoken of either by the angel or by the evangelist, whose account of it is exceedingly rare.

“For his life will be taken from the earth.” *(From Jerome.)* This means that he would live not on earth but in heaven. When the eunuch of Queen Candace was being reproved by this testimony in the Acts of the Apostles, and did not understand what he was reading, Philip interpreted it concerning the passion and the name of the Savior. He understood, and was immediately baptized in the blood of the Lamb whom he had been reading about; he deserved to be called a man, and was sent as an apostle to the Ethiopian nation.

He, therefore, who was handed over to Pilate because he himself willed it, and who did not answer so that he might ascend the cross, condemned for our sake, was led like a sheep to the slaughter and became silent like a lamb before its shearer. “For Christ our Passover was sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5). John the Baptist pointed him out, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1).

He is also often shown in the Apocalypse of John the Evangelist as the slain Lamb (Rev. 5). Concerning himself he speaks in Jeremiah: “But I was like a gentle lamb led to the sacrifice, and I did not know” (Jer. 5). For although he knew no sin, he was made sin for us (2 Cor. 5); and just as a lamb does not resist when led to sacrifice, so he suffered by his own will, in order to destroy him who held the power of death, humbling himself even to death, and death on a cross (Heb. 2).

This is the Lamb in whose type the lamb was sacrificed, whose blood smeared on the doorposts drove away the destroyer of Egypt. He not only redeemed us with his blood but also covered us with his wool, so that he might warm us, chilled by unbelief, with his garment. And we might hear the Apostle speaking to us: “As many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Rom. 6). And elsewhere: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 13).

As for what follows, “From distress and from judgment he was taken away,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “ἐν τῇ ταπεινώσει ἡ κρίσις αὐτοῦ ἤρθη”—that is, “In his humiliation judgment was taken away from him”—this signifies either that he ascended victoriously to the Father from tribulation and judgment, or that the judge of all found no truth in the judgment but was condemned without any guilt by the riot of the Jews and the voice of Pilate, so that the prophet marveled that the God of all had surrendered himself to suffering.

Paul speaks of him: “For if they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (2 Cor. 2). It follows: “Who will declare his generation?” This is understood in two ways. It must either be understood of his divinity, since it is impossible to know the mysteries of divine birth. Concerning this he himself speaks in Proverbs: “Before all the hills he begot me” (Prov. 8). In accordance with what we read elsewhere: “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. 11)—that is, no one.

Or it may be understood of the virgin birth, which can scarcely be explained. When the angel said to Mary, “You will conceive and bear a son,” she replied: “How shall this be, since I have not known a man?” The angel then said to her: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1). Thus the mysteries of this birth are spoken of either by the angel or by the angels, while its narrator is exceedingly rare.

“Philip opened his mouth and, beginning from this Scripture,” and so forth. *(From Primasius.)* Philip is interpreted as “mouth of the lamp,” and the meaning is beautiful: the mouth of the lamp opened its mouth when it brought the obscure things of prophecy into the light of knowledge. Although, according to the historical sense, this circumlocution can also indicate that his discourse, which was then to follow, would be somewhat longer.

“As they went along the road, they came to a certain water.” Today there is a village called Bethsur or Bethsoro in the tribe of Judah or Benjamin, for those traveling from Aelia to Hebron, at the twentieth milestone. Near it a spring boils up at the foot of a mountain and is swallowed by the same earth from which it arises. The Acts of the Apostles report that the eunuch was baptized by Philip at the spring of this village. For there is also another Bethsur in the tribe of Judah, one thousand paces distant from Eleutheropolis.

“And the eunuch said: ‘Behold, here is water; what prevents me from being baptized?’ And he ordered the chariot to stop; and both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him.” O how remarkable was the power of the teacher in the chariot! The eunuch was reading the sacred writings but did not know of whom he was reading. Yet he earnestly desired to know, with a devout mind, the one whom he was unknowingly reading about in the book.

Philip the philosopher came and showed him Jesus, who lay hidden, enclosed in the letter. According to another tradition, Philip said to the eunuch: “If you believe with your whole heart, you will be saved.” The eunuch answered: “I believe in Christ, the Son of God.” At that hour he was baptized, became faithful and holy, was changed from a disciple into a teacher, and thereafter became a preacher and the apostle of his nation.

“When they had come up from the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away,” and so forth. There are some who testify, as Jerome reports, that the angel did this through the Holy Spirit. For we also read of something similar having happened when Habakkuk carried food to Daniel.

“Philip, however, was found at Azotus.” Azotus is a notable town of Palestine, called in Hebrew [the term is absent from the supplied source], *Asdod*. It lies within the territory of the tribe of Judah and is one of the five cities formerly belonging to the Philistines. It had been assigned to Judah but was not retained by that tribe, because it was wholly unable to expel the ancient inhabitants.

“And, passing through, he evangelized all the cities until he came to Caesarea.” This is called Caesarea of Palestine. Philip is later described as having a house there, which is still shown today, together with the chamber of his four virgin daughters who prophesied.

There are two cities named Caesarea in the Promised Land. One is Caesarea of Palestine, on the shore of the Great Sea. It was formerly called Pyrgos, that is, “the Tower of Strato,” but King Herod of Judea built it more nobly and beautifully and made it much more useful against the force of the sea. In honor of Caesar Augustus he named it Caesarea. He also built there a temple of white marble. In that city Herod, his grandson, was struck by an angel; the centurion Cornelius was baptized; and the prophet Agabus bound Paul with his belt (Acts 21).

The other is Caesarea Philippi, which the Gospel mentions as a tetrarchy. It was built at the foot of Mount Lebanon and was named in honor of Caesar. There is also a third Caesarea, the metropolis of Cappadocia, which Luke mentions in this way: “Going down to Caesarea, he greeted the Church.”

Here Smaragdus passes from the mention of the city Caesarea to the names of the regions and places that occur in the Acts of the Apostles. The same material is found in Jerome.

But since cities have been mentioned at this point, we have thought it necessary to mention here a number of the cities, places, and provinces of this book.

Acheldemach is in Aelia, on the southern side of Mount Zion. To this day, in accordance with the Jews’ counsel, it covers undistinguished dead persons with earth and leaves others to decay in the open air.

Asia, which is called Asia Minor, is surrounded on every side by the sea. Its provinces are Phrygia, Pamphylia, Cilicia, Lycaonia, Galatia, and many others.

Arabia lies between the gulf of the Red Sea, which is called the Persian Gulf, and the one called the Arabian Gulf. It contains many peoples: Moabites, Ammonites, Idumeans, Saracens, and many others. It is said to signify “sacred,” because it produces fragrant perfumes. The Greeks called it εὐδαίμων, “fortunate,” and our people called it “Blessed.”

Antioch is a city of Syria in which the apostles Barnabas and Paul were ordained. There is also another Antioch in Asia, where, while preaching to the Jews, the same men said: “It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you first. But since you rejected it, behold, we turn to the nations” (Acts 13).

Alexandria is a city of Egypt, where the tomb of blessed Mark the Evangelist is venerated today in the church.

Amphipolis is a city of Macedonia. There is another of the same name in Syria.

Apollonia is a city of Macedonia. There is another in Africa, which is called Pentapolis.

Athens is a city of Achaea, devoted to the study of philosophy. Its harbor, Piraeus, is described as having once been fortified by a sevenfold wall.

The Areopagus is the council-house of Athens. Its name is interpreted as “the court of Mars,” because Mars was once judged there together with two hundred and twelve gods.

The Forum of Appius takes its name from a forum at Rome, named after a former consul called Appius; the Appian Way also received its name from him.

Babylon is the metropolis of the kingdom of the Chaldeans. There the tongues of those who were building the tower were divided, and from this it is also called Babylonia. Herodotus and many others who wrote Greek histories report that it was laid out as a square, extending sixteen thousand paces from corner to corner of its walls—that is, sixty-four thousand paces around the entire circuit.

Bithynia is a province of Asia Minor. It is also called Greater Phrygia.

Beroea is a city in Macedonia, which nobly received the word of the Lord.

Cappadocia is a region at the head of Syria, toward the north.

Cyrene is a city in Libya, whose region is called Pentapolis because it is especially distinguished by five cities.

Crete is a Greek island, once famous for one hundred cities; hence it was also called Centipolis.

Cyprus is an island in the Pamphylian Sea, once notable for fifteen towns and famous for its wealth, especially its copper.

Cilicia is a province of Asia, through which the river Cydnus flows.

Charra is a city of Mesopotamia, where the patriarch Abraham had his dwelling.

Corinth is a maritime city of Achaea.

Cenchreae is the harbor of the city of Corinth.

Chios is an island near Bithynia. In the Syrian language its name signifies mastic, because mastic grows there.

Damascus is a celebrated city of Phoenicia, which once held primacy throughout Syria and is now the metropolis of the Saracens. Hence their king Nauvias dedicated there a famous basilica for himself and his people, while the Christian inhabitants in the surrounding area frequent the church of blessed John the Baptist.

Derbe is a city of the province of Lycaonia.

The Elamites, the princes of Persia, were named from Elam, the son of Shem.

Ephesus is a city in Asia, the work of the Amazons, where the Evangelist John rests.

Phoenicia is a province of Syria, whose parts include Samaria and Galilee and many others.

There are two Galilees: one, Galilee of the Gentiles, near the territory of the Tyrians, in the tribe of Naphtali; the other around Tiberias and the lake of Gennesaret, in the tribe of Zebulun.

Gaza is a notable city of Palestine, which among the ancients was the land of the Canaanites.

Galatia is a province of Asia, taking its name from the Gauls. They had been summoned by the king of Bithynia to assist him, and, after winning the victory, divided the kingdom with him. Thereafter, mingling with the Greeks, they were first called Gallo-Greeks and later Galatians.

Hadrumetum is a city in the region of Byzacena in Africa.

Adria is the name of a city opposite Ravenna. It also gave its name, Adriatic, to the sea on whose shore it lies.

Joppa is a maritime town of Palestine, in the tribe of Dan.

Iconium is a city of Lycaonia. There is another in Cilicia.

There are two provinces called Libya: one is Cyrenaica, of which it was said, “the parts of Libya that are around Cyrene”; the other belongs to the Ethiopians.

Lydda is a city of Palestine situated on the shore of the Great Sea. It is now called Diospolis.

Lycaonia is a province of Asia. There is another region of the same name in Lesser Phrygia.

Lystra is a city of Lycaonia.

Lycia is a province of Asia.

Media takes its name from Madai, the son of Japheth. Between the river Indus and the regions mentioned here are Arachosia, Parthia, and Assyria, all of which Sacred Scripture often calls by the name Media.

Macedonia is a province of the Greeks, made more famous by the achievements of Alexander the Great.

Miletus is a city in Asia, where Paul addresses the elders of Ephesus.

Nazareth is a village in Galilee, near Mount Tabor. From it the Lord Jesus was also called a Nazarene. It has a church at the place where the angel entered to announce the Gospel to blessed Mary, and it has another where the Lord was raised.

Neapolis is a city of Caria, which is a province of Asia.

Pontus is a region of many peoples beside the Pontic Sea, which separates Asia from Europe. Because of the great inflow of the mouths of the Danube, it is known to be sweeter than the other seas.

Pamphylia is a province of Asia.

Paphos is a city on the island of Cyprus.

Perga is a city in the province of Pamphylia.

Philippi is a city in the first part of Macedonia.

Ptolemais is a city of Judea, near Mount Carmel. There is another Ptolemais in the Pentapolis region of Africa.

Puteoli is a colonial city of Campania; it is also called Ceadicta.

Rhodes is the most famous of the Cyclades islands. It is twenty thousand paces from the port of Asia.

Rhegium is a maritime city of Sicily.

Shechem is the city of Jacob, now called Neapolis. It lies near the tomb of Joseph, where a church has now been built from the stone of Mount Gerizim.

Mount Sinai is in the region of Midian, above Arabia. It is also called Horeb. Hence it is said: “And they made a calf at Horeb,” although Moses wrote that this was done at Sinai.

Saronas, which is interpreted as “level” or “plain,” is a region that, when Peter preached there, immediately produced the fruit of faith.

Sidon is a city of Phoenicia, famous for its skill in making glass.

Seleucia is a notable city of Syria, situated on the promontory of Syria near Antioch.

Salamis is a city on the island of Cyprus, now called Constantia.

Samothrace is an island in the Pacatic Gulf.

Syria—called in Hebrew [term uncertain; absent from the supplied source]—is the region between the Euphrates River and the Great Sea, extending as far as Egypt. It contains very large provinces in which there are twelve peoples.

Samos is an island in the Aegean Sea. It is said that earthenware vessels were first discovered there; hence such vessels were called Samian.

Smyrna is a city in Asia, in the province of Lycia, which Luke mentions when he says: “Sailing, we came to Smyrna of Lycia.”

The Syrtes are sandy places in the Great Sea, very terrifying and dangerous.

Syracuse is the metropolis of Sicily, beneath the promontory of Pachynus.

Tarsus is the metropolitan city of Cilicia, made glorious by the Apostle Paul.

Tyre is the metropolis of Phoenicia, in the tribe of Naphtali. Its greatest renown rests on its shell-purple dye and purple cloth.

Troas is a maritime city of Asia.

Thyatira is a city of Libya, which is a province of Asia.

Thessalonica is a city of Macedonia.

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER 20
“Mary stood outside at the tomb, weeping. As she wept, she stooped down and looked into the tomb, and she saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been placed. They said to her, ‘Woman, why are you weeping?’ She said to them, ‘Because they have taken away my Lord, [Col. 0257A] and I do not know where they have placed him.’ When she had said this, she turned back and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus. Jesus said to her, ‘Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?’ Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, ‘Lord, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have placed him, and I will take him away.’ Jesus said to her, ‘Mary.’ She turned and said to him, ‘Rabboni,’ which means ‘Teacher.’ Jesus said to her, ‘Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father. But go to my brothers and tell them: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, my God and your God.’ Mary Magdalene came, announcing to the disciples, ‘I have seen the Lord,’ and that he had said these things to her.”

But Mary stood outside at the tomb, weeping. [Col. 0257B] (From Augustine.) We must consider how great was the force of love that kindled this woman’s mind. Even when the Lord’s disciples had withdrawn from the tomb, she did not withdraw; she was seeking the one whom she had not found. She wept while seeking, and, set ablaze by the fire of her love, she burned with longing for the one whom she believed had been taken away. Her eyes, which had sought the Lord and had not found him, were already overflowing with tears. She grieved more that he had been removed from the tomb than that he had been killed on the cross, because no memory even remained to them of so great a teacher, whose life had been taken from them. Thus it happened that she alone saw him then—the one who remained—because, surely, perseverance is the strength of good works, as the Voice of Truth says: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Luke XXI).

[Col. 0257C]

As she wept, she stooped down and looked into the tomb, and saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, etc. (From Gregory.) Let us therefore consider what fruit the force of love produces in this woman, who loved in this way and again bends toward the tomb at which she had looked. The account continues: “She saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been placed.” What does it mean that two angels are seen at the place of the Lord’s body, one sitting at the head and the other at the feet? It means, surely, that in Latin the word ἄγγελος means “messenger,” and that the one who was to be proclaimed on the basis of his passion is both God before the ages and man at the end of the ages. The angel sits, as it were, at the head when it is preached through the apostle that “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I), and he sits, as it were, at the feet when it is said: “And the Word became flesh.”

(From Gregory.) We may also understand the two angels as the two Testaments, one earlier and the other later. These angels are joined to one another at the place of the Lord’s body, because both Testaments, with one and the same understanding, announce that the Lord was incarnate, died, and rose again: the earlier Testament sits, as it were, at the head, and the later Testament at the feet.

They said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping?” As though they had said: “There is no need to weep for one who is dead; you ought to believe that he is alive.”

[Col. 0258A]

She said to them, “Because they have taken away my Lord,” etc. Calling him her Lord, she signifies the lifeless body of her Lord by referring to the whole through a part, just as we all confess Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, as our one Lord—which of course includes at once the Word, soul, and flesh. Yet she says that he was crucified and buried, although only his flesh was buried: “And I do not know,” she says, “where they have placed him.” This was the cause of her greater grief: she did not know where to go to console her sorrow. But the hour was near when her sadness would be turned into joy.

When she had said this, she turned back and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus. It should be noted that Mary, who still doubted the Lord’s resurrection, turned back in order to see Jesus. Through this very doubt she had, as it were, turned her back on the Lord’s face, since she did not at all believe that he had risen. But because she loved and doubted, she saw but did not recognize him—the one whom love had shown her. Doubt concealed the one whose continuing ignorance is expressed when the text adds: “And she did not know that it was Jesus.”

Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping?” etc. He asks the cause of her grief in order to increase her longing, so that when she named the one whom she was seeking, her ardor might burn more intensely.

Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, “Lord, if you have carried him away,” etc. Perhaps this woman was not mistaken even in her apparent error when she believed Jesus to be the gardener. Was he not spiritually a gardener to her, who planted in her heart, through his love, the green and flourishing seeds of virtues? But what is the meaning of this: having seen the one whom she believed to be the gardener, although she had not yet told him whom she was seeking, she said to him, “Lord, if you have carried him away, tell me”? Let no one accuse the woman because she called the gardener “Lord” and Jesus “Teacher.” There she was asking; here she was recognizing. There she honored the man from whom she sought a favor; here she remembered the teacher from whom she distinguished and learned what was human and what was divine. She called him “Lord,” although she was not his maidservant, so that she might reach the Lord whose servant she was. Thus she said in one way, “They have taken away my Lord,” and in another, “Lord, if you have carried him away.” In the first case, she spoke from the truth; in the second, from honor.

She was therefore seeking, and she did not say whom she was seeking. When she had said, “Lord, if you have carried him away,” this is what the force of love does; this is what it habitually accomplishes in the mind: the one whom it is always thinking about, it believes no one else can fail to know. Rightly, then, this woman does not name the one she is seeking, yet she says, “If you have carried him away,” because she does not think that the one whom she continually mourns with longing is unknown to another.

He said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him, “Rabboni,” which means “Teacher.” After he had addressed her by the common designation appropriate to her sex, and she was not recognized, he called her by name, as though he were openly saying: “Recognize the one by whom you are recognized.” To the perfect man also it is said: “I know you by name.” Since “human being” is a common designation for all of us, whereas Moses has a proper name, it is rightly said that he is known by name—as though the Lord were openly saying: “I know you not generally, like the others, but individually, above the rest.” Therefore Mary, because she is called by name, recognizes her Creator and immediately calls him “Rabboni,” that is, “Teacher,” because he was both the one whom she was seeking outwardly and the one who was teaching her outwardly to seek.

[Col. 0259A]

Jesus said to her, “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father.” (From Augustine.) He said, “Do not touch me,” so that in this woman the Church from the Gentiles might be represented, which did not believe in Christ until he had ascended to the Father. Or certainly Jesus wished to be believed in this way—that is, to be touched in this particular way—as the one who is himself and the Father one. Otherwise he is not rightly touched, that is, not rightly believed.

(From Gregory.) The Evangelist does not now add what the woman did; rather, he indicates it by what she heard when he said to her: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father.” These words show that Mary wished to embrace the feet of the one whom she recognized, but the Teacher said to her: “Do not touch me.” This was not because, after the resurrection, the Lord refused to be touched by women, since it is written concerning the two women at his tomb: “They approached and held his feet.” But the reason why he should not be touched is also added when the text continues: “For I have not yet ascended to my Father.” In our heart Jesus ascends to the Father when he is believed to be equal to the Father. For whoever does not believe him equal to the Father still does not have Jesus ascending to the Father in his heart. Therefore he truly touches Jesus who believes the Son coeternal with the Father.

“Go to my brothers and tell them: I am ascending to my Father,” and so forth. He does not say “our Father”; therefore “my” in one way and “your” in another. “My” by nature, “your” by grace; and “my God” and “your God.” Nor does he say here, “our God.” Here too, therefore, “my” in one way and “your” in another. “My God,” under whom I too am man; “your God,” among whom I am also mediator. Since he calls him “your” God, why does he not commonly say “our” God? By speaking distinctly, he shows that he possesses the same Father and God in a different way from us: “I am ascending to my Father,” namely, by nature, “and your Father,” by grace; “to my God,” because I descended, “and your God,” because you ascended. Since I too am man, God is my God; since you have been freed from error, God is your God. Thus the Father and God are distinctively mine, because the one who begot me as God before the ages created me as man with himself at the end of the ages.

[Col. 0259D]

“Mary Magdalene came announcing,” etc. Behold, the guilt of the human race is cut away at the point from which it arose. Because a woman gave a man death in paradise, a woman announces life to men from the tomb. She tells the words of her Life-giver, just as she had told the words of the death-bearing serpent—as though the Lord were saying to the human race, not in words but in deeds: “From the hand from which the drink of death was brought to you, receive the cup of life.”

## HARMONY

The readings of these two passages are harmonized in this respect: the angel spoke to Mary, and he also spoke to Philip. Philip evangelized Jesus to the eunuch; Mary announced Jesus to the apostles.

[Col. 0260A]

## FRIDAY

### FIRST EPISTLE OF THE APOSTLE PETER, CHAPTER III

“Christ died once for our sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might offer us to God, put to death indeed in the flesh but made alive in the spirit. In it he also came spiritually and preached to those who were in prison, who formerly had been unbelieving when they were awaiting God’s patience in the days of Noah, while the ark was being built. In it a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water. And now baptism, corresponding to this figure, saves you—not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but an appeal of a good conscience to God, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who is at the right hand of God.”

“Christ died once for our sins,” etc. [Col. 0260B] (From Bede.) Whoever, then, suffers as a righteous person imitates Christ; whoever is corrected through scourging imitates the thief who recognized Christ on the cross and entered paradise with Christ after the cross. Whoever, even amid scourging, does not cease from his sins imitates the thief on the left, who went up onto the cross because of his sins and after the cross fell into hell. For this reason he recalls that Christ died once, so that he may also remind us that eternal reward will be given for our temporal sufferings.

“So that he might offer us to God, put to death indeed in the flesh,” etc. This concerns the mortification of the flesh and the vivification of the spirit possessed by those who labor for the Lord through endurance. The apostle Paul also says: “Although our outward self is being corrupted, yet the one within is renewed day by day” (II Corinthians IV). Christ therefore offers us to God the Father when, after the mortification of the flesh, we rejoice in being sacrificed for him—that is, he displays our praiseworthy life in the sight of the Father. Or certainly he offers us to God when, freed from the flesh, he introduces us into the eternal kingdom.

It is fitting that in the words “made alive in the spirit,” Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, does not refer to the human spirit—which is made more alive when the flesh has been mortified, as the Prophet says concerning the Lord: “To revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite”—but rather refers them to the grace of the Holy Spirit, who grants everlasting life to those who mortify their flesh. He also uses this testimony against the Arians, who contradict the equality of the Holy Trinity, thereby asserting the indivisible unity of the divine operation: “Let the Father make alive, let the Son make alive, let the Holy Spirit make alive.” Accordingly, the Son too may be said to make alive, since it is written: “For just as the Father raises the dead and makes alive, so also the Son makes alive whom he wishes.” The Holy Spirit is likewise declared by this testimony, in which it is said of the Son that he might offer us to God, “put to death indeed in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit.” Therefore, since their operation is one, their essence or substance cannot be different.

“In it he also came spiritually and preached to those who were in prison,” etc. He who in our times came in the flesh and preached the way of life to the world also preached before the Flood, in the spirit, to those who were then unbelieving and had lived according to the flesh. For he himself was present through the Holy Spirit in Noah and the other saints who lived at that time, and through their good conduct he preached to the wicked people of that age so that they might turn to better things. He calls them confined in the flesh because they were weighed down by carnal desires. Hence Scripture says concerning them: “All flesh had corrupted its way” (Genesis VI).

When he says “in it,” he signifies “in that which he had previously stated,” namely, “so that he might offer us to God.” Even then, if any had wished to believe in the Lord’s preaching, which he displayed through the life of the faithful, he rejoiced to offer them to God the Father. But those who reviled the good as though they were evildoers were put to shame when the Flood came.

The words “in it” can also be understood in both ways: “in it,” that is, in the spirit, he came spiritually and preached to those who were confined in the flesh, so that after the same preaching a crown of praise might arise for those who believed, and confusion for those who persisted in unbelief. Some manuscripts read: “In it he also came in the spirit and preached to those who were in the flesh.” This refers to the same intention of the wicked and unbelieving, whose understanding is darkened by the shadows of the heart. They are rightly said to have been confined in prison even in this life: in that prison, namely, amid inward darkness—that is, blindness of mind—and unjust deeds they are burdened, until, released from the flesh, they are cast into outer darkness, into the prison of eternal condemnation, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “The judge will hand you over to the officer, and you will be thrown into prison” (Matthew V).

Yet the saints too, while in this life, rightly proclaim that they are placed in prison when they long for the joy of their heavenly homeland, according to the Psalmist: “Lead my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name” (Psalm CXLI). There is a great difference between the two prisons. The wicked are in the prison of sins and ignorance. The righteous, although placed in the prison of tribulations, enjoy the light of righteousness with hearts expanded toward God. The apostles Paul and Silas signified this when, at midnight, at the beginning of their imprisonment, although bound and scourged, they sang a hymn of praise to God with the most joyful voice.

Someone interpreted this passage as referring to that consolation of which the Lord says to the apostles: “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Matthew XII). The Psalmist also speaks of it: “My eyes have failed at your word, saying: When will you comfort me?” (Psalm CXVIII). The holy ones resting in hell desired that consolation which, when the Lord descended into the underworld, was preached even to those who were in prison and had formerly been unbelieving in the days of Noah. Thus, he said this.

But the catholic faith holds that, when the Lord descended into the underworld, he led out from there not the unbelieving but only his own faithful, bringing them with him into the heavenly kingdoms. Nor did he preach salvation to souls stripped of their bodies and condemned in the prison of hell—the salvation they had loved before death—but to those confined in the prison of sins in this life. To them, whether through himself or through the example or words of his faithful, he daily shows the way of life. Concerning them he says:

“They were formerly unbelieving, awaiting God’s patience.” In the days of Noah, while the ark was being built—for the building of the ark itself was a preaching of God’s patience. Noah devoted himself to the work of the ark for a hundred years, showing through the daily execution of his labor what was going to happen to the world, because Paul says: “Do you not know that God’s patience leads you to repentance?” and so forth.

Another translation renders this passage as follows: “Christ died once for our sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might bring us to God, put to death in the body but made alive in the spirit. In this spirit he also preached to those who were in the flesh, who formerly had not believed in those days, while patience was awaiting.”

[Col. 0262B]

“In the days of Noah, while the ark was being built, in which a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water. And now baptism, corresponding to this figure, saves you.” He says that the form of baptism corresponds to the ark and to the waters of the Flood. This is entirely right, since the construction of the ark from smoothed timbers signifies the building of the Church, which is formed from the gathering of faithful souls by the architects of the Word.

The fact that, when the whole world was perishing, a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water signifies that, in comparison with the Gentiles, Jews, heretics, and false believers who perish, the number of the elect is much smaller. Hence it is said concerning the narrow gate and constricted way that leads to life: “Few are those who find it” (Matthew VII). And again: “Do not fear, little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke XII).

[Col. 0262D]

“Not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but an appeal of a good conscience to God.” For where is there a good conscience unless there is also an unfeigned faith? The apostle Paul teaches that “the end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (I Timothy I).

Therefore, the fact that the water of the Flood did not save those outside the ark but undoubtedly killed them prefigured every heretic who, although possessing the sacrament of baptism in other respects, is plunged by those same waters into hell, while the ark is lifted up to heaven. The number eight itself—the souls saved through water—signifies that the holy Church receives the washing of baptism as a sacrament of the Lord’s resurrection. Just as he rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we, cleansed from sins through the water of regeneration, may walk in newness of life (Romans VI).

The eighth day, that is, the day after the seventh day of the week, when the Lord rose from the dead, displayed both an example of the resurrection that is to come and the mystery of a new manner of life, by which, while placed on earth, we might live a heavenly life. Peter himself explains this further when he says:

“Through the resurrection of the Lord Jesus Christ, who is at the right hand of God.” Having swallowed up death, so that we might become partakers of eternal life, he proceeded into heaven. For just as he rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God, so also he signified through baptism that the way of salvation and entrance into the heavenly kingdom is open to us.

[Col. 0263A]

He rightly says, “swallowing up death.” What we swallow we cause to disappear entirely through the power of our body once it has been taken in. The Lord swallowed up death, and when he rose from the dead he consumed it so completely that it could no longer prevail against him through any contact with corruption. Although the appearance of a true body remained, every stain of former weakness was altogether absent.

The same thing is promised to us at the end, as the apostle says when speaking of our resurrection: “Then the saying that is written will come to pass: Death has been swallowed up in victory” (I Corinthians XV). It is rightly said, “swallowed up,” because when we too have become partakers of eternal life, the power of bodily immortality will remove every blemish of past corruption, just as a flame ordinarily consumes a drop of water cast into it by the power of its heat.

[Col. 0263B]

## ANOTHER EXPOSITION

“Christ died once for our sins.” He says “once” because Christ, having risen from the dead, no longer dies, and death will no longer rule over him (Romans VI).

“Righteous.” To him the Psalmist says: “You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is upright” (Psalm CXVIII). Daniel says: “To you, O Lord, belongs righteousness, but to us confusion of face” (Daniel IX).

“For the unrighteous.” Concerning us Daniel says: “We have sinned, we have acted unjustly, we have committed iniquity” (Daniel III).

“So that he might offer us to God, put to death indeed in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit.” (From Augustine.) He says “put to death in the flesh,” that is, not possessing carnal desires. Paul exhorts us to this mortification when he says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication” (Colossians II), and all vices. And again: “If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live” (Romans VIII). Unless we first die to sin, we cannot live to God through righteousness.

When he says “made alive in the spirit,” this means made alive in the soul, for the soul is understood as spirit. Or the mortification of the flesh and the vivification of the spirit are understood to take place in baptism. We are baptized into the death of Christ—undoubtedly into that death by which he died to sin once for all—so that we too may be separated from sin and live to God.

(From Cassiodorus.) “Put to death in the flesh” may otherwise be understood as meaning that we should not interpret the letter of the Law carnally. “Made alive in the spirit” means that, understanding the meaning of the Law spiritually, we should live. Christ did not withdraw us from the law of sin so that we might serve the oldness of the letter—that is, receive circumcision, observe Sabbaths, or follow the other things contained in the old letter of the Law—but so that we might serve the Law of God in newness of spirit, that is, by receiving, through the gift of the Spirit, the spiritual meaning of everything written in it.

It is said of Christ: “Put to death in the flesh, made alive in the spirit.” Thus one may also say of a human being: “Wasted away in the flesh, justified and made alive in the spirit.”

“In it.” The phrase is understood to mean “in that spirit,” namely the one of which he earlier says: “Made alive in the spirit.”

“And to those who were in prison.” That is, shut up in the ark or in the prison of the body.

[Col. 0264A]

“Coming spiritually, he preached.” He preached to the same people to whom he later came visibly, incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. At that time he preached to them spiritually by breathing into them. For he said to Noah: “My spirit will not remain in man forever, because he is flesh.” And again: “I will wipe out the human being whom I created from the face of the earth, from human beings to animals, from reptiles to birds of the heavens, for I regret that I made them.” Again the Lord said to Noah: “The end of all flesh has come before me. The earth is filled with iniquity, and I will destroy them along with the earth. Make yourself an ark of smoothed wood,” etc. (Genesis VI).

“They were formerly unbelieving, awaiting the Lord’s patience.” That is, although they had formerly been unbelieving, when they heard Noah preaching the things that he had received after hearing them from the Lord, and when they saw the construction of the ark, they believed that the period of a hundred years would be extended, awaiting the Lord’s patience, and they were saved in the ark.

“In which a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water.” That is, four men—Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth—and their four wives: Puarfara, Parfia, Catafluia, and Fluia.

(From Isidore.) Noah, whose name is interpreted as “rest,” signifies Christ, who says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls.” Noah alone is found righteous among that people, and seven persons are granted to him because of his righteousness. Christ alone is righteous, and the seven Churches, because of the sevenfold Spirit who illuminates them, are gathered into one Church, as though into one ark.

The fact that Noah constructed the ark from incorruptible wood signifies the Church, which Christ builds from human beings who will live forever. The ark represents the Church, which floats upon the waves of this world. Just as Noah and his family were then saved through water and wood, so now the household of Christ is saved through baptism and the passion of the cross. Hence the text continues:

“And now baptism, corresponding to this figure, saves you.” Just as the water then saved those who were in the ark, so now baptism preserves those who remain within the unity of the Church by wiping away sins. And just as those who were outside the ark then perished, so now those who are outside the Church will perish.

[Col. 0264D]

“Not the removal of dirt from the flesh.” That is, not baptism that removes the dirt of the flesh, but that which washes away the stains of the mind. For baptism is interpreted as washing or immersion.

“But an appeal of a good conscience to God.” The priest’s question is: “Do you believe in God the almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ his Son, and in the Holy Spirit?” The response of a good and sincere conscience is: “I believe.” This response saves a person and frees him from eternal destruction.

“Through the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is at the right hand of God.” This means: “He rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God.” This sitting signifies the equality of his power with the Father.

[Col. 0265A]

## GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, LAST CHAPTER

“The eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them. And when they saw him, they worshiped him, but some doubted. And Jesus came and spoke to them, saying: ‘All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age.’”

“The eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them.” (From Jerome.) After the resurrection, Jesus is seen on a mountain in Galilee and is worshiped there, although some doubt. Yet their doubt increases our faith, since the side wounded by the spear and the hands fixed by nails are shown more clearly to Thomas.

“And Jesus came and spoke, saying: ‘All authority has been given to me,’” etc. Authority was given to the one who shortly before had been crucified, who had been buried in a tomb, who had lain dead, and who afterward had risen. Authority was given to him in heaven and on earth so that the one who had previously reigned in heaven might reign on earth through the faith of believers.

“Go, therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” First they teach all nations; afterward they immerse those who have been taught in water. For it cannot happen that the body receives the sacrament of baptism unless the soul has first received the truth of faith. They are baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, [Col. 0265C] and of the Holy Spirit, so that, since they share one divinity, there may be one gift; and the name of the Trinity is the one God.

“Teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you.” This is the principal order. He commands the apostles first to teach all nations, then to immerse them in the sacrament of faith, and after faith and baptism to prescribe what must be observed. And lest we think that the things he commanded are insignificant or few, he adds: “Everything that I have commanded you,” so that those who believe and have been baptized in the Trinity may do everything that has been commanded.

“And behold, I am with you all days until the consummation of the age.” By promising that he will be with his disciples until the consummation of the age, he shows that they will always live and that he will never depart from believers. But since he promises his presence until the consummation of the world, he does not fail to know the day on which he knows he will be with the apostles.

(From Chrysostom.) How did he say, “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age,” and again: “These are my words,” he says, “when I was still with you”—that is, when I was still mortal, as you are? He was with them by the presence of his body, but he was not with them according to the condition of mortality. Now he is with us through the presence of his majesty, but he is not with us through bodily presence.

## HARMONY

The readings of these two passages are harmonized in holy baptism. The apostle says: “Baptism, corresponding to this figure, saves you.” The Gospel says: “Teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Matthew, last chapter).

## SATURDAY IN THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

### EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PETER, CHAPTER II

“Put away, therefore, all malice and all deceit, hypocrisy and envy, and every kind of slander. Like newborn infants, desire rational, guileless milk, so that by it you may grow toward salvation—if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet. As you come to him, a living stone rejected by human beings but chosen and honored by God, you yourselves also, like living stones, are being built upon [Col. 0266B] into spiritual houses, acceptable sacrifices to God through Jesus Christ. Therefore Scripture contains this: ‘Behold, I place in Zion a chief cornerstone, chosen and precious, and everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.’ To you, therefore, honor who believe; but to those who do not believe, ‘the stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner,’ and ‘a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.’ They stumble at the word and do not believe; they were appointed to this also. But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for acquisition, so that you may proclaim the mighty works of him who called you from darkness into his marvelous light. Once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people; once you had not obtained mercy, but now you have obtained mercy.”

“Put away all malice and all deceit, hypocrisy and envy, and every kind of slander. Like newborn infants, desire rational, guileless milk,” etc. (From Bede.) “You have been reborn recently,” he says, “and through baptism have become children of God. Therefore now, through the pursuit of a good manner of life, be such as newborn infants are by the innocence of their age: entirely ignorant of malice and every kind of deceit, of pretending, envying, slandering, and being enslaved to other vices of this kind.

“Just as they naturally desire milk forever, so that they may be able to grow toward salvation and reach the point of eating bread, so you too should first seek the simple beginnings of faith from the breasts of Mother Church—that is, from the teachers of both Testaments, who have either written the divine words or proclaim them to you with the living voice. By learning well, you may attain nourishment from the living bread that descended from heaven, that is, through the sacraments of the Lord’s incarnation by which you were reborn and are nourished, and may attain contemplation of the divine majesty. ‘Desire,’ he says, ‘rational and guileless milk, so that by it you may grow toward salvation’ (I Peter II).”

By commanding the desire for the milk of the Word, he touches upon those who come unwillingly and reluctantly to hear the sacred readings, ignorant of that thirst and hunger of which the Lord says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matthew V). For this reason they reach the perfection of salvation more slowly, by which they could be nourished with the solid food of the Word—that is, understand divine mysteries or accomplish greater good works.

[Col. 0267A]

“If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet.” “In this way,” he says, “once the malice and filth of your heart have been dismissed and cleansed, desire the spiritual nourishment of Christ, if you understand how great is the abundance of divine sweetness. For one who tastes nothing of heavenly sweetness in the soul need not wonder if he does not avoid defiling himself with earthly allurements.”

The Psalmist rightly urges us to taste and see how sweet the Lord is (Psalm XXXIII), because there are some who do not perceive God as something that tastes sweet on earth, but only as something that produces an outward sound when shaken. Even if they grasp certain hidden things through understanding, they cannot experience their sweetness. And although they know them, they are ignorant, as I said, of how they taste.

And since in the same Psalm from which he took this verse it is written beforehand, “Come to him and be enlightened,” blessed Peter rightly adds:

“As you come to him, a living stone, rejected indeed by human beings but chosen and honored by God.” He also takes this testimony concerning the stone from the Psalm, where it is written: “The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner” (Psalm CXVII). Lest anyone, in a Jewish manner, think that the prophet sang of a material stone that, in the construction of any earthly house, would not be set in place contrary to human planning by divine judgment, he deliberately adds the word “living”: “As you come to him,” he says, “a living stone,” so that he might signify Christ. He is rightly called a stone because, coming in the flesh, he deigned to insert himself into the building of the holy Church in order to strengthen it.

He is living because he could say: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). He was rejected by human beings when they said: “We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX). He was chosen by God when he himself says: “Yet I have been appointed king by him,” etc. (Psalm II). And he was honored because, after the death of the cross, God exalted him and granted him the name that is above every name, etc. (Philippians II).

And you, like living stones, are being built up into spiritual houses. “You are being built up”—he says this because no spiritual structure can stand without the Lord Jesus Christ, that is, the living stone. [Col. 0267D] For no one can lay any other foundation besides him, and through participation in him the faithful become living stones, though through unbelief they had been dead stones—that is, hard and insensitive stones—to whom it would rightly be said: “I will take from you your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh.” But, like living stones, they are fitted for a spiritual building; through the discernment of a learned teacher, their superfluous thoughts are cut away, and they are squared as though by the stroke of an axe. And just as the rows of stones in a wall are supported one by another, so each of the faithful is supported by the righteous who preceded him in the Church. They too support those who follow, through teaching and endurance, up to the last righteous person. When he is supported by those who came before, he will himself have no later person whom he must support. [Col. 0268A] But the one who supports the entire building, while himself being supported by no one, is Christ the Lord; hence the prophet calls him the precious stone, laid as the foundation.

“You are being built up,” he says, “into spiritual houses.” Thus he says that they become spiritual houses, although there is one house of Christ, gathered from elect angels and human beings. In the same way, although there is one catholic Church spread throughout the whole world, it is often called in the plural, “Churches,” because of the many assemblies of the faithful, distinguished by different tribes, peoples, and languages. It is called one, as it is said in the Apocalypse of John: “I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify these things to you in the Churches.” Nor should it be passed over that some manuscripts have the singular: “You are being built up into a spiritual house.” Others again have: “Be built into a spiritual house,” in which the very unity of the whole holy Church is more suitably commended. [Col. 0268B] When he had said, “You are being built up into spiritual houses,” or “into a spiritual house,” he adds:

A holy priesthood. That is: you yourselves are a holy priesthood, existing upon the foundation of Christ. Thus he calls the whole Church a holy priesthood, although in the Law only the house of Aaron possessed the name and office. For plainly we are all members of the High Priest, and we are all marked with the oil of gladness; what follows therefore applies to everyone:

To offer spiritual sacrifices through Jesus Christ. “Spiritual sacrifices” means our works, almsgiving, and prayers, understood in distinction from bodily sacrifices. The words “through Jesus Christ,” which are given at the conclusion, apply to everything stated above. [Col. 0268C] For by his grace we are built up in him upon wise master-builders—that is, the ministers of the New Testament—and we become a spiritual house through his Spirit, fortified against the rains, winds, and rivers of temptations. We are able to participate in the holy priesthood and to perform anything good and acceptable to God only through him. For just as a branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, he says, unless you remain in me.

For this reason Scripture says: “Behold, I lay in Zion a chief cornerstone,” and so forth. He sets down this testimony from Isaiah (Isa. XXVIII) to confirm what he had promised: when he had asserted and affirmed that, for the sake of his firmness, the Lord Savior is called by the prophets a stone, he says that those who come to him come to a living stone. [Col. 0268D] He then adds:

“And everyone who believes in him,” and so forth. This follows from what he had said: “And you, like living stones, are being built up.” The Apostle’s statement beautifully corresponds to this prophecy: those who come to the living stone, or believe in him, will not be put to shame. In the verse of that psalm, after it is said, “Come to him and be enlightened,” it is immediately added: “And your faces shall not be put to shame.” John says something similar: “And now, little children, remain in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not be put to shame by him at his coming” (II John II).

Therefore, honor belongs to you who believe. This is that honor: that you may not be put to shame by him at his coming, [Col. 0269A] but, as he himself says: “If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him” (John XIII).

But for those who do not believe, “the stone which the builders rejected.” Just as they rejected him while building their own works, refusing to place him as the foundation of their hearts, so they too will be rejected by him at his coming, when he will refuse to receive into the building of his house, which is in heaven, those who rejected him. This distinction between the honor of believers and the rejection of unbelievers extends to this point. From here he again speaks of believers:

“This has become the cornerstone.” For just as a cornerstone joins two walls, so the Lord joined the people of the Jews and the nations in one fellowship of faith. He then immediately adds concerning unbelievers:

[Col. 0269B]

“And a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.” Hence Paul too says: “We preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, but to the nations foolishness” (II Cor. I).

“For those who stumble at the word and do not believe, to which they were also appointed.” They stumble, therefore, because, precisely when it happens that they hear the word of God, they are offended in mind, since they refuse to believe what they hear. To heighten their foolishness he adds: “And do not believe in that to which they were also appointed.” They were appointed to this—that is, they were made human by nature for this purpose: to believe God and obey his will. Solomon bears witness to this when he says: “Fear God and keep his commandments; for this is the whole of man” (Eccl. XII). Man was naturally made for this: that, fearing God, he should obey his commandments.

[Col. 0269C]

Some manuscripts have: “To which they were also appointed.” This may be understood in accordance with what Paul says concerning the Lord: “For in him we live and move and have our being” (Acts XVII).

But you are “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition.” This is a testimony of praise formerly given through Moses to the ancient people of God, which the Apostle Peter now rightly gives to the nations—those, namely, who have believed in Christ. Like a cornerstone, he united the nations to the salvation which Israel had possessed in him. He calls them a chosen race because of their faith, distinguishing them from those who, by rejecting the living stone, themselves became rejected.

[Col. 0269D] They are a royal priesthood because they are united to his body, and he is the supreme king and true priest, granting his people a kingdom, while, as king and high priest, cleansing their sins through the sacrifice of his blood. He calls them a royal priesthood so that they may remember to hope for an everlasting kingdom and always to offer God sacrifices of blameless conduct.

They are also called a holy nation and a people of acquisition, in accordance with the Apostle Paul’s exposition of the prophetic statement: “My righteous one lives by faith” (Hab. II), followed by: “But if he draws back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him. We, however,” he says, “are not of withdrawal unto destruction, but of faith unto the acquisition of the soul” (Heb. X). And in the Acts of the Apostles: “The Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops to govern the Church of the Lord, which he acquired with his blood” (Acts XX).

[Col. 0270A] We have therefore become a people of acquisition through the blood of our Redeemer, just as the people of Israel were once redeemed through the blood of the lamb from Egypt. Hence, in the following verse also, he recalls the mystical history of old and teaches that it is to be fulfilled spiritually by the new people of God, saying:

“So that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you from darkness into his marvelous light.” For just as those who were delivered from Egyptian slavery through Moses sang a triumphant song to the Lord after crossing the Red Sea and the drowning of Pharaoh’s army, so we ought, after receiving the remission of sins in baptism, to return thanks worthy of heavenly benefits.

[Col. 0270B] For the Egyptians signify not only those who afflicted the people of God, but also, since they are interpreted as “darkness” or “tribulations,” they plainly signify the sins that pursued us but were destroyed in baptism. The deliverance of the children of Israel and their being led into the land once promised also corresponds to the mystery of our redemption. Through that redemption, with the grace of Christ illuminating and guiding us, we make our way toward the light of our heavenly dwelling. That light of grace was also shown by the pillar of cloud and fire, which throughout their journey protected them from the darkness of night and led them by an indescribable path to the promised dwelling places of their homeland.

“Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God; once you had not obtained mercy, but now you have obtained mercy.” These verses plainly indicate that he wrote this Epistle to those who had come to faith from the nations. Formerly alienated from the society of God’s people, they were then united [Col. 0270C] to his people through the grace of faith and obtained the mercy which, while hoping for it, they had not known.

He takes these words from the prophet Hosea, who, foretelling the calling of the nations, says: “I will call those who were not my people, ‘my people,’ and her who had not obtained mercy, ‘she who has obtained mercy’; and in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of the living God” (Hos. II).

## ANOTHER EXPOSITION

Putting aside all malice. By saying “all malice,” he has summed up in one word the mother of every crime.

And all deceit. Although deceit especially concerns deceiving one’s neighbor, the person who truly recognizes himself as a sinner [Col. 0270D] puts away all deceit from himself: what he retains in his heart, he confesses with his mouth.

And hypocrisy. Hypocrisy, otherwise called pretense, exists in a person when he conceals one thing in his heart and displays another in his actions: he shows good on the surface while holding evil in his breast.

And envy. The devil envied Adam’s blessedness and happiness; therefore he persuaded him to sin, and thus through the devil’s envy death entered the world.

And all slander. Slander is blasphemy, suspicious criticism, an estimation of evil works, and every poisonous word spoken about a brother in his absence. Alternatively: “Malice” here is understood as the malice [Col. 0271A] of the pagan nations; “deceit,” that of the Jewish people; “hypocrisy,” that of heretics; “envy,” that of the Jewish rulers; “slander,” that of the scribes and Pharisees.

Like newborn infants. This is an example of that little child of whom the Lord says: “Unless someone becomes like this little child, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVIII). And concerning such children he says: “Let the little children come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven.” Through the grace of baptism, the chaste mother, the Church, gives birth to this holy, pure, and innocent infancy.

Reasonable, without deceitful intent. That is: be reasonable and sincere in understanding, and without the deceitfulness of fraud, like little children.

Desire the milk. That is: suck the abundant breasts of eternal wisdom, [Col. 0271B] and, desiring the teaching of the Gospels and the Apostles, be filled with it.

So that by it you may grow unto salvation. That is: receive the word of the New and Old Testament sincerely, so that you may be able to reach the bread that came down from heaven, growing unto salvation.

For the Lord is sweet. (From Cassiodorus.) This taste does not belong to the palate of the mouth, but to the soul’s sweetest perception. He is sweet to those who have spiritually absorbed his goodness and have tasted of his gift with devoted understanding.

To whom you come, a living stone. Here the stone is understood as Christ, concerning whom Daniel says: “I saw a stone cut from the mountain without hands, which filled the whole earth” (Dan. II). And the Psalm says: “The stone which [Col. 0271C] the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” He is called living because on the third day he rose, alive from the dead; he dies no more, and death shall no longer rule over him. Everyone who believes rightly and lives justly comes to him.

Rejected indeed by human beings. That is, by the Jews, who cried out to Pilate: “Take him away; crucify such a man! We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX).

But chosen by God. As God the Father says concerning him through Isaiah: “Behold my servant, my chosen one” (Isa. LXII). And in the Gospel: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. XVII).

And honored. Our Lord Jesus Christ was honored by the glory of his resurrection, by his ascension into heaven, by his sitting at the Father’s right hand, and by his receiving authority over all [Col. 0271D] powers, as he says: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. ult.). For he was given the name that is above every name, so that at his name every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.

And you yourselves, like living stones. Since you have been raised and given life in Christ, the living stone. For, as the Gospel says: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. III).

You are being built up. That is, upon the foundation of the Apostles and prophets, which is Christ Jesus, concerning whom the Apostle says: “As a wise master builder, I laid the foundation.” And again: “No one can lay another foundation [Col. 0272A] besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus.”

Into a spiritual house. The spiritual house is the Church, built from the living stones and souls of the righteous.

And a holy priesthood. That is: strive to be a holy and spiritual priesthood, not like the carnal priesthood of the Old Testament according to Aaron, but according to Christ’s sanctification.

To offer spiritual sacrifices. Spiritual sacrifices are the prayers of the saints. “Let my prayer,” says the Psalm, “be directed like incense in your presence.” Alternatively, spiritual sacrifices are the pure bodies of the righteous, concerning which Paul says: “I appeal to you by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies as a living, holy sacrifice, [Col. 0272B] pleasing to God” (Rom. XII).

Acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. The people of Israel offered carnal sacrifices through many priests; we offer spiritual sacrifices through one high priest, Jesus Christ, the true and eternal priest, to whom it was said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CX).

For this reason Scripture says. The prophecy of Isaiah contains the following words (chapter XXVIII).

“Behold, I lay in Zion a chief cornerstone.” Zion, which is interpreted as “watchtower,” signifies the Church gathered from both peoples. The stone, Jesus Christ, is placed in its foundation because of the beginning of faith, in its corner because of the union of the two peoples, and at its summit because of the perfection of all [Col. 0272C] good works.
