For he himself is the alpha and the omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end (Rev. I).

Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame. The hope of the good will not be put to shame, because what they now believe faithfully and firmly, they will truly receive and possess with joy forever.

Therefore, honor belongs to you who believe. Great honor is indeed granted to those who believe in Christ: that they should be brothers of the Lord Jesus Christ and sons of the Most High Father; that they should be heirs of God the Father and fellow heirs with Christ. Great, I say, is the honor given them: that they should shine like the sun in the kingdom of the Father and sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

Great is the honor of those to whom the Son of God says: “As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you; remain in my love [Col. 0272D]. You are my friends; and I no longer call you servants, but friends” (John XIV). Great is the honor of those to whom he says: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John XVI). And again: “I will see you, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.” To them he says: “The Father himself loves you, because you love me and believe.”

Great is the honor of those for whom the Son, entreating the Father, says: “Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you have given me, so that they may be one as we are” (John XVII). And again: “The glory which you have given me I have given them, so that they may be one as we are one. I in them and you in me, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them as you loved me.”

Great is the honor of believers, for whom [Col. 0273A] he says: “Father, I desire that those whom you have given me may be with me where I am, so that they may see my glory, which you have given me.”

But for those who do not believe, “the stone which the builders rejected.” (From Cassiodorus.) At that time the Jews alone throughout the world seemed to be builders, because while the other nations sacrificed to idols, they alone worshiped God. Yet they did not complete the structure of their faith, because, in the manner of madmen, they despised the very one who was the strongest cornerstone.

He is said to have become the cornerstone because he joined together the people of the circumcision and the nations. For “corner” derives from the Greek word γόνυ, which in Latin is genu, “knee”; through this bending it reproduces the form of a corner with corresponding shape. Alternatively, Christ is called the cornerstone because he joined [Col. 0273B] the two Testaments, or because, making peace between earthly and heavenly things, he joined the earthly to the heavenly and the heavenly to the earthly.

And a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense for those who stumble at the word and do not believe. This applies to those who do not believe in the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, or who do not believe that divinity exists in him, but, blaspheming him in the Jewish manner, say that he was merely a friend of tax collectors and a drinker of wine (Matt. XI). Christ became for them an offense and a scandal. For they stumbled over him and perished through unbelief.

To which they were also appointed. Human beings are said to have been appointed in Christ because they were made through him. “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I); in him we are, we live, and we move.

[Col. 0273C]

But you are a chosen race. The Lord himself says to the Apostles: “You did not choose me, but I chose you”; and again: “I chose you from the world; therefore the world hates you” (John XIV). The chosen race may also be understood according to Abraham as the people of the nations, for it was said to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed.”

A royal priesthood. There is no saint who lacks the office of the priesthood spiritually, since he is a member of the eternal, supreme, and heavenly Priest, who, by offering himself to the Father for us, united us to his body.

A holy nation. In comparison with the nation of the Jews, which was in Egypt, the Christian people, sanctified in the [Col. 0273D] baptism of Christ, are called a holy nation. Concerning them the Lord also says on their behalf: “I sanctify myself, so that they themselves may be sanctified in truth.”

A people of acquisition. Just as the people led out of Egypt through Moses was acquired for God, so the Christian people, redeemed by the precious blood of Christ, delivered from the gloom and darkness of unbelief, are daily acquired for God.

So that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you from darkness into his marvelous light. You are to proclaim the mighty works of Christ, who called you from the darkness of unbelief to faith, and from the gloom of ignorance to true wisdom, which is Christ. Concerning him he adds: “Into his marvelous light.”

Concerning Christ [Col. 0274A] Simeon also says: “For my eyes have seen your salvation, which you prepared before the face of all peoples: a light for revelation to the nations and the glory of your people Israel,” and so forth (Luke XX). The Lord himself says of himself: “I am the light of the world.” And John says of him: “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John I).

Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God. He speaks of the people of the nations, who formerly existed scarcely at all as the Lord’s people, without the Law, the prophets, or the word. Concerning them the Lord himself says in the Psalm: “The people whom I did not know”—that is, to whom I did not come and did not send prophets—“served me,” that is, believed in me (Ps. XVII). For everyone who believes also serves; this was accomplished among the nations, which had not been sought out by Christ in the flesh.

[Col. 0274B]

Who obtained mercy. That is, before the calling and baptism.

But now you have obtained mercy. The understood meaning is: you have obtained mercy through the faith of baptism and the forgiveness of sins, and, moreover, you have obtained him to whom the Psalmist says: “My God, my mercy” (Ps. LVIII).

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER XX

“On the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came early, while it was still [Col. 0274C] dark, to the tomb, and she saw the stone taken away from the tomb. Therefore she ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and said to them: ‘They have taken the Lord from the tomb, and I do not know where they have put him.’ Then Peter and the other disciple went out and [Col. 0274D] came to the tomb. Now the two were running together, and the other disciple outran Peter and came first to the tomb. And when he had stooped down, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not enter. Then Simon Peter came, following him, and entered the tomb, and saw the linen cloths lying there, and the cloth that had been over his head, not lying with the linen cloths, but folded separately in one place. Then the other disciple also entered, who had come first to the tomb, and he saw and believed. For they did not yet understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead.”

“On the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came early, while it was still dark, to the tomb, and she saw the stone taken away from the tomb,” and so forth. (From Augustine.) Just as in the beginning woman was the originator of guilt for man, and man the executor of error, so now she who had first tasted death was the first to see the resurrection. And so that she might not bear perpetual disgrace among men on account of her guilt, she who had transmitted guilt to man also transmitted grace.

He says “on the first day of the week,” which Christian custom now calls the Lord’s Day because of the Lord’s resurrection; Matthew alone among the Evangelists called it “the first of the Sabbath.”

“Therefore she ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and said to them: ‘They have taken my Lord from the tomb, and I do not know where they have put him.’” Troubled by excessive love, she did not find the one whom [Col. 0275A] she sought. She ran to announce this to the disciples, so that they might either search with her or grieve with her over the removal of the Lord whom she did not hesitate to call “Lord,” although she was seeking only his body in the tomb.

“Then Peter and the other disciple went out and came to the tomb. Now the two were running together, and behold, the other disciple outran Peter and came first to the tomb.” Here one should notice and commend the recapitulation: the narrative returns to what had been passed over and joins it on as though it followed directly. For after he had already said, “They came to the tomb,” he went back to narrate how they came, and said: “Now the two were running together,” and so forth. Here he shows that the other disciple, by whom he signifies himself, outran [Col. 0275B] Peter and arrived first at the tomb. Yet, following the manner of Holy Scripture, he narrates everything as though about another person.

“And when he had stooped down, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not enter.” That Mary Magdalene came to the tomb while it was still dark is narrated according to the historical hour; according to the mystical interpretation, it signifies the understanding of one who is seeking. Mary was seeking in the tomb the Author of all things, whom she had seen dead in the flesh; and because she did not find him there, she believed that he had been stolen.

It was still dark, therefore, when she came to the tomb. She ran quickly and announced it to the disciples, but those who loved more than the others ran more than the others—namely, Peter and John. The two were running together, but John [Col. 0275C] outran Peter. He came first to the tomb, but did not presume to enter.

“Then Simon Peter came, following him, and entered the tomb.” This running of the two disciples contains a great mystery. For what is signified by John, who came first to the tomb but did not enter, except the synagogue? And what is shown by Peter except the Church gathered from the nations, which was called later but entered first?

The nations and the synagogue ran together through the succession of this world, but they did not come with equal understanding. The synagogue came first to the tomb but did not enter, because it received certain commandments of the Law and heard the prophecies concerning the Lord’s incarnation and passion, but refused to believe in the dead man.

John saw the linen cloths lying there, but did not enter, because the synagogue recognized the mysteries of Holy Scripture and yet delayed entering by faith into belief in the Lord’s passion. It had long and extensively prophesied him; it saw him present and rejected him; it despised him as a human being and refused to believe that God had become mortal in the flesh. What does this mean, then, except that it ran more quickly and yet stood empty before the tomb? [Col. 0275D]

But Simon Peter came after him and entered the tomb, because the Church from the nations, following later, recognized the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus; it acknowledged that he had died in the flesh and believed that he was God living. The text continues:

“And he saw the linen cloths lying there, and the cloth that had been [Col. 0276A] over the head of Jesus, not lying with the linen cloths,” and so forth. (From Gregory.) Why is the cloth of the Lord’s head not found in the tomb with the linen cloths, except because, as Paul bears witness, God is the head of Christ, and the incomprehensible mysteries of divinity are separated from our weak understanding, while his power transcends the nature of creation?

It should also be noted that the cloth is said to have been found not only separately but also folded. The beginning and end of a cloth that is folded cannot be seen. Rightly, therefore, the cloth of the head was found folded, because the height of divinity neither began to exist nor ceased to exist.

It is well said, “in one place,” because God is not in the division of minds. God is in unity, and those deserve to possess his grace who do not divide themselves from [Col. 0276B] one another through the scandals of sects.

The cloth may also signify the passion of Christ our Lord, whose mysteries of passion are folded away from unbelievers, because although they saw him mortal in the flesh, they did not believe him to be immortal God. The cloth that had been over his head is therefore found separately, because the passion of our Redeemer is far removed from our passion: he endured his passion without guilt, whereas we endure guilt; he willingly chose to submit to death, whereas we come to it unwillingly. The text continues:

“Then the other disciple also entered, who had come first to the tomb.” After Peter entered, John entered as well: the one who had come first entered later. It is known that at the end of the world [Col. 0276C] Judea too is gathered into the faith of the Redeemer, as Paul bears witness, saying: “Until the fullness of the nations enters, and thus all Israel may be saved” (Rom. II).

“And he saw and believed.” What, then, did he see, and what did he believe with his mouth? He saw the linen cloths lying there and believed what the woman had said: that the Lord had been taken from the tomb. It was still dark in the tomb—that is, in their minds—and therefore the text continues:

“For they did not yet understand the Scriptures, that he must rise from the dead.” Then the disciples returned again to themselves—that is, to the place where they lived and from which they had run to the tomb.

## HARMONY

In the name of the stone and in the signification of the two [Col. 0276D] peoples, a fitting harmony is made between these two readings. In the cornerstone, according to the Apostle, the two peoples are joined; and in the two Apostles, according to the Gospel, the two peoples are represented. John represented the Jews, while Peter represented the people of the nations.

## SUNDAY WITHIN THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

## THE FIRST EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE JOHN, CHAPTER V

“Whatever is born of God conquers the world. And this is the victory that conquers the world: our faith. Who is it that conquers the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ—not in water only, but in water and blood. And the Spirit [Col. 0277A] is the one who testifies, because Christ is the truth. For there are three who testify in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one. And there are three who testify on earth: the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and these three are one. If we receive human testimony, the testimony of God is greater, because this is the testimony of God which is greater: that he has testified concerning his Son. Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony of God in himself.”

“Whatever is born of God conquers the world.” (From Augustine.) The divine commandments are not burdensome because all who devote themselves to them with true devotion despise both the adversities and the allurements of this world with an equal mind, even loving death itself as an entrance into the heavenly homeland. And lest anyone trust that he can overcome the luxuries or labors of the world by his own [Col. 0277B] strength, he suitably adds:

“And this is the victory that conquers the world: our faith.” That faith, namely, which works through love; that faith by which we humbly seek the help of the one who says: “In the world you will have distress, but take courage; I have conquered the world” (John XV).

“Who is it that conquers the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?” He conquers the world who, believing that Jesus is the Son of God, joins to that faith works worthy of it. But is faith and confession of his divinity alone sufficient for salvation? Consider what follows.

“This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ.” He who was the eternal Son of God became [Col. 0277C] human in time, so that those whom he had created through the power of his divinity he might restore through the weakness of his humanity. He came through water and blood—namely, through the water of baptism and the blood of his passion.

“Not in water only, but in water and blood.” He did not merely deign to be baptized in water for our cleansing, in order to consecrate and deliver to us the sacrament of baptism; he also gave his blood for us and redeemed us through his passion, so that, continually nourished by its sacraments, we might be sustained unto salvation.

“And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because Christ is the truth.” When the Lord was baptized in the Jordan, the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove, bearing [Col. 0277D] witness that he is the truth—that is, the true Son of God, the true mediator between God and human beings, and the true Redeemer and reconciler of the human race (Matt. III). Truly he was clean from every stain of sin; truly sufficient to take away the sins of the world.

The Baptist himself, understanding this when he saw the arrival of that same Spirit, said: “He who sent me to baptize with water said to me, ‘Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.’ And I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John I).

Therefore, because the Spirit testifies that Jesus Christ is the truth, he himself calls himself the Truth. The Baptist preaches him as the truth; the son of thunder proclaims the truth in the Gospel. Let the [Col. 0278A] blasphemers be silent, those who dogmatize that he was a phantom. May their memory perish from the earth, those who deny that he is truly either God or human.

“For there are three who testify: the Spirit, the water, and the blood.” The Spirit gave testimony that Jesus is the truth, descending upon him after his baptism. For if he were not the true Son of God, the Holy Spirit would by no means have come upon him with such a manifestation.

The water and the blood also gave testimony that Jesus is the truth, because they flowed from his side when he had died on the cross. This could in no way have happened if he did not possess the true nature of flesh. Moreover, the fact that, before his passion, when he was praying, his sweat became like drops of blood running down upon the earth also bears witness to the truth of the flesh he assumed (Luke XXII).

[Col. 0278B] Nor should it be left unmentioned that in this too the blood and water bore witness to him: they flowed abundantly from the side of the dead man, contrary to the nature of the body, and for that reason suited to the mysteries and appropriate as a testimony to the truth. This signified that the Lord’s body itself would live more fully after death, raised in glory, and that his very death would give us life. The fact also that his sweat flowed upon the earth like drops of blood bore witness, through a sacred mystery, that he would wash the whole Church throughout the world with his blood.

“And the three are one.” These things remain undivided, and none of them is separated from its connection with the others, because true humanity cannot exist without [Col. 0278C] divinity, nor can divinity be believed without true humanity. But in us these are one not by the nature of the same substance, but by the same working of the mystery.

For, as the blessed Ambrose says: “The Spirit renews the mind; the water avails for the washing; the blood serves as the price.” The Spirit made us sons of God by adoption; the water of the sacred font washed us; the Lord’s blood redeemed us. One is invisible and the other visible, and testimony follows the sacrament through the spiritual mystery.

If we accept human testimony, the testimony of God is greater. For this is the testimony of God, which is greater, etc. Great is the testimony of man, which he bears concerning the Son of God, saying: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand” (Ps. CXIX). And, speaking in the person of that Son of God: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son” (Ps. II). Likewise, in the person of the Father speaking about the Son: “He himself will call upon me, ‘You are my Father, my God, and the protector of my salvation’” (Ps. LXXXVIII). “My Father,” because I am the Son of God; “my God,” because I am human; “the protector of my salvation,” because I am to suffer and be saved from death. “And I will make him my firstborn, highest among the kings of the earth.” This is a great testimony, true and worthy of all acceptance. This is God’s testimony concerning the Son; but far greater is God’s testimony, which he himself bore concerning his Son when, addressing him from heaven, he said: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17). Great is the testimony of the forerunner, who bore witness to the Son of God, saying: “I baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.” Greater is that of the Father, who also visibly sent the Holy Spirit upon him, although he was always full of the Spirit.

Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony of God within himself. Whoever believes in the Son of God in such a way that he practices in his actions what he believes has the testimony of God within himself: namely, that he too may rightly be counted among the sons of God. The only Son of God himself promises this to his faithful, saying: “If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him.” If, then, you have deserved to possess the testimony of God, if you possess God as an unimpeachable witness to your faith, what harm can human disgrace or persecution do you? For if God is for us, who can be against us?

[Col. 0279B]

## ANOTHER EXPOSITION

Everything that is born of God—that is, the chosen and spiritual race—overcomes the world through the faith by which it believes that Jesus is the Son of God. It overcomes that world which lies in wickedness, concerning which the Savior says: “Take courage, because I have overcome the world.” This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ: through the water of baptism and the blood of martyrdom, giving us in these two things an example, so that we may follow his footsteps.

It is the Spirit who bears witness that Jesus is truth. The Spirit, namely, the Holy Spirit, who descended upon him in the form of a dove. For the Lord himself also says of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” Or this spirit may be understood as the spirit that bears witness that Jesus is truth—that is, a true human being, to whom both water and blood truly bear witness as to flesh. And not only these, but also the spirit of the man who was in him, concerning which the Gospel says: “He bowed his head and gave up his spirit.” It bears witness—that is, it demonstrates—that Jesus is truth, that is, a true human being, consisting of soul and body. For he assumed both, so that he might redeem both.

Because there are three who bear witness: the Spirit, the water, and the blood. That is, the Holy Spirit, and the Father, who says: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water” (Jer. II), and the blood, that is, Christ, true God and man. For “blood” is understood as man. “And these three,” he says, “are one,” that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For the humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ did not make a quaternity in the Trinity; rather, the undivided Trinity always remains. Alternatively:

The water of baptism, the blood of martyrdom, and the reception of the Holy Spirit bear witness to human salvation; through the Spirit’s operation, the mystery of salvation is accomplished as one for the human race.

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, FINAL CHAPTER

“Now when it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were shut where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in their midst and said to them: Peace be with you. And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. The disciples therefore rejoiced when they saw the Lord. Then he said to them again: Peace be with you. As the Father sent me, so I send you. When he had said this, he breathed upon them and said to them: Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained. But Thomas, one of the twelve, who is called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came. The other disciples therefore said to him: We have seen the Lord. But he said to them: Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe. And after eight days his disciples were again inside, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came, although the doors were shut, and stood in their midst and said: Peace be with you. Then he said to Thomas: Put your finger here, and see my hands, and bring your hand and put it into my side, and do not be unbelieving, but faithful. Thomas answered and said to him: My Lord and my God. Jesus said to him: Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed. Jesus indeed performed many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book. But these have been written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and so that, believing, you may have life in his name.”

“When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were shut where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in their midst,” and so forth. (From Gregory.) What is astonishing if, after his resurrection, when he was already destined to live forever, he entered through closed doors, when, coming to die, he came forth without opening his mother’s womb? But because the faith of those who looked upon that body, which could be seen, doubted, he immediately showed them his hands and his side. He offered flesh to be touched, which he had brought in through closed doors. The nails had pierced his hands; the lance had opened his side. The traces of the wounds were preserved there for the healing of doubting hearts. In this he displayed two marvels, utterly contrary to one another according to human reasoning: after the resurrection he showed his body to be both incorruptible and yet tangible. For what is touched must necessarily be subject to corruption, and what is not corruptible cannot be touched. Yet in a marvelous and immeasurable manner our Redeemer presented a body that was both incorruptible after the resurrection and tangible, so that by displaying its incorruptibility he might invite us to the reward, and by offering it to be touched he might form us in faith. Thus he demonstrated himself to be both incorruptible and tangible, plainly showing that after the resurrection his body would possess the same nature but another glory.

He says to them: “Peace be with you.” He offered peace, he who came on account of peace; and to those to whom he had previously said, “I leave you my peace; I give you my peace,” he now says, “Peace be with you.” This is the peace which, at Christ’s birth, the angels proclaimed to the world.

“And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. The disciples therefore rejoiced when they saw the Lord.” (From Bede.) It would have been little for him to offer himself to be seen by their eyes if he had not also offered himself to be handled by their hands. By showing the disciples his bones and flesh to be touched, he clearly signifies the condition of the true resurrection, both that which has taken place in him and that which is to take place in us. It is not as Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, wrote: “Our body in the glory of that resurrection will be intangible, subtler than winds and air.” Rather, in that glory of the resurrection our body will indeed be subtle through the effect of spiritual power, but it will also be tangible through the truth of its nature. Nor should the Apostle’s statement be thought contrary to this assertion, that “flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God.” In this passage the Apostle, by the terms “flesh and blood,” signifies not the substance of the true body but the corruption of mortality, as he immediately explained, saying: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption.”

Then he says to them again: “Peace be with you.” (From Gregory.) Repetition of the words is confirmation. By saying “Peace be with you” a second time, he shows that the things in heaven and the things on earth have been reconciled through his blood.

“As the Father sent me, so I send you.” The Father sent the Son, whom he ordained to become incarnate for the redemption of the human race. He willed that he should come into the world for suffering, yet he loved the Son whom he sent to suffer. The Lord likewise sends the chosen apostles into the world, not to worldly joys, but to sufferings, just as he himself was sent. Therefore, just as the Son is loved by the Father and yet is sent to suffering, so the disciples are loved by the Lord and yet are sent into the world to suffer. Thus he says: “As the Father sent me, so I send you”—that is, I love you with the same love with which the Father loves me, whom he caused to come to endure sufferings, even while sending me amid the scandals of persecutors.

“When he had said this, he breathed upon them and said to them: Receive the Holy Spirit.” We must ask what it means that our Lord gave the Holy Spirit once while remaining on earth and once while presiding in heaven. For the Holy Spirit is nowhere else clearly shown to have been given except then, when he is received through the breathing, and afterward, when he is shown coming from heaven in various tongues. Why, then, is the Spirit first given to the disciples on earth and afterward sent from heaven, unless there are two commandments of charity: love of God and love of neighbor? The Spirit is given on earth so that the neighbor may be loved; he is given from heaven so that God may be loved. Therefore, just as there is one charity and two commandments, so there is one Spirit and two gifts. First from the Lord while he remained on earth, afterward from him in heaven, because through love of neighbor one learns how one ought to arrive at love of God. By breathing upon them he signified that the Holy Spirit is not the Spirit of the Father alone but also his own.

“Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain,” and so forth. (From Bede.) Behold the charity that is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit: it forgives the sins of those who share in it. But it holds fast the sins of those who do not share in it. Therefore, after he said, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” he immediately added this concerning the forgiveness and retention of sins. It must be understood that those who first had the Holy Spirit received him so that they themselves might live innocently and might benefit certain people through preaching. For this reason, after the Lord’s resurrection they openly received him, so that they might benefit not merely a few but many.

“But Thomas, one of the twelve, who is called Didymus, was not,” and so forth. (From Gregory.) This one disciple was absent; when he returned, he heard what had happened, but refused to believe what he heard. The Lord came again and offered his side to the unbelieving disciple to touch, showed him his hands, and by displaying the scar of his wounds healed the wound of his unbelief. What do you observe in these events, dearly beloved brothers? Do you suppose it happened by chance that this chosen disciple was then absent, afterward came and heard, hearing doubted, doubting touched, and touching believed? This did not happen by chance but by divine dispensation. For heavenly mercy acted wonderfully, so that the doubting disciple, while touching the flesh of his master’s wounds, might heal in us the wounds of unbelief. Thomas’s unbelief benefited us more for faith than the faith of the believing disciples. For while he is brought back to faith by touching, our mind, setting aside every doubt, is strengthened in faith.

“Then the other disciples said to him: We have seen the Lord. But he said to them: Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and put my finger,” and so forth. When John says that the apostle Thomas was not with them at that time, while according to Luke the two of them—one of whom was Cleopas—returned to Jerusalem and found the eleven gathered together, along with those who were with them, it must undoubtedly be understood that Thomas had gone out from there before the Lord appeared while they were saying these things.

“And after eight days his disciples were again inside, and Thomas was with them; Jesus came through closed doors and stood in their midst and said to them: Peace be with you. Then he said to Thomas: Put your finger here, and see my hands,” and so forth. (From Gregory.) In this way he allowed the disciple to doubt after his resurrection, yet did not abandon him in his doubt, just as before his birth he willed that Mary should have a betrothed, although that man did not come to her wedding. Thus the doubting and touching disciple became a witness of the true resurrection, just as the bridegroom of Christ’s mother had been the guardian of her spotless virginity.

(From Bede.) He showed not only his hands and feet, on which the marks of the nails were clearly visible, but, as John testifies, he also showed the side that had been pierced by the lance. By displaying the scar of his wounds, he healed the wound of their doubt and unbelief. But just as after the resurrection he deigned to strengthen the disciples’ faith and hope by displaying the places of the nails and the lance, so on the day of judgment he will come displaying both these signs of his passion and the cross itself, to confound the impiety of the proud and the unbelief of the faithless. Namely, he will openly show to all angels and human beings that he himself is the one who died at the hands of the impious and for the sake of the impious; and they will see, as it is written: “They will look upon him whom they pierced, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him” (Zech. XII).

It should rightly be noted that pagans commonly construct a slander at this point and mock, with foolish chatter, the faith in the resurrection that we hope for. “If your God,” they say, “was unable even to heal the wounds inflicted upon him by the Jews, but, as you say, carried the traces of his scars with him into heaven, with what presumption do you think that he will restore your limbs from the dust to completeness?” They should be answered: Our God, who was able, whenever he wished and in whatever manner he wished, to raise from the tomb the flesh that had already been glorified by perpetual immortality, also raised it in whatever condition he wished. For it does not follow that he who is proved to have done greater things was unable to do lesser ones. Rather, by the grace of his dispensation, he who did the greater refrained from doing the lesser: he who destroyed the realms of death did not wish to erase the signs of death.

First, he did this so that through them he might establish in the disciples the faith in his resurrection; next, so that, pleading with the Father for us, he might display above all what kind of death he had endured for the life of mortals. Third, so that he might continually renew for those redeemed by his death the signs of that same death, showing how mercifully they had been helped, and so that they might never cease to sing the mercies of the Lord in eternity, but might say, they who have been redeemed by the Lord: “For he is good, for his mercy endures forever.” Finally, so that at the judgment he might also announce to the faithless, among their other crimes, how justly they are condemned, by displaying the scars of the wounds that he received from them.

It is as though some exceedingly brave soldier, by order of his king, had labored in single combat for the safety of his entire people, had received many wounds but nevertheless killed the enemy, seized his spoils, and brought victory to his people. When asked by the physician to whom he was entrusted for healing whether he wished to be healed in such a way that no trace of his wounds would remain, or rather in such a way that the scars would remain while all deformity and ugliness were entirely removed, he might answer that he preferred to be healed in such a way that, after recovering his former condition of complete health and beauty, he would forever carry with him the signs of so great a triumph. So the Lord, for the sake of the perpetual sign of victory, chose to carry into heaven the scars of the wounds of his passion suffered for us rather than abolish them. Yet none of this prejudices the faith in our resurrection, concerning which the true promise is proclaimed: “Not a hair of your head will perish.”

[Col. 0283D]

Thomas answered and said to him: “My Lord and my God.” Jesus said to him: “Because you have seen me, you have believed.” Since Thomas saw and touched him, why is he told, “Because you have seen me, you have believed”? He saw one thing and believed another. Divinity could not be seen by mortal man; therefore he saw a human being and confessed him as God, saying: “My Lord and my God” (Luke XXI). Thus he believed by seeing: when he contemplated the human being, he exclaimed that this was the true God, whom he could not see.

Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed. In this statement we have been especially marked out: we who retain him in our minds although we have not seen him in the flesh. We have been marked out, but only if we follow our faith with works. For he truly believes who practices in his actions what he believes. When he says, “Blessed are those who have not seen me and have believed,” he uses the past-tense verb as though he knew that what was still future had already been accomplished in his predestination. But, as we have said, these words specifically designate the faith of the nations.

Jesus indeed performed many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book. The evangelist indicates that Jesus performed very many signs and miracles of salvation and preaching that were not written down because of the multitude of things he accomplished.

But these have been written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and so that, believing, you may have eternal life in his name. For whoever believes that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, by believing has the Son himself within him; and by having the Son, he also has life. For he himself said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). Moreover, he will possess eternal life with the saints, where there will be secure certainty, everlasting happiness, and indescribable joy. There that saying will be fulfilled: “I will be their God, and they will be my people” (Jer. XXXI)—that is, I will be the one from whom they are satisfied; I will be their life, salvation, strength, abundance, glory, honor, peace, and every good thing. Thus the Apostle’s saying will be fulfilled: “That God may be all in all.” He himself will be the end of our desires: he will be seen without end, loved without weariness, and praised without exhaustion.

## HARMONY

Although the harmony is also fitting in many words and meanings, it is especially appropriate in the point where it says that Jesus is the Son of God: thus the agreement between these two readings is most suitably established.

## SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

## THE FIRST EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PETER, CHAPTER II

“Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example so that you might follow his footsteps. He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but entrusted himself to him who judged him unjustly. He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood, so that, having died to sins, we might live for righteousness; by whose bruising you were healed. For you were once like wandering sheep, but now you have returned to the shepherd and bishop of your souls.”

“Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example so that you might follow his footsteps; he committed no sin,” and so forth. (From Bede.) You hear that Christ suffered for us, and you rejoice because Christ died for you. But attend to what follows: “Leaving us an example so that you might follow his footsteps.” It is an example of tribulations, not pleasures; of insults, disgrace, pains, reproaches, thorns, the cross, wounds, and death. It is written in the Psalm: “Because of the words of your lips, I have guarded difficult ways” (Ps. LXI). What words of God’s lips are meant, if not those by which he promises eternal life?

“He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood,” and so forth. Having previously addressed servants in particular, he now admonishes everyone in general, so that each may also recall what the Lord God endured for them. Indeed, he instructs the whole Church concerning what its author endured for its liberation. For he does not say “your sins,” but, including himself, says: “He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood.”

“For you were like wandering sheep.” Why does he call them both sheep and wandering, when those who lead their lives in error are more properly reckoned under the name of goats than of sheep? Unless it is because the Lord knows those who are his, and sustains many who have long lived badly, although he foresees that they will nevertheless be saved among the number of his sheep.

[Col. 0285B]

“But now you have returned to the shepherd,” and so forth. He touches upon the Gospel parable in which the merciful shepherd, leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the desert, came to visit the one that had wandered. For what is said there—that after finding it he placed it joyfully upon his shoulders—is anticipated here by the blessed Peter, who says: “He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood,” because he evidently wished to redeem us in such a way that, hanging upon his shoulders, he carried the wood on which he bore away our sins.

“To the shepherd,” he says, “and overseer of your souls.” He is the shepherd because he gives us the pastures of eternal life and, in the present, provides the pasture of temporal graces. He is the overseer of your souls because “the dawn from on high has visited us,” to illuminate those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death. He visits that soul in us daily because he has given light, not so that it may fail but so that it may be preserved—indeed, so that it may increase and grow through his help.

Some manuscripts have the Greek itself: ἀλλὰ ἐπιστράφετε νῦν ἐπὶ τὸν ποιμένα καὶ ἐπίσκοπον τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν, “but now return to the shepherd and overseer of your souls.” In Latin, *episcopus* is called “overseer,” because “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers,” so that he may deliver them from all their tribulations.

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER X

“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep. But the hired man, and he who is not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees; and the wolf snatches and scatters the sheep. The hired man flees because he is a hired man and has no concern for the sheep. I am the good shepherd, and I know my own, and my own know me. As the Father knows me, so I know the Father; and I lay down my life for my sheep. And I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one fold and one shepherd.”

“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep.” When the Lord wished to show the work of the good shepherd, he set himself forward as an example, saying: “The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep.”

(From Gregory.) The way of despising death has been shown to us, and a form has been set before us in which we should be impressed. First, we must mercifully expend our outward possessions for his sheep. Finally, if necessary, we must also offer our own death for those same sheep. He who does not give his possessions for the sheep—when will he give his life?

We have explained, or rather, by the Lord’s teaching we have understood, who the shepherd is, who the door is, who the doorkeeper is; we have also learned who the sheep are, as well as who the thieves and robbers are. But now let us consider the hired man and the wolf. Concerning them the Lord himself said:

“But the hired man, and he who is not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming, and leaves the sheep and flees.” He is called not a shepherd but a hired man because he feeds the Lord’s sheep not out of intimate love but for temporal wages. The hired man is one who holds the position of shepherd but does not seek the profit of souls. He gapes after earthly advantages, rejoices in the honor of leadership, is fed by temporal gains, and delights in the reverence shown him by people. These are the hired man’s wages: that, in exchange for the work he performs in governing, he should find here what he seeks, while remaining excluded in the future from the inheritance of the flock.

“And the wolf snatches and scatters the sheep.” The wolf snatches and scatters the sheep when he draws one person into luxury, inflames another with greed, raises another up in pride, and divides another through anger. He spurs one person on with envy and trips another through deceit. Thus the wolf scatters the flock when the devil kills the faithful people through temptations. But against these things the hired man is inflamed by no zeal and stirred by no fervor of love. Since he seeks only outward advantages, he negligently tolerates the inward losses of the flock.

“But the hired man flees because he is a hired man,” and so forth. The sole reason for the hired man’s flight, then, is that he is a hired man. It is as though it were said openly: He cannot stand in danger for the sheep who, in presiding over the sheep, does not love the sheep but seeks earthly profit. While he embraces honor and rejoices in temporal advantages, he fears to set himself against danger, lest he lose what he loves.

Likewise, the wolf comes upon the sheep when any unjust and rapacious person oppresses the faithful and humble. But he who seemed to be a shepherd and was not one leaves the sheep and flees because, fearing danger to himself from that person, he does not dare resist his injustice. He flees not by changing his location but by withdrawing his assistance; he flees because he saw injustice and remained silent; he flees who hides himself beneath silence.

But there is another wolf who every day, without ceasing, tears apart not bodies but minds: namely, the evil spirit, who prowls around the folds of the faithful, laying ambushes and seeking the deaths of souls.

“I am the good shepherd.” Since our Redeemer earlier made known the faults of the false shepherd, he again shows the form in which we ought to be impressed, saying: “I am the good shepherd.” And he adds: “I know my own”—that is, I love them—“and my own know me”—that is, they obey by loving.

[Col. 0287A]

“As the Father knows me, and I know the Father, and I lay down my life for my sheep.” It is as though he said openly: It is evident that I both know the Father and am known by the Father because I lay down my life for my sheep. That is, by the love with which I die for the sheep, I show how greatly I love the Father. But because he had come to redeem not only Judea but also the Gentiles, he adds:

“And I have other sheep that are not of this fold, and I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one fold and one shepherd.” The Lord had regard for our redemption—we who have come from the Gentile people—when he said that he would bring other sheep also. Brothers, you see this happening daily; today you see it accomplished among the reconciled nations. He makes one fold out of two flocks, as it were, because he joins the Jewish and Gentile peoples in his faith, as Paul bears witness when he says: “He himself is our peace, who made both one.” By choosing the simple from both nations for eternal life, he leads the sheep into his own fold.

## HARMONY

A fitting harmony between these two readings is found both in the sheep and in the shepherd.

## SECOND SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

## THE FIRST EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PETER, CHAPTER II

“I beseech you, as strangers and pilgrims, to abstain from carnal desires, which wage war against the soul. Conduct yourselves honorably among the Gentiles, so that, when they speak against you as evildoers, they may observe you by your good works and glorify God on the day of visitation. Be subject for God’s sake to every human authority, whether to the king as preeminent, or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers but the praise of the good. For this is the will of God: that by doing good you should silence the ignorance of foolish people. Live as free people, yet not as those who use freedom as a covering for evil, but as servants of God. Honor everyone, love the brotherhood, fear God, honor the king. Servants, be subject with all fear to your masters, not only to the good and gentle but also to the difficult. For this is grace in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

“I beseech you, as strangers and pilgrims.” (From Bede.) In Latin, *advenae*—strangers—are called in Greek προσήλυτοι, *proselytoi*. The Jews used this name for those born among the nations who believed in God, received his circumcision, and wished to live according to Jewish custom and the law of God. Some of their number were among those who believed in Christ through the apostles’ preaching on the holy day of Pentecost, when the apostles received the Holy Spirit in the appearance of fire; for Scripture says that Jews and proselytes were also present (Acts II).

But if we can truthfully say to God with the Prophet, “For we are strangers with you on the earth, and pilgrims, as all our fathers were,” we too must believe that the Epistles of the blessed Peter were written to us and read as though they had been sent to us.

“Abstain from carnal desires, which wage war against the soul.” When the flesh is weakened and subdued by flattering desires, the army of vices is already firmly armed against the soul. He appropriately calls them strangers and pilgrims, so that they may place their minds less upon earthly things, remembering that they have a homeland in heaven. For in this life the usual difference between the elect and the reprobate is that the elect, now pilgrims and exiles, await their homeland in the future; and the less they delight in the fleeting joys of the present, the more they hope to receive future joys without end and to reign with Christ forever. The reprobate, however, have their homeland here; they know only how to yearn for the desires of this life. Therefore, after this life they are confined to perpetual exile, where, deprived of every pleasure, they suffer only adversity amid torments.

“So that, when they speak against you as evildoers, they may observe you by your good works and glorify God on the day of visitation.” It often happens that pagans who criticized the faith of Christians, asking why they had abandoned their gods, afterward, when they observed their chaste conduct and unconquered spirit in Christ, ceased to slander them and instead began to glorify and praise God, who was proved good and just by the goodness and justice of his worshipers.

“They glorify God,” he says, “on the day of visitation”—that is, at the time of repayment, when they will see how great is the glory to be given you by God. Let unbelievers recognize this even now, when they see you persistently following him through opposing dangers.

“Be subject for God’s sake to every human authority.” By “every human authority” he means every human rank, every person, and every principality to which divine arrangement may wish you to be subject. This is what he means by “for God’s sake,” because “there is no authority except from God, and whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance.” He explains this authority further by adding:

“Whether to the king as preeminent, or to governors as sent by him.” He mentions only the king and governors, and not masters as well, because in this passage he specifically instructs those who, as we said above, are the masters of servants. Subsequently he admonishes servants concerning how they should serve their masters. He therefore teaches the faithful—servants, that is, of the eternal King—to submit also to the powers of the world, lest anyone be able to reproach the faith and Christian religion on the grounds that through it the rights of human society are disturbed. For what was said—“to every human authority”—can also rightly be understood as referring to masters of both the faithful and the unbelieving.

“For the punishment of evildoers but the praise of the good.” This does not mean that all governors sent by kings know how either to punish evildoers or to praise the good. Rather, he simply describes what the conduct of a good governor ought to be: that he restrain those who do evil and reward those who act well. Even if he acts unjustly and condemns the good, what he does nevertheless contributes to their praise if they patiently endure his wickedness and wisely resist his foolishness.

Hence Paul also says: “Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it.” He does not say “from it” in the sense of praise bestowed by it, but “from it” as the occasion or source. For even if worldly authority does not praise you—indeed, even if it persecutes you, kills you with the sword as it did Paul, or crucifies you as it did Peter—you will have praise from it, when, through what it has done wickedly, your patience in virtue earns a crown of praise for you as a just and innocent person.

The following words also show that the blessed Peter intended this meaning:

“For this is the will of the Lord: that by doing good you should silence the ignorance of foolish people.” This, then, is the praise of the good, for which he says governors are sent by the king: the good use the ignorance of foolish governors for their own perpetual praise by acting well.

“Live as free people, yet not as those who use freedom as a covering for evil.” Those who act well as free people are those who, the greater the freedom they enjoy among human beings, subject themselves all the more strictly—indeed, all the more freely—to divine service. Those also act well as free people who, following the example of the patriarch Joseph, although oppressed by human servitude, are compelled by no means to become servants of vices.

But they turn their freedom into a covering for evil when, the less they are restrained by the yoke of human service, the more broadly they are enslaved to the dominion of sins. When they serve vices with impunity, they call it freedom. Under this name they conceal their guilt.

The passage can also be understood generally according to the Apostle Paul’s statement: “You were called to freedom, brothers; only do not use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh.” We are rightly called free because through baptism we have been released from the bonds of sins, because we have been redeemed from demonic servitude, and because we have been made sons of God. Yet through the gift of freedom we have not received a greater ability or license to sin. On the contrary, if we sin, we immediately become servants of sin, having lost our freedom. Whoever thinks that he has been freed by the Lord so that he may sin more freely turns his freedom into a covering for evil. The blessed Peter wishes us to be free from servitude to guilt, so that we may remain good and faithful servants of our Creator. Therefore he adds next:

But as servants of God. Honor everyone, love the brotherhood, fear God, honor the king. He [Col. 0289D] therefore urges that fitting honor be shown to all, and, in accordance with the Lord’s command, that we render to Caesar what belongs to Caesar and to God what belongs to God. And rightly, among other things, he commands free persons to love the brotherhood, so that they may remember that those who are subject to them by a temporary condition have also been made their brothers in Christ, invoking together with them the Father who judges without partiality.

Servants, be subject with all fear to your masters, not only to the good and moderate, but also to the difficult. *Dyskoloi* (δύσκολοι) means “difficult,” without scholarly training. He calls them “undisciplined,” using a word derived from the Greek expression. For in Greek *scholē* (σχολή) is called the place in which young men ordinarily devote themselves to literary studies and have leisure to listen to teachers [Col. 0290A]; hence *scholē* is interpreted as “leisure.” Accordingly, in the Psalm where we sing, “Be at leisure and see, for I am the Lord,” the Greek has *scholasate* (σχολάσατε) for what we call “be at leisure.” The *scholastici*, therefore, are the educated; the *dyscoli*, the unlearned and rustic. Yet he wishes subjects to obey both, explaining more openly how above he commanded us to be subject to every creature. Another edition has “the difficult” instead of “the difficult people,” and the holy bishop Fulgentius gives the passage in his works as follows: “Serving with love, not only the good and moderate, but also the more difficult.”

But if, while doing good and enduring patiently, you bear it, this is grace in Christ Jesus. For this is grace before God: in this you were called, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, [Col. 0290B] etc. We should note carefully how greatly he glorifies the condition of servants, affirming that those who do good and are beaten without any fault by cruel and wicked masters are imitators of the Lord’s Passion.

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER XVI

> “A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me, because I am going to the Father.” Therefore some of his disciples said to one another: “What is this that he says to us: ‘A little while, and you will not see me; and again a little while, and you will see me, because I am going to the Father’?” So they were saying: “What is this ‘little while’ that he says to us? We do not know what he is talking about.” But Jesus knew that they wanted to question him, and he said to them: “Are you asking one another about this, because I said, ‘A little while, and you will not see me; and again a little while, and you will see me, because I am going to the Father’? [Col. 0290C] Amen, amen, I say to you: you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy. When a woman gives birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come; but when she has given birth to the child, she no longer remembers her anguish, because of her joy that a human being has been born into the world. And you therefore now have sorrow, but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.”

A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me. These words apply especially to those who deserved to cling to his discipleship while he preached in the flesh and, after the sorrow of his Passion, [Col. 0290D] to rejoice when they had seen his resurrection and ascension. There was also a short interval from that hour of the night in which he was handed over to the hour of his Passion, during which the disciples saw him bodily. And again there was a short interval during which he lay shut up in the tomb, destined to rise on the third day, and could not be seen by them. This is what he says: “A little while, and you will not see me.” But when he says, “Again a little while, and you will see me,” he signifies the period after the resurrection during which he lived with the disciples and appeared to them in many ways, until he ascended into heaven while they watched, as is read in the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles. This is also what he means by saying, “Because I am going to the Father,” as though he were plainly saying: “Because shortly I shall be hidden from your sight [Col. 0291A] within the enclosure of the tomb; and again shortly afterward, once the power of death has been destroyed, I shall appear for you to behold, because the time has come for me, having completed the dispensation of the mortality I assumed, to return already to the Father with the triumph of the resurrection.” These words of the Lord, as I have said, apply particularly to those who were able to see his resurrection, though the apostles at that time could not understand them. The compassionate teacher, understanding their ignorance, therefore answered according to the uncertainty in their souls, as though he were about to explain what he had said: “A little while, and you will not see me; and again a little while, and you will see me.”

Therefore Jesus knew that they wanted to question him, and he said to them: “Are you asking one another about this, because I said, ‘A little while, and you will not see me; and again a little while, and you will see me’? [Col. 0291B] Amen, amen, I say to you: you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful,” etc. This applies both to their condition and to that of the whole Church. Lovers of Christ wept and lamented when they saw him seized, bound by his enemies, led before the council, condemned, crucified, killed, and buried. Lovers of the world rejoiced—those whom the Lord calls “the world” because of their base thoughts—when they condemned to the most shameful death him whose very sight was burdensome to them. The disciples were sorrowful when he had been placed in death; but when his resurrection was recognized, their sorrow was turned into joy. After seeing the power of his ascension, they were lifted up by still greater joy and praised and blessed the Lord, as the evangelist Luke [Col. 0291C] testifies. This saying of the Lord also applies to all the faithful, who strive to reach eternal joys through present tears and tribulations: “Those who sow in tears, so that they may reap in joy: going forth, they went and wept” (Ps. CXXV), so that they may receive the reward of their labor in eternal blessedness. But the world—that is, lovers of the world—will rejoice: those who disdain to prepare themselves for eternal joys through tears and afflictions. “You will be sorrowful” through labors and tribulations, “but your sorrow will be turned into the joy of eternal blessedness.”

When a woman is in labor, she has sorrow because her hour has come. He calls the holy Church a woman because of the fruitfulness of her good works. And because she never ceases to beget spiritual children for God, this woman [Col. 0291D], when she is in labor, has sorrow because her hour has come.

But when she has given birth to the child, she no longer remembers her anguish, because of her joy that a human being has been born into this world. For clearly, as long as the holy Church is devoted in this world to the advancement of spiritual virtues, she never ceases to be exercised by the world’s temptations. But when, having overcome the struggle of labor, she reaches the palm of victory, she no longer remembers, he says, the anguish that preceded, because of the joy of the reward received: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to come, which will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII). She does not remember the anguish, he says, because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world. [Col. 0292A] For just as a woman rejoices when a human being has been born into this world, so the Church is filled with worthy exultation when the people of the faithful have been born into the future life. For that birth she labors and groans greatly in the present, suffering as though in labor. Nor should it seem strange to anyone that one who has departed this life is said to have been born. For just as someone is customarily said to be born when he emerges from his mother’s womb and comes forth into this light, so one who has been released from the bonds of the flesh and raised to eternal light can most properly be called “born.” Hence ecclesiastical custom has established that we call the days of the blessed martyrs or confessors of Christ—on which they passed from this age—their *birthdays*, and that their solemn celebrations are called not funerals but birthdays.

[Col. 0292B]

And therefore you now have sorrow, but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you. This is readily understood of the disciples themselves, because they had sorrow when the Lord had suffered and been buried, but after the glory of the resurrection had been accomplished, they rejoiced when they saw the Lord. No one took their joy from them. Although they suffered tribulations and persecutions in this world, they always rejoiced in hope of the future reward, because they were worthy to suffer insults for the name of Jesus: “Again I will see you, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.” The Lord therefore sees the elect after their sorrow when, having condemned their assailant, he rewards their patience: “I will see you,” that is, “when I have taken you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be.” In that vision of perpetual glory, [Col. 0292C] your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you, because there will be no adversary, no persecutor, no one to inflict sorrow on your souls, while “the God of gods will be seen in Zion,” and when Christ appears, then you also will appear with him in glory, as the Apostle says.

## THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

### THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE JAMES, CHAPTER I

> “Every good giving and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow caused by turning. For of his own will he begot us by the word of truth, so that we might be in some sense the beginning of his creation. Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, [Col. 0292D] and slow to anger. For the anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God. Therefore, putting away all filthiness and abundance of wickedness, receive with gentleness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.”

Every good giving and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights. (From Bede.) After teaching that the vices by which we are tempted do not come from God but are shown to be present in us by ourselves, he teaches conversely that whatever good we do, we have received from God as giver. For this reason he calls him the Father of lights, because he recognizes him as the author of spiritual gifts. To this agrees the statement of the Apostle Paul: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (I Cor. I).

[Col. 0293A]

With whom there is no change or shadow caused by turning. Because there is no mutability in God’s nature, nor does his light, like the light of this world, suffer interruption through any shadow of alteration. It is therefore clear that he sends us only gifts of light, and not also the darkness of errors.

Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth. And the Lord says in the Gospel: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John XIV). And in the prophet Hosea: “I will love them spontaneously” (Hos. XIV). Since, therefore, he had said that every good giving and every perfect gift descends from God, he appropriately establishes this by adding that it was not through our merits but through the favor of his own will that, through the water of regeneration, he changed us from children of darkness into children of light.

[Col. 0293B]

So that we might be in some sense the beginning of his creation. Lest, when he says “begot,” we should think that we become what he himself is, he shows that a certain primacy has been granted to us in creation through this adoption. Someone has translated this verse as follows: “Willingly he begot us by the word of truth, so that we might be the firstfruits of his creatures,” that is, so that we might be better than the other creatures whom we see. For the law commands the firstfruits of crops and animals to be consecrated to the Lord. He commanded the firstfruits of gold and silver to be brought for the work of the tabernacle—that is, the very best things in the metals (Exod. XXII, XXIII). And concerning the ancient people of God, the prophet Jeremiah said: “Israel was holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his produce” (Jer. II).

But know this, my beloved brothers. “It is very well known,” he says, “to you that you have fallen into [Col. 0293C] vices through yourselves; but that you are enlightened by the Lord has come about not through your own foresight, but because heavenly grace has gone before you.”

Let every person be quick to hear, etc. Here he instructs the listener by moral precepts, and rightly first admonishes everyone to apply the ear more quickly to one who teaches, but to open the mouth for teaching slowly, since it is foolish for anyone to wish to preach to others what he himself has not learned. Whoever therefore loves wisdom should first, as he admonished above, ask it from God. Then, as a humble hearer, he should seek a teacher of truth and, in the course of action, restrain his tongue with the greatest care—not only from idle speech, but also from proclaiming the truth he has just learned. Hence Solomon, writing about the distinction of times, says: [Col. 0293D] “A time to be silent, and a time to speak” (Eccl. III). Hence the Pythagoreans, endowed with the instruction of natural science, order their pupils to be silent for five years, and only then permit them to preach.

And slow to anger. For the maturity of wisdom is perceived only with a tranquil mind. It is written: “Anger rests in the bosom of a fool” (Eccl. VII). He does not forbid the swiftness of anger in such a way as to approve slowness in every respect; rather, he urges us to take care that, even in a time of disturbance and quarrels, anger not steal upon us. Or, if it should perhaps steal upon us, let us restrain its force within the barriers of the mouth, so that when the hour of danger has passed we may more freely purge it completely from our heart in due time. Or certainly he commands us to be slow to anger so that we do not turn the serenity of our face into harshness for every possible reason. But when a definite reason exists [Col. 0294A]—for example, when we see that those nearest to us, especially those entrusted to us, cannot otherwise be corrected—let us display toward them the severity of words or even the judgment of discipline, while nevertheless keeping the condition of our mind serene, as far as human nature permits. I believe that Phinehas, Samuel, Elijah, and Peter were slow to anger, and yet they slew sinners either by word or by the sword. Moses too, although he was a very gentle man, left Pharaoh, whom he saw to be incorrigible, exceedingly angry, threatening him with a punishment that he also carried out in deed.

For the anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God. The meaning is straightforward: whoever carelessly subjects himself to the vice of anger, even if he appears just to human beings [Col. 0294B], is not yet perfectly just in the divine judgment. Yet it can be understood more profoundly in light of what is said by the Lord: “But you, Lord of hosts, judge with tranquility.” Whatever human judge, having lost tranquility of mind, judges a delinquent—even if he judges justly—cannot imitate the righteousness of the divine judgment, into which disturbance cannot fall.

Therefore, putting away all filthiness and abundance of wickedness, receive with gentleness the implanted word. First he commands both body and mind to be cleansed from vices, so that they may be worthy to receive the word of salvation. For one who does not first turn away from evil cannot do good. By “all filthiness” he means both that of the flesh and that of the soul. [Col. 0294C]

“Wickedness,” properly speaking, refers to the depravity of the inner person. “Receive,” he says, “the implanted word”—that is, the word of God, which we implant in your hearts by preaching; receive it by learning. Or certainly it should be understood in this way: receive now more perfectly the word that was implanted in us on the day of redemption, by which God willingly begot us, fulfilling also in works what you already hold in mystery.

Which is able to save your souls. Even if meanwhile you suffer temptations in the body or are brought to completion by death at the hands of the faithless.

[Col. 0294D]

## ANOTHER EXPOSITION

Every good giving and every perfect gift is from above. This can be understood both generally of all things and specifically of every virtue given by God. The good gift may also be understood specifically as continence within marriage, and the perfect gift as virginity. Nor is there any obstacle to understanding the good gift as given in the grace of baptism and the perfect gift as given in the bestowal of the Holy Spirit.

Coming down from the Father of lights. God is called the Father of lights because from him all lights were made—whether invisible lights, such as the angels, concerning whom God said at the beginning, “Let there be light”; or those souls to whom Jesus said, “You are the light of the world”; or, generally, the visible lights of the sun, moon, and stars.

With whom there is no change. For he who said, “I am who I am” (Exod. III) will not be changed. [Col. 0295A] Motion and time, increase and decline, do not belong at all to the divine nature.

Nor shadow caused by turning. For he who is always the light of light, the creator and source of every light, is not overshadowed by darkness after the light, as one day is after another.

Of his own will he begot us. Certainly by grace, not by nature. For only the Word is substantially and properly called the Son of God. The others are called sons by the power received from him: “But as many as received him,” says the Apostle, “to them he gave power to become the sons of God” (John I).

By the word of truth. God the Father is Truth, and his Son is the Word. If Christ is the Truth, the Gospel is the word of truth: “Through the Gospel,” Paul says, “I begot you.”

[Col. 0295B]

So that we might be in some sense the beginning of his creation. The beginning of creation consists of the rational angels in heaven, Adam on earth, the patriarchs in the Church of the Old Testament, and the apostles in the Church redeemed by Christ’s blood. For to one of them it is said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI), which Church the Apostle Paul calls a new creation.

Let every person be quick to hear, but slow to speak. For the Apostle knew that those to whom he sent his letters wished to hold and teach the primacy of speech rather than to be taught; therefore he admonishes them to preserve humility. Quickness in hearing makes a person teachable; slowness in speaking makes one gentle.

[Col. 0295C]

Slow to anger. Since he could not wholly avoid what occurs naturally, he prohibited hastiness, because delayed anger diminishes. Alternatively: “slow to anger,” that is, according to the law of the Old Testament, slow to vengeance. For, the Apostle says, “the law produces anger” (Rom. V)—that is, “an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth.”

For the anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God. By “the anger of man” he means human anger, which, according to the practice of the Old Testament, always desires to exercise vengeance, and therefore does not accomplish the righteousness of the New Testament, where it is written: “Do not resist evil” (Matt. V). Alternatively: “The anger of man does not accomplish righteousness,” with this understood: the anger of God, which is spoken of in human terms, does accomplish righteousness—as in Sodom, in Pharaoh, in Egypt, at the Red Sea, and among the people of Israel themselves in the wilderness. Hence the Psalmist [Col. 0295D] sings: “The Lord was angry in fury against his people” (Ps. CV). In many places we read of the anger of the Lord, which always produces the most upright righteousness through the most just judgment.

Therefore, putting away all filthiness. Some have wished to understand “filthiness” in this passage specifically as idolatry. Others understand it as the filthiness of fornication, whether with women, men, or beasts, and similar things. Finally, so that you might understand it generally of every kind of wickedness, he added “the abundance of wickedness.” For just as a living root germinates shoots in the earth, so wickedness hidden in the heart generates vices.

With gentleness receive the implanted word, which is able to save your souls. “With gentleness,” [Col. 0296A] that is, without anger and dispute. Receive by right faith, in a pure mind, the word implanted and sent by God and received in our minds, so that where sin abounded, grace might abound all the more. “The word,” he says—that is, the word of faith, the word of the Gospel. Finally, it is the Word of which John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John I). He is also called the Savior because he is able to save our souls.

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER XVI

> “I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’ But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart. But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go away. For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; [Col. 0296B] but if I go away, I will send him to you. And when he has come, he will convict the world concerning sin, and concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment: concerning sin, indeed, because they did not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I am going to the Father, and you will no longer see me; concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has been judged. I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth has come, he will teach you all truth. For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.”

I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, “Where are you going?” (From Augustine.) [Col. 0296C] He indicates that he will go to the one who sent him in such a way that no one asks, since they would see with the eyes of the body that it was happening openly. For a cloud received him when he ascended from them, and they did not question him in words as he went into heaven, but accompanied him with their eyes (Acts I).

But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart. He certainly saw what those words of his were doing in their hearts.
