For since they did not yet possess inwardly the spiritual consolation they were destined to have through the Holy Spirit, they feared losing what they saw outwardly in Christ.

But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go away. [Col. 0296D]

It is expedient that the form of a servant be withdrawn from your sight, so that the love of his divinity may be more suitably fixed in your minds. It is expedient that I carry the form known to you from earth into heaven, so that through this you may yearn for that place with greater desire.

For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you. But if I go away, I will send him to you. He does not say this because, while he was present on earth, he could not himself give the Spirit to the disciples, since it is plainly read that after the resurrection he appeared to them, breathed on them, and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit.” Rather, while he was present on earth and dwelling bodily with them, they were unable to raise their minds toward him in order to thirst for the gifts of heavenly grace. But after he ascended into heaven, they transferred all their desire there as well. Thus they had already become capable of the Holy Spirit: [Col. 0297A] they were no longer sorrowful over his death, but rejoiced in the gift of his promise. It is clear, and requires no laborious exposition, why he called that same Spirit the Paraclete, that is, the Comforter. For the coming of the Spirit comforted and revived the hearts of the disciples, which his departure would have made sorrowful. This does not mean that the Holy Spirit was previously absent from the hearts of the disciples or from the ancient saints, but that he had not before been given in such manifest fullness as he is read to have been given after the ascension, on the tenth day, to the one hundred and twenty persons. Yet in no work of any person of the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit was the activity of the whole Holy Trinity absent. It was necessary, however, that the Trinity be revealed in such a way that, although there is no difference of substance, the distinction of the persons would nevertheless be commended individually.

[Col. 0297B]

And when he has come, he will convict the world. What does he mean by saying, “When he has come, he will convict the world”? Did Christ, while he was in the world, not convict the world concerning all the matters that follow? But Christ convicted only the Jewish nation, whereas the Holy Spirit, spread through his disciples throughout the whole world, is understood to have convicted not one nation but the entire world. In what does he convict it? In this: that through the Holy Spirit love was poured into their hearts, and love casts out fear, so that they were not afraid to convict the world—that is, lovers of the world.

Concerning sin, and concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment. Christ himself explained this statement, saying: “Concerning sin, because they do not believe in me.” He set the sin of unbelief down as a particular sin. For just as faith is the source of virtues, so [Col. 0297C] persistence in unbelief is the foundation of vices, as the Lord solemnly attests when he says: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God” (John III). He said “judged,” that is, “condemned.”

Concerning righteousness, because I am going to the Father, and you will no longer see me. Christ was the righteousness of the disciples: they believed that the Lord whom they saw as truly human was also truly the Son of God, and they continued to worship him with steadfast love even though they knew that he had been taken from them bodily. The righteousness of the other faithful—that is, of those who did not see the Lord in the flesh—is that they believe and love in their hearts the true God and true human being. By this righteousness, the unbelievers are indeed convicted: [Col. 0297D] they heard the word of life just as the faithful did, yet refused to believe in righteousness. For the wickedness of the evil is shown to be condemnable not only by its own depravity but also by comparison with the righteous.

The Holy Spirit therefore convicts the world concerning sin, because they did not believe in Christ. He also convicts it concerning the righteousness of believers, because they refused to follow the example of those who knew that he had ascended to the Father and would no longer dwell bodily on earth, yet could not by any means be separated from his love. This is what he says: “Because I am going to the Father, and you will no longer see me.” You will not see me after I have ascended as you now see me, surrounded by mortal and tangible flesh; [Col. 0298A] rather, you will see me coming in majesty for judgment and, once judgment has been completed, appearing with the saints in greater glory. It follows:

But concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has been judged. He calls the devil the ruler of the world, because he holds primacy in the hearts of unbelievers, whom he wished to be understood here by the name “world”: people who, in a perverse order, love the world rather than the world’s Creator. He has been judged by the Lord, who said: “I was watching Satan falling like lightning from heaven.” He was judged by him when he himself was casting out demons and giving the disciples power to tread upon every power of the enemy. The world is therefore convicted concerning judgment because the devil was judged, when the archangels were terrified by the example of one condemned for pride, so that human beings might not presume to resist God’s will.

[Col. 0298B]

Let human beings believe in Christ, so that they may not be convicted concerning the sin of their unbelief, by which sin all sins are held captive. Let them pass into the number of the faithful, so that they may not be convicted concerning the righteousness of those whom, though justified, they refuse to imitate. Let them beware of the future judgment, lest they be judged together with the ruler of the world, whom they imitate even though he has been judged. Indeed, lest the hard pride of mortals imagine that it will be spared, it must be terrified by the punishment of the proud angels.

I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth has come, he will teach you all truth. It is certain that, when the Spirit came from above, the apostles obtained far greater knowledge of the truth than they had previously been able to possess in the flesh, and they were inflamed [Col. 0298C] with a much greater desire to contend for the truth. Nevertheless, no one should think that in this life anyone can comprehend all truth. Hence the blessed Apostle Paul himself, who was caught up to the third heaven and heard there secret words that it is not permitted to a human being to speak, says: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part” (I Cor. XIII). “But when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be abolished.” We must therefore understand his statement about the Spirit—“He will teach you all truth”—as though he were saying: “He will spread love in your hearts, and love will make you love all truth.” Taught inwardly by its instruction, may you advance from virtue to virtue and become worthy to reach the life in which the eternal brightness of supreme truth and true sublimity—that is, the contemplation of your Creator [Col. 0298D]—will appear to you.

For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak. The Spirit does not speak from himself but from the Father, for the Son is born from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. He does not speak from himself—that is, without communion with the Father and the Son—for the Holy Spirit is not divided from the Father and the Son; rather, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one work. But whatever he hears he will speak. He will hear through unity of substance and the distinct property of knowledge. He does not speak from himself because he does not exist from himself. For the Father alone is not from another; the Son is begotten from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. The Spirit therefore hears from the one from whom he proceeds, because he is not from himself but from the one from whom he proceeds, from whom he has his essence and understanding, and from that same one also his knowledge. His hearing from him is therefore nothing other than knowledge.

[Col. 0299A]

As for what he added—“And he will announce to you the things that are to come”—it is evident that some of the saints, in the Holy Spirit, foretold future things. But these words of the Lord should be considered more profoundly, since they can apply to all the saints. The Spirit, therefore, announces the things to come when he brings to our memory the joys of our heavenly homeland, when through the gift of his inspiration he makes known to us the festivals of that heavenly city. He announces what is to come when, drawing us away from love of present things, he inflames our hearts and desires with the kingdom promised in heaven.

[Col. 0299B]

He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you. The Spirit glorified Christ because through him such love was kindled in the hearts of the disciples that, casting aside bodily fear, they confidently proclaimed the effect of his resurrection, although shortly before, at the time of his Passion, they had been fearful. Hence it is written: “And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts IV), “and they spoke the word of God with confidence” (Acts II). The Spirit glorified Christ when, filled with spiritual grace, holy teachers performed so many and such great miracles in Christ’s name that they converted the whole world to faith in Christ, and endured so many and such great struggles of suffering for Christ’s name. He glorifies Christ as he spreads brightness in our hearts and inspires love of the eternal homeland.

[Col. 0299C]

Because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you—that is, from my Father. The Holy Spirit receives from the Father because he proceeds from the Father, from whom the Son also is born. He who is born from no one proceeds from no one; the Father alone is such. “All things whatever the Father has are mine”; therefore he said: “Because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.” He spoke of those things that pertain to the Father’s own divinity, in which he is equal to the Father, and in which the Holy Spirit is also equal to the Father and the Son. For the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one substance, one nature, one majesty, one glory, and one eternity; and there is one almighty God, invisible and incomprehensible to every creature: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

## HARMONY

[Col. 0299D]

The harmony of these two readings is established in the name of righteousness and in the gift and sending of the Holy Spirit.

## THE FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

### THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE JAMES, CHAPTER I

> “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves. For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he will be compared to a man looking at the face of his birth in a mirror. For he looked at himself and went away, and immediately forgot what he was like. But whoever has looked intently into the law of perfect freedom and has remained in it, not becoming a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, this person will be blessed in his doing. But if anyone thinks that he is religious [Col. 0300A], not restraining his tongue but deceiving his heart, this person’s religion is vain. Religion pure and undefiled before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their tribulation and to keep oneself undefiled from this world.”

Be doers of the word, and not hearers only. Paul likewise says concerning those who observe the law: “It is not merely the hearers of the law who will be justified before God, but the doers of the law are righteous” (Rom. II). And in the Apocalypse, when John had said, “Blessed is the one who reads, and those who hear the words of the prophecy of this book,” he immediately added: “And keeps the things written in it” (Apoc. I).

For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he will be compared to a man looking at the face of his birth in a mirror, etc. By “the face of his birth” he means the face of infancy, [Col. 0300B] which has not yet reached the maturity of a man. It is the custom of women to look at themselves in mirrors so that, if they notice anything dirty or improperly arranged, they may correct it for the better and take care to please their husbands. In a moral sense, this is fitting for our souls. We ought to look at ourselves in the mirror of the Gospel, or of all the divine Scriptures, and, having laid aside our dirt and adorned the conduct of our souls, strive to please Christ, our true husband.

Whoever has looked intently into the law of perfect freedom and has remained in it. He calls the Gospel the perfect law, for the law brings nothing to perfection. And elsewhere: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the spirit of adoption as sons” (Rom. VIII). And again: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is [Col. 0300C] freedom” (II Cor. III); and the Lord himself says: “If the Son makes you free, you are truly free” (John VIII).

Not becoming a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, etc. Blessedness is prepared not by hearing the word uselessly but by carrying out the work, just as the Lord says when speaking to the disciples: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them” (John XIII).

If anyone thinks he is religious, yet does not bridle his tongue, etc. Above he had admonished them not merely to hear the word of God but also to do it. Now he adds that even if someone appears to practice through his deeds the commandments of the Lord that he has learned, yet if he has not also restrained his tongue from slanders, lies, blasphemies, foolish talk, even from excessive talk itself, and from the other things by which people commonly sin, he boasts in vain of the righteousness of his works. [Col. 0300D] Thus Paul too, approving the general saying of the poet, says: “Bad company corrupts good morals” (I Cor. XV).

Pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father is this. He appropriately added “before God and the Father,” because there are people who seem religious to human beings while they are regarded as profane by God. Hence Solomon also says: “There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end leads to death” (Prov. XIV).

To visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself undefiled from this world. Since he had said that the doer of the work would be blessed in his deed, he now states which deeds especially please God: namely, mercy and innocence. For in commanding that orphans and widows be visited in their affliction, he indicates everything that we ought to do mercifully toward our neighbor. How great this is will be disclosed at the very time of judgment, when the Judge will say: “As often as you did it to one of these my least brothers, you did it to me.” Moreover, in commanding us to keep ourselves undefiled from this world, he shows all the things in which he teaches us to preserve ourselves chaste. Among these are also the matters he had admonished us above to observe: that we should be slow to speak and slow to anger.

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER XVI

“Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you. Until now you have asked nothing in my name; ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be full. I have spoken these things to you in figures. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will announce the Father openly to you. On that day you will ask in my name. And I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf. For the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and believed that I came forth from God. I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father.” His disciples say to him: “Behold, now you are speaking openly, and saying no figure. Now we know that you know all things, and that you have no need for anyone to question you. By this we believe that you came forth from God.”

“Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you. Until now you have asked nothing in my name; ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be full.” (From Bede.) This can be understood in two ways: either that they had not asked in his name because they had not known that name as it ought to be known, or that they had asked for nothing because, in comparison with the things they ought to have asked for, what they had asked for must be regarded as nothing.

“Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be full.” It is as though he said plainly: “Ask the Father not for the fleeting joys of the world, which are always mixed with sorrow and must end in grief, but for that unique joy whose fullness is diminished by no disturbance whatsoever and whose eternity is dissolved by no end. If you persist in asking for such things, then without doubt you will receive what you ask, provided that the conduct of the one asking agrees with his mind.” For it brings little benefit to seek heavenly things by praying well if one does not cease to become entangled in earthly things by living perversely.

“I have spoken these things to you in figures; the hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will announce my Father openly to you.” They were still little children and had not yet been able to understand how the Father was in the Son and the Son in the Father, nor the other matters belonging to the profound mysteries of divinity. Therefore the Lord seemed to speak to them in figures, as though in a riddle; but he promised them an hour in which he would speak openly to them about the Father. He evidently signified that hour in which, after accomplishing his passion and resurrection, he would give them the grace of the Holy Spirit. For then, specially instructed within and kindled with a special love, the more perfectly they grasped everything that mortals had to grasp concerning the knowledge of divinity, the more ardently they took care to ask for and desire only those things that would help them to merit the vision of God.

“On that day you will ask in my name.” That is, you will begin to ask for only those things that seem to pertain to the salvation of your souls and to eternal joys, and especially so that you may understand what it means when I said, “I and the Father are one,” or how the Father is in me and I in the Father. Then those who ask ask in his name because, in the sound of that name, they understand nothing other than the very reality that is called by that name. They can in some fashion consider our Lord Jesus Christ, insofar as he is human, to intercede with the Father for us; but insofar as he is God, to hear us together with the Father. I think he signified this when he said: “And I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf.” For what he says—“I will ask”—can not improperly be understood as referring not to the present but to the future: once the saints have been received into inward peace, there will no longer be any need to ask anything concerning them, since they will be given such great blessedness that nothing greater can exist.

“For the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and believed that I came forth from God.” What he said—“because you have loved me”—must not be understood as though they had first loved Christ, but rather in this way: the Father had preceded them with a gratuitous love and, by loving them, had raised them up to love and believe in the Son. Because they had preserved the love of the Son, once recognized, and faith with a pious and attentive heart, the Father had rewarded them with greater gifts of paternal love. He loves them together with the Son and the Holy Spirit, and judges them worthy of love. The addition, “because you have loved me,” must be understood in the same way: whoever rightly possesses the Son loves him together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. And because the nature of their divinity is inseparable and their gifts of virtue are one and the same, this is what it means that you love and believe that I came forth from God.

“I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father.” He came forth from the Father and came into the world because he appeared visibly to the world in his humanity, though he was invisible with the Father in his divinity. [Col. 0302D] He came forth from the Father because he appeared not in the form in which he is equal to the Father, but in an assumed creaturely form, made lower. And he came into the world because, in the form of a servant that he had assumed, he also presented himself to be seen by the lovers of this world. Again he left the world and returned to the Father because he removed from the sight of the world’s lovers what they had seen and taught his own lovers to believe that he was equal to the Father. He left the world and returned to the Father because through his ascension he brought the humanity he had assumed to the invisible things of the Father’s majesty.

These words of the Lord are indeed mystical and, as he himself testifies, were spoken in figures. But the disciples to whom they were spoken were still so carnal that they understood their depth not at all. They understood neither the hidden meaning of the words nor even their own ignorance, supposing that what had been spoken simply and clearly was plain, whereas to those who did not understand it was a figure. Thus they immediately replied:

“Behold, now you are speaking openly, and saying no figure.” They therefore thought that he was speaking openly, although they were not yet able to comprehend the mysteries of his words. But when they add:

“Now we know that you know all things, and that you have no need for anyone to question you. By this we believe that you came forth from God,” they plainly show that, when the Lord spoke to them, he was chiefly discussing what they enjoyed hearing and what they wanted to ask; anticipating them, he freely brought these matters forth himself. Hence they rightly believe and confess that he knows all things, as God, and that as the Son of God he came from God. For knowing the secrets of thoughts is an evident sign of divinity.

## AGREEMENT

In the name of God the Father, the agreement of these two readings is made.

## AT THE GREATER LITANY

## THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE JAMES, CHAPTER V

“Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, so that you may be saved. For the continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful. Elijah was a human being like us, subject to suffering, and he prayed in prayer that it might not rain upon the earth; and it did not rain for three years and six months. And again he prayed, and the heavens gave rain, and the earth yielded its fruit. But if anyone among you wanders from the truth and someone brings him back, he ought to know that whoever brings a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins.”

“Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, so that you may be saved.” (From Bede.) In this statement there must be this distinction: we should confess our daily and lighter sins to one another, as equals, and believe that they are saved through one another’s daily prayer. But the uncleanness of a more serious leprosy we should disclose to the priest according to the law, and according to his judgment we should take care to be purified in whatever manner and for however long he commands.

“For the continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful. Elijah was a human being like us, subject to suffering, and he prayed in prayer that it might not rain upon the earth; and it did not rain for three years and six months.” He fittingly establishes by an example how powerful the continual prayer of a righteous person is, since Elijah, praying only one prayer, held back the heavens for so long, turned away the rains from the earth, and denied fruits to mortals. Then again, when he wished, when he recognized that the time had come, when he saw that the heart of the proud king and the idolatrous people had been bent toward repentance by the long wasting of famine, he prayed only one prayer, and restored to the earth the fruits and waters that he had denied. Thus it follows:

“And again he prayed, and the heavens gave rain, and the earth yielded its fruit.” Therefore once, both first and later, he prayed—and this was one Elijah—and obtained so much. How much, then, is accomplished by the frequent prayer of many righteous people? [Col. 0304A] But lest our weakness tremble, thinking that it cannot do things like that great prophet who deserved to be carried to heaven in a fiery chariot, the blessed James wisely began his account of Elijah’s prayer in this way: “Elijah was a human being like us, subject to suffering.” He was indeed a human being, although second to no human being in virtue; he was like us in the origin of his flesh, and subject to suffering like us, both in the weakness of mind and of flesh. He showed that he was weak in the flesh by seeking food from the widow of Zarephath. He showed also that he was subject to suffering in mind when, after restoring the waters to the earth and destroying the prophets and priests of the idols, he was terrified by the threats of a single woman and fled through the desert. How great, however, is the merit before God of praying for the weak and, when they confess their sins, restoring them to the health they had lost, is shown by what follows:

“But if anyone among you wanders from the truth and someone brings him back, etc.” Since in the earlier parts of this epistle our tongue is restrained from malicious or idle speech, its conclusion appropriately shows what we ought especially to say. We are therefore commanded to pray and sing psalms to the Lord whenever we are assailed by adversities. Likewise, we are to confess our sins to one another and pray for one another so that we may be saved, devoting as much care as we can to the health of our neighbors—not merely their temporal health, but rather their eternal health. For if it is a great reward to rescue flesh that will eventually die from death, how great will be the merit of freeing from death a soul that will live forever in the heavenly homeland?

It should certainly be noted that some copies read, “he will save his soul from death,” and that from the ambiguous Greek σώσει ψυχὴν ἐκ θανάτου (“he will save a soul from death”) it can be interpreted both in this way and correctly. Indeed, whoever corrects one who is wandering thereby acquires for himself greater joys of heavenly life: “He will save,” it says, “his soul from death.”

“And he covers a multitude of sins.” Whoever turns a sinner back from error both hides his sins from the sight of the inward Judge by the superimposition of a better life, and, by caring for his neighbor, also conceals from the gaze of the One who sees all the errors in which he himself has offended, according to the Psalmist’s saying: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered.” The blessed James does not forget what he said above: “Do not become teachers in great numbers, my brothers.” There he removes those who were imperfect in their own conduct and in the office of teaching because they sought it through boasting. Here, however, he teaches those who are instructed in every respect what they ought to do for the salvation of their neighbors through fraternal love. For what is said here to be done by a teacher is elsewhere said to be done by charity, as the blessed apostle Peter says: “For charity covers a multitude of sins.” Nor should it be passed over that this restoration of one who is wandering is accomplished not only by speaking but very often also by doing good. For if someone, even while his tongue is silent, shows his neighbors examples of good action and turns them toward admirable works of almsgiving, hospitality, or other virtues that they had neglected, he certainly performs the office of a teacher and, for the salvation of the brother whom he has corrected, will receive a sure reward from the merciful Judge.

## ANOTHER EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED JAMES, CHAPTER V

(From Bede.) This James was the son of Alphaeus, and is also called the brother of the Lord. For there were three sisters: the Lord’s mother, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee. This James is said to have been of such great holiness that Josephus says Jerusalem was overthrown on account of his death. After the Lord’s passion, he happily completed his martyrdom in the thirtieth year.

“Confess your sins to one another, and so forth.” (From Cassiodorus.) “To confess” is an ambiguous expression, but it is understood differently according to the circumstances. Those who give thanks to the Lord confess, and those who lament their sins also confess. But the former is in joy, while the latter is in tears; the former is recognized in holy gladness of mind, the latter in contrition of heart.

“For the continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful.” For it is written: “The Lord will hear the prayers of the righteous”; and the Lord himself says: “Whatever you ask in prayer, believing, you will receive.”

“It did not rain for three years, etc.” Here the three ages of the world are signified. The first is from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Moses; the third from Moses to the coming of the Lord, when the Lord Jesus Christ himself came and irrigated the parched soil of our heart with the rain of faith and baptism. By heaven, which gave the rain, teachers are understood; by rain, their spiritual teaching; by earth, the Church is signified; and by fruit, holy virtues are understood. “The heaven,” he says, “gave rain, and the earth yielded its fruit.” The three years and six months of sterility can also signify the barren times under Antichrist, which we believe will afterward become fruitful through the grace of the Lord.

“Whoever brings a sinner back will save his soul.” That is, he will free his soul from eternal death, from the perpetual death due to the soul for its sins.

“And he covers a multitude of sins.” Whether the sins of the one whom he brings back or his own, the one who brings him back covers them through repentance. For the Psalmist says: “Blessed are those whose sins are covered.” By the work of charity he covers his own evil and harmful sins. For the Apostle says: “Charity covers a multitude of sins.”

[Col. 0305D]

## THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER XI

“Which of you will have a friend and go to him at midnight and say to him: ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, because a friend of mine has come to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him.’ And the one inside, answering, will say: ‘Do not trouble me; the door is already shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything.’ And if he persists in knocking, I tell you, even if he will not get up and give him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence he will rise and give him as many as he needs. And I say to you: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened [Col. 0306A] to you. For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. Which of you fathers, if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will he give him a serpent instead of a fish? Or if he asks for an egg, will he offer him a scorpion? If you, then, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him!”

“Which of you has a friend and will go to him at midnight and say to him: ‘Friend, lend me three loaves,’ etc.” The Savior, asked by his disciples, teaches not only the form of prayer but also the persistence and frequency with which one should pray. The friend to whom one comes at midnight is understood to be God himself. In the midst of tribulation we ought to beseech him and earnestly request three loaves—that is, an understanding of the Trinity by which the labors of the present life may be consoled. The friend who comes from a journey is our spirit, which departs from us whenever it wanders outside toward the pursuit of earthly and temporal things. It returns and desires to be refreshed by heavenly nourishment when, having returned to itself, it begins to meditate on things above and spiritual matters. Of this friend the one who had asked beautifully adds that he has nothing to set before him, because, after the darkness of the world, when the soul sighs for God, it wants to think of nothing, speak of nothing, or look upon anything except him. It strives only to contemplate the joy of the highest Trinity and to arrive at a fuller vision of it.

“And the one inside, answering, will say: ‘Do not trouble me; the door is already shut,’ etc.” The friend’s door is the understanding of divine speech, which the Apostle prays may be opened to him so that he may speak the mystery of Christ. It is shut during a famine of the word, when understanding is not given. And those who, distributing evangelical wisdom like bread, preached throughout the world are now the children of the master of the house, in secret rest with the Lord; nevertheless, by praying, one is made able to receive. They desire understanding from God himself, even if no human being is present through whom wisdom may be preached.

“And if he persists in knocking, I tell you, even if he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence he will rise and give him as many as he needs. And I say to you: Ask, and it will be given to you,” etc. This is a comparison from the lesser. If a human friend rises from bed and gives, compelled not by friendship but by annoyance, how much more will God give, who without annoyance most generously bestows what is asked! But he wishes to be asked for this purpose: that those who ask may become capable of his gifts. Therefore, lest the friend who has come from a journey perish from hunger—that is, lest the spirit that has recently recovered from the vanity of its error waste away any longer from lack of spiritual desire—let us ask for the feasts of the word by which it may be nourished; let us seek the friend who gives; let us knock at the door where hidden things are kept. For he has given great hope, and he continues to give it, for he does not deceive by promising.

“For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.” Therefore, in accordance with the preceding parable of the friend who asks, perseverance is necessary, so that we may receive what we ask, find what we seek, and have what we knock for opened. For if something is given to the one who asks, if the seeker finds, and if the door is opened to the one who knocks, it is evident that the person who is not given anything, who finds nothing, and for whom nothing is opened has not asked, sought, or knocked properly.

“Which of you fathers, if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone?” Bread is understood as charity, because of the greater appetite for it. It is also so necessary that without it the other things are nothing, just as without bread a table is empty. Its opposite is hardness of heart, which he compared to a stone.

“Or if he asks for a fish, will he give him a serpent instead of a fish?” The fish is faith in invisible things, either because of the water of baptism or because it is caught from invisible places. Since faith is not broken even when surrounded by the waves of this world’s barking, it is rightly compared to a fish. He set the serpent against it because of the poisons of deceit, which the serpent first sowed in the first human being by giving evil counsel.

[Col. 0307B]

“Or if he asks for an egg, will he offer him a scorpion?” In the egg hope is indicated. An egg is not yet a fully formed offspring, but it is expected as it is warmed. Against it he set the scorpion, whose poisonous sting must be feared from behind, just as the opposite of hope is to look backward, whereas hope stretches toward the things that lie ahead.

“If you, then, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him?” How do evil people give good things? He called them evil as lovers still of this world and sinners. The things they give must be called good according to their judgment, because they regard them as good, although by the nature of things these things are indeed good but temporal and belonging to this weak life. [Col. 0307C] And whoever is evil gives them not from his own possession: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness,” the Lord who made heaven and earth and everything in them. How much, then, should we hope that God will give good things to us when we ask, and that we cannot be deceived into receiving one thing instead of another when we ask him, since even when we are evil we know how to give what is asked of us? We do not deceive our children. And whatever good things we give, we give not from our own resources but from his.

Alternatively: the apostles, who by the merit of their election had surpassed the goodness of the human race, are in every respect called evil in view of the goodness above. For nothing is stable in itself, nothing immutable, nothing good except divinity alone. All creatures, in order to obtain the blessedness of eternity or immutability, attain it not through their own nature but through participation in and grace from their Creator. The statement that “your heavenly Father will give the good Spirit to those who ask him” shows that the Holy Spirit is the fullness of God’s good gifts, and that the things administered by God do not subsist apart from him, because all the benefits received from the grace of God’s gifts flow from this fountain.

## AGREEMENT

In the petition of prayer and in the acceptance of the gift, the agreement of these two readings is made.

## ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

## READING FROM THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, CHAPTER I

“I made the first account, O Theophilus, concerning all the things that Jesus began to do and teach until the day on which, after giving commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up. To them also he presented himself alive after his passion by many proofs, appearing to them for forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God. And while eating with them, he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to await the promise of the Father, which you have heard, he said, from my mouth: ‘For John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.’ Therefore those who had assembled asked him, saying: ‘Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?’ But he said to them: ‘It is not for you to know the times or moments that the Father has established by his own authority, but you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and throughout all Judea and Samaria and to the ends of the earth.’ And when he had said these things, while they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes. And while they were looking toward heaven as he went, behold, two men stood beside them in white clothing, and they said: ‘Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking toward heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.’”

“I made the first account, O Theophilus, concerning all the things that Jesus began to do and teach.” (From Bede.) He says that he wrote in the Gospel about all Christ’s deeds and words—not because he was able to include everything, lest he contradict John, who says: “Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples that are not written in this book” (John, final chapter)—but because he selected from everything what he would make his account about, judging that the things he chose were suitable and sufficiently appropriate to the duty entrusted to him. Theophilus is interpreted as “lover of God” or “loved by God.” Therefore, whoever is a lover of God holds that this was written here for himself, for his own soul; because Luke the physician wrote it, he will find salvation. And it should be noted that he says: “What Jesus began to do and teach.” He says first “to do” and afterward “to teach,” because Jesus is a good teacher who instructs by doing and teaches nothing except what he has done.

“Until the day on which, after giving commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up,” etc. The transposition that disrupts the order of the words should be read as a hyperbaton: “until the day on which he was taken up, giving commands” before his ascension—that is, giving the apostles the commands that are read either here or in the Gospels. The sense, then, is: “I wrote about Jesus from the time when he began to perform signs and teach until the day on which, after completing these things, he returned to the place from which he had come, appearing to them for forty days, speaking about the kingdom of God, and eating with them,” etc.

To instruct the apostles in faith in his resurrection, the Lord repeatedly appeared alive to them after his passion, ate food, and offered for them to touch the same flesh that he had raised from the dead. But in a higher mystery, through this forty-day association with the disciples, he signifies that he will fulfill by his hidden presence what he had promised: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.” This number designates the temporal and earthly life, either because of the four seasons of the year or because of the four winds of heaven. For after we have been buried with Christ through baptism into death, as though we had crossed by the road through the Red Sea, we need the Lord’s guidance in this wilderness to lead us to the heavenly kingdom. By rewarding us with the denarius of his image and the presence of the Holy Spirit, he blesses us with the true rest of the jubilee.

“But you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.” The apostles had not yet been baptized—not with water, however, but with the Holy Spirit. We understand them already to have been baptized, either with John’s baptism, as some think, or, what is more credible, with Christ’s baptism. For the ministry of baptizing had not been lacking, so that he might have baptized servants through whom he could baptize others; nor had the memorable ministry of that humility been lacking when he washed their feet. Therefore, when the Lord said, “John indeed baptized with water,” he by no means added, “But you will baptize,” but rather, “You will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.” For neither the apostles nor their successors, who baptize in the Church to this day, can baptize in any other way than John did—that is, in water. But once the name of Christ has been invoked, the inward power of the Holy Spirit is present; while the human minister supplies the water, that power purifies both the souls and bodies of those baptized. This did not happen in John’s baptism, for the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified (John VIII).

[Col. 0309C]

“Therefore those who had assembled asked him, saying: ‘Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?’” Since he had appeared to them and spoken about the kingdom of God, and had promised that the Holy Spirit would come not many days later, they consequently questioned him about that same kingdom: namely, whether, when the Holy Spirit arrived, they should believe that it would immediately be restored in the present, or that it was reserved for the saints in the future. For the disciples were still carnal and, after Christ’s resurrection had been completed, believed that the kingdom of Israel would come immediately, in accordance with Cleopas’s statement: “But we were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel.” The Evangelist had also said earlier that, when the Lord was about to come to Jerusalem, they thought that the kingdom of God would immediately be revealed.

But the prophecy had to be fulfilled in which the Father is addressed in song: “But you have rejected and despised and delayed your Christ” (Ps. LXXXVIII). The Father rejected and despised the Son when he abandoned him in his passion as he cried: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. XX). He delayed him so that the one whom the saints at that time thought would reign would be awaited as coming in his majesty on the day of judgment. Hence the Lord himself, indicating that both the spiritual Israel and the heavenly kingdom had been promised by the prophets, says:

“It is not for you to know the times or moments that the Father has established by his own authority.” He means that the time of that kingdom is so hidden that it is revealed only to the Father’s knowledge. When he says, “It is not for you to know,” he shows that he himself knows it also, since all that belongs to the Father belongs to him; but it is not expedient for mortals to know, so that, always uncertain about the coming of the Judge, they may live each day as though they were to be judged on the following day.

“But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you,” etc. “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “will come upon you. It will not, as you suppose, bring the kingdom of Israel, or the kingdom of God in Israel, but will grant you power to testify about me. The time of that kingdom is so far off that first not only this city of Jerusalem but all the boundaries of Judea, then the neighboring peoples of Samaria, and finally even the most distant regions around the circuit of the world will be traversed by the fame of the Gospel.”

“And when he had said these things, while they were watching, he was lifted up.” Mark, recalling another saying of the Lord, says: “And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven.” But because Luke more significantly added, “When he had said these things, he was lifted up,” he plainly shows that the Lord ascended into heaven after completing the discourses he had mentioned.

“And a cloud received him from their eyes.” Wherever creation performs service for its Creator, the stars bear witness: at his birth they cover him with cloud; the clouds receive him as he ascends; and they will accompany him when he returns for judgment.

“Behold, two men stood beside them in white clothing.” White clothing is more suited to exaltation than to humiliation. Therefore, when the Lord ascends, angels appear in white clothing; when the Lord was born, they are not said to have appeared in white clothing, because the one who appeared humble as God in his birth was shown exalted as a human being in his ascension. The place also corresponds: the one who was born in a humble little city returned to heaven as a human being from a lofty mountain.

“This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven.” The angels appear for two reasons: namely, to console the sadness of the ascension by recalling his return, and to show that he truly went into heaven, not merely as though into heaven, as Elijah did.

“He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.” That is, he will come to judge in the same form and substance of flesh in which he came to be judged. He gave that flesh immortality; he did not remove its nature. His divine glory also, which once appeared to the three disciples on the mountain, will be seen by all the saints after judgment, when the wicked will be taken away so that he may not see the glory of God.

## THE GOSPEL OF MARK, LAST CHAPTER

“When the eleven disciples were reclining at table, Jesus appeared to them and reproached them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him risen. And he said to them: ‘Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned. These signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them. They will lay hands on the sick, and they will be well.’ And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God. But they went forth and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word through the signs that followed.”

“When the eleven disciples were reclining at table, Jesus appeared to them,” etc. How can this be the final appearance, as though they would not see him afterward? It is the final appearance in which the apostles saw the Lord on earth, when he ascended into heaven. This took place on the fortieth day after his resurrection. Was he then going to reproach them because they had not believed those who had seen him risen, when they themselves had seen him so many times after the resurrection? Let us therefore understand that, after the many manifestations by which he had been present to the disciples for forty days, he appeared to the eleven as they were reclining for the last time—that is, on the fortieth day. And because he was about to ascend from them into heaven, let us understand that on that day he chiefly wished to reproach them for not having believed those who had seen him risen, before they themselves saw him, since after his ascension the Gentiles, who had not seen him, were destined to believe when the apostles preached the Gospel. After that reproach Mark continues:

“And he said to them: ‘Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes,’ etc.” (From Augustine.) Since they were going to preach that whoever did not believe would be condemned, and since that person would not have believed what he had not seen, should not the apostles themselves first have been rebuked because, before they had seen the Lord, they had not believed those to whom the Lord had appeared?

(From Gregory.) But concerning what he said to them—“Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature”—was his Gospel really to be preached to senseless things or brute animals, so that it should be said to the disciples, “Preach to every creature”? Rather, by the name “every creature” every nation of the Gentiles can be understood. For earlier it had been said, “Do not go along the way of the Gentiles” (Matthew 10). But now it is said, “Preach to every creature,” so that the preaching which the Jews had first rejected might then become our assistance, when that people, in its pride, had rejected it as a testimony to its own condemnation.

[Col. 0311D]

“Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved. But whoever does not believe will be condemned.” Perhaps each person says to himself: “I have already believed; I shall be saved.” He speaks truly, if he holds the faith through his works. For true faith is that which, in conduct, does not contradict what the word declares. Hence Paul says of certain false believers: “They profess that they know God, but in their deeds they deny him” (Romans 2). Hence John says: “Whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar.” But since it is said, “Whoever does not believe will be condemned,” what shall we say here about little children, who by reason of their age are not yet able to believe? There is no question concerning adults. In the Church of the Savior, therefore, little children believe through others, just as through others they drew the sins that are remitted to them in baptism.

[Col. 0312A]

“Signs will accompany those who believe: In my name they will cast out demons,” and so forth. Does the fact that we do not perform these signs mean that we do not believe at all? These signs were necessary at the beginning of the Church. For, in order that it might grow in faith, it had to be nourished by miracles, just as when we plant young trees, we pour water over them for as long as it takes to see that they have grown strong in the ground. But once they have taken root, the watering ceases. Hence Paul says: “Tongues are for a sign, not to believers but to unbelievers” (1 Corinthians 14). Or should we consider more subtly these signs and powers that still remain?

The holy Church spiritually performs every day what it then performed bodily through the apostles. For when its priests, through the grace of exorcism, lay hands upon believers and rebuke the evil spirits for dwelling in their minds, what else are they doing but casting out demons? And all the faithful who now abandon the worldly words of their former life and utter the holy mysteries, recounting, as far as they can, the praise and power of their Creator—what else are they doing but speaking in new tongues? When by their good exhortations they remove wickedness from the hearts of others, they take up serpents. And when they hear poisonous suggestions but are not at all drawn into evil action, they drink what is deadly, but it does them no harm. Whenever they see their neighbors weakened in good works, they come to their aid with all their strength and strengthen by the example of their own conduct the lives of those who were faltering in their actions—what else are they doing but laying hands upon the sick so that they may be well? These miracles are greater in proportion as they are more spiritual; they are greater in proportion as through them not bodies but souls are raised up.

“And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken,” and so forth. We must consider what it means that Mark says, “He sits at the right hand of God,” whereas Stephen says, “I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.” What does it mean that Mark testifies that he saw him sitting, while Stephen testifies that he saw him standing? We know that sitting belongs to one who judges, while standing belongs to one who fights or gives assistance. Since, therefore, our Redeemer was taken up into heaven, now judges all things, and will come at the end as judge of all, Mark describes him as sitting after his ascension, because after the glory of his ascension he will be seen as judge. But Stephen, engaged in the struggle of his suffering, saw him standing, because he had him as his helper: so that Stephen might overcome on earth the unbelief of his persecutors, Christ fought for him from heaven by his grace.

[Col. 0312D]

“But they went forth and preached,” and so forth. What should be considered here, what committed to memory, except the command of obedience? Signs followed obedience. A substantial question nevertheless remains: how could the same evangelist have written that the angel said to the women, “Go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he told you,” and yet have reported nowhere afterward in his Gospel that the Lord was seen there by the disciples? We should understand what was said in this way by the angel and by the Lord as a prophetic statement.

For Galilee is interpreted as “migration” or “revelation.” First, according to the meaning “migration,” what else should be understood by “He will go before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he told you,” except that the grace of Christ was to migrate from the people of Israel to the Gentiles? The apostles, preaching the Gospel to them, would in no way have believed unless the Lord himself had first prepared the way in human hearts. This is what we understand by “He will go before you into Galilee.” Their joyful amazement when, with difficulties broken through and overcome, they saw an entrance opened to them in the Lord through the illumination of the faithful is signified by “There you will see him”—that is, you will find his members. There and in those who receive you, you will recognize his living body.

According to the other interpretation, by which Galilee means “revelation,” this should no longer be understood as referring to the form of a servant, but to that form in which he is equal to the Father—the revelation he promised his beloved in John when he said: “I also will love him and will show myself to him.” That will be the revelation, like the true Galilee, when we shall be like him and see him as he is. It will also be the happier migration from this world into that eternity, if we embrace his commandments in such a way that we may deserve to be separated to his right hand. For then those on the left will go into eternal fire, but the righteous into eternal life.

CONCORDANCE

At the Lord’s assumption and ascension, these two readings are brought into concord.

SUNDAY AFTER THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

FIRST EPISTLE OF BLESSED PETER, CHAPTER 4

“Be prudent and vigilant in prayers. Above all, have continual mutual charity among yourselves, because charity covers a multitude of sins. Be hospitable to one another without murmuring. As each has received grace, administer it to one another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God. If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God; if anyone ministers, let him do so as from the strength that God supplies” [Col. 0313D] “so that God may be honored in all things through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

“Be prudent and vigilant in prayers.” In view of the uncertainty of the end, the Lord also commanded us in the Gospel always to pray and keep watch. Speaking of the day of judgment, he says: “Watch, therefore, at all times, praying that you may be counted worthy to escape all these things that are to come and to stand before the Son of Man.” We are rightly commanded to keep watch in prayers, so that when we stand at prayer every carnal and worldly thought may depart, and the mind may think at that time of nothing except what it is praying for. The enemy frequently steals upon us and, subtly deceiving us, turns our prayers away from God, so that we have one thing in our heart and utter another with our voice, whereas God ought to be prayed to not by the sound of the voice but by the sincere intention of the soul.

[Col. 0314A]

“Above all, have continual mutual charity among yourselves.” He rightly adds “continual,” so that we may always be able to love. Yet we cannot always remain vigilant in prayers, because of the weakness of the flesh; nor can we always devote ourselves fully to the virtues that he goes on to mention. Therefore hospitality, teaching, the administration of gifts or of spiritual communion to our neighbors, and other such practices must be carried out both through the service of the body and at appropriate times. But charity itself, by whose prompting these external actions are performed and which presides over the inner person, can always be possessed inwardly, even though it cannot always be displayed publicly.

[Col. 0314B]

“Because charity covers a multitude of sins,” and so forth. This is especially true when one says truthfully to God: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” Certainly, it is established that all the good works we perform can dissolve and cover the faults we have committed. But this is said especially of charity, through which we forgive our neighbors what they owe us, because it is most just before God that, according to the measure of mercy by which we have measured others, he should measure back to us. Conversely, the wise man terrifyingly rebukes the hard-hearted when he says: “Man keeps anger against man, and from God he seeks healing.” Nor should it be doubted that, in the case of one who through charity does whatever he can for the correction of his neighbor—admonishing, reproving, and disciplining him—charity itself covers a multitude of sins.

[Col. 0314C]

“If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God.” That is, let him fear saying or commanding anything contrary to God’s will or contrary to what is clearly commanded in the holy Scriptures, lest he be found to be like a false witness of God, or a sacrilegious person, or one introducing something foreign to the Lord’s teaching, or certainly one suppressing and passing over something pleasing to God. For he himself most explicitly commands the preachers of truth concerning those whom they had instructed for life, saying: “Teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matthew, last chapter). For he commands them to hand on to their hearers all the things he himself commanded—not other things, nor these only in part, but all of them—for observance.

“If anyone ministers, let him do so as from the strength that God supplies.” The more certainly each person knows that he cannot have from himself what he gives, the more humbly should he bestow upon his neighbor every good that he can.

[Col. 0314D]

“So that God may be honored in all things through Jesus Christ.” In accordance with the command of Jesus Christ himself, who says: “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 6). God is therefore honored in our actions when, in everything we do well and according to his will, we attribute it not to our own merits but to his grace. Conversely, the evil things we do we attribute solely to our own wickedness, laziness, or ignorance.

[Col. 0315A]

GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER 15

“When the Paraclete has come, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me. And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning. I have spoken these things to you so that you may not be scandalized. They will exclude you from the synagogues; but the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God. And they will do these things to you because they have not known the Father nor me. But I have spoken these things to you so that, when their hour comes, you may remember that I told you.”

“When the Spirit, the Paraclete, has come, whom I will send to you from my Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father.” In many passages of the holy Gospel we find that, before the coming of the Holy Spirit, the disciples were less capable of understanding the mysteries of divine majesty and less strong in enduring the adversities of human wickedness. But when the Spirit came to them, an increase of divine knowledge was granted along with steadfastness for overcoming the assaults of human persecution.

Therefore he promised that they would be strengthened by the coming of the Holy Spirit, either for confidence in preaching or for steadfastness in suffering. We know that this happened in the very leader of the apostles: previously, at the voice of a single maidservant, he was afraid to confess Christ, but afterward, strengthened by the Holy Spirit, he preached him openly and more steadfastly than all the others to many thousands of Jews. We read that three thousand men believed and were baptized at his preaching, and that not long afterward even five thousand believed.

When he says, “who proceeds from the Father,” and immediately adds, “whom I will send,” he signifies that the same Holy Spirit proceeds equally from the Father and the Son and is equally sent by the Father and the Son. But, because of the distinction of the persons, he is here said to proceed from the Father and to be sent by the Son; and within that same distinction of persons, he declares that the Spirit’s operation and will are one with the Father’s will. He also comes of his own accord, being equal to the Father and the Son, so that it may be understood that the will and operation of the Holy Trinity are one.

[Col. 0315D]

“He,” he says, “will bear witness concerning me, and you will bear witness.” What they had received inwardly through the Spirit’s teaching, they carried out outwardly by speaking and ministering to others after casting away fear. For the Spirit himself both illumined their hearts for knowledge of the truth and raised them to the height of truth so that they might teach what they knew.

“When the Paraclete has come, he will bear witness concerning me.” It is as though he were saying: “They hated and killed those whom they saw, but the Paraclete will bear such witness concerning me that he will make them believe in me without seeing.”

“And you,” he says, “will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.” The Holy Spirit will bear witness, and you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning. You can preach what you know; but, since you are not doing so now, the fullness of that Spirit is not yet present in you.

[Col. 0316A]

“I have spoken these things to you so that you may not be scandalized. They will exclude you from the synagogues.” The merciful teacher took care to foretell to the disciples the future battles with wicked people, so that the coming of these events might trouble them less. Adversities that are foreknown are usually endured more lightly than those that suddenly come upon people unexpectedly, as it is written in secular literature: “Often sudden accidents are accustomed to weary even the bravest soldiers in battle.”

“But the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God.” The Jews thought that they were offering service to God by pursuing the ministers of the New Testament with hatred and death. But, as the Apostle testifies concerning them, “they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.” The zealots for the Law therefore think that they are offering service to God when they inflict death on the heralds of grace, but in vain. They defend the Law given through a servant, while they refuse to accept the grace offered by the Son himself. They vainly imagine that they please God the Father while striving to despise, and even to persecute and blaspheme, the Son of God.

He said that two things would come upon them from the Jews: namely, that they would exclude them from the synagogue and that they would kill them. These events would contribute to the accumulation of that people’s condemnation and would advance the salvation of the Gentiles, just as Paul said to those Jews in the Acts of the Apostles: “Since you have judged yourselves unworthy of the word of God, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13).

For thus the Lord commanded us: “Behold, I have given you as a light to the Gentiles, so that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth” (Isaiah 49). It follows:

[Col. 0316C]

“And they will do these things because they have not known me nor my Father.” Since the Son is in the Father and the Father is in the Son, and whoever sees the Son also sees the Father, it is plainly evident that all who obstinately reject faith in the Son are proved not to know the Father either.

“But I have spoken these things to you so that, when their hour comes, you may remember,” and so forth. It is a great consolation for the disciples to remember that their teacher had foretold what they would suffer, so that they might know that they had the same one as their helper and rewarder, in whose name they had been told that they would suffer such things.

[Col. 0316D]

“I did not tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you.” What are the things he did not tell them from the beginning—also concerning the Holy Spirit, whom he was to send to them from the Father, and concerning the consolation and strengthening of that same Spirit, by which they would be consoled and strengthened? He did not tell them these things from the beginning because, since he was with them, they ought not to have feared in a free spirit all the adversities of the world or the scandals and persecutions of the Jews. “I did not tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you,” because his presence consoled them.

CONCORDANCE

These two readings are brought into concord in the duty of charity.

ON THE SATURDAY OF PENTECOST

READING FROM THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, CHAPTER 19

“When Apollo was at Corinth, it happened that Paul, having passed through the upper regions, came to Ephesus and found certain disciples. He said to them: ‘Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?’ But they said: ‘We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.’ He said: ‘In what, then, were you baptized?’ They said: ‘In John’s baptism.’ Paul then said: ‘John baptized with a baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, in Jesus.’ When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied. There were about twelve men in all. Entering the synagogue, he spoke boldly for three months, disputing and persuading them concerning the kingdom of God.”

“When Apollo was at Corinth, it happened that Paul, having passed through the upper regions, came to Ephesus and found certain disciples. He said to them: ‘Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?’ But they said,” and so forth. (From Bede.)

Since the rule of the Church is that the faithful are baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, the question arises how Luke, throughout the whole text of this little book, testifies that baptism was given only in the name of Jesus Christ. Blessed Ambrose resolves this by saying that the mystery is fulfilled through the unity of the name. Whether you say “Christ,” and thereby designate God the Father, by whom the Son was anointed, and the Son himself, who was anointed, and the Spirit with which he was anointed—for it is written: “Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit”—or whether you say “Father,” you have likewise indicated his Son and the Spirit of his mouth, provided that you also comprehend this in your heart. Or whether you say “Spirit,” you have indicated God the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds, and the Son, since you have named both the Son and the Spirit, so that authority may be joined to reason.

Scripture also indicates that one may rightly be baptized in the Spirit, when the Lord says: “But you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit,” just as the Apostle says: “For we were all baptized in one Spirit into one body.” It is especially fitting, in another sense, that we should be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, because, as the Apostle says: “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death,” and so forth (Romans 6).

[Col. 0317D]

For all who came to the apostles to be baptized as believers were instructed and taught by them. After being instructed and taught concerning the sacrament of baptism and the other rules of faith, they received the most holy mystery of baptism.

“Catechumen” is interpreted as “one who hears” or “one who is instructed.” The human race hears and is instructed before it comes to baptism. What it had once heard through Moses—“Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy 6)—and what it was instructed in through the Law and the Prophets, namely, the worship of the one true God, it now receives through the ministry of priests, so that, becoming one who hears, it may be able to be instructed and, abandoning the rite by which it served creatures, may serve God the Creator alone.

On their faces, moreover, the sign of the cross is made by the priest through exsufflation, so that the devil may be driven away and a way prepared for Christ.

[Col. 0318A]

The devil, who through his enticing persuasion had dwelt in the human race, which at its beginning had received the breath of life, is compelled by Christ’s power and by the most sacred sign, through the ministry of priests, to depart. Christ is also read to have breathed upon his disciples and rebuked unclean spirits. Hence that same evil spirit is exorcised, so that he may leave and withdraw from the creature whom he had long possessed through the sin of the first man.

And because, according to the Apostle, there is no agreement between Christ and Belial, nor any fellowship between light and darkness, let darkness go out and let Christ, the true light, enter. Moreover, exorcism is a word of rebuke or adjuration. Hence exorcists are also read to have existed in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 19), and the holy Church includes the ministry of exorcists among its ecclesiastical orders.

[Col. 0318B]

For it must be known that, since exorcism is performed, the one who is undoubtedly exorcised is he who is contrary to baptism, to the salvation of the faithful, and to every virtue. Once he has been exorcised or expelled, the seasoning of the divine word is given to believers. Therefore those who are to be baptized receive salt in the sacrament, so that by its taste they may receive the seasoning of wisdom, may not lose the savor of Christ, and may not become tasteless and foolish.

After exorcism and exsufflation comes the handing over of the Creed. The word “symbol,” Greek σύμβολον (*symbolon*), is interpreted in Latin as “indication,” “sign,” or “contribution.” It is an “indication” because through it the integrity of the faith is indicated. It is a “sign” because, when it is rightly retained and understood, the faithful are distinguished from unbelievers. It is a “contribution” because in it the apostles contributed the whole integrity of the faith.

[Col. 0318C]

What all of them retained in their hearts with equal sincerity of faith, they confessed with their mouths; and, each contributing his own formulation, they produced the symbol—that is, the complete contribution of the faith. As they were about to depart from one another, they established together the standard of future preaching, lest, departing from one another geographically, they should preach anything different or discordant. It was most fitting and useful that those who had one soul and one heart in the Lord, whom the breath of the Holy Spirit enlivened and whom the confession of one faith adorned, should be united in this way. For those bound together by the bond of one faith could neither be divided nor ought to be divided in any respect.

The faith contained in this Creed must be understood by those who are to be baptized in such a way that they believe in God the almighty Father, creator of all visible and invisible things, who alone is not from another. For this reason alone he is called “unbegotten.” They must believe in Jesus Christ, his Son, through whom all things were made, true God and the true only-begotten Son of God—not made or adopted, but begotten, of one substance with the Father, and in every respect so equal to God the Father that he cannot be inferior in time, rank, or power. They must believe that he who was begotten is as great as he who begot him.

They must also believe that he was born of the Holy Spirit and Mary ever-virgin—that is, that, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, the same Son of God assumed a true body from the Virgin, so that he who was the Son of God the Father in divinity became, in humanity, the son of a human mother.

[Col. 0319A]

They must also believe that, in the last age, he descended from the Father for the redemption of the world, although he never ceased to be with the Father; that he became truly human so that, as man, he might free the human race; and that he who, without beginning, possesses eternity with the Father and the Holy Spirit assumed, at the end of the ages, a complete human being of our nature, so that the Word became flesh by assuming humanity, not by changing his divinity.

They must also believe that he endured suffering and death—not through the power of divinity, but in the weakness of humanity—that he died by a true death of the flesh, rose again through a true resurrection of the flesh, and by his resurrection bestowed upon us the hope of resurrection. This means that, just as he rose alive from the dead on the third day, so we too shall rise at the end of the ages in the same flesh in which we now live.

[Col. 0319B]

They must also believe that he ascended into heaven in the same body that he assumed from the Virgin, in which he endured suffering and rose again; that he is now in that same body; and that in it he will come for judgment. When all have been raised, he will give to some the sentence of eternal punishment for their sins and to others the reward of eternal blessedness for the merits of their righteousness.

They must also believe in the Holy Spirit, true God, proceeding from the Father and the Son, equal in every respect to the Father and the Son in will, power, eternity, and substance; and that in this holy Trinity there are no ranks by which anyone can be called superior or inferior.

They must also believe that there is a holy catholic Church—that is, a universal Church—not believe in the holy Church; rather, believing in the Trinity, they must believe that the holy Church is a gift of that same holy Trinity. Those who depart from communion with it are called schismatics and heretics and are punished with eternal damnation. Those who remain in its communion are both members of Christ and receive remission of sins and belong to eternal life.

[Col. 0319C]

Since little children, therefore, do not yet possess the use of reason and cannot understand these things, when they reach an age capable of understanding, they must be taught both the mysteries of the faith and the mysteries of their confession; they must truly believe and carefully guard their confession.

We have plainly said that, although they cannot yet speak, those who receive them from the laver of the font confess and speak for them. Nor is it without reason that it is fitting for those who are liable to the sins of others also, through the confession of others and by the ministry of baptism, to receive remission of original sins.

[Col. 0319D]

The nostrils and ears are therefore touched with spittle, and *Ephphatha* is said. The nostrils are touched so that they may follow Christ in the fragrance of perfumes and say, “Draw me after you; we will run” (Song I), and with the Apostle confess, saying, “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (II Cor. I), and become members of him to whom it is said: “And the fragrance of his garments is above all aromatics.” The ears also are touched, so that, hearing the words of God and doing them, they may resemble, according to the Gospel, the wise man who built his house upon a rock (Matt. VII), and that with spiritual hearing they may always listen to spiritual things, so that they may be able to say with David: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (Ps. LXXXIV). And with Isaiah: “The Lord God opened an ear for me, but I did not resist” (Isa. L). “I did not turn back,” so that, hearing spiritually the things spoken spiritually, they may attain the benefits of spiritual works.
