Since, therefore, the divinity, in assuming humanity, made a kind of salve from the union of the two substances in the one person of the Son of God, by which it might enlighten the human race, which had been born blind from its first parents, the ears and nostrils are rightly touched with spittle. For he who, by spitting, had touched the tongue of the mute, had made mud with spittle, and had opened the eyes of the man born blind, now, through the ministry of priests, grants spiritual hearing to those who are to be baptized, gives them the capacity to speak rightly—that is, to confess the true faith—and opens their nostrils, so that they may receive the good fragrance of Christ.

The breast of the one who is baptized must always be filled with the nectar of divine fragrance and be anointed with spiritual unction. Hence the breast and shoulders of those who are to be baptized are also touched with oil, so that, smeared with the unction of that holy oil—that is, of the Spirit—of which the Apostle says, “His anointing teaches you about everything” (I John II), they may be protected in front and behind; that is, they may be watchful against all things, whether prosperous or adverse, and, in imitation of the heavenly creatures, be full of eyes before and behind—that is, looking toward the past and the future—and not lose custody of their salvation.

Their breast is touched so that they may be able to say with David: “And his mercy will go before me” (Ps. LVIII). Their shoulders are touched so that with the same David they may say: “And his mercy will follow me”: that is, the things before them, so that they may will what is good; the things behind them, so that they may not will in vain.

Under the name of the heart, the mind is often signified, as in the saying: “With my whole heart I have sought you” (Ps. CXVIII). Under the name of oil is understood the anointing of the Holy Spirit, or works of light and mercy. The place of the heart is fortified on both sides by anointing—that is, in front and behind—so that the Christian’s mind may everywhere abound both in the richness of the Holy Spirit and in works of light and mercy.

It abounds well in these things if, by renouncing the devil and his works, it rejects his dominion, and if, through the anointing of that oil, the yoke that weighed upon it becomes rotten, so that the prophetic saying may be fulfilled: “The yoke will rot before the oil” (Isa. X). For *to renounce* is commonly used for *to despise*, *to cast out*, *to resist*, or anything else that can be expressed by this word in that sense.

This renunciation is rightly followed by the confession of the Holy Trinity: “So that where sin abounded, grace might abound all the more” (Rom. V). The faithful renounce Satan, who is also called the devil, so that they may serve the Lord Savior more freely, because, according to the same Lord’s saying, “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. VI).

They also renounce his works, because his works are opposed to the works of the Savior. On earth they likewise renounce his pomps, which are certainly Satan’s works, but which seem to be distinguished from his other works by the fact that in them pride is represented in a particular way—pride of which he is the author and by which he was cast down. His pomps, therefore, are ambition, arrogance, vainglory, and other things of this kind, which are known to proceed from the fountain of pride.

The baptismal font likewise bears the likeness of Christ’s tomb, which is said to have been new, because whoever is buried with Christ in it and rises with him must, according to the same Apostle, walk in newness of life. The font has six steps: three in the descent and three in the ascent, which seem to signify three nights and three days. Baptism is not repeated for this reason: Christ also dies no more than once. Sins committed after baptism are wiped away by the tears of repentance, almsgiving, and the other offerings of good works, not by repeating baptism.

Meanwhile, when the Lord’s body is to be buried, the purest linens and spices are used. Likewise, the one who desires to be buried with Christ, if his age already permits it, although he is dead through original sin—which he still bears—must nevertheless burn with the offering of good works and be clothed in clean garments. Concerning these the prophet prays that priests may be clothed when he says: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. CXXXI).

Since, therefore, everything in the rite of baptism breathes of mysteries and overflows with sacraments, it was fitting that the new human being should receive new garments and, cleansed from the filth of the old guilt, be clothed in the brightness of white garments. For Moses first washed Aaron and his sons with water and afterward clothed them in linen garments. Our true Moses, who frees the people from Egyptian slavery—that is, from the error of paganism—and who is the mediator between God and humanity, purifies us with the ineffable water of his sacrament and adorns us with the garments of good works.

The heads of the baptized are therefore anointed with chrism, so that, anointed for the kingdom and priesthood of the Church, they may receive the prerogative of the Christian name and become members of him who redeemed them and is their head. The heads of those who are regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit are therefore covered with a mystical veil, so that what Peter says may be addressed to them: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession” (I Pet. II). By this veil both the royal diadem and the covering of the priestly head are signified.

And since the head often signifies the mind in sacred Scripture, according to the saying, “Lift up your heads” (Luke XXI), the minds of the reborn must possess the ornaments of royal dignity and the coverings of the priestly crown. Thus they may be fortified against vices by a priestly covering, spiritually adorned with the jewels of virtues, and anointed with the sacred chrism. Through these also the Spirit of sevenfold grace is granted by the anointing of chrism, so that they may deserve to become not merely the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, who is of one substance with the Father and the Son, but the dwelling place of the entire Holy Trinity.

The Paraclete Spirit is also called the Spirit of sevenfold grace because of the mystery of the number seven, in which complete perfection is understood. For seven is composed of the whole of the first even number and the whole of the first odd number: of the whole first even number, which can be divided, and of the whole first odd number, which cannot be divided. In the number three there is the mystery of the Trinity; in the number four, that of the Gospel. For whether three is multiplied by four or four by three, the number twelve is reached, because the mystery of the Holy Trinity and the teaching of the Gospel were spread through the twelve apostles into the four regions of the world: east and west, north and south.

This Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, the same Lord granted to the apostles and, through the ministry of the apostles and their successors, to his holy Church. Although his gifts proceed from the fountain of one Spirit, they seem in some way to possess distinct properties.

For it is one thing to have wisdom and another to have understanding, since many indeed have wisdom concerning eternal things but are entirely unable to understand them. Wisdom therefore fills the mind in which it dwells with hope and certainty concerning eternal things. Understanding, because it penetrates hidden matters, illuminates, by restoring it, the heart that it has touched. Counsel, by preventing someone from acting rashly, fills the mind with reason. Fortitude, when it does not fear adversity, gives confidence to the trembling mind. Knowledge, when it drives away ignorance, enlightens with its light the one whom it has filled. Piety allows the one whom it has filled to abound in works of mercy. Fear, while restraining the mind lest it become proud of present things, strengthens it concerning the future by restoring hope.

Thus these virtues support one another by a kind of mutual assistance, so that, while one gives aid to another, the order and condition of life may be most suitably arranged. Wisdom is lesser if it lacks understanding. Understanding is very useless if it does not rest upon wisdom. For when it penetrates higher things without the weight of wisdom, its lightness raises it only to make it fall more heavily.

Counsel is worthless when it lacks the strength of fortitude, because what it discovers through deliberation, being without power, it cannot bring to completion in action. Fortitude is also greatly weakened unless it is supported by counsel, because the more it sees that it can accomplish, the more disastrously virtue rushes headlong without the moderation of reason.

There is no knowledge if it does not possess the usefulness of piety, because when it neglects to carry out the good things it has learned, it binds itself more tightly for judgment. Piety is also very useless if it lacks the discernment of knowledge, because, when no knowledge enlightens it, it does not know how to show mercy.

Fear itself, unless it also possesses these virtues, certainly rises to no good work, because, while it trembles at everything, through fear of itself it remains sluggish and idle in good works.

It must therefore be observed with the greatest care, and the help of the Holy Spirit himself must be implored: that wisdom may not exalt us; that understanding, while running subtly, may not go astray; that counsel, while multiplying itself, may not confuse us; that fortitude, while giving confidence, may not precipitate us; that knowledge, while knowing but not loving, may not puff us up; that piety, while inclining beyond what is right, may not twist us; and that fear, while trembling more than is just, may not plunge us into the pit of despair.

“And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied. They were about twelve men in all,” etc.

The question is frequently debated whether those who, perhaps through ignorance, had not been baptized, but had nevertheless been baptized by some persons of the right faith, ought to be baptized again. I think that this question is explained in this chapter. For what difference is there between someone’s being baptized then, before the beginning of Christ’s baptism, and being baptized now without succession from that same baptism, when John himself, although he had baptized those who believed in the faith and name of Christ who was to come, proclaimed that they had to be baptized again, saying: “I baptize you with water, but he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit”?

Yet the judgments of the Lord are a great abyss. Behold, Asia, recently unworthy even of the apostles’ visitation, has now been exalted both by the sacred apostolic number and by the prophetic gift. It should be noted that the Holy Spirit here, among the twelve disciples, and above, among the one hundred and twenty—which is the number twelve multiplied by ten—displayed signs of his coming: the former in Jerusalem, the latter in Ephesus, which is a city of the Greeks. I believe this was done to show that, whether someone believes from the Jews or from the Gentiles, the Spirit fills only those who share in the unity of the catholic and apostolic Church.

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER XIV

“If you love me, keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you for ever: the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it has not seen him and does not know him. But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you. I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you. Yet a little while, and the world no longer sees me. But you see me, because I live and you shall live. On that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you. Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, that one is the one who loves me. But whoever loves me will be loved by my Father; and I will love him and manifest myself to him.”

“If you love me, keep my commandments.” What does it mean that the Paraclete Spirit is to be given to those who love God and keep his commandments, when God cannot be loved and his commandments cannot be kept except through the Holy Spirit? It means nothing other than that one who loves God through the Holy Spirit deserves, by loving, to have more; and, by having more, to love more. *Paraclete* is interpreted “Consoler,” and the Holy Spirit is rightly called the Paraclete, because he raises and refreshes the hearts of the faithful with desires for heavenly life, lest they fail amid the adversities of this age.

“And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete.” Thus showing that he himself is a Paraclete. They had previously had a Paraclete, namely the Lord himself dwelling with them in the flesh; by both the sweetness of miracles and the aid of preaching they were customarily raised and strengthened, lest they be scandalized by the persecution of unbelievers. He said “I will ask” with reference to his humanity, though by his divinity he gives together with the Father.

“That he may remain with you for ever.” For he remains for ever with the saints: in this life he continually enlightens them invisibly within, and in the life to come he introduces them eternally to contemplate the form of his majesty.

“The Spirit of truth, whom this world cannot receive, because it has not seen him and does not know him.” By “world” he means people devoted to the love of this world. The world—that is, worldly people—cannot receive him, because they do not possess the invisible eyes of charity, by which alone the Holy Spirit can be seen, known, and understood by being known.

“But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.” He will be in you so that he may remain for ever. Before the Passion, unbelievers too saw the Lord Savior in the flesh; but that he was the Son of God, and that the Paraclete had been sent into the world by the Lord, only believers could know. The unbelievers could neither see the Holy Spirit with their eyes nor know him with their minds, because he did not appear to the disciples clothed in humanity. Rather, he chose to come to them and remain with them in such a way as to consecrate within their hearts a dwelling most pleasing to himself. This is what he says: “But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.” He who remains invisibly in this life with the elect visibly displays to them the grace of his knowledge.

“I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you.” To unbelievers it seemed that, by dying on the cross, the Lord would leave his disciples orphans. But he did not leave them orphans: after his Passion he showed himself alive to them by many proofs for forty days, and ten days after his Ascension bestowed on them from heaven the chrism of the Holy Spirit. No one who recognizes that the nature of the holy Trinity is inseparable in power and operation can doubt that Christ himself came to them there.

“Yet a little while, and the world will no longer see me.” It was a little while until the time when the Passion was completed, after which the reprobate were unable to see him. For only the righteous, who had been saddened by his death, deserved to see the joy of his resurrection.

“But you see me, because I live and you shall live.” What is meant by “Because I live, and you shall live”? Why did he say that he himself lives in the present, but that they would live in the future, except that he promised them the life of the flesh that would surely rise again, such as was first shown in himself? Since his resurrection was soon to occur, he used the present tense to signify its swiftness; but because theirs is deferred to the end of the age, he did not say “you live,” but “you shall live.” Thus, in two words, one present and one future, he elegantly and briefly promised two resurrections: his own, soon to come, and ours, to follow at the end of the age.

“On that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me,” etc. On what day, unless it is the day of which he said, “and you shall live”? The apostles knew that Christ was then in the Father through the unity of indivisible divinity; they knew that they were in Christ through acceptance of faith and his sacraments. They knew that, in order truly to live, Christ was in the Father and Christ was in them through love and the observance of his commandments. The holy Church of God also knows this, but far better and more fully on that day of which he said, “and you shall live,” the day on which they begin truly to live—that is, the day of resurrection—when they know all that ought to be known more perfectly because they behold, without end and more nearly, the very fountain of knowledge. To promise this blessedness to all, and not only to the apostles, he immediately added:

“Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, that one is the one who loves me. But whoever loves me will be loved by my Father; and I will love him and manifest myself to him.” Here it must be considered with every care that truly to love Christ is not merely ambiguously to confess love itself with the lips, but to keep in action Christ’s commandments, which we possess by learning. “Whoever has my commandments,” he says, “and keeps them, that one is the one who loves me”: whoever has them in memory and keeps them in life; has them in speech and keeps them in conduct; has them by hearing and keeps them by doing; or has them by doing and keeps them by persevering—that one, he says, is the one who loves me. Notice that, having said in the present tense, “whoever loves me,” he added in the future, “will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.” For even now the Son loves his lovers together with the Father, but now he loves them so that they may live rightly by the faith that works through love. Then he will love them so that they may attain the vision of truth which they had tasted through faith. Nor did he add without reason, “and I will manifest myself to him.” He will manifest himself in his humanity to all at the judgment; but to the righteous and holy alone he will manifest, for eternal blessedness, the glory of his divinity, in which he is equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit.

## CONCORD

The concord of these two readings consists in the reception and gift of the Holy Spirit.

## PENTECOST SUNDAY

### READING FROM THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, CHAPTER II

“While the days of Pentecost were being fulfilled, all the disciples were together in one place. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a violent wind coming, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And divided tongues, as of fire, appeared to them, and one rested upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in different tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance. Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. When this sound occurred, the multitude assembled and was bewildered, because each one heard them speaking in his own language. They were all astonished and wondered, saying: ‘Behold, are not all these who speak Galileans? And how have we each heard our own language, in which we were born? Parthians and Medes and Elamites, and those who dwell in Mesopotamia, Judaea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya around Cyrene, and Roman visitors, Jews also and proselytes, Cretans and Arabs—we hear them speaking in our own languages the mighty works of God.’”

“While the days of Pentecost were being fulfilled, all the disciples were together in one place.” (From Bede.) This was in the upper room, to which they are related above to have ascended. Whoever desires to be filled with the Holy Spirit must necessarily transcend the dwelling of the flesh by contemplation of the mind. As the forty days during which the Lord conversed with the disciples after the resurrection signify the Church of this pilgrimage with the risen Christ, so the fiftieth day, on which the Holy Spirit is received, fittingly expresses the perfection of blessed rest, in which the temporal labor of the Church will be rewarded with the eternal denarius. For the number forty itself, when its aliquot parts are reckoned, adds up to the denarius and makes fifty. Half of forty is twenty; its fourth part, ten; its fifth, eight; its eighth, five; its tenth, four; its twentieth, two; its fortieth, one. And twenty, ten, eight, five, four, two, and one make fifty. The figure of this calculation is very plain: the present conflict secretly produces for us the everlasting joy of jubilee, as the Apostle says: “For our present momentary and light tribulation works in us beyond measure unto the height an eternal weight of glory.” But our true blessedness is that, glorying in the immortality of body and soul, we should be satisfied by the eternal vision of the supreme and blessed Trinity. For our body consists of four well-known qualities; and in the inward person we are commanded to love God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind. This is the denarius of perfect life: to rejoice in the present vision of divine glory.

Yet it should be noted, according to the historical sense, that among the ancients the days of Pentecost—that is, the fiftieth day, on which the Law was given—were reckoned from the slaying of the lamb. Here, however, it is reckoned not from the Lord’s Passion but, as blessed Augustine says, from the day on which the Holy Spirit was sent. By his coming, returning in the pattern of the ancient sign, he most plainly consecrated the Lord’s Day to himself. At this point in time he also showed that the true Pascha should be celebrated on the Lord’s Day. For as here, so there God appeared in a vision of fire, as Exodus says: “And all Mount Sinai smoked because the Lord had descended upon it in fire.”

“And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a violent wind coming,” etc. The Lord appeared through fire, as blessed Pope Gregory expounds, but inwardly he effected speech through himself. Neither was the fire God nor was that sound God; rather, by what he displayed outwardly he expressed what he effected inwardly. For he who inwardly made the disciples fervent with zeal and instructed by the word showed fiery tongues outwardly. Thus the elements were applied as signs, so that their bodies might perceive fire and sound, while their hearts were instructed by invisible fire and a soundless voice.

“And divided tongues appeared to them,” etc. The Holy Spirit appeared in fire and tongues because he makes all whom he fills both fervent and speaking: fervent from himself and speaking about himself. At the same time he indicated that the holy Church, spread throughout the ends of the world, was to speak in the voices of all nations.

“And one rested upon each of them.” That he is said to have rested is an indication of royal power, or certainly because rest is indicated in the saints.

“And they began to speak in other tongues.” The humility of the Church gathers again the unity of tongues which the pride of Babylon had scattered. Spiritually, the variety of tongues signifies the gifts of diverse graces. Nor is it unfittingly understood that the Holy Spirit first gave to human beings the gift of tongues, by which human wisdom is both learned and taught outwardly, so that he might show how easily he can make people wise through the wisdom of God that is inward to them.

“Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men,” etc. I think it fitting to inquire who these were, and from what captivity they were Jews, since the captivity in Egypt or Babylon had already been ended. The Romans had not yet come for captivity, although it too was already impending as the avenger of the sin committed against the Savior. It remains, therefore, to understand the captivity that occurred under Antiochus, which had happened not many years before.

“Because each one heard them speaking in his own language.” It is asked here, since each one heard them speaking the mighty works of God in his own language, whether those who spoke used the various languages of each individual, so that each of them now spoke in this language and now in another and thus passed through them all; or whether the wonder rather consisted in this: that whatever language the speech of those speaking had been uttered in, it was understood by each hearer in his own language. For example, when any one apostle was speaking in the Church, the rest necessarily being silent, one had to speak and one speech had to reach the hearing of all; that same speech possessed this power in itself, that, although the hearers were from diverse nations, each received the sound and grasped the meaning of that one speech which had been uttered by the apostle according to his own language—unless perhaps the miracle seemed more to be heard in this way than spoken.

“They were all astonished and wondered, saying: ‘Behold, are not all these who speak Galileans? And how have we each heard our own language, in which we were born? Parthians and Medes and Elamites, and those who dwell in Mesopotamia and Judaea and Cappadocia?’” Here “Judaea” does not signify the whole nation, but a part of it, namely the tribe of Judah and Benjamin, in distinction from Samaria, Galilee, Decapolis, and the other districts in the same province. Although they all spoke one Hebrew language, each nevertheless had its own distinct manner of speaking. Hence Peter, at the Lord’s Passion, was betrayed as a Galilean by his speech.

“Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya around Cyrene, and Roman visitors, Jews also and proselytes,” etc. They called *proselytes*, that is, newcomers, those who, though deriving their origin from the Gentiles, preferred to choose circumcision and Judaism, as Achior is related to have done in the book of Judith (Judith XIV). Therefore, they say, not only those who were Jews by nature had assembled from the diverse world, but also those born from the uncircumcision who had attached themselves to their law.

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER XIV

“If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him. He who does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me. I have spoken these things to you while remaining with you. But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything and remind you of everything that I have said to you. I leave you peace; I give you my peace. I do not give it as the world gives. Let not your heart be troubled or afraid. You have heard that I said to you, ‘I am going away, and I am coming to you.’ If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I. And now I have told you before it happens, so that, when it has happened, you may believe. I will no longer speak much with you. For the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me; but this is so that the world may know that I love the Father, and that, just as the Father commanded me, so I do.”

“If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.”

The proof of love, therefore, is the display of works. Hence the same John says in his Epistle: “Whoever says, ‘I love God,’ and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (I John III). We truly love God if we observe his commandments and restrain ourselves from our own pleasures. “And my Father will love him,” because the works that the Father does, the Son likewise does; whoever loves the Son also loves the Father, and whoever is loved by the Son is loved by the Father.

“And we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.” For to the one who truly loves God, and does not withdraw from the love of God even in the time of temptation, the Father and the Son come by a spiritual approach and have their dwelling with him. For that person truly loves whose mind is not overcome by wrongful pleasure through consent. Everyone is separated from heavenly love in proportion as he delights in lower things.

Love distinguishes the saints from the world. It makes them dwell together in one house; in that house the Father and the Son make their dwelling, for they also grant love itself. At the end they grant them their manifestation as well, concerning which a disciple asked and learned that one reaches this manifestation through love.

“He who does not love me does not keep my words.” These are the people who never see the Father and the Holy Spirit, but see the Son for a brief time—not so that they may be blessed, but so that they may be judged. They do not see him in the form of God, where he is, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, equally invisible, but in the form of a human being, in which he wished to be present to the world: contemptible in suffering, terrifying in judgment.

“And the word that you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me.”

Why did he first say “words” in the plural, but now “word” in the singular? Perhaps there he indicated the words of preaching, while here he indicated himself, who is the Father’s Word. Therefore he said that it was not his own, since he is not from himself but from the Father—just as he is not his own image but the Father’s, nor his own son but the Father’s. Rightly, therefore, he attributes to the author whatever the equal Son does, since from him he has the very fact that he is equally equal to him.

“These things I have spoken to you while remaining with you.” The dwelling of which he spoke above is spiritual and is given only to the saints. The dwelling of which he now speaks is bodily; he spoke only of his bodily presence, which both the righteous and the wicked were able to see. The former gives eternal blessedness to those who have been delivered; the latter visits those who are to be delivered in time. “These things,” he says, “I have spoken to you while remaining with you”: he was speaking with them in bodily presence, visibly together with them.

“But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything,” etc.

He said many things in the hearing of unbelievers that found no place in their hearts, because the Holy Spirit was not teaching them inwardly. Every day he says many things through holy preachers, which those who hear do not receive inwardly, because the Holy Spirit does not inwardly remind them of what they have heard outwardly. Of him it is rightly promised: “He himself will teach you everything.” For unless that same Spirit assists the heart of the hearer, the teacher’s speech is useless. No one should attribute to the human teacher what he understands from the teacher’s mouth, because unless there is one who teaches within, the teacher’s tongue labors outwardly in vain.

The Jews therefore heard Christ preaching in one way, and the apostles in another: the former for judgment, the latter for salvation, because the Spirit taught their minds the things they had heard outwardly with their ears.

“I leave you peace; I give you my peace.” I leave you in peace; in peace I shall find you. Here I leave; there I give. I leave it to those who follow; I give it to those who go before. I have left my peace to us in this age; I shall give my peace to us in the age to come. I have left us my peace so that we may love one another. I shall give us my peace where we can never disagree with one another.

Why does he say, “I give you my peace,” and not, “I leave you my peace”? Perhaps peace will be different now and then. Here we wage war against vices; therefore he did not add “my.” There, in eternal peace, there will be eternal tranquility and harmony, and such peace as he possessed with himself, who had no sin in himself.

“Not as this world gives do I give to you.” That is, not as impure people often agree with one another in their wickedness, but as those who agree with one another in holiness and are joined together in the love of Christ.

“Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it be afraid. You have heard that I said to you, ‘I am going away, and I am coming to you.’”

Their hearts could be troubled and afraid because he was going away from them, although he was going to come to them; perhaps the wolf might attack the flock during this interval while the shepherd was absent. But although the human being was departing from them, God was not abandoning them; and the same Christ was both human and God. Thus he was going away insofar as he was human, and remaining insofar as he was God.

Therefore God, whom no place contains, departs from the hearts of those who abandon him, and comes—not with his feet but in their conduct—to those who turn to him; not by face but by faith, and they approach him not in the flesh but in love.

If you loved me, you would surely rejoice, because I am going to the Father, and so forth. By that whereby the Son is not equal to the Father, he was going to the Father, in whom he will come to judge the living and the dead; but by that whereby he is equal to the Father, he never departed from the Father, but is wholly with him everywhere through his divinity, which no place contains. Let us acknowledge the twofold substance of Christ: the divine, by which he is equal to the Father, [Col. 0330B] and the human, by which the Father is greater. Yet the two together are not two Christs but one Christ, lest there be a quaternity rather than the Trinity, God. For just as one human being consists of a rational soul and flesh, so one Christ is God and human being. Accordingly, we confess Christ as God, rational soul, and flesh—in all these together and in each individually.

Who is it, then, through whom the world was made? Christ Jesus, but in the form of God. Who was crucified under Pontius Pilate? Christ Jesus, but in the form of a servant. Likewise, considering each element of which a human being consists: Who was not abandoned in hell? Christ Jesus, but in the soul alone. Who will rise, having lain for three days in the tomb? Christ Jesus, but in the flesh alone. Thus Christ is spoken of in each of these particulars; yet all these together are not two or three Christs, but one Christ. [Col. 0330C] Therefore he says: “If you loved me, you would surely rejoice, because I am going to the Father.” Human nature ought to rejoice because it has been assumed by the only-begotten Word, so that it might be established immortal in heaven; for in this way he said that he would go to the Father. Certainly he was not going to the one who was with him; rather, going to him meant departing from us, changing and making immortal what he had assumed from us as mortal, and establishing at the Father’s right hand that by which he had been on earth for us. Then the Lord Jesus himself added:

“And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe.” He is speaking of what would happen: that after his death they would see him alive and ascending to the Father. For they could doubt whether he was the Son of God when they saw him about to die; but [Col. 0330D] when they saw him risen, they believed in the one about whom they had previously doubted. Their faith was confirmed—the faith he had foretold to them, since by his mouth he promised what he was going to do and by his deed fulfilled what he had foretold. Then what does he say?

“I will no longer speak much with you, for the prince of this world is coming.” Who else but the devil?

“And he has nothing in me”—that is, absolutely no sin. For by this he shows that the devil is prince of sinful human beings, not of God’s creatures. Whenever “world” is used in a negative sense, it refers only to those who love this world and not God. Far be it from us to believe that he is prince of heaven and earth and of all the creatures that are generally [Col. 0331A] called “the world.” The whole world, therefore, serves its Creator, not its deceiver; its Redeemer, not its destroyer; and it is governed by divine providence, not overthrown by the enemy’s cunning—except for the human beings who are his members, who of their own will, and not from any necessity, subject themselves to the devil.

Hence the Apostle also says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood,” that is, against human beings, “but against the powers and rulers of this darkness” (II Cor. VII), that is, of sins, which remain in the darkness of iniquity. These are designated as rulers because they are angels who have deserted [God]. Yet there are people who are rescued from them by God’s grace, not by their own merits. Of these the Apostle says: “For once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light.” Thanks be to God, who has rescued us, as the same [Col. 0331B] Apostle says, from the power of darkness and “transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his glory.” In him the prince of this world—that is, of this darkness—had nothing, because God had come without sin, nor had the Virgin borne his flesh from the propagation of sin. And as though someone had said to him, “Why then will you die, if you have no sin to which the punishment of death was due?” he immediately added:

“But so that the world may know that I love the Father, and that I do just as the Father commanded me.” While reclining, he was speaking to those reclining; but when he said, “Let us go,” where was he going except to the place from which he was to be handed over? He was handed over to death, although he had no merit deserving death; but he had the Father’s command that he should die.

[Col. 0331C]

## SUNDAY IN THE OCTAVE OF PENTECOST

### READING FROM THE BOOK OF THE APOCALYPSE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE JOHN, CHAPTER IV

“I saw an open door in heaven, and the first voice that I heard was like a trumpet speaking with me, saying: ‘Come up here, and I will show you what must take place soon.’ After this I was immediately in the spirit. And behold, a throne was set in heaven, and one seated upon the throne. And the one seated was like the appearance of a jasper stone and a sardius; and a rainbow was around the throne, like the appearance of an emerald. And around the throne were twenty-four seats, and upon the twenty-four thrones were twenty-four elders seated, clothed all around in white robes, and on their heads golden crowns. And from the throne proceeded flashes of lightning, voices, and thunder; and seven burning lamps before the throne, which are the seven spirits of God. And before the throne there was something like a glassy sea, resembling crystal; and in the midst of the throne and around the throne were four living creatures full of eyes before and behind. The first living creature was like a lion, the second living creature like a calf, the third living creature having a face like a human being, and the fourth living creature like a flying eagle. And each of the four living creatures had six wings, and around and within they were full of eyes; and they had no rest day or night, saying: ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty, who was, who is, and who is to come.’ And when the four living creatures gave glory, honor, and blessing to the one seated upon the throne, who lives for ever and ever, the twenty-four elders fell before the one seated upon the throne and worshiped the one who lives for ever and ever.”

“I saw an open door in heaven.” (From Bede.) That is, the faith of Christ’s birth, passion, and resurrection in the Church. The open door indicates Christ born and suffering, for he himself says: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X). And elsewhere: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John VI). What he says, “in heaven,” signifies the Church, which deserved to be heaven because it is God’s dwelling place.

“And the first voice that I heard was like a trumpet speaking with me.” For just as the sound of a trumpet is, so is the voice of preachers when they invite their hearers to faith. By saying “the first voice,” he means the first voice in this vision.

“Saying: ‘Come up here, and I will show you what must take place soon.’” When he says, “Come up here,” he does not mean moving from one place to another, but “come up,” that is, understand and believe. For the Church invites unbelievers to Christ and to baptism. Everyone who believes that Christ was born and suffered ascends to the height of the Church and sees future things with spiritual affection. Hence it follows:

“After this I was in the spirit.” That is, I did not feel my body, as though my spirit alone were outside the body in a spiritual vision.

“And behold, a throne was set in heaven.” That is, the Church perfected in faith.

“And one seated upon the throne.” That is, Christ was seated above the Church. Hence Isaiah also says: “I saw the Lord seated upon a high and exalted throne” (Isa. VI), that is, above the Church, happily raised up in exalted faith and in the hope of eternal life.

“And the one seated was like the appearance of a jasper stone and a sardius,” and so forth. Jasper has a color like the sea, sardius like blood. By jasper baptism is understood; by sardius, martyrdom. These comparisons suit the Church, with which Christ is clothed.

The rainbow is an arc in the sky, signifying the New Testament. It has three colors: water, sulfur, and fire. By water baptism is understood; by sulfur, repentance; by fire, martyrdom. For water came in the Flood, sulfur descended upon Sodom, and fire will come at the time of judgment.

Alternatively: the rainbow around the throne signifies the Gospel around the Church. The emerald likewise has the color of water and fire, signifying baptism and martyrdom.

“And around the throne were twenty-four seats, and upon the twenty-four thrones were twenty-four elders seated.” Twenty signifies the Decalogue doubled; four signifies the four Gospels. Or the twenty-four elders signify the twelve patriarchs and the twelve apostles.

“Clothed all around in white garments.” This means, in the work of chastity. Hence Solomon says: “Let your garments be white at all times” (Eccl. IX), that is, let your flesh be cleansed from every stain of pollution and adorned with the purity of chastity.

“And on their heads golden crowns.” That is, the principal gifts of the mind, or the palms of wisdom and immortality.

“And from the throne proceed flashes of lightning.” That is, from the Church proceed many great miracles.

“And voices and thunder.” That is, the voices of preachers, together with promises and threats.

“And seven burning lamps before the throne.” The throne of God is the Church. He explained what the lamps are when he said: “which are the seven spirits of God,” that is, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

“And before the throne there was something like a glassy sea, resembling crystal.” The glassy sea signified baptism, which is said to resemble crystal because of its purity.

“And in the midst of the throne and around the throne were four living creatures, full of eyes before and behind.” The four living creatures signify the four Gospels. They are full of eyes before, because they preach the future judgment; they are full of eyes behind, because they give testimony from the Old Testament. Or they are full of eyes before because they carefully consider what must be done, and behind because they diligently remember what must be mourned.

“And the first living creature was like a lion,” and so forth. In the anagogical sense, Christ was a lion in the resurrection, a calf in the passion, a human being in the flesh, and an eagle in the ascension.

In the moral sense, the lion, described as the strongest of beasts, signifies those who are stronger in faith; the calf signifies the merciful in the Church; the human being signifies the humble, who say: “I have been humbled exceedingly; give me life, Lord”; the eagle signifies the exalted, who say with Paul: “Our citizenship is in heaven.” These living creatures had six wings, because throughout the six ages of the world they do not cease to proclaim the law of the Old and New Testaments. Although the law of the New and Old Testaments is one, it appears divided into six parts: the law of nature, the law of the letter, the law of the prophets, the law of the Gospels, the law of the apostles, and the ecclesiastical law.

“And around and within they were full of eyes.” They have eyes within and outside who illuminate the Church inwardly and outwardly with the testimonies of the divine Scriptures.

“And they had no rest day or night.” That is, in prosperity and adversity, as the Psalmist says: “I will bless the Lord at all times,” that is, in prosperity and adversity. For day is frequently understood as prosperity and night as adversity.

[Col. 0333D]

“Saying: ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts,’” and so forth. Here the Trinity and unity are understood, because they proclaim three persons and one God, and demonstrate the mystery of both Trinity and unity.

“Who was, and who is, and who is to come.” “Who was,” as in: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word.” “Who is,” as in: “Say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you.’” “Who is to come” means, implicitly, to judge the living and the dead.

“And when the four living creatures gave glory, honor, and blessing to the one seated upon the throne, the twenty-four elders fell down and worshiped the one who lives for ever and ever, and they cast their crowns before the throne, saying: ‘You are worthy, Lord our God, to receive the kingdom.’” All the elect fall before the throne and worship God, and cast their crowns before him, because whatever dignity they possess they attribute not to themselves but to him, and they return to him the glory of praise, from whom they acknowledge that they received the strength for their struggle.

## ALSO, AN EXPOSITION BY BEDE ON THIS SAME READING

“I saw an open door in heaven.” Appropriately, the one who is about to ascend looks upon the heavenly door, since he is promised that lofty mysteries will be opened to him. Or, because Christ is the door, whoever believes that he was born and suffered ascends to heaven—that is, to the height of the Church—and sees future things through a special spiritual effect, as he says:

“And immediately I was in the spirit, and the first voice that I heard was like a trumpet speaking,” and so forth. It was certainly like the earlier voice that had said: “What you see, write in a book.”

[Col. 0334B]

“And behold, a throne was set in heaven, and one seated upon the throne.” The Lord inhabits the Church, which has been established in a heavenly manner of life. Pope Gregory interprets the throne of God in the vision of Micaiah as the angelic powers, over whose minds he presides on high while arranging all things below.

“And the one seated was like the appearance of a jasper stone and a sardius.” The color of jasper signifies water, and that of sardius fire; by these two we know that judgment is carried out. For, as he says: “As it was in the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matt. XXIV).

“And there was a rainbow around the throne, like the appearance of an emerald.” The rainbow, produced when the sun illuminates the clouds and first made after the Flood as a sign of reconciliation, indicates that the Church is protected through the intercession of the saints, whom the Lord enlightens. It is rightly compared to the emerald stone because of its intense greenness. The more perfectly they await the imperishable inheritance by faith, the more powerfully they protect others also through prayer.

Since we have said a little about these three stones, let us discuss these and the other precious stones at somewhat greater length. Isaiah also speaks of them: “Behold, I will lay your stones in order, and I will establish you upon sapphires,” and so forth. Immediately, as though explaining this, he adds: “All your children shall be taught by the Lord” (Isa. LIV).

“The first foundation, jasper.” There are many kinds of jasper. One appears green and as though tinged with flowers; another resembles emerald but is of a dense color, and they say that it drives away all phantoms. Another shines like snow and the foam of sea waves, as though mixed with blood.

Jasper, therefore, signifies the unfading greenness of faith. This faith is infused through the sacrament of the Lord’s passion by the water of baptism and, as merits advance, is equipped with every flower of spiritual grace. Whoever possesses it drives away vain fears, as the Apostle Peter admonishes: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour; resist him, firm in faith” (I Pet. IV).

“The second, sapphire.” Moses explained both the color and the mystery of this stone when, describing God’s appearance, he said: “Under his feet there was something like a pavement of sapphire stone, and something like the sky when it is clear” (Exod. XXIV). Ezekiel likewise says that the place where God’s throne is located has the likeness of sapphire (Ezek. I), and that the glory of the Lord rests in this color. It prefigures the one who bears the image of the heavenly, and who can say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven.”

“The third, chalcedony,” which retains something like the appearance of a pale lamp flame and has a brightness beneath the open sky, not in a house. By it are represented those who, supported by heavenly desire, remain hidden from human beings and perform their fasting, almsgiving, and prayers as though in secret. But when they are commanded to come into public service, whether for teaching or for other needs of the saints, they immediately shine and burn like a lamp of brilliance: they burn, plainly, with love, and shine through speech.

“The fourth, emerald,” which is of such excessive greenness that, staining green grasses and leafy gems, it even colors the air around it through the reflected greenness. There are many kinds, but the Scythian are the noblest; the Bactrian occupy second place, and the Egyptian third.

It signifies souls ever green with faith. They hope in the imperishable inheritance, preserved eternally in heaven (I Pet. V), and strive both to conceive it in their minds through hope and to spread it among their neighbors by preaching.

“The fifth, sardonyx.” Drawing whiteness from the onyx and redness from the sardius, it received its name, sardonyx, from both. There are many kinds. One resembles red earth. Another appears two-colored, as though blood were shining through a human fingernail. Another consists of three colors: black below, red above, and white in the middle. Those are compared to people made ruddy by bodily suffering, white through purity of spirit, but despised in their own eyes through humility.

“The sixth, sardius,” which is entirely blood-colored, signifies the glory of the martyrs, of which it is said: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.” It is rightly placed sixth, since our Lord was incarnate in the sixth age of the world and was crucified on the sixth day for the salvation of the whole world.

“The seventh, chrysolite,” which shines like gold and has burning sparks. By its appearance are figured those who, shining with the understanding of heavenly and true wisdom, pour forth words of exhortation to their neighbors, and even signs of virtues, like sparks of fire. Of such people the orator says:

“Love presses upon their minds,
and ardor seethes in their words.”

[Col. 0335D]

Because this is accomplished solely by the gift of spiritual grace, chrysolite is most fittingly present as the seventh foundation; for the grace of the Holy Spirit is often represented by the number seven.

“The eighth, beryl.” Beryl, as though you were to consider water struck by the sun’s radiance, produces a reddish and beautiful color; but it does not shine unless it is polished and shaped into a hexagonal form. Its splendor is sharpened by the reflection of its angles.

It signifies people who are indeed discerning in intellect but shine still more brightly through the light of heavenly grace. It is said that it burns those who hold it in the hand; this clearly shows that whoever is joined to a holy person is refreshed by the fire of that person’s good manner of life.

[Col. 0336A]

“The ninth, topaz.” The topaz stone is as rare to find as it is precious in value. It is said to have two colors: one of the purest gold, and the other shining with an ethereal brightness. It is said to be so marvelous even to kings that they recognize that they possess nothing like it among their riches.

Its most beautiful natural quality is worthily compared to the beauty of the contemplative life. Holy kings, whose heart is in God’s hand, rightly prefer this life to all the riches of good works and all the jewels of virtues. They embrace the sweetness of heavenly life in their minds with greater ardor the more frequently they have been struck by the splendor of heavenly grace. Holy people therefore possess a golden color, and at the same time an ethereal color from the flame of charity, arising from the contemplation of heavenly sweetness.

[Col. 0336B]

That it is said to be found on the island of Thebaid, which is called Topazion and from which it received its name, is to be understood in two ways: first, because those regions—namely, the regions of Egypt—are especially abundant in flocks of monks; and second, because whoever dwells near the sun of justice is adorned with the brilliance of ethereal light.

It is fitting that the perfection of the active life is placed in the eighth order, and the jewel of contemplative sweetness in the ninth—either because nine orders of angels, whose life it imitates, are found in Holy Scripture.

“The tenth, chrysoprase.” Chrysoprase is a mixture of green and gold, also drawing from it a kind of purple radiance, with golden drops interspersed. It is born in India. It signifies those who, earning the greenness of their eternal homeland through the radiance of perfect charity, also reveal it to others through the purple light of their martyrdom. Because, in despising this life, they prefer eternal glory, they follow the example of the Lord appearing in the flesh. Now, as it were in India—that is, near the rising of the sun—they display the brilliance of their merits.

“The eleventh, hyacinth.” Hyacinth is found in Ethiopia. The finest kind has a blue color, neither sparse nor clouded by density, but shining through a temperate mixture and producing a pleasing flower. Yet it does not gleam uniformly; its appearance changes with the sky. In clear weather it is transparent and pleasing, but under clouds it vanishes before the eyes and fades.

It indicates souls always devoted to heavenly contemplation and drawing, so far as is permitted to mortals, somewhat near to an angelic manner of life. In them the whole conduct of life is governed by the watchfulness of discretion, lest, becoming clever through excessive subtlety of understanding, they dare to seek things too high or investigate things too difficult.

“For the glory of the Lord is to conceal a word”—that is, to speak cautiously and philosophically about God or the human Christ—or, again, lest they sink through sluggish indifference to the weak beginnings of faith and the elementary stages of God’s words. Rather, walking along the royal road, protected on the right and left by the weapons of righteousness, they proceed like a hyacinth surrounded by clouds.

“For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. I); and, as though seen in clear light, he says: “We speak wisdom among the mature” (II Cor. II).

[Col. 0337A]

“The twelfth, amethyst.” Amethyst is purple, mixed with a violet color and something like the radiance of a rose, gently emitting certain little flames. Yet there is also something in its purple that is not wholly fiery but appears reddish, like wine.

Its purple beauty therefore signifies the character of the heavenly kingdom; its rose and violet colors signify the humble, truly desirous, and precious death of the saints.

In jasper, therefore, the greenness of faith is figured; in sapphire, the height of heavenly hope; in chalcedony, the flame of inward charity. In emerald, the strong confession of that same faith amid adversities. In sardonyx, humility among the virtues of the saints. In sardius, the revered blood of the martyrs. In chrysolite, the spiritual voice of preaching amid miracles. In beryl, the perfect work of preachers. In topaz, their ardent contemplation. In chrysoprase, both the work and reward of blessed martyrs. In hyacinth, the heavenly raising of teachers to lofty things and their humble descent to human concerns for the sake of the weak. In amethyst, the constant memory of the heavenly kingdom in the minds of the humble.

Each precious stone is assigned to its own foundation. Although all are perfect, and although the city of our God is adorned and founded upon his holy mountain by the light of spiritual grace, nevertheless “to one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge, to another the grace of healings, to another kinds of tongues, to another faith in the same Spirit,” and so forth.

“And around the throne were twenty-four seats, and upon the twenty-four thrones were twenty-four elders seated.” He had seen the Church, because of the fellowship of faith, in one seat; and he sees that same Church, generated through the two Testaments from patriarchs and apostles, in twenty-four seats. He sees it seated because of its judicial dignity in Christ. Its members also will sit and judge all things, but in one head and through one head.

For how could the saints sit in judgment, standing at the judge’s right hand? The twenty-four elders may also be understood as those who complete the perfection of works—which is commended by the number six—through the clear preaching of the Gospel. For four times six makes twenty-four.

“Clothed all around in white garments, and on their heads golden crowns.” This means clothed in good works and, through the perpetual memory of the mind, seeking the joys above. For the mind is often understood under the name “head.”

“And from the throne proceed flashes of lightning, voices, and thunder.” This is what Mark says: “But they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word by the accompanying signs” (Mark, final chapter).

“And seven lamps before the throne, which are the seven spirits of God.” He calls one spirit sevenfold. For the spirit is one; sevenfoldness is perfection and fullness. Once the Holy Spirit has been mentioned, the water of baptism appropriately follows, through which that same Spirit is believed to be received.

“And before the throne there was something like a glassy sea, resembling crystal.” Because of true faith, baptism is referred to here, in which nothing other than what it bears inwardly is seen outwardly. The crystal, which is made from water into ice and a precious stone, likewise figures the grace of baptism.

“And in the midst of the throne and around the throne were four living creatures, full of eyes, before and behind.” The circuit of God’s throne—that is, the fathers of the Church—is filled with the light of the Gospel and with knowledge of past and future things.

“And the first living creature was like a lion,” and so forth. These living creatures are interpreted in many ways. The blessed Augustine, following the order of this book, says that Matthew is understood as the lion, since he narrates Christ’s royal lineage; and it was the lion from the tribe of Judah who conquered. He is the lion’s cub from Judah, in whom, as king, the king is feared. He is worshiped by the Magi; there also the king settles accounts with his servants. The king makes a wedding feast for his son, and finally the king separates the sheep from the goats.

Luke is represented by the calf, which was a great sacrificial victim; for in his Gospel not only do the beginnings concerning the temple and sacrifices vary, but it concludes in this way: “And they were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God.”

The face of a human being signifies Mark, who said nothing about the Lord’s royal or priestly power but simply narrated the deeds of Christ as a human being.

The eagle is John, who gazes intently upon the birth of the Word, as upon the rising of the sun.

The living creatures sometimes signify the evangelists and sometimes the whole Church, whose strength is shown in the lion, whose sacrificial offering is shown in the calf, whose humility is shown in the human being, and whose sublimity is shown in the flying eagle.

“Each of them had six wings.” Through the perfection of its teaching, the Church raises people to lofty things. The number six is called perfect because it is completed by its own parts: one, which is one-sixth of six; two, which is one-third; and three, which is one-half—all together make the same number six.

Alternatively, the six wings of the four living creatures, which together number twenty-four, indicate the twenty-four books of the Old Testament. These support the authority of the evangelists and establish the truth.

“And around and within they were full of eyes.” The holy Church watches over itself vigilantly both before God and before human beings. The Psalmist had looked upon its inner eyes when he said: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within.” He refers to its outer eyes when he immediately adds: “In golden fringes, clothed around with variety.”

Alternatively, whether one attends to the literal sense or seeks allegory, one always finds light in the Gospel. Another translation has it this way: “Full of eyes before and behind,” because the light of the Gospel illuminates the riddles of the Law and pours the radiance of new grace upon the world.

“And they had no rest day or night, saying: ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty,’” and so forth. The holy living creatures affirm throughout all the ages of the world the one dominion of the Godhead, the omnipotence, and the eternity of the Holy Trinity, while the perpetual praise of intellectual creation remains in the heavens.

“The twenty-four elders fell before the one seated upon the throne and worshiped the one who lives for ever and ever.” While the living creatures resound with praise—that is, while the evangelists preach Christ’s dispensation—the whole Church, which consists of leaders and peoples—for this number doubled signifies the number twelve—immediately falls on its face and worships the one who lives for ever and ever. They cast their crowns before God’s throne, assigning to him whatever virtue and whatever dignity they possess, since he created all things from nothing.

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER III

“There was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. He came to Jesus by night and said to him: ‘Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher; for no one can perform these signs that you perform unless God is with him.’ Jesus answered and said to him: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: Unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.’ Nicodemus said to him: ‘How can a human being be born when he is old? Can he enter his mother’s womb again and be born?’ Jesus answered: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: Unless someone is born of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. What is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of spirit is spirit. Do not be surprised that I said to you: You must be born again. The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.’ Nicodemus answered and said to him: ‘How can these things happen?’ Jesus answered and said to him: ‘You are a teacher in Israel, and you do not know these things? Amen, amen, I say to you: We speak what we know, and we testify to what we have seen, and you have not accepted our testimony. If I have spoken earthly things to you and you do not believe, how will you believe if I speak heavenly things to you? And no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven. And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.’”

“There was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews; he came to Jesus by night.” This ruler of the Jews came to Jesus by night, desiring through a private conversation with him to learn more fully the mysteries of the faith. Through the open manifestation of signs he had already grasped, to some extent, their beginnings. Because he prudently investigated the things he sought from him, he deserved to obtain them.

[Col. 0339D]

“Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher, for no one can perform these signs that you perform unless God is with him.” He confessed that Jesus had come from God to bring heavenly instruction to the world. Through the miracles he understood more wisely that God was with him, although he did not yet recognize that Jesus himself was God. But since he approached with good reason the one whom he knew as a teacher of truth, eager to be taught, he deserved to be instructed perfectly in the knowledge of his divinity. He also learned the mysteries of both his births, namely, the divine and the human, as well as of his passion and ascension. Furthermore, with the Lord revealing it, he learned the manner of the second generation, the entrance into the heavenly kingdom, and many other mysteries of evangelical teaching.

[Col. 0340A]

“Jesus answered and said: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: Unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.’” This statement shines so much more clearly for all the faithful because it is certain that without its light the faithful cannot exist. For who can obtain forgiveness of sins without the washing of regeneration and enter the kingdom of heaven?

But Nicodemus, who came to Jesus by night, did not yet know how to grasp the mysteries of light. The night in which he came signifies the ignorance by which he was still oppressed. He had not yet been joined to the number of those to whom the Apostle says: “Once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. IV). Rather, he remained among those to whom Isaiah says: “Arise, shine, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen over you” (Isa. LX).

[Col. 0340B]

“Nicodemus said to him: ‘How can a human being be born when he is old?’” and so forth. Since he still did not understand the second birth, but had already become concerned for his salvation, he necessarily asked whether the one birth that he knew could be repeated, or in what manner regeneration could be accomplished, lest, remaining without it, he be unable to share in heavenly life.

It must be noted that what he said about bodily birth must also be understood of spiritual regeneration: plainly, after it has once been completed, it cannot be repeated. Whether a heretic, a schismatic, or any criminal person is baptized in the confession of the Holy Trinity, one who has been baptized in this way cannot be rebaptized by good Catholics, lest the confession or invocation of so great a name appear to be annulled.

[Col. 0340C]

And because Nicodemus, anxious after the Lord’s first response, carefully inquired how it should be understood, he deserved to be instructed more plainly. He deserved to hear that the second birth is not bodily but spiritual.

Jesus answered: “Amen, amen, I say to you: Unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” Explaining the manner of this birth afterward and distinguishing it completely from bodily birth, he says:

What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit. The nature of the spirit is invisible, while that of the flesh is visible; and therefore bodily generation is carried out visibly. Through visible growth, the one who is born in the flesh advances by stages of age; spiritual generation, however, takes place entirely invisibly.

[Col. 0340D] For certainly the person being baptized is seen to descend into the font, is seen to be immersed in the waters, and is seen to rise from the waters. But what he has undergone in that washing of regeneration cannot at all be seen. Only the devotion of the faithful knows that a sinner descended into the font, but rose purified; a son of death descended, but a son of resurrection rose; a son of transgression descended, but a son of reconciliation rose; a son of wrath descended, but a son of mercy rose; a son of the devil descended, but a son of God rose. Only the Church, that mother who gives birth, knows this; to the eyes of the foolish, however, the person appears to emerge from the font just as he entered it. They think that the whole rite is merely a game, and so, when at the end they see the glory of the saints, they will say with groaning [Col. 0341A] amid torments: “These are the ones whom we once held in derision and as an object of reproach” (Wis. 5). “How then have they been counted among the sons of God?”

The Apostle John says: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be.” Thus, what is born of the Spirit is spirit. For the one who is invisibly regenerated by water and the Spirit is changed into a new human being, and from being carnal becomes spiritual. He is therefore rightly called not only spiritual but also spirit, because just as the substance of the spirit is invisible to our sight, so the one who is renewed by the grace of God invisibly becomes spiritual and a son of God, although visibly he appears to everyone as flesh and as a son of man.

“Do not marvel that I said to you, You must be born again,” [Col. 0341B] and so forth. “The Spirit breathes where he wills,” because he has the power to illumine by the visitation of his grace the heart of whomever he chooses. “And you hear his voice” when, in your presence, the one who is filled with the Holy Spirit speaks; “but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes,” because even when you are present, if the Spirit fills someone for a time, you cannot see how he entered or how he departed, since his nature is invisible. “So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.” For when the Spirit acts invisibly, he begins to be what he was not.

Thus the unbeliever does not know where he comes from or where he goes—that is, he comes from the grace of regeneration into the adoption of the children of God, and he goes into the possession of the heavenly kingdom. While Nicodemus was still asking how these things could happen,

Jesus answered and said to him: “You are the teacher in Israel,” [Col. 0341C] and so forth. He was not attempting to honor one who was called a teacher while ignorant of the heavenly mysteries, but was summoning him to the way of humility, without which the heavenly door cannot be found.

“Amen, amen, I say to you, we speak of what we know and testify to what we have seen,” and so forth. He called these things earthly, as we found in the preceding reading, when he spoke of the passion and resurrection of his body, which he had taken from the earth: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” Yet they did not believe the word he spoke; indeed, they could not even understand that he was speaking not of another temple but of the temple of his body. If, then, they could not grasp earthly things when they heard them, how much less are they capable of grasping heavenly things—that is, the mysteries of divine generation?

The Lord nevertheless adds further heavenly [Col. 0341D] mysteries and instructs him concerning earthly matters, seeing that he attends wisely and diligently to what he hears. His ascent to eternal life is heavenly; his earthly exaltation, however, is toward temporal death. Accordingly, he speaks of heavenly things:

“And no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven,” and so forth. It is rightly asked how the Son of Man can be said either to have descended from heaven or already to have been in heaven at the time when he was speaking these things on earth. The flesh of Christ, therefore, did not descend from heaven, nor was it in heaven before the time of the ascension. But because there is one person of Christ existing in two natures, the Son of Man is rightly said both to have descended from heaven and to have been in heaven before his passion, because what it could not possess in its own nature, it possessed in the Son of God, by whom it was assumed.

It must also be asked how it was said, “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven,” when all the elect confidently expect to ascend into heaven, since the Lord promises them: “Where I am, there my servant will be also.” The solution to this question is made perfectly clear by the fact that Christ Jesus, the man who is mediator between God and humanity, is the head of all the elect, and all his elect are members of that same head. The Apostle says: “He gave him as head over the whole Church” (1 Cor. 6), and again: “You are the body of Christ and members, each from a member.”

No one ascends into heaven except Christ in his body, which is the Church. He first ascended in himself, in the sight of the apostles, who were its more exalted members; thereafter, ascending daily in his members, he gathers himself into heaven. Whoever desires to ascend into heaven must be joined to the one who descended from heaven and is in heaven by the true unity of faith and love, understanding plainly that no one can ascend into heaven by any other order than through the one who descended from heaven. Hence he says elsewhere: “No one comes to the Father except through me.”

“And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.” By the marvelous art of heavenly instruction, the Lord leads the teacher of the Mosaic law to the spiritual meaning of that same law. He recalls the history of the past and explains that it was made a figure of his passion and of human salvation.

The Book of Numbers relates that the people of Israel, wearied in the wilderness by the hardship of the long journey and by labor, murmured against the Lord and Moses. Therefore the Lord sent fiery serpents among them. When many had been wounded and killed by their bites, and the people cried out to Moses and he prayed, the Lord commanded him to make a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign. “Anyone who has been bitten,” he said, “who looks at it shall live,” and so it happened (Num. 21).

The bites of the fiery serpents are therefore the poisons and incitements of vices, which destroy with spiritual death the soul they touch. And rightly was the people who murmured against the Lord struck down by the serpents’ bites, so that by the outward order of the scourge they might recognize how much inward destruction they were suffering through their murmuring.

The lifting up of the bronze serpent, by which those who had been bitten were healed when they looked upon it, is the passion of our Redeemer on the cross; by faith in him alone the kingdom of death and sin is overcome. [Col. 0342D] Sin is rightly represented by serpents, since sin drags both soul and body toward destruction—not only because serpents are fiery and venomous and exist to kill, but also because our first parents were persuaded to sin through a serpent and, by sinning, were changed from immortal to mortal.

The Lord is rightly shown by the bronze serpent, because he came in the likeness of sinful flesh. Just as the bronze serpent had an appearance resembling that of the fiery serpents but possessed no trace of venom in its members, and by its being lifted up healed those bitten by the serpents, so the Redeemer of the human race assumed not sinful flesh but the likeness [Col. 0343A] of sinful flesh. By suffering the death of the cross in that flesh, he would free those who believed in him from every sin and even from death itself.

“So that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.” The meaning of this saying is clear: whoever believes in Jesus not only escapes the punishment of perdition but also receives eternal life. Here lies the difference between the figure and the reality: through the former, life was prolonged for a time; through the latter, life is given to remain without end.

[Col. 0343B] But we must carefully ensure that what the understanding rightly perceives is advanced by corresponding conduct, so that our confession of the true faith, through devout and sober living, may deserve to attain the perfection of the life promised to us. Yet because these things are said of the Son of Man, who could be lifted up upon the cross and suffer death, the Lord took care also to disclose to Nicodemus the mystery of his divinity, lest he should think him merely the Son of Man from whom everlasting life was to be expected. He showed that the one and the same Son is both Son of God and Son of Man, the Savior of the world.

## THE SECOND WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

### READING FROM THE LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE JOHN, CHAPTER 4

“God is love. In this the love of God has been revealed among us: God sent his only-begotten Son into the world so that we might live through him. In this consists love—not that we loved God, but that he first loved us and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice for our sins.

“Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another. [Col. 0343C] No one has ever seen God. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love is perfected in us. By this we know that we remain in him and he in us: because he has given us of his Spirit.

“And we have seen and testify that the Father sent his Son as the Savior of the world. Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him and he in God. And we have come to know and have believed the love that God has for us.

“God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him. In this love has been perfected with us, so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment, because as he is, so are we in this world.

[Col. 0343D] “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment. Whoever fears has not been perfected in love.

“Let us therefore love God, because he first loved us. If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar. For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see? And we have this commandment from God: whoever loves God must love his brother also.”

“God is love.
