In this the love of God has been revealed among us: God sent his only-begotten Son into the world so that we might live through him.” As the Lord himself says: “No one has greater love than this, that someone should lay down his life for his friends.” Christ’s love for us was proved there, because he died for us.

[Col. 0344A] Where was the Father’s love for us proved? In this: that he sent his only Son to die for us, as the Apostle Paul also says: “He did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all; how will he not also give us all things with him?” (Rom. 8).

“And in this consists love—not that we loved God, but that he first loved us,” and so forth. We did not love him first; rather, he loved us for this purpose, that we might love him. Grace precedes a human being so that he may love God and, through love, do good works. Hence the Psalmist says: “My God, his mercy will come before me” (Ps. 58).

“And he sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice for our sins.” This is the greatest sign of divine love toward us: before we even knew how to ask him for forgiveness for our sins, he sent his Son to us, so that he might freely grant pardon to those who believe in him and call us to share in the glory of the Father.

[Col. 0344B] In some manuscripts this verse is read as follows: “And he sent his Son as a sacrificer [litator] for our sins.” A *litator* is a sacrificer. For the Son of God sacrificed himself for our sins, offering not the victims of animals but himself. Hence Paul rightly admonishes us: “Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma” (Eph. 5). John adds this in harmony with that statement as he exhorts us, saying:

“Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.” What follows—“No one has ever seen God”—requires a fuller discussion, since the Lord promises that those who are pure in heart will see God, and says of the saints that their angels in heaven always see the face of the Father.

[Col. 0344C] John himself places this statement in his Gospel, where he also adds how God may be seen: “The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he himself will declare him.” The blessed Father Ambrose explained this as follows:

“And therefore no one has ever seen God, because no one has perceived or grasped with mind or eyes that fullness of divinity which dwells in God.” The word “seen” must be referred to both. Finally, when it is added, “The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he himself will declare him,” vision of minds rather than of eyes is indicated. Appearance is seen, but power is declared: [Col. 0344D] the former is grasped by the eyes, the latter by the mind.

Likewise, the blessed Augustine, discussing the same question in his book *On Seeing God*, says:

“Therefore, when the only-begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father declares him by an ineffable declaration, the rational, pure, and holy creature is filled with an ineffable vision of God, which we shall then attain when we have been made equal, because just as these visible things are known through the senses of the body, so no one has ever seen God. For if he has at some time been seen in that manner, he was not seen as this nature is seen, but he was seen by his will, appearing in whatever form he wished, while his nature remained hidden and unchangeable in itself. In the manner in which he is seen as he is, he may perhaps now be seen by some of his holy angels. By us, however, he will then be seen in this way when we have been made equal to him.”

[Col. 0345A] Later, explaining the statement of Saint Ambrose, he says:

“For no one has ever seen God, either in this life as he is, or even in the life of the angels as these visible things are perceived by bodily sight, because the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, will himself declare him. For it was said that what he will declare pertains not to the vision of bodily eyes but to the vision of minds.”

Again, after much further discussion:

“He has urged us to purify our hearts for that vision in which we shall see God as he is. Since visible things are called visible according to the customary bodily manner of speaking, God is called invisible so that he may not be believed to be a body. Will he defraud pure hearts of the contemplation of his substance, when this great and supreme reward is [Col. 0345B] promised to those who worship and love God? The Lord himself said this while he visibly appeared to bodily eyes and promised that he, though invisible, would be contemplated by pure hearts: ‘Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him.’ His nature, together with the Father, is invisible in equal measure, just as it is equally incorruptible, for the Apostle immediately continued, saying: ‘To the King of the ages, invisible, incorruptible,’ commending the divine substance to human beings as far as he could by preaching.”

God, therefore, the invisible King, must be sought not with the eyes but with the mind. Yet just as, if we wished to see the sun, we would purify the bodily eye by which light can be seen, so, if we wish to see God, we must purify the eye of the heart by which God can be seen: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5).

[Col. 0345C] But since this vision is hoped for in the future, what are we to do while we still dwell in the body and are away from the Lord? What consolation are we to use while we are not yet permitted to enjoy the divine vision?

“If we love one another, God remains in us.” But no one should think that this love in which God remains is preserved by some base and idle gentleness—or rather, not gentleness but laxity and negligence. This is not love but weakness. Let love be fervent in correcting and improving itself: if good conduct delights us, let evil conduct be amended and corrected. If, then, we love one another with sincere and disciplined love, God remains in us, manifested through the works of that love, although he does not yet appear visibly.

[Col. 0345D]

“And his love is perfected in us.” It must be asked how he can say that the perfection of divine love consists in mutual love, since the Lord declares in the Gospel that it is not a great thing if we love those who love us, unless that same love also reaches our enemies, about whom this passage seems to say nothing at all.

Perhaps we ought to love our enemies precisely out of regard for fraternal love, so that they may not remain enemies forever but may repent of the devil’s snares and be joined to us in brotherly fellowship. “If we love,” he says, “one another, God remains in us, and his love is perfected in us.” Begin to love, and you are being perfected. You have begun to love, and God has begun to dwell in you, so that by dwelling in you more perfectly he may make you perfect.

[Col. 0346A]

“By this we know that we remain in him and he in us,” and so forth. How do you know that he has given you of his Spirit? Question your inmost being: if it is full of love, you have the Spirit of God. The Apostle Paul bears witness to this when he says: “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”

“And we have seen and testify that the Father sent his Son as the Savior of the world” (Rom. 5). Let no one despair of salvation. Although the diseases of sin that oppress us may be great, the physician who saves is almighty. Let everyone remember only that the same Son of God who came gentle in order to save will come severe in order to judge.

“Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him and he in God.” He speaks of a perfect confession of the heart, one that cannot be corrupted by the deceit of heretics who offer evil counsel, shaken by the torments of persecuting pagans, made to stumble by the example of carnal brothers, or weakened by the sluggishness of one’s own frailty.

[Col. 0346B] There are indeed those who deny even in words that Jesus is the Son of God; many such people are reported to have existed at the very time when John wrote these things. There are also those who confess him in words but deny him by their deeds. Therefore the one who now says, “Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him and he in God” (1 John 4), had said shortly before: “If we love one another, God remains in us,” plainly indicating that whoever has love for his brothers testifies that Jesus is the Son of God.

“And we have come to know and have believed the love that God has for us.” We have come to know that Jesus is the Son of God [Col. 0346C] and that the Father sent him as the Savior of the world. We have believed the love that God has for us, because although he had only one Son, he did not wish him to remain alone; rather, he adopted brothers for him, who might possess eternal life together with him.

“God is love.” He said this above; behold, he says it again. He could not commend love to you more fully than by calling God “love.” Perhaps you were going to despise God’s gift; surely you do not despise God himself?

“And whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him.” The one who contains and the one who is contained dwell in one another. You dwell in God so that you may be contained; God dwells in you so that he may contain you, lest you fall. For the Apostle says of love itself: “Love never falls” (1 Cor. 13). How can the one whom God contains fall?

[Col. 0346D]

“And in this love has been perfected with us, so that we may have confidence,” and so forth. Whoever has confidence on the day of judgment has perfect love within him. What does it mean to have confidence on the day of judgment? It means not to fear the coming of the day of judgment. When someone first turns to repentance from evil deeds, he begins to fear the day of judgment, lest, when the just Judge appears, he himself be condemned. As he advances and is encouraged by a good way of life, however, he learns not to fear what he once feared, but rather to desire that the one awaited by all nations should come, hoping that he will be crowned with the saints because of his good works.

How we can have confidence on the day of judgment, he reveals more fully by adding:

“Because as he is, so are we in this world.” [Col. 0347A] Can a human being really be like God? We must remember what was said above: the word “as” does not always indicate equality but may indicate a certain likeness. For example, you say, “As I have ears, so does the image have ears.” Is it altogether the same? Yet you still say “as.”

Since, then, we have been made in the image of God, why should we not be like God—not in equality, but according to our measure? Hence confidence is given to us on the day of judgment, because “as he is, so are we in this world,” namely, because in this world we imitate the perfection of love whose example he daily offers us from heaven.

Concerning this the Savior says in the Gospel: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5).

[Col. 0347B] “Fear is not in love”—that is, in such love as knows how to do good even to enemies and to love them in imitation of divine goodness.

“But perfect love casts out fear”—that is, the fear of which it is said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” Through this fear, when beginning works of righteousness, a person fears lest the severe Judge of righteousness should come and, finding him insufficiently disciplined, condemn him.

That love casts out fear which, on account of the merit of righteousness, has confidence on the day of judgment. Perfect love also removes from the soul fear of present adversities. The Psalmist sought to possess this love when he prayed: “Deliver my soul from fear of the enemy.” He possessed it when he said: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, distress, famine, or persecution, nakedness, danger, or the sword?” (Rom. 8).

[Col. 0347C] “Because fear has punishment.” The conscience of sins torments the heart, since justification has not yet been accomplished. Therefore the Psalmist speaks of that perfect righteousness: “You have turned my mourning into joy; you have removed my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness, so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced” (Ps. 29)—that is, so that there may be nothing to prick my conscience. Fear pricks, but do not fear: love enters and heals what fear wounds.

[Col. 0347D] “Whoever fears has not been perfected in love.” Fear indeed has punishment, although, just as desired health follows a physician’s incision, so desired love follows fear. Nor should these words of the blessed John be thought contrary to what the Psalmist says: “The fear of the Lord is holy and endures forever” (Ps. 13).

There are two kinds of fear. One is the fear by which people fear God lest they be sent into hell; this is the fear that introduces love. But it comes in order to depart. If you still fear God because of punishments, you do not yet love the one whom you fear in this way. You do not desire good things but avoid evil ones. Yet by avoiding evil you correct yourself and begin to desire good.

Once you have begun to desire good, there will be in you holy fear—namely, fear lest you lose those very good things. This is not fear of being sent into hell, but fear lest the presence of the Lord leave you—the Lord whom you embrace and desire to enjoy forever.

[Col. 0348A]

“Let us therefore love God, because he first loved us.” Let us love him because he first loved us. For how could we love him unless he had first loved us? Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 13).

We shall be perfect in love if, just as he loved us first for no reason other than our salvation, so we love him for no reason other than love of him alone. Yet because there are those who love God only in words, the passage wisely adds:

“If anyone says, ‘I love God,’” and so forth. How do we prove that he is a liar? Listen: “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?”

What follows from this? Whoever loves his brother loves God. [Col. 0348B] It is necessary that whoever loves God should love love itself, for God is love. And lest anyone dare say, “What prevents me from loving God even if I do not love my brother?” the text rightly adds:

“And we have this commandment from God: whoever loves God must love his brother also.” How can you love the one whose commandment you hate? Who would say, “I love the emperor, but I hate his laws”? Such a person is not a true lover of God. Rather, observe how the Psalmist says: “I have loved your commandments, Lord,” and therefore confidently adds: “Give me life in your mercy” (Ps. 118).

## THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER 16

“A certain rich man existed, who was clothed in purple and fine linen, and he feasted splendidly every day. And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, who [Col. 0348C] lay at his gate, covered with sores, desiring to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him anything. Moreover, dogs came and licked his sores.

[Col. 0350B] “It happened that the beggar died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died and was buried in hell. And lifting up his eyes while he was in torments, he saw Abraham far away and Lazarus in his bosom. And he himself cried out and said: ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame.’

“And Abraham said to him: ‘Son, remember that you received good things during your life, and Lazarus likewise bad things. [Col. 0348D] But now he is comforted, while you are tormented. And in all these matters a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can anyone cross from there to us.’

“And he said: ‘Then I beg you, father, to send him to my father’s house, for I have five brothers, so that he may testify to them, lest they too come to this place of torment.’ And Abraham said to him: ‘They have Moses and the prophets; let them listen to them.’ But he said: ‘No, father Abraham; but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’ And he said to him: ‘If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead.’”

“A certain rich man existed,” and so forth. (From Bede.) [Col. 0349A] Almost no one doubts that purple is the color of royal dress, dyed from marine shellfish. For shellfish, when cut around with iron, release tears of purple color with which wool is dyed. Fine linen [*byssus*], however, is a kind of linen that is exceptionally white and soft, which the Greeks call *papátōn* [παπάτων].

The Lord had previously instructed them to make friends for themselves from the mammon of unrighteousness, so that, when we depart from this life, they may receive us into eternal dwellings. When the Pharisees heard this, they mocked him. But he supported what he had proposed with examples, showing that the rich man clothed in purple was tormented irreversibly in hell because he had neglected to make the poor Lazarus his friend, by whom he might have been received into the dwellings of life.

Some people think that the precepts of the Old Testament are stricter than those of the New. But they are deceived by careless consideration. [Col. 0349B] In the former, it is not stinginess but theft that is punished; property unjustly taken is there punished by fourfold restitution. Here, however, this rich man is not reproved for taking what belonged to another but for failing to give what belonged to him. He is not said to have oppressed anyone by force, but to have exalted himself in the possessions he had received.

From this, then, we must gather with the utmost seriousness what punishment is due to one who seizes what belongs to another, if the condemnation of hell strikes one who does not give what belongs to him. There are also some who do not think that wearing delicate and expensive clothing is a sin. But if it were not a fault, the word of God would never so attentively emphasize that the rich man who is tormented in hell had been clothed in fine linen and purple. No one seeks especially fine clothing except for empty glory, so that he may appear more honorable than others.

[Col. 0349C] We can gather the seriousness of this fault even from the opposite case: if the rejection of cheap clothing were not a virtue, the Evangelist would not have said of John: “He was clothed in camel’s hair.” But we must pay especially close attention to the order of the narrative in the mouth of Truth concerning the proud rich man and the humble poor man.

Behold, it says: “A certain rich man existed.” And immediately it adds:

“And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus.” Certainly, among the people, the names of the rich are usually better known than those of the poor. What, then, is the reason that, when the Lord speaks of a poor man and a rich man, he gives the poor man’s name but does not give the rich man’s name, except that God knows and approves the humble but is ignorant of the proud?

[Col. 0349D] Hence, to some who were proud of the power of their miracles, he will say at the end: “I do not know where you are from” (Matt. 7); “Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity.” But to Moses it is said: “I know you by name” (Exod. 33).

Thus he says of the rich man, “A certain man”; of the poor man, “A beggar named Lazarus,” as if he were plainly saying: “I know the humble poor man; I do not know the proud rich man. I know the former through approval; I disregard the latter through the judgment of rejection.”

“He lay at his gate, covered with sores, desiring to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table, and dogs came and licked his sores.” The beggar Lazarus, covered with sores, lay before the rich man’s gate. In this matter the Lord carried out two judgments.

[Col. 0350A] The rich man might perhaps have had some excuse if the poor and ulcerated Lazarus had not lain before his gate—if he had been far away, if his poverty had not been an unwelcome sight to the rich man’s eyes. Conversely, if the rich man had been far from the eyes of the ulcerated poor man, the poor man would have endured less temptation in his mind.

But by placing the needy and ulcerated man before the gate of the rich man, who abounded in luxuries, the Lord, in one and the same circumstance, both imposed upon the rich man an accumulation of condemnation because he saw the poor man and did not show compassion, and tested the poor man daily by the sight of the rich man. Poverty alone would certainly have been enough to afflict him, even if he had been healthy; illness alone would have been enough, even if assistance had been available.

But in order to test the poor man more fully, both poverty and illness wasted him away. Moreover, he saw the rich man going out supported by a retinue of attendants, while he himself, in sickness and poverty, was visited by no one. That no one came to visit him is testified by the dogs, which freely licked his sores.

Through one and the same circumstance, therefore, almighty God displayed two judgments when he allowed poor Lazarus to lie before the rich man’s gate: the impious rich man increased the punishment of his own condemnation.

“It happened that the beggar died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died and was buried in hell.” (From Augustine.) Abraham’s bosom is the rest of the blessed poor, theirs being the kingdom of heaven, into which they are received after this life. The burial of hell is the depth of punishments, which after this life devours the proud and the merciless.

[Col. 0350C] “And lifting up his eyes while he was in torments, he saw Abraham far away and Lazarus in his bosom. And he himself cried out and said: ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame.’”

Oh, how great is the sublimity of God’s judgments! How strictly the recompense of good and evil deeds is carried out! It was said above that in this life Lazarus sought the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him anything. Now, concerning the punishment of the rich man, it is said that he desires water to be dripped into his mouth from the tip of Lazarus’s finger.

The one who refused to give even the smallest morsel from his table, once placed in hell, was reduced to seeking even the smallest relief. But we must pay close attention to why the rich man, placed in the fire, asks that his tongue be cooled.

[Col. 0350D] It is customary for sacred eloquence sometimes to say one thing while suggesting another through that same statement. Above, the Lord had described this proud rich man not as wasting his time in talk but as feasting excessively. He did not describe him as guilty of loquacity, but as sinning through gluttony, together with pride and stinginess.

But because loquacity commonly abounds at banquets, the one who is said here to have feasted badly is said to burn more grievously in his tongue in hell. What follows must be weighed with very great fear:

“And Abraham said to him: ‘Son, remember that you received good things during your life, and Lazarus likewise bad things. But now he is comforted, while you are tormented.’”

[Col. 0351A] Behold, when it says, “You received good things during your life,” it indicates that this rich man too had possessed something good, from which he received good things in this life. Again, when it says of Lazarus that he received bad things, it plainly shows that Lazarus too had some evil that needed to be cleansed.

But the fire of poverty cleansed the evils of Lazarus, while the happiness of a passing life rewarded the good things of the rich man.

And in all these things a great chasm has been fixed between you and us, so that those who wish to cross over from here to you cannot, nor can they cross from there to here. Here it must be carefully considered how it can be said, “Those who wish to cross over to you cannot,” for there is no doubt that those who are in hell desire to cross over to the lot of the blessed. But how is it said that those who have already been received into the lot of blessedness wish to cross over to those who are tormented in hell? Yet just as the reprobate desire to cross over to the elect—that is, to depart from the affliction of their punishments—so it belongs to the righteous to cross over in mind, through mercy, to those who are afflicted and placed in torments, and to wish to free them. But those who wish to cross over from the seat of the blessed to the afflicted and those placed in torments cannot, because although the souls of the righteous possess mercy in the goodness of their nature, once joined to the justice of their Creator they are then bound by such uprightness that they are moved by no compassion toward the reprobate. But after hope has been taken away from the rich man burning there, his mind hastens toward the relatives whom he had left behind, because the punishment of the reprobate eventually teaches them, though uselessly, to love, so that even then they spiritually love their own whom here, while loving their sins, they did not love themselves. Hence it now follows:

[Col. 0351C]

“I beg you therefore, father, to send him to my father’s house, for I have five brothers,” etc.

Here it should be noted how many things are heaped upon the burning rich man for his punishment. For both knowledge and memory are preserved for his penalty. He recognizes Lazarus, whom he despised, and he remembers his brothers, whom he left behind. His retribution in regard to the poor man would not be complete if he did not recognize him in the retribution, and his punishment in the fire would not be complete if he did not fear for his own the very thing he himself suffers. Thus, in order that sinners may be punished more severely in their torment, they both see the glory of those whom they despised and are tortured by the punishment of those whom they loved uselessly. It should indeed be believed that, before the retribution of the final judgment, the unjust see certain righteous people in repose, so that, seeing them in joy, they may be tormented not only by their own punishment but also by the good fortune of those others. The righteous, however, always behold the unjust in torment, so that their joy may increase from seeing the evil from which they mercifully escaped, and so that they may give greater thanks to their Redeemer, the more they see in others what they themselves could have suffered had they been neglected. For those who see the glory of their Creator can see nothing that takes place in creation without being able to behold it.

And Abraham said to him: “They have Moses and the prophets; let them listen to them.” But the one who had despised the words of God thought that his followers could not listen to these; therefore the rich man answered:

[Col. 0352A]

“No, father Abraham; but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.”

To him the truthful sentence is immediately spoken:

“If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead.”

For, plainly, those who despise the words of the Law will fulfill the commands of the Redeemer, who rose from the dead, all the less easily because these commands are more subtle; and it is certainly clear that those who refuse to fulfill his sayings also refuse, without doubt, to believe in him.

But whom does this rich man signify allegorically—the one who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day—if not the Jewish people? It possessed an outward observance of life and used the delights of the Law it had received for splendor, not for usefulness. And whom does Lazarus, covered with sores, figuratively express if not the Gentile people? When converted to God, it was not ashamed to confess its sins; thus it had a wound in its skin. For in a wound of the skin, poison is drawn from the inward parts and bursts outward. What, then, is confession of sins except a kind of breaking open of wounds? In confession, the poison of sin is beneficially opened, although it had been festering harmfully in the mind.

But wounded Lazarus desired to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him any. For that proud people despised admitting any Gentile to knowledge of the Law. Since it possessed the teaching of the Law not for charity but for arrogance, it swelled with pride as though over riches received; and because words flowed from its knowledge, they fell from its table like crumbs.

But, on the other hand, dogs licked the wounds of the man lying there. In sacred language, preachers are sometimes understood by dogs. For when a dog’s tongue licks a wound, it heals it; so holy teachers, when they instruct us in the confession of our sin, touch the wound of the mind with their tongue, as it were. And because by speaking they rescue us from sins, they restore us to health by touching our wounds. Hence Lazarus is rightly interpreted as “helped,” because those who heal his wounds through correction by the tongue help him toward deliverance.

Now it happened that both died: the rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen was buried in hell, while Lazarus was led by angels into Abraham’s bosom. What does Abraham’s bosom signify except the secret repose of the Father, of which the Truth says: “Many will come from the east and the west, and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. But the sons of this kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness” (Matthew 8).

The one who is said to have been clothed in purple is rightly called a son of the kingdom. From far away he raises his eyes to see Lazarus, because while unbelievers are below through the punishment of their condemnation, the faithful also, before the day of the final judgment, look upon the repose above them, though they can in no way thereafter contemplate their joys. What they see is far away because they do not attain there by merit.

He is shown to burn more intensely in his tongue when he says: “Send Lazarus, so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame.” The unbelieving people held the words of the Law in their mouth, but despised keeping them in practice. There, therefore, it will burn more intensely where it showed that it knew what it refused to do. It desires to be touched by the tip of the finger because, given over to eternal punishments, it longs to share even in the smallest degree in the activity of the righteous.

He is answered that he received good things in this life because he thought he possessed all his joy in transitory happiness. Here the righteous too can receive good things, and yet not receive them as recompense, because while they desire better things—that is, eternal things—the good things that were present, although truly good, seem to them, amid their holy desires, to be nothing.

Among these things it must be noted that he is told: “Remember, son.” For Abraham calls him son, yet does not free him from torment, because the faithful fathers who preceded this unbelieving people, seeing that many had strayed from their faith, do not rescue them from torments through any compassion, although they recognize them as sons according to the flesh.

The rich man, placed in torment, says that he has five brothers, because that same proud Jewish people, already condemned in great part, knows that the followers whom it left on earth are devoted to the five bodily senses. Thus he expresses by the number five the brothers whom he left behind, because, placed in hell, he grieves that they do not rise to spiritual understanding.

He asks that Lazarus be sent to them, and he is told that they have Moses and the prophets. But he says that they will not believe unless someone rises from the dead. He is immediately answered: “If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe him if someone rises from the dead.”

Certainly the Truth says concerning Moses: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5). What is said in Abraham’s reply is therefore fulfilled. The Lord rose from the dead, but because the Jewish people refused to believe Moses, it also scorned believing in him who rose from the dead. And because it refused to understand Moses’ words spiritually, it did not reach God, about whom Moses had spoken.

## Third Week after Pentecost

### First Epistle of the Blessed Apostle John, Chapter 3

“Do not marvel if the world hates you. We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love remains in death. Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that every murderer does not have eternal life remaining in him. By this we have come to know the love of God: that he laid down his life for us; and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers. Whoever possesses the substance of this world and sees his brother suffering need, yet closes his heart against him—how does the love of God remain in him? My little children, let us not love in word or with the tongue, but in deed and in truth.”

“Do not marvel if the world hates you” (From Bede). By “the world” he means lovers of the world. Nor is this surprising, because those who love the world cannot love a brother separated from love of the world and intent only upon heavenly desires. Religion is an abomination to the sinner, as Scripture testifies.

“We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brothers.” Let no one falsely exalt himself over his virtues; let no one fear the poverty of his strength beyond measure. Whoever is full of brotherly love gives clear evidence, for he belongs to the lot of the elect and has deserved to have a portion in the land of the living.

“Whoever does not love his brother remains in death.” He means the death of the soul. “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18). The life of the flesh is the soul; the life of the soul is God. The death of the body is to lose the soul; the death of the soul is to lose God. Hence it is clear that all of us are born dead in soul in this light, carrying original sin from Adam. But by the grace of Christ, through regeneration, it is brought about for the faithful that they can live in soul. The word of baptism and the mystery of faith benefit only those who sincerely love the brothers; they carry them from death to life. Therefore it must be noted that he does not say, “Whoever does not love will come into death,” as though he were speaking of the eternal punishment that awaits sinners in the future. Rather, he says, “Whoever does not love remains in death”—in that death, certainly, from which he could rise even in this life if he perfectly loved his brothers. For this reason God says in the Apocalypse: “Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection; over these the second death has no power” (Apocalypse 20).

“Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (From Augustine). If someone despised brotherly hatred, would he not also despise murder in his heart? He does not move his hands to kill a person, yet he is already held by the Lord as a murderer: the other lives, but this one is already judged a killer.

“And you know that every murderer does not have eternal life remaining in him.” Even here he may be seen to live among the saints through faith, yet he does not have perpetual life remaining in himself. For when the time of retribution comes, he will be condemned with Cain, who was from the evil one; so too will the one be condemned who is held guilty of murder by discord, dissension, and lack of peace with his brothers. It must be noted that he does not say absolutely, “A murderer does not have life remaining in him,” but “every murderer”—that is, not only the one who attacks his brother with a sword, but also the one who pursues him with hatred.

“By this we have come to know the love of God,” etc. We have learned what perfect love ought to be in us from the example of the Lord’s Passion. “No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends.” Hence Paul also says: “God commends his love toward us, because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5).

The blessed Peter was admonished to possess this love when the Lord said: “Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep.” He answered that he loved him, and immediately heard: “When you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go.” “This he said,” the Gospel declares, “to signify by what death he would glorify God” (John, final chapter). To the one to whom he had entrusted his sheep after he confessed his love, he taught that, as testimony to perfect love, he should lay down his life for those same sheep.

“And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.” But someone might say: “How can I possess this love?” Do not quickly despair of yourself; perhaps it has been born in you, but is not yet perfect. Nourish it, lest it be suffocated. And, you ask, how do I know that love has been born in me, so that I may nourish it? Listen to what follows:

“Whoever possesses the substance of the world and sees that his brother is in need,” etc. Here is where love begins: if you are not yet able to die for your brother, be able now to give your possessions to your brother. For if you do not sympathize with your brother who is suffering hardship, then the love of the Father, from whom both of you have been regenerated, certainly does not remain in you.

“My little children, let us not love in word or with the tongue, but in deed and in truth.” In deed, that is, when a brother or sister is naked and lacks daily food, let us give them what the body requires. Similarly, when we see them lacking spiritual gifts, let us provide for their need whatever we can. In truth, let us bestow these same benefits upon them with a sincere intention, not for human praise, not for ostentation, and not to the injury of others who, though endowed with greater possessions, have done nothing of the kind. For whatever mind is stained by such blemishes cannot contain the purity of truth, even if it appears to devote works of love to its neighbors. “By this we know that we are from the truth”: that is, when we perform works in truth, it is evident that we are from the truth, which is God, since in our measure we imitate his perfection.

### Gospel of Luke, Chapter 14

“A certain man made a great supper and invited many. And he sent his servant at the hour of supper to say to those who had been invited that they should come, because everything was now ready. And they all began together to make excuses. The first said: ‘I have bought a farm, and I must go out and see it; I ask you to excuse me.’ Another said: ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to test them; I ask you to excuse me.’ And another said: ‘I have taken a wife, and therefore I cannot come.’ And the servant returned and reported this to his master. Then the head of the household, becoming angry, said to his servant: ‘Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor and the weak, the blind and the lame.’ And the servant said: ‘Lord, it has been done as you commanded, and there is still room.’ And the Lord said to the servant: ‘Go out into the roads and hedges and compel them to enter, so that my house may be filled. But I tell you that none of those men who were invited will taste my supper.’”

“A certain man made a great supper and invited many” (From Jerome). Who is this man except the one of whom it is said through the prophet: “And he is a man, and who will know him?” He made a great supper because he prepared for us satisfaction in inward sweetness. He invites many, but few come, because sometimes those who are subject to him through faith contradict his eternal banquet by living badly.

“And he sent his servant at the hour of supper to say to those who had been invited that they should come,” etc. What is the hour of supper except the end of the world, in which we certainly are, as Paul long ago bears witness, saying: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come.” If, then, it is already the hour of supper when we are called, we ought to excuse ourselves from God’s banquet all the less, since we see that the end of the age has drawn near. This banquet of God is called not lunch but supper because supper remains after lunch. And because God’s eternal banquet will be prepared for us at the end, it was right that it should be called not lunch but supper.

But whom does this servant, who is sent by the head of the household to invite the guests, signify except the order of preachers? “Everything is now ready” to remove our distaste, because, to wipe away the tepidity of our mind, that unique Lamb who took away the sins of the world has been slain for us at the Lord’s supper.

“And they all began together to make excuses.” God offers what ought to have been requested; without being asked, he wishes to give what could scarcely have been hoped for, since he deigns to grant it when sought. Yet he is despised: he announces that the delights of eternal resurrection are ready, and still all make excuses. Some say, “We do not wish to make excuses; we rejoice that we are both invited to and will reach that banquet of heavenly refreshment.” They speak truly, if they do not love earthly things more than heavenly things, and if they are not more occupied with bodily matters than spiritual ones. Thus the very reason for the excuses is added when it immediately follows:

“The first said to him: ‘I have bought a farm, and I must go out to see it,’” etc. What is signified by the farm except earthly property? Therefore he went out to see the farm who thinks only about outward things because of his possessions.

“And another said: ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to test them; I ask you,’” etc. What do we understand by the five yoke of oxen except the five bodily senses? They are rightly also called yokes because they are doubled in both sexes. Since these bodily senses cannot grasp inward things but know only what is external, and, abandoning what is within, touch what is outside, curiosity is rightly signified through them. For curiosity is a serious vice: while it leads someone’s mind outward to investigate the life of another, it always hides his own inward life from him. For this reason it is said of the same five yoke of oxen: “I am going to test them,” since testing sometimes belongs to curiosity.

But it must be noted that both the one who excuses himself because of the farm and the one who excuses himself in order to test the yoke of oxen mingle words of humility with their excuse, saying:

“I ask you, excuse me.” When he says “I ask,” yet disdains to come, humility sounds in his voice, but pride in his action. And behold, each perverse person recognizes this when he hears it, yet does not cease doing what he recognizes as wrong. For when we say to someone acting perversely, “Convert; follow the Lord; abandon the world,” where are we calling him except to the Lord’s supper? But when he answers, “Pray for me, because I am a sinner; I cannot do this,” what else is he doing except asking and making excuses? By saying, “I am a sinner,” he indicates humility; by adding, “I cannot convert,” he displays pride.

“And another said: ‘I have taken a wife, and therefore I cannot come.’” What is understood by the wife except carnal pleasure? Although marriage is good and was established by divine providence for the propagation of offspring, some people seek through it not the fruitfulness of children but the desires of pleasure. Therefore an unjust thing can not incongruously be signified by a just thing.

The supreme head of the household thus invites us to the supper of the eternal banquet, but one person is occupied by earthly care, another is consumed by shrewd attention to the actions of others, and the mind of another is defiled by carnal pleasure. Each person, full of distaste, does not hasten to the feasts of eternal life.

“And the servant returned and reported these things to his master. Then the head of the household, becoming angry, said to his servant: ‘Go out quickly into the streets and lanes, and bring in here the poor and the weak, the blind and the lame.’” Behold: the one who clings to earthly property more than is right refuses to come to the Lord’s supper; the one who sweats through the labor of curiosity rejects the nourishment of life prepared for him; the one who clings to carnal desires spurns the food of the spiritual banquet.

Since the proud refuse to come, the poor are chosen. Why is this, except because, in Paul’s words, “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Corinthians 1)? The poor and weak are those who are weak in their own judgment and in their own eyes. For the poor may also be, as it were, strong: those who, placed in poverty, are nevertheless proud. The blind are those who possess no light of understanding. The lame are those who do not have straight steps in action.

Since the vices of character are signified by weakness of the limbs, it is plainly clear that just as those who were called and refused to come were sinners, so these too who are invited and come are sinners. But proud sinners are rejected, while humble sinners are chosen. The Lord therefore chooses those whom the world despises, because contempt itself often recalls a person to himself.

The poor and weak, the blind and lame, are called and come, because the weak and those despised in this world often hear God’s voice all the more quickly, since in this world they have nothing in which to take delight. But after the poor have been led to the supper, let us hear what the servant adds:

“Lord, it has been done as you commanded, and there is still room.” Many such people were gathered from Judea to the Lord’s supper, but the multitude from the Israelite people that believed did not fill the place of the heavenly banquet. A large number of Jews has already entered, but there is still room: space remains in the kingdom where the multitude of the Gentiles should be received. Hence the same servant is told:

“Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter, so that my house may be filled.” When the Lord invites people from the lanes and streets to the supper, he signifies that people who knew how to observe the Law within civic society. But when he commands that his guests be gathered from the roads and hedges, he plainly seeks to gather a rustic people—that is, the Gentiles.

It must be noted that in this third invitation he does not say “invite,” but “compel them to enter.” For there are some who understand that good things ought to be done but desist from doing them. As we said above, it often happens to these people that the adversity of this world strikes them amid their carnal desires. Frequently they waste away through a long illness, collapse under the weight of injuries, or are afflicted by heavier losses. But, reproved amid their own desires, they turn their hearts to the Lord.

Those who, broken by the adversities of this world, return to the love of God and are corrected concerning the desires of the present life—what are they except people compelled to enter? But the sentence that follows immediately is exceedingly fearful. For he says:

“But I tell you that none of those men who were invited,” etc. Behold: he calls through himself, calls through angels, calls through apostles, often calls through miracles, often calls through scourges, sometimes calls through the prosperity of this world, sometimes through adversity. Let no one despise him, lest, while making excuses when called, he be unable to enter when he wishes to do so.

## Fourth Week after Pentecost

### Epistle of the Blessed Apostle Peter, Chapter 5

“Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of visitation, casting all your anxiety upon him, because he cares for you. Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, strong in faith, knowing that your brothers throughout the world undergo the same suffering. But the God of all grace, who has called you into his eternal glory in Christ Jesus, after you have suffered a little, will himself perfect, confirm, strengthen, and establish you. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.”

“Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of tribulation,” etc. He grants this grace to the humble: the more they have been humbled for his sake during the time of struggle, the more gloriously they will be exalted by him at the time of retribution.

Humiliation can be understood in many ways here: first, that by which a person beginning the way of virtue is beneficially humbled for the cleansing of the sins he has committed; then, that which, through the spontaneous devotion of the mind, the more perfect offer to God or to their neighbors in peace concerning the things around them; and also that by which, when storms of persecution assail, the unconquered mind is armed through the virtue of patience. Every kind of devoted humility is followed by this reward: those who humble themselves during the time of their pilgrimage will be exalted at the time of his visitation.

“Be sober; watch, because your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.” In explaining this sentence, let us present not our own words but those of the blessed Cyprian:

“He prowls around each of us and, like an enemy besieging enclosed walls, examines and tests whether any part of the body is less stable and less secure, through whose hearing he may penetrate inward. He offers alluring and easy pleasures to the eyes, so that through sight he may destroy chastity. He tests the ears with melodious music, so that by the force of sweeter sound he may loosen the hearing and soften Christian strength. He provokes the tongue with abuse; he incites the hand to the wantonness of slaughter through insulting injuries, so that he may make a person fraudulent. He sets unjust profits before us, so that he may capture the soul with money; he introduces harmful shortcuts. He promises earthly honors so that he may deprive us of heaven; he displays false things so that he may steal away the true. And when he cannot deceive secretly, he openly threatens, directing the terror of turbulent persecution against us—always restless and always hostile in order to overcome the servants of God, crafty in peace and violent in persecution. Therefore the mind must stand equipped against all the devil’s deceitful ambushes and open threats, armed and always as ready to resist as the enemy is always ready to attack.”

“Resist him, strong in faith, knowing that the same suffering is inflicted upon your brotherhood that is in the world,” etc. “Be all the stronger in faith,” he says, “and have all the greater confidence for overcoming the devil’s cunning, since it is clear that you are not tempted alone. The very suffering that wearies you is also common to that Church of Christ which is throughout the whole world—that is, to your brotherhood. And since the righteous have always suffered from the foundation of the world, let it shame you that you alone among all are unable to endure.”

### Another Exposition

“Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God”—that is, under the power of God. The hand of God is understood as both his Son and his power.

The Son, where he says: “Send forth your hand from on high; rescue me and deliver me.”

Power, where he says: “Into your hands I commend my spirit,” and similarly elsewhere.

“So that he may exalt you.” For the Gospel says: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted.”

“At the time of visitation”—that is, on the day of judgment.

“Casting all your anxiety,” etc.—so that, instructed by him, you may be able to resist your enemies bravely. The Psalmist says: “Cast your care upon God, and he himself will nourish you.”

“Because he cares for you.” For “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers”; and whoever touches them is as one who touches the apple of his eye.

“Be sober”—that is, temperate, for sobriety signifies temperance.

“Watch.” This vigilance is understood spiritually, not carnally. “Our struggle,” says the Apostle, “is not against flesh and blood, but against spiritual wickedness.”

“Because your adversary the devil,” etc. Sometimes the devil is called a lion because of open persecutions; sometimes he is named a dragon because of hidden ambushes.

“Resist him, strong in faith”—following the example of Christ resisting the devil in the desert.

“Knowing the same suffering,” etc.—that is, knowing that the same suffering which you endure is also endured without ceasing by your brotherhood throughout the world, which is the universal Church.

“The God of all grace”—that is, of manifold grace. For every good that a person possesses, he receives through God’s grace in order to possess it.

[Col. 0360A]

“Who has called us,” etc. The glory of this age is temporal, while the glory of the age to come is eternal.

“In Christ Jesus our Lord”—that is, through the incarnation of Jesus Christ our Lord.

“After you have suffered a little”—that is, after a brief suffering we are called into eternal rest. As in the prophetic saying: “See that I have labored a little, and have found great rest for myself.”

“He himself will perfect, confirm, strengthen.” He will perfect the body, confirm the mind, and strengthen the spirit; or, he will perfect us through eternal reward, confirm us in good works, and strengthen us in faith in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

### Gospel of Luke, Chapter 15

“Tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to Jesus to hear him. And the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying: ‘This man receives sinners and eats with them.’ And he spoke this parable to them, saying: ‘Which of you is the man who has a hundred sheep, and if he loses one of them, does he not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that was lost until he finds it? And when he has found it, he places it upon his shoulders, rejoicing; and when he comes home, he calls together his friends and neighbors, saying to them: “Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost.” I tell you that thus there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance. Or what woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp, overturn the house, and search carefully until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying: “Rejoice with me, because I have found the drachma that I had lost.” Thus, I tell you, there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.’”

“Tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to Jesus,” etc. Because not only can a righteous person sin through sluggishness, but a sinner can also recover through diligence, after it had been related that salt which had lost its savor ought to be thrown outside, a company of penitents is immediately described as admitted inside. They drew near to hear the word of God and were received not only for conversation but also for eating together.

When the Pharisees saw this, they disdained it, because true righteousness has compassion, while false righteousness has disdain. Yet the righteous too may rightly be indignant at sinners: one thing is done from the pattern of pride, another from zeal for discipline. But because these people were sick in such a way that they did not know themselves to be sick, the heavenly physician heals them with gentle remedies, offers them a kindly example, and presses down the swelling of the wound in their hearts. For he says:

“Which of you is the man who has a hundred sheep,” etc. Behold: in a marvelous dispensation of mercy, the Truth offered a comparison in which a human being could recognize himself, yet which specially pertained to the author of humanity.

Because the number one hundred is perfect, he had a hundred sheep when he created the nature of angels and of human beings. But one sheep was lost when humanity, by sinning, abandoned the pastures of life. He left the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness because he left the highest choirs of angels in heaven.

But why is heaven called a wilderness except because a wilderness is called an abandoned place? Humanity abandoned heaven when it sinned. The ninety-nine sheep remained in the wilderness when the Lord was seeking one on earth, because the number of rational creatures—namely, angels and human beings—which had been created to see God, was diminished when humanity was lost. And so, in order that the perfect total of the sheep might be restored in heaven, lost humanity was sought on earth.

“And when he has found it, he places it upon his shoulders, rejoicing.” He placed the sheep upon his shoulders because, taking human nature upon himself, he himself bore our sins.

“And when he comes home, he calls together his friends,” etc. Having found the sheep, he returned home because our shepherd, after restoring humanity, returned to the heavenly kingdom. There he found friends and neighbors: the choirs of angels, who are his friends because they continually preserve his will in their own steadfastness. They are also his neighbors because through the constancy of vision they enjoy his brightness.

It must be noted that he does not say, “Rejoice with the sheep that has been found,” but “with me,” because our life is his joy, and when we are brought back to heaven, we complete the solemnity of his joy.

“I tell you that thus there will be joy in heaven,” etc. There is more joy in heaven over converted sinners than over righteous people who remain standing, because often those who know themselves not to be burdened by any great weight of sins do stand on the way of righteousness and commit nothing unlawful, yet do not anxiously long for their heavenly homeland. They allow themselves the use of lawful things in proportion to their memory that they have committed no unlawful deeds, and often remain sluggish in practicing outstanding good works because they feel very secure that they have committed no serious evils.

By contrast, sometimes those who remember having done certain unlawful things are pierced by their very sorrow, grow ardent in the love of God, and exercise themselves in great virtues. Thus there is more joy in heaven over the sinner who is converted than over the righteous person who remains standing, because even a commander in battle loves more the soldier who, after fleeing, returns and presses the enemy fiercely than the one who never turned his back and never did anything courageous.

Yet amid these things it must be known that there are many righteous people whose life contains such great joy that no repentance of sinners can in any way be preferred to them. Many are conscious of no evils in themselves, yet they exert themselves in such ardent affliction as though they were distressed by every sin. They reject all lawful things, gird themselves nobly for contempt of the world, rejoice in lamentation, humble themselves in everything, and, just as some lament sins of action, so they lament sins of thought.

From this, then, it may be gathered how much joy it gives God when a righteous person weeps humbly, if there is joy in heaven when an unrighteous person condemns through repentance what he has done wrongly.

[Col. 0362B] Or what woman having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, etc. He who is signified by the shepherd is also signified by the woman; for he is himself God, and he is also the Wisdom of God, because the image is represented on the drachma. The woman lost the drachma when humanity, created in the image of God, withdrew through sin from the likeness of its creator. But the woman lights a lamp, because the Wisdom of God appeared in human form. For a lamp is light in an earthen vessel. Light in an earthen vessel is divinity in the flesh. Once the lamp has been lit, the woman turns the house upside down, because as soon as his divinity shone forth through the flesh, all our conscience was shaken. The house is overturned when the human conscience is disturbed by consideration of its guilt. Once the house has been overturned, the drachma is found, because when the human conscience is disturbed, the likeness of the creator is restored in the human being.

[Col. 0362C] And when she has found it, she calls together her friends, etc. Who are these friends or neighbors, if not those heavenly powers already mentioned above, who are as close to the heavenly Wisdom as they approach it through the continual vision granted by grace? But we must consider why this woman is said to have had ten drachmas. The Lord created the natures of angels and human beings in order that they might know him; and when he willed them to endure unto eternity, he plainly created them in his likeness. The woman had ten drachmas because there are nine orders of angels; but, so that the number of the elect might be completed, the human being was created as the tenth. The human being did not perish from his creator even after the Fall, because eternal Wisdom, shining forth through the flesh by its miracles, restored him from the light of the earthen vessel.

[Col. 0362D] Thus, I say to you, there will be joy before the angels, etc. To practice repentance is both to mourn the evils one has committed and not to commit the things that ought to be mourned. For whoever mourns some sins in such a way that he nevertheless commits others either still does not know how to practice repentance or pretends not to. What good does it do if someone laments the sins of lust while still panting with the passions of greed? Or what benefit is there if he already grieves the faults of anger while still wasting away in the flames of envy? But what we are saying is still far too little: the person who mourns sins must, by mourning, refrain altogether from committing them. For one must think with the utmost care that whoever remembers having committed unlawful acts should strive to abstain even from certain lawful things, so that by this means he may make satisfaction to his creator; and whoever has committed forbidden acts ought to cut himself off even from things that are permitted.

## THE FIFTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

### READING FROM THE LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0363A] > “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us. For the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the children of God. For creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope, because creation itself will also be set free from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. For we know that every creature groans and labors in childbirth until now. And not only it, but we ourselves also, who have the first fruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we await the adoption of the children of God, the redemption of our body in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

[Col. 0363B] “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us.” If anyone considers that, in order for a person to become a son of the Most High God, an heir of his goodness, and a sharer in the glory of Christ—the only-begotten Son of God—even if he remains blameless in the observance of all God’s commandments and the Lord’s ordinances, and perseveres in them with an ever-watchful mind; if he compares with the future glory that will be revealed in the saints, the things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the human heart,” all the kinds of punishment that human nature can endure, whether externally or internally, he can understand how Paul, considering these matters more deeply, said: “I consider, then, that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us.” Nothing worthy of, or comparable to, the future glory can in fact be found. For how can you compare what is mortal with what is immortal, visible things with invisible, temporal things with eternal, or perishable things with things everlasting?

[Col. 0363C] “For the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the children of God.” What creation is it that awaits the revelation of the children of God? “This creation,” he says, “which is now subjected to vanity.” It is subjected not willingly or of its own accord, but by the will of the one who subjected it. Therefore it has been subjected for his sake—not, however, on the condition that it remain forever subject to vanity, but with a certain hope. And he recalls what this hope is when he says: “For creation itself,” he says, “will also be set free from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.”

[Col. 0363D] “For creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope, because creation itself will also be set free,” etc. What is this vanity to which creation is said to be subjected, and what is this corruption from whose slavery it hopes to be set free? It seems to me that these words refer to the material and corruptible substance of bodies. For corruption rules nothing other than the body. The inner human being, however, who was created according to God and made in the image of God, is incorruptible and invisible; according to its proper nature it can even be called incorporeal. The outer human being, on the other hand, is called corporeal and corruptible. Therefore Paul also said: “For although our outward human being is being corrupted, the inward one is being renewed.” The renewal of the inner human being is that of the rational being, the mind in the knowledge of God and in its capacity for the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0364A] But, so that we may briefly and concisely commit something concerning such profound matters even to these little pages, let us gather an image from the very substance of the inner human being—that is, of the soul and mind. How is creation subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope? Let us, if it seems appropriate, place Paul himself before us. His soul or mind, which is his inner human being, surpasses and rises above everything corporeal, everything visible, everything subject to the senses and to sight, and becomes capable of the divine nature itself. Yet this soul, so great and of such a kind, is subject to the slavery of the body’s corruption and bound to its vanity.

[Col. 0364B] Consider the necessities of the body: the desire for food, the foulness of digestion, the shamefulness of producing offspring—how offspring is conceived, how it is born, how it is nourished—and see how much vanity and how much corruption there is in these things. To this the noble and rational creation of the soul is subject, though unwillingly. Yet it is subjected in hope, awaiting the time when it will be set free, when the time of the freedom of the children of God has arrived. This is what the Apostle was also saying more plainly elsewhere about himself: “While we are in this dwelling, we groan” (II Cor. V).

[Col. 0364C] If you also consider the angels according to Paul’s statement that “all ministering spirits are sent for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation” (Heb. I), you will understand that they undergo something of this kind and are subject to this condition. I believe that they too are unwilling, but are subjected because of him who subjected them in hope. For who can resist his will? I am also led by prophetic utterances to understand something of this kind concerning the archangels. What greater vanity and corruption could you find than waging wars in this world and stirring up battles between kings and nations?

[Col. 0364D] See, then, that even in these matters the chief duty of the archangelic work is found, as the prophet Daniel bears witness when he says that the archangel speaks to him and tells him that he fought against the prince of Persia: “No one,” he says, “came to my aid except Michael, your prince.” Through each of these points, therefore, it is shown that rational creation is subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope. For hope consists in the expectation that one day it will cease from these bodily and corruptible things. This rational creation has the expectation that the revelation of the children of God will take place. For their sake the angels are sent to minister, so that they too may receive the inheritance of salvation together with those whom they have served; so that of heavenly and earthly beings there may be one flock and one shepherd, and God may be all in all.

[Col. 0365A] “For we know that every creature groans,” etc. Although creation is subjected unwillingly, nevertheless, because it yields to the will of the one who subjected it, it displays a certain affection and love toward those for whose sake it appears to be subjected; it grieves over their pains and groans over their groanings. But if, as is found in other copies, we read “it groans together and labors in childbirth,” we shall understand the sense to be that the Apostle says he has begotten through the Gospel those whom he brings to the light through faith in Christ. Or, as he said of others: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV). Creation, therefore, labors in childbirth for those whom it regenerates unto salvation.

[Col. 0365B] “Not only it, but we ourselves also,” etc. In this statement we understand rather the following point: in accordance with what we discussed above, there are many ministering spirits sent for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation. Under these, each believer is trained, as it were under guardians and administrators, until the time fixed by the father—that is, until the soul reaches the lawful age of perfection. At that point, having surpassed the spirit of slavery that he received in fear, by which he was guarded as under a pedagogue, he becomes worthy to receive the Spirit of adoption, the first fruits of the Spirit, through which, adopted as a son, he may be joined to the firstborn of the Church who are in heaven.

And just as it differs greatly to be a son rather than a slave, so the Holy Spirit differs greatly from the ministering spirits. Paul says that he and those like him possess the first fruits of this Spirit. Let this be one way in which we have been able to investigate the meaning of this passage.

[Col. 0365C] Let us now consider another. We read in the Apostle Paul himself that many gifts or graces of the Holy Spirit are called “spirits,” when he says: “Now, since you are zealous for spiritual gifts, seek that you may abound for the building up of the Church” (I Cor. XII). And elsewhere: “The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets” (II Cor. XIV). He says that the spirits of the prophets are subject to them, not as inferiors to a superior, but because one who possesses the spirit of prophecy is not compelled to speak unwillingly, as are those who have unclean spirits. Rather, he speaks when he wishes and when reason requires it; but when it does not seem appropriate to speak, he remains silent, knowing well that there is a time for speaking and a time for keeping silent.

[Col. 0365D] Therefore it is not said as an insult that the spirits are subject to the prophets, but as a matter of ordering, just as we understand the statement concerning the Savior: “Then the Son himself will also be subject to the one who subjected all things to him” (I Cor. XV). Here too he is called subject not as an inferior. For how can he be called inferior who is the Son and is all that the Father is? “For all things that are yours,” he says, “are mine.” But he is said to be subject in those whom he subjects to the Father who believe in him, because he says that he is in each one of them, and declares that in them he is hungry, thirsty, and naked, and confesses that in them he is fed and clothed. Therefore he himself is also said to be subject in them. But let these matters be understood as expressed in a certain excess of meaning.

Let us now return to the subject. Paul calls the various gifts of the Spirit “many spirits.” Whatever this multitude of gifts comprises, the Apostles undoubtedly received the highest and greatest gifts, so that they might be capable—as Paul himself says—of being “ministers of the New Testament” and of filling the Gospel “from Jerusalem and all around as far as Illyricum” (II Cor. III). This gift of the Holy Spirit, therefore, which was bestowed upon them more sublimely and excellently than upon others, he rightly called the first fruits of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0366A] And therefore he says: “But we ourselves also,” by which he seems specifically to designate apostolic dignity. “We ourselves,” he says—that is, the Apostles—“who have received the first fruits of the Spirit,” who were chosen for this purpose, that we might receive the first fruits of the Spirit, “we ourselves also groan inwardly.” He says that no creation is so free from pains and groanings that even we ourselves, who have received the highest and choicest gifts from the Holy Spirit, still grieve and groan, awaiting the adoption as sons—that is, the perfection—of those whom we were sent to teach and instruct, until we see them make such progress that they may deserve to be adopted as sons.

Let us nevertheless add a third interpretation. The same Apostle again says concerning the Lord Jesus Christ that he is “the firstborn of all creation.” Perhaps, therefore, just as he is called the firstborn of all creation in a certain sense, so the Holy Spirit may also be called the first fruits of the many spirits.

[Col. 0366B] But if you understand the statement, “We ourselves also who have the first fruits of the Spirit,” as spoken of all who appear to have obtained the grace of baptism, then we must hope for what the same Apostle said: “If the first fruits are holy, so is the whole lump; and if the root is holy, so are the branches” (Rom. XI). Even so, the first fruits of that whole lump—which appears to indicate the multitude of the faithful—were necessarily seen to be placed in the Apostles. For it is written: “God placed in the Church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers” (Ephes. II). Since these were placed first, they will appropriately be believed to possess the spiritual first fruits of grace.

[Col. 0366C] “Awaiting the adoption of the children of God.” Let us now see how he says that he awaits the adoption of the children who earlier said: “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God.” And again, how does he hope for the redemption of the body when elsewhere he said: “Christ redeemed us”? But, as it seems to me, he resolves this himself in the statement that follows. For he says: “In hope we were saved.” Therefore the fact that we are children, that we have been redeemed, and that we have been saved rests in hope.

[Col. 0366D] For now we see “through a mirror in an enigma.” Through a mirror, therefore, and in an enigma we have received both adoption and redemption. For the fullness of time has come, and God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, “to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive the adoption of children” (Gal. IV). We therefore receive adoption, but the adoption that is through a mirror and in an enigma. When what is perfect has come, then we shall obtain adoption face to face.

[Col. 0367A] “The redemption of our body,” etc. When he said “the redemption of our body,” I think that the body of the whole Church is indicated, just as he says elsewhere: “You are the body of Christ and members individually” (Coloss. II). The Apostle therefore hopes for the redemption of the whole body of the Church, and he does not think that perfection can be given to each of the individual members unless the whole body has been gathered together as one.

It can also be understood in this way: by “the redemption of our body” he meant that which will occur in the resurrection, when not only souls but also bodies will come before the tribunal of Christ, “so that each may receive what belongs to the body according to what he has done” (Rom. XVI).

**Here ends Origen’s exposition.**

### (From Augustine)

[Col. 0367B] There is no kind of creation that cannot be recognized in the human being, as though every creature in humanity groaned together and grieved while awaiting the revelation of the children of God. Through the resurrection of the body, even if not in every human being, all creation will nevertheless be freed from slavery to corruption, because all creation exists in each individual. And if this passage in the Apostle’s letters can be understood in some other way, it does not follow from the same words that we should believe the sun, moon, and stars to groan together until, at the end of the world, they are freed from slavery to corruption.

Some also say that Adam and Eve are “creation,” through whom the first fruits of the human race were produced. The serpent, once promising them divinity, subjected them to vanity and made them serve corruption—not merely because they sinned by themselves, but also through the serpent’s instigation. They too, they say, will be set free, so that they may no longer serve the corruption of death.

They also say that all those who were righteous before the coming of Christ are “all creation,” because they too, not yet having received the promise, await it, while God provides something better for us. And not only they, but we ourselves also, in whose days the mysteries of redemption have been fulfilled, because we do not yet possess them but have been saved in hope, although we have seen the things that many righteous people desired to see.

## ANOTHER EXPOSITION

[Col. 0367C] “For I consider that the sufferings are not worthy of comparison,” etc. By this he wishes to commend the future glory, so that we may endure present troubles more easily.

“With the future glory that will be revealed in us.” He says “will be revealed” because it is now hidden with Christ in God, and what we shall be has not yet appeared. For we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (I John III).

[Col. 0367D] “For the expectation of creation.” Different people explain this passage in different ways.
