Either all creation awaits the time of the resurrection, because then it will be changed for the better, when there will be a new heaven and a new earth, and then—that is, at the time of the resurrection—the revelation of the children of God will appear. Or all creation—that is, rational, angelic creation—awaits this fulfillment in human beings. For Peter says that the angels desire to see the glory of the saints.

“For creation was subjected to vanity.” That is, human creation was subjected to transgression through sin.

“Not willingly.” That is, not by its own will, but deceived by the serpent, through that hope in which it had heard: “You will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. II).

“But because of him who subjected it in hope.” What this hope is, hear from what follows: “For creation itself will also be set free from the slavery of corruption.” It heard this when the Lord said to it: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go”; this is understood as the corruption of death.

“Into freedom.” As the Lord says: “If the Son makes you free, you will be truly free” (John VIII).

[Col. 0368A] “Of the glory of the children of God.” For human beings alone, and no other irrational creature, will deserve to obtain the glory of the children of God.

“For we know that every creature,” etc. Not heaven, not earth, not the sea, nor any irrational creature, but the angels, who rejoice when people repent just as they grieve over those unwilling to be converted. Or the entire mixed population of the faithful of the Church may also be understood as “all creation,” as in the command: “Preach the Gospel to every creature.”

[Col. 0368B] “Not only it.” That is, not only the angelic creation, which is more kindly disposed toward us, nor only that human creation which is common and unlearned, but we ourselves also, the disciples of Christ, who are the first fruits of the acquisition and have received splendid charisms as the first fruits of the Spirit, by which we might enrich the world. We await “the redemption of our body,” that is, of the whole Church, which will reign with Christ forever.

## THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0368C] > “Be merciful, just as your Father also is merciful. Do not judge, and you will not be judged. Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you: a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing, they will pour into your lap. For with the same measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you. And he also told them a parable: Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit? A disciple is not above his teacher. Everyone who is perfect will be like his teacher. Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not consider the beam that is in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me remove the speck from your eye,’ while you do not see the beam in your own eye? Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.”

“Be merciful, just as your Father also is merciful.” (From Bede.) God is merciful toward the ungrateful and wicked, either through his manifold mercy, by which he also saves animals by granting temporal goods, or through the singular grace by which he glorifies only the elect, inspiring them with heavenly gifts. But whether you understand it in this way, or in that way, or in both ways, it is accomplished through the great goodness of God, which we are commanded to imitate if we wish to be children of God.

[Col. 0368D] [Col. 0369A] “Do not judge, and you will not be judged; do not condemn,” etc. At this point, I think that nothing else is commanded us except that we interpret for the better those deeds concerning which it is uncertain with what intention they are performed. For the statement, “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. VII), refers to manifest acts that cannot be done with a good intention, such as sexual immorality, blasphemies, thefts, drunkenness, and any other things concerning which we are permitted to judge.

Regarding kinds of food, however, because any human food can be consumed without the fault of desire, with a good intention and a simple heart, the Apostle forbids those who ate meat and drank wine to judge those who abstained from such foods. “Let the one who eats,” he says, “not despise the one who does not eat, and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats” (Rom. XIV).

The same applies to what he says elsewhere: “Do not judge anything before the appointed time, until the Lord comes, who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the intentions of hearts” (I Cor. VI). There are certain intermediate actions whose intention we do not know, because they can be performed either well or wickedly. It is rash to judge such actions, especially so as to condemn them. Their time of judgment will come when the Lord brings to light the hidden things of darkness and discloses the intentions of hearts.

There are two matters in which we must beware of rash judgment when it is uncertain what kind of person someone who now appears either wicked or good will ultimately be.

[Col. 0369B] “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you.” He commands us to forgive injuries and to give benefits, so that our sins may be forgiven and eternal life may be given to us. In this brief but outstanding statement he gathers together and concludes everything he had commanded at length concerning conduct toward enemies.

[Col. 0369C] “A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing, they will pour into your lap.” Something similar is said elsewhere: “So that they may receive you into the eternal dwellings” (Matt. VI). It is not the poor themselves who will repay the reward, but Christ will repay it to those who have given alms. Yet they are said to give it into their lap because they provided the occasion for earning it: when, being needy, they were pitied; or, raging wickedly, they were endured with the patience of the stronger and sustained by their beneficence, and were sometimes drawn to the faith itself by sweet grace.

“With the same measure with which you have measured, it will be measured back to you.” And the Apostle, exhorting the Corinthians to almsgiving, says among other things: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows in blessings will also reap from blessings.” It can also be understood of everything we do in mind, hand, or tongue, because, he says, “you will repay each according to their works.”

[Col. 0369D] “And he also told them a parable: Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit?” The meaning of this statement depends on what precedes, where he commands alms to be given and injuries to be forgiven. If anger against one who uses violence and φιλαργυρία—love of money—against one who asks have blinded you, can you, with your own mind corrupted, cure his vice? Or will only the one who inflicted the injury be held guilty, and not you also, who did not know how to bear it?

But if the wickedness of the other person finds you gentle and tranquil in heart, he will be moved to repentance and you will be rewarded for your patience, because, with a seeing eye—that is, a serene heart—you sought to lead a blind man toward the light.

[Col. 0370A] “A disciple is not above his teacher; everyone who is perfect will be like his teacher.” If the teacher, who as God certainly had the power to avenge his own injuries, preferred instead to make his persecutors gentler by enduring them, then it is necessary that disciples, who are mere human beings, follow the same rule of perfection.

“Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not consider the beam that is in your own eye?” This too refers to what precedes, where he warned that a blind person cannot be led by a blind person—that is, that a sinner cannot be corrected by a sinner. Many people, overcome by pride, hatred, φιλαργυρία—love of money—or greed, or by some other crime, judge these things slight or nonexistent and sharply rebuke those whom they see suddenly agitated by anger, as though a speck had rushed upon them and changed the eye of their mind from its customary purity. Forgetting the Lord’s command, “Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned” (Matt. VII), they prefer to criticize and condemn rather than to improve and correct.

[Col. 0370B] “And how can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me remove the speck from your eye,’ while you do not see the beam in your own eye?” You act in this way toward your brother if, for example, you rebuke in hatred what he did in anger. As much as a beam differs from a speck, so much does hatred differ from anger. Hatred is anger grown old, as though through age itself it had acquired such magnitude that it deserved to be called a beam. It can happen that, if you are angry with someone, you may wish him to be corrected. But if you hate someone, you cannot wish him to be corrected. Therefore it is called impossible for one who carries a beam in his own eye to remove the speck from his brother’s eye.

[Col. 0370C] [Col. 0370D] “Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.” That is: first drive hatred from yourself, and afterward you will be able to correct the person whom you love. Great care must truly be taken to avoid the troublesome class of hypocrites—that is, pretenders—who receive every fault and accusation with hatred and envy, yet wish to appear to be advisers.

Therefore we must watch with pious caution, so that whenever necessity compels us to rebuke or reprimand someone, we first consider whether the vice is one we have never had or from which we have been free. If we have never had it, let us consider that we are human beings and could have had it. But if we have had it and no longer have it, let the memory of our common weakness touch us, so that our rebuke or reprimand may be preceded not by hatred but by mercy. Whether it proves effective for the correction of the person for whose sake we do it, or for his ruin, is uncertain, for the outcome is unknown.

Nevertheless, let us be secure concerning the simplicity of our own eye. But if, on examining ourselves, we find that we are in the same vice as the person whom we were preparing to rebuke, let us neither rebuke nor reprimand him. Instead, let us groan together with him, and invite him not to obey us but to strive together with us. Rebukes should therefore be used rarely and only under great necessity, and even then we must insist that we serve not ourselves but God. The end is that we do nothing with a divided heart: removing from our own eye the beam of envy, malice, or pretense, so that we may be able to remove the speck from our brother’s eye.

[Col. 0371A] ## THE SIXTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

### LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PETER, CHAPTER III

[Col. 0371B] > “Be all of one mind in prayer, compassionate, lovers of the brotherhood, merciful, modest, humble. Do not repay evil for evil, or insult for insult, but on the contrary, bless, because you were called to this, so that you may possess the inheritance of blessing. For whoever wishes to love life and to see good days must restrain his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit. Let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it, because the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil. And who is there who will harm you if you are zealous for what is good? But even if you suffer for righteousness’ sake, you are blessed. Do not fear their fear, and do not be troubled. But sanctify the Lord Christ in your hearts.”

“Be all of one mind in prayer, compassionate, lovers of the brotherhood,” etc. (From Bede.) Since above he taught, with appropriate discernment, about different persons, conditions, and sexes, he now admonishes everyone in common, in the cause of the Lord’s faith, to have one heart and one soul.

[Col. 0371C] [Col. 0371D] “Because you were called to this, so that you may possess the inheritance of blessing,” etc. The inheritance of blessing can also be understood as that blessing with which the Church perpetually blesses the Lord in the future life. Hence even now, rejoicing in hope of the future, it sings: “I will exalt you, my God and king, and I will bless your name forever and unto ages of ages” (Ps. CXLIV).

Therefore, whatever each person desires to find in the future, let him strive to meditate upon and practice it in the present: namely, to bless both the creator and his neighbor with a sincere voice, and to make himself worthy of divine and fraternal blessing alike. For “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. XXXII), and his ears are toward their prayers; but “the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.” Since the blessed Peter had forbidden us to repay evil for evil, indeed had commanded us to bless those who curse, he rightly establishes by prophetic testimony that, through his heavenly regard, both the good and the wicked are always seen. Thus we may remember that our patience, by which we endure the wicked, and our benevolence, by which we wish good for our persecutors, will be rewarded with an eternal prize; and that our persecutors, if they refuse to repent, will be punished with a fitting penalty. But if they repent, then for their salvation—which we had entreated from the Lord—we too shall receive the crown of righteousness with rejoicing.

[Col. 0372A] “And who is there who will harm you if you are zealous for what is good?” He is speaking of the things that come upon us from adversaries through insulting words, losses of temporal goods, and bodily torments. For when these and similar things are inflicted upon the faithful, they can by no means harm those who are zealous for what is good and do so with understanding. Rather, they bring the palm of repentance to those who endure them with equanimity.

On the contrary, such things greatly harm those who, by accumulating punishment, ask for eternal punishment. If someone is overcome by such adversities and is defeated by them, it is not the person who inflicted the evil who harmed him, but he harmed himself by refusing to endure these things patiently. Nor did the house that the wise man built fail to fall because it did not withstand the violence of storms, but because it was founded upon the rock (Matt. VII). Nor, again, did the house that the foolish man foolishly built fall because it was struck by storms, but because it had been placed upon sand. Adversity struck and tested both alike; but the firmness of the foundation granted one the crown of perseverance, while the folly of the structure laid the other low beneath the blows.

[Col. 0372B] “But even if you suffer for righteousness’ sake, you are blessed.” Not only, he says, does the one who inflicts evil upon those doing good do you no harm, but when the enemy persecutes you because of the good things he detests, he provides you with the occasion for greater blessedness, exercising the strength of your patience, in accordance with the Gospel statement: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. V).

“Sanctify our Lord Jesus Christ in your hearts.” What is it to sanctify the Lord in your hearts except to contemplate, with the deepest affection of the heart, the holiness of him whose glory is incomprehensible? This is our greatest defense against the snares and violence of the terrifying enemy: namely, always to contemplate how much power to conquer he is able to give to those who hope in him, whose immeasurable holiness shines forth.

[Col. 0372C] ## ANOTHER EXPOSITION OF THE SAME LETTER

“Be all of one mind in prayer.” The unity of the brotherhood, like an impregnable city, is not open to the snares of enemies. For, as Solomon says, holy Church has “an army set in battle array” (Song VI), which tyrants and persecutors, together with their author the devil, cannot break into. For when Christ guards it, persecution does not overcome martyrs, carnal pleasure does not overcome virgins, greed does not overcome the merciful, and ambition for temporal glory does not overcome the humble.

“Compassionate.” For just as we ought to rejoice with those who rejoice, so also to weep with those who weep, as the Apostle Paul did when he said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (Rom. XII).

[Col. 0372D] “Lovers of the brotherhood.” (From Augustine.) Whoever loves human beings ought to love them either because they are righteous or so that they may become righteous. In the same way, he ought to love himself either because he is righteous or so that he may become righteous.

Let us observe how greatly the Apostle John commends brotherly love: “Whoever loves his brother,” he says, “remains in the light, and there is no scandal in him.” And again: “Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God, and everyone who loves is born of God and knows God.” And the Lord says: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another; and by this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another.”

[Col. 0373A] “Merciful.” For it is written: “To practice mercy is more pleasing to God than sacrifices” (John XIII); and Scripture says: “Whoever is inclined toward mercy will be blessed” (Prov. XXII). And the Lord says: “Be merciful, because your Father also is merciful” (Matt. V).

##
### The Humble

For it is written: “God will destroy the memory of the proud, and he has left the memory of the humble” (Psalm 108). And the Lord says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matthew 11); and again: “Upon whom shall I look,” says the Lord, “unless upon the humble and quiet” (Isaiah 66)?

### Not Returning Evil for Evil

For it is written: “Do not say, ‘I will repay evil for evil’; wait for God, and he will deliver you.” And again: “Whoever wishes to take vengeance will find vengeance from God, and he will keep account of that person’s sin” (Ecclesiasticus 28).

[Column 0373B]

### Or a Curse for a Curse

For in this we must hold to the example of the Lord, who, when he was cursed, did not curse.

### But, on the Contrary, Blessing

As it says: “Bless those who curse you; bless, and do not curse” (Romans 12).

### Because You Were Called to This, That You Might Possess the Blessing of the Inheritance

The blessing of the inheritance is the whole abundance of heavenly virtues, in which the saints will indeed be heirs of God and fellow-heirs with Christ, when they hear: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25).

### For Whoever Wishes to Love Life

That is, eternal life: a blessed life that will remain forever without end.

[Column 0373C]

### And to See Good Days

In which the saints rejoice with the saints in heaven. They are called “days,” not because of the interruption of night, but because of the perpetuity of light.

### Let Him Restrain His Tongue from Evil

That is, from the evil of detraction, cursing, and murmuring; or, more generally, the tongue must be restrained altogether from evil. For James says: “If anyone thinks that he is religious, but does not restrain his tongue and deceives his own heart, his religion is worthless” (James 1). For Scripture also says: “Whoever guards his tongue guards his soul” (Proverbs 21).

### And His Lips, So That They Do Not Speak Deceit

“Deceit” is meant here, not “sorrow”: fraud, when one thing is held in the heart and another is uttered from the mouth.

[Column 0373D]

### Let Him Turn Away from Evil and Do Good

That is, let him destroy vices and build virtues; let him abandon the things to which the devil incites him and perform the things Christ has commanded.

### Let Him Seek Peace and Pursue It

That is, by praying and reading diligently, and by asking humbly, let him seek Christ, who has become our peace, and imitate him. For “to follow” means “to imitate”; or, according to the Apostle, let him pursue peace and holiness, without which no one will see God.

### Because the Eyes of the Lord Are upon the Righteous

That is, the gaze of divinity.

### And His Ears Are Open to Their Prayers

That is, the divine hearing by which he deigns to hear the prayers of the righteous.

### But the Face of the Lord Is against Those Who Do Evil

Why is the face of the Lord against those who do evil? Hear what follows: “To destroy their memory from the earth”—that is, from the land of the living—according to the saying: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written among the righteous” (Psalm 69).

[Column 0374A]

### And Who Is He Who Can Harm You?

“None,” is understood, in accordance with the sense of this passage. Sufferings and persecutions do not make people wretched; rather, they make them blessed.

### If You Are Zealous for What Is Good

That is, for the good God, of whom it is written: “No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10); or, more generally, if you are zealous for all good things—that is, if you are imitators of the virtues.

### But Even If You Suffer Anything for Righteousness’ Sake, You Are Blessed

“You will be,” is understood. Peter had heard the Lord expressing this sentiment when he said: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake,” and so forth (Matthew 5).

[Column 0374B]

### Do Not Fear Their Fear

That is, do not fear the persecutors, so that you may not be disturbed in faith. The Lord also warned of this when he said: “Do not fear those who kill the body,” and so forth, “but rather fear him who has power to cast soul and body into Gehenna.”

### But Sanctify the Lord Christ in Your Hearts

Where is the Lord, who sanctifies all things by creating them, unless in a devout heart and a chaste breast? Thus the Lord Jesus must be sanctified in our hearts, so that we may be called by his name—that is, Christians—and so that we may consider nothing holier than his name. For we sanctify him in hope, faith, and charity, by believing, worshiping, and adoring him, so that we may likewise deserve to be sanctified and justified by him.

[Column 0374C]

## THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER 5

“Now when the crowds were pressing upon Jesus to hear the word of God, he himself was standing beside the lake of Gennesaret. And he saw two boats standing beside the lake. The fishermen, however, had gone down and were washing their nets. And going up into one boat, which was Simon’s, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And sitting down, he taught the crowds from the boat. When he had ceased speaking, he said to Simon: ‘Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.’ And Simon answered and said to him: ‘Master, having labored throughout the whole night, we have caught nothing; but at your word I will let down the net.’

[Column 0374D]

And when they had done this, they enclosed a great multitude of fish. Their net was breaking, and they beckoned to their companions who were in the other boat to come and help them. And they came and filled both boats, so that they were nearly sinking. When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at Jesus’ knees, saying: ‘Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man.’ For astonishment had seized him and all who were with him at the catch of fish which they had taken. Likewise also James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were Simon’s companions. And Jesus said to Simon: ‘Do not fear; from now on you will be catching human beings.’

[Column 0375A]

And when they had brought the boats to land, leaving everything, they followed him.”

### “When the Crowds Were Pressing upon Jesus to Hear the Word of God, and He Himself Was Standing,” etc. (From Bede)

They say that the lake of Gennesaret is the same as the Sea of Galilee, named from the neighboring province. It is called the Sea of Tiberias from the nearby city, which was formerly called Chinnereth but, rebuilt by Herod the tetrarch in honor of Tiberius Caesar, was named Tiberias. Moreover, Gennesar is so called from the nature of the lake itself: because its waters are ruffled, it is said to produce a breeze for itself from within itself; in Greek it is therefore called, as it were, “generating a breeze for itself.” For the water does not lie flat like that of a pond, but is stirred by frequent and rippling winds; its water is sweet when drawn and suitable for drinking. [Column 0375B]

Yet, according to the usage of the Hebrew language, every gathering of waters, whether fresh or salt, is called “sea.” This lake, lying between the streams of the Jordan, extends one hundred and forty stades in length and forty in width.

Therefore, since the present age is signified by the lake or sea, the Lord stands beside the sea. After conquering the mortality of passing life and entering, in the flesh in which he suffered, the stability of perpetual rest, the gathering of the crowds around him is a type of the nations converging in faith. Concerning them Isaiah says: “And all nations shall flow to him; many peoples shall go forth and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” (Isaiah 2).

### “And He Saw Two Boats beside the Lake”

The two boats placed beside the lake signify circumcision and uncircumcision. Jesus is rightly said to have seen them, because

[Column 0375C]

in both peoples the Lord knows those who are his; and by seeing—that is, by visiting them mercifully—he advances their hearts through the waves of this age toward the tranquility of the life to come, as toward the firmness of the shore.

### “The Fishermen, However, Had Gone Down and Were Washing Their Nets”

The fishermen are the teachers of the Church. Having been caught in the net of faith and lifted from the deep into the light, we are brought by them, like fish to the shore, to the land of the living. For the utterances of preachers are, as it were, nets of fishermen: those whom they have caught, they do not allow to escape from the faith. Hence the nets are called, as it were, “that which retains.” These nets are now let down for a catch, and now, having been washed, are folded up, because not every time is suitable for teaching: now the teacher’s tongue must be exercised, now care must be taken of oneself.

[Column 0375D]

### “Going Up into One Boat, Which Was Simon’s, He Asked Him to Put Out a Little from the Land, and Sitting Down He Taught the Crowds from the Boat”

Simon’s boat is the primitive Church, concerning which Paul says: “He who worked through Peter in the apostleship to the circumcision also worked through me among the Gentiles” (Galatians 1). It is rightly called “one,” because the heart and soul of the multitude of believers were one (Acts 3). From it he taught the crowds, because from the authority of the Church he teaches the nations even to this day.

### “When He Had Ceased Speaking, He Said to Simon: Put Out into the Deep and Let Down Your Nets for a Catch” (From Augustine)

That he first asked Simon to put the boat out a little from the land signifies either that the word should be used moderately with the crowds, so that neither earthly things are commanded to them nor are they withdrawn from earthly things into the depths of the mysteries in such a way that they understand nothing at all; or that the preaching should first be directed to the Gentiles in the nearer regions, so that what is said afterward to Peter—“Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch”—may pertain to the more distant nations to whom preaching is later to be delivered.

[Column 0376A]

### “And Simon Answered and Said to Him: Master, Having Labored Throughout the Whole Night, We Have Caught Nothing; but at Your Word I Will Let Down the Net”

“Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 126). Unless the Lord illumines the hearts of the hearers, the teacher labors in the night. Unless the instruments of disputation are let down in the word of heavenly grace, the preacher casts the dart of his voice in vain, because the faith of peoples comes beforehand not through the wisdom of a composed discourse but through the gift of divine calling.

[Column 0376B]

### “And When They Had Done This, They Enclosed a Great Multitude of Fish; Their Net Was Breaking” (From Gregory)

The net was breaking because of the multitude of fish, since now, together with the elect, so many reprobates enter into the confession of faith that they even rend the Church itself through heresies. The net is broken, but the fish does not escape, because the Lord preserves his own even amid the scandals of their persecutors.

### “And They Beckoned to Their Companions Who Were in the Other Boat to Come and Help Them”

The other boat, as we said earlier, is the Church from the Gentiles. Since the one boat is not sufficient for the fish, it too is filled with the elect, because “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2), and with him the number of his elect is certain. When he does not find in Judaea as many believers as he knows to have been predestined to faith and eternal life, he seeks, as it were, another boat to receive his fish, and fills the hearts of the Gentiles also with the grace of faith.

And the companion boat is rightly summoned when the net is broken, since Judas the betrayer was caught first, and Simon Magus, a most wicked fish, was caught first. Earlier, Ananias and Sapphira were deceitfully attempting to enter the net of faith (Acts 5); earlier, as John testifies, many of his disciples went back and no longer walked with him (John 6). Then Barnabas and Paul were called to the salvation of the Gentiles (Acts 13).

[Column 0376C]

### “And They Came and Filled Both Boats, So That They Were Nearly Sinking”

The filling of these boats increases until the end of the age. But the fact that, once filled, they sink—that is, are pressed down toward submersion—does not mean that they are submerged; nevertheless, they are endangered. The Apostle explains this when he says: “In the last days perilous times will come, and people will be lovers of themselves,” and so forth (2 Timothy 3).

For the boats’ sinking means that people, having been lifted by faith from the age, fall back into it through the perversity of their conduct. Peter himself, while still placed in weakness, demonstrates this in the present passage; hence what follows.

[Column 0376D]

### “When Simon Peter Saw This,” etc. (From Augustine)

For all carnal people in the Church repel from themselves, in a certain sense, the governance of spiritual persons, in whom the person of Christ is especially prominent. They do not say this with the voice of their tongue to the good ministers of God, so as to drive them away; rather, by the voice of their conduct and actions they persuade them to withdraw, lest they be governed by the good.

They do this all the more forcefully because they pay them honor and yet, by their deeds, urge them to depart from them. Thus Peter’s falling at the Lord’s feet signifies their display of honor. But his conduct in saying, “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man,” signifies that good and spiritual men ought not, being disturbed by the sins of the crowds, to abandon their ecclesiastical office in order to live, as they suppose, more safely and peacefully.

### “And Jesus Said to Simon: Do Not Fear”

The Lord strengthens the fear of carnal people and, by consoling them, raises the spirits of the weak, lest anyone—whether trembling because of his own conscience

[Column 0377B]

and guilt, or astonished at the innocence of others—fear to set out upon the path of holiness. What follows, however:

[Column 0377A]

### “From Now on You Will Be Catching Human Beings”

Pertains especially to Peter himself. The Lord explains to him what this catch of fish signifies: namely, that just as he now catches fish through nets, so at some time he will catch human beings through words. The entire order of this event shows what is daily enacted in the Church, of which he himself is a type. But what is added is:

### “And When They Had Brought the Boats to Land, Leaving Everything, They Followed Him”

This can signify the end of time, when those who have clung to Christ will entirely withdraw from this kind of age.

[Column 0377C]

It must be understood, however, that this is not the same calling described by Matthew and Mark, in which the Lord is said to have called two fishermen from their boats, first Peter and Andrew, and then the sons of Zebedee.

For Luke does not now say that they were called by the Lord; he merely indicates that Peter had been told that he would catch human beings. Nor was this said as though he would never again catch fish. For after the Lord’s resurrection we read that they went fishing. From this it can be understood that they returned, as was their custom, to catching fish, so that what Matthew and Mark relate might happen afterward, when he called them two by two.

At that time they did not follow him after bringing the boats from the land, as though concerned to return, but followed him as one who was calling and commanding them to follow.

[Column 0377D]

## ON THE VIGIL OF SAINT JOHN

## READING FROM THE PROPHET JEREMIAH, CHAPTER 1

“Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, and before you came forth from the womb I sanctified you, and I appointed you as a prophet among the nations. And I said: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God! Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am a child. And the Lord said to me: Do not say, ‘I am a child,’ for you shall go to all to whom I send you, and you shall speak everything that I command you. Do not fear their presence, for I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord. And the Lord stretched out his hand and touched my mouth, and the Lord said to me: Behold, I have given my words in your mouth. Behold, I have appointed you over nations and over kingdoms, to uproot and to destroy and to overthrow,

[Column 0378A]

and to scatter and to build and to plant, says the Lord Almighty.”

### “Before I Formed You in the Womb, I Knew You, and Before You Came Forth from the Womb I Sanctified You, and I Appointed You as a Prophet among the Nations”

This does not mean that Jeremiah existed before conception, as the heresies suppose; rather, the Lord foreknew that he would exist. For to him things not yet done are already done, according to what the Apostle says: He calls “those things that are not as though they were” (Romans 4).

Some understand this passage as referring to the Savior, who is properly the prophet of the nations and, through the apostles, called all peoples. For he truly was sanctified in the womb before he was formed in the virginal womb, and before he came forth from his mother’s womb; and he was known to the Father, since he is always in the Father, and the Father always in him.

[Column 0378B]

### “And I Said: Ah, Ah, Ah, Lord God! Behold, I Do Not Know How to Speak, for I Am a Child. Do Not Say, ‘I Am a Child,’ for You Shall Go to All to Whom I Send You, and You Shall Speak Everything That I Command You. Do Not Fear Their Presence, for I Am with You to Deliver You, Says the Lord”

When he came in a human body, he says at the beginning: “I do not know how to speak, for I am young”—young on account of the dispensation, old according to the fact that he is the firstborn of every creature. Young because he came at the consummation and at the final period of this age. Therefore he says: “I do not know how to speak.”

For I know how to speak certain greater things; I know your utterance, I am your Word. To you I know how to speak; to human beings I do not know how to speak. I am young.

[Column 0378C]

### “And the Lord Stretched Out His Hand and Touched My Mouth,” etc.

By the word of God that doctrine shall be undermined and destroyed which Jesus will consume with the spirit of his mouth and destroy by the appearance of his coming (2 Thessalonians 2)—namely, every sacrilegious and perverse doctrine he will destroy forever.

Moreover, those things that are raised up against the knowledge of God and trust in their own wisdom, which is foolishness with God, he will scatter and cast down, so that corresponding things may be built in their place, and in place of the former things that have been destroyed and uprooted, those things may be constructed and planted that accord with ecclesiastical truth. Thus may be fulfilled what the Apostle says: “You are God’s building, God’s cultivation” (1 Corinthians 3).

Many understand this passage as referring to the person of Christ. [Column 0378D] Jeremiah is interpreted as “the exalted one of the Lord,” who destroyed the kingdoms of the devil that he had shown him upon the high mountain, overthrew the opposing powers, and erased on the cross the record of errors. Concerning these things he speaks figuratively, after the historical truth, in the Psalm: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate on vain things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together as one” (Psalm 2). In place of these things—uprooted, destroyed, overthrown, and dragged down into the lower regions—the Church of God is built.

## THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER 1

“There was in the days of Herod, king of Judaea, a certain priest named Zacharias, of the division of Abijah; and his wife was from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. They were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without

[Column 0379A]

reproach. And they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in their days.

Now it happened, while Zacharias was serving as priest in the order of his division before God, that according to the custom of the priesthood he was chosen by lot to offer incense. He entered the temple of the Lord, and the whole multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of incense.

Then an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right side of the altar of incense. And Zacharias was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him. But the angel said to him: ‘Do not fear, Zacharias, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John. And there will be joy and exultation for you, and many will rejoice at his birth. For he will be great before the Lord, [Column 0379B] and he will drink neither wine nor strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb, and he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God. And he himself will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers toward the children and the unbelieving toward the wisdom of the righteous, to prepare for the Lord a perfected people.’”

### “There Was in the Days of Herod, King of Judaea, a Priest Named Zacharias” (From Bede)

The sacred and holy nobility of the Lord’s precursor descended gloriously not only from his parents but from his ancestors, so that he might preach more freely that faith in his coming had not been conceived through sudden inspiration but received rather through ancestral succession.

[Column 0379C]

### “Of the Division of Abijah”

The twenty-four orders of priests serving in the ministry of the house of the Lord were divided by lot by Solomon. Among them, the eighth lot fell to the family of Abijah, from which Zacharias arose.

It is not without reason that the first herald of the New Testament is born in the eighth division, because just as the Old Testament is often expressed by the number seven on account of the Sabbath, so the New Testament is sometimes expressed by the number eight on account of the mystery of the resurrection. Therefore, since the hall of the heavenly kingdom is entered only through observance of both Testaments, it is rightly related that in Solomon’s temple there was a mystical ascent of fifteen steps.

### “And His Wife Was from the Daughters of Aaron”

Thus the praise is complete, encompassing lineage, character, office, deed, and judgment: lineage in his ancestors, character in righteousness, office in the priesthood, deed in obedience to the commandment, and judgment in observance of the ordinances.

[Column 0379D]

### “They Were Both Righteous before God”

Blessed is the one who is righteous and praiseworthy in the sight of God. It happens, of course, that people praise one who is not praiseworthy and disparage one who is in no way worthy of disparagement. God alone is a just judge both in praise and in blame.

### “Walking in All the Commandments and Ordinances of the Lord without Reproach”

Very often a harsher righteousness provokes the complaints of people; but what is tempered avoids, through the grace of its own sweetness, even the complaint of envy.

### (From Ambrose)

For when we fulfill God’s commandment but scatter the filth of vainglory upon our conscience in order to please people, we do not fulfill it without reproach.

[Column 0380A]

### “Now It Happened, While Zacharias Was Serving as Priest,” etc.

The one who is chosen by lot is not apprehended by human judgment. Therefore the one whom he represented was being sought: the true priest forever, to whom it is said: “You are a priest forever” (Psalm 110), who would reconcile God the Father to the human race not by the blood of victims but by his own blood.

At that time blood was poured out and the priesthood was instituted in figure. Now, because the truth has come, let us leave the figure and follow the truth. Then there were successive turns of service; now there is perpetuity.

Whom else did the priest Zacharias signify except that priest whose sacrifice would not be shared with the others, who would not sacrifice for us in temples made by hand, but in the temple of his own body would wipe away our sins?

[Column 0380B]

### “He Was Chosen by Lot to Offer Incense,” etc.

The offering of incense in the Holy of Holies by the high priest, while all the people waited outside the temple, was commanded on the tenth day of the seventh month. This day was called the Day of Expiation, or Propitiation. Among us, because of the varying course of the moon, from which the Hebrews calculate the months, it begins sometimes in September and sometimes in October, since the month in which Passover is celebrated holds the beginning of the year, as the Lord says: “This month shall be the first month for you among the months of the year. On the tenth day of this month each person shall take a lamb,” and so forth.

The true high priest Jesus fulfilled the mystery of this day when, having completed the dispensation of the flesh in his own blood, he entered the secrets of heaven to make the Father propitious toward us and to intercede for the sins of those who still wait before the doors in prayer and love his coming.

### “Then an Angel of the Lord Appeared to Him,” etc.

The angel is rightly seen in the temple, because the coming of the true priest was already being announced and a heavenly sacrifice was being prepared, in which angels would minister. Would that an angel also stand by us when we sorrow or offer sacrifice. Do not doubt that an angel assists when Christ assists. Christ is sacrificed, for Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.

[Column 0380D]

### (From Bede)

The angel rightly appears both in the temple and beside the altar and on the right, because he proclaims the coming of the true priest, the mystery of the sacrifice, and the joy of the universal and heavenly gift. For just as present things are often signified by the left, so eternal good things are often announced by the right.

### “But the Angel Said to Him: Do Not Fear, Zacharias,” etc.

In saying that the prayer had been heard, he immediately promises the wife’s childbirth. This does not mean that the one who had entered to offer sacrifice for the people could, abandoning the public vows, have prayed to receive children; rather, what he says—“Your prayer has been heard”—signifies the redemption of the people.

What he adds, “Your wife will bear you a son,” discloses the order of that same redemption: namely, that the son born to Zacharias would prepare the way by proclaiming the redemption of that people.

[Column 0381A]

### “And There Will Be Joy and Exultation for You,” etc.

It should be noted that many rejoice at the birth of the precursor. At the Lord’s birth, however, the angel announces great joy, which will be for all the people, because the one came to proclaim salvation to many, while the other came to grant it to all who are willing.

### “And He Will Be Great before the Lord” (From Ambrose)

This declares not greatness of body but greatness of soul. Before the Lord there is greatness of soul and greatness of virtue, and there is also smallness of soul and childhood of virtue.

### “He Will Drink Neither Wine nor Strong Drink” (From Bede)

[Column 0381B]

“Strong drink” is interpreted as drunkenness. In Hebrew, [the Hebrew term is not preserved in the supplied text]; by this word the Hebrews signify every drink capable of causing intoxication, whether made from fruits, crops, or any other material.

For it is fitting that a vessel devoted to heavenly grace be chastened from the allurements of the age, and that one who desires to be filled with the must of the Holy Spirit not be made drunk with wine, in which there is wantonness.

### “And He Will Be Filled with the Holy Spirit Even from His Mother’s Womb” (From Ambrose)

There is no doubt that this was truly promised by the angel, since holy John, before he was born, while still placed in his mother’s womb, manifested the grace of the Spirit he had received. To one who possesses the spirit of grace nothing is lacking, and the one into whom the Holy Spirit is poured has a fullness of great virtues.

### “And He Will Turn Many of the Children of Israel to the Lord Their God”

When John, bearing witness to Christ and baptizing peoples in faith in him, is said to have turned the children of Israel to the Lord their God, it is plainly evident that Christ is their Lord and God.

[Column 0381C]

### “And He Himself Will Go before Him in the Spirit and Power of Elijah”

He is rightly said to go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, because just as Elijah was the herald of the coming Judge, so John became the herald of the Redeemer.

Hence the two were wholly alike in their manner of life: both pursued the deserts, lived on simple food, wore rough clothing, and bore despised girdles; both endured the madness of a king and a queen. Elijah divided the Jordan when he was seeking heaven; John turned people toward the saving bath by which heaven is sought. John lives with the Lord on earth; Elijah is manifested with him in glory.

[Column 0381D]

### “To Turn the Hearts of the Fathers toward the Children, and the Unbelieving toward Wisdom,” etc.

To turn the hearts of the fathers toward the children is to pour into the peoples, by preaching, the spiritual understanding of the ancient saints. The wisdom of the righteous, however, is not to presume upon righteousness from the works of the Law, but to seek salvation through faith.

## ON THE NATIVITY OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

## READING FROM ISAIAH, CHAPTER 49

“Listen, islands, and attend, peoples from afar. The Lord called me from the womb; from my mother’s womb he remembered my name. And he made my mouth like a sharp sword; under the shadow of his hand he protected me. And he made me like a chosen arrow;

[Column 0382A]

in his quiver he hid me. And he said to me: ‘You are my servant, Israel, because I will be glorified in you.’ And now thus says the Lord, who formed me from the womb as a servant for himself: ‘I have given you as a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.’ Kings shall see and rise up; princes shall bow down before the Lord your God and the Holy One of Israel, who chose you.”

### “Listen, Islands, and Attend, Peoples from Afar” (From Jerome)

After the calling of the remnant of Israel and the rejection of the people remaining in unbelief—concerning whom he had said: “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isaiah 48)—he turns to the Churches gathered from the Gentiles and speaks to them under the name of “islands.” They lie exposed to the plots of persecutors, like islands to the waves of the sea, and are battered rather than moved by shipwreck raging on every side.

[Column 0382B]

And lest anyone think that our interpretation is forced and that what is said does not pertain to the Gentiles but to the synagogues of the Jewish people:

### “And Attend, Peoples or Nations, from Afar”

That is, from the farthest ends of the earth, as the Seventy translated: διὰ χρόνου πολλοῦ στήσεται—“After a long time he will stand.” This means: not at the time in which these things are being said, but after many times have passed. It follows:

### “The Lord,” He Says, “Called Me from the Womb, from My Mother’s Womb,” etc.

What now seems obscure to the hearers will later become known to all the nations, when Gabriel says to Joseph concerning the virginal birth: “You shall call his name Jesus, for he himself will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1).

[Column 0382C]

### “And He Made My Mouth like a Sharp Sword”

He also made his mouth like a sharp sword, so that with the spirit of his mouth he might slay the impious. Concerning this sword he himself speaks in the Gospel: “I have not come to send peace upon the earth but a sword” (Matthew 10), separating the wicked from the good.

For he came to divide a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.

### “And Under the Shadow of His Hand He Protected Me”

He asserts that he is protected under the shadow of God’s hand, so that the lowliness of the flesh might be covered by the power of divinity, when the angel announced to the Virgin: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1).

[Column 0382D]

### “And He Made Me like a Chosen Arrow”

When he says “a chosen arrow,” he shows that God has many arrows, but not all are chosen. These arrows are the Prophets and Apostles, who run throughout the whole world, concerning whom it is sung elsewhere: “Your arrows are sharp, O Most Mighty; the peoples shall fall beneath you.” And again: “The arrows of the mighty are sharp, with burning coals of desolation” (Psalm 45).

Christ, however, among many arrows and many sons, is one chosen arrow and the only-begotten Son. He hid it in his quiver—that is, in the human body—so that the fullness of divinity might dwell bodily in him.

Rare is the faith of believers, to whom it is also said above: “You are a hidden God, and we did not know.” As a result of being wounded by this arrow, the bride speaks in the Song of Songs: “I am wounded by love” (Song of Songs 4).

[Column 0383A]

### “You Are My Servant, because I Will Be Glorified in You”

He is a servant because, although he was in the form of God, he graciously assumed the form of a servant (Philippians 2). He shows that the one who was formed from the womb is called a servant; he also says in the Psalm: “From my mother’s womb, you are my God.”

And he is “Israel” because he was born from the seed of the Jews. That this cannot be understood of any other servant is shown by what is joined to it: “Because I will be glorified in you.” For he himself also says in the Gospel: “Father, glorify your name” (John 12). In the Psalm he says: “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and lyre” (Psalm 56)—that is, the chorus of all virtues.

### “I Have Given You as a Light to the Nations, That You May Be My Salvation to the End of the Earth”

That is, so that you may illumine the whole world and cause my salvation, through which all may be saved, to reach the end of the earth. We know that this was accomplished through the preaching of the apostles, concerning whom the Psalmist prophesies: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 19).

[Column 0383B]

### “Kings Shall See and Rise Up, and Princes Shall Bow Down before the Lord Your God and the Holy One of Israel, Who Chose You”

These things will happen when Christ comes in the glory of his Father with his angels and sits upon his throne of glory to judge the living and the dead (Matthew 25). Then all will bow down because of the Lord their Father, for he is faithful who chose him.

Or it should be understood in this way: kings, whose hearts are in the hand of God, and the princes of the Church will bow down before him, because the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, is faithful.

For what follows can also be understood of Christ. He says: “In an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.” The Apostle uses this testimony when he says: “At an opportune time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you. Behold, now is the acceptable time; now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6).

The acceptable and opportune time, and the day of salvation, are the Savior’s passion and resurrection. To him the same Father says in what follows: “I have given you as a covenant of the people, to raise up the earth and possess the scattered inheritances, to say to those who are bound, ‘Come out,’ and to those who are in darkness, ‘Reveal yourselves.’”

[Column 0383C]

“Of the people” is understood to mean the Jewish people, namely those among them who wished to believe. He raised up the earth that lay in the errors of idolatry, and he will possess the scattered inheritances that had no lord as inhabitant. He says to those who were bound by the chains of sins: “Come out,” for each person is bound by the cords of his sins.

And to those who sat in darkness and could not see the light he says: “Reveal yourselves.” For after all these people have been converted and have looked upon the bright light of Christ, they will feed in the ways and paths of the sacred Scriptures, and they will say: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing. In a place of pasture he has settled me; beside the waters of refreshment he has led me” (Psalm 23).

[Column 0383D]

## THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE, CHAPTER 1

“Elizabeth’s time for giving birth was fulfilled, and she bore a son. And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had magnified his mercy toward her, and they rejoiced with her.

And it happened on the eighth day that they came to circumcise the child, and they were calling him by the name of his father, Zacharias. But his mother answered and said: ‘Certainly not; he shall be called John.’ And they said to her: ‘There is no one among your kindred who is called by this name.’

Then they made signs to his father concerning what he wanted him to be called. And asking for a writing tablet, he wrote, saying: ‘John is his name.’ And they were all astonished.

Immediately his mouth and tongue were opened, and he spoke, blessing God. And fear came upon all their neighbors, and all these things were spoken of throughout the whole hill country of Judaea.

[Column 0384B]

And all who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying: ‘What, do you suppose, will this child be?’ For the hand of the Lord was with him.

And Zacharias, his father, was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying: ‘Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and accomplished the redemption of his people.’”

Elizabeth’s time to give birth was fulfilled, and she bore a son. (From Bede.) Holy Scripture is accustomed to use the word “fulfillment” only in connection with the birth, death, or deed of the good, signifying that their life possesses the fullness of perfection. Thus: “Elizabeth’s time to give birth was fulfilled.” “Mary’s days were fulfilled, so that she might give birth.” “Solomon fulfilled the building of the house of the Lord.” Abraham, or some other patriarch, died “old and full of days”; and “when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son.” On the other hand, the days of the wicked are empty and void: “Men of blood and deceit shall not halve their days” (Psalm 54).

And the neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had magnified his mercy toward her, and they rejoiced with her. (From Augustine.) The birth of the saints brings joy to many, because it is a common good. Justice is indeed a common virtue; therefore, at the birth of the just, the promise of future life is proclaimed, and the grace of the virtue that will follow is signified beforehand by the rejoicing of the neighbors.

And it came to pass on the eighth day; they came to circumcise the child, and they called him by the name of his father, Zachariah, but his mother answered and said, “By no means; he shall be called John.” The holy Evangelist remarkably thought it necessary to mention beforehand that many thought the infant should be called by his father’s name, Zachariah, so that you may understand that the mother did not reject the name of some degenerate person, but that the name infused by the Holy Spirit was the one that had previously been announced by the angel to Zachariah. Indeed, that mute man could not communicate his son’s name to his wife, but through prophecy Elizabeth learned what she had not learned from her husband.

And they said to her, “No one in your family is called by this name.” They gestured to his father, asking what he wished him to be called; and asking for a writing tablet, he wrote, saying, “John is his name,” and they were all astonished. “John is his name,” he said—that is, we are not imposing a name on him, because he has already received a name from God. He has his own name, which we have recognized, not chosen. Nor should you be surprised that a woman asserted a name she had not heard, when the Holy Spirit, who had instructed the angel, revealed it. She who had prophesied Christ could not be ignorant of the Lord’s herald. And it is fittingly added, “For no one in his family is called by this name,” so that you may understand that the name belongs not to the family but to the prophet.

Immediately his mouth and tongue were opened, and he spoke, blessing God; and fear came upon all their neighbors. Because the voice of one crying in the wilderness had been born, the parent’s tongue was rightly released. The father who rejoiced that the herald of the Word had been born to him ought not to remain silent in praise; for faith now freed the lips that unbelief had bound. But if someone wishes to investigate these matters allegorically as well, John’s celebrated birth marks the dawning exaltation of the grace of the New Testament. His neighbors and relatives preferred to impose his father’s name rather than John’s, because the Jews, who were joined to the Law as though by kinship through its observance, desired rather to pursue the righteousness that comes from the Law than to receive the grace of faith. But the mother strives to communicate the name John—that is, “the grace of God”—by her words, and the father by his writing. For the Law itself, as well as the Psalms and the Prophets, openly proclaim the grace of Christ in their statements, while that ancient priesthood bears witness to him through the figurative shadows of ceremonies and sacrifices. Zachariah fittingly speaks on the eighth day after the child’s birth, because through the Lord’s resurrection, which took place on the eighth day after the seventh day of the week, the hidden mysteries of the legal priesthood were revealed, and the tongue of the Jewish priests, which the bonds of unbelief had tightened, was released into the rational speech of understanding.

And throughout all the hill country of Judea all these things were being proclaimed. And all who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying, “What, do you suppose, will this child be?” For the hand of the Lord was with him. “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his purposes” (Psalm 110). Behold: the single silence of Zachariah, imposed not only as punishment for his unbelief but also as a sign that promotes faith, when removed astonishes all his neighbors with wonder and fear. Fame spreads throughout all the surrounding hill country concerning the prophet’s birth. All who could hear were stirred to inquire more carefully about the manner and condition of the child who had been born, so that by such and similar auspices this future prophet of Christ might be commended, and that they might provide, so to speak, advance signs for the forerunner of the Truth and prepare the way for him.

And Zachariah his father was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying, “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and accomplished the redemption of his people.” How great is the abundance of heavenly grace, if the devotion of our faith is ready to receive it! Behold: speech, which alone was taken from the unbelieving man, was restored to the believer together with the spirit of prophecy. The Lord visited his people as though they were wasting away from a long illness, and, as though sold under sin, redeemed them by the blood of his only Son. Since blessed Zachariah knew that this was soon to be accomplished, he narrates it in prophetic fashion as though it had already happened. It should also be noted that he is said to have visited and redeemed his people, not because, when he came, he found them already his, but because by visiting them he made them his. The same thought appears in the verse sung at the end of Proverbs concerning this people: “Who will find a strong woman?” (Proverbs, at the end). For he did not find that same woman—namely, the Church—already strong, that is, possessing devoted faith; rather, by betrothing her to himself he made her strong, perfecting her through the exaltation of her faith.

## ON THE VIGIL OF SAINT PETER THE APOSTLE

### READING FROM THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, CHAPTER 3

“Peter and John were going up into the temple at the ninth hour, the hour of prayer. And a certain man who had been lame from his mother’s womb was being carried; they placed him daily at the temple gate called Beautiful, so that he might ask alms from those entering the temple. When he saw Peter and John beginning to enter the temple, he begged to receive alms from them. But Peter, looking at him with John, said, ‘Look at us.’ And he fixed his attention on them, hoping to receive something from them. But Peter said, ‘Silver and gold I do not have, but what I have I give you: In the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, rise and walk.’ And taking him by his right hand, he lifted him up. Immediately his feet and ankles were strengthened, and leaping up, he stood and walked. And he entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God. And all the people saw him walking and praising God; and they recognized him, because he was the one who sat asking for alms at the Beautiful Gate of the temple. And they were all filled with amazement and astonishment at what had happened to him.”

Peter and John were going up into the temple at the ninth hour, the hour of prayer. As the apostles were about to enter the temple at the ninth hour, they first heal the lame man, who had long been helpless; then, laboring until evening, they instruct many thousands of people in the word of faith. For the teachers of the Church, coming at the end of the world, preach first to languishing Israel and afterward also to the Gentiles. These are the laborers whom the master of the household brings into the vineyard at the ninth and eleventh hours (Matthew 20).

And a certain man who had been lame from his mother’s womb was being carried. The people of Israel were rebellious not only against the incarnate Lord (John 10), but also against the Law given from the earliest times. Thus they were lame from their mother’s womb. This was well prefigured in Jacob, who wrestled with the angel and was blessed, yet walked with a limp: the people prevailed against the Lord in his Passion, and in some respects were blessed through faith, but in others were lame through unbelief.

They placed him daily before the temple gate called Beautiful, and so forth. The Beautiful Gate of the temple is the Lord, through whom, if anyone enters, he will be saved. Israel, weakened and unable to go to this gate, is brought there by the voices of the Law and the Prophets, so that from those entering the interior places of wisdom it may ask for the help of hearing the faith. They place the prophecies of future things before their hearers as though at the gate. But it is Peter’s role to lead him into the temple; to him, in return for his strong confession, were given both the name “rock” and the keys of heaven.

“Silver and gold I do not have.” The former tabernacle did possess ordinances of ritual justification, and the holy worldly sanctuary was adorned with gold and silver; but the blood of the Gospel shines forth as more precious than the metals of the Law. That people, which had previously lain in feeble-mindedness before gilded doors, enters the temple of the heavenly kingdom, saved in the name of the Crucified One (Hebrews 7). Otherwise, blessed Peter, remembering the Lord’s command—“Do not possess gold or silver” (Matthew 10)—customarily did not store for himself the money laid at the apostles’ feet, but reserved it for the needs of the poor who had abandoned their possessions.

And taking him by his right hand, he lifted him up, and so forth. The one whom he raises by his word he also strengthens with his right hand, because the teacher’s speech has little force in the hearts of his hearers unless it is also commended by examples from his own conduct.

And leaping up, he stood and walked, and entered the temple with them. A splendid order of perfection: first to raise the one who had been lying down, then to seize strength, and thus enter the gate of the kingdom with the apostles.

And they were filled with amazement and astonishment, and so forth. “Astonishment” here means terror. In another sense, *ecstasy* is used when the mind is not carried away by fear but is taken up by some inspiration or revelation.

## GOSPEL OF JOHN, LAST CHAPTER

“Jesus said to Peter, ‘Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?’ He said to him, ‘Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.’ He said to him, ‘Feed my lambs.’ He said to him again, ‘Simon, son of John, do you love me?’ He said to him, ‘Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.’ He said to him, ‘Feed my lambs.’ He said to him a third time, ‘Simon, son of John, do you love me?’ And Peter was grieved because he said to him a third time, ‘Do you love me?’ And he said to him, ‘Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you.’ He said to him, ‘Feed my sheep.’ Amen, amen, I say to you: when you were younger, you girded yourself and walked wherever you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go.’ But this he said, signifying by what death he would glorify God.”

Jesus said to Peter, “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” The Lord’s present question shows us the power of perfect love. Perfect love is that by which we are commanded to love the Lord with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength, and our neighbor as ourselves. Neither of these loves is effective without the other, nor is either perfect without the other, because neither can God truly be loved without the neighbor, nor the neighbor truly be loved without God.

He said to him, “Feed my lambs.” As though he were saying openly: This alone is the true proof of an undivided love for the Lord, if you strive to exercise diligent care and labor toward the brethren. For whoever neglects to provide his brother with the work of mercy that he is able to offer shows that he loves his Creator less justly, since he disregards his commands in supporting the need of his neighbor.

He said to him again, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” And he replied, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” Simon is called “John,” which means “obedient by the grace of God.” Therefore, rightly, when the first of the apostles is questioned about his love, he is called “Simon, son of John”—that is, “obedient by the grace of God”—so that it may clearly be shown to all that the fact that he obeys God’s commands with greater obedience than the others, and embraces him with more ardent love, is not a matter of human merit but of divine gift. Carefully, temperately, and in a simple voice he says, “Lord, you know that I love you”—which is openly to say: “I know that I love you with an undivided heart, as you know better than I; how much the others love you, however, is unknown to me, but everything is known to you.”

Peter was grieved because he said to him a third time, “Do you love me?” And he said to him, “Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.” In provident compassion the Lord asks Peter three times whether he loves him, so that by this threefold confession he might loose the bonds that Peter had tied by denying him three times. As often as fear of his Passion had caused him to deny that he knew him, so often, recreated by the Resurrection, he testifies that he loves him with his whole heart. But the shepherd must hold this firmly in his heart: he must remember that those placed under his authority are not his own, but the flock of his Lord, in accordance with what is said to Peter: “If you love me, feed my sheep.” “My,” he says, “not yours. I know that my sheep have been entrusted to you. If you love me perfectly, remember to govern them as mine, seeking in them my glory, my dominion, and my gains, not your own.”

(From the Vulgate tradition.) *Dilectio* retains a higher quality than *amor*; therefore, when the Lord says, “Simon, son of John, do you possess *dilectio* for me?” Peter does not dare to confess that he possesses the full measure of *dilectio*, but humbly professes that he has *amor* for him. For *dilectio* is found to be superior to *amor*. Accordingly, when the Lord questions Peter with a third designation and does not say, as in the previous two instances, “Do you possess *dilectio* for me?” but “Do you have *amor* for me?” Peter is grieved that in the third question he did not say, “Do you possess *dilectio* for me?”—as though he were now being questioned not about the higher rank of *dilectio* but about the lower grace of *amor*.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: when you were younger, you girded yourself and walked wherever you wished; but when you grow old, stretching out your hands, another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go.” As though he were saying plainly: You will one day prove how greatly you love me when, contending even unto death for the life of my little ones, you endure with strong steadfastness of mind all the bodily torments that the adversary desires to inflict, so that they too may be saved in body and mind. The stretching out of his hands signifies the position of his limbs, by which he was to be fitted to the cross. The girding by another expresses the imposition of the bonds by which the persecutor was to restrain him. Being led where he did not wish to go indicates the bitterness of death and suffering itself, which his bodily weakness recoiled from, though the spiritual steadfastness of his soul rejoiced to endure every adversity for the Lord. For he was not seeking his own will but the will of the one who sent him, Christ.

But this he said, signifying by what death he would glorify God. Peter indeed glorified God by his death when, by this sign, he showed everyone how greatly God should be revered and loved, preferring, when given the choice, to undergo the torments of the cross rather than cease preaching the heavenly Word.

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT PETER

### READING FROM THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, CHAPTER 12

“King Herod stretched out his hands to afflict some of those belonging to the Church. He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword. And when he saw that this pleased the Jews, he proceeded to seize Peter also. Now it was during the days of Unleavened Bread. After he had seized him, he put him in prison, delivering him to four squads of soldiers for custody, intending after Passover to bring him out before the people. So Peter was kept in prison, but prayer was being made without ceasing by the Church to God for him. When Herod was about to bring him out, on that very night Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, while guards before the door were keeping watch over the prison. And behold, an angel of the Lord stood by him, and a light shone in the prison room. Striking Peter’s side, he awakened him, saying, ‘Rise quickly.’ And the chains fell from his hands. The angel said to him, ‘Gird yourself and put on your sandals.’ And he did so. And he said to him, ‘Wrap your garment around you and follow me.’ And going out, he followed him, and he did not know that what was happening through the angel was real; he thought that he was seeing a vision. After passing the first and second guard posts, they came to the iron gate that leads into the city, which opened for them of its own accord. And going out, they proceeded along one street. And immediately the angel departed from him. And Peter, coming to himself, said, ‘Now I truly know that the Lord sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all the expectation of the Jewish people.’”

King Herod stretched out his hands to afflict some of those belonging to the Church. (From Josephus.) History relates that this Herod was struck by an angel in the third year of Claudius and the seventh year of his own reign.

He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword, and so forth. (From Bede.) Concerning this James, Clement of Alexandria relates a memorable story:

“And the man,” he says, “who had brought him before the judge for martyrdom—that is, James—was himself moved and confessed that he was a Christian. Both were led together to execution. As they were being led along the road, he asked James to grant him forgiveness. After a brief deliberation, James said, ‘Peace be with you,’ and kissed him; and so both were beheaded together.”

“Delivering him to four squads of soldiers,” and the rest. Just as a centurion had one hundred men, so a squad had four soldiers under its command.

Striking Peter’s side, he awakened him, and so forth. The striking of Peter’s side recalls Christ’s Passion, from whose wound our salvation flowed. To us also, held fast by chains of affliction, the apostle Peter himself offers such comfort, saying: “Since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same thought.”

“Gird yourself and put on your sandals.” And he did so, and so forth. We read that both the prophets and the apostles used belts. Peter had loosened his belt for a time because of the harshness of the prison, so that, with his tunic hanging down around his feet, he might in some measure temper the night’s cold. Thus he offers an example to the weak: when we are tested either by bodily discomfort or by human injury, we may relax something of the strictness of our chosen discipline. And because it is said, “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12), and “with your feet shod in readiness for the gospel of peace” (Ephesians 6), we are spiritually commanded to resume the insignia of virtue and of preaching the Word.

They came to the iron gate that leads into the city, which opened for them of its own accord, and so forth. The gate leading to the heavenly Jerusalem was narrow—indeed, iron—but it has now been made passable for us by the footsteps of the apostles, who conquered the iron door with their own blood. Concerning this Arator says:

> What wonder if iron doors yield to Peter,  
> whom God appoints guardian of the heavenly court,  
> making him retain the summit of his Church?  
> He commands him to overcome hell.

And Peter, coming to himself, said. That is, he returned from the height of contemplation to the condition that had previously existed in ordinary understanding.

“Now I truly know that the Lord sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod,” and so forth. That each one of us has an angel is found both in the *Book of the Shepherd* and in many passages of Holy Scripture. The Lord also says concerning little ones: “Their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matthew 18). And Jacob says of himself: “The angel who rescued me from all evils” (Genesis 48). Here too, the disciples believed that the angel of the apostle Peter had come.

## GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER 16

“Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi and asked his disciples, saying, ‘Who do people say that the Son of Man is?’ And they said, ‘Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, and others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.’ Jesus said to them, ‘But who do you say that I am?’ Simon Peter answered and said, ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.’ And Jesus answered and said to him, ‘Blessed are you, Simon Barjona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I say to you: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.’”

Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi. This Philip was the brother of Herod, whom we mentioned above. He was tetrarch of the regions of Ituraea and Trachonitis; in honor of Tiberius Caesar he named the city Caesarea, which is now called Paneas, and it is in the province of Phoenicia.

And he asked his disciples, saying, “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” (From Jerome.) He did not say, “Who do people say that I am?” but “Who do people say that the Son of Man is,” so that he would not appear to be asking boastfully about himself. Note that wherever “son of man” is written in the Old Testament, the Hebrew has [term absent in the supplied source], “son of Adam.” Likewise, where we read in the Psalm, “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” the Hebrew has [term absent in the supplied source], “sons of Adam.” He fittingly asks, “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” because those who speak about the Son of Man are human beings. But those who understand his divinity are called not human beings but gods.

And they said, “Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.” I am astonished that certain interpreters seek out the causes of each individual error and weave a very long discussion about why some thought our Lord Jesus was John, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets, when they could have erred about Elijah and Jeremiah just as Herod erred about John, saying, “John, whom I beheaded, has risen from the dead, and powers are at work in him” (Mark 6).

“But who do you say that I am?” Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” The prudent reader should observe that, from what follows and from the wording of the discourse, the apostles are called not human beings but gods. For after he had said, “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” he added, “But who do you say that I am?”—as though he were saying: Since they are human beings, they form human opinions; but you, who are gods, whom do you consider me to be?
