Peter confesses on behalf of all the apostles: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” He calls him the living God in contrast with those who are thought to be gods but are dead—Saturn, Jupiter, Ceres, Liber, and the other monstrous idols.

Jesus answered and said to him, “Blessed are you, Simon Barjona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” What flesh and blood could not reveal—that is, human teaching—was revealed by the grace of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, from this confession he receives his designation, because he has received the revelation from the Holy Spirit, whose son he is also to be called. For *Barjona* in our language means “son of a dove.” Others take it simply to mean that Simon—that is, Peter—is the son of John, according to the question in another passage: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” He replied, “Lord, you know.” They believe that the text has been corrupted through scribal error, so that instead of *Bar Joanna*—that is, “son of John”—*Barjona* was written, with one syllable removed. *Joanna* is interpreted as “the grace of the Lord.” Both names, however, can be understood mystically, since both the dove and the grace of God signify a spiritual gift. The statement, “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you,” can also be compared with the apostolic narrative in which he says, “Immediately I did not consult flesh and blood” (Galatians 1). There, “flesh and blood” means the Jews, so that it may also be shown in another sense that Christ, the Son of God, was revealed to him not through the teaching of the Pharisees but through the grace of God.

“And I say to you.” What does he mean by saying, “And I say to you”? Since you said to me, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” I say to you—not with an empty word that has no effect, but because for me to say is to accomplish—that you are Peter.

“For you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.” Just as he gave the apostles light, so that they might be called the light of the world, and just as the other names they received were derived from the Lord, so he gave Simon, who believed that Christ was the rock, the name Peter. In accordance with the metaphor of the rock, therefore, he rightly says to him, “I will build my Church upon you.”

(From Fulgentius.) Either “upon this rock,” that is, upon the one whom you have confessed with your mouth, saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” or “upon this rock,” upon Peter’s confession.

“And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” I understand the gates of hell to be vices and sins, or certainly the teachings of heretics, through which people who are enticed are led to Tartarus. Let no one, therefore, think that this refers to death, as though the apostles were not subject to the condition of death; their martyrdoms shine forth as evidence of the contrary.

“And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.” Bishops and presbyters, failing to understand this passage, assume something of the arrogance of the Pharisees, so that they either condemn the innocent or imagine that they can absolve the guilty, although before God it is not the priests’ sentence but their life that is examined. We read in Leviticus concerning lepers, where they are commanded to show themselves to the priests, and if they have leprosy, then to be declared unclean by the priest (Leviticus 14). This does not mean that the priests make lepers unclean, but that they have knowledge of who is leprous and who is not, and can discern who is clean and who is unclean. Therefore, just as there the priest makes the leper clean or unclean, so here the bishop or presbyter binds or looses—not those who are innocent or guilty in themselves, but, in accordance with his office, when he has heard the varieties of sins, knows who should be bound and who should be loosed.

## ON THE VIGIL OF SAINT PAUL

### READING FROM THE LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE GALATIANS, CHAPTER 1

“For I make known to you the Gospel that was preached by me: it is not according to man. For I did not receive it from man, nor did I learn it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ. For you heard of my former way of life in Judaism, how excessively I persecuted the Church of God and devastated it, and advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries in my own nation, being more abundantly zealous for the traditions of my fathers. But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me so that I might proclaim him among the nations, immediately I did not consult flesh and blood. Nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia, and again returned to Damascus. Then after that I went to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and I remained with him fifteen days. But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the brother of the Lord. Now concerning what I write to you, behold, before God, I do not lie.”

“I make known to you the Gospel that was preached by me: it is not according to man. For I did not receive it from man, nor did I learn it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ.” The very word ἀποκάλυψις (*apokalypsis*), that is, “revelation,” properly belongs to Scripture, and was used by none of the wise men of the world among the Greeks. It signifies that revelation which he saw when, going to Damascus, he was deemed worthy to hear Christ’s voice on the road, and, his eyes having been blinded, to behold the true light of the world. For if Paul’s Gospel is not according to man, and he neither received nor learned it from man but through a revelation of Jesus Christ, then Jesus Christ who revealed the Gospel to Paul is certainly not merely a human being; and if he is not a human being, he is consequently God. This does not mean that we deny the humanity assumed by him, but only that we deny that he is merely human. There is a difference between receiving and learning: one receives through another, who is first introduced so that one may be led to faith and believe that what is written is true; but one learns when one comes to understand, once explained and opened, those things that had been represented through riddles and parables—not with a human being as revealer, but with Christ, who revealed them to Paul.

“For you heard of my former way of life in Judaism, how excessively I persecuted the Church of God and devastated it,” and so forth. How elegant is the observation and weight of the words! “You heard,” he says, “of my way of life—not formerly pleasing, and not merely in Judaism, not in the Law of God—how excessively I persecuted the Church of God, not as the others did.” Here too there arises astonishment: it was not one of those who lightly persecuted the Church of God who was converted to the faith, but the man who surpassed the others in persecution. By calling it the Church of God, he either signifies that Christ himself is God, or that the Church belongs to the same God who was formerly the giver of the Law.

“But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace,” and so forth. Not only here but also in the Letter to the Romans Paul writes that he was set apart for the Gospel of God, and Jeremiah is said to have been known by God and sanctified before he was formed in the womb (Jeremiah 1). We may understand “the womb of my mother” as the Law, which was pregnant with Christ. Paul says that he was separated from its carnal observance through the grace of Christ. But the text does not say that he “revealed his Son to me,” as though it meant: “He revealed his Son to me.” For something can be revealed to the person in whom it was not previously present. But in the person in whom it is revealed, what is revealed is something that was previously in him and afterward became manifest. The same applies to the Gospel statement: “Among you stands one whom you do not know.” And elsewhere: “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into the world.” From this it is clear that knowledge of God is present by nature in everyone. No one is born without Christ, or without within himself the beginnings of wisdom, justice, and the remaining virtues.

Hence many people, without the faith and Gospel of Christ, do some things wisely or virtuously: they obey their parents, extend a hand to the needy, do not oppress their neighbors, and do not seize what belongs to others. The passage can also be understood differently in Paul: the Son of God is revealed because, when Paul preached him, the nations recognized the one whom previously they did not know.

“Immediately I did not consult flesh and blood.” Or, as the Greek has it more accurately, οὐ προσανεθέμην σαρκὶ καὶ αἵματι (*ou prosanethemen sarki kai haimati*), “I did not consult flesh and blood.” Clearly, after Christ’s revelation Paul did not confer with flesh and blood, because he did not wish to cast pearls before swine or give what is holy to dogs. Consider what is written about sinners: “My spirit shall not remain in these people, because they are flesh” (Genesis 6). With such people, who were flesh and blood, the Apostle did not discuss the Gospel that had been revealed to him. Rather, he gradually turned them from flesh and blood into spirit, and only then entrusted to them the hidden mysteries of the Gospel.

“Nor did I go to Jerusalem,” and so forth. What benefit is there in this religious interpretation if I read that Paul, after Christ’s revelation, immediately went into Arabia and returned from Arabia to Damascus, but do not know what he did there? His departure and return give me an opportunity for deeper understanding. Arabia, which is interpreted as “low-lying” and “western,” signifies the Old Testament. As soon as Paul believed, he turned to the Law, the Prophets, and the mysteries of the Old Testament, already situated in the west, seeking Christ in them—the Christ whom he had been commanded to preach among the nations. Having found him there, he did not remain there longer, but returned to Damascus, that is, to the blood and Passion of Christ. From there, strengthened by prophetic reading, he proceeded to Jerusalem, the place of vision and peace—not so much to learn something from the apostles as to compare with them the Gospel that he had taught.

“Then after three years I went to Jerusalem to visit Peter.” He did not go to look at his eyes, cheeks, and face—to see whether he was thin or fat, whether his nose was hooked or straight, or whether his forehead was covered with hair or, as Clement reports in his *Periods*, whether he was bald on his head. Nor do I think it accorded with apostolic dignity, after so much preparation over three years, that he wished to observe something merely human in Peter. Rather, he looked at him with the eyes with which he also appears now in his Epistles; with these eyes Paul saw Cephas, the eyes with which Paul himself is now seen by every prudent person. For the fact that he went to Jerusalem to see the Apostle does not indicate a desire to learn—since he too had the same source of preaching—but rather the offering of honor to the earlier apostle.

“And I remained with him fifteen days.” He did not need extensive instruction, since he had prepared himself for so long to see Peter. And although it may seem superfluous to some to observe even the numbers found in Scripture, I nevertheless think that the fifteen days during which Paul stayed with Peter signify complete knowledge and perfected teaching. For there are fifteen songs in the Psalter, and fifteen steps by which the just person ascends to sing to God and stand in his courts.

“But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the brother of the Lord.” The other apostles too are called the brothers of the Lord, as in the Gospel: “Go, tell my brothers: I am going to my Father and your Father” (John, last chapter). But just as Job and the other patriarchs were indeed called servants of God, while Moses was singularly eminent, so that it was written of him, “Not so with my servant Moses,” in the same way blessed James was specially called the Lord’s brother on account of his outstanding character, incomparable faith, and considerable wisdom. He was also called this because he was the first to preside over the Church that had first been gathered from the Jews as believers in Christ.

But the reason why certain persons, apart from the Twelve, are called apostles is that all who had seen the Lord and afterward proclaimed him were called apostles, as it is written to the Corinthians: “He appeared to the eleven, then he appeared also to James, then to all the apostles.” For others also were appointed apostles by those whom the Lord had chosen, as he says to the Philippians: “I considered it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my fellow soldier, and your apostle” (Philippians 2). And concerning such men it is written to the Corinthians: “Whether apostles of the churches, to the glory of God” (2 Corinthians 8). Silas and Judas, too, were called apostles by the apostles.

“But what I am writing to you—behold, before God, I am not lying.” This may be understood simply, so that the meaning is: “What I am writing to you is true, and I confirm it with God as witness, for it is embellished neither by any verbal artifice nor by any falsehood.” Or it may be taken in a deeper sense, so that it reads: “What I am writing to you is before God,” that is, worthy of God’s sight, because I am not lying; and just as “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous,” while “he turns his face away from the sight of the wicked,” so now the things being written are before God, since I, who write them, am not lying—things that would not be before the Lord if I were lying.

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT PAUL

### READING FROM THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, CHAPTER 9

> “But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest and asked him for letters to Damascus, to the synagogues, so that, if he found any men or women belonging to this Way, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. And as he was making the journey, it happened that he was approaching Damascus. And suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. And falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him: ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’ He said: ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And he: ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting; it is hard for you to kick against the goad.’ And trembling and astonished, he said: ‘Lord, what do you want me to do?’ And the Lord said to him: ‘Rise and enter the city, and there you will be told what you must do.’ Now the men who were accompanying him stood astonished, hearing the voice but seeing no one. Saul rose from the ground, and when his eyes were opened he saw nothing. Taking him by the hands, they led him into Damascus. And for three days he was unable to see, and he neither ate nor drank. Now there was a certain disciple in Damascus named Ananias. And the Lord said to him in a vision: ‘Ananias.’ And he said: ‘Here I am, Lord.’ And the Lord said to him: ‘Rise and go to the street called Straight, and seek in the house of Judas a man named Saul, a Tarsian; for behold, he is praying. And he saw a man named Ananias entering and laying his hands upon him, so that he might regain his sight.’ But Ananias answered: ‘Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints in Jerusalem. And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who invoke your name.’ But the Lord said to him: ‘Go, for this man is a vessel chosen for me, to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name.’ And Ananias went and entered the house, and laying his hands upon him, he said: ‘Saul, brother, the Lord Jesus has sent me—the one who appeared to you on the road by which you were coming—so that you may see and be filled with the Holy Spirit.’ And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. And rising, he was baptized; and when he had taken food, he was strengthened.”

“But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord” (from Bede). That is, afflicting those present with slaughter and terrifying those absent with threats.

“Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” He did not say, “Why are you persecuting my members?” but, “Why are you persecuting me?” For he himself, in his body—which is the Church—still suffers the wicked. And he declares that the benefits bestowed upon his members have been done to him, when he says: “I was hungry and you gave me food” (Matthew 25); and, explaining this, he added: “As long as you did it to one of the least of my brothers.” “I am the one whom you are persecuting.” He did not say, “I am God,” or “I am the Son of God,” but rather: “Receive the weakness of my humility, and lay aside the scales of your pride.”

“But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you must do,” and so forth. He did not immediately show him what had to be done, but gave advance notice that it would be done later in the city, so that afterward he might stand more firmly in good works, having first been utterly overthrown and fallen away from his former error.

“And when his eyes were opened he saw nothing,” and so forth. He could never have seen properly again unless he had first been blinded. By excluding his own wisdom, which had been thrown into confusion, he rightly entrusted everything thereafter to faith.

“And for three days he was unable to see,” and so forth. Because he had not believed that the Lord had conquered death by rising on the third day, he is now instructed by his own example: the darkness of three days would be changed when the light returned.

“For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name,” and so forth. He ought not, he says, to fear him as a persecutor, but rather to embrace him as a brother, because he is ready to endure with the saints the various sufferings that he had inflicted upon them.

“And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes,” and so forth. The whole body of a dragon is said to be woven together with scales. Since the Jews were called serpents and offspring of vipers, and since Saul had followed their faithlessness, he had covered the eyes of his heart as though with serpentine skin. But when the scales fell from his eyes under the hand of Ananias, it was shown outwardly on his face that he was now receiving the true light in his mind.

### THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER 19

> “Then Peter answered and said to him: ‘Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what then will there be for us?’ But Jesus said to them: ‘Amen I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And everyone who has left house or brothers or sisters, or father or mother or wife or children or lands, for my name’s sake, will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life.’”

“Then Peter answered and said to him: ‘Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what then will there be for us?’” (from Jerome). Great confidence! Peter was a fisherman; he had not been rich. He sought food by his hands and by his craft, and yet he speaks confidently: “We have left everything.” For everyone who abandons the will to possess leaves everything. But because it is not enough merely to leave things, he adds what is perfect: “and we have followed you.” We have done what you commanded; therefore, what reward will you give?

“But Jesus said to them: ‘Amen I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.’” He did not say, “You who have left everything,” for the philosopher Socrates did this too, and many others despised riches; but he said, “You who have followed me,” which properly characterizes the apostles and believers. “In the regeneration,” when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, when the dead rise incorruptible from corruption, you also will sit upon the seats of those judging, condemning the twelve tribes of Israel because they were unwilling to believe in you who believed.

(From Augustine.) Here we learn that Jesus will judge together with his disciples. Hence elsewhere he said to the Jews: “If I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they themselves will be your judges” (Matthew 14). Nor should we think that he and only twelve men will sit upon twelve thrones to judge. For by the number twelve a certain entire multitude of judges is signified, because of the two parts of the number seven, by which universality is often signified. These two parts—that is, three and four—multiplied one by the other make twelve. For four times three and three times four are both twelve.

Otherwise, since we read that the apostle Matthias was appointed in the place of Judas the betrayer, the apostle Paul, who labored more than all of them, would have no place from which to judge. Yet he clearly shows that he belongs with the other saints to the number of the judges when he says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Corinthians 6). The same reasoning applies to those who are to be judged under this number twelve. For because it was said, “judging the twelve tribes of Israel,” the tribe of Levi, which is the thirteenth among them, will not be judged; nor will they judge only that people and not the other nations together with it.

When he says “in the regeneration,” he undoubtedly wished the resurrection of the dead to be understood by the name “regeneration.” For our flesh will be regenerated through incorruption, just as our soul has been regenerated through faith. What, then, shall we say about Paul? Will he judge as the thirteenth? Just as in the one hundred and fifty-three fish there is understood a great number of saints; and in the five virgins, countless virgins; and in the five brothers of the man who was tormented in the underworld, the thousands of the Jewish people; and in the seven thousand men of whom it is said to Elijah, thousands of thousands—so in the twelve thrones are signified not twelve men but a great number of the perfect.

The world is contained by its four designated regions. From all these regions people are called into the Trinity; since three times four makes twelve, it signifies a perfect number. Thus the twelve tribes of Israel are the whole Israel: just as those who will judge are from the whole world, so those who will be judged will also be from the whole world.

“And everyone who has left house or brothers or sisters, or father or mother or wife or children or lands, for my name’s sake, will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (from Bede). The meaning, therefore, is this: Whoever has left bodily things for the sake of Christ’s Gospel will receive spiritual goods. In comparison and according to their worth, these will be as though a small number were compared with the number one hundred. For from brothers and companions in his purpose, who are bound to him by a spiritual bond, he receives a far more precious love, even in this life. Read the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and they held everything in common” (Acts 4). Nor was there anyone needy among those who had left their possessions for the Lord. Of these the Apostle also says: “As having nothing and possessing everything.”

It is also possible to understand what he says—“he will receive a hundredfold”—as referring symbolically, in this present age, to houses, brothers, sisters, mothers, children, and lands, together with persecutions, in a higher sense. For the number one hundred, transferred from the left hand to the right, although it seems to retain through the bending of the fingers the same form that the number ten had on the left, nevertheless greatly surpasses it in magnitude. For all who, for the sake of the kingdom of God, hope for eternal things, even in this life, which is filled with persecutions, taste with certain faith the joy of that kingdom; and while awaiting the heavenly homeland, rightly signified by the right hand, they enjoy the sincere love of all the elect together.

## THE SEVENTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

### READING OF THE LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER 6

> “All of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death. For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be [planted together] in his resurrection. Knowing this, that our old man was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, and that we might no longer serve sin. For whoever has died has been justified from sin. But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we will also live together with him, knowing that Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer rule over him. For in that he died, he died to sin once for all. But in that he lives, he lives to God. So you also must consider yourselves to be dead indeed to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

“All of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death” (from Jerome). The Apostle commanded that, because Christ died and was buried for us and rose again, we too should crucify our wills and desires in likeness to his passion and imitate in baptism the mystery of his death, burial, and resurrection.

(From Origen.) One must first die to sin, so that one may be buried with Christ; for burial is owed to the dead, and no living person is ever buried. If you are still alive to sin, you cannot be buried with Christ or placed in his new tomb. For your old man is alive, and therefore you cannot walk in newness of life.

What is the reason that, although the Lord himself told his disciples to baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, the Apostle assumes in baptism the name of Christ alone? It is that in the present passage he wished to examine not so much the nature of baptism as the death of Christ. In likeness to that death, he would persuade us also to die to sin and be buried with Christ. It would certainly not have been appropriate, when he was speaking of death, to mention either the Father or the Holy Spirit. For “the Word became flesh,” and rightly, where there is flesh, death is discussed. Nor was it appropriate for him to say: “All of us who have been baptized in the name of the Father,” or “in the name of the Holy Spirit, have been baptized into his death.”

“For we were buried with Christ through baptism into death.” If we were buried with Christ, according to what we said above—that is, according to the fact that we died to sin—then, when Christ rises from the dead, we too will rise together with him; and when he ascends into heaven, we will ascend together with him; and when he sits at the right hand of the Father, we will be said to sit together with him in the heavenly places, as the Apostle himself says elsewhere: “He raised us up together with Christ and made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 1).

“So that, just as he rose,” and so forth. The newness of life is present when we have put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new, who was created according to God and is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of the one who created him. For the Apostle also says: “Although our outward man is being corrupted, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4).

Observe those who advance in faith and shine daily in virtues: how they continually add better things to their good works and seek more honorable things in place of honorable ones; how they grow in understanding, knowledge, and wisdom. You will understand that they are renewed every day. Let us therefore walk in newness of life, showing ourselves daily as new—and, so to speak, more beautiful—to the one who raised us with Christ, gathering the beauty of our face in Christ as in a mirror. He, rising from the dead, ascended from earthly humility to the glory of the Father’s majesty, so that they may see our good works and glorify our Father who is in heaven (Matthew 6). Thus we shall rightly be said to have risen together with Christ through the glory of the Father.

“For if we have been planted together,” and so forth. He presents the death of Christ as that of a certain planted tree, with which he wants us to be planted together, so that, when our root receives the sap of its root, it may produce branches of righteousness and bear fruits of life. Christ, therefore, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God, is himself the tree of life, into which we must be planted together. By a new and gracious gift of God, his death becomes for us the tree of life.

The Apostle rightly did not say, “If we have been planted together with his death,” but “in the likeness of his death.” Christ died to sin in such a way that he committed no sin at all. We cannot die in such a way that we know nothing of sin. Yet we can possess a likeness of his death, so that by imitating him and following in his footsteps we abstain from sin. This, then, is what human nature can receive: that it may become like his death by imitating him and not sinning. To be wholly and completely ignorant of sin belongs to Christ alone.

Therefore he wants us to be planted together in the likeness of his death, by which he died to sin once for all, so that we may also be planted together in his resurrection. In both cases one must understand the phrase “planted together”: in the likeness of his death and in the likeness of his resurrection.

“Knowing this, that our old man was crucified together with him.” Our old man is to be understood as the former life that we led in sins. We bring about its end and a certain destruction when we receive within ourselves faith in the cross of Christ. Through this faith the body of sin is so destroyed that our members, which served sin, no longer serve it, but God.

“So that the body of sin might be destroyed, and that we might no longer serve sin” (from Origen). We must examine more carefully how he says “the body of sin,” since the expression seems to admit two interpretations: either he calls our body the body of sin, or he says that sin itself possesses a particular body that must be destroyed by those who ought no longer to serve sin.

Since either interpretation can be admitted in this passage, we shall explain what seems to us to be the case regarding both. If we suppose that sin has a body of its own, it will appear that, just as it was said of those who have been restored into the new man, “You are the body of Christ and members in part” (1 Corinthians 12), so it can also be said of those who have not yet crucified the old man that they are the body of sin and its members. The devil is the head of this body, just as Christ is the head of the body of the churches, which has neither spot nor wrinkle (Ephesians 4).

The members from which this body of sin consists may be understood as those which the Apostle listed above as being members upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, wantonness, greed, contention, anger, deceit, quarrels, dissensions, heresies, envy, revelries, and things of this kind. It is fitting to say that the body consists of all these members and to call it the body of the old man. If someone destroys it through the cross of Christ and is changed into the new man, who was created according to God, he will no longer be said to serve sin. Without doubt, he serves sin as long as he is subject to any of those things that we explained above to be members of sin.

But if the Apostle is understood to have called our own body the body of sin, then this will certainly be accepted according to the interpretation by which David also speaks of himself: “For I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins” (Psalm 50). On account of this sin the Church also received from the Apostle the tradition of giving baptism even to infants.

(From Primas.) Or “so that the body of sin might be destroyed,” that is, so that not merely some part but all vices might be destroyed, since one vice is a member of sin, while the body is the totality of sins, whose fullness is original sin. Christ, however, was crucified not in part but whole, so that we might die completely to sin and live to God.

Or it may mean that our body is destroyed from the service of sin and becomes the slave of righteousness, whereas it used to belong to sin. For “everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8).

Or “the body of sin” may be understood as the person who, still outside baptism, is subject to the condition of original sin and has not yet received any beginnings of life, but is wholly alienated from salvation.

“For whoever has died has been justified from sin.” That is, he has been separated from sin; for a dead person does not sin at all. Or, as we said above, having died to the errors of his former life, he has been renewed in Christ and made his member, and he resists desires and passions.

“But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we will also now live together with Christ” (from Origen). In this statement the Apostle brings to a conclusion everything that he had constructed above, and says: “If we have died with Christ”—through the things that we demonstrated above—“we believe that we will also live together with him.” He did not say, “and we have lived together,” just as he said, “we have died,” but “we will live together,” to show that death is at work in the present, whereas life is in the future, namely, when Christ, who is our life hidden in God, is revealed.

“Knowing that Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more.” Resurrection is understood in two ways. One is the resurrection by which, in mind and faith, we rise with Christ from earthly things so that we may think about heavenly things. The other will be the general resurrection in the flesh. The former belongs to the first coming of the Lord; the latter will be in the second. Therefore the Apostle, in a definitive statement, established that Christ would no longer die, so that those who will live together with him might also be secure in the eternity of life.

“Death will no longer rule over him.” One may say more briefly that here he calls death the common and intermediate death by which Christ died, as the same Apostle says, “according to the Scriptures.” There is nothing absurd in the fact that the one who assumed the form of a servant endured the dominion of death, which undoubtedly rules over all who, placed in the flesh, are reckoned under the condition of servitude.

But another person, who observes a deeper meaning in these words of Paul through the power of the Spirit, says that the death of which he had said that it would no longer rule over Christ is to be understood as that final enemy itself which was represented by the sea-monster that swallowed Jonah. Christ entered into this death as Jonah entered the belly of the sea-monster—namely, into the place that the Savior himself called “the heart of the earth.” He says that the Son of Man would be there for three days and three nights, following the example of Jonah (Matthew 12), in order to release those who were held there by death. Hence the Apostle rightly says in the present passage that death will no longer rule over him.

For he will not again give himself over to the dominion of the tyrant, nor will he again empty himself so as to assume the form of a servant and become obedient unto death (Philippians 2), lest he again, in the form of a servant—although placed there by will and not by necessity—suffer the dominion of the tyrant and of death. This is what he says: “For in that he died to sin, he died once for all.”

“But in that he lives, he lives to God.” To live to God is to be understood as meaning that, when what he had emptied himself of while existing in the form of God and taking the form of a servant had been completed, and when he had become obedient unto death, he again remains in the form of God and equal to the Father. Hence he rightly says in what follows: “So you also must consider yourselves to be dead indeed to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” Through imitation of Christ, let us die to sin, becoming separated from it, and live to God, joining ourselves to him and becoming one spirit with him.

“So you also must consider yourselves,” and so forth. Whoever thinks that he is going to die does not sin. For example, if desire for a woman draws me, or desire for silver, gold, or estates presses upon me, and I place in my heart the thought that I have died in Christ, desire is immediately extinguished and driven away; sin is extinguished, fury ceases, anger and hatred subside. In this way one is found to die to sin and to live to God.

What else does he mean by saying “alive to God in Christ Jesus” except living in wisdom, righteousness, peace, and sanctification—all of which Christ is?

(From Primas.) Or “consider yourselves to be dead to sin”: just as your head died once for all, so you, having been made his members, should follow the examples of his life, so that you may owe nothing further to death; that is, so that death may have no place in you to be pursued. But he lives to God who follows the footsteps of Christ in humility, sanctification, and piety.

### THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER 5

> “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not kill.’ But whoever kills will be liable to judgment. But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to the council. Whoever says, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the Gehenna of fire. Therefore, if you offer your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go first to be reconciled to your brother. And then, when you come, offer your gift.”

“Amen, amen, I say to you: unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees,” and so forth (from Augustine). This means: Unless you fulfill not only those least commandments of the Law that initiate a person, but also these commandments that I add—I who did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it—you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.

The righteousness of the Pharisees is that they do not kill. The righteousness of those who are to enter the kingdom of God is that they do not become angry without cause. Not killing is therefore a small matter, and whoever violates that commandment will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. But whoever fulfills it—not killing—will not immediately be great and fit for the kingdom of heaven; nevertheless, he ascends a certain step. He will be perfected if he does not become angry without cause. If he perfects this, he will be much farther removed from murder.

Therefore, the one who teaches us not to become angry does not abolish the commandment of the Law that we must not kill; rather, he fulfills it, so that we may preserve innocence both outwardly, by not killing, and in the heart, by not becoming angry.

“You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not kill.’ But whoever kills will be liable to judgment.” Under the Law, judgment was given so that the person who killed would himself also be killed.

“But I say to you.” That is: I, the new man, speak new things to you who are new.

“Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (from Augustine). We must observe how great the difference is between the righteousness of the Pharisees and that of Christians, which introduces a person into the kingdom of heaven. There, murder makes one liable to judgment; here, anger likewise makes one liable to judgment.

“Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to the council” (from Jerome). This word properly belongs to the Hebrews. For *Raca* is called κενός (*kenos*), that is, “empty” and “vacant”; we may call such a person, in the common insult, “brainless.” If we are going to give an account for an idle word, how much more for an insult?

It is also significantly added: “whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca.’” No one is our brother except one who has the same father as we do. When, therefore, he likewise believes in God and knows Christ, the wisdom of God, by what reasoning can he be branded with the epithet of folly?

(From Augustine.) What is the difference between being liable to judgment, being liable to the council, and being liable to the Gehenna of fire? The last expression sounds most serious and indicates that certain stages proceed from lighter matters to more serious ones, until one reaches the Gehenna of fire. Therefore, if it is lighter to be liable to judgment than to be liable to the council, and likewise lighter to be liable to the council than to be liable to the Gehenna of fire, then it must be understood that it is lighter to become angry with one’s brother without cause than to say “Raca,” and again lighter to say “Raca” than to say “Fool.”

For guilt itself would not have degrees unless sins were also mentioned progressively. *Raca* is obscure, because it is neither Greek nor Latin. Some have wished to derive its interpretation from Greek, supposing that it means “ragged,” for in Greek a rag is called *rachus*. More probably, however, it is said to be a word signifying nothing else but expressing the movement of an indignant mind, like the interjections found among grammarians: when spoken by someone grieving, “alas,” or by someone angry, “ha!” Such expressions belong properly to their respective languages and are not easily transferred into another language. This is why both the Greek and Latin translator retained the word itself, since they could not find a way to interpret it.

There are therefore stages in these sins. First, someone becomes angry and retains the movement conceived in the heart. If he then forces out the voice of an indignant person, the disturbance itself—expressing nothing specific but testifying through its outburst to the movement of the mind by which the person at whom we are angry is struck—is certainly more serious than if the anger were suppressed in silence. But if not only the voice of indignation is heard, but also a word that now clearly indicates and marks a definite reproach against the person to whom it is directed, who could doubt that this is more serious than merely uttering the sound of indignation?

Thus in the first case there is one thing: anger alone. In the second there are two: anger and the voice that signifies anger, together with the expression in that voice of a definite reproach.

Now consider also the three forms of liability: judgment, council, and Gehenna of fire. In judgment, there is still room for a defense. In the council, although judgment is also usually present, the distinction itself compels us to acknowledge that here the pronouncement of the sentence seems to belong to the council. For the matter is no longer being argued with the accused as to whether he should be condemned; rather, those who judge deliberate among themselves what punishment should be inflicted on one whom they agree must be condemned.

But the Gehenna of fire has neither an uncertain condemnation, as judgment does, nor the punishment of one already condemned, as the council does. In the Gehenna of fire both the condemnation and the punishment of the condemned are certain.

“Gehenna” is a compound name, [the source is incomplete here]. For there was a valley of the sons of Hinnom near Jerusalem, in which many corpses of the dead lay; hence the name Gehenna appropriately corresponds to the underworld.

“Therefore, if you offer your gift before the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar,” and so forth (from Jerome). He did not say, “If you have something against your brother,” but “if your brother has something against you,” so that a more demanding necessity of reconciliation might be imposed upon you. Therefore, as long as we cannot appease him, I do not know whether we can consequently offer our gifts to God.

He plainly teaches that one who is not at peace with his brother cannot rightly offer to the Lord the sacrifice of peace.

(From Augustine.) If it comes to mind that our brother has something against us—that is, if we have injured him in some way—then he has something against us. We have something against him if he has injured us; in that case there is no need to go to him for reconciliation. You will not ask forgiveness from one who has wronged you, but only forgive him, just as you desire the Lord to forgive you what you have committed.

Therefore, one must go toward reconciliation when it comes to mind that perhaps we have injured our brother in some way. But one must go not with bodily feet, but through movements of the soul, so that with humble affection you may prostrate yourself before your brother, toward whom you have run with loving thought, in the presence of the one to whom you are about to offer your gift.

Spiritually, our temple is the inner person; the altar is faith; the gift is prophecy, teaching, prayer, hymn, psalm, and anything else of this kind belonging to spiritual gifts. In this way, even if he is present, you will be able to soften him and restore him to friendship with an undeceitful heart, asking forgiveness—provided that you have first done this before God. Go to him not with the sluggish movement of the body, but with the swiftest affection of love; and then, returning—that is, directing your attention back to what you had begun to do—you will offer your gift.

## THE EIGHTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

### READING OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER 6

> “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity for iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness for sanctification. For when you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness. What fruit, therefore, did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed? For their end is death. But now, having been freed from sin and having become servants of God, you have your fruit for sanctification, and the end is eternal life. For the wages of sin are death, but the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

“I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity for iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness for sanctification” (from Origen). Through these words the Apostle instills a certain shame in his hearers, so that they may at least give to righteousness and sanctification what they previously gave to uncleanness and iniquity.

What, then, is so human—that is, what is so easy, so free of burden, and such that no weakness of the flesh can excuse it at all? For righteousness ought to be honored much more and much more earnestly.

“But I,” he says, “act humanely and in an ordinary manner; I ask for the same things and require similar things. Formerly your feet ran to the temples of demons; now let them run to the Church of God. Formerly they ran to shed blood; now let them run to save blood. Formerly your hands were extended in order to seize what belonged to others; now let them be extended in order to distribute what belongs to you. Formerly your eyes looked around for a woman in order to desire her; now let them look around for the poor, the weak, and the needy, in order to show compassion. Your ears took pleasure in empty talk or in disparaging good people; now let them turn to hear the word of God, to the explanation of the Law, and to receiving the discipline of wisdom. And let the tongue that has become accustomed to insults, curses, and shameful speech now turn to bless the Lord, uttering sound and honorable speech at all times, so that it may give grace to those who hear.”

(From Primasius.) I say “human” because of the weakness of your flesh; that is, I ought indeed to demand greater things from you in return for divine service, but accommodating myself and tempering my demands to your weakness, I proclaim and recommend things that are human and possible, so that, just as you were ready to pursue harmful and hostile things, so you may be eager to perform things that are beneficial and conducive to salvation.

For when you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness. Therefore, when someone serves sin, he is free from righteousness—that is, he is alien to righteousness. Here he calls “free” what is “alien,” and rightly so, for no one can serve both sin and righteousness, as it is said: “No one can serve two masters.” It should certainly be noted that there is both a blameworthy freedom and a praiseworthy servitude. For to be free from righteousness is a crime; but to be a servant of righteousness is praiseworthy. When he says that one becomes a servant of righteousness, understand at the same time that one becomes a servant of wisdom, piety, chastity, and all the virtues together. Conversely, whoever is a slave of sin is at once a slave of evil desire, anger, rage, immodesty, robbery, and every vice and crime.

What fruit, therefore, did you have then, in those things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. (From Primasius.) It is as though he said: What sort of fruit did you have in the practice of that deed, at the mere recollection of which there is even shame? In the worship of God, however, this itself is already fruit: that you live, sanctified through baptism.

(From Origen.) Divine Scripture teaches that there is fruit both of good things and of evil things, as the Savior himself says in the Gospels: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad.” If someone, therefore, turns his mind and purpose toward righteousness, he undoubtedly becomes ashamed and reproaches himself for his former deeds, which he performed while subject to sin, because the end of those things is death. But what death, I ask? It is certain that this is not the ordinary death. No one turns to righteousness after death, nor is ashamed of former evil deeds. What, then, is meant? Does he perhaps appear to call it the death of sin, since “the soul that sins shall itself die”? Or can it rather be understood that he calls that death by which we die to sin with Christ and put an end to vices and crimes, so that afterward he seems to have said: “For the end of those things is death”?

But now, freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit in sanctification, and its end is eternal life. He compares fruits with fruits: he declares that the fruits of sin, for which they now—that is, after being freed from sin and made servants of God—are ashamed, end in death. But the fruits of righteousness, which consist in justification, he says attain eternal life as their end.

For the wages of sin are death. For among Roman soldiers, money was paid out as wages for the labor of military service. Thus the payment for labor is its fruit; it is called *stipendium* from *stips*, a contribution to be weighed out. For the ancients were accustomed to weigh money rather than count it. Therefore whoever serves as a soldier of sin will receive death as the wage—that is, the recompense—for his labor in wickedness.

But the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. He did not likewise say “the wages of righteousness,” because righteousness did not exist in us before he rewarded us. It was not acquired through our labor, but granted and forgiven as a gift of God.

## THE GOSPEL OF MARK, CHAPTER VIII

“When there was a great crowd with Jesus, and they had nothing to eat, he called his disciples and said to them: ‘I have compassion on the crowd, because they have now been with me three days and have nothing to eat. And if I send them away fasting to their homes, they will faint on the way; for some of them have come from a great distance.’ And his disciples answered him: ‘From where can anyone satisfy these people with bread here in the wilderness?’ And he asked them: ‘How many loaves do you have?’ They said: ‘Seven.’ And he ordered the crowd to sit down on the ground. Taking the seven loaves, giving thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples to distribute, and they distributed them to the crowd. They also had a few small fish; he blessed these as well and ordered them to be distributed. They ate and were satisfied, and they collected what remained of the fragments, seven baskets. There were about four thousand who had eaten, and he dismissed them.”

“When there was a great crowd with Jesus, and they had nothing to eat,” and so forth. (From Bede.) In this reading we should consider, in our one and the same Redeemer, the distinct operation of his humanity and divinity. For who does not see that the Lord’s compassion for the crowd, lest they should fail either through hunger or through the exertion of a longer journey, is an expression of feeling and of compassion for human weakness? But that he satisfied four thousand people with seven loaves and a few small fish is the work of divine power.

Mystically, however, this miracle signifies that we cannot pass safely through the way of the present world unless the grace of our Redeemer refreshes us with the nourishment of his word. Typologically, the difference between this meal and that of the five loaves and two fish is that there the letter of the Old Testament was signified as being full of spiritual grace, whereas here the truth and grace of the New Testament is shown to be offered to the faithful. Certainly both meals took place on a mountain, as the account of the other Evangelists makes clear, because Scripture rightly understood from both Testaments teaches us the height both of heavenly commandments and of rewards. Both proclaim with one voice the height of Christ, who is the mountain of the house of the Lord on the summit of the mountains. Whoever builds upon him the city or house of the Lord—that is, the Church—and raises it up through the height of good works, displaying it openly to all the nations, draws it away from lowly pleasures, refreshes it with the bread of heaven, and kindles in it a desire for heavenly sweetness by giving it the pledge of spiritual food.

“I have compassion on the crowd, because they have now been with me three days and have nothing to eat.” (From Gregory.) The crowd remains with the Lord for three days on account of the healing of its sick, when the elect, enlightened by faith in the holy Trinity, earnestly and persistently beseech the Lord for their own sins and those of their people—that is, for the illnesses of their souls. Likewise, the crowd remains with the Lord for three days when the multitude of the faithful, turning away through repentance from the sins it has committed, converts to the Lord in deed, speech, and thought.

“And if I send them away fasting to their homes, they will faint on the way.” The Lord does not wish to send them fasting to their homes, lest they faint on the way, because converted sinners plainly faint on the way of the present life if they are sent away in their own conscience without the nourishment of holy teaching. Therefore, lest they grow weary on this pilgrimage, they must be fed with sacred admonition.

“For some of them have come from a great distance.” There is one who, having experienced no fraud and no carnal corruption, hastened to the service of almighty God. He did not come from a distance, because through incorruption and innocence he was near. Another, stained by no immodesty and no disgrace, but having experienced only marriage, turned to spiritual service. He too did not come from a distance, because, having used a permitted union, he did not stray into unlawful things.

Others return to repentance and turn to the service of almighty God after sexual sins, others after false testimony, others after theft, others after acts of violence, and others after committing murder. These plainly come to the Lord from a distance. For the more each person has gone astray in an evil deed, the farther he has withdrawn from almighty God. Let nourishment therefore be given even to those who come from a distance, because when sinners are converted, the food of holy teaching must be provided for them, so that they may recover in God the strength they lost in their crimes.

Likewise, whatever Jews have believed in Christ have come to him from nearby, because they had been instructed about him in the writings of the Law and the Prophets. Believers from the Gentiles, however, certainly came to Christ from a distance, because they had received no prior warning about faith in him from the memorials of the sacred writings.

“And his disciples answered him: ‘From where can anyone satisfy these people with bread here in the wilderness?’ And he asked them: ‘How many loaves do you have?’ They said: ‘Seven.’” It is fitting that seven loaves are placed in the ministry of the New Testament, in which, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, the sevenfold grace is more fully revealed to all the faithful both for belief and for reception. They are not reported to have been barley loaves, as were the five by which five thousand people were satisfied, lest once again, as under the Law, the life-giving nourishment of the soul be concealed beneath bodily sacraments; for the kernel of barley is covered by a very tenacious husk.

“And he commanded,” and so forth. Above, at the meal of the five loaves, the crowd sat down upon green grass. Now, when it is to be nourished by seven loaves, it is ordered to sit down upon the ground, because through the Scripture of the Law we are commanded to trample down and restrain the desires of the flesh. “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isaiah XL). In the New Testament, however, we are commanded also to leave behind the earth itself and temporal possessions. Or certainly, because the mountain on which the crowd was refreshed with the Lord’s loaves signifies, as we said above, the height of our Redeemer, there it is refreshed upon grass, here upon the ground. There the greatness of Christ is covered, on account of carnal people and earthly Jerusalem, by carnal hope and desire. Here, with every carnal desire removed, the guests of the New Testament were held by the foundation of enduring hope, like the solidity of the mountain itself, with no grass interposed.

“And taking the seven loaves, giving thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples to distribute, and they distributed them to the crowd.” The Lord took the loaves and gave them to the disciples, so that they might distribute what they had received to the crowd, because, granting the apostles spiritual gifts of knowledge, he wished the nourishment of life to be distributed throughout the world to his Church through their ministry.

That he broke the loaves which he was to give to the disciples signifies the opening of the mysteries by which the world was to be nourished for eternal salvation. For when the Lord himself says, “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matthew X), what else did he show must be opened to us by him than the bread of life? We could not penetrate by ourselves to behold its inner contents. Concerning this, the Prophet, lamenting the pitiable hunger of certain people, says: “The little ones asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them.” This is to say in other words: The unlearned sought the nourishment of the word of God, and, when teachers failed, there was no one to disclose to them the secrets of Scripture.

After receiving the loaves to be broken, the Lord gives thanks, both showing how much he rejoices in the salvation of the human race and instructing us always to give thanks to God whenever, by the generosity of heavenly grace, we refresh either the body with earthly bread or the soul with heavenly nourishment.

“And they had a few small fish, and he blessed these as well and ordered them to be distributed.” If the seven loaves signify the Scripture of the New Testament, in whose reading we find the inner banquets of our minds through the grace of the Holy Spirit, what are we to understand by the small fish which the Lord likewise blessed and ordered to be distributed to the crowd? We understand them as the saints of the time in which that Scripture was composed, or those whose faith, life, and sufferings that Scripture contains. Rescued from the turbulent waves of this age and consecrated by divine blessing, they have offered us the inward refreshment of examples from their life and death, lest we fail during the passage through this transitory world.

“And they ate and were satisfied.” They eat of the Lord’s loaves and fish and are satisfied who, hearing the words of God and observing the examples, hasten to be stirred and rise toward the progress of a more upright life. To them the Psalmist’s saying plainly applies: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise God,” and so forth (Psalm XXI).

“And they collected what remained of the fragments, seven baskets.” After the crowds have been satisfied, the apostles collect what remained and fill seven baskets, because there are higher commandments of perfection—or rather, exhortations and counsels—which the general multitude of the faithful cannot attain by observing and fulfilling them. Their execution properly concerns those who, through the greater fullness of the grace of the Holy Spirit, surpass the ordinary way of life of God’s people in the sublimity of mind and deed. To such people it is said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have,” and so forth (Matthew XIX).

Hence it is fitting that the baskets in which the fragments of the Lord’s food are stored are said to have been seven, on account of the sevenfold grace of the Spirit. Since baskets are customarily woven from rushes and palm leaves, they are rightly used as a sign of the saints. The rush, for its part, is accustomed to grow upon waters. The palm adorns the victorious hand, and the elect are rightly compared with vessels made of rushes when they place the root of their heart in the fountain of life, lest it dry up through being separated from the love of eternity. They are also likened to things woven from palm leaves when they retain in a pure heart the joyful remembrance of eternal recompense derived from it.

It is fittingly said that although the crowd could not contain the remnants of the Lord’s meal, it nevertheless ate and was satisfied, because there are some who, although they cannot leave all that is theirs, are nevertheless filled when, hungering and thirsting for righteousness, they reach eternal life by hearing the commandments of God’s Law.

“There were about four thousand who had eaten, and he dismissed them.” It is fitting that there were four thousand, so that by this number too they might be shown to have been fed with evangelical nourishment.

## THE NINTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

### READING FROM THE LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER VIII

“We are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live. For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God. For you did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’ For the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are sons of God. And if sons, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, and fellow heirs with Christ.”

“We are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh.” (From Origen.) We are undoubtedly debtors to those things which we have received from the Spirit; but to the flesh, he says, we are not debtors. For God did not make us in his image so that we would be subject to the service of the flesh, but rather so that the soul, serving its Creator, might itself make use of the flesh in service and ministry. (From Primasius.) He does all this to show them that the Law is not necessary, since it was given to the carnal.

“For if you live according to the flesh, you will die.” (From Origen.) What is it to live according to the flesh except to fulfill the desires of the flesh? For elsewhere also he says: “Do not provide for the flesh in its desires.” He is not denying that care should be taken for the flesh in necessary matters, but only in its desires. Thus here also: “If you live according to the flesh,” he says, “you will die.” He signifies the death of eternal punishment. He says this in order to show that the desires of the human body occupy the greatest share of the passions.

“But if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.” (From Origen.) Whoever, therefore, acts according to the Spirit and puts to death the deeds of the flesh will live because of the Spirit of life dwelling in him. One puts the deeds of the flesh to death in this way: love is a fruit of the Spirit; hatred is a deed of the flesh. Hatred, therefore, is put to death and extinguished through love. Likewise, joy is a fruit of the Spirit, whereas the sorrow of this age, which produces death, is a deed of the flesh. This sorrow is therefore extinguished if the joy of the Spirit is in us. Peace is a fruit of the Spirit; dissension and discord belong to the flesh. But it is certain that discord is put to death through peace. Likewise, through the patience of the Spirit, the impatience of the flesh is extinguished; goodness destroys wickedness, gentleness ferocity, self-control intemperance, and chastity immodesty. In this order, whoever through the Spirit has given life to the deeds of the flesh will live.

“For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God.” It is as though he said: Whoever is deemed worthy to be governed by the Holy Spirit, or to live according to the teaching of the Holy Spirit, is led by the Spirit of God—that is, governed or moved by him. For although there are many sons of God, as Scripture says, “I have said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Psalm LXXXII), nevertheless there is one Son by nature, the Only-Begotten from the Father, through whom all are called sons. Likewise, although there are many spirits, there is one who truly proceeds from God himself and grants to all the others the name and grace of his sanctification.

“For you did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear.” (From Primasius.) The Jews received a spirit that compelled no one to slavery through fear. For fear belongs to slaves, while love belongs to sons. As it is written: “A slave will fear his master, and a son will love his father.” Therefore, those who were unwilling to perform works out of love should be compelled by the necessity of fear; but let us perform everything willingly, so that we may prove ourselves to be sons.

(From Augustine.) Whoever performs the work of the Law out of fear of punishment, not from love of righteousness, is by this very fact not a friend but rather an enemy of the Law, which he wishes did not exist; nor is one cleansed by an act when one is unclean in will.

“But you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’” Whoever calls him Father professes himself to be a son. Therefore, in character, the son ought to be found like his father, lest, even on account of the name falsely assumed, he be subjected to a greater punishment.

Likewise, you Romans have been called into adoption as sons, not like the Jews, who, subjected to the authority of the Law, were held in slavery. As for what he added, “Abba, Father”: he repeated a word from the native language, as though he had said, “Father, Father.” For *Abba* means the same as *Father*, but *Abba* is Hebrew, while “Father” is Greek and Latin. Therefore, to teach that both peoples would believe in him and that he was to be invoked by both, the Apostle used both languages, so that those from the people of Israel might cry “Abba,” while we who came to the faith of Christ from the Gentiles might cry “Father.”

“The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit,” and so forth. The Spirit of adoption himself, through whom one is adopted as a son, bears witness to and confirms our spirit that we are sons of God. After we have passed from the spirit of slavery into the spirit of adoption, when no fear remains in us and we do nothing because of fear of punishment, but accomplish everything because of love for the Father—

“And if sons, then heirs—heirs indeed of God,” and so forth. After this, the Apostle now constructs a syllogism from what follows and says: If we have received the Spirit of adoption, then we are sons. And if we are sons, then without doubt we are also heirs, for a slave awaits wages, while a son hopes for an inheritance.

Another then adds an increase to the conclusion: “Heirs indeed,” he says, “of God, and fellow heirs with Christ.” A person becomes God’s heir when he is deemed worthy to receive what belongs to God—that is, the glory of incorruption and immortality, and the hidden treasures of wisdom and knowledge. He becomes a fellow heir with Christ when Christ transforms “the body of our humiliation” so that it is conformed “to the body of his glory,” and also when he is deemed worthy to attain what the Savior himself said: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XIII).

There is also this dignity of Christ’s fellow heirs: the Father indeed gave all judgment to the Son, but the Son also says to his fellow heirs: “You also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” In this way Christ brings his heirs not only into a share of the inheritance, but also into participation in his power.

## THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER VII

“Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will know them by their fruits. Do people gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles? Thus every good tree produces good fruits, but a bad tree produces bad fruits. A good tree cannot produce bad fruits, nor can a bad tree produce good fruits. Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire. Therefore, you will know them by their fruits. Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven—he will enter the kingdom of heaven.”

“Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing,” and so forth. (From Jerome.) This can indeed be understood of all who promise one thing in appearance and speech but demonstrate another in their conduct. But it is to be understood especially of heretics, because they seem to surround themselves with the garment of a certain piety through continence, chastity, and fasting, while inwardly, possessing a poisoned mind, they deceive the simpler hearts of their brothers. Thus, from the fruits of their souls, by which they draw the innocent to ruin, they are compared with ravenous wolves.

“You will know them by their fruits.” (From Augustine.) The Lord said of certain people who clothe themselves in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves—and lest human weakness be unable to recognize the wolf beneath the sheep’s skin, he said: “You will know them by their fruits.” We look for the fruits of love and find the thorns of dissension: “You will know them by their fruits.”

(From Bede.) What are the fruits by which the good or the evil are recognized? The Apostle shows this when he says: “The works of the flesh are evident: fornication, uncleanness, licentiousness, service of idols, sorcery, enmities, contentions, rivalries, anger, quarrels, dissensions, heresies, envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity, and things like these.” For by these fruits each person’s character is recognized.

“Do people gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?” I think that the thorns and thistles of the age are the cares of the world and the pricks of vices, concerning which it was said to the sinful man: “Your land shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you.” The fig and the grape signify the sweetness of a new way of life, for which the Lord hungers within us, and the fervor of love, which gladdens the human heart. But grapes are not gathered from thorns, nor figs from thistles, because a mind still weighed down by the habit of the old human being can pretend, but cannot bear the fruit of the new human being.

“Thus every good tree produces good fruits, but a bad tree produces bad fruits. A good tree cannot produce bad fruits, nor can a bad tree produce good fruits.” (From Augustine.) The tree is the soul itself, that is, the human being himself; the fruit is the human being’s works. Therefore a bad person cannot do good works, nor a good person evil works. If, then, he wishes to do good, let him first become good. The person must first be changed, so that the works may be changed. For if a person remains in what is bad, he cannot have good works; if he remains in what is good, he cannot have evil works. Let each person therefore be a good tree; let him not suppose that he can have good fruits while the tree remains bad. There will be no good fruit unless the tree is good. Change the heart, and the work will be changed. Uproot greed and plant love. For just as greed is the root of all evils, so love is the root of all good things.

“Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.” (From Bede.) Every perverse person who refuses here to produce the fruit of good works quickly finds the prepared burning of Gehenna.

“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven—he will enter,” and so forth. Just as above he had said that those who possess the clothing of a good life are not to be received because of the wickedness of their doctrines, so now, conversely, he asserts that faith is not to be granted even to those who, although strong in the integrity of their faith, live disgracefully and destroy the integrity of their teaching through evil works. Both are necessary for God’s servants: that conduct be proved by speech and speech by conduct.

This statement may seem contrary to the following: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit.” But it is the manner of Scripture to take words as standing for deeds, as is immediately demonstrated in what follows, when those who boast of knowing the Lord without works are refuted and hear from the Savior: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know you” (Matthew VII). The Apostle speaks in this sense as well: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him.”

## THE TENTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

### READING FROM THE FIRST LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER X

“Let us not desire evil things, as they desired them. Nor become idolaters, as some of them did, as it is written: ‘The people sat down to eat and drink, and they rose up to play.’ Nor let us commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication, and twenty-three thousand fell in one day. Nor let us test Christ, as some of them tested him, and perished by serpents. Nor murmur, as some of them murmured, and perished by the destroyer. All these things happened to them as examples. They were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have arrived. Therefore, whoever thinks that he stands should take heed lest he fall. No temptation has overtaken you except a human one. But God is faithful, and he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear; rather, with the temptation he will also provide a way through, so that you may be able to endure it.”

“Let us not desire evil things, as they desired them.” (From Isidore.) At the thirteenth station, which is called “the graves of desire,” the people, growing weary of the heavenly bread, desired the Egyptian meats, and a great fire suddenly consumed many of them. From this we learn that those who by their way of life leave the world and reject the Egyptian pots—that is, the fervors of carnal desires—must not murmur against the heavenly bread, nor seek the poisonous fare of the Egyptians, who have abundant meats, but must seek the simple food of manna, that is, the pure heavenly life.

Otherwise, if after receiving the angelic manna, which is the life or teaching that is in heaven, we again desire the Egyptian meats—that is, the carnal pleasures of this world and the desires of our former ways—we will consume nausea and immediately be tormented by the Lord’s fire. Our desire also becomes burial mounds, so that we are whitewashed tombs, which appear beautiful to people outwardly but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead (Matthew XXIII).

“Nor become idolaters, as some of them did,” and so forth. He touches upon those who rejoiced in an idol, thinking themselves free from guilt, and compares them with those who made a calf for themselves in the wilderness and worshiped it while playing; but many of them were killed and perished (Exodus XXXII, Numbers XXI), so that the death of those people may be understood to signify the destruction of vices. For the Apostle commands us to rage against such vices when he says: “Put to death, therefore, your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, licentiousness, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols” (Colossians III).

“Nor let us commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication,” and so forth. Balaam had indeed given counsel to King Balak to place women in a brothel, with altars before their doors, so that when the sons of Israel came, they would first sacrifice to idols and then enter to the women. Hence it was that Israel committed fornication with the daughters of Midian.

But what is meant by the fact that this Balaam concluded, by a well-founded calculation, that the people of God could be deceived, giving counsel that, on the side where he knew the sons of Israel to be weak, more destructive snares should be laid for them? He did not doubt that, when women were made available to them, they would immediately collapse in the ruin of fornication, because he knew that the desirable parts of their souls were corrupted.
