Thus, in the figure of Balaam, they test each of us through the crafty malignity of wickedness, constructing treacherous snares especially around those affections of the soul in which they perceive that we are sick. For example, when they see that the rational parts of our soul have been corrupted, they attempt to deceive us by that same method.

But Phinehas the priest, moved by zeal in order to appease God’s anger, pierced Zimri and the Midianite prostitute with a dagger. This signified that through the Lord’s cross not only idolatry but also every carnal affection and worldly desire is put to death, and that God is then appeased when the vice of the flesh is extinguished.

“Nor let us test Christ, as some of them did,” and so forth. This means: Do not test him in the pressure of tribulation, since he tests you through tribulations. The Book of Numbers relates that, when the people of Israel were struck in the wilderness, they murmured under the burden of the long journey and its labor; therefore the Lord sent fiery serpents among them. The venom of the fiery serpents is consequently the poison of vices, which kills by spiritual death the soul that it touches. It was fitting that the people who murmured against the Lord should be struck down by the bites of serpents, so that from the order of the external scourge they might recognize how much destruction they suffered inwardly by murmuring. For sins, which drag both soul and body to destruction, are rightly expressed through serpents.

“Nor murmur, as some of them murmured,” and so forth. When he says that they perished “by the destroyer,” this is understood either of the striking angel or of the devouring fire.

“All these things happened to them as examples; they were written for our correction.” (From Primasius.) They received in accordance with their deeds all that happened to them. Nevertheless, these things were written so that we would not think we may sin with impunity. For if he did not spare those who were still children or inexperienced, how much less will he spare us, who receive the perfection of the Law, if we do such things?

(From Jerome.) In that Scripture called the Old Testament, the New Testament lies hidden, as though in the dregs of bodily sacraments. Circumcision of the flesh signifies circumcision of the heart. The temple signifies the Lord’s body. The promised land signifies the kingdom of heaven. There is a type or figure of present, past, and future things not yet known.

The humility of catechumens is a type of past things: they bear the figure of Adam expelled from paradise and fearing the divine presence because of the consciousness of his offenses; for this reason they also walk in public with their heads covered. The vestment of Aaron, which bore the names of the twelve tribes inscribed upon stones, is a type of present things, showing that he somehow intercedes for all peoples. The two sons of Isaac are a type of future things, in whom the two Testaments are displayed.

“Upon whom the ends of the ages have arrived.” That is, upon whom the whole perfection of righteousness falls, as it is written: “For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness” (Romans X).

“Therefore, whoever thinks that he stands should take heed lest he fall.” (From Primasius.) That is, lest he fall into idolatry or into giving scandal to his brothers. He falls because of the very thing in which he boasts that he stands: he falls because he is proud.

“No temptation has overtaken you except a human one.” A human temptation can be understood as an ordinary and, as it has been said, bearable affliction. As he says elsewhere: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh” (Romans IV), that is, something that can easily be undertaken and fulfilled with good will. Who gives counsel either to himself or to others if he is deceived in some matter through ignorance of temporal things? For he acts temporally in this as well and does not maintain the manner of acting that he ought to maintain. A human temptation may be such as this: to be angry is human; to carry anger through to its completion is diabolical.

“But God is faithful, and he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear.” (From Augustine.) He is faithful, for he promised that, on account of his name, he would be present to those enduring tribulation, as in the saying: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord delivered them from them all” (Psalm XXXIII). May he himself make you stand firmly and grant the strength to endure—the same one who taught you to pray, saying: “Do not permit us to be led into temptation” (Matthew VI).

“But with the temptation he will also provide a way through, so that you may be able to endure it.” That is, he will not permit a greater tribulation to come upon you than you can bear, but he will provide a way through—that is, he will cause to arise for you what you can endure, or enable you to gain profit for your soul from the tribulation itself.

## THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER XVI
“Homo quidam erat dives, qui habebat villicum...”—“There was a certain rich man who had a steward, and this man was reported to him as having squandered his possessions. And he called him and said to him, ‘What is this that I hear about you? Give an account of your stewardship, for you can no longer be steward.’ But the steward said within himself, ‘What shall I do? For my master is taking the stewardship away from me. I am unable to dig; I am ashamed to beg. I know what I shall do, so that, when I have been removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses.’ And summoning each of his master’s debtors, he said to the first, ‘How much do you owe my master?’ And he said, ‘A hundred measures of oil.’ And he said to him, ‘Take your written obligation, sit down quickly, and write fifty.’ Then he said to another, ‘And you, how much do you owe?’ He said, ‘A hundred cors of wheat.’ He said to him, ‘Take your document and write eighty.’ And the master praised the dishonest steward, because he had acted shrewdly, for the sons of this age are shrewder in their own generation than the sons of light. And I say to you: Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings.”

“There was a certain rich man who had a steward, and this man was reported to him as having squandered his possessions, and he called him and said to him, ‘What is this that I hear about you? Give an account of your stewardship, for you can no longer be steward.’” (From Augustine.) In this steward, whom the master was expelling from his stewardship and whom he praised because he had provided for his future, we must not take everything as an example for imitation. We are not to commit fraud against our master in any matter so that we may make alms from that fraud; nor may those whom we wish to receive us into eternal dwellings rightly be understood as debtors of God and our Lord. Rather, they signify the just and holy, who introduce into eternal dwellings those who have shared earthly goods with them in their necessities. These parables are also spoken in an opposite sense, so that we may understand that, if the master could praise the man to whom he had done an injustice, how much more do those please the Lord God who perform such works according to his command. Indeed, from the word “steward” we learn that those who possess money should be regarded not as stewards of their own household but rather as administrators of another’s property. If, following the example of this servant, they carefully foresee the time when their stewardship and accounting must end, then, easily stripped both of their delight in earthly things and of their love for them, they will take greater care to acquire friends for themselves in the future than to amass wealth in the present.

“But the steward said within himself: ‘What shall I do? For my lord is taking the stewardship away from me; I am unable to dig.’” Once the stewardship has been taken away, we cannot dig, because, when this life has ended—the life in which we are permitted to work—we may no longer seek the fruit of a good way of life with the mattock of devoted contrition.

“‘I am ashamed to beg,’” and so forth. Begging is a matter of shame, namely that worst kind of begging by which those foolish virgins are said to have begged. When the time of the wedding approached and the oil of virtues had run out, they said to the wise: “Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out” (Matt. 25). Solomon likewise says: “Because of the cold the sluggard would not plow; therefore he will beg in summer, and nothing will be given to him.”

“And summoning each of his master’s debtors, he said to the first: ‘How much do you owe my master?’ And he said, ‘A hundred measures of oil’; and he said to him, ‘Take your written obligation, sit down quickly, and write fifty.’ Then he said to another, ‘And you, how much do you owe?’ And he said, ‘A hundred cors of wheat’; and he said to him, ‘Take your document and write eighty.’” A *cadus* is, in Greek, an *amphora*, containing three urns. A *corus* comprises thirty *modii*. As for the fact that, from one hundred measures of oil, he had the debtor write fifty, and from one hundred cors of wheat eighty, I think it has no other significance than this: whatever each Jew does similarly for priests and Levites should abound in the Church of Christ, so that his righteousness may exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees. Whereas they gave tenths, these should give halves, just as Zacchaeus gave not from his produce but from his actual possessions. Or perhaps, by giving double tenths, or two tenths, he should surpass the expenditures of the Jews. Unless someone thinks the passage should be understood simply to mean that anyone who relieves the need of any poor person among the saints, whether by a half or certainly by a fifth—for twenty or fifty are the proportions of one hundred—should be granted a definite reward for his mercy.

“And the master praised the dishonest steward, because he had acted shrewdly, for the sons of this age are shrewder in their own generation than the sons of light.” Let the wise men of this age hear, so that they may abandon foolish wisdom and learn God’s wise foolishness. Let them learn how highly divine equity has valued their wisdom, since it says that they are not truly wise but wise in their own generation. This accords with what is said elsewhere: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight.” By calling lovers of eternal life “sons of light,” he also reproves those who are wise enough to do evil but do not know how to do good, declaring them to be sons of darkness. They are called sons of light and sons of this age just as others are called sons of the kingdom and sons of perdition: each person is named the son of the one whose works he performs.

“And I say to you: Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings.” He calls this money, which we possess temporarily, “the mammon of iniquity,” because *mammon* is interpreted as “wealth.” Yet this wealth belongs only to the unjust, who place in it the hope and abundance of their blessedness. When the just possess such money, it is indeed money for them, but it is not their wealth; their wealth is heavenly and spiritual. By spiritually supplying their need through these things, they will be enriched with an abundance of blessedness once the poverty of misery has been excluded. If those who give alms from the mammon of iniquity make friends for themselves, by whom they may be received into eternal dwellings, how much more ought those who bestow spiritual nourishment—those who give food to their fellow servants at the proper time—to be uplifted by the most certain hope of the supreme recompense.

[Col. 0419C]

## ELEVENTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

### READING FROM THE LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS, I, CHAPTER XII

“You know that, when you were Gentiles, you went to the mute idols, being led along as you were directed. Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Jesus is accursed.’ And no one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit. Now there are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; and there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of workings, but the same God, who works all things in all. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. To one, indeed, through the Spirit is given a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, the grace of healings in one Spirit; to another, the working of miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, the discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, the interpretation of words. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing them individually as he wills.”

“You know that, when you were Gentiles,” and so forth. The meaning of the speaker seems to be opened only somewhat by these words: when you were Gentiles, you rendered obedience to magicians or to the diviners of idols, who led you to mute and lifeless images. But now, since you have accepted the religion and ought to possess a more receptive understanding, willingly assent to salvation, obey the truth more readily, and receive with attentive mind what I commit to your knowledge. (From Origen.) “Being led,” by whom or by what? Clearly, you were led by wicked spirits to works of sin.

“Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says,” and so forth. Whoever anathematizes—that is, whoever rejects the Lord Jesus with a certain detestation—does not possess the Holy Spirit. Whoever believes in the Lord Jesus possesses the Holy Spirit. And since we read, “Whoever does not have the Son does not have the Father,” from this testimony we can recognize that whoever does not believe in Christ should not be believed to possess the Holy Spirit, just as we read in the Letter to the Romans: “But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. 8). Thus, just as the Lord does not acknowledge workers of iniquity even if they have performed miracles, so God is denied by evil works.

“And no one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit.” This means that someone confesses the Lord Jesus without cause if he does not believe wholly in the Holy Spirit; or he confesses him in words without cause if he denies him by his deeds. He teaches the Corinthians that, unless they say “Lord Jesus” in the Holy Spirit—that is, while conducting themselves in good works—the Lord Jesus cannot benefit them in any other way.

“There are divisions of graces,” and so forth. This means that not only the gift of tongues but various kinds of charisms are distributed by the Lord. He wishes to show that the graces of the Holy Spirit are divided, not the Spirit himself.

“And there are divisions of ministries,” and so forth. These are the ecclesiastical ministries and offices that are distributed. He mentions these ministries as being ordered in what follows by the Holy Spirit—that is, by God’s arrangement—when he says: “He appointed some in the Church, first apostles, then prophets,” and so forth. By saying, “but the same Spirit” and “but the same God,” he shows that he is speaking entirely about the divinity of the Holy Spirit.

“And there are divisions of workings.” That is, through these different powers various works are performed. The meaning is that the same Holy Spirit works all these things in all, that is, in the faithful and believers.

“To each is given the manifestation,” and so forth. The manifestation of the Spirit means that it may be made manifest that a person has received the Holy Spirit for the benefit and salvation of many. They are not enriched with the gifts of grace solely for their own sake, but for the sake of the faithful as well. Or it may be for the benefit of unbelievers, so that they may believe, and so that believers may be strengthened. Or “the manifestation of the Spirit” may mean that, through spiritual teaching, he makes each person’s conscience manifest, just as he says below, that through prophetic correction the secrets of the heart are made manifest. Or it may mean that, once enlightened by the Spirit, the human mind recognizes things through spiritual discernment.

“To one, indeed, through the Holy Spirit is given a word of wisdom.” That is, so that he may be able to discuss and teach wisely, suitably, and rationally what he has received through the inspiration of grace.

“To another, a word of knowledge.” Knowledge consists either in revealing mysteries, knowing or recounting past events, or proclaiming future judgment.

[Col. 0421A]

“To another, faith in the same Spirit.” Here faith is understood in two ways: not only as faith that receives the Trinity with an understanding heart, but also as faith that, with ardent perfection, can perform signs and wonders. Of this the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain,” and so forth (Luke 17).

“To another, the grace of healings in one Spirit.” That is, the grace by which he grants health to the sick.

“To another, the working of miracles.” Through this he can give sight to the blind, release the possessed, and raise the dead.

“To another, prophecy.” Through this he teaches moral matters and proclaims what is to be feared or hoped for concerning the day of recompense.

“To another, the discernment of spirits.” That is, so that he may examine with prudent judgment what kind of spirit is approaching and what in human action comes from God or from the adversary.

“To another, the interpretation of words.” That is, because he could interpret more profoundly what another was saying in a foreign language.

“One and the same Spirit works all these things,” and so forth. Here he shows that above he has been discussing all the powers of the Holy Spirit, and that throughout his discourse he has proclaimed the Spirit himself to be God and Lord.

“Distributing them individually as he wills.” He distributes; he is not himself divided. They are called divisions as the members of the body are called divisions, because ears do not have the same function as eyes, and the remaining members are likewise distributed among different offices in harmony. Yet, when we are healthy, although they are different, they are one and equal—not greater in one place and lesser in another—but, since they are one body, they rejoice together in a common and equal well-being.

## THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER XIX

“When Jesus drew near to Jerusalem, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: ‘If you too had known—and indeed on this your day—the things that are for your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes. For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart; they will surround you and hem you in on every side; they will cast you down to the ground, and your children who are within you. And they will not leave in you one stone upon another, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.’ And entering the temple, he began to cast out those who were selling and buying in it, saying to them: ‘It is written, “My house is a house of prayer”; but you have made it a den of thieves.’ And he was teaching daily in the temple.”

“When Jesus drew near to Jerusalem, seeing the city, he wept over it.” (From Bede.) The compassionate Redeemer wept over the overthrow of the faithless city, which was brought upon it by Vespasian and Titus, the Roman rulers.

“Saying, ‘If you too had known.’” Supply: “you would weep”—you who now rejoice because you do not know what is impending. For the ruin that threatened the city was unknown to the city itself, that is, to the city’s people.

“And indeed on this your day, the things that are for your peace.” Since it gave itself over to the pleasures of the flesh and did not foresee the evils that were to come, it possessed its own day, which could have been a day of peace for it. “But now they are hidden from your eyes.” For if the evils that threatened it had not been hidden from the eyes of its heart, it would not have rejoiced in its present prosperity.

“For days will come upon you, and your enemies,” and so forth. No one who has read the history of the city’s destruction is unaware that all these things were done by Vespasian and Titus.

“And they will not leave in you one stone,” and so forth. The city’s own subsequent migration also bears witness to this. Since it is now built in the place where the Lord was crucified outside the gate, that earlier Jerusalem, as is said, was utterly destroyed. The guilt for which the punishment of its destruction was inflicted is added below.

“Because you did not recognize,” and so forth. The Creator of all graciously deigned to visit this city through the mystery of his incarnation, but it did not remember his fear and love.

“And entering the temple,” and so forth. The one who had foretold the evils that were to come and immediately entered the temple in order to cast out those who were selling and buying in it clearly made known that the people’s ruin arose chiefly from the guilt of the priests. The house of prayer had therefore become a den of thieves, because those who gathered in the temple knew how either to persecute bodily those who did not give gifts or to kill spiritually those who did give them.

“Seeing the city,” and so forth. He did this once when he announced that the city was going to perish. Our Redeemer does not cease to do the same thing daily through his elect, whenever he sees that some have passed from a good life to reprobate conduct. He mourns those who do not know why they are mourned, those who, in Solomon’s words, “rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2). If they had recognized the condemnation threatening them, they would weep for themselves with the tears of the elect.

“And indeed on this your day, the things that are for your peace.” The perverse soul has its own day here: it rejoices for a passing time, and the things that are present are peaceful for it. While it rejoices in temporal things, while it is exalted by honors, while it is relaxed in fleshly pleasure, and while it is terrified by no fear of future punishment, it has peace in its own day. But on an alien day it will have the stumbling-block of its grievous condemnation. There it will be afflicted where the righteous will rejoice.

“But now they are hidden from your eyes.” The perverse soul, devoted to present things and relaxed in earthly pleasures, hides from itself the evils that follow, because it refuses to foresee the future things that would disturb its present joy. Since it abandons itself to the delights of the present life, what else does it do than go toward the fire with closed eyes?

“For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart.” Who have ever been greater enemies of the human soul than wicked spirits? They besiege it as it leaves the body; while it is given over to the love of the flesh, they foster it with deceptive pleasures. They surround it with a rampart when, bringing before the eyes of its mind the sins it has committed, they hem it in and draw it into fellowship with their own condemnation.

“They will surround you and hem you in on every side.” Wicked spirits hem the soul in on every side when they recall to it not only the sins of its deeds but also those of its speech and, further, of its thoughts, so that the soul, which earlier spread itself widely through many crimes, is finally constricted by them all in the retribution.

“And they will cast you down to the ground, and your children who are within you.” The soul is then cast down to the ground by the thought of its guilt when the flesh that it believed to be its life is forced to return to dust. Its children fall into death when the illicit thoughts that now proceed from it are scattered in the final punishment of life. As it is written: “On that day all their thoughts will perish” (Ps. 145). These harsh thoughts can also be understood through the symbolism of stones.

“And they will not leave in you one stone upon another.” When a perverse mind adds a still more perverse thought to a perverse thought, what else does it do than place one stone upon another? But in the destroyed city no stone will be left upon stone, because when the soul is led to its punishment, the entire structure of its thoughts is scattered.

“Because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.” Almighty God customarily visits every perverse soul in many ways. He visits it continually through a commandment, sometimes through a scourge, and sometimes through a miracle, so that it may hear truths of which it was ignorant and, though still proud and contemptuous, may either return, pierced by sorrow, or, overcome by benefits, blush for the evil it has done. But because it does not recognize the time of his visitation, it is finally handed over to the enemies with whom it is joined in perpetual fellowship of condemnation at the eternal judgment.

“And entering the temple he began to cast out those who were selling,” and so forth. Just as the temple is in the city, so the life of religious people is in the faithful populace. Often some assume the religious habit, but when they receive a place among the sacred orders, they turn the office of holy religion into an exchange for earthly business. Those selling in the temple are people who distribute for a reward what belongs by right to certain persons. To sell justice is to preserve it in exchange for receiving a reward. Those buying in the temple are people who, while unwilling to pay their neighbor what is just and while refusing to do what is owed by right, buy sin by giving a reward to their patrons.

“My house is a house of prayer, but you have made it a den,” and so forth. When perverse people sometimes occupy a place of religion, they kill there with the swords of their wickedness, where they ought to give life to their neighbors through the intercession of their prayer. The temple and house of God is also the very mind and conscience of the faithful. Whenever it produces perverse thoughts that harm its neighbor, thieves sit there as in a den and kill those who walk innocently when they drive the swords of injury into people who are guilty of nothing. The mind of the faithful is no longer a house of prayer but a den of thieves when, having abandoned innocence and the simplicity of holiness, it attempts to do what enables it to harm its neighbors. But because we are continually instructed against all these perversities by the words of our Redeemer in the sacred pages, what is said to have been done then is still being done, when it is said:

“And he was teaching daily in the temple.” When he carefully teaches the minds of the faithful to avoid evils, Truth teaches daily in the temple. But we are truly taught by the words of Truth if we look upon our final evils with fear and without ceasing, in accordance with this saying: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin.”

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT FELICITY

### READING FROM THE BOOK OF PROVERBS, LAST CHAPTER

“Who will find a strong woman? Her price is far away and from the remotest ends. The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he will have no need of spoils. She will repay him with good and not evil all the days of her life. She sought wool and flax, and worked with the counsel of her hands. She became like a merchant’s ship, bringing her bread from afar. And she rose at night and gave plunder to her household and food to her maidservants. She considered a field and bought it; from the fruit of her hands she planted a vineyard. She girded her loins with strength and strengthened her arm. She tasted and saw that her commerce was good; her lamp will not be extinguished at night. She put her hand to strong things, and her fingers grasped the spindle. She opened her hand to the needy and extended her palms to the poor. She will not fear for her household because of the cold of snow, for all her household are clothed in double garments. She made herself a variegated garment; fine linen and purple are her clothing. Her husband is noble at the gates when he sits with the senators of the land. She made and sold a linen garment, and gave a girdle to the Canaanite. She considered the paths of her household, and did not eat bread in idleness. She opened her mouth to wisdom, and the law of kindness is on her tongue. Strength and beauty are her clothing, and she will laugh on the last day. Her sons rose up and called her most blessed; her husband also, and he praised her. Many daughters gathered riches; you have surpassed them all. Deceptive is grace and vain is beauty; the woman who fears God is the one who will be praised. Give her from the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her at the gates.”

“Who will find a strong woman?” (From Bede.) The Catholic Church is called the strong woman, whom John is said to have seen in the Apocalypse clothed with the sun, that is, with Christ. She does not cease to beget spiritual children for God from water and the Holy Spirit. She is therefore called strong because, for faith in her Creator, she despises all the adversities and prosperities of the world alike. When he appeared in the flesh, he found her weak, but by his visitation he made her strong. Seeing the human race entangled in many errors, Solomon said: “Who will find a strong woman?” As if he were saying: What patriarch or prophet, or who among those of such virtue or merit, could gather for himself from the many unbelieving nations of the world one Church of the elect and make it strong and unconquerable against all adversaries by his grace? The implied answer is: no one except Christ.

“Far away.” He uses “far away” to indicate the passage of time, that is, from the days of Solomon to the Virgin’s childbirth.

“And from the remotest ends is her price.” He says “from the remotest ends” because “his going forth is from the summit of heaven” (Ps. 18), and because he offered himself to the Father as the price of redemption for our salvation. Hence the Apostle says: “He loved us and handed himself over for us” (Eph. 5). In another sense, the price of the holy Church has been placed far away because the incarnation of the Word of God, his life among human beings, his passion, and his resurrection are far removed from our condition.

“The heart of her husband trusts in her.” He calls the Lord the husband of the holy Church, who also deigned to become her price. Just as a man who has a strong, faithful, and chaste wife trusts in her because she cannot defile herself against his will even by an adulterous thought, and because he desires through constant friendship to turn as many people as possible toward her husband, so our Redeemer trusts in the Church joined to him. For he knows the spirit of grace and the power of charity that he has infused into her inmost heart. Therefore he does not doubt that she can remain uncorrupted in the integrity of her faith and persist steadfastly so as to gather many into the unity of that same faith.

“And he will have no need of spoils.” The Church strips the devil when, through her preachers, she recalls to the way of truth those whom he had deceived, and she never ceases to free souls deceived by diabolical fraud, until, when the course of the world is completed, the predetermined total of her members has been fulfilled.

“She will repay him with good and not evil.” The Church, or each individual soul, repays Christ with good when, responding to the gifts of life received from him, it lives rightly and strives to make known to others what, with his help, it has been able to know or do. In the opposite way act those who repay the good received from the Lord with evil: either by defiling with heretical filth the mysteries of faith that they have received, by blaspheming through evil works the faith they maintain in their profession, or by corrupting good conduct through evil conversations.

“All the days of her life.” He repays the Lord with good throughout all his days who takes care to persevere until the end of his present life in those things that he has begun well. To this is similar the Gospel saying: “Let us serve him in holiness and righteousness before him all our days” (Luke 1).

“She sought wool and flax, and worked with the counsel of her hands.” Even in the literal sense the holy Church customarily observes these things, in accordance with the prophetic saying: “When you see the naked, clothe him, and do not despise your own flesh,” and so forth (Isa. 58). She does not do these things needlessly but with deliberation, so that she may hear from her husband, the Lord, at the judgment: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world, for I was naked and you clothed me,” and so forth (Matt. 25). Mystically, the works we perform for our neighbors are signified by wool, because piety and simplicity have one garment. In flax, the chastisement or mortification of our flesh is indicated.

“She became like a merchant’s ship, bringing her bread from afar.” He calls a merchant an *institor*, because the ancients gave him this name for his diligent persistence in seeking and multiplying merchandise. Thus the holy soul became like a merchant’s ship. It passes across the waves of desire for the present age and meditates only on the eternal joys that it hopes to receive in heaven. To obtain them, it acts zealously with all its strength and strives to overcome every adversity courageously. Of this he rightly adds: “Bringing her bread from afar,” because in all that it does well in temporal matters, it expects only an eternal reward and desires the nourishment of that living bread which said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6), and which lovingly promises its hearers: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11).

“And she rose at night and gave plunder to her household, and food to her maidservants.” Someone rests, as it were, at night when a member of the faithful, interrupting external concerns, begins spiritually to devote himself to himself and does not cease to care for himself through sacred readings, holy prayers, or private tears. He rises from the night when he carefully girds and prepares himself also to undertake the care of his neighbors. He gives plunder to his household when, by teaching, he reconciles to the fellowship of those who preceded them in faith people whom he has been able to rescue from the ancient enemy. He gives food to the maidservants when he refreshes humble people who obey his commands, so that they do not grow weary in their labor, by recalling the heavenly reward.

“She considered a field and bought it.” By “field” he means possession of the heavenly inheritance, concerning which Jacob says: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27). The Church, or the elect soul, considered and bought this field because it diligently learned what the joys of eternal life are and labored with all its power to obtain them. In another sense: she considered the field—that is, the entire world—and bought it when, sending teachers, she bestowed the talent of the word so that she might subject believers to Christ’s most blessed service.

“From the fruit of her hands she planted a vineyard.” She planted a vineyard when, in the field of the world, she made a Church from new peoples of believers and firmly established it through instruction in evangelical truth. She planted this vineyard from the fruit of her hands because the apostles and their successors instructed believers not only by word but also by miracles and by the teaching of good works. Even to this day, and until the end of the age, the holy Church diligently seeks those whom she may convert to the faith. Whoever she finds teachable, she buys for the service of Christ with the money of the word, and she strives to plant Christ’s vineyard in them—or rather, to make them Christ’s vineyard.

“She girded herself with strength,” and so forth. The Church girded her loins with strength when, intent upon desires for heavenly things, she disdained to succumb to carnal enticements. She strengthened her arm when she prepared herself to perform works of virtue. It is rightly said first that she girded her loins with strength and afterward strengthened her arm, because the action of a good work can in no way be acceptable to God unless a person first restrains the flowing of lust from both flesh and mind.

“She tasted that her commerce was good.” Her commerce is surely that of the field of which he said above: “She considered a field and bought it” (Prov. 31). Therefore the Church, or the holy soul, tasted with the inmost desire of her mind and recognized that the commerce of imperishable life was good—the commerce by which, after abandoning temporal enticements, she bought eternity in heaven.

“Her lamp will not be extinguished at night.” The lamps of those people are extinguished at night who, as the Lord says, “believe for a time and in the time of temptation fall away.” The lamps of those people will also be extinguished in the middle of the night who, when the judge comes, do not have the oil of charity in the vessels of their hearts. But the lamp of the holy Church is not extinguished at night, because, when she rests from business, she gives herself more freely to the activity of contemplating the light from above.

“She put her hand to strong things.” By “strong things” he means works perfected in the love of Christ, as the Lord himself says: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who slander and persecute you” (Matt. 5). And also: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess, and give to the poor” (Matt. 19). Elsewhere he speaks of this strength: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11).

“And her fingers grasped the spindle.” Women customarily hold the spindle in the right hand and the distaff in the left. The wool is wound around the distaff; it is drawn out as thread and, through spinning, passes onto the spindle. The right hand signifies eternal life, and the left signifies God’s present gifts: the abundance of possessions, the peace of the times, bodily health, and knowledge of the Scriptures. When, with God’s generosity, we receive these and similar good things, we carry them in the left hand like wool wound around the distaff. But when we begin to exercise them for the love of heavenly things, we transfer the wool of the spotless Lamb from the distaff to the spindle—that is, from the left hand to the right—because from the gifts of our Redeemer and from the examples of his works we make for ourselves a robe of heavenly glory and a garment of charity and of the wedding feast. The fingers with which she is said to grasp the spindle indicate the very intention of discernment by which each person acts.

[Col. 0428A]

“She opened her hand,” and so forth. This may be understood of works of almsgiving generally performed for the poor. But it is better understood of the word of God, which grants the garment of salvation to souls. The Church opened her hand to the needy when she revealed the mysteries of faith to those ignorant of them through the workers of truth. She extended her palms to the poor when she scattered preachers of eternal salvation widely among the nations.

“She will not fear,” and so forth. The cold of snow signifies the hearts of reprobates, frozen in the body by their faithlessness. In them iniquity abounds and charity grows cold. Therefore the Church will not fear for her household because of the cold of snow, since she believes the Lord’s promise that the gates of hell will not prevail against her (Matt. 16).

“For all her household are clothed in double garments.” They are clothed with wisdom to repel the doctrines of heretics. They are clothed with wisdom to endure the battles of perverse enemies. Or the members of the Church’s household are dressed in a double garment, one of works and the other of the mind—that is, of faith and action. They are imbued with the sacraments of their Redeemer and formed by his examples. Or they are clothed in double garments because they possess the promise of the present life and of the future life: now they are aided in their temporal pilgrimage, and then they will live forever in their homeland, sustained by divine grace in perpetual happiness.

“She made herself a variegated garment.” A variegated garment, which is usually made extremely strong through its varied weave, signifies the Church’s strong works and the diverse ornaments of her virtues. Concerning these the Psalmist sang in praise of the supreme King: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, clothed round about with variety” (Ps. 44).

“Fine linen and purple are her clothing.” Fine linen signifies the purity of a chaste way of life; purple signifies the outpouring of precious blood. Hence the Fathers beautifully said that the holy Church, blooming with the flowers of the elect, has lilies in peace and roses in war. The Church is clothed in fine linen when the elect discipline their bodies and subject them to service; she is clothed in purple when they practice this same continence not for popular approval but in order to obtain the blessedness of the everlasting kingdom.

Noble at the gates is her husband. The husband of the holy Church, or of any faithful soul, is the Lord. He appeared ignoble when he stood before the governor’s tribunal to be judged, when he endured insults, scourging, spittle, the cross, and death; but he will appear noble when he comes [Col. 0428D] to judge the world in righteousness, with all the angels accompanying him. Then all the nations will be gathered before him (Luke XXII).

When he sits with the senators of the earth. For he himself, who is now thought contemptible by many—namely, pagans, Jews, heretics, and Christians living wickedly—will be revealed to all as noble and exalted when the end of the world has come and he has opened the entrance to the heavenly homeland, sitting with the senators of the earth, that is, with those to whom he himself promises, saying: “Amen, I say to you, you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew XIX).

[Col. 0429A]

She made and sold a linen cloth. In the fine weaving of the sindon, a linen cloth, is signified the subtle interweaving of holy preaching, in which one rests gently, because through it the mind of the faithful is refreshed by heavenly hope. Hence animals are shown to Peter in a linen cloth (Acts X), because the souls of sinners, gathered together mercifully, are held within the soothing repose of faith. The Church therefore made and sold this sindon, because she gave by speaking the faith that she had woven by believing, and received from unbelievers a life of upright conduct.

And she handed over the girdle to the Canaanite. The Church handed over the girdle to the Canaanite because, through the vigor of righteousness manifested, she binds the unstable works of paganism, so that what is commanded in word may be maintained in life, as in the saying: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke XII). This is well indicated by the name Canaan, who [Col. 0429B] was also born among the Gentile people and whose name is interpreted as “changed”: the Gentiles converted to the faith are signified. By this most blessed exchange, they migrated from vices to virtues, from the devil to Christ, and the prophecy of the Psalm was fulfilled: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people”—that is, vices and sins—“and your father’s house” (Psalm XLIV), that is, the ancient enemy; “and the king will desire your beauty.”

Strength and beauty are her clothing. Strength is for enduring the wickedness of the perverse; beauty is for practicing the grace of virtues. Strength, because she suffers persecution for righteousness; beauty, because she practices righteousness. The Psalmist spoke a similar sentence about the Lord, saying: “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty; [Col. 0429C] the Lord has clothed himself with strength” (Psalm XCII). When the Lord preached the Gospel of the kingdom, some were pleased and others displeased; some spoke well, while others slandered, wounded, insulted, and reviled him. To those, therefore, who were pleased, he put on beauty; to those who were displeased, strength. Imitate the Lord, then, so that you may be his garment: be beautiful toward those who take pleasure in your good works, and be strong against detractors.

And she will laugh on the last day. She will laugh, that is, she will rejoice in the recompense of the heavenly kingdom, she who grieved in the struggle of the present life. For it is the custom of Scripture to use laughter for joy. Thus the Lord also says: [Col. 0429D] “Blessed are you who now weep, because you will laugh” (Luke VI). And blessed Job says: “But the mouth of the truthful will be filled with laughter.”

She opened her mouth to wisdom. She opened her mouth to speak only for the purpose of teaching wisdom, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Let no evil word proceed from your mouth, but only such as is good for the building up of faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians IV). Or certainly, she opened the mouth of her heart in order to learn inwardly from wisdom itself the truth that she would teach outwardly to others. Since the Church does both, what follows aptly agrees with either interpretation:

And the law of kindness is on her tongue. This is that law which does not immediately punish sinners in the manner of the Mosaic law, but mercifully recalls them to the remedies of repentance. [Col. 0430A] An example of this kindness is manifestly commanded by Wisdom himself, God and our Lord and Savior, when a sinful woman was brought before him: “If anyone is without sin,” he said, “let him first cast a stone at her” (John VIII). Thus, taking pity on her, he absolved her from the crime that had been committed, on the condition that she sin no more.

She considered the paths of her house, and did not eat her bread in idleness. She did not eat her bread in idleness because she displays through her works before the eyes of the eternal Judge what she has understood from sacred discourse. Likewise, the house of the strong woman is the dwelling of the heavenly homeland; the paths of that house are the commandments of righteousness, by which one reaches the eternal dwelling of life. The soul carefully considers these paths when it [Col. 0430B] examines diligently by what actions it must reach the things above and does not cease diligently practicing what it has learned must be done.

Nor does she eat her bread in idleness when, receiving the sacrifice of the Lord’s body, she strives to imitate in action what she celebrates in the sacred ministry, taking great care lest, by eating the Lord’s bread and drinking the cup unworthily, she eat and drink judgment upon herself (I Corinthians I). Rather, by suffering for Christ, shedding tears, and persisting in good works, she follows as far as she is able the example of his sufferings.

It can also be understood simply: the strong woman does not eat her bread in idleness, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “If anyone does not work, neither should he eat” (II Thessalonians III). He himself also says of himself: “These [Col. 0430C] hands have ministered to the needs of myself and those who are with me” (Acts XX). Hence, rightly reproving luxurious widows, he adds: “At the same time they also learn to go about from house to house; and not only idle, but also talkative and curious” (I Timothy V).

Her sons rose up and proclaimed her most blessed. What she certainly knew would happen, he relates in prophetic manner as though it had already happened: the sons of the Church will rise, namely, all the elect, endowed at the last with the immortality of the flesh. Then they will proclaim their mother most blessed—the mother who begot them for God from water and the Holy Spirit, but who is now despised by unbelievers as though she were wretched. Indeed, as the Apostle says: “If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are more pitiable than all people” (I Corinthians XV).

Since we wage war in the present life for the sake of the life to come, rightly, when [Col. 0430D] what we shall be has appeared, we will proclaim our mother most blessed. Gathered from all the righteous, she is called the one dove, bride, and friend of Christ. This statement can also suitably be understood as referring to the present time, whenever any of the faithful, having passed beyond the hardships of the world, is brought to the heavenly kingdoms. To sit belongs at times to humiliation, while to rise belongs to glory. The sons of the Church therefore rise and proclaim her most blessed when, exalted by heavenly blessings, they behold how great is the blessedness of that homeland of which they have deserved to become participants, and celebrate it with due praise in the divine vision.

Her husband will praise her. Her husband [Col. 0431A] will praise her when he rewards in the future the good things that he himself gives in the present world, saying at the judgment: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food,” and so forth (Matthew XV).

He himself, the firstfruits of those who sleep, rose from the dead; but on the day of judgment he will demonstrate more manifestly to all those whom he judges worthy of his praise how great is the glory of his own resurrection. The words with which he praises her are shown next.

Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all. By “many daughters” he means the Churches of the heretics and the crowds of wicked Catholics. They are called daughters either of Christ or of the Church because they too have been reborn through the sacraments of the Lord and have received adoption as sons, [Col. 0431B] though they did not preserve it. Hence John also says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (I John II).

They gathered riches, namely, good works: prayers, fasts, almsgiving, affliction, chastity of the flesh, restraint of the tongue, meditation on the Scriptures, and so forth. These things are true riches when the spirit performs them with pure sincerity of mind. But when they are done without the faith that works through love, they benefit those who do them nothing. Those daughters also gathered riches in vain, of whom the Lord says: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will confess to them, ‘I never knew you.’”

But the Catholic Church [Col. 0431C] surpasses all such daughters, following the footsteps of her Redeemer with pure faith and perfect works.

Grace is deceitful, etc. The grace of praise that she receives from human beings is deceitful. The beauty of chastity or of good works that a soul without the fear of God displays to everyone is vain.

The woman who fears God will herself be praised. That soul whose conscience is sincere is true and worthy of praise, because it preserves the fear of God in all things. For fear is the beginning and guardian of every virtue, as Scripture says: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs I). And again: “Whoever fears God will neglect nothing” (Ecclesiastes VII).

Hence blessed Job both flourished incomparably in virtues during prosperity and remained unconquerable before the enemy in adversity. For he could [Col. 0431D] truly say: “I have always feared God, as though waves were swelling over me, and I could not bear his weight” (Job III).

The grace of pretenders, therefore, is deceitful; the beauty of the work of fools is vain. But the Church, preserved in fear during the time of her sojourn, will offer burning lamps of virtue to her Bridegroom when he comes to judgment. Rightly praised by God, she will enter with him through the gate of the heavenly kingdom. How he praises her is taught in the final verse.

Give her the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her at the gates. These are the words of that husband of whom it was said: “Her husband will praise her”—that is, of our Lord and Savior, who at the end will command the angels to bring the Church, after the struggle of this life [Col. 0432A] and after the threshing and affliction of earthly things, into the joys of the heavenly kingdom and to gather her as his companion in immortal life, in accordance with the Gospel saying: “But gather the wheat into my barn” (Matthew XIII).

“Give her,” he says, “the fruit of her hands,” because she took care to bear the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, kindness, goodness, modesty, self-control, faith, and patience. Repay her the reward due for this.

“And let them praise her at the gates,” that is, at the judgment, or at the entrance to the heavenly homeland. Let it not be the empty favor of human beings, but the works themselves that she performed, examined and approved, praise her and reward her—by him whose grace, in giving these things, brought them to perfection. May he graciously grant that, in the future, we may deserve to be praised by him, because in the present life we have praised him with worthy service. Amen.

[Col. 0432B]

## THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER XII

“When he was speaking to the crowds, behold, his mother and brothers were standing outside, seeking to speak with him. But someone said to him: ‘Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you.’ And answering the one who told him, he said: ‘Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?’ And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said: ‘Behold, my mother and my brothers. Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.’”

When Jesus was speaking to the crowds, behold, his mother and brothers were standing outside, seeking to speak with him. (From Jerome.) The Lord was occupied with the work of discourse, with teaching the peoples, and with the ministry of preaching. [Col. 0432C]

(From Bede.) It is clear that when the Lord, being asked about his mother and brothers, appears to withdraw from the ministry of the word, he is not refusing the services of filial piety, since the commandment is: “Honor your father and your mother” (Exodus XX). Rather, he shows that he owes himself more to the mysteries of the Father than to maternal affection, commending the same to us by his example as well as by his word, when he says: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew X).

Mystically, however, the mother and brothers of Jesus are the synagogue, from whose flesh he was born, and the Jewish people, who, while the Savior teaches within, are unable to enter when they come. They neglect to understand his words spiritually; for the one who entered his house beforehand occupies it, because, while Judea delayed, the Gentiles flowed together to Christ and, the nearer they came in faith, the more capaciously they received in mind the mysteries of eternal life, in accordance with the Psalm’s saying: “Draw near [Col. 0432D] to him and be enlightened” (Psalm XXXIII).

But someone said to him. (From Jerome.) It seems to me that the one who reports this did not report it by chance and simply, but was laying a trap, to discover whether he preferred flesh and blood to spiritual work. Therefore the Lord did not scorn to go out as though denying his mother and brothers; rather, answering the one who laid the trap, he stretched out his hand toward the disciples and said: “Behold my mother and my brothers.” These are my mother, who daily give birth to me in the minds of believers; these are my brothers, who do the works of my Father.

And behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you. He preferred the apostles to his kin, so that we too might prefer the spirit to the flesh in the comparison of loves.

[Col. 0433A] We understand the brothers of the Savior as his cousins, the children of Mary, the sister of the Lord’s mother and therefore his maternal aunt, who is said to have been the mother of James the younger, Joseph, and Jude. In another place in the Gospel we read that these were called the Lord’s brothers.

(From Bede.) His relatives stand outside seeking to see the Lord when the Jews, not seeking the spiritual meaning in the Law, have fixed themselves outside upon the observance of the letter and, as it were, force Christ to go out to teach carnal things rather than consenting to enter themselves to learn spiritual things.

But he answered the one who told him: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” etc. (From Gregory.) Since the one who does the will of God is called the Lord’s sister and brother, because of both sexes being gathered into the faith, this is not surprising. [Col. 0433B] It is, however, highly astonishing how the Lord’s mother can also be spoken of. For he graciously called his faithful disciples brothers, saying: “Go and announce to my brothers.”

Therefore, since someone can become the Lord’s brother by coming to the faith, it must also be asked how he can become his mother. But we should know that the one who believes and becomes the brother and sister of Jesus becomes his mother by preaching. For one gives birth, as it were, to the Lord when one pours him into the heart of a hearer; and one becomes his mother if, through one’s voice, the love of the Lord is generated in the mind of one’s neighbor.

## THE TWELFTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

### READING FROM THE LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS, I, CHAPTER XV

“I make known to you the Gospel that I preached [Col. 0433C] to you, which you also received, in which you stand, through which you are also saved. I make known the manner in which I preached to you, if you hold fast, unless you believed in vain. For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he was seen by Cephas and afterward by the Eleven. Then he was seen by more than five hundred brothers at once, of whom many remain until now, while some have fallen asleep. Then he was seen by James, then by all the apostles. Last of all, as to one untimely born, he was seen also by me. For I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God. But by the grace [Col. 0433D] of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain.”

For I make known to you the Gospel, etc. (From Primasius.) Here, passing over the order of preaching, he turns to the doctrine of the resurrection, because some of the Corinthians were doubting the resurrection.

Which you also received. That is, which you received as something handed down. He says this so that they might not appear not to have believed it.

In which you stand. That is, persevering in good works, raised up toward heavenly things by its teaching.

Through which you are also saved. That is, through whose teaching you hope for the salvation of souls and also from various bodily infirmities, because without faith in the resurrection the hope of salvation perishes altogether.

[Col. 0434A]

In what manner I preached to you. It is as though he said: The whole purpose of our preaching is this—that you believe the resurrection, which is the reward of all who have believed in Christ. Otherwise all the labor of fasts and all the tribulations that you endure for Christ in this life are useless.

If you hold fast to it, unless you believed in vain. That is, unless you have forgotten, or certainly unless you do not hope to rise again to receive the reward of your faith or labor, you believe in vain.

For I delivered to you as of first importance. That is, from the beginning when I preached to you, I delivered the mystery of the resurrection, which is established as belonging to our faith—or as the first principle of it.

What I also received. He says that he received it either from the Law, from the elders, or from the Lord himself through revelation.

That Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures. [Col. 0434B] So that the blessed Apostle might establish with greater authority what he preached—that this is Christ the Savior of the world—he says: “The one whom Moses and the prophets announced.” Therefore he recalls that Christ was foretold according to the Scriptures, as in the passage: “He is led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he is silent,” and in the passage: “He was handed over because of our iniquities, and by his bruising we were healed” (Isaiah LIII), along with many other things concerning his Passion that you will find in the divine Scriptures.

And that he was buried. As in the passage from Isaiah: “He will give the wicked for his burial and the rich for his death.” Likewise, he himself says: “His burial was removed from the midst…”

And that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures. In Hosea you have: [Col. 0434C] “He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we will live in his sight” (Hosea VI).

And that he was seen by Cephas. That is, by Peter; for Cephas is a Syriac name. He appeared to Peter, as it is written in the Gospel, that he appeared to Simon.

And afterward by the Eleven. This is to be understood as referring to the time when he entered to them though the doors were shut. Not all the appearances are written in the Gospel, but only those sufficient for the faith of the hearers.

Then he was seen by more than five hundred brothers at once, of whom, etc. To establish greater faith, he introduced a multitude of witnesses. Many of them are said to be living and therefore able, if questioned, to say what they saw; many others are said already to be sleeping in death.

Then he was seen by James. He appeared separately to James [Col. 0434D] of Alphaeus. For they report that James of Alphaeus himself testified at the Lord’s supper, saying that he would not eat bread until he saw Christ rising from the dead.

Then by all the apostles. Many here wish all seventy apostles to be understood, those whom the Lord sent in pairs to preach.

Last of all, etc. He was seen by him on the road, when light surrounded him, or in the temple. He says this so that they would not think that he was relating what he had merely heard rather than what he had seen.

He calls himself “as one untimely born” because he had died to the Synagogue and had been born to the Church as one untimely born, whose life would have been despaired of unless he had been forcefully drawn in by the Lord’s grace (I Corinthians XV). He was drawn [Col. 0435A] in by preaching, not by chains.

And, through astonishment at the novelty, he who was in vices was perfect in training in the Law [the syntax is uncertain]. Or he was called untimely born for this reason: his mother, the synagogue, conceived him wrongly and gave birth to him imperfectly.

For I am the least of the apostles. He says this about himself out of humility; otherwise, he was least in time, not in labor. For elsewhere he says: “I labored more than all of them.”

Who am not worthy to be called an apostle, etc. Explaining why he is not worthy, he says: “Because I persecuted the Church of God.” By his example he teaches us that, even if we make progress in the present, it is better to grieve over past sins. For it is better to remember sins that have been forgiven than to forget sins that were committed. It is written: “My son, if you have sinned, do not add again to it, but pray concerning your former sins” (Ecclesiasticus XXI).

[Col. 0435B]

But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain. The grace by which we were redeemed did not seek labor, exertion, or merit. But the daily grace after baptism expects the daily service of labor.

## THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER XVIII

“Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a publican. The Pharisee, standing, prayed this to himself: ‘God, I give you thanks that I am not like the rest of humanity: robbers, unjust, adulterers, or even like this publican. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of everything I possess.’ But the publican, standing at a distance, would not even lift his eyes toward heaven, but struck his breast, saying: ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner.’ [Col. 0435C] Amen, I say to you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a Publican. (From Bede.) The publican praying humbly belongs to those members of the aforementioned widow—that is, of the Church—about whom it was said above: “But will God not avenge his elect who cry out to him?” The Pharisee, however, boasting of his merits, belongs to those concerning whom the terrifying sentence is added at the conclusion: “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on the earth?”

The Pharisee, standing, prayed this to himself: “God, I give you thanks that,” etc. [Col. 0435D] There are four forms in which all the pride of the arrogant is revealed. They consider either that they possess good things from themselves, or, if they believe they have received them from above, they think they received them because of their own merits; or they boast of possessing what they do not possess; or, despising others, they desire to appear uniquely to possess what they do possess.

The Pharisee is discovered to have suffered from this plague of boasting. He descended from the temple without justification because, attributing the merits of good works to himself as though they were uniquely his, he placed himself above the praying publican.

I fast twice a week; I give tithes of everything I possess. The prophet Ezekiel writes concerning the living creatures of heaven shown to him: “Their whole body was full of eyes all around” (Ezekiel I). The four bodies of the four living creatures are described as full of eyes [Col. 0436A] because the action of the saints is examined from every side: it eagerly provides for good things and carefully avoids evil.

But we often, while attending to one matter, end up neglecting another; and wherever we neglect, there we plainly have no eye. For behold, the Pharisee had an eye for displaying abstinence, showing mercy, and giving thanks to God, but he had no eye for preserving humility. What good is it if nearly an entire city is carefully guarded against the enemy’s attacks, if one opening is left exposed through which the enemy may enter?

But the publican, standing at a distance, would not even lift his eyes, etc. [Col. 0436B] What confidence in forgiveness this offers rightly to penitents! The publican, who fully recognized the guilt of his wickedness, wept and confessed; and although he came to the temple unjustified, he returned from the temple justified.

Typically, the Pharisee is the Jewish people, who boast of their merits on the basis of the justifications of the Law. The publican is the Gentile, who, placed far from God, confesses his sins. One withdrew in pride and was humbled; the other deserved to draw near through lamentation and was exalted.

For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. This can rightly be understood both of the two peoples mentioned above and of every proud or humble person, just as we read elsewhere: “Before destruction the heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled” (Proverbs XVI).

Therefore, from the words of the exalted Pharisee, by which he deserved to be humbled, we can conversely take a pattern of humility by which we may be exalted. Just as he, [Col. 0436C] considering both the vices of worse people and his own virtues, was lifted up to destruction, so let us, considering not only our own sluggishness but also the virtues of those who are better, humble ourselves toward glory. Thus each of us should entreat this suppliantly and submissively within himself:

“Almighty God, have mercy on your suppliant, because I am not like the innumerable servants of yours who are exalted through contempt of the world, glorious through the merit of righteousness, angelic through the praise of chastity, or like many of those who, after public crimes, deserved through repentance to become devoted to you. Even if I do anything good through the generosity of your grace, I do not know with what intention I do it or by what strict judgment it will be weighed by you.”

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT LAWRENCE

### READING FROM THE SECOND LETTER OF THE APOSTLE PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER IX

“Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly; and whoever sows with blessings will also reap with blessings. Let each one give as he has determined in his heart, not with sadness or from compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver. God is able to make every grace abound in you, so that, always having all sufficiency in all things, you may abound in every good work, as it is written: ‘He scattered, he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever and ever.’ And he who supplies seed to the sower will also provide bread for eating. And he will multiply your seed and increase the growth of the fruits of your righteousness.”

[Col. 0437A]

Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. (From Primasius.) That is, whoever gives little to the needy will receive little reward; each person will receive eternal rewards according to works of mercy.

And whoever sows with blessings will also reap with blessings. As the devotion has been, so will the recompense be. Whoever, with a grateful heart and in sufficient measure, provides either alms of temporal goods or words of preaching to one in need will receive sufficient and abundant rewards from the Lord. For the miser will not have a reward for what he gives unwillingly. Almsgiving becomes an eternal blessing for the giver and a present benefit for the recipient.

Let each one give as he has determined in his heart, not with sadness or from compulsion. That is, let him give to the poor as much as he has decided [Col. 0437B] or chosen, not under compulsion but voluntarily. Tobias says to his son: “If you have much, give much; if you have little, share a little with the needy” (Tobit IV).

For God loves a cheerful giver. Solomon says: “In every gift make your face cheerful” (Ecclesiasticus XXXV). Indeed, in the language of the divine Scriptures, the Lord desires his giver to be cheerful.

God is able to make every grace abound in you. Let those who give alms not fear poverty. For this reason he places God’s power first in the work of mercy. By “every grace” he means either an abundance of crops and an increase of fruits, or an abundance of understanding and insight into wisdom.

So that, always having all sufficiency in all things. [Col. 0437C] It is as though he said: The Lord will give you every sufficiency, both spiritual and bodily, so that you may be able to fulfill every good work with a free mind, whether devotion in mercy or instruction in teaching.

“He scattered, he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever and ever.” That is, he divided and gave to many. He gave not to one but to many because the prayer of many is greater than that of one. From temporal goods, if they are distributed well, eternal righteousness is acquired.

And he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for eating, etc. We understand this in the holy Gospel as spoken about the seed of the word, where the Lord, explaining the parable of the seed to his disciples, says: “The seed is the word of God” (Matthew XII). It is as though the Apostle said to preachers: God, who gave you the ministry of teaching, [Col. 0437D] does not withdraw bodily food. Or, he who by distributing has granted you the means to give will certainly not allow you to hunger.

And he multiplied your seed. That is, he will increase your goods—or your words. “Give, and it will be given to you,” says the Lord. Whoever, for God’s sake, gives either the word of preaching or the nourishment of mercy will receive it multiplied, both here and in the future.

And increase the growth of the fruits of your righteousness. By the growth of the fruits of righteousness he means either material resources or the teaching of words. For, as Solomon says, the wise person “will be satisfied by the fruit of his lips.”

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0438A]

“Amen, amen, I say to you: Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit. Whoever loves his life will lose it, and whoever hates his life in this world preserves it for eternal life. If anyone serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also will my servant be. If anyone serves me, my Father who is in heaven will honor him.”

Amen, amen, I say to you: Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit. He was speaking of himself as having to be put to death and multiplied: put to death in the unbelief of the Jews, multiplied in the faith of all peoples.

[Col. 0438B]

Whoever loves his life will lose it. This can be understood in two ways. “Whoever loves it will lose it,” that is, if you love it, you will lose it. If you desire to preserve your life in Christ, do not fear dying for Christ.

There is another interpretation: “Whoever loves his life will lose it.” Do not love it in this life, lest you lose it in eternal life.

And whoever hates his life in this world preserves it for eternal life. Thus, where it was said above, “whoever loves,” the words “in this world” are understood. That person will therefore lose it. But whoever hates it in this world certainly preserves it for eternal life.

A great and wondrous sentence! How can love of one’s life cause a person to perish, while hatred keeps one from perishing? If you have loved wrongly, then you have hated; if you have hated rightly, then you have loved. Blessed are those who hate in order to preserve, lest they lose by loving here.

Here the name [Col. 0438C] “life” designates the present life, or even the pleasure of this life, which must be lost so that you may happily find in the kingdom of God your will, which you bravely overcame in this world. For the holy martyrs hated this present life for Christ’s name, preferring to lose this present life rather than deny Christ.

If anyone serves me, let him follow me. What does “let him follow me” mean except “let him imitate me”? Those serve Jesus Christ who do not seek their own interests but those of Jesus Christ. This is what “let him follow me” means: let him walk in my ways, not his own, as it is written elsewhere: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked” (I John II).

Even if he offers bread to the hungry, he should do it from mercy, not from boasting; he should [Col. 0438D] seek nothing other than the good work, with his left hand unaware of what his right hand is doing (Matthew VI), that is, so that the intention of acquisitiveness may be removed from works of charity.

And where I am, there also will my servant be. The reward of love and the price of the work for one who serves Christ is to be with Christ. Let us hear what fruit, what reward, what recompense he promises him.

If anyone serves me, my Father who is in heaven will honor him. With what honor, except that he may be with his Son? What he said above—“Where I am, there also will my servant be”—he explains when he says: “My Father will honor him.” An adopted son can never receive [Col. 0439A] greater honor than to be where the Only-Begotten is—not made equal to the Godhead, but made a companion of eternity.

## THE THIRTEENTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

### READING FROM THE SECOND LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER III

“Such confidence we have through Christ toward God—not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God. He also made us competent ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the spirit. For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life. Now if the ministry of death, formed in letters on stones, was in glory, so that the children of Israel could not gaze upon the face of Moses because of the glory of his face, which is being brought to an end, [Col. 0439A] how will the ministry of the spirit not be more glorious? For if the ministry of condemnation is glory, much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory.”

[Col. 0439B]

Such confidence we have through Christ toward God. It is as though he said: That confidence is unconquerable which comes not from us but from Christ; through our faith, grace commends us more than any human letter does.

Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything. That is, by our own wisdom or power we accomplish nothing in the cause of your salvation. He wishes to show that, in saving the Gentiles, he neither thinks nor does anything by his own judgment or ability. Indeed, a few humble, uneducated, and almost rustic men could never have saved [Col. 0439C] the whole world without God’s grace.

He prefaced this because he was about to say that he had undertaken a ministry so much greater than Moses’ as the New Testament is greater than the Law, which, by means of mysteries that foreshadowed it, retained Christ hidden within itself. He does not claim anything for himself, but seeks through his teaching, which is in Christ, to recall them more easily from the false apostles.

Who made us competent ministers of the New Testament. That is, fit to fulfill the office of apostleship.

Not of the letter, but of the spirit. That is, not of the carnal law, but of spiritual commandments.

[Col. 0439D] For the letter kills. (From Augustine.) “Where, O death, is your contention? Where is your sting?” He explains the sting: “The sting of death,” he says, “is sin,” and he adds a remarkable statement: “The power of sin is the law.” For sin is stirred up more vehemently when it is forbidden, but only if the letter is present and grace absent. The law is the letter. Here is the law: “You shall not covet.” I say that unless grace assists you, you will covet more vehemently. This is what is meant by “the letter kills.” (From Primasius.) If you consider the former period of the law, then the letter was killing transgressors if they failed either to observe the Sabbaths or to offer carnal sacrifices.
