But now it kills in this way: if the carnal ceremonies involved in offering bulls and calves are observed—ceremonies that the observance of grace has now removed—for if they are observed now, they kill.

[Col. 0440A] But the Spirit gives life. That is, the spiritual understanding of the law bestows eternal salvation. This should not, however, be taken generally from the entire text of Scripture, for there are some things that must now be observed according to the order of history, such as: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI), and similar passages.

What if the ministry of death, engraved in letters on stones, was in glory? That is, if the law among the ancients granted present glory to those who followed it according to the letter, how much more does it now glorify those who carry it out spiritually.

[Col. 0440B] So that the children, etc. Because the visible glory of carnal works is emptied through the spiritual glory of the Gospel—but it is emptied in such a way that it advances toward something better through inner understanding, just as infancy is emptied through adolescence and old age, and just as seed is emptied into fruit. The fruit is indeed better than the seed, but fruit never rises without seed; the seed does not perish but is multiplied in the fruit. Thus it is emptied so that it may be enlarged, as he himself says: “But when that which is perfect has come, that which is partial will be brought to nothing” (1 Cor. XIII).

How much more, etc. That is, ours, which is not brought to nothing because it is perfect.

For if the ministry of condemnation is glory. Above he called the law’s ministry “the ministry”; now he has called it “the ministry of condemnation.” It is the ministry of death because, by itself alone, it did not free from death. It is also the ministry of condemnation because, without any remedy of repentance, it consigned the guilty to present destruction.

Much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory. It truly abounds unto glory, that is, eternal glory, because righteousness justifies freely, without observance of the legal commandments.

[Col. 0440C] ## THE GOSPEL OF MARK, CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0440D] “Jesus went out from the borders of Tyre and came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, through the midst of the region of the Decapolis. And they brought him a deaf and mute man, and they begged him to lay his hand upon him. And taking him aside from the crowd, he put his fingers into his ears, and, spitting, touched his tongue. And looking up to heaven, he groaned and said to him: ‘Ephpheta,’ which means ‘to open.’ And immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was loosed, and he spoke correctly. And he charged them to tell no one. But the more he charged them, the more abundantly they proclaimed it, and they were astonished beyond measure, saying: ‘He has done all things well; he makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.’”

[Col. 0441A] Jesus went out from the borders of Tyre and came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, through the midst of the region of the Decapolis. (From Bede.) Decapolis is, as the name itself indicates, a region of ten cities beyond the Jordan toward the east, around Hippo, Pella, and Gadara, opposite Galilee. Therefore, when it is said that the Lord came to the Sea of Galilee through the midst of the region of the Decapolis, this does not mean that he entered the very borders of the Decapolis. For it is not said that he crossed the sea by boat, but rather that he came as far as the sea and reached the place that looked toward the central region of the Decapolis, situated far beyond the sea.

And they bring him a deaf and mute man, and they begged him to lay his hand upon him. The deaf and mute person is one who neither opens his ears to hear God’s words nor his mouth to proclaim them. Such people must be offered to the Lord for healing by those who, through long practice, have already learned to speak and hear the divine utterances, so that those whom human frailty cannot help may themselves be saved by the right hand of his grace.

[Col. 0441B] And taking him aside from the crowd. For he takes the sick man aside from the crowd when, illuminating a mind weakened by sins with the visitation of his mercy, he withdraws it from the customary ways of human society and calls it to follow the paths of his commandments.

[Col. 0441C] He put his fingers into his ears. To put fingers into the ears means that, through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, he opens the ears of the heart to understand and receive the words of salvation. For the Lord himself bears witness that the Holy Spirit is called the finger of God when he says to the Jews: “If I cast out demons by the finger, by whom do your sons cast them out?” (Matt. XII). Another evangelist, explaining this, says: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Luke XII); and the magicians in Egypt, having been overcome, said: “The Spirit of God is here” (Exod. VII). The law, too, was written on stone tablets by the finger of God. Therefore, the fingers of God put into the ears of the man who was to be healed are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, by which he recalls hearts that have wandered from the way of truth to hear and learn the knowledge of salvation. And because confession ought to follow upon the light of truth once it has been recognized, it is appropriately added:

And, spitting, he touched his tongue. The Lord touches the tongue while spitting when he trains the mouths of catechumens for the confession of faith, and, by the touch of his mercy, forms mouths that have long been speechless to utter words of wisdom. For the Lord’s spittle signifies the taste of wisdom, which, as the wise man testifies, says: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High as the firstborn.”

And looking up to heaven. He looked up to heaven in order to teach that from there speech is to be sought for the mute, hearing for the deaf, and healing for all infirmities.

[Col. 0441D] He groaned. He groaned, not because he himself needed to ask the Father for anything with a groan—the Father who, together with him, grants all things to those who ask—but in order to give us an example of groaning when we invoke the aid of heavenly mercy either for our own errors or for those of our neighbors.

And he said to him, “Ephpheta,” which means “to open.” When he said “Ephpheta,” that is, “to open,” this properly concerned the ears. The ears had to be opened for hearing, while the tongue had to be released from the restraints of its slowness so that it could speak.

[Col. 0442A] And immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was loosed, and they spoke correctly. For that person alone speaks correctly—whether by confessing God or by preaching to others—whose hearing divine grace opens so that he may listen and obey the heavenly commandments, and whose tongue the Lord trains to speak by the touch of wisdom, which he himself is. Such a person can rightly say with the Psalmist: “O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise” (Ps. L). And with Isaiah: “The Lord has given me a learned tongue, that I may know how to sustain him who has fallen. He raises with a word; morning by morning he raises my ear to hear as a teacher” (Isa. L).

[Col. 0442B] And he charged them to tell no one; but the more he charged them, the more abundantly they proclaimed it, and they were astonished beyond measure, saying: “He has done all things well; he makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.” If he knew that they would proclaim him all the more the more he commanded them not to proclaim him—he who knew both the present and future wills of human beings—why did he command this, except that he wished to show the sluggish how much more diligently and fervently they ought to proclaim him when he commands them to preach, since those who had been forbidden to speak could not remain silent?

## THE FOURTEENTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

## THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE GALATIANS, CHAPTER III

[Col. 0442C] “Promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. He does not say, ‘and to offspring,’ as referring to many, but as referring to one: ‘and to your offspring,’ who is Christ. Now I say this: the covenant confirmed by God is not annulled by the law made four hundred and thirty years afterward, so as to abolish the promise. For if the inheritance comes from the law, it no longer comes from the promise. But God granted it to Abraham through the promise. Why, then, the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, having been ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not of one party; but God is one. Is the law, then, contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not. For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly be from the law. But Scripture confined everything under sin, so that the promise might be given to those who believe through faith in Jesus Christ.”

[Col. 0442D] Promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. (From Jerome.) The straightforward sense woven through this passage has this force: the Apostle teaches that the promises made earlier to Abraham cannot be destroyed by the law given afterward, and that what came later cannot prejudice what came first. The promises were given to Abraham four hundred and thirty years earlier, namely, that all nations would be blessed in him; the observance of the law, however—that whoever did it would live by it—was given to Moses on Mount Sinai four hundred and thirty years later.

He does not say, “and to offspring,” as referring to many, but as referring to one: “and to your offspring,” who is Christ. The Apostle interpreted Abraham’s offspring as Christ. Traversing all the Scriptures in thought and memory, I have never found “offspring” written in the plural, but whether in a good or bad sense it is always singular.

[Col. 0443A] Now I say this: the covenant confirmed by God. He calls the promises made to Abraham a covenant. They cannot be annulled by a human being, since even human covenants retain their legal force and cannot be dissolved if they have been formally established.

Here, certainly, if we ask whether this covenant, which he says was confirmed by the Lord and could not be weakened by the law made four hundred and thirty years later, should be understood as new or old, who would hesitate to answer “new”? Yet it was hidden in prophetic mysteries until the time came when it would be revealed in Christ.

[Col. 0443B] Which was four hundred years afterward, etc. (From Jerome.) The calculation of the years in this passage—from the time when the Lord spoke to Abraham, saying, “In your offspring all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XII, XXII), to Moses the lawgiver—whether they amount to four hundred and thirty, or how in Genesis the Lord himself promises Abraham that after four hundred years his descendants would leave the land of slavery, is no small question. Many have asked it, and I do not know whether anyone has solved it.

[Col. 0443C] (From Primasius.) No one should think this contradictory because in the book of Genesis God says to Abraham: “Know this with certainty: your offspring will be strangers in a land not their own; they will enslave them and afflict them for four hundred years” (Gen. XV), whereas here the Apostle adds thirty years. What he means is this: in the seventieth year of his life Abraham received the promise from God. From that time until the beginning of the Mosaic law, four hundred and thirty years are completed in the following manner. From the time of the promise until Abraham’s hundredth year, when Isaac was born, twenty-five years are counted; afterward, in Isaac’s fifth year, the child Isaac began to be afflicted by Ishmael, as the same Apostle recalls in this very epistle. It is therefore clearly shown, according to the word of God spoken to Abraham, that thirty years after the promise his offspring began to suffer under persecutors.

For if the inheritance comes from the law, etc. It is as though he said: the offspring who is Christ, in whom all nations would be blessed, was granted not from the law, which did not yet exist, but from the promise made to Abraham.

[Col. 0443D] Why, then, the law, etc. (From Jerome.) Someone could have said here: Why was the law given after the four hundred and thirty years of the promise, when, once the law had been given, suspicion could arise that the pledge had been destroyed, and when the law, while the promise remained, had no beneficial purpose? The Apostle, foreseeing this question, proposes it to himself in what follows, saying: “Why, then, the law?” He answers himself: “It was added because of transgressions, until the holy one should come to whom the promise had been made.” After the people’s offense in the wilderness, after they worshiped the calf and murmured against God, the law was brought in to prohibit transgressions. (From Augustine.) The law was added because of transgressions so that human beings might receive commandments, trusting proudly in their own powers; then, failing in those powers and becoming transgressors as well, they would seek a liberator and Savior. Thus the fear of the law, having made them humble, would lead them like a pedagogue to faith and grace, and would either compel or teach them not to transgress until Christ came, concerning whom he says: “The offspring to whom he had made the promise.”

[Col. 0444A] Ordained through angels. (From Primasius.) Here he indicates that Moses received the law through an angel of the Lord, as Stephen says: “This is he who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai” (Acts VII). (From Jerome.) Throughout the Old Testament, wherever an angel is first said to have appeared and afterward is introduced as speaking as God, the one who appeared is indeed an angel from among the many ministers, whoever he may have been; but in him the mediator speaks, saying: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. III).

[Col. 0444B] By the hand of a mediator. (From Primasius.) We should understand the mediator to be Jesus Christ, of whom it is also written to Timothy: “There is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. II). By the “hand” of the mediator we should understand his power and might. Some think that Moses was the mediator. For Moses, they say, stood between God and the people; thus he himself says to the people: “Face to face the Lord spoke with us on the mountain from the midst of the fire; I was the intermediary and stood between the Lord and you at that time, to announce his words.” (From Jerome.) Since the order of the reading is confused and disturbed by hyperbaton, it seems that it should be rendered for us as follows: “The law was placed through angels by the hand of a mediator, ordained through angels because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made.” The offspring undoubtedly signifies Christ, concerning whom Matthew says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matt. I).

[Col. 0444C] Now a mediator is not of one. “Of one party” is understood: a mediator is not of one party but between two, so that he stands in the middle.

But God is one. He adds this so that no one might think Christ entirely separated from the unity of the divine nature because he had undertaken the office of mediator.

[Col. 0444D] Is the law, then, contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not. It is as though he said: the law does not take away God’s promises but prepares people for them. Just as the mediator between God and human beings stood between the one who gives and the one who receives the law, so the law itself, which intervened after the promise and before its fulfillment, must not be thought to exclude the promise merely because, following afterward, it might seem to abolish what came first. Rather, because it could not give life or grant what the first promise had pledged, it is clear that it was given to guard the promise, not to overthrow it.

For if a law had been given, etc. It did not give life because it could not remove original sin, or certainly because life was to be given not through the blood of goats or bulls but through the blood of Christ.

[Col. 0445A] Righteousness would truly be from the law. He called the gift of the promised inheritance “righteousness,” as though he said: if a law had been given that could bestow life and provide what the promise had pledged, then the promise would truly be thought to have been excluded by the law. But now, because it was added on account of transgressions, as we said above, it rather convicted as sinners those to whom, after the promise, it was given for protection—or, so to speak, as a prison—so that those who deliberately refused to await the promise of the innocent one might, being hindered by legal bonds and reduced to servitude under commandments, be kept until the coming of the future faith in Christ, which would bring the promise to its fulfillment.

[Col. 0445B] But Scripture confined everything under sin. (From Primasius.) When Christ came, those who were under the law of Moses were confined under sin if they wished to remain any longer in observance of the law. For those who served the shadow of the law while the truth was present were accursed. This is also shown by the fact that no one could be found who fulfilled all the commandments of the law. Or, when he says that everything was confined under sin, he means that he discovered everything enclosed under sin, so that people could not escape sin unless they believed in Christ; thus it was necessary for believers to reach the promised salvation through faith alone. Alternatively, “confined” means that we were held in many divisions, occupied in different observances and detained in the school of the law for instruction in the faith, which was to be revealed in Christ’s time.

[Col. 0445C] So that the promise might be given to those who believe through faith in Jesus Christ. (From Jerome.) That is, it was necessary that faith in Christ alone should save those who believe. Nor should Scripture be judged the author of sin because it is said to have confined everything under sin, since a commandment imposed by right of law rather reveals and condemns sin than causes it. In the same way, a judge is not the author of crime when he convicts wicked people; rather, he confines them and declares them guilty by the authority of his judgment, so that afterward the ruler, if he wishes, may release those who are liable to punishment through clemency.

## THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER X

[Col. 0445D] [Col. 0446A] “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For I say to you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it. And behold, a certain lawyer stood up, testing him and saying: ‘Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?’ But he said to him: ‘What is written in the law? How do you read?’ He answered: ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.’ And he said to him: ‘You have answered correctly. Do this and you will live.’ But he, wishing to justify himself, said to Jesus: ‘And who is my neighbor?’ Jesus, taking up the question, said: ‘A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers. They also stripped him, inflicted wounds upon him, and went away, leaving him half dead. Now it happened that a certain priest was going down the same road, and when he saw him, he passed by. Likewise a Levite, when he was near the place and saw him, passed by. But a certain Samaritan, journeying, came near him, and when he saw him, he was moved with compassion. He approached and bound his wounds, pouring in oil and wine. Then he placed him on his own beast, brought him to an inn, and took care of him. The next day he brought out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying: ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I return.’ Which of these three seems to you to have been neighbor to the man who fell among robbers?’ He said: ‘The one who showed mercy to him.’ And Jesus said to him: ‘Go and do likewise.’”

[Col. 0446B] Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. (From Bede.) Not the eyes of the scribes and Pharisees, who saw only the Lord’s body, but those blessed eyes that are able to recognize his mysteries. Of them it is said: “You have revealed them to little ones” (Matt. XI). Blessed are the eyes of the little ones, to whom the Son deigns to reveal both himself and the Father.

But I say to you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it. “Abraham rejoiced that he might see Christ’s day; he saw it and was glad” (John X). Isaiah also (Isa. VI), and Micah, and many other prophets saw the glory of the Lord; but all of them saw it from afar, through a mirror and in a mystery. The Apostles, however, having the Lord present with them, dining with him, and learning through questioning whatever they wished (Acts I).

[Col. 0446C] And behold, a certain lawyer stood up, testing him and saying: “Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?” The lawyer who questioned the Lord about eternal life in order to test him seems, I think, to have taken the opportunity for testing from the Lord’s own words, where he said: “Rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” Yet by this very testing he shows how true the Lord’s confession is when he speaks to the Father: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones.”

But he said to him: “What is written in the law? How do you read?” He answered, etc. While answering the lawyer, the Savior shows us the perfect path of heavenly life. To the lawyer, who first put forward the words of the law concerning love of God and neighbor, he says:

[Col. 0446D] “You have answered correctly; do this and you will live.” He declares most openly that love alone—love not displayed merely in words but proved by the performance of works—is what leads to perpetual life.

But he, wishing to justify himself, said to Jesus: “Who is my neighbor?” The Lord tempered his answer in such a way that he taught that anyone who shows mercy is a neighbor to everyone. Yet this same parable also specifically signified the Son of God himself, who deigned to become our neighbor through his humanity.

[Col. 0447A] Jesus, taking up the question, said: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho.” This man is understood as Adam in the human race. Jerusalem is that heavenly city of peace; having fallen from its blessedness, he came down into this mortal and wretched life, which is aptly signified by Jericho, interpreted as “moon.” It is always uncertain because of the varied labors and errors of decline.

And he fell among robbers. Understand the robbers as the devil and his angels, among whom the one who was going down fell. For unless he had first become inwardly swollen with pride, he would not so easily have yielded when tested outwardly. The saying is entirely true: “Before destruction the heart is exalted” (Prov. XVI).

They also stripped him. They deprived him, namely, of the garment of immortal glory and innocence. This is the first robe with which, according to another parable, the prodigal son is clothed when he returns through repentance (Luke XV); and, having lost it, the first parents recognized that they were naked and put on tunics of skins belonging to mortal nature (Gen. III).

And having inflicted wounds upon him. The wounds are sins. By violating the integrity of human nature, they implanted, so to speak, a seedbed for the increase of death in its weakened inner parts.

They went away. They went away not by ceasing their ambushes in any respect, but by concealing the frauds of those same ambushes.

Leaving him half dead. They left him half dead because they were able to strip him of the blessedness of immortal life but could not abolish the faculty of reason. Insofar as a human being can understand and know God, he is alive; but insofar as he wastes away through sins and fails in misery, he is at once dead and disfigured by a deadly wound.

[Col. 0447B] [Col. 0447C] Now it happened, etc. The priest and the Levite who, after seeing the wounded man, passed by signify the priesthood and ministry of the Old Testament. There, through the decrees of the law, the wounds of the world in its sickness could be displayed but not healed, because, as the Apostle says, it was impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of calves and goats.

[Col. 0447D] But a certain Samaritan, journeying, came near him, and when he saw him, etc. The Samaritan, whose name means “guardian,” signifies God. The Prophet rightly begs him to keep him from encountering these robbers: “Guard me,” he says, “from the snare they have set for me and from the stumbling-blocks of those who work iniquity” (Ps. CXL). Descending from heaven for us human beings and for our salvation, he undertook the journey of this present life and came near the one who was wasting away from the wounds inflicted upon him—that is, having been made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a man (Phil. II), he became near through sharing our compassion and a neighbor through the consolation of mercy.

He approached and bound his wounds, etc. He restrained the sins he found in human beings by reproving them, instilling hope of pardon in the penitent and fear of punishment in sinners. He binds the wounds when he commands: “Repent.” He pours in oil when he adds: “For the kingdom of heaven is near.” He also pours in wine when he says: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.”

[Col. 0448A] And placing him on his own beast, etc. His beast is the flesh in which he deigned to come to us. He placed the wounded man upon it because he bore our sins in his body upon the wood; and, according to another parable, he placed upon his shoulders the sheep that had wandered and, having found it, carried it back to the flock (Luke XV). Thus to be placed upon the beast means to believe in the incarnation of Christ, to be initiated into his mysteries, and at the same time to be protected from the enemy’s attack. The inn is the present Church, where travelers returning from this pilgrimage to their eternal homeland are refreshed. He rightly brought him to the inn after placing him on the beast, because no one enters the Church unless baptized and united to the body of Christ.

[Col. 0448B] And the next day he brought out two denarii, etc. The next day means after the Lord’s resurrection. Before this, indeed, he had illuminated those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death through the grace of his Gospel; but after the resurrection had been celebrated, the splendor of perpetual light shone forth more fully. The two denarii are the two Testaments, in which the name and image of the eternal King are contained. For Christ is the end of the law. These denarii are given to the innkeeper after being brought forth on the next day, because then he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures. On the next day the innkeeper received the denarii, by whose value he was to care for the wounded man, because the Holy Spirit, coming upon them, taught the Apostles all truth, so that they would be able to devote themselves to instructing the nations and preaching the Gospel.

[Col. 0448C] And whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I return. The innkeeper spends more than he received in the two denarii when the Apostle says: “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give advice.” Likewise, the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel, but “we have not used this authority, lest we burden any of you.” When he returns, he will repay the debt he promised, because when the Lord comes for judgment he says: “Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of the Lord your God” (Luke XII).

[Col. 0448D] Which of these three seems to you to have been neighbor? etc. According to the letter, the Lord’s judgment is clear: no one is more our neighbor than the one who shows mercy. For the citizen of Jerusalem, it was not the priest or the Levite of the same people—indeed, not one born and raised in the same city—but a resident of a foreign nation who became neighbor because he showed greater mercy. In a more sacred understanding, since no one is more truly our neighbor than the one who healed our wounds, let us love him as the Lord our God; let us love him as our neighbor, for nothing is so near as the head is to its members; and let us also love the one who imitates Christ.

And Jesus said to him: “Go, and you also,” etc. That is, to show that you truly love your neighbor as yourself, devote yourself to doing whatever you are able to do to assist him in his bodily or spiritual need.

## THE FIFTEENTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

## READING FROM THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE GALATIANS, CHAPTER V

[Col. 0449A] [Col. 0449B] “Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh. For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh. These are opposed to one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law. Now the works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, licentiousness, debauchery, service of idols, sorceries, enmities, contentions, jealousies, angers, quarrels, dissensions, sects, envies, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, longsuffering, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity. Against such things there is no law. Those who belong to Christ have crucified their own flesh with vices and desires.”

[Col. 0449C] Walk by the Spirit, and desire, etc. This must be understood in three ways. First, we may say that those who have put the works of the flesh to death by the Spirit and have sown in the Spirit so that they may reap eternal life from the Spirit, whenever they feel the pleasure of the flesh begin to tickle them, do not fulfill its desire. In another way, we say that those walk by the Spirit and do not fulfill the desire of the flesh who spiritually depart from Egypt and draw spiritual food and drink from the spiritual rock; they walk in all things spiritually, not fulfilling the letter or desire of the carnal law, but reaping the fruits of spiritual understanding (1 Cor. X). In a third way, some say that the desire of the flesh belongs to those who are little ones in Christ, while the way of the Spirit belongs to mature men. “Walk by the Spirit,” that is, in the gravity of the Spirit, on the path of the mature man; and “you will not fulfill the desire of the flesh,” that is, of the little ones.

[Col. 0449D] For the flesh desires against the Spirit, etc. The flesh delights in present and fleeting things, while the Spirit delights in things perpetual and future. The flesh fears cold, rejects hunger, is weakened by vigils, burns with lust, seeks soft things, and desires what is pleasant. The Spirit, by contrast, seeks the things opposed to the flesh and capable of weakening it. Alternatively, “the flesh desires against the Spirit” means that the literal and carnal understanding of Scripture struggles against allegory and spiritual teaching. “The Spirit against the flesh” means that what is higher resists what is lowly, the eternal what is fleeting, and truth what is shadow.

But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law. This means: if you devote yourselves entirely to spiritual actions, the law is not necessary for you, since it was given not to spiritual but to carnal people. When he says “you are led by the Spirit,” that is, “you are governed by the Spirit,” he signifies not the spirit of a human being but the Holy Spirit, of whom the Apostle says elsewhere: “The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God” (Rom. VIII). By following this Spirit we become spiritual and cease to be under the law.

[Col. 0450A] Now the works of the flesh are manifest. That is, they are known to everyone—or certainly manifest only to those who believe in Christ. For many Gentiles glory in their disgrace and think that, if they have satisfied some pleasure, they have won a victory through shame. It is also elegantly said that he placed “works” in the flesh but “fruit” in the Spirit, because vices come to an end in themselves and perish, whereas virtues grow and overflow with fruits.

[Col. 0450B] Which are fornication. The first work of the flesh, then, is fornication, which he placed at the beginning so that there might be no uncertainty about what follows. Everything that a human being does is outside the body, but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body. The fornicator is guilty of a greater crime because he takes the members of Christ and makes them members of a prostitute: “The two will be one flesh.” One who is not faithful and does not believe in Christ makes his own members members of a prostitute. But one who believes and commits fornication makes the members of Christ members of a prostitute.

Uncleanness, licentiousness. The second work of the flesh is called uncleanness. The third is licentiousness, for uncleanness follows as the companion of licentiousness. Just as in the old law (Lev. XV), concerning shameful crimes committed in secret—which it is most disgraceful even to name, lest they pollute both the mouth of the speaker and the ears of those who hear—the Scripture spoke generally, saying: “Make the children of Israel ashamed of, or reverent before, every uncleanness,” so here it has called the other extraordinary pleasures, and even the acts of marriage themselves if they are not carried out modestly and honorably, as though in the sight of God and solely for the service of children, “uncleanness” and “licentiousness.”

[Col. 0450C] Service of idols. Idolatry holds the fourth place in the catalogue of the works of the flesh. For once someone has mingled himself with luxury and pleasure, he no longer looks toward the Creator. In another sense, all forms of idolatry delight in feasting, gluttony, the belly, and the things below the belly.

Sorceries. And lest sorceries and magical practices, which are arts, might perhaps not seem to be forbidden in the New Testament, they too are named in fifth place among the works of the flesh. For it often happens through magical arts that the wretched both love and are loved.

Enmities. Enmity, which is placed sixth after sorceries, shows what guilt it has by being set beside an obvious crime. As far as depends on us, we should be enemies of no one but should have peace with everyone.

Contentions. Contention occupies the seventh place among the works of the flesh. “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward everyone, teachable, patient, correcting with gentleness even those who argue against him” (2 Tim. III).

Jealousies. In eighth place comes jealousy, which in Greek is more significantly and more familiarly called ζῆλος (*zēlos*), “zeal” or “jealous rivalry.” I do not know which of us is free from this evil. The patriarchs were jealous of their brother Joseph. Mary the prophetess and Aaron the priest of God were also deceived by this passion against Moses.

Angers. Anger follows in ninth place. It does not produce the righteousness of God and is a form of fury. The difference between an irascible person and an angry person is that the irascible person is always angry, whereas the angry person is stirred up for a time. And I do not know how anyone can possess the kingdom of God when the person who becomes angry is separated from the kingdom.

[Col. 0450D] [Col. 0451A] ##
### Quarrels

In the tenth place are placed quarrels, which the Greeks, using another significant term, call *ἐριθείας* (*eritheias*), since a quarrel is called *μάχη* (*machē*). They exclude one from the kingdom of God. *Εριθεία* (*eritheia*) is when someone is always ready to contradict, contends with womanish bickering, and provokes the person who is contending; among the Greeks this is also called *φιλονεικία* (*philoneikia*).

### Dissensions

In the eleventh place are placed dissensions, which are works of the flesh. They arise when someone, being by no means perfect, does not speak with the same understanding and the same judgment, saying, “I am of Paul,” “I of Apollos,” “I of Cephas,” and “I of Christ.” The same dissension is also found among gifts themselves; it may occur between husband and wife, father and son, brother and brother, fellow servant and fellow servant, soldier and comrade, craftsman and a craftsman of the same trade. Sometimes dissension also arises in explanations of the Scriptures, from which heresies—also called sects by another name—boil up.

### Sects

In the twelfth place are placed sects, so called either from following (*sectari*) or from division. For if the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God, then sects too, which are now placed among the works of the flesh, are not friendly to Him; all doctrines of falsehood that oppose God are hostile to Him.

### Envy

In the thirteenth place follows envy, which is always tormented by another’s happiness and is divided into a twofold passion: either there is something in oneself that one does not want to exist in another, or, seeing another to be better, one grieves that one is not like him. A certain writer of the modern poets (*Neoterici*), beautifully translating a Greek verse and playing upon envy in elegiac meter, said:

> Nothing is more just than envy, which immediately  
> Gnaws at and tortures its very author’s mind.

### Drunkenness

Drunkenness holds the fourteenth place among the works of the flesh. For the drunkards will not possess the kingdom of God. “Woe,” says the Prophet, “to you who are powerful for drinking wine and mighty for mixing drunkenness”; and the Lord says: “Beware lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and the cares of this life” (Luke XXI).

### Revelries

The fifteenth, which is the last among the works of the flesh, is revelry: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (I Cor. X). In Latin manuscripts, adultery, immodesty, and homicides are reported as written in this catalogue of vices; but it should be understood that no more than fifteen works of the flesh are counted, and we have discussed them.

### “And things similar to these”

It would have been lengthy to explain all the works of the flesh; therefore he summed them all up in a single statement, saying, “and things similar to these.”

### “Which I foretell to you,” etc.

Where had he foretold this earlier? Certainly where he says: “Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, so as to obey its desires” (Rom. VI). Sin possesses all these forms. Therefore, in the soul in which sin has reigned, the kingdom of God cannot reign.

### “For those who do such things”

It must therefore be noted and mourned that he has entirely excluded from the kingdom those who quarrel, dissent, and are angry, together with idolaters, sorcerers, and homicides.

### “For the fruit of the Spirit is love”

What other fruit among the fruits of the Spirit ought to hold the first place except love? Without it the other virtues are not reckoned to be virtues, and from it everything good is born. Indeed, both in the Law and in the Gospel it holds the first place: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. XXII).

### Joy

The second fruit of the Spirit is joy. Even the Stoics, who make finer distinctions among words, judge it to be something different from gladness. They say that joy is an exultation of the soul rejoicing over things worthy of exultant gladness. It should be noted that joy follows love: for whoever loves someone always rejoices in that person’s happiness.

### Peace

The third fruit of the Spirit is peace. From it Solomon too, who came beforehand as a type of Christ, received his name; and concerning the Church the Psalmist sings: “His dwelling has been established in peace” (Ps. LXXV). Among the eight blessings of the Gospel it is written: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. V).

### Long-suffering

The fourth fruit of the Spirit is long-suffering, or patience, since we can interpret *μακροθυμίαν* (*makrothymian*) in either way. Its opposite is faintheartedness. The patient person, however, who endures everything, is a wise man; and when he is greatly increased in this quality (*ἐπίτασις*, *epitasis*), he is called very wise, as it is also written in Proverbs: “The long-suffering man is rich in prudence” (Prov. XIV).

### Goodness

The fifth fruit of the Spirit is goodness. The Stoics define it in this way: “Goodness is a virtue disposed spontaneously toward doing good.” The followers of Zeno likewise define it: “Goodness is a virtue that benefits,” or “a virtue from which usefulness arises.”

### Kindness

The sixth fruit of the Spirit is kindness, or gentleness, since among the Greeks *χρηστότης* (*chrēstotēs*) conveys both meanings. It is a virtue that is mild, pleasant, tranquil, and suited to companionship with every good thing; it invites intimacy with itself, is sweet in speech, and moderate in conduct.

### Meekness

The seventh fruit of the Spirit is meekness. It is opposed to anger, quarrels, and dissensions, and is never provoked by things contrary to it. Through it Moses, the servant of God, deserved to receive the testimony of Scripture, which says: “Moses was meek, more than all human beings upon the earth.”

### Faith

The eighth fruit of the Spirit is faith, which elsewhere is also placed among three things—hope, faith, and love. From faith comes everything that acts, since what we hope will come, though it is not yet present, we possess by faith, hoping to hold what we believe.

### Moderation

The ninth fruit of the Spirit is moderation. It always follows peace, always pursues peace, and, even when injured, never becomes angry.

### Self-control

The tenth fruit of the Spirit is self-control. We must understand this not only with respect to chastity, but also with respect to food and drink, speech, anger, mental agitation, and the desire to disparage others.

### Chastity

The eleventh fruit of the Spirit is chastity. Chastity exists among virgins, among those who practice continence, among widows, and within marriage.

### “Against such things there is no law”

That is, there is no Law against the Spirit. The Law was not established for the righteous, but for the unrighteous and disobedient, the ungodly and sinners. The Law says to me: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not kill; you shall not bear false witness,” and so forth (Exod. XX). If, while love—which is the fruit of the Spirit—reigns in me, I do none of these things, the commandments of the Law are superfluous for me. Therefore, whoever fulfills the fruit of the Spirit spiritually does not remain under the Old Testament.

### “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh,” etc.

If all the vices have been crucified together, and the flesh, as though hanging upon the cross, desires nothing, why do we need the Law, which was given to restrain vices? It should also be noted that he says those belong to Christ who have crucified the flesh with its vices and desires, in opposition to those who think faith alone is sufficient.

## THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER XVII

> “As Jesus entered Jerusalem, he was passing through the middle of Samaria and Galilee. And as he entered a certain village, ten leprous men met him. They stood at a distance and lifted up their voices, saying: ‘Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.’ When he saw them, he said: ‘Go, show yourselves to the priests.’ And it happened that, as they went, they were cleansed. But one of them, when he saw that he had been cleansed, returned, glorifying God with a loud voice, and fell on his face at his feet, giving thanks. And he was a Samaritan. Then Jesus answered and said: ‘Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner?’ And he said to him: ‘Rise, go; your faith has saved you.’”

### “As Jesus entered Jerusalem,” etc.

The lepers can not unreasonably be understood as those who, lacking knowledge of the true faith, bring forth various doctrines of error. They do not conceal their ignorance; rather, they bring it into the light as though it were the highest expertise and display the boastfulness of their speech. Moreover, there is no false doctrine that does not mix in something true. Thus truth mixed disorderly with falsehood, appearing in a single discussion or narrative of a human being like colors in a single body, signifies leprosy—as though human bodies were varied and spotted by true and false colors in different places.

These people must be avoided by the Church so completely that, if possible, they should remain at a great distance and call upon Christ with a loud cry. Hence what follows appropriately:

### “They stood at a distance and lifted up their voices,” etc.

They rightly name Jesus “Master” in order to be saved, because they signify that they had gone astray in his words. They humbly call him their Master, who must save them; and when they return to knowledge of the Master, they immediately return to the pattern of salvation.

### “When he saw them, he said: ‘Go, show yourselves to the priests.’”

The Lord is found to have sent none of those to whom he granted these bodily benefits to the priests except lepers. This was because the Jewish priesthood was a figure of the future royal priesthood, which exists in the Church, where all who belong to the body of Christ, the supreme and true chief priest, are consecrated.

Whoever, whether through heretical perversity, pagan superstition, Jewish unbelief, or even fraternal schism, has been deprived by the Lord’s grace of a condition resembling a variegated color, must come to the Church and display the true color of the faith he has received.

The other vices, however, like illnesses and diseases of the soul and the senses, the Lord heals and corrects inwardly by himself, in the conscience and understanding. Finally, after hearing the Lord’s voice—“Why are you persecuting me? I am Jesus whom you are persecuting” (Acts IX)—Paul was nevertheless sent to Ananias, so that through that priesthood established in the Church he might receive the sacrament of the doctrine of faith and have his true color approved.

### “And it happened that, as they went, they were cleansed.”

They had not yet received the sacraments of baptism, nor had they yet reached the priests spiritually; nevertheless, their cleansing was made evident through the pouring out of the Holy Spirit.

### “But one of them, when he saw that he had been cleansed, returned,” etc.

This one who returned glorifying God signifies the devoted humility of the one Church toward Christ. He rightly falls before the Lord’s feet and gives thanks. The person who truly gives thanks to God is the one who, restraining the thoughts of his own presumption, humbly sees how weak he is in himself; who attributes no virtue to himself; who recognizes that the good things he does come from the mercy of the Creator. He falls on his face because he is ashamed of the evils he remembers having committed.

### “And he was a Samaritan.”

*Samaritan* is interpreted as “guardian.” By this name that people is most suitably signified which, by giving thanks to the one from whom it received, attributes everything it has received to him, as though singing these words from the Psalm: “I will keep my strength toward you, for you, God, are my protector; my God, his mercy will come before me” (Ps. LVIII).

### “Then Jesus answered and said: ‘Were not ten cleansed, and where are the nine?’”

If one is added to nine, a certain image of unity is completed. This produces such a combination that the number cannot proceed farther unless it returns again to one, and this rule is preserved throughout the infinity of number. Thus the nine need the one in order to be joined together in a certain form of unity and become ten. The one, however, does not need them in order to preserve unity.

Therefore, just as the one who gave thanks, approved and praised as a sign of the unique Church, was so honored, so the nine who did not give thanks, having been rejected, were excluded from the fellowship of unity. Consequently, they will remain in the number nine as imperfect; and rightly the Savior inquires where they are, as though he did not know them. For God’s knowing is his choosing, and his not knowing is his rejection.

### “Was no one found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner?”

According to the bodily sense, it is easy to see that a person may not have leprosy and yet may not be good in mind. According to the significance of this miracle, however, it troubles the observer to consider how a person who has been cleansed can be called ungrateful.

Yet it is also easy to see that someone may attain sound and true doctrine within the fellowship of the Church and discuss everything according to the rule of Catholic teaching, distinguishing the creature from the Creator, and thus show himself to have lacked the variegation of falsehoods, as though leprosy, while nevertheless being ungrateful to God and to the Lord who cleansed him.

For, lifted up by pride, he is not brought low by the devout humility of giving thanks, and he becomes like those of whom the Apostle says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Rom. I). In saying that they knew God, he shows that they had indeed been cleansed of leprosy; but he immediately accuses them of ingratitude.

### “And he said to him: ‘Rise, go; your faith has saved you.’”

The person who devoutly fell before God is commanded to rise and go. Whoever, recognizing his weakness with discernment, lies humbly prostrate is commanded, through the consolation of the divine word, to rise for strong works and, as his merits increase day by day, to advance gradually toward greater perfection.

But if faith saved the one whom it inclined to give thanks to his Savior and cleanser, then unbelief destroyed those who neglected to give glory to God for the benefits they had received.

## THE SIXTEENTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

## THE READING FROM THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE TO THE GALATIANS, CHAPTER IV

> “If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit. Let us not become desirous of empty glory, provoking one another, envying one another. Brothers, even if someone is overtaken in some offense, you who are spiritual should instruct such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ. For if anyone thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. Let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone and not in another. For each person will bear his own burden. Let the one who is instructed in the word share with the one who instructs him in all good things. Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap. For the one who sows in his flesh will also reap corruption from the flesh; but the one who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit. Let us not grow weary in doing good. For in due time we shall reap, if we do not grow weary. Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to all, and especially to those who belong to the household of faith.”

### “If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit.”  
*(From Jerome.)*

Let us use this testimony against those who do not wish to understand the Scriptures spiritually. Who is the one who lives by the Spirit except our hidden inner person? He sometimes also lives according to the flesh; but when he has lived by the Spirit, he walks by the Spirit. When he wishes to walk in the flesh, though living, he is dead. The perfect man in Christ always lives by the Spirit.

*(From Primasius.)* If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit—as though he were saying: If we have life through the Spirit, let us conduct ourselves spiritually and not serve the Law carnally.

### “Let us not become desirous of empty glory.”

We rightly call those desirous of glory who desire the glory of God, praise worthy of virtue, and something that displays the divine gaze. On the other hand, whoever performs almsgiving, prolonged prayer, or chastity—whether in marriage, widowhood, or virginity—for the praise of human beings possesses empty glory.

Glory sometimes signifies virtue and sometimes vice. If I seek glory from human beings, it is a vice and is called empty glory. Concerning such glory it is written: “They do everything so that they may be glorified by human beings” (Matt. VI). If I seek glory from God, it is virtue. Concerning such glory the Lord says: “Those who glorify me, I will glorify” (I Kings II).

### “Provoking one another, envying one another.”  
*(From Jerome.)*

We have joined this passage to what comes before. If we live by the Spirit, we obey the Spirit, serving one another not through the Law but through love. We must not quarrel over interpretations of the Scriptures, saying, “Circumcision is better,” or, “No, the foreskin is better.” “History must be rejected, and allegory followed.” Or rather: “Allegory is vain and shadowy, supported by the roots of no truth.” From such disputes, provocations and envies likewise arose at that time between Jews and Gentiles.

### “Brothers, even if someone is overtaken in some offense.”  
*(From Primasius.)*

Human weakness is overtaken in lighter sins, which occur unexpectedly and without forethought. It is not, however, an unexpected seizure when some sin is committed after prolonged and deliberate planning.

### “You who are spiritual should instruct such a person.”  
*(From Jerome.)*

He also urges the spiritual person not to cease extending a hand to one who has fallen. Appropriately, he calls the person overtaken in an offense “overtaken,” showing by the very word the frailty of human condition, so that the person may be worthy of pardon: he erred as a human being. In the end, he was not overtaken by many sins but by some particular fault.

The spiritual preacher should apply a spirit of gentleness and meekness in correcting the sinner. He should not be harsh, angry, or sad in his desire to correct the one who has erred; rather, he should encourage him, promising salvation and offering pardon.

Alternatively, if someone is weak in faith and is still nourished with the milk of infancy, and cannot pass so quickly from legal observance to spiritual sacraments, then you who are stronger in faith and have become spiritual should bear his burden, lest through your knowledge the brother perish for whom Christ died.

### “In a spirit of gentleness”

To the Corinthians also he says: “Shall I come to you with a rod?” (I Cor. IV). Here, however, he says to the spiritual: “Instruct him in a spirit of gentleness.” There he speaks to those who, after sinning, did not recognize their error and refused to submit to their superiors and be corrected through repentance. Here, however, when the sinner recognizes his wound and has handed himself over to the physician to be healed, a rod is not necessary but a spirit of gentleness.

### “Considering yourself, lest you also be tempted.”  
*(From Primasius.)*

It is as though he were saying: You too are human, and you can be tempted in some matter and need assistance; therefore you must sustain the one who is tempted. For those who have been placed under the condition of weakness rightly support the weak.

### “Bear one another’s burdens.”  
*(From Jerome.)*

The person who helps a burdened poor man weighed down by poverty bears his brother’s need. He makes friends for himself from unrighteous wealth, so that he may hear from the Lord: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world; for I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink,” and so forth (Matt. XXV).

### “And so you will fulfill the law of Christ.”  
*(From Primasius.)*

The law of Christ is love. Concerning it the same Lord says: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John XIII). If, therefore, we love God and our neighbor, let us have mercy on the poor, just as the Lord has had mercy on us.

### “For if anyone thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.”  
*(From Jerome.)*

If someone does not wish to bear the burdens of others and, without mercy, is content only with his own work and virtue, not seeking what belongs to others but what belongs to himself—loving only himself and not God—he deceives himself.

The sentence can be distinguished in two ways. Either: “If anyone thinks himself to be something when he is nothing,” or in this way: “If anyone thinks himself to be something,” with “when he is nothing” following. In either case, the meaning is that the person judges himself to be something through his own work and labor, not through clemency toward his neighbor, and is content only with his own virtue. Through this very arrogance he becomes nothing and deceives himself.

### “Let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone and not in another.”

The meaning is this: You who consider yourself spiritual and stronger than another’s weakness must consider not the weakness of the person lying fallen but your own strength. For if someone else cannot pass perfectly from Judaism to Christianity, that does not make you a perfect Christian. But if your own conscience does not reproach you, you have glory in yourself and not in another.

It can also be understood in another way: Whoever has a conscience of good work and, examining himself, does not condemn his work should not glory in it before another, but should have glory in himself and say: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

### “For each person will bear his own burden.”

This seems contrary to what he said above: “Bear one another’s burdens.” But there he commanded us to sustain one another in this life when we sin and to help one another. Here he speaks of the judgment of the resurrection: we will be judged either sinners or saints according to our own work, not on the basis of another’s sin or comparison with someone worse.

### “Let him who is instructed share,” etc.

He commands weaker and carnal disciples that, just as they reap spiritual things from their teachers, so they should provide carnal things to their teachers in all good things—that is, food, clothing, and everything else that human beings count among goods. Hence Job also says: “If we receive good things from the hand of the Lord” (Job II). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you, though evil, know how to give good things to your children” (Matt. VII).

Alternatively, he gives the disciples the command that they should share with those who instruct them in the word, obey them, and make themselves teachable and accommodating in all things that are good and spiritual, not things corrupted by heretical or Jewish perversity. “To be instructed” means to be taught, educated, and corrected.

*(From Primasius.)* It must be asked how the disciple is said to share with the teacher in the word, since the teacher rather instructs the disciple through the word. But he wished “word” to be understood as the fruit of devotion and the generosity of good work. Scripture also commonly uses “word” for “deed,” as in the statement about David: “Because you have done this thing” (II Sam. III). Moses likewise says: “How has this thing become publicly known?”

### “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked.”

That is, the person who wishes to lie to God or to be a transgressor of the commandment deceives himself.

*(From Jerome.)* Foreseeing in the Spirit that those who are instructed and ought to provide the teachers’ expenses might plead poverty and say, “My field has dried up this year through drought; hail has destroyed my vineyard; I have nothing from which to give what is commanded,” he added: “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked.” He knows your hearts; he is not ignorant of your resources. An excuse in words can deceive a human being, but it cannot deceive God.

### “For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap.”  
*(From Primasius.)*

That is, he will receive things of the kind he has done, unless repentance follows sin.

*(From Primasius.)* He urges them to present what has been commanded, calling it seed, so that they may not think lost what they will receive multiplied with interest.

### “For the one who sows in his flesh will also reap corruption from the flesh, but the one who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.”

Everything we say, do, and think is sown in two fields: flesh and Spirit. If the things that come forth from hand, mouth, and heart are good, then, sown in the Spirit, they will overflow with the fruits of eternal life. If they are evil, received from the field of the flesh, they will cause a harvest of corruption to sprout for us.

Alternatively, the person who understands the Law carnally also expects carnal promises, things that are corrupted in the present world. But the person who is a spiritual helper sows in the Spirit and from the Spirit reaps everlasting life.

It should also be observed that the phrase “sows in his flesh” is written with the addition of “his.” But of the person who sows in the Spirit it does not say “in his spirit,” but simply “in the Spirit.” For whoever sows good does not sow something in his own spirit, but in the Spirit of God, from whom he will also reap eternal life.

### “Let us not grow weary in doing good, for in due time we shall reap, if we do not grow weary.”

He exhorts to persevering diligence those who expect the reward of good work in this life, not knowing that, just as in seed there is one time for sowing and another for harvest, so in the present life there is a time for sowing, and in eternity there will be a time for harvesting. No one can harvest that crop if he grows weary; for “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X).

*(From Primasius.)* Now is the time for sowing, not for harvesting. Therefore, let us not seek to receive our reward here, lest the tender plant, cut down by the winter’s frost, be useless and there be nothing to harvest in the future. For it will be said to us: “You have received your good things,” and again: “They have received their reward.”

### “Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to all.”  
*(From Jerome.)*

As we have said, the time of sowing is the present life, in which we are permitted to sow. When it has passed, the time for working is taken away.

*(From Primasius.)* This is the final season for those who sow. Therefore, let us hurry to sow all the fields; above all, let us fill those that are most fertile, lest at harvest time we begin to hunger while others feast.

### “And especially to those who belong to the household of faith.”  
*(From Jerome.)*

Let us imitate our Father, who is the fountain of goodness, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust. Let us do good to everyone, especially to those who belong to the household of faith—that is, to Christians, who have the same Father.

It seems to me that this passage can also be joined to what comes before, so that he calls the teachers the household of faith, to whom above he had commanded their hearers to provide everything considered good—that is, to pagans and Christians, to the good and the evil. Let us show mercy to everyone, lest we deny them what God does not deny. Nevertheless, let us show it especially to those who offer devoted service to the particular worship and religion of the faith.

## THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER VI

> “No one can serve two masters. For either he will hate one and love the other, or he will endure one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and Mammon. Therefore I say to you: Do not be anxious about your life, what you shall eat, nor about your body, what you shall wear. Is not the life more than food, and the body more than clothing? Look at the birds of heaven, for they neither sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth more than they? Which of you, by thinking about it, can add one cubit to his stature? And concerning clothing, why are you anxious? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they do not labor or spin. But I say to you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these. If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, you of little faith! Therefore do not be anxious, saying: ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ For the Gentiles seek all these things. Your Father knows that you need all these things. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.”

### “No one can serve two masters.”  
*(From Augustine.)*

He goes on to show who the two masters are when he says: “You cannot serve God and Mammon.” Among the Hebrews or Syrians, *Mammon* means riches. The Punic name corresponds as well, for in Punic *mammon* means profit.

*(From Jerome.)* Let the greedy person hear this; let the Christian hear it: he cannot serve both riches and Christ. Yet he did not say, “Whoever has riches,” but “whoever serves riches.” The person who is a slave to riches guards riches as a slave. But the person who has shaken off the yoke of slavery distributes them as a master.

### “For either he will hate one and love the other, or he will endure one and despise the other.”

Whoever serves Mammon will endure a harsh and destructive master. Entangled in his own desire, he is subjected to the devil; nevertheless, he endures him, while he despises the other. He did not say, “He hates him,” for scarcely anyone’s conscience can hate God; but he will despise him, that is, he does not fear him.

### “Therefore I say to you: Do not be anxious about your life, what you shall eat, nor about your body, what you shall wear.”

Understand that the one who gave the soul will much more easily give food, and that the one who gave the body will much more easily give clothing.

At this point it is usually asked whether this food pertains to the soul, since the soul is incorporeal while this food is corporeal. But let us understand “soul” as referring to this life, whose support is nourishment. According to this meaning it is said: “Whoever loves his soul will lose it,” and “the Good Shepherd lays down his soul” (John X, 2). If we do not understand it of this life, it will contradict the statement: “What will it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matt. XVI).

### “Is not the life more than food, and the body more than clothing?”  
*(From Jerome.)*

The meaning of what he says is this: the one who has provided greater things will certainly provide lesser things.

“Look at the birds of heaven, for they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and God feeds them” (Matt. VI). This should therefore be understood simply: if the birds are fed by God’s providence without care or hardship—birds that exist today and will not exist tomorrow, whose souls are mortal and which, once they cease to exist, will never exist again—how much more will human beings, to whom eternity is promised, be governed by God’s will?

### “Are you not worth more than they?”  
*(From Augustine.)*

That is, you are dearer and worth more, because you are rational.

### “Which of you, by thinking about it, can add one cubit to his stature? And concerning clothing, why are you anxious?”

That is, the one in whose power and dominion it was made that your body should be brought to this stature can clothe it by his providence.

### “Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they do not labor or spin.”

A lesson concerning clothing had also to be given, just as one was given concerning food. But these examples should not be examined allegorically in such a way that we seek what the bird or the lilies signified. They were set forth so that greater things might be impressed upon us through lesser things.

### “But I say to you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.”  
*(From Fulgentius.)*

“In all his glory” means in all the variety of his clothing and luxuries, or in the greatness of his kingdom; “like one of these” is understood to mean “like one of these lilies.”

*(From Hilary.)* Indeed, neither silk, which is the purple of kings, nor the designs of weavers can be compared with flowers. What is as red as the rose? What is as white as the lily? As for the violet, that its purple is surpassed by no purple dye is more an indication of the eyes than of speech.

### “If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven,” that is, into the fire

Here it is understood that above he spoke of lilies not specifically of one plant but generally of many grasses.

### “How much more will he clothe you, you of little faith!”

The person who is little in faith is the one who is not perfect in love. For love believes all things. Faith begins from a small measure but grows until it reaches what is perfect. Hence the apostles also say to the Lord: “Increase our faith.” Paul calls faith complete when he says: “And if I have all faith,” and so forth (I Cor. XIII).

### “Therefore do not be anxious, saying: ‘What shall we eat?’ or what, etc.”

Labor must be undertaken; anxiety must be removed. The statement “Do not be anxious,” and so forth, should be understood of bodily food and clothing. With regard to spiritual foods and clothing, however, we must always be anxious.

### “But seek first the kingdom of God.”

Here “first” does not refer to order but to quality, as though he were saying: Seek what is most important before all else—above all, the kingdom of God and his righteousness—and it will be given to you. Moreover, that is, apart from the kingdom, whatever else is necessary will be added to you.

## THE SEVENTEENTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

## THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE EPHESIANS, CHAPTER III

> “I ask you not to grow weary in my tribulations for you, which are your glory. For this reason I bend my knees before the Father of my Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, and that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts. Being rooted and grounded in love, may you be able to comprehend, with all the saints, what is the breadth, length, height, and depth; and to know the love of Christ, which surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God. To him who is able to do far more abundantly than we ask or understand, according to the power that works in us, to him be glory in the Church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.”

I beseech you not to lose heart because of my tribulations for you, which are your glory. (From Jerome.) This, then, is what the Apostle asks and earnestly begs from the Lord: that they not lose heart in his afflictions. For he saw that he had preached the Gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, had gone to Rome, and had proceeded—or intended to proceed—to Spain; that the whole world was being taken away from the power of its ruler for his teaching. People were abandoning idols, and the temples were being left desolate, filled with squalor and filth. For this reason the entire army of demons and the whole host of hostile powers, forming a battle line against him, fought so that through tribulations and hardships he might cease preaching the Gospel of Christ and, exhausted, finally rest. This, therefore, is what he says: “I ask that you not lose heart because of my tribulations for you.” For everything that I suffer, everything that troubles and constrains me, is for the sake of your salvation, while I desire to announce the Gospel to you; and my tribulations are your glory. It may also be explained according to what he expressed more fully: “For this reason I ask that you not lose heart because of my tribulations for you, which are your glory.” It can also be understood that he asks on behalf of the Ephesians that they not grow weary and lose heart amid the Apostle’s afflictions. Indeed, what follows agrees more closely with this interpretation.

For this reason I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord. Just as there are outward and inward eyes, so there are knees of the outward and inward person. For when the Apostle says, “At the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Philippians II), this refers not to the knees of the body, but to the submission of the mind, the inclination of the soul, and the obedience of the heart. In explaining these matters specifically, we do not immediately abolish, according to the literal sense, the practice of prayer by which we adore God supplicantly with the knee placed upon the ground. But just as that practice edifies the simple, so we teach that true kneeling takes place in the mind, because many who bend their bodily knees do not bend their souls at all, while others, though praying to God with their bodies upright, have bowed themselves more deeply in spirit.

From whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named. It should not be read as it has been added in the Latin manuscripts, “to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” but simply “to the Father,” so that the name of God the Father may be applied not only to our Lord Jesus Christ but to all rational creatures. Notice that he did not say, “from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth was born or created,” but “from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named.” For it is one thing to deserve the title of fatherhood, and another to share in nature. Thus, just as the one who alone is good makes others good, and the one who alone is true bestows the name of truth, so the Father alone, who is the Creator and the cause and substance of all things, grants to the rest that they may be called fathers. The question is why every fatherhood in heaven is also named from him. Just as we call our patriarchs and prophets fathers, so, I think, the angels and the other powers have leaders of their own kind in heaven, whom they gladly call fathers. For an archangel can be called an archangel only in relation to angels; and dominion, principality, and powers are not so called unless they have lower beings subject to them. It can therefore also be said that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ is Father according to substance, and that the Only-Begotten is not a son by adoption but by nature. The other creatures, too, have earned the name of fatherhood by adoption.

That he may grant you, and so forth. Therefore he says, “I bend my knees to the Father,” so that he may grant you the power of his glory—that is, participation in his majesty—and strengthen and confirm you through the Holy Spirit, because no strength exists apart from the Holy Spirit. Let him strengthen and confirm you in the inner person. For we do not desire the outward but the inward person to be strengthened, so that once Christ has dwelt in the inner person, he may dwell in the principal part of that inner person, namely, in your hearts. All this will take place through faith, if we believe in him. Hence he says, “that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts.” This dwelling, which is built through the beginning of faith, has its roots and foundations in love. This is the life of hearts, in which we live forever and ever, from the beginning of faith until the end of sight.

Rooted, and so forth. This is the communion of a certain divine and heavenly commonwealth. From it the poor are filled—not seeking what belongs to themselves, but what belongs to Jesus Christ. Concerning the bread with which such people are filled, the Apostle says in one place: “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body” (I Corinthians X).

What is the breadth, and so forth. When love is exercised in good works of affection, it can be extended in every direction, as though for the purpose of offering assistance; this is its breadth. Now it endures adversity with perseverance in what it has truly held fast; this is its length. It does all this in order to attain the eternal life promised to it on high; this is its height. From this worship there arises the love in which we are, so to speak, founded and rooted, where the reasons for God’s will are not searched out; this is its depth. Height is, of course, a common term for what is high and what is deep. But when it is said of what is high, the excellence of its elevation is commended; when it is said of what is deep, the difficulty of investigation and understanding is meant. Hence it is also said to God: “How greatly your works have been magnified, O Lord; your thoughts have become exceedingly deep” (Psalm CIII).

To know also the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, and so forth. In this mystery the figure of the cross is displayed. He who died because he willed to do so died in the manner he willed. He therefore did not choose such a kind of death without reason, unless it was so that in it also he might become the teacher of this breadth, length, height, and depth. Its breadth is in the wood fixed transversely above, and this refers to good works, because the hands are extended there. Its length is in what is visible from that wood down to the earth. There one stands, so to speak—that is, one persists and perseveres—and it is also bestowed. Its height is in the part of the wood that remains above the transverse beam, toward the head of the crucified one, because the expectation of those who hope for good things is directed toward what is above. The part of the wood that is not visible, fixed and hidden, from which the whole structure rises, signifies depth: the gratuitousness of grace, in which the understanding of many is worn down as they strive to investigate it, until at last it is said to them: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Romans IX).

Now to him who is able, and so forth. (From Jerome.) Here he shows that he asked according to human weakness for what seemed beneficial to them. But, as regards the truth of the matter itself, he attributes to God a greater power to bestow than is requested.
