He will provide beyond what we ask or understand, according to the power that works in us.

To him be glory in the Church, and so forth. Therefore, to that God be glory, first in the Church above, which has neither spot nor wrinkle and which can consequently receive the glory of God because it is the body of Christ; then in Christ Jesus, because in the body of the assumed man, whose members are all believers, the whole divinity dwells bodily. This glory is not extended merely through the present age and then brought to an end in the ages to come; rather, it remains, grows, and increases through all generations, forever and ever, in ineffable eternity.

## THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER VII

> “Jesus went into a city called Naim, and his disciples and a large crowd went with him. When he drew near the gate of the city, behold, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow, and a large crowd from the city was with her. When Jesus saw her, he was moved with compassion for her and said to her: ‘Do not weep.’ Then he approached and touched the bier. Those who carried it stopped, and he said: ‘Young man, I say to you, arise.’ The dead man sat up and began to speak, and he gave him to his mother. Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying: ‘A great prophet has arisen among us,’ and, ‘God has visited his people.’”

Jesus went into a city called Naim, and his disciples and a large crowd went with him. Naim is a city of Galilee, two miles from Mount Tabor toward the south, near Endor, which is a large village four miles from the same mountain toward the south. For Nain is interpreted as “wave” or “commotion.”

When he drew near the gate of the city. The gate of the city through which the dead man was being carried out, I think, represents one of the bodily senses. For the person who sows discord among brothers and speaks iniquity on high is carried out dead through the gate of the mouth. Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her passes judgment of love through the gate of the eyes. Whoever willingly opens his ear to idle stories, obscene songs, or slanders makes this the gate of death for his soul.

Behold, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother. This dead man, who was carried outside the city gate while many looked on, signifies a person overcome by the deadly funeral of crimes. The same death of the soul is no longer concealed in the bedchamber of the heart, but is exposed to the knowledge of many through indications in his speech or conduct, as though through the gates of his city. He is rightly said to have been the only son of his mother, because, although the virgin mother Church, gathered from many through the washing of baptism, is one, perfect, and undefiled, each individual believer rightly acknowledges himself to be a son of the universal Church. For every chosen person, when instructed in the faith, is a son; when he instructs others, he is a mother. Did he not act with a mother’s affection toward little ones when he said: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you”?

And she was a widow, and a large crowd from the city was with her. Every soul remembers and acknowledges that the Church is a widow, redeemed by the death of her Bridegroom and Lord. By divine providence, a large crowd followed the Lord, and a large crowd followed the widow, so that, having seen so great a miracle, many might become witnesses and many praisers of God.

When Jesus saw her, he was moved with compassion for her and said: “Do not weep.” “Stop,” he says, “weeping as for one dead whom you will soon see rise alive.” The Evangelist beautifully testifies that God was first moved with compassion for the mother and then raised the son, so that in the one he might show us an example of the piety to be imitated, and in the other establish faith in the power to be marveled at.

Then he approached and touched the bier, and those who carried it stopped. The bier on which the dead man is carried out is the heedlessly secure conscience of a despairing sinner. Those who carry him to burial are either unclean desires, which drag a person into destruction, or the poisonous enticements of flattering companions. These, while lifting up sins with their favors, heap them up and bury sinners beneath them with contempt, as beneath a mound of earth. Concerning them it is said elsewhere: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matthew VIII). The dead bury the dead when sinners flatter others like themselves with harmful approval and, by piling up the mass of evil flattery, crush them so that they may never gain any hope of rising again.

When the Lord therefore touched the bier, the bearers of the funeral stopped, because the conscience, touched by fear of the heavenly judgment, restraining both the abundance of carnal pleasures and the crowd of those who praise unjustly, returns to itself and hastens to answer the Savior who calls it to life. Hence it rightly follows:

And he said to the young man: “I say to you, arise.” And the dead man sat up, began to speak, and he gave him to his mother. The dead man sat up when the sinner comes back to life through inward compunction. He begins to speak when, by displaying the signs of restored life, he shows them to all who had mourned his sin. He is returned to his mother when, through the decrees of priestly judgment, he is joined to the communion of the Church.

[Col. 0466A]

Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, and so forth. The more hopeless the death of the soul that is restored to life, the more people are corrected by the same example. Look at the prophet David; look at the Apostle Peter. The higher their standing, the more grievous their fall. The more grievous the fall, the more welcome the mercy of the one who raises them. And the more welcome the Lord’s mercy appeared in them, the more certain the hope of salvation appeared to all penitents, so that all who hear may rightly say:

“God has visited his people.” Not only by once incorporating his Word, but also by continually sending this into our hearts: that we ought to be raised up.

## THE EIGHTEENTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

### THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE EPHESIANS, CHAPTER IV

> “I beseech you, I who am imprisoned in the Lord, to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. One body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling. One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all and through all and in us all. He is blessed forever and ever. Amen.”

Therefore I beseech you, I who am imprisoned in the Lord, to walk worthily, and so forth. (From Jerome.) He could write this while imprisoned in Christ’s bonds and confined in prison for martyrdom. It is better, however, if we understand him to be imprisoned by the love of the Lord. There is also another interpretation, whether it should be accepted being left to the reader’s judgment: that this body may be called the bond of the soul, and that because Paul received a body for the ministry of the Gospel, he was consequently called Christ’s prisoner. He is to be considered walking who enters through him who says, “I am the way,” and does not turn aside either to the right or to the left (Isaiah XXX; Proverbs IV), but turns his foot away from every evil way; and in him is fulfilled: “The steps of a man are directed by the Lord” (Psalm XXXVI).

With all humility and gentleness, with patience. Whoever knows that he is earth and ashes and will shortly dissolve into dust will never be lifted up by pride. Whoever, having contemplated God’s eternity, considers the brief span of human life, almost like a moment, will always have death before his eyes and will be humble and cast down. All humility, moreover, is found not so much in speech as in the mind, so that our conscience knows us to be humble and we never judge ourselves to know, understand, or be anything. Gentleness is likewise that disposition which is disturbed by no passion, and especially is not shattered by anger and fury. Whoever possesses it will attain the blessedness promised by the Lord’s voice.

Bearing with one another in love. This seems to me to signify the same thing as what is written to the Galatians: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians VI). We say that those bear or endure one another’s burdens in love who are rich and relieve the poverty of the poor. Whoever does not have love neither consoles a sinful brother nor a person in need; he despises the Apostle’s admonition: “We who are stronger ought to bear the infirmities of the weak and not to please ourselves” (Romans XV).

Eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. It is rightly said to the Ephesians, who had already attained the unity of the Holy Spirit, that they should be eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. For diligence in preserving is commanded to the one who possesses something, while effort toward acquiring it is commanded to the one who does not possess it.

One body. Either one simply understands this as the one body of Christ, which is the Church, or certainly as that which he deigned to assume from the Virgin, so that they should not think that he became embodied as many times as he appeared in the Old Testament.

[Col. 0467B]

One Spirit. For there is one giver and sanctifier of all; or certainly “one body” refers to life and action, which in Greek are called πρακτικὸς βίος (*praktikos bios*, “the practical life”), while “one Spirit” refers to knowledge and contemplation, which have their proper activity in the heart and are called by them θεωρία (*theoria*, “contemplation”).

Just as you were called in one hope of your calling. When someone is a member of the Church and is not separated from its one Spirit, he will consequently be in the one hope of calling. It may be asked how there can be one hope of calling when there are different dwelling places with the Father. To this we shall answer that the kingdom of heaven is one hope of calling, as it were one good belonging to God the Father, while there are various dwelling places in one house. “One is the glory of the sun, another of the moon, and another of the stars” (I Corinthians XV). Or perhaps something more subtle is indicated: that at the end and consummation of all things everything will be restored to its original state, when we all become one body, are re-formed into a perfect man, and the Savior’s prayer for us is fulfilled: “Father, grant that just as you and I are one, so these also may be one in us” (John XVII).

One Lord and one faith, one baptism, one God and Father, and so forth. There is one Lord and one God, because the lordship of the Father and the Son is one divinity. Therefore faith is also said to be one, because we believe similarly in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Baptism is one as well, for we are baptized in the same manner into the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and we are immersed three times, so that the Trinity may appear as one sacrament. We are not baptized in the names of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, but in one name, which is understood to be God. “One baptism” can also be understood in this way: although we are baptized three times because of the mystery of the Trinity, nevertheless the baptism is considered one. There is also one baptism in water, Spirit, and fire, and the baptism of which the Lord speaks: “I have a baptism with which to be baptized” (Luke XII), and elsewhere: “You shall be baptized with my baptism” (from the Vulgate). Whoever believes rightly in the Father necessarily believes also in the Son and the Holy Spirit; no one offers faith separately to any one person of the Holy Trinity, for one service is rightly owed to the divine unity. The grace of baptism is likewise inseparably bestowed in the one name of the Trinity. Therefore the apostolic mouth proclaims one God, one faith, and one baptism.

Who is above all, and through all, and in us all, who is blessed forever. The differing prepositions in the statement, “One God and Father of all, who is above all and through all and in all,” suggest different interpretations. God the Father is above all, because he is the author of all; the Son is through all, because he passes through and moves throughout all things; the Holy Spirit is in all, because nothing exists without him. Some think that the words “above all and through all and in all” should be referred to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together: the Father is above all because he is the author of all; the Son is through all because all things were created through the Son; and the Holy Spirit is in all, because he is given to believers, we are the temple of the Holy Spirit, and the Father and the Son dwell in us.

## THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER XIV

> “When Jesus entered the house of a certain leader of the Pharisees on the Sabbath to eat bread, they were watching him. And behold, a certain man who had dropsy was before him. Jesus responded and said to the lawyers and Pharisees: ‘Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?’ But they were silent. Then he took him, healed him, and dismissed him. And responding to them he said: ‘Which of you, if his donkey or ox falls into a well, will not immediately pull it out on the Sabbath day?’ And they could not answer him concerning these things.
>
> “He also told a parable to those who had been invited, observing how they chose the places of honor, and he said to them: ‘When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place, lest someone more honored than you has been invited by him; and when the one who invited you and him comes, he says to you, “Give this man your place,” and then you begin with shame to occupy the lowest place. But when you are invited, go and recline in the lowest place, so that when the one who invited you comes, he may say to you, “Friend, move up higher.” Then you will have glory before all those reclining with you. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.’”

When Jesus entered the house of a certain leader of the Pharisees on the Sabbath to eat bread, and they were watching him, behold, a certain man who had dropsy was before him. (From Bede.) The disease of dropsy takes its name from watery fluid. For in Greek, ὕδωρ (*hydōr*) means “water.” It is a subcutaneous fluid arising from a disorder of the bladder, accompanied by swelling from inflation and foul breath. It is characteristic of a person with dropsy that the more abundant the disordered fluid becomes, the more intensely he thirsts. Thus he is compared with one whom an overflowing stream of carnal pleasures burdens. He is compared with the avaricious rich man, who, the more abundant his wealth is—wealth he does not use well—the more ardently desires such things.

And Jesus responded and said to the lawyers and Pharisees, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?” But they were silent. The statement that Jesus “responded” refers to what had been said previously: “They were watching him.” The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, but they rightly remain silent when questioned, because they see that whatever they say will be turned against them. If it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath, why are they watching to see whether the Savior will heal? If it is not lawful, why do they themselves heal animals on the Sabbath?

Then he took him, healed him, and dismissed him. By a providential arrangement, the Lord heals the man with dropsy before the lawyers and Pharisees and immediately afterward argues against avarice, so that through this bodily illness the illness of the heart might be more clearly expressed. Indeed, after many of his arguments of exhortation, it is added: “The Pharisees, who were avaricious, heard all these things and mocked him.” A person with dropsy thirsts more the more he drinks, and every avaricious person multiplies his thirst: once he has obtained what he desires, he pants even more eagerly for other things to desire.

And responding to them he said: “Which of you, if his donkey or ox falls into a well, will not immediately pull it out on the Sabbath day?” Thus he convicts the Pharisees who were watching him, so that he may condemn them for avarice. “If you,” he says, “hurry on the Sabbath to rescue a donkey or ox, or any other animal that has fallen into a well—not caring for the animal but for your own avarice—how much more ought I to free a human being, who is far better than an animal?” He appropriately compared the man with dropsy to an animal that had fallen into a well, for he was suffering from fluid, just as that woman whom they said had been bound for eighteen years and whom he freed from the same bondage. He compared him to an animal that is untied in order to be led to water. He rightly placed both an ox and a donkey in the two passages, whether we understand these to signify the wise and the foolish alike, or, as was said above, the two peoples: the one whose neck the yoke of the law had worn down, and the one whom any deceiver found, like a brute animal that offered no resistance, and dragged away into whatever error he wished. When the Savior came, he found them all bound by Satan’s chains and all plunged into the deepest well of desire. “For there is no distinction: all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Romans III).

He also told a parable to those who had been invited, observing how they chose the places of honor, and said to them: “When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place.” This admonition of the Savior is clear according to the literal sense: it teaches that humility is praiseworthy not only before God but also before human beings. But since the Evangelist does not call this a parable without reason, we should briefly consider what it signifies mystically as well. That the union of Christ and the Church is called a wedding is evident in many passages, one of which is: “Can the children of the wedding fast while the bridegroom is with them?” (Matthew IX). Another is: “The kingdom of heaven has become like a king who made a wedding for his son and sent his servants to call those invited to the wedding.” Whoever attends this wedding after being invited—that is, whoever is joined to the members of the Church through the grace of faith—should not recline in the first place. That is, he should not exalt himself by boasting of his merits as though he were higher than the rest. Rather, according to the parable in another passage, he should strive to appear clothed in a wedding garment, that is, radiant with the splendor of virtues, but should adorn the very display of those virtues with the place of devoted humility.

Lest someone more honored than you has been invited by him, and the one who invited you and him comes and says to you, “Give this man your place,” and then you begin with shame to occupy the lowest place. The one who gives place to a more honored guest is the person who, made too confident and secure by reliance on the distance he has traveled in his way of life, finds himself surpassed by the vigorous life of those who have followed in Christ. He occupies the lowest place with shame when, recognizing better qualities in others, he humbles whatever seemed lofty to him in his own conduct, saying with the Prophet: “I am needy and in labors from my youth; having been exalted, I was humbled and confounded” (Psalm LXXXVII).

But when you are invited, go and recline in the lowest place. “The greater you are,” he says, “humble yourself in all things.” And the Psalmist boasts: “I have been humbled exceedingly, Lord; revive me according to your word” (Psalm CXVIII), clearly signifying that he could be revived by the Lord if he himself held a humble opinion of his virtues.

So that when the one who invited you comes, he may say to you: “Friend, move up higher.” When the Lord comes and finds someone humble, he will bless him with the name “friend” and command him to move up higher. “Whoever humbles himself like this little child is greater in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XVIII).

Then you will have glory before all those reclining with you. It is beautifully said, “Then you will have glory,” so that you do not begin seeking now what is reserved for you at the end. For, as Solomon says: “The inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end” (Proverbs XX). This may also be understood of the present life: the person who is found reclining in the lowest place is exalted when the Lord comes. For the Lord enters his wedding every day; every day he judges the conduct, places, and appearance of those reclining at the feast. Looking down upon the proud, he often grants such great gifts of the Spirit to the humble that, deservedly, the assembly of those reclining together—that is, of those resting in faith—glorifies them with unanimous admiration and, leaping forth in wonder to praise its Creator, says: “Your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honored by me; their dominion has been exceedingly strengthened” (Psalm CXXXVIII).

For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. With this conclusion he clearly teaches that the preceding saying of the Lord is to be understood typologically. For it is not immediately true that everyone who exalts himself before human beings will be humbled, or that whoever humbles himself in the sight of human beings will be exalted by them. On the contrary, sometimes a person who raises himself either to the pinnacle of dignity or to any other glory he seeks does not cease to be exalted until the end. Likewise, any humble and modest person may remain until the end of life in the modest position with which he is content. Therefore, because according to the judgment of truth everyone who carelessly elevates himself on account of his merits will be humbled by the Lord, while whoever prudently humbles himself because of his good deeds will be exalted by him, the preceding saying of the Redeemer—which forbids seeking the places of honor at weddings—plainly agrees with this same meaning.

## THE NINETEENTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

### THE FIRST EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER I

> “I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace that was given to you in Christ Jesus, because in everything you have been enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you, so that you lack nothing in any grace, as you await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ. He will also confirm you to the end, blameless on the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

[Col. 0471B]

I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God that was given to you in Christ Jesus. I give thanks because you possess knowledge, the mother of virtues. But I want you to know that true knowledge is that which agrees in the unity of souls. As is customary, he first attracts them with gentle speech and wins their attention with flattering praise.

Because in everything you have been enriched in him. By saying this, the Apostle shows that when they came to the faith of Christ, they were then enriched with every grace—that is, with all virtues and with the wisdom that establishes prophets and friends of God.

In every word and in all knowledge. That is, with the learning of both the Old and the New Testament. By saying, “You have been enriched,” and adding, “In every word and in all knowledge,” he clearly shows in what they were rich.

[Col. 0471C]

Just as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you. That is, the mystery of both volumes of Scripture, which either prophesied Christ’s coming or revealed it. Concerning this he says: “Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old” (Matthew XII). These confirm the hearts of believers.

So that you lack nothing in any grace. As Solomon says: “All good things came to me together with her” (Proverbs, final chapter), that is, together with wisdom.

As you await the revelation, and so forth. He said “revelation” because our life is now hidden with Christ; then it will be revealed bodily in the age to come.

He will also confirm you, and so forth. As the Prophet says: “Confirm me in your words.” And also: “Confirm, O God, what you have worked in us.”

## THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER XXII

> “The Sadducees approached Jesus, and one of them, a lawyer, questioned him, testing him: ‘Teacher, which is the great commandment in the law?’ Jesus said to him: ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the first and greatest commandment. The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend the whole law and the Prophets.’
>
> “When the Pharisees had assembled, Jesus questioned them, saying: ‘What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?’ They said to him, ‘David.’ He said to them: ‘How then does David in the Spirit call him Lord, saying: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies beneath your feet”? If David calls him Lord, how is he his son?’ And no one could answer him a word, nor did anyone dare from that day onward to question him any further.”

The Sadducees approached Jesus, and one of them, a lawyer, questioned him, testing him: “Teacher, which is the great commandment in the law?” and so forth. (From Bede.) Understand “first of all” as referring not to order but to dignity—that is, “greatest of all” or “first.” Above all, each of us must establish it deep within the heart as the single foundation of devotion. Therefore the first and greatest commandment is knowledge and confession of the divine unity, together with the performance of good works. Good works are accomplished through love of God and neighbor. The Apostle briefly commends this in other words when he says: “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision has any power, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love.” This response shows that a serious question was often debated among the scribes and Pharisees: which commandment was first or greatest in the divine law. Some praised sacrifices and offerings, while others, with greater authority, preferred the works of faith and love, since many of the fathers before the law had pleased God solely through faith working through love, without any practice of victims and sacrifices, and had held the highest place with him. No one, however, was ever found to have pleased God by holocausts and sacrifices alone, without faith and love. The scribe declared that he too held this opinion.

Jesus said to him: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the greatest,” and so forth. (From Augustine.) Love, by which we love God and our neighbor, securely possesses the whole magnitude and breadth of the divine utterances. For the one heavenly Teacher teaches us and says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,” and so forth. If, therefore, you do not have time to examine all the holy Scriptures, to penetrate all the coverings of their words—for whatever is rolled up is examined—and to enter all the secrets of the Scriptures, hold fast to love, on which everything depends. In doing so, you will hold fast to what you have learned there, and you will also hold fast to what you have not yet learned. For if you know love, you know something from which even that which you perhaps do not know depends; and in whatever you understand from the Scriptures, love is evident. Therefore, the person who holds love in his conduct holds both what is open and what is hidden in the divine words. This is what is meant by: “The Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth.”

Having assembled the Pharisees, Jesus questioned them, saying: “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?” (From Jerome.) Those who had assembled to tempt Jesus and were trying to ensnare the truth by a deceitful question provided the occasion for their own refutation. They are asked about the Christ: whose son is he? Jesus’ question benefits us even today in disputing with the Jews. For those who confess that Christ will come as an ordinary and holy man rightly assert that he is of David’s lineage. Let us therefore, taught by the Lord, ask them: if he is merely a man and only David’s son, how does David call him his Lord? Not through an uncertain error or by his own will, but in the Holy Spirit.

They say to him, “David.” He says to them, “How then…” and so forth. (From Bede.) They are not reproved because they say that he is David’s son, but because they do not believe that he is the Son of God. For he is both David’s Lord, remaining God before the ages, and he appeared as David’s son, being born as a man at the end of time. The subjection of the enemies by the Father to the Son signifies not the Son’s weakness, but unity of nature, since one acts through the other. For the Son also subjects the enemies to the Father, because he glorifies the Father upon the earth. “Sit at my right hand,” and so forth.

(From Fulgentius.) Here “sitting” signifies stability. Appropriately, after the labor of his Passion, the Son is told: “Sit,” that is, “as victor in glory.” “At my right hand” signifies not a place but equality with the Father. “Until” signifies the infinite “forever,” as in: “Until you grow old, I am he,” as though he said: “Sit always, because your enemies will always be placed beneath your feet.” The feet of the Lord are understood either as his Incarnation or as the apostles themselves.

And no one was able to answer him a word, nor did anyone dare from that day onward, and so forth. The Pharisees and Sadducees, seeking an opportunity for slander and to find some word that might lie open to ambush, had been refuted in their arguments. They questioned him no further, but handed him over, now openly apprehended, to the Roman authority. From this we understand that the poisons of envy can indeed be overcome, but that they are slow to come to rest.

Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples, saying, and so forth. What is more gentle, what is kinder, than the Lord? He is tempted by the Pharisees, their snares are shattered, and, according to the Psalmist, “The arrows of infants became their wounds” (Psalm 63). Nevertheless, because of the dignity of the priesthood and of their name, he urges the people to submit to them, considering not their works but their teaching. When he says, “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon Moses’ seat,” he indicates by “seat” the teaching of the Law. Thus we must also understand what is said in the Psalm: “He did not sit in the seat of pestilence.” And when he overturns the seats of those selling doves, we must understand this as referring to doctrine.

(From Augustine.) That seat, therefore, was not theirs but Moses’, compelling them to speak good things even while they did not do good things. Thus they carried out their own practices in their own lives. But their seat did not permit them to teach their own things as though they were another’s. Many therefore benefit others by saying what they do not do, but far more would benefit them by doing what they say.

But they bind heavy and unbearable burdens and place them upon people’s shoulders, while they themselves are unwilling to move them with a finger. (From Jerome.) This is directed generally against all teachers who command great things but do not do even lesser ones. It should be noted, however, that the shoulders, the finger, the burdens, and the bonds by which they are tied are to be understood spiritually.

But they do all their works in order to be seen by people. Therefore, whoever does anything in order to be seen by people is a scribe and a Pharisee.

For they enlarge their phylacteries. When the Lord had given the commandments of the Law through Moses, he added at the end: “You shall bind them upon your hand, and they shall be immovable before your eyes” (Deuteronomy 6). The meaning is: “Let my commandments be upon your hand, so that they may be fulfilled in action; let them be before your eyes, so that you may meditate upon them day and night.” The Pharisees, interpreting this badly, wrote the Decalogue of Moses—that is, the ten words of the Law—on little pieces of parchment, folded them, and tied them to the forehead, making them like a crown for the head, so that the text might continually move before their eyes. To this day the Indians, Persians, and Babylonians do this, and whoever possesses such an object is judged among the peoples to be religious. They called these little strips themselves *pistariola*, “phylacteries,” because whoever had them was thought to possess them for his protection and defense. The Pharisees did not understand that these things were to be carried in the heart, not on the body; otherwise, chests and coffers have books but do not possess knowledge of God.

They enlarge their tassels. Moses had also commanded that they make hyacinth-colored tassels at the four corners of their cloaks, so that the people of Israel might be distinguished. Just as circumcision in the body marked some difference belonging to the Jewish people, superstitious teachers, courting popular favor and seeking profits from women, made the tassels large and tied very sharp thorns into them, so that while walking or sitting they would sometimes be pricked and, as though recalled by this admonition, be drawn back to the service of God and the duties of his worship.

(From Origen.) Such was the small and short tassel prescribed by the Law, which the woman suffering from a flow of blood touched on the Lord’s cloak. But she was not pricked by the Pharisees’ superstitious thorns; rather, she was healed by touching him.

They also love the first couches at banquets, the first seats in the synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called by people “Rabbi.” But you must not be called “Rabbi,” for one is your teacher, and you are all brothers. The Lord reproves them in the remaining matters: namely, why they seek the first couches at banquets and the first seats in the synagogues, pursue their appetites and glory in public, and are called by people “Rabbi,” which in Latin means “teacher.”

(From Augustine.) Are the Scriptures of God therefore to be thought contradictory to themselves? And for that reason is what is written, “Honor your father and your mother” (Exodus 20), to be neglected? Although we may understand “father” as God himself and “mother” as the Church, nevertheless the order of all things must be preserved. The Lord does not abolish the honor due to parents when he says, “Do not call anyone your father on earth.” Rather, those whom he was raising to the hope of eternal life, whom he was saving, he taught concerning these temporal and transitory relationships that they should extend themselves toward him as Father—toward the one whom they were to succeed not as dead persons, but with whom they were always to live. Therefore we have fathers, and we are fathers, in many ways; but in one unique and eternal way, God alone is Father.

And do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven. Nor be called teachers, for one is your teacher, Christ, and the one who is greater among you shall be your servant. (From Jerome.) No one is to be called teacher or father except God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. He is Father because all things are from him; he is Teacher because all things are through him, or because through the dispensation of the flesh we have all been reconciled to God. When we call a man “father,” we pay honor to his age; we do not present him as the author of our life. He is also called “teacher” by participation in the true teaching. And, not to repeat endlessly: just as the one God by nature and the one Son do not prevent others from being called gods and sons by adoption, so the one Father and Teacher do not prevent others from being called fathers and teachers in an extended sense.

Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. Seek the exposition of this saying above, in the eighteenth week after Pentecost.

## On the Nativity of Saint Michael the Archangel

### Epistle from the Apocalypse of John, chapter 1

“God signified what must soon take place, and he signified it by speaking through his angel to his servant John, who bore witness to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, to everything that he saw. Blessed is the one who reads and hears the words of this prophecy and keeps what is written in it, for the time is near. John to the seven churches that are in Asia: Grace to you and peace from him who is, and who was, and who is to come, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne, and from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth. He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood, and made us a kingdom and priests for his God and Father. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.”

In those days God signified what must soon take place. (From Bede.) This is what “he signified” means: he wove the same Apocalypse together with mystical expressions, lest it become commonplace by being clear to everyone. “Soon,” that is, the things that are to come upon the Church in the present age.

Speaking through his angel. The Lord the Father spoke through his Son, because Christ is called the Angel of Great Counsel. Or the angel appeared to John in the form of Christ, as will become clearer in what follows.

(From Primasius.) “What must soon take place”: everything that occurs in time has a beginning, a course, and an end. After the beginning of the Church, which had already been founded through the preaching of the apostles, it was necessary to reveal how it would be spread more widely and by what end it would be contained, so that the preachers of this truth, relying upon the confidence born of this knowledge, might undertake it without hesitation: the few against the many, the unarmed against the armed, the humble against the proud, the weak against the noble, the living against those who were spiritually dead. When he says “he signified,” he also reveals something of future events and mysteries. He did not wish us to remain satisfied with the surface of the letter; by the word “signification” he made us attentive to searching more deeply into the mysteries. Rightly, indeed, he added that these things had been shown to the disciple by Christ through his angel; for it is clear that Christ, God and the only Son, has always appeared to mortals through an assumed creature, not through the essence of his divinity, both before the Incarnation and after the Ascension. Therefore the one who knew him as Teacher bore witness, in the assumed humanity, to the invisible Word; and lest anyone think that only “Word” was intended, he again added the name “Jesus Christ,” which he knows belongs to the form of the man who was assumed.

To his servant John. When he says this to the whole Church, he wished to reveal in one person the Church that he founded in unity. Therefore he says that he made it known to his servants—not merely to one among many, but rather through one person to all. Just as Peter alone received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, yet the whole Church, raised up, was deemed worthy to use that authority.

Blessed is the one who reads and those who hear the words of this prophecy. By saying “the one who reads” and “those who hear,” he indicated the persons of teachers and learners: by the zeal of reading he removed laziness, and upon those who kept the words he bestowed blessedness.

And keep what is written in it. Since it belongs to both groups to keep them, it is appropriate for both. For it is not the hearers of the Law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the Law will be justified (Romans 2).

For the time is near. That is, so that each of the things that must be said may be fulfilled.

John to the seven churches that are in Asia. This means: to the one sevenfold Church. The number seven often represents unity, because the whole is formed from the first odd and the first even number—that is, from three and four—as from unlike elements. The distinction between soul and body also embraces the unity of this number: three pertain to the soul and four to the body. For it is said that God must be loved with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind. The body, meanwhile, has four qualities: hot and cold, dry and moist. Therefore it is also sung: “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Psalm 118).

Grace to you and peace from him who is, and who was, and who is to come. Although, according to the Apostle, “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5), or, as he himself testifies, “He who sent me is with me,” because of the unity of one and the same nature, this passage must nevertheless be referred properly to the person of the Son. He “is,” because he remains the same; he “was,” because with the Father he created all things; he “is to come,” because he will come to judge.

And from the seven spirits who are before his throne. Because of the sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit, he is called the sevenfold Spirit: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, counsel and fortitude, knowledge and piety, and the fear of God. The gifts of the one Spirit are always lawfully commended when peace and grace are wished upon the devout from the seven spirits.

And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness. In the humanity he assumed, he bore witness to the Father when he preached, saying, “I have made your name known to them, and I will make it known” (John 17). Showing what had long been denied to the Jews, he says: “I did not declare your name, Adonai, to them” (Exodus 3). Believe in the Son, and knowledge of the Father is likewise revealed. For he would not be called Son unless he had a Father, nor Father unless he had a Son. Each, therefore, is known through the proclamation of the other, because the Father is truly recognized in the Son and the Son in the Father. Or he is called “witness” because by his death he testified to the New Testament. For a testament is not confirmed until after the death of the man.

The firstborn from the dead. Because he was the first to rise from the dead, and he first demonstrated in himself what he had testified concerning the resurrection of the dead.

And ruler of the kings of the earth. That is, of the apostles and of all the saints.

He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood. Having also suffered, he freed us from sin by his own blood. Rising again, he is rightly proclaimed the firstborn from the dead.

### The Gospel of Matthew, chapter 18

“His disciples came to Jesus, saying: ‘Who, do you suppose, is greater in the kingdom of heaven?’ And Jesus, calling a little child, placed him in their midst and said: ‘Amen, I say to you, unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. And whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me. But whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it is better for him that an ass’s millstone be hung around his neck and he be sunk into the depth of the sea. Woe to the world because of stumbling blocks. For it is necessary that stumbling blocks come; nevertheless, woe to the person through whom the stumbling block comes. But if your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter life maimed or lame than, having two hands or two feet, to be cast into the eternal fire. And if your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than, having two eyes, to be cast into the hell of fire. See that you do not despise one of these little ones. For I say to you: their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.’”

His disciples came to Jesus, saying: “Who, do you suppose, is greater in the kingdom of heaven?” (From Jerome.) It was written above that the Lord said to Peter: “Go to the sea and cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up; when you open its mouth, you will find a stater. Take it and give it to them for me and for you.” From this occasion they supposed that the apostle Peter had been placed above all the others, since in the payment of the tribute he had been associated with the Lord. Therefore they ask: “Who is greater in the kingdom of heaven?” Jesus, seeing their thoughts and understanding the causes of their error, wishes to heal their desire for glory through a contest in humility.

And Jesus, calling a little child, placed him in their midst and said: Either he simply called any little child, in order to point to childhood and demonstrate its innocence; or he certainly placed himself, as a little child, in their midst—he who had come not to be served but to serve—in order to give them an example of humility. Others interpret the little child as the Holy Spirit, whom he placed in the hearts of the disciples so that he might change pride into humility.

Amen, I say to you: unless you turn and become like little children… You are not commanded to have the age of little children, but their innocence. What they possess through their years, you must possess through deliberate effort, so that you may be little children in malice, not in wisdom.

Therefore, whoever humbles himself like this little child is greater, and so forth. Like this child, whose example I give you: he does not persist in anger, he does not remember an injury, he is not delighted when he sees a beautiful woman, he does not think one thing and say another. So too, unless you possess such innocence and purity of spirit, you cannot enter the kingdom of heaven. Or otherwise: whoever humbles himself like this little child is greater in the kingdom of heaven. Whoever imitates me and humbles himself as my example, lowering himself as much as I lowered myself by taking the form of a servant, will enter the kingdom of heaven.

And whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me. Whoever is such as to imitate Christ’s humility and innocence receives Christ in himself. He wisely moderates his answer: lest the apostles, when honor was offered to them, think that they were honored on their own account, he added that they were to be received not for their own merit but in honor of their Teacher.

But whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble. Notice that the one who is scandalized is a little one, for the greater do not receive stumbling blocks.

(From Bede.) It should rightly be noted that in our good works we must sometimes beware of causing our neighbor to stumble, but at other times disregard it as nothing. As far as we can do so without sin, we must avoid causing our neighbors to stumble. But if offense is taken at the truth, it is better to allow offense to arise than to abandon the truth.

It is better for him that he be hung, and so forth. He speaks according to the custom of the province, by which among the ancient Jews this was the punishment for greater crimes: they would sink a person into the depths after fastening a stone to him. It is better for him because it is far better to receive a brief punishment for guilt than to serve eternal torments. For the Lord will not judge twice for the same thing.

(From Gregory.) Likewise, the ass’s millstone expresses the circuit and labor of secular life, while the depth of the sea signifies ultimate damnation. Therefore, whoever has been led into the appearance of holiness but destroys others either by word or by example would plainly have been better off if earthly actions had bound him to death under an outward form, rather than sacred offices presenting him to others as an example in guilt. For if he alone fell, the punishment of hell would in some way have tortured him more tolerably.

Woe to the world because of stumbling blocks; for it is necessary that stumbling blocks come, and so forth. (From Jerome.) This does not mean that stumbling blocks must come in such a way that those who cause them would be without guilt. Rather, since it is necessary that stumbling blocks arise in this world, each person is exposed to them through his own fault. At the same time, Judas, who had prepared his mind for betrayal, is struck by the general sentence.

But if your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter life maimed or lame than, having two hands or two feet, to be cast into the eternal fire, and so forth. (From Bede.) Since above he taught us not to cause those who believe in him to stumble, he now consequently admonishes us how greatly we must beware of those who strive to cause us to stumble—that is, to drive us toward the ruin of sin by their word or example. He calls our hand a necessary friend, whose work and help we need daily. But if such a person wishes to harm us in the matter of the soul, he must be excluded from our society, lest, if we wish to share in this life with one who is lost, we perish with him in the future. In the foot, as in the hand, he teaches that dear but incorrigible persons must be separated from us, lest through the uncleanness of those whom we cannot correct, we ourselves become polluted and perish. Such persons may be called “hands” because of their necessary work for us, being suited to our needs in their service and activity. In the eye also, which is to be torn out because of stumbling, the same persons are indicated: carnally our friends, but spiritually our adversaries. We need their counsel and foresight, but they seek to deceive us with wicked advice and turn us aside onto the path of error.

*Skándalon* (σκάνδαλον) is a Greek word, which we may render in Latin as “stumbling block,” “ruin,” or “a striking of the foot.” Some translate *skándalon* in Greek as *scrupulus* in Latin. Therefore, whoever causes his brother to stumble gives him, by word or deed, an occasion of falling that is not right.

(From Jerome.) It may also be understood simply in this way: if someone seems so necessary to us that he is like a hand, foot, or eye—useful, diligent, and sharp in perception—but causes us to stumble and, through a discordance of character, drags us into hell, we must not, for the sake of his temporal advantages, use or cherish him at the risk of our souls.

See that you do not despise one of these little ones. As far as it lies within you, do not despise them; rather, for the sake of your own salvation, seek their healing also.

For I say to you: their angels in heaven, and so forth. Great is the dignity of souls, since each one has, from the beginning of its birth, an angel appointed for its protection. Hence we read in the Apocalypse of John: “To the angel of Ephesus, of Thyatira, and to the angel of Philadelphia” (Revelation 1, 2, 3), and “write to the angels of the four remaining churches.” The Apostle also commanded that women’s heads be veiled in the churches because of the angels.

## The Twentieth Week after Pentecost

### Epistle of Blessed Paul the Apostle to the Ephesians, chapter 4

“Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who has been created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth. Therefore, laying aside falsehood, speak truth, each one with his neighbor, because we are members of one another. Be angry and do not sin. Do not let the sun go down upon your anger. Do not give place to the devil. Let the one who stole steal no longer; rather, let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something from which to give to the one who suffers need.”

Be renewed in the spirit of your mind. (From Jerome.) We are not renewed in understanding without the spirit, nor in the spirit without understanding. Rather, we are renewed together in the spirit of our understanding. Just as we sing with the spirit and also sing with understanding, and pray with the spirit and also pray with understanding, so may the spirit of our understanding be renewed. When our understanding has become pure and cleansed, free from every stain of filthy mixture, then the spirit is joined to it, and the two are bound together by a kind of bond of unity, so that it is no longer called simply “spirit,” but “the spirit of understanding.”

And put on the new man. I think this is the same as what is said elsewhere: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ.” For he is the new man, with whom all believers must clothe and cover themselves. What in the man assumed by our Savior was not new—the conception, birth, delivery, infancy, teaching, life, power, and finally the cross and Passion, in which he stripped the principalities and powers and exposed them to public display, as well as the resurrection and ascension into heaven? Whoever, therefore, can imitate his conduct and express all his virtues in himself—being gentle as he was gentle, humble of heart, and laying down his life for his friends as he laid it down for his sheep; when beaten, not answering back; when cursed, not returning a curse, but overcoming pride through humility—this person has put on the new man and can say with the Apostle: “I live, now not I, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2).

Who was created according to God. It must therefore be considered that “creation” and “formation” are mentioned only with reference to great works. For example, the world was created and a city was founded. From this we should observe that this new man, who was created according to God in Christ, is a great work of God and stands above the other creatures, since he is said to have been formed as the world was formed, the beginning of the ways of God and the first creation of all the elements.

In righteousness and holiness, and so forth. Jesus, therefore, was truly created in righteousness and the holiness of truth, because he is the true God and Son of the true God, and in him the whole religion and righteousness of God were completed in truth.

[Col. 0481A]

Therefore, laying aside all falsehood, speak truth, and so forth. The Apostle did not command simply, as some think, nor merely in a moral sense, that after abandoning falsehood we should speak truth with our neighbors. Otherwise, if we speak truth only with our neighbors, then concerning anyone who is not a neighbor they say that falsehood may be spoken. The same would also follow from the commandment in the Law: “You shall not commit adultery with your neighbor’s wife” (Exodus 20). If “neighbor” means only a relative or friend, it would rightly promise adultery with strangers. But he calls every human being a neighbor, since everyone has been born from the same parent as we have.

Because we are members of one another. When he says, “We are members of one another,” he seems to me to signify a deeper mystery and to speak of those who are our neighbors in faith and virtue. For believers are members of believers, and Christians of Christians; no others are truly members of one another. Therefore he commands that each person speak with his neighbor whatever is mystical and secret, whatever is full of God’s truth. He must not give what is holy to dogs or cast his pearls before swine, but whoever possesses the oil of truth should lead them into the bridegroom’s chamber, the king’s storeroom and inner treasury.

Be angry and do not sin. The term “anger” has a twofold meaning, not only among us but also among philosophers: either when, provoked by an injury, we are stirred by natural impulses; or when, after the impulse has subsided and the fury has been extinguished, the mind can exercise judgment and nevertheless desires vengeance against the one thought to have caused the injury. I therefore think that the first kind of anger is intended here, and that it is permitted to us as human beings to be moved at the sight of something unworthy, so that the tranquility of the mind may be disturbed like a gentle breeze, but that we must not swell up and be lifted by the force of a whirlpool of fury.

Do not let the sun go down upon your anger. If we understand this simply of the sun that is seen by the eyes of the flesh, we commit sin whenever we become angry and our anger persists after the sun has set. But we do not sin whenever, for example, becoming angry from the first hour until the eleventh, we do whatever indignation, fury, and anger have suggested. By this interpretation nothing seems more absurd to me, as though someone could rage from sunrise to sunset in crimes so great that in his entire life he could not expiate them with tears. Or would anger not rather have its place during the day, since night naturally gives rest from fury, and when sleep follows, even if we are angry, we postpone our anger until the day?

Because the true sun also sets upon wicked prophets, according to what is written: “The sun set upon your prophets at midday” (Amos 8), and likewise sets upon all sinners, granting them none of the light of its rising, the Apostle now commands us not to do such things, overcome by fury, that the sun may set upon us and the ruling power of the heart be wrapped in darkness. Some think this should be understood simply in the same way as the passage in the fourth Psalm, from which this appears to have been taken: “What you say in your hearts, and in your chambers be pricked” (Psalm 4). That is: whatever you sin in the day, whether in deed, word, or thought, cleanse it through repentance during the night that follows; let anger be brief and not be postponed until the following day.

Do not give place to the devil. “Devil” is a Greek word, *diabolos* (διάβολος), which in Latin is called “accuser.” In the Hebrew language he is called *Satan*, meaning “adversary” or “opponent.” The Apostle calls him *Belial*, that is, “without a yoke,” because he cast from his neck the service of God; Aquila translated this as “apostate.” Therefore, he says, do not give place to the devil, whether by becoming angry or by sinning in any other way. Sin is the devil’s place. For the devil, like a roaring lion, seeks an entrance through which he may break in, and when we have given him a place, he enters. Before he comes, however, he usually sends certain arrows ahead and makes a thought the forerunner of his arrival. If we nourish this thought after receiving it in our heart, he himself will dare to enter.

Let the one who stole steal no longer. Since those who live amid the business of this life are compelled, for the sake of food and necessary uses, either to buy or sell certain things and to seek profits through trade, he now warns the Ephesians not to incur the crime of theft under the pretext of gain. He calls everything acquired to another’s loss “theft.” It may also be understood in a higher sense: “Let the one who stole steal no longer,” in reference to what is written concerning false prophets: “Everyone steals words from his neighbor” (Jeremiah 23), and: “All who came before me were thieves and robbers” (John 10). He forbids these people to commit spiritual thefts.

Rather, let him labor, and so forth. He does not say, “Rather, let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may not be in need, have food, and trouble no one.” Instead he says, “Let him labor with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something from which to support and share with those in need.” Therefore, whoever labors only so that he himself may not be in need and withdraws his hand from others, even if he applauds himself, has not fulfilled the Apostle’s command. The person who does good is the one who turns away from evil and does good, and who works in the field of his soul so that he may be filled with spiritual bread and be able to provide for the hungry and for the one suffering need, giving food to his fellow servants at the proper time.

### The Gospel of Matthew, chapter 9

“Jesus went up into a boat, crossed over, and came to his own city. And behold, they brought to him a paralytic lying on a bed. When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic: ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven.’ And behold, some of the scribes said within themselves: ‘This man blasphemes.’ When Jesus saw their thoughts, he said: ‘Why do you think evil in your hearts? Which is easier to say, “Your sins are forgiven,” or to say, “Rise and walk”? But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins,’ then he said to the paralytic: ‘Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house.’ And he rose and went to his house. When the crowds saw this, they were afraid and glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings.”

Jesus went up into a boat, and so forth. (From Figulus.) Mark does not say that this happened in his city, which is called Nazareth, but in Capernaum, unless perhaps the whole of Galilee can be called Christ’s city, wherever in it Christ might have been. For Nazareth and Capernaum are in Galilee. Or it should be read in this way: “And going up into a boat, he crossed over and came to his own city,” that is, Nazareth; Matthew omitted what happened there.

The sea that the Lord crossed signifies this present world. The boat into which he went sometimes signifies his body, sometimes the cross, sometimes his holy soul in particular, or generally the whole Church. His city, which is called Nazareth and to which he came mercifully, is interpreted as “pure” or “guarded”; it signifies the whole Church in general.

And behold, they bring him, and so forth. The healing of this paralytic indicates the salvation of the soul that, after a long paralysis caused by carnal allurements, sighs for Christ. First of all, it needs ministers who raise it up and bring it to Christ—that is, good works—and teachers who offer the hope of healing and the help of intercession. According to Mark’s account, these ministers are rightly found to have been four, either because the whole power and preaching of the preachers is established upon the four books of the Gospel, or because there are four virtues by which the confidence of the mind is raised toward obtaining health. These virtues are praised in relation to eternal wisdom: it teaches sobriety and wisdom, justice and virtue, and nothing is more useful for human beings in life. Some, changing the names, call them prudence, fortitude, and justice.

And when he saw their faith, he said to the paralytic. It should rightly be considered how great is the value of each person’s own faith before God, since the faith of others had such value that the whole man, that is, both outwardly and inwardly already healed, suddenly rose, and the errors of some were forgiven because of the merit of others. For the Gospel does not say: “When Jesus saw the faith of the one who was brought,” but “the faith of those who brought him.”

Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven. (From Jerome.) O marvelous humility! He calls “son” one who was despised, weak, and dissolved in all the joints of his limbs—one whom the priests did not deign to touch—or perhaps he calls him “son” because his sins are forgiven. In a tropological sense, the soul sometimes lies in the body, its virtues dissolved in every limb. A perfect teacher brings it to the Lord to be healed, and once it has been healed by his mercy, it receives such strength that it immediately carries its bed.

(From Bede.) In preparing to heal the man of paralysis, the Lord first loosens the bonds of his sins, so that he might show that the man had been condemned by the dissolution of his limbs because of the dissolution of his sinful actions, and that he could be healed by the restoration of his limbs only after those sins had been forgiven.

[Col. 0484A]

And behold, some of the scribes said to themselves, “This man blasphemes.” Or, according to Mark: “Who can forgive sins except God alone?” The scribes speak rightly, since no one can forgive sins except God, who also forgives through those to whom he grants the power of forgiving. Therefore Christ is proved to be true God, because he can forgive sins as God.

And when Jesus had seen their thoughts, he said: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” He shows himself to be God, who can know the hidden things of the heart; and, as it were, while remaining silent he says: “By the same majesty and power with which I perceive your thoughts, I can also forgive human beings their offenses. From this, understand what the paralytic is about to receive.”

Which is easier to say: “Your sins are forgiven” [Col. 0484B] or to say: “Rise and walk”? (From Jerome.) There is a great difference between saying and doing. Only the one who forgave knew whether the paralytic’s sins had been forgiven. But “Rise and walk” could be confirmed both by the man who rose and by those who saw him rising. Thus a bodily sign is produced so that the spiritual one may be proved; and we are given to understand that bodily weaknesses very often occur on account of sins. For there are five different kinds of causes on account of which we are afflicted in this life with bodily troubles.

(From Bede.) Either the righteous are burdened by bodily illness in order that their merits may be increased through patience, as in the case of blessed Job and Tobias; or for the protection of their virtues and observance of the commandments, lest they perish when tempted by pride, as happened to the Apostle Paul, to whom, so that he might not be exalted by the greatness of his revelations, [Col. 0484C] “a thorn in the flesh” was given (2 Cor. XI); or for the recognition and correction of our sins, as with this paralytic whom we are discussing, who could not be healed of his illness until his sins had first been forgiven; or for the glory of God in those who are saved, whether by God himself or through his servants, as with the man born blind in the Gospel (John IX), and Lazarus, whose illness was not unto death but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God might be glorified through it (John XI); or as the beginning of eternal condemnation, which is the condition of the reprobate, as with Antiochus and Herod, who showed everyone, by the misery of their present afflictions, what torments they would suffer in perpetual Gehenna. To them the Prophet’s words apply: “With a twofold destruction, destroy them.” Hence it is necessary that, in all the temporal adversities we suffer, [Col. 0484D] we give thanks to the Lord with humility and, conscious of our weakness, rejoice over the remedies bestowed upon us.

“But that you may know that the Son of Man,” etc. He himself is both God and the Son of Man: as man, Christ is able, through the power of his divinity, to forgive sins; and as God, Christ is able, through the weakness of his humanity, to die for sinners.

Then he said to the paralytic: “Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house,” etc. Spiritually, then, to rise from weakness is for the soul to withdraw itself from carnal desires, in which it had lain sick. To take up the bed is to separate even the flesh itself—restrained by the reins of continence—from earthly pleasures through hope of heavenly rewards. After taking up the bed, to go home means to return to paradise, for this is the true home. For the home that first received the human being was lost not by right but through fraud, and was at last restored by him who owed nothing to the deceitful enemy. In another sense, the man who had been ill brings his bed home when the soul, having received forgiveness of sins, returns with its very body to the inner guardianship of itself, lest after pardon it admit anything for which it might again justly be punished.

But when the crowds saw this, they were afraid and glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings. How wonderful is the power of divine might, when, with no interval of delay, swift healing accompanies the Savior’s commands! Rightly do those who had been present, their hearts struck by the weapons of blasphemous accusation, turn in astonishment [Col. 0485B] to praise such great majesty.

## The Twenty-First Week after Pentecost

### The Epistle of Blessed Paul the Apostle to the Ephesians, Chapter V

“See, therefore, how carefully you walk, not as unwise people but as wise, making the most of the time, because the days are evil. Therefore do not become foolish, but understand what the will of God is. And do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, but be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord, giving thanks always for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God the Father, submitting to one another in the fear of Christ.”

[Col. 0485C]

“See, therefore, how carefully you walk, not as unwise people but as wise,” etc. (From Jerome.) It is rightly said to the Ephesians that they should walk carefully, since they had trained faculties for discerning good and evil; and, testing everything, they retained what they had determined to be good. Whoever watches how he walks and how carefully he sets his step, lest he should strike his foot against a stone, and says, “Your word, Lord, is a lamp to my feet” (Psalm CXVIII), is certainly wise.

“Making the most of the time, because the days are evil.” (From Augustine.) To make the most of the time means this: when someone brings a lawsuit against you, give up something so that you may be free for God and not for lawsuits. What you lose is the price of time. Just as you lose money—that is, give it to another—in order to buy something, so lose money in order to buy yourself peace. [Col. 0485D] For there is an ancient proverb: “The pestilence asks for one coin; give it two, and let it depart.” What else did God say than “making the most of the time,” when he said: “If anyone wishes to go to court with you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well”? Because the days are evil. Two things make the days evil: human wickedness and misery. Otherwise, these days, insofar as they concern the duration of the hours, are orderly. They follow their cycles, the seasons proceed, the sun rises and sets, times pass, and they are burdensome to no one unless human beings are burdensome to themselves. Thus misery and human wickedness make the days evil. Ever since Adam fell from paradise, there have never been days except evil ones. Children are born, and they begin with crying; after I do not know how many days, they laugh. When the prophet was crying, it was because of his own calamity. [Col. 0486A] Tears are witnesses to misery. What was he prophesying? Surely that he would be in toil or in fear? Even if he had lived well and been righteous, placed amid temptations he was always afraid. For the Apostle says: “All who desire to live a godly life in Christ will suffer persecution.” See, then, how the days are evil!

(From Gregory.) We redeem the time when we restore by weeping the active life that we lost through dissipation.

(From Jerome.) We redeem the time because the days are evil when we spend time in good works, buying and making our own what human wickedness had put up for sale. No one who seeks the necessities of this life and thinks about riches and anxieties—which the Gospel calls thorns—can redeem time for himself. But when we redeem the time because the days are evil, we somehow change it, turn evil days into good ones, and make them belong not to the present age but to the age to come.

“Therefore do not become foolish, but understand what the will of God is.” In every action, therefore, we must first consider what God wills; and after making a judgment, we must then do what has been found pleasing to him.

“Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit.” Just as we cannot serve two masters, God and Mammon, so we cannot be filled simultaneously with the Spirit and with wine. Whoever is filled with the Spirit possesses prudence, gentleness, modesty, [Col. 0486C] and chastity; whoever is filled with wine possesses foolishness, rage, shamelessness, and lust. I think that all this is signified by the single word “debauchery.” The wine “in which there is debauchery” may also be understood as that of which Moses sings: “The fury of dragons is their wine, and the incurable fury of asps.” All who are drunk with the thoughts of this age drink it; they go mad, vomit, and fall headlong.

“Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts.” (From Jerome.) Whoever abstains from the drunkenness of wine, in which there is debauchery, and is instead filled with the Spirit, can receive all these things spiritually. We learn psalms, hymns, and songs most fully in the Psalter. Hymns are those that proclaim the strength and majesty [Col. 0486D] of God and continually marvel at either his benefits or his deeds; all the psalms contain this, since “Alleluia” is placed either before or after them. Psalms, properly speaking, belong to the ethical sphere, so that through the instrument of the body we may know what should be done and what avoided. But whoever discusses higher matters and, as a subtle disputant, expounds the universe and the order and harmony of all creatures, sings a spiritual song. Or, to speak more plainly for the simpler-minded: the psalm refers to the body, while the song refers to the mind. We must therefore sing, make melody, and praise the Lord more with the mind than with the voice; that is what is meant by “singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord.” [Col. 0487A] Let young men hear this—let those hear it who have the duty of singing psalms to God in the Church: it is not with the voice but with the heart that one must sing, in fear, in conduct, and in knowledge of the Scriptures. If he has good works, he is a singer pleasing to God. Let Christ’s servant sing in such a way that it is not the singer’s voice but the words being read that please.

“Giving thanks to the Lord always for everything.” This must be considered in two ways: we should give thanks to God both at all times and for everything that happens to us. Thus the mind should burst forth in gladness to the praise of God not only for what we consider good, but also for what constrains us and comes against our will. It is a virtue proper to Christians to give thanks to the Creator even for what is considered adverse.

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and the Father.” [Col. 0487B] Whoever, as we have said, gives thanks to God the Father should give those thanks through Christ Jesus, the mediator of God and human beings, because we cannot approach the Father except through him.

“Submitting to one another in the fear of Christ.” And in another passage: “Through love serve one another.” Let bishops hear this, let presbyters hear it, let all the orthodox hear it: they must understand that they are subject to those subject to them, and imitate the Apostle who says: “Though I was free from all, I made myself a servant to all, that I might win the more” (1 Cor. IX). But what he says, “in the fear of Christ,” must be understood in this way: that this submission should not be made for human glory but because of the fear of Christ, since we fear offending him.

## The Gospel of Matthew, Chapter XXII

[Col. 0487C]

“Jesus spoke with his disciples in parables, saying: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son. And he sent his servants to call those who had been invited to the wedding feast, but they were unwilling to come. Again he sent other servants, saying: “Tell those who have been invited: Behold, I have prepared my meal; my bulls and fattened animals have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast.” But they paid no attention and went away, one to his farm, another to his business. The rest seized his servants and, after treating them shamefully, killed them. When the king heard this, he became angry and, sending his armies, destroyed those murderers and burned their city. Then he said to his servants: “The wedding feast is indeed ready, but those who had been invited were not worthy. Go therefore to the crossroads, and [Col. 0487D] invite to the wedding feast everyone whom you find.” And his servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found, both good and bad; and the wedding feast was filled with those reclining at table. But when the king entered to see those reclining at table, he saw there a man who was not dressed in a wedding garment. And he said to him: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” But he was speechless. Then the king said to the attendants: “Bind his feet and hands and cast him into the outer darkness. There there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” For many are called, but few are chosen.’”

“Jesus spoke with his disciples in parables, saying: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son.’” (From Gregory.) The assembly of the righteous is called the kingdom of heaven. The kingdom of heaven is the Church of the righteous, because the hearts of the elect desire nothing on earth; and because they sigh for heavenly things, the Lord already reigns in them as though in the heavenly realms.

(From Jerome.) This king who made a wedding feast for his son is almighty God. He made the wedding feast for our Lord Jesus Christ and the Church, which has been gathered both from the Jews and from the nations.

(From Gregory.) In this, the Father makes a wedding feast for the Son: he joined the holy Church to him through the mystery of the incarnation. The womb of the virgin mother was the bridal chamber of this bridegroom, and so the Psalmist says: “He himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber” (Psalm XIX). Like a bridegroom he came forth from the bridal chamber, for God, having become incarnate in order to join the Church to himself, came forth from the incorrupt womb of the virgin.

“And he sent his servants to call those who had been invited to the wedding feast, but they were unwilling to come.” He therefore sent servants to invite friends to this wedding feast. He sent once; he sent again, because the preachers of the Lord’s incarnation were first the prophets and afterward the apostles. Thus he sent servants twice to invite them, because he both foretold the future incarnation of the Only-Begotten through the prophets and announced its fulfillment through the apostles.

(From Jerome.) “He sent his servant to call those who had been invited to the wedding feast”—without doubt, Moses, through whom he gave the Law to those invited. But if we read “servants,” as many copies have it, this should be referred to the prophets, whom those invited scorned to follow.

[Col. 0488C]

“Again he sent other servants, saying: ‘Tell those who have been invited: Behold, I have prepared my meal; my bulls and fattened animals have been slaughtered, and everything is ready.
