Come to the wedding feast.’ But they paid no attention.” The prepared meal, and the slaughtered bulls and fattened animals, may be understood metaphorically as the spiritual riches of the king; or, certainly, the greatness of the doctrines and the fullness of the teaching of God’s Law may be understood.

(From Gregory.) What do we understand by the bulls and fattened animals, most beloved brothers, except the fathers of the New and Old Testaments? What are signified by the bulls except the fathers of the Old Testament? Since they had received from the promise of the Law the command to strike down their adversaries in requital of hatred, what else were they, so to speak, than bulls, who struck their enemies with the horn of bodily strength? What, however, are signified by the fattened animals except the fathers of the New Testament, who, receiving the grace of inner richness, are lifted by the wing of their contemplation in mind from earthly desires to lofty things? “My bulls and fattened animals have been slaughtered, and everything is ready,” as though it were said more openly: “Look upon the deaths of the fathers who came before, and consider the remedies for your life.”

“And they went away, one to his farm, another to his business.” To go to one’s farm is to devote oneself excessively to earthly labor; to go to business is to long for profits through secular activity. Since one person, intent upon earthly labor, and another, devoted to the activities of this world, neglects to contemplate the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation and to live according to it, he refuses to come to the king’s wedding feast as though he were going to a farm or a business. And often, what is more serious, some not only reject the grace of the one who calls but even persecute it. Hence it follows:

“But the rest seized his servants and, after treating them shamefully, killed them.” (From Jerome.) Among those who do not receive the truth of the Gospel there is great diversity. Those who, being occupied with other matters, were unwilling to come are guilty of a lesser offense than those who, despising the affection of the inviter, turned kindness into cruelty and either treated the king’s captured servants shamefully or killed them.

“But when the king heard this, he became angry and, sending his armies, destroyed those murderers and burned their city.” Let us understand the armies as either avenging angels, concerning whom it is written in the Psalms (Psalm LXXVII), “A sending through evil angels,” or as the Romans under the leadership of Vespasian and Titus, who, after killing the peoples of Judea, burned their treacherous city.

(From Gregory.) He destroyed the murderers because he destroys those who persecute; he burned their city with fire because not only their souls but also the flesh in which they dwelt is tormented by the flame of eternal Gehenna. He is said to have destroyed the murderers by sending armies because all judgment is carried out through angels.

“Then he said to his servants: ‘The wedding feast is indeed ready,’” etc. If in Scripture we understand “roads” as actions, we understand “the crossroads” as the failures of actions, because those often come easily to God who are accompanied by no prosperity in earthly activities.

“And his servants went out into the roads and gathered all [Col. 0489C] whom they found,” etc. (From Jerome.) The people of the nations were not in the roads but at the crossroads. It is asked, however, how some good people were found among those who were outside, among the wicked. The Apostle treats this passage more fully in his letter to the Romans: the nations, naturally doing the things of the Law, condemn the Jews who did not fulfill the written Law. Among the pagans themselves there is also infinite diversity, since we know that some are inclined toward vices and rush into evil, while others, because of the honesty of their behavior, devote themselves to virtues.

(From Gregory.) Behold, the very character of those reclining at table now openly shows that by this wedding feast of the king the present Church of God is signified, in which the wicked gather together with the good. It is mixed with a diversity of children. The good alone are nowhere except in heaven, and the wicked alone are nowhere except in hell. But this life, situated between heaven and hell, just as it stands in the middle, so receives in common the citizens of both parts.

“But when the king entered to see those reclining at table, he saw there a man,” etc. What, then, should we understand the wedding garment to be except love? For he enters the wedding feast but does not enter with a wedding garment who, standing in the holy Church, has faith but does not have love. Love is rightly called the wedding garment, because our Creator possessed it in himself when he came to the wedding feast in order to join the Church to himself. It was solely through God’s love that his Only-Begotten united the minds of the elect to himself. Hence Paul says: [Col. 0490A] “For God so loved the world that he gave his Only-Begotten Son for us” (John III). Therefore, since he came to human beings through love, he made known that this same love is the wedding garment.

We are the brothers who recline at the wedding feast of the Word, who already have a place in the Church, who are nourished by the feasts of sacred Scripture, and who rejoice that the Church has been joined to God. Behold, the king enters the wedding feast and examines the condition of our heart; and to the one whom he does not find clothed with love he immediately says in anger: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” It is very astonishing, most beloved brothers, that he calls this man both a friend and a reprobate—as though he were saying more plainly, “Friend and not friend”: friend through faith, and not a friend through conduct.

(From Jerome.) Those who had been invited, gathered from hedges, corners, marketplaces, and various places, had filled the king’s banquet. But afterward, when the king came to see those reclining at his feast—that is, those resting, as it were, in his faith—in order to visit the guests on the day of judgment and distinguish the merits of each, he found one who was not clothed in a wedding garment. This one signifies all who are joined to wickedness; the wedding garment signifies the Lord’s commandments and the works fulfilled according to the Law and the Gospel, which form the clothing of the new human being. Therefore, if at the time of judgment someone is found under the name of Christian not to have a wedding garment—that is, the garment of the heavenly human being—but instead a defiled garment, namely, the cast-off garments of the old human being, he is immediately rebuked and told: “Friend, how did you come in here?” [Col. 0490C] He calls him a friend because he was invited to the wedding feast; he accuses him of shamelessness because he has polluted the cleanliness of the wedding feast with a filthy garment.

“But he was speechless.” At that time there will be no place for shamelessness or opportunity for denial, since every corner and the world itself will be witnesses to the sins.

(From Gregory.) Because this cannot be said without a groan: in that final severity of rebuke, every argument of excuse ceases, since the one who rebukes outside is he whom the witnesses of conscience accuse within.

“Then the king said,” etc. Then, through the severity of the sentence, feet and hands are bound—the feet and hands of those who now refused to be bound from evil works through improvement of life. Or certainly punishment then binds those whom guilt now binds from good works. The feet of those who neglect to visit the sick, and the hands of those who give nothing to the needy, have already been bound from good work by their own will. Therefore, those who now willingly bind themselves in vice are then bound unwillingly in punishment.

“Cast him,” etc. By the inner darkness we mean blindness of heart; by the outer darkness, the eternal night of condemnation. Then, therefore, each condemned person is cast not into inner but into outer darkness, because there he is unwillingly thrown into the night of condemnation who here willingly fell into blindness of heart. There is also said to be weeping and gnashing of teeth, so that teeth gnash there which here rejoiced in gluttony. Eyes weep there which here were occupied with unlawful desires, [Col. 0491A] so that each member may undergo the punishment to which it had here willingly subjected itself in the service of its particular vices. (From Jerome.) Through the weeping of the eyes and the gnashing of the teeth, the greatness of the torments is shown by a metaphor drawn from the bodily members.

“For many are called, but few are chosen.” (From Augustine.) He calls the righteous few in comparison with the many unrighteous. Yet, considered in themselves, spread throughout the whole world, growing among the weeds and remaining with the chaff until the day of harvest and winnowing, they are numerous. For in comparison with the chaff, the grains may be called few, although, gathered by themselves into a heap, they fill the Lord’s granary.

(From Gregory.) Behold, we have all now been called through faith, [Col. 0491B] and have come to the wedding feast of the heavenly king; we both believe and confess the mystery of his incarnation and partake of the feasts of the divine Word. We know that we have been called; whether we are chosen, we do not know. Therefore, the more necessary it is that each of us humble himself, the more he is unaware whether he has been chosen.

## The Twenty-Second Week after Pentecost

### To the Ephesians, Chapter VI

“Finally, be strengthened in the Lord and in the strength of his might. Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the Devil. For our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers and authorities, against the world-rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Therefore take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and, having accomplished everything, to stand firm. Stand therefore, with your loins girded in truth, and clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, and with your feet shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace. In all things take up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one. And take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.”

“Finally, be strengthened in the Lord and in the strength of his might.” (From Jerome.) What he says, therefore—“Be strengthened in the Lord and in the strength of his might”—is understood wholly in Christ, so that those who believe may be strengthened in all the virtues understood in relation to him. And prudently, after the particular commandments concerning what husbands and wives, fathers and children, masters and servants must observe, he now gives a general command to everyone together: strengthened in the Lord and in his power, they should prepare themselves against the Devil.

“Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist the schemes of the Devil.” From what we read below, and from what is said about the Lord and Savior throughout all the Scriptures, it is most clearly proved that all the weapons of God with which we are now commanded to be clothed are to be understood as the Savior, so that it amounts to saying one and the same thing: “Put on all the armor of God,” as though he had said, “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ.” For if the belt is truth and the breastplate is righteousness, while the Savior is called both truth and righteousness, there is no doubt that he himself is both the belt [Col. 0492A] and the breastplate. What other weapons of God can we suppose that one should put on who must fight against the Devil’s cunning, except the virtue that is Christ? Whoever is clothed with him according to all that is understood concerning him will be able to resist all the Devil’s schemes.

The Devil is a Greek name, meaning “accuser.” But according to the idiom of the Hebrew language, since the tribe of Zebulun also has a certain resemblance to this word, he may be called καταρύων (*kataruōn*), that is, “flowing downward.” This signifies that he gradually flowed down from virtue into vice and fell from heavenly things to earthly ones.

“For our struggle is not against flesh and blood,” etc. I think that struggles against flesh and blood occur when the flesh desires against the spirit and provokes us to perform its works: fornication, impurity, debauchery, and other things like these. But it is not a human temptation, nor a struggle against flesh and blood, when Satan himself, transformed into an angel of light, tries to persuade us to regard him as an angel of light, or when he does something similar through every kind of virtue, signs, and lying wonders, through every deception of wickedness. Rather, one might say that a principality, power, ruler of darkness, and spiritual wickedness speaks in the words: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers and authorities,” and the rest that follows.

He says this so that we may learn that even the vices we think are being supplied to us by flesh are not from flesh or blood, but are suggested by certain spiritual wickednesses. For there are certain demons who serve loves and love songs, and the Prophet also mentions them, saying: “They were seduced by the spirit of fornication.” Others promote anger, fury, and wars; others preside over enmities and stir up hatred among human beings. Since the Apostle wishes, they say, to teach us that these kinds of vices are not generated by the nature of the body and the material of flesh and blood but by the impulse of demons, he therefore says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers and authorities,” and the rest.

But it is against the rulers of those darknesses that hang over this world and spread the error of unbelief over human beings, and against the spiritual wickednesses that dwell in the heavenly places. This does not mean that demons live in the heavenly places, but that the air above us has received this name; hence the birds that fly through the air are called “birds of heaven.” This, however, is the opinion of all teachers: that this air, which divides heaven and earth by occupying the space between them and is called the void, is filled with hostile powers.

(From Augustine.) Our struggle is not against flesh and blood—that is, against a human being—but against rulers and authorities, that is, demons, who are spiritual forces of wickedness, against the rulers of the world. He explains what the world is whose rulers they are when he says: “the rulers of the darkness of this world.” The world is full of those who love these things and of unbelievers; the Apostle calls them darkness, and their ruler is the Devil [Col. 0493A] with his angels. These darknesses are not unchangeable, but can at some time be changed and become light; and it is said to them: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.”

(From Primasius.) Likewise, “flesh and blood” means a human being, but the struggle is against the rulers and authorities who have usurped rule over the people of this world. They deceive ignorant souls through sins. The struggle is against the rulers of this world’s darkness: “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.” Against spiritual enemies, spiritual weapons must be taken up, so that the dissimilarity of our nature may be protected by the strength of these weapons. Against them we struggle in the heavenly places, that is, for the promise of heavenly rewards.

(From Augustine.) Because he says “in the heavenly places,” and this seems ambiguous, it should be said that the phrase may be understood as applying to everything, so that the meaning is: “Our struggle is not against authorities in the heavenly places, nor against the rulers of these darknesses in the heavenly places, nor against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.” We should also know that, apart from the present passage, we have never read the expression “rulers of the world” in either the Old or the New Testament. The Apostle Paul coined this expression because, when discussing invisible matters with the Ephesians, he needed to adapt new names to them.

“Therefore take up,” etc. Paul, by the spirit of prophecy, saw future temptations and persecutions arising for the Ephesians after this letter; he therefore urges and admonishes them to do everything by which they may stand firm in the faith of the Gospel and not fall during persecution. The present time shows what “the evil day” means: the time of which he had said above, “making the most of the time, because the days are evil,” on account of the distress and labors of this life, since we do not reach the palm of victory without sweat and struggle. Or it may refer to the day of consummation and judgment, concerning which Joel says: “The day of darkness and tempest is near, the day of cloud and gloom,” and the rest (Joel II).

Therefore, so that a person may be able to resist the Devil on that day—for he is the accuser of our brothers—let him take up all the armor of God. For this is what the Greek word πανοπλία (*panoplia*) signifies: “complete armor.” It has not been translated into Latin merely as *arma*, “weapons,” but means that one is girded with every weapon and every armament, as is explained in what follows. Let him know that he can then stand if he has performed every virtue, so that, full of all virtues, he may plant his foot firmly and not be moved from the battle line.

“Stand therefore, with your loins girded in truth.” (From Primasius.) Be perfect, with the loins of your mind girded—that is, prepared manfully for every battle and freed from all the cares of the world.

(From Jerome.) No one doubts that in Scripture all the members of the soul are called by reference to the members of the flesh and body. I think that one of these members is now called the loins, which we are commanded to gird with Truth: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke XII). I also think that this signifies what is meant by John’s having a leather belt around his loins. He was not among the unclean who, because of the discharge of semen, were cast outside the camp (Lev. XIII) and could not dwell with the ark of the Lord (Num. VIII). In accordance with this, whoever is girded with truth—that is, with Christ—will not easily be led astray into false doctrines.

“Clothed with the breastplate of righteousness.” (From Primasius.) Just as a breastplate is woven together from many rings, so righteousness is joined together from various kinds of virtues. It covers not only the conscience of the breast but also the continence of the belly, and it extends even to the thighs in order to restrain lust.

(From Jerome.) Whoever is surrounded by the many-layered garment of righteousness neither, like a stag, receives an arrow in his liver, nor falls into desires and rages. Rather, he will be pure in heart, having God as the craftsman of this breastplate, the one who fashions all the weapons for each of the saints.

[Col. 0494B]

“And with your feet shod,” etc. Observe more carefully that he has called a certain virtue of the soul “feet,” with which we walk in the one who says: “I am the way” (John XIV). Concerning them we sing: “Direct our feet, Lord, into the way of peace.” These feet must be shod with the readiness of the Gospel of peace. Whoever therefore has peace is shod with the Gospel of Christ, and for that reason has become a person of peace. He neither does anything warlike or tumultuous nor will he be condemned together with those who are unprepared.

“In all things taking up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the darts,” etc. It is as though he had said: “Carry the shield of faith in every work, so that, covered and protected, you may receive the arrows that come against you and skillfully turn them aside in every direction by the art of war.” The darts of the Evil One are obvious: he wishes to shoot them into our hearts through the worst thoughts. One of these he cast into the heart of Judas, so that he might betray the Savior (John XII). Thus the enemy can have no beginning of wounding if we hold the shield of faith. On it, not only are the incoming darts shattered, but the very fire of the darts is extinguished. Unbelief too is hostile to faith; where the shield of faith is present, it will have no power.

“And take the helmet of salvation.” Because of this helmet of salvation, all the senses in our head remain whole. For if Christ is the head of the man, it follows that all our understanding, mind, thought, speech, and counsel—provided that we are wise—should be in Christ. The head also, which is the chief part of the heart, in which all the senses are situated, will not be shaken when surrounded by the helmet of salvation.

And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. *(From Primasius.)* No soldier dares set out for battle without a sword. He can in some measure defend himself, but he cannot kill the enemy; just as he is sometimes stripped of all his weapons by a bold foe and slain, so without the word of God every righteousness is unprotected. The faithful person, like a brave and strong warrior, will cut down, kill, and slaughter all sects opposed to the truth. Holding the sword of the Spirit—that is, the word of God—in his hand, the Savior is called both Truth and Righteousness. No one doubts that he himself is also the belt, the breastplate, the preparation of the gospel of peace, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God: a living and effective utterance, concerning which the Apostle says: “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts of the heart; and no creature is invisible in his sight, but all things are naked and open to his eyes.”

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER 4

“Now there was a certain royal official whose son was ill at Capernaum. When he heard that Jesus had come from Judea into Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son, for he was beginning to die. Jesus therefore said to him: ‘Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.’ The royal official said to him: ‘Lord, come down before my son dies.’ Jesus said to him: ‘Go; your son lives.’ The man believed the word that Jesus had spoken to him, and he went away. Now, as he was going down, his servants met him and announced to him, saying: ‘Your son lives.’ Therefore he asked them the hour at which he had improved. And they said to him: ‘Yesterday, at the seventh hour, the fever left him.’ The father therefore recognized that it was at that hour when Jesus had said to him: ‘Your son lives’; and he himself believed, and his entire household.”

### There was a certain royal official whose son was ill at Capernaum. *(From Gregory.)*

“Royal official” is a diminutive name derived from “king”; and therefore perhaps this man, who sought healing for his son, is called a royal official because he did not possess complete faith. Capernaum, moreover, is interpreted as “most beautiful field” or “village.”

When he heard that Jesus had come from Judea into Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son, for he was beginning to die. Jesus therefore said to him: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.” Why, then, does he say, “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe,” when the man believed before he saw the sign? The one who was seeking salvation for his son undoubtedly believed; but remember what he asked, and you will clearly recognize that he doubted in faith. For he asked him to come down and heal his son. Thus he was seeking the Lord’s bodily presence, although the Lord was nowhere absent in spirit; he believed less in the one whom he did not think able to give healing unless he were bodily present. For if he had believed perfectly, he would undoubtedly have known that there was no place where God was not. He therefore asked healing for his son, and yet doubted in faith, because he believed the one to whom he had come to be powerful enough to heal, but nevertheless thought God absent while his son was dying.

The royal official says to him: “Lord, come down before my son dies,” and so forth. Here we must carefully observe that, as we learn from another Evangelist, a centurion came to the Lord, saying: “Lord, my servant lies paralyzed in the house and is grievously tormented.” Jesus immediately replied to him: “I will come and heal him.” What does it mean that the royal official asks him to come to his son, and yet that he refuses to go bodily? The centurion does not invite him to come to the servant, and yet he promises to go bodily. He does not deign to be bodily present for the royal official’s son, but he does not disdain to go to the centurion’s servant. What does this mean except that our pride is exposed? We venerate in human beings not the nature by which they were made in the image of God, but honors and riches. Our Redeemer, however, to show that what is exalted among human beings is to be despised by the saints, and what is despised among human beings is not to be despised, did not wish to go to the royal official’s son, but was ready to go to the centurion’s servant.

The man believed the word that Jesus had spoken to him, and went away. He was beginning to have faith in Jesus’ word; and he who came partly doubtful departed faithful, and therefore deserved his son’s recovery.

Now, as he was going down, his servants met him, saying that his son was alive. Therefore he asked them the hour at which he had improved, and they said to him: “Yesterday, at the seventh hour, the fever left him.” The number seven is sanctified in the gifts of the Holy Spirit, in whom healing is given, as is evident, to all who believe. For in the Holy Spirit, who is God’s gift, there is forgiveness of all sins for believers. And if the number seven is divided into three and four, it signifies the Holy Trinity. In the number three there is the perfection of all creatures; in the number four, because of the four elements, the four regions of the world, and the four seasons of the year, all things consist and are governed, since all things were created from him, through him, and in him; for “in him we live and move and are.”

The father therefore recognized that it was the hour when Jesus had said to him, “Your son lives,” and he himself believed, and his entire household. When the son’s recovery was announced to him, many Samaritans believed on the word alone; but at that miracle only that household believed. This event points forward to the multitude of the faith of the Gentiles and the smallness of the faith of the Jews. The Gentiles believed through the word alone—that is, through apostolic preaching. The Jews, however, saw signs performed by the very Son of God, and yet only a few of them believed.

## THE TWENTY-THIRD WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

## THE LETTER TO THE PHILIPPIANS, CHAPTER 1

“We are confident in the Lord Jesus that he who began a good work in you will himself bring it to completion, until the day of Christ Jesus. It is right for me to think this concerning all of you, because I have you in my heart and in my bonds, both in the defense and confirmation of the gospel, since you are all partners in my joy. For God is my witness, how I long for you all in the bowels of Jesus Christ. And this I pray: that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and in every understanding, so that you may approve what is better, and be sincere and without offense until the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.”

### We are confident in the Lord Jesus that he who began a good work in you will himself bring it to completion.

It is as though he had said: “Trusting that the teaching begun among you will be obtained, or that the grace of knowledge will be completed in you by being generously bestowed.”

### Until the day of Christ.

That is, until the day when you depart from the body, after which each person is reserved for the Lord’s coming; or, until the day of Christ—that is, until the day of judgment.

### It is right for me to think this concerning all of you.

It is as though he had said: “Love makes me think this concerning you: that you will complete the work you have begun until the day, whether of death or of judgment, because love hopes for all things.”

### Because I have you in my heart and in my bonds.

It is as though he had said: “I love you so much that neither the force of tribulation nor the anxiety of defending myself can remove the memory of you from me.”

### Both in the defense and confirmation of the gospel.

The confirmation of the gospel is the steadfast endurance of the preacher.

### Since you are all partners in my joy.

It is as though he had said: “This is what I think and believe concerning you: just as you are partners in my tribulation, so you will also be partners in my eternal joy.” Or: “Since I know that you have believed the gospel, you rejoice with me equally both in my tribulations and in its defense.”

### For God is my witness, how I long for you all in the bowels of Jesus Christ.

It is as though he had said: “I desire you as the very bowels of Christ,” or, “I desire that you may be in his bowels.”

### And this I pray: that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and in every understanding.

It should be noted that he asks those who already possess knowledge to receive still greater knowledge, so that they may prevail in being sincere in all things; or, “in knowledge and understanding,” that is, in the understanding of the letter and of the spiritual mystery.

### So that you may approve what is better, and so forth.

Sincerity is a substance that preserves its own nature, is not disfigured by any external corruption, and always advances toward what is better, not toward what is worse. Or “sincere,” that is, not returning evil for evil, nor giving offense through a bad example.

### Filled with the fruit of righteousness through Jesus, and so forth.

That is: not only that you may be sincere and free from every corruption, but also that you may abound in the fruit of righteousness, following the example of Christ, who not only has no malice but also overflows with goodness. When he says, “to the glory and praise of God,” it is as though he said: “So that God may be glorified and praised in your actions,” or, “so that glory may be present in your works and praise in your words.”

## THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER 18

“The kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants. And when he had begun to settle accounts, one was brought to him who owed ten thousand talents. Since he had nothing with which to repay, his master ordered him to be sold, together with his wife and children and everything he had, and payment to be made. Falling down, that servant begged him, saying: ‘Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.’ The master of that servant, moved with compassion, released him and forgave him the debt. But when that servant had gone out, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii. And seizing him, he was choking him, saying: ‘Pay what you owe!’ His fellow servant, falling down, begged him, saying: ‘Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.’ But he was unwilling; instead, he went away and put him in prison until he should repay the debt. When his fellow servants saw what had happened, they were greatly saddened. They came and reported to their master everything that had taken place. Then his master summoned him and said to him: ‘Wicked servant, I forgave you the entire debt because you begged me. Should you not therefore also have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?’ And his master, being angry, handed him over to the torturers until he should repay the entire debt. So also my heavenly Father will do to you, unless each of you forgives his brother from your hearts.”

### The kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants. *(From Augustine.)*

That one who was brought to his master as a debtor owing ten thousand talents, and whom he ordered to be sold, together with his wife and children and everything he had, and payment to be made, is to be understood as a debtor to the ten commandments of the Law. Because of his greed and his deeds, he had to pay the penalties as though they were his wife and children; this is his price. For the price of one sold is understood as the punishment of one condemned. When it says that he was unwilling to forgive his fellow servant, but went away and put him in prison, and so forth, this is to be understood as meaning that he held such an attitude against him that he wished him to suffer punishment. The fellow servants who reported what had happened to their master can be understood as the Church, which both looses one and binds the other.

*(From Jerome.)* He therefore instructed Peter, by the comparison of a king, a lord, and a servant who owed ten thousand talents, that the servant, having begged his lord, obtained pardon, and that he too should forgive his fellow servants who had sinned in lesser matters. For if that king and lord so readily forgave a servant who owed ten thousand talents, how much more ought servants to forgive lesser offenses committed by their fellow servants! To make this clearer, let us speak by way of example. If any of us have committed adultery, murder, sacrilege, or greater crimes—debts of ten thousand talents—let these be forgiven when they ask, so that they too may forgive those who have sinned in lesser matters. But if, because of an insult received, we are implacable, and because of a bitter word maintain lasting quarrels, do we not seem rightly to deserve imprisonment, and, following the example of our own conduct, bring this upon ourselves, so that forgiveness for our greater offenses is not granted?

## AUGUSTINE, ALSO

Peter asked the Master how often he should forgive a brother who had sinned against him, and asked whether seven times would be enough. The Lord answered him: “Not only seven times, but up to seventy times seven.” Then he told a very fearful parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who settled accounts with his servants, among whom he found a debtor owing ten thousand talents.”

Every human being is both a debtor and has a debtor. He is God’s debtor and has his brother as a debtor. For who is there who is not God’s debtor, except one in whom no sin can be found? And who is there who does not have a debtor who is his brother, except one against whom no one has sinned? Every person, then, is a debtor who has a debtor, and the just God establishes this rule concerning your debtor: what he does with his debtor, you must also do with yours.

There are therefore two works of mercy that free us, which the Lord himself briefly set forth in one place in the Gospel: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you.” “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” pertains to pardoning. “Give, and it will be given to you” pertains to offering a benefit or alms. Do you wish to be forgiven? Forgive. Release, and you will be released. Do you wish to receive? Give, and it will be given to you.

But this can trouble us, as it troubled Peter: “How often must I forgive?” he says. “Is seven times enough?” “It is not enough,” says the Lord. “I do not say seven times, but up to seventy times seven.” Now count how often your brother has sinned against you. If you can reach the seventy-seventh or seventy-eighth offense, so that you pass 490, then begin your vengeance. Is this really what he means? Is it truly arranged so that if he sins 490 times you forgive him, but if he sins 560 times you are now permitted not to forgive? I dare to say: even if he sins 490 times, forgive him; and if he sins a hundred times, forgive him. Why should I say “so many times” and “so many times”? Forgive him absolutely as often as he sins. For the Lord did not say 490 without reason, since there is no offense that we ought not to forgive.

Look at that servant himself, whose debtor was found to be a debtor. He owed ten talents, I think, because, to put it mildly, the ten talents signify ten sins. I do not wish to say that one talent encompasses all sins. But how much did that servant owe? He owed a hundred denarii. That is already more than 490, and yet the Lord was angry because he did not forgive him. Not only are a hundred more than 490, but a hundred denarii may perhaps amount to a thousand asses. But what is that in comparison with ten talents?

By this, then, let us all be prepared to forgive every offense committed against us, if we wish to be forgiven. Every day we prostrate ourselves and say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” What debts? All of them, or only some portion? We shall answer: “All.” So therefore must you act toward your debtor. You establish this rule; under this condition you speak; by this agreement and arrangement you bind yourself to God.

What, then, does 490 signify? Listen, brothers: a great mystery, a wondrous sacrament. Matthew began with Abraham and reached Joseph by descending. Luke, however, began to count by ascending. Why did one descend and the other ascend? Matthew was commending the generation of Christ by which he descended to us; therefore, when Christ was born, he began to count by descending. Luke, however, began to count when Christ was baptized. There is the beginning of ascent, and so he began to count by ascending.

By counting, he completed seventy-seven generations. Consider carefully from whom he began to count today: he reached Adam himself, who first sinned and generated us under the obligation of sin. He reached Adam, and seventy-seven generations are counted: from Christ to Adam, seventy-seven; from Adam to Christ, seventy-seven. If, therefore, no generation has been omitted, no offense is passed over where it ought not to be forgiven. For he counted seventy-seven generations for this reason: the Lord commended that number for the remission of sins, since he began counting from baptism, where all sins are loosed.

Then inquire more diligently into the secret meaning of the number itself, and search out its hidden places. Knock more diligently, so that the righteousness established by the Law may be opened to you. The Law is commended in ten commandments; therefore that debtor of ten talents is the renowned Decalogue, written by the finger of God and delivered to the people through Moses, God’s servant. That debtor of ten talents, therefore, signifies all sins, on account of the number of the Law.

He also owed ten denarii; this does not depart from the same number. For ten times a hundred is one thousand, and ten times ten is one hundred: both the ten talents and the ten times ten belong to the same numerical pattern. Thus neither case departs from the legitimate number, in which you will find both kinds of sins: both are debtors, and both lament and seek pardon. But that evil, ungrateful, unjust servant was unwilling to repay what he had received; he was unwilling to provide what had been provided to him, though he was unworthy of it.

See, therefore, brothers: whoever begins from baptism comes out free. His debt of ten thousand talents has been forgiven. When he goes out and finds his fellow servant to be a debtor, let him observe that same sin, which, I think, is well signified by the number eleven. For the Law is ten, while sin is eleven: the Law by ten, sin by eleven. Why is sin represented by eleven? Because it is a transgression of ten, so that one comes to eleven. In the Law a limit has been fixed; you have crossed it, and you have sinned. Whenever you cross ten, you come to eleven.

This is why there is a great mystery in the command to construct the tabernacle. Many numbers are mentioned there in a great sacrament. Among other things, coverings of goat hair were commanded to be made—not ten, but eleven—because by goat hair the confession of sins is shown.

*(From Jerome.)* The Apostle Peter, prompted by the example, asks how often he ought to forgive a brother who sins against him, and in his question he offers a proposed answer: “Up to seven times?” The Lord replies: “Not up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven,” that is, 490 times, so that he should forgive a brother who sins that many times in a day, however often he might be able to sin.

*(From Augustine.)* You ask further whether you wish to know whether all sins are contained in this number, seventy-seven. He therefore said “all sins” when he said seventy-seven, because eleven multiplied by seven makes seventy-seven; that is, where sin is signified, eleven is multiplied by seven. He therefore wished all sins to be forgiven, since he prefigured them by the number seventy-seven.

Let no one hold anything against himself by refusing to forgive, lest something be held against him when he prays. For God says: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven.” “But I have forgiven first; forgive afterward, you too.” For if you do not forgive, I will recall you, and whatever I had forgiven you I will charge against you again. Truth does not lie; Christ does not deceive or err, who added and said: “So also your Father who is in heaven will do to you.”

You have found the Father; imitate the Father. If you do not wish to imitate him, you will be disinherited. “So will your heavenly Father do to you,” he says, “if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts.”

Do not say with your tongue, “I forgive,” while in your heart you postpone punishment and threaten vengeance. God knows where you speak; a human being hears your voice, but God examines your conscience. If you say, “I release,” then release. It is better to cry out with your mouth and forgive in your heart than to flatter with your mouth while being cruel in your heart.

Now let undisciplined children observe this. Discipline must be given to children, yet they do not wish to be struck. When we want to discipline them, they write this out for us: “I have sinned; forgive me.” “I have forgiven you.” They sin again: “Forgive me.” “I have forgiven you.” They sin a third time: “Forgive me.” “Here is the third time; I have forgiven you.” Now, the fourth time, let him be struck. And he says: “Forgive me.” “I have forgiven you.” “I have forgiven you a fourth time, a fifth time, a sixth time, and a seventh time; now let him be struck.”

Does he become weary at seventy-seven times, so that through this written record the severity of discipline falls asleep and, with discipline suppressed, unpunished wickedness grows fierce? What, then, should be done? Let us correct with words, and, if necessary, also with blows; but let us do this out of love. Let us forgive the offense and drive from our hearts whatever harm comes from our brother.

For this reason the Lord added: “From your hearts,” so that when discipline is imposed from the heart through love, gentleness may not depart. Let us therefore understand these things, my brothers, so that we may love our brothers who have sinned with all our heart, may not abandon love toward them, and may exercise discipline when necessary, lest, by abolishing discipline, wickedness increase and we begin to be accused before God. For it has been read to us: “Reprove the one who sins in the presence of all, so that the others may have fear” (1 Tim. IV).

Certainly, when one is alone with another, it is true: distinguish the circumstances, and you resolve the question. If the sin is secret, reprove him in secret; if the sin is public and open, reprove him publicly, so that he may be corrected and the others may be afraid.

### So also my Father, and so forth.

This is a fearful sentence, if God’s judgment is bent and changed according to our own thinking: if we do not forgive small offenses against our brothers, great offenses will not be forgiven us by God. And because someone may say, “I have nothing against him; he himself knows. He has God as his judge. I do not care what he wishes to do. I have forgiven him,” he confirms his sentence and overturns every pretense of false peace, saying: “If you do not forgive each of you his brother from your hearts.”

## THE TWENTY-FOURTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

## THE LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE PHILIPPIANS, CHAPTER 3

“Be imitators of me, and observe those who walk in this way, as you have us for an example. For many walk—those of whom I often told you, and now tell you even weeping—as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction; their god is their belly; and their glory is in their shame, for they set their minds on earthly things. But our citizenship is in heaven. From there also we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will reform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory, according to the operation of his power, by which he is also able to subject all things to himself.”

### Be imitators of me.

That is: follow me; faithfully imitate me, not the false apostles.

### And observe those who walk in this way. *(From Augustine.)*

“Observe” is said in two senses: either for imitation, as here, or for avoidance, as he says to the Romans: “Observe those who cause dissensions and offenses” (Rom. XVI).

### As you have us for an example.

That is, the example of our teaching.

### For many walk, of whom I often told you.

He speaks of those who, removing the hope of Christ’s passion by which sins have been forgiven, placed their hope in the ceremonies of the Law. It may also be interpreted of the Jovinianists, who turned the hardships of fasting and all bodily tortures into luxury and banquets.

### And now I tell you even weeping, as enemies of the cross of Christ.

It should be noted with what feeling he desired the salvation of all, since he even mourned the enemies of the cross of Christ, who were rushing voluntarily toward destruction.

### Their end is destruction, and so forth.

“For those who sow in the flesh,” says the Apostle, “will also reap corruption from the flesh.” Those who think they serve God in this way—if they eat, and the pleasures of the belly and the desires of the flesh are fulfilled—are said to have their belly as their god. They do not listen to the Prophet who says: “When you have eaten and drunk, do you not eat and drink for yourselves?” Their glory, he says, is in circumcision, in the shame—that is, in the shameful part of the body. “Those who set their minds on earthly things,” he says, are those who observe the law according to the flesh.

### But our citizenship is in heaven.

A person enslaved to earthly vices cannot say this.

### From there also we await a Savior, and so forth.

It is as though he had said: “Our head is in heaven, where we already dwell through desire. Since he is heavenly, and since he is our head, we await him coming from heaven.”

### Who will reform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body, and so forth.

He showed this, indeed, in his death, when, with wine and those drinking it, he conformed one of the dead to his body, showing an example of resurrection among the dead and the living.

### According to the operation of his power, and so forth.

It is as though he had said: “He not only strengthened us by the example of the resurrection, but also made all things subject to his body; and according to this power by which he subjected all things to himself, we understand that he can do all things and is the Son of the Almighty.”

### Therefore, my most beloved brothers.

It is as though he had said: “Because you are perfect in faith, perfect in conduct, placing your hope in the faith of Christ alone and living in a heavenly manner, I rejoice in you at the present time and will be crowned in the future.”

### I ask Euodia and I urge Syntyche to think the same thing in the Lord.

That is, to have one and the same understanding of the faith and to believe equally in the Lord.

### I also ask you, Germane, my companion.

When he says “Germane,” he uses a proper name; for the man was called Germanus. By “companion,” however, an associate in office or faith is understood.

### Help those women who labored with me in the gospel.

These women were religious and learned, and the Apostle urges Germanus to help them. When he says, “who labored with me,” “in preaching the word of faith” is understood. They taught within their own sex from house to house, but remained silent in the churches. For Paul himself removes the office of preaching from women in the Church, where he says: “Let women keep silence in the church.”

### Together with Clement and my other fellow workers.

Clement was a philosopher and a man of great learning, who later became bishop of the Roman Church.

### Whose names are in the book of life.

That is, in eternal memory. Concerning this the Psalmist says to the Lord: “Your eyes saw my unformed substance, and in your book they will all be written” (Ps. CXXXVIII). And the Lord says to the apostles: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Matt. V). Conversely, David says concerning the reprobate: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous.”

### Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice.

It is as though he had said: “Rejoice in the Lord, you who do not rejoice in worldly joy.” For blessed are those who mourn, because they will be comforted. When he repeats, “Again I say, rejoice,” this is either so that their joy may be confirmed more and more, or so that they may be strengthened in the Lord through the joy of body and soul in prosperity and adversity.

### Let your moderation be known to all people.

Let your moderation be known to Jews and Gentiles, and to all who persecute you. “Moderation” means gentleness, or modesty, or integrity. For it is written: “Let them see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

### The Lord is near; be anxious about nothing.

It is as though he had said: “Because the Lord is near those who are troubled in heart, do not be anxious about the evils that are coming upon you, since you know that God is your defender.” This can also be understood according to the Gospel: “Do not consider what you shall eat or what you shall wear. He knows what you need, and before you ask he knows it” (Matt. VI).

### But in every prayer.

That is, not with murmuring or sadness, lest, afflicted by tribulations, you murmur in some way and your prayer become unworthy of God’s ears. I urge you to do all things peacefully through prayer.

### And supplication with thanksgiving.

“Prayer” is what is offered for past sins; “supplication” is for acquiring virtues; “thanksgiving” is for God’s benefits.

### Let your petitions be made known before God.

This is not to be understood as though your petitions become known to God, who knew them even before they existed. Rather, let them become known to us before God through endurance, not before human beings through boasting. Or perhaps they are also to become known to the angels who are with God, so that they may in some manner offer them to God and consult him concerning them, and, having learned from his command what ought to be fulfilled, may bring it to us either openly or secretly as necessity requires. For the angel said to a man: “When you were praying, I offered your prayer in the presence of God’s glory.”

### And the peace of God, which surpasses every understanding, and so forth.

Whose understanding does it surpass, if not ours, or perhaps even that of the holy angels? Certainly not God’s. If, therefore, the saints and God’s angels will live by God’s peace, they will surely live in that peace which surpasses every understanding. There is no doubt that it surpasses ours. But if it also surpasses the angels, so that he seems not to have excluded even them when he says “every understanding,” we ought to understand the statement in this sense: the peace by which God himself is at peace, just as God knows it, cannot be known by us in the same way, nor by any angel.

It therefore undoubtedly surpasses every understanding—not, of course, God’s own understanding. But since we too have become participants in his peace according to our measure, we shall possess the greatest peace within ourselves, among ourselves, and with him, insofar as our highest capacity extends. In their own measure the holy angels know it; human beings, however, are now far below them, however greatly they may excel in the advancement of the mind. We must consider how great a man it was who said: “We know in part and prophesy in part, until that which is perfect comes.”

## THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER 22

“The Pharisees went away and took counsel so that they might trap him in his speech. And they sent their disciples to him with the Herodians, saying: ‘Teacher, we know that you are truthful, and teach the way of God in truth, and that you do not care about anyone. For you do not regard the person of human beings. Tell us, therefore: What do you think? Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?’ But Jesus, knowing their wickedness, said: ‘Why do you test me, hypocrites? Show me the coin of the tribute.’ And they offered him a denarius. And Jesus said to them: ‘Whose image and inscription is this?’ They said to him: ‘Caesar’s.’ Then he said to them: ‘Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.’”

### The Pharisees went away and took counsel so that they might trap him in his speech, and so forth. *(From Jerome.)*

Recently, under Caesar Augustus, Judea had been subjected to the Romans when the registration was proclaimed throughout the whole world; it had become tributary, and there was a great disturbance among the people. Some said that, for the sake of the security and peace under which the Romans served on behalf of everyone, tribute ought to be paid. The Pharisees, however, who applauded themselves for their righteousness, contended against this, saying that the people of God, who paid tithes, gave first fruits, and offered the other things written in the Law, ought not to be subject to human laws.

Caesar Augustus had appointed Herod, the son of Antipater, a foreigner and proselyte, as king over the Jews. Herod presided over the tributes and obeyed Roman authority. Therefore the Pharisees sent their disciples with the Herodians—that is, with Herod’s soldiers—or with those whom the Pharisees, mocking them because they paid tribute to the Romans, called Herodians and regarded as not devoted to divine worship. Some Latin writers absurdly think that the Herodians were those who believed Herod to be the Christ, but we nowhere read this at all.

### Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth, and that you do not care about anyone; for you do not regard the person of human beings. Tell us, therefore: What do you think? Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?

This was a flattering and fraudulent question. It provoked the respondent to fear God more than Caesar and to say that tribute ought not to be paid, so that the Herodians, hearing it immediately, might seize him as the instigator of rebellion against the Roman rulers.

### But Jesus, knowing their wickedness, said: Why do you test me, hypocrites?

The first virtue of a respondent is to recognize the mind of those questioning him, and to call them not disciples but testers. A hypocrite, therefore, is one who is one thing and pretends to be another: who acts one way in deeds but presents another through words.

### Show me the coin of the tribute; and they offered him a denarius.

Wisdom always acts wisely, so that those who test it may be refuted by their own words. “Show me,” he says, “a denarius.” A denarius is a kind of coin that was reckoned as ten coins and bore Caesar’s image.

### And Jesus said to them: Whose image and inscription is this?

Those who think that the Savior’s question expresses ignorance rather than dispensation should learn from the present passage that Jesus certainly could have known whose image was on the coin, but asked so that he might respond appropriately to their speech.

### They said to him: Caesar’s. Then he said to them: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.

We should understand “Caesar” not as Augustus, but as Tiberius, his stepson, who succeeded him and under whom the Lord also suffered. All the Roman kings, beginning with Gaius Caesar, who had seized the imperial power, were called Caesars.

When he says, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s,” let us understand this as the coin, tribute, and money; and “the things that are God’s” as tithes, first fruits, offerings, and sacrifices. In this way, he himself paid tribute for himself and Peter, while rendering to God the things that are God’s by doing the Father’s will.

*(From Bede.)* Alternatively: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” Just as Caesar requires from you the impression of his image, so does God. Just as the coin is returned to Caesar, so the soul is returned to God, illumined and marked by the light of his countenance. Hence the Psalmist says: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. IV).

This light is the whole of the human being, and the true good, which is seen not with the eyes but with the mind. He said that it was marked upon us, just as a denarius is marked with the image of the king. For the human being was made in the image and likeness of God, which he corrupted by sinning. His good, therefore, is true and eternal if, by being born again, he is marked anew.

# The Twenty-Fifth Week after Pentecost

## To the Colossians, Chapter I

> “We do not cease praying and asking for you, that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in [Col. 0506A] in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, so that you may walk worthily of God, pleasing him in all things, bearing fruit in every good work, and increasing in the knowledge of God, strengthened with every virtue according to the power of his glory, in all patience and long-suffering with joy.”

We do not cease praying and asking for you. That is, from the time we heard of your love and charity, and of the faith that you have in God, we do not cease praying that you may be filled with spiritual virtues, concerning which he continues:

That you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding. One is filled with wisdom and understanding when one knows not only the historical meaning but also the spiritual understanding.

[Col. 0506B]

So that you may walk worthily, pleasing God in all things. Those walk worthily of God who, pleasing him in all things, exercise themselves as follows.

Bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God. Here he has plainly explained what he had said above obscurely: how God grants both the will and the ability to do good, so that they may bear fruit in virtues and overcome an ingrained habit, or conquer the weakness of the mind in its passions of the flesh.

Strengthened with every virtue according to the power of his glory. That is, according to his will, so that you too may patiently endure all things as he did.

In all patience and long-suffering, with joy, in Christ Jesus, and so forth. For true long-suffering and patience must be shown where malice is exercised by someone.

## The Gospel of Matthew, Chapter IX

> “While he was saying these things to them, behold, one ruler came and worshiped him, saying: ‘Lord, my daughter has just died; but come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live.’ And Jesus rose and followed him, with his disciples. And behold, a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment. For she said within herself: ‘If I only touch his garment, I shall be saved.’ But Jesus, turning and seeing her, said: ‘Take courage, daughter; your faith has saved you.’ And the woman was saved from that hour.”

While he was saying these things to them, behold, one ruler came and worshiped him, saying: “Lord, my daughter has just died, but come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live.” And Jesus rose and followed him, with his disciples. This is the eighth sign, in which the ruler asks that his daughter be raised, unwilling to be excluded from the mystery of true circumcision. But a woman suffering from an issue of blood enters between them and is healed in the eighth place, so that the ruler’s daughter, excluded from this number, may come to the ninth, according to what is said in the Psalm: “Ethiopia shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God” (Psalm LXVII), and: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans XI).

(From Primas.) The ruler of the synagogue is most suitably understood as Moses himself; hence, according to Luke, he is properly called Jairus, that is, “illuminating” or “illumined.” For he who received the words of life to give to us, and through them illumines others, is himself illumined by the Holy Spirit, so that he may write or teach life-giving admonitions. According to Luke, he had an only daughter, that is, the synagogue, which, formed by legal instruction alone, was as though born as Moses’ only child. At about the twelfth year of her age—that is, as the time of puberty approached—she was dying, because, nobly raised by the prophets, after she had reached the age of understanding, and after she ought to have borne spiritual fruits for God, she suddenly became overwhelmed by the sickness of error and hopelessly abandoned the paths of spiritual life. And unless Christ came to her aid, she would have fallen entirely into a terrible death.

And behold, a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years came up behind him and touched him, and so forth. In the Gospel according to Luke it is written that the ruler’s daughter was twelve years old. Observe, therefore, that this woman—that is, the people of the Gentiles—began to suffer at the time when the Jewish nation came to believe. For unless vice is shown by comparison with virtues, it is not recognized. This woman, suffering from a flow of blood, does not come to the Lord in a house or in a city, because according to the Law she was excluded from cities. Rather, she comes to the Lord as he walks along the road, so that while he proceeds toward one person, another may be healed. Hence the Apostles also say: “It was necessary for us to preach the word to you, but since you have judged yourselves unworthy of salvation, we are turning to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII).

For she said within herself: “If I only touch his garment, I shall be saved.” The Church approaches the Lord and touches him because she draws near through the truth of faith. She approaches behind him or beside him—that is, in accordance with what he himself says: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John XII); and elsewhere it is commanded: “You shall walk after the Lord your God.” Or else this is because, not seeing the Lord present in the flesh, after the mysteries of his temporal dispensation had been completed, she has already begun through faith to follow in his footsteps.

She touches the fringe of his garment and stops the flow of blood, because blessed—and truly in need of cleansing—is the one who touches even the edge of the word with the hand of faith. For very few are so worthy as to recline upon his breast or to anoint his head with precious nard; yet great also was the one who said that he was unworthy to carry his sandals, and great too was she who deserved to anoint his feet and wipe them with her hair.

But Jesus, turning and seeing her, said: “Take courage, daughter; your faith has saved you,” and the woman was saved, and so forth. (From Jerome.) He calls her “daughter” because her faith has saved her. He did not say, “Your faith will save you,” but “Your faith has saved you”: because you have believed in me, you have already been saved.

# On the Feast of Saint Andrew

## The Epistle of Blessed Paul the Apostle to the Romans, Chapter X

> “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. For Scripture says: ‘Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.’ For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, rich toward all who call upon him. For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved. How then will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how will they believe him whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without a preacher? And how will they preach unless they are sent, as it is written: ‘How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, of those who proclaim good things!’ But not all obey the Gospel. For Isaiah says: ‘Lord, who has believed our report?’ Therefore faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ. But I ask: Have they not heard? Indeed, ‘Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.’”

For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. (From Origen.) Whoever truly and not falsely confesses the Lord Jesus with his mouth also believes and confesses him with his heart. He must be subject to wisdom, righteousness, truth, and everything that Christ is, and must no longer allow mammon to rule him—that is, he must no longer allow greed, injustice, immodesty, or falsehood to rule him. For once the soul has confessed Jesus Christ as Lord, it must serve none of these.

For Scripture says, and so forth. This is said in Isaiah: “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame” (Isaiah XXIII). But everyone who sins is put to shame, just as Adam sinned, became ashamed, and hid himself. Whoever still incurs the shame of sin does not appear to believe.

For there is no distinction, and so forth. There is, he says, no distinction between Jews and Greeks, since it is clear that all were previously under sin, and that all who now believe have been saved through faith in Jesus Christ. The righteousness of God, coming through Christ to all who believe, whether they are Jews or Gentiles, cleanses them from their former crimes, justifies them, and makes them capable of the glory of God.

For the same Lord, and so forth. If righteousness, truth, wisdom, and sanctification—which altogether is Christ—rule over us, then the Lord becomes rich toward us in all things. For these are his riches, since in him are hidden the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. Yet he did not say that he bestows these riches upon all people, but upon all who call upon his name. For not everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord can be saved; rather, the one who performs works worthy of invocation will himself be saved.

(From the Vulgate.) He says: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth.” Here there is the tetragrammaton, which the Hebrews say designates the ineffable name of God. In another passage it is written: “They will call upon me, and I will not answer them.” Here, however, the statement is made absolutely: “Whoever calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.” Unless, in this invocation, we understand that a sincere invocation is intended—that is, one expressed with humility of heart, in which God is invoked together with confession of the true doctrine.

How then will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? The Jews did not believe in Christ, and therefore they do not call upon him in whom they did not believe. For what he says above—“Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord”—he taught must be referred to Christ the Lord. Enos, Moses, Aaron, and Samuel also called upon the Lord, and he himself heard them. Without doubt they called upon Christ Jesus. And if calling upon the name of the Lord and praying to the Lord are one and the same thing, then just as Christ is invoked, so Christ must be prayed to; and just as we offer prayers first of all to God the Father, so also to the Lord Jesus Christ; and just as we offer petitions to the Father, so we offer petitions to the Son; and just as we offer thanksgiving to God, so we render thanks to the Savior. For divine Scripture teaches that one honor is to be given to both, Father and Son, when it says: “Let all honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (John V).

Or how will they believe him whom they have not heard? We can understand this either of the Lord himself, while he was present in the flesh, or of his Apostles preaching about him, whom they were unwilling to hear. For the Lord himself says: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke X). It can also be understood in this way: even now and always Christ, as the Word and Reason, speaks in each person’s heart, teaching piety and urging righteousness. He testifies concerning chastity, purity, and all the virtues together, just as he himself says: “My sheep hear my voice.”

And how will they hear without a preacher? In this he more clearly shows that Christ is heard through the speech of preachers, in whom, according to what we said above, Christ is shown to speak and teach.

And how will they preach unless they are sent? A difficulty seems to arise for me in this statement. For if we understand it to mean that they do not preach because they are not sent, and that without a preacher they will not hear, and not believing they will not call upon him, and not calling upon him they will not be saved, it follows that the cause of their not being saved must be attributed to the fault of the one who did not send preachers. But let us turn instead toward the interpretation that preserves the more correct path of understanding.

When he says, “How will they preach unless they are sent?” let us understand him as though the Apostle were saying: “We, the heralds and preachers of Christ, cannot preach, nor would any power of announcing remain with us, unless he himself who sent us were present with us. But if you are unwilling to hear us when we preach, the fault is now yours. And if, though hearing, you do not believe; and though not believing, you do not call upon him; and though not calling upon him, you cannot be saved—then, because they have been sent for preaching, it is concerning those who have been sent by him that it is written:

How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim good things. Those are beautiful and comely feet that walk along the road of life. According to him who said, “I am the way,” understand as beautiful and comely the feet of those who proclaim the Gospel, who deserve to walk along such a way (Isaiah LII). These are the feet concerning which he says that he has run the course, and that he runs so as to obtain—that is, the vigor of the soul by which one strives and prepares oneself for heaven. You will also properly understand these feet to be firm, the feet that Jesus washes for his disciples and dries with the towel with which he is girded.

Although the word “evangelize” itself means “to announce good things,” the good things are understood to be those announced by the holy Trinity to the Apostles, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For this is what the Evangelists announce according to the Lord’s command: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew, at the end).

But not all obey the Gospel. Not all among the Gentiles believed the Gospel, nor did all among Israel; nevertheless, more—and far more among the Gentiles than among Israel—believed.

But Isaiah says: “Lord, who has believed our report?” “Who?” is said because of the rarity; yet Isaiah seems to prophesy these words from the person of the Apostles, to whom the office of preaching had been entrusted. They themselves, observing the rarity of those who believed, especially among the people of Israel, said to the Lord: “Lord, who has believed our report?”

Therefore faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ. Here “the word of Christ” signifies the whole preaching concerning Christ. For not only those who heard the word from the Lord himself believed; there are many more who heard when others preached him, just as the Lord himself says: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.” Thus every word that the Apostles, and anyone else who preached Christ, proclaimed, this Apostle declares to be the word of Christ.

But I ask: Have they not heard? Indeed, “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” This is taken from the Psalm, where it says: “There are no speeches or words whose voices are not heard” (Psalm XIX). In this passage the Gentiles are undoubtedly understood through the variety of languages and speeches.

It should be observed that sound has gone out into the earth, while not sound but words have reached the ends of the world. By “earth” in this passage he means unskilled and unteachable people, to whom not words—in which the reasoning of faith and the exposition of wisdom are contained—but the sound of faith, while it remains simple preaching, has reached. By “the ends of the world” he means the more learned and prudent. For “the end” indicates the perfection of things. To such people, therefore, he declares that not merely voices but words and reason have reached.

[Col. 0510D]

## The Gospel of Matthew, Chapter IV

> “As Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. And he said to them: ‘Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men.’ Immediately they left their nets and followed him. And going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in a boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them. Immediately they left their nets and their father and followed him.”

As Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee. (From Eucherius.) Because of the neighboring regions, this sea is called by many names: the Sea of Galilee, Lake Chinnereth, the Lake of Gennesaret, the Sea of Tiberias, the Salt Lake, and others.

He saw two brothers, Simon who is called Peter, and so forth. Why are they called fishermen? So that no one might think that the word of God spread more widely through the eloquence of preachers. It is not the sons of kings or scribes who are first recorded as being called, but fishermen.

(From Jerome.) Fishermen and uneducated men are sent to preach, lest the faith of believers should be thought to arise not through the power of God but through eloquence and learning.

(From Fulgentius.) They are called in pairs and sent in pairs, appropriately. For Scripture says: “Woe to the one who is alone, because when he falls he has no one to lift him up.” There is, in fact, a twofold teaching: love of God and love of neighbor. Filled with this, they preach the good Testament, that is, of the Law and of the Gospel.

For they were fishermen, and he said to them, and so forth. (From Origen.) It seems to me that it did not happen by chance that Peter and Andrew and the sons of Zebedee were found to be fishermen by trade. Paul, however, was by trade a tentmaker. Those men, called from the art of catching fish, are changed and become fishers of men when the Lord says: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men.” There is no doubt that Paul too, because he was called as an Apostle by my Lord Jesus Christ, was changed through a similar transformation of his trade: just as they were changed from fishermen of fish into fishers of men, so he was transferred from making earthly tents to constructing heavenly tabernacles.

For Paul constructs heavenly tabernacles by teaching each person the way of salvation and showing the road to blessed dwellings in heaven. Paul makes tabernacles when, filling the Gospel of God from Jerusalem and all around as far as Illyricum, he constructs churches; in this way he too makes tabernacles.

And going on from there, and so forth. (From Fulgentius.) At first a person casts the nets of his desire into the sea of this age, in order to catch dead works as though they were fish. But Christ comes mercifully and, through compunction of spirit, changes the former instruments, so that, casting once again the net of good desire into the sea of the world, he may bring fish of good virtues in the vessel of the flesh to the harbor of life, leaving behind the fugitive devil—for this is the interpretation of Zebedee.

The four names of the Apostles signify two peoples. Simon is interpreted as “obedient,” while Peter is interpreted as “recognizing”; he signifies the Jewish people, who first obeyed the Lord’s commands and recognized their Creator. James, whose name is interpreted as “supplanter,” signifies the same people. Andrew is interpreted as “manly”; he signifies the people of the Gentiles, who act manfully in the faith of Christ. John, whose name is interpreted as “the grace of the Lord,” signifies the same people. For the Gentiles were saved by the grace of God.

These four names are also contained in the character of each individual: Simon is present in obeying God; Peter in recognizing one’s sin; Andrew in manfully enduring hardships; James in supplanting the vices of the flesh; and John in receiving the grace of God.

Alternatively, these four names are to be understood as the four principal virtues. A person is obedient when he possesses the prudence to recognize sins. He is manly when he has acquired temperance for enduring labor. He is a supplanter when he has received the fortitude to conquer vices. He has the grace of God when he has found true righteousness for fulfilling the commandments.

# The Readings for the Advent of the Lord Begin

## The Fourth Week before the Nativity of the Lord, that is, the First Sunday of Advent

## To the Romans, Chapter XIII

[Col. 0512B]

> “Knowing that it is already time for us to rise from sleep. For now our salvation is nearer than when we believed. The night has passed, but the day has drawn near. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. Let us walk honorably as in the day, not in revelries and drunkenness, not in beds and immodesties, not in strife and rivalry, but put on the Lord Jesus Christ.”

Knowing that it is already time for us to rise from sleep. (From Origen.) There are souls, eyes, ears, hands, feet, and so forth. We say that each of these is not a bodily member but a virtue, by which one must be moved toward each task. Thus the soul’s sleep is understood according to its eyes. For if it does not do what belongs to God at the proper time but grows sluggish through idleness, it is rightly said to sleep.
