Therefore Paul, the herald of Christ, traveling throughout the world, announces that the light has already arrived for those lying in the sleep of idleness, and that it is time to rise from sleep and leave behind the time of ignorance.

For now our salvation is nearer than when we believed. Our salvation—that is, the future life in heaven—draws nearer each day as the days decline. The periods that have passed increase, while those that remain are undoubtedly reduced; therefore our salvation becomes nearer every day. This is our redemption, which is everlasting life, concerning which the Lord also says: “Lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near” (Luke XXI).

The night has passed, but the day has drawn near. By night he means the time when ignorance ruled over humanity. By day he names the time when, with darkness diminished, the knowledge of truth arrived through the coming of the sun of righteousness. Or night is unbelief, while light is faith. Or night is the present world until the judgment, while day is the time after the end of the age.

It must be understood, however, that the coming of this light and day can be taken in two ways: generally, for all, and specifically, for each individual. Generally, when the day of the future age arrives, in comparison with which the span of this present world is called darkness. Individually, when Christ is in a person’s heart and makes it day for him, whereas ignorance generates darkness for him.

Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light, so that we may walk honorably as in the day. The works of darkness are those actions that are alien to God, which are called works of the flesh in those who have surrendered their flesh to luxury and immodesty rather than to holiness and the Lord. The armor of light is the assumption of all the virtues, in which we walk honorably and confidently as in the day.

Not in revelries and drunkenness. A revelry is a contribution to a common table. Or revelries are dishonorable and luxurious banquets, accompanied by the vilest drunkenness.

Not in beds and immodesties. “Beds” are so called from foul lying together; such behavior seems suited not so much to rational human beings as to wild animals and beasts. Immodesty means irreligion and shameful conduct without restraint.

Not in strife and rivalry. What he mentioned above are vices of the flesh; these are vices of the soul. Nevertheless, all are called works of the flesh and of darkness, because strife and rivalry truly belong to those who live according to the flesh and walk in darkness. Whoever is in the light and walks honorably as in the day does nothing through strife or empty glory. Here rivalry is understood as envy.

But put on the Lord Jesus Christ. He now explains what he said above: let us put on the armor of light. Christ becomes the armor of light for all his saints. We have often said that Christ is wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, truth, and all the virtues. Whoever assumes these is said to have put on Christ. For if Christ is all these things, necessarily whoever possesses these things also possesses Christ.

## The Gospel of Matthew, Chapter XXI

> “When they drew near Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples, saying to them: ‘Go into the village that is opposite you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me. And if anyone says anything to you, say: “The Lord has need of them,” and immediately he will let them go.’ Now all this happened so that what had been spoken through the Prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Tell the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, gentle, sitting upon a donkey and a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.’ The disciples went and did as Jesus commanded them. They brought the donkey and the colt, placed their garments upon them, and made him sit upon them. Very many from the crowd spread their garments on the road. Others were cutting branches from the trees and spreading them on the road. The crowds that went before and those that followed were crying out, saying: ‘Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’”

When they drew near Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives. (From Jerome.) Bethphage is interpreted as “house of the mouth” or “house of the jaws,” because it was a village of the priests. It bore the type of confession and was situated on the Mount of Olives, where there is the light of knowledge and rest from labors and sorrows.

Then Jesus sent two disciples, saying to them. (From Bede.) It is not without reason that he mentions two disciples sent to bring the animals to the Lord. The two orders of preachers are understood: one among the Gentiles and the other among the circumcision. They are rightly sent as two, either because of knowledge of the truth and purity of action, or because the mystery of the twofold love—of God and of neighbor—was to be preached throughout the whole world.

Go into the village that is opposite you. (From Jerome.) It was opposite the Apostles and unwilling to accept the yoke of instruction. These disciples who were sent signify teachers, destined by their preaching to penetrate the unlearned and barbarous places of the whole world, like the walls of a village set opposite them.

And immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her; untie them and bring them to me. As the holy preachers entered the world, they found the people of the nations entangled in the bonds of unbelief. Each person was bound by the cords of his own sins, and not only the nations but also the Jews, for all had sinned and lacked the glory of God.

The donkey, which is subject to the yoke and domesticated, signifies the synagogue, which had borne the yoke of the Law. The wild and free colt of the donkey signifies the people of the nations, upon whom no human being had yet sat, because none of the rational teachers had placed upon them the bridle of correction—one that would restrain the tongue from evil or compel them to enter the narrow way of life. No one had imparted to the people of the nations the garments of salvation by which they might be warmed spiritually, persuading them toward what was useful. A human being would have sat upon that colt if someone using reason had corrected it by suppressing its foolishness.

And if anyone says anything to you, say: “The Lord has need of them,” and immediately he will let them go. In Luke it is written that “their owners said to them: ‘Why are you untying the colt?’” This is entirely appropriate. For it had many owners, since it was not devoted to one doctrine or superstition, but was miserably dragged about according to the will of unclean spirits into various and diverse errors, moving toward mute idols wherever it was led.

Now all this happened so that what had been spoken through the Prophet might be fulfilled, saying: “Tell the daughter of Zion,” and so forth. This is written in the prophet Zechariah: “Daughter of Zion” (Zechariah IX). Historically, he means the whole of Jerusalem, or Zion, which was situated on the citadel. Spiritually, however, it signifies the holy Church, to which Christ deigned to come.

When he says, “Your king,” it is as though he says: not a stranger, not a foreigner, but your own—gentle, that is, not fierce or savage like the others. For he himself says concerning himself: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matthew XI).

The disciples went and did as Jesus commanded them, and they brought the donkey and the colt. Those who had opposed the untying of the colt fell silent when they heard the Lord’s name. They had resisted the teachers who came for the salvation of the nations and defended their own darkness until, through the testimony of miracles, the power of the true possessor and Lord shone forth. After the power of the Lord’s sovereignty appeared, the complaints of the adversaries gave way, and the free assembly of believers was brought to God, whom it would carry in its heart.

And they placed their garments upon them, and made him sit upon them. The garments of the Apostles may be understood as instruction in virtues, exposition of the Scriptures, or certainly the various teachings of the churches. With these he covers human hearts, previously naked and cold, so that they may become worthy of Christ as their possessor.

Very many from the crowd spread their garments on the road. While the donkey carries the Lord, many spread their garments on the road, because the holy martyrs, stripping themselves of the covering of their own flesh, prepare the road with their blood for the simpler servants of God, so that they may proceed with unhindered step in their minds toward the walls of the heavenly city, where Jesus is led.

Likewise, our Savior travels toward Jerusalem seated upon the little donkey whenever the soul of an individual believer, guiding its own beast, leads it toward the peace of inward vision. He also does so when he presides universally over the holy Church, which he sets aflame with desire for heavenly peace. Many spread their garments on the road because they subdue their bodies through abstinence, either to prepare his way to God or to offer good examples to those who follow.

Others were cutting branches from the trees and spreading them on the road. Those cut leaves or branches from trees who gather words and sayings from the Fathers and teachers in the instruction of truth, and submit these on the road of God to the mind of the listener through humble preaching.

The crowds that went before and those that followed were crying out, and so forth. The Jewish people went before, while the Gentile people followed. Since all the elect—whether those who could be in Judea or those who now exist in the Church—believed in the mediator between God and humanity, both those who went before and those who followed cried out “Hosanna.”

“Hosanna” means “savior” in the Latin language. From him those who came before sought salvation, and those who are present now seek it; and they confess that he who comes in the name of the Lord is blessed, because there is one hope and one faith among the peoples who precede and those who follow.

# The Third Week before the Nativity of the Lord

[Col. 0515D]

## That is, the Second Sunday of Advent

## The Epistle of Blessed Paul the Apostle to the Romans, Chapter XV

> “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction, so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope. May the God of patience and consolation grant you to think the same thing among yourselves according to Jesus Christ, so that with one mind and one mouth you may honor God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore receive one another, just as Christ also received you, for the honor of God. For I say that Jesus Christ became a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers. But the Gentiles are to honor God for his mercy, as it is written: ‘Therefore I will confess to you among the Gentiles and sing to your name.’ And again he says: ‘Rejoice, Gentiles, with his people.’ And again: ‘Praise the Lord, all Gentiles, and magnify him, all peoples.’ And again Isaiah says: ‘There shall be a root of Jesse, and he who rises to rule the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles will hope.’ May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope and in the power of the Holy Spirit.”

Whatever things were written were written for our instruction. (From Origen.) It was written for our sake that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman, so that we might know that these are allegorically the two Testaments.

It was written for our sake that the people ate manna and drank water from the rock, so that we might understand that they drank spiritual food and drink. They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them. The rock was Christ. These things and similar ones were written for our instruction; they were revealed through the coming of the Savior. Whoever understands what was written will undoubtedly find what follows: that through the wisdom and consolation of the Scriptures we may have hope in God. The one who neither believes nor understands the Scriptures cannot have this hope.

May the God of patience and consolation grant you to think the same thing among yourselves according to Jesus Christ. This is a great blessing of God: that all may think and feel as one, and that each person may wish for his neighbor what he wishes for himself. The grace of unanimity is of great value. Hence the Savior says: “If two or three agree together on anything, whatever they ask from God will be done for them” (Matthew XVIII).

The Jews say concerning those who are called the sons of Korah in the Psalter, whose names are found in Exodus—namely, Assyr, interpreted as “instruction”; Elkanah, interpreted as “possession of God”; and Abiasaph, interpreted as “assembly of the father”—that when their father sinned, they separated themselves from the wicked assembly together with Dathan and Abiram. Separated from them, they poured out prayers to God with one accord and were heard. They merited not only pardon for their punishment but also the grace of prophecy. God further granted them that they should not be ordered to prophesy anything sorrowful. Therefore all the Psalms bearing their names contain nothing sorrowful against sinners or anything harsh. We have brought this forward to show how great unanimity is.

So that with one mind and one mouth you may honor God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. One mouth is said to exist wherever one and the same meaning and speech proceed through all who are diverse. Since it can happen that some agree with one another in evil and think alike for the worse, he therefore added: “according to Jesus Christ.”

Therefore receive one another, just as Christ also received you, for the honor of God. He refers to the passage where, because of differing opinions concerning clean and unclean foods, they were disagreeing with one another, as though he were saying: Do not judge anything concerning the uncleanness of animals, just as Christ reckoned the uncleannesses of believers. He covered no one’s offense and imputed sin to no one, but received all for the honor of God. Those whom Christ received he teaches to act in such a way that, seeing their good works, people may glorify the Father who is in heaven.

I say that Christ Jesus became a minister of the circumcision for the sake of God’s truth, to confirm the promises made to the fathers. This can be understood in two ways: either that he himself received circumcision in his flesh, so that, coming from the seed of Abraham, he might fulfill in himself what had been promised to the fathers; or that he is said to have been, in his flesh, a minister of circumcision. Concerning this the same Apostle says: “It is not the one who is a Jew openly, nor is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh, but the one who is a Jew inwardly, and circumcision of the heart, which takes place by the Spirit, not by the letter; his praise is not from human beings (Romans 2), but from God.” Through this kind of circumcision it is certain that the promises made to the fathers have been fulfilled.

But the Gentiles are to honor God because of his mercy. They should do so because God has freely granted them mercy; for the one to whom more is forgiven ought to love more.

As it is written: “Therefore I will confess to you among the Gentiles, and I will sing to your name.” *(From Primasius.)* He removes the Jews’ arrogance while teaching that the salvation of the Gentiles had been foretold, although it had not been announced to them personally: Christ confesses among the Gentiles. And again he says:

“Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and magnify him, all you peoples.” This is the voice of the apostles, summoning the newly baptized people, as though he were saying: “All you Gentiles who, having abandoned your idols, have approached God through faith, praise him.” Hence David says: “Magnify him, all you peoples,” and he exhorts those who had been converted from the Jews. This was proclaimed by the title that Pilate placed above the cross, written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—that is, “King of the Jews.”

And again Isaiah says: “There shall be a root of Jesse, and he who rises to rule the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles will hope.” For Jesse is interpreted in our language as “he is to me.” Therefore, at Christ’s coming, everyone who believes in him appropriately says: “He is to me”—as though he were saying: “The one of whom Moses said, ‘He who is’ has sent me to you—he is to me; that is, I believe in him. And he is the one who arose from the root of Jesse, and in him the Gentiles will hope.”

Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope and in the power of the Holy Spirit. Since above he had said, “In him the Gentiles will hope,” he gratefully joins this to it: “the God of hope.” If the earlier passage had read, “In him the Gentiles believe,” he would undoubtedly have added, “the God of faith.” But because he placed the Gentiles in relation to hoping, he therefore invokes the God of hope upon those who hope in him, and prays that the gift of blessing bestowed upon them may be increased. This blessing is that they may be filled with all joy and all peace, which is rightly understood of Christ, who by his blood made peace not only among the things on earth but also among those in heaven. What it means to be filled with all joy and peace seems difficult to explain. The peace of believers in hope must concern the future, where perpetual joy and secure peace remain; the abundance of hope, however, consists in virtues.

# THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER 21

> “There will be signs in sun and moon and stars, and on earth distress of nations because of the bewilderment caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves, while people wither from fear and expectation of what is coming upon the whole world. For the powers of heaven will be shaken. And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty. But when these things begin to happen, look up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.” And he told them a comparison: “Look at the fig tree and all the trees. When they now put forth fruit from themselves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near. Amen I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all things happen. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.”

“There will be signs in sun and moon and stars, and on earth distress of nations because of the bewilderment caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves.” When he says, “There will be signs in sun and moon and stars,” he indicates, as it were by a herald, the forerunners of that approaching judgment. Among these is the prophet’s saying: “The sun will be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes” (Joel 2). Likewise, what Luke says, “and on earth distress of nations,” I think is the very thing that Matthew, describing the times of Antichrist, says: “For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor will be.” But Luke’s addition, “because of the bewilderment caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves,” heralds what John saw: that, among the other changing things of the age, the sea would have its place.

“While people wither from fear and expectation of what is coming upon the whole world; for the powers of heaven will be shaken.” I believe that this sentence denotes the very coming of the Judge, when, according to the parable in another passage, all—the wise and the foolish virgins alike—awakened by an unusual cry, trim their lamps; that is, they reckon up the works they have with them, for which, in the greatest fear, they await the event of the eternal judgment now and immediately impending. Therefore, when fear comes upon the whole world and expectation of a strict examination, many who seemed to flourish in this world, when they see themselves without fruit, will wither. Then faith which had lived without works will fade, tested by the fire of the just Judge.

“And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty.” *(From Gregory.)* They will see in great power and majesty him whom, while he was placed in humility, they refused to hear, so that they may then feel his power more strictly, in proportion as they now refuse to bend the neck of their heart to his patience. But because these words have been said against the reprobate, the discourse immediately turns to the consolation of the elect. For it adds:

“But when these things begin to happen, look up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.” “When,” he says, “the plagues of the world become frequent, when the terror of judgment is displayed by the shaking of the powers, raise your heads”—that is, make your hearts glad—“because, while the world of which you are not friends is ending, the redemption you have sought draws near.” To raise one’s heads, then, is altogether to lift our minds to the joys of the heavenly homeland. The Lord further shows, by a provident comparison, that the world ought to be trodden underfoot and despised. For it follows:

“And he told them a comparison: ‘Look at the fig tree and all the trees. When they now put forth fruit from themselves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near.’” He plainly teaches, therefore, that just as the coming summer is recognized from the fruit of trees, so the kingdom of God is known to be near from the ruin of the world. These words surely show that the fruit of the world is its ruin. For it grows in order to fall; it buds in order that whatever it has budded may be consumed by disasters. The kingdom of God is rightly compared to summer, because then the clouds of our sorrow pass away and the days of eternal life shine with the brightness of the sun. All these things are confirmed with great certainty when the sentence is added which says:

“Amen I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all things happen.” *(From Bede.)* What the Lord thus declares carries great weight; it is, so to speak—if it is permitted to say so—his oath: “Amen I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all things happen.” By “generation” he means either the whole human race or, particularly, the Jews.

“Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.” We must understand the heaven that will pass away to be not the ethereal or starry heaven, but the aerial heaven, from which both “birds of heaven” and “clouds of heaven” take their name. But if heaven and earth will pass away, one may wonder how Ecclesiastes says, “A generation passes away and a generation comes, but the earth stands forever” (Ecclesiastes 1). Yet the explanation is clear: heaven and earth pass away in the form they now possess, but they continue to subsist without end in their essence. For “the form of this world passes away.” And the angel says to John: “There will be,” he says, “a new heaven and a new earth.” These are not to be created as other things, but these very things are renewed. Heaven and earth, therefore, both will pass away and will be, because they will be cleansed by fire from the form they now have, yet will always be preserved in their own nature.

# THE SECOND WEEK BEFORE THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD, THAT IS, THE THIRD SUNDAY OF ADVENT

## THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER 4

> “Let a person regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Here now it is required among stewards that someone be found faithful. But to me it is a very small matter that I should be judged by you or by a human day. Nor do I judge myself, for I am conscious of nothing against myself; but I am not thereby justified. The one who judges me is the Lord. Therefore do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the counsels of hearts. And then each person’s praise will come from God.”

“Let a person regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God.” That is, not as Christ’s equals. This means that you should not honor even the apostles with excessive praise—not to mention false apostles—as he said elsewhere: “Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” For a human being is the minister of baptism, but God is its author, as we read: “The one upon whom you see the dove descending—he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1).

“Here now it is required among stewards that someone be found faithful.” This is the voice of one asking a question: “Here it is required”—that is, in the present age. You now suppose that you can judge human consciences. When he says “it is required,” the words “by human beings” are understood: “that someone be found faithful?” This may refer either to the one who is sent or to those to whom he is sent, so that he may be found a faithful and wise servant. Alternatively, it is as though he were saying: “Here perhaps someone among the stewards presumes to exalt their merits and has dared, before the time of judgment, to judge consciences.”

“But to me it is a very small matter that I should be judged by you or by a human day; nor do I judge myself, for I am conscious of nothing against myself.” When he says, “To me it is a very small matter,” it is as though he said, “It is nothing to me that I should be judged by you.” He called it human judgment because truth and justice are frequently frustrated in it. By “a human day” he meant the revelation brought about by human judgment: “Nor do I judge myself,” he says—that is, “I do not condemn myself, because I know of no evil in myself, nor am I conscious of any.” Alternatively: “To me it is a very small matter”—that is, it is of no consequence to me to be something merely because of a human day, that is, because I am captivated by human praise or favor. Thus it is written: “I did not desire the day of man”—that is, I did not seek the consolation whose pleasantness can captivate a carnal mind. “Nor do I judge myself”—that is, I do not declare myself to possess any merit, because I place greater trust in my conscience than in praise arising from another person’s evaluation. *(From Augustine.)* When can I judge my own conscience? When will I be able to examine the disposition with which I do whatever I do? To the extent that human beings can judge another, a person can certainly judge himself more; but God judges a person more deeply than a person judges himself. For a human being sees the face, but God sees the heart.

“But I am not thereby justified.” That is, not at this time—or, even if I have committed no crime, it does not follow that I have not sinned. If Paul says this, what should we say, who are far removed from his merits? Alternatively: “I am not thereby justified”—that is, even this does not contribute to my righteousness, if I refuse to be praised because I know myself unworthy of praise.

“The one who judges me is the Lord.” It is as though he were saying: All these things, which a person believes he can establish by the judgment of his own estimation, must be reserved for divine judgment. God knows how to judge not only deeds but also thoughts (Ecclesiastes 2).

“Therefore do not judge before the time,” and so forth. That is, do not pass judgment concerning a person’s praise before the time of judgment, because it is written: “Do not praise a person during his lifetime.”

“And then each person’s praise will come from God.” Here he clearly shows that he is speaking about human praise, when he says that the truth of a person’s merits consists in God’s praise alone. The truly praiseworthy person is the one whom God praises, for he knows all hidden and unseen things.

## THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER 11

> “When John heard in prison about the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples and said to him: ‘Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?’ And Jesus answered them: ‘Go and report to John what you have heard and seen: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, the poor are evangelized. And blessed is the one who is not scandalized by me.’ As they were departing, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John: ‘What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? But what did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses. But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. This is the one of whom it is written: Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’”

“When John heard in prison about the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples and said to him: ‘Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?’” *(From Bede.)* “The one who is to come”—that is, the one whom the prophets proclaimed would come. He does not say, “Are you the one who has come?” but, “Are you the one who is to come?” The meaning is: “Send word to me—since I am to be killed by Herod and descend to the underworld—whether I must announce you there also, having announced you to those above, or whether it is unfitting for the Son of God to taste death and whether you are going to send another for these mysteries.”

“And Jesus answered them: ‘Go and report to John what you have seen and heard: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, the poor are evangelized, and blessed is the one who is not scandalized by me.’” *(From Fulgentius.)* They heard one set of things and saw another: they heard that the deaf were hearing and that the poor were being evangelized, while they saw the blind seeing, the lame walking, and the lepers cleansed.

“Report to John,” and so forth. It is as though he were saying: “Tell John that I am the one of whom the prophet said: ‘God himself will come and save us’ (Isaiah 35). The blind see, so that the prophetic word may be fulfilled: ‘Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened.’ The lame walk, so that this may be fulfilled: ‘Then the lame man shall leap like a stag.’ The deaf hear, so that this may be fulfilled: ‘And the ears of the deaf shall be opened.’

“Spiritually, John signifies the Law. Therefore John in prison signifies the Law bound among the Jews. He sent two scribes and Pharisees: ‘Are you the Law?’ it asks Christ, so that he may proclaim it. Jesus answered: ‘The blind see,’ as though he were saying: ‘That time has come when the blind, who previously did not see the sun of righteousness, now see it.’ The saying ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’ is fulfilled in them.

“And the lame, who clung to earthly things and thought very little about heavenly things, now run through the humility of gentleness toward the land of the living, so that this may be fulfilled in them: ‘Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land.’

“And the lepers, who languished under the immense burden of their vices, now receive consolation through repentance, so that this may be fulfilled in them: ‘Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.’

“And the deaf, who had no ears with which to hear, now drink in righteousness through the ears of their hearts, so that this may be fulfilled in them: ‘Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.’

“And those who were previously dead to God and alive to the world now, through repentance, take pity on their souls and live, so that this may be fulfilled in them: ‘Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.’

“And those who were previously poor in virtues are filled with the Holy Spirit and evangelize, so that it may be said of them: ‘How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of those who evangelize peace, who evangelize good things’ (Isaiah 52).”

“And blessed is the one who is not scandalized.” *(From Gregory.)* What, then, does it mean to say, “Blessed is the one who is not scandalized by me,” except that, in clear language, he signifies the rejection and humility of his death? It is as though he plainly said: “I certainly perform wondrous things, but I do not disdain to endure things that are rejected, because by dying I follow the same path.” People must be very careful not to despise death in me while venerating my signs.

“As they were departing, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John: ‘What did you go out into the wilderness to see?’” and so forth. He introduced this not by asserting but by denying it. A reed, as soon as a breeze touches it, bends to one side or the other. What, then, is signified by the reed except a carnal mind, which, as soon as it is touched by praise or criticism, inclines in any direction?

If the breeze of human praise blows from human lips, such a mind becomes cheerful, is exalted, and bends itself entirely, as it were, toward that side. But if the wind of criticism bursts forth from the place whence the breeze of praise had come, it immediately bends, as though toward the opposite side, toward the force of anger. John was not a reed shaken by the wind, because neither favor made him complacent nor anyone’s anger made him harsh; prosperity could not lift him up, nor adversity bend him.

“But what did you go out to see—a man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses.” John is described as being clothed in camel’s hair. Those who avoid enduring harsh things for God, but devote themselves only to external matters and are softened by the present life, seeking pleasure, belong not to a heavenly kingdom but to an earthly one. Let no one suppose that sin is absent from luxury and devotion to clothing; for if this were not a fault, the Lord would never have praised John for the harshness of his clothing.

Although the statement that John was not dressed in soft clothing can also be understood symbolically. He was not dressed in soft clothing because he did not nurture the life of sinners with flattering words, but rebuked it with the force of harsh denunciation, saying: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matthew 3).

“But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.” The ministry of prophets is to speak of things to come, but not also to point them out. John, therefore, is more than a prophet, because he both prophesied beforehand about the one who would come and announced him by pointing him out.

“This is the one of whom it is written: ‘I send my angel before your face, who prepared your way before you.’” In Greek, ἄγγελος (*angelos*) is called *angelus* in Latin, “messenger.” Rightly, therefore, the one who is sent to announce the heavenly Judge is called an angel, so that the name may preserve the dignity which his activity fulfills. It is another name, certainly, but he is not inferior in the dignity of his life.

All who are counted among the priesthood are also called angels, as the prophet attests when he says: “The lips of a priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.” Moreover, every believer, insofar as he is able and insofar as he receives the grace of heavenly inspiration, becomes an angel when he recalls his neighbor from wickedness, takes care to exhort him to good works, or announces eternal kingdom or punishment to one who has gone astray, as he applies the words of holy admonition.

# THE FIRST WEEK BEFORE THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD, THAT IS, THE FOURTH SUNDAY OF ADVENT

## THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE PHILIPPIANS, CHAPTER 3

> “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice.”

For an exposition of this epistle, see the twenty-fourth week after Pentecost.

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER 1

> “The Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to him to question him: ‘Who are you?’ And he confessed and did not deny it; he confessed: ‘I am not the Christ.’ And they questioned him: ‘What then? Are you Elijah?’ And he said: ‘I am not.’ ‘Are you the prophet?’ And he answered: ‘No.’ Therefore they said to him: ‘Who are you, so that we may give an answer to those who sent us? What do you say about yourself?’ He said: ‘I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, “Make straight the way of the Lord,” as the prophet Isaiah said.’ And those who had been sent were from the Pharisees. And they questioned him and said to him: ‘Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?’ John answered them, saying: ‘I baptize in water; but among you stands one whom you do not know. He is the one who will come after me, who was made before me, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie.’ These things took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.”

“The Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to John to question him: ‘Who are you?’ And he confessed and did not deny it; he confessed: ‘I am not the Christ.’” These words commend John’s humility. Although he possessed such great virtue that he could have been believed to be the Christ, he chose to stand firmly within his own identity, lest human opinion vainly carry him beyond himself. For “he confessed and did not deny it; he confessed: ‘I am not the Christ.’” Because he said “I am not,” he plainly denied what he was not, but he did not deny what he was. Speaking the truth, he became a member of the one whose name he did not deceitfully claim for himself.

“And they questioned him: ‘What then? Are you Elijah?’ And he said: ‘I am not.’” There is a danger that those who understand poorly may think John said something contrary to Christ. Christ had said: “Elijah has already come,” and he himself is John the Baptist. When questioned, John answered: “I am not Elijah.” Both spoke the truth. If you ask about personal identity, John is John and Elijah is Elijah. John rightly answered concerning the identity of his own person: “I am not Elijah.” But the Lord rightly spoke concerning the foreshadowing: “He himself is Elijah.” Neither John nor the Lord spoke falsely. John came in the very foreshadowing in which Elijah was to come according to his own personal identity.

John, therefore, was Elijah in spirit, but he was not Elijah in person. What the Lord acknowledges concerning the spirit, John denies concerning the person. It was right for the Lord to give the disciples a spiritual judgment concerning John, while John, among carnal crowds, answered not concerning his spirit but concerning his body.

“Are you the prophet? And he answered: ‘No.’” He does not say that he is a prophet because he knows himself to be greater than the prophets: the one whom the prophets said would come, he pointed out with his finger, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold the one who takes away the sins of the world.”

“Therefore they said to him: ‘Who are you, so that we may give an answer to those who sent us? What do you say about yourself?’ He said: ‘I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, “Make straight the way of the Lord,” as the prophet Isaiah said.’” John asserts that he is a voice because the word follows it. First John’s voice sounds, so that the Word may follow. The voice is therefore said to precede the Lord’s coming, because through its mystery the Father’s Word is heard by human beings—the Word of whom John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

The voice also cries in the wilderness because it announces the consolation of the Redeemer to deserted and abandoned Judea. What he cries out, he indicates when he adds: “Make straight the way of the Lord, as the prophet Isaiah said” (Isaiah 40). The way of the Lord is made straight to the heart when the word of truth is heard humbly. The way of the Lord is made straight to the heart when it is prepared for the commandment of life.

“And those who had been sent were from the Pharisees. And they questioned him and said to him: ‘Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?’” Because this was said not out of a desire to know the truth but out of the malicious zeal of rivalry, the Evangelist quietly made it known when he added: “And those who had been sent were from the Pharisees.” It is as though he were saying plainly: Those who do not know how to seek teaching are questioning John about his actions in order to envy him.

“John answered them, saying: ‘I baptize in water.’” John washed the bodies of those being baptized not with the Spirit but with water, yet he did not cleanse them from sin through forgiveness. Why, then, did he baptize, if baptism did not remit sins? It was so that, preserving the order of his mission as forerunner, he might precede by baptizing the Lord who was to baptize, just as by being born he had preceded the one who was to be born. He who became Christ’s forerunner by preaching thus became his forerunner by baptizing as well, through an imitation of the sacrament.

“But among you stands one whom you do not know.” The Savior is therefore said both to have stood among human beings and to have been unknown, because, appearing in the flesh, he stood visibly in body but invisibly in majesty.

*(From Bede.)* Luke says at this point: “He himself will baptize us in the Holy Spirit and fire”—that is, both in the purification of sanctification and in the testing of tribulation. The same Holy Spirit can also be understood under the name of sanctifying fire, because he kindles hearts through love and illuminates them through the wisdom with which he fills them.

“He is the one who will come after me, who was made before me.” *(From Gregory.)* This is said as “made before me,” as though it meant “placed before me.” He came after me because he was born later. But he was made before me because he was preferred to me. Yet by saying this a little earlier he also disclosed the reasons for his precedence: “He was before me.” It is as though he were saying plainly: “Although he was born after me, he surpasses me because the limits of the time of his birth do not confine him.” For the one who was born in time through his mother was generated timelessly by the Father. John reveals how great a humility of reverence he possesses by adding:

“Whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie,” and so forth. It was the custom among the ancients that if someone did not wish to take as his wife the woman who belonged to him, the man who came as the bridegroom by right of kinship would untie his sandal. What, then, did Christ appear among human beings to be, except the Bridegroom of the holy Church? John himself says of him: “The one who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3). But because people thought John was the Christ—a notion which John himself denies—he rightly declares that he is unworthy to untie the strap of his sandal. It is as though he were saying plainly: “I cannot uncover the Redeemer’s footprints, because I do not presume, unworthily, to claim the name of bridegroom.”

This may nevertheless be understood in another way. Who does not know that sandals are made from dead animals? The incarnate Lord, coming in the flesh, appeared as though wearing sandals, for in his divinity he assumed the dead matter of our corruption. But the human eye is not sufficient to penetrate the mystery of this incarnation. The strap of the sandal is therefore the bond of the mystery. John is unable to untie the strap of his sandal because even he, who recognized the incarnation through the spirit of prophecy, is not sufficient to investigate its mystery.

To untie the sandal is to uncover the limbs that it covers. Who, by contemplation, could explain the Word plainly—that is, the divine discourse—once the verbal covering had been removed, unless perhaps by explaining it through certain images? This is what he says: “I am not worthy”—that is, “I am not sufficient to reveal all Christ’s mysteries completely, with the veil of words removed.”

“These things took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.” Bethany is a village at the second mile from Aelia [Jerusalem; the source reads *Elia*], on the side of the Mount of Olives, where the Savior raised Lazarus. It is fitting that the forerunner of our Lord is said to have baptized in Bethany, for Bethany is interpreted as “house of obedience,” indicating that all must come to Christ’s baptism through the obedience of faith.

Thus far, with Christ’s help, we have completed expositions of many Sundays and festivals. From this point onward we shall set forth expositions of the holy martyrs, virgins, and confessors.

# ON THE FEAST OF THE APOSTLES

## THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER 8

> “We know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called saints according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified. What then shall we say about these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all—how will he not also, with him, freely give us all things? Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect? God is the one who justifies. Who is the one who condemns? Christ Jesus, who died—indeed, who also rose again—who is at the right hand of God and who also intercedes for us. Who, then, will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or persecution, or the sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter.’ But in all these things we conquer through the one who loved us. For I am certain that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither powers, neither things present nor things to come, neither strength, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

“We know that for those who love God all things work together for good.” All things work together for good to such an extent, and those who love God praise them together with him, that the Spirit himself also assists and the divine nature does not disdain to be the guide of the journey toward good.

“For those who are called saints according to his purpose.” That is, according to what he purposed—not by works of the Law or legal sacrifices, but by faith alone and the outpouring of his blood—to save those whom he had foreknown would believe. Those whom he freely called to salvation he glorified all the more as they worked.

“For those whom he foreknew he also predestined.” To predestine is not the same as to foreknow, because foreknowledge precedes predestination in reasoning. For those whom he foreknew as good, he makes blessed through predestination. Therefore, those whom he foresaw would become conformed to Christ in life, he willed and purposed to make conformed to him in glory, as he said: “He will configure the body of our humility to be conformed to the body of his glory” (Philippians 3).

“So that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.” Insofar as he is called the only-begotten, he has no brothers—that is, according to his divinity. But insofar as he is called the firstborn, he has brothers—that is, according to his humanity. Hence there is also the saying: “The firstborn from the dead,” so that he might hold the primacy through the resurrection of the dead.

“And those whom he predestined, he also called.” Let us not think that predestination forcibly acts upon those who are unwilling. By calling, he gathers the willing, not the unwilling. They are called so that they may believe through preaching. Those who believe are justified through baptism and afterward glorified—that is, either now through the virtues of grace or later in the blessed resurrection of the age to come.

“And those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified,” and so forth. Those who are called according to the good purpose and good will which they possess toward the worship of God are the ones who are said to be called according to his purpose. These are the ones who are called and justified, and the justified are glorified. That glory is present in the present age, of which the Apostle says: “We all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory”; in the future, when the body of our humility rises into glory.

*(From Augustine.)* What he said above—“to be conformed to the image of his Son”—is understood in this way: just as he has an immortal body, so we shall have an immortal body, being conformed in this respect—not to the image of the Father or of the Holy Spirit, but only to that of the Son, because sound faith receives this teaching: “The Word became flesh.” It may also be understood in this way: just as he became mortal for us, so we shall become conformed to him in immortality.

“What then shall we say about these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?” He wishes to show that no one can harm or hinder those who love God and are loved by God, preventing them from attaining the glory that has been promised, because the perfect love within them drives out every cause of mortal fear.

*(From Origen.)* How God is for us is clear from what he explained above: that the Spirit of God dwells in us; that Christ is in us; that we are led by the Spirit of God and have received the Spirit of adoption; that we are children of God and heirs and co-heirs of Christ; that we have received the first fruits of the Spirit; that the Spirit himself intercedes for us; that all things work together for our good; and that we have been called according to his purpose, foreknown, justified, predestined, and glorified. Using all these points as a kind of recapitulation, and repeating them together, he says: “What then shall we say about these things?” That is, about all the things we have said above: If God is for us in such a way that he has granted all these things to us, who can be against us?

“He who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all.” He permitted him to be handed over so that the freedom of the one who handed him over might remain, and so that through the Lord’s sufferings an example of patience might be set before us. But pay attention to the words “for us all”: he did not hand him over for some only, as the error of predestination supposes, but for all.

*(From Origen.)* The Father handed over his own Son not only for the saints, nor only for the great, but also for the least—all who are in the Church. Therefore no one in the Church should be a cause of scandal or be despised.

How will he not also give us all things with him? What can he have that is more precious, which he would refuse us, when he did not refuse his only Son? It is as though he were saying: There is no visible or invisible creature that can be compared with the Son. Even if the Creator himself has been given to us, how will he not give us every creature together with him? This too should be understood in two ways. For if we have Christ within us, insofar as he is Word, Wisdom, Truth, Justice, Peace, and all the other things written concerning him, then all things will be given to us together with this fullness of virtues, so that we may possess with Christ all things whatsoever God created, visible and invisible, hidden and manifest, temporal and eternal. In another way, he gave us all things with him: to him as heir, but to us as co-heirs, so that together with him we might likewise be granted the enjoyment of the whole creation.

[Col. 0528B]

Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect? God, who justifies. It seems to me that, when he says, “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect?” he is speaking of the devil. For there is no one so elect and so great whom he would not dare to accuse, except the one who committed no sin, who also said: “Now the prince of this world has come, and he finds nothing in me.” But although the devil displays the wickedness of his ruler, when God justifies and removes the iniquity of his elect, what will the accuser accomplish?

[Col. 0528C]

Who is he who condemns? Christ Jesus, who died—indeed, who also rose again—who is at the right hand of God, and who also intercedes for us. But since Christ died for them, or rather rose from the dead, and stands at the Father’s right hand and intercedes for them, who will be able to condemn them?

Alternatively: It seems that this speaks implicitly against the Jews. Will you be able to accuse Christ’s faithful who come from the Gentiles, who, believing in grace, disregard the legal commandments, and are shown to be righteous by signs and works of power? Or will anyone dare to accuse those who have been washed and sanctified through regeneration on account of their former sins—which is to be understood? Will God, who justifies, accuse them? Will Christ condemn those who live in his justifications, for whom he died and for whom he intercedes with the Father, standing on their behalf as an indefatigable advocate? For Christ is said to intercede with the Father for us because he continually shows him the human being whom he assumed as our pledge, as it were.

*(From Augustine.)* When, he says, we have been fixed and rooted in the love of God through all these benefits that we have received, who will be able to separate us from it? If tribulation comes, we shall say to God: “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Psalm 4). If distress occurs, we shall seek the breadth of God’s wisdom and knowledge, in which the world will not be able to constrict us; rather, mystically and spiritually, through the divine Scriptures, I shall ride across the broadest fields. If I suffer persecution and confess my Christ before human beings, I am certain that he too will confess me before his Father who is in heaven (Matthew 10). If hunger comes, it cannot trouble me, for I have the bread of life that came down from heaven (John 2). Nakedness does not shame me, for I have put on the Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 13). I shall not fear danger, for “the Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” The sword cannot terrify me, for I have with me the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword. For the love of him who loved us and drew our affection to himself makes us feel bodily anguish and pain; therefore, in all these things we overcome.

[Col. 0529A]

*(From Origen.)* These things seem capable of separating us from the love of God: death, and perhaps angels, principalities, and powers opposed to us; certainly the present things, which are unstable and fleeting. But “the depth” may likewise be understood, while the future life, height, and creation in some way attempt to separate us from the love of God. It does not seem pointless to explain this, unless someone should perhaps say that the Apostle speaks hyperbolically: that is, we are not turned aside from God’s love not only by things that can happen, but not even by things that cannot happen at all.

[Col. 0529B]

*(From Augustine.)* Let no one separate us from it by threatening death, for that very thing by which we love God cannot die. Unless, by not loving God, one should mean that death itself is not to love God. Let no one separate us from it by promising life. No one separates water from the very spring. An angel does not separate us; for, when we cling to God, no angel is more powerful than our mind. Power does not separate us—namely, the power that holds authority over the darkness in this world—for the mind clinging to God is altogether higher than the whole world. Present afflictions do not separate us; indeed, we feel them to be lighter in proportion as we cling more closely to him from whom they strive to separate us. The promise of future things does not separate us, for God promises more certainly whatever good is to come, and nothing is better than God himself, who is already present to those who cling to him well.

[Col. 0529C]

For I am certain. He did not say, “I suppose,” but “I am certain”: neither the death nor the life of Christ’s faithful separates them from his love—that is, neither persecution, which now inspires hope of life and now threatens the terror of death—nor the hostile power that transforms itself into an angel of light is to be heeded. Nor the powers, because the vessels of the strong will be plundered, he who has been bound through Christ.

Nor height nor depth—that is, neither astrology nor necromancy, since the former searches the height above and the latter the underworld below.

[Col. 0529D]

Nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. Even if another creature—that is, one from another region, set apart within another order of nature—could rise from the underworld, it would not be able to separate us from the Creator, to whom the soul must remain joined even through death.

[Col. 0530A]

## THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER 15

> “This is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you. No one has a greater love than this, that someone should lay down his life for his friends. You are my friends if you do what I command you. I shall no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything that I heard from my Father I have made known to you. You did not choose me, but I chose you, so that you should go and bear fruit, and your fruit should remain, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name he may give you.”

[Col. 0530B]

This is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you. *(From Augustine.)* Why did Christ love us, except so that we might be able to reign with Christ? For this reason we ought to love one another: that we may have God and remain in God. If those who love one another thereby love God, this is love: that God may be all in all (1 Corinthians 15).

No one has a greater love than that someone should lay down his life for his friends. In this Christ’s love surpasses ours, because he came to lay down his life for his enemies, yet with the purpose of making friends out of enemies. Martyrdom, however, is not granted to everyone, though kindness toward one’s brothers is required of everyone. Whoever does not give his true substance to a brother in need, how will he give his life for his brother in persecution?

[Col. 0530C]

The strength of this love, however, is to distribute what is one’s own in time of peace for Christ’s love, so that one may be able to give oneself up in disturbance for his name.

You are my friends if you do what I command you. Great is the dignity of being God’s friend, but we must consider by what steps one reaches this height. He adds: “If you do what I command you.” It is as though he were openly saying: You rejoice in the summit; consider through what labors one comes to the summit. Great is the mercy of our benefactor: we were not worthy to be servants, yet we are called friends. Therefore he adds:

[Col. 0530D]

I shall no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. The service of fear is one thing, and the service of love another. The Truth itself expresses these two forms by way of example in this same Gospel, saying: “A servant does not remain in the house forever, but the son remains.” The son serves the father because of love, while the servant serves because of fear. Concerning this service the Lord said: “I no longer call you servants, but friends,” because they are sons, not servants, and therefore also friends; for “a servant does not know what his master is doing.” He does not know his master’s will who serves his master through the bitterness of fear and not through the sweetness of love, as though he were serving a father.

But I have called you friends, because everything that I heard from my Father I have made known to you. What are all the things that he heard from the Father and wished to make known to his servants, in order to perfect them as his friends, except the joys of inward love and the festivals of the heavenly homeland, which he daily impresses upon our minds through the inspiration of his love? Yet this knowledge, which now advances only in part, will be perfected in the fullness of knowledge. Concerning this the Apostle says: “When that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be abolished” (1 Corinthians 13). For the Lord said that he had done for his disciples what he knew he would do.

[Col. 0531A]

You did not choose me, but I chose you. This is the gracious favor that goes before us, so that we may become friends instead of servants. Therefore let pride not steal upon us, as though we were receiving something on account of our merits: we were children of wrath, but now through grace we have become children of God. Without him we can do nothing, as the Truth itself said shortly before: “Without me you can do nothing.”

And I appointed you to go and bear fruit. “I appointed” you to grace; I planted you so that you might go by willing, and bear fruit by acting. For he said “go” with reference to willing, because intending to do something is already to go in the mind. What kind of fruit they ought to bear he adds:

[Col. 0531B]

And that your fruit should remain, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name he may give you. The name of the Son is Jesus; Jesus is called “Savior,” or also “salutary.” Therefore he asks in the Savior’s name who asks for what pertains to true salvation. For if something harmful is requested, it is not requested in Jesus’ name.

## ON THE FEAST OF ONE CONFESSOR

## THE LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS, II, CHAPTER 1

> “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation, so that we too may be able to console those who are in every distress, through the consolation with which we ourselves are consoled by God. For just as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so also through him our consolation abounds. Whether we are afflicted for your consolation and salvation, or whether we are consoled for your consolation, which produces endurance of the same sufferings that we also endure, our hope for you is firm, knowing that just as you are partners in the sufferings, so also you will be partners in the consolation, in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

[Col. 0531D]

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus, and so forth. The unstated sense is that our Lord blesses God because the saints receive consolation so that they themselves may console others.

The Father of mercies. That is, because mercy was born from him, although it is not therefore younger than he is.

And the God of all consolation, who consoles us. He said “of all consolation” because he consoles them fully and perfectly in their labors, and balances consolation against tribulation, as he said in the psalm: “According to the multitude of my sorrows within me, your consolations delighted my soul” (Psalm 93).

In every tribulation and consolation. That is, not in some things, but in all things.

[Col. 0532A]

So that we too may be able to console those who are in every distress. That is, for this reason he frees us, so that we may ourselves be able to console others. He gives us a model for consoling others, and through the consolation by which, according to God’s will, we ourselves console others, we recognize that God abandons no one. He will reward all the more greatly in the future those whom he consoles in the present age.

For just as the sufferings of Christ abound in us. That is, sufferings endured for Christ’s name.

So also through Christ our consolation abounds. Through this consolation he himself is instructed on the way by manifest vision at the time of his summons, and when he or Peter was being released from prison.

Whether we are afflicted for your consolation and salvation, and so forth. That is, there are two causes of our tribulation: either when we preach your salvation, which is Christ, or when through our affliction we provide you an example of endurance.

Knowing that just as you are partners in the sufferings, so also you will be partners in the consolation. “Knowing,” that is, holding fast with the firmest hope.

## THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER 14

> “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. Whoever does not carry his cross and come after me cannot be my disciple. For which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the cost required to complete it? Otherwise, after he has laid the foundation and is unable to finish, all who see it will begin to mock him, saying: ‘This man began to build and was unable to complete it.’ Or what king, going to engage in war against another king, does not first sit down and consider whether he can meet, with ten thousand, the one who comes against him with twenty thousand? Otherwise, while he is still far away, he sends an embassy and asks for terms of peace. So therefore, every one of you who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple.”

[Col. 0532C]

If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father, mother, wife, and so forth. *(From Bede.)* One may ask how we are commanded to hate our parents and those related to us by flesh, when we are also commanded to love our enemies. Certainly the Truth said of a wife: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19), and Paul said: “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the Church” (Ephesians 6). Behold, the disciple commands that a wife be loved, while the Master says: “Whoever does not hate his wife cannot be my disciple.” Does the judge announce one thing and the herald proclaim another? Or can we both hate and love at the same time?

[Col. 0532D]

But if we weigh the force of the command, we can do both through discernment: we should love those joined to us by kinship of flesh, insofar as we know them to be our neighbors, but we should hate and avoid them insofar as we endure them as adversaries on the way of God. To show that this hatred of those close to us does not proceed from lack of affection but from love, the Lord immediately added, saying: “And even his own life.” We hate our own life when we do not comply with its carnal desires, when we break its appetite and resist its wishes. Thus what is rejected and led toward something better is loved, as it were, through hatred. In the same way, we must show discernment in our hatred of those close to us, so that in them we may love what is of God and hate what obstructs us on God’s path.

[Col. 0533A]

And whoever does not carry his cross and come after me cannot be my disciple. The cross derives its name from torment, and we carry the Lord’s cross in two ways: either when through abstinence we afflict the flesh, or when through compassion for our neighbor we regard his necessity as our own. Whoever displays sorrow over another’s need carries a cross in the mind. To carry the cross and follow the Lord is to practice either abstinence from the flesh or compassion for one’s neighbor with the intention of eternity. For whoever practices these things with a temporal intention indeed carries the cross, but refuses to follow the Lord.

Since sublime commandments have been given, a comparison with the building of something lofty is immediately added, when it says:

[Col. 0533B]

For which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the cost required to complete it? Everything we do must be preceded by careful consideration. For behold, according to the voice of the Truth, whoever builds a tower first prepares the cost of the building. If, therefore, we wish to construct the tower of humility, we must first prepare ourselves against the adversities of this age. This is the difference between an earthly and a heavenly building: the earthly building is constructed by gathering expenses, whereas for the heavenly building we expend by distributing our resources. We spend on the former if we gather what we do not possess; we spend on the latter if we also abandon what we possess. We must consider what is said:

[Col. 0533C]

Otherwise, after he has laid the foundation and is unable to finish, all who see it will begin to mock him, saying: “This man began to build and was unable to complete it.” For, in the Apostle’s words, we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings. In everything we do, we must consider our hidden adversaries, who are always intent upon our works and always rejoice in our failure. The Prophet, observing them, says: “My God, in you I trust; I shall not be put to shame, and let not my enemies mock me” (Psalm 26). When we are intent upon good works, unless we vigilantly guard against evil spirits, we suffer as mockers those whom we have as persuaders to evil.

[Col. 0533D]

Or what king, going to engage in war against another king, does not first sit down and consider whether he can meet, with ten thousand, the one who comes against him with twenty thousand? Otherwise, while he is still far away, he sends an embassy and asks for terms of peace. A king comes against a king on equal terms for battle, yet if he realizes that he is unable to prevail, he sends an embassy and asks for terms of peace. With what tears, then, ought we to hope for pardon, since at that fearful examination we shall not come to judgment on equal terms with our king? Our condition, weakness, and lesser circumstances produce this inequality, though perhaps by then we have hidden the guilt of our evil deeds and avoided every wrong outwardly.

[Col. 0534A]

Are we capable of giving an account of our thoughts? The one who comes against us with a doubled army to confront a single army examines us, scarcely prepared in works alone, both concerning our works and our thoughts. Therefore, while he is still far away, let us send an embassy and ask for terms of peace. He is said to be far away who is not yet seen as present through judgment. Let us send our tears as an embassy; let us send works of mercy; let us sacrifice offerings of appeasement on his altar. This is our embassy, which appeases the coming king.

[Col. 0534B]

So every one of you who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple. By this conclusion the Lord most clearly teaches what it means to build a tower or to make peace with a stronger king: it means to be his disciple. To prepare the expense for completing the tower and to send an embassy to obtain peace means nothing other than renouncing all that one possesses.

There is, to be sure, a difference between renouncing everything and abandoning everything. To abandon everything, set aside the cares of the world, and long only for eternal desires belongs to the few who are perfect. But it belongs to all the faithful to renounce everything they possess—that is, to hold worldly things in such a way that they are not themselves held by them; to have a temporal possession for use but an eternal one in desire; and to govern earthly things while directing the whole mind toward heavenly things.

[Col. 0534C]

## ON THE FEAST OF MANY SAINTS

## THE LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PETER, CHAPTER 1

> “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy regenerated us into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, into an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance, kept in heaven for you, who are guarded by God’s power through faith for salvation, ready to be revealed at the last time, in which you will rejoice. Now, if necessary, you are distressed for a little while by various trials, so that the testing of your faith may be much more precious than gold, which is tested by fire. Therefore, Christ having suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same disposition. For whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sins, so that for the remaining time in the flesh he may live no longer according to human desires but according to the will of God. The God of all grace, who called you into his eternal glory in Christ Jesus after you had suffered a little, will himself perfect, confirm, strengthen, and establish you. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.”

[Col. 0534D]

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus, and so forth. *(From Bede.)* In this way he offers praises of blessing to God the Father while showing that our Lord and Savior is both God and human. When he says “the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” he calls him the God of our Lord Jesus Christ because he remembers that the Lord Jesus himself became human. He calls him the Father of our Lord because he does not doubt that this same Lord of ours has always existed as the Son of God.

[Col. 0535A]

Who according to his great mercy regenerated us into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, into an inheritance, and so forth. God is rightly blessed by us, since although we had been generated in our merits for death, he regenerated us by his mercy for life. He did this through the resurrection of his Son, since he loved our life so greatly that he appointed him to die for it, and by destroying that death through the resurrection he showed us the hope and example of rising again. He died so that we would not fear dying; he rose from the dead so that we might hope that we too would rise through him.

[Col. 0535B]

Into an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance. “Incorruptible,” he says, because of the heavenly life, which is touched neither by old age, disease, death, nor any grief. “Undefiled,” because no unclean person can enter it. “Unfading,” because even in the minds of blessed human beings that heavenly way of life cannot become worthless through long familiarity, as the luxury and delights of the present age commonly do, when even through divine familiarity and use they sometimes turn into distaste.

Kept in heaven, and so forth. He says “kept in you” instead of saying “kept for you,” that is, kept for this purpose: that it may now be given back to you in heaven at the appointed time. Or certainly it is kept in heaven and in you, because he who gave believers the power to become children of God also gave them the power to receive an inheritance from him—not as those who deserve it by their own merit, but by persevering to the end, so that they may be saved.

[Col. 0535C]

Therefore he says that the inheritance is kept for those whose merits, with the Lord’s help, he knows will reach it, because those who do not preserve their father’s discipline do not deserve to receive an inheritance from him.

Who are guarded by God’s power, and so forth. The Lord also says in the Gospel: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John 14), and again: “It is not mine to give, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.” Seats, therefore, are prepared in the kingdom of God; dwelling places are prepared in the Father’s house; salvation is prepared in heaven. Let the one who desires to receive it only make himself worthy. But because no one can become worthy of eternal salvation by his own effort and strength alone, it is rightly stated beforehand that you are guarded by God’s power through faith. No one can be kept in good things by the power of his own freedom; rather, we must seek his help in all things, so that we may be perfected by the one from whom we received the beginning of good action.

[Col. 0535D]

In which you will rejoice, though now, if necessary, you are distressed by various trials. What he says—“in which”—means “in that [time]”: salvation will be revealed at this last time, concerning which the Lord says: “Again I shall see you, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John 16). “Now for a little while it is necessary to be distressed.” It is necessary, he says, to be distressed, because one can reach eternal joys only through sorrow over the passing age and through afflictions. He says “for a little while” because, when eternal reward is given, everything that seemed grievous and bitter amid the tribulations of the age will appear brief and light.

[Col. 0536A]

So that the testing of your faith may be much more precious than gold, which perishes, and so forth. The Book of Wisdom likewise compares the sufferings of the saints with gold tested by fire, saying: “As gold in the furnace the Lord tested the elect, and as a burnt offering he accepted them” (Wisdom 3). Those whom he tests as though in the furnace of tribulation he takes up in the joy of reward as an offering pleasing to him. The endurance of the saints is rightly compared with gold, because just as nothing among metals is more precious than gold, so nothing is more worthy of praise before the Lord than this. Hence it is written: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 115).

[Col. 0536B]

Just as gold enclosed in a furnace is tested by the fires, and once tested outside the furnace displays the brilliance that it possesses, so the steadfastness of the faithful appears contemptible and foolish amid the afflictions of the faithful. But when the time of reward arrives, after the contest of tribulations has ended, then their virtue shows how great its glory was and how greatly it advanced through the flames of suffering.

Therefore, since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same disposition. After he had established the example of the Lord’s resurrection and of our cleansing, which takes place in baptism through the sacrament of the ark and the Flood, he returns to what he had begun to say: by imitating the work of our Redeemer, let us patiently endure the wickedness of the evil amid the good things we do.

[Col. 0536C]

It should be noted how strictly he speaks when he says: “Since Christ suffered in the flesh.” For, as blessed Ambrose says: The flesh suffered, while the divinity was free from death; the body submitted to suffering according to the law of human nature. But can the divinity die, when the soul cannot? “Do not fear,” he says, “those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.” Therefore, if the soul cannot be killed, how can the divinity?

For whoever has suffered in the flesh, and so forth. Whenever one of the righteous submits his body to the violence of persecutors for martyrdom, there is no doubt that, until the end of his life, insofar as human nature permits, he abstains from sins.
