What could he think about the committing of sin or about carnal desires, except what he could turn over in his mind concerning the will of God, when he was either fastened to wood, surrounded by blows of stones, overcome by the bites of beasts, placed upon flames of fire, pierced by the lashes of scorpions, or afflicted by any other kind of punishment, and was compelled to desire only this: that, when the contest had ended, he might receive the crown of life?

[Col. 0536D]

Blessed Peter therefore desires us always to imitate the mind of such people when, setting before us the example of the Lord’s Passion, he commands us to arm ourselves with the same disposition against the wickedness of evil people and against the allurements of vices. He wants it understood that even while resting in the peace of the Church, if we put on the disposition of one who suffers patiently, then, with the Lord’s help, we easily avoid falls into sin and subject all human desires to the commands of the divine will.

[Col. 0537A]

Therefore be prudent, and so forth. We are rightly commanded to keep watch in prayers, so that whenever we stand at prayer every carnal and worldly thought may depart. The mind should think of nothing except what it is praying for. For the enemy frequently creeps in, subtly deceiving us, and turns our prayers away from God, so that we have one thing in our heart and utter another with our voice. We ought to pray to God with sincere intention not only in voice but also in the sense of the mind.

Above all, have mutual love among yourselves, and so forth. He rightly adds “continual,” because we are always able to love, but because of the weakness of the flesh we cannot always keep watch in prayers. Love itself, however, by whose impulse these outward actions are performed and which presides in the inner person, can always be held there, even though it cannot always be displayed publicly.

[Col. 0537B]

If anyone speaks, and so forth. He fears that, contrary to God’s will or to what is clearly commanded in the holy Scriptures, someone might say or command something and be found to be a false witness of God or a sacrilegious person, either introducing something alien to the Lord’s teaching or omitting and passing over something pleasing to God. For the Lord most clearly commands preachers of the truth, concerning those whom they instruct: “Teaching them to observe everything whatsoever I have commanded you” (Matthew, final chapter). He commands them to hand on for observance what he himself commanded, not other things, and not in part, but everything, to their hearers.

[Col. 0537C]

If anyone ministers, let him do so as from the strength that God supplies. The more certainly each person knows that he cannot possess from himself the good that he supplies, the more humbly let him bestow upon his neighbor every good that he can.

So that God may be honored in all things through Jesus Christ. This accords with the command of Jesus Christ himself, when he says: “Let them see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 6). God is therefore honored in our actions when we attribute everything that we do well and according to his will not to our merits but to his grace.

[Col. 0537D]

And when the chief shepherd appears. Just as Christ is called King of kings, Lord of lords, and Prince of princes, and shepherd of shepherds, so here the Apostle is understood to have said “chief shepherd.”

You will receive the unfading crown of glory. He said “unfading” because it will not grow old. The crown signifies the eternity of life together with everlasting rewards.

[Col. 0538A]

The God of all grace, who called us into his eternal glory in Christ Jesus after we had suffered a little. The same God is called “of all grace” because grace is manifold. Every good that a human being has is received through God’s grace; all glory is given by him and referred again to him.

He himself will perfect, confirm, strengthen, and establish you; to him be glory forever and ever. He called us into eternal glory—that is, into eternal life—in Christ Jesus, that is, through his incarnation. Or he called us in the sense of the saying: “Come to me, all you who labor,” and so forth (Matthew 11). He will perfect us in faith and perseverance in good works, and in the future, when he says generally to all his saints: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you” (Matthew 25). Or he will confirm us in faith and strengthen us in works. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER 12

> “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands. And be like people waiting for their lord when he returns from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks they may immediately open to him. Blessed are those servants whom, when he comes, the Lord finds watching. Amen, I say to you, he will gird himself, make them recline, and, passing by, minister to them. And if he comes during the second watch, and if he comes during the third watch, and finds them so, blessed are those servants. But know this: if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly have watched and would not have allowed his house to be broken into. You too must be ready, because at an hour when you do not expect it, the Son of Man will come.”

[Col. 0538B]

Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning. *(From Bede.)* Since he had shown that many people either submit to the Lord throughout the whole age or serve him with an eye to worldly advantage, he aptly and briefly teaches his own disciples both to gird their loins, because of continence from love of worldly things, and to have burning lamps, so that they may do this with a true end and right intention. Alternatively, we gird our loins when we restrain the luxury of the flesh through continence.

[Col. 0538C]

We hold burning lamps in our hands when through good works we show our neighbors examples of light. For our Redeemer can in no way be pleased with one without the other.

And be like people waiting for their lord, and so forth. The Lord went away to a wedding when, rising from the dead and ascending into heaven, he joined to himself, as a new human being, the heavenly multitude of angels. He will return when he is made manifest to us through judgment. Concerning servants who wait, it is rightly added:

[Col. 0538D]

So that when he comes and knocks they may immediately open to him. He comes when he hastens to judgment. He knocks when, through the afflictions of illness, he indicates that death is near. We open to him immediately if we receive him with love. Whoever trembles at leaving the body and fears to see as judge the one whom he remembers having despised does not wish to open to the Judge who knocks. But whoever is secure in hope and conduct immediately opens to him who knocks, because he receives the Judge gladly. When he recognizes that the time of approaching death has come, he rejoices in the glory of the reward. Hence it is also added:

[Col. 0539A]

Blessed are those servants whom, when he comes, the Lord finds watching. The one who keeps the eyes of the mind open to the sight of the true light watches. The one who preserves through action what he believes watches. The one who drives away the darkness of the body and negligence watches.

I truly tell you: he will gird himself, make them recline, and, passing among them, minister to them. He girds himself—that is, he prepares himself for recompense; he will make them recline—that is, he will refresh them in eternal rest. For our reclining means resting in the kingdom. The Lord ministers as he passes by because he satisfies us with the illumination of his light. “Passing by” means that he returns from judgment to the kingdom; or certainly, after judgment, the Lord passes over to us when he raises us to the contemplation of his divinity through the form of his humanity. For to pass over is to lead us into the contemplation of his brightness: when, after the judgment, we also see in divinity the one whom we behold in humanity at the judgment.

[Col. 0539B]

And if he comes during the second watch, and if he comes during the third watch, and finds them so, blessed are those servants. The first watch is the earliest period, that is, childhood. The second is adolescence, or youth, which the authority of sacred speech treats as one, saying: “Rejoice, young man, in your adolescence” (Ecclesiastes II). The third is understood as old age. Whoever was unwilling to keep watch during the first watch should at least guard the second; and whoever neglected in childhood to turn from his wickedness toward the paths of life should at least awaken during youth. And whoever was unwilling to keep watch during the second watch should not lose the remedies of the third watch: whoever does not awaken to the paths of life in youth should at least come to his senses in old age. To shake off the sluggishness of our mind, even external losses are brought forward by way of comparison, so that through them the soul may be roused to guard [Col. 0539C] itself. For it is said:

But know this: if the householder had known at what hour the thief would come, he would surely have kept watch and would not have allowed his house to be broken into. From this preceding comparison an exhortation is also added, when it says:

You also must be ready, because you do not know at what hour the Son of Man will come. For while the householder is unaware, the thief breaks into the house, because, while the spirit sleeps in neglect of its own vigilance, sudden death comes and breaks into the dwelling of our flesh. It kills the one whom the master of the house finds sleeping, because, since the spirit did not foresee the coming losses at all, death carries him off unawares to punishment. He would resist the thief if he kept watch, because, anticipating the coming of the Judge who secretly snatches away the soul, he would meet him through repentance, lest he perish unrepentant. Our Lord therefore wished the final hour to remain unknown to us so that it might always be feared, and so that, since we cannot foresee it, we might prepare for it without interruption.

But Peter said to him: Lord, are you telling this parable to us, or also to everyone? That is: are you saying it specifically to us apostles, or also to all who are to be saved?

And the Lord said: Who, then, is the faithful and prudent steward whom his lord will appoint over his household, to give them their measure of wheat at the proper time? By the measure of wheat the proper manner of speech is signified. For lofty matters ought to be concealed from many hearers and opened only to a few, lest something incapable of being contained by a narrow heart be given to it and spill outside. Hence Moses, coming forth from God’s secrecy, veils his shining face before the people, because he certainly does not disclose the inner mysteries of brightness to the crowds. The speech of teachers, therefore, ought to be formed according to the quality of their hearers, so that it may suit each one individually and yet never depart from the art of common edification.

Blessed is that servant whom his lord, when he comes, finds doing so. Truly I tell you, he will appoint him over all that he possesses. As great as the difference in merit is between good hearers and good teachers, so great is the difference in their rewards. When he comes and finds the former keeping watch, he will make them recline, and, passing among them, will minister to them. But when he finds the latter faithfully and prudently distributing the grain of the word to the household entrusted to them, he will appoint them over all that he possesses—that is, over all the joys of the heavenly kingdom—not, of course, so that they alone may hold dominion over them, but so that they may enjoy eternal possession of them more abundantly than the other saints. For “those who are instructed will shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who teach many to righteousness like stars forever and ever.”

## ANOTHER GOSPEL, LUKE XIX

> “A certain nobleman went into a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself and then return. Calling his servants, he gave them ten minas and said to them: ‘Do business until I come.’ But his citizens hated him, and they sent a delegation after him, saying: ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’ And it happened that, when he returned after receiving the kingdom, he ordered the servants to whom he had given the money to be called, so that he might know how much each had gained by trading. The first came, saying: ‘Lord, your mina has gained ten minas.’ And he said to him: ‘Well done, good servant; because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.’ And another came, saying: ‘Lord, your mina has made five minas.’ To this one he said: ‘And you, be over five cities.’ And another came, saying: ‘Lord, behold your mina, which I kept laid up in a cloth; for I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man: you take up what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow.’ He said to him: ‘I judge you from your own mouth, wicked servant. You knew that I am a severe man, taking up what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow; why, then, did you not put my money in the bank? Then, when I came, I could have collected it with interest.’ And he said to those standing by: ‘Take the mina away from him and give it to the one who has ten minas.’ And they said to him: ‘Lord, he has ten minas.’ But I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away.”

[Col. 0540D]

A certain nobleman went into a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself and then return. The nobleman is the one to whom the blind man above cried out, “Son of David, have mercy on me,” and to whom, as he came to Jerusalem, they sang: “Hosanna to the Son of David. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.” The distant country is the Church from the Gentiles, concerning which the same nobleman says: “But I have been appointed king by him”; and the Father says: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth.” This inheritance and possession is called a distant country for two reasons: either because it cried out to God from the ends of the earth, or because salvation is far from sinners, and although God is present everywhere, the true God is nevertheless far from the understanding of those who worship idols. But those who were far away have been brought near in the blood of Christ.

Calling his ten servants, he gave them ten minas, and so forth. The number ten pertains to the Law because of the Decalogue. The householder therefore calls ten servants because he chose disciples instructed in the letter of the Law. He gives them ten minas because he reveals that the sayings of the Law are to be understood spiritually. After his passion and resurrection, he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures. The mina, which the Greeks call μνᾶμ [mnâm], is weighed at one hundred drachmas, and the speech of all Scripture, because it suggests the perfection of heavenly life, shines as though with the weight of the number one hundred.

And he said to them: Do business until I come. Having examined, he says, the words of the Law and the Prophets through mystical interpretation, offer them to the peoples, and receive from them a confession of faith and uprightness of conduct, in accordance with what the Psalmist commanded his hearers, saying: “Take up the psalm and give the tambourine”—that is, receive the praise of preaching with the intention of the heart, and bring the devotion of action into the discipline of the flesh.

But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying: We do not want this man to reign over us. He calls the impious Jews his citizens, concerning whom he elsewhere testifies: “But now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father.” They hated him not only while he was present, even to the death of the cross, but, after his resurrection, they also persecuted the apostles and rejected the preaching of the heavenly kingdom.

And it happened that he returned after receiving the kingdom. This signifies the time when he who appeared to them in humility will come in the most manifest and eminent glory, when he said: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John XIX).

And he ordered the servants to whom he had given the money to be called, so that he might know how much each had gained by trading, and so forth. “So that he might know,” he says—not because anything is hidden from him, to whom it was most truly said, “Lord, you know all things,” but he says “to know” in the sense of making everyone know. For then everyone’s works and thoughts are openly displayed to all.

[Col. 0541D]

The first came, saying: Lord, your mina has gained ten minas. The first servant is the order of teachers sent to the circumcision. He received one mina with which to do business, and was commanded to preach one God, one faith, one baptism, and one Lord. This same mina gained ten minas because by teaching he joined to himself the people established under the Law.

And he said to him: Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities. The servant is faithful in a very little when he does not adulterate the word of God, but speaks “as from God, before God, in Christ.” For whatever gifts we receive in the present, in comparison with those of the future, are little [Col. 0542A] and slight. The ten cities are souls coming through the word of the Law to the grace of the Gospel; and then he who has worthily entrusted to them the money of the word is rightly placed over them in glory.

And another came, saying: Lord, your mina has made five minas. This servant is the assembly of those who were sent to preach to the uncircumcised. As he went out to preach, the Lord had entrusted to him one mina—that is, the one and same faith entrusted also to the circumcision. But this mina made five minas because it converted to the grace of evangelical faith the Gentiles who had previously been enslaved to the senses of the body.

And he said to him: And you, be over five cities. That is, shine as great and exalted on account of the faith and conduct of those souls whom you had instructed. Since by teaching he had changed them from darkness, he is rightly said to have been placed over five cities, because he is honored not only for his own progress but also for that of his hearers, whom he called to the light.

And another came, saying: Lord, behold your mina, which I kept laid up, and so forth. To tie up money in a cloth is to hide the gifts one has received in the idleness of a sluggish body. There are people who flatter themselves with this perversity: “It is enough for each person to give an account of himself; why should one preach to others, so that one may also be compelled to give an account of them?” Yet even those to whom the Law was not given and who did not sleep after hearing the Gospel are without excuse before the Lord, because through creation they were able to know the Creator. This is what it means to reap where he did not sow: to hold even those guilty of impiety to whom the word of the Law or the Gospel was not ministered. Avoiding this seeming danger of judgment, they rest in sluggish torpor from the ministry of the word; this is like tying up in a cloth what they received.

He says to him: I judge you from your own mouth, wicked servant. He is called a wicked servant because he is both lazy and inactive in carrying on the business, and insolent and proud in accusing the judgment of his Lord.

You knew that I am a severe man, taking up what I did not deposit, and so forth. (From Jerome.) What he thought he had said as an excuse is turned into his own guilt. “If,” he says, “you knew me to be harsh and cruel, and to pursue what belongs to another and reap where I had not sown, why did such a thought not instill fear in you? [Col. 0542D] You should have known that I would seek my own more diligently, and you should have put my money—or silver—into the bank.” The Greek term ἀργύριον [argyrion] signifies both things. “The words of the Lord,” he says, “are pure words, silver tested by fire.” Money and silver, therefore, signify the preaching of the Gospel and the divine word, which ought to have been put into the bank—that is, impressed upon the ready and prepared hearts of the faithful. Into what bank, namely? Into the minds of the hearers. No money other than the Lord’s is to be deposited, so that every word of the teacher may follow the meaning of Scripture. For by saying here that it is not just any money but his own that should be lent at interest to the money-changers, the Lord is explained by the Apostle, who says: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God.”

[Col. 0543A]

And when I came, I would surely have collected it with interest. Whoever receives the money of the word from a teacher and purchases it by believing must repay it with interest through action, so that he may carry out in deed what he learned by hearing. For with interest even money that was not given is received; or, certainly, the person who, from the interest of the word he has received, strives to understand other things as well—things he has not yet learned from the preacher’s mouth—pays interest.

And he said to those standing by: Take the mina away from him, and give it to the one who has ten minas; and they said to him: Lord, he has ten minas. He rightly loses the grace bestowed upon him because he neglected to communicate it by preaching to others, so that it may be increased for the one who labored in it—just as Saul lost the royal anointing through pride, while David earned it through obedience. That the mina taken away from the wicked servant was ordered to be given to the one who had ten minas mystically indicates, as I think, that, when the fullness of the Gentiles enters, all Israel will be saved, and that then the abundance of spiritual grace, which we now exercise sluggishly, will be bestowed upon the teachers of that people.

But I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away. (From Augustine.) This saying refers to what precedes. It teaches that even one who has God’s gift—that is, uses it well—can lose it. Since this exchange of graces usually takes place in the present life, it should be noted that the examination by the returning Lord is even now carried out in part, but then will be fulfilled universally. For every day he returns after receiving the kingdom from the Father, because he continually observes the state of the Church as it journeys on earth. Every day, amid so great a number of faithful servants, he lends money to one who will do business with it. In one he examines the measure of completed work; the one who labors faithfully and prudently he endows with a greater gift of grace, while he deprives the other who pursues soft idleness, wilted leisure, and pleasures.

## ON THE FEAST OF MANY HOLY MARTYRS

### READING FROM THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE HEBREWS, CHAPTER XI

> “The saints through faith conquered kingdoms, practiced righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the force of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, recovered strength from weakness. They became mighty in war; they routed the camps of foreigners; they received back their dead through women by resurrection. Others were stretched out, refusing deliverance, so that they might obtain a better resurrection. Others experienced mockeries and scourging, and moreover bonds and prisons. They were stoned, they were cut apart, they were tested, they died by the killing of the sword. They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, distressed, afflicted—people of whom the world was not worthy. They wandered in deserts, mountains, caves, and caverns of the earth. And all these, having been tested, were found approved by the testimony of faith in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

[Col. 0544A]

The saints through faith conquered kingdoms, practiced righteousness, obtained promises, and so forth. Faith is of things hoped for that are not seen; for no one hopes for what he sees, but what we do not see we await with patience. Faith cannot be called faith unless a person is more assured concerning things that are not seen than concerning those that are seen.

They stopped the mouths of lions. Here, I think, he is speaking of Daniel.

They quenched the force of fire; they escaped the edge of the sword. Here, I think, he is speaking of the three boys.

They recovered strength from weakness. Here he refers, I think, to the time when they returned from Babylonia. By “from weakness” I understand him to mean “from captivity,” when the affairs of the Jews were already in despair, when they were scarcely different from the dead.

They became mighty in war; they routed the camps of foreigners. Here he seems plainly to be speaking of the Maccabees, although it can also be understood of Joshua, Samson, David, and others like them.

They received back their dead through women by resurrection. He refers to what happened concerning the Prophets, signifying Elisha and Elijah, who raised the dead.

Others were stretched out, refusing deliverance, so that they might obtain a better resurrection. It is therefore clear that they refused deliverance in order to obtain a better resurrection—not one like the resurrection received by the sons of those women. Here it seems to me that he signifies John and James. “Being stretched out” is said of beheading; for they chose rather to die, although they themselves were raising others, so that they might obtain a better resurrection.

Others experienced mockeries, and moreover bonds and prisons.

He says this so that, whenever someone is held in the same cause, or in the same suffering or sadness, he may receive consolation from the likeness of one who suffers with him. Even if you regard some suffering as worse, it is of no benefit if it did not arise from the same cause; if you do not suffer for righteousness, it profits nothing. For the Gospel says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matthew V).

They were stoned, they were cut apart, they were tested, they died by the killing of the sword. Here he uses the plural for the singular. In the Old Testament, we read of only one righteous man stoned for righteousness: Naboth the Jezreelite. Only Isaiah was cut apart; but many were tested and died by the killing of the sword.

They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, distressed, and so forth. All these things seem to be said of the sons of the Prophets who lived in the wilderness. In the New Testament the Apostle bears witness to them as faithful witnesses, so that, kindling the hearts of the sluggish by the example of those holy men, he may rouse and restore them.

## GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER V

> “When Jesus saw the crowds, he went up the mountain. And when he had sat down, his disciples came to him. And opening his mouth, he taught them, saying: ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled. Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God. Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are you when people revile you and persecute you and speak every evil against you falsely because of me. Rejoice and exult, for your reward is abundant in heaven.’”

When Jesus saw the crowds, he went up the mountain, and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him. (From Augustine.) If it is asked what the mountain signifies, it is rightly understood to signify the greater commands of righteousness, because those given to the Jews were lesser. Yet the one God, through his holy prophets and servants, according to the most orderly distribution of times, gave lesser commands to the people who still had to be bound by fear, and through his Son gave greater commands to the people whom it was now fitting to set free by love. He teaches while seated, which pertains to the dignity of the teacher’s office; and his disciples approach him so that those who drew nearer in mind to the fulfillment of his commands might also be physically closer in order to hear his words.

(From Fulgentius.) Rightly does the exalted God ascend to an exalted place, so that he may preach exalted things to exalted people; and plainly the new Law is preached in the mind, because the old Law was given to Moses on the mountain.

[Col. 0545C]

And opening his mouth, he taught them, saying. By opening his mouth he shows that he is about to bring forth a deep and hidden discourse; for he is said here to open his mouth because he earlier opened the mouths of the Prophets.

Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. The beatitude ought not to have begun elsewhere, since it is to arrive at the summit of wisdom. “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord,” and, conversely, the beginning of every sin is pride. Therefore, by “poor in spirit” are understood the humble and God-fearing: those who do not possess a spirit that puffs itself up.

Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth. I believe it is that earth of which it is said in the Psalms: “My portion is in the land of the living” (Psalm XXVI). For it signifies a certain solidity and stability of perpetual inheritance; he himself is the rest and life of the saints. The meek are those who do not resist evil but overcome evil with good.

Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Blessed are those who mourn over sins; they shall be comforted by the Holy Spirit, who is therefore called the Paraclete—that is, the Comforter—so that, having lost temporal things, they may enjoy eternal joy.

Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled. Here he speaks of lovers of the true and unshaken good. They shall be filled with that food of which the Lord himself says: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John VI), where he speaks of righteousness; and with that water of which whoever drinks will have within him “a spring of water welling up to eternal life.”

Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. He calls blessed those who help the wretched, because they are repaid in such a way that they are freed from misery.

Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. As it is written elsewhere: “Seek him in simplicity of heart.” For this is a pure heart: a simple heart. And just as this light cannot be seen except by pure eyes, so God will not be seen unless that which can see him is pure.

Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God. In peace there is perfection, where nothing is opposed; therefore the peacemakers are sons of God, because nothing resists God. Peacemakers within themselves are those who bring all the movements of their soul into harmony and thereby become the kingdom of God. Here the following poetic lines are appropriate:

> Peace nourishes the soul; concord preserves peace.  
> Peace restrains strife; concord binds people together in unity.  
> Strife fears peace; discord flees from peace.  
> Peace drives away hatred; peace nourishes chaste love.

Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. He does not mean those persecuted on account of wickedness, but those persecuted because of division within Christian unity. For Hagar also suffered persecution from Sarah, and the one who inflicted it was holy, while the one who suffered it was wicked. He significantly added, “for righteousness’ sake”: many suffer persecution on account of their sins and are not righteous. (From Jerome.) At the same time, consider that the eighth beatitude of true circumcision ends in martyrdom.

Blessed are you when people revile you and persecute you and speak every evil against you falsely because of me. That curse is to be despised, and it creates blessedness, which proceeds from the false speaker’s mouth. Hence he specifically defines what a blessed curse is: every curse spoken against you falsely because of me. Therefore, where Christ is the cause, there the curse is to be desired.

Rejoice and exult, for your reward is abundant in heaven. I do not know who among us could fulfill this—to have our reputation torn apart by insults and yet exult in the Lord. One who pursues empty glory cannot fulfill it. We must therefore rejoice and exult [Col. 0546D] so that a reward may be prepared for us in the heavens. Elegantly, we read in a certain volume: “Do not seek glory, and you will not grieve when you are without glory.”

(From Augustine.) “In heaven” means in spiritual realms, where wisdom and righteousness dwell. Hence the Apostle says: “Our commonwealth is in heaven” (Philippians II). (From Jerome.) When he says, “Blessed are the poor,” he rejects greed. “Blessed are the meek” excludes anger and indignation. “Blessed are those who mourn” opposes the world’s sorrow, which produces death. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst” restrains gluttony, or desire for every kind of pleasure, through fasting. “Blessed are the merciful” casts down pride by humbly suffering with others. “Blessed are the pure in heart” forcefully tears out fornication and every defilement of the body. “Blessed are the peacemakers” humbles empty glory through love of peace. “Blessed are those who suffer persecution” casts away sloth and every love of wandering about.

## ON THE FEAST OF VIRGINS

### GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER XIII

> “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field. When a man finds it, he hides it, and for joy over it goes and sells all that he has and buys that field. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls. When he has found one precious pearl, he goes and sells all that he has and buys it. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind. When it was full, they drew it out, and sitting beside the shore, they chose the good into their vessels, but threw the bad outside. So it will be at the consummation of the age. The angels will go out and separate the wicked from the midst of the righteous and throw them into the furnace of fire. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth there. Have you understood all these things?’ They said to him: ‘Yes.’ He said to them: ‘Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old.’”

The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field. When a man finds it, he hides it, and for joy over it goes and sells all that he has and buys that field. Delayed by the frequent obscurities of the parables, we go beyond a clause-by-clause interpretation, so that we seem almost to have passed from one kind of interpretation to another.

(From Jerome.) This treasure, in which all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden, is either God the Word, who appears hidden in the flesh of Christ, or the holy Scriptures, in which knowledge of the Savior is stored. When someone finds him in them, he ought to despise all the profits of this age so that he may possess the one whom he has found. As for what follows—“when a man finds it, he hides it”—this is said not because he does so out of envy, but because he hides him in his heart out of fear, as one who guards him and does not wish to lose him, preferring him to his former possessions.

Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls. When he has found one precious pearl, he goes and sells all that he has and buys it. In other words, the same thing is said here as above. The good pearls sought by the merchant are the Law and the Prophets, and knowledge of the Old Testament; but the one most precious pearl is knowledge of the Savior, the mystery of his passion, and the secret of his resurrection. When the merchant, like the Apostle Paul, finds it, he despises as refuse and rubbish all the mysteries of the Law and the Prophets and his former observances, in which he had lived blamelessly, so that he may gain Christ. The discovery of the new pearl does not condemn the former pearls; rather, in comparison with it, every other gem becomes less valuable.

[Col. 0548A]

Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind. When it was full, they drew it out, and sitting beside the shore, chose the good into their vessels, but threw the bad outside. So it will be at the consummation of the age. The angels will go out and separate the wicked from the midst of the righteous, and so forth. Once Jeremiah’s prophecy had been fulfilled—“Behold, I am sending many fishermen to you” (Jeremiah XVI)—after Peter and Andrew, James and John, the sons of Zebedee, heard, “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men,” they wove for themselves from the Old and New Testament a net of evangelical doctrines. They cast it into the sea of this age, where to this day it is stretched amid the waves, catching from the salty and bitter whirlpools whatever falls into it—that is, both good and bad people, and the best and worst fish. But when the consummation and end of the world have come, as he explains more clearly below, the net will be drawn out onto the shore. Then the true judgment for separating the fish will be displayed; and, as though in a very tranquil harbor, the good will be placed in the vessels of the heavenly dwellings, while the bad will be received by the flame of Gehenna to be scorched and dried up.

Have you understood all these things? They said to him: Yes. This saying is directed particularly to the apostles, and he says to them, “Have you understood these things?” He does not wish them merely to hear, like the people, but to understand, as future teachers.

Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old. The apostles were instructed scribes and notaries of the Savior. They inscribed his words and commands, through the mysteries of the heavenly kingdoms, on tablets of fleshly hearts, and they possessed the wealth of the householder, bringing forth from the treasure of their teachings new things and old, so that whatever they preached in the Gospel they might prove by the words of the Law and the Prophets. Hence the bride also says in the Song of Songs: “New things together with old, my cousin, I have kept for you.”

### GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER XXV

> “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride. Five of them were foolish, and five wise. But the five foolish, after taking their lamps, did not take oil with them. The wise, however, took oil in their vessels with their lamps. Since the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and slept. But at midnight a cry arose: ‘Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him.’ Then all those virgins arose and trimmed their lamps. But the foolish said to the wise: ‘Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out.’ The wise answered, saying: ‘Perhaps there will not be enough for us and you; go rather to those who sell it and buy some for yourselves.’ While they were going to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready entered with him for the wedding, and the door was shut. At last the other virgins came, saying: ‘Lord, Lord, open to us.’ But he answered and said: ‘Truly I tell you, I do not know you.’ Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.”

The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins. (From Gregory.) Since it is established that no reprobate enters the kingdom, one may ask why it is said to be like foolish virgins. But it should be understood that sacred Scripture often calls the present Church the kingdom of heaven. Elsewhere the Lord says: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather from his kingdom”—that is, from the present Church—“all scandals.” And elsewhere he says: “Whoever loosens one of these commandments and teaches people so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XIII)—that is, in the Church. Therefore here also the present Church is signified by the ten virgins. Each person subsists in the five senses of the body. The five doubled make ten. And because a multitude of the faithful is gathered from both sexes, the holy Church is proclaimed like ten virgins. Since the wicked are mixed with the good, and the reprobate with the elect, it is rightly said to be like both wise and foolish virgins.

Five of them were foolish, and five wise. It seems to me, therefore, that the five virgins signify continence divided in five against the enticements of the flesh. The appetite of the soul must be restrained from the pleasure of the eyes, the pleasure of the ears, the pleasure of smelling, tasting, and touching. But because this continence is practiced partly before God, so as to please him through the inner joy of continence, and partly only before human beings, so as to capture human glory, five are called [Col. 0549C] wise and five foolish, although both groups are virgins, since both practice continence, even though they rejoice in different sources of encouragement.

Some interpret this parable of the ten foolish and wise virgins simply as referring to virgins. Some, in accordance with the Apostle, are virgins both in body and in mind; others preserve only the virginity of their bodies, but either do not possess other works corresponding to their purpose, or, while their parents’ guardianship preserves them, have nevertheless married in mind. But it seems to me that this comparison pertains not to virginal bodies but to the whole human race, including churchmen, Jews, and heretics, who are called virgins because they glory in knowledge of the one God.

[Col. 0549D]

Who took their lamps. They are called lamps because they testify with their hands to the works performed according to this continence; for it is said: “Let your works shine before people.”

They went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride. By the name “bridegroom,” Christ is understood, concerning whom the Gospel says: “The sons of the bridegroom will not fast as long as the bridegroom is with them.” Therefore those who are not Christians cannot go out to meet Christ the bridegroom. He speaks of one body, comprising both sexes, bridegroom and bride; but we understand by reason what applies to the Lord and what applies to the Church, as elsewhere: “As for a bridegroom, he placed a headdress upon me, and as for a bride, he adorned me with an ornament.” He spoke of one body, that is, Christ and the Church.

[Col. 0550A]

But the five foolish ones, having taken their lamps, did not take oil with them. (From Augustine.) For many, although they hope greatly in Christ’s goodness, nevertheless have no joy while living continently except in human praise; therefore they do not have oil with them. For I think that joy itself is signified by oil: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness.” But whoever does not rejoice for this reason—that he is pleasing to God inwardly—does not have oil with him.

For by oil the brightness of glory is signified. The vessels, moreover, are our hearts, in which we carry all that we think. The foolish virgins do not take oil with them because they do not have glory within their conscience: for they often display their good works to both the elect and the reprobate, but only those come to the bridegroom with oil who seek inward glory from what they have done outwardly. Hence it is also said through the Psalmist concerning the holy Church of the elect: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Psalm 44).

But the prudent took oil in their vessels with their lamps. They placed the joy of good works in their heart and conscience. Thus the Apostle also exhorts us: “Let a person examine himself,” he says, “and then he will have glory in himself, and not in another.”

(From Gregory.) The prudent have oil in their vessels because they retain the brightness of glory within their conscience, as Paul bears witness when he says: “Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience.”

But while the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and slept. (From Augustine.) He says “all,” because from both kinds of continent people—whether those who give glory for their good work to God, or those who rest in human praise—people die during this interval, until, at the Lord’s coming, the resurrection of the dead takes place.

(From Gregory.) While the Judge delays his coming to the final judgment, the elect and the reprobate are lulled in the sleep of death. To sleep, indeed, is to die; but before sleep, to become drowsy is, before death, to grow weak with respect to salvation, because through the burden of illness one arrives at the sleep of death. Consequently it is said, “they slept,” because afterward they are to be awakened.

But at midnight, etc. (From Gregory.) The cry concerning the bridegroom takes place at midnight because the day of judgment steals upon us in such a way that it cannot be foreseen when it will come, since the Lord himself says: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows” (Matthew 24). And the Apostle says: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians 5). Through the cry of the angels and the trumpets of the powers that precede it, Christ’s coming resounds. It is a tradition of the Jews that Christ will come at midnight, in imitation of the Egyptian time when the Passover was celebrated and the doorposts of our foreheads were consecrated with the blood of the lamb. Hence I think that the apostolic tradition has remained, namely, that on the day of the Paschal vigil it is not permitted to dismiss the people before midnight, but that, awaiting Christ’s coming, they should remain standing in the Church.

Then they all arose, etc. (From Gregory.) Then all the virgins rise, because the elect and the reprobate are awakened from the sleep of their death; they trim their lamps because they reckon up the works they have with them, for which they expect to receive eternal blessedness.

(From Augustine.) They prepared their lamps—that is, the accounts of their works that they must render. For we must be presented before the tribunal of Christ, so that there each person may receive what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.

But the foolish said to the wise: “Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out.” (From Gregory.) What is it that they then ask from the prudent for oil, except that, when they find themselves empty within at the Judge’s coming, they seek testimony from without? As though, deceived in their own confidence, they were saying to their neighbors: “You see us being rejected as though without works; tell us what you have seen in our works.” But the lamps of the foolish virgins go out because their works, which appeared bright to people outwardly, are darkened inwardly at the Judge’s coming, and do not reach their recompense, because for them they received from people the praises they loved.

(From Jerome.) Their lamps were shown to be in danger of being extinguished: they shone in part, yet did not possess unfailing light or enduring works. If, therefore, anyone has a virginal soul and loves chastity, he must not be content with mediocre things, which quickly fade and wither when the heat arises, but must pursue perfect virtues, so that he may have everlasting light.

The prudent answered, saying: “Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you.” (From Augustine.) For each person will give an account for himself, and no one will be assisted before God by another’s testimony, since the secrets of hearts are visible to him. And scarcely does each person suffice for himself, so that his conscience may bear witness on his behalf.

(From Gregory.) On that day—for I am speaking of certain people who rest in the peace of the Church—the testimony of each person scarcely suffices for himself; how much less for himself and his neighbor? And immediately they add by way of rebuke:

“Go instead to those who sell, and buy some for yourselves.” (From Augustine.) They should not be thought to have given advice, but rather to have recalled their crimes indirectly.

(From Gregory.) The sellers of oil are flatterers. For whoever, having received any gift of grace, offers the brightness of glory through his empty praises, sells what is, as it were, oil. Concerning this oil the Psalmist says: “But let not the oil of the sinner make my head fat” (Psalm 140).

But while they went to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready entered with him to the wedding, and the door was shut. (From Augustine.) While they were going, the bridegroom came—that is, while they were inclining themselves toward outward things and seeking to rejoice in solid realities, because they did not know inward joys. He came who judges, and those who were ready—that is, those for whom conscience bore good testimony before God—entered with him to the wedding, that is, where the pure soul is joined to the eternal Word of God and made fruitful. The door was shut—that is, after those had been received who have been changed into angelic life. “For we shall all rise,” he says, “but we shall not all be changed” (1 Corinthians 15). The entrance to the kingdom of heaven is shut: for after the judgment there is no place for prayers or merits. If only one could taste in the palate of one’s heart what is meant here, what wonder is contained in the words, “the bridegroom came”? What sweetness? “They entered with him to the wedding”—what bitterness? “And the door was shut.” How great then will be the joy of the elect, who are worthy to rejoice in his vision and to enter with him together into the wedding—who rejoice in the bridegroom’s wedding, and yet are themselves the bride, because in that eternal bridal chamber of the kingdom God is joined to our vision, so that he who is our vision may never be torn away forever from the embraces of his love. Then the door of the kingdom is closed to those who mourn, though now it is opened daily to the penitent. For then there will indeed be repentance, but it will no longer be fruitful, because whoever now wastes the fitting time when it comes will then by no means find forgiveness.

Finally the other virgins also come, saying: “Lord, Lord, open to us.” (From Jerome.) The confession contained in the title “Lord” is indeed excellent, and its repetition is likewise an indication of faith; but what good does it do to invoke with the voice one whom you deny by your works?

(From Gregory.) There the person who here refused to hear what God commanded can no longer obtain from God what he asks. Whoever has lost the fitting time for repentance comes uselessly with prayers before the door of the kingdom.

(From Augustine.) It is not said that they bought oil; therefore we must understand that, with no joy in others’ praises now remaining, they return amid distress and great affliction to imploring God. But great is his severity after the judgment, whose ineffable mercy was bestowed before the judgment.

But he answered and said: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know.” (From Jerome.) “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2), and “the one who is ignorant will be ignored” (1 Corinthians 14). The Lord does not know the workers of iniquity.

(From Gregory.) They offer prayers, but they are not known, because then God abandons as strangers those whom he does not now acknowledge as his own through the merit of their life.

Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour. If each person knew at what time he would depart from the present age, he could assign one period to pleasures and another to repentance. But to the sinner who promised a life of repentance, God did not promise tomorrow. Therefore we must always fear the final day, which we can never foresee.

(From Augustine.) Each person does not know not only the time of that final moment when the bridegroom will come, but also the day and hour of his own sleep. Whoever is prepared will be found prepared until sleep—that is, until death, which is owed to all—even when that voice sounds at midnight by which everyone will be awakened. But when he says that the virgins came out to meet the bridegroom and the bride, I think this should be understood in such a way that the thing called the bride is constituted from those very virgins, just as, when all Christians are running together into the Church, sons are said to run together to their mother, since, with the sons gathered together, the one called their mother is thereby constituted.

[Col. 0553]

# SUMMARY OF THE EPISTLES AND GOSPELS READ IN CHURCHES THROUGHOUT THE CYCLE OF THE YEAR

Containing within itself, like a cornucopia, the marrow and kernel of the whole teaching of piety, without anyone’s biting it, written for the use of the ministers of the Church and appended to Smaragdus.

[Col. 0553A]

# ON THE VIGIL OF CHRIST’S NATIVITY

## EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER 1:

Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, etc.

1. The Gospel of God is found throughout all Scripture, which contains every good thing and is useful for teaching, etc. (2 Timothy 3.)

2. The confession concerning Christ is that he is the Son of God and the son of David—that is, true God, at the same time made true man from the seed of David. Catholic faith knows that both of these are written, and confesses both to be true. If you say that he is God alone, you deny the remedy by which you were healed. If you say that he is man alone, you deny the power by which you were created.

3. The goal of apostolic preaching is the obedience of faith in the name of Jesus: so that, by obeying the truth, souls may be purified through the Holy Spirit with brotherly love. Grace and eternal life follow this.

## READING FROM ISAIAH, CHAPTER 62:

“For Zion’s sake I will not be silent,” etc.

1. The longing for Christ’s coming among the ancients, since he is our righteousness and salvation, through whom we are defended from the injury of all creatures and saved as through a most merciful friend.

2. He does not merely desire him to be present, but cries out that God has been manifested in the flesh, which is the mystery of piety, undeniably great (2 Timothy 3).

3. The praises, victories, and triumphs of Christ’s Church: she is no longer to be called forsaken; the Lord’s will is in her, and the Lord is pleased with her. These things contend with the titles of the Church of the wicked—δίς διαπασῶν, “twice through all” [the phrase is uncertain].

## GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER 1:

“Now the generation of Christ was thus.”

1. Christ is the son of man because he is from the seed of Abraham. Christ is the Son of God because he is from the Holy Spirit.

2. Ministering spirits are angels, who are sent into service for the sake of those who are heirs of salvation (Hebrews 1). Here they serve Mary and Joseph.

3. The sum of the Gospel is contained in the name Jesus, as the angel explains: *Ieschua* signifies salvation among the Hebrews, and he is our salvation, life, and resurrection, through whom we have been saved and delivered.

[Col. 0553C]

# ON THE NIGHT OF THE NATIVITY

## READING FROM THE PROPHET ISAIAH, CHAPTER 9:

“The people of the nations who walked,” etc.

1. Christ the Lord is rich toward all who call upon him, Jews and nations alike, and he has called them from darkness into his marvelous light (1 Peter 3).

2. The promise to Abraham has been fulfilled, so that his seed would be like the sand of the sea and the stars of heaven (Genesis 15).

3. What Christ is, why he came, and what we have through him—all are expressed with remarkable emphasis in this catalogue of names: “Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God,” etc.

## GOSPEL FOR THE NIGHT OF THE NATIVITY, LUKE, CHAPTER 2:

“There went out,” etc.

1. Christ our Lord. In the year 3962 from the beginning of the world’s creation according to the Hebrew truth, and in the year 5201 according to the Septuagint.

[Col. 0554A]

Two thousand three hundred and six years from the Flood.

Two thousand and fourteen years from Abraham’s birth.

1059 years from Moses and the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt.

1031 years from Solomon and the first building of the Temple.

519 years from its rebuilding under Darius.

751 years from the founding of the city of Rome. In the third year of the 194th Olympiad.

When Caesar Augustus, by God’s ordering, established the firmest peace, he was born in Bethlehem of Judea.

2. The sum of the Gospel and the preaching concerning Christ is proclaimed by the angel: “Do not fear; I announce joy. A Savior has been born for you.” The emphasis is on “Savior” and “for you.”

3. The angels are present with the Lord of angels at his conception, birth, and indeed throughout the whole course of Christ’s life; and the angels’ song contains the Gospel when it announces peace and the εὐδοκία—“good pleasure”—of God.

[Col. 0554B]

# ON THE DAY OF THE NATIVITY

## EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS, CHAPTER 1:

“In many parts and in many ways.”

1. The ineffable goodness of God, who in these last days has spoken to us in his Son, so that through him, who is in his bosom, he might announce all things to us. How, then, shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation? (Hebrews 2.)

2. Testimonies to Christ’s divinity, full and varied, from the Scriptures—Psalms 2, 96, 103, 44, and 101—so that we may know that the one who came to announce the remission of sins is God, and may not doubt God’s will.

3. Christ himself made purification for sins and sat at the right hand of Majesty on high, so that believers may know that Christ has forgiven their sins and that he reigns, conquers, and triumphs. That great, marvelous, and astonishing mystery surpasses understanding, as Chrysostom notes: our flesh sits above and is worshiped by angels, archangels, cherubim, and seraphim. Chrysostom is overwhelmed as he considers this. Therefore accursed is the heresy that denies Christ’s true humanity.

## GOSPEL FOR THE DAY OF THE NATIVITY, JOHN, CHAPTER 1:

“In the beginning was the Word,” etc.

1. The sum concerning Christ is to believe that he is true God and man, who created all things and was given to human beings as life and light, although few receive him. Thus John sets it forth, thus Paul, and thus all Scripture.

2. How the natures could be joined together, God knows. The Christian can answer many questions with “God knows”; this is Chrysostom’s most useful rule.

3. When you hear “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” consider all that the ancient saints occupied themselves with. Why did God become man? Clearly, so that the Church might have her head (Ephesians 1; Colossians 1); so that the structure of the Temple might have its cornerstone (Psalm 117); so that every creature might have a mediator (Galatians 3); so that the whole army of heaven might have its king (Luke 1; Revelation 19); so that God’s school might have its teacher (Joel 2); so that the city of Jerusalem might have its Temple (Revelation 2); so that the Temple of the heavenly Jerusalem might have its priest (Hebrews 7); so that all might have their sacrifice in the Temple; so that all the sheep of God’s pasture might have one common shepherd (John 10); so that all the children of God, and every creature, might have the firstborn brother (Romans 8).

Now, when you hear “flesh,” consider Christ’s extreme humiliation; in that humiliation, the forgiveness of sin and satisfaction; and, beyond that, the overflowing love of the Father, who delivered up his Son for us.

[Col. 0555A]

# ON THE NATIVITY OF SAINT STEPHEN

## ACTS, CHAPTER 7:

“Stephen, full of grace,” etc.

1. A description of Stephen’s person: a man full of grace and courage and endowed with many splendid and holy gifts, a type of the Church’s deacons. The bishop and the deacon have similar conditions; see this in Paul. Hence we should be ashamed, who fight in diametrical opposition to them.

2. A type of the wicked who attack the truth: what they cannot accomplish by truth, they attempt through false accusations and slanders. This has always been the lot of Christians, that they should be burdened with lies. Hence the many apologies of Tertullian, Justin, Quadratus, and Miltiades; hence the slanders of our own times: blasphemy against God, contempt for the saints, trampling upon the sacraments, and proscription of good works.

3. The person defended by God is stronger than the person persecuted by the world. What a marvelous consolation for those facing death for the truth, who see Christ standing and helping them.

## GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER 23:

“Behold, I send to you,” etc.

1. Here you have the cause of the killing of all the prophets: it was pride of heart.

2. When someone suffers punishment for another’s sin, according to that saying of Exodus 21: “You shall repay the sin of the parents upon the children, to the third and fourth generation.”

3. A most sweet comparison, in which Christ compares himself to a hen and us to chicks, by whom alone we escape from kites—that is, from devils—through faith in Christ, just as we fell away through unbelief. And we hear the dreadful judgment, together with the unbelieving Jews: “Your house shall be left desolate” (Matthew 23).

[Col. 0555C]

# ON THE NATIVITY OF JOHN THE EVANGELIST

## EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS, CHAPTER 1:

“Blessed be God and Father.”

1. Our salvation proceeds from God’s election, so that whoever glories may glory in the Lord, and so that the saints may know that they cannot fall away.

2. Election is followed by a righteous life pleasing to God, in which faith works through love. For believers make their calling and election firm through works of faith (2 Peter 1).

3. In Christ, the beloved Son of God, there is redemption through his blood, for the remission of sins, so that no one may glory in works.

## GOSPEL OF JOHN, LAST CHAPTER:

“Jesus said to Peter: Follow me.”

1. Concerning the breaking of our own will into the will of God. Often we are compelled to recognize that God’s will is other than ours, not by a voice from heaven, nor through a prophet, revelation, dream, or rapture of mind, but by events themselves or by circumstances calling us to something other than what we had determined. Augustine, Letter 65 to Paulinus and Therasia.

2. An example concerning those who look at another’s calling and another’s works, when they ought fearlessly to follow Christ who calls them: “For obedience is better than sacrifice.”

3. The authority of John the Evangelist and the dignity of his testimony: he reclined upon Jesus’ breast; he wrote; his testimony is true. His whole purpose is directed toward our believing in the name of the only-begotten Son of God and, by believing, our having life through his name.

[Col. 0555A]

# ON THE NATIVITY OF THE INNOCENTS

## REVELATION, CHAPTER 14:

“I saw above Mount Zion.”

1. Christ is the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, protecting his Church—that is, the number of God’s people—against the beast.

2. The Church sings a new song to the Lamb who stands: that is, she celebrates God through praise and imitation, confession of faith, and a righteous life.

3. The innocence of true Christians: they are virgins, chaste and modest, without blemish and blameless in the way (Psalm 119).

## GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER 2:

“Behold, an angel of the Lord.”

1. From the very beginnings of life, let us prepare ourselves for temptations and ambushes by Christ’s example.

2. God’s care for his own, according to the saying: “From my mother’s womb he remembered my name.” The angel appears and commands him to flee into Egypt; he recalls him from Egypt into the land of Israel.

3. An example of impiety in Herod, which continues until the consummation of the age, while the Church endures persecution.

[Col. 0556B]

# ON THE OCTAVE OF THE NATIVITY

## TO TITUS, CHAPTER 2:

“The grace has appeared.”

1. He embraces the whole of Christianity clearly and wonderfully in brief. Having denied impiety, let us live soberly, justly, and piously—that is, μετανοεῖτε, “repent” (Mark 1; Matthew 3).

2. Christ is preached and commended, and what he did for our sake: he gave himself for us, redeemed us from all iniquity, died for our sins, and rose again for our justification.

3. Those who believe this are followers of good works. Here you have the root together with its fruits, faith together with works, and the fact that without grace there is no good work.

## GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER 2:

“When the eight days were completed.”

1. Christ is circumcised so that we might be circumcised spiritually; he is presented to the Lord so that he might teach us to present ourselves to God. He observes the figures of the Law, though he is the Law’s author.

2. An example of the Christian person in Simeon, who was pious and just and in whom the Holy Spirit was.

3. He departs from this world in peace who understands that God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself (2 Corinthians 5).

[Col. 0556C]

# FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THE NATIVITY

## EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE GALATIANS, CHAPTER 4:

“As long as the heir is a child.”

1. He distinguishes the time of the Law from the time of grace: the Law was given through Moses, while grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (Hebrews 9). He speaks of worldly sanctity, which could not make its worshiper perfect, imposed in foods, drinks, washings, and fleshly ordinances, until the time of correction.

2. The fullness of time is the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of salvation, when God is manifested in the flesh and the Son of God becomes the Son of a virgin.

3. The dignity of believers: they are sons and heirs through God, not through merit or nature, but through the Spirit of grace, who cries in our hearts, “Abba, Father.”

## GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER 2:

“Joseph and Mary were marveling.”

1. Christ is for some a resurrection, for others a downfall. Faith is to believe and be built up. Unbelief is ruin and collapse.

2. A consolation: where there is no contradiction, there is no word of God. If Christ is appointed for downfall and resurrection, then so are the members of Christ. Hence the Apostles: “Lord, who has believed our report?” (Isaiah 53; John 13; Romans 10.)

3. The works of faith in Anna the prophetess: prayer and fasting. She is therefore not condemned; rather, faith is taught first, then works, so that we may do good works. “God looked upon Abel and upon his offerings” (Genesis 4).

[Col. 0557A]

# ON THE DAY OF THEOPHANY

## READING FROM ISAIAH, CHAPTER 60:

“Arise, shine, Jerusalem.”

1. The Church is gathered throughout the whole world through the preaching of the Gospel. Christ reigns in her, and all good things are found there—now indeed obscure, but destined through Christ to become clearer day by day, so that very many may join her.

2. Where the Church is not, there is no salvation, and the nations are wretched where the word of God is unknown.

3. Whoever embraces the faith of Christ in Germany cannot fail to love those who invoke God’s name in the most distant regions—Sabaea, Panchaea, Arabia, among the Damascenes, Armenians, and Assyrians—for there is one God, one faith, one religion, and in Christ all the elect are one and perfected into one.

[Col. 0557B]

## GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER 2:

“When Jesus had been born.”

1. An example of the calling of the nations into the obedience of faith.

2. The Scripture of the Old Testament clearly expresses the time of Christ’s coming, the place of his birth, and the manner of his birth, life, and death. Here, concerning the place of his birth, you have the testimony from Micah 5.

3. An example of impiety in Herod; those who seek themselves under the title of piety act as Herod does today. Here again you have a memorable example of hope, faith, and God’s care for his own.

[Col. 0557B]

# FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THEOPHANY

## EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER 12:

“I beseech you.”

1. Rational worship, which must be performed through soul and spirit: true religion in Christianity consists in presenting ourselves to God as a living, holy, acceptable sacrifice.

2. Christians must not be conformed to the world, which lies wholly in evil. Having abandoned the will of the nations, which consists in wantonness, lusts, drunkenness, revelries, and drinking parties, let them give themselves wholly to the will of God.

3. A marvelous and most beautiful comparison concerning the fellowship of members with one another in one body—a comparison also used by Cicero in *On Duties*, Book 3—which binds us together for the mutual building up of Christ’s body, so that we may benefit one another.

## GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER 2:

“When Jesus was twelve years old.”

1. What is asserted about Christ’s childhood apart from the Scriptures is not far removed from fables. This was the desire of the corrupt age of the previous generation to spoil everything and misuse the titles of illustrious people; thus many ψευδεπιγραφαί—“false writings under another’s name”—arose.

2. Here there is a most fitting example that the glory of God and the salvation of souls must be dearer to us than any affection for parents; for God must be preferred to parents and to all things.

3. A pattern for forming Christian youth: Christ was subject to his parents; he progressed in wisdom and age, and in favor with God and human beings. By this Lesbian rule let us form our children; let us give them the discipline of marriage, and Christian commonwealths will be happy to possess such seed.

[Col. 0557A]

# SECOND SUNDAY AFTER THEOPHANY

## EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER 12:

“Having gifts according to the grace that has been given to us,” etc.

1. A necessary command: each person must serve his calling, each must adorn his own assigned place, and the shoemaker must not go beyond the shoe.

2. But here let us likewise examine which callings please God, so that no one may please himself without contributing to the building up of his neighbor.

3. The best rule here for discerning spirits is the analogy of faith. Hence monks, Anabaptists, and those who boast of revelations are expelled together with the company of the spirit of error.

## GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER 11:

“A wedding took place at Cana of Galilee.”

1. Honorable marriage and an undefiled marriage bed, which Christ honored with his most chaste mother and holy disciples, by the presence of himself and his followers and by the generous and sweet-smelling miracle of wine.

2. Christ is nowhere flattering toward his mother, as is learned from this and other passages of the Gospel. He teaches that bodily kinship did nothing for his mother unless she had blessed faith, and that parents must be obeyed when they do not impede divine things.

3. Christ is the one who irrigates the vineyards, who turns rain into wine through the root of the vine, and who accomplishes suddenly at a wedding what he accomplishes in the plant every year over a longer period of time. Let us only acknowledge God’s works and use his creatures with thanksgiving.

[Col. 0558B]

# THIRD SUNDAY AFTER THEOPHANY

## EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER 12:

“Do not be wise,” etc.

1. The root of Christianity is poverty of spirit and modesty of mind, which cannot tolerate μεγαφρονεῖν—“thinking highly,” or “being high-minded”—nor bear pride of mind.

2. Let peace and harmony so bind and join all Christians together that, with common zeal, they are concerned for one another, so that they benefit all—Jews, nations, friends, and enemies—and no one is harmed. This will be to heap coals of fire upon the heads of such people.

3. What Tertullian says concerning patience, all Christians should know from this passage to have been spoken by God to them: “Vengeance belongs to me, and I will avenge; patience belongs to me, and I will reward patience.”

[Col. 0558C]

## GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER 8:

“When Jesus had come down from the mountain.”

1. True faith breaks itself wholly into the will of God, so that a person endowed with it wishes to belong to God whether healthy or sick, dead or alive.

2. The power of Christ’s divinity: by a word he heals the leper.

3. Christ declares himself Lord and τέλειον—“fulfillment”—of the Law. He touches the leper, although this was forbidden in the Law, teaching that the leprosy of the soul, namely sin, is to be feared more.

[Col. 0558C]

# FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER THEOPHANY

## EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER 13:

“Owe no one anything.”

1. When John was living in Ephesus into extreme old age and could scarcely be carried to the Church in the hands of his disciples, since he was unable to say much, he used to say nothing else at each gathering except this: “Little children, love one another.” At last, wearied, they said to their teacher, “Why do you always say this?” He replied, “Because it is the Lord’s command, and if it alone is done, it is sufficient.” Jerome, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians. Paul speaks here most beautifully in the same spirit.

2. Here Paul gathers the commands of the second table of the Decalogue into a clear and brief compendium concerning love, which is the goal of the Law (1 Timothy 1).

3. Love, and do whatever you wish, and you will not sin.

## GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER 8:

“When Jesus entered the boat.”

1. A figure of the future temptations of the Church, by which the Apostles were exercised. Although they were neither lame nor blind nor suffering from any other illness, and although they saw very many people being healed each day and thereby saw his omnipotence—to whom the winds and the sea obey—and retained a firm memory of his benefits, they were nevertheless brought into this storm.

2. This is a consolation for all Christ’s faithful: he is present with his own until the consummation of the age and does not leave them orphaned, so that they may not despair in the midst of dangers.

3. Συλλήβδην—“in a word”—let us all and each of us cry out, princes, monks, bishops, spiritual and worldly people, in this storm of the Church and amid these things so wretchedly afflicted: “Lord, save us; we are perishing!” Let us not doubt that we shall rouse the Lord so that he may have mercy on us.

[Col. 0559A]

# SUNDAY IN SEPTUAGESIMA

## FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER 9:

“Do you not know that those who run in the stadium?”

1. The Christian life is not at all soft and delicate, but laborious and full of sweat. Yet God, the judge of the contest, wishes to reward it; this is set before our eyes through beautiful comparisons.

[Col. 0559B]

2. Those who were going to compete in the long jump, as Philostratus says in his little book *On Athletes*, abstained from intercourse and other pleasures. It is disgraceful, then, if we conduct ourselves more sluggishly for the prize of eternal life than the common crowd does for a worthless reward.

3. An example is offered for imitation: Paul, in his speech, life, and good deeds, and likewise the ancient fathers, who shared in the mystery of baptism and in spiritual food and drink not merely in name but in reality.

## GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER 20:

“The kingdom of heaven is like a householder.”

1. Parables are comparisons drawn from familiar things, the simplest mode of teaching, and especially suited to the uneducated. As for individual words, we should not be anxiously curious in these matters, when the substance of the meaning can be clear.

2. This is a very difficult passage concerning predestination. Why does he not call everyone at once, but calls one at this hour and another at a later hour? For from God’s predestination it follows that someone believes or does not believe, is freed from sin or is not freed, so that we may know that our salvation rests not in our powers but solely in God’s power. Hence we have hope against sin and Satan.

3. “Because the last will be first, and the first last, and many are called, but few are chosen”: a boundary is thus set for rash and lofty spirits who wish to investigate God’s inscrutable counsels—whether they are predestined or not, and so forth. Whoever wishes to be a wise and faithful steward should follow Paul’s order in the concise Epistle to the Romans, the epitome of Christianity, and above all inquire about Christ in the Gospel, so that a person may acknowledge his own sins and Christ’s grace, fight against sin, and, once he has begun to be under the cross and passion, will then teach predestination correctly. For not all wineskins are capable of this new wine.

[Col. 0559D]

# SUNDAY IN SEXAGESIMA

## SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER 11:

“You gladly tolerate fools.”

1. Paul’s glorying and triumph, unlike the bloody triumphs of certain people who, although they ought to be fathers, are tyrants and, instead of Catholics, are κακόλυκοι—“evil wolves”—in labors, etc. This is the decoration of war; the crown of righteousness remains laid up for that day.

2. Necessity pressed upon Paul, so that what he had concealed for fourteen years he was afterward compelled to disclose. So many dangers threatened the Christian religion from false apostles, worldly philosophy, and Jewish superstition. If Paul had not stood against all of these with every foot, as they say, and had not had daily care for all the churches, evangelical doctrine would have been in the gravest danger. These things rightly condemn the sluggishness of bishops and ministers of the Church and ought to spur us on to render our ministry fully approved.

[Col. 0560A]

3. Plutarch writes about the benefit to be taken from enemies. Here we clearly have an example that the thorn in the flesh—that is, the persecution of wicked people—was useful to Paul. Thus enemies sometimes also benefit us, teaching us sobriety and modesty; and here weakness perfects virtue, and infirmity completes power.

## GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER 8:

“When a very large crowd was gathering, and people were hurrying from every city.”

1. The comparison of the sower exhorts all people to receive the Gospel discourse with eager minds and to apply what they have learned to the practice of piety. For this is the faith of the elect and the acknowledgment of the truth leading to the hope of eternal life.

2. Hence, by the exclamation, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear,” he rouses the hearer. We must not cease from sound teaching, even if it does not always bear fruit in everyone; only a fourth part of the seed produces perfect and complete fruit.

3. Christ is the best interpreter of his own discourse, and here he is the sower. The heart of a human being is the earth or soil; the seed is the Gospel discourse.

[Col. 0560B]

# SUNDAY IN QUINQUAGESIMA

## FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER 13:

“If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have love,” etc.
