1. Love is necessary, but the gifts of tongues, prophecy, and miracles are not necessary. “By this,” says Christ, “all will know that you are my disciples” (John 13), and without the effort to do good to one’s neighbor no one will see God. Therefore this one thing is necessary and must be pursued.

2. The use of charity extends most broadly; hence it is a perpetual gift, diffused throughout the whole life of Christians. It possesses the most beautiful qualities: it is patient, it is kind; charity does not envy, charity is not [Col. 0560C] boastful, it is not puffed up, it is not disdainful, it does not seek its own interests, it is not provoked, it does not devise evil, it does not rejoice over injustice but rejoices with the truth; it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails.

3. Christianity has beginnings, growth, and a summit; it has its own stages and advances through those stages. Therefore let us strive to arrive altogether at the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, at mature manhood, at the measure of the fully developed age of Christ.

## GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER XVIII

“Jesus took the twelve disciples.”

1. The frequent mention of the Lord’s passion and resurrection: for this is the Gospel that we have received, in which we must stand, and through which we attain salvation. Christ died for our sins and rose again for our justification. 1 Cor. XV.

[Col. 0560D]

2. The apostles’ dullness: they understood none of these things, and this saying was hidden from them. Hence there was need of the Spirit as teacher and prompter, John XIV, so that what, because of obscurity or slowness of understanding, they had been unable to commit to memory, they might afterward understand fully, as future teachers of the world.

3. He remedies the apostles’ weakness by restoring sight to a blind man: “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened,” Isa. XXXV. This was a testimony to the Messiah.

[Col. 0560B]

## SUNDAY INVOCAVIT IN LENT

### SECOND EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER VI

“We urge you not to receive the grace of God in vain,” etc.

1. The time of the grace of God exhibited in Christ is the acceptable time and the day of salvation, about which the prophets spoke in harmony. For the Gospel was promised in the Holy Scriptures concerning his Son. Rom. I. And truly it is the time of grace and the day of salvation, for unspeakable blessings have come through Christ. Our curse was cast upon him, and his blessing flowed from him wholly into us.

[Col. 0561A]

2. The Christian life is described here with remarkable brevity: let us give no offense, so that our ministry may not be reproached.

3. The apostles are true deceivers, that is, those who teach a person to despise what he has and hope for what he does not have, to look toward what is unseen and eternal, and to abandon what is seen and temporal.

### GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER IV

“Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, to be tempted by the devil.”

1. Christ is tempted by the devil immediately after his baptism, being led by the Spirit into the wilderness, so that we may know that adversities too are the work of the divine will, and that baptism is an anchor amid temptations. Therefore let us not lose heart in temptations, but act manfully and stand firm in faith, 1 Cor. XV, knowing that through Christ’s baptism we have been made stronger.

[Col. 0561B]

2. The devil is Proteus and Vertumnus, who attacks by various devices; but he must be overcome through endurance, and we must never believe him, even if he commands something useful or cites Scripture, which he does wickedly.

3. The angels applaud us and minister to us if we overcome the tempter.

[Col. 0561B]

## SUNDAY REMINISCERE  
*(Smaragdus calls this the first Sunday in the first month.)*

### 1 THESSALONIANS, CHAPTER IV

“We ask and exhort you in the Lord.”

1. Paul gives commandments, but through our Lord Jesus. For he is the beloved Son, concerning whom the heavenly Father testifies: “Hear him.”

2. A concise statement of the will of God: whoever wishes to obey it will easily recognize it from any teaching, John VII: “The will of God is your sanctification.”

[Col. 0561C]

3. He exhorts us to avoid impurity of life through fear of punishment: the Lord is an avenger of all these things, as in 1 Cor. VI: “Do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God?”

### GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER XV

“Jesus departed and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a woman,” etc.

1. Christ was a minister of the circumcision, for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers. But the Gentiles should glorify God for his mercy. Here, as a prelude to the calling of the Gentiles into the obedience of faith, contrary to his own commandment—which he had given for a time—he goes into the way of the Gentiles, for the Lord is rich toward all who call upon him.

2. How much persistent and fervent prayer can accomplish. The woman did not desist, although she had been rejected and treated indignantly. She follows behind, crying out in a lamentable voice: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.”

[Col. 0561D]

3. The patience and faith of the foreign woman.

[Col. 0561B]

## THIRTIETH SUNDAY, OR, IF YOU PREFER, SUNDAY OCULI

### EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS, CHAPTER V

“Be imitators of God as beloved children, and walk in love.”

1. Christians are temples of the Holy Spirit, who is in them, as Paul testifies, 1 Cor. VI: “Do you not know,” he says, “that your bodies are members of Christ?” And immediately he adds: “Do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit dwelling in you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? For you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God now in your body.” And in 2 Cor. VI he says the same thing: “What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For you are the temple of the living God, as God said: ‘I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people,’” etc. They are also sons of God by adoption, as Paul speaks of Christians in Eph. I: “He predestined us,” he says, “for adoption as sons.” Rom. VIII: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again for fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’” Therefore they are also holy, just as God is holy.

[Col. 0562A]

2. The immeasurable love of God and of Christ toward us: he both freely forgave sin and gave his Son as an offering for our sins.

3. Let us love in return the one who loves us in this way, shunning every kind of shamefulness and vice. Those who act otherwise and are disobedient will face God’s vengeance.

### GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER XI

“Jesus was casting out a demon, and it was mute; and when he had cast it out,” etc.

1. Christ’s miracles are acts of beneficence: he frees a wretched man from a demon that was *κωφόν* (*kōphon*), that is, deaf and mute. Thus, through signs and teaching, he leads people to recognize his omnipotence.

[Col. 0562B]

2. Because the Jews persisted in wickedness, he answers them—not indeed from Scripture, which they denied, but from things that commonly occur. At the same time he answers them gently, teaching us to be mild toward enemies who curse us.

3. Christ’s perpetual war with Satan, and the fact that the blessed are doers, not hearers, of the word.

[Col. 0562B]

## FRIDAY AFTER SUNDAY OCULI

### GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER IV

“Jesus, wearied from the journey.”

1. Jesus is wearied from the journey, so that he may bless weariness for us, just as below he weeps, so that he may bless tears. Throughout the Gospel he is described as weak, so that we may know that we have a high priest who can sympathize with our weaknesses.

2. The water that Christ gives is the Holy Spirit. In him we cry, “Abba, Father”; through him we become true worshipers, who worship in spirit and truth.

[Col. 0562C]

3. Since salvation was also promised to the Gentiles, Christ teaches by the likeness of the harvest, the sowers, and the reapers that the time is at hand for preaching the Gospel throughout the whole world.

[Col. 0562C]

## SATURDAY AFTER SUNDAY OCULI

### GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER VIII

“Jesus went to the Mount of Olives.”

1. In Scripture eighteen persons are counted who are commanded to be stoned for various crimes. The Hebrews had four kinds of execution: strangulation and striking with the sword were the least severe; stoning and burning were the most severe. They demand that the adulteress be stoned.

2. The Lord writes on the ground twice, to teach that the wretched should descend into themselves and that the sinful woman ought indeed to be punished, but not by sinners; that the law should be fulfilled, but not by transgressors.

3. Christ answers in such a way that he neither openly acquits nor condemns her, but indicates why he had come—namely, so that she should not continue to sin.

[Col. 0562D]

## TWENTIETH SUNDAY, THAT IS, SUNDAY LAETARE

### EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS, CHAPTER IV

“It is written that Abraham,” etc.

1. The distinction between the Old and New Testaments, and between the two peoples: one is subject to the slavery of the law, while the other, through faith, is freed from the burden of the law.

2. Prophetic testimonies concerning the multitude of the Gentiles that would flock from every direction to the Gospel of Christ.

3. The hostility of those attached to the carnal law toward those who embrace the spiritual law of the Gospel and the freedom that comes through Christ.

### GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER VI

“Jesus went across the Sea of Galilee.”

1. Here there are two miracles, or a miracle within a miracle. For he satisfies five thousand men with a few loaves, and, through the Lord’s providence, twelve baskets were left over—no fewer than twelve. These are proofs of God’s unspeakable power.

[Col. 0563A]

2. Observe that when Christ heals a paralytic, raises the dead, and calms the storms of the sea, he does not give thanks; but before food he gives thanks, to teach that whenever we eat or drink, it should be done with thanksgiving.

3. Those devoted to luxuries should consider the abstinence of the ancients, whose table consisted of barley loaves and cheap bread, with side dishes of little cost and a few small fish.

[Col. 0563A]

## MONDAY AFTER SUNDAY LAETARE

### GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER II

“The Passover of the Jews was near.”

1. He drove out those who were buying and selling twice: once at the beginning of his ministry, as John relates; and a second time, when the time of his passion was approaching, when he also used more severe chastisement and called it a den of robbers, as in Matt. XX.

2. By this act Christ wished to show that avarice would become the deadly plague of his Church, and that nothing can be sincere and holy where the pursuit of money reigns.

3. Christ’s zeal: because of the house of God, he threw himself into the midst of the fury of the crowd and the priests. See Augustine, so that every Christian, as a member of Christ, may be consumed by zeal for the house of God.

[Col. 0563B]

## WEDNESDAY AFTER SUNDAY LAETARE

### GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER IX

“As Jesus passed by, he saw a man blind from birth.”

1. So that John the evangelist might declare how blind the Jews were, and that an envious mind distorts everything, he describes this miracle so carefully and at such length.

[Col. 0563C]

2. The *parrhesia*—the boldness—of the blind man, who confesses Christ before the crowd while the priests rage and rave, teaching us to spare no one who speaks against Christ.

3. Christ reveals himself to those who seek him with pious affection; to others he conceals himself. Here there is an example in the blind man and the Pharisees, elsewhere in the Magi and Herod, and repeatedly among the crowds and the Pharisees. The same matter was also prefigured in Saul, David, and Jonathan.

[Col. 0563C]

## FRIDAY AFTER SUNDAY LAETARE

### GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER XI

“There was a certain man who was ill, Lazarus.”

1. Among the miracles by which Christ confirms his divinity, this is the chief: through it he teaches that he is Lord of life, death, and illnesses.

2. Just as he splendidly proves his divinity, so also he proves his humanity, because he groaned in spirit, troubled himself, and wept.

3. A consoling saying for all who dread death is what Christ says here: “I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me, even though he has died, will live.” Know here what Augustine says: faith is the soul of your soul.

[Col. 0563A]

## FIFTH SUNDAY IN LENT, WHICH IS SUNDAY JUDICA

### EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS, CHAPTER IX

“Christ, appearing as high priest,” etc.

1. Christ alone is the true and eternal priest according to the order of Melchizedek, always ready for his office and to intercede with the Father for us.

2. Christ is the sole and only offering for our sins; through his blood he obtained eternal redemption—for those who have believed, believe, and will believe.

[Col. 0564A]

3. Let him be accursed who establishes anything else, who multiplies the one offering, who refuses to acknowledge Christ as Savior and mediator of the New Testament, made by God our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption. 1 Cor. I.

### GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER VIII

“Which of you can convict me of sin?”

1. The distinction between the elect and the reprobate, between God’s children and the devil’s children. The former hear the word of God; the latter do not hear it.

2. The insults of the Jews against Christ, calling him a Samaritan and demon-possessed. He rejects the one charge and defends himself modestly; he rebukes the Jews severely.

3. From Abraham to Christ there were 2,025 years, for he was born in the forty-first year of Augustus and suffered in the fourteenth year of Tiberius. Here Christ is declared to be God in these words: “Before Abraham was, I am.”

[Col. 0564A]

## PALM SUNDAY

### EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE PHILIPPIANS, CHAPTER II

“Have this mind among yourselves.”

[Col. 0564B]

1. Christ Jesus was given to us as a gift and an example: as a gift, because he was made for us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption. 1 Cor. I. As an example, so that from him we may learn to be gentle and humble in heart. Matt. XI.

2. The unspeakable counsel of God: Christ had to suffer and thus enter into his glory, and be given the name that is above every name. This is the folly of preaching through which he saves believers. 1 Cor. I.

3. The Christian who seeks true and eternal glory should strive to enter by this way, the way by which Christ entered, and by no other. “If we die with him, we shall also live with him; if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him.” 2 Tim. III.

## HERE BEGINS THE PASSION OF OUR LORD JESUS, ACCORDING TO MATTHEW, MARK, LUKE, AND JOHN

[Col. 0564C]

1. The foundation of the Lord’s passion is the articles of faith, and the saying in John III: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.”

2. In former times, concerning the Lord’s passion, people were accustomed seriously to consider three things among themselves. First, the event itself, as the evangelists describe it in great harmony. Second, the manner of the event, marked by the most steadfast patience and, indeed, by the whole chorus of virtues. Third, the cause of Christ’s passion: each person should think within himself, “You—you are the cause,” as though Christ had suffered for him alone. Therefore, whatever you read or hear, think as though Christ were saying: “I did this for your sake. Follow in my footsteps; humble yourself; be patient; take up your cross and follow me. A servant is not greater than his master.”

3. It is wonderfully consoling for a Christian, who can say with Augustine and the ancients: “All my hope is in the death of my Lord. His death is my merit [Col. 0564D] and my refuge, my salvation, life, and resurrection; my merit is the Lord’s mercy. I am not without merit, so long as the Lord of mercies has not failed. Although the Lord’s mercies are many, I too am rich in merits. The more powerful he is to save, the more secure I am.”

## SUMMARY OF THE LORD’S DISCOURSE, FROM CHAPTER XIII [OF JOHN] TO CHAPTER XVIII

### Chapter XIII

1. Charity was the cause of Christ’s death: he loved his own to the end and omitted nothing that was fitting for one who loves. Thus, as those who are loved, let us love Christ in return, and for his sake let us bring our neighbor to salvation—the end of our faith.

2. The Father gave everything into Christ’s hand: sin, death, his enemies, and even the traitor himself, whom he could have destroyed like a fig or split apart like a rock; but Christ willingly endures passion and death.

[Col. 0565A]

3. The evangelist, about to speak of such great humility in Christ, first wished to commend his majesty: that he had come forth from God and was going to God.

4. Contemplate Christ in this form of humility, washing the feet of his disciples; it will be an antidote against the plague of ambition. Who would not be ashamed to lift up his neck when he sees this? Hence he says, “I have given you an example.” Nor is it enough to know these things; blessed are those who do them.

5. Consolation for the disciples: “Whoever receives anyone whom I send receives me; and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me.”

6. Our weakness is troubled in Christ: he died for us and is troubled for us. Let the arguments of the philosophers perish, those who deny that disturbances of the soul can befall the wise. God makes foolish the wisdom of this world. Christ is troubled and distressed so that he may bless and soothe all these things for us.

7. Judas breaks that great oath, “Do not transgress Salem and the table,” he who, one of the number of the twelve [Col. 0565B], betrayed Christ.

8. The judgment of God, by which God blinds the hardened: after the morsel, Satan entered into him. Ps. LXVIII: “Pour out your anger upon them.”

9. He calls his passion his glorification, so that we may know that the forms of the cross are saving; thus, if a Christian is afflicted, he should not be ashamed but rather glorify God in this portion. 1 Pet. III.

10. Christ’s new commandment concerning charity, by which he wishes his own to be recognized. Faith makes disciples; charity testifies who they are.

11. We cannot bear the cross by our own strength. This is evident from Peter’s presumption. Therefore those who are to become confessors and martyrs must be clothed with power from above.

### Chapter XIV

1. As Christ is about to depart from his own, he consoles them with many assurances.

2. He departs to prepare a place and to take them to himself. In his Father’s house there are many dwelling places.

[Col. 0565C]

3. He himself is the way, the truth, and the life.

4. If it is asked what people in all the centuries before Christ’s coming did, since Christ is the way, the truth, and the life, the answer is: the salvation of religion was lacking to no one who was worthy; whoever lacked it was unworthy.

5. When he has gone to the Father, his disciples will perform greater miracles than he himself did.

6. He consoles them with the promise: if they ask anything in his name, he will do it.

7. He wishes to give another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, so that he may remain with them forever.

8. A terrifying judgment upon the world, which cannot receive the Spirit of truth.

9. He does not wish to leave them orphans, for he is the Father of orphans and the judge of widows.

10. He elegantly and briefly promises a twofold resurrection: his own, which would soon occur, and ours, which will come at the end of the age. When he says: “Because I live, you also will live.”

[Col. 0565D]

11. He repeatedly mentions love, by which he drives away sadness, as though he were saying: “You ought not to be so saddened by my death that you yourselves must also be crucified, if you truly love me.”

12. He does not answer openly when Judas Lebbaeus asks him, so that they may prepare themselves for the Lord’s spiritual presence. For he wishes not to show himself to the world, since it does not love Christ, but to come to his own. God is the Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

13. Christ’s departure is the cause of many great blessings.

14. The two operations of the Holy Spirit: to teach and to remind; to teach all things and to suggest all things.

15. Promise and consolation: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace.”

16. The peace of the world is not true peace; it flees the cross. The proof of the peace Christ gives is the cross, for “we glory in afflictions.” Rom. V.

[Col. 0566A]

17. The devil is called the prince of this world and the ruler of this darkness, that is, of wicked people—not because he rules heaven or earth.

18. Satan has nothing in Christ, for God came *ἀναμάρτητος* (*anamartētos*), “without sin,” and a virgin bore his flesh, not from the propagation of sin.

### Chapter XV

1. We are consoled through the parable of the vine and the branches.

2. We are cleansed by Christ’s word and, by obeying the truth through the Holy Spirit, with brotherly love.

3. Without works no one can be in Christ.

4. Great consolation: “If you remain in me and my words remain in you, whatever you wish, ask, and it will be done for you.”

5. The greatest consolation is to trust that the Father loves us, when he says to our soul, “I am your salvation,” as the Psalms are full of saying.

[Col. 0566B]

6. The love of God is like a chain joined to our love. Therefore at one time he speaks of two commandments and at another of one, for no one could attain the first without the other. At one point he says: “On these hang the law and the prophets.” At another: “Whatever you wish people to do to you,” etc.

7. The proof of the greatest love is that he shared the Father’s secrets with them: “Everything I have heard from my Father,” which Augustine understands according to the hope of things to come.

8. He consoles them against external persecutions, so that they may believe that these occur through God’s good will.

9. The Jews will have no excuse because of Christ’s teaching and works. They hated Christ without cause. Malice and folly were the cause of their unbelief.

10. A passage concerning the authority of the apostles: clothed with power from above, they were witnesses of the resurrection and had been with Christ from the beginning, so that they could testify to what they had heard and seen.

### Chapter XVI

[Col. 0566C]

1. The fate of the Gospel and of those who profess it: they are to be the offscouring of the world.

2. Let us arm ourselves with Christ’s word against the scandal of the cross.

3. In temptations, consider that you suffer from evil people both because of Christ and because of virtue.

4. Christ’s going to the Father is the inauguration of his kingdom. It is a great thing to know that Christ reigns, rules, triumphs, and conquers.

5. The Spirit of truth reproves the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment. Therefore the preaching of the Gospel concerns everyone—for all have sinned and fallen short of the righteousness of God—and it must be salt for corrupt flesh.

6. The Spirit will lead into all truth; therefore no new doctrine is to be expected.

7. An example of the apostles’ ignorance and unbelief: they did not understand or believe many things. There is a similar example of Christ’s concern for his own, whom he bears however they may be. Hence we too, who are strong, ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak and not please ourselves, but our neighbor, for his edification. Rom. XV.

[Col. 0566D]

8. The Christian profession is not delicate or ease-loving for a time; rather, sorrow is turned into joy, and the momentary lightness of afflictions produces an eternal weight of glory. The prophet used the image of childbirth in calamities.

9. We need no advocate besides Christ. Indeed, Christ makes the brethren equal with himself and co-heirs: “I do not say to you that I will ask the Father for you; the Father himself loves you.”

10. Great consolation: “Take courage; I have conquered the world”—spoken by the one who is the truth. For it is impossible for the world to say, “I have conquered Christ.”

### Chapter XVII

1. In temptations let us flee to God, and, following the example of Christ our teacher, who teaches by deeds and words, let us be attentive in prayer when we are tempted.

[Col. 0567A]

2. All flesh has been given to Christ, so that he may be God not only of the Jews but also of the Gentiles, rich toward all who call upon him.

3. Eternal life is believing that God has had mercy on us because of Christ, who is the mediator between God and human beings.

4. Christ’s glory with the Father before the world existed; therefore he is God.

5. Consolation: just as Christ prays for himself, so he also prays to the Father for all who were to believe until the end of the world. Below: “I do not pray for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word.”

6. Christ’s terrifying judgment concerning the world: “I do not pray for the world, but for the elect.”

7. The security of God’s elect, whom Christ guards so that none of them may perish.

8. The world hates believers, just as it hates Christ himself, the head of believers.

9. The saints have affliction in the world, but in temptations they do not succumb, because of Christ’s grace.

[Col. 0567B]

10. Christianity and the Church: believers should be one and perfected into one, against disagreements of opinion.

[Col. 0567B]

## HOLY SATURDAY

### EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE COLOSSIANS, CHAPTER III

“If you have risen with Christ.”

1. Christ’s resurrection admonishes us to seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. He does not say where the sun, moon, or angels are, but where Christ is.

2. The elements of the world are avarice and luxury, fornication, uncleanness, softness, and similar vices.

3. Those whose life is Christ must have their earthly members mortified. Now we are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be.

### GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER XXVII

“Now, when evening had come on the Sabbath.”

1. The article of the resurrection is the foundation of our faith. Hence the evangelists are so diligent concerning it.

[Col. 0567C]

2. The steadfastness of the women who ministered to Christ even at the point of danger.

3. The sex that was most condemned is the first to enjoy the contemplation of good things.

[Col. 0567C]

## HOLY SUNDAY OF EASTER

### FIRST EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER V

“Purge out the old leaven.”

1. Christianity means that we walk in newness of life, wholly free from the leaven of sin; for through baptism we become unleavened.

2. The Jews celebrated Passover in shadow; we celebrate it in truth and light. They sacrificed a sheep; our Lamb is Christ. The doorposts were marked with blood; our foreheads are marked with Christ’s blood.

3. Those who live purely celebrate Passover daily—not with the leaven of the old malice and wickedness, but with food and bread unfermented by any leaven, that is, with harmless, simple, sincere conduct.

[Col. 0567D]

### GOSPEL OF MARK, LAST CHAPTER

“Mary Magdalene and Mary of James.”

1. A truly evangelical, indeed angelic, voice: “Do not be afraid.” Since Christ has risen from the dead, we have a living hope and all fear has fled. Death is not death, for Christ by the grace of God tasted death for everyone. Heb. II.

2. The courage of the women, their devout love toward Christ, their generosity with money, and their spirit, which despised even the dangers of death.

3. Let us imitate these women, so that we too may not abandon the Lord in temptations. You have no less than these women: “Whatever you did for one of these least ones, you did for me.” Matt. XXV.

4. The witness to the resurrection appears in splendor and brightness, because God is both terrible and gentle.

[Col. 0568A]

## EASTER MONDAY

### ACTS, CHAPTER X

“Peter, standing in the midst, said,” etc.

1. Who Christ is, why and how he came, and what he brought: namely, that he is true God and human being, through whom we have peace.

2. John the Baptist was the first and greatest herald of Christ’s Gospel.

3. The almighty Lord Jesus is judge of the living and the dead. All the prophets bear witness to him: all who believe in him receive forgiveness of sins through his name. This is our faith.

### GOSPEL OF LUKE, LAST CHAPTER

“Two disciples went out.”

1. While the two disciples, Cleopas and Ammaon, were speaking about him, Christ appears, as Ambrose testifies, in accordance with the saying, “Where two or three are gathered, there am I in the midst of them.” He opens their minds—he who is the key of David—so that they may understand the Scriptures.

[Col. 0568B]

2. We must believe not only particular passages but also universally the prophets and the Scriptures concerning Christ. For Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and repentance and forgiveness of sins had to be preached in his name.

3. Christ’s particular custom was to give thanks to the Father before food and then to distribute broken bread among his own. Theophylact understands the breaking of bread as referring to the Lord’s flesh, and says: “The flesh of the Lord has great power; the eyes of those who receive it are opened.”

[Col. 0568B]

## EASTER TUESDAY

### READING FROM THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, CHAPTER XIII

“Paul rose and, with his hand,” etc.

1. Salvation is brought through Christ to everyone, but it is first conferred upon those to whom the prophecies were revealed and from whose race Christ came.

[Col. 0568C]

2. Jesus, whom the malice of human beings, by God’s will, delivered to death, God’s power raised from the dead on the third day, in accordance with the predictions of the prophets.

3. Very true testimonies to this resurrection were given. He was seen, heard, and touched for forty days, speaking to his own about the kingdom of God.

### GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER XXIV

“Jesus stood in the midst of the disciples.”

1. Before and after his passion Christ prays for peace, for peace, harmony, and charity are marks of Christians. Not content to say it once, he repeats: “Peace be with you.” Hence the Christian people of today should be ashamed of wars, disagreements, and lawsuits.

2. Confirmation of the true resurrection and of the true body, since he eats with the disciples of fish, roasted food, and honeycomb.

3. Christ, who is the *τέλειον* (*teleion*), the perfection, of the law and the prophets, opens the minds of the apostles so that they may understand the Scriptures.

[Col. 0568D]

## EASTER WEDNESDAY

### READING FROM THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, CHAPTER III

“Peter opened his mouth.”

1. The mystery of the Trinity appears in Peter’s words: “The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers.” He wisely distinguishes the persons and unites the nature.

2. Christ, the victim for the sins of the world, was sacrificed by the Jews, not without their guilt; yet that guilt is remitted through repentance.

3. Therefore repentance, conversion, and the forgiveness of sins must be preached to Jews and Gentiles. Ezek. XVIII: “I do not desire death,” etc.

### GOSPEL OF JOHN, LAST CHAPTER

“Jesus revealed himself again.”

1. After the resurrection the apostles returned to the fishing trade. Thus the Lord appears to those who are laboring and speaks in their manner, as though he were about to buy something from them.

[Col. 0569A]

2. The nature of the Word and the fishing for human beings are shown here: nothing is caught except through Christ’s word.

3. The apostles’ poverty: it is easy to endure poverty and to live from honest labor. This is opposed to idleness.

[Col. 0569A]

## EASTER THURSDAY

### READING FROM THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, CHAPTER VIII

“The angel of the Lord spoke to Philip.”

1. From Isa. LIII Philip explains to the Ethiopian the substance of evangelical doctrine: namely, that Christ is the Son of God, through whom God had determined and through his prophets had promised to give salvation to all who believe in him; that he is true God and human being, righteousness, sacrifice, and the one satisfaction.

2. The Ethiopian professes faith and, consenting to Jesus Christ, is baptized by Philip.

3. Although faith in Christ will save, the institution of baptism must nevertheless not be despised.

[Col. 0569B]

### GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER XX

“Mary stood near the tomb.”

1. Christ appears to Mary, who is weeping at the tomb, in a lowly and ordinary form—that is, as a gardener.

2. Mary represents the Church from among the Gentiles, which did not believe in Christ until he had ascended to the Father.

3. A wonderful consolation—for ascending pertains to the flesh—is the Lord’s saying: “Tell my brothers, ‘I am ascending to my God and your God, my Father and your Father.’” For it is a great, marvelous, and astonishing thing that our flesh sits above and is worshiped.

[Col. 0569B]

## FRIDAY AFTER EASTER

### FIRST EPISTLE OF PETER, CHAPTER III

“Christ once suffered for our sins.”

1. Christ died, the just for the unjust and the ungodly. Hence God commends his love toward us: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Rom. V. Therefore let us love and be grateful.

[Col. 0569C]

2. The fruit of Christ’s death in Christians is the mortification of the flesh and the vivification of the spirit. Therefore, disregarding the will of the Gentiles, we must live according to the will of God.

3. After his ascension Christ preaches to the spirits who are in prison and disobedient—externally through the apostles and apostolic men, internally through his own breath—so that they may not trample upon the Son of God, regard the blood of the covenant as profane, or despise the Spirit of grace.

### GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, LAST CHAPTER

“The eleven disciples went.”

1. The greatest consolation of believers is to know that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Christ.

2. A compendium of the doctrine of piety and of the sacrament of baptism: they are to teach what he himself commanded and baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so that the heavenly Father may be acknowledged as the creator, ruler, and restorer of all things; the Son as the redeemer of the human race; and the Holy Spirit as the teacher of all righteousness and truth, the patron and comforter of all who trust in God through Christ.

[Col. 0569D]

3. Christ, who has authority over all flesh, who conquered the world, who is our salvation, life, and resurrection—the presence of whose majesty is with you until the consummation of the age.

[Col. 0569D]

## SATURDAY IN THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

### FIRST EPISTLE OF PETER, CHAPTER II

“Putting aside all malice.”

1. Reborn through baptism, let them be like newborn infants, free from all malice; for Christianity is true rebirth.

2. The dignity of Christians: they are to be a spiritual house, a holy and royal priesthood, a people who have come into possession of a gain.

[Col. 0570A]

3. Let us be grateful to the gracious Lord and to Christ, the living stone, and let us proclaim the virtues of him who called us out of darkness into his marvelous light.

### GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER XX

“On the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene.”

1. The devotion of this woman, who sought Christ with such assiduity.

2. When you hear that Christ rose naked, leaving behind the linen cloths, cease from the senseless pomp of funerals.

3. The evangelist’s diligence in asserting the truth of the resurrection.

[Col. 0570A]

## SUNDAY IN THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

### FIRST EPISTLE OF JOHN, CHAPTER V

“Whatever is born of God.”

1. The world has poverty, exile, disgrace, prisons, lashes, and death; faith conquers all these things, believing that Jesus is the Son of God.

[Col. 0570B]

2. Christ testified by three witnesses that he is the Savior of the world: water, blood, and Spirit.

3. The Father’s philanthropy—his love for humanity—is unspeakable, since he testifies in so many ways concerning his Son, our redeemer.

### GOSPEL OF JOHN, LAST CHAPTER

“When it was evening on that day.”

1. Christ’s first word after the resurrection is “Peace,” so that we may know that Christ and the preaching of the Gospel are peace, which gladdens the conscience.

2. The Gospel includes the power to loose and to bind: it looses when it forgives sins; it binds when it judges all the ungodly who despise the word of God.

3. Thomas’s doubt—for all things work together for the good of the elect—was beneficial; for through it he confesses Christ’s divinity and humanity more fully, saying: “My Lord and my God.”

[Col. 0570B]

## SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

### FIRST EPISTLE OF PETER, CHAPTER II

“Christ suffered for us.”

[Col. 0570C]

1. Whoever rejoices because Christ died for him should pay attention to what follows: “Leaving you an example, so that you may follow his footsteps.”

2. A teaching for the whole Church: what Christ, the author of the Church, endured for its liberation.

3. Christ is the shepherd, caretaker, visitor, and bishop of our souls.

### GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER X

“I am the good shepherd.”

1. Christ is that good shepherd who gives his life for his sheep.

2. The distinction between the hireling and the good shepherd, by which Christ marks the Pharisees, who could not bear that many were attaching themselves to Christ while abandoning them, although they were nothing but thieves and robbers.

3. The calling of the Gentiles and the Jews into the obedience of faith, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd.

[Col. 0570C]

## SECOND SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVES OF EASTER

### FIRST EPISTLE OF PETER, CHAPTER II

“I beseech you as strangers.”

1. The apostolic spirit beseeches, exhorts, and invites us to true innocence of life: we are foreigners and, as it were, guests reborn for heaven.

2. The order of the world is not to be disturbed on the pretext of religion, insofar as this can be done without endangering Christ’s glory, lest anyone turn liberty into an occasion for the flesh—which, alas, many do.

3. The office of magistrates is necessary for the world: for the praise of those who do right and for the punishment of those who do wrong, Romans XIII; 1 Peter II.

### GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER XVI

“A little while, and you will not see me, etc.”

1. He recalls and explains the time before and after the resurrection: what it means not to see him for a little while, and then to see him again.

2. Christ’s concern for us: he comes to the aid of those who hesitate and answers before we ask.

[Col. 0571A]

3. He foretells afflictions and shows from the example of a woman in labor from where consolation is to be expected.

[Col. 0571A]

## THIRD SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVES OF EASTER

“Every good gift and every perfect gift.”

1. Whatever good there is in us comes from the Father of lights; therefore, “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”

2. We are the firstfruits of God’s creatures—that is, his most excellent creatures. Therefore we must not speak rashly or indulge in anger.

3. An exhortation to gentleness and self-denial.

### GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER XVI

“I am going to him who sent me.”

1. The benefit of Christ’s departure to the Father: ascending on high, he led captivity captive, gave gifts to humanity, filled all things, and gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers for the building up of Christ’s body, Ephesians IV.

[Col. 0571B]

2. The preaching of the Gospel will not be sound unless exhortatory speech also reproves vices. For the Spirit of truth reproves the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment; and Paul exhorts his Timothy: “Reprove, beseech, rebuke, with all patience and doctrine.”

3. The Spirit of truth will lead into all truth, so that we do not vainly await new doctrines from the Spirit, against erroneous spirits and impostors.

[Col. 0571B]

## FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVES OF EASTER

### EPISTLE OF BLESSED JAMES, CHAPTER I

“Be doers of the word, etc.”

1. It is not enough to profess the Gospel in words, unless we also express it in deeds.

2. The likeness of someone looking at himself in a mirror and then going away shows how empty this is. Christ expresses the same thing through the likeness of the person building upon rock and the person building upon sand, Matthew VII.

3. The whole of true religion and piety is expressed with remarkable brevity: to keep oneself unstained by the world and to raise up one’s needy neighbor mercifully.

### GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER XVI

“Amen, I say to you, if you ask anything.”

1. A promise concerning Christ’s priesthood and intercession, by which he makes consciences completely certain that their prayers are heard.

2. The eternal Gospel is not parabolic or proverbial, nor is it to be interpreted linguistically, nor is it merely verbal. “I will announce openly concerning my Father,” says Christ.

3. The dignity of Christians: without an intercessor, they are powerful enough to appeal to the Father and cry, “Abba, Father.” “The Father himself loves you,” says Christ the mediator.

[Col. 0571C]

## ON THE GREATER LITANY

### EPISTLE OF JAMES, CHAPTER V

“Confess your sins to one another.”

1. Christ can be moved by prayers if we mutually forgive one another.

[Col. 0571D]

2. The great power of the persistent prayer of a righteous person is proved by the example of Elijah.

3. The most acceptable worship to God is to turn a sinner back from error; for he does not desire the death of the sinner.

### GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER XI

“Which of you will have a friend?”

1. When the disciples ask him, Christ teaches not only the form of prayer in the Lord’s Prayer, but also the persistence and frequency with which one ought to pray.

2. The comparison proceeds from the lesser case: if a human friend rises from bed and gives something—not out of friendship but because he is compelled by annoyance—how much more will God give, who is without annoyance? He gives most generously and is rich toward all who call upon him; he will give good things to those who ask him.

3. Perseverance is necessary, so that we may receive what we ask, find what we seek, and have the door opened when we knock.

[Col. 0572A]

## ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

### READING FROM THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, CHAPTER I

“I made the first account, etc.”

1. The foundation of our religion is that Jesus truly died, truly rose again on the third day, and, having made purification for sins through himself, sat at the right hand of Majesty on high.

2. Speaking to the apostles for forty days about the kingdom of God and eating with them, he proves by many arguments that the resurrection was real.

3. The apostles are promised the baptism of the Spirit and power from on high, by which, clothed with power, they will be witnesses of the resurrection not only in Judea and Samaria but to the ends of the earth. Here the breadth of Christ’s kingdom is displayed.

### GOSPEL OF MARK, CHAPTER XVI

“While the eleven disciples were reclining at table.”

1. Unbelief and hardness of heart remained in the apostles until the Lord’s ascension; yet the Lord was patient toward them.

2. The commission to teach the Gospel throughout the whole world and to every creature—that is, to the Church.

3. Confirmation of evangelical preaching through the signs that followed, and the power of miracles whenever a situation calls for a miracle.

[Col. 0572B]

## SUNDAY AFTER THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

### FIRST EPISTLE OF PETER, CHAPTER IV

“Be prudent.”

1. Sobriety, watchfulness, prayer, charity, and hospitality are fitting for Christians.

2. Let us say nothing foreign to the teaching of God, lest we be found false witnesses of God and sacrilegious.

3. The glory of God—so that God may be glorified in all things through Christ—the public good, and public integrity should be the aim of all Christians, especially of those who preside over the ministry of the word.

### GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTERS XV AND XVI

“But when he comes.”

1. Before the coming of the Holy Spirit, the disciples were neither capable of the mysteries of the kingdom nor strong enough to endure adversity; after receiving the Spirit, they became entirely different men.

2. It belongs to the apostles to bear witness concerning Christ, and the testimony of blood is immense.

3. No danger, not even death itself, ought to deter anyone from confessing evangelical truth; for the crown of righteousness is laid up, which the Lord will award on that day.

[Col. 0572C]

## SATURDAY, ON THE VIGIL OF PENTECOST

### READING FROM THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, CHAPTER XIX

“It happened when Apollos was there.”

1. Imperfect Christianity is corrected in certain people.

2. Those who err not through malice but simply acknowledge their error frankly: an example is found in the imperfect disciples whom Paul encountered at Ephesus.

3. Believers must be baptized not into the name of John, so as to be John’s followers, but into the name of Christ—or of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—so as to be Christians.

### GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER XIV

“If you love me, keep my commandments, etc.”

1. Love and observance of God’s commandments follow faith. 2 Peter I: “Supply virtue in faith, knowledge in virtue, self-control in knowledge, endurance in self-control, godliness in endurance, love of the brethren in godliness, and love in love of the brethren.”

2. He comforts the apostles by sending them another Comforter, namely, the Holy Spirit, who will remain with them forever.

3. Christ’s fatherly saying is: “I will not leave you orphans”; for he is the Father of orphans and the judge of widows.

[Col. 0573A]

## PENTECOST SUNDAY

### READING FROM THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, CHAPTER II

“When the day of Pentecost was being fulfilled.”

1. While they were gathered together with one accord and persevering in prayer and supplication, the Holy Spirit came.

2. He came in tongues as though of fire, so that the effectiveness of the Spirit might be shown: he makes people ardent and gives them speech.

3. This passage indicates how necessary knowledge of languages is for apostolic men. On this matter, see Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book II, chapters 11–12.

## ON THE DAY OF PENTECOST

### GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER XIV

“If anyone loves me.”

1. The Triune God—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—comes to the one who loves Christ and keeps his word.

2. The Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, is promised; he will teach all things and bring all things to remembrance.

3. True peace, which surpasses all understanding, is promised to Christ’s disciples—a peace that the world cannot give.

[Col. 0573B]

## EIGHTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

### READING FROM THE BOOK OF REVELATION, CHAPTER IV

“I saw a door opened in heaven.”

1. Faith in Christ’s birth, passion, and resurrection is commended in the Church, and the course of the Church is described.

2. Unbelievers are invited to the Church and to baptism.

3. There is one Church, united by the fellowship of faith, of all the elect from the beginning of the world to the consummation of the age. Day and night it does not cease to say: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty.” This is the illustrious religion and faith of Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Samuel, David, all the prophets, Stephen, John the Baptist, Peter, Paul, James, Chrysostom, Augustine, and others.

### GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER III

“There was a man of the Pharisees.”

1. A teaching for receiving those who are weak in faith, such as Nicodemus—and there are many such today. Here we see our most merciful God Christ not rejecting Nicodemus’s cold disposition, not rebuking him, and not considering him unworthy of his teaching, but addressing him at length with gentleness and opening to him the reason for justification.

2. The essence of salvation is set before us in weighty words, with great insistence and emphatic repetition: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” Likewise: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.”

3. He teaches through whom we are reborn and justified—namely, through Christ, whose righteousness alone is accepted before God. He descended from heaven, the Son of Man, and is in heaven. From this we learn what Christ is: our righteousness, sanctification, and redemption; why he came; and what we have through him—namely, eternal life.

[Col. 0573D]

## SECOND SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

### FIRST EPISTLE OF JOHN, CHAPTER IV

“God is love.”

1. It is wonderfully consoling that he calls God love. By this expression, as by the strongest bond, he binds us to himself, so that we may never be torn or separated from him who loves us so intensely. We also have the command that those who love God must love their neighbor.

2. A fitting blessing at table: if we do not forget charity, we will order everything for edification, whether we eat or drink. This is opposed to the very common crime of slander, from which a Christian should recoil, saying: “May our food be Christ and our drink be faith”; let us joyfully drink the sober intoxication of the Spirit.

[Col. 0574A]

3. A necessary exhortation: let us conduct ourselves so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment and not be put to shame by him at his coming. For who will endure these thunderclaps: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know you. Go, you accursed, into eternal fire”?

### GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER XVI

“There was a certain rich man, etc.”

1. The example of unbelief is found in the rich banqueter, who lived according to the will of the Gentiles—in debauchery, lusts, drunkenness, feasting, and mercilessness. Eternal damnation follows such a life. The example of faith is found in Lazarus, who lived out the time that remained according to the will of God and endured extreme poverty with equanimity. Thus he had God as his helper, and he attained Abraham’s bosom—that is, a dwelling in a certain hidden rest.

2. A teaching against Christian Epicureans, animals of the belly, who want to fill their stomachs here and their minds elsewhere, passing from one pleasure to another. Let no one go astray: God is not mocked. Hence Luke, chapter VI: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation here. Woe to you who are filled, for you will hunger. Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep.”

3. It is vain to expect truth from the dead or certainty about the condition of the departed. We must listen to Moses and the prophets, and to Christ, the fulfillment of the Law and the prophets; whoever does not listen to him will be destroyed from among the people, Acts III.

[Col. 0574B]

## THIRD SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

### FIRST EPISTLE OF JOHN, CHAPTER III

“Do not marvel if the world hates you.”

1. The word “world” often signifies the whole Church, as in John, chapter III: “The Son of Man did not come to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him.” Likewise, 2 Corinthians VI: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.” Sometimes, as in the present passage, it refers to people devoted to pleasure and impiety, the world that hates Christ’s disciples.

[Col. 0574C]

2. An encomium of brotherly love, which transfers a person from death to life. “Whoever does not love his brother remains in death.”

3. A teaching about loving one’s neighbor—not in word or tongue, but in deed and truth—and about distributing the world’s goods among the needy. Hence usurers, inhospitable people, merciless people, and greedy men are in a ruinous condition.

### GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER XIV

“A certain man made a great supper.”

1. The parable of those invited to the supper presents the Jews and the Gentiles: that is, all nations indiscriminately are called, so that the assembly of the Church might be filled. The Jews were called first, for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers; the Gentiles, moreover, were called so that God might be glorified for his mercy, Romans XV.

2. The hindrances and obstacles of those who do not come to the prepared supper are profit from earthly possessions, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life. Hence there is a little flock that delights in innocence, truth, and righteousness; yet it has pleased the Father to give the kingdom to these little ones, Luke XII.

3. A dreadful judgment is threatened against unbelieving Jews: “None of those men who were invited will taste my supper.” Such punishments will be inflicted on the one who tramples underfoot the Son of God, regards the blood of the covenant—or the sacred reality—as profane, and insults the Spirit of grace, Hebrews X.

[Col. 0574D]

## FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

### FIRST EPISTLE OF PETER, CHAPTER V

“Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God.”

1. Humility of spirit, poverty of spirit, and true modesty must be firmly implanted in the minds of Christians—a most beautiful teaching against pride, the root of every evil.

2. Wonderful consolation: we are cared for by God, who has a mighty hand. Therefore let us cast our thought upon him and, as the Hebrew word explains the Psalm more clearly, our burden—that is, whatever weighs us down.

3. By faith, sobriety, vigilance, and with all our might, as the saying goes, we must stand against the devil, the enemy who prowls about deceitfully. God, the giver of every grace, grants these things to his own; he restores, supports, strengthens, and establishes them, so that whoever boasts may boast in the Lord.

### GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER XV

“Those who were drawing near.”

1. Christ does not shrink from the company of sinners where there is hope of repentance. From this comes both an example and a teaching: we must not seek to please ourselves, but our neighbor, for his edification.

2. The substance and core of the three parables—of the hundred sheep, the lost drachma, and the prodigal son—are the same: namely, that a sinner who sincerely repents must be received with joy.

3. There is more joy in heaven over converted sinners than over righteous people who remain standing. Let us not seize this as an occasion for the flesh, but produce fruits worthy of repentance.

[Col. 0575B]

## FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

### EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER VIII

“For I consider that they are not, etc.”

1. Paul consoles the brethren by pointing to the reward and future glory that will be revealed in us: an exceedingly great consolation, the inheritance of heaven and brotherhood with the Son of God.

2. He consoles them by the example that every creature groans and awaits the revelation of the children of God, which will occur in the resurrection of the body. Here the struggle between faith and unbelief, hope and despair, is set before us. The angels also desire the glory of the saints.

3. The supreme consolation lies in adoption as children of God, for the Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God. If children, then heirs—heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ.

[Col. 0575C]

### GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER VI

“Be merciful.”

1. God’s goodness is set before the children of God for imitation, so that we may be beneficial and merciful toward the grateful and the ungrateful. The power of Christianity is the ability to do good to unwilling, ungrateful, and uncomprehending people.

2. It belongs to the Christian to interpret the doubtful words and deeds of his neighbor in the better sense, with regard to the intention behind them.

3. Through the likeness of the speck and the beam, Christ censures the blind philanthropy of human nature: being offended by the vices of others while flattering our own, keeping our own sack behind us and that of others before our eyes. True goodness, however, is more lenient in judging others and more severe in examining itself.

[Col. 0575C]

## SIXTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

### FIRST EPISTLE OF PETER, CHAPTER III

“Be all of one mind.”

1. In remarkable brevity, the apostolic spirit of Peter embraces the whole doctrine of godliness. The commandment of charity is explained: let us all be of one mind, similarly disposed, endowed with brotherly love, and so forth.

[Col. 0575D]

2. A rule for living, so that we may have good days and life: we must govern the tongue, this small member from which uncontrollable evils arise; turn away from evil and do good.

3. For Christians, what appears to the world to be calamity is blessedness—namely, suffering adversity on account of righteousness. “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake,” Matthew V.

### GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER V

“When the crowds were pressing upon Jesus.”

1. Just as Christ’s life was devoted to the public good and especially to the glory of God, so too the life of Christians must be. He teaches while silent, while opening his mouth, on the mountain, at sea, in the countryside, in the temple—everywhere acting as Savior.

2. In the narrative of the event according to the flesh, an image is presented of the Church being born and becoming abundant. Its mystery is this: Christ, together with his ministers, the apostles and preachers, catches human beings floating upon the transient things and storms of this life.

3. Observe carefully that when Christ entrusts the sheep to Peter after Peter has thrice confessed his love, he says here: ζωγρῶν ἀνθρώπους, that is, “you will be catching human beings alive.” This is contrary to the cruelty of those who prefer to kill Jews, Turks, and unbelievers and send them to hell rather than win them alive for God.

[Col. 0576A]

## ON THE VIGIL OF JOHN THE BAPTIST

### READING FROM THE PROPHET JEREMIAH, CHAPTER I

“Before I formed you in the womb.”

1. The admirable clemency and predestination of God, who appoints his prophets for the salvation of peoples and sanctifies them while they are still in their mothers’ bodies: an example is found in Jeremiah and John the Baptist.

2. The likeness between the two is this: each began to prophesy as a boy; each was of priestly descent; each summoned the people to repentance, preferring to save those who turned back rather than destroy those who transgressed.

[Col. 0576B]

3. The excellence of God’s word and of those ministers whose mouths the Lord touched: they are God’s building and God’s cultivation, and they announce the word that is over nations and kingdoms. Here all flesh must humble itself under the mighty hand of God.

### GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER I

“There was in the days of Herod the king.”

1. Zachariah and Elizabeth, the parents of John, provide an example worthy of imitation by all parents. Both were righteous before God, living blamelessly according to all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord.

2. Barrenness is not always because of sin, for the wives of the patriarchs were barren—Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel—and here Elizabeth. Children are the reward of marriage; if God gives them, they should be consecrated to the one who gave them, namely, God.

[Col. 0576C]

3. A catalogue of John’s praises and office: he will be great before the Lord and will be filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb. He will be Elijah in spirit and power. Here you have the aim of the preaching office: to turn people to the Lord God and to prepare for the Lord a perfect people.

[Col. 0576C]

## ON THE NATIVITY OF JOHN THE BAPTIST

### READING FROM ISAIAH, CHAPTER XLIX

“Listen, islands, and attend, peoples from afar.”

1. The goodness and love of God toward the human race are proclaimed. After the calling of the remnant of Israel and the rejection of the people who remain in unbelief, he gathers Churches from the Gentiles, as though from the farthest islands.

2. The Church lies exposed to the attacks of persecutors like the waves of the sea and is battered by shipwreck raging on every side, but it is not submerged, because it has Christ God as its protector.

[Col. 0576D]

3. Christ was given as a light to the Gentiles, to be salvation to the ends of the earth. Thus, through the preaching of John the Baptist and the apostles, he illumines the whole world, so that kings and princes—whose hearts are in the hand of God—may worship him.

[Col. 0576D]

## ON THE DAY OF JOHN THE BAPTIST

### GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER I

“The time was fulfilled for Elizabeth.”

1. Children and offspring are the reward of marriage; these, in turn, should be consecrated to God. Thus parents are saved through the generation of children if they continue in faith, charity, and love.

2. The giving of names was extremely celebrated and especially serious among the ancients. Hence Pliny and Plutarch also record that the Gentiles gave names derived from deeds, fortune, appearance, virtue, and bodily condition—Soteres, Eudemones, Physchones, Evergetes, Philadelphos, and so forth—and that the ancient Germanic names included Friderich, Gothart, Gotlieb, and others. The name John is not a name of lineage but of grace, and it was fitting that the herald of the new law—which would abolish the traditions of the ancients and turn carnal worship into the grace of the Spirit—should be called John.

[Col. 0577A]

3. The signs of his preaching ministry: “The hand of the Lord was with John,” the forerunner of truth. The whole doctrine of godliness is also set forth in a few words through Zachariah, filled with the Holy Spirit: God has visited his people, as though wasting away from a long illness and as though sold under sin, redeeming them with the blood of his only Son.

[Col. 0577A]

## ON THE VIGIL OF THE APOSTLE PETER

### READING FROM THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, CHAPTER III

“Peter and John went up.”

1. Love of meeting and gathering in the Church is set before us here by the example of the apostles, so that we may pray and hear the law of God. Many psalms testify that David and the other saints desired to be in the assembly and to celebrate the feast with believers. Psalm XLII: “As the deer longs for springs of water, etc.”

[Col. 0577B]

2. The humility and lowliness of the apostles, entering the temple without pomp or an entourage and possessing neither gold nor silver, are set against those who, while falsely claiming the apostolic title, are Sardanapaluses and Croesuses.

3. The healed blind man offers an example of gratitude. For he entered the temple with the apostles, walking, leaping, and praising God. This shows the proper use of temples: the praise of God, in contrast to those who profane these temples, built so that the people might be taught, God might be invoked with one accord, praise might be offered, and the sacraments might be used, by means of ironic ceremonies and commerce.

### GOSPEL ON THE DAY OF SAINT PETER, JOHN, CHAPTER XXI

“Simon, son of John, do you love me, etc.?”

1. Christ is the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, indeed the chief shepherd. How highly he values his sheep we understand fully from this threefold questioning about love.

[Col. 0577C]

2. After Peter had thrice confessed his love, Christ entrusted his sheep to him, so that we may know that no one is fit for the priesthood unless, neglecting everything else, he has nothing but Christ—that is, truth, innocence, and godliness.

3. An example concerning those who look at another person’s calling and work: there we must break our will into conformity with God’s will and hear the Lord saying, “You follow me.” See Augustine’s Letter LXV to Paulinus and Therasia.

[Col. 0577C]

## ON THE VIGIL OF SAINT PAUL

### EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE GALATIANS, CHAPTER I

“For I make known to you the Gospel, etc.”

1. The Gospel, by which the destruction of punishments, the forgiveness of sins, sanctification, righteousness, adoption as children of God, the inheritance of heaven, and brotherhood with the Son of God are announced to us, is not through a human being or from human beings, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ. Thus our consciences may be certain and may know whom they believe—him who is powerful to save.

[Col. 0577D]

2. The secret of divine providence in Paul: from a blasphemous persecutor and violent man he becomes God’s chosen instrument, bearing the name of Christ before the Gentiles, kings, and the children of Israel, Acts IX and XXII; 1 Timothy I.

3. The apostolic office is wholly heavenly and admits no human affections. Therefore Paul does not confer with flesh and blood; he does not cast pearls before swine, nor give what is holy to dogs.

[Col. 0577C]

## ON THE NATIVITY OF SAINT PAUL

### READING FROM THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, CHAPTER IX

“But Saul, still breathing out…”

1. The calling to the apostolic office does not arise from our powers or free will, but solely from God’s mercy. Hence Scripture describes the calling of Saint Paul so carefully—as it does the callings of other great men, Moses, Samuel, Isaiah, and Jeremiah—so that we may understand both the Lord’s mercy and the power that turns a wolf into a sheep: striking in order to heal, casting down in order to raise up, blinding in order to illumine.

[Col. 0578A]

2. Great consolation: Christ makes the persecutions suffered by believers his own. For Christ lives in them, and just as everything belonging to Christ is ours, so in turn what is ours belongs to him. Therefore he says, “Why are you persecuting me?”—not “my people”—and the power of the deity inspires terror.

3. Examples of those who truly obey are found in Ananias, who says, “Here I am, Lord,” and in Paul, who says, “Lord, what do you want me to do?” You also have the steadfast preaching that Christ is the Son of God.

### GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER XIX

“Behold, we have left everything.”

1. It belongs to the apostles and to all Christians to leave everything—that is, to abandon the desire to possess—and to love all things with contempt, as honest usufructuaries customarily use possessions, not as absolute masters and owners. 1 Corinthians VII: “The form of this world is passing away”; those who use this world should be as though they did not use it.

[Col. 0578B]

2. Here we learn that Jesus will judge together with his disciples. Matthew XII: “They themselves will be your judges.” 1 Corinthians VI: “The saints will judge the world.”

3. Great consolation and promise: whoever has left carnal things for the sake of Christ’s Gospel will receive spiritual goods, which are like the number one hundred compared with a very small number. “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, what God has prepared for those who love him,” Romans VIII. “The momentary lightness of our affliction produces beyond measure an eternal weight of glory,” 2 Corinthians IV.

[Col. 0578B]

## SEVENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

### EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER VI

“All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus…”

1. Baptism is the sacrament of repentance and the beginning of Christianity. Since Christ died, was buried, and rose again for us, we too must crucify our wills and desires in likeness to his passion and imitate in baptism the mystery of his death, burial, and resurrection.

[Col. 0578C]

2. The chief work of faith is the struggle of the spirit against the flesh. Let no one think that the Christian life is soft and delicate: to destroy the body of sin and no longer serve sin—this is the work; this is the labor.

3. An exhortatory sermon about Christ, urging people to abstain from vices. The most effective remedy against them is for a person to consider himself mortal; and it is consoling, so that through him we may be secure concerning the eternity of life.

### GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER V

“Amen, amen, I say to you.”

1. Christ’s philosophy from the beginning of chapter V, concerning the beatitudes, must be carefully observed, and likewise his subsequent explanation of the divine law. He does not disparage the ancient law but shows the old law to be imperfect by comparison with the new.

[Col. 0578D]

2. The distinction between the righteousness of the Pharisees, which concerns itself only with external matters, and that of Christians, from whom the heart is required.

3. Concerning reconciliation and forgiveness; the time of anger, whether opportune or inopportune; and the many evils that arise from anger. These are necessary passages, in which we see that Christ’s chief concern is charity and that the sacrifice most acceptable to God is one that even laypeople, according to Chrysostom, ought to offer.

[Col. 0578D]

## EIGHTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

### EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER VI

“I speak in human terms because of your weakness.”

1. The apostle’s gracious exhortation is that we devote ourselves to righteousness and sanctification, which is God’s will, abandoning every desire of the Gentiles, which consists in impurity.

2. According to Origen, the Apostle brought a certain shame upon them, so that they might at least devote to righteousness and sanctification as much as they had previously devoted to impurity and iniquity.

[Col. 0579A]

3. He compares fruits with fruits, because the wage of labor is its fruit: “The wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life.” Here our merits and righteousness are excluded, and faith in Christ Jesus is commended.

### GOSPEL OF MARK, CHAPTER VIII

“When there was a great crowd with Jesus.”

1. An example of Christ’s continual benevolence, by which he teaches that nothing will be lacking to those who cling to him with sincere trust.

2. Arguments for the divine and human natures in Christ: the fact that he is moved by compassion belongs to his humanity; the fact that he feeds four thousand people with seven loaves and a few small fish is the work of divine power.

3. After giving thanks, he broke the bread and gave it to the disciples to set before the people. Hence the teaching that we should eat and drink with thanksgiving, for he himself opens his hand and fills every living thing with blessing. A prayer before food from Chrysostom:

> “Blessed is God, who has fed me from my youth, who gives food to all flesh. Fill our hearts with gladness and joy, so that, always having enough for every good work, we may abound in Christ Jesus our Lord, with whom, together with the Holy Spirit, glory, honor, and dominion are yours forever. Amen. Glory to you, Lord; glory to you, Holy One; glory to you, King, for you have given us food. Fill us with joy and gladness in the Holy Spirit, so that we may be found acceptable in your sight, without shame, when you render to each according to his works.”

[Col. 0579B]

## NINTH SUNDAY

### EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER VIII

“We are debtors, not to the flesh.”

1. Paul’s exhortation teaches that it is necessary to do good works, for we are debtors.

2. He confirms this exhortation by punishments and rewards: “If you live according to the flesh, you will die. But if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.”

[Col. 0579C]

3. The dignity of believers, who through the Holy Spirit recognize and call upon God: in this they cry, “Abba, Father”; they are children and heirs, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ. These things wonderfully console terrified consciences.

### GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER VII

“Beware of false prophets.”

1. Christ’s serious teaching—as the Greek expression προσέχετε also indicates—is that we must beware not only of open enemies, who are pigs and dogs, but also of hidden ones, who, although corrupted by depraved living, nevertheless put forward the appearance of virtue. Paul says the same in Romans XVI.

2. Christ’s gentleness must be observed. He does not say, “Punish such people; kill them,” but rather, “Take care that you are not harmed by them”; beware lest, being incautious and unprotected, you fall into their snares.

3. Through a comparison drawn from the common example of human beings, he teaches how the good are to be recognized from the bad: the works of the flesh and the fruit of the Spirit, Galatians V. He also requires faith, without which God’s commandments are not kept and good works are not performed.

[Col. 0579D]

## TENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

### FIRST EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER X

“Let us not desire evil things.”

1. “The things that were written were written for our admonition,” so that we may not think we can sin with impunity. He who did not spare the little ones or the inexperienced will not spare us, who have received the perfection of the law.

2. Through various dreadful examples he exhorts us: since by baptism we have been incorporated into Christ’s household, we must be free from every association with vices. We must not desire evil things; we must not be worshipers of idols; we must not be defiled by sexual immorality; we must not put Christ to the test; we must not grumble.

3. Consolation from the faithfulness of God, who, for the sake of his name, has promised a future to those who endure tribulation for him. Psalm XXXIII: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous.” He will not permit us to be tested beyond what we can endure.

### GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER XVI

“There was a certain rich man who had a steward.”

1. Christ removes the opinion held by most mortals: that we are not masters of the things we possess, but their caretakers and stewards.

2. He also teaches that a Christian must take every opportunity to do good to his neighbor: to support, console, exhort, and teach him. Such kindness will not perish but will be preserved for the life to come.

3. Our negligence is censured: people who serve the world are anxious about bodily life, while we are not more diligent in providing for eternal things.

[Col. 0580B]

[Col. 0580]

## ELEVENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

### FIRST EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER XII

“You know that when you were Gentiles…”

1. He exhorts the Corinthians, having abandoned impious religion and impious customs and rites, to adopt true and holy religion and godly conduct, so that whatever they do may appear to be done through the inspiration of the Spirit.

2. The commendation of God’s grace: when a person lacks it, a spirit of confusion drives him into idolatry; when he possesses it, he believes with the heart unto righteousness and confesses with the mouth unto salvation.

3. The graces and gifts of the Holy Spirit are divided, not the Spirit himself: divisions of gifts, ministries, and activities. All these things are for the salvation and benefit of many.

### GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER XIX

“When Jesus drew near.”

1. Christ weeps because the Jews, in their remarkable blindness, did not recognize the time of the approaching grace—or, after its arrival and its presence among them, did not acknowledge grace.

2. Jerusalem, which stubbornly rejected the mercy of God visiting her, felt the time of vengeance with the utmost severity. Josephus records in *The Jewish War* that ninety-seven thousand captives were seized throughout the entire war, while during the whole period of the siege eleven hundred thousand perished. Concerning the woman who, driven by hunger, cooked her son, see Book VII, chapter 81.

3. Christ enters the Temple and drives out those buying and selling, wishing to show that avarice and commercial gain would be the deadly plagues of his Church, which that Temple prefigured.

[Col. 0580C]

## On the Feast of Saint Felicity

### Reading from the Last Chapter of Proverbs

**“Who can find a strong woman?”**

1. In metaphorical speech, the Catholic Church is described as a strong woman, whom John is said to have seen in the Apocalypse clothed with the sun—that is, with Christ.

2. The husband of this woman is Christ, the head of the Church, and the Church is subject to Christ, Ephesians 5.

3. The various conditions of bridegroom and bride are set forth, in which the choir of virtues is discerned: for Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, in order to sanctify her after cleansing her with the washing of water through the word, so that he might present her to himself as a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle.

### Gospel of Matthew, Chapter 12

**“Behold, your mother and your brothers.”**

1. By this present example Christ teaches us not to prefer flesh and blood to spiritual work. Certainly, God’s commandment is, “Honor your father and your mother”; yet here Christ teaches that one owes more to paternal mysteries than to maternal affections.

2. The importunity of the mother and brothers is shown: they ought to have entered and listened with the crowds, or waited outside until the end of the discourse. Instead, as Chrysostom testifies, moved by ambition and display, they summon him outside so that they might appear to command Christ.

3. The common nobility shared with Christ by all genuine Christians is to do the will of God. Let us be energetic in this.

[Col. 0581A]

## Twelfth Sunday after Pentecost

### Reading from the First Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians, Chapter 15

**“I make known to you the Gospel.”**

1. The Gospel is clearly and briefly summarized in its entirety—the Gospel in which one must stand and through which we obtain salvation: Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and he rose again according to the Scriptures.

2. Christ is that Savior of the world whom Moses and the prophets announced; therefore Paul recalls that he was foretold in the Scriptures.

3. In asserting the resurrection, the Apostle is painstaking. He was seen by Cephas, then by the Eleven, afterward by more than five hundred brothers, by James, by all the apostles, and finally by Paul. For whoever denies the article of the resurrection will deny many things that we rightly believe: that the word we have heard is true, that the apostles teach rightly, that they are apostles of God, that God is truthful, and that God exists.

### Gospel of Luke, Chapter 18

**“Two men went up into the Temple.”**

1. This is a parable about humility opposed to pride. Pride is contempt for God; Christ speaks against it often, since this passion afflicts human beings above all.

2. The question is asked why the Pharisee is condemned when he recites his own praises, while Job, doing the same, is crowned. The answer is that the Pharisee spoke by condemning others, with no compelling reason. Job was compelled by his friends and by his calamities to declare his innocence.

3. The teaching is that everyone who humbles himself will be exalted. Therefore let us learn here that each person should entreat God before him in supplication and submission: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”

[Col. 0581C]

## On the Feast of Saint Lawrence

### Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians, Chapter 9

**“He who sows sparingly.”**

1. By the comparison of the sower and the reaper, the Apostle exhorts us to be generous and spontaneous in doing good.

2. This benefaction will not perish, for whatever is bestowed out of love for God upon the saints, God counts as bestowed upon himself, Matthew 10 and 25.

3. Munificence, by which the poverty of the saints is relieved, is a good part of piety and righteousness: Psalm 91 [as cited]: “He distributed, he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures.”

[Col. 0581D]

### Gospel of John, Chapter 12

**“Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth.”**

1. By the parable of the grain thrown into the earth, Christ shows the usefulness and abundant fruit of his death and passion. For Christ’s death is our merit, our refuge, our salvation, our life, and our resurrection.

2.
