The exhortation following the proposed parable, by which we are commanded to lose our souls, does not mean that each person should kill himself—for that is an unforgivable crime—but that he should kill within himself the carnal affection of the soul, by which the present life delights us to the detriment of the future life. The same applies to parents: whoever loves them must “lose” them, not kill them in the manner of parricides, but kill their carnal affection with the spiritual sword of the word of God.

3. There is a most delightful promise and dignity for those who minister to Christ: “The Father will honor them.” That is, they will be with Christ, the Son of God. An adopted child cannot receive greater honor than to be where the only-begotten Son is.

[Col. 0582A]

## Thirteenth Sunday after Pentecost

### Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians, Chapter 3

**“We have such confidence.”**

1. In the matter of the salvation of souls, we can accomplish nothing by our own wisdom or power; all our competence comes from God. Therefore the Church should earnestly pray for ministers of the word: “Grant your servants that with all confidence they may speak your word; let them speak the utterances of God and minister in power, so that God may be glorified through Christ.”

2. The offices of the Law and the Gospel. The Law is letter: “You shall not covet.” I say: unless grace assists you, you will covet more ardently. This is what is meant by, “The letter kills, but the spirit changes the heart and gives life.”

3. The glory of the Law and the Gospel. He calls the commandments of the Law “the ministry of condemnation”; the Savior’s grace, “the ministry of righteousness,” to which he ascribes an abundance of grace. He judges rightly concerning the nature of things as a divine man, Cyril of Alexandria, *Commentary on John*, on the words, “Grace for grace.”

[Col. 0582B]

### Gospel of Mark, Chapter 7

**“Jesus departed from the region of Tyre.”**

1. The miracle by which the Lord heals a deaf and mute man, or **μογιλάλον**—“speech-impaired”—testifies that the Messiah is present, of whom Isaiah foretold: “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped,” Isaiah 35.

2. This is a type of the evangelical teacher: he takes the man aside, away from the crowd. In the same way, one must lead people away from the broad road on which many walk toward destruction and bring them back to the company of the little flock, which loves truth, innocence, and righteousness.

3. Praise belongs to God alone: “He has done all things well.” No mortal does everything well; Christ is God.

[Col. 0582B]

## Fourteenth Sunday after Pentecost

### Epistle of Paul to the Galatians, Chapter 3

**“The promises were spoken to Abraham.”**

1. The promises were given to Abraham four hundred and thirty years earlier: in his seed, which is Christ, all nations would be blessed. And Jesus Christ became a minister of circumcision for the truth of God, in order to confirm the promises made to the fathers.

2. The Law was established because of transgressions, so that man might receive commandments, proudly trusting in his own powers; then, failing in them and even becoming a transgressor, he would seek a liberator and savior.

3. The Law was given so that grace might be sought; grace was given so that the Law might be fulfilled. If there were no Law, there would be no conscience; sin would not be recognized; we would not be humbled, and thus we would not desire grace. Therefore he enclosed all things under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ.

### Gospel of Luke, Chapter 10

**“Blessed are the eyes that see.”**

1. This is the blessedness of Christ’s disciples, to whom the Son of God revealed himself and the Father, and opened the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, hidden from the wise and prudent.

2. The two commandments concerning love of God and neighbor comprise what is best; yet it is not knowledge but observance that gives life.

3. Who is one’s neighbor? The Jews interpreted the word “neighbor” as referring to members of their own nation, thinking that they were permitted to hate those who were not neighbors. Christ declares that anyone—whether Gentile or Jew—who needs my works of mercy, to whom an act of compassion must be shown, is my neighbor.

[Col. 0582D]

## Fifteenth Sunday after Pentecost

### Epistle of Paul to the Galatians, Chapter 5

**“Walk by the Spirit.”**

1. The chief work of faith is the struggle of the spirit against the flesh, so that no one may think the Christian life is soft and idle. Sins continually attack us: these are the Moabites and Ammonites, our enemies, with whom we must make no truce but remain perpetually in combat.

2. The works of the flesh are adultery, fornication, and so forth. Those who do such things will not be heirs of the kingdom of God.

3. The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, and so forth. Against such things there is no law. Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.

### Gospel of Luke, Chapter 17

**“As Jesus entered Jerusalem.”**

1. How abominable a vice ingratitude is, and how rightly the Jews were rejected because of it while the Gentiles were admitted into the obedience of faith.

2. Christ observed the legal ordinances, as is clear from the account of his life: his circumcision, his offering in the Temple, and his sacrifice of the paschal lamb. Therefore, in accordance with the commandment of the Law, Leviticus 14, he ordered those cleansed of leprosy to show themselves to the priests.

[Col. 0583B]

3. Foreigners were more ready for faith than Israel. Hence, “The first will be last, and the last first”; and to the foreigners it is said, “Your faith has saved you.” To the Jews: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits,” Matthew 21.

[Col. 0583B]

## Sixteenth Sunday after Pentecost

### Epistle to the Galatians, Chapter 4

**“If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit,” etc.**

1. It belongs to Christians to produce the fruit of the Spirit and to remain far from the works of the flesh.

2. Those who have fallen into sin must be restored and raised up gently and kindly.

3. The law of love is especially the law of Christ. Paul calls it building up one’s neighbor: considering all the members of the same body as one, regarding everyone as one in Christ, rejoicing in the advantages of one’s brothers as in one’s own, remedying their disadvantages as though they were one’s own, correcting the one who errs with gentleness, teaching the ignorant, raising up the fallen, consoling the downcast, helping the laboring, and assisting the needy. In short, we must direct all our resources and efforts toward benefiting as many as possible in Christ—first the members of the household of faith, then everyone—so that love may be accompanied by affection.

### Gospel of Matthew, Chapter 6

**“No one can serve two masters.”**

1. The philosophy of Christ, which promises eternal blessedness, requires the whole person and spits out those who limp in both directions. For righteousness has no partnership with injustice, light no communion with darkness, nor Christ agreement with Belial; the believer has no share with the unbeliever, 2 Corinthians 6.

2. Christ relieves us of anxiety about temporal matters by the example of the birds, the lilies, and the grass of the field; indeed, by his most delightful promise, when he says, “Your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things,” so that our hearts may not be weighed down by the cares of this life, Luke 21. He also teaches us to keep our conduct free from avarice, content with what is present, Hebrews 13, knowing that the Lord says, “I will never leave you nor forsake you.”

3. He teaches that the kingdom of God must first be sought—that is, faith in Jesus Christ—and his righteousness, that is, faith working through love. For the kingdom of God is not in word but in power. Thus **προστεθήσεταί ὑμῖν ταῦτα πάντα**, “all these things will be added to you.” He did not say “they will be given,” but “they will be added,” so that we may learn that the things granted in the present are altogether insignificant when compared with the greatness of those that are to come.

[Col. 0583D]

## Seventeenth Sunday after Pentecost

### Epistle of Paul to the Ephesians, Chapter 3

**“I beseech you, do not lose heart.”**

1. The cross of Christ and the chains of the apostles and apostolic men, which they bear for their sincere profession of the Gospel, are an adornment to Christians, not a disgrace. It is glory before God if someone suffers as a Christian; let him not be ashamed, but rather glorify God in this respect, 1 Peter 4. See Augustine, *To Boniface*, Letter 50.

2. “The weapons of our warfare,” powerful through God for the demolition of strongholds, are prayers by which, with knees bent and from the innermost affection of the mind, we beseech God our Father and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

3. The aim of our prayers is that we may be filled with all the fullness of God and know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so that with all the saints we may attain its breadth and length, and so forth. Love demonstrates that faith is true. This faith comprehends that there is nothing so high, low, long, or broad over which Christ does not have power and in which he cannot help; nor does it fear death or hell.

### Gospel of Luke, Chapter 7

**“Jesus went to a city called Nain.”**

1. The account of the dead only son of a widowed woman, whom the Lord restored to life, shows Christ to be Lord of life and death. Therefore, amid death, hope must not be placed in the saints.

2. Christ consoles by words and helps by deeds. He is the father of orphans and the judge of widows. By words: “Do not weep”; by deed, because he says, “Young man, I say to you, arise,” and returns him alive to his mother.

3. These events, carried out according to the historical account, possess the meaning of spiritual teaching. The widowed mother bears the image of the Church, whose son lies dead; the sinner comes back to life through inward contrition. See Bede and Erasmus’s paraphrase.

[Col. 0584B]

## Eighteenth Sunday after Pentecost

### Epistle of Paul to the Ephesians, Chapter 4

**“I, a prisoner in the Lord, beseech you.”**

1. Paul’s exhortation is clear: the whole pattern of our life should display true modesty of spirit, gentleness, and mildness, which constitute the Christian life, Matthew 11: “Learn from me to be meek and humble in heart.”

2. Unity is strongly commended for preservation through the bond of peace. For there is one body, one spirit with God, and one spirit with our brothers. Here we Christians should be ashamed of sects, schisms, and individual opinions, 1 Corinthians 1. Paul entreats us by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ that we all speak the same thing, that there be no dissensions among us, but that we be an undivided body, of the same mind and the same judgment. For unity to stand, calmer dispositions are necessary, with stomachs not so raw on every side.

3. One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, and so forth. Let these things also inflame us toward ecclesiastical unity and mutual love, so that the Churches are not disturbed because of the sublimity of doctrines, since one ought to endure martyrdom sooner than sever unity. See Eusebius.

[Col. 0584D]

### Gospel of Luke, Chapter 14

**“When Jesus entered the house of a certain ruler.”**

1. Christ heals a man with dropsy on the Sabbath in the presence of the interpreters of the Law and the Pharisees. He teaches that when a great benefit results, one should not be concerned if evil people take offense, and that the religion of those who are offended by a person’s salvation is perverse.

2. Christ so refutes the Pharisees who observed such things that he condemns both their avarice and their true violation of the Sabbath.

3. The parable of those invited both calls us to true humility and exposes the Pharisees’ counterfeit holiness.

[Col. 0584D]

## Nineteenth Sunday

### First Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians, Chapter 1

**“I give thanks to my God always for you.”**

1. Those who come to the faith of Christ are enriched with every grace—that is, with all virtues, wisdom, and knowledge, which establish prophets and friends of God.

2. The joy and mutual rejoicing of the saints arise when they see people advancing in evangelical knowledge.

3. The most powerful consolation for the elect is to await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ on the day of judgment, which makes them blessed in hope.

### Gospel of Matthew, Chapter 22

**“The Sadducees approached Jesus.”**

1. The first and greatest commandment is the knowledge and confession of the divine unity together with the performance of good works. Good works are perfected through love of God and neighbor, as Paul says in these words: “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love.”

2. The Hebrews say that the highest degree of worshiping the Creator is to serve him out of love, and not in order to receive payment or a reward: with the whole heart, since the heart alone makes one’s work good or evil; with the whole soul, so that even if the situation demands it, one does not hesitate to expose one’s soul for him—that is, one’s bodily life; with all one’s strength, so that one would rather incur the loss of all one’s possessions than turn away from the love of God.

3. He drives one question in with another as a nail with a nail, from Psalm 109, concerning the divinity of the Son. This question and interrogation, as Jerome testifies, continues to benefit us to this day against the Jews.

[Col. 0585B]

## On the Feast of Saint Michael the Archangel

### Epistle from the Apocalypse, Chapter 1

**“God signified the things that must take place.”**

1. The Church, founded through the preaching of the apostles, was destined to be propagated more widely, so that preachers of the truth, relying confidently on this knowledge, might undertake their task without hesitation: the few against the many, the unarmed against the armed, the humble against the proud, the weak against the noble, the spiritually living against the spiritually dead.

[Col. 0585C]

2. The Savior Jesus bears distinguished titles: “who is, who was, and who is to come,” “the faithful witness,” “the firstborn,” and “the ruler of the kings of the earth.” From this the confidence of believers’ hearts is increased.

3. The ineffable love of Christ, who loved us, washed us from our sins in his blood, and made us a kingdom and priests to his God and Father: let us return love to him who loves in this way.

### Gospel of Matthew, Chapter 18

**“His disciples approached Jesus, saying, ‘Who, do you think,’” etc.**

1. By the example of a little child, an age endowed with innocence and simplicity, Christ teaches true modesty of spirit and **ταπεινοφροσύνην**, “humility,” the root of Christianity, and condemns the desire for ambition.

2. We must be neither an offense to ourselves nor a stumbling block to others who are hastening toward the kingdom of heaven. By the example of the foot, hand, and eyes, he teaches that every affection that draws us away from concern for eternal salvation must be cut off.

[Col. 0585D]

3. The little and despised in the eyes of the world are held in such continual regard by God that even their angels are their tutors and guardians.

[Col. 0585D]

## Twentieth Sunday

### Epistle of Paul to the Ephesians, Chapter 4

**“Be renewed in the spirit of your mind.”**

1. Through baptism we have been grafted into the new man, Christ, and must be renewed, so that injustice being removed, evangelical innocence and holiness may take its place.

2. Let the disciples of truth shudder at every lie and deal truthfully with their neighbor.

3. Let anger, shouting, and abuse depart so completely from Christians that no trace of them remains in the soul.

### Gospel of Matthew, Chapter 9

**“He entered the boat, crossed over, and came to his own city.”**

1. This is an example of burning faith in the paralytic himself, who ordered—or allowed—himself to be lowered, and likewise in those who carried the sick man.

2. The healing of the paralytic proves that it is equally easy for Christ, the Son of Man, to remove illness by a word and to forgive sins.

3. Christ displays his power and, through friends and enemies, opens up the vastness of his wisdom. He is himself both God and the Son of Man; therefore he does not blaspheme.

[Col. 0586A]

## Twenty-first Sunday after Pentecost

### Epistle to the Ephesians, Chapter 5

**“Therefore see carefully how you walk.”**

1. Since the whole world lies in the power of evil and the days are evil, from the time Adam fell from paradise, Christians must walk cautiously and carefully and understand the will of God, which is the substance of our salvation.

2. What drunkenness, pleasure, merriment, and feasting are worthy of Christians? Christ is our food, faith our drink; let us joyfully drink the sober intoxication of the Spirit.

3. At all times and for everything that happens to us, let us give thanks to God—not only for what we consider good, but also for what constrains us and comes against our will. For the distinctive virtue of Christians is to give thanks to the Creator amid adversities. Yet this is the work; this is the labor.

### Gospel of Matthew, Chapter 22

**“Jesus spoke with his disciples in parables, saying: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like a king,’” etc.**

1. This parable, like the preceding one about the vineyard, signifies God’s great patience, providence, and care toward the Jews, as well as their ingratitude toward God, their rejection, and the calling of the Gentiles. It also indicates what the discipline of life should be and how bitter a punishment awaits the negligent.

2. Yet how does he invite them? Not to labors, afflictions, and sweat, but to a wedding feast and delights—“For my bulls and fattened cattle have been slaughtered,” he says. Nevertheless, the negligent did not come; therefore they are without excuse.

3. The parable teaches that nothing can be so necessary that spiritual things should not be preferred to it.

[Col. 0586C]

## Twenty-second Sunday after Pentecost

**“Finally, be strengthened in the Lord.”**

1. With Jesus as their champion, who does not abandon or forsake his own, Christians are strong, powerful, and robust.

2. The armor and panoply of Christians against demons and their instruments, wicked human beings, are these: truth as a belt; innocence and righteousness as a breastplate; greaves of pure affections, desiring nothing except heavenly things; faith as a shield; a watchful mind as a helmet; and the sword of the word of God.

3. From this passage all spiritual weapons must be sought, so that, fortified on every side, we may be able to stand against the assaults of the devil.

### Gospel of John, Chapter 4

**“There was a certain royal official.”**

1. The account of the royal official—so called either because he was of royal descent or because he held some other princely office—provides an example of the calling of the Gentiles into the obedience of faith. It also shows that the Jews were rightly rejected for their unbelief and that the Gentiles were admitted into fellowship with the kingdom of God.

2. Christ prescribes a pattern of humility and shows that God is not swayed by respect for persons: he goes to the centurion’s servant but does not go to the royal official’s son.

3. This is an example of the power of faith, together with a declaration of faith.

[Col. 0586C]

## Twenty-third Sunday after Pentecost

### Epistle to the Philippians, Chapter 1

**“We are confident in the Lord Jesus that he who began,”** etc.

1. Since Christianity has beginnings, growth, and maturity, it belongs to love—which hopes all things—to be persuaded concerning those who have begun to be Christians that they will persevere.

2. God grants the beginnings of piety; he brings to completion in the elect what he began, until the day when Jesus Christ will come and repay eternal reward for righteous deeds, so that no one may glory in himself or in his own powers, but in the Lord.

3. He sets forth the example of Christ, who not only possesses no malice but also overflows with goodness, so that we too may be not only sincere and free from every corruption but also abundant in the fruit of righteousness.

### Gospel of Matthew, Chapter 18

**“The kingdom of heaven is like a king.”**

1. Christ himself explains the meaning of the parable of the king who settles accounts with his servants in a fearful statement: “So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive your brother from your heart their trespasses.”

[Col. 0587B]

2. He does not say, “Your Father,” but “My Father,” to show that these people are unworthy to have God called their Father, since they are so wicked that they pursue human beings with hatred and are unwilling to forgive.

3. This parable chiefly contains two things: that we acknowledge ourselves to be sinners and that we forgive the sins of others. The latter is easier because of the former. Hence the very true saying of the ancients: “No one is harmed except by himself.” See Chrysostom.

[Col. 0587B]

## Twenty-fourth Sunday

### Epistle of Paul to the Philippians, Chapter 2

**“Be imitators of me, and observe them.”**

1. The Apostle urges the Philippians to imitate him as an elect exemplar and instrument of God, not the false apostles, who removed the hope of Christ’s passion—through which sins are forgiven—and placed it in the ceremonies of the Law. This also rebukes those today who, neglecting true piety, place their confidence in the cold and plainly ridiculous ceremonies of human beings.

2. This is a description of the false apostles: enemies of the cross of Christ, concerned with earthly things, whose god is their belly, whose glory is in their shame, and whose end is destruction.

3. Our citizenship is in heaven, from which we await the Savior, the Lord Jesus, who will transform our humble body. Here believers possess both the evangelical goal and marvelous consolation in the saving forms of the cross, knowing that what is corruptible will put on incorruption and what is mortal will put on immortality.

### Gospel of Matthew, Chapter 22

**“The Pharisees went away and took counsel,”** etc.

1. When questioned about paying the census tax to Caesar, Christ responds to the Jews with serpentine wisdom, pointing out that they were concerned about what they owed Caesar but did not care instead about what was owed to God.

2. The Jews paid tribute when their possessions had come into Roman hands, and they had seen Theudas and Judas punished as seditionists for this reason. By this question, therefore, they attempt to cast Christ under a similar suspicion and hand him over to the governor as a factional agitator. But no plan can prevail against the Lord.

3. When you hear, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s,” do not doubt that this refers only to things that do not obstruct piety and religion. For whatever harms virtue and faith is not Caesar’s tribute or tax, but the devil’s tribute and levy. Tertullian, in the *Apology*: “I will not call the emperor God, either because I do not know how to lie, or because I dare not mock him, or because he himself would not wish to be called God if he is a human being.” Theodoretus says the same in Book 5, chapter 20.

[Col. 0587D]

## Twenty-fifth Sunday

### Epistle of Paul to the Colossians, Chapter 1

**“We do not cease praying for you.”**

1. The Apostle’s perpetual prayer is offered for the Colossians, whose faith in Christ and love toward the saints he had heard of.

2. To have believed the Gospel is the beginning of salvation, but salvation is completed and perfected by pious actions. Paul prays and nourishes them so that they may be filled with the knowledge of God’s will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding.

3. Christianity is an exceedingly serious matter and does not tolerate sluggishness or cowardice. We must walk worthily of God, please him in all things, bear fruit and grow in every good work, and be strengthened with every virtue. Away with the Sardanapaluses and the herd of swine, together with the people of the Asatori.

### Gospel of Matthew, Chapter 9

**“While he was speaking these things to them, behold, a certain ruler approached.”**

1. Jesus was ready to do good to all who asked something with simple confidence, whether they were poor or rich, Jews or foreigners. He restores to life the dead daughter of Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue, and on the way frees the woman with a hemorrhage from her flow of blood. Everywhere Jesus is present; everywhere he is a benefactor.

2. There is a sign of true flesh in Christ: it can be touched. Hence Luke says, “Someone touched me.”

3. He brings the woman forward publicly, not for ostentation, but to reveal the woman’s faith. Hence he also called her “daughter”; certainly her faith made her a daughter of Christ.

[Col. 0588B]

## On the Feast of Saint Andrew

### Epistle of Paul to the Romans, Chapter 10

**“With the heart one believes unto righteousness.”**

1. Here the basis of justification and regeneration is explained, which depends on faith, not on ceremonies. When the Spirit of God is granted to a person so that he may mortify his flesh, he ceases from his evil way of life; things opposed to God become displeasing to him. From that mortification arises the desire to live according to God’s will. “With the heart we believe unto righteousness, and with the mouth we confess unto salvation” for the sake of others.

2. God’s common order is that faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God. Therefore, when we receive the word and the Spirit working faith within us, so that we desire to amend our lives, this is a sign of new regeneration.

3. Beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize peace and proclaim good things; yet believers in the Gospel are rare. “The gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and few are those who find it,” Matthew 7. Hence a dreadful judgment awaits the world, which does not wish to receive the Spirit of truth.

[Col. 0588C]

## Readings for Advent

## First Sunday of Advent

### Epistle of Paul to the Romans, Chapter 13

**“Knowing that the hour has come.”**

1. By reference to the time, Paul urges us, recovering from the sleep and darkness of our former life, to awaken. And let us embrace love, the sum of all the commandments.

2. There are three kinds of vices from which a harvest of innumerable evils arises. The first is feasting and drunkenness; the second, beds and wantonness; the third, quarrels and rivalries. This third kind, Augustine says in Letter 64 to Aurelius, is more serious in our order.

3. Christ is wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and truth; sobriety, chastity, peace, love, and every virtue. Whoever takes these up is said to have put on Christ.

### Gospel of Matthew, Chapter 21

**“When they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage.”**

1. The three evangelists who wrote in Greek mention only the colt. Matthew, however, the only one who wrote in Hebrew for the Hebrews, also reports that the untied she-ass was brought to the Lord, to show that the salvation of that same Hebrew people, if it should repent, must not be despaired of. Jerome.

2. He often went up to Jerusalem, but never so openly, because the cross was at the doors. He fulfills a twofold prophecy, one by deed and the other by words. By deed, because Zechariah wrote that he would sit upon a she-ass like a king. The second signifies the calling of the unclean Gentiles, because he will rest among them; for they will come and worship him.

3. The whole Gospel is presented to us with marvelous brevity in the words of Zechariah: “Behold, your king comes to you, meek,” and so forth. Emphasis is present in every word. Let us only cry out, “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” and let us recognize the time of visitation.

[Col. 0589A]

## Second Sunday of Advent

### Epistle to the Romans, Chapter 15

**“Whatever was written was written for our instruction.”**

1. The sacred writings make one learned for salvation through faith, which is in Christ Jesus. “Whatever was written was written for our instruction, so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope.” All the writings contain faith and love and teach us to please everyone for the good.

2. The chief expression of our profession is peace and unanimity. Therefore he prays to God, the author of patience, that after the example of Jesus Christ he may make us perfected in unity.

3. Christ is the rich Lord toward all who call upon him, Jews and Gentiles. He was promised to the circumcised, while the Gentiles possess him through the purest generosity: they who once were not a people are now God’s people; they who once had not obtained mercy have now obtained mercy, 1 Peter 2.

### Gospel of Luke, Chapter 21

**“There will be signs in the sun and moon.”**

1. Christ enumerates various but absolutely certain signs of the approaching final day, here in Luke and elsewhere in Matthew. Chrysostom, so great a man, is seized with horror when he reads these things and groans from the depths of his heart: “O our negligence! How do we prepare ourselves for that dreadful day, so that we may flee from the wrath to come?”

2. The second coming of Christ is foretold with power and great majesty. Then all, from Adam until Christ’s coming, will render an account of their works; angels will minister, and the gates of heaven, closed since the beginning of the age, will be opened.

3. By the beautiful comparison of the fig tree, the trees, and summer, he foretells to the elect the kingdom of God and redemption—that is, the perfect liberation of body and soul. Therefore, when these things begin to occur, he wishes them to lift up their heads and remain steadfast in spirit, asserting under oath that his words will not pass away.

[Col. 0589C]

## Third Sunday of Advent

### First Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians, Chapter 4

**“Let a person regard us in this way.”**

1. Even the apostles—not to mention the false apostles—should not be honored with excessive praise. Therefore he says elsewhere, “Was Paul crucified for you?” They should be regarded as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Concerning the praise that may rightly be accepted by ministers of the Church, so that one accepts neither all nor nothing, see Augustine, Letter 84 to Aurelius.

2. Among the qualifications of a minister, faithfulness is required; elsewhere Luke adds prudence. Faithfulness consists in concealing none of God’s counsels; prudence consists in distributing everything at its proper time and in its proper order for the building up of the body of Christ, with simple prudence and prudent simplicity.

3. Since all things are clear to the eyes of God, to whom all judgment concerning hidden matters must be entrusted, we must take care not to anticipate the Lord’s judgment. For only the one whom God praises is praiseworthy, since he knows all hidden and unseen things.

[Col. 0590A]

### Gospel of Matthew, Chapter 11

**“When John heard in prison about the works of Christ,”** etc.

1. John’s disciples were sent as a delegation to Christ, not because John doubted that Christ was the Messiah, nor because he had been frightened by prison and changed his confession, but because his disciples were entertaining some human notion about Christ. To prevent them from leaving behind material for a pernicious opinion and becoming “Johannites” rather than Christians, he sent them away.

2. What are Christ’s deeds—“the blind receive sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have the Gospel preached to them”—except pure acts of kindness testifying from the prophecies that the Messiah is present?

3. Great is the praise of John, the voice crying in the wilderness, for his constancy, his life, and the Scripture. Among those born of women no one greater than John the Baptist has arisen.

[Col. 0590A]

## Fourth Sunday of Advent

[Col. 0590B]

### Epistle to the Philippians, Chapter 4

**“Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice,”** etc.

1. It belongs to Christians always to rejoice in the Lord, even amid afflictions, knowing that affliction produces patience, patience endurance, and endurance hope; moreover, hope does not put us to shame. And the Lord is near.

2. The Christian life is a profession of moderation. Let this be known to all people, so that the good may become better through the example of Christians, and the wicked may either be won over or broken.

3. Conditions of proper prayer, by which the Church and the saints pray, through which the peace of God that surpasses all understanding is attained.

## GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER I:

“The Jews sent from Jerusalem priests and Levites.”

1. What John’s testimony is not—namely, that he is not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet—and what it is: namely, [Col. 0590C] “the voice of one crying in the wilderness.”

2. Because Christ was born of an obscure lineage, and Christ’s way of life was ordinary—for he lived among the multitude as one of them—and Christ’s clothing differed in no way from that of the common people, whereas John’s birth was most celebrated, his life extremely austere, his garment of camel’s hair, his food locusts, and so forth, the Jews would have preferred to have John rather than Christ as their teacher. Therefore they send the most distinguished envoys, priests and Levites, from Jerusalem itself, to draw John by flattery to this point: that he might call himself the Christ.

3. The distinction between John and Christ, and between their two baptisms, together with John’s testimony, which is an argument for Christ’s divinity: “I am not worthy to untie his sandal strap,” and so forth.

(The summaries of the Epistles and Gospels for the feasts of apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins follow, in the order preserved by Smaragdus.)

[Col. 0590D]

[Col. 0590]

## ON THE FEAST OF THE APOSTLES

### PAUL’S LETTER TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER VIII:

“We know that for those who love God…”

1. This is a consoling passage, whose argument is drawn from usefulness. That is, whatever affliction comes from the flesh, the world, or Satan benefits us; and it is a work of God’s mercy, which we interpret as wrath.

2. In a most beautiful progression he teaches from where our salvation comes: those whom God had foreordained, he also called through the Gospel; those whom he called, he justified by faith; and finally he will glorify them. This necessity of predestination, teaching God’s mercy—that he foreordains without any merits—is pleasing to the spirit and hateful to the flesh.

3. The greatest arguments and supreme consolations concerning God’s beneficence toward us: he did not spare his own Son, and so forth. Let us return love for having been so loved, and let nothing separate us from the love of God, by which we are joined to him through Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0591A]

## GOSPEL OF JOHN, CHAPTER XV:

“This is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you.”

1. Christ’s commandment is that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he gave the commandment. If this alone is done, it is sufficient (I John III). See what Jerome writes in his Letter to the Galatians.

2. God’s ineffable grace: he calls them friends, not servants; he has made known to them everything he heard from the Father; he chose them; and he promises that he will give whatever they ask of the Father. To say nothing else, to be Christ’s friend is a dignity exceeding the limits of human nature, and this friend is more necessary than fire and water.

3. His friends, however, are those who do everything he has commanded, whom he chose to bear lasting fruit. Lasting fruit is the righteousness of evangelical discipline. This stands against the sloth of those who say to Christ, “Lord, Lord,” but do not do the will of the Father who is in heaven.

[Col. 0591A]

## ON THE FEAST OF ONE CONFESSOR

[Col. 0591B]

### PAUL’S SECOND LETTER TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER I:

“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

1. Paul calls the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ by a new title: “the Father of mercies and God of all consolation,” so that he may teach us to trust and to cast all our care and all our burden upon him.

2. Just as the sun receives light not merely so that it itself may shine but also so that it may illuminate other things, so God consoles the Apostles in every tribulation, so that through them others may be consoled by word and example.

3. In sum: God abandons no one. Those who are companions in sufferings will also be companions in consolation, and in the future he will reward much more greatly those whom he consoles in the present age.

### GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER XIV:

“If anyone comes to me and does not hate…” and so forth.

1. Let no one love parents, brothers, [Col. 0591C] wife, or children above Christ. In this matter, to be cruel is a form of piety, for Christ says: “Whoever does not renounce everything that he possesses cannot be my disciple.” See Jerome’s letter to Heliodorus and Augustine, Letter 39.

2. This ram of piety, by which faith of the Gospel is shaken, must be blunted against the wall: “My mother and my brothers are those who do the will of my Father who is in heaven.”

3. By two parables—one about a man building a tower and calculating the expense, the other about someone preparing to fight a king—Christ shows that prudence is necessary in following Christ, and that strength of spirit must be assessed before one declares oneself a follower of Christ.

[Col. 0591C]

## ON THE FEAST OF MANY SAINTS

### THE FIRST LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PETER, CHAPTER I:

“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord.”

1. Christians have a living hope because Jesus Christ rose from the dead, into an inheritance immortal, undefiled, and unfading, preserved in heaven. [Col. 0591D]

2. Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God. If we suffer with him, we shall reign with him; if we die with him, we shall live with him.

3. Christ was given to us as a gift, to be our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, and as an example, so that, since Christ suffered in the flesh, we too may arm ourselves with the same understanding.

### GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER XII:

“Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning.”

1. By the likeness of servants who are ready for service, the Lord teaches our diligence: that we should stand firm in faith, be watchful in the business of salvation, do no evil, and devote ourselves to good works.

2. Christ most earnestly wished his followers to live by this principle: that they should always await that final day of judgment prepared, as though it were about to come at once. It is evident that Peter, Paul, Jerome, and countless others lived by this principle. [Col. 0592A]

3. Hilary, following Origen, understands the thief to be the devil; others understand him to be the final day. By the master of the household, each one of us is meant. Yet it was said to everyone: “Watch” (Mark XIII). The day and hour are unknown. Death is certain, the day uncertain, the hour still more uncertain. Therefore let the wise man take thought for his soul.

### ALSO, THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, CHAPTER XIX:

“A certain nobleman went to a distant country.”

1. The parable of the nobleman concerns Christ’s kingdom, that is, the evangelical kingdom, into which tax collectors, prostitutes, soldiers, Greeks, Romans, Scythians, Gauls, Goths, Sarmatians, Germans, and everyone else must be drawn by the word of preaching. Hence we ought also to study the Agarenic and Arabic languages—let me say nothing of the three celebrated languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—so that we might one day draw Turks and Hagarenes into the obedience of faith. For faith comes through hearing, and the tongue serves it; and it is a great disgrace that, while the twelve apostles, like leaven placed in three measures of flour, leavened the whole world, we Christians, though innumerable, produce so little fruit—or rather, none at all. [Col. 0592B]

2. The distant country is the Church of the Gentiles. That illustrious man, Christ, went away so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter; he will return so that all Israel may be saved.

3. A lesson for ministers of the word: in the work of evangelical preaching, we must be as faithful and industrious as possible and win many for Christ, thereby receiving an unfading crown when Christ, the prince of shepherds, returns—the true noble and illustrious man. Otherwise, the one who has but does not have—that is, does not use what he possesses—loses God’s gift; whereas the one who has and possesses—that is, uses it well—is increased by it.

[Col. 0592B]

## ON THE FEAST OF MANY MARTYRS

### PAUL’S LETTER TO THE HEBREWS, CHAPTER XI:

“By faith the saints conquered kingdoms.”

[Col. 0592C]

1. What power faith possesses: it is the substance of things hoped for and the proof of things not seen.

2. Outstanding examples are drawn from the Old and New Testaments, by which the majesty and power of faith are displayed. Joshua and David conquered kingdoms; Samuel practiced righteousness; Joshua and David again obtained the promises. David and Samson shut the mouths of lions; Aaron and the youths in Daniel extinguished the power of fire; Elijah and others escaped the edge of the sword; Jonathan, Asa, and Jehoshaphat turned back attacks by foreigners. Others were tortured. See Jeremiah XX, Judges XVI, Tobit II, Job XIX. See Eusebius’s Chronicle and Theodore’s Book V, chapter 39, concerning the various kinds of punishments and refinements of torments by which the godly were tortured.

3. What the Apostle here attributes to faith, Chrysostom attributes to Christ’s cross. See Homily 55 on Matthew, where he calls it the sign and symbol of our salvation, for the Lord’s Passion is the foundation and origin of our blessedness. “Therefore,” he says, “when you sign yourself with the cross, consider with yourself the whole purpose of the cross, and extinguish the fires of anger and the remaining passions. This sign, in ancient and in our own times, has opened closed doors; it has extinguished the power of poisons; it has restrained savage beasts; it has healed deadly serpent bites. It must be preserved not merely by the finger on the body, but by great faith in the mind.” Thus far he.

### GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER V:

“When Jesus saw the crowds…”

1. Christ Jesus, the heavenly teacher and orator, sets forth the sum of heavenly philosophy—that is, an explanation of the divine law—with clear brevity and most gentle invitations and promises.

2. Some orators are grand, serious, and expansive; others are restrained, subtle, brief, intermediate, or moderate. Christ is everything, and the best of all: by his speech he teaches, delights, and moves the minds of his hearers, promising the kingdom of heaven, consolation, an inheritance of the earth, mercy, [Col. 0593A] the vision of God, adoption as God’s children, and a great reward in heaven.

3. Poverty of spirit is the root of every good, just as pride of mind and μεγαφρονεῖν—“thinking great thoughts,” or arrogance—are the root of every evil. From this arise the greatest evils, those that have nearly brought destruction upon the whole world.

[Col. 0593A]

## ON THE FEAST OF VIRGINS

### GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER XIII:

“The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field.”

1. Just as the parables of the mustard seed and the leaven display the great power of the Gospel, which was destined entirely to overcome the whole world, so the parable of the treasure and the pearl shows that the Gospel is of the highest value and must be preferred above all things.

2. The preaching of the Gospel is hidden and concealed in the world, and supreme blessedness lies concealed within that preaching. It is found only if you seek carefully, just as a treasure hidden in a field is ordinarily sought.

3. Christ himself interprets the parable of the net cast into the sea, showing the many paths to destruction. Thus it was not without reason that he elsewhere said that broad is the way that leads to destruction, and so forth, in order to enlarge and instill fear. Hence he also mentions the furnace, the gnashing of teeth, weeping, and so forth. “Indignation, anger, affliction, and anguish against every human soul that does evil” (Romans II). [Col. 0594A]

### GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, CHAPTER XXV:

“The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins.”

1. Virginity, because of its excellence, is not commanded; it is a sublime state that even among the ancients could not be practiced by those ancient and holy men. Nevertheless, as a sublime virtue it will not suffice unless the work of faith and the labor of charity are present.

2. Let each person take care for himself, lest we go astray. God is not mocked; no one will be able to defend us if we do not have oil in our lamps.

3. Christ repeatedly says, “Watch,” because you do not know the day or the hour, showing that ignorance of the end of this life is beneficial. Therefore, with that Pauline conclusion, we gladly sound the retreat: “Watch, stand firm in the faith, act courageously, be strong; let everything among us be done with charity.” This is the Christian life. Those who have lived in this way, when Christ appears, will have confidence and will not be put to shame by him at his coming; instead, they will enter with Christ the bridegroom into the wedding feast.

[Col. 0593B]

# THE DIADEM OF MONKS BY SMARAGDUS, ABBOT

[From the *Bibliotheca Patrum Maxima*, volume XVI.]

[Col. 0593B]

## PROLOGUE OF THE REVEREND FATHER SMARAGDUS

[Col. 0593C]

We have compiled this little book of our work from the sayings of many orthodox Fathers, with Christ’s help. Passing through their flowering meadows, fragrant with good odors, we gathered little flowers, as though readily to hand; and from that flower-bearing field, full of the Lord’s blessings, we gathered what we perceived to be necessary for monks and endeavored to assemble it in this small book.

These are matters that may soothe the hearts of perfect monks and raise them more eagerly and more loftily toward desire for their heavenly homeland; they may also strengthen and alarm the hearts of weak monks and lead them to regular correction. And because it is written in the Rule of blessed Benedict: “As soon as the brothers rise from supper, let them all sit together, and let one read the Conferences or Lives of the Fathers, or certainly something that edifies those who hear it,” therefore in this little book we have collected a small amount from the Conferences of the Fathers and from their ways of life and teachings, but much from various Doctors, and thus completed the whole in one hundred chapters.

And because it is the custom of monks to read the Rule of blessed Benedict daily at the morning chapter, we wish this little book to be read daily at their evening chapter. And because we read in the same Rule of blessed Benedict that whatever good we begin, we should earnestly ask God to bring it to completion with the most fervent prayer, for this reason we place the chapter on the duty of prayer first in this book.

[Col. 0594C]

# CHAPTER ONE: ON PRAYER

The remedy for the soul of one who burns with the assaults of vices is this: whenever he is touched by any vice, he should immediately submit himself to prayer, because frequent prayer extinguishes the attacks of vices. We must devote our minds to prayer and knocking with such perseverance that, by the greatest concentration, we overcome the importunate suggestions of carnal desires that clamor against our senses; and we must persist until, by persisting, we conquer. For negligent prayers cannot obtain, even from the person himself, what they seek.

When someone prays, he summons the Holy Spirit to himself; but when the Spirit has come, the temptations of demons that plunge themselves into human minds flee at once, unable to endure his presence. Prayer belongs to the heart, not to the lips. For God does not attend to the words of the one who pleads, but looks upon the heart of the one who prays. If the heart prays silently and the voice is quiet, although this may be hidden from human beings, it cannot be hidden from God, who is present to the conscience. It is better to pray with silent heart and without the sound of the voice than with words alone, without the mind’s attention. What makes our words reach the most secret ears of God is not speech but desire.

Even if we ask for eternal life with our mouth but do not desire it in our heart, we remain silent while crying out. But if we desire it from the heart, even when we are silent with our mouth, we cry out while remaining silent. (Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXII, chapter 18.)

Hence, in the wilderness, the people resound with their voices, while Moses remains silent amid the clamor of words; yet, though silent, he is heard by the ear of divine compassion. He is asked: “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exodus XIV). There is therefore within desire a secret cry that does not reach human ears and yet fills the hearing of the Creator.

One should never pray without a groan. For remembrance of sins produces sorrow. (Thus far Gregory.) For when we pray, we call our sin to mind, and then we recognize more fully that we are guilty. Therefore, when we stand before God, we ought to groan and weep, remembering how grave are the crimes we have committed and how terrible are the punishments of hell that we fear.

Let the mind preserve after prayer the condition in which it presents itself during prayer. For prayer accomplishes nothing if one again commits the sin for which forgiveness has already been requested. The one who undoubtedly receives the desired effect of prayer is he who does not repeat by transgressing what he asks to have washed away by praying.

We truly pray when we think of nothing else. Indeed, we believe that divine gifts are obtained when we stand before God with a simple devotion as we pray. When we stand for prayer, we must be watchful and devote ourselves to prayer with our whole heart, so that every carnal and worldly thought may depart and the mind may then think of nothing except the very thing for which it prays.

Therefore the priest also prepares the minds of the brethren by saying, “Lift up your hearts,” so that when the people respond, “We have them toward the Lord,” they may be reminded that they ought to think of nothing other than the Lord.

Let the one who is injured not cease to pray for those who injure him; otherwise, according to God’s judgment, he sins by not praying for his enemies (Matthew V). Just as medicine does no good for a wound if the iron remains in it, so prayer does nothing for one whose pain still remains in the mind or hatred in the breast.

The sacrifice of prayer is received more willingly when it is seasoned, in the sight of the merciful Judge, with love of one’s neighbor. A person truly makes this sacrifice complete when he offers it also for his adversaries.

Such must be the devotion toward God of one who prays: that he does not despair of the effect of prayer. We pray in vain if we have no confidence of hope. “Let each person ask in faith,” says the Apostle James, “without doubting” (James I). And the Lord says: “Whatever you ask in prayer, believing, you will receive” (Matthew XI).

Once an old man came to Mount Sinai, and as he was leaving, a brother met him on the road and, groaning, said to the old man: “We are afflicted, Abba, because of the drought, for it has not rained upon us.” The old man said to him: “Why do you not pray and ask God?” He replied: “We do pray and continually entreat God, and it does not rain.” The old man said: “I believe that you do not pray attentively enough. Would you like to know that this is so? Come, let us stand together in prayer.”

And stretching out his hands toward heaven, he prayed, and immediately rain descended. When that brother saw it, he was afraid, and falling down, he did obeisance to the old man. For the Lord also said to his disciples: “Have faith. Truly I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and cast into the sea,’ and does not doubt in his heart, whatever he says will be done for him” (Matthew XI).

We also read that this happened through the prayers of blessed Gregory of Neocaesarea. When he wished to build a church in a suitable place and saw that it was narrower than the work required, he came to the place at night, knelt down, and prayed to the Lord to move the mountain farther away in accordance with the faith of the one asking. In the morning, when he returned, he found that the mountain had left the builders of the church as much space as the work required.

Holy Scholastica likewise placed her hands and head upon the table and prayed for rain, and immediately rain descended from heaven upon them. (Rufinus, Book VII of the *History*.)

For this reason, too, the prayers of the righteous are heard more slowly: so that, while they are delayed, they may be increased with greater rewards. Prayer is poured forth more suitably in private places when it is uttered with God alone as witness. For it is not the many words of the one praying that win over God, but the greater and sincere concentration of prayer.

Some people asked Abba Macarius: “How ought we to pray?” The old man said to them: “There is no need to speak much in prayer, but to stretch out the hands frequently and say: ‘Lord, as you will and as you know, have mercy on me.’”

Hence blessed Benedict says: “Let us know that we are heard not through much speaking, but through purity of heart and compunction of tears.” Therefore prayer ought to be brief and pure, unless it is extended by the movement of inspiration from divine grace. In the assembly, however, prayer must be made altogether brief.

[Col. 0596B]

# CHAPTER II: ON THE DISCIPLINE OF PSALMODY

We must obey with all our strength the one who admonishes us through the Prophet, saying: “Sing psalms wisely” (Psalm XLVI); that is, let us not seek the sound that pleases the ear, but the light of the heart, and let us fulfill in our works what we sing with our tongue. (Basil, *Brief Rule*, 279.)

He also sings wisely who understands what he sings in the psalm. For no one acts wisely who does not understand what he is doing. What taste is among all foods, by which one distinguishes what flavor something has, such is prudence and understanding in the words of Holy Scripture.

Therefore, if someone applies his soul to each word of psalmody as taste is applied to distinguishing the flavor of foods, he is the one who has fulfilled what is said: “Sing psalms wisely” (Psalm XLVI).

It is good always to pray in the heart, and it is also good to glorify God with the sound of the voice through spiritual hymns. To sing with the voice alone, without the heart’s attention, is nothing. [Col. 0596D] Rather, as the Apostle says: “Admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to God” (Colossians III). That is, singing psalms not only with the voice but also with the heart. Hence elsewhere: “I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind” (I Corinthians XIV).

Just as we are governed by prayers, so we take delight in the study of psalms. The usefulness of psalmody consoles sad hearts, makes minds more grateful, delights the fastidious, awakens the sluggish, and invites sinners to lamentation. For although the hearts of the fleshly may be hard, as soon as the sweetness of a psalm resounds, it bends their minds toward a feeling of devotion.

Although it is not the modulation of the voice but only the divine words spoken there that ought to move the Christian, nevertheless, somehow a greater compunction of heart arises from the singer’s melody. Many are found who, moved by the sweetness of song, mourn their sins and are more readily bent to tears by the very part from which the most delightful sweetness of psalmody has sounded.

In the present life prayer is poured out only as a remedy for sins, but the chanting of psalms displays the perpetual praise of God unto everlasting glory, as it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm LXXXIII).

Whoever faithfully and attentively performs the ministry of this work is, in a certain sense, joined to the angels. Hence the same Psalmist says elsewhere: “In the sight of the angels I will sing psalms to you” (Psalm CXXXVII). The power of psalmody is shown here: whoever sings psalms among human beings with a pure heart seems also to sing above with the angels.

Hence the Apostle also says: “Admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing in your hearts to God” (Colossians III). We must therefore sing, chant psalms, and praise the Lord more with the mind than with the voice. For this is what is meant by “singing in your hearts.”

When the voice of psalmody is performed with the heart’s attention, through that attention a path to the heart is prepared for almighty God, so that he may pour into the attentive mind either the mysteries of prophecy or the grace of compunction.

Hence it is written: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me, and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God” (Psalm XLIX). And also: “Sing to the Lord, sing a psalm to his name; make a way for him who rides upon the sunset—the Lord is his name” (Psalm LXVII). For he has ridden upon the sunset who, by rising again, trampled down death. When we sing to him, we make a way for him to come to our heart and kindle us with the grace of his love.

[Col. 0597C]

# CHAPTER III: ON READING

By prayers we are cleansed; by reading we are instructed. Both are good, if possible; if not possible, it is better to pray than to read. Whoever wishes always to be with God ought frequently to pray and frequently to read. For when we pray, we speak with God himself; but when we read, God speaks with us.

All progress proceeds from reading and meditation. What we do not know, we learn through reading; what we have learned, we preserve through meditation.

Reading the holy Scriptures bestows a twofold gift: either because it trains the understanding of the mind, or because, drawing a person away from the vanities of the world, it leads him to the love of God. (Isidore, *Sentences*, Book III, chapter 8.)

The study of reading is also twofold. First, how the Scriptures are to be understood; second, with what usefulness or dignity they are spoken. For everyone should reasonably first be ready to understand what he reads, and then capable of expressing what he has learned.

The law of God contains both a reward and a punishment for those who read it: a reward for those who preserve it by living well, but a punishment for those who despise it by living badly.

Holy Scripture calls the mind of its reader to the heavenly homeland, changes the reader’s heart from earthly desires to the embrace of heavenly things, exercises it with more obscure sayings, and with humble speech caresses the little ones; by the practice of reading, it removes weariness from the reader. For those whom it assists with humble words, it raises up with sublime ones.

Holy Scripture somehow grows together with its readers: it is, as it were, rediscovered by unskilled readers, and yet it is always found to be new by the learned.

It is said to the prophet Ezekiel: “Son of man, whatever you find, eat it” (Ezekiel III). Whatever is found in Holy Scripture is to be eaten, because its small matters shape a simple life, while its great matters build subtle understanding.

By reading the commandments of Holy Scripture, we revive, though we lay dead in guilt. Hence through the Psalmist it is said to almighty God: “I will never forget your words, for by them you have given me life” (Psalm CXVIII).

Holy Scripture has been made for us a light on the path amid the darkness of the present life. Hence Peter says: “To which you do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (II Peter I).

When the word of Holy Scripture seems tepid to a reader, the meaning of the divine utterance does not stir his mind, and no light of understanding shines forth in his thought, let him seek the order of living well. If, through the step of his heart, he discovers how to set down the foot of good works, he finds as much progress in the sacred utterance as he himself has made progress within it.

Often it happens that someone perceives the words of Holy Scripture to be mystical if, kindled by the grace of heavenly contemplation, he raises himself toward heavenly things. For the wondrous and ineffable [Col. 0598C] power of sacred speech is recognized when the soul of the reader is penetrated by heavenly love.

[Col. 0598C]

# CHAPTER IV: ON THE LOVE OF GOD AND NEIGHBOR
*(Isidore, Book II of the Sentences, chapter 3.)* Charity consists in love of God and of neighbor. He preserves love of God who is not separated from charity toward his neighbor. Whoever withdraws from fraternal fellowship is deprived of participation in divine charity. Nor can he love God who is known to err in loving his neighbor. Christ is God and man. Therefore, whoever hates a human being does not love the whole Christ.

*(Isidore, same work.)* Although some may appear to share in faith and holy works, nevertheless, because they are deprived of the charity of fraternal love, they possess no increase of virtue. For, as the Apostle says: “If I deliver my body to be burned, but have not charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13). Without the love of charity, even if one believes rightly, one cannot attain blessedness. For so great is the power of charity that even prophecy and martyrdom are considered nothing without it. No reward is equal to charity. Charity indeed holds primacy among all virtues. Hence the Apostle calls charity “the bond of perfection” (Colossians 3), because all the virtues are bound together by its bond.

*(Thus far Isidore.)* The first virtue of obedience is in charity. This charity is distinguished in two commandments, so that God and neighbor may be loved; and right action is perfected through the completion of the Decalogue, so that once good deeds have begun, no evil deeds are then committed. There are two commandments of charity, namely love of God and love of neighbor, through which the words of Sacred Scripture give us life, because in the divine utterances we grasp the love of God and neighbor.

*(Gregory, Moralia, Book VII, chapter 10.)* Through love of God, love of neighbor is begotten, and through love of neighbor, love of God is nourished. For whoever neglects to love God plainly does not know how to love his neighbor. We make fuller progress in the love of God if, within the embrace of that same love, we are first bound by charity toward our neighbor. Since, therefore, love of God generates love of neighbor, when the Lord was about to say through the Law, “You shall love your neighbor,” he prefaced it by saying, “You shall love the Lord your God” (Matthew 22; Luke 10; Deuteronomy 6), so that he might first establish the root of his love in the soil of our breast, and afterward brotherly love might sprout through its branches. Love of God grows strong through love of neighbor, as John testifies when he rebukes certain people, saying: “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” 

*(Gregory, cited work.)* This divine love, however, is born through fear, but as it grows it is changed into affection. Often almighty God makes known how far each person is from the charity of God and neighbor, or how much progress he has made in it (1 John 4). Disposing everything in a wondrous order, he brings some low through scourges and supports others through prosperity. And while he temporarily abandons some, he reveals what evil lies hidden in the hearts of others. For often those whom we had honored as incomparably fortunate pursue us in our misery.

Our journey on earth proceeds with an unhindered step if God and neighbor are loved with an undivided mind. For neither is God truly loved without one’s neighbor, nor is one’s neighbor truly loved without God. The Holy Spirit is read as having been given to the disciples twice: first by the Lord dwelling on earth (John 20), and afterward by the Lord presiding from heaven (Acts 2). On earth, therefore, the Spirit is given so that one may love one’s neighbor; from heaven, so that one may love God. But why first on earth and afterward from heaven, unless it is plainly shown that, in accordance with John’s words, “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4).

Let us love and embrace our neighbor, who is near us, so that we may be able to reach the love of him who is above us. Let the mind consider in its neighbor what it may present to God, so that it may deservedly rejoice perfectly in God together with its neighbor. Then we shall reach that joy of the heavenly assembly, of which we have now received the pledge of the Holy Spirit, if with all our love we strive toward this end—namely, the love of God and neighbor. Every commandment concerns love alone, and all are one commandment.

*(Gregory, Homily 27 on the Gospels.)* Whatever is commanded is made firm in charity alone. The Lord’s commandments, therefore, are both many and one: many through the diversity of their works, one in the root of love. He himself indicates how the love of God and neighbor is to be maintained: in many passages of his Scripture he commands that friends be loved in him and enemies be loved for his sake.

Let us therefore love, beloved brothers, the Lord our God as he commanded: let us love him with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength, because he first loved us (Deuteronomy 6; Matthew 22; Luke 10). Thus John, who reclined at the supper upon that fountain of love, says in his epistle: “Brothers, let us love the Lord, because he first loved us” (1 John 4). Human frailty could not love the Lord unless he first loved our nature. He loved us before we existed, and therefore he created us to exist; he gave us life, nourished us, guarded us, brought us to the bath of regeneration, renewed us, governed us, and brought us to intellectual maturity. He accomplished all these things for us mercifully and through an excess of love.

Let us therefore open the eyes of our hearts, beloved brothers, and recognize ourselves as so loved by Jesus Christ our Lord that we do not doubt that his blood was shed for us. Let us raise our hearts to the love of our Creator, and not love him only a little or in part, but let us love him with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength (Deuteronomy 6; Matthew 22; Luke 10), and let us prefer the love of no created thing to the love of our Lord Jesus Christ. For he himself says: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10). Truly, if we love God with all our heart, we must prefer to his love neither the love of parents, nor of friends, nor of children.

But if we love the Lord, we must love our neighbor also, as ourselves, because “on these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matthew 22; Romans 13). Therefore, whoever does not love God and neighbor does not fulfill the Law and the Prophets. For it is written: “We have this commandment from God, that whoever loves God should love his brother also” (1 John 4). And: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13). And again: “Beloved, let us love one another, because charity is from God. Everyone who loves his brother is born of God and knows God” (1 John 4). “If you love one another, God remains in us, and his charity is perfected in us” (same passage).

Blessed, therefore, is the love of charity, which embraces everyone, loves everyone, and cherishes everyone. Truly blessed is it, which nourishes virtues and destroys sins. It suppresses anger, excludes hatred, drives away greed, restrains quarrels, and likewise puts all vices to flight. “It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things” (1 Corinthians 13). It is secure amid insults, calm amid anger, beneficent amid hatred, and firm in truth. It is not torn away by wicked attackers, not stolen by robbers, not consumed by fire, and not divided by heresy. It stands undivided, remains unconquerable, endures beyond explanation, perseveres unshaken, and rejoices incorruptibly. For it is the bond of all virtues, the glue of souls, the harmony of minds, and the fellowship of the elect. So that it may not be broken by adversity, it strongly strengthens the mind; so that it may not be lifted up by prosperity, it prudently moderates it; so that it may not be overcome by anger, it restrains it rationally.

[Col. 0601A] Truly, as I see it, this is the noblest and most excellent virtue. Let us therefore hold fast to it, brothers, with whatever strength we possess, so that it may be with us, remain with us, rise with us, proceed with us, rejoice with us, and feast with us. For it is fitting that so royal a virtue should continually be present in the congregation of brothers.

[Col. 0601A]

## CHAPTER V. On Observing the Commandments of God

After discussing love, let us see what the author of love himself commands us to observe. For he says: “If you love me, keep my commandments, and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you forever” (John 14).

Let us therefore attend, brothers, to how greatly our Lord Jesus Christ loves us: together with promising us his love, he requires our love and says that the Holy Spirit will remain with us forever if, after his love, we keep his commandments. From him all good things are bestowed upon us; from him we are first given both the will to do good and the ability to act. We are loved by him so that we may love him; we are loved by him so that we may love him in return. We are known so that we may know; we are helped so that we may act, and by acting may grow rich in virtues.

Therefore, if the love of God and neighbor delights us, it follows that we should do what he commanded. For we love to the extent that we act. Indeed, no one can sincerely love God who does not faithfully fulfill his commandments. For he himself says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word. And my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him. Whoever does not love me does not keep my words.”

The Apostle John too, filled with love of the Lord, says in his epistle: “By this we know that we have come to know him, if we observe his commandments” (John 14). Whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him. “Whoever keeps his word, truly in him the charity of God is perfected” (1 John 2).

Job also says of himself: “My foot has followed his steps; I have kept his way and have not turned aside from it. I have not departed from the commandments of his lips, and I have hidden the words of his mouth in my breast” (Job 23).

The Lord himself, admonishing the Israelite people concerning love of him and observance of his commandments, says: “And now, Israel, hear the precepts and judgments that I teach you today, so that by doing them you may live in them” (Leviticus 18). “Observe and take care lest at any time you forget the Lord your God and neglect his commandments, judgments, and ceremonies that I command you today” (Deuteronomy 8). “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God require of you except that you fear the Lord your God, walk in his ways, love him, serve him with all your heart and all your soul, and keep his commandments and ceremonies that I command you today, so that it may be well with you?” (Deuteronomy 10).

“But if you listen so as to do all his commandments, the Lord will make you higher than all the nations that dwell upon the earth. You shall be blessed in the city and blessed in the field; blessed shall be the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your land. The Lord will send blessing upon your storehouses and upon all the works of your hands” (Deuteronomy 28).

Hence the Apostle John also says: “By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and do his commandments. For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments, and his commandments are not burdensome” (1 John 5). The Lord himself likewise says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John 14).

*(Gregory, Homily 30 on the Gospels.)* The proof of love is the exhibition of works. We truly love God if, while observing his commandments, we restrain ourselves from our own wills. For whoever still pours himself out through unlawful desires plainly does not love God, because he contradicts him by following his own will.

[Col. 0602A]

## CHAPTER VI. On Fear

For it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 110). “The fear of the Lord is glory, boasting, joy, and a crown of exultation. The fear of the Lord will delight the heart and give gladness and joy for length of days” (Ecclesiasticus 1). “Fear the Lord and turn away from evil, because it will be well with the one who fears God at the end, and he will be blessed in the days of his completion” (Proverbs 3). “The fullness of wisdom is to fear God” (Ecclesiasticus 1). The generation of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, riches, life, and glory.

The fear of the Lord drives out sin and restrains vice; it makes a person cautious and attentive. For whoever is without fear cannot be justified. Where there is no fear, there is the dissolution of life. Where there is no fear, there is wickedness. Where there is no fear, there is an abundance of crimes. Those who fear the Lord will not disbelieve his word, and those who love him will keep his way. Those who fear the Lord will prepare their hearts and sanctify their souls in his sight. Those who fear the Lord will keep his commandments and have patience until they behold him (Ecclesiasticus 2).

The fear of the Lord is not to despise a poor righteous person and not to honor a worse man because he is rich. For David says: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling” (Psalm 2). And: “Fear the Lord, all you his saints, for those who fear him lack nothing” (Psalm 33). And: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways” (Psalm 127). Moses also says: “Walk after the Lord your God, fear him, keep his commandments, and obey him” (Deuteronomy 13, according to the Septuagint).

The Apostle also says: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Philippians 2). Solomon again says: “The crown of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, filling one with peace and the fruit of salvation; and both are gifts of God” (Ecclesiasticus 1). “You who fear the Lord, wait for his mercy and do not turn away from him, lest you fall. You who fear the Lord, believe in him, and your reward will not be lost. You who fear the Lord, love him, and your hearts will be enlightened” (Ecclesiasticus 2).

Blessed is the one to whom it has been given to possess the fear of God. “The fear of the Lord is like a paradise of blessing, and above every glory they covered him” (Ecclesiasticus 40). In praise of fear Solomon further says: “The fear of the Lord will add days” (Proverbs 10).

Let us therefore fear, brothers, with that fear of the Lord “which endures forever and ever” (Psalm 18); with that pure fear which may add to the days of this present age eternal days, perpetual days, everlasting and immortal days—indeed, one day without evening and without end, a day filled with blessed joy, filled with unfailing light, supported by angelic companionship; a day, I say, which night does not interrupt, darkness does not obscure, cloud does not darken, summer heat does not make unbearable, and winter cold does not make sluggish; a day which for us will be one with the saints, shared with the angels, eternal with both; which may grant us fellowship with the angels in blessed joy, make us companions of the patriarchs, count us among the prophets, and make us companions of the apostles in exultation.

And since the Apostle John says in his canonical letter: “There is no fear in charity, but perfect charity casts out fear; for fear has punishment, and whoever fears is not perfected in charity” (1 John 4), we must understand two kinds of fear distinctly and carefully.

There are therefore two fears. One is the fear by which people fear God lest they be sent into Gehenna. This is the fear that introduces charity, but it comes in order to depart. For if you still fear God because of punishments, you do not yet love the one whom you fear in this way: you do not desire good things, but avoid evil ones. Yet because you avoid evil, you correct yourself and begin to desire good things. Once you have begun to desire good things, there will be in you a holy fear—namely, fear lest you lose those very good things—not fear lest you be sent into Gehenna, but fear lest the presence of the Lord whom you embrace, and whose eternal enjoyment you desire, should depart from you.

A certain brother asked an old man: “How does the fear of the Lord enter the soul?” The old man said: “If a person has humility and poverty, and does not judge another, then the fear of God comes into him.”

A certain old man said: “May fear and humility, scarcity of provisions, and mourning remain in you.” Another old man said: “Whatever you hate, do not do to another” (Tobit 4). If you hate one who speaks evil to you, do not speak evil of anyone yourself. If you hate one who slanders you, do not slander anyone yourself. If you hate one who holds you in contempt or attacks you with insults, do none of these things to anyone. Whoever, therefore, can keep this saying has enough for salvation.

A certain old man said: “The life of a monk is this: action, obedience, meditation, and not judging, not speaking against others, and not murmuring.”

For it is written: “You who love the Lord, hate evil. The life of a monk is this: not to enter in with the unjust, nor to see evil with his eyes, nor to act inquisitively, nor to hear empty things, nor to seize what belongs to another, but rather to give away his own; not to be proud in heart, nor to devise evil, nor to fill his belly, but to do everything with discernment” (Psalm 96). Behold, in these things is the monk.

Abba Jacob said: “Just as a lamp illuminates a dark room, so the fear of the Lord, if it comes into a person’s heart, illuminates him and teaches him all virtues and the commandments of God.”

Some of the fathers asked Abba Macarius the Egyptian: “How and when do you eat, and when do you fast, that your body is so dry?” The old man said to them: “Just as wood in a person’s hand, by which brushwood is turned in the fire, dries out, so, if a person keeps his mind in the fear of God, that fear of God consumes his bones.”

[Col. 0604A]

## CHAPTER VII. On Wisdom, Which Is Christ
