As Scripture says, “The crown of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; the beginning of wisdom is to fear God; and the fullness and root of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” (Ecclesiasticus 1). Let us therefore fear the Lord, dearest ones, and prepare our souls to receive wisdom, so that by living wisely, piously, and justly, we may deserve to possess everlasting kingdoms together with wisdom itself.

For it is written: “Those who keep her will be justified by her, and she will readily be seen by those who love her, and will be found by those who seek her” (Wisdom 6). It is written: “The desire for wisdom leads to everlasting kingdoms” (same passage).

Therefore Solomon says: “I desired, and understanding was given to me; I called, and the spirit of wisdom came to me, and I resolved to possess her as light. I loved her above health and every beauty, because her radiance is unfailing. All good things came to me together with her, and innumerable honor through her hands, and I rejoiced in all things, because this wisdom went before me. For she is an inexhaustible treasure for human beings; those who use her become participants in the friendship of God.

“For in her is a spirit intelligent, holy, unique, manifold, subtle, mobile, eloquent, undefiled, certain, sweet, loving what is good, acute, unhindered, beneficent, humane; steadfast, compliant, possessing every virtue, observing all things, and penetrating all intelligent spirits. For wisdom is more mobile than anything that moves. For she is the vapor of the power of God and a pure emanation of the glory of almighty God. She is the radiance of eternal light, the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness” (Wisdom 7).

For, as it is said, “she is more beautiful than the sun and, compared with the arrangement of the stars, is found to surpass it in light. For night follows light, but wisdom conquers wickedness” (same passage). As it is said: “She reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly. For she teaches sobriety and wisdom, justice and virtue, than which nothing is more useful for human beings in life” (Wisdom 8).

Wisdom is a great treasure: whoever finds it will find life, and whoever possesses it will have the crown of immortality. For it is she who makes people steadfast in faith, reliable in speech, gracious in eloquence, cheerful in giving, humane in mercy, gentle in answering, discerning in judgment, mild in prosperity, secure in adversity, sharp in understanding, transparent in action, radiant in countenance, and strong in conflict (same passage).

From where, then, does wisdom come, and where is the place of understanding? It is hidden from the eyes of all living things. God understands its way, and he himself knows its place. For he said to humanity: “Behold, the fear of the Lord—that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding” (Job 28).

Let us therefore love her, brothers, so that we may be loved by her. Wisdom herself, who is Christ, says: “I, wisdom, dwell in counsel, and I am present among learned thoughts. Counsel is mine and equity; prudence is mine, and strength is mine. I love those who love me, and those who watch for me early will find me. With me are riches and glory. My fruit is better than gold and precious stone. I walk in the ways of justice, so that I may enrich those who love me and fill their treasuries” (Proverbs 8).

For God loves the one who loves wisdom. Wisdom prepares life for her children, supplies justice to those who love her, and gives prudence to those who cherish her. In temptation she walks with that person; preparing a straight path for him, she uncovers her hidden things and stores up for him knowledge and understanding of prudence. Therefore, whoever holds fast to her will inherit eternal life.

[Col. 0605B]

## CHAPTER VIII. On Prudence

Prudence is the adornment of all virtues, the glory of speech, and the beauty of language, as it is written: “An ornament of gold is prudence, instruction, and like a bracelet on the right arm” (Ecclesiasticus 21). Prudence is the guardian of the mouth, the governance of action, the moderation of the heart, the restraint of the tongue, and the balance and weighing of all words and things.

For it is written: “The words of the prudent will be weighed on a balance” (Ecclesiasticus 21). Hence Paul also says: “Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (Colossians 4).

Let us also love, brothers, this most illustrious virtue, which may order the governance of our spirit and strengthen the discernment of our mind. For it is written: “The wise person is governed by much prudence” (Proverbs 14).

Let us love prudence, which may direct the steps of our works and order the actions of our thoughts. For it is written: “A prudent man directs his steps” (Proverbs 15).

Let us love prudence, which may build a spiritual house for us and strongly strengthen what has been built on high. For it is written: “A house will be built by wisdom, and by prudence it will be strengthened” (Proverbs 24).

Let us love prudence, which may provide us with adornments of character and an abundance of virtues; which may instill the law of truth in our mouth, adorn our speech with wisdom and understanding in many ways, place a golden ornament upon our words, and bestow a silver gift upon our lips; which may provide our conduct with continual guardianship, fitting honor, and glory.

[Col. 0605D]

## CHAPTER IX. On Simplicity

The virtue of prudence is indeed great, but it must be tempered by the virtue of simplicity. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matthew 10).

And concerning Job, a simple man, the Lord says to the devil: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth, a simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil?” (Job 1).

Let us therefore love, brothers, this great virtue, which comes forth from the treasure of the Most High. Although it is necessary for all Christians, it is especially necessary for monks, who ought to adorn their way of life with the practice of simplicity.

[Col. 0606A] For it is written: “Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart, because he is found by those who do not test him; but he appears to those who have faith in him” (Wisdom 1).

Let us therefore love simplicity of heart, so that our actions may be directed by it along the way of salvation. For it is written: “The simplicity of the upright will guide them” (Proverbs 11).

Let us obey the words of Paul, that outstanding preacher, who admonishes us, saying: “I want you to be wise in what is good and simple in what is evil” (Romans 16). The hearts of the elect ought always to be sharpened by prudence for what is good, while simplicity must temper the sharpness of prudence, lest prudence exceed the measure of uprightness or simplicity grow dull through the deceit of ignorance.

*(Gregory, Moralia, Book V, chapter 3.)* Concerning Jacob it is written that he was “a simple man, dwelling in a house” (Genesis 25), because all who avoid being scattered among external concerns remain simple in thought and in the dwelling of their conscience, lest, while they gape after many things outside, they become alienated from themselves and depart from their thoughts.

Let us therefore run along the paths of simplicity, so that through it we may deserve to reach more quickly the homeland of perpetuity, where we may deserve to receive the robe of immortality and the rewards of simplicity.

[Col. 0606B]

## CHAPTER X. On Patience

Concerning this virtue of patience the Lord says: “In your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21). And Paul, his disciple, says: “As God’s elect, holy and beloved, put on the heart of mercy, kindness, humility, modesty, and patience, bearing with one another in charity” (Colossians 3; Ephesians 4).

Solomon also says: “A man’s instruction is known through patience, and his glory is to pass over wrongdoing” (Proverbs 19). The Apostle James, preaching, says: “Let patience have its perfect work, so that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing” (James 1). And Paul says again: “Reprove the restless, comfort the fainthearted, support the weak, and be patient toward all” (1 Thessalonians 5).

Let us therefore run, beloved brothers, along this way of patience, and love it, because it has no stumbling block, but in the future it will repay those who run along it with full and eternal joy.

For great is the virtue of patience, brothers: it does not injure those who injure it, but loves them; it forgives injuries to the one who injures it and does not return them; it does not harm the one whom it could harm, but spares him.

For patience is the root and guardian of all virtues. Through patience we possess our souls (Luke 21). The Lord therefore showed that patience is the guardian of our condition, because in it he taught us to possess ourselves.

*(Gregory, Pastoral Care, Part III, admonition 10; Cyprian, On the Good of Patience.)* True patience is to endure the evils of others with equanimity and to be moved by no grief against the one who inflicts those evils.

The virtue of patience, therefore, brothers, commends us to God, guards us from every evil, and preserves us. It moderates anger, restrains the tongue, and governs the mind. It preserves peace, carries out discipline moderately, breaks the impulse of lust, suppresses violence, and extinguishes the fire of hostility. It restrains the power of the rich, relieves the poverty of the poor, makes people humble in prosperity, strong in adversity, and gentle in the face of injuries and insults. It conquers temptations and endures persecutions.

It is patience that strongly fortifies the foundations of our faith, nobly advances the growth of our hope, and directs the actions of our life. It patiently governs us so that we may be able to keep the way of Christ, and confirms us immovably so that we may persevere as children of God.

This virtue, dearest brothers, we must love with joy and embrace with all our strength. We shall soon receive the fruit and reward of patience if we persevere with it to the end. Thus the Apostle James says: “Behold, the judge stands before the door, and may he return to you the rewards of patience and to your adversaries the punishment they deserve” (James 5). He says “before the door” because he is near us: the Lord Jesus Christ is ready both to forgive sins when we ask and to return the rewards of patience.

They used to tell of Abba Isidore, who was a presbyter in Scetis, that if someone had a brother who was weak, fainthearted, or abusive and wanted to expel him, Isidore would say: “Bring him to me.” Taking him in, he would heal that brother’s spirit through his patience.

Once robbers came to a certain old man’s monastery and said to him: “We have come to take everything that is in your cell.” He said: “Take, children, whatever seems good to you.” So they took whatever they found in the cell and went away. But they forgot there a small bag that had been hidden in the cell. The old man followed them, calling out: “Children, take what you forgot in the cell.”

They, astonished at his patience, turned back and restored everything to his cell. And they all repented, saying to one another: “This truly is a man of God.”

[Col. 0607C]

## CHAPTER XI. On Humility

Although this virtue of humility ought to belong to all Christians, it ought especially to dwell and rest in the hearts of monks. Hence Isidore says *(Sentences, Book III, chapter 19)*: “The highest virtue of a monk is humility; his greatest vice is pride. A person should then consider himself a monk when he has regarded himself as the least, even when he has performed greater works of virtue.

“Those who abandon the world yet follow the virtues commanded without humility of heart fall more grievously, as though from a height, because through the exultation of virtues they are cast down more disastrously than they could have slipped through vices.

“The conscience of a servant of God should always be humble and sorrowful—humble, so that it does not become proud, and usefully sorrowful, so that the heart does not dissolve into wantonness.”

*(Thus far Isidore.)* Concerning this supreme virtue the Lord says: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18). Hence the Apostle James also says: “Let the humble brother glory in his exaltation” (James 1), because every brother who humbly suffers adversity for the Lord will receive from him the kingdom’s rewards on high.

Hence the blessed Apostle Peter also says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5). He says “all,” namely elders and young men, to whom he appears to commend the virtue of humility toward one another—humility in governing some and in humbly obeying others. He teaches all to commend humility to one another by example and also by word, because he knew that all had to beware the vice of pride, which cast the angels from heaven.

He next explains what grace he promises to give the humble, saying: “Humble yourselves, therefore, under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of visitation” (1 Peter 5). He grants this grace to the humble: the more greatly they have been humbled for his sake in the time of struggle, the more gloriously they will be exalted by him in the time of recompense.

Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit” (Psalm 33).

All humility, however, is found not so much in speech as in the mind, so that our conscience may know us to be humble and we may never suppose ourselves to know, understand, or be anything. King and prophet David wonderfully retained the summit of humility when he said: “Lord, my heart is not exalted, nor are my eyes lifted up” (Psalm 130), and so forth.

He says again: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Psalm 50). And again: “See my humility and my labor, and forgive all my sins” (Psalm 24). If, then, a humbled heart is a sacrifice to God, he offered a sacrifice when he said: “Lord, my heart is not exalted,” and so forth.

If some hermit devoted to his cell were to say such things, he would shine with great praise for patience. But because a king clothed in purple and an outstanding prophet said this, the Church spread throughout the world praises his example of humility.

Humility rises honored above all the eminent virtues especially because the condescension of Majesty itself assumed it.

Abba Antony said *(Athanasius, Life of Antony)*: “I saw all the snares of the enemy stretched out over the earth, and, groaning, I said: ‘Who, do you think, can pass through these?’ And I heard a voice saying: ‘Humility.’”

Abba Serapion said: “I performed more bodily labors than my son Zacharias, but I did not attain the measure of his humility and silence.”

Abba Moses said to Brother Zacharias: “Tell me, what should I do?” He took the hood from his head, placed it beneath his feet, and, trampling upon it, said: “Unless a person is trampled down in this way, he cannot be a monk.”

An old man was asked why he was troubled by demons and replied: “Because we have cast away our weapons, which are insults, humility, poverty, and patience.”

An old man was asked what perfection was and replied: “The perfection of a human being is humility. For to the extent that someone has progressed in humility and has bowed down, to that extent he will be raised up toward advancement, because humility is a great and divine work.”

The way of humility is this: a person should undertake bodily labors, regard himself as a sinner, and place himself under obedience in all things; he should not attend to the sins of others, but always look upon his own, and pray to God for them without ceasing.

[Col. 0609A]

[Col. 0609]

## CHAPTER XII. On Peace
No one exalts himself more before God than the one who humbles himself before himself for God’s sake. For this reason the humble person is exalted by God, so that he may be called a son of God and an heir of Christ. All the more should he pursue peace, because a son of peace ought to seek and pursue peace. Thus the Apostle admonishes us, saying: “Pursue peace with everyone, and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Heb. XII). The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God” (Matt. V). Indeed, among his divine commandments and saving teachings, when he was already near his Passion, the Savior commended and entrusted this precept and commandment to us for observance. For he says: “I give you my peace; I commend my peace to you” (John XIV).

[Col. 0609B] The Lord, ascending into heaven, left us this inheritance, and through his most faithful king and prophet David commanded us to follow it. For he says: “Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it” (Ps. III). If we wish to follow this with a sincere heart, we shall be heirs of Christ. But if we desire to be Christ’s heirs, we must live in the peace of Christ. If we are sons of God, we must be peacemakers. For God’s sons ought to be peaceful and humble, gentle in mind, simple in heart, pure in speech, innocent in spirit, harmonious in affection, and faithfully and unanimously joined to one another.

[Col. 0609B]

## CHAPTER XIII. On Obedience

Concerning obedience, the blessed Apostle Peter says: “[Therefore,] having girded the loins of your mind, being sober in all things, hope perfectly in the grace that is offered to you in the revelation of Jesus Christ, as obedient children” (I Peter I). He rightly wishes those to be children of obedience whom he had said in the preface were chosen for the sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience, and for the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ (ibid.).

Obedience, therefore, ought to possess something of its own even in adversity, and likewise, in prosperity, ought in every way not to possess something of its own, so that in adversity it may be all the more genuine the more completely it separates the mind from the present glory which it receives divinely. Obedience is commanded by the almighty Lord to be preserved even unto death, just as the Truth says: “I can do nothing of myself, but as I hear, I judge” (John V). He judges as he hears. Then also he will obey the Father when he comes as judge of this world. (Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXXV, chapters 22–23.)

Lest obedience seem burdensome to us until the end of our present life, our Redeemer shows that he preserves it even when he comes as judge. What wonder, then, if sinful man submits himself to obedience during the brief span of the present life, when the mediator of God and human beings does not abandon it even when he rewards the obedient?

It must be understood that evil is never done through obedience, but that sometimes the good being done ought to be interrupted through obedience. For the tree in paradise was not evil, yet God forbade the human being to touch it (Gen. II). But so that the well-created human being might grow more fully through the merit of obedience, it was fitting that he should even be prohibited from doing what was good, so that the virtue of his action might be all the more genuine: by refraining from what was good, he would show himself more humbly subject to his Creator. For it is written: “Obedience is better than sacrifices” (Eccles. IV). Obedience is rightly placed before sacrifices, because through sacrifices another’s flesh is slaughtered, but through obedience one’s own will is slaughtered. Therefore, the sooner a person appeases God, the more he restrains the pride of his own will before God’s eyes and sacrifices himself with the sword of the commandment.

Hence, when Abba Basil was asked how brothers ought to obey one another, he replied: “As servants of the Lord, according to what the Lord commanded: ‘Whoever wishes to be great among you must become the last of all and a servant; just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve.’” (Cassian, *Institutes*, book IV, chapters 23, 27.)

An old man planted a dry piece of wood in the desert. Wishing to test the brother’s obedience, he said to him: “Water this piece of wood every day until it bears fruit.” Now the water was far from them. After the brother had done this for three years, the piece of wood became green and produced fruit. The old man took some of its fruit, carried it to the church, and said to the brothers: “Take and eat the fruit of obedience.”

The old man used to say that God seeks nothing so much from those who are beginning their conversion as the labor of obedience.

A certain layman renounced the world and came to a monastery, bringing his little son with him. The abbot took the child, kissed him, and said to his father: “Do you love this child?” He replied: “Yes.” Again he said to him: “Do you cherish him?” He replied: “Yes.” Then the abbot said to him: “Take him, then, if you love him, and throw him into the blazing furnace.” His father took him and threw him into the blazing furnace, and immediately the furnace became like dew. By this deed he gained glory in that time, like the patriarch Abraham.

The old man said: “The brother who gives his soul over to obedience to a spiritual father receives a greater reward than the one who withdraws alone into the desert. Those who seclude themselves in the desert have withdrawn from the world by their own decision; but this order, which has given itself to obey, casting aside all its own wills, depends upon God and upon the command of its spiritual father. Therefore it receives greater glory than the others.”

Therefore, O sons, obedience performed for God’s sake is good. Pay attention, then, sons, to some trace of this virtue. Obedience is the salvation of all the faithful. Obedience is the mother of all virtues. Obedience is the discoverer of the kingdom of heaven. Obedience opens heaven and raises the human being from earth. Obedience dwells together with the angels. Obedience is the food of all the saints. For by it they were weaned, and through it they attained perfection.

[Col. 0610D]

## CHAPTER XIV. On Those Who Despise the World

(Isidore, *Sentences*, book III, chapter 16.) Those things that are dear to lovers of the world, the saints shun as though they were adversities; they rejoice more in the world’s adversities than they delight in its prosperity. It is clear that those to whom this world prospers for every advantage are alienated from God. But everything in this world is contrary to the servants of God, so that when they experience these adversities they may be stirred more ardently toward heavenly desire.

Great grace shines before God in the one who has become contemptible to this world. For truly, the one whom the world hates must be loved by God. For this reason holy men desire to despise the world and call back the movement of their minds to heavenly things, so that there they may gather themselves again, from where they have flowed away, and withdraw themselves from where they have been scattered. (Ibid., same passage.)

Whoever, after renouncing the world, longs for the heavenly homeland with holy desires is raised up from this earthly attention as though on certain wings. He perceives with groaning the place where he fell, and with great joy he fixes his attention on the place where he will arrive. (Isidore, *Sentences*, book III, chapter 17.)

Holy men, renouncing the world completely, die to this world in such a way that they delight in living for God alone. To the extent that they withdraw themselves from the conduct of this age, they contemplate with the inner vision of the mind the presence of God and the fellowship of the angels. The monk’s life is a path without stumbling, without the hindrance of desire and love. For when someone is drawn away from companionship with the world, neither desire binds him when he consents to it, nor does it torment him when he experiences it.

It is good to be physically removed from the world, but it is much better to be removed from it by the will. For the perfect man, both are necessary. The perfect man is one who is separated from this age in body and in heart. As Jeremiah says, the wild ass despises the city (Jer. II), and so does the monk despise the common conduct of secular citizens. These men desire the adversities of our life and despise its prosperity, so that while this life is disregarded by them, the future life may be found.

[Col. 0611C]

## CHAPTER XV. On Repentance

Every sinner ought to have a twofold groaning in repentance, clearly because he both failed to do the good that he ought to have done and did the evil that he ought not to have done. When we do not rise to good works, we must mourn ourselves in two ways, because we did not do what was right and performed what was wrong.

Through blessed Moses, one turtledove is commanded to be offered for sin, and another as a burnt offering (Lev. V). A burnt offering is so called because it is wholly burned. Thus we offer one turtledove for sin when we give forth a groan for our fault. We make a burnt offering of the other when, because we neglected good things, we set ourselves wholly aflame and burn with the fire of grief.

Blessed Job, progressing after his sufferings and examining himself in severe reproof, says: “Therefore I condemn myself and do penance in dust and ashes” (Job XLII). (Gregory, commentary on Job XLII, 1; book XXXV, chapter 2.)

To do penance in dust and ashes is, after contemplating the highest Being, to recognize oneself as nothing other than dust and ashes. In sackcloth, the harshness and contrition of sins are shown; in ashes, the dust of the dead is signified. Therefore both are customarily applied to repentance, so that in the sackcloth of contrition we may recognize what we have done through our faults, and in the dust of ashes consider what we have become through judgment.

Every faithful person, knowing that thoughts will be examined minutely at the judgment, examines himself inwardly and scrutinizes himself intensely before the judgment, so that the strict Judge may come all the more peacefully and see that the heart he wishes to examine has already been punished for its fault. For when we punish ourselves, he does not judge us at the final examination. Paul bears witness to this when he says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (I Cor. XI). (Gregory, same passage.)

What we do outwardly, unless we wipe it away with repentance intervening, is preserved in the hidden recesses of God’s judgments under a certain concealment, so that at some time it may emerge from the seal of secrecy into the public judgment. But when we are worn down by the rod of discipline for the evils we have done and mourn them through repentance, he marks and heals our iniquity, because he neither leaves much of it here nor preserves it for punishment at the judgment.

Let the righteous judge himself in this life, so that he may not be judged by God with eternal condemnation. A person takes judgment upon himself when, through worthy repentance, he condemns his own evil deeds. The bitterness of repentance makes the mind examine its deeds more carefully and recall with tears the gifts of God that it despised.

Nothing is worse than to recognize one’s fault and not mourn it. Every sinner ought to have a twofold weeping in repentance: either because through negligence he failed to do good, or because through audacity he committed evil. He did not do what he ought to have done, and he did what he ought not to have done.

That person performs repentance worthily who laments his guilt with legitimate satisfaction, condemning and mourning what he has done, and weeping over it more deeply the more readily he had inclined toward sinning. That person performs repentance worthily who so mourns past evils that he does not commit them again in the future. For one who mourns sin and commits sin again is like someone washing an unbaked brick: the more he washes it, the more mud he makes.

However much a person may be a sinner and ungodly, if he turns to repentance he is believed able to obtain pardon. Each person must hasten to God through repentance while he can, lest, if he is unwilling while he can, he should be unable altogether when he wishes too late. Therefore the Prophet says: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isa. LV).

If, while a person can still sin, he repents and corrects his life from every crime while he is alive, there is no doubt that, when he dies, he passes into eternal rest. But for one who practices repentance in the danger of death after living wickedly, just as his condemnation is uncertain, so his remission is doubtful.

Although the forgiveness of sins comes through repentance, a person ought not to be without fear, because the satisfaction of repentance is weighed by divine judgment, not human judgment. Therefore, since God’s mercy is hidden, it is necessary to weep without interruption. The penitent ought never to have security concerning his sins. For security produces negligence, and negligence often leads the unwary person back to the vices he had left behind.

When vices have been driven out of a person through repentance, if afterward, through intervening security, any fault should creep in, the former pleasures of vice immediately creep in more greedily, and, beating upon the person, drag him more heavily into his customary deeds, so that “the last state of that person is worse than the first” (Matt. XII).

[Col. 0613A]

## CHAPTER XVI. On Confession

Hence James says: “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James I). In this statement there ought to be such discernment that we confess daily and slight sins to our equals, and believe that we are saved through their daily prayer. But the uncleanness of more serious leprosy we must submit to the priest according to the law, and, at his direction, take care to be purified in the manner and for the length of time he commands (Lev. XIII).

Hence David also says: “Reveal your way to the Lord and hope in him” (Ps. XXXVI). The density of sins is a kind of veil, by which our way—that is, our life—is clothed in darkness and wrapped around. We reveal it when we most readily confess our dark offenses.

Again David himself says: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is everlasting” (Ps. CV). He indicates that this confession is to be applied as a remedy for the fullness of sin. It is also undoubtedly directed toward the praise of the Lord, since it is a greater glory of mercy to spare the one who confesses than to preserve the one who lives without offense.

And lest anyone be frightened by the multitude of his faults, he adds: “For he is good.” Who would doubt returning to one whom he hears is able to come to his aid most quickly? He adds: “For his mercy is everlasting.” Having heard that the Lord is good, lest human negligence hold anyone back from diligent and assiduous supplication, he declares the cause of the remedy, so that a person should hasten by the Lord’s gift to swift confession.

Therefore, brothers, let us confess to our Lord, because he is good and forgives sins. (Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXII, chapter 13.)

It is a testimony of humility both for each person to recognize his own iniquity and, once recognized, to disclose it by confession. It is a customary vice of the human race both to commit sin by falling and, after committing it, to betray it by refusing to confess, defending it by denial, and multiplying it by defending what has been exposed.

The signs of true confession are present if, when each person calls himself a sinner, he does not contradict another who says the same thing about him. It is written: “The righteous person is his own accuser at the beginning” (Prov. XVIII).

We must take the greatest care both willingly to acknowledge the evils we have committed and not to deny them when others reproach us for them. For it is a vice of pride that what someone deigns to confess about himself, as though voluntarily, he disdains to have said about him by others.

[Col. 0613D]

## CHAPTER XVII. On Compunction

(Isidore, *Sentences*, book II, chapter 12.) Compunction of heart is humility of mind with tears, arising from remembrance of sin and fear of judgment. For those who have been converted, that affection of compunction is more perfect which drives away from itself every affection for carnal desires and fixes its attention wholly, with the mind’s complete devotion, upon contemplation of God.

Compunction is evidently twofold, by which the soul of every chosen person is moved for God’s sake: either when it considers the evils of its deeds, or when it sighs with desire for eternal life. There are four qualities of affection by which the mind of the righteous person is pricked with healthy sorrow: remembrance of past crimes, recollection of future punishments, consideration of one’s pilgrimage throughout the length of this life, and desire for the heavenly homeland, so that one may be able to reach it as quickly as possible.

When a sinner is pierced by the memory of sins and moved to lamentation, he should know that he is being given life by God’s presence when, remembering what he has lost, he is inwardly ashamed and already punishes himself by repentance according to his own judgment. For Peter wept when Christ looked upon him (Luke XXII). Hence the Psalm also says: “He looked, and the earth was moved and trembled” (Ps. XCVI).

Of this virtue of compunction David says: “My tears have been my bread day and night” (Ps. XLI). (Here ends Isidore.)

The soul feeds upon its own mourning when it is raised by weeping to the joys above. Within, it endures the groaning of its pain, but it receives nourishment for refreshment in the measure that the force of love flows forth from here through tears.

The mind of each of the elect places before its eyes, on one side, the strictness of justice and, on the other, the merit of guilt. It sees what punishment it deserves if the mercy of the One who pardons were absent—he who customarily rescues it from eternal punishment through present lamentation.

Almighty God afflicts the minds of worldly people, which previously wandered amid the waves of this world, through the coming of the Holy Spirit, with the sorrow of repentance, so that, with their pride healthfully crushed, they may lie in humility—those whom previously the high wave of their vanity and prosperity had lifted upon this sea of the world. (Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXIII, chapter 21.)

There are four conditions by which the soul of righteous men is intensely afflicted in compunction. It is afflicted when it remembers its evils, considering where it was; when, fearing the sentence of God’s judgments, it asks itself and considers where it will be; when, carefully attending to the evils of the present life, it sorrowfully considers where it is; or when it contemplates the good things of the heavenly homeland and, because it has not yet attained them, mournfully sees where it is not.

Hence the Psalmist says: “You gave us drink in tears by measure” (Ps. LXXIX). Care must be taken by those who mourn the sins of their deeds that they wash away completed evils with complete lamentation, lest they be more tightly bound by the debt of the deed committed and pay less in tears of satisfaction. For it is written: “You gave us drink in tears by measure.” That is, each person’s mind should drink the tears of its compunction in repentance to the extent that it remembers having dried up from God through its faults.

[Col. 0614D]

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Hope and Fear of the Elect

Often the mind of a righteous person both mourns what it remembers having done perversely and not only abandons its evil deeds but also punishes them with the bitterest lamentations. Yet, while it remembers what it has done, it is terrified by great fear of judgment.

Each chosen person has already converted perfectly, but still does not raise himself perfectly into security. For while he weighs the severity of the final examination, he trembles anxiously between hope and fear, because he does not know what the just Judge, when he comes, will reckon concerning what he has done and what he will pardon.

He remembers what evils he has committed, but does not know whether he has worthily mourned what he committed. He fears that the enormity of his guilt may exceed the measure of his repentance. Often the Truth has already released the guilt, but the afflicted mind, while deeply anxious about itself, still trembles concerning pardon.

Thus the holy man even here receives mercy, but does not know that he has received it. A person abandons his sin by correcting and repenting, yet still fears the strict Judge concerning the retribution for it.

There, then, every righteous person freely sings the mercies of the Lord in eternity: where there is no longer doubt concerning the pardon of sin; where the memory of his guilt no longer troubles his secure mind; where the soul does not tremble under accusation, but exults freely in his forgiveness.

Those oppressed by fearful dread must be admonished to trust in the mercy they request, lest they perish through the force of immoderate affliction. (Gregory, *Pastoral Care*, part III, admonition 30.)

For the Lord would not mercifully place sins to be mourned before the eyes of delinquents if he had wished to strike them down strictly by himself. It is clear that he wished to conceal from his judgment those whom, going before them in mercy, he made judges of themselves. Hence Paul says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (I Cor. XI).

[Col. 0615B]

## CHAPTER XIX. On Those Who Return to Sin After Tears

(Isidore, *Sentences*, book II, chapter 16.) He is a mocker, not a penitent, who continues to do what he repents of; nor does he seem to ask God as a submissive person, but to mock him as a proud one. “A dog returns to its vomit,” and so does the penitent return to sin (Prov. XXVI).

For many continually shed tears and do not cease sinning. We see some receive tears for repentance but not possess the effect of repentance, because through inconstancy of mind they sometimes shed tears in remembrance of sin, but at other times, when their former practice revives, they commit again what they had mourned.

Whoever wishes to mourn past sins while continuing to devote himself to worldly activities does not possess cleansing, because he still does what he could mourn in repentance. Isaiah says to sinners: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. I). Therefore the person is washed and clean who mourns past sins and does not again admit what must be mourned. He is washed but not clean who mourns what he has done but does not abandon it, and after his tears repeats what he had mourned.

Thus elsewhere divine speech reproves the penitent soul that sins again, saying: “How vile you have become, repeating your ways” (Jer. II). (Here ends Isidore.)

Therefore, whoever mourns past faults must observe this condition and mourn his admitted sins in such a way that he does not again commit what must be mourned. It is written in the book of Ecclesiasticus: “He who is washed by a dead person and touches him again, what profit is there in his washing?” (Ecclus. XXXIV). (Gregory, *Pastoral Care*, part III, admonition 31.)

Whoever does not preserve innocence of life after tears neglects to remain clean after washing. They are washed but not at all clean who do not cease to mourn what they have committed but again commit what must be mourned.

A person is washed by a dead person when he is cleansed from sin by tears; but after baptism he touches the dead person when he desires guilt after tears. Hence Solomon says: “As a dog that returns to its vomit” (Prov. XXVI). When a dog vomits, it casts out the food that had weighed down its chest; but when it returns to its vomit, it is burdened again with what had relieved it.

Those who mourn what they have committed cast out through confession the wickedness with which they had been badly filled and which weighed down the innermost parts of their minds; but when they repeat it after confession, they take it up again.

And the pig, when washed in the mud wallow, becomes dirtier (II Peter II). Likewise, the person who mourns the sin he has committed but does not abandon it subjects himself to nearly a graver fault: he both despises the pardon he could have obtained through weeping and, as though rolling himself in muddy water, soils himself, because by withdrawing purity of life from his tears he makes even those tears themselves filthy before God’s eyes. (Here ends Gregory.)

[Col. 0616B]

## CHAPTER XX. On the Life or Conduct of Monks

A monk must always carefully consider the reverence due to his habit in his actions, speech, and thoughts. He must completely abandon the things of the world and make his conduct before God’s eyes correspond to what his habit displays before human eyes.

For chosen monks, when passing prosperity smiles upon them, pretend as though they do not know the world’s favor, and with a firm step trample inwardly the things by which they are raised outwardly. Chosen monks do not resound with the clamor of wicked action, nor are they carried away by the turbulent desire for temporal passions; but they flee from being excessively occupied with the necessary concerns of the present life.

Often monks who are doing good works still feel the scourges of their father, so that they may come to the inheritance all the more perfect because the discipline of the one who lovingly strikes them daily cleanses them even from the smallest matters.

True monks, renouncing the world completely, die to this world in such a way that they delight in living for God alone. To the extent that they withdraw themselves from the conduct of this age, they contemplate with the inner vision of the mind the presence of God and the fellowship of the angels; and the more they cast themselves down outwardly by despising themselves, the more they are inwardly nourished by contemplation of revelations. For those whom the valley of humility holds outwardly in weeping, the ascent of contemplation raises inwardly. (Isidore, *Sentences*, book III, chapter 18.)

There are certain precepts given to the faithful who live a common life in the world, and other precepts given to those who renounce the world. The former are told to manage all their possessions well; the latter are told to abandon all their possessions. The former are bound by general precepts; the latter, by living more perfectly, transcend general precepts.

For perfection it is not enough to renounce all one’s possessions unless one also denies oneself. But what is it to deny oneself except to renounce one’s own pleasures? Let the person who was proud become humble; let the person who was angry strive to become gentle. For if someone renounces everything he possesses but does not renounce his own character, he is not Christ’s disciple.

The person who renounces his possessions denies what belongs to him; but the person who renounces wicked habits denies himself. Hence the Lord says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matt. XVI).

[Col. 0617A]

## CHAPTER XXI. On Those Who Love a Quiet Life

(Gregory, *Moralia*, book IV, chapter 34.) Because holy men desire nothing from this world, they are undoubtedly oppressed by no inner tumult. They drive every disordered movement of desire from the chamber of the heart with the hand of holy conduct, and, despising all transitory things, they do not suffer the insolence of thoughts arising from them.

For they desire only the eternal homeland, and because they love none of the things of this world, they enjoy great tranquility of mind. Great rest of mind consists in expelling the tumult of earthly desires from the heart’s secret place and, with a single intention toward the eternal homeland, breathing after the love of inner quiet.

David sought withdrawal from the tumult of temporal things when he said: “One thing I asked of the Lord; this I shall seek, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord” (Ps. XXVI). And again: “Behold, I have gone far away in flight and have remained in solitude” (Ps. LIV). The one who flees goes far away when he raises himself from the crowd of temporal desires into the heights of contemplation of God; he remains in solitude when he perseveres in a remote intention of mind.

Abba Antony said: “The one who sits in solitude and rests is rescued from three battles: hearing, speech, and sight.” (Simeon Metaphrastes, *Life of Arsenius*.)

Abba Arsenius prayed, saying: “Lord, lead me to salvation.” And a voice came to him, saying: “Arsenius, flee from people, be silent, rest, and you will be saved.”

Abba Moses said: “The person who flees from people is like a ripe grape; but the person who associates with people will be like an unripe grape.”

Abba Nilus said: “The person who loves quiet remains impenetrable to the arrows of the enemy; but the person who mingles with the crowd will receive frequent wounds.”

[Col. 0617C]

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Elect Who Leave Everything

(Gregory, *Moralia*, book XI, chapter 30.) At the end of the age those who are now unjustly judged for God’s sake will come as judges with God. Then their light will shine more widely in proportion as the hand of their persecutors now constricts them more harshly. Then it will be revealed to the eyes of the reprobate that those who willingly abandoned all earthly things were supported by heavenly power.

For whoever, stirred here by the goad of divine love, has abandoned his possessions will undoubtedly obtain there the summit of judicial authority, so that the one who now chastises himself voluntarily in consideration of judgment may then come as judge together with the Judge.

Our Redeemer pronounces the sentence of judgment with the holy preachers of the Church, just as he himself says in the Gospel: “You who have left everything and followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX).

All who are now perfect in the Church have learned the uprightness of their perfection through the Gospel. Therefore, united to our Redeemer and joined to his majesty, those who now follow perfect works according to the Gospel precepts will be seen as judges with him.

Whoever in this age obeyed the Lord’s precepts will afterward come as a judge with him to judge the peoples, just as it is said to the preachers who left everything: “You also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” For it is right that those who perfectly abandon the present age in response to God’s words should dispute with God concerning the peoples in judgment.

And those who were his companions in voluntary poverty or in peace in this life will afterward come as judges with God. It is written: “He summoned the heavens above and the earth, that he might judge his people” (Ps. XLIX). (Gregory, *Moralia*, book XV, chapter 15.)

He summons the heavens above when those who, leaving all their possessions, maintained a heavenly way of life are called to sit with him in judgment and come as judges with him. The earth also is called above when those who had been bound to earthly activities nevertheless sought heavenly gains more than earthly ones in those activities. To them it is said at the end: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; naked, and you clothed me” (Matt. XV).

The elect, leaving everything, are not judged but reign. They even transcend the precepts of the law through the virtue of perfection, because they are not content merely to fulfill what divine law has commanded all, but seek with a more excellent desire to offer more than they could have heard in the general precepts.

[Col. 0618B]

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Mortification of Monks

The Apostle Paul says: “Consider yourselves dead indeed to sin, but alive to God” (Rom. VI). Sin does not reign in the dead, nor does the desire for sin live in them. For the concupiscence of the flesh is immediately extinguished in such a person; fury rests, anger ceases, hatred is driven away, and all vices together come to rest. This is to die to sin and to live for Christ.

The Apostle himself also says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III). Christ was crucified, died, and was buried for us; and in his likeness we crucify our wills and desires.

Christ, however, was not crucified to sin in part, but wholly, so that we might live for God. The person lives for God who follows Christ’s footsteps in humility, sanctification, and devotion.

A monk is mortified when he chastises his body through continual fasting; when he restrains his appetite within the necessary measure; when, abstaining not only from more delicate foods but even from inferior ones, he holds himself back; when he permits nothing to his flesh for the sake of desire, but only what is necessary to sustain life. (Gregory, *Moralia*, book V, chapter 3.)

When spiritual monks fully desire their mortification, the nearer they come to the end, the more ardent they show themselves in their work. Therefore they do not grow weary through labor; rather, they increase against their labors. When they already consider the rewards to be nearer, they sweat more gladly in their work.

All monks, leaving the world, do not cease to punish with tears the things in which they have sinned. They afflict themselves with deep sorrow because, having been cast far from the face of their Creator, they are not yet in the joys of the eternal homeland.

Sometimes monks do not reach the desires they contemplate precisely so that, through the delay itself, the bosom of the mind may be broadened toward those desires; and what could have been weakened by entanglement is arranged in such a way that, being repulsed, it may grow more abundantly.

Many monks desire to mortify themselves in the present age so that, if permitted, they might already contemplate perfectly the face of their Creator. But their desire is delayed so that it may progress, and it is nourished by the delay that it may grow.

The good monk completely withdraws from the restless desire of this world, abandons the tumult of earthly activities, and, through devotion to quiet, his mind intent upon the virtues, sleeps as though watchful.

No monk is led to contemplate inner things unless he diligently withdraws from those things that entangle him outwardly. Hence the Truth itself says: “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. VI). Hence Paul says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (II Tim. II).

Through the Prophet the Lord admonishes us, saying: “Be still and see that I am God” (Ps. XLV), because inner knowledge is by no means conceived unless one ceases from outward entanglement.

Again Paul says: “If we have died with him, we shall also live with him” (II Tim. II). For if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him (Rom. VI), because just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ (I Cor. XV).

And if we endure tribulations for him, just as he endured for us, we shall reign with him, because we must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations (II Tim. II). “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III).

[Col. 0619C]

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Contemplative Life
Active life is innocence in good works; contemplative life is speculation concerning heavenly things. The former is common to many, but the latter belongs to few. Active life makes good use of worldly affairs, whereas contemplative life, renouncing the world, takes delight in living for God alone. Whoever first makes progress in the active life ascends well to contemplation. For rightly is one raised up in the latter who is found useful in the former. Just as one who has been buried is deprived of every earthly business, so one who devotes himself to contemplation is turned away from active occupation.

Holy men, just as they emerge from the hidden place of contemplation

[Col. 0619D] into the public sphere of action, so again they return from the public manifestation of action to the secrecy of inward contemplation, so that inwardly they may praise God, where they received what enables them to work outwardly for his glory. (Gregory, *Moralia*, book IX, chapter 23.) Just as it is the nature of an eagle always to fix its eye upon the sun’s ray and not turn it aside except for the sake of food alone, so the saints sometimes turn back from contemplation to active life, considering that those higher things are so useful that nevertheless these humble things are somewhat necessary for our need.

Great is the exertion of the mind in the contemplative life: when it raises itself toward heavenly things, when it stretches its spirit toward spiritual realities, when it strives to transcend everything that is perceived bodily, when it constricts itself in order to expand. At times

[Col. 0620A] it indeed prevails, overcomes the resisting darkness of its blindness, and furtively and subtly touches something of the unbounded light. But immediately it is driven back upon itself and, from that light toward which it passes by breathing deeply, returns with sighs to the darkness of its own blindness.

It is written in the Book of Genesis: “Abraham buried his wife in a double tomb” (Gregory, *Moralia*, book VI, chapter 25). The active life is, as it were, a tomb, because it covers those who are dead to evil works; but the contemplative life buries one more completely, because it entirely separates one from all the activities of the world.

A certain brother went to the cell of Abba Arsenius and looked through the window. He saw the old man wholly as though he were fire, absorbed in contemplation. That brother was worthy to behold such things. They said of Abba Sisoes that, unless he quickly lowered his hands

[Col. 0620B] when he stood at prayer, his mind was carried away into higher things. Therefore, if another brother happened to pray with him, he would quickly lower his hands, lest his mind be carried away and he be delayed.

A certain old man said that continual prayer quickly corrects the mind. One of the Fathers said: Just as it is impossible for anyone to see his face in troubled water, so the soul cannot pray contemplatively to God unless it has been purified from alien thoughts.

[Col. 0620B]

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Desire for the Heavenly Kingdom

Great is the cry of the saints, and great is their desire; for each person cries out the less, the less he desires. And he expresses a voice all the louder in the ears of the

[Col. 0620C]

unbounded Spirit, the more fully he pours himself into the desire for him. Often our desires are heard precisely because they are not fulfilled quickly, and what we urgently ask to be accomplished is brought to a better outcome by the very delay.

Our desires are prolonged by delay so that they may grow; they grow so that they may become strong enough for what they are about to receive. They are stirred up in the contest so that they may be increased by greater rewards in the recompense. The labor of the struggle is prolonged so that the crown of victory may increase.

As much as just men desire to cling to heavenly things through the ray of contemplation, so much do they refuse to build themselves up on earth, where they know themselves to be strangers and guests, as Paul testifies when he says: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians III).

(Gregory, *Moralia*, book V, chapter 3.) Holy men do not cease to mortify themselves with the sword of the sacred word, cutting themselves off from the importunity of temporal desires and useless cares, and from the love of clamorous disturbances; inwardly they hide themselves before the face of God in the bosom of the mind.

[Col. 0620D] Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “You shall hide them in the hiding-place of your face, from the turmoil of men” (Psalm XXX), so that, while their mind is wholly stretched toward the love of God, it may not be torn apart by any useless disturbance.

The Apostle Paul, through contemplation, had seen his disciples as dead and hidden, as it were, in a tomb; to them he said: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians III). Whoever desires to mortify himself rejoices greatly in the rest found in contemplation, so that, dead to the world, he may be hidden from it, and, with all the disturbances of outward affairs

[Col. 0621A]

quieted, may hide himself within the bosom of inward love.

Sometimes the mind of a just person is admitted to an unusual sweetness of inward savor; and, suddenly breathed upon by an ardent spirit, it is renewed in some manner. The more it tastes something of this sweetness, the more eagerly it longs for it, and within itself desires that which it senses to possess more sweetly within.

Abba Theonas said: Our mind is hindered and called back from the contemplation of God; therefore we are led captive into carnal passions.

Abba Arsenius said to a certain brother: Whatever virtue you may possess, strive that your inward work according to God may prevail over the passions of the outward person.

Abba John used to say that he had once made a plait for two baskets, but spent it all on one basket and did not

[Col. 0621B]

realize it. For his mind had been occupied in the contemplation of God.

Abba Serapion said: Just as the emperor’s soldiers, when they stand before him, do not dare to look to the right or to the left, so, if a monk stands in the presence of the Lord and is attentive every hour in his fear, there is nothing by which the adversary can terrify him.

Abba Hyperichius said: Let your thought always be in the kingdom of heaven, and soon you will receive it as an inheritance. He said again: Let the monk’s life be made according to the imitation of the angels, burning up and consuming sins.

Abba Matois said: The nearer a person approaches God, the more clearly he sees himself to be a sinner. For the prophet Isaiah, seeing the Lord, called himself wretched and unclean (Isaiah VI).

A certain old man said: Just as no one dares to harm one who is beside the emperor, so Satan

[Col. 0621C] will be unable to harm us if our soul clings to God.

[Col. 0621C]

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Lax Conduct of Monks

(The same, book II of the *Sentences*, chapter 10.) Many are led back to their former errors by lax conduct, and are weakened over the course of their lives. One who is lukewarm in his conduct does not perceive that idle words and empty thoughts are harmful. But if he awakens from the lethargy of his mind, he immediately fears as dreadful and atrocious the things he had considered trivial.

Every art of this world has energetic lovers and people most ready to carry it out. This happens because it has the remuneration for its work in the present. But the art of divine love has many followers who are weak, lukewarm, and frozen by laziness and inertia.

[Col. 0621D] This happens because their labor is deferred not for a present but for a future reward. Therefore, while the recompense of their labor does not immediately follow, they grow weak, their hope almost dissolved.

Hence great glory is prepared for those who complete the beginnings of good conduct and life with more solid growth, and are prepared all the more brightly to merit recompense the more firmly they both begin and complete the labors of the difficult journey.

(Gregory, *Moralia*, book XII, chapter 26.) Some gird themselves for virtue in the first heat of their conversion; but as progress advances, while they devote themselves excessively to earthly affairs, they are obscured by the dust of lowly desire.

There are some who, after following perverse paths, desire to pursue holy ways.

[Col. 0622A] But before good desires have been strengthened in them, as we have said, some prosperity of the present age overtakes them. It entangles them in outward affairs and, by drawing their mind back from the heat of inward fervor, extinguishes it as though with cold; whatever seemed to appear in them of late fervor, it destroys.

If a weak and lukewarm monk perhaps begins to do something good, before he grows strong in it through the length of time, he slips away toward outward things and perversely abandons what he had seemed to begin rightly. For the mind grows very cold in earthly activities if it has not yet been made firm by inward gifts.

It must be known above all that this usually happens to monks who do not follow God with pure and simple

[Col. 0622B]

devotion, as it is written in the Book of blessed Job: “The assembly of the hypocrite is barren” (Job XV).

(Gregory, *Moralia*, book XII, chapter 27.) They would not lose the good things they had begun if they had not been hypocrites. Hypocrites too gather good works, but their gathering itself is barren, because through what they do they do not seek to receive fruit in the eternal recompense. They appear fruitful and green in their works to human eyes, but in the sight of the hidden Judge they appear fruitless and dry.

The perverse minds of monks do not cease to turn over within themselves the turmoil of temporal affairs, even when they are at leisure. For in their thoughts they preserve images of what they love; and although they do nothing outwardly, nevertheless within themselves they labor in quiet under the weight of unrest. If the administration of those same

[Col. 0622C]

affairs is entrusted to them, they utterly abandon themselves.

For, intent upon worldly cares, we become inwardly all the more insensitive the more diligent we appear toward the things outside.

(Gregory, homily 17 on the Gospels.) Through use and concern for earthly desire the mind becomes hardened, and, becoming hard through the activity of the world itself, it cannot be softened toward the things that belong to the love of God.

Holy Church says of its weakened members: “They made me keeper of the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep” (Song of Songs I). Our vineyard is, of course, our actions, which we cultivate through the practice of daily labor. But, placed as keepers in the vineyards, we do not guard our own vineyard at all, because, when we become entangled in foreign activities, we neglect the ministry of our own activity.

Abba Sisoes said: Make yourself contemptible, and throw your desires behind your back. Be free and secure from worldly cares, and you will have rest.

An old man said: This is the monk’s life: work, obedience, meditation, so that he does not judge, slander, or murmur; so that he does not act inquisitively, nor take pleasure in hearing what belongs to others. For it is written: “You who love the Lord, hate evil” (Psalm XCVI).

[Col. 0622D]

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Abstinence

This is perfect and reasonable fasting: when our outward person fasts, the inward person prays. Through fasting, prayer penetrates heaven more easily. For then, having become spiritual, a person is joined to the angels and united more freely to God.

Through fasting also the hidden mysteries of heavenly things are revealed

[Col. 0623A], and the secrets of the divine sacrament are disclosed. Thus Daniel, when an angel revealed them, was found worthy to know the sacramental mysteries. This virtue reveals both manifestations of angels and their announcements.

Fasts are strong weapons against the temptations of demons. For through abstinence they are quickly overcome. Hence our Lord and Savior also teaches us to overcome their assaults through fasts and prayers, saying: “This kind of demon is not driven out except through prayer and fasting” (Mark VI).

Unclean spirits thrust themselves more readily into those places where they see more food and drink. As long as the saints dwell in the life of this age, they carry their body dried out by the desire for heavenly dew. Hence it is said in the Psalm: “My soul has thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh

[Col. 0623B]

longs for you” (Psalm LXII). The flesh thirsts for God when it abstains and withers through fasting.

Abstinence both gives life and kills: it gives life to the soul and kills the body. Fasts are acceptable to God when accompanied by good works. But those who abstain from food and act wickedly imitate demons, who have no food but always have wickedness.

A person abstains well from food when he fasts from acts of malice and from the ambitions of the world. A fast that is restored in the evening by filling oneself with food is despised. For abstinence cannot be reckoned where fullness of the stomach has followed. A fast that is compensated in the evening with delicacies is despised.

When we subdue our bodies through abstinence, what else do we offer to almighty God but bodily sacrifices?

[Col. 0623C] As Paul says: “That you may present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (Romans XII).

The distinguished psalmist David, indicating that there is no abstinence without harmony, says: “Praise him with tambourine and chorus” (Psalm CL). In the tambourine, dry hide resounds; in the chorus, voices sing together in harmony. What is signified by the tambourine except abstinence, and by the chorus except the harmony of charity?

(Gregory, *Pastoral Care*, part III, admonition 23.) Therefore, whoever practices abstinence in such a way as to abandon harmony praises with the tambourine, but does not praise with the chorus.

A certain old man said: For this reason I cut off carnal pleasures from myself, so that I may also cut off the occasions of anger. For I know that anger always fights against me on behalf of pleasures, troubles my mind, and drives away my understanding.

Abba John

[Col. 0623D]

, who was small in stature, said: If some king wishes to hold a city of enemies, he first takes control of their water and provisions. Then, when the enemies are endangered by thirst and hunger, they are subjected to him. If a person lives in fasting and hunger, his enemies, who trouble the mind, are first weakened.

[Col. 0623D]

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Continence

Continence is given by God, but “ask, and you shall receive” (Wisdom VIII; Matthew VII; Luke XI). It is granted when God is besought with inward groaning.

Virginity is a twofold good, because in this world it loses the anxiety of the age, and in the future receives the eternal reward of chastity. Isaiah testifies that virgins are more fortunate in eternal life when he says: “Thus says the Lord

[Col. 0624A]

to the eunuchs: I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that shall not perish” (Isaiah LVI).

There is no doubt that those who persevere in chastity and virginity become equal to the angels of God. The beauty of chastity is to be loved; once its delight has been tasted, it is found sweeter than that of the flesh. Chastity is the fruit of sweetness, the undefiled beauty of the saints. Chastity is security of mind and health of body.

The incorruption of the flesh is of no benefit where there is no integrity of mind, nor does bodily purity avail one who is polluted in mind.

An old man said that security, silence, and hidden meditation produce chastity; the monk’s glory consists in abstinence from food and from excessive talk of the tongue.

Abba Poemen said: Just as the prince’s sword-bearer

[Col. 0624B]

stands continually beside him, always ready, so the soul must always be ready against the spirit of fornication.

Abba Antony used to say: It is fitting to know that there are three bodily movements: one is natural, another comes from fullness of food, and the third from the assault of demons. But against all of them it is good to guard what is written: “With all vigilance guard your heart” (Proverbs IV).

[Col. 0624B]

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Enduring Divine Correction

(Isidore, book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 4.) A sinful person ought not to murmur under the scourges of God, because he is especially corrected through the very thing by which he is chastised. Everyone bears what he suffers more lightly if he examines his own evils, for which a just recompense is inflicted upon him.

[Col. 0624C]

Let the person who suffers evils learn not to murmur, even if he does not know why he suffers them; and by this let him judge that he suffers justly, because he suffers from the one whose judgments are never unjust. Whoever endures scourges and murmurs against God accuses the justice of the Judge. But whoever recognizes that he suffers what he endures from a just Judge, even if he does not know for what he suffers, is already justified by this: that he accuses himself and praises God’s justice.

(Gregory, on chapter IV of Job, book V, chapter 26; Isidore, book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 4; Gregory, *Moralia*, book VII, chapter 3.) For great benefit, the mind of a just person is agitated by various trials of suffering according to divine judgment. If he gives thanks to God for them and attributes them to his own fault, acknowledging that he is worthy of such things, then what he endures from suffering will be reckoned to him as virtue, because he recognizes divine justice and understands his own guilt.

[Col. 0624D]

The mind of the just weighs not only what it endures, but already fears what remains. It sees what it suffers in this life and fears that afterward it may suffer more grievous things. It mourns because it has fallen from the joy of paradise into the exile of this blindness; it fears that, when the exile is left behind, eternal death may follow.

Thus it already endures the sentence in punishment, but still fears the threats of the eternal Judge because of guilt. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “Your wrath has passed over me, and your terrors have troubled me” (Psalm LXXXVII). For after the wrath of the inward Judge has passed over, terrors also trouble us, because we already suffer one thing from condemnation and still fear another from eternal vengeance.

(Thus far Gregory.) The monk’s glory, however, is patience in his tribulations and long-suffering with charity. The more holy men humble themselves outwardly by despising themselves, the more they are inwardly nourished by contemplation of revelations. Those whom the valley of humility holds outwardly in weeping, the ascent of contemplation raises inwardly.

[Col. 0625A]

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Scourges of God

(Isidore, book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 1.) God’s mercy is ordered in such a way that he first cleanses a person here from sins through scourges and afterward frees him from eternal punishment. God’s chosen one is worn down by the pains of this life so that he may gain the rewards of the future life in greater perfection.

God by no means spares the delinquent: for he either strikes the sinner

[Col. 0625B] with a temporal scourge for purification, leaves him to be punished by eternal judgment, or the person himself punishes through repentance what he has wrongly committed. Thus it is rightly said that God does not spare the delinquent.

Through temporal scourges the just advance toward eternal joys. Therefore the just ought to rejoice in punishments, while the wicked ought to fear in prosperity. God withdraws neither mercy nor justice from the just or the reprobate. He judges the good here through affliction and rewards them there through mercy; he rewards the wicked here through temporal kindness and punishes them there through eternal justice.

In this life God spares the wicked and yet does not spare the chosen; in the other life he will spare the chosen, but will not spare the wicked. The one whom the Lord loves is corrected more severely if he has sinned, as the prophet Amos says:

[Col. 0625C]

“You only have I known out of all the nations of the earth; therefore I will visit all your iniquities upon you” (Amos III). For “the Lord disciplines the one whom he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives” (Hebrews XII).

(Isidore, in the same place.) It is greatly necessary for the just person in this life both to be tested by vices and struck by the scourge, so that, while he is assailed by vices, he may not become proud of his virtues; and while he is worn down by pain of mind or body, he may be withdrawn from the love of the world.

(Isidore, at the cited place.) God deals more harshly with his chosen ones in this life so that, while they are struck by the stronger goads of the scourge, they may take pleasure in no delight of the present life, but may desire without ceasing the heavenly homeland, where assured rest is awaited.

The sick are to be admonished so that they may recognize themselves as God’s children precisely insofar as the scourges of discipline chastise them. For if he did not intend to give an inheritance to his corrected

[Col. 0625D]

children, he would not take care to educate them through hardships.

The stones of the Lord’s sanctuary were hewn outside so that they might be placed in the construction of the temple without the sound of a hammer (1 Kings VI). For now we are struck outside through scourges, so that afterward we may be arranged within God’s temple without discipline and blows; thus whatever is superfluous in us may now be cut away by blows, and then only the harmony of charity may bind us together in the building.

The sick are to be admonished to preserve the virtue of patience, so that they may continually consider how many evils our Redeemer endured from those whom he had created. Why, then, is it thought harsh that a human being should endure scourges from God for evils, if God himself endured such great evils from human beings for the sake of good?

[Col. 0626A]

Or who of sound understanding would be ungrateful for his own chastisement, if the one who came here without sin did not depart from here without scourging?

[Col. 0626A]

## CHAPTER XXXI. On Bodily Illness

(Isidore, book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 3.) Seeing that some people refuse to be corrected by their own choice, God touches them with the goads of adversity. Foreknowing also that some may sin greatly, he chastises them with bodily illness for their salvation, so that they may not sin; for it is more beneficial for them to be broken by sickness unto salvation than to remain healthy unto condemnation.

Those who are stronger and healthy benefit from becoming ill and not sinning, lest through the vigor of health they be defiled by illicit desires for greed and luxury. There is a harmful health that leads a person to disobedience, and there is a health-giving illness

[Col. 0626B] that, through divine correction, breaks the mind’s hardness.

Holy Syncletica said: The devil sometimes deliberately brings illnesses against the one who is to be tested, so that by making monks fainthearted through them he may disturb the charity they have toward God.

But even if the body is broken and inflamed by severe fevers, and even if the affliction is intolerable, if you are a sinner who endures these things, remember the punishments of the future age, the eternal fire, and the torments of judgment. In this way you will not faint under what happens in the present; indeed, you will rejoice because God has visited you. Keep that famous saying on your lips: “The Lord has chastened and chastened me, but he has not given me over to death” (Psalm CXVII).

If you are iron, expect fire to be applied to you

[Col. 0626C]; for if you are just and suffer these things, you are being promoted from great things to greater. You are gold, but through fire you will become more fully tested.

If you are chastised by fevers or by the chill of cold, remember what Scripture says: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment” (Psalm LXV).

If illness becomes burdensome to us, let us not grieve as though, because of illness and bodily wounds, we were unable to stand for prayer or sing psalms aloud. All these things will contribute to the destruction of bodily desires, since fasts and labors were appointed for us because of shameful pleasures.

If, therefore, this illness blunts what is excessive, there is reason to observe these things. For just as a strong and powerful medicine cuts away deadly diseases from bodily illness, so it is a great virtue when, amid illnesses, patience is practiced and thanksgiving is offered to God.

If we lose our eyes, let us not bear it heavily. For we have lost an instrument of pride, and with our inner eyes we behold the glory of the Lord. If we have become deaf, let us not be troubled, because we have lost the hearing of vanity. Our hands have been weakened by some illness, but we have inward hands ready against the temptations of the enemy. Illness possesses our whole body, but the health of our inward person increases.

[Col. 0626D]

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Tribulation of the Just

(Isidore, book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 58.) Let the just person recognize that he is being tested in adversity, not cast down. Holy men fear the prosperity of the world more than its adversity

[Col. 0627A], because the prosperity of the world casts down God’s servants, whereas adversity makes them wiser.

Therefore the steadfastness of holy men ought to bear adversity in such a way that it cannot be broken. The eyes of God are more especially upon the just when heavenly providence permits them to be afflicted by the wicked. For then eternal joys are prepared for them, when they are tested by present tribulation.

All the tribulations of this life are compared to passing waters, because if some tribulation occurs in this life, it does not remain but quickly passes away. Whoever carefully considers the rewards of the future life bears all the evils of the present life with equanimity, because by the sweetness of that life he moderates the bitterness of this one, and by its eternity he disdains the fleeting brevity of this.

Since those who are weighed down by bodily pain do not desire the evils of greed, luxury, and other

[Col. 0627B]

vices, the trial of the world benefits salvation more than prosperity. For prosperity leads to what is worse, while the pain of trial advances one toward what is better.

Everyone ought to prepare his mind for temptation. For temptation weighs less when it is expected; but it presses harshly if it arrives unexpectedly. It is the mark of a wise person to meditate beforehand upon every adversity; no misfortune should occur that his counsels have not anticipated.

(This is Isidore, at the cited place.) This is why the just are allowed to be afflicted by the unjust: so that, while they hear of the future good things they desire, they may also suffer the present evils they dread; and, while love summons them toward an easier departure, torment may drive them onward.

The Psalmist David says: “You are my

[Col. 0627C]

refuge from the distress that surrounded me; my joy, redeem me from those who surround me” (Psalm XXXI). See: as though in the night, he names distress, yet calls his deliverer “my joy” amid his straits. Outside there was night in the surrounding distress, but inside songs resounded from the consolation of joy.
