Each chosen person, while telling that he is surrounded by distresses and nevertheless calling God his joy, undoubtedly sings a song in the night so that he may arrive happily at the day of the life to come.

A certain old man said: If temptation comes upon a person—for tribulations are multiplied on every side—and he becomes fainthearted and murmurs, yet if bodily illness overtakes you, do not become fainthearted or receive it with distress, because the Lord himself is thinking about everything for you. Do you live without him? Therefore you ought to bear it patiently and ask him to grant you what is expedient: namely, that you do what his will is, and sit patiently, eating what you have in charity.

[Col. 0627D]

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Temptations

(Isidore, book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 5.) In this life the mind of the just is assailed by many temptations of calamities; hence it desires to be utterly removed from this age, so that it may be free from hardships and find secure stability there.

The devil does not tempt the chosen more than God’s will permits. By tempting them, however, he serves the progress of the saints. Even unwillingly, the devil serves the saints’ benefit when he does not deceive them through his temptations

[Col. 0628A]

but rather instructs them.

God’s servant must carefully understand and at the same time avoid the enemy’s ambushes, and must be simple in the innocence of his life while nevertheless being prudent with that simplicity. Whoever does not mix prudence with simplicity is, according to the prophet, “a dove without a heart,” that is, without understanding (Hosea VII). It is called a dove because it is simple; but it is said to have no heart because it is ignorant of prudence.

In the eyes of the chosen, the devil’s terror is contemptible. He is feared as a lion by unbelievers; by the strong in faith he is despised as a worm and, when offended, is driven away in an instant.

The devil is a slippery serpent. If one does not resist his head—that is, his first suggestion—he slips wholly into the inward heart without being perceived. The beginnings of diabolical temptations are weak; if they are not guarded against but pass through use into habit

[Col. 0628B], they become powerful at the end, so that they are either never overcome or overcome only with difficulty.

Although the devil desires to overthrow a person throughout the whole of life, he nevertheless strives more intensely to deceive at the end. Hence at the beginning it was said to the serpent concerning the first-formed human being (Genesis III): “And you shall lie in wait for his heel.” For the devil intends to trip up at the end the person whom he did not deceive during the course of his former life.

Therefore, although someone may be just, it is never safe for him to be secure in this life. In humility he must always be cautious, and must always fear anxiously lest he fall at the end.

The devil does not possess holy people by holding them captive, but persecutes them by tempting them. Because he does not reign within them, he fights against them from outside; and having lost dominion within, he stirs up war

[Col. 0628C]

outside.

When the devil seeks to deceive someone, he first examines that person’s nature, and then approaches from the side where he sees the person to be most inclined toward sin. The devil tempts people from the side where he sees that they can easily be bent toward vices by an excess of bodily humor, so that he applies temptation in accordance with the distribution of that humor.

Read about Balaam, who, in the figure of the devil, commanded that harmful snares be set against the Lord’s people from the side where he perceived that they would most easily fall (Numbers XXIV). For when someone diverts water in a particular place, he does not send it by another route but where he directs its force.

It is one thing for the devil to enter someone’s mind, and another for him to inhabit it. He enters even the hearts of the saints when he insinuates evil suggestions; but he does not

[Col. 0628D]

dwell in them, because he does not lead them over into his own body [variant: “transfer them”]. Those who are in his body, however, he inhabits, because they themselves are his temple.

Even if the devil slips into the minds of the chosen, he does not rest in them as he does in the hearts of the reprobate. For the heat of faith immediately rouses him so that he departs from the chosen.

Some whom the devil had already devoured with greedy mouth are again, through the hidden mercy of divine judgment, snatched from his mouth and restored to salvation. Often the divine power has drawn from the ancient enemy’s jaws, through repentance, many whom he held submerged in the abyss of lust.

The just person suffers many adversities in his soul at the instigation of demons, but he cannot be destroyed by such temptations with respect to eternal life, because the merciful Lord does not reckon as guilt leading to condemnation what a person, unwillingly suffering it, bears by permission of his divine majesty.

[Col. 0629A]

We sin where we turn aside through desire or will. But where we are forcibly subjected, even if there is no crime or disgraceful act, there is nevertheless misery as though for a crime and disgraceful act. Yet whoever praises God for the misery inflicted upon him is undoubtedly free from the crime.

[Col. 0629A]

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Many Kinds of Sins
(Gregory, Book IV, chapter 26, on chapter 3 of Job.) Sin is committed in the heart in four ways, and perpetrated in deed in four ways. It is admitted into the heart through demonic suggestion, sensual pleasure, the mind’s consent, and the defense of pride. It is committed in deed now secretly, now openly, now through habit, now through despair. [Col. 0629B] Thus, through these stages, one both sins in the heart and perpetrates sin in deed.

(Isidore, Book II of the Sentences, chapters 17, 18, 19, 21, and 25.) Sin is practiced in three ways: through ignorance, weakness, and deliberate action. It is graver to sin through weakness than through ignorance, and graver to sin deliberately than through weakness. For one sins deliberately when one does evil with intention and deliberation of mind. Through weakness, however, one sins by accident or rashness. More wicked still are those who sin deliberately: they not only fail to live well, but also, if they can, turn those who live well away from the truth.

There are venial sins that beginners cleanse through daily satisfaction, yet which perfect men avoid as though they were grave crimes. What, then, ought people to do concerning great crimes, when even the perfect mourn their lesser offenses as though they were most serious? Greater sins ought not to be committed through experience of lesser sins, lest those who do not know how to be corrected by small faults be struck more harshly because of great crimes. By divine judgment, those fall into more grievous guilt who disdain to discipline their lesser deeds.

Many fall from one crime into another: although they possess knowledge of God, they neglect his fear; and although they know him intellectually, they do not honor him through their conduct. Therefore they are allowed, by divine judgment, to commit deeds deserving punishment and, as a penalty, to add a worse crime to the crime already committed.

Often one sin is the cause of another, because when it is committed another arises from it like its offspring, just as lust commonly arises from excessive indulgence of the belly. Sin is also admitted as the punishment of sin when, because of the merit of a given sin, God abandons a person and that person proceeds into a worse sin, by which the one who committed it is further defiled. Thus the preceding sin is the cause of the following sin, while the following sin is the punishment of the preceding offense. Preceding sins, therefore, are the cause of subsequent crimes, so that the sins that follow are the punishment of those that preceded them.

The punishment of preceding sins is itself called hardening, proceeding from divine justice. Hence the prophet says: “You have hardened our heart, so that we would not fear you” (Isaiah 63). It is one thing not to sin out of love for God; it is another not to sin out of fear of punishment. For the one who does not sin out of love of God’s charity abhors every evil, embracing the good of righteousness; nor does that person sin when sin is pleasing, even if impunity for the crime is promised. [Col. 0630A] But whoever restrains vices in himself solely through fear of punishment, although he does not carry out the sinful act, nevertheless lives with the will to sin and grieves that what the law clearly forbids is unlawful for him. Therefore the one who does what is good by loving righteousness receives the reward of a good deed, not the one who unwillingly observes it solely through fear of punishments.

Every sin is feared more before it is committed. Once it has become habitual, however, although it is serious, it is considered light and committed without any fear. Through these sources, as through successive steps, every sin grows. Evil thought gives birth to pleasure, pleasure to consent, consent to action, action to habit, and habit to necessity. Thus, entangled in these bonds, a person is held fast by a certain chain of vices, so that one cannot be torn away from it unless divine grace takes hold of the hand of the fallen.

To admit sin is to fall into a pit. To establish a habit of sinning is to narrow the mouth of the pit, so that the one who has fallen cannot escape. Yet sometimes God also frees such people, when he changes their despair into the freedom of conversion. Through his mercy sins are forgiven; under his protection, a person is prevented from proceeding into worse sin by sinning further. Therefore those who trust that they can be saved in this way must fear lest, while we wait to be healed from vices, we multiply them and fail to attain salvation. Let us therefore strive either not to fall or, having turned back quickly, to rise from our fall.

Delay in sinning makes the crime monstrous. Hence the prophet also says: “Woe to those who drag iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as though with a cart rope” (Isaiah 5). One drags iniquity like a cord when one delays turning back to God. To drag iniquity is to delay iniquity. Hence the Psalmist also says: “They have prolonged their iniquities; the righteous Lord has cut off the necks of sinners” (Psalm 128).

[Col. 0630C]

## CHAPTER XXXV. How one may rise after a fall

(Gregory, *Pastoral Care*, Part III, admonition 29.) Those who have experienced sins of the flesh should at least after their shipwreck fear sinning, and should shudder at the dangers of their ruin, now that they have learned them. Those who have fallen should be told to consider their past sins and avoid those that threaten, so that they may recall their transgressions and blush to be defiled by future ones.

Those who have experienced sins of the flesh should be admonished to observe with vigilant care how, after our offenses, God expands the lap of his mercy toward us when we return to him. Through the prophet he says to us: “Your eyes shall see your teacher, and your ears shall hear the word of one admonishing behind your back: This is the way; walk in it,” and so forth (Isaiah 30). Almighty God admonishes us as though following behind us, because even after guilt he persuades us to return to him. He recalls the one who has turned away, does not regard the offenses committed, and expands the lap of his mercy for the one who returns. We hear the voice of one admonishing behind us if, after our sins, we return with a humble and contrite heart. We ought, therefore, to blush before the mercy of the one who calls us if we do not wish to fear his justice, because he is despised with all the graver wickedness inasmuch as, though despised, he does not disdain still to call.

(Gregory, Homily 10, Book I, on Ezekiel.) Through the prophet Micah the Lord says: “You shall come as far as Babylon; there you shall be delivered” (Micah 4). Babylon is interpreted as “confusion.” Often, after someone has fallen into the confusion of vices, that person returns to repentance, ashamed of the evils committed, and raises himself from his falls by living well. What, then, does this person do except come as far as Babylon and there receive deliverance? Sometimes a person, ashamed of the evils committed, rises up against himself and returns to a state of uprightness by doing good. He is therefore delivered in Babylon who is shown, through divine grace, to have been saved even from confusion.

The prophet speaks of transmigration when he rebukes those who have fallen in transmigration from a state of uprightness into the vices of error. A brother asked an old man: “If a monk falls into sin and is afflicted because, having advanced, he has reached a worse state, must he labor until he rises again?” The old man replied: “A monk who falls into temptation is like a house that has fallen. If he is sober in his thought, he rebuilds it, finding materials useful for construction, since he already has the foundations, stones, sand, and the other things necessary for building; thus his structure quickly advances. So it is with a monk: if he falls into temptation and turns back to the Lord, he has a great deal of equipment—meditation on divine law, psalmody, and manual labor—which are the foundations of a spiritual building.”

[Col. 0631C]

[Col. 0631]

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On thought

(Isidore, Book II of the *Sentences*, chapter 25.) The cause of sin is twofold: deed and thought. One of these is called iniquity, which is carried out in deed; the other is injustice, which is admitted in thought. Action must be cut off first, and thought afterward; first evil deeds, then desires. Yet actions proceed in turn from thought, and thought arises from action. Even if someone abstains from evil deeds, that person will not be innocent because of the wickedness of evil thought alone. Hence the Lord says through Isaiah: “Take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes” (Isaiah 2). For we sin not only through deeds but also through thoughts, if we take pleasure in them when they unlawfully arise.

Just as a viper is killed when it is torn apart by its young while they are still in the womb, so our thoughts, nourished within us, kill us; conceived inwardly, they consume us with viperous poison and slay our soul with a cruel wound. Whenever someone is reached by divine illumination, that person is immediately assaulted by the troubles of shameful thoughts. But God’s servant, through the judgment of the fear of God, rejects temptations from himself and drives away shameful thoughts by introducing good thoughts.

Great vigilance must be applied to guarding the heart, because the source of either good or evil lies there. For, as it is written, “From the heart proceed evil thoughts” (Matthew 15). Therefore, if we resist wicked thought first, we do not fall into sinful action.

(Thus far Isidore.) Often from good works we learn how much purity of life we should construct in thought. Almost all good works proceed from thought, but some acute insights of thought arise from action. For just as action is taken up from the mind, so the mind is in turn instructed by action. It is very necessary that, when a thought is carried out into action, the eye of the mind should immediately be recalled to deeds already performed. Sometimes one sins in thought alone, and because the guilt does not reach action, neither does repentance reach torment.

(Gregory, *Moralia*, Book X, chapter 39; Book XVI, chapter 20; Book IV, chapter 33; Book II, chapter 5.) Yet an affliction merely imagined raises the mind more quickly, because indeed iniquity merely imagined pollutes it. Often what has already been erased from the sight of the judge through intervening tears returns to the mind through thought; the conquered fault tries once more to creep into pleasure and is renewed by prolonged assault in the old struggle, so that what was previously in the body afterward comes to reside in the mind through persistent thought.

When nothing is done outwardly in deed, but sin is committed only inwardly in thought, the mind binds itself under strict guilt unless it cleanses this through watchful lamentation. Often the ear of the heart is closed when a crowd of earthly thoughts roars around it; and the less the sound of tumultuous cares is restrained within the secret chamber of the mind, the less the voice of the presiding judge is heard.

Sometimes, during the very sacrifice of our prayer, unwelcome thoughts intrude and are able to snatch away or stain what we offer to God amid our tears. All who either desire unlawful things or wish to appear as something in this world are pressed down in their hearts by dense tumult of thoughts.

The sea signifies the human mind, and the thoughts of the mind are like the waves of the sea: sometimes they swell through anger, become calm through God’s grace, and flow away bitterly through hatred. The human mind, enduring so many temptations, is moved as though by so many winds. Often the tumult of thoughts weighs down the human mind; anger disturbs it, and when anger departs, foolish joy takes its place.

A certain brother asked some of the Fathers whether a person is polluted when thinking about filthy things. Some answered: “Yes, he is polluted; we who are uneducated cannot be saved.” But this pertains to salvation: if we do not carry out bodily the things we think about. A certain old man said: “We are not condemned because evil thoughts enter us, but if we use the thoughts badly and give them our assent. It happens both that we suffer shipwreck through thoughts and that we are crowned because of thoughts.”

[Col. 0632D]

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On speech

(Isidore, Book II of the *Sentences*, chapter 29.) When we do not avoid certain small words of vice, we slide into great guilt of the tongue; and when we freely and fearlessly commit certain deeds that are not serious, we slide through the habit of sinning into more grievous crimes. Empty words ought not to be found in the mouth of a Christian. For just as good conversations correct bad morals, so corrupt conversations corrupt good morals (1 Corinthians 15).

A guard is placed over the mouth (Psalm 140) when someone confesses not to be righteous but—what is more truthful—a sinner. He places his hand over his mouth (Job 39) who covers the excesses of his tongue with good works. He places his hand over his mouth who conceals the faults of evil speech beneath the covering of good action.

There is a fourfold rule of speaking, by which one must consider what, when, to whom, and how something should be said. The good person speaks well when humbly announcing what is right. One speaks well in the heart when one does not counterfeit charity. One speaks well with the mouth when one proclaims the truth. One speaks well through deeds when one builds up others by good example.

The wicked return evil for good and adversity for prosperity. The good return good for evil and prosperity for adversity. Against verbal abuse, the strength of patience must be applied, so that the temptation of speech that attacks outwardly may depart, conquered by the virtue of endurance.

A certain one of the Fathers said that once, when some elders were sitting and speaking about edifying matters, there was among them one who was perceptive. He saw angels moving their hands and washing them. But when the conversation turned to worldly matters, the angels departed, and pigs, full of filth, rolled about among them and polluted them. When they again spoke about edification, the angels returned and washed them.

On one occasion some old men came to Abbot Antony, and Abbot Joseph was also with them. Wishing to test them, Abbot Antony began a discussion about the holy Scriptures and asked the younger men what this or that word meant. Each answered as best he could. But he said: “You have not yet found it.” Finally he said to Abbot Joseph: “How do you understand this word?” He replied: “I do not know.” Abbot Antony said: “Truly Abbot Joseph alone has found the way, since he answered that he did not know.”

A brother asked an old man: “If one of the brothers brings me reports from outside, do you wish me, Father, to tell him not to bring them to me?” The old man replied: “No.” The brother said: “Why?” The old man answered: “Because we ourselves have not been able to keep this.” The brother said: “What, then, should be done?” The old man replied: “If we wish to preserve silence, the measure itself is sufficient for our neighbor.”

[Col. 0633C]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On silence

The tongue must be restrained with discretion, not bound irrevocably. For it is written: “The wise man will remain silent until the proper time” (Sirach 20), so that, when he judges the occasion opportune, he may set aside the discipline of silence and devote himself to useful purposes by saying what is appropriate.

Concerning the discipline of silence and speech, Solomon says: “A time to be silent, and a time to speak” (Ecclesiastes 3). The times of alternation must be weighed with discretion, lest, when the tongue ought to be restrained, it flow uselessly through words, or, when it can speak profitably, it restrain itself sluggishly.

(Gregory, *Moralia*, Book VII, chapter 26.) Considering the great usefulness of silence, the Psalmist says: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Psalm 140). He does not ask that a wall be placed over his mouth, but a door, which can evidently be opened and closed. Hence we too must speak cautiously, so that the voice may open the mouth with discretion and at the proper time, and silence may close it again at the proper time.

Each person must be admonished that, if he loves his neighbors as himself, he should not remain silent about what he rightly rebukes in them. The medicine of the voice contributes to the salvation of both: the one who commits the wrongful action is restrained, and the heat of pain in the one who suffers is moderated through the wound being opened.

(D. Gregory, *Pastoral Care*, Part III, admonition 15.) Those who observe the faults of their neighbors and nevertheless press down their tongue in silence are like people who, after seeing wounds, withhold the use of medicine; they become the authors of death precisely because they were unwilling to cure the poison they could have healed.

A brother asked a young monk: “Is it good to speak or to remain silent?” The boy replied: “If the words are idle, leave them aside. But if they are good words, do not prolong them; cut short what you are saying and be silent.”

A certain old man said: “Devote yourself to silence, think of nothing, and attend to your thought, whether resting in bed or rising with fear of God. If you do this, you will not fear the attacks of the wicked.”

Abbot Pastor said: “Abbot Moses asked Brother Zacharias, when he was dying: ‘What do you see?’ He answered him: ‘Nothing is better than silence, Father.’ He said to him: ‘It is true, son. Be silent.’”

Someone said to Abbot Ammon: “If there is a necessity to speak with a neighbor, do you think I should speak with him about the Scriptures or about the sayings and judgments of the elders?” The old man replied: “If you cannot remain silent, it is better to speak about the sayings of the elders than about Scripture. There is no small danger in doing otherwise.”

An old man said: “If a person has words but does not have deeds, he will resemble a tree that has leaves but no fruit. For just as a tree full of fruits is also green with leaves, so speech accompanies the person who has good works.”

[Col. 0634C]

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On excessive talk

It is written: “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Proverbs 10). And: “Whoever uses many words harms his soul” (Sirach 20). And: “The talkative man shall not be established upon the earth” (Psalm 139). If we exalt ourselves in much speaking, we will not be acquitted before the Lord. Therefore it is better that, entreating the Lord, we say: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Psalm 140). And: “Do not incline my heart to words of wickedness” (ibid.).

(Gregory, Book VII, chapter 25, on chapter 6 of Job.) Those who devote themselves to excessive talk should watch attentively how far they decline from a state of uprightness while they dissipate themselves through multiplied words. The human mind, enclosed like water, gathers upward because it returns to the place from which it descended; when released, however, it is lost because it uselessly spreads itself into low places. Whoever is dispersed through superfluous words from the discipline of silence is carried outside himself through many channels. Thus the mind is not able to return inward to knowledge of itself, because, scattered through excessive talk, it excludes itself from the secret chamber of inward reflection. It exposes itself completely to the wounds of the ambushing enemy, because it does not surround itself with the fortification of watchfulness.

It is written in Proverbs: “Like an open city without the circuit of walls is a man who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking” (Proverbs 25). Because it lacks the wall of silence, the city of the mind lies open to the enemy’s arrows; and when it casts itself outside itself through words, it shows itself open to its adversary.

(Gregory, *Pastoral Care*, Part III, admonition 15.) Often the sluggish mind is driven through successive stages into a pit. When we neglect to avoid idle words, we arrive at harmful ones: first we take pleasure in speaking about the affairs of others, afterward our speech gnaws away at the lives of those about whom we speak through detraction, and finally the tongue bursts forth into open insults. Through the unbridled tongue, goads are sown, quarrels arise, torches of hatred are kindled, and the peace of hearts is extinguished.

(Gregory, *Moralia*, Book VII, chapter 37.) That one who devotes himself to excessive talk can in no way hold to the uprightness of justice is attested by the Prophet, who says: “The talkative man shall not be established upon the earth” (Psalm 139). Hence Solomon says again: “In much speaking sin will not be absent” (Proverbs 10). The prophet Isaiah says: “The cultivation of justice is silence” (Isaiah 32), clearly indicating that the justice of the mind is laid waste when restraint is not practiced in immoderate speech.

Hence James says: “If anyone thinks he is religious, yet does not bridle his tongue but deceives his heart, that person’s religion is vain” (James 1). Wicked people, being as light-minded in understanding as they are rash in speech, neglect to consider what they say before speaking; but what a shallow conscience conceives, an even more shallow tongue immediately brings forth.

Truth itself admonishes us, saying: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matthew 12). An idle word is one that lacks either the reason of just necessity or the purpose of pious usefulness. If, then, an account is demanded for idle speech, let us consider what punishment awaits excessive talk, in which one also sins through harmful words.

Abbot Sisoes once said: “Believe me, believe me: for thirty years now I have not prayed to God because of sin in any other way than by saying: ‘Lord Jesus Christ, protect me from my tongue.’ Yet even now, every day, I fall and sin through it.”

Abbot Macarius the Elder said to the brothers in Scetis: “After the church services, flee, brothers.” One brother said to him: “Father, where can we flee farther than this solitude?” He answered by placing his finger on his mouth: “This is what I say must be fled.” Then he entered his cell, closed the door, and sat alone.

Abbot Sisoes said: “Our exile consists in this: that a person keep his mouth.” Abbot Hyperichius said: “A monk who does not restrain his tongue in the time of anger will never be able to restrain his other passions.”

Abbot Longinus said to Abbot Lucius: “I have three thoughts: one is to go into exile.” The old man replied: “If you do not restrain your tongue, wherever you go you will not be an exile. But restrain your tongue here, and you will be an exile even here.”

A brother asked Abbot Sisoes: “I desire to guard my heart.” The old man said to him: “How can we guard our heart if our tongue has an open door?”

A brother asked Abbot Pastor: “How ought a monk to sit in his cell?” He replied: “As far as outward matters are concerned, he should perform manual labor, eat once, remain silent, and meditate. Inwardly, he can make progress in his cell by rebuking himself for his own faults wherever he goes.”

[Col. 0636A]

## CHAPTER XL. On conference

(Isidore, Book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 14.) Although reading is useful for instruction, when conference is added it provides greater understanding. It is better to confer than to read. Conference makes a person teachable, [Col. 0636B] for when questions are proposed, uncertainty about matters is removed, and hidden truth is often confirmed through objections. What is obscure or doubtful quickly becomes clear through conference.

Just as conference usually instructs, so contention destroys. For, abandoning the meaning of truth, it generates disputes and, by fighting with words, even blasphemes against God.

Reading needs the assistance of memory. If memory is naturally slower, it is nevertheless sharpened by frequent meditation and strengthened through constant reading. Often a lengthy reading, because of its length, erases the reader’s memory. But if it is brief, and once the book has been set aside the thought is reviewed in the mind, then it is read without labor; and by recalling what has been read, it does not slip from memory.

Silent reading is more acceptable to the senses than reading aloud. The intellect is more fully instructed when the reader’s voice is silent and the tongue moves in silence. For reading aloud both tires the body and dulls the sharpness of the voice.

(Thus far Isidore.) Abbot Pelagius said: “A soul living according to Christ’s will ought either faithfully to learn what it does not know or openly to teach what it knows. If it can do both but does not wish to do so, it suffers from the disease of madness. For the beginning of departing from God is distaste for instruction.”

Abbot Pastor said: “He who is querulous is not a monk; he who slanders his brother is not a monk; he who is angry is not a monk. But the one who is truly a monk is always humble and tranquil, full of charity, keeps the fear of God before his eyes, and guards his heart.”

An old man was asked what is meant by what is read, “the narrow and constricted way.” The old man replied: “The narrow and constricted way is for a person to do violence to his thoughts and, for God’s sake, cut off his own desires.” This is also what is written: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (Matthew 7).

An old man said: “Every morning and evening a monk ought to consider within himself what he has done of the things God wills and what he has not done. By reflecting in this way on his whole life and practicing repentance, he can be a monk.”

An old man said: “Whether you are sleeping, rising, or doing anything else, if God is before your eyes, the enemy will be unable to frighten you in anything. If such a thought remains in a person, the power of God also remains in him.”

[Col. 0637A]

## CHAPTER XLI. On love of neighbor and fraternal correction

Two things must be preserved regarding love of neighbor: first, that one inflict no evil; second, that one render good. The first is to take care not to harm; the second is to learn to do every good thing.

Friendship is a fellowship of souls. It begins with two, since love cannot exist among fewer than two. A friend is truly loved when he is loved not for his own sake but for God’s sake. Whoever loves a friend for his own sake embraces him foolishly. Deeply submerged in earthly things is the one who loves a mortal human being carnally more than is fitting.

(Isidore, Book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 32.) One who still serves the contagions of vices ought not to correct the vices of another. For it is improper to accuse someone else of what one still reproves in oneself. Whoever truly wishes to heal and correct a brother’s weakness should strive to make himself useful to his brother, admonishing the one he wishes to correct with a humble heart. He should do this out of compassion, as though facing a common danger, lest he too be subjected to temptation.

Just as spiritual men await the correction of another’s sin, so the insolent mock and insult those who offend. As far as they are concerned, they consider such people incurable; they do not incline their hearts toward compassionate mercy, but hate and blaspheme those who come before them.

Many consider their correction an act of charity. Many others, however, turn the very fact that they are corrected out of charity into an insult and affront. Thus it happens that they become worse through the very means by which they could have been corrected through obedience.

The righteous receive correction salutarily whenever they are reproved for their faults. Truth is burdensome to the wicked, and the discipline of righteousness is bitter; they take pleasure only in what flatters their own weakness. The hearts of the reprobate are slippery and yielding in consenting to evil, but exceedingly hard in consenting to good. Of such people Solomon says: “Whoever instructs a mocker does himself an injury” (Proverbs 9 and 15). Concerning the good person he says: “Teach the righteous, and he will hasten to receive it.” The wicked person turns hatred against the one who corrects him.

(Gregory, Book XX, chapter 21, *Moral Exposition on Job*, chapter 19.) If we remain silent about correcting someone because we fear that hatred will rise up against us, then we are certainly seeking not God’s gain but our own. We must know above all that sometimes, when the wicked are reproved, they become worse and pursue us with great hatred. We therefore spare them, not ourselves, if out of love for them we cease reproving them. Hence it is necessary for us sometimes to endure in silence what they are, so that by seeing in us what they are not, they may learn.

A righteous person must not at all fear that, while someone is being corrected, the person will inflict insults; rather, one must fear that, drawn into hatred, the person may become worse. Great care must be taken lest excessive talk drag the tongue along and extend it into the wantonness of detraction, lest malice arouse hatred and bend it toward the arrows of cursing.

Hence Solomon says: “Reprove the wise person, and he will love you; reprove the fool, and he will add to his hatred of you. Whoever loves discipline loves understanding; whoever hates the one who reproves him is a fool” (Proverbs 9 and 12).

But since the Apostle says: “Correct the restless, comfort the fainthearted, support the weak, and be patient toward all” (1 Thessalonians 5), it is necessary to set down here the pious examples of the Fathers’ correction.

Once a brother offended within the community and was expelled. After being expelled from the community, he went into a reed-filled marsh and wept there. It happened that some other brothers, going to Abbot Pastor, heard him crying. They went down to him, found him bound by great distress, and urged him to go to that solitary old man, but he did not consent, saying: “I will die in this place.”

The brothers went to Abbot Pastor and told him about him. He asked them to go to the man and say: “Abbot Pastor calls you to him.” When they had said this to him, he went to him. Seeing him afflicted, the old man rose, kissed him, and rejoicing with him, asked him to take food. He did so.

A brother asked Abbot Pastor: “I have committed a great sin, and I want to repent for three years.” Abbot Pastor said to him: “That is much.” The brother said: “Do you command one year?” The old man again said: “That is much.” Those who were present said: “Up to forty days.” The old man again said: “That is much.” And he added: “I think that if a person repents with all his heart, God will accept even three days of repentance.”

Abbot Joseph asked Abbot Pastor: “How is it necessary to fast?” Abbot Pastor said: “I want a person who eats every day to take a little away from himself, so that he is not satisfied.” Abbot Joseph said to him: “Then when you were young, did you not fast for two days at a time?” The old man said: “Believe me, brother, I fasted for three days at a time, and even for a week. But the great old men tested all these things and discovered that it is good to eat every day while taking a little away from oneself. They showed us this royal road, because it is lighter and easier.”

[Col. 0638C]

## CHAPTER XLII. On zeal in pastoral duty

(Gregory, on Ezekiel, Book I, Homily 12.) Every spiritual zeal of a teacher burns the teacher’s heart, because he is greatly tormented when he sees the weak abandoning eternal things and taking pleasure in temporal ones. No sacrifice is so pleasing to almighty God as zeal for souls, as the Psalmist says: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Psalm 68).

How pleasing to the almighty Lord is the burning of the heart that is undertaken for spiritual zeal is clearly shown when the Law commands fine flour to be offered in sacrifice. For it is written: “It shall be fried in a pan sprinkled with oil, and the priest who lawfully succeeds his father shall offer it hot as a most fragrant odor to the Lord, and it shall be wholly burned upon the altar” (Leviticus 6).

The fine flour is fried in the pan when the pure mind of the righteous is burned through the ardor of holy zeal. It is commanded to be sprinkled with oil when it burns and shines before almighty God through the inward organs of charity and mercy. Hence it is commanded to be offered hot to the Lord as a most fragrant odor, because if zeal does not possess love, the fine flour offered from the pan has lost its heat.

It must be carefully noted who is commanded to offer the fine flour: namely, the priest who has lawfully succeeded his father. That priest lawfully succeeds his father who shows by his conduct that he is a son of almighty God and who does not differ from inward nobility through the ignobility of his works.

The fine flour is commanded to be wholly burned upon the altar, so that it may become a whole burnt offering. The fine flour in the pan, therefore, is the pure mind of the righteous amid the affliction of spiritual zeal. It is fried through concern for souls and is reckoned to the Lord not merely as a sacrifice but also as a whole burnt offering.

Let us therefore take an iron pan and place it as an iron wall between us and the city (Ezekiel 4), that is, let us assume strong zeal, so that afterward we may find this strong fortification between ourselves and the soul of our hearer. We shall find this iron wall if we now hold it firmly: by teaching, guarding, persuading, rebuking, soothing, and frightening; acting sometimes gently and sometimes more severely.

(Thus far Gregory.) Above all, the person moved by zeal for uprightness must take care that anger does not pass beyond the rule of the mind. Considering the time and measure appropriate for punishing sin, that person must restrain the disturbance of the rising spirit through careful reflection, repress hostility, and order ardent impulses according to equity, so that he may be the more just an avenger of another’s fault because he first conquered his own.

Whoever is moved by zeal for uprightness should correct the faults of offenders in such a way that he himself, before correcting, grows through patience. He should judge his own fervor by rising above it, lest, excited beyond measure by that very zeal for uprightness, he wander far from uprightness.

[Col. 0639C]

## CHAPTER XLIII. On discretion in teaching
(Isidore, Book III of the Sentences, chapters 43, 44, 46.) The same doctrine is not to be applied to everyone; rather, the exhortations of teachers should vary according to the character of each person. For some are corrected by harsh rebuke, while others are corrected by gentle exhortation. Just as skilled physicians treat various bodily illnesses with different medicines, so that the remedy varies according to the variety of wounds, so the teacher of the Church will apply to each person the appropriate remedy of instruction and will announce what is fitting for each according to age, sex, and profession. For the first virtue of prudence is to assess the person whom one ought to teach.

Different action is required toward those entrusted to our governance if they offend, and toward those who have not been entrusted to us. If they are righteous, they are to be revered; but if they offend, they are to be corrected, as charity requires and opportunity permits, though not with the severity used toward those entrusted to our rule. Because of the people’s evil merit, the teaching of preaching is withdrawn. Because of the hearer’s good merit, speech is granted to the teacher. It lies within God’s power to give the word of instruction to whomever He wishes, or to take it away from whomever He wishes. This happens either because of the merit of the speaker or because of that of the hearer: sometimes the sermon is withdrawn from the teacher because of the people’s guilt, and sometimes it is granted because of the merits of both parties [another reading: “for the benefit of both”].

Whoever receives the office of teaching should sometimes, for a time, remain silent about the deeds of his neighbor when he does not at once judge that they should be corrected. For if he can correct them and dissimulates, it is true that he shares in another’s error. Often holy teachers, because of the obstinacy of the wicked and because they cannot reform the unrighteous, decide to remain silent toward them; but, unable to endure the heat of the spirit by which they are moved, they again burst forth into rebuke of the wicked.

Those who preside are condemned because of the wickedness of their subjects if they either fail to teach the ignorant or fail to rebuke sinners. For the Lord says to the prophet: “I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. If you do not speak so that the ungodly may turn from his way, he shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezekiel 3).

He who presides ought to care for those who are perishing, so that by his rebuke they may either be corrected from their sins or, if they prove incorrigible, be separated from the Church. Whoever is not corrected by a gentle word of chastisement must necessarily be rebuked more sharply. What cannot be healed gently must be cut away with grief. Whoever neglects to be corrected privately after being admonished about his sin must be rebuked publicly, so that the wound which cannot be healed secretly may be corrected openly.

Manifest sins are not to be cleansed by secret correction. Those who do harm openly must be rebuked openly, so that while they are healed by public reproof, those who had sinned by imitating them may be corrected. While one person is rebuked, many are amended. It is better that one be condemned for the salvation of many than that many be endangered through one person’s license.

Thus speech must be addressed to the offender in the manner demanded by the salvation of the one being corrected. If it is necessary to sprinkle the harshness of rebuke with some remedy of healing, one must nevertheless retain gentleness in the heart. Teachers sometimes strike their subjects with severe rebukes, yet they do not withdraw their charity from those whom they correct. (Thus far Isidore.)

Great is the subtlety of discernment required in the discipline of teaching, so that every ruler may know how both discreetly to spare and devoutly to cut away the faults of sinners. Those who forgive sins without correcting them, or who strike as though correcting without forgiving, possess the spirit of discernment.

It is written in the Book of Genesis: “If you offer correctly but do not divide correctly, you have sinned” (Genesis 4, according to the Septuagint). [Gregory, Book III of the *Exposition of Morals*, chapters 9 and 10, and Book I on Ezekiel, Homily 11.] To divide offerings correctly is to weigh each of our good efforts with discernment. [Col. 0640D] Whoever neglects to do this sins even when offering correctly. Often, while we undertake something with good zeal and carelessly neglect to discern the end by which it will be judged, we do not know what outcome it will have; and sometimes what is thought to be a cause of virtue becomes an accusation of crime. We therefore offer correctly when we perform a good work with good zeal; but we do not divide correctly if we postpone exercising discernment in a good work.

Abba Antony said: “There are some who wear out their bodies through abstinence, and because they lack discernment, they have become far from God.”

Abba Daniel used to say that to the extent the body grows strong, the soul becomes dry; and to the extent the body has been dried up, the soul grows strong.

Abba Pastor said: “Malice never drives out malice. If someone has done you harm, do good to him, so that by your good deed you may destroy his malice.”

An old man was asked by a brother: “How can I find God? Through fasts, labors, vigils, or mercy?” He replied: “Through all that you have listed—and through discernment. For I tell you that many have afflicted their flesh, and because they did this without discernment, they departed empty-handed, possessing nothing.”

[Col. 0641A]

## CHAPTER XLIV. On Divine Gifts

Almighty God, by the secret governance of His inner judgment, grants to one the word of wisdom, to another complete faith, to another the gift of healings, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, and to another the interpretation of speech (1 Corinthians 12). (Gregory, Book XX of the *Morals on Job*, chapters 18 and 11.)

Our Creator and Disposer governs all things in such a way that whoever might become proud because of the gift he possesses is humbled by the virtue he does not possess. Thus, when He raises each person up through an abundant grace, He also subjects one to another through their unequal gifts.

The almighty Lord orders everything so that, while each gift belongs to all through a certain bond of charity, all things become the possession of each individual. Each person possesses in another what he himself has not received, while he humbly offers for another’s possession what he has received.

The holy Church is the body of its heavenly Head. In it, one who sees lofty things is an eye; one who performs upright deeds is a hand; one who runs about attending to everything is a foot; one who understands the voice of the commandments is an ear; and one who distinguishes the stench of evil from the fragrance of good is a nose. For just as bodily limbs mutually provide their appointed services, they make one body out of themselves all together.

By a wondrous plan our Author and Disposer bestows on one what He denies to another, and denies to one what He bestows on another. Therefore, whoever strives to do more than he has received strives to exceed the measures assigned to him. If one of the faithful—perhaps someone given only to expound the hidden meanings of the commandments—also attempts to shine through miracles, or if someone whom the gift of heavenly power strengthens solely for miracles also strives to disclose the hidden things of divine law, he stretches out his foot toward destruction because he does not heed the limit of his own measure.

They said of Abba Hor that he never lied, never swore, never cursed anyone, and, unless necessity required it, never spoke to anyone.

Once Abba Hilarion came from Palestine to Abba Antony on the mountain, and Abba Antony said to him: “You have come well, morning star [*lucifer*], who rises in the morning.” Abba Hilarion replied: “Peace to you, pillar of light, who support the world.”

An abba said that a certain man had lived alone in the desert for forty years. When Abba John questioned him, he replied: “Ever since I became a solitary, the sun has never seen me eating.” Abba John answered him: “Nor has it seen me angry.”

They said of Abba Arsenius that he kept vigil throughout the night. When he wished to sleep toward morning, he would say to sleep: “Come, wicked servant.” Then he would steal a little sleep while sitting, and immediately rise.

[Col. 0642A]

## CHAPTER XLV. On the Grace of God

(Gregory, Book I on Ezekiel, Homily 9.) Through the grace of almighty God we can indeed strive toward good works, but we cannot complete them unless He Himself, who commands, helps us. We must understand that our evil deeds belong solely to us. Our good deeds, however, belong both to almighty God and to us. For He precedes us by inspiring us to will, and follows after us by helping us, so that we do not will in vain but can accomplish what we will.

When grace precedes and good will follows, what is the gift of almighty God becomes our merit. Paul explains this well in a brief statement, saying: “I labored more than all of them” (1 Corinthians 15). But, lest he seem to attribute what he had done to his own virtue, he added: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (ibid.).

(Isidore, Book II of the *Sentences*, chapter 5.) Sometimes, when we sin, God does not withdraw His grace from us, so that the human mind may rise toward hope in divine mercy. For all good things are given to us by Him, grace preceding us. A person’s progress is God’s gift; no one can correct himself by himself, but only through God, as the prophet testifies: “I know, Lord, that a man’s way is not his own, nor does it belong to a man to walk and direct his steps” (Jeremiah 10).

Spiritual grace is not distributed to everyone but is granted only to the elect. The gifts of grace are given to one person in one form and to another in another; no one is granted to possess one gift in such a way that he has no need of another. It is beyond doubt that those whom certain people surpass in excellence of virtue may, through God’s sudden preceding grace, surpass others in the short path of holiness, so that while they are last in conversion, they suddenly become first in the summit of virtue.

When each person receives some good gift, he should not desire more than he has merited, lest, while attempting to seize another limb’s function, he lose what he has merited. For whoever, not content with his own function, steals another’s, disturbs the entire order of the body.

A brother asked an old man: “If I am in some place and tribulation arises for me, and I have no one to whom I can entrust myself and disclose the suffering of my soul, what should I do?” The old man said to him: “Believe in God, for He will send His grace and will satisfy you if you ask Him in truth.” He added: “For I have heard that something of this kind happened in Scetis. There was a man who endured temptations. Having no confidence in anyone to whom he could confess, he packed his bag in the evening so that he could leave. And behold, at night the grace of the Lord appeared to him in the form of a virgin and said to him: ‘Go nowhere, but remain here with me; none of the things you have heard will harm you.’ Believing her words, he sat down, and his heart was immediately healed.”

[Col. 0642A]

## CHAPTER XLVI. On Good Subjects

(D. Gregory, *Pastoral Care*, Part III, Admonition 5, 11.) Subjects must be admonished not to criticize their superiors rashly if they perhaps see them doing something blameworthy, lest, while rightly rebuking evil, they plunge themselves into deeper things through the impulse of pride. Subjects must be admonished not to become bolder against their superiors when they observe their faults; rather, even if some of their deeds are very wrong, they should judge them within themselves in such a way that, constrained by fear of God, they nevertheless do not refuse to bear the yoke of reverence under them.

Benevolent subjects must be admonished to rejoice in the good of others in such a way that they also desire to possess good of their own; they should praise the deeds of their neighbors with love in such a way that they also multiply them by imitation. Otherwise, if in the contest of the present life they stand as devoted supporters but lazy spectators of another’s struggle, they will remain without a prize after the contest because they do not labor now in the contest, and then, afflicted, will look upon the palms of those whose labor they now continue to observe in idleness.

We sin greatly if we do not love the good deeds of others but do nothing deserving of reward; and if we do not imitate, as far as we can, those things we love. The good deeds of others are truly ours when we love them in others, even if we cannot imitate them; what lovers love becomes theirs.

(Gregory, Book XXV of the *Exposition of Morals*, chapter 22.) Those who advance through great virtues in the bosom of the holy Church should not despise the lives of their superiors when they see them occupied with external matters. For the fact that they themselves safely penetrate inward things is due to the help of those who labor outwardly against the storms of this age.

What grace of its whiteness would linen retain if rain touched it? Or what brilliance and splendor would scarlet or hyacinth display if the dust that covered them defiled them? Let there therefore be above a strong texture of goat-hair cloth suited to the dust, and within a hyacinth-colored material suitable for adornment. Let those who devote themselves solely to spiritual matters adorn the Church. Let those whom the burden of bodily affairs weighs down cover the Church. Therefore, let no one who already shines spiritually within the holy Church murmur against his ruler for attending to external matters. If you shine safely within like scarlet, why do you accuse the goat-hair cloth that protects you? (Thus far Gregory.)

Abba Joseph asked Abba Pastor: “Tell me, how can I become a monk?” The old man replied: “If you wish to find rest both in this age and in the age to come, say in every matter, ‘Who am I?’ and judge no one.”

A brother asked Abba Pastor: “What shall I do? I become fainthearted while I sit.” The old man said to him: “Judge no one, despise no one, condemn no one, and slander no one. Then God will grant you rest, and your sitting will be without disturbance.”

A holy man, hearing of someone who had sinned, wept bitterly and said: “He today; I tomorrow.” Nevertheless, however you see someone sinning before you, do not judge him; rather, judge yourself, the sinner, more than him.

Often something is done by those of greater rank as a matter of prudent administration which those of lesser rank consider an error. Often many things are said by the strong which the weak judge precisely because they do not understand them. Thus some subjects extend the hand of criticism against this, but immediately fall away from life itself through their rashness. Levites therefore stretched out a hand as though to help, but, because he transgressed, lost his life (2 Samuel 6), since whenever the weak criticize the deeds of the strong, they themselves are rejected from the lot of the living.

[Col. 0644A]

## CHAPTER XLVII. That the Monk’s Treasure May Be Stored in Heaven

The Lord admonishes us, saying: “Store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys” (Matthew 6). And concerning how each person may attain the perfection of monastic life, He says again: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come and follow me” (Matthew 19; Mark 10; Luke 19).

Let us therefore, brothers, place our treasure in heaven, where we need not fear an enemy or invader. Let us store the treasure of our deeds and virtues in heaven, where we need not fear either a hidden thief or a violent robber. For our homeland is paradise. In our homeland, where we shall afterward be received, we must now store up many treasures of good virtues, so that after the end of this age we may deserve to receive fruits multiplied a hundredfold.

“For the saints,” says the prophet, “shall possess double in their land” (Isaiah 61)—that is, in the land of the living they shall possess together blessedness of mind and body: “where the Lord Jesus Christ will reform the body of our lowliness, making it like the body of His glory” (Philippians 3).

(Cyprian, *On Mortality*, at the end.) A great number of our beloved awaits us there. A large crowd of parents, brothers, and sisters longs to see us; secure already in their own immortality, but still concerned for our salvation. There the choir of patriarchs, the company of prophets and apostles and virgins, and the entire assembly of all the saints longs to behold us. O what great joy it is to enter the fellowship of all these saints and to come into their blessed embrace! O what supreme and perpetual happiness it is there to behold the glorious choirs of the apostles, to see the sacred number of the rejoicing prophets, and to stand among the white-robed assembly of virgins, martyrs, and confessors!

Abba Hyperichius said: “The monk’s treasure is voluntary poverty. Therefore, brother, store up treasure for yourself in heaven, for the ages are there for resting without end.”

Abba Evagrius used to say: “When you sit in your cell, gather your mind to yourself, remember the day of death, and then you will see the mortification of your body. Consider destruction, accept sorrow, avoid the vanities of this world. Be modest and watchful, so that you may always remain in the same purpose of quiet and not grow weak. Remember also the good things stored up for the righteous. Have confidence before God the Father and His Christ, before the angels and powers and all the people of the kingdom of heaven; think upon His gifts, rest, and joy. Rejoice, exult, and be glad over the good things stored up for the righteous, and hasten to enjoy them.”

[Col. 0644A]

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On Counsel

Solomon admonishes us concerning this virtue of counsel, saying: “Listen, my son, to counsel and receive discipline, so that you may be wise at your end” (Proverbs 19). “My son, do nothing without counsel, and afterward you will not regret it” (Ecclesiasticus 32). “The astute person does everything with counsel” (Proverbs 13). “Those who do everything with counsel are governed by much wisdom” (ibid.). “Thoughts are scattered where there is no counsel” (Proverbs 15). “Where there are many counselors, they are confirmed.” “The heart delights in ointment and various fragrances, and the soul is sweetened by the good counsels of a friend” (Proverbs 27). “War is begun with deliberation, and there is safety where there are many counsels” (Proverbs 24). “The knowledge of the wise will overflow like a flood, and his counsel remains like a fountain of life” (Ecclesiasticus 21).

A good counsel is indeed a great matter and exceedingly necessary for monks. All those on earth who wished to ascend to the heavenly homeland loved this virtue of counsel. Through this virtue of counsel the martyrs, so that they might receive eternal life from the Lord, handed over their mortal bodies to death. Through this virtue of counsel virgins and confessors persevered in the Lord’s service to the end.

Serious counsel of the heart drives out all instability of wandering. There are souls that, moved lightly, desire now one thing and now another. Almighty God does not lightly regard these light fluctuations of minds; by abandoning the wandering of the heart He judges it. But when He looks upon it through grace, He fixes the wandering mind in the stability of counsel. When almighty God mercifully deigns to regard the light movements of a person, He immediately forms him into maturity of constancy and, by the regard of heavenly grace, suddenly brings his heart to the gravity of counsel.

In every work you are thinking of doing, think first of God, and carefully examine whether what you are thinking is according to God. If it is right before God, complete it; but if it is perverse, cut it away from your soul.

Let us also, brothers, do everything with counsel, for it is written: “Before all your works let a truthful word go before you, and before every action let there be firm counsel; and in all these things beseech the Most High, that He may direct your way in truth. For if the great Lord wills, He will fill you with the spirit of understanding, and like showers He will send you the words of His wisdom; He will open your mouth in prayer, direct your counsel toward good, and your memory will not be erased forever” (Ecclesiasticus 37, 39).

At the beginning of his monastic life Abba Evagrius came to an old man, seeking counsel, and said to him: “Tell me, abba, a word by which I may be saved.” The old man said to him: “If you wish to be saved, when you go to someone, do not speak before he questions you.” Evagrius, moved by this saying, replied: “Believe me, I have read many books, but I have never found such instruction.” And he departed, greatly advanced.

Abba Pastor said: “Whoever teaches and does not do what he teaches is like a canal that satisfies all who come to it and washes away their filth, but cannot cleanse itself; all filth and impurity remain in it.”

A brother asked Abba Pastor: “What does that passage mean which is written: ‘Whoever is angry with his brother without cause’?” (Matthew 5). He replied: “Whatever your brother may wish to burden you with, do not become angry against him until he casts out your right eye; otherwise you are angry with him without cause. But if someone wishes to separate you from God, be angry for this reason.”

[Col. 0646A]

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the Sanctification of Heart and Body

Among other things, Paul speaks as follows about sanctification in his Letter to the Thessalonians: “This is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication” (1 Thessalonians 4). “This is the will of God,” he says—that is, this pleases God: that you be sanctified equally in heart and body. For if this had not pleased Him, He would not have commanded us, saying: “Be holy, because I also am holy, the Lord your God” (Leviticus 19 and 20).

But truly and without any doubt, the sanctity by which the devout and the magnificence by which the great are made holy before God consist in the sanctification of that same Creator of ours, as it is written: “Holiness and magnificence are in His sanctification” (Psalm 95). Hence the Lord also says: “Keep my commandments and do them; I am the Lord who sanctify you” (Leviticus 20).

Although this virtue of sanctification ought to be present in all Christians, it is especially suitable and becoming to the priestly order. Hence the Lord says to Moses: “You shall clothe Aaron and his sons and sanctify them, so that they may serve me as priests” (Exodus 28). And so that the priest may not be defiled by the dead, because he is consecrated to his God and offers the bread of the Presence: “Let him be holy, because I am holy, the Lord who sanctify you” (Leviticus 21).

For unless a sacrifice is offered to God by a priest sanctified in heart and body, it will not be pleasing to Him, since He knows that the priest’s heart is polluted by the contagion of fornication. Therefore, in this passage the Apostle urges not only the Thessalonians (1 Thessalonians 4) but all who believe in Christ to abstain from fornication, because just as chastity of the flesh is preserved through humility of mind, so through pride of heart one proceeds into the uncleanness of lust.

(Isidore, Book II of the *Sentences*, chapter 39.) For this reason demons associate more familiarly with the lustful and the proud than with other sinners, because through bodily lust the devil binds them with his chains, so that, separated from God and joined to demons, they cannot possess the kingdom of heaven with the saints.

The Apostle John also speaks thus about this virtue of sanctification: “Everyone who has this hope in him sanctifies himself, just as he is holy” (1 John 3). Many say that they have hope of heavenly life in Christ, but by living carelessly they empty this confession of its force. The person who strives to devote himself to good works gives clear evidence of heavenly hope, being certain that no one will attain the likeness of God in the future except by imitating God’s holiness in the present through sanctifying himself—that is, by denying ungodliness and worldly desires and living soberly, justly, and devoutly (Titus 2).

Whoever has hope in the Lord sanctifies himself, insofar as he can, by looking to Him in all things and earnestly seeking His grace, who said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15), and saying to Him: “Be my helper; do not abandon me” (Psalm 26). Thus He sanctifies us, just as He Himself is holy (1 John 3). But He is holy by eternity, while we are holy by faith.

In ancient times bishops, presbyters, and deacons were ordained as husbands of one wife (1 Timothy 3). Now, however, since purity has increased for the sake of holiness, the rule of the sacred canons forbids all of them every carnal union. In the Old Testament, during the time when the priests were serving at the altar, they abstained from intercourse with their wives (Exodus 28); now, however, since every day we must either prepare the Lord’s body at the altar or receive it, we must abstain daily from carnal intercourse.

Hence Paul admonishes Timothy, saying: “Be an example to the faithful in speech, in conduct, in charity, in faith, and in chastity” (1 Timothy 4). Whoever ought to provide others an example in speech must not be ignorant of the proper manner of speaking but must carefully consider what he ought to say, to whom, when, and how, so that his speech may not be foolish but, according to the Lord’s command, seasoned with the salt of wisdom (Matthew 5).

He provides others a good example in conduct who lives chastely, devoutly, and justly in this age (Luke 14). He provides others a good example in charity who loves God with all his heart, all his mind, and all his strength, and his neighbor as himself (Deuteronomy 6; Matthew 22; Luke 10). He provides others a good example in faith who lives well by believing rightly and preserves right faith by living well. He provides others a good example in chastity who, loving the beauty of chastity, not only preserves it in his body but also guards it from evil thoughts in his mind, because bodily purity is of no benefit where the mind is not whole.

[Col. 0647C]

## CHAPTER L. On the Divine Call to Mercy

The call of divine mercy—which occurs in different ways, at different ages, and at different times—is made not because of human merit but always freely by God alone, who is merciful, as the Apostle says: “The gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11). He also says to Timothy: “He delivered us and called us with His holy calling, not according to our works but according to His purpose and grace” (2 Timothy 1).

They are called in different ways, as has been said: some, divinely inspired, are called while bodily healthy; others are afflicted with bodily illness; still others are oppressed by various losses or different tribulations. They are also called at different ages: some in infancy, others in adolescence, others in youth, others in old age, and still others in extreme old age. They are called at different hours of the day: some early in the morning, others at the third hour, others at the sixth, others at the ninth, and still others at the eleventh hour.

None of all these is called into uncleanness; all are called by the holy God to sanctification of heart and body. For the holy God always wishes to have holy ministers, as He Himself says in the Gospel: “For their sake I sanctify myself, so that they too may be sanctified in truth” (John 17).

An old man said: “There were two neighboring brothers, one a stranger and the other a native. The stranger was somewhat negligent, while the native was very diligent. It happened that the stranger fell asleep in peace. The old man who lived near them, being watchful, saw a multitude of angels escorting his soul. When he came to heaven to enter, a question arose concerning that soul. Then a voice came from above, saying: ‘It is clear that he was somewhat negligent, but because he was a stranger, open to him.’

“After this the native fell asleep, and all his relatives came to him. But the old man did not see angels coming to escort his soul. Amazed, he said: ‘How did that stranger, though more negligent, receive such glory, while this man, though diligent, deserved nothing of the kind?’ A voice came to him and said: ‘When this diligent man came to sleep, he opened his eyes and saw his parents weeping, and his soul was comforted. But the stranger, although more negligent, saw none of his own; he groaned and wept, and God comforted him.’”

They said of Abba Sisoes that on the day of his death, while the fathers were sitting around him, his face shone like the sun. He said to them: “Behold, the choir of prophets and apostles is coming.” Again he said: “Behold, angels have come to receive me.” Once more his face became like the sun, and they all were afraid. He said to them again: “See, the Lord is coming, saying: ‘Bring me the chosen vessel of the desert.’” Immediately he gave up his spirit, and the whole place was filled with radiance and the fragrance of sweetness.

[Col. 0648C]

## CHAPTER LI. On the Love and Grace of God

The Apostle speaks as follows concerning this chapter: “But God, who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which He loved us, when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ. By whose grace we have been saved; and He raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ, so that He might show the surpassing riches of His grace in goodness toward us in Christ Jesus. For by grace we have been saved through faith” (Ephesians 2).

God is said to be rich in mercy because He is almighty and the earth is full of His mercy. God is called rich in mercy because He mercifully draws all sinners to repentance and mercifully grants them perseverance in it. He is also called rich because of the great love with which He loved the human race. Almighty God loved us so greatly that He handed over His Son to death for us, as it is written: “God did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all” (Romans 8).

For it is a great and extraordinary love to hand over the only-begotten Son for sinful servants and to love those same rebellious servants as sons. Therefore, brothers, we ought to consider how greatly the Lord loves us, since He deigned to love sinners so greatly. When we were dead because of our transgressions, He made us alive in Christ Jesus (Ephesians 2), granting us, through His mercy, one and the same everlasting life with Him.

The soul is called dead when it is said to be stained with deadly vices, as the Apostle says: “And you, when you were dead in your transgressions and sins, in which you once walked openly” (Ephesians 2). Sin is called the death of the soul, as the prophet says: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18).

A person’s soul sins in two ways: by not doing what it was commanded to do, and by doing what was forbidden. “By whose grace,” he says, “we have been saved”—that is, not by the former works of our life, but by faith alone and the grace of baptism we have received the forgiveness of our sins.

Our Lord Himself, who is rich in mercy, brothers, because of the great love with which He loved us, raised us up together and made us sit in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus. Consider, brothers, what thanksgiving we ought to offer to our Creator, since in our nature our Creator and Redeemer, Christ, both rose from the dead and ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father.

In this nature of ours we too have risen with Him, ascended, and sit at the right hand of the Father. Hence the holy man, who while living in the flesh has his way of life in heaven, does not hesitate to say that the saints already sit and reign with Christ at the Father’s right hand.

How great is the magnitude of the benefit and how manifold the grace by which He has made us sit with the Lord and reign with Christ is shown by this: we who once were held by the law of hell now reign in Christ and sit with Him. Truly abundant is the grace that not only forgave sins but also placed us, raised together with Christ, at the right hand of God.

An angel said to a certain bishop: “God loved this world so greatly that He gave His only-begotten Son for it” (John 3). Since, then, He chose to die for human beings when they were enemies, will He not much more, once they have become members of His household and repented of what they had done, release them from punishments and grant them the good things He has prepared?

Know this, then: no human sins overcome the mercy of God. Let them only wash away through good deeds the evil things they committed long ago by patience. Since God is merciful, He knows the weaknesses of your race, the force of its passions, and the power and cunning of the devil. When people fall into sins, He as though forgives them and awaits their correction, showing patience toward them. But when they turn back and entreat His goodness, He sympathizes with them as with the weak, immediately releases them from their torments, and grants them the good things prepared for the righteous.

[Col. 0649B]

## CHAPTER LII. On the Fact That the Saints Are Called Sons of Light
The apostle John says: “We announce to you that God is light, and there are no darknesses in him at all” (1 John 1). Therefore, deservedly, those who are sons of God are called sons of light by the Apostle, when he says: “For you are all sons of light and sons of day; you are not of night or of darkness” (1 Thess. 5). For just as they are called sons of love or sons of peace because they possess love and peace within themselves, so they are also called sons of light because they possess within themselves the light of faith and knowledge. Hence Paul says elsewhere: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as sons of light” (Eph. 5).

Or they are called sons of light—that is, sons of God—as the Lord says: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8). And “sons of day,” he says, that is, of the Lord Jesus Christ, who said to his disciples: “Are there not twelve hours of the day? Whoever walks in the day does not stumble” (John 11). He wished himself to be signified by the day, and the apostles by the hours. For he himself is spiritually the true day, because it was said of him: “The sanctified Day has shone upon us.” The twelve hours, as has been said, are his twelve apostles, because, to show that he himself was the day, he chose twelve apostles.

Whoever does the truth and comes into the light is light, and a son of light and of day (John 3). For just as no one exists from himself, so no one is illumined from himself; rather, he is illumined by the one of whom it is written: “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). Whoever rises from the darkness of ignorance and from sins, and is illumined by the one who said, “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8), is deservedly called a son of light and of day. For we are sons of God by imitation, not by nature, as the Savior says: “So that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5).

[Col. 0650B]

## CHAPTER LIII. On Hope

Concerning this chapter on hope, the Apostle Paul likewise says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Heb. 11). For no one hopes for what he sees, but “what we do not see, we await with patience” (Rom. 8).

Hope is the expectation of future good things; it expresses an attitude of humility and the obedience of diligent service. It is called hope because it is as though it were a foot—*pes*—for advancing. Conversely, despair is so called because it has no ability to advance: for when someone loves sin, he does not hope for future glory. The person who faithfully keeps God’s commandments awaits confidently.

Hope is rightly called blessed by the Apostle, because through it we shall deserve to be sons and heirs of God: “Indeed, heirs of God, and fellow-heirs with Christ. When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (Rom. 8). There sin will not rule over us, and eternal life will be granted to us. There we shall possess the splendor of the sun and the fellowship of the angels.

Hence the Apostle says elsewhere: “Because of the hope that has been laid up for us in heaven” (Col. 1). For the hope of future good things is not yet visible to bodily eyes; rather, it has been laid up for us in heaven. Concerning this hope the same Apostle says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2).

For the hope of all the elect is also eternal life, which is still laid up for us in heaven in Christ: “But when Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3). Elsewhere the same Apostle says: “But our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God the Father, who loved us and gave us eternal consolation and good hope through grace” (2 Thess. 2).

It is called good hope because it is written: “Those who hope in the Lord will not lack any good thing” (Ps. 33). It is also called the hope of mercy: “For mercy will surround those who hope in the Lord” (Ps. 31). Peter calls it living hope (1 Pet. 2), because it promises us eternal life. According to the character of its gift, it also receives an addition to its name.

In this passage, “good hope through grace” may be understood even more clearly and sublimely as the Lord Jesus Christ himself, who alone, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is good. Concerning him the Psalmist sings: “The Lord is my hope, from my youth” (Ps. 70).

[Isidore, *Sentences*, book II, [Col. 0651B] chapter 4.]

We must greatly fear both that, because of the hope of forgiveness which God promises, we should persist in sinning, and that, because he justly punishes sins, we should despair of forgiveness. Rather, avoiding both dangers, we should turn away from evil and hope for forgiveness from God’s mercy.

[Col. 0651B]

## CHAPTER LIV. That We Should Pray Without Ceasing

It seems to me that praying without ceasing can happen in two ways: either through the intention of the heart or through works of mercy.

A person prays through the intention of the heart when, inflamed by the desire for heavenly contemplation, he is wholly devoted to the love of his Creator. For the continual persistence of the love of God is prayer without ceasing.
