Prayer also takes place without ceasing when the treasure of almsgiving is stored up in heaven, as the Lord says: “Store up treasures for yourselves in heaven” (Matt. 6). For the person who stores up treasure in heaven—whether he walks, sits, eats, drinks, speaks, keeps silent, or sleeps—his treasure, deposited in the sight of the Lord, prays to the Lord without ceasing.

Hence the Lord himself says: “Hide your alms in the bosom of the poor, and they themselves will pray for you to the Lord” (Sir. 29; Luke 11).

Some also hold that the person prays without ceasing who strives to preserve himself afterward in prayer as he first presents himself in it. This is likewise said to have happened with Hannah as she prayed: she remained in the very disposition of compunction in which she had prayed until she obtained from the Lord her God what she had asked (1 Sam. 1).

They said of Abbot Arsenius that on Saturday evening, as Sunday was dawning, he would leave the sun behind him, extend his hands toward heaven, and pray until the sun rising on Sunday morning illumined his face; and then he would sit down.

On one occasion some monks came to Abbot Lucius. They were called Euthicae, that is, “those who pray.” The old man asked them: “What is the work of your hands?” They answered: “We do not engage in any manual labor, but, as the Apostle says, ‘we pray without ceasing’” (1 Thess. 5).

The old man said to them: “Then you do not eat?” They answered: “Indeed, we eat.” He said to them: “When you eat, then, who prays for you?” Again he asked them: “Do you not sleep?” They answered: “We sleep.” The old man said: “And when you sleep, who prays for you?” They could find nothing to answer him.

The old man said: “Forgive me, brothers, for you are not doing as you said. But I will show you that, while working with my hands, I pray without ceasing. I sit, with God’s help, soaking a few palm leaves; I make a braid from them and say: ‘Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy. And according to the multitude of your mercies, blot out my iniquity’” (Ps. 50).

And he said to them: “Is this prayer or not?” They answered: “It is.” He said to them: “When I remain working and praying all day, I make approximately sixteen coins. From these I put two at the door, and I eat the remainder. Whoever takes those two coins prays for me during the time when I eat or sleep. Thus, by the grace of God, what is written is fulfilled in me: ‘Pray without ceasing’” (1 Thess. 5).

[Col. 0652B]

## CHAPTER LV. That We Should Be Simple, Like the Sons of God

A person is blameless who, insofar as human frailty permits, strives to lead a life without fault. Fault gives rise to complaint against God or one’s neighbor when an offense has been committed. Therefore, the person lives without blame who does not lead a life sullied by vices and does not commit an offense for which complaint could justly be brought against him.

“And be simple,” the Apostle says, “like the sons of God” (Phil. 2). God is simple by nature. Those who are already sons of God by adoption and desire to be sons by imitation must therefore be simple, like doves (Matt. 10). For it is written: “The simplicity of the upright will guide them” (Prov. 11).

[Gregory, *Moralia*, book XII, chapter 19.]

Nothing is happier than a simple heart: for the person who displays innocence toward others has nothing to fear from others. His simplicity is, as it were, a fortress of strength; he is not afraid of suffering what he does not remember having done.

“Blameless, without reproach” (Phil. 2). Paul teaches and desires that the sons of God be most adorned and honorable. For the person who sins is stained. The stain is the sin itself, which stains and contaminates the one who commits it.

With God’s help, the sons of God can live undefiled and without reproach if they do not perform works deserving reproach, even though they may be reproached by the malicious. “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 118).

The holy Syncletica said: “Let us become prudent like serpents and simple like doves” (Matt. 10), so that we may understand his snares with discernment. For the command to become prudent like serpents was given so that we would not be unaware of the devil’s attacks and devices. Indeed, something similar is overcome by another similar vice. The simplicity of the dove, moreover, indicates purity of action.

[Col. 0652B]

## CHAPTER LVI. That We Should Do Everything Without Murmuring

Whoever murmurs against the commands of the Lord or of his teacher undoubtedly hesitates to receive the rewards of his labor. All those among the children of Israel who murmured against the Lord and Moses in the wilderness perished in that same wilderness from the bites of poisonous serpents, and did not receive an inheritance among their brothers in the land of promise (Num. 14 and 21).

Therefore, if any one of us desires to have an inheritance among God’s elect, as among brothers, in the land of the living, he must live without murmuring in the present age. A person murmurs all the more about present labor the more he despairs of receiving an eternal recompense for his work. For the person who does not doubt the hope of recompense, even when placed amid difficult works, does not murmur at his teacher and Lord.

The son who is disciplined by his father in order to receive an eternal inheritance ought not to murmur, but rather to rejoice in his father’s discipline. When a perverse mind is corrected through reprimand or urged toward good through the sweetness of preaching, it becomes worse because of the correction and is thereby inflamed with the iniquity of murmuring—precisely where it ought to have been restrained from iniquity.

Whoever is struck because of sin, unless he resists by murmuring, begins to be just by that very fact: he does not accuse the justice of the one who strikes him. Hence Paul also says: “Do not murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by serpents” (1 Cor. 10; Num. 21).

The Book of Numbers relates that the people of Israel, wearied in the wilderness by the long journey and labor, murmured; therefore the Lord sent fiery serpents among them. The venom of the wounds inflicted by the fiery serpents signifies the poisons of vices, which destroy by spiritual death the soul they touch.

And rightly was the people murmuring against the Lord laid low by the bites of serpents, so that from the order of the outward scourge it might recognize how great an inward destruction it was suffering through murmuring.

Abbot Joseph said that there are three honorable orders in the sight of the Lord. The first is when a person becomes ill and temptations are added to him, and he receives them with thanksgiving. The second is when someone performs all his works purely before the Lord and seeks nothing human in them. The third is when someone remains in submission, obeys spiritual commands without murmuring, and renounces all his own wishes.

[Col. 0653C]

## CHAPTER LVII. On the Circumcision of Vices

Concerning this chapter Paul says: “For we are the circumcision, who serve God in the Spirit and glory in Christ Jesus” (Phil. 3). It is as though he were saying to those circumcised in the flesh: “You are the circumcision of the skin of your foreskin; we are the circumcision of our heart and body. You cut away from yourselves God’s good creation; we spiritually circumcise vices from ourselves.”

Therefore, “we are the circumcision, who serve God in the Spirit”—not you, who bring the mark of circumcision upon your bodies. When he says, “We are the circumcision, who serve God in the Spirit,” it is as though he were saying: “We are the righteousness of spiritual circumcision, because, having been made spiritual through righteousness, we spiritually serve our Creator.”

For he did not say, “We are circumcised,” or “We have circumcision,” but, “We are,” he says, “the circumcision”—that is, we are the purity and righteousness of spiritual circumcision, possessing spiritual righteousness and purity.

In the Law and the Prophets we are commanded to be circumcised in two ways: in flesh and in heart. In the flesh, where it says: “Circumcise the flesh of your foreskin” (Gen. 17; Deut. 10); in the heart, where it says: “Circumcise the foreskins of your hearts” (Jer. 4).

We are circumcised in the flesh when we cut away from ourselves carnal vices—that is, adulteries, fornications, impurity, gluttony, drunkenness, and all other things of this kind, which operate through the desire of the flesh. We are circumcised in the heart when we cut away from ourselves spiritual vices—that is, pride, boastfulness, anger, quarrelling, hatred, envy, and the like.

The rejection of all these vices and the assumption of good virtues make a person righteous. Paul calls this righteousness of circumcision, by which people are made righteous, “circumcision.”

“We who serve God in the Spirit,” he says (Phil. 3), for “God is Spirit” (John 4). And just as those who worship God must worship in spirit and truth, so those who serve God must serve him in spirit and truth.

“And we glory in Christ Jesus.” It is as though he were saying: “We who serve God in the Spirit do not glory carnally in circumcision of the flesh, but spiritually in Christ Jesus, from whom we have also received the virtue of faith, through which we glory in him.”

The fact that the Lord was circumcised on the eighth day and, after the thirty-third day following his circumcision, was brought to the temple so that an offering might be made for him and he might be called holy to the Lord (Luke 2) signifies mystically that no one is worthy to be presented before the Lord’s presence unless he has been circumcised of his vices, and that no one can perfectly enter the joys of the heavenly city unless he has been freed from the bonds of mortality.

The apostle James also urges us to perform this circumcision of carnal and spiritual vices, saying: “Putting aside all impurity and abundance of wickedness, receive with meekness the implanted word” (James 1). First he commands the body and mind to be circumcised of vices, so that we may be worthy to receive the word of salvation.

He calls every impurity that of both flesh and soul; but he indicates that wickedness pertains only to the perversity of the inner person. The apostle Peter likewise admonishes us to carry out this circumcision of vices, saying: “Beloved, I urge you, as sojourners and exiles, to abstain from carnal desires” (1 Pet. 2).

He clearly teaches us to abstain from carnal desires because they are always at war against our soul. When the flesh is weakly subjected to enticing desires, the army of vices is firmly armed against the soul.

Abbot Ammonas said that he had remained for fourteen years in Scetis, entreating God night and day to grant him the power to overcome the flesh.

[Col. 0654D]

## CHAPTER LVIII. On the Fruit of Righteousness

The apostle James says: “The fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace” (James 3).

[Col. 0655A]

Everything we do in this life is seed for future recompense. That recompense itself is the fruit of present works, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap. The one who sows in the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh; but the one who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit” (Gal. 6).

Therefore it is rightly said that “the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.” The fruit of righteousness is eternal life, which is repaid for works of righteousness, because those who seek peace follow it. With that peace to which they devote themselves, as with the best seed, they sprinkle the soil of their heart, so that through the daily growth of good works they may reach the fruit of heavenly life.

Concerning this it is written elsewhere: “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy” (Ps. 125). Hence Paul also says: “Filled with the fruit of righteousness through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God” (Phil. 5).

In his Epistle to the Galatians he called this fruit of righteousness the fruit of the Spirit, saying: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity” (Gal. 5).

He wants us to be filled with this manifold fruit on the day of Christ Jesus, to the glory and praise of God. For concerning all the good things we have received from him, we ought to return glory and praise not to ourselves but to him, saying with the Psalmist: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. 113).

Once two brothers came to a certain old man. It was the old man’s custom not to eat every day. When he saw the brothers, however, he received them joyfully and said: “Fasting has its own reward. Again, the person who eats out of love fulfills two commandments, because he abandons his own will and fulfills the commandment by refreshing the brothers.”

One of the Fathers said: “Unless you first hate vices, you will not be able to love. Unless, therefore, you hate sin, you will not do righteousness.” It is written: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 33).

Nevertheless, in all these matters the purpose of the mind is required everywhere. Adam, standing in paradise, transgressed God’s commandment; Job, sitting in the dung, kept it. Hence it is clear that God seeks from a person a good purpose, and that the person should always fear him.

[Col. 0655C]

## CHAPTER LIX. That We Should Return to the Innocence of Childhood

[Col. 0655D]

The Lord says in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18). The Lord commanded this not only to the apostles but also to all who believe in him and desire to enter the kingdom of heaven.

We are not therefore commanded to possess the age of little children, but to maintain the conduct of innocence. What they possess through the years of childhood, we are to possess through the purity of innocence, so that we may be children in malice, not in wisdom.

Hence the Lord himself says again: “Whoever humbles himself like this little child is greater in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18). It is as though he were saying: “Just as this little child, whose example I give you, does not persist in anger, does not remember an injury, is not delighted when he sees a beautiful woman, and does not think one thing while saying another—so you also will not be able to enter the kingdom of heaven unless you possess such innocence and purity of mind.”

The apostle Peter explains how we can attain the innocence of childhood, saying: “Therefore, putting aside all malice and all deceit and hypocrisies and envies and all slanders, like newborn infants, long for rational milk without deceit, so that by it you may grow into salvation” (1 Pet. 2).

It is as though he were saying: “Since you have already been reborn through the water of baptism and have become sons of God through the grace of the Holy Spirit in baptism, now, through your devotion to a good way of life, be what infants are by the nature of their harmless age”—that is, having no malice, deceit, hypocrisies, or slanders (Eph. 4), so that all bitterness, fury, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy, together with all malice, may be removed from you.

Returning in this way to the infancy of innocence, desire to receive within yourselves the word of the holy Scriptures as though it were maternal milk, so that, growing through it, you may advance toward eating the bread that came down from heaven and gave life to the world (John 6).

Paul says of himself and his followers: “We became little children in your midst, as a nurse cherishes her own children” (1 Thess. 2). For he knew the Gospel saying spoken by the Lord: “Whoever humbles himself like this little child is greater in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18).

Therefore he humbled himself among his disciples, both to provide them an example of humility and to acquire for himself the reward of humiliation. Yet we must consider how he can commendably say here, “We became little children,” when elsewhere he says: “I wish that we might not become little children” (1 Cor. 14)—how they voluntarily became little children while not wishing to be little children.

But Paul himself explains what kind of little children he wants us to be when he says: “Be little children in malice” (1 Cor. 14). And he reveals what kind of little children he does not want us to be when he adds: “I wish that we might not become little children, tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine” (Eph. 4).

Thus we rightly become little children in two ways: by possessing and by not possessing. We possess humility, purity, and innocence; we do not possess malice, deceit, and envy.

The apostles became little children by not possessing malice, deceit, or envy. They became great by possessing humility, purity, and innocence, and also by possessing the abundance of teaching with which Paul, like a nurse, cherished his children. He also said to them: “As little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3).

[Col. 0656D]

## CHAPTER LX. On the Fact That the Righteous Are Called Living Stones

Peter says in his Epistle: “You yourselves, like living stones, are being built up into spiritual houses” (1 Pet. 2). He says that they are being built up because no spiritual building can stand without the Lord Jesus Christ, the living stone. “No one can lay any foundation other than him” (1 Cor. 3).

Through participation in him, the faithful become living stones—those who had been dead stones through unbelief, hard and insensitive. To them it would rightly be said: “I will take away from you the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. 36)—a heart teachable for receiving evangelical doctrine—so that, like living stones, they may be fitted for a spiritual building. Through the discernment of a learned teacher, their superfluous deeds and thoughts are cut away, and they are squared as though by the stroke of an axe.

For a square stone, whichever side it is turned toward, stands equally firm.

[Gregory, *On Ezekiel*, book II, homily 21.]

The righteous person who is not lifted up by prosperity, not broken by adversity, not cast down by insults, and not drawn toward evil by persuasion is a square stone.

Just as stones in a wall are supported one by another, so the faithful are supported by the righteous who preceded them in the Church. They themselves also support those who follow through teaching and endurance, and in this order righteous people support one another until the final righteous person.

When the final righteous person is supported by those who came before, he will have no one after him whom he must support. But the one who supports the entire building and is himself supported by no one is the Lord Christ. Hence the prophet calls him a precious stone, laid as a foundation (Isa. 28).

The Apostle likewise calls the elect living stones, thereby indicating their zeal for good action. Dead stones—that is, material stones—remain insensibly wherever the builder places them, or even fall down when they slip.

Blessed Peter therefore does not want us to imitate the insensibility of such stones, but to be built as living stones upon Christ the foundation, so that, with God’s grace helping us, we may live soberly, justly, and piously in this age (Titus 2).

Whoever, with Christ’s gift and help, strives tirelessly to devote himself to good works is therefore built by Christ into his house as a living stone. In a living and holy temple, stones cannot be placed unless they are living and holy.

We must therefore strive with every effort to be stones of the kind concerning which it is written: “Living stones roll upon the earth” (Zech. 9, according to the Septuagint). When we have become living stones, hewn on every side, let us be built into a temple and, with the apostles and prophets, become God’s holy dwelling, spiritual and not made by human hands (Heb. 9).

[Col. 0657C]

## CHAPTER LXI. On Enduring Temptations

“Blessed is the man,” says the apostle James, “who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life, which God promised to those who love him” (James 1). This resembles the saying in the Apocalypse: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life, which,” he says, “God promised to those who love him” (Rev. 2).

He clearly admonishes us that we ought to rejoice all the more in temptations, the more certainly it is evident that God often lays a greater burden of temptations upon those whom he loves, so that through the exercise of temptations they may be tested as perfect in faith.

When they have truly been proven faithful—that is, perfect and complete, lacking in nothing—they will rightly receive the promised crown of eternal life.

There are two kinds of temptation: one that deceives and another that tests. With regard to the temptation that deceives, it is written: “Let no one, when tempted, say that he is tempted by God. For God tempts no one” (James 1). With regard to the temptation that tests: “God tested Abraham” (Gen. 22). Concerning this temptation the Prophet also asks the Lord: “Test me, O Lord, and try me” (Ps. 25). It is written elsewhere: “The furnace tests the vessels of the potter, and temptation through tribulation tests righteous people” (Sir. 27).

[Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, book I, homily 16.]

Temptation occurs in three ways: suggestion, delight, and consent. Suggestion comes from the enemy; delight and consent come from our frailty. If, when the enemy suggests, we do not wish either to delight in sin or to consent to it, the temptation itself becomes for us an occasion of victory, through which we may deserve to receive the crown of life.

Job was tempted in many ways. But because he had preferred neither his possessions nor the health of his body to divine love, he could indeed be tempted by hostile suggestion, but he could in no way consent to sin or even take delight in it.

Abbot Anthony said to Abbot Pastor: “This is the great work of a person: that each one should set his own fault before the Lord and await temptation until the final moment of his life.”

A certain old man used to say: “When we are tempted, then we are humbled more deeply. For God, knowing our weakness, protects us. But if we boast, he removes his protection from us, and we perish.”

They related of a certain old man that, while sitting in his cell and enduring temptations, he saw demons openly and despised them. When the devil saw that he was being defeated by the old man, he came and, appearing to him, said: “I am Christ.”

When the old man saw him, he closed his eyes. The devil said to him: “I am Christ. Why have you closed your eyes?” The old man replied: “I do not wish to see Christ here, but in the life to come.” Hearing this, the devil disappeared.

[Col. 0658C]

## CHAPTER LXII. On Knowledge of Our Lord Jesus Christ

The apostle Peter says: “May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ, as all things belonging to his divine power, for life and godliness, have been granted to us through the knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and virtue” (2 Pet. 2).

It is as though he were saying: “May grace be multiplied to you in this respect: that you may know our Lord Jesus Christ perfectly. And may you also learn through him how all things belonging to his divine power have been granted to us by his grace, sufficient for attaining life and preserving godliness.”

For the more perfectly a person knows the Lord, the more deeply he perceives the greatness of his promises. Hence Paul says: “To know him and the power of his resurrection” (Phil. 3). Knowledge of the mystery of his incarnation, passion, and resurrection is the perfection of life and the treasure of wisdom.

Through knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, we recognize all the mysteries of his divinity by which we are saved. Scripture teaches us that we come to recognition of Christ in three ways.

First, we must believe that he is the Son of God the almighty Father, and that with the Father and the Holy Spirit he is one God in the Trinity.

Second, we must love him with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength (Matt. 32), because, as John says: “Everyone who loves is born of God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know him” (1 John 4).

Third, we must keep his commandments, as the same John testifies when he says: “Whoever says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2). “By this we know that we have come to know him: if we keep his commandments,” and the power of his resurrection.

We recognize the power of Christ’s resurrection when we believe that God raised him from the dead and raised us with him through his power (1 Cor. 6), rescued us from the condemnation of death, and, once rescued, placed us as sons at the Father’s right hand in an eternal inheritance.

For on the eighth day, when the Lord rose from the dead, he displayed for us an example of the future resurrection and the mystery of a new way of life.

[Col. 0659B]

## CHAPTER LXIII. On the Glorification of Our Lord Jesus Christ in the Saints

Concerning the Lord Jesus Christ, the apostle Paul says: “When he comes to be glorified in his saints” (2 Thess. 1). He who is naturally always glorious in his own glory and always remains glorified will, at the judgment—when he comes to judge the living and the dead, and the age by fire—glorify his saints. He will appear glorious and glorified together with them, making them radiant with the splendor of his power.

As the same Lord says to the Father: “The glory that you gave me, I have given them” (John 17). And elsewhere: “The righteous,” he says, “will shine like the sun in the kingdom of my Father” (Matt. 13).

Clothed in this glorious and everlasting glory, the elect will appear with Christ at the judgment. He will come—yes, he will come—to appear glorified in his saints, he who appeared despised to the wicked in his passion.

He who at his first coming appeared humble and small before Pilate and the Jewish priests will appear at his second coming as God, glorious, great, and exalted, and will be shown to be wonderful in all who believed.

For our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who is always wonderful in his divinity, became wonderful for us also in his humanity: wonderful in his conception, wonderful in his birth, wonderful in his resurrection, and wonderful also in his ascension.

He will still appear wondrous in all who—as we must believe—have believed, at the revelation of the final judgment, so that, made wondrous by that wondrous one, they may live with him glorified forever.

He is the wondrous God of whom Isaiah says: “His name will be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God,” and so forth (Isa. 9). David likewise says: “Wonderful is God in his saints” (Ps. 67).

The Christian peoples have seen and believed the glory of his resurrection, but at the judgment only the elect will see the glory of his majesty.

[Col. 0660A]

## CHAPTER LXIV. That We Should Walk Worthily of God and Be Filled with Knowledge of His Will
After receiving the water of holy baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of the bishop’s hands, it is of the utmost importance that a person be filled with knowledge of God’s will (Col. I), so that he may do what is God’s will and live in all things according to his will. For to the extent that each person possesses knowledge of God’s will, to that extent he will also possess fear of his majesty, retain love toward him in his heart, be able to walk worthily of God, please him, and bear fruit in every good work.

Therefore, he walks worthily of God who daily increases through good works the faith he received through the Lord’s grace in baptism; who puts to death his members that are upon the earth, so that he may live spiritually for God and please him to whom he has shown himself faithful by living justly and piously. “Pleasing God in all things” (ibid.).

No one, therefore, can please God and attain true blessedness except through the mortification of vices and the assumption of virtues, through right faith and holy action. Nor in this age—provided, that is, that time for action is available—does anyone obtain the grace of sanctification without these two things; nor in the future will he possess eternal life: “bearing fruit in every good work” (ibid.).

He bears fruit well in every good work who, having received the seed of the word in his heart, brings forth, like good and excellent soil, “one thirtyfold, another sixtyfold, and another a hundredfold fruit in patience” (Luke VIII).

It should be noted that in this passage he silently rebukes the sluggish minds of those who do not grow toward what is better and do not advance in virtues by doing good, but believe that they alone are sufficient either because they do not do evil or because they have left the world bodily. They do not know that through the exercises of wisdom, meditation on the holy Scriptures, and the practice of good works, a new person is daily formed, growing and pleasing to God.

Abba Pastor said: “Just as bees are driven away by smoke so that the sweetness of their works may be taken away, so bodily repose drives the fear of the Lord from the soul and removes every good work from it.”

He said again: “All bodily repose is an abomination.”

[Col. 0660C]

## CHAPTER LXV  
### That we ought not to please all people

Paul says here: “If I still wished to please people, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. I). That is: if I had agreed with the Jews in a carnal observance of the law, or with Christians living wickedly in their wickedness, I would not be a servant of Christ.

This is in no way contrary to what he says elsewhere: “Be without offense to Jews and Gentiles and the Church of God, just as I also please everyone in all things” (I Cor. X). Explaining why he pleased everyone, he immediately adds: “not seeking what is useful to me, but what is useful to many, so that they may be saved” (ibid.).

Since he sought the benefit and salvation of all, he rightly said that he pleased everyone. Good monks, following this apostolic example, ought not to be content merely to seek what is suited to their own benefit, but rather what is suitable for their neighbors, considering not what belongs to each person individually, but what belongs to others.

He who considers only what is his own (Phil. II)—that is, what is necessary for himself alone—and does not care about his brother’s salvation or his temporal welfare undoubtedly turns aside from the path of charity, in which the salvation of all souls consists.

But he who is concerned for his own welfare and salvation and for those of his neighbors, and strives to offer whatever benefit he can to his brothers as though they were his superiors, acquires for himself, through this humble obedience, more abundant joys of heavenly life.

Paul therefore both pleases people and does not please them. He pleases all who live well, justly, and rightly, in all their conduct, words, and actions; but, since he stands as an opponent of all who live wickedly and badly, he pleases them neither in words nor in conduct.

For in this broad and magnificent Church of Christ, stretched throughout the four quarters of the world, there are two kinds of people: those who will good and those who will evil. Paul pleases those who will good in all things, but displeases those who will evil in all things.

For just as grain is mixed with chaff on the threshing floor, so the good are still mixed with the evil in the Church that dwells on earth. Concerning this mixture of the evil and the good, we read in the Epistle Paul sent to Timothy: “In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware; some indeed for honor, others for dishonor” (II Tim. II).

By the great house of the great Lord may be understood the Church of Christ, spread throughout the whole world. In it there are golden vessels—namely, the hearts of people filled with spiritual understanding and shining with various virtues like refined gold. There are also silver vessels, bright with the splendor of eloquence and radiant with the ministry of preaching.

There are also wooden vessels: proud, foolish, and insensible hearts. There are also earthen vessels, fragile and earthly, taken from the earth and devoted to earthly actions.

But the golden and silver vessels in this great Church of Christ are worthy of honor. For the Apostle says: “Those who have served well should be considered worthy of double honor” (I Tim. V).

The wooden and earthen vessels, however, are rightly held in dishonor, because, possessing a foolish and proud mind, they have not kept the just commandments of their Lord.

Saint Syncletice said: “We ought to govern our souls with discernment; and, while remaining in the community, we should not seek what is ours or serve our own will, but obey our spiritual father according to faith.”

A certain old man said: “I have never desired to do something useful to me while causing loss to my brother. I hold this hope: that my brother’s gain is a work of fruitfulness for me.”

[Col. 0661D]

## CHAPTER LXVI  
### That we ought mutually to forgive one another’s offenses

The Lord says in the Gospel: “If you offer your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matt. V).

Although this command is to be observed historically, it must always also be fulfilled by us spiritually. Spiritually, our temple is our inner person; the altar is our faith; and the gift is prophecy, teaching, prayer, hymn, and psalm.

If a brother who has something against us is present, we can appease him not with feigned but with sincere intent and call him back to grace by asking pardon—provided that we do this before God not with sluggish bodily movement but with the swiftest affection of love.

Concerning this passage the Apostle Paul also says: “Bearing with one another in charity, and forgiving one another, if anyone has a complaint against another, just as the Lord has forgiven us” (Col. III).

The Apostle urges us to bear with one another—that is, patiently, for Christ and out of brotherly love, to bear one another’s dispositions, actions, and words, and all our burdens. For whoever loves his brother as himself patiently bears and endures everything for him. “Charity,” according to the Apostle, “endures all things and bears all things” (I Cor. XIII).

“Forgiving one another,” the Apostle says, “if anyone has a complaint against another” (Col. III). Someone has a complaint against another when that person injures him, even without cause. “Just as the Lord has forgiven you, so also do you.”

It is as though he said: Just as the Lord forgave you all your sins through the water of holy baptism, so you also ought to forgive your brothers from your hearts—not some sins, but all the offenses committed against you. For it is most just before God that, according to the measure of his mercy by which he forgave our offenses, we should forgive our brothers all the sins they have committed against us.

Thus we may freely say to God: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI). For this reason we should be ready to pardon all the offenses committed against us, if we desire to be pardoned ourselves.

Let no one retain anything against himself by refusing to forgive, lest it be held against him because he has not forgiven. For the Lord says concerning the wicked servant who refused to forgive his fellow servant’s offense: “His lord was angry and delivered him to the torturers until he should repay the whole debt” (Matt. XVIII).

His example warns us to beware, as he says: “So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if you do not forgive each one his brother from your hearts” (ibid.).

Do not say with your tongue, “I forgive,” while postponing forgiveness in your heart. God examines your conscience.

Do you therefore wish God to forgive you all your debts? You too must forgive all your debtor’s offenses. This is the rule you establish; by this pact and agreement you bind yourself to God when you say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI).

The Lord also says elsewhere: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke VI).

An old man was asked, “What is humility?” He replied: “If you forgive your brother who sins against you before he has repented before you, and if you do good to those who do evil to you.”

Abba Antony said: “Death and life depend on one’s neighbor. If we gain our brother, we gain God; but if we scandalize our brother, we sin against Christ.”

Abba Hyperius said: “To rescue your neighbor from sins without reproach—how great a virtue that is, since God does not reject those who convert.”

Do not have a word of malice or wickedness in your heart against your brother, so that you may be able to say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI).

Concerning this passage it is also written elsewhere: “That you may be without complaint and simple, like the children of God” (Phil. II).

A person is without complaint who, insofar as human frailty permits, strives to lead a blameless life. Sin committed against God or one’s neighbor gives rise to complaint. Therefore, a person lives without complaint who does not lead a life stained by vices and does not commit an offense for which complaint may justly be brought against him.

[Col. 0663A]

## CHAPTER LXVII  
### That we are children of God and heirs, and that he is our inheritance and we are his

Paul says here: “Because you are sons of God, he sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. IV).

We would never dare to say, “Our Father who art in heaven,” unless it were from the consciousness of the Spirit dwelling within us. To demonstrate that we have been adopted by God as sons, he gave us his Spirit, which shows the Father’s sign to be present in his children, so that we may dare to say “Abba,” which means “Father”—something the Jews had previously not been permitted to say.

Therefore we are no longer servants but sons. And if sons, then “heirs through God” (Gal. IV). That is, if we are sons, the Father’s inheritance is consequently owed to us. Just as, by receiving the Spirit of God’s Son, we have become sons, so, changed from slavery into freedom, we may be heirs of God the Father and co-heirs of Jesus Christ, his Son.

The Apostle says the same elsewhere (Col. I): “Giving thanks to God the Father, who has made us worthy to share in the lot of the saints in light.”

The portion of the lot of the saints is the gathered assembly, joined together in one fellowship, of all the elect. As he says elsewhere: “May the Lord multiply you” (I Thess. III)—that is, in the number of his elect—so that you may be holy and without blemish, gathered, as it were, in the bosom of the saints.

Thus the portion of the lot of the saints comes to be in light and is illumined by light when it comes to be in Christ, and is illumined by Christ, because inheritance is often signified by a lot, as it is written: “By lot he divided their land by the cord of distribution” (Ps. LXXVII).

Let us say that, just as the whole people of the elect is the Lord’s portion and cord of inheritance, Scripture saying: “The Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob is the cord of his inheritance” (Deut. XXXII), so the Lord himself is the portion and inheritance of the lot of the saints, for he said to Aaron: “I am your portion and inheritance in the midst of the children of Israel” (Num. XVIII).

Since we share fellowship with the apostles and all the saints, let us give thanks to God the Father and pray that he may make us worthy to share in the lot of the saints in light (Col. I)—that is, that we may deserve to be the Lord’s portion, lot, and inheritance, and that we may happily possess the Lord our Savior himself as our eternal lot and inheritance, and, in the light—that is, illumined in him and through him—remain blessed forever.

[Col. 0664A]

[Col. 0664]

## CHAPTER LXVIII  
### How a person may gain Christ

If a monk puts to death his members that are upon the earth and, taking up his cross, follows Christ (Col. III; Matt. XVI), and, dead to the world, fastens the trophy of his mortification to the wood of the Lord’s Passion, so that he can say with Paul, “Through the law I died to the law, that I might live for God; I have been crucified with Christ” (Gal. II), he will be able to gain Christ.

For Christ is called Truth, Charity, Wisdom, Justice, and Sanctification. Whoever acquires all these things for himself by living well undoubtedly gains Christ. Or certainly, whoever gains his brother—who is a member of Christ—by preaching and displaying a good example gains Christ.

Blessed Augustine says: “If you happen to see anything perverse, strive to correct it, and do not cease to amend it. Do whatever you can for the person whose role you bear. Do not cease to gain Christ, because you have been gained by Christ.”

According to the meaning of this statement, whoever understands that Christ became human, suffered, died, rose from the dead, and ascended into heaven for his sake, and follows him on a straight course, rejecting everything that belongs to the world, so that he may grasp Christ, by whom he has been grasped, happily gains Christ.

The same Apostle says elsewhere: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world” (Gal. VI).

A monk ought not to glory in his own righteousness or in any doctrine, but in faith in Christ’s cross, through whom he hopes that all his sins will be forgiven. Therefore the monk and the world ought to be mutually dead to one another: the world to the monk and the monk to the world.

The monk ought not to desire anything that belongs to the world, nor should the world possess anything to desire in the monk. Therefore only he can glory in Christ’s cross who takes it up and follows the Savior; who crucifies his flesh with its vices and desires; who has died to the world; and who does not contemplate the things that are seen, but those that are unseen and eternal (Matt. XVI; Gal. V; II Cor. IV).

[Col. 0664C]

## CHAPTER LXIX  
### That the Lord’s virtues should always be proclaimed by monks

The Apostle Peter says here: “That you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you from darkness into his marvelous light” (I Pet. II).

Just as those who were liberated from Egyptian slavery through Moses sang a song of triumph to the Lord after crossing the Red Sea and the drowning of Pharaoh’s army (Exod. XV), so we too, after receiving forgiveness of sins in baptism, ought to return thanks worthy of the heavenly benefits and always proclaim his virtues.

If almighty God were silent about his own virtues, no one would recognize him and no one would love him. He therefore proclaims his virtues, not so that he himself may benefit from human praise, but so that those who have come to know him through praising him may attain an everlasting inheritance.

[Gregory, *Moralia*, book XVIII, chapter 5.]

For this reason God makes his praises known, so that by hearing him we may be able to know him, by knowing him love him, by loving him follow him, by following him attain him, and, having attained him, enjoy his vision.

The Prophet says here: “He will proclaim the power of his works to his people, so that he may give them the inheritance of the nations” (Ps. CX).

It is as though he openly said: For this reason he makes known the strength of his activity, so that those who hear of it may grow rich in spiritual gifts.

To advance in spiritual gifts is to walk worthily in God and to advance from day to day in holy virtues, until one is able to reach the vision of the Almighty, so that it may be said with the other saints concerning him: “They will go from virtue to virtue; the God of gods will be seen in Zion” (Ps. LXXXIII).

He will be seen by us in Zion—that is, in heavenly contemplation—who first called us through faith to his kingdom and glory, and afterward called us through sight, when we shall see him face to face and hear that desirable voice saying: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV).

In that kingdom, glory and eternal life remain forever.

Blessed Job, speaking about this proclamation of virtues under the figure of our Redeemer, says: “Earth, do not cover my blood” (Job XVI).

[Gregory, *Moralia*, book XIII, chapter 23.]

For the earth did not cover Christ’s blood, because the holy Church has already proclaimed the mystery of its redemption throughout every part of the world. The blood of redemption that is received is the cry of our Redeemer.

Therefore, so that the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion may not be idle in us, we ought to imitate what we receive and proclaim to others what we revere.

Blessed Job says again: “Let not my cry find a place to hide in you” (Job XVI).

His cry finds a place to hide in us if the tongue is silent about what the mind believes. But, so that his cry may not remain hidden in us, each person must, according to his own measure, make known to his neighbors the mystery of his own vivification.

[Col. 0665C]

## CHAPTER LXX  
### That it has been granted to the saints to suffer for Christ

Thus, among other things, the Apostle Paul says: “It has been granted to you for Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Phil. I).

It should be noted that both the faith by which we believe in Christ and the sufferings that we endure for him are granted to us by God the Father for Christ’s sake. For it is not granted to others, but to those who love Christ, to suffer for Christ.

Therefore we ought not to grieve in sufferings for Christ; rather, we should greatly rejoice and exult, because the apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, since they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus (Acts V).

The one who inflicts evils on those who do good not only does them no harm, but also provides them with a cause of greater blessedness, according to the Gospel saying: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V).

Paul says elsewhere: “For this reason I also suffer these things, but I am not ashamed” (II Tim. I). By “this reason” he means the preaching of the Gospel and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.

To suffer for Christ ought not to be a disgrace to the faithful, but a great cause of glory. “Christ,” the Apostle says, “has become righteousness for us” (I Cor. I). To suffer for Christ, therefore, is to suffer for righteousness.

For the Lord says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V).

Let those who persecute the elect for righteousness be ashamed, because eternal torments await them. Let not the elect be ashamed, for, in exchange for brief tribulations, eternal joy and the kingdom of heaven will likewise be granted to them.

Peter says here: “If you suffer anything for righteousness, you are blessed” (I Pet. III).

He means: Not only does the one who inflicts evil on those who do good harm you nothing, but when the enemy persecutes you because of the good things he hates, he provides you with the cause of greater blessedness by exercising the strength of your patience.

He says again: “For it is better, if the will of God should so will it, to suffer while doing good than while doing evil” (ibid.).

This statement condemns the foolishness of those monks who, when rebuked by their brothers for their faults or even excommunicated, do not endure patiently. But if they suffer without fault either verbal insults or any adversity from their superiors, they immediately erupt in anger; and those who previously seemed innocent make themselves blameworthy and guilty through impatience and bold murmuring.

If I were given a choice, I would prefer to be judged or to suffer adversity without fault rather than, with fault, to be subjected to beatings or excommunications. For the just person who suffers without fault imitates Christ; but the person corrected by blows imitates the thief who recognized Christ on the cross and entered paradise with Christ after the cross.

Whoever does not cease from his faults even amid blows imitates the thief on the left, who went up onto the cross because of his sins and, after the cross, fell into hell.

Saint Syncletice said: “Even if the body is shattered by infirmities and inflamed by severe fevers, do not fail under your pressures; rather rejoice, because the Lord has visited you, and say: ‘The Lord has chastened and chastened me, but he has not handed me over to death’” (Ps. CXVII).

“If you are iron, expect fire to be applied to you. You are gold, but through fire you will become more thoroughly tested” (I Pet. I).

And if you are just and suffer these things, you will be promoted from great things to greater.

A certain brother asked an old man: “Tell me one thing that I may keep and by it live.” The old man said to him: “If you can endure insult and bear it, that is a great thing, greater than all virtues. Whoever patiently bears contempt, injury, and loss can be saved.”

[Col. 0666D]

## CHAPTER LXXI  
### That Christ gave himself up for love of us

The Apostle Paul says: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins” (Gal. I).

He says the same elsewhere: “Who loved us and gave himself up for us” (Eph. V).

Christ loved our life so greatly that he laid down his own life for it. The Lord Jesus Christ gave himself over to death so that he might rescue us from the danger of death and, once rescued, adopt us as sons to the Father.

He died so that we would not fear dying. He rose so that through him we too might be able to rise. “He rescued us from the present evil age” (Gal. I, 7), so that he might grant us both glory and eternal life.

The Son of God rescued us from the wicked captor so that he might restore us to our proper Lord. Christ rescued us from the present evil age when he changed our life, nourished in vices, into a better life.

He so changed and raised our manner of life to a higher level that with Paul we can say: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III).

Paul rightly says that his own manner of life and theirs is in heaven: they have left earthly things and think with their whole desire about heavenly things; with a pure and devoted mind they desire not the earthly and perishable things but those that are heavenly and eternal.

For it was the will of God the Father that the Lord Jesus Christ should be handed over for our sins. And it was Christ’s will to do the Father’s will, as the same Lord says through the Prophet: “To do your will, my God, I have desired” (Ps. XXXIX).

“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them” (Eph. II).

This means that what we live, what we hope for, what we understand, and what we are able to believe belongs to him, because he is our creator and we are his workmanship.

For we are said to have been created in Christ Jesus for this purpose—not created because we did not previously exist, but reborn in Christ and created for the good works that God prepared so that we might walk in them.

“Rooted and founded in charity” (Eph. III). Charity is Christ; and we ought to be so rooted and founded in charity—that is, in Christ—that we persevere firmly in his love.

“For no one can lay another foundation apart from that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III).

“Doing the truth in charity, let us grow in all things in him who is the head, Christ” (Eph. IV).

For Christ is truth, Christ is charity, and Christ is justice, sanctification, and peace (I Cor. I). Therefore whoever does all that Christ is, and also keeps his commandments, does the truth and daily grows in charity—that is, in Christ.

[Col. 0667D]

## CHAPTER LXXII  
### Concerning the Apostle’s statement: “Do not extinguish the Spirit”

It is as though he said: Do not extinguish by wicked living the grace of the Holy Spirit, which you received when you were baptized through the laying on of hands and the anointing of chrism (I Thess. V); rather preserve it whole and inviolate in your heart and body.

Accordingly, the same Apostle says to the Ephesians: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. IV).

For we received the seal of the Holy Spirit on the day on which we were baptized and confirmed, and we must certainly preserve it faithfully.

By this seal of the Holy Spirit, therefore, the person who believes in God is sealed by him so that he may preserve and display it on the day of redemption, pure and sincere, mutilated in no respect.

The Apostle John likewise says: “And let the anointing that you received from him remain in you” (I John II).

It is as though he said: With the Lord’s help, take care to preserve whole in your heart and body the grace of the Holy Spirit that you received in baptism. This is what it means: “Do not extinguish the Spirit.”

[Note: [Col. 0667D] Chrysostom beautifully explains what it means to extinguish the Spirit in his *Homily on the Epistle to the Thessalonians*, chapter V, homily 11.]

The anointing of which John speaks and the Spirit of whom Paul says, “Do not extinguish the Spirit,” may be understood as the very charity of God, which is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. V).

This charity very quickly inflames the heart it fills to observe God’s commandments; but among those who live wickedly it is extinguished through hatred, envy, and discord.

The spirit of preachers is also extinguished. They proclaim the word of salvation to their hearers, but the malice of hearers who contradict, resist, and provoke them makes them prefer silence to preaching. Thus, through the provocation of their hearers, the word is taken away from preachers.

Therefore the Lord says to Ezekiel: “I will make your tongue cling to your palate, and you will be mute and no longer as a man who rebukes, because it is an exasperating house” (Ezek. III).

A certain old man came to another old man, and one of them said: “I am dead to this world.” The other replied: “Do not trust in yourself until you have departed from this body. For if you are dead, Satan is not dead.”

Abba Pastor said: “A person ought always and unceasingly to breathe humility and fear of God, just as he breathes the air that he draws in or expels through his nostrils.”

He said again: “To cast oneself down in the presence of God, not to exalt oneself, and to put one’s own will behind one’s back are the tools with which the soul works.”

[Col. 0668C]

## CHAPTER LXXIII  
### Concerning the harmful curiosity of monks

The Apostle Paul says: “We urge you, brothers, to be quiet, to attend to your own business, and to work with your hands” (I Thess. IV).

It is as though he said: Abstain from every vice of restlessness and curiosity, so that, having become quiet, you may attend to your own business.

A person attends to his own business who, putting aside the vice of curiosity, is unceasingly concerned for his salvation. But a monk attends to another’s business when, through the vice of curiosity, he forgets to examine his own sinful life and carefully investigates another’s.

Accordingly, he says to the same people in a second Epistle: “For we hear that some among you walk restlessly, doing nothing but acting curiously” (II Thess. III).

In this brief statement Paul rebukes many vices of monks: restlessness, idleness, curiosity, and excessive talk, in which, according to Solomon (Prov. X), sin is not avoided.

Restlessness, which is also called curiosity by another name, is therefore a great vice. It permits neither the body to be quiet nor the soul to remain without sin. For while a person busily goes around other people’s homes or curiously investigates what belongs to others, he undoubtedly gives offense in many ways.

The vice of curiosity is also continually accompanied by idleness. “Idleness is the enemy of the soul” (Ecclus. XXXIII).

It is therefore better for monks to be obedient to their superiors in every obedience that benefits them; and, in silence—that is, removed from every vice of restlessness, curiosity, and excessive talk—to work with their hands, eat their own bread, and understand as applying to themselves the Psalmist’s saying: “You shall eat the labors of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. CXXVII).

An old man said: “For this reason we do not advance: because we do not know our own measure and do not have perseverance in the work we have begun. Yet without any labor we wish to possess the virtues.”

Abba Pastor said that Abba Isidore once addressed the assembly of the brothers, saying: “Brothers, surely we came to this place to labor? And now I see that there is no labor here. Therefore I am leaving the assembly and going where there is labor and where I find no rest.”

The brothers urged a certain old man to rest from his severe labor, but he answered them: “Believe me, children: Abraham will repent when he sees the great and splendid gifts of God, because he had not striven more in labors.”

[Col. 0669B]

## CHAPTER LXXIV  
### Concerning the rule established by the apostles

The Apostle Paul says here: “Peace and mercy be upon all who follow this rule” (Gal. VI).

The teaching of God is a certain rule of speech that judges between what is just and what is unjust. Whoever follows it will have within himself the peace that surpasses all understanding, and after peace he will obtain mercy.

The Christian generation is a new creation, because Christ, the new human being, came into the world and gave the world new commandments; and upon those who observe them there are peace and mercy.

The same Apostle says: “Nevertheless, having reached the point to which we have come, let us think the same thing and remain in the same rule” (Phil. III). That is: let us remain in the ministry of faith to which we have come at Christ’s call; let us think nothing in our manner of life outside the discipline of the rule, but think what is common and modest; and let us remain in the evangelical truth and in the same rule of faith.

In this passage the rule is called the Catholic faith. It is called a rule from the fact that it leads and governs rightly. Hence those institutions of the Fathers that teach the Catholic Church to live rightly are called canons. *Canon* in Greek (*kanōn*), in Latin *regula*—“rule.”

Paul says elsewhere: “We announce to you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks restlessly and disorderly” (II Thess. III).

This announcement must not be disregarded by its hearers, because it is supported by royal authority, having been proclaimed in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Although it is full of apostolic charity, it nevertheless contains royal authority, which leads the salutary multitude of all the faithful toward the right rule of souls.

He says: “That you withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks restlessly and not according to the tradition that they received from us” (II Thess. II).

From the apostle of the saints the Church therefore received firm authority to withdraw from wicked people. The apostles handed down to the faithful the rule of walking well—that is, of living well, justly, and piously—which the Church of all the faithful must hold firmly if it wishes to direct its life according to theirs.

The life of the apostles themselves has therefore become the standard of this rule for all Christians. Hence it follows: “For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us” (ibid.).

It is as though he said: Because we have often already foretold this to you in words and shown it by examples, you therefore know how you ought to imitate us. Nevertheless, willingly do what we exhort you to do, if you wish to hold the rule of faith handed down by us.

A certain old man said: “It is written: ‘The just will flourish like a palm tree’” (Ps. XCI).

This saying signifies a good deed—lofty, upright, and sweet. For in the palm there is a single central core, and it is white, containing within itself the whole operation of the tree.

Likewise, in a just man there is found one simple heart, looking only toward God. It is also white, possessing the illumination of faith, and every action of the just person is in his heart. The sharpness of its thorns is also a defense against the devil.

[Col. 0670C]

[Col. 0670]

## CHAPTER LXXV  
### That monks should be watchful
The apostle Paul admonishes us, saying: “Let us not sleep as the rest do, but let us keep watch” (I Thess. V). That is, let us not sleep as the other unbelievers, unjust and wicked, who, weighed down by the sleep of ignorance and of the body, and burdened by the mass of their sins, are unable to foresee what will happen to them in the future. They sleep so heavily and disgracefully that they do not open the eyes of their hearts to guard themselves; they think nothing of future glory, but always of the present life. They do not think of the things that are unseen and eternal, but always of those that are seen, perishable, and temporal. We, however, should not sleep as they do, but keep watch.

Hence the evangelist Mark also salutarily admonishes us, saying: “Keep watch, therefore, because you do not know when the Lord will come. Lest, when he comes suddenly, he find you sleeping” (Mark XIII). “Blessed are those servants whom, when the Lord comes, he finds watching” (Luke XII). For he keeps watch who keeps his eyes open for the sight of the true light. He keeps watch who preserves by his deeds what he believes. He keeps watch who drives away from himself the darkness of the body and of negligence.

Hence also the same apostle says elsewhere: “Whether we keep watch or sleep, let us live together with Christ” (I Thess. V). That is, whether we keep watch for the guarding of our salvation, or sleep away from the harmful cares of this age, let us live together with him—that is, let us always be in Christ and with Christ, who died for us and rose again (ibid.).

Concerning this salutary watching and sleeping, Solomon says in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song V). As if he were saying: The more I rest, as though asleep, from earthly cares, the more freely my heart keeps watch for the contemplation of its Creator. For that soul will always live with the Lord forever which, cleaving to him here through love, never turns away from him. Hence the Lord also says: “Whoever loves me, let him follow me. And where I am, there my servant also will be” (John XII). That is, living with me forever, he will reign perpetually in glory and immortality.

Abba Evagrius said: “If you are losing heart, pray as it is written. Pray, however, with fear, trembling, and labor, soberly and attentively. One must pray in this way especially because of our wicked and malicious invisible enemies, who above all strive to hinder us in this.”

He said again: “When an opposing thought comes into your heart, do not seek one thing through prayer in place of another, but sharpen against the thought that attacks you the sword of tears.”

### CHAPTER LXXVI. On the Struggle of the Virtues

(Isidore, *Sentences*, book II, chapter 37.)

Holy men are cleansed more truly from the filth of vices when individual virtues are set against each individual vice. For against the assaults of vices one must fight with contrary virtues: against lust of the heart, purity must be applied; against hatred, love must be prepared; against anger, patience must be set forth; against fear, confidence must be employed; against sadness, joy must be applied; against acedia, strength; against avarice, generosity; against pride, humility must be opposed. Thus the several virtues suppress the vices that arise against them.

Abstinence subdues lust, for to the extent that the body is weakened by hunger, the mind is recalled from unlawful desire. Endurance fights against anger. Hope of eternal joy overcomes the sorrow of grief. The sweetness of inner tranquility soothes the troubled mind when it is afflicted by external things. Charity is prepared against envy, and against the fires of anger the tranquility of gentleness is applied.

When we oppose the dominion of vices, when we resist the wickedness that separates us from God, when we violently withstand habit, and, trampling perverse desires underfoot, claim for ourselves against these things the right of our innate freedom, we resist the armies of vices in the fiercest conflict. When we strike our faults through repentance and wash away the stains of filth with tears, we struggle bravely against vices.

Abba Agathon said: “I have never gone to sleep while according to my own will retaining resentment in my heart against anyone; nor have I allowed another to sleep while harboring anything against me.”

Abba Macarius said: “Take courage, son, for I too, for twenty years, was satisfied neither with bread, nor with water, nor with sleep. I received bread by weight and water by measure; as for sleep, leaning only against walls, I hastened to snatch a little.”

Abba Isidore said: “If we have no thoughts, we are like beasts. But if the enemy demands what belongs to him, we too must fulfill what belongs to us. Let us persist in prayer, and the enemy is put to flight. Devote yourself to the contemplation of God, and you conquer. Perseverance in good is victory. Fight, and you will be crowned.”

Abba John said: “Humility is the door of God, and the fathers, driven by many insults, entered rejoicing into the city of God, because humility and the fear of God surpass all virtues. Therefore the monk must possess humility before all else. For this is the first commandment among the eight beatitudes of the Savior, who says: ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven’” (Matt. V).

### CHAPTER LXXVII. On Hatred and Fraternal Correction

The apostle Paul says: “If anyone does not obey our word through the letter, mark that person, and do not associate with him, so that he may be put to shame; and do not regard him as an enemy, but correct him as a brother” (II Thess. III). As if he were saying: If the authority of our letter does not correct him, inform us by your letters who he is, so that he may be corrected by us, or even excommunicated through our letter. And do not associate with the excommunicated person until, submitting to the apostolic commands, he consents to obey; and thus, having at last been put to shame by both us and you, let him come to his senses and, having been corrected, obey our commands.

Here the Apostle gives a clear indication that we should have no association with an excommunicated person, neither in action, nor in counsel, nor in any other fellowship. In one and the same person we can love his brotherhood and hate his vices at the same time. For one thing is that he is a brother; another is that he is a vicious man. Let us therefore love in him our brotherhood, and hate his viciousness. Let us persecute the vice in him, and, once he has been corrected, love him as ourselves.

Hence blessed Gregory says (*Homily 37 on the Gospels*): “Thus, indeed, we ought to show discernment in our hatred toward our neighbors, so that in them we may love what makes them human, and hate what obstructs us along the way of God.”

A certain old man said: “A man must put himself to death with respect to every evil thing before he leaves the body, and he must harm no one. And unless a man has in his heart that he is a sinner, God will not hear him. What does it mean to have in one’s heart that one is a sinner? It means that someone bears his own sins and does not see the sins of his neighbor. For when a man has abandoned his own will, then God is reconciled to him and receives his prayer.

“For if we have seen our own sins, we do not see the sins of our neighbor. It is foolish for a man who has his own dead person to leave him and go away to weep for the dead person of his neighbor. For when the hand of the Lord struck down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, there was no house in which a dead person did not lie” (Exod. XII). “For there is no one who lives and does not sin” (III Kings VIII). Therefore each person ought to mourn his own dead person—that is, his own sin.”

The prophet calls sin a dead person when he says: “Whoever washes from a dead person and touches a dead person again”—that is, whoever mourns sin and then commits sin again—“his washing profits nothing” (Ecclus. XXXIV).

### CHAPTER LXXVIII. That the Monk Should Have the Loins of His Mind Girded

The apostle Peter says: “Therefore, having girded the loins of your mind in truth, being perfectly sober, hope in the grace that is offered to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ” (I Pet. I). As if he were saying to the monks: The greater the grace promised to you, the more diligently take care to be worthy of it, so that you may be able to receive it. And he rightly says, “hope in the grace that is offered to you at the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ,” because whoever awaits the Lord’s coming with the loins of his mind girded—that is, chaste in both mind and body—rightly hopes for it when he is revealed.

Hence the apostle Paul also says: “Stand therefore, having your loins girded in truth” (Eph. VI), that is, stand perfected, with the loins of your mind girded; in other words, prepared manfully for every battle and freed from all the cares of the world.

It is beyond doubt that in Scripture all the members of the soul are called according to the members of the flesh and body. Among these I think that the loins are now one member, which we are commanded to gird by the Truth. “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke XII). Hence the prophet also says: “Gird your loins over your breasts” (Isa. XXXII). As if he were saying: Cut away lusts in your heart, lest outwardly you fall shamefully into fornication. For one who is chaste in body but not in heart has no reward in the promise, because according to the saying of the Truth: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V).

[Gregory, *Moralia*, book VIII, chapter 19.] If, therefore, fornications are first prohibited in the heart, they do not break out into action. There are some righteous people who, girded to attain the summit of perfection, abandon everything outwardly while seeking higher things inwardly. They strip themselves of their possessions; they divest themselves of the glory of honor; through continual attachment to a beloved sorrow they afflict themselves; they refuse to possess consolation from external things; and, while drawing near in mind to inner joys, they put to death within themselves every bodily delight of life.

To such people Paul says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III). The Psalmist had expressed their voice when he said: “My soul longs and fails for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. LXXXIII). The soul longs and fails for the courts of God when, desiring eternal things, it does not remain in the love of temporal things.

[Thus far Gregory.]

The Psalmist says again: “My soul fails for your salvation” (Ps. CXVIII). Therefore, for the soul of the righteous to fail for God’s salvation means to abandon the goods of the present life by choosing eternity, to seek what will remain, and to place no confidence in temporal things.

### CHAPTER LXXIX. On the Mortification of Vices

Hence the apostle Paul says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, and so forth” (Col. III). These vices and sins are called our members because through our members they perform their own functions, to which the Apostle forbids us to consent, saying: “Do not present your members as weapons of iniquity to sin, but present yourselves to God” (Rom. VI).

For all sins and vices in general form one body of the devil; the particular vices that follow are called its members. Hence it is also written in the Epistle to the Romans: “Knowing this, that our old man was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed” (ibid.), that is, crimes and sins, which he collectively calls one body and says is destroyed through a good life and the catholic faith.

Every uncleanness and lust is called fornication by one name. Unless it is first removed from the thought of the heart, it breaks out into action. But if it has been nourished by pleasure or consent, it grows into a serpent, so that with deadly poison it kills the one who nourishes it. Therefore it must not be nourished, but put to death by us, lest we be put to death by it. Let it be crucified by us, lest we be crucified by it.

Hence Paul says again: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. IX). If all vices have been crucified together, and the flesh, hanging as though on a cross, desires nothing, why do we need the law, which was given to restrain vices? It should also be noted that he says those belong to Christ who have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires, against those who think faith alone is sufficient.

There was a certain great old man among those who possessed foreknowledge, who affirmed: “The same power that I saw standing over baptism I also saw over the monk’s garment when he receives the spiritual habit.”

A certain old man was given the grace to see what was happening, and he said: “I once saw a brother in a coenobium meditating in his cell, and behold, a demon came and stood outside the cell. While that brother was meditating, the demon was unable to enter. But when he ceased meditating, then the demon entered the cell.”

### CHAPTER LXXX. On the Grace of Tears

It is written that Achsah, the daughter of Caleb, sighed and said to her father: “Give me a blessing. You have given me a southern and dry land; add also a watered one.” And her father gave her an upper watercourse and a lower watercourse (Josh. XV). This signifies that we must seek from our Creator and Father, God, the grace of tears with great groaning.

There are some who have already received other gifts of the Lord, signified by the southern land, but have not yet received the grace of tears.

[Gregory, *Dialogues*, book III, chapter 34.] The soul thirsting for God is first pierced by fear, and afterward by love. At first it afflicts itself with tears, because, recalling its evils, it fears that it will suffer eternal punishments for them. But when fear has been consumed by a long anxiety of grief, a certain assurance born of hope for pardon arises, and the mind is kindled with love of heavenly joys.

The one who first wept lest he be led to punishment afterward begins to weep most bitterly because he is delayed from the kingdom. For the mind contemplates what the angelic choirs are, what the fellowship of holy spirits is, and what the majesty of the eternal vision of God is; and it grieves more because it is absent from everlasting goods than it had previously wept when it feared eternal evils. Thus perfect compunction arising from fear draws the soul toward compunction arising from love.

The soul receives the upper watercourse when it afflicts itself with tears through desire for the heavenly kingdom. It receives the lower watercourse when, by weeping, it fears the punishments of hell.

They said of Abba Arsenius that throughout the whole time of his life, while sitting at his manual work, he kept a cloth in his lap because of the tears that frequently flowed from his eyes.

Saint Syncletica said: “For those who first turn to the Lord, there is labor and a great struggle; afterward they have indescribable joy. Just as those who wish to kindle a fire are first filled with smoke and thus obtain what they want, so we must kindle the divine fire within ourselves with tears and labors. For it is written: ‘Our God is a consuming fire’” (Deut. IV; Heb. XII).

An old man said: “Just as we carry the shadow of our bodies everywhere with us, so we ought to carry weeping arising from compunction with us wherever we are.”

Abba Hyperius said: “Night and day the monk labors, keeping watch and remaining in prayers; and by piercing his heart he produces tears and more swiftly calls forth the mercy of God.”

### CHAPTER LXXXI. That Holy Monks Are Called Sons of God

Hence the Lord says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. V). Perfection is in peace, where nothing resists. Therefore the peacemakers are sons of God, because nothing in them resists God. They are peacemakers within themselves who, composing all the movements of their soul, become the kingdom of God.

If we are sons of God, we ought to be peacemakers. The sons of God ought to be peaceful, humble, meek in mind, simple in heart, pure in speech, innocent in spirit, harmonious in affection, and united with one another in complete accord.

Hence the apostle John also says: “See what kind of love the Father has given us, that we should be called and should be sons of God” (I John III). Great is the grace of our Creator, which he has granted us, so that we may both love him and know him, and love him in such a way that sons love a father—although it would already be a great thing if we could love him as faithful servants love their masters.

How we ought to become sons of God the same John testifies: “As many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name” (John I). Through faith, therefore, and love we become sons of God.

Great benevolence, great mercy! The Only-Begotten was born, and he did not wish to remain alone. God sent into this world the Only-Begotten whom he had begotten and through whom he had created all things, so that he would not be alone but would have adopted brothers. For we were not born from God in the way that the Only-Begotten was, but we have been adopted by his grace. First we received, as a divine gift, the power of adoption; afterward we attained the status of being worthy to be sons of God.

Hence the same John says again: “Beloved, now we are sons of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be” (I John III). Again he says: “We have known and believed the love that God has for us” (I John IV). We have known that Jesus is the Son of God and that the Father sent him as the Savior of the world; and we have believed the love that God has for us. For although he had the Only-Begotten, he did not wish to be alone; rather, so that he might have brothers, he adopted others to him, who would possess eternal life together with him.

Abba Pastor said that a certain brother asked Abba Poemen: “What is meant by what the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friend’” (John XV)? “How does this happen?”
