The old man replied: “If someone hears an evil word from his neighbor, and although he could answer with something similar, nevertheless struggles in his heart to bear the burden and restrains himself lest he perhaps answer him with evil and grieve him, such a person lays down his life for his friend.”

Once Abba Pabo went with the brothers into the regions of Egypt, and seeing certain worldly people sitting there, he said to them: “Rise, greet and kiss the monks, so that you may be blessed. For they frequently speak with God, and their mouths are holy.”

### CHAPTER LXXXII. That Virtues Arise from Virtues and Vices from Vices

All virtues support one another before the sight of the Creator through reciprocal assistance, so that—since one virtue without another is either entirely nothing or very small—they may mutually strengthen one another through their union. No other good is of any value if it is not approved by the testimony of chastity in the eyes of the hidden Judge, whether humility abandons chastity or chastity deserts humility. In the presence of the author of humility and purity, neither proud chastity nor defiled humility can accomplish anything.

Thus vice gives birth to vice, and virtue is conceived from virtue (Isidore, *Sentences*, book II). Vice gives birth to vice, as in David, who, because he did not avoid adultery, committed murder (II Kings XI). Likewise, virtue is conceived from virtue, as the apostles merited the virtue of martyrdom through the virtue of evangelical preaching.

Saint Gregory said that God requires these three things from every person who has received baptism: right faith with the whole soul and strength, restraint of the tongue, and chastity of body.

Abba Evagrius said: “Reading, vigils, and prayer make firm a wandering or wavering mind. Hunger, labor, and solitude cause desire to wither. Psalmody, long-suffering, and mercy restrain anger. But these things must be applied at appropriate times and in suitable measures. Whatever is done inopportunely or without measure benefits only for a short time.”

### CHAPTER LXXXIII. What It Means to Be Nailed to Christ’s Cross

The monk who takes up his cross and follows Christ, putting to death his members upon the earth, dead to the world, conformed to the death of Jesus Christ, and fastened to the wood of the Lord’s Passion—he is nailed to Christ’s cross.

He who follows Christ’s footsteps in such a way that he can imitate his manner of life, being meek as he was, gentle and humble of heart, not answering when struck, not returning abuse when cursed, but conquering pride through humility—such a person can say with Paul: “I am crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II).

Blessed and exceedingly happy is the person in whom Christ lives, who can say through each prayer, thought, and deed, “Christ lives in me,” and, “The life I live, I live in faith in the Son of God” (ibid.).

Christ lives in the one in whom wisdom, justice, truth, sanctification, peace, strength, and the other virtues live. Whoever does not have these cannot say, “Christ lives in me.” Christ also lives in the one who follows his footsteps and is captured by no desire of the world, so that, living for God, he may appear dead to the world: “For everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (I John II).

Monks, having food and clothing, ought to be content with these, because whatever is desired or longed for from this world ought to be foreign to monks and alien to the faith, since it is superfluous.

A certain old man was asked by a brother what he should do to be saved. The old man stripped off his clothing, girded his loins, and stretched out his hands, saying: “Thus the monk ought to be naked of all the world’s material things and crucify himself against the temptations and struggles of the world.”

Abba Hyperius said: “The obedience of a monk is pleasing to God. Whoever possesses it is heard in what he asks and will stand with confidence before the Crucified One. For the Lord came to the cross in this way: ‘Having become obedient unto death’” (Phil. II).

### CHAPTER LXXXIV. That Monks Should Have a Pure Heart and a Good Conscience

Scripture cries out to us, saying: “The end of the commandment is love from a pure heart and a good conscience” (I Tim. I). He says “end,” that is, the perfection of the commandment and of the whole law.

Love, therefore, which makes us dear to God and to human beings, contemptuous of this age, and lovers of every good, is the fountain of all good things, the source of spiritual gifts, and the perfection of all virtues.

The pure heart is one in which there is no deceit and no plotting of evil; in which there is no pretense, but complete purity reigns; in which one thing is not held in the heart and another spoken with the mouth; in which this saying is not found: “They spoke vain things, each one to his neighbor.” For “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). “The one innocent in hands and pure in heart shall receive a blessing from the Lord” (Ps. XXIII).

A good conscience is one in which there are no dead works, but which has been cleansed from every stain of sin. Hence the apostle Paul says to the Hebrews: “He offered himself immaculate to God through the Holy Spirit and cleansed our conscience from dead works” (Heb. IX), that is, from sins. Dead works are understood to mean sins.

Therefore a good conscience is found where there is good and pure innocence, complete simplicity, and unfeigned faith. Without doubt that is a good conscience in which there is no accusation of any vice, which is not gnawed by the guilt of sin or accused by the burden of crimes; which hates no one, harms no one, slanders no one, troubles no one, envies no one, but is agreeable to all, harmful to none, gentle, peaceful, and kind.

Abba Agathon said: “A monk must not allow his conscience to accuse him in any matter.”

Monks ought therefore to understand that, just as angels stand before the Creator with fear and trembling, singing hymns, so monks too ought during the time of prayer to stand before God in psalmody with fear and a pure heart.

The monk’s glory and praise in the sight of angels and human beings is humility and simplicity of heart. The monk’s glory is gentleness of heart and silence.

### CHAPTER LXXXV. That Monks Should Be Rich in Good Works and Lay Up for Themselves a Good Foundation

Monks who are not rich in earthly possessions ought to be rich in holy virtues and good works, because it is not carnal but spiritual riches that free the soul on the day of vengeance and retribution. Hence Solomon says: “Riches will not profit on the day of vengeance, but justice will deliver from death” (Prov. XI).

The good foundation he mentions signifies either Christ or the reward of good works, which each monk lays up for himself in heaven by living well and justly, so that, firmly established there, he may not be moved forever, like Mount Zion (Ps. CXXIV).

“For our eternal house is not made with hands” (II Cor. V). It is built in heaven through good works; if it is founded upon the rock (Matt. VII), that is, upon Christ, it will suffer no ruin from the assault of anything that comes upon it. For it has Christ as its foundation and therefore will fear no impact.

An earthly treasure, because it does not have Christ as its foundation, is dug up and stolen by thieves. But the treasure that holy monks lay up in heaven, because it has Christ as its foundation, is neither dug up by thieves nor stolen. For the Lord himself commands us to lay up treasure there when he says: “Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not dig through or steal” (Matt. VI).

There too the Apostle announces that we shall attain the true life if, while we live in the present, we carefully keep the Lord’s commandments. Without doubt, those attain true life in the age to come who, while still living in the world, daily store up for themselves there the treasure of their good works.

Hence it is written elsewhere: “Place your treasure in the commandments of the Most High, and it will profit you more than gold” (Ecclus. XIX). An earthly treasure preserves deceptive riches; a heavenly treasure prepares both true and eternal life. In comparison with this passing life, that is called the true life in which monks rich in virtues reign happily with Christ forever.

Once Zacharias went to his abbot, Sylvanus, and found him in an ecstatic state, with his hands extended toward heaven. When he saw this, he closed the door and went out. Returning at about the sixth and ninth hours, he found him in the same posture. About the tenth hour he knocked, entered, and found him resting. He said to him: “What happened to you today, Father?”

The old man replied: “I was sick today, son.”

But Zacharias, holding his feet, said: “I will not let you go unless you tell me what you saw.”

The old man answered him: “I was caught up into heaven, and I saw the glory of God. I stood there until now, and now I have been released.”

### CHAPTER LXXXVI. On the Eternal Dwelling Prepared by God for the Saints

“Let us guard our heart with all vigilance” (Prov. IV), brothers, while awaiting Christ the Lord and our God, the Master of the household, who, although he was rich, became poor for our salvation (II Cor. VIII), so that he might make us companions of his riches and reveal us as partakers of the ineffable glory to come.

We must therefore love him without interruption, so that we may deserve to be loved by him as well and enter with him into that dwelling which has been prepared by the Father for the saints. There we shall behold the entire nature of angels and archangels, of virtues and powers, and of all the saints.

There we shall be called sons of God. There the gates of the kingdom will be opened to us, and we shall enter into the inner chambers of the Father. There Christ, the Sun of Justice, will appear to us. There God will transform the body of our lowliness, making it conform to the body of his glory (Phil. III).

There our youth will be renewed like the eagle’s (Ps. CII). There we shall receive from the hand of the Lord a crown of beauty and a garment of joy, and on that day we shall say: “Let our soul rejoice in the Lord, for he has clothed us with the garment of salvation and righteousness and has surrounded us with the clothing of gladness. Like a bridegroom he will place a mitre upon us, and like a bride he will adorn us with an ornament” (Isa. LXI).

There we shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of our Father (Matt. XIII). There we shall find immortal and everlasting ages. There the length of days will be granted to us without disturbances or storms, where the voice of those rejoicing and exulting will always be heard. There a place and an eternal dwelling have been prepared for us in the house of the Lord and within its wall, and an everlasting name that will not be erased.

Let us therefore pray always, beloved brothers, that the merciful and kind Lord may transfer us to that blessed hope, ineffable joy, and eternal dwelling where praise, exultation, and everlasting delight always exist.

If you desire to be heavenly, always abhor and despise the things that are earthly; follow the examples of the perfect and become their imitator. Do not think within yourself, saying: “The labor required by the purpose and discipline of our monastic life is great; but I am small and weak and cannot persevere in this calling.”

O most beloved brother, understand what I say. If you wish to travel to a distant region, you cannot traverse the distances of the entire road in the space of one hour; rather, each day you complete a stage gradually, and after much time and labor you arrive at the homeland you desire.

So it is with the kingdom of heaven, the paradise of delights, and the desirable homeland of monks. One reaches it through prayers and vigils, fasts and continence, tears and obedience, charity and perseverance, humility and justice, and whatever other virtues there may be. These are the stages by which we believe we shall come to the heavenly kingdom and to God the Father. Preserve these things, and do not fear undertaking the beginning of the good way that leads you to eternal life.

### CHAPTER LXXXVII. How a Person Becomes Blessed

Blessed is the one who has hated this world and whose only meditation is upon God.

Blessed is the one who has execrated sin and wickedness, and has loved only God, the kind and merciful Redeemer, and who has continually kept chaste and holy thoughts.

Blessed is the one who has been cleansed from all polluted thoughts and has not been entangled in the affairs of this world, but, wholly free in the Lord, has been freed from all the most vain business of this world.

Blessed is the one who has always remembered that dreadful day and hastened to be washed in fountains of tears, continually caring for the wounds of his soul.

Blessed is the one who has become like a cloud, bringing forth a rain of tears by which he can extinguish the flames of every vice.

Blessed is the one who has walked in the way of the Lord’s commandments (Ps. CXVIII) and, continually conducting himself in holy works, has preserved his soul undefiled.

Blessed is the one who has daily grown in good works through holy discipline, possessing a sure hope in the Lord, so that he may see him in his glory, kingdom, and majesty.

Blessed is the one who has remembered the Lord’s precept and carefully kept his commandments, so that he may do them and live in them.

Blessed is the one who has set a guard over his mouth and a door of restraint around his lips, so that he may not turn aside to words of wickedness (Ps. CXL).

For people become blessed in many ways, as the Lord says in the Gospel:

“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

“Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.

“Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.

“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V).

### CHAPTER LXXXVIII. On the Hour of Departure and the Separation of the Soul from the Body
Blessed is the one who always keeps the day of his departure before his eyes and hastens to be found at that hour prepared and without any fear of sin or evil conscience. Blessed is the one who finds confidence at the hour of his departure, when the soul will be separated from the body—for it is separated with great fear and great pains. For angels will come to take the soul; they will separate it from the body and lead it before the tribunal of the immortal and fearsome [Col. 0681A] Judge. Then, remembering its deeds, it trembles; seeing and considering its actions, it is afraid to depart because of overwhelming dread and fear. Yet, trembling and afraid, it proceeds to the eternal judgment. Therefore everyone ought to live carefully, lest he be seized in his iniquities and his life end together with his guilt. (Isidore, *Sentences*, book III, chapter 62.)

For ignorance of the coming end is uncertain, and while a person does not expect to die, he is taken away. For the devil, the instigator who inflames the living toward vices, strives to drag them, when they suddenly die, into torments; and at an hour they do not know, they are seized by an unforeseen departure and, swallowed up by the abyss, are assigned to be tormented by the eternal fires of Gehenna. Concerning them it is written: “They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they descend to the underworld” [Col. 0681B] (Job XXI).

For apostate angels receive the souls of wicked people as they leave the body, so that those who were persuaders toward vices may themselves be their torturers in punishment. But the end of the righteous is sometimes commended by a most excellent, tranquil summons, so that from this they may be understood to belong to the company of the holy angels: they are taken from this body without harsh distress. Therefore, although piety commands us to weep for such people, faith nevertheless forbids us to mourn. Those should be bewailed whom the abyss of hell swallows, not those whom the palace of paradise receives to be made glad.

We read of a certain old man who, when he was dying in Scetis, was surrounded by the brothers at his bed. They clothed him and began to weep. But he opened his eyes and laughed. Again he began to laugh. This also happened a third time. When the brothers saw this, they asked him, saying: “Tell us, abba, why do you laugh while we are weeping?” He said to them: “The first time I laughed because you fear death. The second time I laughed because you are not prepared. But the third time I laughed because I am going from labor to rest.” Having said this, the old man immediately closed his eyes in death.

They also said of Abba Sisoes that, on the day of his falling asleep, while the brothers were sitting around him, his face shone like the sun. He said to them: “Behold, Abba Antony has come.” After a little while he said to them again: “Behold, the choir of prophets has come.” Again his face shone even more brightly, and he said: “Behold, the choir of apostles has come.” His face shone still more intensely, and behold, he was speaking with certain persons. The elders asked him: “With whom are you speaking, Father?” [Col. 0681D] He said to them: “Behold, angels have come to receive me, and I ask to be allowed to repent a little longer.” The elders said to him: “You have no need of repentance, Father.” But he said to them: “Truly, I do not know whether I have even begun to repent.” And they all understood that he was perfect. Then suddenly his face became like the sun again, and they all were afraid. He said to them: “Look, behold, the Lord is coming, saying: ‘I will take [Al.: bring] to myself the chosen vessel from the desert.’” And immediately he gave up his spirit. Once this had happened, the entire place was filled with a flash of light and the fragrance of sweetness.

[Col. 0681D]

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. On Innocence

The truly innocent person is one who harms neither others nor himself. [Col. 0682A] But whoever harms himself, although he does not harm others, is not innocent. David, trusting in the Lord concerning his own innocence, said: “Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence, and, hoping in the Lord, I shall not be weakened” (Psalm XV). And again: “But I have walked in my innocence; redeem me and have mercy on me” (Psalm XXV).

And when he asked the Lord who would dwell in his tabernacle or who would rest on his holy mountain (Psalm XIV), he heard the divine answer: “The innocent in hands and pure in heart, who has not received his soul in vain, nor sworn deceitfully to his neighbor. He shall receive a blessing from the Lord and mercy from God his Savior” (Psalm XXIII). (John Chrysostom, sermon on Joseph sold by his brothers.)

Rejoice, innocence, and exult; rejoice, I say, because everywhere you are unharmed, everywhere secure: if you are tested, you advance; if you are humbled, you are raised up; if you fight, you conquer; if you are slain, you are crowned. In slavery you are free; in dangers, safe; in custody, joyful. Every guilt is assigned to you, and all wickedness is subjected to you. The powerful honor you, rulers receive you, the great seek you; even those who attack you sometimes desire you. The good obey you; the wicked envy you. Rivals are jealous, enemies fall beneath you; nor can you ever fail to be victorious, even if you lack a just judge among human beings.

They said of Abba Paul that he held in his hands horned serpents, snakes, vipers, and scorpions, and tore them in half. When the brothers saw this, they questioned him, offering him their respect: “Tell us what you have done to receive this grace.” He answered them: “Forgive me, Fathers. If someone possesses purity and innocence, everything is subjected to him, as it was to Adam when he was in paradise before the transgression of the divine commandment.”

[Col. 0682C]

## CHAPTER XC. What It Means to Sanctify the Fast

Since, in recalling the victories of the fasting Lord, we have recognized the triumph of our salvation, let us sanctify our fasts by religious observances. What else is it to sanctify the fast (Joel I) than to will what is holy for the sake of the fast, to do what is just, and to avoid what is wicked?

That person sanctifies the fast who extinguishes the flames of raging anger by the calmness of a gentle mind. That person sanctifies the fast who turns lascivious eyes away from a shameful sight by the reins of chastity. (Maximus, Homily 1, on the Fast of Lent.)

That person sanctifies the fast who scatters the darts of insults after deflecting them with the shield of patience. That person sanctifies the fast who restrains the tumult of disputants by peaceful speech and the skill of a more prudent tongue. That person sanctifies the fast who, like a cultivator of his own breast, cuts out the thorns of vain thoughts rising within him by the evangelical plowshare. That person sanctifies the fast who, with hands moved by compassion according to the extent of his resources, consoles the poverty of the needy.

Above all, that person sanctifies the fast who, attentive in everything to the precepts of the divine law, rejects diabolical temptations from his heart. And therefore, dearest brothers, if we wish to offer fasts pleasing to God, [Col. 0683A] let us be strong in faith, just in judgments, faithful in friendship, patient under injuries, moderate in disputes, shunning foul speech, steadfast against wickedness, sober at banquets, restrained in pleasures, simple in charity, cautious among the deceitful, grieving with the sorrowful, resisting the insolent, sparing in suspicions, silent among evil-speakers, and equal among the humble.

If we wish to sanctify our fasts by virtues of this kind, then, with the Lord granting it, we shall come to the festival of Paschal grace and to the joys of the heavenly promises with unwavering confidence and a more joyful conscience.

[Col. 0683A]

## CHAPTER XCI. What It Means to Fast Well

That person fasts well who sustains his own hunger by satisfying a poor person. That person fasts well who, restraining himself in remembrance of the divine judgment, abstains from every pleasure of enticements. That person fasts well who chastises his flesh, which produces the shoots of vices, through meditation on holy virtues and love of sobriety. That person fasts well who forgives the injuries of his brothers with the gentleness of a peaceful heart. (Maximus, Homily 3, on the Fast of Lent.)

He offers God a most acceptable fast who guards his mind from evil thoughts, his eyes from lust, and his tongue and hands from strife. Thus let chastity sanctify our fast, patience adorn it, kindness foster it, mercy gladden it, humility commend it, so that by a twofold fast of body and soul we may always commend ourselves to divine grace.

[Col. 0683C]

[Col. 0683]

## CHAPTER XCII. On What Is Written: “Many Will Come from East and West and Recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the Kingdom of Heaven” (Matthew VIII)

Many will come from East and West and recline—not lying down bodily, but resting spiritually; not drinking for a time, but feasting eternally. They will recline in the kingdom of God, where there are light and beauty, joy and exultation, glory and blessing, light for the eyes and the long duration of eternal life; where all rejoice, where all are glad; where those blessed Fathers recline; where all the prophets rest; where the apostles and evangelists sit upon glorious thrones; where the multitude of martyrs exults in eternal glory; where the abundance of virgins rejoices forever, bearing [Col. 0683D] the crown of undefiled virginity. (Augustine, Sermon 1, on the Feast of All Saints.)

O sweetest brothers, harmonious gathering, joyful assembly, radiant fellowship! This is the exultation approved and proclaimed from the beginning of the world; this is the rest recounted from the beginning. All who love the Lord have hastened to go there; all from the nations who believe in the Lord and preserve religious devotion are gathered there; let us all proceed there as well.

O devout sons of God, let us hasten there with all our strength. Let nothing call us back, nothing delay us, nothing impede us from hastening to this desirable banquet. Let us drive every negligence from ourselves, every laziness from our soul, and cast away the impediments of the body, so that we may become members of this blessedness and rest, and may be found worthy of this holy feast, as has been said.

[Col. 0684A]

## CHAPTER XCIII. On the Figurative Meaning of the Fact That Every Elect and Perfect Monk and Person Is a Man, a Calf, a Lion, and an Eagle

For every person who is elect and perfect in the way of the Lord is at once a man, a calf, a lion, and an eagle. A man is a rational animal. A calf, however, is customarily slaughtered for sacrifice. A lion is a strong beast, as it is written: “The lion is the strongest of beasts; he will fear no encounter” (Proverbs XXX). An eagle flies up to lofty places and fixes its gaze with unblinking eyes upon the rays of the sun.

Therefore everyone who is perfect through reason is a man. And because he puts himself to death with respect to the pleasure of this world, he is a calf. But because, by that voluntary mortification of his, he possesses the strength of security against every adversity, he is a lion. Hence it is written: “The just man, confident as a lion, will be without terror” (Proverbs XXVIII). And because he contemplates sublimely those things that are heavenly and eternal, he is an eagle.

Therefore, since the just person becomes a man through reason, a calf through the sacrifice of his mortification, a lion through the strength of his security, and an eagle through contemplation, every perfect person may rightly be signified by these holy animals. For every intention and every contemplation of the saints reaches beyond itself, so that they may attain what they desire in the heavens. Whether someone devotes himself to a good work or to heavenly contemplation, what he does is truly good when he desires to please the one from whom he exists. In this matter it must be considered that every good deed performed should always be lifted toward heavenly things through intention.

But because the elect desire both to please almighty God through good works and, through the grace of contemplation, to taste already the eternal blessedness, they stretch out their faces and wings above (Ezekiel I).

[Col. 0684C]

## CHAPTER XCIV. On What the Apostle Says: “The Flesh Lusts,” etc. (Galatians V)

The lust of the flesh is an unclean movement of the soul toward an affection for sordid pleasure. The lust of the spirit, however, is the mind’s ardent striving toward desires for holy virtue. The former, when people consent to it, sends them to everlasting punishment; the latter sends those who consent to it into the kingdom.

For the lust of the flesh first produces the enticements of vices in the thoughts. The lust of the spirit, on the contrary, continually sets holy thoughts against them. The former delights in idle tales and words; the latter in meditation on the Scriptures and the commandments. The former rejoices in spectacles of earthly things; the latter in contemplation of heavenly joys. The former seeks earthly pleasures; the latter draws forth groans and sighs. The former relaxes the body into sleep and laziness; the latter labors in vigils and suitable prayers. The former, through gluttony, burns with the enticements of the belly and desire of the throat; the latter torments and mortifies itself with fasts and abstinence.

[Col. 0684D]

The former, subjected to lust, strives to fulfill through the completion of the will the desires for shameful acts that it pursues through concentrated thought; the latter loves the honor of chastity and modesty. [Col. 0685A]

The former, kindled by the flame of greed, seeks profit and flees the loss of temporal goods; the latter, despising the world, claims Christ alone for itself. The former, envious, permits no one to be superior or equal to it, but wastes away through inward rancor at everyone’s progress; the latter rejoices in everyone’s virtues and, out of charity, places those lesser than itself before itself.

The former, seething, bears nothing calmly, but with an agitated mind raises its voice into tumult; the latter is moved by no provocation, but patiently endures through the gentleness of tranquility. The former is infected by sadness whenever it senses any adversity; the latter is broken by no grief, but even while bearing the troubles of others is not moved from its inward joy. The former is infected by ambition for honors and soothed by human praises or the enticements of empty glory; the latter loves humility and delights in pleasing its only God, who observes the mind. The former, swollen with the arrogance of pride, raises its wretched heart; the latter humbles itself even to the lowest places, lest it fall from its height.

But why say more? The lust of the flesh hurls those who consent to it into a multitude of every vice. The lust of the spirit strengthens the weary mind with hope of future glory, lest it fail.

[Col. 0685B]

## CHAPTER XCV. What the Impulse of the Spirit Is and What the Impulse of the Flesh Is

There are different impulses in the elect and the rejected: in the elect, the impulse of the spirit; in the rejected, the impulse of the flesh. For the impulse of the flesh drives the mind toward hatred, arrogance, uncleanness, plunder, outward glory, cruelty, treachery, despair, anger, quarrels, and pleasures. [Col. 0685C] The impulse of the spirit, however, draws the mind toward charity, humility, self-restraint, generosity of mercy, inward progress, works of piety, faith in eternal things, hope of the joy to come, patience, peace, consideration of immortal life, and tears.

Therefore we must always consider with great care, in everything we do, where the impulse is leading us: whether our thought is driven by the impulse of the flesh or by the impulse of the spirit. To love earthly things, to prefer temporal things to eternal ones, to possess external goods not for necessary use but out of desire for pleasure, to seek vengeance upon an enemy, and to rejoice at the fall of a rival—these are impulses of the flesh.

[Col. 0685D]

On the contrary, to love heavenly things, to despise what passes away, to seek things that pass away not for the fruit of pleasure but for necessary use, and to grieve over the death of an enemy—these are impulses of the spirit. And because all the perfect continually exercise themselves in these virtues, it is rightly said now concerning the holy animals: “Wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there they went” (Ezekiel I).

[Col. 0685D]

## CHAPTER XCVI. On the Fact That Every Just Person Walks Both Before His Own Face and in the Presence of His Own Face

Therefore the just person advances before his own face, because he no longer looks [Col. 0686A] with any desire toward the things he has left behind, and places the foot of good work upon the eternal things he desires under the eye of his contemplation. (Gregory, Book I on Ezekiel, Homily 4.)

To walk before one’s face means to seek what lies ahead. To walk in the present means not to be absent from oneself. For every just person who carefully observes his life and diligently considers how much he grows daily in good things—or perhaps how much he declines from them—because he places himself before himself, walks in his own presence: he vigilantly sees whether he is rising or sinking.

But whoever neglects the guardianship of his life, whether he disregards or does not know what he does, what he says, and what he thinks, does not walk in his own presence, because he does not know what he is like in his habits or actions. Nor is the person present to himself who is not careful to examine and know himself every day. But he truly places himself before himself and is present to himself who observes himself in his actions as though he were another person. [Col. 0686B] (Thus far Gregory.)

Therefore we must diligently see ourselves as we see others, and, as has been said, place ourselves before ourselves; in everything we do, inwardly and outwardly, we must carefully guard ourselves.

[Col. 0686B]

## CHAPTER XCVII. On What Is Written: “Guard Your Heart with All Vigilance” (Proverbs IV)

Perhaps you say: “How can I guard my heart so that it does not think evil?” Hear the explanation briefly. You plainly can, if you meditate on divine and heavenly things. There are, nevertheless, three things that can free the soul from evil thoughts: holy vigilance, prayer, and meditation. Their constancy gives stability to the soul, so that it is occupied with good thoughts and not evil ones.

If you wish to have a pure heart in this world, say with David: [Col. 0686C] “I meditated at night with my heart, and I examined my spirit within me” (Psalm LXXVI). The more you tame your heart through meditation, the more exalted a reward you will attain, and the more brightly you will shine with the light of wisdom and knowledge.

If, as was said above, you wish to have a pure heart, never occupy yourself with empty tales. Whatever is shameful and contrary to holiness, never do it or take pleasure in hearing it. You have already laid aside the things of the world; you have put on Christ the Lord (Romans XIII). Take care not to descend from the roof of the virtues in search of your former garments (Matthew XXIV), nor return from the field to the house; and never let go of the Savior’s fringe, nor of the locks moistened by the dew of night, which you once began to hold.

Be like a house founded upon a rock (Matthew VII); let no breeze of this world [Col. 0686D] shake you, and let no wind of evil desire burn you. Be a most prudent bee; let your works compose a honeycomb, so that you may satisfy Christ with your sweetness. Fly above the vices and you will touch him who says to you: “I am the flower of the field and the flower of the meadow” (Song of Songs II). Pluck flowers through the holy Scriptures, so that you may say with the Prophet: “My heart has poured forth a good word; I speak of my works to the king. My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe” (Psalm XLIV).

Therefore imitate and follow those who deserved to hear these things, whose bearing, speech, gait, and life offer a model to those who observe them. But avoid, as I have said, those whom you see walking in the manner of a turtle dove, curious, talkative, quick to laugh, shameless, immodest, recounting childish and empty tales, slow to run, ready for the table, and ungrateful for fasting; whose eyes, like burning torches, with the wind of the soul blowing this way and that, [Col. 0687A] scatter sparks of desire; who roll about like a wheel and are tormented by their own fire in the frying pan of their mind. For you read: “With the holy you will be holy, and with the perverse you will be made perverse” (Psalm XVII).

Love and cherish the humble and obedient, those who love reading and devote themselves to prayer, as members of Christ. Do not attend to those whom I warned you to avoid. Rather, I want the wicked to fear and imitate you, while the good love and receive you.

[Col. 0687A]

## CHAPTER XCVIII. What Is Signified by God’s Saying to Abraham: “Go Out from Your Land and from Your Kindred, and Come [Col. 0687B] into the Land That I Will Show You” (Genesis XII)

And we, dearest brothers, following the example of blessed Abraham, let us arrive at this command: “Let us go out from our land and from our kindred, and let us come into the land that the Lord will give us after this life.” What is our land from which we are commanded to go out, if not our flesh? (Augustine, Sermon 34, among the appendices.)

Therefore a person goes out well from his land who, despising carnal desires and rejecting his own wills as the devil’s poison, frequently devotes himself to reading or prayer. He goes out well from his land who spurns greed and loves mercy, flees lust, and embraces chastity. He goes out well from his land who abandons wickedness in order to hold fast to charity, despises pride, [Col. 0687C] and pursues humility.

What, then, is it to go out from one’s land except to leave behind all sins and carnal vices? “And come,” says the Lord, “into the land that I will show you” (Genesis XII). Therefore, if we leave our land, we shall come to the land that the Lord shows us. But what is this land that the Lord deigns to show us? Without doubt, let us believe that it is the land of which the Prophet said: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm XXVI).

Therefore, when the land of our body serves great crimes, it is recognized as the land of the dying. But when it has devoted itself to virtues, it is changed by a most blessed migration into the land of the living. This, then, dearest brothers, we can accomplish not outside ourselves but within ourselves, with God’s grace, if we wish.

For if we leave sins and devote ourselves to virtue, we shall have happily gone out [Col. 0687D] from the land of the dying and shall happily come into the land of the living. Therefore let the one who used to curse bless; and let the one who used to slander always strive to bring forth what is good. Let the one who used to preserve anger in his heart hold fast to patience. Let the one who used to seize the possessions of others strive to distribute from his own possessions. Let the one who used to practice fraud in business and seek worldly profits through false weights or double measures strive through repentance or mercy to lift his soul away from every fraud and every iniquity.

Do this, then, dearest brothers, and the God of peace and love will be with you (2 Corinthians XIII).

[Col. 0688A]

[Col. 0688]

## CHAPTER XCIX. On the Martyrdom That Takes Place in the Peace of the Church

(Augustine, Sermon 250, on the seasons.)

Let no one say, brothers, that in our times there can be no contests of martyrs. Our peace, too, has its martyrs. For, as we have often stated, to restrain anger, flee lust, guard justice, and despise greed is a great part of martyrdom.

It was not inappropriately said: to despise greed, to restrain anger, to flee lust. Greed must be despised because it procures unjust profits for us in order to make us its own. We would belong to ourselves if it did not belong to us. Greed is unjust; like fire, the more it receives, the more it seeks.

Anger, however, must be restrained, because it harms those who do harm before it harms those who are harmed. [Col. 0688B] As for our advice that lust must be fled, the apostle Paul clearly demonstrates this. Although he preached that all vices must be resisted, when he spoke against lust he did not say “resist,” but “flee fornication” (1 Corinthians VI). Thus, with God’s help, we must resist the other vices in the present, but overcome lust by fleeing.

Therefore flee from the assault of lust if you wish to obtain victory. And do not be ashamed to flee if you desire to win the palm of chastity. Hence, dearest brothers, all Christians, but especially clerics and monks, must flee unworthy and dishonorable intimacy; for without any doubt, whoever does not wish to avoid intimacy that is suspect quickly falls into ruin. [Col. 0688C]

Among all the contests of Christians, the battles of chastity alone are especially severe: there is daily combat and rare victory. Chastity has drawn a formidable enemy, one who is conquered and feared every day. Therefore, as has already been said, let no one deceive himself with false security or dangerously presume upon his own strength, but let him hear the Apostle saying: “Flee fornication.”

[Col. 0688D]

And therefore, dearest brothers, let us continually implore God’s help against deadly flatteries and against the devil’s assistants, who neither fear nor blush to maintain suspect intimacy, lest they deceive us by their example; let us ask that he deign to free us from the snare of the hunters (Psalm CXXIV). We know that in all the evils mentioned above, daily martyrdoms cannot be lacking for Christians.

For if chastity, truth, and justice are Christ, just as the one who lies in wait is a persecutor, so also the one who wishes to defend these things in others and preserve them in himself will be a martyr. Therefore whoever loves these things with all the strength of his soul, and shows by both words and example that others should love them, and wherever peace, truth, justice, or chastity is suffering, willingly presents himself to the extent of his power and strives to defend it, will receive the crown of martyrdom when the Lord rewards him.

But someone says: “I am young; I will do what pleases me now, and afterward I will repent.” This is equivalent to saying: “I will strike myself with a cruel sword and afterward go to the physician.” He does not know that a wound is inflicted in a moment, but is scarcely restored to its former health after a long time. For when an adulterer says that he will repent afterward, why does he not fear that a sudden little fever may overtake him, that the opportunity for delay may perish for him, and that eternal damnation may follow?

[Col. 0689A]

## CHAPTER C. On the Two Altars in a Human Being, One in the Body and the Other in the Heart

(Augustine, Sermon 4, on the anniversary of a dedication.)

There are two altars established within us, namely, those of our body and our heart. Accordingly, God asks a twofold sacrifice from us: one, that we be chaste in body; the other, that we be pure in heart.

Therefore let good works be offered on the exterior altar, that is, in our body; and on the altar of the heart, let holy thought give forth fragrances of sweetness. [Col. 0690A] On the altar of our heart, let us always think what is good; on the altar of our body, let us continually perform what is pleasing to God.

For we celebrate the consecration of the altar in due order and with joy when we offer the altars of our heart and body, clean and pure, in the sight of the divine majesty. For I do not know with what face or conscience a person desires to rejoice at the consecration of an altar if he does not strive to preserve purity on the altar of his heart.

We, however, dearest brothers, should strive to act in such a way that we may always deserve to celebrate a twofold festival. And just as we visibly rejoice at the consecration of the temple altar, so may we deserve to possess invisible spiritual joy in the chastity of the body and the purity of the soul.

[Col. 0689A]

## COMMENTARIES OF ABBOT SMARAGDUS ON THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

[Works of Rabanus Maurus, volume IV, p. 246.]

[Col. 0689B]

[Col. 0689]

## HERE BEGINS THE PREFACE COMPOSED IN VERSE

Whoever prefers to climb to the eternal kingdom

Must in mind ascend to the star-bearing heaven;

By holy religion seek the path of life,

By which he may swiftly climb to the golden realms.

For the monks of holy Benedict, Father,

The Rule is a sweet and broad road, a palm of victory;

But harsh for boys and narrow for beginners,

Whom a life of milk has long nourished in its bosom.

This is the holy, shining path, the bright track of heaven,

Which the blessed camps of God desire to follow.

This exalted Rule admonishes all monks

To be without possessions and seek the heavenly realms;

Let them abandon what is their own, so that they may possess all things as their own—

The prosperous heavenly realms that await their companions. [Col. 0689C]

By our fathers, in the sacred song of the law,

This royal road is rightly called the path of rectitude.

This is life for the good and also the rule of salvation,

A bow and weapons for the devout, shining arrows against the wicked.

No unwilling person will fulfill it; everyone who desires it will.

Let it be burdensome to the burdensome, sweet and fitting for the good.

This Rule shows high-soaring monks

The radiant place of paradise that they should desire.

It chastises its children well with maternal love,

Rebuking them as it instructs, while remaining without bitterness.

It patiently nourishes them with a tender blow;

After death it will give many bright rewards.

It opens the road for our friends; it opens the heavenly road.

Let them not be reluctant to run, but go patiently. [Col. 0689D]

It examines life, composes and adorns conduct,

Strikes and balances it, and threatens while moderating;

It destroys what is crooked and tests what is just like gold by fire,

Files and examines it, and balances it by polishing.

[Col. 0690B]

It is a slender rod for sheep, just moderation,

A file cleansing sins and preparing the blessed realms.

It rebukes, entreats, reproves, and willingly corrects

Those whom it joins to itself in brotherly covenant.

It knows how to lead monks to the eternal kingdom

And sweetly join them to the angelic choir.

Although it leads these companions of heaven to the heights,

It is nevertheless a narrow track and a confined road.

The narrow road leads the devout to the lofty halls of the kingdom;

The broad road plunges the wicked into the depths of the black pit.

Let no monk fear to enter the narrow way;

It leads to the star-bearing heaven, the blessed camps.

He will be able easily to climb the heights of heaven

Whom no guilt weighs down with a harmful weight.

No winged being of the ether, burdened with a heavy body, [Col. 0690C]

Can often beat out the ethereal roads by flying.

For no monk pressed down by the weight of sin

Can enter the kingdoms of the starry heaven.

Every monk must wash away what he has done with tears

And suffer no further things that must be washed away.

Meanwhile, let the monk’s discretion govern his mind,

And let the royal middle way lead him.

Let him carefully avoid the right and fear the left;

The duties of the sacred law urge him onward.

Let him not fear sorrowful things, but fear the world’s prosperity;

Then he will be able to climb the blessed kingdoms of heaven.

Whoever loves to gather the shining fruits of the saints

Must be joined to them in all his deeds.

Adorned in conduct and dressed in a chaste body,

He will live, and will always be loved by the Lord. [Col. 0690D]

Let him be silent, humble, most gentle, and kind;

Let him be patient, sober, prudent, and devout.

Of good character and docile, wise and humble in mind,

Penitent, peaceful, and very cautious, let him go.

Meanwhile compunction of heart stirs a fountain [Col. 0691A]

That washes away the soul’s filth and uncleanness.

The outpouring of tears, poured forth with chrism,

Equals the fountain, wiping away black stains as it does;

It also cleanses those washed, the inhabitants of paradise, as is proper;

It makes them citizens who may now, without end,

Offer continual thanks of praise,

Live with the Lord always, and belong to him. [Col. 0691A]

## HERE BEGINS THE PROEM

When I saw a great multitude of monks keenly seeking in the blessed Rule of Benedict interpretations of its words, the meaning of its various statements, and discernment concerning its many judgments, which vary according to the differing measure of faults, I was moved, both by myself and compelled by others, to undertake its exposition. Although the learned have no need of its exposition, its simple explanation is nevertheless pleasing to simple monks who desire, through its observance, to climb to the heavenly kingdoms and who desire frequently to hear even a few words about it. Those who hold fast to its rectitude and hope to enjoy eternal blessedness gladly hear the discourse of the Rule again and again.

With the Lord’s grace assisting, I shall now begin to expound its words in order.

[Col. 0691B]

## EXPOSITION OF THE RULE OF BLESSED BENEDICT

## HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE OF THE RULE OF BLESSED BENEDICT, FATHER OF MONKS

[Col. 0691C]

### “Listen.”

These are the words of blessed Benedict exhorting us. For, filled with the Holy Spirit, he urges us to advance toward better things. There are some who rashly attempt to criticize him, saying: “He should have said *ausculta*, ‘listen,’ not *obsculta,’” unaware that just as one correctly says *obaudi*, “obey,” *obtempera*, “comply,” *obsecunda*, “assist,” and many other such forms, so *obsculta* can also be said most correctly.

### “O son.”

The interjection “O” has different meanings according to different senses. At times it expresses wonder, as in: “O how beautiful is a chaste generation!” (Wisdom IV). At times it expresses grief, as in: “O all you who pass along the way, look and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow” (Psalm CV). At times it contains the meaning of a wish, as in: “O Lord, save us. O Lord, grant prosperity” [Col. 0691D] (Psalm CXVII). It appropriately has this force here as well.

For he also chose to call him “son” whom he wished to have as an imitator. There are four ways in which people are called sons: by nature, by imitation, by adoption, and by instruction. Here, however, the person is called a son not by nature or adoption, but by instruction or imitation, because he is urged to listen to the teacher’s precepts.

### “Precepts.”

Precepts are teachings about what must or must not be done: what must be done, such as “Love the Lord your God,” “Honor your father,” and the rest; what must not be done, such as “You shall not kill,” “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not steal” (Exodus XX), and similar commands.

What he says, “of the Master,” is understood to mean Christ. Although several are called masters by an improper usage—as in the passage in Ecclesiastes concerning the law and its legislators: “What was given through the counsel of masters by one shepherd”—nevertheless, God alone is by nature Master and Father. For he himself says: “Do not call anyone father on earth. For one is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. XX). “Do not be called masters, because your one Master is Christ.” When we call a human being “father,” we pay honor to his age; we do not indicate that he is the author of our life. A master, however, may truthfully be called so through association with the true Master: just as by nature there is one God, and the Son does not prevent others from being called gods and sons by adoption, so one Father and Master does not prevent others from being called fathers and masters in an improper sense.

[Col. 0692B] “Master” is understood as leader, governor, instructor, or teacher. Its etymology derives from the Greek word *steron* [uncertain reading]. In Greek, *steron* is said to mean “station.” Therefore, in Latin, a master is called *major visitatione* [“greater in visitation,” or, as the bracketed gloss has it, “in station”].

And incline the ear of your heart. The ear of our heart is then truly inclined to hear when the admonition of the devoted Father, that is, the Lord, is willingly heard by us and effectively fulfilled, when it is received humbly and held with a pure heart. Seeking this ear, the Lord said: “Whoever has an ear for hearing, let him hear” (Matt. XI). The bodily ear of a human being is so called from hearing or drawing in; but the ear of the heart draws in the understanding of speech.

And the admonition. Properly speaking, admonition occurs when what a person had fallen away from is brought back to his memory. Through Adam’s disobedience, we all in general withdrew from the joy, exultation, and glory of paradise; but we must return to what we lost through disobedience by imitating the obedience of Christ, who “became obedient to the Father unto death” (Phil. II).

Of the devoted Father. Properly, the devoted Father is he who powerfully forgives the impieties of others’ hearts. To him the Psalmist says: “I said, I will confess my injustices against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the impiety of my heart” (Ps. XXXI). God is called devoted because of his clemency, kindness, and mercy. The piety of the Father is justice, which, as Augustine says, is properly understood as the worship of God. Properly, God alone is called Father, because, as the Apostle says, “from him every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named” (Eph. III). For in the Gospel he also says: “Do not call anyone father on earth. For one is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. XX). And through the prophet he himself speaks, saying: “You will call me Father, and you will not cease to walk after me.” The whole Church likewise cries out universally: “Our Father, who art in heaven.”

When he says, “receive willingly,” this means diligently, with the utmost care, and with complete willingness. To receive means to accept or take up.

He added: And fulfill it effectively. “Effectively” is understood as easily, readily, quickly, perseveringly, or attentively. This adverb comes from the noun *efficax*, because an effective action has no difficulty in its execution.

So that by the labor of obedience you may return to him from whom through the sloth of disobedience you had withdrawn. When he says “to him,” God is understood. From God, as was said above, whether generally in Adam and Eve, or individually each one of us, we withdrew through the vice of disobedience and the sloth of the heart. Blessed Benedict exhorts us to return to him through the humility and labor of obedience. Obedience is called humility and compliance, because one humbly obeys or complies with the person commanding.

The labor of obedience is called every human action of ours which, having been justly commanded by the Lord, is humbly fulfilled by those who hear, according to the distribution of grace. Concerning the goodness of obedience, Solomon says: “An obedient man speaks of victories” (Prov. XX). Indeed, an obedient man speaks of victories because, when each of the elect submits himself to God with his whole heart through the humility of obedience, humbly fulfills his commands, and gives thanks for all these things not to himself but to God, he is freed from the guilt of disobedience by God’s mercy and, triumphing over the disobedient devil, ascends victoriously into heaven.

An obedient man speaks of victories when each person tramples vices and bravely overcomes the battles of the vices, so that with Paul he may say: “But in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Rom. VIII). For the victory of so great a triumph, he attributes glory not to himself but to God.

We return to God through the labor of obedience when we humbly fulfill with all our strength what has been commanded us; when we hate our own will and do not carry out the desires of the flesh (Gal. V); when we patiently endure persecution for justice (Matt. V; Rom. XII); when we return neither evil for evil nor insult for insult (1 Pet. III); when we keep neither deceit in our heart nor reserve time for anger (Eph. IV); when we fulfill the Lord’s commands daily by our actions (Jas. I) and obey our elders’ orders in everything; when we devote ourselves frequently to prayer (Rom. XII), and by vigils, fasts, tears, many labors, and various afflictions bring our chastised body into servitude; when we take up our cross, deny ourselves, and hasten to follow after Christ (1 Cor. VII; Col. IV; 1 Cor. IX).

The labor of obedience is altogether every chastisement of the body for God’s sake, every affliction of the heart, lowliness, every contempt and rejection of monks. This is the narrow and constricted way that leads those who walk along it to eternal life (Matt. XVI; Mark VIII; Luke IX). Those who labor faithfully on it and persevere to the end will deserve to hear, invited to the satisfaction and refreshment of eternity: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you,” says the Lord (Matt. XI).

Just as humility is called obedience because one obeys, so pride is called disobedience because one disobeys. Sloth is called laziness or delay. Hence those who are found slow and lazy in good work are called slothful. Through this vice, which nourishes all evils, all evils grow together, while all good things lie dormant and at rest so that they may not be brought to completion.

Of this vice Solomon says: “Sloth sends sleep” (Prov. XIX). Sloth sends sleep into the sluggish mind: when it finds someone lukewarm and slow in good works, so that he may not grow in goodness, it closes the eyes of his heart and binds his hands. Through the same Solomon it is said: “Because of the cold the lazy man would not plow” (Prov. XXVII). The lazy man does not plow because, bound by sloth at the time of slothfulness, he pretends not to do the good things he ought to do. While he fears small evils, he neglects to perform the greatest good.

Of the lazy man it is rightly added: “He will beg in summer, and it will not be given to him” (Prov. XX). For whoever does not sweat in good works in the present age, when the time of repayment has come, hungers with an empty mind, deprived of the gift of reward.

On the contrary, Solomon says of the ant: “The people of the ants are a weak people; they prepare food for themselves in the harvest” (Prov. XXX). By the ants, surely, the strenuous life of monks is signified, because, in comparison with the lovers of this world, they seem like tiny ants through the grace of humility. In the present life, as in a harvest, they do not cease gathering the fruit of good works, by which they may rejoice in the future.

Again, it is written concerning the obedient and the disobedient: “The mind of the just will meditate obedience, but the mouth of the wicked, perversity” (Prov. XV, X). The humble monk, while striving through love of eternal life to obey the command of his elders, first meditates obedience in his thought. But the disobedient, while he scorns to fulfill the orders of his superiors, contradicts them with insolent words.

Such a person, imitating Adam’s disobedience, withdraws from God. The humble monk, imitating Christ’s obedience, returns to the Lord. Adam sinned, but neither recognized his sin nor asked forgiveness for it. Christ, however, committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth (1 Pet. II); but, in order to redeem us from sin, he “became obedient to the Father unto death” (Phil. II). Innocent, he endured suffering and death for us, leaving us an example so that, by imitating him, we might follow in his footsteps (Isa. LIII).

When Adam fell, we all fell, and we lost all good works. In Christ, however, we rose again (1 Pet. II; 1 Cor. XV) and received greater things that will remain without end—provided, however, that we hold fast to his footsteps perseveringly. Adam subjected us to every evil through his own fault, but Christ’s coming freed us through grace. To say everything in brief: Adam’s disobedience took paradise from us; Christ’s obedience gave us the kingdom. Therefore, having withdrawn from God through the sloth of disobedience, let us return to God through the labor of obedience, so that this may be fulfilled in us: “They returned to their own region by another way” (Luke II).

To you, therefore, my speech is addressed. Many at this point try to change *meus* into *mihi*, as though correcting it, not knowing that many learned teachers have used this form of expression. Thus, in one place blessed Gregory says: “Let these things be said by me to them.” And elsewhere: “For now my speech is turned to you.”

Speech (*sermo*) takes its name from *serere*, “to sow” or “to string together.” It is a discourse or a conversation, which does not consist of only one word; rather, because it strings together many words, it is called speech—for example, the speech of Hilary, the speech of Augustine, and those of others.

Whoever renounces his own wills. “To renounce” is customarily used to mean despise, reject, contradict, or whatever else this word can express in this sense. For the renunciation of monks—or, indeed, of all the faithful—takes place in two ways.

First, all the faithful renounce Satan, who is also called the devil, in baptism, so that they may serve the Lord the Savior more freely, since, according to the Lord’s own saying, “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. VI). His works are renounced because his works are contrary to the works of the Savior. His pomps are renounced; these are certainly Satan’s works, but they seem to be distinguished from his other works by the fact that in them pride is represented in some fashion—pride of which he is the author and which cast him down from heaven.

His pomps, therefore, are ambition, arrogance, vainglory, and other things of this kind, which proceed from the fountain of pride.

Second, monks and Christian believers renounce their own wills, following the example of the Lord, who said: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John VI, VII). Scripture also says: “Turn away from your own wills” (Ecclus. XVII).

What belongs to each person is called his native, private, or individual will. “Will” takes its name from *velle*, “to wish.” It is the power of the mind to deliberate, and the purpose of one’s judgment.

This is to live according to man, not according to God. He lives according to man who lives according to himself and according to his own will: who goes with whom he wishes and where he wishes; sleeps as much as he wishes and when he wishes; speaks when and for as long as he wishes; eats and drinks what he wishes, where he wishes, as much as he wishes, and when he wishes; laughs when and as much as he wishes; and, finally, does and pursues whatever is pleasing to his eyes, whatever is sweet to his nostrils, and whatever is agreeable to the other senses of his flesh.

But the person who lives according to God is not carnally delighted by all these things. Spiritual things spiritually build him up, and he restrains every desire of the flesh by the delight of spiritual desire. He prefers future things to present things, subjects the flesh to the spirit, and wishes everything he does to proceed not from his own will but from the will of his God, whom he desires with all his strength to please.

About to serve the Lord Christ, the true King. The Lord is so called because he rules over all his creation, or certainly because every creature serves his dominion. “Christ” is named from *chrism*. For *chrism* in Greek is called *unctio* in Latin, “anointing.” This name is also applied to the Lord Jesus Christ, whom God the Father anointed not with visible but with invisible and spiritual oil. Hence in the Acts of the Apostles it is said to the Father: “They gathered together in this city against your Son, whom you anointed” (Acts IV). To the Son himself the Psalmist says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness,” and so forth (Ps. XLIV).

He is therefore rightly called the true king because he created all things, rightly sustains, governs, protects, and rules them. Although the saints are improperly called kings, as in the Psalm: “And now, kings, understand” (Ps. II), and in Job: “He sets kings upon the throne,” nevertheless Christ the Lord is truly King, because he is the Son of the true King. Hence the Psalmist says: “Give the king your judgments, O God, and your justice to the Son of the King” (Ps. LXXI).

The saints are therefore kings of the world because they know how not to succumb to the movements of their temptations but to govern them and rule over them. They are kings of the world because, set above all the movements of the flesh, sometimes they restrain the appetite of lust, sometimes temper the heat of avarice, sometimes bend the glory of pride, sometimes overwhelm the suggestions of envy, and sometimes extinguish the fire of anger. Yet they accomplish all these things not by their own strength but by the Lord’s work. And because they receive from the Lord the ability to do these things, they are called kings not properly but improperly.

Christ the Lord is truly proved to be the true Christ, King of kings and Lord of lords (1 Tim. VI), because, just as every creature is known to have been made through him (John I), so it is proved to be rightly governed and directed through him.

There are soldiers of the world, and there are soldiers of Christ. The soldiers of the world take up weak and slippery weapons; the soldiers of Christ take up weapons that are most powerful and glorious. The former fight against enemies so that they may bring themselves and those whom they kill to eternal punishment; the latter fight against vices so that after death they may attain eternal life as their reward. The former fight to descend to Tartarus, the latter to ascend to glory; the former to be handed over with demons to hell after death, the latter to possess the kingdom perpetually with angels; the former to be joined forever to demons, the latter to rejoice forever with angels; the former to mourn forever with the devil, the latter to exult with Christ.

The Apostle Paul includes both kinds of soldiers in one statement, saying: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs” (2 Tim. II), showing that there are soldiers of God, just as there are also soldiers of the world. Thus the twofold warfare signifies two kinds of soldiers. Spiritual warfare brings some to the heavenly camp through the freely given grace of the heavenly commander; bodily warfare compels others to labor with the world according to the will of an earthly king.

The soldiers of the world are held subject to passions and desires; the soldiers of God crucify their flesh with its vices and desires. The former are nourished by feasts, the latter by virtues. The former strive to seize what belongs to others; the latter patiently endure the loss of their own possessions or mercifully desire to distribute them. The former acquire things by which they may be raised up through false praises; the latter seek things by which they may be honored with eternal rewards.

To the former vanity grants the appearance of joy; to the latter truth confers true joys. The former look after their own interests; the latter after the common good. The former, themselves destined to perish, hasten to preserve perishing things; the latter desire to possess things that will never perish, so that they may not perish eternally. For the former, living is labor and dying punishment; for the latter, “to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” The former fight against visible enemies; the latter against invisible enemies. Avarice makes the former cruel; mercy makes the latter kind. Envy makes the former quarrelsome; gentleness makes the latter peaceful.

Through pride the former quarrel for their own honors; through humility the latter consider one another superior to themselves. Through the former Babylon is ruled; through the latter, and over the latter, the heavenly Jerusalem is administered by the Lord. Prosperity raises up the soldiers of the world, while adversity casts them down; but the soldiers of God remain unmoved both in adversity and in prosperity.

You take up the strongest and most glorious weapons of obedience. Blessed Benedict called the weapons of obedience “strongest” because the labor of obedience surpasses all human labors that are performed voluntarily. For what can be stronger than for a person to make himself a servant of another in all things? And, though free and honored, to display himself to everyone as a vile and despised slave, rejected and abject, so that he may say: “But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the abjection of the people.”

What is stronger than, when struck on the cheek, to offer the other; to leave one’s cloak to the person taking one’s tunic; when pressed into service for one mile, to go two? And in all these things to rejoice that one has been considered worthy to suffer insults for the Lord’s name?

For what can be stronger or harder than for a person voluntarily to submit himself to another in every obedience and patiently endure the harsh and contrary injuries inflicted within that obedience? What is harder than to be content with every lowliness and extremity, ready for everything imposed upon him, and to declare himself lower and more contemptible than all others not only with his tongue but also in his heart? Wherever he may be, sit, or walk, he is always to have his head bowed and his eyes always fixed on the ground, considering himself guilty because of his sins and saying: “Lord, I am not worthy to look upon and see the height of heaven because of my injustices.”

Let us see why blessed Benedict called the weapons of obedience strongest and most glorious. They are strongest because, as we said above, the labor of obedience surpasses all the labors of the human race that are performed voluntarily. The weapons of obedience are strongest so that a person may deny himself to himself; glorious so that he may follow Christ. Strongest, so that he may turn away from evil; glorious, so that he may do good. Strongest, so that he may not return evil for evil; glorious, so that he may return good for evil. Strongest, so that he may not curse the one who curses him; glorious, so that he may even bless him.

Strongest in refusing to hold hatred in his heart; glorious in loving the enemy and neighbor as himself. Strongest in rejection; glorious in action. Strongest in endurance; glorious in obedience. Strongest in continual fasting; glorious in restoring the poor. Strongest: “Let your loins be girded”; glorious: “and your lamps burning.” Strongest in enduring illness; glorious in visiting other sick people. Strongest so that he may not be dissolved by the lie of vanity; glorious so that he may speak truth with heart and mouth. Strongest in patiently enduring injuries; glorious in not doing what must be endured. Strongest in restraining the appetite of the stomach; glorious in loving frugality and restraint. Strongest in chastising the body; glorious in loving chastity.

We may also say this truthfully: just as in the present life the weapons of obedience are strongest in action, so they will be glorious in eternal reward. To the extent that they are strongest in the practice of the present life, to that extent they will be glorious in future rest. To the extent that they are harsh and burdensome on the rugged road, to that extent they will be pleasant and light upon arrival. To the extent that they are despised in the present, to that extent they will be honored in the future.

To the obedient the Apostle says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. III). Concerning these same people the Lord says to the Father: “Father, those whom you have given me, I will that where I am, they also may be with me, so that they may see my glory. And I have given them the glory that you gave me” (John XVII). And they hear him say with the apostles: “Amen, I say to you, that you who have left everything and followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX).

First of all, whenever you begin any good work. “First of all,” that is, at the beginning of one’s way of life or of the initiation of a good work, he says. Understand, monk, that there are ambushes between you and the ancient serpent. Crush his harmful head as far as you prevail, because, as far as he is able, he will not cease to lie in wait for your heel.

You then prudently crush the serpent’s head if you neither consent to nor receive the beginning of his evil suggestion; and if you receive it by thinking, you do not nourish it by meditating upon it. That man crushes the serpent’s head well who neither chews over his suggestions in thought, nor cherishes them with delight, nor nourishes them through meditation, nor brings them to the commission of sin by consenting to them or feeding them. In this way, the one who crushes the serpent’s head drives the devil’s entire body away from himself.

For the crafty and slippery serpent, once he has sunk the head of his suggestion, strives to glide in completely, so that from the one by whom he has been received evilly he may receive everything evilly, and, having been received evilly, may possess him evilly in bondage. Therefore, let the good monk crush the serpent’s head—that is, the devil’s suggestion—at the beginning, lest at the end he become its possession. Let him crush it well, lest he be crushed evilly; let him strike, lest he be struck; let him kill, lest he be killed. And while he is a strong victor in all these things, let him return not praises to himself but thanks to his Creator, from whom he received the ability to conquer, lest, having been conquered, he perish.

Therefore, the prudent monk should direct all the watchfulness of his concern toward the heel of his final life, lest, unwary, he perish from the serpent’s poisonous bite. For what is signified by the human heel? Is not the final moment of life meant? What does the crafty enemy lying in wait strike with his deadly tooth if the unsound mind withdraws from guarding itself?

Therefore, monk, hear the counsel of your salvation and carefully guard the heel of your work, lest at the end of your life, deceived by some error, you slip into a wrong path. Where you hoped to receive a reward, may you not, deceived, find loss; where you hoped joyfully to climb into heaven, may you not there be plunged sadly into Tartarus; and, unwary, may you not suddenly lose what you could have acquired and possessed eternally after a long time.

For what benefit is there in beginning a good work and not completing it? Scripture does not say, “The one who has begun,” but “the one who has persevered will be saved” (Matt. X and XXIV).

Among the other kinds of sacrifices, the tail is commanded to be offered to the Lord. Just as the heel indicates the end of the body, so the tail indicates its end. The person sacrifices the tail well to the Lord who perseveres to the end in a good work. We offer the victim’s tail to the Lord when we complete a good work with a persevering ending.

Joseph, whose name is interpreted as “increased,” is also described as wearing a long tunic. The tunic in which he was clothed signifies perseverance in good works. He walks adorned with a long tunic who, having clothed his actions with virtues, advances toward perseverance in the good he has begun and does not leave unfinished the good he began to do.

Therefore, let the prudent monk extend the tunic of his good work as far as the ankle, lest he suffer the hostility of the enemy of the human race, and lest, naked of the tunic of perseverance, he be plunged into the depths of hell, or, partly clothed and partly mutilated, be preserved forever for condemnation in disgrace. Thus, let the long garment consistently adorn and protect the monks’ feet, so that at the end of life it may happily return them to God, where they will attain eternal rewards together with the glory of happiness.

Ask him to bring it to completion through the most urgent prayer. But so that these things may come to you, whoever you are, monk, by God’s generosity, ask for them not slowly, not lukewarmly, but through the most urgent prayer. Hear the Apostle admonishing us concerning perseverance in prayer. He says: “Devote yourselves to prayer, keeping watch in it” (Rom. XII). And again: “Watch and pray” (Col. IV). Elsewhere he says: “For it is necessary always to pray and never to grow weary” (Matt. XXVI; Mark XIII; Luke XVIII). “The continual prayer of the righteous,” says the Apostle, “is very powerful” (Jas. V).

The prayer of Elijah shut the hinges of heaven; the prayer of Daniel closed the mouths of lions; the prayer of the three youths extinguished the furnace of fire; the Church’s prayer loosed Peter’s chains; the prayer of Cornelius penetrated the Lord’s ears; the prayer on the cross opened paradise to the thief.

Let it not weary the monk to pray persistently, because he has within himself as an inhabitant the Lord whom he prays to. For the Apostle says: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of the Lord dwells in you” (1 Cor. III; 2 Cor. XVI). Those who become the temple and dwelling place of the Lord are quickly heard by their inhabitant. They carry within themselves the one whom they ask; indeed, they are heard by him by whom they are carried.

Therefore, whoever wishes to bring a good work to perfection must frequently devote himself to prayer. Prayer is called supplication or petition. It is called *oratio*, as it were, “the reason of the mouth” (*oris ratio*). A sequence of words without meaning, however, is not the reason of the mouth.

That he has deigned to count us among the number of sons. The Lord first mercifully deigned to count us among the number of sons when we received him through faith, as the evangelist John says: “But to as many as received him, he gave power to become sons of God” (John I); when we received not the spirit of servitude in fear but the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. VIII).

Having received the adoption of sons, we renounce the devil, his works, and his pomps in baptism. Afterwards we are counted among the number of sons when, through the grace of conversion, we leave the world and follow Christ, hearing the prophet’s voice saying: “Hear, daughter, and see, and forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. XLIV).

We have forgotten the father who is the world, which nourished us by nursing us badly, and we have followed the Father who is Christ, who nursed us well by chastising us. The good nurse therefore exhorted us, saying: “You will call me Father, and you will not cease to walk after me” (Jer. III).

Great is the dignity of God the Father! We do not deserve to be counted among servants, yet he does not disdain to count us among sons. Great, I say, is the dignity, that although by nature we are sons of wrath and sinners from infancy, we should mercifully be called sons of God and heirs—heirs indeed of God, and fellow heirs of Christ (Eph. II; Rom. VIII).

Great is the exaltation of the monks’ goodness before God the Father. They are permitted to shine like the sun in the kingdom of heaven (Dan. XII) and to sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. XIX). From the Lord, together with the apostles, they will hear: “As the Father has loved me, I also have loved you; remain in my love” (John XV).

And it is said: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends. And I will see you, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you. And whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John XVI). Great is the dignity of those for whom the Son intercedes with the Father, saying: “Holy Father, keep them in your name, so that they may be one, as we also are one. And I will that where I am, they also may be with me, so that they may see my glory; and I have given them the glory that you gave me” (John XVII).

He must never at any time become saddened by our evil deeds. “Deeds” takes its name from doing and action. Our works, whether good or evil, signify our deeds.
