If our works are righteous, the Lord rejoices and exults in these deeds of ours. But if they are wrong, he is saddened by them, punishes them, and condemns and judges us.

Just as God the Father rejoices in his chosen sons, so he is saddened by the reprobate. Solomon says in Proverbs: “A wise son makes his father glad, but a foolish son is the grief of his mother” [Col. 0700D] (Prov. X). For not only is God the Father saddened by a wicked son, but the holy mother, the Church, is also saddened.

The Apostle likewise says: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, in whom you were sealed” (Eph. IV). We grieve the Holy Spirit when we do what is displeasing to him and refuse to do what pleases him. Christ is the author of all good things, while the devil is the author of evils. He rejoices over those whom he sees perfecting themselves and growing in holy deeds; but he is saddened by those whom he sees entangled in and devoted to the devil’s deeds.

God is said to be saddened not properly but improperly. The expression is taken from our own usage. For God, who is always himself and unchanged, is never saddened, because he is never changed.

[Col. 0701A]

Thus, at all times we must obey him by means of his own good gifts in us. “Times” are so called from the movement of the stars. Hence, when God established these things, he said: “Let them be for signs and for times and for days and years” (Gen. I)—that is, for some changeable movement, in which one thing has passed earlier and another later, since they cannot exist simultaneously.

Times are divided into moments, hours, days, years, lustrums, ages, and actions. Properly speaking, neither a hundred years, nor one month, nor a day, nor an hour is one time, because when one thing passes away, another arrives, and one cannot be simultaneously the same.

When he says, “thus he must be obeyed,” Christ the King is understood, whom above he said the monk was armed to serve through obedience. “He must be obeyed” means that one must obey, serve, or comply. When he says “at every moment,” understand that this is spoken both in prosperity and in adversity.

When he adds that we must obey him by means of his good gifts, he shows that we possess nothing of our own by which we are able to obey him. Therefore, since we cannot even have the will from ourselves, let us hasten to obey him at every moment with what comes from him.

We obey God concerning his good gifts when, for the virtues we have received, we give thanks not to ourselves but to him; when we proclaim his commands with our mouth and fulfill them in our works, as he himself says: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John XIV); when, denying ourselves and carrying the cross, we follow the Lord with a joyful heart; when, having received the seed of the word in a good and excellent heart cleansed of every dregs of evil, we return one thirtyfold, another sixtyfold, and another a hundredfold fruit (Matt. XIII; Mark IV); when, having received the talent of money, we return to the Lord with great profit (Luke VIII; Matt. XVIII); when we forgive the one who sins against us not only seven times but up to seventy-seven times (Matt. XXV); when, invited to the wedding feast of the supreme King, we recline wearing the wedding garment (Matt. XXII), lest, like the one who refused to forgive his brother who had sinned against him, or like the one who buried his master’s money in the earth and hid it, or like the one who attended the wedding without a wedding garment, we deserve to be bound hand and foot, shut out in the outer darkness, and condemned to everlasting punishment.

Hence it follows:

So that not only may an angry father never disinherit his sons, but neither may the Lord, when angered by our evils and therefore to be feared, hand over the worst of servants to everlasting punishment—those who have refused to follow him to glory.

When he says “an angry father,” understand that this is not said properly of the Lord, but by an abusive figure of speech. For in accordance with human usage you will find many such expressions and others like them spoken of the Lord in the sacred Scriptures. He is called angry because he is moved by anger—that is, agitated by anger—which is said of the Lord in two ways: either when he chastises every son whom he receives into glory, or when he strikes every wicked person whom he hands over to punishment.

He is called our Father because he created us so that we might exist, recreated us through the grace of baptism, and bestowed upon those reborn the Holy Spirit, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. VIII); and he commanded us to pray to him, “Our Father who art in heaven” (Matt. VI). “Father” is a name of dignity and honor, and in God himself this is truly and perfectly established. For the Apostle says of him: “From whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named” (Eph. III). And the very Spirit whom we received in baptism bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God. But if children, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, and fellow-heirs with Christ (Rom. VIII).

In another passage the Apostle calls this inheritance “incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading,” and promises us that it is kept for us in heaven. For he who gave us the power to become children of God has also given us the power to receive an inheritance in heaven—provided that we persevere in salvation to the end.

He called the heavenly inheritance incorruptible because it is touched neither by old age, nor defiled, nor corrupted by death, nor constricted by the sadness of repentance, nor by filth, nor by the restraint of frugality. It receives nothing from outside by which it could be corrupted or violated. He described it as undefiled because it always remains whole and inviolate in itself, and is constrained neither by the limit of heirs nor by an extended measuring-rope. No hidden thief defiles it; no violent plunderer carries it away. It always remains undefiled, always incorruptible.

He called it unfading because it withers neither by the cutting of the sickle nor by being violently scorched beneath the sun’s heat. It remains forever green, forever immortal. In its children it is flourishing, in its virtues fruitful, in its delights pleasant, in its heirs splendid, in its possessors glorious, and in the gifts of its rewards always exalted. In it are eternal life, everlasting immortality, perpetual power, enduring peace, assured sanctification, and true justification. In brief: Christ is our inheritance, in whom all goodness is present.

Therefore we must take the greatest care lest an angry father exclude us from this most radiant splendor, and lest the Lord, when angered by our evils and therefore to be feared, hand over the worst of servants to everlasting punishment. It should be noted that those who were first called children by believing rightly and living well are afterward called the worst of servants when they live badly.

For two kinds of servants are found in the divine Scriptures: one good, the other evil. The good are those of whom the Lord says through Isaiah:

> “Behold, my servants shall eat, and you shall hunger. Behold, my servants shall drink, and you shall thirst. Behold, my servants shall rejoice, and you shall be ashamed. Behold, my servants shall praise because of the exultation of their heart, and you shall cry because of the sorrow of your heart, and because of the contrition of your spirit you shall howl” (Isa. LXV).

And concerning them the Lord says in the Gospel: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things” (Matt. XXV).

The evil kind of servants are those of whom it is written: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin; but a slave does not remain in the house forever” (John VIII). And: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all that debt,” and so forth (Matt. XVIII). Concerning these he also says here that he may hand over the worst of servants to everlasting punishment.

For the Lord does not hand anyone over to punishment; rather, the person who does not hesitate to sin hands himself over to punishment. For it is written: “Flee sin as from the face of a serpent” (Ecclus. XXI). Therefore the one who neither fears nor flees sin hands himself over to the serpent, the devil, to be tormented. The one who continues to sin while living softly and dissolutely hands himself over to everlasting punishment.

Punishment is so called because it binds and chastises sinners in torments. Punishment is understood as the monstrous Gehenna of sinners, everlasting torments, eternal penalties, unending burning, certain destruction, true death, eternal anguish, perpetual pain, continuous groaning, and everlasting ruin. There, according to Isaiah, “their worm does not die, and their fire is not quenched” (Isa. XIV).

They say that the worm is the devil and his angels, who gnaw at the souls of the rejected with the tooth of malice like worms, and hand them over to unquenchable and eternal fire, to burn and be tormented forever. To this truly terrible punishment are rightly handed over those who refuse to follow Christ to glory—to that glory of which the Psalmist says: “The saints shall exult in glory” (Ps. CXLVII).

And “follow” is rightly placed, because, as the Apostle says, he is called: “The God of all grace, who has called us to his eternal glory, so that when Christ, our life, appears, we too may appear with him in glory” (I Pet. V). He calls glory eternal life, complete and everlasting joy. There are certain security, secure tranquility, tranquil delight, blessed eternity, and eternal happiness. There is perfect love, no fear, an everlasting day, and joyful movement. There the assembly of the saints shines with their resplendent merits; eternal salvation overflows; truth reigns. There are understanding without error, memory without forgetfulness, thought without disturbance, charity without hypocrisy, perception without offense, safety without weakness, health without pain, life without death, ease without impediment, fullness without weariness, and complete health without sickness.

So let us finally arise at some time. “Let us arise” is rightly said of those who are idle and weighed down by the sleep of sloth, because the soul devoted to sleep and burdened by the inertia of negligence and delay rests like a sleeper, badly drowsing on the bed of idleness. For he says, “Let us arise”—that is, let us prudently raise ourselves from that place of negligence in which we have lain for a long time, oppressed by harmful sluggishness.

Let us lift our hearts, together with our hands—that is, with good works—to the Lord. We have long clung to the world, weighed down by evil deeds and bent down by perverse habits. For the wicked spirits say to a soul living softly and dissolutely, “Bend down, so that we may pass over you.” If it obeys their evil suggestions, it will perish, badly trampled beneath their feet. But if it perseveres uprightly in the work of God, it will be able to say with Elijah: “The Lord lives, in whose sight I stand” (III Kings XVII). And with Paul: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III).

When he says “finally, at some time,” unless I am mistaken, he signifies a delay of time. For he compounded one adverb of time from two: *tandem* means the same as *aliquando*. It is as if he said: If we do not wish to exercise ourselves in good works in the time of our first age—that is, in youth—then at least let us come to our senses in old age, and, though late converted to the ways of life, let us not lose the remedies of salvation.

“While Scripture arouses us and says.” For it is not the waking soul but the sleeping one that is aroused. The soul sleeps when it forgets its Lord and does not remember his commandments. It watches when it continually keeps the memory of its Lord in its heart and observes his commandments in its works. The soul sleeps when it does not amend past offenses and thinks nothing about the future. It watches when it laments past sins and does not commit again what must be lamented.

The soul sleeps when, advancing along the broad and spacious way, it thinks nothing of the future life or glory, but, sleeping with closed eyes and becoming daily worse, hastens toward eternal destruction. It watches when, thinking of eternal life and future glory, it walks along the narrow and constricted way, daily grows in virtues and is renewed, and does not cease to labor in order to reach knowledge of its Creator.

“It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep.” Here he uses “hour” for “time.” The duration of any time may appropriately be called an hour, as it is written in the Gospel: “The householder went out at the third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hour to hire laborers for his vineyard” (Matt. XX). For “hours” are used there for periods of time.

He says, “It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep”—that is, it is time for us to awaken from the heaviness of mind and the torpor of negligence in order to observe the Lord’s commandments. Solomon exhorts us concerning this, saying: “Do not love sleep, lest poverty overwhelm you” (Prov. XX). To love sleep is to embrace the torpor of the mind through laziness and to think nothing of the future, because poverty—that is, eternal misery—overwhelms the soul that is falsely secure.

“And with our eyes opened.” Those, namely, of which Solomon says: “Open your eyes, and be filled with bread.” To open the eyes is to direct the understanding of the mind toward the light of justice. To be filled with bread is to refresh the mind with the spiritual food of divine knowledge.

“To the deifying light.” That is, the divine light, which bestows understanding upon the soul.

“With attentive ears.” That is, with attentive minds.

“Let us hear divine things.” That is, things full of God, filled with divinity.

“Crying out daily, what does the voice admonish us, saying: ‘Today, if you hear his voice’?” The word “today” has the etymology “on this day.” But here it also signifies “always,” or “at every time,” because he who admonishes salutarily and teaches mercifully must be heard continually and at every hour. The Apostle forcefully expressed the power of this saying: “But exhort one another every day” (Heb. III). It is called “today” as long as today lasts.

“If you hear his voice.” He says “his,” that is, the voice of that good shepherd who says: “I am the good shepherd; and my sheep hear my voice, and follow me, and I know them; and no one snatches them from my hand. And I will give them eternal life” (John X).

In the Law and the Prophets, in the Gospel and the Apostles, the voice of the Lord is heard sounding in many ways; but it is heard and heeded by a good and excellent heart. By hard and stony hearts it is indeed heard, but not heeded. Therefore the souls that harden their hearts so as not to hear the voice of that good and true shepherd neither follow him nor are his sheep; they do not know him, nor are they known by him. For whoever is ignorant will be ignored. They will neither be freed from the hand of the robber nor placed in pastures, nor will they receive everlasting life.

“Do not harden your hearts.” Thus the Apostle says elsewhere: “Let none of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Heb. III). Those harden their hearts who refuse to perform what they rightly understand from God’s commandments. Concerning them Solomon says: “Slothfulness brings on sleep” (Prov. XIX). The lazy person, while thinking rightly, seems to be awake; but by doing nothing good, with a hardened heart and drowsy understanding, he sleeps in the bed of his sluggishness.

Those, I say, harden their hearts who hear the preacher but refuse to imitate the one who acts; who do not obey the voice of the Lord saying: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXIII); who do not hear: “Put off the old man with his deeds; put on the new man, who was created according to God in justice and the holiness of truth”; who do not renounce the world and, carrying the cross, follow Christ.

“And again: ‘Whoever has ears to hear’” (Matt. XIII; Mark IV; Luke VIII). Here he requires the ears of the heart, not of the body. He has ears to hear who fulfills in action what he understands in his heart. He has ears to hear in his heart who entrusts the Lord’s commandments to his memory and preserves what has been entrusted to him, so that he may return it to the Lord with manifold increase. He does not have ears to hear who neither retains the Lord’s commandments in memory nor fulfills them in works, neither stores them in his heart nor practices them in action.

“Let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Rev. II). “Let him hear,” he says—that is, let him understand. What Spirit? The almighty Spirit, the Holy Spirit, that Spirit who bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God, and of whom the Apostle says: “You are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you” (I Cor. III; II Cor. XVI).

The Holy Spirit is called “Spirit” according to the fact that he breathes or inspires something. He is called the Holy Spirit of God because he is the holiness of the Father and the Son. For although the Father is spirit and the Son is spirit, and the Father is holy and the Son is holy, he is properly called the Holy Spirit, as the holiness that is consubstantial with both.

“Church” is Greek; in Latin it is translated as “assembly,” because it calls everyone to itself. Although it is one and universal—that is, catholic—seven churches are written to by John in the Apocalypse (ch. I), on account of the uniform fullness of the Spirit: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and fortitude, of knowledge and piety, and of the fear of the Lord.

“And what does he say? ‘Come, children, hear me.’” Great is the piety and mercy of the Holy Spirit, who invites each person to hear him even before the habit of conversion has been acquired. Those whom he invites to the grace of conversion he calls children. For he is the one who says through the prophet: “You shall call me Father, and you shall not cease to walk after me” (Jer. III).

“I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. XXXIII). Concerning this fear the Psalmist also says elsewhere: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever and ever” (Ps. XVIII). For the more attentively someone loves the Lord, the more diligently he fears offending him.

It is a paternal voice, a voice of compassion, admonishing us not to be afraid of what we have heard about fear. For this is not a fear that is dreaded, but one that is loved. Human fear has bitterness; this fear has sweetness. The former compels one into servitude; the latter draws one into freedom. Finally, the former fears confinement; the latter opens the kingdoms of heaven.

In praise of fear Solomon says: “The fear of the Lord adds days” (Prov. X). Therefore fear the Lord, O monk—but with that fear which remains holy forever and ever; with that chaste love which will add to the days of this present time for you eternal days, everlasting days, immortal days, and unending days. Rather, it will add one day without evening and without end: a day full of blessed joy, filled with unfailing light, supported by angelic companionship; a day that night does not interrupt, darkness does not obscure, and cloud does not cover; a day that the heat of summer does not make unbearable and the cold of winter does not make sluggish.

That day will be one for you with the saints, shared with the angels, eternal with both. It will grant you, in blessed joy, fellowship with the angels; make you a companion of the patriarchs; count you among the prophets; and make you a companion of the apostles in their exultation. For it is written: “Those who fear the Lord have hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and protector” (Ps. CXIII). And elsewhere: “The fullness of wisdom is to fear God; and the crown of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, filling one with peace and the fruit of salvation” (Ecclus. I). And: “You who fear the Lord, believe him, and your reward shall not be taken away. You who fear the Lord, love him, and your hearts shall be enlightened” (Ecclus. II). And: “How great is the one who has found wisdom! Yet he is not above those who fear God” (Ecclus. XXV).

Blessed is the one to whom it is given to possess the fear of God. “The fear of the Lord is like a paradise of blessing” (Ecclus. XL), because in it there is confidence of strength; through it the fruit of salvation and peace springs forth.

Hear further and attend carefully, O monk, to what the Lord promises through the prophet to those who fear him: “For you who fear my name, the sun of justice shall rise, and healing shall be in his wings; and you shall go out and leap like calves from the herd,” and so forth (Mal. IV).

And you, O monk, must fear the name of the Lord, so that Christ, the sun of justice, may rise for you, drive away the darkness of your mind, remove ignorance from your heart, and pour in the light of understanding. May he grant you to live justly here and, after death, bestow eternal life.

“Run while you have the light of life.” Here he does not seek bodily running, but the progress of souls. Hence the Psalmist says: “They shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Ps. LXXXIII). And elsewhere: “I have run in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. CXVIII). For here too “running” signifies observance of the commandments and the progress of souls.

“While you have the light of life,” he says—that is, while you live, while the span of this life is granted to you. For the person who abandons the error of his former way of life and turns to better ways of living also has the light of life within him, as the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. V).

The person also has the light of life within him who possesses the one who said: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness” (John VIII). Therefore he continues plainly here:

“Lest the darkness of death overtake you.” In this passage “darkness” is understood as death or the devil. We may also, not inappropriately, understand here the darkness that the Lord calls “outer darkness” in the Gospel.

Those who, while they live, do not strive to separate themselves from vices and refuse to grow in virtues are rightly overtaken by the darkness of death and mourn as condemned in hell. We call the inner darkness the blindness of the heart; the outer darkness, the eternal night of condemnation.

Thus each condemned person is sent not into inner darkness but into outer darkness, because there he is thrown unwillingly into the night of condemnation, whereas here he willingly fell into blindness of heart. There, it is said, are weeping and the gnashing of teeth: teeth gnash there that here rejoiced in gluttony; eyes weep there that here were occupied with unlawful desires. Thus each individual member is subjected to the punishment of the vices to which it was here subject and in whose service it was employed.

In the weeping of the eyes and the gnashing of the teeth, through a metaphor drawn from bodily members, the magnitude of the torments is shown. Darkness is so called because it holds shadows. Darkness is not some substance; rather, where light is absent, darkness occurs. As darkness is nothing except the absence of light, so death is nothing except the deprivation of life. Death is called *mors* either from *morsus*, “a bite,” or because it is bitter.

“And the Lord, seeking his laborer among the multitude of the people to whom he cries these things, says again.” Among the multitude the Lord seeks a few laborers, because “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX). He seeks laborers now, in the present life, to whom afterward he will mercifully cry: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you,” says the Lord (Matt. XI).

For it is written: “He who works his land shall be filled with bread; but he who pursues idleness shall be in poverty” (Prov. XII). He diligently works his land who diligently cultivates the secrets of his heart through daily exercises, meditation on the law, and watchfulness of mind, as through agriculture; and, like bread, does not cease to refresh the sense of his inner person with invisible nourishment, lest he perish from hunger for ignorance.

He, I say, who works the land of his body by keeping nightly vigils, pouring out abundant tears for his sins, disciplines his body by bringing it into servitude, mortifies his flesh by fasting, and torments it with various afflictions—he shall be filled with heavenly bread and eternal rewards.

“Who is the person who desires life and longs to see good days?” (Ps. XXXIII). This question is framed in such a way that everyone assents to it. For who could say, “I do not want life,” or “I do not desire to see good days”? But would that we sought perpetual life as earnestly as we fix our hearts upon this temporal life.

He does not call “good days” those in which we are occupied with fleeting pleasures, but those that are truly good and are spent in supreme holiness. “Who is the person,” he says, “who desires life”—that is, blessed, perpetual, immortal life, without death, without end, and without labor, because in this life a person is born for labor. To that life he comes without labor and in order to live forever.

That is the blessed life. Those who reach it after completing good works will be like the blessed angels and will reign without end with their God. What they believed here, they will see there: contemplating the substance of their Creator with pure hearts, they will rejoice with eternal exultation. Possessed by divine love and mutual love, they will cling to one another forever in happiness.

Having received their bodies in incorruption and immortality, they will receive citizenship in the heavenly homeland; made its citizens forever, they will carry away the promised rewards. There such great joy and such an abundance of heavenly delights will overflow for them that they will give thanks to their gracious Rewarder for such gifts and will suffer no weariness from the very perfection of the blessings that overflow.

But if, upon hearing this, you answer, “I am the one,” God says to you:

What is God? God is that which no opinion can reach. For he is more than can be said or conceived. Each nature forms a conception of God according to its capacity. And as one nature differs from another, so one judgment differs from another. Since he is above all things, it is necessary that he surpass the minds of all.

Human beings, so far as they can extend the eye of the mind, perceive what God is by opinion, not by definition. There is no doubt that the angels, who are superior to human beings, have a greater understanding of God. The archangels have still more by that very fact. The cherubim and seraphim, who are said to be nearest to God, have greater conceptions of God; yet they do not fully comprehend what God is, because “no one knows the Father except the Son, nor does anyone know the Son except the Father.”

Thus, as it appears to human beings, God is spirit, simple in nature, inaccessible light, invisible, immeasurable, infinite, perfect, needing nothing, eternal, wholly immortal; the one from whom all things received their beginning; worthy of reverence from those who love him and of fear; outside of whom nothing exists—indeed, in whom all things exist, whatever is above or below, highest or lowest. He is almighty, holding all things, truly rich in all things, because there is nothing that is not his; good, just, and merciful.

He is also severe, so that by fear the things well created by him may be preserved, lest negligence produce the ruin of life. And, not to omit what is more marvelous, his clemency is so great that, though he suffers insults from those whom he made, he bears with them and first calls them to peace.

“If you wish to have true and perpetual life.” Life is so called because of vigor, or because it holds the power of being born and growing. It is called true and perpetual either on account of Christ, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV), or on account of the eternity by which one lives in it.

Death follows upon this present life; death never follows upon that one. Therefore this life is called deceptive, while that one is called truthful. This life, briefly terminated, is called temporary; that one perpetual. This life is mortal; that one eternal. This life is miserable; that one glorious. This life is full of pains and labors; that one remains joyful in health and repose. This life languishes in hatreds and failures; that one, always fruitful, rejoices in charity and virtues.

Concerning these matters blessed Augustine says in his *Exposition of the Gospel*: “Therefore the Church knows that two lives have been divinely foretold to it. One is in faith, the other in sight. One is in pilgrimage, the other in eternity. One is in labor, the other in rest. One is on the way, the other in the homeland. One fights with an enemy, the other reigns without an enemy. Thus one is good, but still miserable; the other better and blessed.” Whoever reaches it happily will enjoy eternal joy in the kingdom.

“Keep your tongue from evil” (Ps. XXXIII). “Keep,” he says: abstain, restrain, control, curb, or compress. “From evil” means from every kind of evil—namely, detraction, cursing, murmuring, mockery, reproach, unjust rebuke, lying words, idle speech, and the like.

For it is written: “Whoever secretly slanders his neighbor, him I will persecute” (Ps. C). And: “Nor shall the revilers possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI). And: “Those who murmured perished from the serpents” (I Cor. X). And: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. I). And: “You shall destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. V), and many similar passages.

See, O monk, why it is said, “Keep your tongue from evil.” If the Lord persecutes the slanderer, if revilers do not possess the kingdom of God, if murmurers perished from serpents—that is, from demons—and if God will destroy all who speak lies, then we must keep our tongue from evil with complete vigilance, lest we perish forever with those who are perishing.

And let us hear further what the Apostle James says about the evil of the tongue. He says: “The tongue is a fire, the universe of iniquity. The tongue is placed among our members; it defiles the whole body and sets on fire the wheel of our birth, being set on fire by Gehenna. For every nature of beasts, birds, and serpents, and also of other creatures, is tamed and has been tamed by human nature; but no human being can tame the tongue—a restless evil, full of deadly poison. With it we bless God and the Father, and with it we curse human beings, who were made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth proceed blessing and cursing; these things ought not to be so,” and so forth.

“And do not let your lips speak deceit.” Let the good monk imitate the Lord as far as he can, and let him neither harbor deceit in his heart nor speak it with his lips. For the Lord did not do evil, nor was deceit found in his mouth (Ps. XI; I Pet. II). God will destroy deceitful lips—namely, those of people who have spoken evil in their heart and from their heart.

Deceit is hidden malice adorned with flattering speech. It is properly called fraud, ambush, or deception: it occurs when we deceive a listener, so that what is believed to offer help appears instead to bring harm. It is rightly prohibited, because it is always contrary to a pure conscience.

“Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXIII). Many do good but do not turn away from evil. By day they celebrate a fast, and by night they commit adultery. They give alms to the poor, and they seize plunder from the poor. They offer a cup to the poor, and they themselves drink to drunkenness. They give a morsel to the hungry, and they themselves eat to excess. In brief, in public they do what is lawful, while in secret they do not cease to do what is unlawful. Acting in this way, they refuse to separate the left hand from the right.

There is another class of people, and especially of monks, who turn away from evil but do not work any good. They abandon earthly labors in the world and pursue idleness in the monastery. Concerning such people the Lord says: “The tree that does not produce good fruit shall be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. VII; Luke III). And in the Apocalypse the Lord says: “Because you are neither cold nor hot, but lukewarm, and you make me nauseated, I will begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Rev. III).

Hence idleness is also described as an enemy of the soul. Therefore, to turn away from evil and to do good in a singular and proper sense belongs to the elect. For a farmer or gardener does not sow the seeds of his crops upon thorns, thistles, or nettles; rather, he first cleanses the field of these and then casts the suitable grain of seed. In the same way each of the elect first cleanses the field of heart and body from vices and afterward casts the seeds of virtues. In this way every person turns away from evil and does good.

“Seek peace and pursue it” (Ps. XXXIII). The Prophet knew that in this contest of the world the most faithful do not possess peace with the body, and that here they are engaged in continual struggle with their vices. Therefore he says beautifully, “Seek peace,” so that although they do not possess it here, they may nevertheless pursue it always with the greatest diligence. Here he commands, “Pursue it,” as though it were going before them.

Let us therefore seek it diligently and pursue it attentively, because we cannot find it there unless we seek it here more carefully. It will then be granted to be possessed when we behold the author of peace himself.

Peace is serenity of mind, tranquility of soul, simplicity of heart, the bond of love, and fellowship in charity. It removes quarrels, restrains wars, suppresses anger, tramples the proud, loves the humble, calms the quarrelsome, reconciles enemies. It is gentle toward all; it does not seek what belongs to another; it counts nothing as its own; it teaches love for what it does not know how to hate; it does not know how to exalt itself or become inflated.

Therefore let the one who has received it hold onto it; let the one who has lost it seek it again; let the one who has missed it search for it, because whoever is not found in this peace is rejected by the Father, disinherited by the Son, and likewise made alien from the Holy Spirit.

“And when you have done these things.” That is, the things mentioned above.

“My eyes are upon you.” This is the Lord’s voice, the voice of mercy, the voice of compassion. He mercifully enables human beings to do these things, because human weakness can do nothing except what divine majesty grants it the power to do.

“And when you have done these things,” he says—that is, when you have kept your tongue from evil and your lips have not spoken deceit; when you have turned away from evil and done good; when you have sought peace and pursued it—“then my eyes are upon you.”

Here the eyes of the Lord mean the divine regard, which is mercifully opened over the righteous. For “the Lord looked upon Peter,” and immediately Peter remembered the Lord’s word and wept bitterly (Luke XXII), because he had denied the Lord three times.

Therefore the eyes of the Lord—that is, the divine regard—grant the righteous both memory and understanding, and deliver them from eternal death and everlasting hunger. Thus it is also written in another psalm: “The eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him, to deliver their souls from death and to feed them in famine” (Ps. XXXIII).

He added: “And my ears are attentive to your prayers” (Isa. LXV). In this passage the ears of the Lord are understood as divine hearing, which the Psalmist sought with all his strength, saying: “Incline your ear, my God, and hear me” (Ps. XLIV and LXXXV). And: “Attend with your ears, O Lord, to my prayer” (Ps. CXXIX). And: “Let your ears be attentive to the prayer of your servant” (Ps. XVI), and a thousand such passages.

Solomon also included both together in his prayer—that is, the eyes and ears of the Lord—saying: “Let your eyes be open and your ears attentive to the prayers of your servants.” Although the Lord frequently hears sinners, much greater and swifter hearing is promised to the righteous, when he shows that he has ears prepared for their prayers.

Therefore do not fear, O righteous monk, the persecutions of human beings or the labors of the world. For the eyes of the Lord are upon you to deliver you, and his ears are upon you to hear you. But keep his ways, hope in him, and say with the Apostle: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Rom. VIII).

God is for us, so that his eyes may regard us. God is for us, so that his ears may hear us. God is for us, so that he may predestine us. God is for us, so that he may call us. God is for us, so that he may justify us. God is for us, so that he may glorify us. If God is for us, who can be against us?

He predestined us before we existed; he called us when we had turned away; he justified us when we were sinners; he glorified us when we were mortal. If God is for us, who can be against us—against those predestined, called by God, justified, and glorified? Whoever wishes to oppose us, let him prepare himself, if he can wage war against God. For where have we heard, “If God is for us, who can be against us?” No one can harm us unless someone conquers God.

“And before you call upon me, I will say to you: ‘Behold, here I am.’” O speech full of gentleness and kindness! He does not wait for the prayer to be completed, but grants the petition beforehand. For the Lord knows what we need before we ask him. And this is because we are the temple of God, and the Spirit of the Lord dwells in us. God, the inhabitant, hears his dwelling place with the greatest speed.

What is sweeter to us than this voice of the Lord inviting us, dearest brothers? Truly this voice of the Lord is sweet to holy monks, because it invites them to that great abundance of his sweetness which he has hidden for those who fear him. He has become their inhabitant, so that he may hear them even when they do not call upon him. He has become the way and the homeland, so that through him they may come to him. He has become shepherd, door, and pasture, so that, governed by him, they may enter through him, go in and out, and find pasture.

Behold, in his compassion the Lord shows us the way of life. Therefore the Lord himself, as was said above, has become for us the way, the truth, and the life. The royal way, certainly, so that as we walk through him we may not turn aside to the right or to the left, but reach eternal life, which he himself is. There no weeping or groaning can exist; there all the saints will have perfect love, no fear, and everlasting joy.

For there their will shall be certain and their desire absent, because, enjoying the heavenly goods to which they longed to attain, nothing will be lacking to them that they might desire afterward. In that region of perpetual security and peace they will be perfectly blessed, suffering neither the goads of fear nor those of pain.

Therefore, with our loins girded by faith or by the observance of good works (Eph. VI). For most elegantly, and in prophetic manner, blessed Father Benedict has here placed a twofold girding of monks. He knew that faith without works is dead, and works without faith are empty. Therefore he wished the monks’ girding to be woven not from one strand but from both. Isaiah likewise placed this very thing twice in the Lord, saying: “And righteousness shall be the girdle of his loins, and faith the belt of his reins” (Isa. XI). For the one set faith, and this one also set faith; the one set righteousness, and this one the observance of good works. Every observance of good works is appropriately called righteousness, as it is written: “You shall faithfully carry out what is just” (Deut. XVI).

We gird the loins of our mind with faith if we think rightly concerning the Holy Trinity and believe in it faithfully. We gird our loins with the observance of good works if we diligently exercise ourselves in good works, as the Apostle says: “Stand therefore with the loins of your mind girded” (Eph. VI)—that is, prepared manfully for every battle and freed from all the cares of the world. And the Lord says to Job: “Gird up your loins like a man” (Job XXXVIII). For Holy Scripture calls those men who walk along the Lord’s way with strong and unrelaxed steps. To gird one’s loins manfully means to restrain, whether in action or in thought, the lust of the flesh and of the mind.

But why is it said to blessed Job, “Gird your loins like a man,” unless because one kind of lust is the lust of the flesh, by which we corrupt chastity, while another is the lust of the heart, by which we boast of chastity? Therefore it is said to him: “Gird your loins like a man,” so that he who had previously conquered the lust of corruption might now restrain the lust of pride, lest he become proud of his patience or chastity.

In the Old Testament we read of a leather belt around the loins, but in the New Testament of a golden belt around the breast. To prevent adultery, a leather belt is to be worn around the loins, so that a woman may not be looked upon for the purpose of lust; a golden belt is to be worn around the breast, so that by the guidance of the Gospel we may proceed along its paths. The guidance of the Gospel means the guidance of Christ; for Christ does not lead one way and the Gospel another. Rather, the deeds of the Lord, or his most holy words, are called Gospels; and those who follow them along straight paths are led to the heavenly kingdoms.

But we must carefully consider who these people are who proceed under the guidance of the Gospel, who follow, and toward what they are heading. They are certainly those to whom the Lord says: “Amen, I say to you, you who have left everything and followed me: in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX). And the man to whom he says: “Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Mark X). And: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. XVI), and similar passages.

We know who they are: those who leave everything, those who sell and give to the poor, and those who deny themselves and take up their cross. Whom do they follow? Christ, namely, who says to them, “and have followed me,” and, “come, follow me.” Let us see how they follow. He follows Christ who adheres to his commands, who walks in the footsteps of his teaching, who pursues his footprints and paths, and who imitates what Christ taught and did, as Peter exhorts us, saying: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, that we should follow his footsteps” (I Pet. II)—an example of tribulations, not pleasures; of insults, not joys; of scourges, sufferings, reproaches, thorns, the cross, and death.

Where, then, are those heading who run under the guidance of the Gospel? We shall see more clearly if first we hear the Lord calling them. For the Lord says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI). Again he says: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV), and similar passages.

It is clear, then, where those are heading who proceed under the guidance of the Gospel: namely, toward such great glory that when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, they too may sit upon twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel; that they may receive eternal refreshment; and that they may receive the kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world. Therefore the words of blessed Benedict appropriately follow, as he says:

## So that we may deserve to see him who called us in his kingdom

Concerning the grace of calling, the Apostle Paul says to the Galatians: “I marvel that you are so quickly transferred from him who called you into the grace of Christ” (Gal. I). And of himself he likewise says: “He who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace” (ibid.). Again, elsewhere he says: “I therefore beseech you, I who am bound in the Lord, to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience, supporting one another in charity, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. One body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling” (Eph. IV).

Here blessed Benedict says, “he who called us,” and this is understood either first as calling to the grace of faith, or later as calling to the religious state and way of life.

If we wish to dwell in the tabernacle of his kingdom, we cannot reach it except by running there through good works. For it is evident that those who do good and do not do evil will possess the tabernacles of the heavenly kingdom. Thus the Apostle Paul says concerning the wicked: “Neither adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the covetous, nor the revilers, nor the drunkards, nor the rapacious shall possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI).

But if we desire to possess the kingdom of God, let us present ourselves in all things as ministers of God: in great patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distress, in blows, in prisons, in seditions, in labors, in vigils, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in gentleness, in the Holy Spirit, in sincere charity, in the word of truth, in the power of God; through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left; through glory and dishonor; through infamy and good reputation; as deceivers and yet truthful; as unknown and yet known; as dying, and behold, we live; as chastised, and not put to death; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as needy, yet enriching many; as having nothing, yet possessing all things (II Cor. VI).

And by running through these and other good works, we shall deserve to be inhabitants of the tabernacle of the heavenly kingdom.

[Col. 0714C]

But let us ask the Lord with the Prophet, saying: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle? Or who shall rest upon your holy mountain?” (Ps. XIV). Although other teachers understand the tabernacle here as the present Church, blessed Benedict, no less filled with the Holy Spirit, wished the heavenly dwelling—which is the eternal kingdom—to be understood by “tabernacle.” Hence the Lord also says: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal tabernacles” (Luke XVI).

The mountain itself is understood as our Lord Jesus Christ, concerning whom Isaiah says: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared upon the top of the mountains” (Isa. II). In him the souls of all the elect rest forever, as the same Lord says to them: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart; and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI).

After this question, brothers, let us hear the Lord answering and showing us the way to his tabernacle, saying: “He who enters without blemish and does justice; who speaks truth in his heart; who has not practiced deceit with his tongue; who has not done evil to his neighbor and has not accepted reproach against his neighbor” (Ps. CXXXVI).

He who, when the wicked devil suggested something to him, rejected the devil from the sight of his heart together with his suggestion, reduced him to nothing, seized his little thoughts, and dashed them against Christ. Those who fear the Lord do not make themselves proud because of their good observance; rather, believing that the good within them is not accomplished by their own power but by the Lord, they magnify the Lord who works in them, saying with the Prophet: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. CXIII).

Let us examine each point, and, as the Lord grants, discuss them all.

### He who enters without blemish

Blessed Augustine said that this sentence was the Prophet’s question, while blessed Benedict said that it was the Lord’s answer. But since, according to Ezekiel, the living creatures follow the wheels, both understood this sentence well—indeed, both understood it most rightly. When the Lord was asked who would dwell in his tabernacle, he answered: “He who enters without blemish,” as if he were saying: “He who lives without fault and guards himself from the contagion of sin will enter my tabernacle.”

“Blemish” means sin. For even in the Lord’s sacrifice an animal was not offered unless it was unblemished; the Lord’s sacrifice accepts nothing blemished. Hence the bridegroom says to the bride: “You are beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song IV).

### And does justice

It is called “justice” because it is the state of what is right. For justice is equity or rectitude. But since justice consists of works and faith, he fully practices justice who, believing rightly, exercises his whole self in good works.

He enters without blemish who lives without fault. He practices justice who diligently does the good that prevails. He enters without blemish who mourns the sins he has committed and does not again commit sins that must be mourned. He practices justice who carefully keeps the Lord’s commandments in all things.

### Who speaks truth in his heart

A human being speaks with the tongue and mouth, not with the heart. But because the mouth speaks only what is supplied to it by the heart, it is rightly said here, “who speaks truth in his heart.” As if he were saying: “It is not enough for the tongue merely to speak truth with the mouth, unless it has received that truth from a sincere heart.” Whether the tongue speaks good or evil, its source supplies this to the heart, as it is written: “For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Luke VI).

There are some who, filled with an evil spirit, pretend to say one thing with their mouth while contemplating another in their heart. Of such people Solomon says: “The hypocrite deceives his neighbor with his mouth” (Prov. XI). Therefore the Lord says: “He who speaks truth in his heart, he shall dwell in my tabernacle.”

### Who has not practiced deceit with his tongue

To practice no deceit with the tongue is the same thing as speaking truth in the heart. Sometimes deceit is brought forth by the tongue, as the Psalmist says here; sometimes it is simultaneously contemplated by the lips and the heart, as you find in Solomon: “An enemy is recognized by his lips when he has plotted deceit in his heart” (Prov. XXVI).

Deceit is brought forth only by the tongue when a person appears to be a friend in speech but is an enemy in his heart. Deceit is contemplated both by the lips and by the heart when a person shows himself to be an enemy in his heart and mouth alike.

### Who has not done evil to his neighbor

“Neighbor” is to be understood here as every human being. Hence it is written: “You shall not commit adultery with your neighbor’s wife” (Lev. XVIII)—that is, with the wife of no human being. Because of the closeness of blood, every human being is called the neighbor of another human being. For human blood is distinguished from the blood of other animals.

### Who has not accepted reproach against his neighbor

“He has not accepted,” he says—that is, he has not regarded it as pleasing or listened to it willingly. We call those things “accepted” which we show to be pleasing to us. He accepts reproach against his neighbor who receives the words of the slanderer with a willing spirit. This commonly happens to those who do not wish to love their neighbor as themselves. From this source comes the ability to listen willingly to the words of the slanderer.

But he who loves his neighbor as himself does not wish to hear reproach against his neighbor any more than he wishes to hear it against himself.

If someone should say, thinking in his heart: “Who is the human being who lives among human beings without blemish, so that he neither does evil to his neighbor nor speaks deceit with his lips, since it is written, ‘There is no one who lives and does not sin’ (III Kings VIII)?” let him hear the Apostle Paul answering him: “And such indeed were some of you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified,” and so forth (I Cor. VI).

### Who rejects the wicked devil

“Devil” is interpreted in Hebrew as “flowing downward,” because, pressed down by the weight of pride, he fell as he descended. In Greek, however, *diabolos* means “accuser,” because just as “accuser” comes from accusation, “proud” from pride, and “unjust” from iniquity, so “wicked” comes from wickedness.

“Suggesting something to him”—that is, sins and vices.

“Rejecting him together with the suggestion from the sight of his heart, he reduced him to nothing.” The righteous rejects the devil when he consents neither to him nor to his suggestion. He reduces him to nothing when he neither receives nor nourishes his insinuations.

Therefore the annihilation of the devil is the perfection of the monk. The devil is then considered strong in himself when the wretched monk is overcome by him. But he is annihilated when he is conquered and rejected as weaponless by a perfect monk.

### And seized his little thoughts and dashed them against Christ

“His little thoughts”—that is, the devil’s. They are the evil beginnings of his suggestions, which must be seized lest they grow into evil; and they must be dashed against the rock, that is, against Christ, so that they may perish, lest they perhaps acquire the strength of a fortress and wage harmful wars against us.

### Those who fear the Lord do not make themselves proud because of their good observance

That is, they do not set themselves up or consider themselves exalted, as though they could accomplish some good by their own powers, especially since the Lord said to the Apostles: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV). For a human being receives from the Lord both the will to do good and the ability to do it.

A person is called “exalted” because he raises himself above his proper measure, when he seems great to himself because of the works he performs.

“But believing that the good within them is accomplished not by themselves but by the Lord”: the proud desire what they do not accomplish to be praised in them. The humble shrink from having whatever good they do acknowledged. The proud refuse to admit that their vices were produced by themselves, yet boast shamefully that their good works were accomplished by their own strength.

The humble, because they have committed sins, willingly confess and accuse themselves; and they attribute all their good works not to themselves but to divine favor. They affirm that these works were accomplished in them not by themselves but by the Lord. They magnify the Lord working in them, saying with the Prophet: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. CXIII).

He magnifies the Lord working in him who attributes the glory for his good works not to himself but to the Lord. He ought to magnify the Lord working in him because without him he is unable to do anything good.

For the Prophet knew that it is not for a human being to direct his own ways, but that, when the Lord disposes them, it belongs to the Lord to direct his steps. Therefore he attributes glory to the one from whom he knows he has received every good thing. The Apostle says: “Whatever you do, do all in the name of the Lord” (Col. III).

Therefore let the Church attribute everything to that name, from which and in which it receives the power to do what is right; and let it humbly and truthfully say with the Prophet: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory.”

Likewise the Apostle Paul attributed nothing of his preaching to himself, saying: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (I Cor. XV). Formerly Paul had been a blasphemer and persecutor of the Church; but, called by the grace of God and separated from the womb of the Synagogue, he had now become a faithful and upright preacher in the Church. Therefore he said: “By the grace of God I am what I am”—that is, by myself I was depraved; by the grace of God I am upright. By myself I was a persecutor; through the grace of the Lord I am now a defender of the Church. By myself I was a blasphemer and impious; through the grace of the Lord I have become faithful and devout.

And this is what “By the grace of God I am what I am” means: not through my merits, but by the grace of God I have been made faithful from unbelieving, a shepherd from a wolf, a defender from a persecutor, upright from depraved, devout from impious, a Christian from a Jew, and an apostle from a Pharisee. This is what “By the grace of God I am what I am” means: I am not what wickedness once made me, but what the Lord’s grace has now willed me to be.

Again he himself says: “He who glories, let him glory in the Lord” (I Cor. I). For, as was said above, a human being has nothing good except what he receives from the Lord. If he receives it, let him not glory as though he had not received it, lest the giver perhaps withdraw what he gave, and the one who gloried in another’s possession remain empty.

Elsewhere the Apostle says: “Not from ourselves; it is the gift of God—not from works, lest anyone should glory” (Eph. II). Therefore let us give glory with all our strength not to ourselves but to the name of the Lord, by which we have been saved and in which we faithfully hope to be saved forever. For there is no other name in the whole world by which the people may be saved.

Hence the Apostle also says: “To him be glory in the Church and in Christ Jesus, throughout all generations of the age of ages. Amen” (Eph. III). This, then, is the name before which every knee bows—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confesses that this name, namely, the Lord Jesus Christ, is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. II).

Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them, I will compare him to a wise man who built his house upon rock. The floods came, the winds blew, and they struck that house, and it did not fall, for it had been founded upon rock” (Matt. VII).

The wise man does not build upon sand—that is, upon himself, because he is dust and will return to dust—but upon the rock, namely that of which the Apostle says: “The rock was Christ” (I Cor. X). He builds his house upon it: that is, he places the beginning of his first way of life as the foundation of his house, the middle of good action as the middle of its wall, and perseverance in perfection as the completion of his endurance upon that foundation.

Concerning this the Apostle says elsewhere: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III). From this foundation he receives strength so that the house—that is, every work of the monk—may be built, and strength so that, when struck by storms, that is, by the tribulations of temptations, it may not be destroyed.

But the foolish man builds upon sand because he attributes the glory for his work not to God but to himself. The wise man builds upon rock because, for all his good works, he attributes no praise to himself but gives thanks to God; and he humbly attributes everything to his giver because he recognizes that he received everything from him.

In another sense, this parable applies especially to the disobedient. For we read: “Everyone who hears my words and does not do them, I will compare him to a foolish man who built his house upon sand,” and so forth (Matt. VII). That is: when the drops of sufferings have poured in, when floods and torrents and the assaults of tribulations have arrived from the multitude of negligences; when the winds have blown—those winds, certainly, that fly through this air, ready to winnow Christ’s threshing floor, wherever they find chaff to seize and scatter for their mockery—then they will rush upon that house which has been built without the foundation of obedience, and its fall will be great.

Therefore neither rain, nor rivers descending with force, nor the strongest winds will be able to shake a house founded upon rock. From this you may understand that if a person does not betray himself and is not shaken by himself, no temptation that comes upon him will be able to overthrow or move him.

But the other building is easily overturned—not because of the violence of temptation, for otherwise that building too would have been cast down, but because of the weakness of its foundation, that is, its purpose. Sand is a movable and fruitless thing, and without doubt signifies the instability and fickleness of souls.

Having fulfilled these things, the Lord expects us every day to answer his holy admonitions with deeds. In completing these things, the Lord looks back to the good things mentioned above concerning the inhabitant of the tabernacle; for Christ the Lord fulfilled what was said above, fulfilling it in word and deed. He preached in word what he fulfilled in action. For he himself fulfilled in himself what he commanded the inhabitant of the tabernacle to fulfill.

He entered the world without the blemish of sin; he lived in the world without sin; and he ascended into heaven without the contagion of sin. The prince of this world came to him, but found nothing in him that he could condemn.

Although he, the just Lord, loves righteousness and always and everywhere practices righteousness, he practiced it above all when he bound the proud and powerful devil, entered his house, and took away his vessels, which the devil had unjustly held. Having washed them in the fountain of baptism, he consecrated them to perpetual service.

He speaks truth in his heart because he is the truth, and what he promises with his mouth he completes in deed. For he says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). He did not practice deceit with his tongue, because he committed no sin, and deceit was not found in his mouth.

He did not do evil to his neighbor; on the contrary, he did good to him when he descended from Jerusalem to Jericho—that is, from heaven into the world—and became related and near, through the flesh, to the human race. He found it wounded by robbers—that is, by demons—with many wounds of sins. He poured in wine and oil—that is, the severity of repentance and the refreshment of forgiveness. He placed it upon his beast—that is, joined it to his body—and led it to the inn—that is, making it faithful and joining it to the body of the Church.

And to the innkeeper—that is, the governor of the Church—he gave the command to care for it, preaching and governing it through the New and Old Testaments, as though through two denarii.

Behold how the Lord Jesus Christ did not do evil to his neighbor but, showing mercy toward him, did him good. He is wise because he is the wisdom of the Father. He founded his house upon his rock because he founded the Church upon himself.

And this is what is meant by “the Lord completing these things”: he fulfilled all that was contained above, both by preaching in words and by completing it in works. He expects us every day to respond to these holy admonitions with deeds.

We say that someone “responds” to another when we return corresponding works in exchange for his deeds. Therefore to respond to God is to return our service for his gifts that preceded us. We render true service to God when, trusting in love, we do not fear him.

For this reason, the days of this life are prolonged for us as a respite for correcting our evils, as the Apostle says: “Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance?” (Rom. II). The Apostle Peter likewise says concerning this matter: “The Lord is not delaying his promise, but acts patiently for your sake, not wishing anyone to perish but all to return to repentance” (II Pet. III).

Again he says: “Therefore, beloved, while you await these things, strive to be found by him undefiled and unblemished in peace; and consider the long-suffering of our Lord to be salvation” (ibid.).

Therefore let us not waste, through negligence of the body, the respite of our days granted to us by the Lord, but let us hasten to correct what we have negligently done for a long time. Otherwise, after the dissolution of this flesh, we may join those reprobates who are described in the Book of Wisdom and, practicing fruitless repentance, groaning in the sorrow of our heart, say to ourselves:

“We fools went astray from the way of truth; and the light of righteousness did not shine for us, and the sun of understanding did not rise for us. We grew weary in the way of vanity and destruction, and we traveled difficult paths; but we did not know the way of the Lord. What did pride profit us? Or what did the boasting of riches bring us? All those things passed like a shadow, and we were consumed in our wickedness” (Wis. V).

For the Lord does not rejoice in the destruction of the living; rather, he wishes to save those who repent than to destroy those who offend. As he himself says through the Prophet:

For the merciful Lord says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.”

When, therefore, brothers, we had asked the Lord about the inhabitant of his tabernacle, we heard the command concerning dwelling there. But if we fulfill the duty of the inhabitant, we shall be heirs of the kingdom of heaven (Ezek. XVIII, XXXIII).

Here blessed Benedict uses “hear” in place of “heed” or “obey.” As if he were saying: “Then we have truly heard, if we fulfill the duty of the inhabitant,” just as the Lord says in the Gospel: “My sheep hear my voice” (John X)—that is, they obey it.

But if we do not fulfill the duty of the inhabitant, we have by no means heard the command concerning dwelling there. Thus the same Lord says to the Jews: “He who is of God hears the words of God; therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John IX). Elsewhere, seeking the ears of the heart, he said: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. XI, XIII; Luke VIII).

Therefore he does not hear the voice of the Lord who does not retain in his heart and fulfill in deed what he hears. But if someone here should prefer to understand “hearing” in this manner, the sentence must be rendered as follows: “But if we fulfill the duty of the inhabitant, we too shall be inhabitants of that same tabernacle mentioned above.”

Therefore our hearts and bodies must be prepared to serve in the holy obedience of the commandments.

How are our bodies to be prepared for service? Hear the Apostle beseeching us. He says: “I beseech you, therefore, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your reasonable service. And do not conform yourselves to this age, but be transformed in the renewal of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Rom. XII).

And elsewhere he says: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires. Nor present your members as weapons of iniquity to sin; but present yourselves to God as living from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness to God. Let not sin dominate you” (Rom. VI).

How, again, are our hearts to be prepared? The same Apostle says: “Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh.” Again he says: “If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit. Let us not become desirous of empty glory, provoking one another and envying one another” (Gal. V).

Our hearts and bodies are then prepared for the Lord’s service if we cast away from ourselves dead works—that is, sins—the works of darkness and the works of the flesh and of darkness, and put on the weapons of light and the fruit of the Spirit, which are the virtues of souls.

The works of the flesh are adultery, fornication, uncleanness, immodesty, lust, service of idols, sorcery, enmities, contentions, rivalries, indignation, provocations, dissensions, sects, heresies, envy, anger, quarrels, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and the like. I forewarn you, as I have already warned you, that those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God.

But the fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, faith, modesty, gentleness, self-control, and chastity. Against such things there is no law. Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires (ibid.).

And to the Corinthians, concerning the preparation of heart and body alike, he says: “In all things let us present ourselves as ministers of God: in great patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distress, in blows, in prisons, in seditions, in labors, in vigils, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in gentleness, in the Holy Spirit, in sincere charity, in the word of truth, in the power of God; through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left; through glory and dishonor; through infamy and good reputation; as deceivers and yet truthful; as unknown and yet known; as dying, and behold, we live; as chastised, and not put to death; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as needy, yet enriching many; as having nothing, yet possessing all things” (II Cor. VI).

## And what human nature finds somewhat difficult

By “nature” he means natural ability, character, and the mind’s cleverness. Nature is so called from the fact that it causes something to be born. It has the power of generating and making. Human nature is fragile, for it cannot bring to completion the good it wishes to do unless it has deserved to receive help from the Lord.

Hence the Apostle says: “For to will is present with me, but I do not find the ability to accomplish it” (Rom. VII). Therefore what follows here is appropriate:

## Let us ask the Lord to command that the help of his grace be supplied to us

Fulgentius explains the difference between *ministrare* (“to minister”) and *subministrare* (“to supply” or “provide assistance”) in this way: in one of them the service of humility is shown, while in the other a judgment of abundance and power is displayed. From the one who ministers, service is rendered; from the one who supplies, assistance is provided beforehand.

## And if, fleeing the punishments of Gehenna, we wish to reach everlasting life

Gehenna is a place of fire and sulfur. The place of future punishment, where sinners are to be tortured, is designated by this name. For the punishment of the condemned in Gehenna is twofold: it burns the mind with sorrow and the body with flame.

Just as the fire of the furnace did not burn for the punishment of the three young men, yet burned to consume the bonds of their chains, so the fire of Gehenna will shine for the wretched to increase their punishments, but will not shine for the consolation of joys.

While there is still opportunity, while we are in this body, and while it is possible to fulfill all these things through this way of light, we must run and do now what will profit us forever. “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.” Let us have leisure for this, and see how sweet the Lord is; and while there is time, let us do good to all. For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap. Those who sow in the present life with tears will reap with joy in the age to come.

Therefore we must run—not with our feet, but with our life and conduct—so that in this life we may acquire what we know will profit us eternally: namely, that we may possess in the present age the virtues mentioned above, charity, joy, peace, and all the others, and that with them and for their sake we may live in the future.

## Therefore we must establish the school of the Lord’s service

“School” is a word of Greek origin and means a place in which adolescents customarily devote themselves to literary studies and have leisure to listen to teachers. Hence *schola* is interpreted as “leisure” or “release from other occupations.” Indeed, in the Psalm where we sing, “Be at leisure and know that I am the Lord” (Ps. XLV), the Greek has Σχολάσατε (*Scholasate*).

Therefore, just as boys in school learn with discipline the things necessary for them and acquire what will benefit them in the future, so monks in the school of the monastery’s rule must diligently learn and effectively fulfill both what enables them to live honorably in the present and what will make them happy in the future.

## In this institution we hope to establish nothing harsh, nothing burdensome

For the institution of the regular life contains nothing harsh or burdensome for those who willingly embrace it. “My yoke is easy,” says the Lord, “and my burden is light” (Matt. XI). For those who are unwilling and wish to fulfill their own desires, all good things are harsh and all are burdensome. “Institution” is understood as arrangement or ordering.

## But if anything should proceed somewhat more strictly, as the rule of equity dictates

Equity is truth, and the justice of truth. Reason is a certain movement and power of the mind that sharpens mental perception and distinguishes truth from falsehood. When the human mind judges rightly, it is reason. When it breathes, it is spirit.

## For the correction of vices

Vices are nothing. But where goodness is absent, there is vice. For every nature is the work of God. The works called vices are acts, not things.

Although they are said to do something by themselves and through themselves, the devil accomplished everything through them; or they are called condemned because he himself is condemned on their account. A human being, when attracted by them through free choice, draws them toward his own perception.

Therefore in the future age there will be no vices. They will be condemned in their author, the devil, when he, having been condemned to Gehenna, will no longer have the power to cause these things to be done in order that human beings may sin.

## Or for the preservation of charity should proceed

Charity is Greek and is translated into Latin as *dilectio*, “love,” because it binds two persons together. Hence the Apostle says to the Colossians: “Above all, have charity, which is the bond of perfection” (Col. III).

For love begins from two persons: the love of God and of neighbor. Charity ought not to be temporary but continually maintained. Hence the Apostle Peter says elsewhere: “Above all things, have continual mutual charity among yourselves” (I Pet. I). Perfect charity, preserved forever, embraces eternal love of God and neighbor.

Do not immediately flee the way of salvation, terrified by fear. [Col. 0723A] As it is written: “For whoever puts his hand to the plough and looks back is not fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9). For the fearful are not admitted to battle under the Law, lest they perish in their fear and make others fearful. For it is not the one who has begun, but the one who has persevered, who will be saved. “No one serving as a soldier for God,” says the Apostle, “entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (2 Tim. 2). For “the one who competes in the contest is not crowned unless he has competed lawfully.”

Which must be begun only at a narrow entrance. The way that leads to life is narrow and constricted; the way that leads to death is broad and spacious. The Lord also says to his disciples: “Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke 13). For we must enter the kingdom of heaven through many tribulations.

[Col. 0723B]

But through progress in manner of life and faith. By “progress in manner of life” he means an increase of virtues and advancement of the soul, in which the monk ought daily to increase and grow. Thus the Apostle, praying for us, says: “We pray that you may walk worthily of God, pleasing him in all things, bearing fruit in every good work and increasing” (Col. 1). Every day, therefore, the monk, made new and becoming new, ought to grow from virtue to virtue; and, forgetting what lies behind, to stretch himself toward what lies ahead, until he reaches the appointed prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. The apostles also show us that faith makes progress—that is, increase and advancement—when they say to the Lord: “Lord, increase our faith” (Luke 17). Faith is the confession of divinity and the solid foundation of religion. Faith is the belief by which we confess God; worship and religion are what we offer to him because we believe in him. Faith is so called from the fact that what has been agreed upon between both parties—so to speak, between God and humanity—is brought about. Properly speaking, faith exists when what is believed has not yet been seen. For we can no longer believe what we see.

With an enlarged heart. By “with an enlarged heart” he means enlarged—that is, made great and spacious—because the more a person advances in God’s service, the more joyfully he strives to grow in the breadth of his commandments, as the Psalmist says: “I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118).

With the indescribable sweetness of love. That sweetness is called indescribable of which the Psalmist says: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you and perfected for those who hope in you” (Ps. 30). The Apostle also calls it indescribable when he says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2).

The way of God’s commandments is run. As was said above concerning the first point: “I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart.” The Apostle also says: “So run that you may obtain” (1 Cor. 9). Here he signifies not the running of the feet but of conduct. “Walk from virtue to virtue, until the God of gods is seen in Zion”: this is the soul’s running. But so that this running may be more swift, the body must be disciplined, as the same Apostle says: “I therefore run,” he says, “not as though uncertainly; I fight, not as one beating the air, but I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Cor. 9). Elsewhere the Apostle himself says: “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course; I have kept the faith. Henceforth the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the just judge, will award me on that day” (2 Tim. 4).

So that, never departing from his instruction. “From his,” he says, that is, from God’s. “Instruction” means teaching or training.

Persevering in his teaching in the monastery until death. For it is not the one who has begun, but the one who has persevered, who will be saved. The dwelling of a single monk can also be called a monastery. For *monos* in Greek means “alone,” while *sterium* means “station” or “dwelling.” Thus a monastery can be called a solitary dwelling.

Let us share in the sufferings of Christ through patience. The Apostle Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that we might follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2).
