By “let us share through patience,” he means that patience is necessary in sufferings. For he was so patient in suffering for us that, like a gentle lamb, he was led to the sacrifice and did not open his mouth. “Let us share,” he says, that is, let us join ourselves to him.

So that we may also deserve to be sharers in his kingdom. “Sharers” means companions, heirs, or participants. A *consors* is one who joins himself by lot, just as a *concors* is one who joins himself in heart. He is called a *consors* because a portion of good things belongs to him. For the ancients used *sors* to mean “portion.” If we are sons, then we shall also be heirs. But if heirs, then without doubt we shall also be sharers. Amen.

The prologue ends.

It is called a rule, as blessed Benedict says, because it directs the conduct of the obedient. Others, however, say that it is called a rule because it leads rightly and never draws elsewhere; or because it governs; or because it provides a standard for living rightly; or because it corrects what is twisted and wicked.

## CHAPTER ONE. On the four kinds of monks

It is clear that there are four kinds of monks. [Col. 0724D] A monk is so called by Greek etymology because he is solitary. In the books of the *Collations*, they are named *Alonardi*, or *Alonazontai*, by a distinction of the singular and solitary life. Hence it followed that, from the fellowship of their community, [*koino bisatai*, uncertain], and that their cells and lodgings were called *koinobia*. This, therefore, was the most ancient kind of monks; not only first in time but also first in grace. It alone continued for many years, down to the time of Abbot Paul or Antony. Even now we see traces of it remaining in strict monasteries.

Thus the discipline of the cenobites took its beginning from the time of apostolic preaching. For such was the whole multitude of believers in Jerusalem, as it is described in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul; nor did any of them say that anything they possessed was his own, but all things were common to them. They sold their possessions and goods and distributed them to everyone according as each had need” (Acts 4). Such, I say, was the whole Church then, as it is now difficult to find except among a few in monasteries.

The first, the cenobites. Understand “first” here as referring not to chronological order but to greatness of grace. Cenobites are a kind of monks whom we may call those living in common. For a cenobium is a monastery of many people, that is, of those living in common; the term appears to have been formed from Greek and Latin [that is, rendered into Latin]. The Greeks call the common *koinon*. From this number of the perfect—and, so to speak, from this most fruitful root of the saints—the flowers and fruits of the anchorites also emerged afterward. The leaders of this profession are said to have been those whom we mentioned a little earlier, namely Saints Paul and Antony [perhaps: “we mentioned”]. They pursued the secrets of solitude and divine contemplation not, like some, because of faintheartedness or through the disease of impatience, but from a desire for higher advancement.

Serving under a rule or an abbot. He says “serving,” because “the life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7). As it is also written elsewhere: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in righteousness and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2). Placed in this warfare, we ought to implore the Lord with the Prophet, saying: “Judge, O Lord, those who harm me; fight against those who fight against me. Take up arms and shield, and rise to help me” (Ps. 34).

The second kind is that of the anchorites, that is, hermits. For *anachorisis* in Greek is called *eremos*, “desert.” The anchorites are a kind of monks who, after the life of the cenobites, seek the deserts; and because they have withdrawn far from human beings, they are called by this name. Thus *anchorites* may be interpreted as “those who withdraw.”

Those who do not, through the recent fervor of conversion. A novice, compelled by the fervor of compunction, promises to observe all the precepts of the rule. But since it belongs to a human being to arrange his ways, while it belongs to the Lord to direct his steps, a person does not know whether he will reach the goal of perfection.

But through the monastery’s prolonged testing. By “prolonged” he means tested over many periods or days. For just as gold is tested by being heated and refined in a furnace, so a good monk is tested through tribulation in the enclosure of the monastery and under the discipline of the rule. Just as tested gold is fashioned into the diadem of a true king, so a well-tested monk is fashioned into the diadem of Christ the King. As it is written concerning the person of that true King: “He has adorned me with a crown as with a bridegroom” (Isa. 61). For Christ’s crown consists of all the elect, among whom well-tested monks are numbered.

They have learned, already trained by the support of many, to fight against the devil. Just as no one is crowned in the contests of this world without a struggle or contest, so in spiritual conduct and a holy purpose no one can receive an unfading crown or become an heir of eternal life without a struggle. Perfect athletes are always found in the contest without fear and with great eagerness. Thus the most perfect combatants and the most continent monks also contend, always keeping before their eyes the delight of paradise, expecting to enjoy its pleasures, the promised goods, the immortal ages, and the everlasting light. Do you wish to contend in the arena and emerge victorious? Put on the armor of God as a garment—that is, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the other things prescribed by the Apostle.

[Col. 0726B]

And, well trained in the brotherly battle line, they are now able to go from it to the solitary combat of the desert and, without the comfort of another, fight against the vices of the flesh or of thought with only their own hand or arm, God helping them. A battle line is an ordered formation of soldiers prepared to fight against the devil. From it this solitary order of monks goes forth to fight. The fight is so called because at first they began to battle in war with their fists. No one will be crowned without a contest; nor does God’s grace abandon anyone who fights against the vices of the flesh with eagerness and good will. The vices of the flesh are known to all, as the Apostle says: “The works of the flesh are manifest,” he says, “which are fornication, uncleanness” (Gal. 5), and the rest, as has already been stated above. Thus he says “against the vices of the flesh or of thought,” as though he were saying, against the vices of action and of intentions.

Sometimes vices begin in thought and afterward emerge in action. At other times they exist only in thought and do not proceed into action. Hence the law forbids the offering to the Lord of weighty bread. A person is “weighty” who does not shamefully practice vices in action but is frequently polluted by them in the mind. Although he does not commit the wicked deed in action, he nevertheless harbors shameful vices in thought. Against these vices the monk fights with hand or arm, because, without the aid of the brothers and by his own strength or activity—which are signified by the arm and hand—he emerges victorious in the desert with the Lord’s help alone.

The third and most horrible kind of monks is that of the Sarabaites. [Col. 0726D] He says “third,” meaning blackest, darkest, most dreadful, wild, or savage. For the ancients used “most dreadful” to mean exceedingly savage. Sarabaites are interpreted as “Rennuites,” because they refuse to follow the examples or teaching of their elders. This most dreadful and faithless kind of monks emerged—or rather, that harmful plant, having revived, grew again—which had sprouted through Ananias and Sapphira at the beginning of the Church and was cut down by the severity of the Apostle Peter. It was judged so detestable and accursed among monks that no one afterward dared to appropriate it, as long as fear of that strict sentence remained fixed in the memory of the faithful. By that sentence the blessed Apostle did not allow the leaders of the novel crime to be healed by repentance or by any satisfaction, but cut down the most destructive shoot by a swift death.

Who, approved by no rule or by the experience of a teacher, are like gold in a furnace. “Approved by no rule,” he says, that is, tested or instructed by no examination under a rule. For the lives of all who live rightly are undoubtedly called rules. “Experience” means knowledge or teaching, and is derived from “experiment.” The Sarabaites do not imitate the pattern of all these things in order to live, but, corrupted by their own pleasures, dissolve in order to perish. They are not tested as gold by disciplined observance of the rule, but soften like lead under their own desires. Hence it follows:

But softened in the nature of lead. When gold is placed in a furnace, it receives both strength and brilliance. So a good monk, placed in the furnace of the rule, receives strength, so that he may endure adversity with equanimity, and brilliance, so that he may display to all an example of good works. But lead placed in fire softens and perishes. Thus, when a reprobate monk placed under regular discipline grows lukewarm, he perishes. Concerning the former it is said: “As gold in the furnace, the Lord tested him” (Wis. 3). Concerning the latter: “Because you are lukewarm, I will begin to spew you out of my mouth,” says the Lord (Rev. 3).

One, having received the brilliance of gold, ascends to reign with Christ in heaven; the other, softened into the nature of lead, descends to Tartarus to be tormented with the devil. One, increased in virtues, grows toward what is better; the other, having become lukewarm, declines toward what is worse. One flourishes in sacred virtues; the other grows cold amid worldly cares. One truly bears the name of monk; the other bears the name of a counterfeit monk because of his tonsure. Hence it follows:

Still serving the world by their works, they are known to deceive God through the tonsure. That person still serves the world who, placed in the monastic habit, does not cease to do what he did as a secular person. For what is it to continue serving the world by one’s works except to do in the monastery what one did in the world while still clothed in secular attire? He serves the world because he does not cease to do its will; he serves the world because he separates himself from it neither in desire, thought, nor action, but merely pretends through his tonsure and religious habit to be God’s son. In habit and outward religion he appears to the ignorant to be a monk, but by his works he is seen by those who know him to have deceived the Lord. Concerning such people the Lord says: “You will see them in the clothing of sheep, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves; you will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7).

Who, two or three together, or certainly singly, without a shepherd, shut up not in the Lord’s but in their own sheepfolds, make the pleasure of their desires their law. “Without a shepherd” means without an abbot, who appears in the monastery to act in Christ’s place. Christ said: “I am the good shepherd; I feed my sheep; I know mine, because mine know me” (John 10). Since they have no shepherd, they remain shut up not in the Lord’s sheepfolds but in their own. The Lord’s sheepfolds are the monasteries of holy monks, rightly governed by Christ, the supreme shepherd, [Col. 0728A] and placed in a pasture. These men are neither governed nor placed there by him; instead, fulfilling their own desires, they shamefully remain in their own lairs. There they treat everything they do as law, and, fulfilling the desires of their pleasures, they carry out whatever they wish. Hence it is added:

Whatever they have thought or chosen, they call holy; and whatever they have not wanted, they consider unlawful. He says “whatever they have thought,” not whatever they have proved by the authority of the divine Scriptures or by the examples of the fathers. They break their fast with whomever they wish, saying, “It is good and holy to break the fast for a guest.” But to those to whom they do not wish to show hospitality they say, “We are not permitted to break the fast today.” They think one thing in their hearts and choose in their minds to lead a solitary life rather than remain with others under regular discipline, saying: “It is holier to live separately with a secure and private mind than either to impose discipline on others or to receive from others the discipline imposed by the rule.” They do not know what is written: “Woe to the one who is alone, because when he falls he has no one to lift him up” (Eccl. 4).

For many dangers are close to the solitary person. First, he pleases only himself in all his actions and has no one else to approve his work. Then he does not recognize which vices abound in him or which virtues are lacking. He has no one in whom to test his humility; he does not offer obedience to a brother; he does not display patience in fasting. It is therefore better for a monk to live in a monastery under the discipline of one father and in the company of many, [Col. 0728C] and to learn humility from one and patience from another. One teaches silence; another teaches gentleness. He should not do what he wishes; he should eat what he is ordered to eat; he should have as much as he has received; he should pay the measure of his work; he should be subjected to one to whom he does not wish to be subjected. Let him come to service when weary and, walking, fall asleep; and before his sleep is complete, let him be compelled to rise. Having suffered an injury, let him remain silent.

The fourth kind of monks is called the gyrovagues. Throughout their whole life they lodge in the cells of different people, traveling through various provinces for three or four days at a time, always wandering and never stable. *Gyro* means “circuit” or “going around.” Therefore a gyrovague is one who, wandering and roaming, goes around the cells and houses of others alike. They are also called by another name, Circilliones; under the appearance of monks they wander here and there, carrying hypocrisy around for sale. They go through the provinces, sent nowhere, fixed nowhere, standing nowhere, sitting nowhere—always and everywhere.

Serving their own pleasures and the enticements of the appetite. Enticements are illicit, luxurious, pleasure-seeking, or most shameful delights, in which a soft and dissolute monk is frequently entangled.

And since these men are in every respect worse than the Sarabaites, it is better to be silent about all their miserable way of life than to speak of it.

## CHAPTER TWO. What the abbot ought to be like

Wishing in what follows to demonstrate the character of a good shepherd, blessed Benedict first said: [Col. 0729A] “What ought an abbot to be like?” The answer must be affirmative: good, certainly. Such as the Apostle describes when he says: “Blameless, as God’s steward; not arrogant, not irritable, not given to wine, not violent, not greedy for temporal gain, but hospitable, kind, sober, just, holy, self-controlled, so that he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and refute those who contradict it” (Tit. 1). Without doubt, he ought to be such and of this kind.

The abbot who is worthy to preside over a monastery must always remember what is said. For he is called and named *abbas*, that is, “father.” If he is a father, let him nourish his sons—that is, his monks—in the manner of a father; let him love them in the manner of a father; and when necessary, let him chastise, rebuke, entreat, and correct them with the severity of a father. [Col. 0729B] And if necessity requires him to apply the cautery of excommunication or the punishment of rods, let him do so not from hatred of spirit but from paternal love—not for the sake of vengeance but from love of justice. For it is written: “You shall carry out what is just and right” (Deut. 16). And because the just Lord loves justice, the abbot, who appears in the monastery to act in his place, ought to love justice.

And fulfill the name of superior by his deeds. For many abbots rejoice to possess the name of superior, that is, of abbot, but nevertheless fear to undertake the sweat of labor. They desire temporal glory and do not undertake labor for the sake of the commandment. And if it happens that they address a word of exhortation to the brothers for the sake of vain glory, they do so not for an eternal reward. Therefore whoever wishes to bear the name of superior above the others ought to sweat more than the others in good works. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified.

He is believed to act in Christ’s place in the monastery when he is called by Christ’s own title, as the Apostle says: “You have received the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’” The abbot then acts in Christ’s place in the monastery when he governs the flock entrusted to him carefully and justly; when he arranges rightly everything that must be arranged; when he performs temperately everything that must be done; when he teaches in a catholic manner everything that must be taught. He does what must be done, judges with discernment what must be judged, mercifully relaxes what must be relaxed, and binds together the whole flock entrusted to him in the love of charity. He loves the whole flock as a father loves his only son; and then, rightly and reasonably fulfilling the office attached to Christ’s name, he is called *abba*, “father,” by everyone, as by his sons.

Therefore the abbot must neither teach, establish, nor command anything outside the Lord’s precept—God forbid. All teaching consists in two ways, namely words and examples, as the same blessed Benedict says below: “When someone receives the name of abbot,” he says, “he ought to preside over his disciples by a twofold teaching.” Therefore in this twofold teaching the abbot ought to teach nothing that lies outside the Lord’s precept. The fullness of the divine Scriptures is filled with the examples of the fathers and with the words of teachers. He ought not, therefore, to teach what lies outside the Lord’s precept; [Col. 0730A] rather, his teaching must agree most carefully in all things with the Lord’s commandments. From the Lord’s commandments he ought to take everything that he wishes to teach his disciples.

Or establish. By “establish” he means to define or set a measure, which an abbot must not do outside the Lord’s precept. For the abbot’s measure and definition must be made in all things according to the Lord’s commandment, lest, by living too laxly, he plunge them into a snare, or, by excessive abstinence, compel them into harmful murmuring. The abbot’s arrangement must therefore make straight progress along the royal road, lest, if he does too much, he suffer the loss caused by his flock’s failure from weariness on the journey. And if he nourishes it more laxly than is proper, it may slide into Tartarus while living luxuriously.

Or command. By “command” he means to prescribe or order those things that an abbot must not impose outside the Lord’s precept. For if he prescribes and commands his disciples what accords with the Lord’s commandments, he will receive grace from them and an everlasting reward from the Lord. But if he commands what lies outside the Lord’s precept, he inflicts harm on his disciples and injury on his own soul. Therefore he ought neither to teach, establish, nor command anything outside the Lord’s precept.

But let his command or teaching sprinkle the leaven of divine justice into the minds of his disciples. The word “leaven” derives its name from fervor. In this passage it signifies the love of charity, which makes minds fervent for and awakens them to the love of divine justice, until it leads them to such perfection of love [Col. 0730C] that they desire to love nothing except their Creator. Therefore the abbot’s command or teaching ought to sprinkle the leaven of charity into the minds of the monks, so that they may have no taste for anything earthly, love nothing vain, and desire nothing transient; but, always loving and holding fast to divine justice, may hasten to ascend to their Redeemer and to their heavenly homeland.

Let the abbot always remember that, at God’s dreadful judgment, an examination will be made both of his teaching and of his disciples’ obedience. These words do not require exposition; rather, they strike great fear into abbots and monks. At that dreadful judgment there will be an examination of the abbot’s teaching: whether he taught the faithful doctrine of the mystery of the Holy Trinity; whether he himself first fulfilled what he commanded his disciples to do according to the Lord’s precept; and whether he first corrected in himself what he rebuked and amended in others.

There will also be an examination of the disciples’ obedience on that dreadful day: whether, following the Lord’s footsteps, they were humble; whether they made themselves obedient under the hand of their abbot unto death; whether they obediently fulfilled everything their abbot commanded them for the love of Christ; and whether, as though obeying Christ himself—whose place the abbot occupies in the monastery—they obeyed their abbot from the heart. For it is written: “Whoever hears you hears me” (Luke 10). And elsewhere: “Obey your parents in the Lord” (Eph. 6; Heb. 13).

Let the abbot know that the shepherd will bear the blame for whatever benefit the householder is unable to find in the sheep. [Col. 0731A] This sentence would have been very frightening to abbots had it not been healthfully tempered by the following sentence, in which he says:

Only then will he be free. That is, he will be free from guilt to such an extent that:

If the shepherd has devoted every care to a restless or disobedient flock, and has given complete attention to its diseased conduct. The abbot gives his monks every care when he forms them in holy conduct and instructs them with suitable words and holy works. He provides complete attention when, as far as he is able, he supplies what is necessary for their souls and bodies. He provides both care and attention when he adorns them with inward holy virtues and governs outward material matters temperately; when, on account of outward matters, he does not abandon inward care, nor, on account of inward solicitude, leave aside outward provision; but, remaining temperate in both, provides them with care for their souls and attention to their bodies.

Their shepherd, acquitted at the Lord’s judgment, will say with the Prophet to the Lord: “I have not hidden your justice in my heart; I have declared your truth and your salvation.” The abbot’s intention ought to be such that, whenever he can be of benefit, he does not cease from the word of preaching. It is his duty to display the glory of the heavenly Father through the voice of preaching; to reveal how many temptations of the ancient enemy lie hidden along the journey of this life; and gently, yet with great sharpness of zeal, to correct the evils of his subjects, which he ought not to tolerate, lest, if he is insufficiently inflamed against their faults, he himself be held guilty of them all.

Nevertheless, the abbot’s speech, which is made for the sake of justice, truth, and salvation, must sometimes rebuke the vices of his subjects more harshly and at other times admonish them gently. He must distinguish by careful inquiry what to say, to whom, when, and in what manner, and impose judgment on each person according to the measure of the fault, yet with discretion and tranquility of mind. As the Apostle Paul says, the abbot must be “able to exhort in sound doctrine and refute those who contradict it.” For the word of correction is the key that opens: by rebuking, it exposes a fault that often remains unknown even to the person who committed it.

There are, and will be, many monks who do not cease committing faults through ignorance and therefore do not mourn the faults they have committed. Instead, they rise insolently against the one correcting them, contemptuously resisting him, and arrogantly spurning their abbot’s admonition. Concerning such people it is added:

But they, despising, have scorned me. Evil monks despise and scorn their good abbot when they do not humbly obey his commands; when they do not humbly keep his saving instructions but, in their pride, even criticize them; when they disdain to fulfill what is ordered and shamelessly contend to fulfill what is not ordered; when they become lazy and lukewarm, or even idle, in the works they must perform, and at the same time murmuring and querulous in their conduct. Subjects ought to serve their abbot as members serve their head, preserve his commands with the greatest love as though they were the Lord’s authority, and attribute the correction of rebuke to their own negligence, rather than criticize the abbot’s severity or discipline.

And then, finally, punishment itself—the very death—shall prevail over the disobedient sheep entrusted to his care. That death which prevailed over the first disobedient human beings in paradise now prevails daily in the world over disobedient monks. In paradise Adam and Eve abandoned the Lord’s commandments through disobedience, and then for the first time the punishment of eternal death prevailed mightily over them. But our Lord Jesus Christ, who said through his prophet, “I will be your death, O death” (Hos. 13), emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and becoming obedient unto death (Phil. 2); he destroyed death’s dominion, mercifully enlightened the hearts of the obedient, and completely extinguished their punishment.

But then, finally, among the obedient sheep—that is, monks—who abandon the commands of their abbot, indeed of the Lord and Savior, and try to fulfill their own desires, death itself shall prevail as punishment, so that it may rightly be said of them: “Like sheep they have been placed in hell; death shall feed upon them” (Ps. 48). Rightly, those who despise the commands of a good teacher receive such a reward.

Therefore, when someone receives the name of abbot, he ought to preside over his disciples by a twofold teaching: namely, to display all good and holy things more by deeds than by words. [Col. 0732C] Those who preside are the head of their subjects, so that the feet may be able to take the right paths; therefore, without doubt, the head must go first. The abbot who preaches to his subjects in words must show them, by his life, the footsteps of good action. When he speaks words of holy preaching, he must first rouse himself to the practice of good action; he must always exercise lofty deeds first, and then make others zealous to live well. He must first correct himself with strict scrutiny, and then shape the lives of others by his speech. He must first take care to punish his own faults with tears, and then declare the faults of others by punishing them. Before his words resound in exhortation, everything he is about to say must cry out through his deeds. For that voice more readily penetrates the hearts of listeners which the life of the speaker commends, because by showing what he commands in speech, he helps bring it about.

So that he may set the Lord’s commands before receptive disciples in words. The verb “ought” is understood. For in this passage he uses the adverb *ut* in place of the conjunction “and.” By “receptive” he means those who are mindful, suited, or capable of understanding—those who quickly grasp what they hear from their teachers, retain it in memory, and fulfill it in their works. He says “set before,” that is, place first, because receptive and simple disciples, after hearing and quickly understanding the Lord’s commands, strive afterward to fulfill them wisely.

But to the hard-hearted and the more simple-minded. By “hard-hearted” he means stubborn, rigid, or incorrigible. By “more simple-minded” he means unlearned people who possess scarcely any memory or understanding of the divine Scriptures.

To show the divine commands by his deeds. Therefore, as blessed Gregory says, the one who is to preside over the others as an example of good living ought to be spiritually alive after dying to all the passions of the flesh; one who has set aside the prosperity of the world; who fears no adversity; who desires only what is inward; who is not led to covet what belongs to others but gives away what is his; who commits no unlawful acts but mourns as his own the acts committed by others; who in all that he does presents himself as worthy of imitation by the others; who strives to live so that he may demonstrate a good example to his monks throughout his entire life; who first sheds the tears he wishes his hearers to shed, and so kindles them through the compunction of his own heart. And just as he surpasses his subjects who do good works in honor, so also he must surpass them in deeds and life.

But whatever he teaches the disciples to be contrary to the divine commandments, he must judge in his own deeds to be things that must not be done. He teaches that gluttony, drunkenness, the cares of this age, and all vices and sins are contrary to the disciples; from all these he must first abstain, and thus teach others by deeds and words to abstain. For he is chosen as abbot for this reason: that his words may not be emptied of their force by his deeds. The one chosen to correct the faults of others must take care not to commit things for which others could rebuke him. He ought not to undertake the office of preaching if he does not know how to go before others by living well.

Therefore the abbot must first be entirely free from evil works, and thus restrain others with firm authority. For the one who takes care to wash away the filth of others must strive to keep his hands clean, lest, if he holds on to mourning while pursuing what is dirty, whatever he touches become more foul. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Cleanse yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52). For abbots carry the Lord’s vessels: they have received into the faith of their conversion the souls of their neighbors, to be led into the inner sanctuaries. Let them therefore consider within themselves how greatly they must be cleansed, since they carry living vessels in the embrace of their own profession to the temple of eternity. Therefore what the abbot preaches must not be done, he himself must not do; and what he preaches must be done, he himself must first necessarily fulfill in his deeds.

Lest, preaching to others, he himself be found reprobate. A preacher is himself found reprobate when, preaching to others, he says one thing and does another. He practices one thing in speech and another in deeds. What he preaches to others as something to be done, he himself becomes sluggish in carrying out. By his word he shows the way of uprightness, but he neglects to walk in it. He is eager to preach but becomes sluggish in acting. He preaches to others the way of justice that they must hold, but he himself does not wish to submit to the discipline that saves. To him what follows rightly applies.

When God says to the sinner: “Why do you recite my ordinances and take my covenant upon your lips?” (Psalm 49). Nor does what he preaches to others pertain to just anyone, if he himself does not practice what he preaches. For the mouth that dares to recite the Lord’s ordinances and take up the holy covenant ought to be righteous. Whoever neglects to fulfill what he preaches, though he does not cease to fulfill what he judges ought to be done, must neither recite the Lord’s ordinances nor assume the sacred covenant in the office of preaching. For it is written: “Praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclesiasticus 15).

“But you hated discipline and cast my words behind you.” A subject hates discipline when, in wrongful presumption, he murmurs against just corrections. As it is written: “Fools despise discipline.” He casts the Lord’s words behind him when he scorns obedience to the just commands of his abbot or elders. A superior hates holy discipline when he scorns living according to the precepts of the Rule, forgetful of divine Scripture, which says: “My son, do not reject the discipline of the Lord, and listen to counsel and accept discipline, so that it may be well with you” (Proverbs 13; Proverbs 19). For the regular life is saving discipline for those who hold to it. A superior casts the Lord’s words behind him when he himself pretends to fulfill what he preaches to his subjects from the divine Scriptures. Whoever hastens zealously to rebuke the faults of others must carefully consider and condemn his own sins through repentance, lest, while publicly censuring another’s smallest offense, he conceal his own worthless sin as though it were gold. For there are some who always keep the errors of others before their eyes, but consider their own as nothing, consign them to oblivion, and cast them behind their backs. [Col. 0734C] Concerning such people it follows plainly:

“And you saw the speck in your brother’s eye, but did not see the beam in your own” (Matthew 7). An abbot sees a speck in his brother’s eye but does not see a beam in his own when he publicly judges and exaggerates even the smallest faults of his subjects, while making light of and concealing his own greater faults and pretending not to correct them. He sees a speck in his brother’s eye when he reproves the fault of anger, laziness, drowsiness, and other such vices in another’s heart; he does not see a beam in his own when, although he has hatred, drunkenness, pride, and similar crimes in his heart, the abbot does not recognize that he possesses them, seeing and rebuking the minor things in others’ hearts that ought to be censured, while neither seeing nor correcting the serious things in his own heart.

[Col. 0734D]

Let him not show partiality toward anyone in the monastery. For “God is not a respecter of persons” (Acts 10), but in every nation whoever fears him is acceptable to him. Therefore, the abbot must neither distinguish nor favor anyone in the monastery, because God neither distinguishes nor favors a person, but accepts and approves only good works. “To show partiality in judgment is not good,” says Solomon (Proverbs 18). And it is written in Leviticus: “You shall not do what is unjust, nor judge unjustly; you shall not regard the person of the poor, nor honor the face of the powerful. Judge your neighbor justly” (Leviticus 19). Once someone has come from the world to the monastic habit—whether previously free or enslaved, poor or rich, noble or ignoble—the abbot must not distinguish him, but must either correct or love each one according to the merit of his life.

Let no one be loved more than another, unless he is found better in good works or obedience. A monk is rightly loved more than the others by his abbot when he is found better than the others in good works and obedience. For that person is rightly loved by another who is honored by God for good works and holy obedience. It is necessary, I say, that a person who is loved by the immortal God be loved with such love. For such a monk submits himself to obedience before all others for the love of God and exercises himself in every good work; and therefore he is rightly preferred, loved, and cherished by the abbot above all others. [Col. 0735B]

A freeborn man must not be placed before one who has converted from slavery, unless another reasonable cause exists; and if justice so dictates, let the abbot do this in the case of anyone’s rank. Otherwise, let them keep their proper places. When he says that a freeborn man must not be placed before a slave, this is understood to refer to rank or office. It does not mean that, merely because he is freeborn, he should hold a higher place in rank or the office of prior or dean, unless another reasonable cause exists. For it is a reasonable cause that the one who can sing and read better in the Church, or fulfill every office, be assigned a suitable place so that he may worthily fulfill that office. And if he is endowed with such rational understanding and instructed in word and deed that he can be dean or prior, neither his free birth nor his servile status should hinder him. But if a reasonable cause requires it, let him be placed higher in rank and as prior in the monastery. This, however, must be done not only concerning the freeborn or servile order, but concerning anyone’s rank—that is, whether it be the rank of a prior or a junior, of a priest or a Levite, or of the remaining orders. Otherwise, let them keep their proper places: that is, because of the dignity of power or free birth, one should not be placed before another, but each should remain in the place in the order in which he came.

For whether slave or free, we are all one in Christ. “We are all one in Christ,” he says—that is, one body of Christ. Thus the apostle Paul says elsewhere: “In one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Gentiles, slaves or free, and we were all given to drink of one Spirit” (Galatians 1; Ephesians 6; 1 Corinthians 12; 1 Timothy 2). God, the Son of God, who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, redeemed every sex, every age, and every condition from the whole human race, joined them to his body among the number of the elect, and therefore, whether slaves or free, we are all one in Christ. [Col. 0735D]

And under one Lord we bear an equal service as soldiers. The life of good monks in this present world is always established as a military service under Christ. Hence blessed Job says: “A human being’s life is warfare upon the earth” (Job 7). This we bear equally under one Lord, because although we do not live equally, we have equally promised and endure the Lord’s gentle yoke and light burden while living the regular life. This regular life, which is here called warfare, must be observed equally by all monks and may never permissibly be violated by slaves or free, by priors or juniors. And if, because of human frailty, anyone happens to deviate from it, it is necessary that he be corrected by the same penance and that the same discipline be maintained for all. Hence it plainly follows:

“For there is no partiality with God” (Acts 10). We distinguish persons by accepting them, because when they come into this world we find them distinguished. But God, who in the beginning created everyone from one human being and in one condition, neither accepts nor distinguishes persons; rather, he either condemns or justifies each person according to his works. He justly and deservedly condemns the unjust; but he mercifully and freely justifies the just. Those whom he finds living proudly in wicked deeds he humbles and condemns. Those whom he finds living humbly in good works he rewards and exalts. Hence it follows here:

“We are distinguished by him only in this respect: if we are found better than others in good works and humble.” In these two matters the elect are always distinguished from the reprobate: true humility of heart and the performance of good works. For it is the voice of the Head and the body—that is, of Christ and the Church—in the Psalm: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Psalm 42). The Lord therefore does not distinguish persons from persons—that is, freeborn from slaves—but distinguishes works by works and merits by merits, so that he may grant each person rewards according to the works of his own labor. For those whom he finds better than others in good works and the merits of the virtues, and humbler than the rest in purity of heart, he will assign fitting dwelling places in the kingdom of heaven, with a distinction of rewards. The abbot ought to maintain this discernment, the mother of all the virtues, in everything: not to distinguish persons, but to approve each according to his merit and to love all with a sincere heart according to the merits of their works. Hence it follows:

“Therefore, let his love be equal toward all; let discipline be administered to all alike, according to their merits.” In this respect the abbot’s love ought to be equal toward all: he should not distinguish persons in the manner of his affection. He ought to love monks of noble birth equally and those born of servile condition equally. Thus he ought to discern the merits of each in such a way that he does not prefer one person to another. And if a freeborn person or a slave commits one and the same fault, let them undergo one and the same discipline. One should not be lightened in penance because of honor, while another is burdened because of contempt. Rather, the abbot’s judicial severity should be tempered so that one person is not judged more leniently and another more harshly.

In his teaching the abbot must always preserve that apostolic form in which it says: “Reprove, appeal, rebuke” (2 Timothy 4). In this apostolic statement the words of blessed Jerome and blessed Prosper should be placed. Jerome says: “Reprove sinners, warn them not to sin, rebuke those who resist. But let all this be done with patience and according to doctrine.” Prosper, however, said: “The teachers of the Church ought to possess both severity, so that they may reprove, and patience, so that they may endure firmly those unwilling to be corrected, fulfilling the apostolic command, by which he instructed Timothy, saying: ‘Reprove, appeal, rebuke, with all patience and doctrine.’” It is as though he said: “Reprove equals, appeal to elders, rebuke juniors.” But he added “with all patience and doctrine” for this reason: a person corrected gently shows reverence to the one correcting him. Offended, however, by the harshness of excessive rebuke, he accepts neither the rebuke nor salvation.

In this statement, which they reasonably understand as being fulfilled by different persons, we can also undoubtedly understand that it is to be fulfilled in one and the same person at different times. First, the sinner must be reproved because he sins. For no one ought to reprove another unless that person is sinning. As the Lord says in the Gospel: “If your brother sins against you, go and reprove him between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have won your brother” (Matthew 18). Behold, by reproving your brother you have already won him, because, listening to you, he corrected himself. Then appeal to him again, so that, living daily in good works, he may grow in the virtues and arrive at perseverance in good conduct. But if he does not listen to you and does not correct himself, or perhaps returns to his vomit after correction, rebuke him severely and, if you are able, correct him—but always with patience and doctrine. In this way the entire statement can be fulfilled in one and the same person.

At another appropriate time, the sinning monk should be reproved so that he may turn away from evil. If he has corrected himself, he should again, at a suitable time, be appealed to, so that he may not live lukewarmly, but, growing in the virtues, may do good. But if he refuses to correct himself, or, after being appealed to, again at the proper time he must be greatly frightened and rebuked, so that he is treated as a pagan and a tax collector. The exposition of blessed Benedict seems to accord with this interpretation. When he said, “Reprove, appeal, rebuke,” he added:

“That is, mixing times with times, terrors with consolations.” As if he said: “Mix times of appeal with times of reproof, and times of rebuke with times of appeal.” And when the sinful soul has been terrified by the stern and just rebukes of its teacher, consolations should be added to it through paternal love, lest it sink into the pit of despair. Hence blessed Gregory also says: “Gentleness must therefore be mixed with severity. Something should be formed from both, so that subjects are neither wounded by excessive harshness nor relaxed by excessive kindness.” For the abbot must carefully exercise every kind of care, lest any of his sheep perish. Hence it follows:

“Let him show the harshness of a teacher and the loving affection of a father.” “The harshness of a teacher” refers to his gravity, or greatness, or great dignity of honor. At times, *dirus* (“harsh”) is understood as “great” or “worthy.” When he says, “Let him show the loving affection of a father,” this implies that he should possess it within himself. Alternatively, “the harshness of a teacher” means the greatness or terror of the rebuke that the teacher displays toward his subjects so that they may be healed. This harshness—that is, this terror—must necessarily show within itself not hatred but the affection of a loving father. For terror toward delinquent disciples should proceed not from the fuel of hatred but from the love of a loving father, so that the teacher’s prudent terror may correct those who go astray, while the loving father’s affection may encourage those who act well. Hence the appropriate exposition of blessed Benedict’s preceding statement—“Reprove, appeal, rebuke”—is most clearly added. Concerning reproof he says: “That is, he should reprove the undisciplined and restless more severely.”

[Col. 0738B]

Concerning appeal he says: “He should appeal to the obedient, gentle, and patient, so that they may progress toward better things.”

Concerning rebuke he says: “We admonish him to rebuke and correct the negligent and contemptuous.” I think no clearer exposition can be found of this statement of the Apostle than that which blessed Benedict gave.

Nor should he pretend not to notice the sins of offenders. The sins of offenders must not be overlooked, lest the harmful offenses of subjects be prolonged. The sooner a sinner’s fault is to be corrected, the sooner he also obtains forgiveness. Today the abbot quickly corrects one manifest fault; tomorrow, without doubt, he will have another that he must correct. Therefore, let him not delay in pretending not to notice and correct it, as though unaware of the great burden of governing souls that weighs upon him.

[Col. 0738C]

But as soon as they begin to arise, let him cut them off at the root, insofar as he is able. Vices or sins must be cut off at the root at their beginning, lest, once their roots have been fixed and strengthened, they send forth harmful branches and bear the fruits of evil works on those branches. He commanded sins or vices to be cut off at the root, but nevertheless said, “insofar as he is able.” For we cannot cut away sins or vices as much as we wish; rather, let us hasten to cut away the sins of offenders as much as we are able with the Lord’s help.

Remember the danger of Eli, the priest of Shiloh (1 Samuel 2). Because Eli, overcome by false pity, refused to strike his delinquent sons, he struck himself together with his sons by a cruel condemnation before the strict Judge. He was condemned for his sons’ iniquity because he did not rebuke them with the severity and authority of a pontiff, but softened them with paternal gentleness. This judgment must be carefully feared by abbots, lest, when they have treated the faults of their subjects more gently than is fitting, they be struck by the sentence of condemnation from the strict Judge.

Let him correct the more honorable and understanding minds with words at the first or second admonition. By “more honorable” he means more worthy of honor. A person is called honorable, as though possessing a state of honor, because he has nothing shameful. “Understanding” means capable of reason: those who understand what they hear from their teachers and strive to fulfill it in their actions. If they should overstep in some matters—for there is no human being who lives and does not sin—he commanded that they be admonished with words a second time, according to the Lord’s command, because he believed that they could be corrected in this way.

But let him restrain the wicked, hard-hearted, proud, or disobedient by correction in words or body at the very beginning of sin, knowing that it is written: “A fool is not corrected by words” (Proverbs 18). And again: “Strike your son with a rod, and you will deliver his soul from death” (Proverbs 23). By “wicked” he means imprudent people, lacking integrity of mind. By “hard” he means stubborn, obstinate, incorrigible, or rebellious people. He must restrain such people, as well as the proud and disobedient, by correction in words or body at the very beginning of sin, lest the evil of sin grow upward and, when completed, produce for its author the fruit of death, because it is written: “When sin is fully grown, it brings forth death.” Correction is understood as including excommunication, words, and blows. “Let him restrain” means let him check, bridle, or repress. And because it is written, “A fool is not corrected by words,” bodily correction must be imposed upon him through excommunication. And if it is still necessary, let the rod be applied through blows, because it is written: “Strike your son with a rod, and you will deliver his soul from death.” It is better that he be struck here by a father’s rod than that, condemned to hell, he suffer punishment there. It is better that he endure a father’s correction here for a short time than that, eternally condemned in hell, he groan. A father’s correction seems bitter for a little while, but for those who patiently endure it, it produces the sweetest fruits in the future.

The abbot must always remember what is said and know that “to whom more is entrusted, from him more is required.” Let him not, lifted up by pride over those who live well, exalt himself and despise those who live viciously. He must always remember what is said—that is, remember that he is a fragile creation, formed from the soft clay of the earth. Therefore, let him always fear the fall of his frailty and condemn another’s sin humbly and with discernment. Let him seek out another’s hidden faults with careful investigation and, once discovered, strike them with discretion and the utmost caution. Let him sympathize with the one who has been tempted, fearing that he too may at some time be tempted and fall. Let him hear the Apostle saying: “If a person is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted.” As if he said: “When what you see displeases you because of another’s weakness, consider what you are.” And remember what is said: the abbot is called “father.” If he truly is a father, let him love his sons—that is, his monks—with paternal love, and let him show himself to those born under him in such a way that he is both loved and feared by them. Let him be loved by the good and feared by the wicked. In the one person of the abbot there should be both the tender entrails of a loving mother and the strict judgment of a father, so that those whom he nourishes with maternal love he corrects with paternal rigor, and those to whom he offers the breasts of a mother to suckle he holds under a father’s discipline.

Hence blessed Gregory says: “Care must be taken that a ruler display to his subjects both the tenderness of a mother and the discipline of a father, and that those who preside show themselves to be such that their subjects are not ashamed to reveal their hidden matters, so that when the little ones endure the waves of temptations, they may flee to the father’s mind as to a mother’s lap.” The abbot must also know that “to whom more is entrusted, from him more is required.” For the more people entrusted to someone’s care of governance, the more an account is required from him. However many monks each abbot receives under his governance, for that many he will have to render an account to the Lord. And if he saves himself by living well and governs them well and justly, he will receive from the Lord grace for his own salvation and everlasting reward for all of them.

Let him know what a difficult and arduous task he has undertaken: to govern souls. He says that governing a soul is a difficult and arduous task because it is subtle and laborious, exceedingly delicate to comprehend, and narrow when examined; therefore it is laborious and arduous to govern, burdensome and sluggish to correct, and danger threatens every governor who must render an account concerning it.

And to serve the dispositions of many. Since the dispositions of different monks are different, they require different expenditures of care, because different wounds require different medicinal remedies. Therefore blessed Benedict sets down here a different method of treatment for different dispositions, saying:

“To one, indeed, with consolations; to another, with rebukes; to another, with persuasion; and according to the quality or understanding of each, let him conform and adapt himself to all.” In explaining this statement, the words of blessed Gregory should be inserted. He says: “It must also be known that at times the vices of subjects should prudently be overlooked, but the reason why they are overlooked should be indicated. At times, things openly known should be patiently tolerated. At times, they should be investigated subtly and secretly. At times, they should be reproved gently; at other times, rebuked forcefully. But because the same exhortation is not suitable for everyone, since the same quality of character does not bind everyone equally, the speech of teachers must be shaped according to the quality of those listening, so that it may suit each person’s circumstances and yet never depart from the art of common edification.”

According to the quality or understanding of each, the abbot should thus conform and adapt himself, becoming great with the great and small with the small; becoming weak with the weak, so that he may save the weak; becoming a model to the flock, showing a pattern of humility to the humble and providing an example of obedience to the obedient. Similarly, he should provide all his subjects with a pattern of salvation in abstinence, vigils, prayer, and every good virtue. For when, together with Paul, he truly says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not inflamed?” (2 Corinthians 12), and the like, he thus conforms and adapts himself to all and shows his subjects the good model of a good shepherd. And when he rejoices with those who rejoice, weeps with those who weep, has pity on the weak, sympathizes with the afflicted, accommodates himself to the old and the young, patiently bears with those weak in mind, strengthens the frail with kindness, and makes himself composed and suitable for all according to the qualities of every character and the understanding of little ones or simple people.

So that he may not only suffer no loss of the flock entrusted to him, but also rejoice in the increase of the good flock. By “loss” he means the damage, ruin, or diminution of the flock, which the abbot must neither suffer nor desire in the flock entrusted to him, insofar as he is able, nor allow to happen; rather, he should rejoice in its increase—that is, in the enlargement of the good flock. For an increase in the number of the good flock, or growth in the virtues, is the progress and exaltation of a good shepherd. The multiplication of good monks, I say, is the salvation of the souls of rulers and the honor of governors.

It should be noted that he said the shepherd’s joy lies in the increase of the good flock, not of the evil flock. For the multiplication of the wicked is the distress of the good. Their multiplication therefore causes greater loss than their diminution, and the unjust produce grief rather than joy for the just. Through the multiplication of the wicked, the congregation of the good is weakened; conversely, through the increase of the good, the assembly of the wicked is weakened. Through the progress of the virtues, the strength of the vices is diminished.

Above all, let him not, by pretending not to know or by making light of the salvation of the souls entrusted to him, show greater concern for transient, earthly, and perishable things? The abbot must not pretend not to know—that is, pretend ignorance of—the matter concerning which he must render an account to the strict examination of the Lord; nor must he make light of the salvation of his monks and consider the care of earthly things a great matter. He must not care less about the salvation of the souls entrusted to him and show greater concern for material possessions. “The soul is more,” says the Lord, “than food.” For to care anxiously for earthly matters and not care for souls is not a counsel of salvation but of death. To regard a transient, earthly, and perishable thing as of great importance, and to make light of what is permanent and eternal, is not a counsel of salvation but the folly of destruction.

“Making light of” means considering something small, holding it in contempt, or even looking down with a proud spirit upon something great. *Pendere* means “to value” or “to estimate.” Whoever considers himself to be something and, despising another, regards him as small or nothing, makes light in another of what he considers great in himself. Some, forgetting that they have been placed over their brothers for the sake of their souls, devote themselves with all the effort of their hearts to worldly matters. When these things are present, they rejoice; when they are absent, they pant after them day and night amid the fever of their thoughts. For, as right reason demands, we should care less for transient things and more for what will remain forever; we should be less concerned with earthly things and more with heavenly things, less with perishable things and more with lasting things, because we will render an account to God not for earthly possessions but for the souls of our monks. Hence it follows:

“But let him always think that he has received souls to govern, and that he will render an account for them.” Since the substance of the soul is incorporeal, invisible, and of unknown origin, governing it is therefore a laborious, difficult, and arduous task. It requires great labor and skill to reach the purity of its thoughts, and therefore its wound of sin is healed only through prolonged and difficult labor. The soul has willingly received many wounds of sin, but, in order to be healed, it reluctantly accepts much medicine. If the abbot administers spiritual medicines to wounded souls discreetly and reasonably, the soul receives healing and he receives grace from God. But if he neglects to administer spiritual medicines to sick souls, he will be compelled to render an account concerning all his subjects.

And let him not complain of a smaller material possession. “Let him not complain,” he says—that is, let him not murmur. For one who murmurs complains. Whoever murmurs because of the poverty of perishable things makes an unjust complaint against the Lord, not knowing that just as gold is tested in the furnace (Proverbs 17), so the life of monks is tested in the furnace of poverty. By “smaller material possession” he means the scarcity of earthly goods. Here he uses “substance” improperly for earthly things. Properly speaking, substance is so called because every thing subsists through it. It has eight attributes: quantity, knowledge, position, condition, action, passion, place, and time; the Greeks call it *ousia* (οὐσία), “substance.”

Let him remember what is written: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6). We must first seek the kingdom of the Lord—that is, with the greatest effort, the utmost zeal, and the full intention of our hearts—and then hope from him for the earthly support necessary to us. We must first seek his righteousness and afterward hope from him for the earthly substance necessary to us. From the Lord we must seek both the eternal kingdom and earthly support: the former as a permanent good, the latter as transient, yet necessary along the way of this life.

Concerning this statement blessed Augustine says: “What is the difference between the good that ought to be desired and the necessity that ought to be taken up?” He explained this statement when he said: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest.” The kingdom and righteousness of God are therefore our good; this is what should be desired, and in it our end should be established, for its sake we do everything we do. But because we are engaged in warfare in this life in order to reach that kingdom, and life cannot be conducted without these necessities, “these things,” he says, “will be added to us.” But you must first seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness. When he said “first,” he indicated that this must be sought before the other—not in time but in dignity: the one as our good, the other as our necessity. If this necessity is for the sake of that good, it must be sought by you.

And again: “Nothing is lacking to those who fear him” (Psalm 33). Whoever possesses God, through whom all things were created and in whom all things remain and endure, cannot lack anything of spiritual or earthly substance. God is able to prepare for his saints, in the desert of this world, a table full of both spiritual and bodily delights. Whoever fears the Lord with chaste fear, in whom all fullness of things and abundance of virtues abide, cannot lack anything of the substance of spiritual or bodily things. For it is written: “It will be well with the one who fears God forever, and he will be blessed in the days of his completion” (Ecclesiasticus 1). And: “Those who fear the Lord have hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and their protector” (Psalm 113).

Let him know that whoever undertakes to govern souls must prepare himself to render an account. Whoever undertakes the souls of others to govern them, lest he be compelled to render an account concerning them with the Lord, must teach them by the word of right preaching and by the example of good works, so that he may both strive to please the eternal Judge by living well and provide his subjects with an example of good living; he must detect carefully what needs correction in them and correct it quickly, insofar as he is able. He must also heed the counsel of Solomon, who says: “My son, if you have pledged yourself for your friend, you have struck your hand with a stranger, and you have been ensnared by the words of your mouth and caught by your own speech. Do therefore what I say, my son, and free yourself. Run, hasten, rouse your friend,” and so forth (Proverbs 6).

To pledge oneself for a friend is to take responsibility for another’s soul at the risk of one’s own conduct. One’s hand is struck with a stranger when one’s mind is bound to the care of another. He is therefore ensnared by the words of his own mouth when he is constrained by reason, so that his life cannot be released from what he admonishes others to do. Thus, before the strict Judge, he is compelled to perform as much in deed as it is evident that he commanded others by his voice. Whoever is placed before others as an example for living is admonished not only to keep watch by living well himself, but also to rouse his friend through preaching. For it is not enough to watch over oneself by living well if he does not also separate the one under his authority from the body of sin. Therefore, let the abbot live in such a way, guarding himself and rousing others, that he may not render a punishable account to the Lord, but may receive eternal rewards from him with joy.

And whatever number of brothers he knows himself to have under his care, let him recognize with certainty that on the day of judgment he will render an account to the Lord for all those souls, without doubt with his own soul added. According to the number of his monks, the abbot will render an account at the Lord’s dreadful judgment. And if a just account saves him, he will receive a reward both for his own salvation and for governing his brothers. But if his own unjust deeds and the unjust governance of his subjects condemn him, he will receive condemnation according to the number of his evils. For just as concerning the souls of his subjects, so also concerning his own soul the abbot will render an account to the Lord. Therefore, he must watchfully and prudently care for both theirs and his own, and must not neglect either his own life for theirs or their conduct for his own. The abbot must hold outwardly what he has undertaken for their benefit; inwardly, he must preserve what he promised to the Lord for his own salvation.

[Col. 0744A]

And thus, always fearing the future examination of the shepherd concerning the sheep entrusted to him, while he takes care concerning the accounts of others, he becomes concerned about his own. The lesser shepherds of the supreme Shepherd—that is, of Christ, who said, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10)—must always fear the future examination both of their own actions and of the sheep entrusted to them, lest God at some time rebuke them, saying: “You did not bind up what was broken, and you did not bring back what had been cast away” (Ezekiel 34). “And when you yourselves drank the clearest water, you muddied what remained with your feet; and my sheep were feeding on what had been trampled by your feet, and they drank what your feet had muddied,” and so forth.

Let abbots take care not to hear this voice of rebuke, and let them diligently fulfill the concerns of their subjects and not cease to manage their own prudently. Let them thus burn with concern for themselves that they do not withdraw from guarding their subjects. For it is fitting that those who preside over others keep their eyes open and look attentively in every direction. Let them be full of eyes within and without, so that from afar they may foresee the ambushes of the ancient enemy; within, that they may carefully guard themselves; without, that they may provide others with an example of good living.

In this way, while he is vigilant concerning the accounts of others, the abbot becomes concerned about his own—that is, while he is vigilant concerning the accounts of his subjects, he is made concerned about his own. “He becomes concerned,” that is, he becomes concerned about his own accounts, understood as his own reckonings. Let him think carefully that he will render an account to the Lord in the dreadful judgment for his own actions just as for those of his sheep. They distinguish *ratio* (“account” or “reason”) from *ratiocinatio* (“reckoning”) in this way: *ratio* is a certain movement of the mind that distinguishes truth from falsehood; *ratiocinatio* is a rational and subtle discussion. He knows well how to avoid rendering an account with the Lord who knows how both to guard himself and to govern his subjects well.

And when he supplies correction to others through his admonitions, he himself is made free from vices. It is most fitting that the one who ministers the bread of life to others should not perish from hunger himself. For whoever, out of love, offers his brothers the word of salvation is by that very love corrected from vices. For charity covers a multitude of sins, as it is written: “Whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death, and will cover a multitude of his own sins” (James 5). Therefore, rightly, he who by his admonitions frees others from the error of vices will, with the Lord’s help, first be freed from his own vices. Vices are called sins, which in themselves are nothing; but where goodness is absent, there is vice. For every nature is a work. Evil works, which are called vices, are acts, not things. But this name has been acquired through the privation of goodness.

## CHAPTER III. On Calling the Brothers to Counsel

For this reason the brothers are called by the abbot to counsel, because it is written: “Plans are scattered where there is no counsel, but where there are many counselors they are confirmed” (Proverbs 15). Again: “The heart is delighted by ointment and varied fragrances, and the soul is sweetened by the good counsels of a friend” (Proverbs 27). “War is undertaken with deliberation, and there will be safety where there are many counsels” (Proverbs 24).

Whenever some important matters must be undertaken in the monastery. A monastery, as was said above, is also called the dwelling of a single monk. But one must ask: if the dwelling of one person is properly called a monastery, because in the Greek language *monas* means “one,” why is the dwelling of many people placed together in one called a monastery? Perhaps, as I think, it is because there is one faith, one baptism, one heart, and one soul among all monks who live well and justly, as formerly there was among those who rightly believed and lived well in the religious life. For one will remains among all monks who live rightly. They serve one Lord, serve as soldiers under one king, and, having become one body of Christ, worship the same one Redeemer; and therefore the dwelling of them all is not improperly called a monastery.

Let the abbot summon the whole community and state what is under discussion. “What is under discussion” means what is to be deliberated or what is to be investigated. Earlier writers distinguished congregation and convocation in this way. *Congregation* may be said of human beings, brute animals, stones, or any other insensible things, because they can be gathered either by voices or in any other manner. *Convocation*, however, can be made only of rational human beings, who are summoned by their proper names, because being called together belongs specifically to those who know how to hear and discern.

[Col. 0745C]

And, hearing the counsel of the brothers, let him consider it within himself and do what he judges more useful. First, therefore, the abbot should seek counsel from all the brothers assembled together concerning matters to be done in the monastery or concerning any other matters requiring action; he should willingly hear what counsel each person gives, and afterward, in private with only the senior brothers, carefully and keenly discern who has given the more useful and who the less useful counsel. Then he should strive to carry out what he has judged better—that is, what he has discerned. For “to judge” is said to mean “to discern,” as in: “Judge me, O God, and discern my cause” (Psalm 42).

We have said that all are to be called to counsel because the Lord often reveals what is better to a younger person. For it is written: “If something is revealed to a younger person, let the elder be silent” (1 Corinthians 14). Often, for the sake of humility, the Lord reveals to the younger what he conceals from the elders. For God is not a respecter of persons (Acts 10), but in every age, condition, sex, and nation, those who fear God are acceptable to him; and among all these, where he wills, the Spirit of the Lord breathes mercifully and, in his goodness, bestows the grace of wisdom. For he did not distinguish age in Daniel and Samuel, but bestowed grace. “Gray hairs are a human being’s understanding,” says Scripture, “and an undefiled life is old age” (Wisdom 4).

Let the brothers therefore give counsel with complete humble submission, so that they do not presumptuously and insolently defend what seems right to them; rather, let the matter depend upon the abbot’s judgment, so that all obey what he judges more salutary. All monks ought to obey their abbot in such a way that none of them rashly dares to criticize his actions; instead, like sons toward a father or members toward the head, let them all serve and obey him humbly as subjects. If his commands accord with the Lord’s commandments, let them guard and fulfill them with the utmost care, as though they were the Lord’s command, and strive to carry them out with complete love. Let them judge that what is holy, salutary, and necessary for them is what pleases their abbot, not what they themselves have chosen to do. Thus, established in the virtue of obedience and patience, let them not question the abbot’s decrees, but carry them out. And when the rigor of discipline requires that they be rebuked severely, let them bear the correction they have received with magnanimity, attributing their punishment not to the moods of those by whom they were rebuked, but to their own negligences.

But just as it is fitting for disciples to obey their teacher, so it is fitting for the teacher himself to arrange everything prudently and justly. The abbot must always distinguish good from evil by careful examination, diligently consider what is suitable for whom, when, and in what manner, and thus arrange everything prudently and justly. For this reason all the disciples ought to obey him, since he is their rational Father. Therefore, as blessed Gregory says, the one who presides should look around himself, so that he may live both for himself and for his subjects; so that he may conceal within the bosom of his mind the good things they do, while nevertheless offering from them an example of right action for the progress of those who follow; so that, noticing the faults of his subjects, he may correct them without becoming swollen with pride; so that he may gently tolerate some things after correcting them, without by that gentleness loosening the bonds of discipline; and so that, by tolerating certain things, he may overlook them, but without allowing them to grow through his overlooking them. Therefore he must take the greatest care that the one set over the governance of human beings preside within himself, in the inner chamber of his mind, upon the seat of humility, and constantly watch with vigilant eye the one before whom he will one day stand as judge, to be judged concerning these matters; so that, the more anxiously he now trembles before the one whom he does not see, the more confidently he may behold him when he does see him.

In all things, therefore, let all follow the Rule as their teacher. “In all things” means, by implication, in all the precepts of that same Rule. In divine offices and human actions—in food and drink, in clothing and footwear, in vigils and prayers, in sleep and silence, at the appropriate hours, in labors, and in absolutely all the precepts of that same Rule—let all monks follow that Rule as their teacher: subjects and superiors, disciples and teachers, provosts and deans, and all ministers without exception. Moreover, the abbot himself, in all things, just as much as the other monks, should follow the Rule as his teacher. As the text continues:

Nor should anyone rashly depart from it. That is, no one—neither superiors nor subjects—should rashly depart from the Rule itself, that is, inconsiderately or irrationally. He did not say absolutely, “Nor should anyone depart from it,” but added “rashly,” so that you might understand that, if necessity demands it, one may depart from it reasonably, with discretion, great caution, and because of necessity.

Let no one in the monastery follow the desire of his own heart. For everyone who, moved by compunction and sent by the Lord, comes to the monastery wishes to live not according to the judgment of his own heart, but according to the counsel of his abbot and of the Lord; he does not wish to do the will of his own heart, but to obey the commands of the Lord and of his abbot, frequently recalling that saying: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6). There are many monks of limited understanding who say: “The desire of my own heart is good, and therefore I wish to follow it.” They should be answered: “Ask your abbot and the spiritual brothers about it,” because it is written: “Do everything with counsel” (Proverbs 13). If they judge it good and agree that it is good, then do it, because it is no longer merely the desire of your own heart, but has become common to all who agree. But if they do not agree and do not approve it as good, recognize that it belongs to your own heart. And if you wish to be saved, flee from it as from the face of a serpent.

Nor should anyone presume to contend insolently with his abbot, either inside or outside the monastery. To contend insolently means to contend proudly, stubbornly, rashly, or presumptuously. No brother should have such contention with a brother, nor a monk with his abbot. But it must be understood that, by forbidding contention with the addition “insolently,” he permitted friendly or peaceful contention. There is a friendly and beneficial contention which frequently arises between two people according to the nature of the matter at issue, as it is once said to have arisen between blessed Benedict and his disciple Maurus concerning the boy Placidus. Blessed Benedict said that the merit belonged to his disciple Maurus, who, in order to rescue the boy from the river, had walked upon the water. Maurus, on the other hand, contending with him, said that the merit was not his but his teacher’s, since he himself, walking upon the water, rescued the boy unharmed from the river. Although he forbade such a form of friendly contention outside, he certainly did not prohibit it inside when a just matter required it. Outside, he condemned insolent contention; inside, however, he did not forbid friendly contention for the sake of bringing an accusation or for some useful purpose, as was said above. Outside he permitted neither insolent nor friendly contention, because if even friendly contention occurs in public, it gives rise to harmful contempt for the teacher and deadly elation in the disciple. Hence, when blessed Benedict said, “Nor should anyone presume to contend insolently with his abbot,” he did not say “inside or outside,” as some books have it; rather, in the copy he wrote with his own hands, it is found as “insolently, inside or outside the monastery.” From this it is understood that he allowed no contention outside, but permitted friendly contention inside.

If anyone should presume to do so, let him be subject to regular discipline. Regular discipline, in the case of spiritual vices—that is, stubbornness, disobedience, pride, murmuring, detraction, and other vices of this kind—should first be applied, according to the Lord’s command, by admonition once, and a second time by the elders in private. If he does not correct himself, let it be done a third time through public rebuke. If he still does not amend, let it be done a fourth time through the punishment of excommunication. But if he is so perverse that he is not corrected even by this, let him be subjected a fifth time to bodily punishment. If the scourging does not correct him, let the brothers’ prayer be applied on his behalf even a sixth time. If the prayer of the brothers does not benefit him either, let him suffer a sorrowful separation from the brothers and a damaging expulsion from the monastery even a seventh time. In this way, apart from more serious faults and those which Benedict judged otherwise, all regular discipline is understood to have been arranged.

Yet the abbot himself must do everything with fear of God and observance of the Rule.
