The abbot ought to do everything with fear of God, because it is written: “Those who fear the Lord prepare their hearts, sanctify their souls in his sight, and will be filled with peace and the fruit of salvation” (Ecclesiasticus 2). It should also be noted that he commands the abbot to do everything with observance of the Rule, lest, while he preaches to others that the Rule must be fulfilled, he himself become rejected by failing to fulfill it; and lest the abbot or any superior find an excuse for not fulfilling it. Let him read this chapter, and he will plainly discover that just as the subject monk is bound, so too the abbot and every superior are bound by observance of the Rule.

[Col. 0748C]

Knowing without doubt that he will render an account of all his judgments to God, the most equitable Judge. For the Lord himself says to judges: “With whatever judgment you have judged, you will be judged” (Matthew 19). Therefore the abbot must attend most diligently to ensuring that he does not do to another what he does not wish done to himself, because he will render an account to the most equitable Judge, God. Whatever he has sown by his actions in the present life, this he will certainly reap in the future. Blessed Benedict frequently impresses this sentence upon our hearts for the purpose of writing it there, lest, once placed in forgetfulness by us, it be neglected; rather, let it be retained and feared as a terrible judgment.

But if some lesser matters are to be undertaken for the monastery’s needs, let him use only the counsel of the elders, as it is written: “Do everything with counsel, and afterward you will not repent” (Ecclesiasticus 32). For counsel is a great matter, exceedingly necessary for abbots, and not to be undervalued, but to be set above gold and silver. Divine Scripture itself approves this, saying: “Gold and silver are the setting of one’s steps, and good counsel is above both” (Ecclesiasticus 40). “The knowledge of the wise will abound like a flood, and his counsel remains like a fountain of life” (Ecclesiasticus 21).

## CHAPTER IV. What the Instruments of Good Works Are

Just as smiths and other craftsmen have suitable and numerous instruments for fashioning their works, so good monks have suitable spiritual instruments of many virtues. By these, their life is beautifully and according to God’s will ordered in the present, and, once so ordered, they will reign happily with Christ in the future. Blessed Benedict wished to set forth in orderly fashion in this chapter these virtues by which the order of good monks is chastely arranged, so that a monk may walk adorned with them, strike the enemy boldly with them, overcome all the temptations of this age, and join himself to the fellowship of all the saints and angels. We too will endeavor to speak of the praise of all these virtues insofar as the Lord permits.

### First Instrument

First of all, to love the Lord God with all one’s heart, all one’s soul, and all one’s strength (Luke 10). This rule of love has been divinely established in such a way that you should direct toward him all your thoughts, your whole life, and your entire understanding, from whom you yourself have what you offer. When it commands that God be loved with all one’s heart, all one’s soul, and all one’s strength, it leaves no part of our life that ought to be free from the love of God. For a person sins in that part by which he loves God less. If we love him with all our heart, there will be nothing in us by which we serve the desires of sin.

And what is it to love God except to occupy one’s mind with him, conceive an affection for enjoying the vision of him, hate sin, despise the world, love one’s neighbor, preserve the proper measure in that love, and not overturn the established order of love? Those overturn the order of love and do not preserve the proper measure of loving who either love the world, which ought to be despised, or fail to love their neighbors as themselves, or perhaps do not love God as themselves. Those love God perfectly who, by willing what God wills and not willing what he does not will, yield to no sins by which he is offended, and always show themselves ready to love and possess the virtues that he deigns to grant. They strive diligently to observe the word of God, as the Apostle says: “Whoever keeps his word, truly the love of God is perfected in him” (1 John 2). For the one who proves that he has his love by keeping his commandments truly knows God. To know God is to love him. Whoever does not love him clearly shows that he does not know how lovable he is; he has not learned to taste and see how sweet and good the Lord is, since he does not constantly strive to please him in his sight.

Again the Apostle says: “Whoever keeps his commandments remains in him, and he in him” (1 John 3). Therefore let God be your house, and be the house of God. Remain in God, and let God remain in you. Let God remain in you so that he may contain you; remain in God so that you may not fall. Keep his commandments, hold fast to charity, do not be torn away from his faith, so that you may glory in his person and remain secure in him, according to this: “They will rejoice forever, and you will dwell in them” (Psalm 5). “God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4).

### 2. Then, Your Neighbor as Yourself

Thus the Apostle Paul says in his Epistle to the Galatians: “The whole law is fulfilled in one saying: You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Galatians 5). John also says: “Whoever loves his neighbor remains in the light, and there is no scandal in him. Whoever says that he is in the light and hates his brother is in darkness even now” (1 John 2). For the one who did not take care to put on the inner organs of charity could not strip off the darkness of sins.

Love alone, therefore, distinguishes between the sons of God and the sons of the devil, as the Apostle John says: “By this the sons of God and the sons of the devil are manifest” (1 John 3). “Everyone,” he says, “who is not righteous and does not love his brother is not from God.” Those who have charity have been born from God. Whatever else you wish to have, have it; only do not have this one thing, and it benefits you nothing. If you lack other things, have this, and you have fulfilled the law. For whoever loves another has fulfilled the law. Whoever does not love remains in death.

The same Apostle also says: “Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God, and everyone who loves has been born from God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love. Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another” (1 John 4). If we love one another, God remains in us and his love is perfected in us. Let no one therefore suppose that this love, in which God remains and which is perfected in us, can be preserved through some careless, idle relaxation and negligence. That is not charity, but languor. Let charity burn for correction and amendment. If there are good morals, let them delight us; if there are bad ones, let them be amended and corrected. Thus let us love one another with sincere and disciplined charity, and in this way his love is perfected in us.

You have begun to love; God has begun to dwell in you, so that by dwelling in you he may make you perfect. We shall be perfect in charity if, just as he first loved us for the sake of our salvation, so we love him for no reason other than his love. We have this commandment from God: whoever loves God must love his brother. By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God. Therefore the one alone is proved to love his neighbor rightly who is known to burn with love for the Creator.

### 3. Then, Do Not Kill (Matthew 5)

When he says “do not kill,” the prohibition applies not only simply to the killing of the body, but also to the killing of the soul, especially since this is forbidden to monks in the monastic habit and to those established in the religious life. They do not go armed with worldly weapons, by which homicides are committed, but with spiritual virtues, by which souls are saved. But just as there is killing by iron, so there is killing by hatred, by falsehood, and by any serious sin. For it is written: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3); and, “The lying mouth kills the soul” (Wisdom 1); and, “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Leviticus 4; Ezekiel 18).

Blessed Benedict wishes the monk to abstain from all these kinds of killing when he says “do not kill”: neither the bodies of others with iron, nor his own soul through hatred, homicide, or any other sin, because it is written: “A human being kills his own soul through wickedness” (Wisdom 21). It is fitting that not only the monk but every Christian abstain from all these things, because whoever commits any one of them commits homicide, according to the Lord’s judgment: “Whoever kills will be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5).

### 4. Do Not Commit Adultery

Adultery is both committed and called by many names, in body and in soul. For fornication, the worship of idols, the desire of the eyes, and friendship with worldly people arising from desire and greed for possessions are also called adultery. Concerning adultery of both flesh and soul, the Apostle says among other things: “Neither adulterers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6; Romans 13). The Law likewise forbids it, saying: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exodus 20).

Concerning the desire of the eyes, the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5). Concerning the friends of this world and the lovers of temporal things, the Apostle James says: “Adulterers, do you not know that friendship with this world is enmity with God?” (James 4). He rightly calls those people adulterers whom he rebukes for turning away from the love of heavenly wisdom toward the embrace of worldly friendship, and whom he saw, having despised the Creator, serving Mammon instead. He also shows them to be adulterers who, under the faith and confession of Christ’s name, serve the enticements and love of the world.

There is yet another kind of adultery, concerning which the Apostle denies that he is guilty, saying: “For we are not like the many, adulterating the word of God, but from sincerity, as from God and before God, we speak in Christ” (2 Corinthians 2). Adulteries must first be removed from the heart, so that they do not draw a person toward carrying out works of the flesh. For before adultery is completed in action, it is already adultery in thought.

Elijah and John were girded around the loins with leather belts; in Revelation, however, there is a golden belt around the breast. The Rule wishes the monk to have these two belts: let his leather belt always gird his loins and the golden one his breast. Concerning the first, the Lord says: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12). Concerning the other, the prophet admonishes us, saying: “Gird your loins over your breasts” (Isaiah 32). Hence Peter also says: “Therefore, having girded the loins of your mind,” and so forth (1 Peter 1).

The beauty of chastity, therefore, which is compared to a golden belt, must be loved above all by monks. Once its delight has been tasted, it is found sweeter than every delight of the flesh. Chastity is the fruit of sweetness and the beauty offered to the saints, the security of the mind and the health of the body. Through it human beings are lifted to heaven and joined to the angelic choir.

### 5. Do Not Commit Theft

It is also written in the Law: “You shall not steal” (Exodus 20). The Apostle says: “Let the one who stole steal no longer” (Ephesians 4). Elsewhere, among other things: “Neither thieves will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6). Whoever therefore wishes to possess the kingdom of God must guard himself in every way from the evil of theft, lest, while he desires to seize what belongs to another, he lose his own soul and forfeit the heavenly kingdoms.

He commits not a small but a great evil who takes a coin from his brother and the kingdoms of heaven from himself. The monk must understand that theft is not always committed in the same way. Whoever takes a slave from his rightful master and subjects him to another who is not his rightful master undoubtedly commits theft. Therefore whoever, by living wickedly, takes himself away from his own Creator and subjects himself to the devil likewise commits theft. The Lord Jesus Christ created us from the clay of the earth and redeemed us with his own blood; therefore, by his creation we are his slaves, and by his redemption we are his servants.

If anyone among us, as was said, withdraws himself from God’s service by living badly and subjects himself to the devil, he commits the worst theft. He has separated himself from the fellowship of the children, and, having become a servant of demons, has lost both the inheritance and the dwelling-place of the heavenly kingdom. For it is written: “Everyone who sins is a slave of sin. A slave, however, does not remain in the house forever” (John 8).

Similarly, whoever takes the members of Christ and makes them members of fornication and of a prostitute commits theft; and, having become a slave of sin, he does not remain in the house forever—that is, in heaven. Concerning this the Lord said: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John 14). For the one who does not enter through the door but climbs up by another way is a thief and a robber. And because thefts are not committed in one way only, but in many ways, they must not be understood uniformly. We must beware the guilt of all these forms.

### 6. Do Not Covet (Exodus 20; Deuteronomy 5)

He is not speaking of the desire of which David sang: “My soul has desired and fainted for the courts of the Lord” (Psalm 44); and, “My soul has desired to long for your judgments at all times” (Psalm 118); and of which it is written elsewhere: “The desire for wisdom leads to the everlasting kingdom” (Wisdom 6). This desire is a virtue. Rather, he speaks of the desire that is a vice, concerning which the Lord says: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s possession” (Exodus 20; 1 Samuel 15).

Hence James also says: “Each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire” (James 1). “When desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin.” Peter likewise says: “Fleeing the corruption of the desire that is in the world” (2 Peter 1), in accordance with this: “Flee sin as from the face of a serpent” (Ecclesiasticus 21). The Apostle Paul says: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires” (Romans 6). From this it is understood that sin reigns in a human being chiefly through the desire of the mortal body.

John also says: “Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2). By these names of vices he comprehends every kind of vice. The desire of the flesh is everything pertaining to the pleasure and delights of the body, chiefly food, drink, sexual intercourse, and so forth. The desire of the eyes is every worldly curiosity involved in acquiring temporal things and in needless concerns, in distinguishing good and evil, and in criticizing the faults of one’s neighbors.

This vice of desire must be greatly avoided by monks. It easily steals upon the mind and, by pouring in its poison, quickly plunges the soul into death. Therefore, among the Ten Commandments of the Law, just as homicide, theft, and adultery, the evil of desire is forbidden by the Lord; for just as those sins draw a person toward punishment, so desire, having drawn and enticed him, plunges him into the pit of hell.

### 7. Do Not Give False Testimony (Exodus 20; Deuteronomy 5)

False testimony is that by which truth is often mocked, so that things done or said are denied as though they had not been done. There is another kind of falsehood that makes a monk very guilty. Every promise made only in words and not fulfilled in deeds is without doubt proved to be false testimony.

Hence Solomon says: “A lying witness will perish, but an obedient man speaks of victories” (Proverbs 21). For whoever testifies that he serves God but does not carry out his words in deeds will perish forever. Whoever faithfully strives to fulfill what he promises brings his speech to victory, because, while he strives through obedience to conquer his desires, he afterward receives the palm of victory through the justice of the Judge.

The one is also proved to be a false witness who does not understand words in the same sense in which they are spoken. Such were those of whom the Gospel says: “Finally, two false witnesses came,” and so forth (Matthew 26). Monks must also guard most carefully against that kind of falsehood concerning which the Psalmist says: “They went astray from the womb; from the belly they spoke falsehood” (Psalm 57), if they desire to ascend unhindered to the heavenly kingdoms; for, as Solomon says, “A false witness will not go unpunished” (Proverbs 19).

A deceitful witness is found to be liable to three persons: first, to God, whom he despises by falsifying, swearing falsely, and lying; second, to the judge, whom he deceives by pretending, lying, and falsifying; finally, to the innocent person, whom he harms and oppresses by false testimony. For just as the person who gives false testimony against the innocent is condemned before God, so also is the one who readily believes accusers and quickly lends his ear to charges. The speech of a righteous person ought to serve only salvation, not the condemnation of a brother.

### 8. Honor All People (1 Peter 2)

A monk honors all people when, despising himself, he humbles himself before everyone and, considering all others superior, shows himself to be lower than they; when he displays not only humility in his heart but also abasement and self-contempt in his body; when he embraces everyone with fraternal love and reveres them humbly as elders; when he declares himself a sinner above all and proclaims himself an unworthy servant; when he honors the elders as fathers and loves the younger as brothers.

Hence the Apostle Peter says: “Honor everyone; love the brotherhood” (1 Peter 2). Paul likewise admonishes us: “In honor, anticipate one another” (Romans 12). A monk therefore honors all people when he subjects himself to everyone and is regarded as useful, generous, and gracious toward all. In sacred Scripture, honor is understood to be rendered not only through greetings and the duties of obedience, but also through alms, gifts, and offerings.

### 9. What You Do Not Want Done to Yourself, Do Not Do to Another (Matthew 7)

When this sentence is referred to the love of God, all acts of shame die; when it is referred to one’s neighbor, all crimes die. Whoever does not do to another what he does not want done to himself does not inflict evil upon his brother, does not return evil for evil, does not utter a curse for a curse, does not secretly slander his neighbor, and does not envy his good works. Thus, so to speak, he closes every entrance to sin within himself and opens the door of charity and every good virtue.

For while he neither desires nor performs evil toward another, he undoubtedly desires and performs good toward his neighbor as far as his strength permits. This sentence must also be understood in the way stated above concerning the future. No one wishes his dwelling-place to be corrupted, and neither should he corrupt God’s dwelling-place, namely, himself. No one wishes someone to take away his servant and hand him over to another to whom he ought not belong. No one wishes a thief to drive away his beast and deliver it to a robber. No one wishes anyone to plunder his dwelling-place and overthrow his temple.

Therefore what a human being does not want done to himself, he should not do to God: he should not take himself away from God by living badly and hand himself over to the devil. Rather, persevering in good works, let him say with David: “I became like a beast before you, and I am always with you” (Psalm 72). Let him not destroy God’s dwelling-place in himself or overthrow the temple, because it is written: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of the Lord dwells in you” (1 Corinthians 3). Whoever violates the Lord’s temple in himself, God will destroy.

Therefore, by living badly in himself, the monk both takes the Lord’s servant away from the Lord, drives away his beast, and destroys the gift of the Holy Spirit and overthrows the temple. In this way he does to another what he does not want done to himself.

### 10. To Deny Oneself in Order to Follow Christ

“To deny” is understood as to refuse, reject, or prohibit. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16). And what is it to deny oneself to oneself except to lay aside the old person with his deeds? And what is it to follow Christ except to put on the new person, who has been created according to God in righteousness and holiness; to live spiritually, not carnally?

“For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh”—that is, the old person against the new, and the new against the old. Our inner person resists the outer, and the outer the inner. For the flesh always desires useless and perishable things; the spirit seeks what is useful and always sighs for eternal things. The flesh is frequently tormented by the cares and anxieties of the world, stolen away by the enticements of pleasures, inflamed by the desires of the flesh, delighted to live idly, weighed down by the vice of lethargy, depressed by bodily sleep, infected by the laziness of the mind, led astray by gluttonous greed, and stretched beyond measure by excess of food and drink. And when it is luxuriously nourished in all these things, it is dragged toward the shameful act of fornication.

The spirit, which desires to please God through holy works, forbids the body to fulfill these things and those like them. This is what it means to deny oneself in order to follow Christ: to prevent oneself from doing evil and to urge oneself to do good. Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps.

What is it to follow his footsteps except to walk as he walked: to despise all prosperity, as he despised it; not to fear adversity, which he endured; willingly to do what he did; willingly to undergo what he commanded; to hope for what he promised; to follow where he went before; to bestow kindness even upon the ungrateful; not to repay the malicious according to their deserts; to pray for enemies; to love the good; to show mercy to the perverse; to invite those who oppose us; to receive in charity those who have been converted; and to endure the deceitful and the proud with equanimity.

### 11. To Discipline the Body (1 Cor. 9)

The body is so called from corruption, because, once corrupted, it perishes. [Col. 0755B] For it is dissoluble, frail, and mortal. We ought to discipline it—that is, to correct it by fasts, afflict it, and reform it; and, if necessary, even to strike it with blows. For we use *discipline* to mean *strike*, just as Pilate said concerning the Lord: “I will release him after having scourged him” (Matt. 27).

The body is disciplined by fasts, vigils, and many afflictions, concerning which the Apostle Paul says: “I therefore run, not as though uncertainly; but I discipline my body and bring it into servitude,” etc. (1 Cor. 9). For what else is it to discipline the body than to die to vices and sin? And what is it to die to sin except not to live at all for condemnable deeds, to desire nothing carnally, and to pursue no ambition?

Such a person, like one dead in the flesh, no longer slanders anyone, opposes or displeases anyone, uses violence against no one, calumniates [Col. 0755C] or oppresses no one, does not envy the good or insult the afflicted, does not indulge in luxury, does not become drunk, does not burn with the torches of hatred, does not pursue unjust profits, does not cling to the powerful or the rich, is not distracted by restless curiosity or burdened by anxious concern, does not take pleasure in the greetings of others, and is not wearied by the insults of the proud. Pride does not inflate him; vicious ambition does not hurl him headlong; vainglory does not disgracefully display him; contention does not exhaust him; boldness does not make him shameless; injustice, unjust; lack of clemency, savage; fickleness, changeable; obstinacy, stubborn; gluttony, indulgent; disobedience, rebellious; boastfulness, vain; ease, frivolous; cruelty, fierce; disgraceful greed, a devourer; restlessness, impatient; instability, changeable; spiritedness, angry; vanity, talkative; malignity, a mocker.

[Col. 0755D] Removed from worldly enticements, removed from hostilities, removed from the plots of others, removed from robbery, removed from lies and perjuries—in short, removed from every kind of shameful deed and crime—just as one dead in the flesh can neither do nor suffer the things I have mentioned, so those who discipline their bodies in order to live for God, and crucify their flesh with its vices and desires, do not live at all for these and similar vices.

### 12. Not to Embrace Delicacies (2 Pet. 2)

He does not forbid touching or tasting delicacies, but forbids taking them with greed and embracing them with the desire of love. For the fast is despised when it is compensated for in the evening with delicacies, as the prophet says: “Behold, on the day [Col. 0756A] of your fast your own desire is found” (Isa. 58). Here “desire” means delicacies.

The person who prepares delicacies for himself in the evening to satisfy his appetite spends the whole day mentally chewing over the meal. Such a fast is not praised, when the belly is swollen in the evening by the fullness of luxurious foods. Abstinence cannot be reckoned where luxurious satiety of the belly has followed.

Carnal delicacies make the one who is about to eat greedy, but the one who has been satisfied sluggish and sleepy. Spiritual delicacies, however, make the satisfied person eager and joyful. The former, once eaten, produce disgust; the latter increase the desire to eat. The former, through an excess of food, blunt the mind’s perception; the latter pour light into the heart. The former supply drowsiness; the latter, vigils. The former give [Col. 0756B] torpor to body and soul; the latter continually supply the love of the Lord to the pure in heart. The former make one desire a bed; the latter, heaven. The former bring sleep; the latter, the kingdom. The former seek shameful and dark sleeping places; the latter desire to possess holy and radiant glory in heaven with the saints. The former delight in playing with prostitutes in a brothel; the latter in reigning with the angels in heaven. The former desire lustful embraces; the latter hasten to come to the embraces of Christ, so that with him, like a bride with her bridegroom, they may rest forever.

Delicacies are so called because they nourish the eater delicately, or because people take delight in them. They make a person soft, tender, and delicate in God’s service. Spiritual delicacies, by contrast, make a person pure, strong, and firm in order to obtain eternal glory. [Col. 0756C] Therefore the latter are to be desired, but the former are not to be embraced by monks. The following sections show what monks ought to love and embrace.

### 13. To Love Fasting (Dan. 9; Joel 2; Tob. 12)

There are many who fast, but do not love fasting itself. As though it were a burden imposed upon them, they bear the fast under compulsion, but do not love it. Like an animal, they carry a burden but do not taste the sweetness of that same burden. Thus they do not love what they carry.

Just as someone weighed down by a burden wishes to lay down what presses upon him before he reaches his appointed destination, so the sluggish monk wishes to break his fast before the appointed hour. He frequently looks at the clock; and, repeatedly [Col. 0756D] observing the sun’s course, raises his eyes to heaven and, with both voice and desire, already proclaims that the hour of refreshment has arrived.

But a good monk ought not to act in this way. Rather, he should love fasting as a medicine for the soul. By fasting the soul is defended from every danger of enticement; by fasting the temptations of demons are driven away; by fasting the strength of vices is broken; by fasting the pleasure of the flesh is restrained; by fasting the incentives to lust are extinguished. Through fasting prayer penetrates heaven more freely, and the gaze of the fasting mind fixes itself more intently through the gift of compunction.

Through the gifts of fasts, the hidden mysteries of heaven and the secrets of divine revelations are disclosed to human beings. Through the gift of fasting a carnal person becomes [Col. 0757A] spiritual and is joined to the choir of all the saints and angels. Therefore a monk ought to love fasting as a good.

But since we have said that fasting consists in the whole discipline of the body, one must not fast only from desire for food, but from every joy in temporal pleasures. For if this virtue, called abstinence, sanctifies the whole person, it is necessary not only for the body but also for the soul, because the whole human being consists of body and soul.

That abstinence is spiritual and perfect which makes people alien not merely from the enticements of carnal pleasures but from every sin. Although this virtue is necessary for all, it is especially familiar to those whose heart is one and whose soul is one, fused by the fire of divine love. [Col. 0757B] Their life thus becomes one, just as their substance is one, because, for the holy union of souls to be formed and maintained, a well-ordered sharing of possessions is necessary.

Otherwise, what benefit is it to renounce possessions if we do not abandon our own pleasures? If Adam had desired this kind of abstinence in paradise, he would neither have lost his state of blessedness nor been subjected to the misery of corruption and mortality. Who can say how many good things his lack of self-control took from him? He lost the dignity of his intellectual mind and the image of his Creator.

Jerome rejects this in his letters when criticizing Origen, who asserted the same thing. There was no troublesome anxiety to disturb him there, no anxious labor to weary him, no sleep to oppress him, no fear of death to torment him. [Col. 0757C] He had easy nourishment, a healthy body, peaceful movement, a clean heart, no knowledge of evil; he was an inhabitant of paradise, free from sin, capable of God. Finally, who was happier than he, to whom the world was subject, by whom no one was opposed, whose mind was free, and who saw God?

Adam could therefore see God before he sinned, just as the holy patriarchs saw him. But after he disobeyed him, he lost the permission to see him. Therefore the abstinence of fasting ought to be loved, so that in Christ we may attain eternally all the things we lost in Adam—not perishable things, but eternal ones.

### 14. To Refresh the Poor (Tob. 4)

Appropriately, after urging love of fasting, he admonishes us concerning the refreshment of the poor, because we fast most effectively when we distribute to the poor what we take away from our bellies. Hence the prophet admonishes us, saying: “Sanctify a fast” [Col. 0757D] (Joel 1). As though he were saying: What is taken from the body during the fast in order to afflict it, offer to the poor for the sanctification and blessing of the soul.

For it is written: “Stretch out your hand to the poor, so that your propitiation and blessing may prosper” (Eccl. 7). And again: “My son, do not defraud the poor of alms, and do not turn your eyes away from the poor. Do not despise the hungry soul, and do not afflict the heart of the needy. Do not turn your face away from the destitute, nor your eyes from the poor. Incline your ear to the poor and repay your debt. For the commandment’s sake take in the poor, and because of his poverty do not send him away empty; but enclose your alms in the bosom of the poor, and he will pray for you to the Lord” (Eccl. 4).

The angel Raphael also urges us [Col. 0758A] to give alms willingly, saying: “Prayer with fasting and almsgiving is good, which delivers from death and purges sins” (Tob. 12).

The possession of wealth has this one great benefit: that it refreshes the lives of the wretched. Therefore a just accumulation of riches will not harm us if generous distribution is present. From our wealth we ought to extend the gift of mercy to the needy, cover the nakedness of the poor, supply the want of travelers, wipe away the misery of orphans, repel the hunger of the hungry, drive away the thirst of the thirsty, and satisfy the needs of the sick.

We ought therefore to give alms to the poor with great eagerness of mind, because what is cheerfully distributed to the poor is given to the Lord himself. For the Lord himself will say at the judgment to those who will be at his right hand: “Come, [Col. 0758B] blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink,” etc. (Matt. 25).

We have Christ as our eternal rewarder if we extend bread to the poor for his sake. From him we obtain eternal mercy if for his sake we extend a full hand. Let us therefore give food and drink, so that with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob we may deserve to reach the eternal banquet; so that there we may receive heavenly things in place of earthly, everlasting things in place of temporal, great things in place of small, enduring things in place of perishable, and things that remain in place of things that pass away.

There is another twofold kind of almsgiving by which monks ought especially to refresh the poor. One part is to be applied to the sick and afflicted, the other to fools and the [Col. 0758C] ignorant. Whoever shares compassionately with the sick and supplies the afflicted with counsel for consolation undoubtedly refreshes the poor. Likewise, whoever supplies instruction to fools and the word of knowledge to the ignorant deserves to be praised with the proclamations due to one who gives alms.

### 15. To Clothe the Naked (Isa. 58; Matt. 25)

Just as there is bodily nakedness, so there is nakedness of the soul. Bodily nakedness is the lack of clothing; the nakedness of the soul is the lack of virtues. Therefore, just as we ought to clothe the body with garments, so we ought to clothe the soul with virtues.

“I was clothed with justice,” Job says, “and it clothed me as a garment.” The prophet says: “He clothed me with the garment of salvation and surrounded me with the clothing of joy” (Isa. 61). With these and similar garments [Col. 0758D] a monk ought to clothe both himself and others.

When Adam sinned in paradise, he lost the garment of the soul, not of the body. For he lost innocence, immortality, and glory. Likewise, the man who descended from Jerusalem to Jericho was stripped of the garments of his soul by robbers.

Let us therefore clothe the bodily nakedness of the poor with great eagerness, because by doing so we shall regard the Lord himself as our debtor and shall have him as a faithful rewarder. For among other things he will say to us: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world, because I was naked and you clothed me” (Matt. 25).

Let us clothe ourselves inwardly with holy virtues, because it profits nothing to clothe another with garments while leaving oneself [Col. 0759A] naked of virtues. We ought to have mercy on others in such a way that we do not forget ourselves. Thus the divine word admonishes us concerning the work of mercy, saying: “My son, have mercy on your own soul, pleasing God.”

Therefore, insofar as we are able, let us have mercy on others, and let us always carefully have mercy on ourselves, so that we may obtain eternal reward for others and everlasting prizes for our own preservation.

### 16. To Visit the Sick (Matt. 25)

We ought to visit the sick, because in them we visit the Lord. Among the works of mercy he himself will say to us: “I was sick, and you visited me.”

Let us visit the sick also for the sake of compunction, so that with Paul we may be able to say: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (1 Cor. 12). Let us visit them also in expectation of reciprocity—that is, so that when we are sick, [Col. 0759B] we may be visited by the healthy. Let us visit them also for the sake of love, because it is written: “Do not be reluctant to visit the sick, for through them you will be strengthened in love” (Eccl. 7).

The person who provides alms from his possessions to monks also visits the sick. For it is written concerning monks: “The ants are a weak people, yet they prepare their food in the harvest” (Prov. 30). The person who distributes alms to widows and orphans also truly visits the sick. Widows and orphans, who are humble and poor in spirit for the Lord’s sake, are undoubtedly weak in this world because they are not powerful, and in this age they need the assistance of visitation.

Concerning such visitation the Apostle says: “Religion pure and undefiled before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their tribulation [Col. 0759C],” etc. (Jas. 1).

There is also another sickness of the soul, for which monks ought very frequently to visit one another: that of which David said, “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak; heal me, Lord” (Ps. 6). And to make clear what sickness he meant, he added: “And my soul is greatly troubled” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “I said: Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40).

Therefore, wherever we see a brother oppressed by the stain of this sickness, let us devote ourselves to visiting him until he is restored to his former state of salvation. Thus the one sick in body may find the comfort of our visitation, and the one sick in soul, through Christ’s gift, may find everlasting healing. A person is called sick not only when physically ill, but also when troubled and [Col. 0759D] grieved in spirit.

### 17. To Bury the Dead (Tob. 1, 2, 12)

Appropriately, after commanding us to visit the sick, he also commands us to bury the dead, because visitation is owed to the sick, but burial to the dead. For it is written: “My son, shed tears for the dead, and begin to weep as though you had suffered something grievous; and according to the judgment, bury his body, and do not neglect his burial” (Eccl. 38).

It seems very surprising to some people that blessed Benedict commanded monks to bury the dead. “Surely,” they say, “monks will not be able either to leave their own dead unburied or to go through streets and villages burying the dead of others?” But since such things are not appropriate for monks, let us consider the meaning of this passage. [Col. 0760A]

Sin is called “dead,” as in the saying: “Whoever washes after touching a dead person and again touches a dead person gains nothing from his washing” (Eccl. 34)—that is, whoever washes away sin with repentant tears and then commits sin again gains no fruit from the groaning or shedding of tears of repentance.

“For the soul that sins, it shall die.” The young girl whom the Lord raised in the house signifies sin still hidden in the soul. In the only son of his mother whom the Lord raised outside the gate, sin is signified that has already emerged from the soul into public action. Lazarus, whom the same Lord raised after four days (John 11), represents sin committed long ago.

The practice of burial ought therefore to be applied to all these kinds of dead people by everyone, and especially [Col. 0760B] by monks. It is concerning this kind of burial that blessed Benedict commanded monks to bury the dead.

If the sin is still hidden in the conscience, as with the girl in the house, it must be buried there, so that it may not appear in action. If it has already become manifest in action, as with the only son of his mother who had been carried outside the gate, it must be brought to an end there and buried in the grave of the heart, so that, growing further, it may not advance. And if, through long persistence in sin, it has become manifest publicly in every respect and has been judged foul by everyone, as with Lazarus after four days, it must finally be put to death and lie buried, so that it may not continue to sprout and grow in the person.

In this way every monk, and every convert to the Lord, ought to bury the dead—that is, his own [Col. 0760C] sin.

### 18–19. To Aid Those in Tribulation; To Console the Grieving (Eccl. 6)

This virtue is also greatly necessary among holy monks: that one should aid another and one should be consoled by another. As it is written: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6)—that is, charity. Without doubt, charity aids the afflicted and consoles the grieving.

It must nevertheless be understood that sometimes a monk’s tribulation is stirred up externally by a human being, sometimes by a demon, and sometimes solely by his own body. Therefore he frequently has great need of a brother’s assistance in tribulation. We ought not only to help one another, but also to offer assistance to others [Col. 0760D] placed in any kind of necessity.

According to the Apostle’s command, we ought to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep (Rom. 12). Everyone becomes sorrowful in two ways: either through the loss of temporal things or through the loss of spiritual virtues. Concerning the former kind Solomon says: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccl. 1). Concerning the latter Job said: “What shall I do? Even if I am silent, my pain will not be quiet,” etc. (Job 16).

One person grieves carnally, another spiritually. One grieves because he has lost earthly comfort; another because, by sinning, he has lost an abundance of virtues. One grieves because he has lost father and mother; another because, through pride, he has lost [Col. 0761A] humility and through indulgence chastity. One grieves because he has lost both the comfort of his parents and the support of their possessions; another because, by sinning, he has lost both the eternal kingdom and its reward. One grieves because he has become poor in earthly goods; another because he has become poor in virtues. One grieves because he is despised by the world; another because he is separated from God.

Therefore, so that neither may perish in grief, let both receive the consolation of their brothers. Let monks visit both kinds, because they will receive eternal reward from both.

### 20. To Make Oneself Alien from the Affairs of the World

“No one serving as a soldier for God,” says the Apostle, “entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (2 Tim. 2). Hence the Lord says: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses [Col. 0761B] cannot be my disciple” (Luke 12).

Whoever wishes to become alien from the affairs of the world must, by obeying sacred commands, become close to the Lord himself. For the Lord’s command is: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 30).

Therefore, having become alien from worldly affairs, let the monk approach his Creator to be enlightened. Let him continually desire him, love him with his whole heart, and for love of him abandon all harmful worldly actions, hanging all his hope upon delight in him.

Every day let him exercise himself in the field of the divine writings, and there, as in a mirror, carefully examine himself in his entirety. Whatever he finds in himself that must be rejected from worldly conduct, let him reject; whatever he finds must be retained, let him hold willingly and firmly; whatever he finds deformed, [Col. 0761C] let him set right; whatever beautiful, cultivate; whatever sound, preserve; whatever weak, strengthen.

Let him read the commands of his Lord tirelessly, love them insatiably, fulfill them effectively, and learn from them what he must avoid and what he must pursue. Let him believe the promises of the future and live as far removed as possible from the tumult of worldly business.

Let him watch over his spiritual studies, by which he may become better each day. Let him love holy leisure, in which he may conduct the business of his soul. Let him regard the world as dead to him and present himself crucified to the world’s enticements. Let him direct the attention of his mind toward the place he desires to reach.

Let him set before the eyes of his soul the blessedness of the future life and love it. Let him neither fear nor desire anything temporal, and let no desire soften the purpose of his mind. [Col. 0761D] Let him rejoice in temporal things not at all, nor grieve over them, but always extend himself toward that blessed and future life where he may see the substance of God with unveiled face.

### 21. To Prefer Nothing to the Love of Christ (Matt. 10)

We read in the *Life of Blessed Antony* that he reconciled many people who were quarrelling, saying to them all that they ought to prefer nothing in the world to the love of Christ.

Basil says: “Let there be one outlook for you, my son: if you desire to serve the one Lord, cut off carnal love from yourself in every way, lest it exclude the love of God from you.”

Truly, we ought to prefer nothing to the love of Christ—that is, to place nothing before it or esteem anything above it. The love of Christ is charity. For when love is perverse, it is called desire or lust; but when it is upright, it is called charity or love.

Everything that we can do belongs to Christ. We live because he gives us life; we move and exist because he sustains us. We love because he first loved us. In his love he created and gave us life; he nourished and guarded us, and led us to the bath of regeneration; he renewed and governed us, and raised us to intellectual maturity. God has mercifully accomplished all these things for us through love.

Open, therefore, O monk, the eyes of your heart, and recognize yourself as so loved by Jesus Christ that you do not doubt that his blood was poured out for you. Lift your heart toward his love, and love the Lord your God not in a small measure or from some part of yourself, but with your whole heart, your whole soul, and your whole mind, so that you prefer no love to the love of your Lord. [Col. 0762B] Understand this from his own teaching. For he says: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10).

Indeed, if we love God with our whole heart, we ought not in any way to prefer to his love the love of parents or children. Blessed, therefore, is the virtue of the love of Christ, which is called devotion and charity.

God loves everyone, and, as though all were one neighbor, he stores the love of all in the secret chamber of his mind. Truly blessed is this love, which nourishes virtues and destroys sins, suppresses anger, closes hatred away, expels greed, restrains quarrels, and drives away all vices at once.

It endures all things, believes all things, hopes all things; amid insults it is secure, amid anger calm, amid hatred kind, and it always remains firm in truth. It is not conquered by wicked attacks, is not plundered by robbers, is not stolen by [Col. 0762C] thieves, and is not consumed by fire. It remains unconquerable, endures beyond explanation, perseveres unshaken, and rejoices incorruptibly.

For it is the bond of all virtues, the glue of souls, the harmony of minds, the fellowship of the elect, and the exultation of the saints and angels. So that it may not be broken by adversity, it strongly fortifies the mind; so that it may not be exalted by prosperity, it carefully restrains the heart.

Therefore the blessed monk must necessarily hold this most radiant virtue in his mind. Let him always be with it and remain with it; let him rise with it and proceed with it; and here and forever let him live joyfully and perseveringly with it.

### 22–23. Not to Carry Anger through to Action; Not to Reserve Time for Wrath (Eph. 4)

A distinction is made between *anger* and *irascibility*: anger is present indignation, which suddenly [Col. 0762D] arises from some disturbance of the soul; irascibility is a natural and enduring vice. Thus an angry person is stirred up for a time, whereas an irascible person becomes angry frequently and easily. Concerning him it is written: “An angry person digs up sins.”

The Apostle also forbids us to sin through anger, saying: “Be angry, and do not sin. Do not let the sun go down upon your anger, and do not give place to the devil” (Eph. 4).

Consider therefore, blessed monk, that whoever seeks vengeance on a brother through anger builds in his own heart a place for the devil to dwell, and, insofar as it lies within him, prepares the setting of Christ—the true sun.

Flee anger, therefore, with God’s help, and do not return vengeance to your brother through anger. Pay careful attention to what Paul admonishes us [Col. 0763A], saying: “Putting away from you all anger, indignation, and malice” (Col. 3).

James also says: “The anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (Jas. 1). Solomon says: “Jealousy and anger shorten one’s days” (Eccl. 30). And elsewhere: “A person harbors anger against another person and seeks healing from God” (ibid.). Although he is flesh, he harbors anger and asks God for swift and immediate mercy.

Whoever is slow to reconcile himself with his brother is slower to appease God. For one seeks God’s pardon in vain if he quickly neglects to appease his neighbor.

Our Lord himself, the glory and adornment of his entire Church, its teacher and preacher, creator, ruler, and governor, completely removing anger from our relations with our brothers, says: “Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matt. 5).

Monks who wish happily to ascend to the heavenly kingdoms [Col. 0763B] must therefore take the greatest care not to carry their anger into action. Rather, they must be gentle and exceedingly meek toward everyone.

If the fury of irascibility strikes their minds, brotherly love must suppress it. Brotherly sweetness must temper irascibility; brotherly charity must temper spiritedness; brotherly devotion must soften indignation. For irascibility is a great vice.

Through anger wisdom is lost; through anger justice is abandoned; through anger brotherly fellowship is dissolved; through anger the harmony of peace is broken; through anger the law of truth is lost. When the body is driven by the goads of irascibility, it trembles all over, the tongue stammers, the face burns, the throbbing heart quivers, and the troubled eyes grow dim.

Therefore, monk, so that these things may not happen to you, restrain your anger [Col. 0763C] as much as you can, and do everything with calmness and patience, so that here you may govern yourself modestly and patiently and may rejoice forever as the possessor of your soul.

### 24. Not to Keep Deceit in the Heart (Prov. 12 and 26; Ps. 14)

*Deceit* is so called because one person tricks another. A person holds one thing in his heart but pretends to do something else in action. It is the craftiness of the mind, an inward malice adorned with flattering speech.

The more this vice is concealed in the heart, the more it grows in wickedness. Once exposed, however, it is destroyed and healed. For what else is it to keep deceit in the heart than, in a certain sense, to shut the devil up in the mind? He cannot be driven out of a deceitful mind in any other way than through brotherly love.

It is written: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of the Lord dwells in you” (1 [Col. 0763D] Cor. 3). Therefore, if we wish to become a temple of the Holy Spirit, let deceit not lie hidden in our heart. Rather, once exposed, let it diminish, and, as the love of brotherhood grows within us, let deceit completely vanish.

Monks must take the greatest care not to lose the indwelling Holy Spirit by keeping deceit in their hearts. They must beware lest they cease to be a temple of the Holy Spirit and, by harboring deceit, become a dwelling place of the devil.

For one heart cannot retain both the Lord and deceit at the same time. The Lord does not possess deceitful hearts, but innocent ones. He does not love a soul polluted by deceit, but an innocent and pure soul.

Therefore we must cease to keep deceit in our hearts and learn to love our neighbors as ourselves, so that in the present age we may deserve to have the [Col. 0764A] Holy Spirit dwelling within us, and in the future receive the glory and eternal inheritance of children.

### 25. Not to Offer False Peace (Ps. 27; 1 Pet. 3)

That is, not to offer a kiss or forgiveness falsely. *Falsehood* is so called from *speaking*, because it says something other than what is true. To deny or maliciously conceal what is true is falsehood, as with Judas, who turned the sign of peace into deceit and, because he had been a false confessor, represented false peace in the Church.

Since we have spoken of false peace, let us consider the benefits of true peace. True peace is serenity of mind and tranquility of soul, which the Apostle urges us to possess, saying: “Pursue peace and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Heb. 12).

The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God [Col. 0764B]” (Matt. 5). And, already approaching his passion, he commended this command to us, saying: “I give you my peace; I commend my peace to you” (John 14). He added: “I do not give you peace as the world gives it” (ibid.)—that is, not deceitful or false peace, as Judas and his followers give, which blessed Benedict also forbids us to give to one another here.

Instead, as he ascended into heaven, Christ gave us true peace to hold and left it to us as an everlasting inheritance. If we wish to hold and pursue it with a sincere heart, we shall be sons of God and heirs of Christ.

Therefore, if we desire to be sons of God and heirs of Christ, let us live in the peace of Christ. The sons of God ought to be peacemakers, humble, gentle in mind, simple in heart, pure in speech, innocent in spirit, harmonious in affection, and faithfully and unanimously [Col. 0764C] joined to one another.

### 26. Not to Abandon Charity (Rom. 12; 1 Cor. 14)

Charity is perfect love of God and neighbor. Whoever abandons it loses both God and neighbor. This virtue of love embraces eternal love. According to the Apostle, it is granted the special primacy and honor among the virtues, and its excellence remains forever.

We must not abandon it, nor merely possess it for a time. Rather, we must retain it happily forever and never at any time, even for a moment, fall away from it in our minds.

For it is written: “Let your garments be white at all times, and let oil not fail from your head” (Eccl. 9). Oil on the head is charity in the mind. Oil fails from the head when charity descends from the [Col. 0764D] mind.

Hence the Apostle Peter urges us, saying: “Above all, maintain constant mutual charity among yourselves” (1 Pet. 4). Paul says: “Let brotherly charity remain among you” (Heb. 13).

Charity must therefore remain and endure with the sons of God, so that in the present it may teach them to do God’s will and may remain happily with them forever.

Charity is a right will joined to God and inseparably united to him by a kind of fire of the Holy Spirit; kindled, it is borne from him and toward him, alien to every defilement, incapable of corruption, subject to no vice, exalted above all things loved carnally, most powerful among all affections, eager for divine contemplation, and always unconquerable in everything.

It is the salvation of morals, [Col. 0765A] the death of crimes, the life of virtues, the strength of those who fight, the palm of the victorious, and the reward of the perfect. It raises the dead in sins, heals the sick, restores the lost, inspires hope in the despairing, and dwells in peaceful minds.

It is fruitful in the penitent, joyful in those making progress, glorious in those who persevere, and active in absolutely all the faithful. Faith conceives it; hope runs toward it; everyone’s progress serves it; whatever good work exists lives from it; under it obedience grows; through it patience conquers. Without it no one has pleased God or will please him; with it no one could sin, nor will anyone be able to sin.

This is true charity. We must not abandon it but hold it firmly. For this virtue is necessary to us above all: it separates us from the devil, purifies us from sin, and reconciles us to God.

[Col. 0765B] Therefore, no sins can remain in us, nor can anything good be lacking, if charity—the teacher of all good things—is present within us. For, according to the Apostle, if charity is patient and kind, does not envy, does not act wrongly, is not inflated, is not ambitious, does not seek its own interests, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth, bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things (1 Cor. 13), it bestows these good qualities that it possesses upon everyone in whom it is present.

And what could be more perfect in this life for those who abound in such virtues, with charity reigning within them?

### 27. Not to swear, lest one perhaps swear falsely (Matthew 5)

It is not contrary to God’s commandment to swear, since he said, “You shall swear by my name”; but when we make a practice of swearing, we incur the crime of perjury. Therefore, whoever fears swearing falsely must never swear. For it is written: “Let not your mouth consent to an oath” (Ecclesiasticus 23). And, “A man who swears much will be filled with iniquity” (ibid.). The apostle James also strongly admonishes us not to swear, saying: “Above all things, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth, or by any other oath. Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no,’ so that you may not fall under judgment” (James 5).

And our Lord Jesus Christ, the salvation of all and the Savior who wills all to be saved and to be freed from the evil of perjury, admonishes us, saying: “You shall not swear by heaven, because it is God’s throne; nor by the earth, because it is his footstool; nor shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black. Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no’; and whatever is more than this is from evil” (Matthew 5).

Whoever does not swear does not sin and is far from sin. If he should offend, he slips downward, falls, and is spared the punishment of perjury. Thus false swearing is destructive, while true swearing is dangerous. No oath is sound and secure.

Someone said: “It is not an oath when I say, ‘God is my witness,’ or ‘I call God as witness,’ or anything similar.” But what is swearing except calling upon God and rendering justice to God? What is it to say, “God is my witness,” except to swear by God? God himself, by whom he swears, is invisible. He has sworn by the invisible One and is struck by an invisible punishment.

Indeed, when the apostle says, “Above all things, do not swear” (James 5), he makes us cautious concerning our tongue, so that we may pay attention and keep watch lest the habit of swearing creep upon us. “Above all things,” he says, in order to make you especially vigilant against the habit of swearing, so that you might inspect everything and guard all the movements of your tongue with the greatest care.

It follows: “so that you may not fall under judgment.” “For this reason,” he says, “I restrain you from the fault of swearing: lest, by frequently swearing truly, you should at some point also fall into perjury. Rather, you should stand farther from the vice of perjury, inasmuch as you do not wish to swear even truly except under the most immediate necessity.”

But even the one who, although he never swears falsely, nevertheless swears more frequently than necessary falls under the charge of judgment, because he sins through the very superfluous idleness of his speech and offends the Judge, who forbade both every useless word and every oath.

### 28. To speak truth from the heart and mouth (Psalm 14)

Many hold one thing in their hearts and utter another with their mouths. Though they themselves have been deceived by vanity, they strive deceitfully to deceive others. And because truth is not in their mouths, their hearts are therefore vain.

But the monk who desires to follow Christ’s footsteps with a pure heart—Christ who said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14)—must hold truth in his heart and speak it simply from his mouth. For the one who speaks truth in his heart and does not practice deceit with his tongue is said to dwell in the Lord’s tabernacle and rest upon his holy mountain.

Deceit arises in the tongue when truth is hidden in the heart while falsehood sounds from the mouth. For it is vanity and great misery to hold one thing in the heart and present another in speech to a brother. The human creature is subject to vanity and therefore does not stand in feigned truth, but is always inclined to deceive its neighbor.

The monks, however, whom the Lord has deigned to separate from the deceit and vanity of this world, must speak truth from heart and mouth. Truth must always dwell in their hearts, and truth must necessarily sound from their mouths. Truth in thought, truth in speech, truth in deed: in all their actions and throughout them all, truth must shine forth resplendently and remain fixed in them forever.

Truth is in the angels; truth is in the patriarchs and prophets; truth is in the apostles and virgins; truth is in the martyrs and confessors; and truth is in all who dwell in heaven. Truth is in all the saints who live in the world. With and among all these is always our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the way, the truth, and the life, and the salvation and glory of all the saints (John 14).

### 29. Not to return evil for evil (1 Thessalonians 5)

According to the precept of the holy Rule, monks must flee forgetfulness altogether and carefully listen to what the Holy Spirit admonishes them through his ministers. For it is not fitting for a monk to be a forgetful hearer rather than a doer of the work.

Let us therefore hear not only with the ears of the body but also with the mind, and carry out in our works what he admonishes us through Peter, the chief of the apostles, saying: “Be merciful, humble, not returning evil for evil” (1 Peter 3). You see, therefore, that by returning evil for evil you lose both the work of mercy and the duty of humility.

For it is written: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12). The one who, provoked by evils, returns evil is overcome by evil. But the one who, having received evil, returns good overcomes evil with good. For one is said to have overcome another when he has brought that person over to his own side. If, therefore, he makes you repay him in kind, he has conquered you by making you like himself.

The apostle Paul likewise says: “Do not be wise in your own estimation, returning evil to no one for evil” (Romans 12). If inflicting evil is sin, returning evil for evil is not just, but is a similar and more serious sin. For the one who first inflicted evil may have done so suddenly, without premeditation; but the one who returns evil for evil does so voluntarily and deliberately.

Again it is written: “Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath” (ibid.). He gives place to wrath who does not defend himself by taking revenge: who does not return insult for insult, hand for hand, injury for injury, or blow for blow, but prepares himself to receive the other cheek and patiently endures everything adverse that happens to him. Hence what follows:

### 30. Not to inflict injury, but also patiently to endure injury inflicted (1 Corinthians 6)

Injury is insult, abuse, or any injustice. It is called *injury* because it is done contrary to the order of justice. People commonly inflict injury upon others in many ways: sometimes by provoking them with insults, sometimes by taunting them with accusations, sometimes by striking and stripping them, and sometimes even by beating them.

A monk—or indeed every Catholic Christian—must not only refrain from doing these things to others, but must also patiently, even with sorrow, endure injuries inflicted by others. For it is written: “Endure in sorrow, and have patience in your humility, because gold is tested in fire,” and so forth (Ecclesiasticus 2).

Therefore, so that the virtue of patience may be tested in a monk, let him appear strongest in enduring injuries. For, as has been said, just as gold is tested in the furnace of fire, so a monk is tested in the furnace of tribulation. Paul bears witness, saying: “Knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience produces proven character, and proven character produces hope,” and so forth (Romans 5).

Peter likewise says: “So that the proven quality of your faith may be found much more precious than gold, which is tested by fire” (1 Peter 1). The Lord also says in the Gospel: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21). Solomon likewise says: “A man’s instruction is known through patience” (Proverbs 19). Paul also says: “Encourage the fainthearted, support the weak, be patient with everyone” (1 Thessalonians 5). James says: “Let patience have its perfect work, so that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing” (James 1).

And elsewhere: “As gold in the furnace he tested them, and as holocausts he accepted them” (Wisdom 3), because those whom he has tested in the furnace of tribulation he receives in the joy of recompense like a pleasing sacrifice.

For just as gold enclosed in a furnace is assayed, but once tested outside, its brilliance becomes evident, so the steadfastness of good monks appears contemptible in this world; but when the time of recompense arrives, how great it was will easily become apparent.

Therefore, so that we may be able to possess our souls, let us hold firmly to the virtue of patience. And so that we may be perfect and complete in all our actions, let us be patient toward everyone, lacking in nothing.

Great is the virtue of patience: it does not injure the one who injures it, but loves him; it forgives injuries to the one who inflicts them rather than returning them; it does not harm the one whom it could harm, but spares him. Patience commends us to God and preserves us inwardly safe from every evil. It is the virtue that moderates anger, restrains the tongue, and governs the mind. It guards peace, exercises discipline with moderation, and firmly breaks the impulse of lust. It suppresses the violence of rage, extinguishes the fire of hostility, restrains the power of tyrants, and refreshes the poverty of the poor. It makes people humble in prosperity and strong in adversity. It conquers temptations, endures persecutions, and, so that we may be able to hold to the way, Christ governs us moderately and justly.

This virtue, therefore, monks and all Catholic Christians alike ought to love, cherish, and embrace with joy and all their strength.

### 31. To love enemies (Matthew 5)

Because we are children of God, we must imitate our Father insofar as we can. He loved his enemies when he prayed for those who crucified him, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (ibid.).

He also commanded us to love our enemies and pray for them, saying: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven” (ibid.).

Let us therefore love our enemies, because our God loved us first when we were still enemies and reconciled us through the blood of his Son. “God,” says the apostle, “commends his love toward us, because, while we were still sinners”—that is, enemies—“Christ died for us,” reconciling us to God (Romans 5).

For it is a great and spiritual virtue to love enemies, one which no human being has had, has, or will have unless God, the giver of all good things, has granted it to him. Let us therefore love our enemies as God commanded and show them kindness insofar as we can. For it is written: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink,” and so forth (Proverbs 25).

The love of an enemy is preserved most truly when we neither rejoice in his downfall nor waste away at his progress. Great and exceedingly difficult is love of enemies, but for those who fulfill it, it prepares eternal rewards.

Love of enemies makes us children of God and companions of the angels; from enemies it makes friends for us, and from adversaries dear ones, and from the hated most beloved brothers. It joins us to the brotherhood and unites us forever in inseparable love, so that here we may live together in harmony in fraternal affection and hereafter reign together eternally.

Therefore, the more difficult love of enemies is in practice, the happier it will be in recompense; the narrower it is in fulfillment, the more abundant it will be in the gifts received; the more laborious it is here, the more certainly glorious it will be in the future. For love of enemies separates us from the world and happily joins us to God; it distinguishes us from the actions of worldly people and joins us equally to the fellowship of the saints and angels.

### 32. Not to return curses upon those who curse us, but rather to bless them (Luke 6)

Even though fulfilling this may seem impossible to us, Paul admonishes us by his own example, saying: “We are cursed, and we bless; we suffer persecution, and we endure” (Romans 12).

Peter, the chief of the apostles, likewise commands and exhorts us, saying: “Not returning evil for evil, nor cursing for cursing, but, on the contrary, blessing; for to this you were called, that you might possess a blessing as your inheritance” (1 Peter 3).

Whoever wishes to possess eternal blessing as an inheritance must bless his enemy, not curse him. For it is a great, not a small, evil to curse the one who curses us. It seems slight to frivolous people, but the apostle counts it among serious crimes, saying: “Neither drunkards, nor fornicators, nor revilers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6).

As we have said, cursing is a grave sin: it deprives a person of possession of the kingdom, plunges him into the Tartarus of hell, and destroys him like a puff of smoke in eternal fire. For it is written: “Before fire comes vapor and smoke, and before blood, cursing and insults” (Ecclesiasticus 22).

Wherever cursing has settled persistently, it makes children of God into children of wrath, turns heirs into outsiders, and makes the unjust even more unjust. It takes away the kingdom of heaven and plunges one into Tartarus. It removes the glory of the saints and presses one into the pit of hell. It takes Christ’s bride away from him and gives the soul to the devil.

For thus it is written: “While the impious curses the devil, he curses his own soul” (Ecclesiasticus 21). Here Scripture shows that the devil is the soul of the one who curses.

The Lord, however, gave us a mouth and tongue not for cursing but rather for blessing. Yet, as the apostle James says, with the same tongue we bless the Lord and Father, and with it we curse human beings, who were made in the likeness of God; from the same mouth proceed cursing and blessing (James 3).

But let us hear what the same apostle says: “My brothers, this ought not to be so. Does a spring pour forth sweet and bitter water from the same opening?” (ibid.). It is as though he said: Just as sweet and bitter water cannot flow simultaneously from the same vein of a spring, so blessing and cursing cannot simultaneously flow from the same fissure of the heart.

But whoever has become accustomed to blessing God in prayer or preaching while not ceasing to curse human beings—without doubt, the bitterness of his cursing consumes the sweetness of his blessing.

Yet just as great as the evil of the vice of cursing is, so much greater is the good duty of blessing. Through the former, punishment is increased; through the latter, grace and glory. Through the former, reproach is received in hell; through the latter, an everlasting reward in heaven.

[Col. 0770A]

### 33. To endure persecutions for righteousness (Matthew 5)

The Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” He did not say, “They suffer persecution because of their own iniquity,” but deliberately added, “for righteousness.”

Many suffer persecution because of their sins, but they are called neither just nor blessed. Only those who suffer persecution for righteousness are considered just.

For this reason the apostle Peter says: “But even if you suffer for righteousness, you will be blessed” (1 Peter 3). He says not only that the one who inflicts evil upon you when you are doing good does you no harm, but also that when an enemy persecutes you because of the good things you do, he provides you with the occasion for greater blessedness and strengthens the power of your patience.

Peter says again: “For it is better, if God’s will so desires, to suffer while doing good than while doing evil” (1 Peter 3).

This statement elegantly exposes the folly of those who, when reproved for their faults or restrained by brothers or superiors with punishments deserved for their actions, endure it with complete patience. But if, without fault, they suffer insults or any adversity from those close to them, they immediately burst into anger; and those who until then appeared innocent make themselves guilty through impatience and murmuring. They do not know that it would be better for them to suffer injuries for righteousness than for their own iniquity.

Whoever therefore suffers as a just person imitates Christ. Whoever is corrected with blows for his own deeds imitates the robber who recognized Christ on the cross and entered paradise with Christ after the cross. But whoever does not cease from his faults even under blows imitates the robber on the left, who went up onto the cross because of his sins and after the cross fell into Tartarus.

Therefore it is far better to suffer in this present world, though innocent, any kind of persecution for righteousness, and in the future receive the recompense of one’s labor with the children of God, than to be scourged with sinners as a sinner and, after death, to be plunged into hell with the reprobate as one rejected.

### 34. Not to be proud

Through the prophet Jeremiah the Lord threatens the proud, saying: “Behold, I am against you, proud one, says the Lord of hosts, because your day will come, the time of your visitation; and the proud man will fall and collapse, and there will be no one to raise him up; and I will kindle a fire in his cities, and it will devour everything around it” (Jeremiah 50).

And elsewhere it is written: “God will destroy the memory of the proud and will not abandon the memory of the humble” (Ecclesiasticus 10).

Divine Scripture speaks of pride itself in this way: “Pride,” it says, “is hateful before God and human beings. Whoever clings to it will be filled with curses” (ibid.). And, “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (ibid.).

It does not say “of some sin,” but “of every sin,” clearly showing that pride itself is the cause of all sins; for it is not only itself a sin, but no sin could be, can be, or will be committed without it.

A proud will causes God’s commandments to be despised; a humble will causes them to be observed. Pride made demons from angels; humility makes human beings like the holy angels. Pride subjects rebels to the devil; humility joins the humble to Christ.

From pride arise heresies, schisms, detraction, envy, loquacity, boasting, contentions, hostilities, ambition, arrogance, presumption, vanity, restlessness, lying, perjury, and many other evils.

Let us now see by what signs pride may be detected. I pass over those whom their very appearance and bearing reveal as proud—those whose raised neck, grim face, fierce eyes, and terrifying speech proclaim naked pride. I point out only those whom I grieve over and whose examples I declare must be avoided: those who have already converted and made some progress, yet are secretly seized by pride; those whom it casts into the depths of evil by a deceitful condemnation and continually tramples down lest they ever rise from there.

These are the people who do not observe the commands of their superiors but judge them. When rebuked for their negligences, they either insolently rebel or murmur. They dispute over the higher place and rashly strive to put themselves before their betters. They exaggerate the simplicity of spiritual fathers and brazenly boast of their own opinions. They show neither reverence toward superiors in obedience, nor modesty in speech, nor discipline in conduct.

They have stubbornness in their intentions, hardness in their hearts, and boastfulness in their conversation; they are deceitful in humility, persistent in hatred, and impatient of submission; hateful to all good people, sluggish in good work, hard in obedience, and eager to speak about what they do not know; reckless in listening, loud in speaking, and unrestrained in laughter.

These are the signs of rampant pride. By these God is offended and departs, while the devil is invited to come. The devil exults, nourished by all these evils; he enters proud minds to hold, exalt, and cast them down. He cherishes them in order to destroy them; he holds them in order to possess them and exercise every evil through them.

Pride has a twofold distinction: one kind casts down spiritual people who become proud of their virtues; the other is carnal and makes them disobedient to the commands of their superiors. One person is lifted up by spiritual virtues, another by possessions of worldly things. Pride is so called because it wants what is above (*super*) what is.

### 35. Not given to wine (1 Timothy 3, Titus 1)

A person is called “given to wine” when he drinks a considerable amount and is difficult to intoxicate. Hence Isaiah says: “Woe to you who are powerful in drinking wine and mighty in mixing drunkenness” (Isaiah 5).

A certain wise man says: “Wine has destroyed many. When drunk in excess, it produces provocation, anger, and many ruinous consequences. Much-drunk wine is bitterness of soul. Wine was created for joy, not for drunkenness. Sober drinking is health of body and soul; drunkenness, however, is boldness and the offense of the imprudent” (Ecclesiasticus 31).

Drunkenness produces disturbance of mind; it arouses fury of heart and the flame of lust; and it so alienates the mind that the drunkard does not know where he is. Hence the evil committed through drunkenness is not perceived.

Blessed Basil therefore says: “Many have been seized by demons through wine. Drunkenness is nothing other than a most manifest demon.”
