Hence the Prophet says: “Fornication and drunkenness take away the heart” (Hosea 4). To those who sleep as though in mental alienation, the prophet Joel cries out: “Awake, drunkards, and weep, all you who drink wine in sweetness, for it has perished from your mouth” (Joel 1).

### 36. Not excessively gluttonous (Ecclesiasticus 31)

The more excessively gluttony fills the belly with bodily food, the more it empties the mind of spiritual virtues. The more a gluttonous body grows fat, the more the soul, fasting from virtues, grows weak. Gluttony makes the flesh obese and the mind empty; it makes the bodily limbs strong but the soul weak.

Gluttony produces sluggishness; sluggishness brings on sleep; sleep, negligence. Negligence generates a curse, as it is written: “Cursed is everyone who does the work of the Lord negligently” (Jeremiah 48).

Excessive gluttony produces overeating, and overeating produces drowsiness. A drowsy person does not love vigils and does not sing psalmody to God at the proper time. He neither raises his mind to heaven nor ascends to the grace of compunction nor lifts his soul to the heights of contemplation. He is slow to prayer, weary of reading, hard-hearted toward understanding the Lord’s word, sluggish in obeying his superiors, and tepid in carrying out every good work.

But because the Rule does not want a monk to be excessively gluttonous or given to wine, it therefore wants him to be temperate in all things. For, as blessed Ephraem says, this is the general measure of self-restraint: each person should allow himself as much food or drink as the capacity of his strength, body, or age requires—only as much as sustains the flesh, not as much as the desire for satiety demands.

Whoever keeps an unequal balance in either direction will suffer great loss: he neither constricts his belly through the dryness of fasting nor relaxes it through an excess of food. For a mind weighed down by excessive greed cannot send pure prayers to God.

As long as the saints dwell in this life, they bear an emaciated body out of desire for the kingdom of heaven. Hence the Psalmist says: “My soul has thirsted for you exceedingly, and so has my flesh” (Psalm 62). The flesh thirsts for God when it is dried out through abstinence.

For, as was said above, a fast is despised when it is restored by an evening replenishment of food. Abstinence cannot be considered present when satiety of the belly has followed. Therefore immoderate abstinence must not be imposed upon the body, lest, when it is burdened by excessive hunger, it fail to complete the good work it has begun.

The substance of the flesh must be moderated with discretion, lest it either be completely extinguished or be relaxed without measure. Bodily weakness breaks the powers of the soul and causes the mind’s intelligence to wither. Whatever is done with moderation nourishes the health of body and soul.

### 37. Not drowsy

After the correction of gluttony and drunkenness, the correction of drowsiness appropriately follows. Just as the Rule does not want a monk to be excessively gluttonous or given to wine, so it does not want him to be drowsy.

Just as a soldier weighed down by a heavy burden is hindered in battle, so a monk burdened by excessive quantities of food is hindered in keeping vigils. We cannot keep watch when our belly is loaded with rich foods; instead, oppressed by sleep, we lose the fruit of vigils, acquire the greatest harm to our soul, and likewise suffer poverty and want of spiritual virtues.

As it is written: “How long will you sleep, you sluggard? When will you rise from your sleep? You will sleep a little, doze a little, fold your hands a little to sleep, and poverty will come upon you like a traveler, and want like an armed man” (Proverbs 6).

Again: “Do not love sleep, lest poverty overwhelm you; open your eyes, and you will be filled with bread” (Proverbs 20).

We must beware lest our soul itself sleep. The sleep of the soul is forgetting its God. Every soul that forgets its God sleeps; therefore the apostle says: “Rise, you who sleep, and Christ will enlighten you” (Ephesians 5).

A drowsy monk is soft, tepid, and slack in his works. Of him it is written: “The one who is soft and slack in his work is a brother to the one who destroys his own work” (Proverbs 18).

Conversely, of a vigorous worker it is written: “He who works his land will be filled with bread” (Proverbs 12)—that is, the one who subjects his body during his life and brings it into the service of God, so that by working he may please the one to whom he submitted himself by obeying, will be filled after the body’s dissolution by receiving an eternal reward.

In good works a monk must be vigorous and instructed, robust and strong, not soft and slack. Hence Isidore says: “Those who do not pursue the monastic profession with firm resolve: the more loosely they desire the purpose of heavenly love, the more readily they are led back again to love of the world. For an imperfect profession returns to the desires of the present life; and although the monk has not yet bound himself to them in deed, he already binds himself to them through the love of his thoughts.”

[Col. 0773C]

### 38. Not sluggish (Proverbs 26)

That is, not slow or sluggish, not tepid or idle. A person is called sluggish as though he were sick in his feet, for he is slow to walk. Through usage, this name passes also to the soul, so that it is called sluggish when it is idle.

For it is written in Proverbs: “Idleness kills the sluggard, for his hands refuse to do anything” (Proverbs 21). Again it is written there: “The sluggard desires and does not desire, but the soul of those who work will be enriched” (Proverbs 13).

The one who wishes to reign with Christ but does not wish to work for him is rightly marked by the name “sluggard.” He delights in eternal rewards but shuns laborious works. He wishes to have temporal leisure and to receive an eternal reward.

But the soul of those who work for the eternal Lord will be enriched with everlasting gifts in the kingdom. Those who here toil in pious labors for the Lord will rejoice after receiving heavenly refreshment and will hear that desirable voice of the Lord saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11).

Again it is written: “The sluggard is stoned with a muddy stone, and everyone will speak of his disgrace” (Ecclesiasticus 22). And there: “Sluggishness brings on sleep” (Proverbs 19).

Every idle person is called a sluggard: one who, by thinking rightly, is as though awake, although through doing nothing he grows numb. But sluggishness brings on sleep when the person who thinks rightly loses wakefulness by failing to act well.

Again it is written: “Because of the cold the sluggard would not plow” (Proverbs 20). Because of the cold the sluggard does not plow when, broken by the numbness of idleness, he pretends not to do good. When he fears small adversities in carrying out his work, he neglects great things.

Of him it is rightly added: “He will beg in summer, and nothing will be given him” (ibid.). For the monk who does not now labor in good works will beg in the future world like one receiving nothing in summer.

Hence it is written: “I passed by the field of a lazy man, and behold, it was completely covered with nettles,” and so forth (Proverbs 24). What is it to pass through the field of a lazy man except to examine the life of a negligent monk and consider his works? Nettles and thorns fill it because earthly desires and the pricks of vices sprout in the hearts of negligent monks.

### 39. Not murmuring (1 Corinthians 10; Philippians 2)

A monk murmurs either against the Lord’s scourges, against the discipline imposed upon him by his superiors, against the obedience enjoined upon him by his elders, or simply because of the gluttony of his own belly.

If he were not a forgetful hearer, he would have heard consolation from the Scriptures concerning all these things and would not have murmured. For Scripture says: “God scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12). It also says: “My son, do not reject the discipline of the Lord, for whoever loves discipline loves knowledge” (Proverbs 5; 12). Again it says: “Obedience is better than sacrifice” (Ecclesiasticus 4).

A monk must therefore attend to all these authorities of Scripture and live without murmuring, lest he incur the evil of murmuring and lose the reward of his labor.

The apostle forbids us to murmur with great fear, saying: “Nor murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by serpents” (1 Corinthians 10). It is as though he were saying: Guard yourselves from the evil of murmuring. For just as those who murmured against the Lord in the wilderness were torn apart and perished from the bites of serpents, so you too will perish, torn apart by the bites of demons, unless you guard yourselves from the evil of murmuring.

Again it is written: “Therefore guard yourselves from murmuring, which profits nothing” (Wisdom 1). Unjust murmuring profits monks nothing, because it proceeds from a disobedient and contentious mind. By murmuring, a person condemns himself and does not correct the one against whom he murmurs. By murmuring he accuses his teacher and multiplies punishments for himself.

Even if he completes the work assigned to him while murmuring, he acquires not the reward of labor but harm to his soul. For thus it is written in this same Rule of blessed Benedict: “If he obeys discipline with an evil disposition,” it says, “and murmurs not only with his mouth but also in his heart, even if he fulfills the command, it will nevertheless not be acceptable to God, who sees the heart of the murmurer; and for such an act he receives no grace, but rather incurs the punishment of murmuring, unless he corrects himself with satisfaction.”

### 40. Not a detractor (Proverbs 4)

That is, not a defamer, accuser, or reviler. A person is said to detract when he changes good into evil. For one who says that something is evil when it is evil is not to be called the author of detraction, but a friend of truth. In choosing virtues and condemning vices, he obeys the divine will in every respect.

The Lord himself says through the Psalmist David: “The one who detracts from his neighbor, him I persecuted” (Psalm 100).

We must therefore refuse to agree with the detractor to such an extent that, insofar as it lies with us, we agree with the Lord and, together with him, persecute the detractor of our neighbor. In both cases we must look to the welfare of ourselves and of the one who detracts: we must neither willingly listen to him nor permit him to sin.

For, if it can be so, detraction is a greater sin than fornication. The fornicator kills only himself; but the detractor plunges both himself and the one who agrees with him into the pit of death.

Hence it is written in Proverbs: “Remove from yourself a perverse mouth, and let detracting lips be far from you” (Proverbs 4). This can be understood in two ways: we must guard with every care both that our mouth does not speak anything perverse and that our lips do not detract from our neighbor.

And whenever we see others devoted to this vice, we must make them strangers to us—not by agreeing with them, but by driving them far from us—lest both we and they perish in the vice of detraction. For it is written: “My son, fear God, and do not associate with detractors, because their destruction suddenly arises, and the ruin of both” (Proverbs 24)—that is, of the one who detracts and of the one who agrees with the detractor.

It is written: “If a serpent bites in silence, the one who secretly detracts is no less guilty than it” (Ecclesiasticus 10).

Hence James says: “Do not detract from one another, my brothers, for whoever detracts from his brother or judges his brother detracts from the law and judges the law” (James 4).

### 41. To entrust one’s hope to God (Psalms LXI, LXXVII)

Hope is called the expectation of future goods, which expresses an attitude of humility and the obedience of diligent service. It is called “hope” because it is a “foot” for one who advances, as it were, a foot. Hence, by contrast, despair is so called: the capacity to advance is lacking in it, because when someone loves sin, he does not await future glory.

Blessed is the one who entrusts his hope to God and places it in eternal happiness and glory. Blessed is the one whose hope, placed in the Lord so that he may live forever, continually endures. Hence the Psalmist says: “But it is good for me to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord” (Psalm LXXII). For the one who places his hope in him clings well to God, because nothing can be more blessed than to entrust everything to the one who knows how to grant future things to his worshipers.

Hence the Apostle says: “Rejoicing in hope” (Romans XII). But he ought to rejoice entirely in heavenly hope, because, with God’s help, he has now ceased to do what is wrong. For those who do not cease doing evil, deceived by empty hope, seek pardon and eternal life from God; yet they would seek it rightly if they ceased from evil conduct.

Every righteous person ought to have both hope and fear: now hope should raise him up toward eternal joy, and now the terror of Gehenna should bring him down to fear. Therefore let the monk fear the Lord and, hoping in him, continually implore his help, because it is written: “Those who fear the Lord have hoped in the Lord; he is their help and their protector” (Psalm CXIII). Let him ask to be girded with a belt, as it were, of righteousness through mercy, and let him not despair of pardon, because it is written: “But mercy will surround those who hope in the Lord” (Psalm XXXI).

Let him cling to God with right faith and holy works, and say: “The Lord is my hope from my youth” (Psalm LXX). And: “Remember your word to your servant, in which you have given me hope; for it is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in man.”

### 42. When he sees some good in himself, let him attribute it to God, not to himself (James I)

Whatever good the monk sees in himself, he should attribute to God—that is, he should ascribe it to God, give God thanks for it, and not call it his own, but recognize that it belongs to God. For all good things possessed by human beings are supplied by God alone.

For God is spirit: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues” (1 Corinthians XII), and other things of this kind are granted to the holy by the one Lord, to whom every human being ought continually to give thanks. If we have received all good things from the Lord, we ought to give thanks for everything not to ourselves but to him.

“For what do you have, O man,” says the Apostle, “that you did not receive?” Therefore, “let the one who boasts boast in the Lord,” not in himself, as it is written: “My son, let your glorying be in the fear of the Lord” (Ecclesiasticus I, IX).

When he had said, “I know both how to be humbled and how to abound, both how to be filled and how to hunger, both how to have plenty and how to suffer need” (Philippians IV), he added: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (ibid.). He attributed nothing to himself, because he recognized that his ability to do everything lay not in his own strength, but in him who strengthened him.

And elsewhere, when he said, “I labored more than all of them,” so that he would not attribute this to himself but to God, he added: “Not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians XV).

We owe to God what we are, what we live, what we understand, that we are human beings, that we have lived well and justly, and that we understand rightly and in accordance with the Catholic faith. In every respect we owe these things to God. For nothing is ours except the sin and evil that we have committed.

Hence what follows:

### 43. Let him always know that evil was done by himself, and let him attribute it to himself (Hosea XIII)

Whatever evil the monk finds done in himself, let him truly believe that he discovered it as arising from himself or instigated by the devil, not created by God; for God did not make evil, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living.

The devil, although he was a good angel, became evil through pride; and by deceiving the human being, who by nature had been created good, he made him evil and proud. Thus all the evil of sin entered the human race through the fault of the first human being. Through long habit it also holds and operates almost as something natural; and, like a natural law, sin reigns in human members and resists the law of the mind and all the holy virtues.

Hence the Apostle says: “But I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members” (Romans VII).

Therefore let the monk recognize that evil and every sin have been done by himself, and, attributing them to himself, let him say to God: “Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done what is evil before you” (Psalm L). Let him acknowledge and repent, and, weeping, say with the prophet: “Clearly, this iniquity is mine, and I shall bear it.” Again, groaning with David, let him say: “Wash me more thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin, for I know my iniquity, and my transgression is always before me” (ibid.).

Therefore we ought to accuse ourselves of every evil deed and attribute it to ourselves, and repent with our whole heart. But any good in us, as was said above, we should attribute not to our own strength or merits, but to him who dwells in heaven and supplies virtues from his treasure to all the holy.

“For in Christ all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God are hidden” (Colossians II), and through him, who grants them according to his arrangements, all the holy receive their portions. Therefore we ought to honor God not only for the substance of money that we distribute to the poor, but also for all the good works that we perform and for the ministries of grace that we have received; in everything we must seek his praise, not our own.

### 44. To fear the day of judgment

The day of judgment is greatly to be feared by sinners. Although it is gentle toward the righteous, it is exceedingly terrible for sinners and wicked people, who on that day will hear: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew XXV).

Concerning this terrifying day, it is written through the prophet Zephaniah: “The great day of the Lord is near; it is near and comes very swiftly. The sound of the day of the Lord is bitter; the mighty man will be afflicted there. That day is a day of wrath, that day a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and storm, a day of trumpet and blast. There human beings will be afflicted, and they will walk like the blind, because they have sinned against the Lord. Their blood will be poured out like soil, and their bodies like dung” (Zephaniah I).

That day is greatly to be feared by sinners, because at that time and on that day, in the fire of the Lord’s zeal, the whole earth will be consumed at the consummation. The Lord will bring about a swift destruction for all the inhabitants of the earth on that day.

Hence the Apostle also says: “For the expectation of judgment is terrifying, and the jealous fire that will consume the adversaries in judgment” (Hebrews X).

Brothers, we ought now to consider what we shall be able to do when we come to that final judgment of judgment. What shall we do when the judge begins to examine the secrets of our hearts and to disclose not only our deeds and words but also our thoughts? What shall we do when placed beneath the majesty of so great a judge? To whose aid shall we flee, or whose assistance shall we seek, or what excuse shall we be able to offer? By what art of defense shall we fight? What repentance will then come to our aid, which we disdained to practice in this life? What good works will defend us, which we did not perform in this flesh? To which saints shall we flee, whose examples and words we alike despised?

What, then, shall we answer when the Lord begins to say to us in judgment: “If you were able, why did you not do what was good and resist the desires of sins? But if you were not able, why did you not seek my help against sins?”

Therefore it is necessary now, while we live and are able, that we turn away from evil and do good, and continually seek his help in everything, so that, with his assistance, we may persevere to the end in the good work that we have begun. Thus, on the day of judgment, when placed with the lambs on the right, we may hear: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV). Amen.

### 45. To dread Gehenna

Gehenna is a place of fire and sulfur, which they think is named from a valley consecrated to an idol situated beside the wall of Jerusalem. There the Hebrews sacrificed their children to demons. It was the valley of the sons of Hennon, and from this it was called *gehennon*; many corpses of the dead lay there.

The place of future punishment, where sinners are to be tormented, is designated by the name of this place. For the punishment of the condemned in Gehenna is twofold: sorrow burns their minds, and flame burns their bodies.

This place, so terrifying, ought to be dreaded not only by the monk but by every Christian. All the condemned who are to be tormented are thrown there. Concerning them the Lord says: “After binding their hands and feet, throw them into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth; where their worm will not die and their fire will not be extinguished” (Matthew XXII; Mark IX).

This place is exceedingly terrible and greatly to be dreaded: there are the weeping of many, continual groaning, eternal torture, the sharpest pain, and punitive suffering. There the souls of the impious are tormented but do not perish; bodies are punished but do not come to an end. Unquenchable fire endures, so that it may always burn the souls of the rejected and contain them for suffering rather than for illumination, killing those who continually live in its living flames.

For all who are said to be killed in Gehenna are not dealt with in such a way that, once consumed by sufferings, they eventually perish; rather, they live in them under punishment.

We ought continually to bring these and similar things before the eyes of our mind, and to dread with terror the Gehenna of eternal fire. Above all, with the utmost diligence and the most attentive eyes of the mind, we ought to consider how great an evil it is to be excluded from the joy of divine contemplation, to be plunged into the infernal Tartarus and the place of Gehenna, to be deprived of the most blessed fellowship of all the saints and associated with demons, to become exiles from the heavenly homeland and inhabitants of hell—to die to blessed life and live for everlasting death.

There, what gives light is not perceived; what torments is perceived. Everything situated there is filled not with light or joy, but with darkness, pains, and tortures.

### 46. To desire eternal life with every spiritual longing (Philippians I)

The holy monks ought to desire eternal life with every spiritual longing. When they reach it, they will receive many indescribable goods. There are stored up all those things for those who love God of which the Apostle Paul said: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians II).

The monks ought to desire eternal life because there they will cease from hard labors and possess an eternal inheritance and perpetual rest. There they will have a heavenly kingdom and glorious dominion. There they will diligently obtain the fellowship of the patriarchs and the companionship of the prophets. There they will receive fellowship with all the saints and equality with the angels. There, pure in heart, they will see God; and, having been made sons from servants, they will reign with Christ.

Therefore eternal life is to be loved and desired by the holy monks. There they will find that sweetness stored up of which the prophet David said: “How great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you and perfected for those who hope in you” (Psalm XXX)!

There they will receive a spacious possession of paradise and flourishing kingdoms. There they will be clothed in the robe of joy and royal purple. There pain and groaning will flee, and health and everlasting joy will come. Mourning and sadness will flee, and peace and eternal gladness will come.

There they will hear from the Lord: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew XI). And: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV). He will make them recline in eternal glory; and, passing among them, the Lord himself will minister all good things to them. Amen.

### 47. To keep death daily before one’s eyes as something to be feared (Matthew XXIV)

As blessed Isidore says, each person ought to live attentively and always keep watch over the end of his life, because it is written: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Ecclesiasticus VII).

The uncertainty of the approaching departure is unknown; and while a person does not expect to die, he is taken away. Therefore each person ought daily to keep death before his eyes as something to be feared, and ought anxiously to fear lest he be suddenly seized in his iniquities and, together with his life, his guilt come to an end.

For the devil suddenly drags to torments at death those whom he urges toward vices while they are alive. Even if someone is righteous in this life, nevertheless, when he departs from this body he fears that he may be deserving of punishment. No human being is without sin, nor can anyone be secure concerning God’s judgment, since an account must even be given for idle words.

Human life is brief, and therefore we ought always to keep death before our eyes as something to be feared. The present life, because it diminishes day by day, is quickly brought to an end; therefore its mortal danger must be feared. The present life does not last long; rather, just as cloth is completed by threads, so human life is completed day by day, with each passing day.

Therefore, while keeping watch, we ought anxiously to fear death, lest we be suddenly seized by it. For it is written: “Blessed is that servant whom, when the Lord comes, he finds watching” (Matthew XXIV; Luke XII)—that is, fearing death and carefully considering the salvation of his soul.

Blessed, then, is the monk who is always fearful. By fearing the departure of his death, he is always watchful and ready, so that when at midnight the cry is made, “Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him” (Matthew VI), he may without delay go out to meet him with prepared lamps and enter with him joyfully into the bridal chamber as an eternal inhabitant, where, surrounded by the bridegroom’s embraces, he may live happily and blessedly forever. Amen.

### 48. To guard the actions of one’s life at every hour (Deuteronomy IV)

The monk guards the actions of his life well at every hour if he keeps himself, as far as he can, free from the sin of thought, speech, and deed. Every day the monk ought to examine his actions vigilantly and carefully. If he senses that he has become liable to sin in any of these respects, it is necessary for him to hasten to repentance before sunset and, if possible, before he eats, sleeps, or undertakes any work; thereafter he must guard himself from every evil deed.

For we sin not only in deeds but frequently also in thoughts and words. Evil works proceed in turn from evil thoughts, and evil thoughts erupt from evil deeds. Even if someone abstains from an evil deed, he is nevertheless not innocent of wickedness on account of the evil of a single thought.

Hence the Lord cries out to the people through Isaiah: “Take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes” (Isaiah I).

For just as a viper is killed when torn apart by its offspring placed within the womb, so harmful thoughts, if nourished within us, kill us and consume us with viperous poison. Unless they are still small and dashed against the rock—that is, Christ—they kill our soul with a cruel wound, if we illicitly consent to them and unhappily strive to fulfill them.

Great vigilance, therefore, must be applied to guarding our heart, because evil thoughts come out of it, and evil actions proceed from evil thoughts. For this reason we ought anxiously to guard the actions of our life at every hour, lest, having fallen through thought, speech, or action, we be dragged into sin like foolish and unguarded people and, mocked by demons, be torn apart as unarmed.

### 49. To know with certainty that one is watched by God in every place (Proverbs V)

The immensity of the divine greatness is so great that it sees everything, fills everything, and is above everything, beneath everything, within everything, and outside everything; there is no enclosed place where God is not.

Hence David also said: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; and if I descend into hell, you are present” (Psalm CXXXVIII). Therefore every creature of God—whether it is in heaven, on earth, or beneath the earth—is clear and manifest to him.

Hence Paul says: “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts; and no creature is invisible in his sight, for all things are naked and open to his eyes” (Hebrews IV).

Hence Solomon says: “In every place the eyes of the Lord contemplate the good and the wicked” (Proverbs XV).

Since we know that God watches us at every hour and in every place, we ought not to sin in his sight or in the sight of his angels. Rather, in every place, at every hour, and at all times, we ought to live with justice and truth and stand before him in fear and trembling.

And just as blessed Job feared him, so we ought to fear him and truly say with him: “Like swelling waves I have always feared the Lord over me, and I could not bear his burden” (Job XXXI).

### 50–51. To dash the evil thoughts that come to one’s heart against Christ at once, and to disclose them to a spiritual elder

There are passing thoughts, empty and fleeting, which pollute the person thinking them less the more quickly they pass. Concerning these Solomon says: “And the grinders will be idle in a small number” (Ecclesiasticus XII)—that is, thoughts that revolve in the human mind like grinders during a person’s life, and, when the soul leaves the body, will all remain empty and idle.

No one can retain all such thoughts in memory, and no one is ever compelled to confess them. But there are other harmful thoughts that frequently delight the mind and, having persuaded it, seek to plunge it into sin.

Hence Solomon says: “The thought of a fool is sin” (Proverbs XXIV). Again he says: “Evil thoughts are an abomination to God, but a pure word is most beautiful” (Proverbs XV).

Blessed Benedict urges us not to hide these thoughts in the recesses of our heart, but to dash them against Christ and disclose them to a spiritual father. For it is written: “Whoever hides his crimes will not prosper; but whoever confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy” (Proverbs XXVIII).

The monk, therefore, most easily obtains mercy from the Lord if he does not hide his thoughts from his spiritual father, but reveals them with a pure mind and humble heart.

To dash the evil thoughts that come to our heart against Christ means to implore Christ’s help against the allurements of their pleasures, to entrust one’s hope to Christ so that one may emerge victorious, to believe faithfully in him, to hope firmly in him, and, for the victory of triumph, not to please oneself but to give thanks to Christ.

He commands that these thoughts be disclosed to a spiritual father so that from him one may find counsel for salvation and from the Lord the swiftest remedy for sin, as it is written: “I said: I will declare my iniquities against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my heart” (Psalm XXXI).

For merciful God washes away sins more quickly when he does not allow them to proceed into deeds. And a wickedness conceived in thought is dissolved all the more quickly the more strictly it is not bound to the accomplishment of a deed.

How easy forgiveness is in such a case he shows: while a person still promises that he will ask, he obtains what he was promising to ask for; because the guilt had not yet reached action, repentance did not reach torment. Rather, the affliction conceived in thought cleansed the mind to the extent that the iniquity conceived in thought had stained it.

### 52. To guard one’s mouth from evil or wicked speech

Hence Solomon admonishes us, saying: “Remove from yourself a wicked mouth, and let lips that slander be far from you” (Proverbs IV). Hence Paul says: “Let no evil word proceed from your mouth, but only such a good word as is suitable for edification and gives grace to those who hear” (Ephesians IV).

From the monk’s mouth there ought to proceed not an evil or wicked word, but a word of edification and grace. Drawn by the Lord, the good monk runs after him; therefore, so that others may also follow, he ought frequently to utter an exhortatory, not a malicious, word.

For it is written: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’”—that is, whoever among the monks has been worthy to receive the inner light of faith or charity should not cease inviting others to it as well.

We ought therefore to guard our mouths from evil or wicked speech, lest it first infect us with the poison of its own malice and afterward spread deadly venom among others.

For it is written: “The wound of a scourge leaves a bruise” (Ecclesiasticus XXVIII). But the wound of the tongue crushes bones. For, as the Apostle James says, the tongue is full of deadly poison (James III); therefore we must guard it with the greatest care.

It is written: “Whoever guards his mouth guards his soul; but whoever is heedless in speaking will experience evil” (Proverbs XIII). Without doubt, the one who does not cease sowing scandal while he lives will experience evil in the future.

Hence Solomon says: “The foolish man digs up evil, and fire blazes on his lips” (Proverbs XVI). Again he says: “A dart, a sword, and a sharp arrow is the person who speaks evil against his neighbor” (Proverbs XXV).

It often happens that, when we do not avoid certain small evils of vice, we slip into the great crime of the tongue. When we commit certain deeds that are not serious without fear, we slide through the habit of sinning into worse crimes. And when we speak many things carelessly, without doubt we sin either against God or against our brother.

Hence an appropriate admonition follows:

### 53. Not to love speaking much

The monk ought to love silence more than excessive speech. Concerning silence Isaiah says: “The cultivation of righteousness is silence” (Isaiah XXXII). The righteousness of the mind is laid waste when it is not spared from immoderate speech.

Concerning excessive speech Solomon says: “In much speaking sin will not be absent” (Proverbs X). Again it is written: “Like an open city without the enclosure of walls is a man who cannot restrain his spirit” (Proverbs XXIII).

The monk who does not have the wall of silence is exposed to the arrows of the enemy. The enemy overcomes him with so much less effort because he himself fights against himself through excessive speech.

Hence James says: “If anyone thinks he is religious, but does not bridle his tongue and deceives his own heart, that person’s religion is worthless” (James I). Again he says: “Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak” (ibid.).

As blessed Gregory says, those who devote themselves to excessive speech should be admonished and should watch carefully to see from what state of uprightness they fall away while they slip through their many words.

For the human mind is like water: when enclosed, it gathers upward; when released, it is lost, because it disperses itself uselessly in every direction. When it is scattered through superfluous words from the discipline of its silence, it is led outside itself, as if through many streams. Thus it rightly does not suffice inwardly for itself, because, dispersed through excessive speech, it excludes itself from the secret depths of inner contemplation.

### 54. Not to speak vain words or words suited to laughter (Matthew XII)

Vain words are those also called idle words—namely, words that lack either the necessity of a just occasion or the intention of pious usefulness.

Vanity of speech is a great vice, and monks must avoid it in every way. It proceeds from the fuel of vanity and, as if by persuasion and gentle enticement, deceives the frivolous person.

Vanity is a lightness of spirit, an excess of loquacity and idleness that always carries fuel in the heart and always utters vain speech from the mouth. It is a kind of simulation of virtues, an appetite for honors—hollow, diseased, and turbulent; sweet to the wretched, bitter to the mature, dangerous to the stern, and imperious toward subordinates. It captures the frivolous, delights those whom it has captured, harasses the ambitious, inflates the narrow-minded, and humbles the exalted. The puffed-up serve it; the haughty lie beneath it; the lost find it; those destined to fall run toward it.

This is the vanity that does not, as is thought, extinguish certain virtues, but, once admitted, strengthens license for vices. For it does not penetrate minds full of virtues at all; it tests those empty of virtues. It casts down its lovers—namely, those who disgracefully boast of themselves and wickedly delight in being praised by everyone.

These are people who rejoice in the greetings of passersby, favor their flatterers, obey their pleasures, please shameful people, eagerly teach what they do not know, wish to be believed to have understood lofty matters, rejoice in agreeable things, give the names of virtues to their vices, deceive themselves, and mislead those who favor them. They are swift in promising and liars in performance; weighty in speech, shameful in mind, deceitful everywhere; joyful in prosperity, fragile in adversity, inflated in service, anxious in reproach, and immoderate in pleasure.

This is the vice of vanity, which monks ought not to possess at all. Instead, loving and speaking the truth from both heart and mouth, they ought to follow and imitate Christ the Lord, so that with him they may be able to reign happily forever.

This vanity described above dwells in a vain and sinful heart. It always makes people laugh at others and always causes others’ laughter to burst forth. Its sign is often detected both in vain speech and in abundant, uncontrolled laughter.

Hence what follows:

### 55. Not to love excessive or uncontrolled laughter

Monks ought to weep more than laugh, because it is written: “Laughter will be mingled with sorrow, and mourning will occupy the end of joy” (Proverbs XXIV). In the Gospel the Lord says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew V).

We are in a valley of tears; therefore we ought not to laugh but to mourn. We ought to have tears for our sins, tears for the dissolution of the body, tears from longing for our Redeemer and for the fellowship of all the angels and all the saints, tears so that we may be freed from the punishments of hell and from the snares of the devil.

For, as the Psalmist says, “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy” (Psalm CXXV)—that is, those who, while they live in mortal bodies, pour out prayers to the Lord with tears and groaning will, after death, reap the reward of their labor in eternal joy: in that joy, namely, concerning which the Lord says to his disciples: “I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John XVI).

Therefore it is more fitting for a monk to have salutary sadness than empty joy. It is written: “The heart of the wise is where there is sadness, and the heart of fools where there is joy” (Ecclesiasticus VII). Again it is written: “Anger is better than laughter, for through sadness the spirit of the one who sins is corrected” (Ecclesiasticus VII).

The Apostle James also sternly admonishes us, saying: “Be wretched, mourn and weep. Let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow” (James IV). Hence the Lord says: “Woe to you who laugh, for you will mourn and weep” (Luke VI).

A monk, who ought to serve the Lord with a contrite and humbled heart, should not laugh much. Nor should he love uncontrolled laughter—that is, laughter uttered in a loud voice, which shakes the one who utters it—lest he be marked as foolish by people, because it is written: “The fool raises his voice in laughter” (Proverbs XIV). And: “Like the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of a fool” (Ecclesiasticus VII).

It is natural for a human being to laugh, and therefore one cannot entirely forbid a person to do so. But it is permissible to allow laughter when it is restrained, cautious, and decent, since a person cannot entirely abandon what nature compels him to do.

### 56. To hear the holy readings willingly (Luke XI)

Knowledge of sacred reading supplies its practitioners with sharpness of understanding, multiplies their insight, shakes off sluggishness, removes idleness, orders their life, corrects their conduct, produces salutary groaning, and brings forth tears from a contrite heart. It grants eloquence in speaking and promises eternal rewards to those who labor. It increases spiritual riches, restrains vain speech and vanities, and kindles desire for Christ and the heavenly homeland, which ought always to accompany and remain joined to prayer.

For we are cleansed by prayers, but instructed by readings. Therefore whoever wishes always to be with God ought frequently to pray and frequently to read. When we pray, we speak with God; but when we read, God speaks with us.

Every perfected person advances through reading, prayer, and meditation. Through reading we learn what we do not know; through meditation we preserve what we have learned; and through prayer we obtain that what has been preserved by us may be fulfilled.

The reading of the holy Scriptures confers a twofold gift: it either educates the understanding of the mind or leads a person, withdrawn from the vanities of the world, to the love of God.

Hence Paul admonishes Timothy, saying: “While I am coming, attend to reading and instruction; meditate on these things and devote yourself to them, so that your progress may be manifest to all” (1 Timothy IV).

No one can fully know the meaning of sacred Scripture unless, by reading or hearing it continually, he has become familiar with it, as it is written: “Love it, and it will exalt you; you will be glorified by it when you have embraced it” (Proverbs IV).

### 57. To devote oneself frequently to prayer (Matthew VI; Luke XI)

“To devote oneself” means to persist, or to apply oneself closely. Appropriately, after hearing the reading, he commanded us to devote ourselves frequently to prayer.

Prayer does not disagree with reading, nor is reading alien to prayer. At times they express the same thing, and at times different things. But since prayer is called the “reasoning of the mouth,” neither of them lacks the name of prayer; both are rationally guarded, and both are rationally composed.

Each is greatly and necessarily commended to the Lord, so that action may be supported by prayer and prayer by action. Hence Jeremiah says: “Let us lift our hearts with our hands to the Lord” (Lamentations III). A person lifts his heart with his hands when he supports prayer with action.

Paul admonishes us concerning perseverance in prayer, saying: “Devote yourselves to prayer, praying at all times in the Spirit” (Romans XII). Since we offend at all times, as it is written, “We all offend in many ways” (James III), we ought to pray for our offenses at all times. Again Paul says: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians V). Peter says: “Therefore be prudent and watchful in prayers” (1 Peter IV).

Whenever we are touched by any vice, we ought to submit ourselves to prayer, because frequent prayer is an assault upon vices. Prayer ought not to belong only to the lips, but also to the heart. God does not attend to many words; he looks upon the heart of the one praying.

One should never pray without groaning, for remembrance of sins produces sorrow. When we pray, we recall our guilt and recognize more clearly that we are then guilty. Therefore, when we stand before God, we ought to groan and weep, remembering how grave are the crimes we have committed and how dreadful are the punishments of hell that we fear.

Let the mind preserve after prayer the state in which it presents itself during prayer. For prayer accomplishes nothing if one again commits what one is already asking to have forgiven.

Without doubt, the one who receives the desired effect in prayers is the person who does not repeat by sinning what he asks to have washed away by praying.

[Column 0785C]

### 58. To confess one’s evils daily to God in prayer with tears or groaning (Psalm VI)

Confession is understood in two ways: either as praise, as when the Lord says to the Father, “I confess to you, Father of heaven and earth” (Matthew XI; Luke X), or when someone confesses his sins to the one whose mercy is unfailing, so that they may be forgiven.

For, while those who confess remain in this world, God’s mercy comes to their aid. After death, however, repentance, pain, and groaning torment souls but do not free them from the punishment of sin. Guilt must not be concealed, since after death it brings eternal punishment upon the soul.

For, as Cassian says, the devil cannot deceive or overthrow a young monk except one whom he sees hiding his thoughts either through pride or through shame. For the Fathers clearly called that a diabolical thought which a junior is ashamed to disclose to an elder.

It is better to confess one’s sins to the Lord and confidently hope for pardon from his mercy than to hide an offense for a brief time and receive eternal harm to the soul.

Hence Solomon says: “Whoever hides his crimes will not prosper; but whoever confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy” (Proverbs XXVIII).

A person more easily reconciles God to himself when he has not been overcome by human judgment, but voluntarily acknowledges the crime committed. Having made himself his own judge and avenger, he punishes with tears what he previously committed in deeds, and is not ashamed to punish well with weeping what he was not ashamed to commit wrongly.

Again it is written: “Do not be ashamed to confess your sins to the Lord” (Ecclesiasticus IV).

Let each of us certainly confess our sins to the Lord, because if he perseveres in repentance and, after confessing, performs works worthy of repentance, he will receive not only forgiveness of sins but also eternal rewards, having become a citizen of the heavenly city.

And thereafter to amend those very evils. He therefore does penance worthily who so laments past evils that he does not commit them again in the future. For whoever bewails sin and commits sin again is like someone washing an unfired brick: the more he washes it, the more mud he makes. He therefore does penance worthily who no longer commits what he has committed, but promises amendment with satisfaction for what he has done [Col. 0786B]. For each person ought to hasten to the Lord through repentance while he can, lest, if he is unwilling while he can, he may be altogether unable when he wishes too late. Hence the prophet says: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isa. LV). A penitent ought not to have security concerning his sins. For security gives birth to negligence, and negligence draws a person back to his former vices. Rather, the penitent ought to foresee the enemy’s crafty snares against him, so that he may neither return to the vices he has left behind nor continue to do what is evil.

### 59. Not to fulfill the desires of the flesh (Gal. V)

By “desires of the flesh” he means the pleasures or cravings of the body. By “not to fulfill” he means not to bring them into effect [Col. 0786C], that is, not to accomplish them in deeds. Hence Paul says: “Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh” (ibid.). To fulfill the desires of the flesh is to bring the flesh’s lusts and the body’s temporal impulses into the execution of an act. Hence Peter says: “Beloved, I urge you, as resident aliens and pilgrims, to abstain from carnal desires, which wage war against the soul” (I Pet. II). For while the flesh is weakly reproved amid flattering desires, the army of vices is firmly armed against the soul.

Carnal desires are the products of the sordid pleasure and enticement of carnal vices. Enticed by these, the monk delights in empty tales and superfluous words, and delights in spectacles of earthly things and earthly [Col. 0786D] pleasures; he burns with gluttony of the belly and desire of the throat, is consumed by ambition for honors, and is caressed by human praises or the allurements of empty glory. He raises his wretched heart in pride and plunges it, diseased in mind, into a multitude of every vice.

But, by contrast, the monk who takes no pleasure at all in fulfilling the desires of the flesh, armed with holy virtues, fights bravely against the desires and vices of the flesh and battles the assaults of vices with opposing virtues. Against luxury he employs purity of heart; he subdues lust by abstinence. Against hatred he prepares love; against anger he sets patience; against fear, confidence; against avarice, generosity; against pride, humility. Thus he sets one virtue against each vice [Col. 0787A], so that he may not be overcome by them and succumb, but, having overcome them, may stand forth victorious.

### To hate one’s own will

By “one’s own” he means private, or uniquely one’s own—the will that no one else approves and no one declares to be just. For even if it seems good to the person who tries to fulfill it, it is not good for that reason: because it is one’s own and because it has not been approved by the counsel of any Father. Hence it is written: “Do not follow your desires, and turn away from your own will” (Eccl. XVIII). Hence the Lord says: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John VI).

Holy men, renouncing their own wills, die to this world in such a way that they delight in living for God alone. And the more they withdraw themselves from this world’s pleasures, the more keenly in mind they contemplate God’s presence and the continual fellowship of the angels [Col. 0787B]. For no one can attain perfection, after renouncing everything he possesses, unless he has also renounced his own wills. For what is it to deny oneself except to abandon one’s own wills?

### 60. To obey the abbot’s commands in everything (Heb. XIII)

The abbot’s commands ought always to be just and holy. Therefore the disciples ought always and in everything to obey them. For if he commands his disciples in a way contrary to what is proper, they must answer him as the apostles answered: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts V). The abbot’s command, therefore, must never disagree with the Lord’s commandment, lest, while the abbot’s command is obeyed, one depart from the Lord’s commands.

The abbot must therefore be obeyed so that this obedience may also be obedience to Christ [Col. 0787C]. For he himself says to the disciples: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke X). Hence the apostle Paul says: “Obey your leaders and submit to them. For they keep watch as those who will have to give an account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning” (Heb. XIII). Hence Solomon says: “Obedience is better than sacrifice” (Eccl. IV). Again Paul says: “We ask you, brothers, to recognize those who labor among you, preside over you in the Lord, and admonish you, and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves” (I Thess. V).

The abbot appears to act as Christ’s representative in the monastery, and therefore the good of obedience must be offered to him. For if he performs the perfect work, as is fitting [Col. 0787D], he must be imitated by his subjects. Nevertheless, if, because of bodily frailty or weakness of spirit, he refuses to fulfill in deeds what he proclaims in words, let his subjects hear what follows and fulfill by their deeds the command of our Lord Jesus Christ, namely:

### 61. Even if he himself acts otherwise—God forbid—remembering that command of the Lord: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. VI)

Not to wish to be called holy before one is holy, but first to be holy, so that one may more truly be called holy.

When blessed Benedict says this, he wisely and briefly corrects and admonishes the monk, lest he succumb to the vice of boastfulness. For there are some monks who desire not to be holy but to be called holy. They want to possess the name of holiness, but do not want to practice the work of holiness. Therefore whoever desires to possess the name of holiness must first not cease to perform the work of holiness.

The Lord did not say to the children of Israel, “Be called holy, because I too am called holy,” but said: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Lev. XI, XIX, and XX). Therefore whoever wishes to be called holy must first hasten to perform the work of holiness and diligently seek spiritual fruits, filled with which he may justly be called and be holy. No one can properly be called holy unless he has deserved to receive the fruits of the Holy Spirit.

“The fruit of the Spirit,” as the Apostle says, “is love, joy, peace, patience, goodness, kindness, faith, modesty, gentleness” (Gal. V), together with the gathering of all the other virtues [Col. 0788B]. Filled with all these, as has been said, the monk may properly both be called holy and be holy.

### 62. To fulfill God’s commandments daily in deeds

Hence James says: “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only” (James I). Hence Paul says: “It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified” (Rom. II). In his Apocalypse, when John had said, “Blessed is the one who reads and those who hear the words of the prophecy of this book” (Rev. I and XXII), he immediately added, “and keeps what is written in it” (ibid.).

Hence in the Gospel the Lord says: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John XIV). Again he says: “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me” (ibid.)—that is, the one who has them in memory and keeps them in life; who has them in speech and keeps them in conduct; who has them by hearing and keeps them by doing; or who has them by doing and keeps them by persevering.

Again the Lord says: “Whoever hears my words and does them will be like a wise man who builds his house upon rock,” and so forth (Matt. VII). Again the Lord himself says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.). And: “Amen, I say to you, if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death” (John VIII).

Hence through Solomon the Lord admonishes us, saying: “My son, do not forget my law, and let your heart keep my commandments. For they will add length of days, years of life, and peace for you” (Prov. III). Again the same Solomon says: “My son, keep my words, and store my commandments up for yourself; keep my commands, and you will live” (Prov. VII).

### 63. To love chastity (I Tim. V)

Chastity is called incorruption of body and heart. Some have said that chastity is in the mind and virginity in the body; but that is true and genuine chastity which permits neither the mind to be stained nor the body to be polluted. It shines not only in virgins but also in those who practice continence, and gleams with the brightness of its beauty.

Admiring its beauty, Scripture says: “Oh, how beautiful is a chaste generation!” (Wis. IV). Isaiah testifies that virgins will be more blessed in eternal life, saying [Col. 0789A]: “Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that will not perish” (Isa. LVI).

The beauty of chastity, therefore, is to be loved: it separates its lovers from the cares of the world and prepares for them in the heavenly Jerusalem a most exalted and radiant name and place. It grants its devotees the reward of continence and the name of children. It gives an eternal name and joins them to the choir of angels. The beauty of chastity is therefore to be loved, for it makes virgins and those who practice continence equal to the angels.

Chastity of body is sanctified and perfected by humility and purity of heart. For bodily incorruption is of no benefit where there is no integrity of mind. It is of no value for someone to be clean in body if he is polluted in mind [Col. 0789B]. For just as one chaste in heart and body produces a pleasant fragrance for angels and human beings, so one polluted in heart and body spreads a foul stench everywhere. The chaste person shines through the virtue of purity; the polluted person reeks of filthy defilements. The chaste and pure are joined to the holy angels; the unclean are associated with unclean demons. The demons plunge the polluted and defiled into Tartarus, but the holy angels receive the chaste into heaven.

The former, because he was never ashamed to commit evil in darkness, is justly condemned and plunged into a dark abyss; the latter, because he loved the radiance of chastity in the light, will forever reign, radiant, in the light of radiant eternity. Let us therefore love the purity of chastity, which may preserve us chaste in the present life and make us receive eternal rewards in the future.

[Col. 0789C]

### 64. To hate no one

Those who waste away in hatred against a brother and harbor a ruinous deceit against others are to be mourned with tears. For those who separate themselves from fraternal love separate themselves from the kingdom of God. Hence the apostle John says: “Whoever says that he is in the light and hates his brother is still in darkness” (I John II).

Again he says: “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness, walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (ibid.)—that is, because of fraternal hatred he is unknowingly thrown into the hell of Gehenna, and, ignorant and blind, is plunged into the dark punishment of hell.

Again he says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (I John III). He does not move his hands to kill a person, yet he is already held by God to be a murderer. For when the time of recompense arrives, he will be condemned with Cain, who was of the evil one and who is held guilty of this kind of murder, namely hatred [Col. 0789D].

Again he says: “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar” (I John IV). He is proved to be a liar in claiming that he loves God, whom he does not see, since he does not love but hates his brother, whom he does see. For we have received this commandment from God: whoever loves God must love his brother also.

### 65. Not to harbor zeal and envy (James I)

Envy of another’s good punishes its own author. For where the good person prospers, there the envious person wastes away. Thus he is also a member of the devil, through whose envy death entered the world. To be jealous of and envy another’s good is not a small but a great and serious sin.

At the beginning of the world the devil, immediately struck by the malice of envy, was the first to perish, and thus he destroyed others. To envy and begrudge another’s good is the root of all evils and the fountain of vices. Hatred arises from it; hostility proceeds from it. Envy arouses avarice. Through envy the fear of God is despised, the day of judgment is not anticipated, pride is inflated, humility is embittered, faithlessness transgresses, patience is shaken, discord rages, and anger grows fierce. Hence every bond of peace is broken; hence fraternal charity is violated; hence truth is corrupted and unity torn apart; hence the threatening face, the grim expression, pallor in the face, trembling in the lips, and gnashing of the teeth.

Why say more? From the rancor of envy the fountain of all vices springs up, as James says [Col. 0790B]: “Where there is envy and strife, there is instability and every evil work” (James III). Hence what follows appropriately:

### 66. Not to love contentiousness (Phil. II; Titus III)

Contentiousness is called controversy, stubbornness, or quarrelsome dispute. Therefore the monk ought not to love disputes in words, but should instead hold firmly to fraternal love. For if we have died to sin, we ought not to live for the world or speak a contentious word to a brother, since verbal contention is the fuel of every evil, a danger to souls, and the ruin of those who hear.

Hence Paul says to Timothy: “Do not quarrel about words” (II Tim. II). It is useful for nothing except the ruin of those who hear. One must consider how contentiousness shakes those who engage in it uselessly, when it also overthrows those who listen. For if a wicked disturbance had not first existed in the heart, contentiousness would not have come into public view.

Again Paul says: “Lest perhaps there be among you quarrels, jealousies, hostilities, dissensions, and disputes” (II Cor. XII). James also says: “If you have bitter envy and contentiousness in your hearts, do not boast” (James III).

Among carnal monks contentiousness is always accustomed to arise, as it is written: “The wicked person always seeks quarrels” (Prov. XVII). Hence Paul himself says: “For while there is envy and contentiousness among you, are you not carnal and walking according to the flesh?” (I Cor. III).

Through useless contentions, anger is aroused, discord is generated among brothers, hostilities are nourished, quarrels arise, dissensions are produced [Col. 0790D], rivalries emerge, scandals are provoked, and, to put it briefly, every evil arises among brothers. Hence true is what Solomon says: “It is an honor for a person to separate himself from disputes” (Prov. XX).

The Apostle numbers contentiousness among the works of darkness, saying: “Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness” (Rom. XIII). Concerning these works he adds: “Not in revelries and drunkenness, not in beds and sexual immorality, not in contention and rivalry” (ibid.). Contentiousness belongs to those who live according to the flesh and walk in darkness. But the one who is in the light does nothing through contention or conceit, nor through empty glory. Hence what follows:

[Col. 0791A]

### 67. To flee conceit and boastfulness (Ps. CXXX)

Conceit is called vainglory of mind, boldness of heart, confidence in one’s virtues, or rashness and fearlessness of heart. For unless, as blessed Isidore says, hidden conceit of mind comes first, open boastfulness of praise does not follow. “It is more useful,” he says, “to stumble through any vice whatsoever and become humble before God after the fall than to become proud through conceit.”

Sometimes a Christian is attacked by the devil through a double vice: secretly through conceit and publicly through lust. But while someone avoids lust, he falls into conceit; and while he cautiously avoids conceit, he falls into lust. Thus one proceeds from the hidden vice of conceit into the open vice of lust, and from the open vice of lust into the hidden vice of conceit.

But God’s servant, weighing both carefully, avoids lust in such a way that he does not fall into conceit, and avoids conceit in such a way that he does not relax his spirit into lust.

### 68. To honor the elders (Lev. XIX; I Tim. V)

Humility among good subjects is the honoring of elder brothers. No one can sincerely honor an elder unless he possesses a humble mind, not a swollen and exalted one. The honor shown to elders ought to be expressed in words and deeds: in words, by speaking a few reasonable words to him humbly and reverently; in deeds, by having the younger rise when he passes, sit when he commands, keep silent and listen when he speaks, answer humbly when he asks a question, obey when he commands, and, when he passes, ask humbly for his blessing with bowed head. In everything, wherever reason properly requires it, the younger monk should obey the elder [Col. 0791C].

Hence Paul says to Timothy: “Do not rebuke an older man, but appeal to him as a father” (I Tim. V). And: “Children, obey your parents in the Lord” (Col. III). For the Lord also went down from Jerusalem with his parents to Nazareth and was subject to them (Luke II).

Hence through a certain wise man it is said: “With all your soul fear God and honor his priests” (Ecclus. VII). Again he says: “With all your strength love him who made you, and do not forsake his ministers” (ibid.).

But one must also take care lest, having received reverence from the younger, the elder become puffed up with pride and thus nourish scandal. Instead, he should humble himself more and more, love them with paternal affection, and thereby urge them toward humble obedience. Hence what follows:

[Col. 0791D]

### 69. To love the younger

The younger ought to receive a twofold love from their elders. First, because they are brothers. For it is written: “We have received this commandment from God, that whoever loves God should love his brother” (I John IV). Second, because they humbly serve their elders in obedience. Hence it is written: “Let the sensible servant be dear to you as your own soul; treat him as a brother” (Ecclus. VII). If this is to be understood of a servant, how much more must it be understood of a beloved son and brother!

### 70. In the love of Christ, to pray for enemies

The love of Christ makes us love an enemy and also makes us pray for him. For if we are his children, we ought to imitate him insofar as we can. He prayed for his persecutors, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII).

Therefore, to be his children by imitation, just as we already are his children by the grace of adoption, let us love even our enemies according to his command and pray for them. For he himself, commanding us as a ruler, says: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven; for he makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. V).

When he had said, “so that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven,” he added, “who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil,” and so forth, so that, understanding this, we may do good to our enemies, extend our love toward them, and pour out prayer for their salvation. Thus, having already become children of God through adoption, we may also become children through imitation.

“Christ suffered for us,” the apostle Peter says, “leaving us an example, so that we might follow his footsteps” (I Pet. II). We must understand this not only of his Passion but also of loving an enemy and praying for them.

### 71. To return to peace with those who are at odds before sunset (Eph. IV)

Just as the pious mother Church is oppressed by all who live wickedly, or by heretics, yet embraces them with gracious love when they come back to her, so we too must immediately embrace whatever enemies we have endured when they return to us, imitating our mother. For whoever is slow to reconcile a brother to himself is slow to make God favorable to himself.

Hence the Lord says: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matt. V).

Hence the apostle Paul says: “Be angry, and do not sin. Do not let the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. IV). By this he shows that before sunset both the one who is at fault must ask for and receive forgiveness, and the one who has been injured must pardon the one who injured him by forgiving his offense. Anyone who asks forgiveness must quickly be forgiven, for it does no good to be free from fault if one is not ready to grant forgiveness. Guilt increases and grows when fraternal offenses are forgiven too slowly.

[Col. 0792D]

### 72. Never to despair of God’s mercy (Ezek. XVIII)

Even if there are a thousand sins, one must not despair of forgiveness. For God is both compassionate in forgiving and almighty in saving. The only requirement is that each person turn away from evil and do good (Ps. XXXVI). Let him confess his sins to the Lord and perform penance according to the measure of his guilt, because every sinner who turns to the Lord with all his heart will be saved. He himself says to sinners: “Turn to me, and you will be saved” (Isa. XLV).

Again he says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XVIII and XXXIII). Since the merciful Lord does not desire the sinner’s death but life, the sinner himself closes the door of mercy against himself if he despairs of receiving forgiveness of sins from him [Col. 0793A].

Again through the prophet he says: “On whatever day the sinner turns with all his heart to the Lord, he ceases to be a sinner” (Ezek. XXXIII). Hence Jerome says: “Let no one doubt the Lord’s indulgence; let no one despair. For he came sent for this purpose: not to destroy sinners who confess, but to save them. Let no one despair because of the multitude of his crimes, for the merciful and compassionate Lord is ready to forgive.

“If he commanded his disciple Peter to forgive his brother’s sin up to seventy times seven, how much more will that fountain of compassion and forgiveness forgive the offense of those who sin against him and ask forgiveness, even a thousand times a thousand times! He himself washed away the crimes of the whole world; how much more will he wash away the sins of one person.”

The only requirement is that each person turn away from his wickedness and live forever through deeds worthy of the fruits of repentance, filled with the virtue of every good thing.

Behold, these are the tools of the spiritual art. “Behold, these are,” he says—that is, these divine commandments stated above, each of which has already been explained in order earlier. These, then, are the tools of the spiritual art.

It is called an “art” because, bound by the precepts and rules of art, it leads well and justly. For just as there is a bodily art, so there is a spiritual art. But just as spiritual life is better than bodily life, so the art of that life is more refined. Therefore the former requires few tools, while the latter requires very many.

Just as there are tools belonging to smiths, scribes, and other craftsmen, by which their work is completed, so there are tools of the virtues, by which spiritual life is ordered. If the art of governing one’s own soul and the souls of others were not spiritual, Gregory would not say: “With what presumption, then, is pastoral leadership undertaken by the inexperienced, when the governance of souls is the art of arts?”

Hence the apostle Paul says: “I know how to be humbled, and I know how to abound; I know how to be filled, and I know how to hunger; I know how to have abundance, and I know how to suffer want” (Phil. IV). To those who look at these things superficially, none of this seems to be a spiritual art, but simply the necessity of action. Yet if it were not an art, the Apostle would not have said, “I know.” By saying “I know,” he demonstrated that the practice of this work contains an art.

The person whom poverty does not break, does not withdraw from thanksgiving, and does not inflame with desire for temporal things knows how to be humbled. The person who is not puffed up by things received and does not twist them toward the use of empty glory, who does not possess them alone but mercifully shares them with those who love him, knows how to abound.

The person who uses food received not for filling the belly but for restoring strength knows how to be filled. The person who tolerates scarcity of food without murmuring and, because of the necessity of sustenance, does nothing by which his soul may fall into the snare of sin, knows how to hunger.

Therefore the person whom neither pride elevates in abundance nor desire provokes in need knows how to abound and also how to suffer want. Whoever is not exalted in prosperity, is not broken by adversity, is not drawn toward evil by persuasion, and is not recalled from good work by reproaches, filled with spiritual art [Col. 0794A], does not grow weak and deteriorate but, sound, always advances toward what is better.

When these things have been fulfilled by us unceasingly day and night and have been recorded again on the day of judgment—these most sacred commandments of the Lord stated above are recorded for us in the present life so that we may practice them and, practicing them, keep them. They will be recorded again for us in eternal life, so that we may be worthy to receive the rewards due for our labor, namely those which the Lord himself promised to his laborers, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI). And: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV). Concerning this the Apostle said:

That reward will be repaid to us by the Lord which he himself promised: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II).

The workshop, however, in which we diligently practice all these things is the enclosure of the monastery and stability within the community. The word “workshop” (*officina*) is derived from “doing” (*faciendo*) and “work” (*officium*). The monastery enclosures are the dwellings of those who work and of all the monks living there.

Whoever wishes to live in them must have firmness of mind and stability within the community, lest he begin to wander through various regions of the earth, or move from one cell to another, and from his own places to places that are not his own. Otherwise what is written in Solomon’s book may be said of him: “Just as a bird,” he says, “wandering from its nest, so is a man who abandons his place” (Prov. XXVII).

For what is signified by the bird that abandons its nest except the monk who abandons his place and his vocation? Let him rather abandon the wandering of his mind and hold firmly to stability of heart and place, and bring to perfection the good work he has begun, because it is written: “It is not the one who has begun, but the one who has persevered, who will be saved” (Matt. X and XXIV).

What follows concerns obedience.

## CHAPTER V. On Obedience

The first degree of humility is obedience without delay.

Many ask why blessed Benedict in this Rule said that two degrees of humility are first: one, this one that we have in hand; the other, the one placed first among the twelve degrees (chap. VII) [Col. 0794D]. But it must be understood that the former is first in the heart, while this one is first in action. For just as the former is first in order, so this one is second in thought, will, desire, and conversion.

Nevertheless, this one, which is placed first here, is found there to be second in order. For here he says: “Such persons, immediately abandoning what is their own and forsaking their own will,” imitate that saying of the Lord in which he says: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John V and VI).

There, however, he says: “The second degree of humility is that, not loving one’s own will, one does not delight in fulfilling one’s desires, but imitates in deeds that saying of the Lord who says: ‘I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.’”

Behold how it is proved that this same degree, which is placed first here, is found placed second there. But that one is first in order and thought, while this one is first in the execution of the work. That one is first at the beginning of conversion, while this one is first at the beginning of action. That one is first spiritually in the soul, while this one is first bodily in obedience.

Therefore the title of this chapter is prefaced not with “On Humility” but with “On the Obedience of the Disciples.” In that chapter the subject is thought, will, and desire; in this one the discussion concerns the disciples’ obedience. The disciples’ obedience must first be offered to God in the heart and afterward to the teacher in action.

For inwardly, touched by fear, each person goes forth into public obedience like a disciple to a teacher. Unless the fear of the Lord compelled it, one person would never submit to another in the regular life. But, compelled alike by fear and love of the Lord, one person submits to another and one is governed by another.

After the fear of the Lord penetrates the human heart, the person quickly seeks another guide for life, so that where he cannot go by himself, he may arrive under another’s guidance. Therefore here blessed Benedict, arranging the beginning of the work and the way in the most orderly manner for those who wish to reach eternal life, says: “The first degree of humility is obedience without delay.”

As blessed Benedict is about to discuss obedience, he reasonably places here first not the degree of order, as stated above, but the degree of labor. The disciple who wishes to ascend to the kingdom of heaven without delay must fulfill it without delay. The monk who wishes to receive the rewards of his labor without delay must render obedience without delay [Col. 0795C]. The one who obeys humbly fights bravely against the enemy and gains victory without delay.

For it is written: “An obedient man speaks of victories” (Prov. XXI). What wonder is it if sinful human beings submit themselves to obedience during the brief span of the present life, when the mediator between God and humanity himself emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient unto death (Phil. II)? And, holding dear the human being whom he redeemed by death, he showed himself dear to all his saints. Hence what follows:

These words apply to those who consider nothing dearer to themselves than Christ.

A Christian ought to hold nothing dearer than Christ, because he recognizes him—and no other—as his Creator, Redeemer, and Lord. We must therefore hold nothing dearer than Christ, because he held nothing as dear as the assembly of the elect. He deigned to hold us so dear that he did not refuse to pour out his sacred blood for us.
