Let him be dear to us as a Father, and let us be to him as children. Let us therefore love the Lord Jesus Christ, because he first loved us and handed himself over for us. We must place nothing before his love, but love and cherish him above all things, because with him we hope to reign forever.

For he says: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. VI). Who could be so foolish and dull as to refuse to love his own life and salvation [Al., “to exist”]? For Christ is our life [Col. 0796A] and salvation, and he said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV).

While we live in this mortal body, Christ is therefore our hope; Christ is our defense, Christ our governance, Christ our strength, Christ our consolation, Christ our redemption; Christ is our shepherd, salvation, and protection; Christ is our justification, sanctification, and illumination. In the age to come Christ will be our glory; Christ our exultation, Christ our glorification, Christ our peace, Christ our inheritance, Christ our eternity, Christ our law, Christ our brightness, Christ our health, Christ our crown, Christ our wisdom, Christ our kingdom, Christ our reward, Christ our joy, Christ our gift [Col. 0796B], Christ our honor, Christ our refreshment, Christ our rest; Christ is all our good things, all our holy things, all our lovely things, all our desirable things. It is fitting for us to hold nothing dearer than Christ.

For in him and through him we live, move, and exist. Therefore we must hold nothing else dearer than him. But those who wish to reign with Christ forever must obey the one who commands without delay and do what follows, namely:

Because of the holy service they have professed, or because of fear of Gehenna, or because of the glory of eternal life, as soon as something has been commanded by a superior, they know no delay in doing it, as though it had been commanded by God himself.

He said, “Because of the holy service they have professed”—that is, because of the profession which the monk promised before all, before the altar, saying: “I promise my stability, the conversion of my conduct, and obedience before God and his saints.”

If this regular profession is fulfilled in deeds within the monastery until the end of life, it is rightly called holy service, because through it the monk is made holy and joined to the holy Lord. Whether it is for this service—that is, so that they may fulfill it, since it is better not to make a vow than, after making a vow, not to fulfill what was promised—or because of fear of Gehenna—that is, lest they descend into Gehenna and be tormented eternally—or because of the glory of eternal life—that is, so that they may reach that glory and shine, brighten, and gleam like the sun in the presence of the Father—as soon as something has been commanded by a superior, as though it had been divinely commanded, they must know no delay in doing it [Col. 0796D].

Concerning these the Lord said: “At the hearing of the ear he obeyed me” (Psalm XVII; 2 Samuel XXII). That is, at the very hearing by which he heard my voice, he immediately and without delay submitted and obeyed me. This testimony is taken from Psalm XVII, where the Lord praises the Gentile people for the readiness of their belief: they did not see our Lord Jesus Christ with bodily eyes, but quickly believed those apostles who preached about him. Obedient monks now follow their example, readily obeying elders sent by God. And so that they may understand that they obey not merely a human being but rather God, and may commend the obedience they offer to their superiors to the Lord, the giver of all good things [Col. 0797A], let them hear the Lord saying what follows:

> “Whoever hears you hears me” (Luke X).

He is proved to hear the Lord who inclines the ear of his heart to teachers in obedience, and from the Lord receives the reward of his obedience—the one who does not delay humbly obeying his elders. Those, therefore, who deserve to have such a rewarder of their work must always obey with great eagerness of heart. Concerning them it is also added:

> “Therefore, such men, immediately abandoning what is their own and forsaking their own will, as soon as their hands are freed, leaving unfinished what they were doing, follow with deeds, on an obedience-ready foot, the voice of the one commanding.”

These plainly abandon what is their own who, for the benefit of others, leave their own work unfinished and strive to please their neighbors more than themselves. They endeavor to fulfill not their own will but rather that of their neighbors. “As soon as their hands are freed”—that is, detached from all the works at which they were laboring, separated from or released from every activity—they leave unfinished what they were doing. For the sake of the perfection of obedience, every other action must be abandoned, because obedience pleases God more than sacrifice. Obedience is preferred to sacrifices because through sacrifices another’s flesh is slaughtered, whereas through obedience one’s own will is slain. “They follow with deeds, on an obedience-ready foot, the voice of the one commanding.” The foot of obedience therefore draws near so that it may run swiftly and fulfill quickly and without delay what is enjoined upon it. Speed must be offered to the one commanding not only by the body but also by the heart, so that neither bodily sluggishness nor a lukewarm will may resist. Rather, the swift hearer must complete the commander’s voice with a worthy deed, so that when the time of recompense arrives, he may receive a worthy reward from the Lord. For the desire of that reward, what follows must be fulfilled energetically. For he says:

> “And as though in a single moment the master’s command already mentioned and the disciple’s completed work are both accomplished more quickly together in the speed of the fear of God.”

“Moment” derives from a brief span of time, since the work of obedience enjoined is completed in a short time. When the good master’s command, given for the sake of charity, and the obedient disciple’s action are joined together in harmony, they undoubtedly bring forth good fruit, because the conjunction of the Holy Spirit is not fruitless where there is no harmful separation of souls. Hearts joined together in the fear of the Lord quickly bring forth the remedy of salvation for weakened souls.

Those upon whom the love of advancing toward eternal life presses therefore take up the narrow way, as the Lord says:

> “Narrow is the way that leads to life” (Matthew VII).

In this passage blessed Benedict left the pronoun to be understood. If it is supplied, what is said becomes clearer: “Those upon whom the love of advancing toward eternal life presses therefore take up the narrow way, so that, not living according to their own judgment,” and so forth in what follows. In a marvelous manner this has also been arranged by the Lord: the elect ascend by the narrow and confined way to heaven’s broadest homeland, while the reprobate descend by the broad and very spacious way to the narrowest confines of hell. Through the most confined path the saints come to the most spacious kingdom, while through the broad path the wicked reach the narrowest abyss.

The destiny of wicked rich people is changed, and that of holy poor people is changed as well: the former pass from the spacious road of pleasure to the narrow punishments of hell; the latter pass from the narrowness of the present age to the broadest and most radiant glory of heaven. The former pass from the soft and loose road into the narrowness of Tartarus; the latter pass from the narrow and strenuous discipline of the body into heaven’s spacious kingdom. Hence the Lord says:

> “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew XI).

For it is not the one who lives softly and dissolutely who possesses the kingdom of God, but the one who acts manfully for its sake. Hence blessed Jerome says: “Broad is the way of worldly pleasure, which people desire; narrow is the way opened through labors and fasts. Many walk along the broad way, but few find the narrow one.”

### “Not living according to their own judgment”

It is dangerous for a monk to live according to his own judgment, lest he should call good what others judge—and what truly is—not good but evil. While he thinks that he is running along the straight way with open eyes, he may, blind, fall into a ruinous pit, as it is written:

> “There is a way that seems straight to human beings, but its end leads to hell” (Proverbs XIV).

Therefore monks must not serve their own desires [Col. 0798C], but humbly obey the Lord’s commands. They must not obediently serve their own pleasures, but must humbly submit themselves with fear of the Lord to his commands, so that they may be able to say with David:

> “I am a companion of all who fear you and keep your commandments” (Psalm CXVIII).

### “But walking according to another’s judgment and command”

Here he uses “judgment” for discernment or decision. A monk who is good and mortified for Christ must discern the work he ought to do in one way, so that he may receive from the Lord the reward of his work; in another way, he must obey another’s command. The one whose work another discerns and judges runs more sweetly along the way of the Lord’s commandments.

### “Living in monasteries, they desire to have an abbot over them”

“Coenobia” are monasteries of monks, communities of many people living together, and the name appears to be compounded from a Greek expression. In Greek, κοινόν (*coenon*) means what we call “common.” Thus, those living in coenobia—that is, dwelling together with many others—desire to have an abbot over them so that, under his governance, they may run more easily along the way of the Lord’s commandments; under his direction, live more easily; and more pleasantly obtain the rewards promised to them in the future. They know that the more willingly they consent to submit themselves to another’s authority for the love of Christ, the more happily they will rejoice with the Lord himself in the age to come.

And because without doubt such men imitate by their deeds the Lord’s statement:

> “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John VI),

they will unquestionably reign happily with him forever [Col. 0799A].

But this same obedience will then be acceptable to God and pleasing to human beings if what is commanded is carried out neither fearfully, slowly, lukewarmly, with murmuring, nor with a response expressing unwillingness. Obedience is acceptable to God when it is performed swiftly, with a pure heart and without murmuring; it is pleasing to human beings when it is performed without laziness, with eagerness and a cheerful mind. Hence it is added:

### “Not fearfully”

“To tremble” means to fear or to doubt. The one who does not firmly hope in the Lord’s help trembles when carrying out obedience. But whoever trusts in Christ’s assistance will not tremble to obey for Christ’s sake, because it is written:

> “Those who fear the Lord have hoped in the Lord; he is their help and their protector” (Psalm CXIII).

### “Not slowly”

The monk performs obedience who does not desire to receive eternal rewards from it. The one whom love of God does not rouse to obey delays in obeying his elders, delighted by bodily ease. He does not know that “the one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows with blessing”—that is, with an abundance of blessing—“will also reap abundantly with blessing,” namely, eternal life.

### “Not lukewarmly”

“Lukewarmly” means softly, sluggishly, or dissolutely. The monk performs obedience lukewarmly who does not fear what the Lord says about the lukewarm. For he says:

> “Because you are lukewarm and make me nauseated, I will begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Revelation III).

Nor does he conform to Paul, who says:

> “Fervent in spirit, serving the Lord” (Romans XII).

Monks ought to be fervent rather than lukewarm in Christ’s service, so that, kindled by the fire of charity, they may perform what they do not lukewarmly but swiftly and readily. That divine fire which the Lord sent upon the earth, desiring that it should burn, quickly rouses the hearts of good monks to obey, so that the sooner they please him by obeying, the sooner they may desire to reign with him.

### “Or with murmuring”

The one who performs obedience with murmuring receives neither praise from the one commanding nor reward from the Lord, but rather bodily discipline from the abbot and from the Lord the just punishment owed to those who murmur. Unhappily he loses both and painfully acquires both: he loses the grace of praise and reward, and acquires punishment for both body and soul.

### “Or with a response expressing unwillingness”

The monk who condemns obedience with a response expressing unwillingness must either quickly correct both his will and his response, or swiftly fall into the sin of murmuring. But if he quickly corrects both his response and his will, he will not lose the reward of his obedience, because the merciful and compassionate Lord quickly forgives those who repent.

### “Because the obedience offered to superiors is offered to the Lord”

He himself says:

> “Whoever hears you hears me” (Matthew X).

Obedience must be performed with great love of heart and with bodily speed, since the Lord himself receives it as holy and takes it into his own person, so that when the time of recompense arrives he may grant those who perform it the fullest rewards. For he will say to all who have been placed in obedient labor, when the time of eternal refreshment arrives:

> “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew XI).

Therefore the monk who hopes to receive such a reward for obedience must perform it with great eagerness of heart. Hence it follows:

### “And it ought to be offered by the disciples with a good disposition”

> “For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians IX).

This statement is understood not only of the almsgiving specially offered to the poor, but also generally of all the obedience of monks. Whatever a monk does in obedience, he offers entirely to God, to whom he has wholly vowed himself. He offers to God his fasting, vigils, abstinence, the additional prescribed course, and every action of heart and body, from whom he hopes to receive a hundredfold fruit for his labor [Col. 0800B].

Therefore, whoever wishes to receive from the Lord the fruit of his obedience with joy and increase must obey his superiors with joy, because whoever scorns obeying his superiors undoubtedly contradicts the Lord’s command. He says to the disciples and to all teachers:

> “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke X).

The obedience enjoined by superiors must not therefore be despised, but rather loved and cherished and, insofar as strength permits, carried out in deeds with joy. For it is written:

> “In every gift make your face cheerful” (Ecclesiasticus XXXV).

He makes his face cheerful in every gift who offers not with sadness or resentment but with a serene face and joyful spirit: speech to his hearers, bread to the poor, and a humble and obedient heart to his superiors. This person makes his face cheerful in every gift and therefore believes that all his giving has been received and approved by the Lord.

But those who fast without joy, keep vigils without joy, abstain without joy, and perform many other good works without joy or a good disposition do not receive from the Lord the reward of their labor; rather, they receive from the evil one condemnation for their murmuring. Hence it is added:

### “For if the disciple obeys with a bad disposition”

If the disciple obeys with a bad disposition and murmurs not only with his mouth but also in his heart, then, even if he fulfills the command, it will no longer be acceptable to God, who sees the heart of the one who murmurs. For such an action he obtains no grace; rather, he incurs the punishment of those who murmur unless he corrects it with due satisfaction.

The disciple must obey his master with a good disposition, a pure heart, and a humble spirit, so that he may receive from God the grace of his obedience. For when he obeys with a bad disposition, he is held by God as proud, murmuring, and disobedient. God, to whom all things are naked and open, condemns the hearts of those who murmur, even when they are silent.

Therefore whatever monks do, let them do it without murmuring, lest—God forbid—they perish by murmuring under the sentence by which those perished who murmured against the Lord in the wilderness. They perished while eating manna; these perish in the monastery while reciting the Scriptures and, in addition, murmuring. Those died while eating manna; these die daily from spiritual famine while reading and hearing the Scriptures. Those did not enter the promised land because they murmured; these will lose paradise because they murmur and will not enter the promised land—that is, the eternal homeland of heaven.

For what benefit is it to those who murmur to perform externally the work that was enjoined while remaining inwardly empty of the reward? It is therefore better to obey one’s superiors with joy and receive an everlasting reward than to obey with a sorrowful disposition and lose the rewards of one’s labor.

Even if he fulfills the master’s command in deeds, he does not fulfill the Apostle’s command, who said:

> “Do everything without murmuring and hesitation” (Philippians II).

## CHAPTER VI. On Silence

Silence is a virtue of humility and a sign of seriousness, the nurse of virtues and guardian of morals [Col. 0801B]. Hence Solomon says:

> “Whoever guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from distress” (Proverbs XIII).

That is, he frees his soul from the distress of eternal punishment: by loving silence, he guards it from evil and wicked speech, or from foolish talk altogether, and restrains his tongue, saying:

### “Let us do what the Prophet says: ‘I said, I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue’” (Psalm XXXVIII)

He guards his ways well—that is, the actions of his life—who does not offend with his tongue. The tongue is a small member, but it often causes many quarrels and many scandals. Concerning it the apostle James says:

> “No human being can tame the tongue; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison,”

and so forth (James III).

Whoever therefore does not wish to sin with his tongue must first carefully watch over his ways—that is, the actions of his life—lest he suddenly slip with his tongue because he previously neglected to watch over his ways. It follows:

### “I placed a guard over my mouth” (Psalm XXXVIII)

He places a good guard over his mouth whose tongue does not flow shamelessly into evil speech, empty speech, or excessive speech, but, according to Solomon, waits for “a time to be silent and a time to speak” (Ecclesiastes III). Again it is written:

> “A wise person will keep silent until the proper time, but the reckless and imprudent person does not observe the time” (Ecclesiasticus XX).

He also places a guard over his mouth who does not declare himself righteous but, what is more truthful, confesses himself a sinner. Therefore, so that our tongue may not slip into evil speech, let each of us place a guard over his mouth and carefully attend to what the Apostle says about those who speak evil. Among the other evils he names above or below, he says:

> “Neither drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians VI).

But in the Law the Lord commanded the children of Israel, saying:

> “You shall not allow revilers to live in the land” (Exodus XXII).

Therefore, so that the tongue may not drift into empty speech, let us hear what the Psalmist says about empty speech:

> “Each spoke empty words to his neighbor; they spoke with deceitful lips and a double heart. May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips,”

and so forth (Psalm XI).

So that the tongue may not fall heedlessly into excessive speech, let us hear what Solomon says:

> “In much speaking you will not escape sin, and whoever uses many words harms his soul” (Proverbs X).

A guard must therefore be placed over our mouth, lest by speaking without restraint—whether through evil speech, empty speech, or excessive speech—we offend the Lord our God. For, as blessed Augustine says, through the tongue’s lack of restraint, goads are sown, quarrels arise, torches of hatred are kindled, peace is extinguished from hearts, and an abundance of many other vices overflows.

### “I was struck dumb, and was humbled, and was silent from good things” (Psalm XXXVIII)

Blessed Benedict explained this statement in praise of silence, saying: Here the Prophet shows that if one ought sometimes to be silent even from good speech because of silence, how much more must one cease from evil words because of the punishment of sin? Thus someone has said:

> “For an idle word an account is rendered;  
> for an unjust speech punishment is paid.”

“I was struck dumb,” he said—that is, I voluntarily imposed silence upon myself so that I might not sin through loquacity. For it is written:

> “Whoever hates loquacity extinguishes wickedness” (Ecclesiasticus XIX).

Hence Isaiah says:

> “The cultivation of righteousness is silence” (Isaiah XXXII),

indicating that the righteousness of the mind is laid waste when the tongue is not restrained from immoderate speech.

Silence, as has been said, is a virtue of humility, because the more the tongue is bound by the bridle of silence, the more the humbled mind is raised toward the heights. The more it lowers itself under silence, the more it fixes the sharp point of compunction in heaven. And as the humbled mind raises itself toward the grace of compunction, so it humbles itself again toward the grace of compunction. Hence it follows:

### “I was humbled, and was silent from good things” (Psalm XXXVIII)

Unless he had first been humbled, he would not have been silent from either good or evil things. “Humbled” is understood as “thrown down upon the ground.” Whoever therefore truly loves the virtue of silence must sometimes remain silent even from good speech, so that by remaining silent for a time he may nourish the other virtues, which, once nourished, he may wisely bring forth at the proper time.

Hence a certain wise man says:

> “There is one who is silent and is found wise, and there is one who is hateful because he is shameless in speaking” (Ecclesiasticus XX).

It is as though he said: The former, shaping himself into a wise person through silence, nourished himself; the latter made himself hateful by speaking shamelessly. The one who was silent was found wise; the other, because he exceeded the proper measure in speaking, was found shameless.

Therefore, although permission to speak about good and holy matters, in words suited to edification, is granted rarely to perfect disciples because of the seriousness of silence, he says that the Lord’s words are good and holy and suited to the edification of souls. Unless the soul is shaped by them, it will in no way be able to ascend to the homeland of the heavens or receive rewards with the saints.

Concerning these words the Psalmist says:

> “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire,”

and so forth (Psalm XI).

Again he himself says:

> “The judgments of God are justified in themselves, more desirable than much gold and more precious than a precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Psalm XVIII).

> “Your servant also keeps them; in keeping them there is great reward.”

Hence Paul says:

> “We know that the law is good, holy, and righteous” (1 Timothy I).

These are the Lord’s words, which prepare eternal life for those who believe them and do them. Because of the seriousness of silence, disciples are rarely permitted to preach them, lest, while carelessly leaving the confines of their silence, they fall headlong into the pit of pride, or cross the boundary of their silence and suffer harm to their soul. They may lose the beneficial seriousness of silence and fall into the ruinous frivolity of the mind. Hence it follows:

### “For it is written: ‘In much speaking you will not escape sin’” (Proverbs X)

Hence blessed Gregory says: Since no one who serves excessive speech can maintain the uprightness of justice, the Prophet bears witness, saying:

> “The man of many words will not be directed upon the earth” (Psalm CXXXVIII).

Hence blessed Ambrose says: There is a person who indeed longs for silence, but his heart condemns him greatly. Such a person speaks much. There is another who speaks from morning until evening and nevertheless carefully observes great silence with discernment. For it is better to keep silence than to say something malicious. Guilt is more easily avoided by keeping silent than by speaking.

For it is written:

> “Do not be hasty with your tongue, and before you hear, do not answer a word; and in the midst of elders do not add to your speech. Do not speak unless you have been questioned” (Ecclesiasticus IV).

Questioning should open the monk’s mouth. Let there be measure in his words and a balance in his speech; let his words always be restrained. Let him not exceed the proper measure of speaking, and let him always prefer to hear rather than to speak.

And elsewhere:

> “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs XVIII).

The tongue has no hands, but metaphorically it is said to have hands, since “hands” signify works, just as the Psalmist says:

> “Deliver my soul from the sword, my only one from the hand of the dog” (Psalm XXI).

Death and life therefore lie in the hands of the tongue, because, as the apostle James says:

> “From the same mouth proceed blessing and cursing” (James III).

When we speak the truth and bless the Lord who said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV), we hold life in the hands of the tongue, because it is written:

> “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom I);

and:

> “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John III).

Again James says:

> “The tongue is a fire, the universe of iniquity” (James III).

The tongue is a fire because, by speaking wickedly, it devours the forest of virtues and through it nearly all crimes are either continued, perpetrated, or defended. They are continued, as in robberies and sexual violations; perpetrated, as in perjuries and false testimonies; defended when committed offenses are denied to the one making inquiry.

Again he says:

> “See how great a fire sets ablaze how great a forest!” (ibid.).

Just as a fire growing from a small spark often sets a great forest ablaze, so the lack of restraint of the tongue, nourished by its own frivolities, destroys the great substance of good works and many fruits of the spiritual life wherever it reaches. It also frequently consumes countless leaves of speech that had seemed excellent.

For speaking and teaching befit the master; silence and hearing suit the disciple. Speaking and teaching befit the master because through the Prophet it is said to him:

> “Cry out, do not cease, says the Lord; raise your voice like a trumpet and announce to my people their crimes, and declare to the house of Jacob their sins” (Isaiah LVIII).

Again, through the same prophet he is commanded:

> “Climb upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion; speak to the cities of Judah,”

and so forth (Isaiah XL).

Silence and hearing suit the disciple. For it is said to disciples:

> “Whoever has ears for hearing, let him hear” (Matthew XI; Mark IV).

Hence the apostle James says:

> “Let every person be quick to hear but slow to speak” (James I).

Rightly he first urges everyone to lend an ear quickly to the teacher, but to open the mouth for teaching only slowly. Whoever therefore loves wisdom should first ask it from God; then, as a humble hearer, seek a teacher of truth; and while carrying out his duties, carefully restrain his tongue not only from idle speech but also from preaching the very truth he has recently learned.

For it is safer to hear than to preach: when one hears, humility is preserved; but when one preaches, even the slightest boastfulness scarcely fails to steal upon anyone. Hence Jeremiah, describing the way of a well-instructed youth, counts the modesty of silence among the first pursuits of virtue:

> “It is good for a man,” he says, “when he has borne the yoke from his youth, to sit alone and be silent” (Lamentations III).

Therefore, if anything must be asked of the prior, let it be requested with complete humility and submissive reverence, lest one appear to speak more than is fitting. Whoever asks the prior for counsel concerning salvation and words of instruction must ask with complete humility and submission, because humility is the monk’s highest virtue, while pride is his greatest vice.

Each monk should judge himself to be a monk when he considers himself least, even when he has performed the greatest works of virtue. The conscience of God’s servant must always be humble and sorrowful: humble, so that he may not grow proud; and usefully sorrowful, so that his heart may not dissolve into frivolity.

But we condemn absolutely, in every place, buffoonery, idle words, and words that provoke laughter; nor do we permit the disciple to open his mouth for such speech. “Buffooneries” are obscene and shameless jokes, or things deserving ridicule, which must be entirely foreign to monks. It befits a monk to utter words of instruction, not the buffoonery of joking. He ought to possess seriousness of mind, not the frivolity of joking or buffoonery. His speech must be just, honorable, and reasonable—not light, empty, and alien to seriousness.

The monk must therefore meditate on hymns, psalms, and songs, not on empty, vain, or idle words. Often the sluggish mind is driven into a pit by certain stages; while we neglect to avoid idle words, we reach harmful ones. First we take pleasure in speaking about the affairs of others, and afterward we wound the lives of those about whom we speak through detraction.

The Lord warns us to avoid this, saying:

> “For every idle word that human beings speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matthew XII).

If an account is demanded for idle speech, let us consider what punishment awaits excessive speech, in which one also sins through harmful words. Idle words themselves are often words that provoke laughter. Therefore we must all avoid the immoderate indulgence of joking and laughter, through which exceedingly bitter scandals frequently arise among brothers.

Hence Solomon says:

> “As though in laughter, the fool works evil” (Proverbs X).

Who does not know that excessive laughter is the gateway of indiscipline and frivolity, through which the devil subtly serves harmful food to the wretched soul?

## CHAPTER VII. On Humility and Its Many Commendations, Distinguished by Twelve Steps

Divine Scripture cries out to us, brothers, saying:

> “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV).

This must plainly be understood and held by us with the greatest firmness: everyone who carelessly lifts himself up because of his merits—or, worse, without merits—will justly be humbled by the Lord; and whoever humbles himself prudently because of his good deeds will justly be exalted by him.

Hence Solomon says:

> “Humility follows the proud, and glory receives the humble in spirit” (Proverbs XXIX).

Humility follows the proud because the one who persists in living proudly in the present descends after death, humbled, into hell. Concerning the proud it is written:

> “They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they descend to the underworld” (Job XXI).

This is the damnable and miserable humility that follows the proud; and “glory receives the humble in spirit,” that is, the glory of the heavenly kingdom receives all who live with a humbled spirit. Hence the Lord says concerning the humble:

> “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew V).

Again he says:

> “Let the little children come to me, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Mark X).

Thus he calls both little children and the poor in spirit humble, and mercifully promises them the kingdom of heaven after death.

When he says these things, he shows us that every exaltation is a kind of pride. Every pride lies as far below as it raises itself high; and the more deeply it falls, the more loftily it rises. The one lifted up through pride is brought low by God’s justice. Pride, therefore, just as it is the origin of all crimes, is likewise the ruin of all virtues. It is first in sin and last in conflict. It either casts the mind down through sin at the beginning or throws it down from the virtues at the end. Hence it is the greatest of all sins, because through both virtues and vices alike it destroys the human mind.

The Prophet indicates that he guards against this, saying:

> “Lord, my heart was not exalted, nor were my eyes lifted up” (Psalm CXXX).

This psalm preaches humility, teaches temperance, urges patience, and sets forth and composes every humility in those who do good. If a humbled heart is a sacrifice to God, then the one who said, “Lord, my heart was not exalted,” offered a sacrifice (Psalm CXXX). If some hermit devoted to his cell were to say this, he would shine with the praise of great patience; how much more so because it was said by a king clothed in purple and an eminent prophet.

If holy men, even when performing strong deeds, consider themselves lowly, what will those say in their defense who swell with pride without any work of virtue? Whatever the works may be, let them be nothing unless they are seasoned with humility. An admirable action accompanied by pride does not raise a person but weighs him down. Whoever gathers virtues without humility carries dust in the wind. From the very place where he appears to bear something, his worse, prideful eyes are blinded.

> “I have not walked in great things, nor in marvels beyond me” (Psalm CXXX).

This means: I have attributed nothing to my merits; I have contributed nothing from my own knowledge. If I possessed anything good, I gave it all to the glory of God. I did not wish to become known among people as though for marvelous deeds, nor did I seek anything beyond my strength by which I might boast before the inexperienced.

Alternatively: to walk in great things is for each person to think great things about himself; to walk in marvels is to consider something marvelous about oneself. The Prophet denies that he does this when he says:

> “I have not walked in great things, nor in marvels beyond me.”

All humility is found not so much in speech as in the mind, so that our conscience may know us to be humble and so that we may never think that we know, understand, or amount to anything, nor attribute anything to our merits, because we possess nothing of our own except sin.

### “But what if I was not humbly disposed, but exalted my soul?”

In everything we do, we think humbly about ourselves if we hold humility at the root of our good work and look not at those above us but at those to whom we are still inferior. Thus, while we set before ourselves the examples of better people, we may always ascend to greater things through humility.

We exalt our soul when, in this dwelling of the body, we meditate on humble things, as Scripture says:

> “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV).

And again:

> “Humble yourselves before God, and he will exalt you” (1 Peter V).

The more worthless a person is before God, the more precious he is in his own eyes; and the more precious he is before God, the more worthless he is in his own eyes, because God regards humble things and recognizes lofty things from afar. This is usually the finest mark of the elect: they always think less of themselves than they are, and speak humbly of themselves below what they are.

> “As a child weaned from his mother, so you will requite my soul” (Psalm CXXX).

The one who does not lift up his heart, raise his eyes on high, or walk in great things or in marvels beyond him is found to be like a nursing child, as Scripture says:

> “From the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise” (Psalm VIII).

This virtue rises to particular honor among the eminent virtues because the condescension of the Majesty has taken it up. Let us finally consider how highly humility is honored: it is placed, as the opposite of pride, in the twelfth step. Pride plunges into Tartarus through the seven principal vices; humility leads to heaven through twelve steps.

Therefore, brothers, if we wish to reach the summit of the highest humility, the summit of highest humility, as some maintain, is completed in four ways.

First, if the monk has put to death within himself all his wills.

Second, if he has concealed nothing from his abbot—not only of his actions but also of his thoughts.

Third, if he entrusts everything not to his own discernment but to the abbot’s judgment, and knowingly and willingly listens to his admonitions.

Fourth, if in everything he preserves steadfastness in obedience, gentleness, and patience.

Blessed Benedict, however, wished and defined the highest and perfect humility to consist not merely in four but in twelve steps. Humility may also appear highest and perfect if one humbly and patiently fulfills what the Lord says:

> “But I say to you, do not resist evil; but if someone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also,”

and so forth (Matthew V).

The one who patiently and humbly endures these things, and moreover hears what the Lord commanded:

> “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew V),

seems to me to possess the highest humility and to hold the highest summit of humility.

And to that heavenly exaltation, to which one ascends through the humility of the present life, we wish to arrive swiftly. He calls it that heavenly exaltation of which the Lord says: “The saints will shine like the sun in the presence of my Father” (Matt. XIII). And of which Daniel says: “Those who instruct many in righteousness will shine like the stars for everlasting ages” (Dan. XII). Hence the Psalmist also says: “Your friends, O God, have been exceedingly exalted; their sovereignty has been exceedingly strengthened” [Col. 0807C] (Ps. CXXXVIII). The heavenly and supreme exaltation is this: that the holy monks may be like the angels, that they may be sons and heirs of God, and co-heirs of Christ; and that they may hear from the Lord: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV); and that he may make them recline in that same kingdom, and, passing among them, graciously minister all good things to them.

### As Our Deeds Ascend

Our deeds then ascend well to the heights when, by living well from day to day, they advance toward better things; when, strengthened by various and numerous virtues, they humbly rise toward the contemplation of our Creator. And, as though by steps, they climb through the virtues of the soul to the vision of him, so that it may be said of us: “They will go from virtue to virtue, and the God of gods will be seen in Zion” [Col. 0807D] (Ps. LXXXIII).

That ladder must be erected which appeared in Jacob’s dream, by which angels descending and ascending were shown to him (Gen. XXVIII). Without doubt, we understand that descent and ascent to mean nothing other than descending through exaltation and ascending through humility. Although other teachers wished to understand this ladder and the angels descending and ascending upon it differently, blessed Benedict nevertheless wished in this passage to understand it as our life, which, full of virtues, must daily be raised up to heaven. By the ascending and descending angels he understood souls living the regular life. Some of these, by humbling themselves, ascend to heaven; others, growing proud of those very steps of virtue, [Col. 0808A] fall into the depths of Tartarus. In them is fulfilled: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV).

The ladder itself, once erected, is our life in this age, which the Lord raises to heaven when the heart has been humbled. Our ladder—that is, our life—is then rightly raised by the Lord to heaven when our hearts, together with our hands—that is, with good works—are lifted upward by us; when, according to the Apostle’s exhortation, we set our minds on the things above, not on the things that are upon the earth; when, sighing for heaven, we meditate upon and seek heavenly things; when we forget what lies behind and stretch ourselves toward what lies ahead; when, with the full intention of our mind, we pursue the prize of the heavenly calling; when, meditating on heavenly things, we can say with Paul: “Our citizenship is in heaven” [Col. 0808B] (Phil. III).

For we say that the sides of this ladder are our body and soul. He wisely says that our body and soul are the two sides of this ladder, because every human being is composed of both, and, for the love of Christ and eternal life, does good works from both substances as far as he is able; and so that, in the glory of the resurrection, he may receive the rewards of his labor in both substances, he carefully strives in both substances to keep the Lord’s commandments. We then raise our whole ladder to heaven when, with God’s help, we also offer our bodies to him as a sacrifice, as the Apostle exhorts us, saying: “I beseech you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your reasonable service” [Col. 0808C] (Rom. XII). The ladder takes its name from *scandere*, that is, from ascending; and it cannot be complete in any other way than by consisting of sides and steps.

Into these sides divine calling has inserted various steps of humility or discipline, to be climbed. These are called the steps of humility and discipline because these two most beautiful virtues are joined to one another: humility makes a person gentle, while instruction in discipline shapes and makes him learned; humility makes him tranquil and mild, while instruction in discipline makes him prudent and wise. Since it is written: “God loves no one except the one who dwells with wisdom” (Wis. VII), discipline must necessarily be joined to humility; for instruction in discipline is the guardian of humility, and humility is the tempering of instruction.

A “calling” is so named when, for the greatest battle, not only soldiers but also the rest are summoned. Hence *evocare* is understood to mean “to lead out” or “to call forth.” The word is very suitably placed here, because we are summoned, led forth, and called forth daily by the Lord, so that, armed with the twelve steps of humility, we may rise up courageously to battle against the devil; and, under his leadership, triumphing in victory, may reach the kingdom of heaven joyfully by ascending through the twelve steps of humility.

### On the First Step of Humility

The first step of humility, therefore, is for a person always to keep the fear of God before his eyes. This step is rightly placed first among the twelve, both in dignity and in order. It is first in order because it is first in thought, in the heart, and in the will. It is first in dignity because one begins to fear the Lord. For concerning fear it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and the fear of the Lord is the discipline of wisdom. The fear of the Lord is glory, exultation, joy, and a crown of rejoicing; and it will give gladness and joy for length of days” (Ecclus. I). All these good things, and many others, the fear of the Lord will provide for those who continually set it before their eyes and say with blessed Job: “As though swelling waves were over me, I have always feared the Lord, and I could not bear his burden” (Job XXXI).

Let him flee oblivion altogether. Since memory and oblivion cannot both be retained in one dwelling-place of the heart, it is necessary that we drive harmful oblivion from our hearts and retain beneficial memory. When destructive oblivion is driven from the heart’s cloister, then fruitful memory grows and overflows within us. It brings before the eyes of our mind the Lord and his commandments; diligently asks how we may please him and keep his commandments; and attentively considers what must and must not be done. Hence the Lord admonishes the people of the Jews, saying: “Therefore keep watch over yourself and your soul carefully, and do not forget the word of the Lord, lest it depart from your heart all the days of your life” (Deut. IV). Hence the Psalmist says: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his rewards” (Ps. CII).

The memory of the fear of the Lord makes a person [Col. 0809C] cautious, modest, just, upright, honorable, devout, kind, merciful, prudent, humble, gentle, sober, and temperate and provident in all his actions. Conversely, forgetfulness of the mind makes a person foolish, careless, senseless, stupid, imprudent, unjust, injurious, wrathful, envious, impure, harsh, incontinent, mocking, slanderous, puffed up, proud, arrogant, vain, and utterly depraved in all his actions; it also makes him wretched. For he does not bring his Lord and his commandments back to memory, and therefore, like a blind and wandering man, he sins and perishes. But how this harmful oblivion is to be avoided, hear what follows:

And let him always remember all that God has commanded. The memory of God’s commandments then brings salvation to the soul when what is wisely remembered from the Lord’s commandments is effectively fulfilled in deed. For the commandments of the Lord that are remembered but not fulfilled show the soul’s condemnation rather than its salvation. But when remembered and completed in works, they drive sins far away from those who perform them, and promise continual salvation and eternal rewards to those who persevere. They grant glory to those who do them, but threaten eternal Gehenna to those who do not; hence it follows:

And how those who despise God fall into Gehenna because of their sins. Those who despise him are the ones who hear the Lord’s commandments but disdain obeying them. [Col. 0810A] Monks despise God when they refuse to obey their abbot and resist with a stubborn neck. Concerning all the preachers whom he sends, the Lord says: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke X). Gehenna rightly burns up these despisers who scorn the just commandments of the abbot because they could have escaped if they had obeyed the commandments of the Lord and of their abbot.

As fire consumes wood, so Gehenna receives the sins of the disobedient. And just as fire is kindled from wood, so Gehenna is kindled by the sins of those who despise God, so that it may torture each one according to the measure of his offenses. For each person kindles for himself the flame of Gehenna’s fire in proportion to the amount of sin he has supplied to Gehenna. In proportion to the wood of sins that each sinner has carried with him, so much will the wretched man be tortured in Gehenna. And as great and hard as the heap of his sins is there, so great and hard a torment will he find there. In this way the fire of Gehenna burns each person because of his own sins.

Hence blessed Isidore says: “Just as each saint will be glorified in the future judgment according to the measure of his virtues, so also each ungodly person will be condemned according to the measure of his crimes. Nor will the order of future condemnation be lacking in punishment; rather, there will be a distinction of penalties according to the quality of the crimes.”

Hence blessed Gregory says: “The justice of almighty God, foreknowing the future, created from the very beginning of the world the fire of Gehenna, which would begin once to exist as the punishment of the reprobate, but would never end its burning even without wood; [Col. 0810C] it would be for the wretched a death without death, an end without end, a decay without decay. For death lives, the end is always beginning, and decay does not know how to decay; death presses down but does not extinguish; pain tortures but in no way dispels terror; the flame burns but in no way drives away the darkness.”

And let him always turn over in his mind the eternal life prepared for those who fear God. That is, let him always turn over in his heart what is said concerning those who despise God: “The wicked will go into eternal punishment” (Matt. XXV); and concerning those who fear God: “But the righteous into eternal life” (ibid.). There is everlasting glory, great rejoicing, a crown flowering with virtues, a splendor radiant with the illumination of the true Sun, the secure habitation of all the saints, and the whole of an eternal and ever-enduring goodness. [Col. 0810D] Those who reach it, strengthened by the virtues of good works, will be like the blessed angels; they will rejoice happily with their God and reign forever without end.

And let him guard himself at every hour from sins and vices—that is, from those of thought, tongue, eyes, hands, feet, or one’s own will. When he says that one must guard oneself from sins at every hour, this is understood to mean from all evil works carried out in thought, speech, and deed. Hence he appropriately adds “of thought, tongue, hands, feet,” and so forth. From these kindlings, as from certain steps, every sin develops. For evil thought gives birth to pleasure, pleasure to consent, consent to action, action to habit, and habit to necessity. [Col. 0811A] Bound by these chains, a person is held fast in the chain of vices, so that he cannot be torn away from it unless divine grace takes hold of the hand of the one lying prostrate.

Thus we must fit our whole body for service, so that we may be able to offer obedience to our Creator with the full strength of our members. The eye then offers service to God when it avoids looking upon shameful things. The tongue will deserve a reward when it is occupied with blessings. Hearing will please God if it does not mingle with slander. The feet will be able to praise God if they hasten to turn their course away from every evil. The hands bless if they renounce theft and prepare themselves for mercy.

When he says that one must guard oneself from vices, this is understood to mean from the seven principal vices: gluttony, fornication, avarice, anger, [Col. 0811B] sadness, acedia, and vainglory, and from their eighth parent, pride, and from all their harmful little branches, which, like poisonous offspring, are born from poisonous parents. It would be too lengthy to list their catalog here. For in the hearts of the reprobate, one catalog of vices follows another, so that when one has departed, another may succeed it, according to the prophet’s testimony: “What the locust left, the caterpillar consumed; what the caterpillar left, the rust consumed” (Joel I), and so forth.

Again, through the prophet it is said: “All the tribes of the earth will come from the north, and each will set up his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem” (Jer. I). The kingdoms of the north are vices that reign at those very gates—that is, in those very senses of the soul. For we sin from no other source than seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching. Hence it is also said elsewhere: “Death entered through your windows” (Jer. IX).

When he says “or of one’s own will,” this is understood to mean that one must guard oneself from sins and vices arising from one’s own will.

But let him also hasten to cut off the desires of the flesh. This is understood to mean: let him not take pleasure in fulfilling them. For what is more burdensome in this life than to burn with carnal desires? Or what is safer here than not to fulfill the desires of the flesh and to desire nothing of this world? Those who love this world and strive to fulfill the desires of the flesh are disturbed by the turbulent anxieties of the age. But those who die to this world in such a way that they take pleasure in living for God alone have already begun, in a certain manner, to possess here the rest of the future peace for which they await there.

[Col. 0811D] Therefore we must apply our mind with such perseverance in praying and knocking that, by the strongest concentration, we may overcome the intrusive suggestions of carnal desires that clamor against our senses; and we must persist until, by persevering, we conquer.

Let a person always judge that he is watched by God from heaven at every hour, that his deeds in every place are seen by the sight of the Divinity, and that at every hour they are reported by the angels. For the more carefully each person believes that he is watched by God, the more cautiously he ought to live and the more honorably guard his life, lest he offend those eyes of the Divinity that he wishes to have favorable toward him. He sees hidden things and considers what is secret and concealed; no one can escape God’s eyes, which say: “I am God who is near, and not a God far away. If a person is hidden in secret places, will I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?” (Jer. XXIII). Hence the Psalmist says: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers” (Ps. XXXIII).

When he says that the angels report everything at every hour, this is understood from the passage where the angel said to Tobiah: “When you prayed with tears and buried the dead, I offered your prayers to the Lord” (Tob. XII). Moreover, when the Lord had said in the Gospel: “Whoever humbles himself like this little child is greater in the kingdom of heaven, and whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me” (Matt. XVIII), he added shortly afterward: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones. For I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father.” [Col. 0812B] Great is the dignity of souls, that each soul should have, from the beginning of its birth, an angel assigned to its protection, both to guard it lest it sin and never cease reporting to God the good things it has done.

The Prophet demonstrates this to us when he shows God always present in our thoughts, saying: “God searches hearts and reins” (Ps. VII). As Cassiodorus says, this is a power proper to God alone: to examine our hearts and, by the power of his light, penetrate the vigor of our spirit. For although the powers of heaven are much higher than we are, no creature has been granted the ability to know fully the secrets of our thoughts. Only he who judges knows them perfectly in us. He himself says: “All the churches will know that I am he who searches the reins and the heart” [Col. 0812C] (Rev. II). Again it is written: “God is the witness of his reins, and the true examiner of his heart” (Wis. I).

The Lord searches our hearts when he carefully investigates the thoughts of our hearts, so that what is hidden from human beings may become manifest to him. For it is written: “A human being sees the face, but God sees the heart.” He searches the reins when he directs his attention to the most steadfast vigor of our spirit, or when he clearly penetrates bodily pleasures.

And again: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain” (Ps. XCIII). Hence Jeremiah says: “My eyes are upon the ways of human beings. They are not hidden from my face, and their iniquity was not concealed” (Jer. [Col. 0812D] XVI). Hence Solomon says: “The Lord observes a person’s ways and considers all his steps” (Prov. V). Hence David says: “I have kept your commandments and your testimonies, because all my ways are before you” (Ps. CXVIII).

We sin not only by deeds but also by thoughts, if we take pleasure in them when they arise unlawfully. For if we first resist an evil thought, we do not fall into the deed.

And again he says: “You understood my thoughts from afar” (Ps. CXXXVIII). Hence through Solomon it is said: “All the ways of human beings are open to the eyes of the Lord; hell and destruction are before the Lord” (Prov. XVI)—how much more, then, the hearts of human beings. By “from afar” he does not indicate a place but a time, because God not only foresees our deeds but also knows our thoughts before we ourselves realize them.

We should not be afraid if good and evil thoughts enter the mind; rather, we should rejoice if the mind distinguishes an evil thought from good ones through rational understanding, and if, by a more prudent perception, it distinguishes between good and evil, either avoiding recognized evils or doing the good it has understood.

And because “the thought of a human being will confess to you” (Ps. LXXV). The thought of a human being then confesses to God when past sins are condemned before him with humble satisfaction. For when each person is anticipated by divine illumination, he is immediately assailed by the troubles of shameful thoughts, yet he does not hesitate humbly to confess them to the Lord.

For, in order to be vigilant concerning his perverse thoughts, let the useful brother always say in his heart: “Then I shall be blameless before him, if I guard myself from my iniquity” (Ps. XVII). The life of blessed monks is subtly described here. When they recognize that they have attained some grace of the Lord, they take care lest they again become entangled in the calamities of their former iniquity.

For to introduce unlawful thoughts is the work of demons, but to take pleasure in perverse thoughts is harmful. In this passage he uses “iniquity” for “thought.” Everything that is not just is iniquitous. Therefore whoever guards himself from evil thoughts more easily guards himself from evil deeds. Hence he says: “And I shall be blameless before him, if I guard myself from my iniquity” (Ps. XVII). It is as though he were saying: “Then I shall be able to lead a blameless life if an evil thought does not stain me.” For no one whose iniquitous thought pollutes the mind can live without stain. But only that person lives truly blamelessly who guards himself from the iniquity of an evil thought.

And lest anyone say, “To think only, and not to do, is not a great sin,” let him hear what is written concerning evil thoughts. Scripture says: “The thought of a fool is sin” (Prov. XXIV). And so that you may understand what kind of sin it is, the same Scripture says elsewhere: “Perverse thoughts separate from God” (Wis. I). It is not a small but a great sin to be separated from God and joined to the devil. One guards himself well from him who, while iniquitous thoughts are still small, seizes them and dashes them against the rock.

We are forbidden to do our own will when Scripture says to us: “And turn away from your own wills” [Col. 0813D] (Eccles. VIII). It has already been said in many places that no one may ever be permitted to do his own will except by the judgment and approval either of many people or of those in authority. For we call that perfect self-restraint by which a person restrains himself from his own wills. How great the danger is for one who wishes to do his own will rather than the Lord’s is clear from the Apostle, who says: “We too once lived according to the desires of the flesh and of our thoughts, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. II).

And again: “Let us ask God in prayer that his will may be done in us” (Matt. VI). Showing the weakness of the humanity he bore, the Lord said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Luke XXII). And, giving his disciples an example that they should do not their own will but God’s, he added: “Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will.” And elsewhere he says: “I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me” (John VI). If the Son obeyed in doing the will of the Father, how much more must a servant obey and do not his own will but the Lord’s!

We are therefore rightly taught not to do our own will, when we beware of what holy Scripture says: “There are ways that seem right to human beings, but their end plunges down to the depths of hell” (Prov. XVI). This is that broad and spacious way which leads those walking upon it to destruction, by which many perish as they follow their own wills and descend into hell.

[Col. 0814B] Hence a certain wise man says: “The way of sinners is paved with stones, and at its end are the underworld, darkness, and punishments” (Eccles. XXI). Concerning them it is also read in the Book of Job: “They rejoice in games, they hold the tambourine and the lyre, and they are glad at the sound of the organ; they spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they descend to the underworld” (Job XXI).

This may also be understood of those who now appear to be chosen but are not, and therefore are rejected by the Lord, as the prophet says: “The Lord called judgment to the fire, and it devoured a portion of the house” (Amos VII). A portion of the house will indeed be devoured, because hell will also swallow those who now boast that they stand in the heavenly commandments.

It may also appropriately be understood of those whom vices deceive under the guise of virtues. Certain vices appear to have the appearance of virtues, but they are not virtues. Sometimes cruelty is practiced under the pretext of justice, and from this some become confident that they are just, although it is precisely for this that they are most severely rejected by the Lord. Carnal people, moreover, often fail through dullness of mind to recognize as blameworthy the vice that appears worthy of condemnation.

Hence through Solomon it is said: “The Lord knows the ways that are on the right; but those on the left are perverse” (Prov. IV). This is also understood of heretics, whose doctrine appears right to them but is distinguished by Catholic men and judged to be perverse; for it is said that their followers are headed toward Tartarus. Hence Solomon says: “The way of the ungodly is dark; they do not know where they fall” (Prov. IV). Again he says: “On the path of those who are despised there is a chasm” [Col. 0814D] (Prov. XIII).

And let us likewise beware of what was said concerning the negligent: “They have been corrupted and have become abominable in their pleasures” (Ps. LII). They have been corrupted by following the freedom of their own judgment, and have become abominable by following the desires of their own hearts. Concerning them the Apostle says: “People corrupted in mind, rejected, without affection, transgressors, harsh, having a seared conscience,” and so forth (1 Tim. IV).

But in the desires of the flesh let us believe that God is present above us, as the Prophet says to the Lord: “All my desire is before you” (Ps. XXXVII). He does not say, “before human beings,” who cannot see the heart, but “all my desire is before you,” to whom the things in the thought or desire of my heart are not hidden.

Therefore an evil desire must be avoided, because death has been placed beside the entrance of pleasure. Death is so called either from *morsus* (“a bite”) or because it is bitter. It was called death from a bite because Eve took pleasure in eating from the forbidden tree of paradise; persuaded by the devil, she took the fruit, bit it, and immediately swallowed bitter death with the bite. She took pleasure, bit, and at once incurred the danger of death. The pleasure of the fruit entered the soul, and death entered together with it. Therefore blessed Benedict says that death has been placed beside the entrance of pleasure.

For people are now deceived by the devil through the same allurements of pleasure by which our first parents were deceived in paradise. When the devil wishes to deceive someone, he first inflames that person’s nature, and then approaches from the point at which he has seen the person to be suited to sin. The devil is a slippery serpent; if he is not resisted at the head of his suggestion, he slips unnoticed into the innermost heart. But if holy men resist him strongly at the head, his entire suggestion is quickly destroyed. Hence the Psalmist says: “The wicked has been brought to nothing in his sight” (Ps. XIV); and: “Blessed is the one who seizes his little ones and dashes them against the rock” (Ps. CXXXVI).

Hence Scripture commands, saying: “Do not follow your desires” (Eccles. XVIII). The Apostle James says: “Each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire” (Jas. I). Drawn away, that is, from the right path, and enticed into evil. Again he himself says: “Then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it has been completed, produces death” (ibid.).

David was tempted by the sight of another man’s wife, and was drawn away and enticed by his desire. When he had completed the crime conceived within him, he fell under the sentence of guilt leading to death even from his own mouth; yet he escaped it through repentance. Judas was tempted by love of money, and because he was greedy, he was drawn away and enticed by his own desire and led to destruction by giving his consent. Joseph was tempted by the words of his mistress; but because he had neither lustful desire nor pleasure of the flesh, he escaped temptation victorious.

Therefore, if the eyes of the Lord observe the good and the evil (Ps. XXXII), and the Lord continually looks down from heaven upon the children of human beings to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God, and if our works are reported daily to the Lord our Maker by the angels assigned to us (Ps. XIII), then the Lord’s looking upon us is the divine act by which he continually looks upon the good, to defend them from the enemy’s snares, guard them from sins, and make them persevere continually in good works.

The Lord’s eyes looked upon Peter, and he immediately turned back from the fault of denial, recognized the Lord, and corrected his offense by weeping bitterly. The Lord’s eyes therefore observe the good and the evil, so that they may repay good things to the good and evil things to the evil: rewards for good works to the former, and eternal punishment for evil deeds to the latter. He looks upon the former to hear and save them, and upon the latter to destroy and condemn them, as it is written: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers” (Ps. XXXIII). But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth.

He also looks upon the children of human beings to see whether there is anyone among them who understands or seeks God. For that person is considered understanding before God who, in work and prayer, seeks and entreats no other hearer than God himself; who places care, hope, or trust in no one but the Lord Jesus Christ. Care: “Cast your care upon the Lord.” Hope: “The Lord is my hope from my youth.” Trust: “It is good to trust in the Lord.”

He speaks of the angels assigned to us, concerning whom the Lord says: “Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII). It is on their account that the Apostle forbids women to enter the church with their heads uncovered. Concerning them he also says elsewhere that angels have been sent in service for the sake of those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation.

Therefore, brothers, we must beware at every hour, as the Prophet says in the psalm, lest God at some hour see us turning toward evil and having become useless; and lest, while sparing us in this present time—because he is merciful and waits for us to change for the better—he say to us in the future: “You did these things, and I was silent” (Ps. LII).

For the one who turns toward evil is the person who first stood in the good; and whoever first stood in a state of uprightness, if he turns toward evil, has become a useless and wicked servant. Concerning such a soul the Prophet says: “How utterly vile you have become, repeatedly changing your ways” (Jer. II). That soul becomes wretched which, frequently descending from a state of uprightness, commits sin. Thus it has become both wretched and useless; yet forgiveness must not be denied even to such people.

But one must guard against this: he should mourn his past sin in such a way that he does not commit another sin to be mourned, and lest the Lord, seeing him sin frequently and waiting a long time for him to return to repentance, say to him unwilling to repent: “You did these things, and I was silent” (Ps. XLIX).

Earlier the Lord had said to the sinner: “You hated discipline and cast my words behind you” (Ps. XLIX), together with the other evils of sinners recorded there in abundance. Then, adding this, he spoke to the sinner in retribution, as though he were saying: “You have frequently committed these sins mentioned above, and I have not repaid you with the punishment deserved by your evil deed; rather, I was silent and waited for you to turn to repentance. I did not wish to repay evil for your evils, but I was silent and waited to reward you when you repented.”

For the Lord’s silence consists in not repaying the sinner evil for evil, but in waiting a long time for repentance. The Lord would not be silent toward the sinner but would answer him if he were immediately seeking vengeance for his evil deeds. But the one for whom he waits a long time to repent—if he does not repent—he suddenly strikes, so that he may perish.

### On the Second Step of Humility

The second step of humility is for a person, not loving his own will, not to take pleasure in fulfilling his desires, but to imitate in deeds that word of the Lord who says: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John VI).

Just as a person cannot serve both God and Mammon, so he cannot fulfill both his own will and the will of God. A vessel full of one drink cannot be filled with another unless it first empties what is harmful; only then can it be filled by drawing in what is beneficial. Nor can the vessel of one fleshly breast simultaneously contain the desires of the flesh and of divine majesty. As one set of desires departs, another succeeds: as vices depart from the mind, an abundance of virtues takes possession of it.

Therefore the carnal desires must be emptied from the treasury of our breast, so that an abundance of spiritual virtues may be received and spiritual desires coming from God may be retained. Hence it is written: “The tree of life is a desire that comes, and his desire will be given to the righteous” (Prov. XIII). But concerning the desire of the wicked it is written: “The desire of the wicked is a fortress of the worst things” (Prov. XII). And elsewhere it is written: “At the utterance of their desire, a quail rose for them from the sea, and afflictions came upon sinners” (Wis. XIX).

Our wills and desires must therefore be abandoned, so that by our deeds we may imitate that word of the Lord in which he says: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.” What follows is:

Scripture also says: “The will has punishment, and necessity produces a crown.” I confess that, unless I am mistaken, I have never read this in the divine Scriptures; and therefore I wish to seek not the sound of this sentence but rather its meaning. It says: “Pleasure has punishment, and necessity produces a crown.” It is as though it were saying: The broad and spacious way leads to the punishment of death; the narrow and constricted way leads to life, where those who endure necessities for the Lord receive eternal crowns.

Again the Lord says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. XVI; Luke IX). What else is it to deny oneself than to abandon the broad and spacious way and hate one’s own wills? What else is “take up his cross and follow me” than to seize the narrow and constricted way, where one endures many necessities for me? And thus, following me, to come to everlasting joys, where, with me granting it, one receives an eternal crown?

### On the Third Step of Humility
### On the Third Degree of Humility

The third degree of humility is that, for the love of God, one submit oneself in all obedience to one’s superior, imitating the Lord, [Col. 0817D] of whom the Apostle says: “He became obedient unto death” (Phil. 2). For if we love God as we ought, we must be ready not only to submit to our superior in all obedience but, if necessary, even to die for him, just as he died for us, as the Apostle says: “God commends his love toward us, because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Rom. 5). And we must be ready not only to die for him but also to lay down our lives for our brothers, as the same Apostle says: “By this we know his love, that he laid down his life for us; and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers” (1 John 3).

Let us therefore love God as sons love their father, [Col. 0818A] and for love of him let us remain subject to our superiors even unto death. For he, although he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings; and being found in appearance as a human being, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death. “See,” the Apostle says, “what sort of love the Father has given us, that we should be called and should be the children of God” (1 John 3). We shall therefore be perfect in love if, just as he first loved us for the sake of our salvation, so we too are ready, moved solely by love of him, both to submit to our superiors and to die for him.

### On the Fourth Degree of Humility

The fourth degree of humility is that, amid hard and adverse circumstances, or even whatever injuries may be inflicted, one embrace patience with a silent conscience. It frequently happens that the more a monk submits himself to humility and obedience, the more he finds things that he must bear harshly. Therefore, when anyone approaches the service of God, it is necessary for him to prepare his spirit courageously to endure everything, as it is written: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation. Crush your heart and endure” (Eccles. 2). Whether injuries inflicted by another or temptations arising within, let him endure them with a silent conscience and, with God’s help, conquer everything through patience.

For it is written: “In your patience you shall possess your souls.” Hence James says: “Knowing that the testing of your faith produces patience; but patience has its perfect work” (James 1). He means that you are tested by adversities so that you may learn the virtue of patience and thereby show and prove that you carry in your heart a firm faith in the reward that is to come. Paul likewise says: “Tribulation produces patience; and patience, testing” (Rom. 5). For patience produces testing, because the one whose patience cannot be overcome is thereby proved perfect.

The reason for this is that the faithful are exercised through patience, so that by it their faith may be proved to be perfect. Although the just person must provide useful examples to others through prosperous circumstances, he must also be touched by adversities, so that his patience may offer the rest a good example and, after death, he may receive the rewards of his patience. For whoever praises God for an injury inflicted upon him will undoubtedly lose the crimes he has committed and will eventually receive the rewards promised by God.

And let him endure without growing weary or departing, as Scripture says: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10; 24). A reward is promised to those who begin, but it is given to those who persevere. Our way of life is pleasing to God when we complete with a persevering end the good work that we begin.

That monk grows weary or departs who does not bring the regular work he has begun to perfection; who, in the very work he began with fervent spirit, gradually grows weak and lukewarm, and, becoming tepid, withdraws either from the work alone or from both the work and the monastery. He does not place before his eyes what Scripture especially urges upon monks, saying: “Trust in the Lord, and remain in your place” (Eccles. 2). Hence it continues:

“Let your heart be strengthened, and endure the Lord” (Ps. 26). It is as though it said: Act manfully, lest you fall into despair, and do not think that what was promised you long ago has been denied you merely because you do not yet receive it. Endure the Lord and hope in him without failing, so that at the proper time you may reap what you diligently work at here each day.

This exhortation is for good monks and also for all Christians: they must not allow the weakness of the flesh to draw them away from their right purpose, but, persevering in good works, must strive toward perseverance and remain constant in what is regularly enjoined upon them. Thus the hearts of those who endure are strengthened if, placing their hope in the Lord’s power, they strive toward perseverance in good work and, awaiting the Lord’s promises, do not despair of receiving their reward from the Lord.

To show that the faithful must endure everything, including adversity, for the Lord, Scripture speaks even in the voice of those who suffer: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are reckoned as sheep for slaughter” (Ps. 43). To be put to death means to encounter destruction through the long sufferings of the present life.

The strength of a good monk must neither be overcome when struck by various troubles nor yield to any enticements of pleasure; it must not be cast down by adversity or lifted up by prosperity, but must remain strengthened and unshaken against every vice. And just as a sheep led to slaughter neither cries out nor resists, [Col. 0819C] so a monk who possesses patience must not resist injury by crying out, murmuring, or fighting back. Rather, afflicted by many tribulations, he should say to the Lord with the Psalmist: “Because of the words of your lips I have kept to difficult paths.”

And secure in hope of divine reward, let them follow with joy, saying: “But in all these things we conquer through him who loved us” (Rom. 8). The saints, with God and for God, overcome all the tribulations of the present age, acting courageously for the sake of eternal reward. They overcome every adversity, and although they have the Lord, they are overcome by a thousand adversities. “If God is for us, who can be against us?” Hence the Apostle Peter says: “Who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good?” (1 Pet. 3).

He is speaking of what comes upon us from adversaries through insulting words, losses of bodily possessions, and bodily torments. When all these things are inflicted upon the faithful, they cannot harm them; rather, they bring the palm of patience to those who endure them calmly. But if anyone, overcome by such adversities, gives way, it is not the one who inflicted the evil but the person himself, who rejected these things impatiently, who has harmed him.

Elsewhere Scripture says: “You have tested us, O God; you have examined us by fire, as silver is examined by fire” (Ps. 65).
