The testing of monks takes place in the furnace of temptations and various tribulations. “We must,” says the Apostle, “enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations” (2 Cor. 2).

“You have examined us by fire,” he says, “as silver is examined.” The elect are therefore examined by the fire of tribulation, so that, cleansed from every impurity, they may be found worthy to come to the diadem of the eternal King. Unless silver is examined by fire, it remains dirty from its original condition. So also the hearts of human beings, unless they have been cleansed by the fire of the Holy Spirit, naturally remain dirty and unclean.

Therefore, lest they become soft like lead in the furnace of humility and tribulation, they must hold firmly the weapons of endurance and patience. For it is written: “Endure the temptations of the Lord, join yourself to God, and endure, so that your life may increase in the end. Accept everything that is brought upon you, and endure in suffering, and have patience in your humility; for gold and silver are tested in fire, but receptive human beings in the furnace of humiliation” (Eccles. 2).

“You brought us into a snare; you placed tribulations upon our back.” The expression “You brought us into a snare” speaks of the greatness of the tribulation, so that we may understand that every kind of tribulation comes upon the elect in this age, because they expect to receive every kind of glory from the Lord in the future. Whoever expects to receive the rewards of the future life endures all the evils of the present life calmly, because he tempers the bitterness of this life with the sweetness of that one.

What follows—“You placed tribulations upon our back”—agrees with the verse of the Psalm that says: “I was bent down and humbled exceedingly; I roared because of the groaning of my heart” (Ps. 37). Tribulations upon the back signify both a humbled spirit and a bent body. They indicate a body chastised by fasts and a heart contrite and humbled.

Those who do not bear the tribulations of salutary discipline upon their backs walk upright in body and carry a very fierce and swollen spirit. What follows says:

And to show that we ought to remain under a superior, he continues: “You placed human beings over our heads” (Ps. 65). According to the interpretation of blessed Benedict, this signifies abbots, under whom the monastic institution has decreed that monks live and whose commands they must obey. Under them it is fitting for monks to bow their heads and fulfill their just orders.

Moreover, fulfilling the Lord’s command amid adversity and injuries through patience, those who are struck on one cheek offer the other also; those who have their tunic taken away give up their cloak as well; those compelled to go one mile go two; with the Apostle Paul they endure false brothers and persecution; and they bless those who curse them (Matt. 5; Luke 6; 2 Cor. 2; 1 Cor. 4).

Other teachers of justice have interpreted this saying. Blessed Benedict, however, placed it here simply to give us an example of humility and patience. Whoever genuinely strives to fulfill it amid adversity and injuries will be able quickly to ascend to the summit of eternity. No one can fulfill it perfectly unless he has first laid in his heart the foundation of great patience and previously reached the summit of supreme humility.

The person who does not return evil for inflicted injury offers one cheek and the other to the one who strikes him. [Col. 0821A] The person who does not return a curse for a curse gives up his cloak as well as his tunic to the one who takes his tunic. The person who is not overcome by evil but conquers evil with good voluntarily goes two miles with the one who compels him to go one. Such a person undoubtedly endures false brothers patiently with Paul and, by blessing those who curse him, truly fulfills the commandment of humility.

### On the Fifth Degree of Humility

The fifth degree of humility is that a monk not conceal from his abbot, through humble confession, any evil thoughts that come into his heart or any evil deeds secretly committed by him. Hence Solomon says: “The one who hides his crimes will not be rightly directed; but whoever confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy” (Prov. 28).

The bitterness of repentance makes the spirit examine its deeds more carefully and recall with tears the gifts of God that it despised. It is already a large part of justice for a person inwardly to know himself—that he is evil—so that, recognizing his sins and confessing them to another, he may submit himself humbly to divine power. Hence Solomon again says: “Reveal your works to the Lord, and your thoughts will be directed” (Prov. 16). Therefore it is added here:

Scripture urges us concerning this matter, saying: “Reveal your way to the Lord” (Ps. 36). That is: reveal through confession to the abbot, whom the Lord has given you as his vicar, your actions in which the consciousness of sin lies hidden.

“And hope in the Lord” (ibid.), who mercifully grants you forgiveness for what you have committed.

Hence Cassiodorus says: “A kind of veil covers sins; therefore our way, that is, our life, is clothed in a dark covering of concealment. We reveal it when we confess our dark offenses most readily.” Paul revealed his way when he said: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5). He hoped in the Lord when he cried out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?”—“The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7).

Hence Augustine says: “What you have in your heart, make known in speech through confession. Hope in him, and he himself will act”—that is, he himself will forgive your sins and lead your works into love. It continues:

And again he says: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is everlasting” (Ps. 105). Hence Cassiodorus says: “He designates this confession as something to be applied as a remedy for repentance.” Yet there is no doubt that it also belongs to the praises of the Lord, since it is a greater glory of mercy to spare one who confesses than to grant favor to someone living without confession.

And lest anyone be frightened by the multitude of his faults, he added: “For he is good.” Who would hesitate to turn to one whom he hears wishing to come quickly to his aid? He added: “For his mercy is everlasting.” Having heard that the Lord is good, lest human negligence hold anyone back from earnest and diligent supplication, he declares the reason for the remedy, so that one ought rightly to hasten to prompt confession to the Lord.

“Everlasting” signifies the course of this life, in which all who sin are wretched; in which it is permitted for our hearts to be converted and mercy to be sought. For there confession of sin brings condemnation, where judgment is already known to exist.

And again the Prophet says: “I made my sin known to you, and I did not cover my iniquities” (Ps. 31). To make known means to bring one’s offense into confession; to cover means to wish to conceal something in silence or to hide the body through dissimulation. Fools do this, thinking that God can be ignorant of what they do.

But those who know that everything is manifest to him descend to humble confession and vows of repentance, lest they suffer as an enemy the judge whom they could have as a merciful advocate. It continues:

“I said: I will declare my iniquities against myself to the Lord; and you forgave the wickedness of my heart” (Ps. [Col. 0822B] 31). Here the great mercy of the Divinity is revealed: at the mere declaration of devotion he suddenly released the sins, judging a pious intention as though it were the completed action.

In his heart he said to the Lord that he would not conceal what he had done; and, as though he had already disclosed everything, he was forgiven those things that he intended to confess. My confession, therefore, was still in my heart and had not yet reached my lips. I had said, “I will declare against myself,” and nevertheless God, who heard my heart, forgave the wickedness of my sin.

### On the Sixth Degree of Humility

The sixth degree of humility is that a monk be content with every kind of lowliness and extremity. Great grace shines before God in the person who has been contemptible and lowly in this world. For it is truly necessary that the one whom the world hates should be loved by God.

The saints who love lowliness and renounce possessions and honors mortify themselves with respect to every earthly possession so that they may live happily with God in their inheritance. They love lowliness and extremity so that, through the mortification of this life, they may rise stronger to the life that is prepared for them eternally. It continues:

And in everything imposed upon him, let him judge himself to be a bad and unworthy laborer. A monk judges himself a bad laborer because he does not know how his work will be received by the Lord. We work outwardly, but inwardly we do not know how the work is received by the Lord.

He judges himself unworthy because, just as the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us, so our works, even though they are good, are not worthy of obtaining glory or eternal rewards.

Saying with the Prophet: “I was reduced to nothing and did not know” (Ps. 72). This is the voice of humility, not of fear; it is more the speech of a wise person than of one who lacks knowledge; it is the statement of one who humbles himself, not of one who exalts himself. For in this world the just person recognizes himself as foolish, so that he may be found wise before the Lord.

Hence Paul says: “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1). “I did not know,” he said—that is, “I recognized myself as ignorant.” I counted myself foolish and little, and despised myself as though I were without understanding. Whoever now humbly recognizes himself before himself as ignorant will one day rejoice as wise and exalted before God.

“I became like a beast before you, and I am always with you” (Ps. 72). Not a beast in the sense that I possessed foolishness of heart, but one who carried God with his whole body and heart. The Lord’s beast does not refuse to bear whatever burden is placed upon it; rather, enduring patiently, it carries it until it reaches the appointed place.

So also a monk must patiently endure and bear without murmuring whatever has been regularly imposed upon him by the abbot or by any other superior, until he reaches the end of his life, where, having laid down the burden of labor, he awaits from the Lord a fitting reward for his work.

[Col. 0823B]

### On the Seventh Degree of Humility

The seventh degree of humility is that a monk not merely declare with his tongue that he is lower and more contemptible than everyone else, but also believe it with the innermost affection of his heart. Whoever wishes to be higher in the kingdom must become lower in this world; and whoever wishes to be more honored must become more lowly and despised, according to the Lord’s saying: “Whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your servant. And whoever wishes to become greater among you shall be your minister,” and so forth (Mark 10).

A monk should then judge himself to be such when he considers himself the least, lower, and more contemptible of all the others. A monk lives in the monastery for this purpose: that, possessing a humbled spirit, he may offer the others an example of humility.

Hence the Apostle Peter says: “All of you show humility toward one another” (1 Pet. 5). The person who truly shows humility to others is the one who genuinely carries it in his heart; who does not present himself as great and exalted, but, as lowly and despised, composes and adapts himself to what is “great [and] pious” [reading uncertain]; who considers and presents himself as poor in spirit and as a little child in the midst of his brothers.

Hence blessed Gregory says: “It must be known above all that each soul is more precious in the eyes of God the more, for love of the truth, it has been despised in its own eyes.”

Humbling himself and saying with the Prophet: “But I am a worm and not a human being, the reproach of human beings and the outcast of the people” (Ps. 21). “I am a worm and not a human being” is said to intensify humility. A worm seems more humble and more contemptible than all living creatures. Since a worm is nourished from wood, the more fragile it is, the purer it is proved to be.

The monk is compared to it: the more despised, weak, and lowly he has been in this world, the holier and cleaner he is found before God. Of such people Solomon says: “The ants are a weak people that prepare food for themselves in the harvest” (Prov. 30).

But when he says, “the reproach of human beings and the outcast of the people,” he is referring to proud and boorish common people, who always despise the humble and reject the poor. They heap upon them whatever reproaches they can, hurl hostile words at them, and never cease slandering them in secret.

Hence Solomon says: “Bloodthirsty men hate the innocent, but the unjust [read: the just] seek his life” (Prov. 29). This distinction separates the children of God from the children of the devil: the children of the devil love and cherish the world, whereas the children of God love and cherish God. But the children of the devil cannot love a child of God who is separated from love of the world and devoted solely to heavenly desires. For, as he says above, the religion of a sinner is an abomination.

“I was exalted and humbled and confounded” (Ps. 87). This is shown to apply especially to the elect. One of them says that he was exalted when he previously considered human affairs with a puffed-up heart. “I was humbled,” he says, when, through the mercy of divine grace, he came to confession, the healing gift. He was confounded when, by professing repentance, he condemned the things he had done wrongly.

O blessed confusion, which removes eternal reproach! For whatever has fallen under the guilt of the repentant person is restored as absolved throughout everlasting ages.

And again: “It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I may learn your commandments” (Ps. 118). He explains that he tastes that sweetness which is proved to surpass all delights, saying: “It is good for me that you humbled me”—that is, so that I might learn the abundance of your commandments, which previously, puffed up and proud, I could not receive.

This humility touches the glorious heights of Jerusalem. For just as pride plunges one into Tartarus, so humility lifts one to heaven. He subsequently explains what reward this humiliation possesses when he says: “So that I may learn your commandments.” The commandments are learned perfectly when the Lord’s precepts are faithfully fulfilled—when what is understood with a right heart is accomplished in effective work.

### On the Eighth Degree of Humility

The eighth degree of humility is that a monk do nothing except what the common rule of the monastery or the examples of his superiors encourage. It is as though he said: A monk should not devise a new institution according to his own judgment, but should do everything he sees others doing, fully perform what he sees the others perform, firmly observe what is contained in the Rule, and readily complete everything in deeds. Thus, finally, in due order he will reach the pattern of the fathers who came before him.

He should receive an example of humility from Christ, of devotion from Peter, of love from John, of obedience from Abraham, of patience from Isaac, of endurance from Jacob and Job, of chastity from Joseph, of gentleness from Moses, [Col. 0824D] of steadfastness from Joshua, of kindness from Samuel, of mercy from David, and of abstinence from Daniel.

So too, the holy monk should consider the other deeds of the devout: with what labor, moderation, intention, or compunction they are carried out. He should imitate them so that, with Christ’s help, his own work may be extended toward their example.

### On the Ninth Degree of Humility

The ninth degree of humility is that a monk restrain his tongue from speaking and, maintaining silence, not speak until questioned, as Scripture shows: “Sin will not be avoided in much speaking” (Prov. 10). Therefore a monk must restrain his tongue from speaking, lest he fall into the sin of excessive speech.

Silence nourishes many virtues, whereas talkativeness scatters even virtues that have already been nourished. Hence Solomon says: “Like an open city without the circuit of walls is a man who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking” (Prov. 23). An open city without a barrier does not preserve unharmed what it holds within unless, at the appropriate time, it is closed with bolts or a wall. So too, unless a monk restrains his tongue from speaking, he loses through the vice of talkativeness the virtues he holds inwardly, unless he sets a guard and a door over his mouth. It continues:

“And because a talkative man will not be established upon the earth” (Ps. 139). Although those who are eloquent through the abundance of their language can also be called talkative, this name is especially given to those who are wordy through inconsiderate speech.

Thus the Apostle James warns those who are opposed to the wise and speak in a contrary manner: “Let every person be quick to hear but slow to speak” (James 1). Such people are not established upon the earth, because through their instability they frequently go astray. For it is difficult for an unconsidered word to be right.

### On the Tenth Degree of Humility

The tenth degree of humility is that a monk not be quick and ready to laugh, because it is written: “A fool raises his voice in laughter” (Eccles. 21). Lightness of spirit makes a monk always quick and ready to laugh. He does not carry the fear of the Lord in his heart; therefore he wishes to laugh loudly and constantly with loud laughter.

He does not pay attention to what the Apostle James urges us, saying: “Be miserable, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow” (James 4). Hence Solomon says: “Laughter will be mixed with sorrow, and mourning takes possession of the end of joy” (Prov. 24). Again he himself says: “I considered laughter an error, and I said to joy: Why are you deceived in vain?” (Eccles. 2).

Mourning therefore suits a monk more than laughter, because through mourning one comes to joy, as it is written: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5). Through laughter, however, one comes to weeping, as it is written: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall weep and mourn” (Luke 6)!

As was said above, laughter is not altogether forbidden to human beings, because it is naturally known to have been granted to them alone among all creatures. But to avoid the vice of frivolity, being quick to laugh and laughing loudly are forbidden.

[Col. 0825D]

### On the Eleventh Degree of Humility

The eleventh degree of humility is that, when a monk speaks, he speak gently and without laughter, humbly and with gravity, using few and reasonable words.

“Gently”—that is, temperately and calmly—a monk ought to speak, because it is written: “The words of the prudent shall be weighed on the scales” (Eccles. 21). Gentleness proceeds equally from the source of sweetness and peace. Hence Solomon says: “A sweet word multiplies friends, appeases enemies, and a gracious tongue abounds in a good person” (Eccles. 6). Again he himself says: “Well-arranged words are a honeycomb” (Prov. 6). Well-arranged words both dignify the speaker and provide grace to those who hear them.

He added: “And without laughter.” Words full of laughter [Col. 0826A] reveal a monk to be either foolish, frivolous, or certainly vain. A monk should speak humbly and with gravity, because it is written: “Do not be hasty with your tongue” (Eccles. 4); and: “Whoever hates loquacity extinguishes wickedness” (Eccles. 19).

“And let him speak few and reasonable words.” Few, because it is written: “In much speaking you will not avoid sin, and whoever uses many words will injure his soul” (Prov. 10). Reasonable, because it is written: “Whoever restrains his lips is most prudent” (ibid.).

Few, because it is written: “A fool multiplies words. And where there are many words, there is often want” (Eccles. 10). Reasonable, because it is written: “A wise person will remain silent until the proper time, but the frivolous and imprudent will not observe the proper time. And the one who is impudent in speaking is hateful” (Eccles. 20). And: “The person who is inconsiderate in speaking will experience evils” (Prov. 13).

And let him not be loud in voice. As an imitator of Christ, a monk ought to be silent, not loud. For it is written of the Lord: “He will not cry out, nor will his voice be heard outside” (Isa. 42). Silence is more fitting for a monk than shouting. A subdued voice shows propriety, whereas a loud voice shows frivolity. A loud voice often makes a person hateful, while a subdued one makes him lovable.

Hence it is written: “The wise person makes himself lovable in words” (Eccles. 20). He is lovable because he speaks prudent, reasonable, and gracious words. Hence Basil says: “The measure of the voice is determined by the manner of hearing. For if the voice is louder than necessary, when the person to whom one speaks is able to hear, even if we are reading aloud, it is no longer a voice but a shout”—unless, perhaps, the hearing of the person to whom he speaks is impaired and necessity compels him to shout.

Hence Fructuosus says: “It is not fitting for a monk to be loud or ridiculous in speech. Whoever is such a person, and, although often corrected, has not been reformed, must be treated with blows and corrected severely.” It continues:

As it is written: “The wise person is made known by few words” (Eccles. 20). “Is made known,” he says—that is, he makes known outwardly to others what he is inwardly in himself. The wisdom he kept secretly in his heart he shows to others by bringing it forth in speech. The person who was hidden and known only to himself brings himself into public through speaking.

Where this tradition says, “The wise person is made known by few words” (Eccles. 20), another says: “The wise person brings himself forth in words” (ibid.)—that is, he brings forth outwardly in speaking what he is inwardly while silent.

### On the Twelfth Degree of Humility

The twelfth degree of humility is that a monk not only show humility in his heart but also always display it bodily to those who see him. A monk must truly retain humility inwardly and demonstrate it outwardly to those who see him, so that he may please the inward Judge within and offer outwardly to everyone an example of humility.

Thus, shaped by the virtue of humility in both respects, he should be found humble in heart and humble in body: humble inwardly in spirit and humble outwardly in bodily appearance, [Col. 0827A] so that those who see his example may praise and glorify God, who granted him the foundation of humility and steadfastness in work.

That is, in his work, in the oratory. Specifically, while praying, singing psalms, hymns, canticles, or performing any other work of God in that sanctuary, he must always keep his head bowed.

In the monastery, in the garden, on the road, in the field, or wherever he may sit, walk, or stand, he should always have his head inclined and his eyes fixed upon the ground, considering himself at every hour guilty on account of his sins and imagining himself already being brought before God’s fearful judgment. He should always say in his heart what that evangelical publican said, with his eyes fixed upon the ground: “Lord, I am not worthy—I am a sinner—to lift my eyes to heaven” (Luke 18).

How much confidence in forgiveness this rightly gives to penitents: the publican, who perfectly recognized the guilt of his wickedness, wept and confessed. Although he came to the temple unjust, he returned from the temple justified. One, through pride, departed humiliated; the other, through lamentation, deserved to draw near exalted, because “everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Matt. 23).

Therefore, from the words of the proud Pharisee, by which he deserved to be humbled, we can conversely take a model of the humility by which we may be exalted. Just as he, considering the vices of the worse and his own virtues, was lifted up to his injury, so may we, examining not only our own laziness but also the virtues of those who are better, be humbled toward glory.

Thus let each of us entreat this within himself, submissively: “Almighty God, have mercy on your suppliant, because I am not like countless servants of yours who are exalted by contempt for the world, glorious through the merit of justice, angelic in the praise of chastity, or even like many of those who, after public crimes, deserved through repentance to become devoted to you. Even if I do anything good through your gracious gift, I do not know with what end I do it or with what strictness it will be weighed by you.”

And again with the Prophet: “I have been bent down and humbled utterly.” Whoever remembers the height of eternal rest sees how greatly he has been humbled in this corruption of the flesh. Let us therefore mourn and groan in confession, recognize where we are, remember the height of eternal rest, and patiently await what he promised who showed us in himself an example of patience and humility.

He said that he was bent down from a state of exaltation and humbled from the inflation of pride.

And again with the Prophet: “I have been bent down and humbled utterly” (Ps. 118). That is: I who formerly was exalted in the world have now been bent down and humbled under God. I who formerly was exalted in worldly glory have now been bent down and humbled in the poverty of repentance. I who formerly was exalted in worldly appearance have now been bent down and humbled under the hand of almighty God. Or, he was bent down in body and humbled in spirit.

What he says—“utterly”—is understood as meaning from every side and in every respect. For humility, which is the teacher and mother of all virtues, must be held firmly in the heart and demonstrated bodily to everyone.

Therefore, after ascending all these degrees of humility, a monk will soon arrive at that love of God which perfectly casts out fear. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5).

This is the perfect love of which the Apostle John says: “There is no fear in love” (1 John 4)—namely, in such love as knows, in imitation of divine goodness, how to do good even to enemies and to love them. “Perfect love,” he says, “casts out fear” (ibid.), specifically the fear of which it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Eccles. 1). Through this fear, a beginner fears while undertaking works of justice, lest the strict Judge come and condemn him as insufficiently corrected.

But perfect love also drives from the spirit the fear of present adversities. The person who sought to possess it prayed to the Lord: “Deliver my soul from fear of the enemy” (Ps. 63). And the one who said, “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution?” and so forth (Rom. 8), possessed it as well.

Fear indeed spurs us on—but do not be afraid. Love enters, driving out fear and healing what had been wounded by the pain of fear.

Through it, he will begin to observe all the things that he previously kept with no little fear, without any labor, as though naturally, through the force of habit. At first a person comes to the practice of conversion with inward fear and apprehension; but after he has persevered for a long time in Christ’s service and his conduct has persisted in good habit, charity succeeding, he is free from fear and dread. What he formerly did with fearful anxiety, he begins to keep with the love of sweetness; and, as though naturally, he begins gently to observe what he had previously begun to do harshly and fearfully. Hence it follows:

No longer from fear of hell, but from love of Christ, habit itself, and delight in the virtues, which the Lord will now deign to reveal through the Holy Spirit in His worker, cleansed from vices and sins. Many, as was said above, begin to do good from fear of punishments, but complete it through love of Christ. They begin from fear, but as they go from virtue to virtue, they pass into the perfect love of Christ. What previously, through harmful ignorance, they feared to do, they no longer fear to do, instructed now by habit and knowledge. They desire to possess an abundance of virtues, and therefore strive to do good works and hasten to cleanse themselves quickly from vices. Having received the gift of the Holy Spirit, they delight in what is just, holy, and right, and they strive keenly to fulfill what delights them, so that they may deserve to become the temple of Him to whom, from the beginning of their conversion, they vowed that they would belong as monks; so that the apostolic saying may be fulfilled in them: “You are God’s temple, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you” (II Cor. XVI). Taught by that Holy Spirit, they do what must be done; assisted by Him, they bring it to perfection; drawn by Him through desire, they run the course of good action; and by running they advance from virtue to virtue and strive to reach the everlasting prize, where they may be filled with every good and with eternal joy. Amen.

And lest the inexperienced suppose that these twelve degrees of humility were set down by blessed Benedict in confusion, I shall briefly disclose their order. The first degree of humility therefore begins with fear. The second is that the monk fulfill not his own will but the Lord’s. The third speaks of the perfection of obedience. The fourth concerns the endurance of patience. The fifth is that each person disclose his hidden thoughts to his abbot. The sixth is that the monk love lowliness and the lowest place. The seventh is that he proclaim with his voice, believe in his heart, and show by his works that he is inferior and baser than the others. The eighth is that the monk do nothing except what the common rule and the examples of his elders encourage. The ninth is that the monk restrain his tongue from speaking. The tenth is that he not be quick to laugh. The eleventh is that he speak gently and without laughter. The twelfth is that in every place he demonstrate by heart and deed, before all who see him, his humility.

Having ascended all these degrees of humility, the monk will happily come to the vision of the Almighty, where he will enjoy, with his Lord, the blessed joy that will never be taken from him. For “they will go from strength to strength,” that is, they ascend from one degree of virtue to another; and thus they will see the God of gods in Zion and in the heavenly Jerusalem, with exaltation and joy.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the divine offices at night. [Col. 0829C]

In winter, that is, from the Kalends of November until Easter, according to a reasonable calculation, one should rise at the eighth hour of the night, so that one may rest a little longer after midnight and rise having already digested. This phrase, “a little longer after midnight,” may be understood as the whole seventh hour of the night and half of the eighth. Then, when the signal has been struck, let all rise together; and let that remaining half of the eighth hour be distributed among the intervals between the signals, so that the nocturnal praise of the psalms may begin at the ninth hour of the night.

For elsewhere he says similarly: “After rising at the sixth hour, let there be rest after the office, and let the ninth hour be performed in the middle of the eighth hour.” Here he shows that the whole seventh hour of the day and half of the eighth are to be spent sleeping. The same meaning seems to me to be set down here: after six hours of the night, let there still be rest for the whole seventh hour and half of the eighth; then, after the interval marked by the signals, beginning at approximately the half-hour, let them, alert in mind and with unwearied bodies, render the office of divine praise to our Lord Jesus Christ from the ninth hour of the night.

But when he says, “and let them rise having already digested,” this seems to the inexperienced to have been written absurdly and ridiculously; yet to those who understand correctly it is shown to have been usefully and appropriately said. For *digestum* means cooked, consumed, or even carried onward, or certainly evaporated. Hence “let them rise having digested” is understood here to mean that, with the food already cooked in the stomach’s vessel and carried down into the belly, and with sleep evaporated, they should rise.

In another place, concerning this same matter, a certain master of the monks says: “For this reason we have said that the night offices should be joined with the morning offices after the cockcrow, so that the brothers, having digested their sleep, may soberly complete the work of God with an alert and clear mind, and may understand what they say. For this reason an interval is appointed, so that the heaviness of sleep may be ended during the long night. Otherwise, when in the short nights the brothers are compelled to rise before the crowing of the cock, still raw from the beginning of sleep—while, in the very rush of the veins, blood and moisture boil through them, and the members, aroused by the harmony of heaviness in sleep, are still digesting the food they have taken, uncooked in the fire of slaughter—they will flee the gifts of the Holy Spirit when they begin to rise: not awakened but rather killed, with a still heavy head and an undigested belch.”

It follows:

What remains after the vigils is to be devoted to meditation by the brothers who need something from the Psalter or from the readings. Here blessed Benedict does not command them to sleep, as some wish, but to keep watch; he does not command healthy men to rest in their beds, but to devote themselves to meditation. For it is written: “On my bed I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him” (Song III). Christ the Beloved is not found on the bed of carnal pleasures, but in holy labors, sacred vigils, and frequent prayers. He is found not in the torpor of sleep, but in the prayer of vigils and in the compunction of prayer.

Hence Cassian says: “Some, in ignorance, after completing the morning hymns, return again to sleep. This must not be done in any way, lest our purification, acquired through humble confession before dawn, be polluted either by some emerging excess of natural fluids, or be corrupted by the enemy’s illusion, or else lest even the refreshment of a pure and simple sleep, intervening, interrupt the fervor of our spirit and, having been made lukewarm by the torpor of sleep, carry us throughout the whole day thereafter inactive and sluggish.”

Again he himself says: “No one should afterward, following the purification of the nocturnal vigils, dissolve into the repose of sleep again until, when day has come, divine action succeeds nocturnal meditation; lest perhaps the jealous devil contaminate our purity, acquired through psalms and prayers, by some deception of sleep.”

Hence Aurelius says in his Rule: “After the morning prayers it is not permitted to return to sleep.” But, as the Rule says: “From Easter until the Kalends of November mentioned above, the hour at which the vigils are to be performed should be so regulated that, after the very brief interval preserved for the brothers to go out for the necessities of nature, the morning offices, which are to be performed at the beginning of daylight, may immediately follow.”

## CHAPTER IX. How many psalms are to be said at the nocturnal hours.

In winter, after the verse has first been said, “O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me” (Ps. LXIX), the following is to be said three times at the second: “O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise” (Ps. L). Just as, out of reverence for the Holy Trinity, “Holy” is said three times, so in this supplication, through the threefold opening of the lips, prayer is made to the Holy Trinity itself so that, after the opening of the lips, the mouth of the Lord’s servants may worthily announce praise to the Lord. The mouth is both a bodily member and the hidden place of the heart. Hence divine praise is sung effectively.

The third psalm and the *Gloria* are to follow it. The psalm is appointed for action; the *Gloria* is divine praise, which the angels sing in heaven and human beings on earth, just as that divine hymn begins: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II).

After this, Psalm 94 is to be sung with an antiphon, or at any rate chanted. *Antiphon* is interpreted from the Greek as “reciprocal voice,” namely, with two people singing the psalms alternately, changing places in order. The Greeks are said to have invented this kind of psalmody. Among the Latins, however, most blessed Ambrose first established antiphons. [Col. 0831B]

Then let the Ambrosian follow—that is, the hymn. He calls it “Ambrosian,” either because it is divine or heavenly, that is, inspired by God or from heaven. Others wish the Ambrosian to be so called from Ambrose, the master of hymns.

Then let six psalms with antiphons follow. When these have been said, after the verse has been recited, let the abbot give the blessing. That is, after the singer has said the verse, let the abbot say: “Through the prayers of all his saints, may the Lord save and bless us,” or some other blessing of this kind.

With everyone seated on benches, let the readings be read in turn by the brothers from a book. “In turn” means by turns, alternately, or mutually: that is, now this one, now that one; now from this side, now from that.

Three readings are to be given at the lectern. It is called a lectern because from it the divine discourse is either read or preached; for among the Greeks *logos* means “discourse.”

Among these, three responsories are also to be sung. Two responsories are to be said without the *Gloria*. After the third reading, however, the singer is to say the *Gloria*. As soon as the cantor begins to say it, everyone is immediately to rise from his seat, out of honor and reverence for the Holy Trinity.

At the vigils, books of divine authority are to be read, both of the Old Testament and of the New. That is: the books of Moses—Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy; Judges; Ruth; Kings; Chronicles; Job; Psalms; Solomon; the Book of Wisdom; Ecclesiasticus; Tobit; Esther; Judith; Ezra; the Prophets, namely Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi; and Maccabees.

The four books of the Gospels, namely Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. The fourteen Epistles of Paul: one to the Romans; two to the Corinthians; one to the Galatians; one to the Ephesians; one to the Philippians; two to the Thessalonians; one to the Colossians; two to Timothy; one to Titus; one to Philemon; one to the Hebrews; one of James; two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude; the Acts of the Apostles; and the Apocalypse.

Also, the expositions of these books composed by the most renowned orthodox and catholic Fathers. Men are called *orthodox* when they are catholic, right in faith, and approved in life. For among the Greeks *ortho* means “right,” while *doxa* is called “glory.” Thus orthodox men may be called men of right glory. *Catholic*, however, is interpreted as “universal” or “general.” For they are not separated from the universal Church through heresy or schism.

After these three readings with their responsories, let the remaining six psalms follow, to be sung with the *Alleluia*. After these, let the reading of the Apostle follow, to be recited from memory; then the verse and the supplication of the litany, that is, “Kyrie eleison”; and thus let the nocturnal vigils end. For among the Greeks *Kyrie* means “Lord,” while *eleison* is interpreted as “have mercy.” Likewise, *Christe eleison* is interpreted as “Christ, have mercy.”

## CHAPTER X. How the nocturnal praise is to be performed in summer.

From Easter until the Kalends of November, let the entire quantity of psalmody be retained, as stated above, except that the readings from a book are not to be read, because of the shortness of the nights. Instead of those three readings, let one reading from the Old Testament be recited from memory, followed by a brief responsory; and let all the rest be completed as stated—that is, let no fewer than twelve psalms ever be said at the nocturnal vigils, apart from Psalms 3 and 94.

## CHAPTER XI. How the vigils are to be performed on Sundays.

On Sunday one should rise earlier for the vigils. At these vigils the prescribed measure is to be maintained: six psalms, arranged in melody as we established above, and the verse. “Earlier” means sooner, before, in advance. *Temperius* is a comparative formed from the primitive adverb *tempore*, just as *tardius* is formed from *tarde* and *citius* from *cito*. “Arranged in melody” means that the six psalms are sung, composed or formed in the voice. For *modulation* means the sweetness or pleasantness of singing that is produced in a melodious, resonant voice.

With everyone seated in an orderly manner and by rank on the benches, let four readings with their responsories be read from a book, as we said above. Only in the fourth responsory is the singer to say, “Glory.” As soon as he begins it, let everyone rise with reverence.

After these readings, let another six psalms with antiphons follow in order, as before, together with the verses. After these, let four other readings with their responsories again be read in the order given above. For just as he wishes twelve psalms to be sung fully on Sunday, so he wishes twelve readings to be read and the same number of responsories to be sung.

After these, let three canticles from the Prophets be said, those which the abbot has appointed. For the abbot ought to appoint canticles that are suitable to the seasons, festivals, and days.

Let these canticles be sung with the *Alleluia*. Moses first introduced canticles when, after Egypt had been struck by the ten plagues and Pharaoh had been submerged with his people, he went out rejoicing through the unfamiliar paths of the sea toward the desert, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously exalted” (Exod. XV). Later Deborah, a woman of no low standing, is found to have performed this ministry in the Book of Judges; afterward many—not only men but also women—filled with the divine Spirit, are found to have sung the mysteries of God.

After the verse has also been said and the abbot has given the blessing, let four other readings from the New Testament be read in the order given above. After the fourth responsory, let the abbot begin the hymn, *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise you, O God.” When it has been completed, let the abbot read a Gospel lesson, with everyone standing in honor and trembling. When it has been read, let everyone respond, “Amen.” Immediately afterward, let the abbot sing the hymn, *Te decet laus*—“Praise befits you.” After the blessing has been given, let them begin Matins.

He says that the abbot should begin the hymn and read the Gospel lesson; nevertheless, not all abbots ought or are able to do these things. Some ought not, because guilt prevents them; others cannot, because necessity compels them. There are abbots who perform neither the ministry of a priest nor that of a Levite, and therefore cannot read the most holy Gospel. They do not hold the office of cantor, and therefore cannot begin the Ambrosian hymn in a high voice. Yet, with heavenly assistance, they can govern the flock entrusted to them, and for this reason they are chosen to perform the office of abbot.

Nevertheless, if the abbot ought to perform the work well or is able to do so, let him do it. But if he cannot, let him permit one who can to do it, according to what blessed Benedict himself commanded elsewhere, saying: “Let no one presume to sing and lead unless he can fulfill that office, so that those who hear may be edified.”

But what he says—after the Gospel reading has been completed, let everyone respond “Amen”—seems to many to have been said and done improperly. For they say that it is not fitting to respond “Amen” at every ending of the Gospel, and therefore that it seems superfluous to have it written and stated.

They should be answered as follows. *Amen* has two meanings among the Latins: one belonging to a person praying or expressing a wish, when it is used in the sense of “let it be,” as in “And all the people said, Amen, amen,” meaning “let it be, let it be”; and one belonging to a person affirming, as in “Amen, I say to you,” and so forth. You will never find the end of a Gospel without one of these two meanings. Therefore it is not improper but entirely suitable and reasonable for us to respond “Amen” at the end of every Gospel, so that by saying “Amen” we may show either that we faithfully believe what has been foretold or that, by wishing and praying, we desire to obtain what has been promised for our benefit.

Let this order of the vigils be observed equally on Sunday throughout the whole year, in summer as in winter—unless, God forbid, they rise late and something must be shortened from the readings or responsories. Yet every effort must be made to prevent this from occurring. If it does occur, let the person through whose negligence it happened make worthy satisfaction to God in the oratory.

To make worthy satisfaction is to undergo the regular punishment according to the measure of the fault. For someone who is judged severely for a light fault, or lightly for a serious fault, does not seem to make worthy satisfaction. He therefore commands that the person through whose fault it happened make satisfaction in the oratory, so that, because he sinned by acting negligently toward all the brothers, he may be seen by all to be making satisfaction and, for his offense, may seek mercy and forgiveness from the Almighty on behalf of all.

## CHAPTER XII. How the solemnity of Matins is to be performed.

*Solemnity* means a festival of religious observance, an assembly’s joy, which is customarily celebrated with a gathering of gladness. *Solemnity* received its name from the fact that it is customary.

On Sunday at Matins, Psalm 66 is first to be said without an antiphon, straight through. After it, Psalm 50 is to be said with the *Alleluia*. After that, Psalms 117 and 62 are to be said. Then follow the benedictions and praises; one reading from the Apocalypse, recited from memory; the responsory; the Ambrosian hymn; the verse; a canticle from the Gospel; the litany; and it is complete.

## CHAPTER XIII. How Matins is to be performed on ordinary days.

By “ordinary days” he means days of public offices, days that are external or set apart. *Privari* is also used in a bad sense, as Jacob says to Rachel: “Am I in God’s place, who has deprived you of the fruit of your womb?” (Gen. XXX). One also speaks of a “private friend,” that is, one separated from others and joined to the rest more intimately in friendship.

On ordinary days, the solemnity of Matins is to be performed as follows. Psalm 66 is to be said without an antiphon, shortening it slightly as on Sunday, so that everyone may assemble for Psalm 50, which is to be said with an antiphon. After it, two other psalms are to be said according to custom: on Monday, Psalms 5 and 35; on Tuesday, Psalms 42 and 56; on Wednesday, Psalms 63 and 64; on Thursday, Psalms 87 and 89; on Friday, Psalms 75 and 91; and on Saturday, Psalm 142 and the canticle of Deuteronomy, which is to be divided into two *Glorias*. On the other days, one canticle from the Prophets is to be said on its appointed day, as the Roman Church sings it.

After these, let the praises follow; then one reading from the Apostle, to be recited from memory; the responsory; the Ambrosian hymn; the verse; a canticle from the Gospel; the litany; and it is complete.

The morning or evening office must never pass without the Lord’s Prayer being said by the prior, with everyone listening, at the final order, because of the thorns of scandals that are accustomed to arise in a monastery. Thus, bound by the pledge of that prayer—“Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI)—they may cleanse themselves from such a fault. In the other offices, only the final part of that prayer is to be said, so that all may respond: “But deliver us from evil.”

Here *plane*, “plainly,” is sometimes used as an adverb of affirmation, as the Prophet says: “I said plainly: This iniquity is great, and I shall bear it” (Ezek. XIV). But here it is used as the conjunction “nevertheless” or “for.”

The thorns of scandals are understood in this passage to mean anger, quarrels, dissensions, detractions, rivalries, or any contentious disputes that are accustomed to arise among the brothers. While maintaining peace with one another and preserving continual charity, the monks ought to cleanse themselves from these things in the morning and evening. In the morning, so that none of these vices may remain in anyone until sunset, because it is written: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger.” In the evening, so that no vice may remain through the night until sunrise and make the monk guilty of sins and foul in the sight of the Lord in the morning.

Thus, bound—that is, by the promise of the Lord’s Prayer, which says, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI)—each person should forgive his brother from the heart. Then, cleansed, that is, corrected from his vices, let him either in the morning proceed to perform the work of obedience or in the evening proceed to celebrate the nocturnal vigils.

In the other offices—that is, in the celebration of the other hours—only the final part of that prayer, “And lead us not into temptation,” is to be said in a loud voice, so that, after all have heard it, they may respond, “But deliver us from evil.”

## CHAPTER XIV. How the vigils are to be performed on the anniversaries of the saints.

By “the anniversaries of the saints” he means their festivals and solemnities, on which they migrated happily from this world to heaven. They are dead to us, but to God, His angels, and His saints they live forever. They are absent from us, but to them they are visible and present. They are dead to us, but born to them.

No one ought to find it strange if someone who has departed from this life is called “born.” For just as a person is customarily said to be born when, coming forth from his mother’s womb, he enters this light, so he can most rightly be called born when, released from the bonds of the flesh, he is raised into eternal light. Hence ecclesiastical custom has established that the days of blessed martyrs or confessors of Christ who have passed from this world be called, in ordinary speech, their “birthdays”—not funeral observances but birthdays.

At the festivals of the saints, and at all solemnities, let the office be performed as we said it should be on Sunday, except that the psalms, antiphons, or readings belonging to that particular day are to be said. The measure stated above is to be retained.

## CHAPTER XV. At what times the *Alleluia* is to be said.

From holy Easter until Pentecost, let the *Alleluia* be said without interruption, both in the psalms and in the responsories. “Without interruption” means that wherever it ought to be said, both in the psalms and in the responsories, it is not to be omitted casually but is to be said regularly and firmly.

From Pentecost until the beginning of Lent, however, let it be said at the nocturnal offices on every night only with the six later psalms. Although blessed Benedict commands that from Pentecost until the beginning of Lent the *Alleluia* be said at the nocturnal offices with the six later psalms, it nevertheless pleased the synod assembled in the kingdom of the Franks that, just as the Roman leaders of the Church abandon the *Alleluia* in Septuagesima, so the monks established in that kingdom should also abandon it.

On every Sunday outside Lent, let the canticles, Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, and None be said with the *Alleluia*; let Vespers, however, be said with an antiphon. Responsories are never to be said with the *Alleluia*, except from Easter until Pentecost.

## CHAPTER XVI. How the divine offices are to be performed during the day.

As the Prophet says: “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Ps. CXVIII). The phrase “seven times a day” signifies always. This number is customarily an indication of totality, because the whole world revolves through seven days, and by their number the Lord created all the times of the days. This number is said to be especially sacred because of the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, which is mercifully distributed to those who fear God. Hence it follows:

This sacred number seven will be fulfilled by us if, at the times of Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline, we perform the offices of our service, since the Prophet spoke of these hours of the day: “Seven times a day I have praised you.” Concerning the nocturnal vigils, the same Prophet says: “At midnight I rose to confess to you.”

Therefore, at these times, let us offer praises to our Creator for the judgments of His justice: at Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline; and at night let us rise to confess to Him.

Cassian says concerning these same hours: “The arrangement of the hours during which we render services to God throughout the entire day is as follows. Prime is for the beginning of the day; Terce, because the Holy Spirit is first shown to have descended upon the apostles at that hour; Sext, because at that hour our Lord Jesus Christ, the immaculate sacrifice, was suspended on the cross and freed those subject to Him from the eternal bonds of sins; None, because at that hour our Lord, descending to the underworld, freed the souls of the saints that were held shut in darkness and carried them with Himself to heaven at Compline; while the twelfth hour is for the ending of the day, just as Prime is sung at its beginning.”

Prime and Compline, the twelfth hour, were afterward added by the Fathers for the beginning and ending of the day. We read that Terce, Sext, and None were also celebrated by the apostles. For at the third hour the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles as they were engaged in the office of prayer. At the sixth hour, we read that Peter, while praying in a small boat and suddenly in an ecstasy of mind, saw a vessel lowered from heaven, like a linen cloth, having four beginnings. Concerning None we read: “Peter and John were going up into the temple at the ninth hour, the hour of prayer” (Acts III).

We read that evening and morning prayers were offered in the Lord’s temple not only by the apostles but also in the Old Testament. Hence David says concerning Vespers: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight; the lifting up of my hands as an evening sacrifice” (Ps. CXL). Concerning Matins he says: “O God, my God, to you I keep watch from the dawn; and in the morning I will meditate upon you, for you have been my helper” (Ps. LXVII).

## CHAPTER XVII. How many psalms are to be sung at these hours.

We have now set out the order of psalmody for the nocturnal offices and Matins; let us now consider the subsequent hours.

At Prime, let three psalms be said individually and not under a single *Gloria*. The hymn for that hour is to follow the verse, “O God, come to my assistance,” before the psalms begin. After the three psalms have been completed, let one reading, the verse, and “Kyrie eleison” be recited, and let the office be dismissed.

Terce, Sext, and None are celebrated in the same order: the verse; the hymns of those hours; three psalms; a reading; the verse; “Kyrie eleison”; and dismissal. If the congregation is large, let them be sung with antiphons; if it is small, let them be sung straight through.

Let the evening assembly end with four psalms with antiphons. After these psalms, a reading from the Apostle is to be recited; then the responsory, the Ambrosian hymn, the verse, a canticle from the Gospel, the litany, and the Lord’s Prayer; and let the office be dismissed.

Let Compline end with the recitation of three psalms. These psalms are to be said straight through without an antiphon. After them come the hymn of that hour, one reading, the verse, “Kyrie eleison,” and the blessing; afterward let the office be dismissed.

Where he says in other places, “and it is complete,” in this concluding formula he says, “and they are dismissed,” repeating the phrase “let them be dismissed.” For the prayers of the office, which we complete and send to God, are called *missae* because they are celebrated in His honor. In another sense, prayers—that is, collects—said by the priest at the end of the course are called *missae*, meaning sent to God. They are sent by the priest but received by God. Hence, when a litany is celebrated in the Church on some solemn occasion, it is lifted up in a loud voice and, through the ministry of the priest, is already sent to God.

## CHAPTER XVIII. In what order the psalms are to be said.

At all the daytime hours, the verse is always to be said first: “O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me,” followed by the *Gloria*. Hence Cassiodorus says: “We ask for assistance when we are subject to danger, so that, lifted up by some remedy, we may be able to overcome the calamities of various sufferings.”

“Attend,” he says, means “look favorably,” because the Lord recognizes everything even when He is not asked. “Make haste,” therefore, is said to the Lord by one who hastened to be freed from the ruin of this world.

The eloquent Cassianus, discussing the usefulness of this passage at length in the tenth Conference, celebrates it generally with such honor that, whatever the monks undertake, they do not begin without the thrice-repeated use of this verse. By joining it repeatedly with renewed praise, he proves that remembrance of it is exceedingly useful.

Then comes the hymn of each hour. At Prime on Sunday, four sections of Psalm 118 are to be said. At the remaining hours—that is, Terce, Sext, and None—three sections of the same Psalm 118 are to be said.

At Prime on Monday, three psalms are to be said, namely Psalms 1, 2, and 6. And so, on each successive day at Prime, through Sunday, three psalms are to be said in order, up to Psalm 19. Psalm 9 and Psalm 17 are to be divided into two *Glorias*. Thus, at the Sunday vigils, they are always to begin with Psalm 20.

At Terce, Sext, and None on Monday, the nine sections remaining from Psalm 118 are to be said, three at each of those hours. After Psalm 118 has therefore been completed over two days, Sunday and Monday, then on Tuesday at Terce, Sext, or None, three psalms are to be sung, from Psalm 119 through Psalm 127—that is, nine psalms. These same psalms are always to be repeated at the same hours until Sunday, while the arrangement of the hymns, readings, and verses is likewise kept uniform on all days. Thus, on Sunday they are always to begin with Psalm 118.

Vespers is to be sung daily with four psalms. These psalms are to begin with Psalm 109 and continue through Psalm 147, except for those taken from this sequence for use at different hours: Psalms 117 through 127, Psalm 133, and Psalm 142. All the rest are to be said at Vespers.

Since there are three psalms too few, those found to be longer in the sequence stated above are to be divided, namely Psalms 138, 143, and 144. Since Psalm 116 is short, it is to be joined to Psalm 115.

Once the order of the evening psalms has been arranged, let the remaining elements—that is, the readings, responsories, hymns, verses, and canticles—be completed as we prescribed above.

At Compline, the same psalms are to be repeated daily, namely Psalms 4, 90, and 133.

Once the order of the daytime psalmody has been arranged, let all the remaining psalms be divided equally among the vigils of the seven nights, dividing among them, of course, those psalms that are longer, and assigning twelve to each night.

We give this particular warning: if anyone should happen to dislike this distribution of the psalms, let him arrange it differently if he judges that another arrangement is better. Blessed Benedict did not place this distribution of the psalms wholly under the judgment of the one who decides, but he gave this particular instruction: whoever wishes to keep this distribution of the psalms according to his own arrangement may keep it; but whoever judges another arrangement better may retain that one and abandon this one without guilt.

We, however, exhort the person who has promised to live according to this Rule to keep and preserve it firmly, insofar as he is able, and, trusting in God’s mercy, to believe that the heavenly kingdoms will be opened to those who observe it.

It follows: Let this above all be observed, that the Psalter in its complete number of one hundred and fifty psalms be sung over the course of the week. On Sunday let it always be begun again from the beginning at the vigils, for monks show the extreme laziness of their devotion if, over the course of a week, they sing fewer psalms with the customary canticles, when we read that our holy Fathers vigorously completed in one day what we, lukewarm as we are, might wish to perform over an entire week.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the discipline of psalmody.

We believe that the divine presence is everywhere. For, as the Apostle says, “All things are naked and open to the eyes of God,” and “no creature is invisible in His sight” (Heb. IV). Therefore we ought to stand before His eyes as before the eyes of our Creator and Judge.

No one, when seeing his prince or judge and speaking with him, dares to let his eyes wander or look elsewhere. How much more, then, should one who approaches the Lord never move the eye of his heart elsewhere, but remain intent upon Him who searches the kidneys and the hearts! For when we humbly plead with the Lord on account of our sins, we know that we are speaking to the Lord.

We should observe that the eyes of the Lord watch the good and the wicked in every place; but we should believe this without any doubt especially when we are attending upon the divine office. Therefore we must fear lest, if we think of something other than what we ask for, we commit an insult against the divine majesty before whom we seem to be standing.

Therefore let us always remember what the Prophet says: “Serve the Lord in fear” (Ps. 2). And again: “Sing psalms wisely” (Ps. 46). Let the tongue, then, always utter what pleases the Creator, in accordance with the Psalmist’s proclamation: “Serve the Lord,” he says, “in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling.” The Creator is served in fear when good works are joined to devout praises, [Col. 0839C] as it is said elsewhere through the Psalmist: “Sing psalms wisely.” For a person sings psalms wisely when the voice praising God is not contradicted by harmful deeds, and when he diligently and wholeheartedly pursues how he ought to serve the divine power. Thus let our mind advance intent upon singing psalms, so that, impeded by no obstacle of worldly desire and darkened by no vice of time, but always intent upon heavenly things and adorned with humility, purity, and the readiest devotion, it may strive to attain eternal rewards. Thus let the body burn with compunction, so that it may stir within itself the Creator’s mercy.

And: “In the sight of the angels I will sing psalms to you” (Ps. 137). Such should be the solemnity of reverence and the discipline of psalm-singing that what is said may be heard more pleasingly by the Lord than by us [Col. 0839D], as Scripture says: “You will delight in the morning and evening offerings” (Ps. 64). And again: “Sing psalms to the Lord wisely” (Ps. 46). He therefore commands that psalms be sung wisely and with fear. The one singing psalms ought to stand with his body motionless and his head bowed, and to sing praises to the Lord in a measured manner, since he is carrying out his ministry before the Divinity. The Prophet teaches this when he says: “In the sight of the angels I will sing psalms to you” (Ps. 137). For the one who sings psalms must always take care that his mind does not wander elsewhere, lest, when our thoughts have migrated to another concern, God say of us: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29).

[Col. 0840A]

Let us therefore consider how we ought to stand in the sight of the Divinity and his angels; and let us stand for psalm-singing in such a way that our mind accords with our voice. For such a great and solemn duty, let heart and tongue alike be united; the daily debt must be rendered to the Lord with fear. The one who sings psalms should mark in his heart every testimony contained in each thing he says, because, when each verse is noted, the verses advance the soul toward salvation, and in them is found everything that is sought. For the psalm speaks all things for edification, as the Prophet says: “I will sing psalms and I will understand” (Ps. 100).

## CHAPTER XX. On Reverence in Prayer

If we wish to present some request to powerful human beings, we presume to do so only with humility and reverence. How much more, then, must we implore the Lord God of all things with complete humility [Col. 0840B] and pure devotion! If prayer is not offered to carnal human beings without humility when we ask them for some temporary benefits, how much more fitting is it that we should entreat Christ for our sins and offenses with every prayer of which we are capable? There must therefore be no duplicity in prayer. One person must not be found on the lips and another in the heart. Purity of heart excludes every vice and obtains every virtue. Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice, because the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit is wherever there is purity of heart. Hence it also follows:

Let us know that we are heard not in much speaking, but in purity of heart and compunction expressed through tears. Prayer should therefore be brief and pure. Prayer should be brief so that, because of the opportunity afforded by a prolonged prayer [Col. 0840C], they do not fall asleep, or perhaps, while lying there for a long time, the devil does not place various things before their eyes or suggest something else in their hearts. We must therefore pray with fear and supplication, as though the one praying were visibly holding the feet of the present Christ. We ought to pray with such fear that we recognize ourselves to be speaking with God. Let no one believe that he will be heard through much speaking, but rather through purity of heart and an abundance of tears. For it is not the length of a prolonged prayer but the focused attention of a ready mind that stirs the compassion of the merciful judge. We must therefore always pray that he may grant pardon to sinners—he who pours healing through the passion of the cross upon the ailing world—the eternal salvation of the world, Christ Jesus our Lord.

[Col. 0840D]

Unless, perhaps, the prayer is extended through the impulse of inspiration by divine grace. In the assembly, however, prayer must be shortened completely. Therefore our Fathers wisely ordered prayer itself to be brought to a swift conclusion, lest, if we linger in it, some coughing, phlegm, or other bodily disturbance interrupt the sound, and, while the prayer is still fervent, it be swiftly snatched back as though from the devil’s throat. Since he is always hostile to us, he is especially hostile when he sees us inwardly offering prayers to the Lord, hastening to draw our mind away from the intention of prayer either through thoughts or through stirred-up bodily humors. For this reason our Fathers ordered that prayers be brief but frequent. Brief, so that by their very brevity we might be able to avoid the devil’s ambushes, which are especially active when we pray. Frequent, so that through this very frequency [Col. 0841A], as we continually pray to the Lord, we may be able to cleave to him continually.

For the sake of this frequency of prayer, it is also useful that we should not recite longer psalms continuously to the end, but should conclude them in two or three divisions, divided into an equal number of verses, with attention to prayer. We ought to take delight not in a multitude of verses but in the mind’s understanding, following with devotion the words: “I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind” (1 Cor. 14).

And when the prior gives the signal, let them all rise together. This was the custom among the ancient bands of monks: when the signal for each hour was heard, they would all quickly assemble for prayer, apply themselves to prayer together, pray together, and, when the prior gave the signal, all rise together from prayer. But now among us the practice is held differently in different places. To the extent that we are later [Col. 0841B] than the primitive monks, to that same extent we are farther removed in the merit of our life from those ancient Fathers. They were fervent in spirit, serving the Lord; but we are lukewarm and do not do similar things, although we hope in the Lord’s mercy.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Deans of the Monastery

If the congregation is large, let good brothers of proven character and holy conduct be chosen from among them and appointed as deans. They are to exercise care over their deaneries in everything, according to the commands of God and the precepts of their abbot. For the abbot’s precepts must agree with the Lord’s commands; therefore the deans and the other subjects alike must obey them. For the subjects must obey the deans, the deans must obey the superiors, and the entire congregation together must obey the abbot’s precepts.

[Col. 0841C]

Deans were originally so called because they were placed over ten soldiers. Now, however, both those placed over ten and those placed over more are called deans. The dean’s care and instruction toward anyone entrusted to him by the abbot must be as follows: he must first teach him to overcome his own inclinations, diligently training him in this and always deliberately commanding him to do what he recognizes to be contrary to his mind. For experience has taught many that a monk can never restrain his desires unless he has first learned through obedience to mortify his own inclinations. Nor can one [Col. 0841D] extinguish anger, sadness, or the spirit of fornication, nor retain firm and perpetual humility toward the brothers, nor remain longer in the congregation, if he has not first learned to overcome his own inclinations.

Deans should be chosen who are such that the abbot can safely share his burdens with them. They should not be chosen by rank or sequence, but according to the merit of their life and the teaching of their wisdom. The deans appointed over the deaneries must exercise such care over the brothers placed under their authority that no one follows his own inclinations. They must not speak unless questioned, do nothing on their own authority unless commanded, and go nowhere unless assigned to do so. Let them fear their seniors as masters, love them as parents, and do whatever they receive as an order from them. Let them believe whatever their seniors command to be salutary, if they do it without murmuring, with cheerfulness and silence [Col. 0842A], as Moses says: “Hear, Israel, and be silent” (Deut. 4, 6, and 9).

Let one bear another’s burdens; let no one judge another or disparage another. For it is written: “Every slanderer will be uprooted” (Prov. 24). Let each receive from another what he does not possess: let one learn humility from another, charity from another, patience from another, silence from another, and gentleness from another. Let them eat without complaint whatever is set before them, and wear whatever they receive. Let them not conceal from their deans anything they have thought about during each day.

Let the deans be to them like rulers and guardians, as though they would have to render an account to the Lord for them. Let them anticipate the negligence of all, have the power to correct it, and, if they are unable to correct something themselves, not delay in reporting it to the superior.

[Col. 0842B]

The superiors themselves should act so strictly and reasonably in this matter that they never presume to disturb their abbots, except in matters that neither party has been able to expedite. In this, let each show such humility toward the other that no one ever offends anyone, but each remain in the other as though firmly embedded: the juniors in the deans, the deans in the superiors, and the superiors in the abbots, each bearing the other like squared stones in a wall, as the Apostle attests above: “By bearing one another’s burdens, you will thus fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6).

[Col. 0842C]

If any of these deans should be found blameworthy because he has become inflated with pride, and, after being corrected once, twice, and three times, refuses to amend, let him be removed, and another who is worthy be substituted in his place. We establish the same rule concerning the superior. For those who must correct, chastise, and guard others in all things ought not to be proud but humble.

Therefore let the abbots themselves, together with their superiors and deans, examine themselves first, rebuke the juniors in their own likeness, and uproot from their hearts every ferment of worldly service. Thus let them strive to chastise, correct, and amend those entangled in various cares and vices. For example, if they hear a brother speaking without having been questioned, let them admonish him, saying: “What are you doing, brother, when the Rule forbids it? Maintain silence until you are questioned. Say with the Prophet: ‘Set a guard, Lord, over my mouth, and a door of protection around my lips; do not incline my heart to words of evil’” (Ps. 140).

Let wisdom sit upon your mouth [Col. 0842D], with the key of justice and the fear of God; let it open your lips to good words and close them to evil words. If they hear a brother lying, let them admonish him, saying: “Why are you lying, brother, when you know what is written: ‘The mouth that lies kills the soul’” (Wis. 1), and, “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Ps. 5).

If they hear a brother swearing frequently, let them admonish him, saying: “Restrain your tongue, brother! Why do you swear, when it is written: ‘You shall not swear by heaven, because it is God’s throne, nor by the earth, because it is the footstool of his feet, nor shall you swear by your head,’ and so forth; but let your speech be ‘Yes, yes; no, no’” (Matt. 5–6).

If they see someone becoming angry, let them admonish him, saying: “What are you doing, brother? Complete your works in gentleness and charity [Col. 0843A], because it is written: ‘Cease from anger and abandon wrath’” (Ps. 36), and, “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to judgment” (Matt. 7).

Similarly, the superiors ought daily to admonish and chastise brothers occupied by other such various and diverse impediments and vices. For while they diligently do these things each day among the brothers entrusted to them, they themselves make progress and, by admonishing others, cause them to make progress as well.

Many superiors have to restrain monks burdened by many different concerns. Some habitually care, in the manner of natural affection, for their wives and children or for various relatives. Many others, who are not entangled in such matters, are anxious about food. Others are consumed inwardly by the disease of sadness and, like a garment eaten by moths, are devoured inwardly by the greed of their own minds [Col. 0843B]; with this very sickness of resentment, they slip into despair.

Others are inflamed by the spirit of fornication and, often incited by such a stimulus of the flesh, blinded in their inner eye, are led captive, bound by the chain of destruction. Others, puffed up by the spirit of acedia, desire to spend their time in idleness and sleep, and are enticed by curious stories; and, what is worse, they plan to withdraw from their own monastery.

Others are pierced in different places by the weapon of the exaltation of vainglory. Some defend one cause and others another, magnifying their own positions. Because they do not wish to be like Christ’s poor, each slips away into these vain thoughts and, as though he had received nothing from God, exalts himself on the strength of his own abilities. When they find no one to praise them, they themselves leap forth into self-praise.

One boasts in his genealogy and declares himself [Col. 0843C] a prince of his people; another boasts of his parents; another of his brothers; another of his relatives; another of his kinsmen, blood relations, and worthy connections; another of his divine gifts; another of the vigor of youth; another of strength in war; another of traveling through lands; another of craftsmanship; another of wisdom; another of eloquence in argument; another of silence; another of humility; another of charity; another of generosity in gifts; another of chastity; another of virginity; another of poverty; another of abstinence; another of frequent prayer; another of vigilance; another of obedience; another of renunciation of possessions; another of reading; another of writing; another of modulation of the voice.

All these matters that we have touched upon above—whenever someone repeatedly speaks of such things without being asked and without moderation—lead him into the exaltation of vainglory; and, through that very disease, while he strives to defend what he says, he is cast into pride.

[Col. 0843D]

Therefore each person must fight against the vice with which he recognizes that he is engaged in combat, and, once corrected, amend himself concerning it, so that, when amended, he may be saved and may prepare for himself eternal salvation and for his teacher an everlasting reward.

## CHAPTER XXII. How Monks Should Sleep

Let each monk sleep in a separate bed. Hence Isidore says: “Let a light illuminate the place of those sleeping at night, so that, when darkness has been dispelled, the testimony of individual repose may be evident.” The monk’s bed must not be occupied by any shameful thought; rather, as he lies there contemplating God alone [Col. 0844A], he should have both bodily rest and tranquility of heart. Let him repel evil thoughts from himself and reject shameful thoughts by placing good thoughts before himself. For the movements of the mind stir it through their images, and whatever the thought has been while awake, such an image appears during sleep.

Fructuosus says: “Let two not lie in one bed, nor let anyone have permission to sleep outside his own sleeping place. A space of one cubit should separate the individual beds, lest, when bodies draw close to one another, they nourish the sparks of lust.
