In the darkness let no one speak to another, nor let any junior in any way approach another’s bed after Compline.”

Ferreolus says: “Let two persons, however close or friendly, not occupy one small bed on the pretext of secret prayer, which is better directed to God without any witness. In this way the repentant mind may believe that greater freedom for praying has been granted to it [Col. 0844B], since it neither fears anyone as a witness nor regards anyone as a judge of its vigil.”

Let each receive bedding according to the manner of his life and according to the arrangement of his abbot. Bedding is so called because it is where people customarily lie and sit. Augustine says: “A people long and greatly wearied judged that new bedding should be provided, something it had never done before.” Beds were spread in honor of the gods; hence this sacred—or rather sacrilegious—name arose.

If it can be done, let all sleep in one place. If the number does not permit this, let groups of ten or twenty rest with their seniors, who are to care for them. For Isidore also says: “It is fitting for all the brothers, if possible, to remain in one room. If this is difficult, then certainly at least ten should be together, with one dean placed over them as ruler and guardian.”

[Col. 0844C]

Let a candle burn continually in the same cell until morning. This candle should be lit daily before Compline, so that they may see how each person arranges his bed and places himself upon it; and, as he settles into bed, he should frequently sing: “Each night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears” (Ps. 6). Having completed this, let him add and say: “In the night I remembered your name, Lord, and kept your law” (Ps. 118). Thus, so that each devout person may more usefully fulfill this during the time granted for rest, he alone shall possess his bed, as we said above, having with him, in a better exchange for the sleeping brother, the Lord who keeps vigil.

[Col. 0844D]

Let them sleep clothed and girded with belts or cords, and let them not have knives at their sides while sleeping, lest the sleepers accidentally be wounded in their sleep. Hence a certain master says: “When monks sleep, let them sleep clothed and girded, that is, with belts, nets, or a slender strap. We forbid a brother to use a knife at night, lest, when he turns about in sleep while oppressed by it, the knife’s blade should come out through its sheath and pierce his flesh. Or we have said that the brothers should sleep clothed and girded so that, when the hour of God’s work arrives and the signal of the oratory sounds, they may immediately rise prepared during the night. Or the brothers must sleep clothed and girded because a brother is not permitted to touch his naked limbs; for from this [Col. 0845A] impurities of lust are introduced into the mind. When the nakedness of the limbs is touched by contact, the heart is immediately titillated by desire for women, and thus during sleep the defiled limbs are polluted.”

And so that the monks may always be ready, let them rise without delay when the signal is given and hasten to anticipate one another in coming to God’s work, yet with complete solemnity and restraint. Solemnity is understood as the strength or firmness of the soul. Restraint is called gentleness, propriety, or self-control. The monks should always be prepared with these virtues; and when the signal is given, rising quickly for the appointed course, let them make the sign of the cross upon their foreheads and say together in silence: “O God, come to my assistance; Lord, hasten to help me” (Ps. 69).

[Col. 0845B]

The younger brothers must not have beds beside one another, but must be mixed among the seniors. When rising for God’s work, let them moderately encourage one another, for the sake of those who might plead sleepiness as an excuse. The younger brothers must not have beds beside one another; rather, as we said, the superiors have their beds among theirs because of some fault of vice that must be corrected in them. Thus they may sleep more reverently in the presence of an elder, rise guarded and honorably admonished by their seniors, and complete the Lord’s service with eagerness.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Excommunication for Faults

If a brother is found to be stubborn, disobedient, proud, murmuring, or otherwise contrary to the holy Rule, and contemptuous of the commands of his seniors [Col. 0845C], let him, according to the command of our Lord (Matt. 18), be admonished once and a second time privately by his seniors. When it says “otherwise contrary to the holy Rule,” this should be understood as referring not to more serious but to lesser faults. For in the case of more serious crimes, the monk must regularly be subjected to public penance; he is nevertheless to be admonished once and a second time by his seniors.

If he does not amend, let him be rebuked publicly before everyone. If he does not correct himself even then, let him, if he understands what the punishment is, be subjected to excommunication. But if he is shameless, let him be subjected to bodily punishment.

[Col. 0845D]

We have decided to set down here what various Fathers thought about this chapter. One of the Fathers says: “If a brother, at the instigation of the devil, appears stubborn, proud, disobedient, or murmuring, or if, having fallen into any circumstance, he attempts to violate the commands of his seniors or the standard of the holy Rule, let him, according to the Lord’s command, be corrected privately once by his seniors in words. If he refuses to amend, let him then be rebuked by the entire congregation together. If he still refuses to amend, let him then be judged according to the Rule, as the magnitude of his fault requires: that is, let him either be subjected to excommunication, if his understanding is sound enough to grasp it, or, if the stubborn tenacity of a hardened mind and the wickedness of the fault persist, let him be subjected to bodily discipline.”

Hence blessed Fructuosus says: “It is not fitting for a servant of God to be a liar, a thief, a striker, or a perjurer [Col. 0846A]. He ought first to be corrected in words by his seniors, so that he may withdraw from the vice. After this, if he still does not amend, he should be summoned a third time before the brothers, so that he may cease to wander into such errors. If he still does not amend, let him be severely flogged, and, receiving the punishment of excommunication for three months, let him be confined alone in a cell under strict penance, sustained from evening to evening by six ounces of barley bread and a small measure of water.”

Hence blessed Basil also says: “If people are to render an account on the day of judgment for every idle word, nothing ought to be despised as insignificant. For whoever despises small things gradually falls away. And how will anyone dare to call a transgression small, when the Apostle says: ‘Through transgression of the law God is dishonored’” (Rom. 2)? Sin is also called the sting of death; and he did not say this or that sin, but every sin.

[Col. 0846B]

The one who fails to correct and neglects is more merciless than the one who rebukes, just as one who allows poison to remain hidden in a snakebite is more merciless than one who extracts and draws it out. He also destroys charity who, according to Scripture, spares the rod and hates his son. But the one who loves corrects him diligently.

Hence blessed Augustine says in his Rule: “If after the admonition you see him doing the same thing again, or on another day, let whoever can bring this to light expose him as someone wounded who must be healed. First, however, it must be shown to another, or to a third person, so that he may be convicted by the testimony of two or three and restrained with appropriate severity. [Col. 0846C]

“Do not consider yourselves malicious when you report these things. For you are more certainly not innocent if, by remaining silent, you permit your brothers—whom you could correct by reporting them—to perish. If your brother had a wound on his body that he wished to conceal because he feared being cut, would it not be cruel of you to remain silent and merciful to disclose it? How much more, then, ought you to make this known, lest it putrefy more disastrously in his heart.

“Before it is shown to others by whom he is to be convicted, if he denies it, it must first be brought to the superior. If, after being admonished, he has neglected to correct himself, this should be done so that, if he is corrected more privately, the matter may perhaps not become known to the others. But if he denies it, others must be brought in who are unaware of the matter, so that he may now be rebuked before everyone, not by a single witness, but convicted by two or three.

“Once convicted [Col. 0846D], he must, according to the judgment of the superior or even of the priest whose responsibility it is, endure corrective punishment. If he refuses to bear it, let him be expelled from your fellowship, even if he has not himself withdrawn. This is not done cruelly but mercifully, lest through a destructive contagion he destroy many.”

For concerning this chapter the abbots Paul and Stephen also wrote as follows: “If anyone sees another doing something unlawful in any respect, either in word or in deed, and delays reporting it to the prior, let him recognize that he is a nourisher of sin and in every respect equal to the sinner. For he is the harshest enemy both of his own soul and of the one whom he conceals. Because of this, he will be considered accursed and unfaithful before God [Col. 0847A], who hates evil, and before the entire brotherhood: because, through an abundance of wickedness, he did not wish to expose the erring person so that he could correct him; because, out of hatred for discipline, he loved wickedness and stood on every evil path.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. What the Measure of Excommunication Should Be

The measure of excommunication or discipline should be extended according to the measure of the fault; the determination of the fault’s measure rests with the abbot’s judgment. When blessed Basil was asked what corrections ought to be used among the brothers for the amendment of those who offend, he replied: “Let this be placed in the judgment of those who preside: for how long and in what manner they ought to be corrected. For age and education also create a great difference in punishment.”

[Col. 0847B]

Likewise, according to the rule of a certain form of excommunication, what the measure of excommunication should be is shown by the measure of the fault, leaving judgment to those who know what is just. For lighter faults require a lighter correction, while more serious faults require a more fervent condemnation.

Therefore the abbot must take care that, if a brother is found liable for lesser faults, he be deprived of the table until the hour appointed for him. In the case of more serious faults, however, let the punishment be brought to an end through a correction extended for a longer period, whether days, weeks, or months.

If a brother is nevertheless found liable for lesser faults, let him merely be deprived of participation at the table. According to Isidore, the person guilty of a lesser fault is one who loves to be idle; who comes late to the service, to the conference, or to the table; who laughs in the choir or spends his time in stories [Col. 0847C]; who leaves the service or work and goes outside for any reason other than necessity; who loves sluggishness and sleep; who swears frequently; who is excessively talkative; who undertakes an assigned task without a blessing, or, after completing the task, fails to ask for a blessing; who completes an assigned task negligently or late; who accidentally breaks some vessel; who causes damage to a small object; who uses a book negligently; who withdraws somewhere for a moment; who secretly receives letters or any gift from someone, or conceals a letter when receiving it, or replies without the abbot’s consent; who sees or speaks with any parent or layperson without the order of his senior; who is disobedient to a senior [Col. 0847D]; who answers a senior defiantly; who does not restrain his tongue before a senior; who is wanton in speech; who walks indecently; who jokes; who laughs excessively; who speaks, prays, or eats with an excommunicated person; or who does not disclose a nocturnal illusion to the Father.

These and similar matters are to be corrected through the discipline of excommunication. Elsewhere too we find the following counted among lesser faults: if someone stumbles even slightly while chanting a psalm; if he murmurs even lightly; if, after the assembly has ended, he does not hasten quickly back to his cell; if, while carrying out the duties of reading, work, or obedience, he performs what has been assigned too sluggishly; if he stops with someone even briefly; if he holds another’s hand [Col. 0848A]; if he presumes to utter something playful or suited to laughter in the assembly of the brothers; or if he wishes to tell idle stories to the younger brothers or to form friendships with those of immature age. He shall be subjected to rebuke as he deserves.

If anyone finds anything, let him not conceal what he has found, nor hide what ought to be made known. If someone is proved to have kept what he found for the space of one day, let him recognize that he has been defiled by the contagion of theft. If anyone learns that a person who cannot endure the strictness of the monastery is contemplating flight, and does not immediately report it, let him not doubt that he is a participant in that person’s destruction. Such a person must be separated from the assembly of the brothers for as long as the fugitive can be recalled.

If anyone does not strive with all his strength to observe these things that please the Lord, and, after being corrected once and a second time, does not amend [Col. 0848B], it is fitting that the matter be reported according to his age and condition. Up to this point spiritual correction applies to such offenses and similar ones.

But the remaining offenses that are admitted indiscriminately among us and tolerated even by those who themselves deserve correction are these: open insults, manifest contempt, arrogant contradictions, free and unrestrained conduct, familiarity with women, anger, quarrels, hostility and disputes, presumption in undertaking private work, the contagion of love of money, affection for and possession of superfluous things not possessed by the other brothers, and extraordinary and sumptuous eating. These and similar offenses are not corrected by the spiritual rebuke mentioned above, but are either amended through blows or cleansed through expulsion.

[Col. 0848C]

The rule for those deprived of fellowship at the table is this: they shall neither assign a psalm or antiphon in the oratory nor recite a reading until they have made satisfaction. Hence a certain master of monks says: “A brother who has committed a lesser fault and, after the first, second, and third admonition concerning each offense, has not amended, shall be excommunicated from the table, but not from the oratory. Let this excommunication remain without interruption until the guilty person, with his head bowed to his knees in greater humility, has promised thereafter to amend and has made satisfaction.

“That brother who has been excommunicated from the table but not from the oratory shall not assign an antiphon or reading until he has made satisfaction for that fault by the amendment he has promised, having bent his knees before the present abbot or his superior.

“But if excommunicated brothers become so proud [Col. 0848D], or persist in the pride of their hearts and refuse to make satisfaction to the abbot at the ninth hour on the third day, let them, under guard, be beaten with rods until death. If the abbot so decides, let them be expelled from the monastery, because such a life does not require bodily companions or the fellowship of brothers whom death possesses in a proud soul. Such men rightly deserve to be killed with blows and expelled: they are not worthy to be with Christ, the Lord of humility, but should be separated from God’s perpetual promises together with their author, the devil, who was cast from the kingdoms of heaven because of his pride.”

Let him receive his meal after the meal of the brothers, at the measure or hour that the abbot determines to be suitable for him. For example, if the brothers eat at the sixth [Col. 0849A] hour, let that brother eat at the ninth; if the brothers eat at the ninth, let him eat in the evening—until he obtains pardon through appropriate satisfaction.

Satisfaction is called appropriate when repentance is carried out according to the measure of the fault. Care must be taken that a severe penitential punishment is not imposed for lesser faults, nor a light one for more serious faults. The Father or superior must excel in measure, equal weighing, justice, and continual compassionate mercy, so that he may heal the sick person’s wound in such a way as to bring health rather than weakness to the limb. For just as God will judge the life of subjects through the superior, so he will judge the negligence of superiors through himself.

## CHAPTER XXV. On More Serious Faults

That brother who is held by the guilt [Col. 0849B] of a more serious fault. *Noxa* means guilt or criminal offenses. For grievous sins are called harmful (*nocibilia*) or injurious (*noxia*).

Let him be suspended both from the table and from the oratory. Hence blessed Isidore says:

“Liable to a more serious offense is anyone who is drunken, quarrelsome, foul-mouthed, intimate with women, a sower of discord, hot-tempered, stiff-necked and high-headed, swollen with pride in mind or immoderate in a boastful gait; a slanderer, whisperer, or envious person; one who presumptuously appropriates property, who is entangled in the contagion of money, who possesses anything superfluous beyond the regular provision, who defrauds property received or entrusted to him, or entrusted to him only imperfectly. Among these offenses are also the following: if he boasts about things brought with him, or murmurs about them through disobedience; if he causes damage to a greater possession; if he has stolen; if he has committed perjury; if he has spoken falsely; if he has loved arguments or quarrels; if he has openly insulted a brother; if he has stained an innocent person with a false accusation; if with a stubborn spirit he has despised an elder; if he has harbored resentment against a brother; if he has not granted pardon to one who sinned against him and afterward begged forgiveness; if he has played, laughed, or kissed little boys; if he has lain with another in one bed; if outside the common table he has privately or secretly taken anything; if, departing somewhere without the consent of the superior or abbot, he has remained away through midday or longer; if, in order to be idle, he has pretended to be falsely ill. These offenses and similar ones must, according to the prior’s judgment, be cleansed by prolonged excommunication, so that those known to sin gravely may be restrained with sharper severity.

“For the Apostle Paul also lists these grave vices in his Epistle to the Galatians, saying: ‘The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, impurity, licentiousness, the service of idols, sorcery, enmities, contentions, jealousies, angers, quarrels, dissensions, factions, envies, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God’ (Gal. 5).

“And concerning those who are devoted to such vices, the same Apostle speaks condemnatorily in his Epistle to the Romans, saying: ‘Therefore God gave them over to dishonorable passions. Their women exchanged natural use for that which is against nature. Likewise the men, abandoning natural use of woman, burned with desire for one another, males committing shameful acts with males and receiving in themselves the recompense that was fitting for their error. And since they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a debased mind, to do what is improper: filled with all iniquity, wickedness, fornication, avarice, depravity; full of envy, murder, contention, deceit, malignity; whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God, abusive, proud, arrogant, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, foolish, disorderly, without affection, faithless, without mercy. Though they knew God’s justice, they did not understand that those who do such things deserve death—not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them’ (Rom. 1).”

Let these words of the Apostle suffice. Let us see how the other Fathers, and blessed Benedict himself, judge such harmful and grave offenses. The same author says later:

“No one of the brothers is to associate with him in any way, nor converse with him. He is to be alone at the work assigned to him, remaining in the grief of penitence.”

Hence other Fathers also said:

“If a monk commits theft—which may more properly be called sacrilege—we have judged that the following order should be established: if he is a young man, after being beaten with rods, and guilty of so great a crime, he is never to receive clerical office. If he is already a cleric and is caught in this offense, he is to be deprived of the dignity of his rank. For him, after the prescribed satisfaction has been completed, communion may suffice as appropriate to the lightness of his act.”

Hence blessed Ferreolus says:

“We command that one conscious of theft—if we may still call him a monk—be subjected, as an adulterer, to a twofold flogging [the printed reading *secundum flagellis* is uncertain], and be crushed by great affliction, assigning him the same sentence as the fornicator, because he too acted lustfully when he stole. For we not unjustly call those alike whom we find placed together in sacred reading.”

The Lord therefore says through the prophet: “There is no knowledge of God upon the earth” (Hos. 4). And shortly afterward: “Theft and adultery have overflowed” (ibid.). Again, in the psalm: “If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and with adulterers you placed your portion” (Ps. 49). We also read that the Lord said in the Gospel: “Fornications, thefts”—and without delay he adds—“these are the things that defile a person” (Matt. 15).

From this, surely, the servants of these crimes can understand that, just as these vices exercise equal dominion over them, so an equal punishment is owed to them.

Hence blessed Bishop Fructuosus says:

“If a monk pursues little boys, or anyone who, on any occasion, is found blameworthy for shamefully craving something, and the matter has been clearly established through absolutely reliable accusers or witnesses, he is to be publicly flogged; he is to lose the crown he wore on his head; he is to be exposed disgracefully in bare feet to public shame; he is likewise to receive all the spitting and insults directed against him; and, bound tightly in iron chains, he is to be tormented for six months in the confinement of prison. Each week he is to be sustained by a three-day ration of a small amount of barley bread, given in the evening. After those months have been completed, he is to spend the following six months segregated in a small enclosure under the custody of a spiritual elder, content with the work of his hands and continual prayer, subject to vigils, tears, and humility; through the lamentations of penitence he is to receive pardon; and, always under the custody and vigilance of two spiritual brothers, he is to walk about in the monastery, never again to be joined to the young men in private conversation or counsel.”

Knowing the Apostle’s terrible sentence, in which he says that such a man is “handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord” (1 Cor. 5), Jerome says concerning this sentence:

“To hand such a person over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh is to grant Satan power to seize him bodily. When he sees that he will have rest neither for his flesh here nor for his spirit in the future, he may repent of his deed and be saved. Or, in accordance with each person’s merits, one is expelled from the Church in this way and handed over to Satan’s power, so that, while his flesh suffers a kind of destruction through penitence, his spirit may be preserved. Scripture has the custom of understanding the whole person by a part. Or it is so because Scripture also has the custom of showing that carnal acts perish in the flesh, while spiritual conduct is preserved in the spirit.

“Here, too, it shows that one expelled from the Church is to be torn apart by the swift mouths of demons if he persists in refusing to mortify the life of the flesh, so that he may recover holy life and his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus. For Satan cannot take possession of the spirit; it is reserved for the Lord’s judgment.”

The text continues:

“Let him alone receive his food, at the measure or hour which the abbot has determined to be suitable for him.”

Therefore the abbot must consider what kind of discipline or penitence is appropriate to him. He must take into account a childish age, infirm old age, or a delicate, perhaps even weak, body; and according to the condition of each person he must impose the measure of penitence and the weight of discipline, so that discipline may heal him as medicine, not crush him; raise him up with vitality, not burden him with death.

“Let no one bless him as he passes by, nor bless the food that is given to him.”

Concerning this sentence other Fathers said:

“Let him be consoled by no one’s words; let everyone pass him by in silence. When he asks for a blessing, let no one answer him. Whatever is handed to him, let no one make the sign over it. Whatever he does voluntarily or on his own beyond the work assigned to him is to be scattered or destroyed. Thus everywhere he is alone, and his only consolation is his guilt.”

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning those who join the excommunicated without the abbot’s command

If any brother presumes, without the abbot’s command, to join an excommunicated brother in any way, or to speak with him, or to send him a message, let him suffer a similar punishment of excommunication.

Hence blessed Isidore says:

“Let no one be permitted to enter to an excommunicated person without the order of the elder. No one may pray or speak with an excommunicated person. No one at all may eat with an excommunicated person—not even the one who provides him with food.”

Hence Cassian says:

“If anyone has been suspended from prayer on account of some offense, no one is to have permission to pray with him until, after he has lain prostrate on the ground in penitence before all the brothers, pardon has been granted him by the abbot as he begs for it. For whoever, before he is received by the prior, presumes through ill-considered compassion to associate himself with him in prayer or conversation becomes subject to the same condemnation, voluntarily handing himself over to Satan, to whom that man, according to the Apostle’s sentence (1 Cor. 5), had been assigned for the correction of his guilt.

“He sins more gravely in this respect because, by offering him comfort, he makes his heart still harder and does not allow him, since he has been separated from prayer, to think about his satisfaction and pardon; instead, he nourishes to his detriment a greater fuel of pride and obstinacy in the delinquent.”

Hence a certain teacher of monks says:

“If a brother speaks or associates with him, whether openly or secretly, let him immediately incur with him the common penalty of excommunication; let him be guilty before all; let his superior separate him from the others in another work; and let him himself be separated both from that guilty man and from everyone else, alone and immediately alienated from the speech of all. Nor is he himself to have any share in the pardon of the greater offender unless a similar satisfaction of penitence has been performed equally by both: by the former because he was disobedient in vice or sin, and by the latter because he offered the reward of consolation to the author of evil.”

## CHAPTER XXVII. How the abbot ought to be solicitous concerning the excommunicated

“Let the abbot care for delinquent brothers with every solicitude, for ‘a physician is not needed by the healthy but by those who are ill’” (Matt. 9).

“Every solicitude” means every care, every discernment, and every diligence toward delinquent—that is, sinful—brothers. Here he likens delinquent brothers to those who are ill, and compares the abbot to a physician. Without doubt, when the soul sins, it is ill, because it departs equally from goodness and from health. For just as there is bodily sickness, so without doubt there is sickness of the soul. And just as one sick in body needs a physician, so does one whose soul is sick. Wishing to be freed from this sickness, the Psalmist said to the Lord, the physician: “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40).

The good abbot, who holds the Lord’s place in the monastery, ought to care for sick souls, so that they may be healed of sins and vices and, having recovered their former health, may again serve their Creator.

“Therefore he ought to use every means, like a wise physician, to send in secret comforters who are *senipetae*.”

*Senipetae* is a Greek, not a Latin, name, by which, according to the interpretation of blessed Benedict himself,

“wise elder brothers” are understood.

“Let them secretly console the wavering brother.”

He calls him “wavering,” that is, hesitating, afflicted, or changing amid various thoughts.

“And let them urge him toward the satisfaction of humility.”

The satisfaction of humility occurs when a person recognizes that he has sinned through pride and, with heart and body humbled, produces worthy fruits of penitence for his sins. The elder brothers ought to urge him toward this satisfaction of humility, saying:

“Humble yourself through penitence under the mighty hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of visitation; for God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.”

“And let him console him, lest he be swallowed up by excessive sorrow.”

By “excessive sorrow” he means one greater and deeper than the sorrow he previously had when he sinned. “Be swallowed up” means devoured and engulfed. A brother who is sick in spirit is often more distressed by immoderate correction than by the guilt he committed. Therefore, when the wound of sin in those subject to authority is tightened through correction, even strictness itself must exercise great care in the matter, so that it may enforce the rights of discipline against delinquents without losing the compassion of mercy.

Concerning this sentence Jerome says:

“‘Lest he be swallowed up by excessive sorrow’—lest such a person be swallowed up in the whirlpool of vices through despair of pardon and, persuaded by the devil, be led into the greater precipices of unbelief and blasphemy. Therefore I urge you to confirm your love toward him, by which he recognizes that he has received complete pardon.”

But, as the Apostle says (2 Cor. 2), “let love be confirmed in him, and let everyone pray for him.”

Hence Gregory Nazianzen says:

“Paul received into penitence the man who sinned in Corinth with a sin such as was not found even among the Gentiles. He not only received him, but also confirmed love toward him. When he saw his amendment, he explained the reason for his action, saying: ‘Lest such a person be swallowed up by greater sorrow’ (ibid.), that is, weighed down by excessive correction.”

The abbot ought to exercise the greatest solicitude concerning delinquent brothers. “The greatest” means with great zeal, great care, or great struggle, because the abbot ought to care for the souls entrusted to him not softly or sluggishly, but firmly and vigilantly.

Hence it follows:

“And with every discernment and diligence take care not to lose any of the sheep entrusted to him.”

“Discernment” means vigilance, solicitude, or useful attentiveness; “diligence” means skill or foresight. Relying on these, everyone ought to exercise care—not with bodily steps, but with the steps of mind and understanding—not to lose any of his sheep through his own negligence, slowness, or sluggishness.

Good monks are called Christ’s sheep because of the innocence of their life. Concerning them their Lord and shepherd himself said:

“My sheep hear my voice; I know mine, and mine know me; and the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10).

“For he is to know that he has undertaken the care of sick souls, not tyranny over healthy ones.”

Properly speaking, a tyrant is one who rules a republic without lawful authority. Therefore every proud person exercises tyranny in his own manner. Accordingly, they rightly call the pride of the wicked tyranny. “Tyranny” is a Greek name. It means an unjust seizure of kingship, an undeserved honor, unjust power, proud action, and inequitable rule proceeding from a swollen mind and proud heart.

The abbot has not undertaken this ministry in order to exercise it over healthy souls—that is, over strong and well-living monks—but over sick souls, who have not yet been firmly strengthened to endure the sufferings and temptations of the world. He has undertaken the care of healing and restoring them. He has undertaken to care for sinners, strengthen those weak in spirit, make firm those wavering in God’s service, and not overthrow the healthy or those living rightly, nor disturb those who have gone astray.

“And let him fear the prophet’s threat, through whom God says: ‘What was fat you took for yourselves, and what was weak you cast away’” (Ezek. 34).

When he says, “What was fat you took,” this is understood as “you devoured, killed, or consumed.”

Concerning this sentence blessed Augustine says:

“There are very few healthy and fat sheep—that is, those made firm by the food of truth and using the pastures that come from God’s gift. But those wicked shepherds do not spare such sheep. It is little enough that they do not care for the languishing, the sick, the wandering, and the lost; they also kill these strong and fat ones, insofar as they can. Those sheep live by God’s mercy; nevertheless, as far as bad shepherds are concerned, they kill them.

“How do they kill them? By living badly and providing a bad example. Even a strong sheep often observes its superior living badly. If it turns its eyes away from the Lord’s rules and fixes them on a human being, it begins to say in its heart: ‘If my superior lives this way, who am I that I should not do what he does?’ He kills the strong sheep.

“If, then, he kills the strong sheep, what will he do to the others, since by living badly he has killed what he himself did not make strong but found already strong and robust? I say to your charity, and I say again: even if the sheep live, even if they are strong in the word of the Lord and hold to what they heard from their Lord—‘Do what they say, but do not do what they do’ (Matt. 23)—nevertheless, whoever lives badly in the sight of the people kills, insofar as he can, the one who watches him.

“Thus everyone who lives badly before those over whom he has authority kills, insofar as he can, even the strong sheep. Therefore the one who imitates a bad superior dies; the one who does not imitate him lives. Nevertheless, as far as that superior is concerned, he kills both.”

“And let him imitate the pious example of the good shepherd.”

The good shepherd is Christ, who said: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10). He also said of himself: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (ibid.).

The abbot ought to imitate his pious example and love the flock of his sheep—that is, his monks—as Christ loved the human race, so much that he handed himself over to death for it; rising from the dead, he raised it to heaven and joined it to the angelic choir, thus restoring the number of his sheep.

For the abbot ought to correct a monk who has gone astray and, once corrected and likewise loved, join him to the company of his other monks. Then he imitates Christ well,

“who, leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the mountains, went to seek the one sheep that had gone astray.”

He had such compassion for its weakness that he deigned to place it upon his sacred shoulders and carry it back to the flock (Luke 15). The hundred sheep signify the whole company of angels and human beings. One went astray—that is, the human race sinned. He left the ninety-nine in the mountains—that is, the nine orders of angels in heaven—and came to seek the one in the valley of tears. When it is found, there is greater joy over it than over the ninety-nine that had not gone astray.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning those who, though corrected repeatedly, do not amend

If any brother, repeatedly corrected for some offense, does not amend even after excommunication, let sharper correction be applied to him—that is, let the punishment of flogging proceed against him.

“Corrected” means chastised or rebuked. The difference between correcting, chastising, and rebuking is this: we correct with blows, rebuke with words, and chastise with both words and blows.

“But if he does not correct himself even in this way, or perhaps—which God forbid—lifted up in pride, wishes even to defend his deeds, then let the abbot do what a wise physician does.”

He has provided poultices, the salves of exhortation, the medicines of the divine Scriptures, and finally the cautery of excommunication or the wounds of rods.

Chastisements accompanied by mercy and gentleness are rightly called poultices. Exhortations with the soft sweetness of kindness are called salves. The testimonies of the divine Scriptures, or the sacred precepts of the law, are appropriately called medicines. They heal the wounds of sin in souls that guard and observe them. Hence the Psalmist, keeping the Lord’s commandments, said:

“I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40).

The severe rigor of excommunication imposed upon a sinner for sin is appropriately called cauterization. Just as cautery burns and scorches the body, so the rigor of excommunication afflicts the soul, burning it and the body together. Yet this cautery cleanses the humble soul of the rust of sin, while it turns the proud soul into the nature of lead.

Concerning the rod’s lash Solomon says: “Strike your son with the rod, and you will deliver his soul from death” (Prov. 23). And: “If you love your son, give him continual lashes” (Ecclus. 30).

“Even if he sees that all his diligence is accomplishing nothing, let him also apply—which is greater—his own prayer and that of all the brothers for him, so that the Lord, who can do all things, may bring salvation to the sick brother.”

Hence the Apostle also says:

“Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be saved. The continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful. Elijah was a human being subject to suffering like us, and he prayed fervently, and so forth” (James 5).

If one Elijah alone obtained so much, how much more effective will be the frequent prayer of many righteous people. They are therefore commanded to pray and sing psalms to the Lord whenever we are struck by adversities—not only for the health of bodies, but also for the health of souls.

For if it is a great merit to rescue flesh, which will one day die, from death, how great is the merit of freeing a soul from death, so that it may live forever in the heavenly homeland?

“But if he is not healed even in this way, then let the abbot now use the iron of excision, as the Apostle says: ‘Remove the evil person from among you’” (1 Cor. 5).

Hence it is written in the rule of a certain Father:

“If a brother, though repeatedly corrected, refuses to amend, let him be corrected by excommunication according to the measure of his offense. If the correction of the one rebuking him accomplishes nothing even then, he shall be subjected to the punishment of flogging. If he refuses to amend even in this way, but, lifted still higher into the swelling of pride, defends the works or acts for which he is being corrected, then let him be corrected under the governance of the abbot’s knowledge, for it is written: ‘Unhappy is the one who rejects discipline’ (Prov. 15).

“Under the direction of wise judgment, therefore, let care for healing be applied to the wound. If such a wound is not restored to health by the poultices of chastisement and the salves of mercy and gentleness, then let him incur the sentence of excommunication or the punishment of bodily discipline. And if he is not broken either by fear of excommunication or by the punishment of the lash, let the poultice of mercy be increased still further, so that the whole congregation may entreat the Lord for him through the common ministry of prayer, asking that the one held entangled in the devil’s snare may be healed by the Lord’s mercy and compassion.

“If he refuses to be corrected even then, let him be segregated within the enclosure of the monastery from everyone except the custodians and be chastised with various corrections under the discipline of penitence, until his humility becomes manifest to all with credible evidence, because salvation is often granted even against a person’s will. He must be separated from the congregation so that by his vice he may not stain the innocent.

“But tender age, which does not understand the force of excommunication, is to be corrected not by excommunication but by the lash.”

Hence Isidore says:

“One who, though repeatedly excommunicated for a grave vice, neglects to amend must remain subject to condemnation until he lays aside his ingrained vices, so that one whom a single act of correction did not restrain may be judged amendable by repeated severity. Although someone may be immersed in the abyss of frequent and very serious vices, he is nevertheless not to be expelled from the monastery, but restrained according to the nature of his offense, lest one who could have been corrected through prolonged penitence, when expelled, be devoured by the devil’s mouth.”

Blessed Macarius, however, says differently in his Rule:

“One who is repeatedly corrected and does not amend is to be regarded as an outsider, as the Lord said: ‘Let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector.’”

Blessed Basil says:

“One who does not repent of his sin is to be cut off like a rotten member from the body. For it is written that it is better for one of your members to perish than for your whole body to be cast into Gehenna, because it is not yours to wish to spare one whom the Lord has condemned.”

In the Eastern Rule we find the following:

“If anyone is so hard and so alien to the fear of the Lord that he is not corrected by so many chastisements and so many acts of leniency, let him be expelled from the monastery and regarded as an outsider, lest others be endangered by his vice.”

Hence it also follows:

“And again: ‘If the unbeliever departs, let him depart’” (1 Cor. 7).

That is, if he wishes to go, let him go. The abbot must not make much of this or judge himself at fault if his unfaithful monk departs; for if the latter abandons the enclosure of the monastery through his own vice, the stain of that sin does not redound upon the abbot. For one who first departs in mind must afterwards depart also in body, lest there happen in the flock what follows:

“Lest one diseased sheep contaminate the whole flock” (ibid.).

The ancients called it *morbus* (“disease”) in order, by the name itself, to indicate the force of death that arises from it. Between health and disease lies treatment, which, unless it suits the disease, does not lead to health. “Contaminate” means pollute or defile. Contagion is called the defilement of crimes, misery, sickness of mind, calamity, or defilement of mind. *Contagium* is so called from touching; for whatever it touches, it defiles.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Whether brothers departing from the monastery ought to be received again

“If a brother leaves the monastery through his own fault or is expelled, and wishes to return, let him first promise complete amendment of the vice for which he departed; then let him be received in the lowest rank, so that his humility may thereby be tested. If he leaves again, let him be received up to a third time. After that, let him know that every avenue of return is denied him.”

Hence a certain teacher of monks says:

“If a brother frequently leaves the monastery, let him be received when he returns up to the third time. No more after that. What need is there any longer in the monastery for one whom God does not possess? Therefore, after the third correction, he is rightly to be regarded by the monastery as a Gentile and a tax collector.”

Hence Ferreolus says:

“We have decided that a fugitive monk who abandons discipline and loses himself should be recalled as a despiser.”

Hence holy Bishop Fructuosus says:

“When someone has escaped from the monastery through vice, he is not to be received into another cenobium, neither out of human kindness nor with a kiss of peace, but is immediately to be led back to his own abbot with his hands bound behind his back.”

Again he says:

“If, indeed, those apostates have been expelled by everyone and, wandering here and there, unstable and wavering in different places, have been compelled by necessity to ask to return to their own monastery, let them be brought before the assembly of the elders and tested like potter’s vessels in a furnace. When they have been tested, let them be restored to their own monastery, and received not in the first but in the last place.”

Again, from the Rule of a certain author:

“If at any time—which God forbid—a brother departs from the Christian religion and leaves the monastery’s enclosure, then, fleeing outside and afterward remembering his former religion and struck by fear of eternal judgment, returns, let him first of all promise amendment of his entire way of life. Then, if his penitence is recognized as credible, let him finally be received within the monastery’s enclosure. If he does this a second or third time, let him likewise be treated with mercy, but in such a way that, received in the last place among the penitents, he is examined for as long as necessary, until his life is found to be credible.”

## CHAPTER XXX. How children of lesser age are to be corrected

“Every age or level of understanding ought to have its own measures.” That is, the discipline of judgment is not to be applied uniformly to everyone, but is to be imposed with great moderation according to each person’s age or understanding. Children are to be judged one way, adolescents and young men another, the elderly another, and those placed in decrepit old age another.

Therefore, whenever children or those younger in age, or those who are less able to understand how great the punishment of excommunication is, commit an offense, such persons are either to be afflicted with excessive fasts or restrained with rigorous lashes [variants: *acribibus*, “sharp,” and *acrius*, “more harshly”], so that they may be healed.

Concerning such persons Solomon says:

“Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, and the rod of discipline will drive it out” (Prov. 22).

Hence Isidore says:

“Those in the lesser age are not to be restrained by the sentence of excommunication, but according to the nature of their negligence they are to be amended with appropriate blows, so that those whom the weakness of age does not turn away from guilt may be restrained by the discipline of the lash.”

Those brothers who have committed a sufficiently serious offense, whether theft, flight, or a criminal offense, are to be beaten after fifteen years of age.

## CHAPTER XXXI. What the monastery’s cellarer should be like

“The monastery’s cellarer is to be chosen from the congregation as a wise man.”

The cellarer, who distributes the substance of the servants of God and dispenses their food, ought to be endowed with prudence and full of wisdom, so that he may prudently and wisely distribute what is to be distributed and preserve what is to be preserved. For one who is wise according to God is blessed; and Scripture says: “The Lord loves no one except the one who dwells with wisdom” (Wis. 7).

Hence Isidore says:

“It profits nothing to know every kind of prudence while being ignorant of God; it harms those who know the Lord nothing to be ignorant of the world. He knows perfectly who knows God first, and knows these other things not for himself but for God.”

“Of mature character.”

Mature character means gentle and modest character, tempered by experience of many things and by a long period of time. For it is written: “The senses of a human being are gray hairs, and an undefiled life is the age of old age” (Wis. 4).

Therefore gray hair is to be honored and old age revered; and maturity is found not only in the body but also in a person’s understanding, where all good things received from God are composed with discernment, distinguished rationally, and preserved firmly.

“Sober.”

“Sober” means cautious or considered in food and drink, frugal and sparing, temperate in word and deed. Hence Paul says:

“Do not think more highly than one ought to think, but think with sobriety” (Rom. 12), that is, temperately.

The cellarer ought to think temperately, live temperately, speak temperately, and temperately distribute what is to be given to the brothers. Sober in mind, discerning in his work, gracious in speech, and sweet in expression. For it is written:

“The wise person makes himself beloved by his words” (Ecclus. 20).

And: “The one who is wise in heart will be called prudent” (Prov. 16).

And: “The one who is sweet in speech will receive greater things” (ibid.).

“Not a great eater.”

A great eater is called a glutton, a devourer—something that is not fitting for a monk, and especially not for a cellarer. For it is not the prayer of a glutton but of an abstinent monk that penetrates heaven. An abstinent person becomes spiritual, is joined to the angels, and more easily draws near to his Creator, as it is written:

“Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.”

It is therefore good to beware of the belly’s gluttony, lest the soul that lives forever be subjected to the belly through destruction and be ruled by foods destined for destruction.

Concerning the belly and food the Apostle writes:

“Food is for the belly and the belly for food, but God will destroy both the one and the other” (1 Cor. 6).

No one can rule over the other vices unless he has first restrained the gluttony of the belly.

Hence a certain teacher of monks says:

“The brother who is proven by the abbot to be faithful and abstinent is to be appointed cellarer—the one whom the appetite of any desire never conquers, and who does not greatly love eating or drinking—lest greater opportunity be given to the devil, as Scripture says: ‘Do not give an occasion to those who seek it’ (Gal. 5; 1 Tim. 5), and lest provision be seen to be made for brothers who are gluttonous with the appetite of *gastrimargia*, or for gluttons, rather than that they be restrained.”

“Not proud.”

One is called “proud” when lifted up in pride, bold and boastful, or arrogant. Concerning such persons Solomon says:

“Every arrogant person is an abomination to the Lord, and the one who boasts and enlarges himself stirs up quarrels” (Prov. 16).

Arrogance arises from pride. Unless hidden exaltation of mind has preceded it, open boastfulness in praise does not follow.

Divine Scripture rebukes such a person, saying:

“Do not exalt yourself in thought like a bull, lest your strength be struck down and you be left like a dry tree in the wilderness” (Ecclus. 6).

“Not turbulent.”

One is called turbulent when stirred up by the whirlwind of fury, or blinded in the eye of the heart by anger, as it is written:

“My eye is troubled because of anger” (Ps. 6).

Concerning such a person Solomon also says:

“Whoever disturbs his own house feeds the winds” (Prov. 10).

He disturbs his own house who, through light-mindedness, quickly arouses his mind to anger. An impatient cellarer, seeing many people ask him for many things, is troubled in spirit by his volatility and gives those who ask him not a gracious answer but rather an abusive one. He is strictly forbidden to do this, as follows:

“Not abusive.”

An abusive person is one who inflicts injuries or insults upon the brothers. Concerning such people it is written:

“An angry person provokes quarrels” (Prov. 15).

And: “The mouth of the wicked overflows with evil” (ibid.).

And: “The evil person is always seeking quarrels, but a cruel angel will be sent against him” (Prov. 17).

And this: “Among the proud there are always quarrels” (Prov. 13).

Wicked monks are called proud when, neglecting the counsels of their elders, they live by their own laws according to their own pleasure, frequently quarrel among themselves, and often stir up disputes. Against them a cruel angel is sent, because, when they give him a place, the devil—the enemy who wages war against souls—is stirred up against them.

“Not slow.”

A slow person is called lazy, sluggish, or lukewarm. It is not fitting for the cellarer to be slow or lazy, lest this be said of him:

“The lazy person hides his hand under his armpit and does not bring it back to his mouth” (Prov. 26).

It is not fitting for one who ought to provide service to many people to be slow. Rather, he must be quick to hear, quick to serve, slow to make excuses, and slow to anger.

Not prodigal. For “prodigal” means excessively generous, lavish or wasteful, a squanderer or dissipator of the monastery’s goods, or one who uproots the brothers’ resources.

[Col. 0860B]

But fearing God, so that he may be like a father to the whole community. For the cellarer ought both to fear and to love God; and for love or fear of him, he should love the brothers and obey them—toward the younger as a father, toward the older as a son. Yet, possessing fatherly compassion, he should serve everyone suitably and appropriately. For it is written: “Fear God with all your soul, and sanctify his priests. Love him who made you with all your strength, and do not abandon his ministers” (Sirach 7).

Let him care for everything, but do nothing without the abbot’s command. Many say: “He may do nothing without the abbot’s command; how, then, can he care for everything?” But the author explains this when he adds:

[Col. 0860C]

Let him guard what he is ordered to guard. It is as though he said: “Above I said that he should care for everything; let him care for those things which he has been ordered to guard. As for other matters, let him do nothing without the abbot’s command.”

Let him not distress the brothers. Why he should not distress the brothers, hear what follows.

If a brother should happen to ask something of him unreasonably, let him not distress him by despising him, but let him reasonably and humbly refuse the one who asks wrongly. “To ask wrongly,” he says, means asking unreasonably for things that ought not to be requested, or asking for things that may properly be requested but at an unsuitable time. Things requested in this manner are understood or regarded as blameworthy requests. Since the cellarer is forbidden to give in such circumstances, especially when the following is said about him:

[Col. 0860D]

Let him guard his own soul. That is, let him neither offend by giving what ought not to be given nor by answering what ought not to be answered.

Always mindful of that apostolic saying: “He who has ministered well acquires for himself a good standing” (1 Timothy 3). That is the standing which the faithful and prudent steward acquired for himself—the one whom the Lord appointed over his household to give them their measure of grain at the proper time. With him he will hear: “Blessed is that servant whom, when his lord comes, he will find doing so” (Matthew 24), that is, ministering well. “Truly I say to you, he will appoint him over all that he possesses,” that is, over all the joys of the heavenly kingdom. Behold what a good joy he who ministers well acquires for himself [Col. 0861A]: namely, that he may be honored in heaven among the Lord’s stewards and ministers. For whoever labors more in God’s service in the present life will receive a greater reward in the future.

Let him care with every diligence for the sick, the children, the guests, and the poor. Let him minister to brothers afflicted by illness with attentive care and the readiest affection. For it is written: “I was sick, and you visited me” (Matthew 25). For the children, considering the frailty of their age and the tenderness of their bodies, let him provide what is necessary with fatherly affection. Let him supply what the guests require, because it is written: “I was a guest, and you received me” (ibid.). And because it is commanded: “Give to everyone who asks of you” (Luke 6). Let him not withhold alms from the poor, because it is written [Col. 0861B]: “He who closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be heard” (Proverbs 21). Rather, let him cheerfully supply them with what they need, because it is written: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9).

Knowing without doubt that for all these things he will have to render an account on the day of judgment. “We must,” says the Apostle, “stand before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Corinthians 5). Thus each of us will receive a reward worthy of his labor.

Let him regard all the monastery’s vessels and its entire property as he would the consecrated vessels of the altar. Hence the ancient Fathers of the monks said: “A cellarer of such a kind should be chosen that he can, in all things and according to the evangelical order, provide food for his brothers; one who fears the sentence against Judas, who from the beginning was a thief. The man appointed to this office should strive to hear that ‘he who has ministered well acquires a good standing,’ and gains profit for his soul. The brothers should also know that everything handled in the monastery—whether vessels, tools, or anything else—is sanctified. If any of the brothers handles anything carelessly, let him know that he shares in the guilt of that king who drank with his concubines from the sanctified vessels of God’s house, and let him remember what punishment that king deserved. These precepts must be guarded and recited into the brothers’ ears every day, lest they be condemned in their sins.”

Let him consider nothing negligible; let him neither pursue avarice nor be prodigal or a destroyer of the monastery’s resources [Col. 0861D], but let him do everything in due measure and according to the abbot’s command. Hence, according to the Eastern Rule of the Fathers, it is said: “For seasoning the food, the cellarer should provide what is necessary according to the custom of daily expenditure, neither lavishly nor stingily, lest through his fault the monastery’s resources be burdened or the brothers suffer injury. Yet, considering the needs and labor of sick brothers, let him refuse the sick nothing that he has, insofar as they need it. He shall prepare food for various brothers who arrive. This shall be the cellarer’s recurring care: always to return to the counsel of the elders and to inquire about everything, especially those matters which he cannot accomplish by his own judgment.”

[Col. 0862A]

Above all, let him possess humility; and when he has no goods to give, let him offer a good word in reply, as it is written: “A good word is better than an excellent gift” (Sirach 18). Without doubt, whoever possesses true humility in his heart will speak a good word with his mouth; and whether he has something to give or lacks it, let him offer everyone a gracious and good word. It is also written in Ecclesiasticus: “Does not dew cool the heat, just as a word is better than a gift?” (ibid.). Behold, is not a word better than a good gift?

Let him himself keep under his care everything the abbot entrusts to him. Let him not presume to take charge of what the abbot forbids him. Here he shows that if he subjects to his authority anything other than what he has received as an assignment from his abbot, or presumes to handle what has been forbidden to him [Col. 0862B], this will be reckoned not as the merit of obedience but as the guilt of disobedience. For if he did not come to the monastery to do his own will, then nothing that has not been assigned to him ought to concern him.

Let him offer the brothers their allotted ration without any grimace or delay, so that they are not scandalized. “Ration” means the provision of food and the monks’ entire sustenance. For the ancients customarily ate at the ninth hour, and therefore, from the time of that hour—when they took their food—the whole human supply of provisions appropriately received the name *annona*. Many names derive from an action or a time. When he says that he should offer what is to be offered “without any grimace,” this is understood to mean without a troubled heart or altered facial expression; rather, with a cheerful spirit and a serene or pleasant countenance, let him give what must be given and offer what must be offered. *Typus* is a Greek word, which we call “figure” or “form.” In a *typus*, a matter is explained through other things, and inward realities are displayed outwardly. The word *typus* is also used for a plant that swells up from water. Hence the swelling of ambitious and self-satisfied people is likewise called *typus*.

Mindful of the divine word, let him remember what punishment awaits one who scandalizes one of the little ones. It is written in the Gospel: “Whoever scandalizes one of these little ones who believe in me, it would be better for him that an ass’s millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths of the sea” (Matthew 18). What, then, is signified by the ass’s millstone except the round of care for the present age? And what is signified by the sea [Col. 0862D] except this same present age? For it would have been lighter for a monk who scandalizes others while placed in the monastery to be thrown into the sea of this world with an ass’s millstone tied around his neck—that is, to be entangled in worldly cares and to carry out secular business and the round of earthly concerns—than to destroy himself and others by scandalizing them in the harbor of the monastery. Hence blessed Gregory says: “By the ass’s millstone the worldly round and labor are expressed, and by the depth of the sea final damnation is signified. Therefore, when someone who has been led to the appearance of holiness destroys others either by word or by example, it would surely have been better if earthly affairs had bound him to death beneath an outward appearance, than that sacred offices should display him to others as an example in guilt. For if he alone were to fall, the punishment of hell would in some way torment him more tolerably.”

If the community is large, let assistance be provided for him, so that, helped in this way, he may himself fulfill the office entrusted to him with an even temper. Assistance must especially be assigned to him so that he does not perform the office entrusted to him with murmuring. For if, being alone, he cannot complete the laborious ministry assigned to him, he will undoubtedly generate dangerous murmuring among the others.

At suitable times let what must be given be given, and what must be requested be requested. By “suitable times” he means fitting or appropriate times, when both actions are permitted: both the petitioner’s asking and the giver’s giving. For when they ought to devote themselves to reading or prayer and maintain silence, neither may one ask nor may another give, except in a case of necessity, lest both be disturbed from the regular order by indiscriminate asking and giving. Hence what follows:

So that no one may be disturbed or distressed in the house of God. The house of the Lord is the most holy hearts of good monks and their purest dwelling places, in which they provide their Lord with the cleanest habitation. For the Lord himself says: “I will dwell in them and walk among them; I will be their Lord, and they will be my people.” And the Apostle says: “You are God’s temple, and the Spirit of the Lord dwells in you” (2 Corinthians 6; 1 Corinthians 3; 2 Corinthians 16). In this temple—that is, in this house of the Lord—no one may disturb or distress another, because it is fitting that the children of peace should always be peaceable.

[Col. 0863C]

CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning the tools and property of the monastery.

The abbot shall entrust the monastery’s property—tools, clothing, and every other kind of possession—to brothers whose life and conduct he can trust; and he shall assign each item to them, as he judges useful, to be guarded and collected again. The abbot shall keep a written inventory of these things, so that, when the brothers successively take over the items assigned to them, he may know what he gives and what he receives. If anyone handles the monastery’s property sordidly or negligently, let him be corrected; if he does not amend, let him submit to regular discipline.

When blessed Basil was asked how those who work ought to care for the tools and implements with which they work, he replied: “First, they ought to use them as the vessels of God or as things already consecrated to God. [Col. 0863D] Then, as those who cannot obtain the fruits of their devotion and diligence without them.” Again, when asked what should happen if anything among these things perished through negligence or was destroyed through contempt, he replied: “The one who treats it with contempt must be judged like a sacrilegious person. The one who loses it through negligence likewise incurs a similar crime, because everything assigned for the use of God’s servants is undoubtedly consecrated to God.”

Hence Isidore says: “The custody of the instruments and tools shall belong to one whom the Father of the monks has chosen; he shall distribute them to those who work and guard what has been returned. Although all these things remain specially assigned to individuals, nevertheless everything ordered by the Father of the monastery shall belong to the care of the superior.” Hence another master of monks says: “The monastery’s tools shall be kept in one room, and the abbot shall entrust the care of preserving them to one brother whose diligence he has come to know. Each day he shall issue them to the brothers for their work, counting them, and shall likewise receive them back clean from those who took them, and put them away, while the abbot keeps a written inventory of everything.”

CHAPTER XXXIII. Whether monks should possess anything of their own.

Above all, let this vice be cut off from the monastery: that no one presume to give or receive anything without the abbot’s command. A monk ought not to give or lend to anyone anything that he has received from the abbot for the needs of the present time, unless the abbot has ordered it [Col. 0864B]. For what worldly possessions could he give to another brother who, for Christ’s sake, has handed over all his own wishes to the abbot’s authority? Hence blessed Fructuosus says: “A particular practice has been established: no monk is to undertake any work as though he could claim it as his own or distribute it to anyone he wishes on his own authority; nor is he to accept, begin, or perform any work without the instruction and permission of his superior. Rather, in every matter, whatever the abbot or superior commands, that must be done.”

Nor should he possess anything as his own—no object at all, neither a book, nor writing tablets, nor a stylus, but nothing whatsoever; for he is not even permitted to have his own body or wishes under his own control. What can the holy monk possess as his own, when he has not retained either his body or his will under his own authority, but has wholly denied himself in order to follow Christ? What can he possess from the world, when the world has been crucified to him and he to the world? He who has once died to the world by neither desiring nor possessing worldly things—ought he to live again for the world? Once he has left the world, he must not entangle himself in it again.

Rather, he should hope for everything necessary from the Father of the monastery. If the Lord has given the monk his portion, why should he anxiously care for all those necessities? Why should he be concerned about earthly possessions, when the Lord expressly says: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’” (Matthew 6). First we must seek the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0864D], and afterward all these things are to be hoped for not from ourselves but from the Lord through the Father of the monastery. It is therefore unnecessary for a monk to possess anything privately, since the Father supplies everything belonging to the monastery.

Nor may he possess anything that the abbot has not given or permitted. “What the abbot has not given,” he says—that is, into his hands—or “permitted,” meaning either to be given or to be possessed. Here he shows that he may receive nothing either from relatives outside the monastery or from those within, nor exchange anything familiarly with anyone else; but whatever is distributed to him by the abbot and at the abbot’s command, let him willingly keep and enjoy calmly.

Let everything be common to everyone, as it is written [Col. 0865A] (Acts 7), and let no one say or presume that anything is his own. Hence Ferreolus says: “Let him judge as his own only whatever he possesses undivided together with the brothers.” For the reading of the Acts of the Apostles likewise records that, at the time when the Church was rising, Christ’s faithful lived in this way: “No one,” it says, “claimed that any of his possessions was his own, but everything was common to them.” Elsewhere it says: “For if Ananias and Sapphira, concerning their private property, did not deserve to receive faith from the apostles, when they had assigned all their possessions at the apostles’ feet but fraudulently withheld part of what was their own and were condemned by the judgment of sudden death, it was because fraud cannot be committed against God, since nothing is hidden that will not be revealed by him.”

If anyone is found to delight in this most wicked vice, let him be admonished once and again; if he does not amend [Col. 0865B], let him submit to correction. Hence Cassian says: “He must not dare even in speech to call anything his own, for it is a great crime for such words to come from a monk’s mouth: ‘my tunic, my book, my tablets, my stylus,’ and other similar expressions. If such a word should slip from his mouth through inadvertence or ignorance, let him ask pardon by prostrating himself on the ground and making fitting satisfaction through penance.” Another master of monks likewise says: “If anything private, or any other object, is found in someone’s possession, let the abbot condemn him to a severe and lengthy excommunication, so that no one may dare imitate this example of punishment.”

CHAPTER XXXIV. Whether all should receive necessities equally.

[Col. 0865C]

As it is written: “It was distributed to each according to what each had need of” (Acts 4). We do not mean by this that there should be acceptance of persons—which God forbid—but consideration of infirmities. Let the one who needs less give thanks to God and not be distressed; let the one who needs more humble himself because of his infirmity and not become proud because of the mercy shown him. Thus all the members will be at peace.

Hence blessed Augustine says: “Strength and clothing are not distributed equally to everyone, because you are not all equally strong; rather, to each according to what each requires.” For it is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Everything was common to them, and it was distributed to each according to what each had need of” (ibid.). Elsewhere it is written: “Do not consider anything to be your own, but let everything be common to you” (Acts 4). What is distributed to you by the abbot’s command is not to be given equally to everyone, but to each according to what the order of stewardship or the cause of infirmity requires; nevertheless, each should receive according to his need. Nor should those be judged more fortunate who, because of infirmity, are provided with what is withheld from the healthy because of the rigor of observance. And if those whom their parents raised more delicately receive more abundant food or clothing, the brotherhood should not therefore be disturbed that what is denied to the physically stronger by the rule’s constitution is granted to them out of consideration for charity.

Above all, let the evil of murmuring not appear in anyone, for any cause, in any word or sign whatsoever. If anyone is caught doing so, let him be subjected to stricter discipline. Hence Ferreolus [Col. 0866A] says: “Let no murmuring or slander—the practice most familiar to monks—be heard in the community against the abbot or any other brother, lest God’s anger, which often condemned a wretched people because of this offense, likewise be aroused against the crowd of murmurers in their destruction, and lest personal murmuring cause them to lose the promised land, which we rightly understand as the place of future blessedness, promised by divine pledge.” Thus the psalm announces that the followers of this vice are to be condemned: “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I will persecute” (Psalm 100). And again the Apostle rebukes them, saying: “Whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God” (Romans 1; Jude 16). And again: “These are murmurers and complainers, walking according to their own desires, and their mouth speaks arrogance.”

CHAPTER XXXV. Concerning the weekly kitchen servers.

Let the brothers serve one another in such a way that no one is excused from kitchen duty unless prevented by illness or occupied with a matter of serious usefulness; for thereby greater reward and charity are acquired. Bodily illness itself excuses the sick from kitchen duty. The sick are to be borne with out of charity and brotherly love, not compelled to work. By “serious usefulness,” great or considerable usefulness is meant. For “serious” is often used to mean great, large, or perfect, as the Psalmist says: “I will give thanks to you in the great assembly; among a weighty people I will praise you” (Psalm 35). When it says, “For thereby greater reward and charity are acquired,” this means that a greater reward is acquired with God, and charity toward God and human beings is increased. Whoever cheerfully prepares food in all things will receive from everyone the grace of charity and, from the Lord, an eternal reward for all. For it is written: “Whoever labors more will receive a greater reward” (Ecclesiastes 8).

Let assistance be provided for the weak, so that they do this not with sadness, but so that everyone may have assistance according to the size of the community or the character of the place. By “weak” he means fragile, delicate, or infirm. *Imbecillis*—as though “without the consolation of a staff”—is understood to mean one who lacks support. By “according to the size of the community,” the number and quantity of the monks are meant. For according to the size of the community, a smaller or larger number of ministers should be assigned. By “the character of the place,” the construction or arrangement of the monastery is meant. If the monastery is constructed in a suitable place, where, according to this chapter of the Rule, everything necessary is contained within the cloister, the cook needs less assistance from others. But if it is situated in a confined, narrow, or dry place, where they cannot obtain water without labor or have a garden without difficulty, more assistance should be given to the cooks.

If the community is large, let the cellarer be excused from the kitchen, as should those who, as we said, are occupied with more important duties. Let the others serve one another in charity. In the duty of charity, let everyone serve everyone, and, receiving service from one another, let them return service, supporting one another, while each awaits from the Lord a reward worthy of his labor.

The one leaving the weekly service shall clean everything on Saturday. Let him wash the linens with which the brothers dry their hands or feet. Both the one leaving and the one entering shall wash everyone’s feet. Let them return the clean and sound vessels of their ministry to the cellarer. The cellarer, in turn, shall hand them over to the one entering, so that he may know what he gives and what he receives. Hence Cassian says: “When the Lord’s Day has been completed, those entering on the second day of the week, as others again succeed them, shall hand over the implements and vessels with which they have served. They should guard them with such great care and diligence that nothing may be diminished or perish; or they should believe that they will have to render an account not only to human beings but also to the Lord for even the smallest vessels, as for holy and great things, if anything among them should be handled or lost through negligence.” Thus the weekly server must faithfully perform his service, so that he does not allow even a single grain of legume to perish carelessly from his hands. For our Fathers commanded that everything entering the monastery, once admitted, be handled with the greatest reverence as though it were most holy and already consecrated to the Lord. The weekly servers themselves shall perform every service, all diligence, and all cleaning of the monastery; they shall themselves carry water, wash the feet, and wash the cloths, sheets, and towels.

[Col. 0867C]

The weekly servers shall receive, one hour before the meal, individual drinks and bread in addition to their assigned ration, so that at the hour of the meal they may serve their brothers without murmuring or excessive labor. When it says “one hour before the meal,” this is understood to mean that, during that one hour, before the brothers eat, they should receive these things in addition to their assigned ration—that is, in addition to their normal measure of food, which has been established for them communally and according to the Rule. Let them receive individual drinks beyond their measure and a little bread beyond their allotted pound, lest, burdened by service, they also be burdened by fasting.

On solemn days, let them wait until the Masses. When it says, “let them wait until the Masses,” this means until the principal Mass, which is sung solemnly for everyone. For there are many monastic ministers who hear Mass in the morning, eat, and go wherever they wish, saying that they have heard Mass and have therefore eaten. Foreseeing and forbidding this vice, blessed Benedict said: “On solemn days, let them wait until the Masses.”
