The entering and departing weekly servers shall immediately after Sunday Matins prostrate themselves before everyone in the oratory, asking that prayers be offered for them. They faithfully seek this blessing and reward for the labor of the entire week, so that, as Christ’s command is fulfilled in them, a prayer uttered by all the brothers may accompany them; and so that this prayer may commend their completed service to God as a devout sacrifice, and may simply intercede for whatever they have sinned through ignorance or human frailty [Col. 0868A].

The one departing from the weekly service shall say this verse: “Blessed are you, Lord God, who have helped me and comforted me.” After saying it three times, let the departing server receive a blessing. The one entering shall follow and say: “O God, come to my assistance; Lord, hasten to help me.” Let this also be repeated three times by everyone. After receiving the blessing, let him enter.

The departing server shall receive this blessing from the priest: “O God, who said, ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you,’ refresh these your servants with the everlasting reward of their labors. Through the Lord, etc.” The entering server shall receive this blessing: “Help, I ask you, Lord, these your servants who labor in fraternal service, and grant them perseverance without murmuring and the perpetual reward of their own labor. Through the Lord, etc.” [Col. 0868B]

The departing weekly server rightly says to the Lord: “Blessed are you, Lord God, who have helped me,” because the Lord himself helps a person in labor, and he himself promises the laborer the reward of consolation. The entering server rightly says to the Lord: “O God, come to my assistance,” because he is entering upon the work of labor, in which he needs the Lord’s help—namely, the help of the one who said to those willing to labor for him: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). When it says, “After receiving the blessing, let him enter,” this is understood either as entry after the prayer has first been offered by all the brothers or after the priest has gathered the petition [Col. 0868C].

CHAPTER XXXVI. Concerning sick brothers.

Care for the sick must be provided before and above all else, so that they may be served as Christ himself truly would be, because he said: “I was sick, and you visited me” (Matthew 25). And: “What you did for one of the least of these, you did for me” (ibid.). Hence, when blessed Basil was asked with what disposition we ought to minister to sick brothers, he replied: “As though offering service to the Lord himself, who said: ‘When you did it for one of the least of these my brothers, you did it for me’” (ibid.). Hence another Father of the monks says: “What care should be shown to those held by illness is declared by the Author’s compassion when he says: ‘Whatever you want people to do to you, you also do likewise to them’” (Matthew 7) [Col. 0868D]. Although this must be done in all things, this command must especially be demonstrated in care for the sick, because the Lord said: “I was sick, and you came to me” (Matthew 25). Thus care must be sought for the sick as though they were being served in Christ’s presence. For truly, whoever cares for the sick for Christ’s sake ministers to Christ in the sick.

The sick themselves should also recognize that they are being served for the honor of God and should not distress the brothers who serve them through their excessive demands. Hence blessed Basil says: “For preserving the spirit of our service, it is beneficial that the sick who receive service from us should be people to whom service ought rightly to be offered, not people who indulge the flesh and the belly, but rather people who prove worthy in the love of God and his Christ. Through their patience and the merit of their life, they should deserve the service of the brothers, so that they may be held to the glory of Christ and the shame of the devil, as was the holy Job.”

Nevertheless, such people must be borne patiently, because a more abundant reward is acquired through them. Hence blessed Isidore says: “Those who are healthy ought to bear with the sick. Those who are sick, however, should not hesitate to place the healthy and laboring before themselves. Those who are healthy in body ought also to be healthy in mind. Therefore it is fitting that the healthy bear the sick rather than be borne by the sick. For we must patiently bear the sick, so that, when we in turn are sick, we may patiently be borne by the healthy. During the time of their illness, let us acquire an abundant reward by serving them, so that during the time of our illness they may likewise acquire an abundant reward by serving us.” Hence the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6).

Therefore, let the abbot take the greatest care that they suffer no neglect. Let a separate cell be assigned for the sick brothers, with a servant who fears God and is diligent and attentive. Thus the abbot’s concern should be that they have a separate cell with every convenience, so that those who bear the pain of illness in weak flesh may feel no external hardship. A person sufficiently faithful and energetic should also be placed in charge of those who are sick or afflicted by some necessity; he should serve the sick compassionately, observe monastic discipline according to the Rule, reasonably distribute what is appropriate for the sick [Col. 0869C], prepare their food diligently, attend upon them with devoted service, and neither defraud them of what remains nor pollute himself by secretly eating it unlawfully. The sick should be nurtured with such great mercy that they neither seek the affection of relatives nor the delicacies of cities, but that the cellarer and superior provide whatever they need. The sick themselves should be admonished with such care that no murmuring word, however small or slight, proceeds from their mouths; rather, in their illness, with cheerfulness of mind and true contrition of heart, they should always give thanks to God. Without the permission of the superior, no one should dare visit them; nor may relatives or siblings have authority to serve them without the superior’s command. For the sake of preserving their reputation, we have taken particular care that no monk who falls ill should be entrusted, after leaving the monastery, to the attention of his parents; for we judge that he is more likely to be polluted by seeing and hearing worldly spectacles than to be cleansed of his illness.

Let the use of baths be offered to the sick whenever it is beneficial. To the healthy, and especially to the young, let it be granted more reluctantly. Hence Saint Isidore says: “No monk should go to the baths for the sake of washing his body, except solely because of the necessity of illness. If it is beneficial, it should not be postponed on account of the treatment, nor should there be murmuring, because it is not done out of a desire for pleasure but solely as a remedy for health. For the purpose of healing, the use of baths should be undertaken with the greatest diligence. To the healthy, especially the young, let it be granted more reluctantly.”

Hence blessed Augustine says: “A bath should by no means be denied to the sick if necessity compels it; even if he does not wish it, it should be done for his health at the superior’s command. But if he himself wishes it and it happens not to be beneficial, his desire should not be obeyed.”

Meat may also be granted to the sick and to those who are altogether weak, for the restoration of their strength. But once they have improved, let everyone abstain from meat as usual. Hence Augustine himself says again: “Just as the sick necessarily need to receive less, lest they be burdened, so after illness they should be treated in such a way that they may recover more quickly. But when they have regained their former strength, let them return to their happier customary practice, which suits God’s servants all the more because they need less. Let the pleasure of food not hold those who are now vigorous, whom necessity had bound when they were sick. Let them judge those richer who have been stronger in enduring restraint. For it is better to need less than to have more.”

The abbot must recognize and test the matter with careful scrutiny, lest anyone pretend to be ill for the sake of eating his fill. If someone says that he is sick, does not rise for the work of God, and remains lying down continuously, he should not be called to account; but at the meal he should receive only broths, eggs, or hot water, so that, if he is pretending to be ill, hunger may compel him to rise. But whoever claims that he cannot work should likewise be judged unable to eat, since it is consistent with justice that he be unable to do both. If we say that we cannot work, then let us also say that we cannot eat. O monstrous injustice! The head is racked with pain on account of labor, but the belly is not racked by the distension of food? [Col. 0870C]

The abbot must take the greatest care that the sick are not neglected by the cellarers or servants, because whatever is done wrong by the disciples falls under his responsibility. Hence a certain master of monks says: “The abbot should care for the sick in the manner in which he hopes to receive care from the Lord, so that the sick do not experience any neglect from the cellarer. It is the abbot’s responsibility to correct whatever the disciples do wrong. If he does not correct it, the abbot is not freed from the guilt of negligence.”

CHAPTER XXXVII. Concerning the elderly and children.

Although human nature itself is drawn toward mercy for these ages—namely, the elderly and children—the authority of the Rule will also provide for them. Here, *licet* is used in the sense of “although.” It is as though he were saying: “Although human nature itself, naturally full of compassionate feeling, draws a person toward mercy, or toward pity for the elderly and children, nevertheless the authority of the Rule also provides for them.” How it provides for them, hear what follows.

Their weakness should always be taken into consideration, and the strictness of the Rule concerning food should in no way be imposed upon them; rather, compassionate consideration should be shown toward them, and they should anticipate the canonical hours. Hence blessed Isidore says:

> Those, however, who have been worn out by the old age of the body, or are held back by the weakness of tender age, should not be exercised by daily fasts, lest either old age fail before it dies, or the growing child fall before it advances, and perish before learning to do good.

Hence another master of monks says:

> Little children should fast on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, though only on the shorter days—that is, during the winter season. On the other days they should take their meal at the sixth hour. During the summer days, however, little children should take their meal at the sixth hour on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday; on the other days they should be refreshed at the third hour, because on the longer days the strength of the younger age is less, just as it differs in its capacity for endurance.

We permit this relaxation for those children who are under twelve years of age; but whoever is older should be held to the discipline of the adults. For by a just judgment, little children, those advanced in old age, and the sick should all be granted relaxation in the matter of meals on an equal basis.

“Let them anticipate the canonical hours.” By “canonical hours” he means regular hours. For *canon* is interpreted as “rule.” The canonical hours which he asks the elderly and the little ones to anticipate—that is, to take their food earlier—are the sixth and ninth hours. He says, “Let them anticipate the canonical hours,” meaning that if the brothers eat at the sixth hour, those persons should be refreshed at the third hour; and if the brothers eat at the ninth hour, those persons should receive food at the sixth hour.

We command that those elderly men whom we recognize as quiet, simple, humble, obedient, frequent in attendance at prayer, always having Christ in their mouths, weeping over their sins, depending not on their own judgment but on that of their superiors, having completely abandoned affection for their relatives, holding the love of God and of their neighbor with their whole mind, and meditating day and night on the law of the Lord, should be cherished with compassionate mercy like little children and honored like fathers.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the weekly reader

Reading should not be lacking at the meal of the brothers who are eating. Therefore there should be no lack of reading for those who are eating, so that, attending to sacred reading, the brothers may eat their bread with silence, according to the Apostle. For just as the body is restored by bodily food, so the mind should be restored by spiritual food.

Therefore, while seated at table, let them keep silence. Reading should be read every day and at all times while food is being taken, so that both the outer person may be nourished by food and the inner person by the word of God, since it is written: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Deut. 8; Matt. 4).

Nor should whoever happens to take up the book read there by accidental chance. “He should” or “he should dare” is understood. By “accidental chance” he means suddenly or unexpectedly. The reading must indeed be provided for carefully, since it is to be read for the edification of so many men, lest an unprepared reading provide the hearers not with life-giving nourishment but rather generate harmful murmuring. Sacred reading should be read in such a way that, just as food fills the bodies of those eating, so it may fill the hearts of those listening.

The one who is to read for the whole week should enter on Sunday. After entering, following Masses and Communion, let him ask everyone to pray for him, so that God may avert from him the spirit of vainglory. Reasonably, the reader should enter first of all the days in order to read, and thus begin and complete the work of reading for the entire week. This work should not be begun by him without prayer having first been offered, both his own prayer and that of the brothers. In everything that monks are to do, the prayer of the brothers should continually precede them. The prayer of good monks quickly penetrates heaven.

It is therefore a sign of this that the reader should ask everyone to pray for him, so that God may avert from him the spirit of vainglory, because the arrogance of vainglory arises from pride; and unless hidden elation of mind has preceded it, open boasting of praise does not follow.

And this verse should be said in the oratory three times by everyone, with the reader himself beginning:

> “O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.”

Then, having received the blessing, let him enter to read. The opening of the lips is to be sought from the one by whom the distribution of all languages was first made. From him who made the tongues of infants eloquent, the opening of the lips and the illumination of the heart must be sought, so that the reader’s mouth may proclaim to him the service of praise, since the reader knows that his mouth has been mercifully opened by him.

When it says, “and thus, having received the blessing, let him enter to read,” this means that, having received prayer from the brothers and having received the collected blessing from the priest, he should enter to complete the reading. If it is agreeable, this collect may be given to the reader by the priest before the altar after Mass has been completed, with the following words:

> “Turn away, we beseech you, O Lord, from this servant of yours the spirit of vainglory, so that, reading humbly, he may receive the meaning and understanding of the reading. Through Christ, etc.”

And let the greatest silence be kept at table, so that no one’s muttering or voice may be heard there except that of the reader. There is a difference between ordinary silence and the greatest silence: in the latter, no voice and no muttering sounds. Ordinary silence is where people speak, but softly and silently. Thus, in the Gospel, Martha called Mary quietly, saying: “The Teacher is here and is calling you” (John 11). Of this silence the Rule says: “At all times let the monks devote themselves to silence.” But at table and during the night, let the greatest silence be observed.

The brothers should serve one another whatever is necessary for those eating and drinking, so that no one needs to ask for anything. If something is nevertheless needed, it should be requested by the sound of any signal rather than by voice. Hence blessed Fructuosus says:

> If anything is lacking at table, the one in charge should, by giving a signal or by silent gestures, ask and indicate to the server what needs to be brought to or removed from the table.

And elsewhere:

> If anything necessary is needed at table, no one should dare to speak, but should give a signal by sound to those serving.

Nor should anyone presume to ask anything there about the reading itself or about anything else, lest an occasion be given. It is understood: lest an occasion be given either to the wicked devil for tempting, or to the brothers for speaking excessively, as blessed Cassian says:

> While the brothers are being refreshed, sacred readings should be read because of the superfluous and idle stories, and especially the arguments that frequently tend to arise at the table of those eating.

Unless perhaps the prior wishes to say something briefly for the sake of edification. Hence a certain master of monks says:

> At table no one at all, except the abbot or one to whom he himself has given orders, should presume to speak for a common necessity. But all, giving thanks to the Creator in their hearts with attentive minds, should enjoy food and drink in the customary measure. And no one should scrutinize how much another is being refreshed, with wandering and curious eyes; rather, each should look before himself.

The weekly reader should receive the *mixtum* before beginning to read, for the sake of Holy Communion and lest it be burdensome for him to endure fasting. Afterwards, however, he should take his meal with the weekly kitchen servants and servers. When it says “let him receive the *mixtum*,” bread together with wine is meant. In many provinces, bread alone and the wine offered upon the altar are called *mixtum*. He says “for the sake of Holy Communion,” so that, having taken something from it, he may not spit it out and cast it away in his spittle.

The brothers should not read or chant in rotation, but those who edify the hearers should do so. Hence again the master of monks says:

> Let the reader read in an orderly manner, without hurrying, so that the hearers, being occupied with it, may recognize more clearly what they ought to fulfill in their actions. And if anything is ambiguous or obscure, it will be understood more easily when read more clearly.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the measure of food

We believe that two cooked dishes are sufficient for the daily meal, both at the sixth and at the ninth hour, at all tables, on account of the different weaknesses of the brothers, so that perhaps whoever cannot be refreshed by one may be refreshed by the other. Therefore two cooked dishes should suffice for the brothers; and if there are fruits or growing vegetables, a third may also be added.

Hence Isidore says:

> At both times the meal will consist of three dishes: namely, vegetables, legumes, and, if there is a third, fruit.

A certain master of monks likewise says:

> We believe that two cooked dishes are sufficient for the daily meal, both at the sixth and at the ninth hour, at all tables, together with whatever third item of fruit there may be in its raw state.

On feast days, however, out of reverence for the sacred solemnity, the bodies should be refreshed with more foods—that is, with three or four courses—yet in such a way that, the more numerous the foods are, the smaller they should be, so that the bodies may be restored by necessary food and not condemned by excessive satiety.

When food is served at table, no one should eat before the signal for the blessing sounds. When they have heard the signal, let them ask for the blessing with one voice. The abbot follows their voice, saying: “May the Lord deign to bless.” Above all, we decree that no one should presume to give to another from his own measure or to receive from another, except the abbot or the provost, to whom the abbot has entrusted this responsibility.

One weighed pound of bread should be sufficient for each day, whether there is one meal or both dinner and supper. If they are going to have supper, a third of that pound should be reserved by the cellarer and given to those who are to sup.

Hence the same master mentioned above says:

> Half a loaf of bread, weighing a pound, should suffice for each brother each day, according to the pattern of divine provision. When the raven had prepared half a heavenly loaf for Paul, the servant of God, to eat each day, then, whenever they are refreshed at the sixth hour during the summer season or at other times, a third of that loaf of the Lord’s bread, taken by the cellarer from the common stores in the cellar, should be set before the tables in the evening, before that raw dish is brought in.

When it says “one weighed pound of bread,” “previously weighed” or “measured out” is understood. The dish mentioned above also derives its name from *puls*, porridge. Whether only porridge, or something else composed and consumed according to the same manner of mixture, is properly called a *pulmentum*, a dish. By “growing vegetables” are understood the shoots of those same vegetables, which, prepared with vinegar or other fruits, are suitable for eating.

If greater labor has perhaps been performed, it will be within the abbot’s judgment and power, if it is expedient, to increase something. Hence Basil says:

> Those in authority should observe that rule which says: “It was distributed to each according to what each one needed.” Each person should therefore be anticipated, so that, according to his labor, he may also find the consolations of refreshment. As far as vices are concerned, there must be complete abstinence; but as far as food is concerned, its measure and quality should be adjusted according to what use, age, labor, bodily strength, or bodily weakness requires.

Above all, gluttony must be removed, so that indigestion may never creep upon the monk; for nothing is so contrary to every Christian as gluttony, as our Lord says: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke 21). *Crapula* means immoderate greediness. The word *crapula* is derived as if from “raw food” (*cruda epula*), whose rawness weighs down the heart and makes the stomach indigested. Hence the text continues: “and so that indigestion may never creep upon the monk,” that is, an undischarged or obstructed belly.

Concerning gluttony the Lord says: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness,” and so forth. For it is highly useless for a monk to fill and burden his belly with food, and it is contrary to every good work, because the more someone uses food excessively, the more he feeds his belly and the more he dulls the understanding of his mind.

For children of younger age, the same quantity should not be observed, but a smaller quantity than for adults, with moderation preserved in all things. Hence the master says:

> For those over twelve years of age, less than a pound of bread per day should suffice.

Quantity means smallness or largeness. It is derived from *mensura*, “measure,” which expresses how much something is. By it, either more or less is shown. Moderation is temperance, deriving its name from sparing.

The eating of the meat of four-footed animals should be entirely abstained from by everyone, except by the completely weak and the sick. Hence Aurelius says:

> Meat should never be taken as food. Chicks and all poultry should not be served in the congregation. Provision should be made for the sick alone, and they may receive it.

Hence Fructuosus says:

> No one is granted permission either to take or to taste meat—not because we judge God’s creature unworthy, but because abstinence from meat is considered useful and suitable for monks. Nevertheless, a measure of compassion is preserved toward the needs of the sick and toward those traveling a long distance, so that the sick may be sustained by the food of birds, and those destined for a distant journey—if they are expected by a prince or bishop—need not fear tasting it as a blessing and act of obedience, while preserving with themselves their customary continence in the remainder.

If any monk violates this and presumes to eat meat against the Rule’s decree and the practice of the elders, he will be subjected to confinement and penance for six months. When it says “the weak, the sick,” it does not signify two persons, as many think, but only one person. Thus, a weak sick person is one who, oppressed by a long or severe illness, has been reduced to weakness, and to whom meat-based nourishment must be applied for the sake of restoration.

[Col. 0875B]

## CHAPTER XL. On the measure of drink

“Each person has his own gift from God: one in this way, another in that” (1 Cor. 7). When it says “one in this way, another in that,” it means that one has received from God a greater gift of abstinence, while another has received less. Therefore their food and drink must be regulated with great caution, lest, while the one who needs less is being moderated, the one who needs more suffer the deprivation of want. For this reason the text continues:

“And therefore the measure of nourishment for others is established by us with some scrupulousness.” *Scrupulousness* means sadness, anxiety, concern, or distress of mind.

Nevertheless, considering the weakness of the sick, we believe that a *hemina* of wine per person is sufficient for each day. Those to whom God grants the endurance of abstinence should know that they will have their own reward. Here he speaks of the weakness of the sick not as bodily illness but as an inability of the soul. For the body cannot fulfill abstinence outwardly unless the mind inwardly consents to abstinence. There are many who could abstain because health has been granted to them, but who cannot do so because of weakness of mind. A *hemina* of wine weighs one pound; doubled, it makes a *sextarius*.

If the need of the place, labor, or the heat of summer should demand more, it should remain within the prior’s discretion, while he considers in all things that satiety or drunkenness does not creep in. Hence Ferreolus says:

> I think it unnecessary to admonish a monk about drunkenness, since, if he takes even a little wine, he departs from the bodily discipline imposed upon him.

And therefore, if it should ever happen—though it is a shameful thing to say—that a monk is seen to be drunk, I command him, full of zeal and anger, to be suspended from his portion of wine for thirty days, so that during this period everything poured in may be evacuated after digestion has been allowed.

Although we read that wine is altogether not for monks, hear where blessed Benedict read this. For a certain ancient Father says:

> Flesh and wine, or drink in which there is drunkenness, are to be rejected by monks and not accepted by those for whom the world has been crucified through Christ, and they to the world. Nor is there to be a feast for a monk on earth, except perhaps a little at the arrival of the brothers, as though Christ’s food had been made more joyful by the grace of charity.

But since in our times this cannot be persuaded upon monks, let us at least agree to this: that we should not drink to satiety, but more sparingly, because “wine makes the wise apostatize” (Eccl. 10). *To apostatize* means to depart from the way of justice, to transgress from the faith, to turn back, or to defect from the good.

But observe carefully how wine makes the wise apostatize. Noah, a wise, holy, and most ancient man, whom such masses of waters had not overcome, was overcome by a little wine and, sleeping in drunkenness, was stripped naked. Wine made the patriarch Lot apostatize when, against nature, he shamefully had intercourse with his daughters. If, then, the drunkenness of wine did not spare holy and magnificent men, how much more will it overcome a weak and insignificant monk!

Where the need of the place requires that even the measure written above cannot be obtained, but much less is available, or nothing at all, let those who live there bless God and not murmur. Since the Apostle writes to the weak Timothy, saying, “Use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent infirmities” (1 Tim. 5), let the monks receive, according to the means of the monastery, as much wine each day as is offered by the command or dispensation of the abbot, and let them ask for absolutely no more.

Above all, we admonish that they be without murmuring. For it is fitting that monks be without murmuring, lest they perish by murmuring, as those who murmured in the desert also perished and, having lost the name of sons, received another name according to the Apostle: murmurers, complainers, hateful to God.

## CHAPTER XLI. At what hours the brothers should eat

From Holy Easter until Pentecost, let the brothers take their meal at the sixth hour and sup in the evening. Hence blessed Isidore says:

> These are the feasts of monks, during which fasts cease: first, the venerable Lord’s Day, dedicated to the name of Christ, which, just as it is solemn because of the mystery of his resurrection, so among all his servants it will be held as a celebration with the joyful festivity of a votive banquet. Likewise, from the first day of Easter until Pentecost, the fast was dissolved by the holy Fathers on continuous days because of Christ’s resurrection and the coming of the Holy Spirit, so that these days might be celebrated not as an image of labor, which the season of Lent signifies, but in the rest of joy, with the fasts relaxed.

Hence Cassian says:

> From the evening of Saturday, which dawns into the Lord’s Day, until the evening of that same Sunday, and throughout all the days of Pentecost, the Fathers decreed and sanctioned that neither knees should be bent nor the rule of fasts observed.

When it says “let them sup in the evening,” *sera* is used for “late,” just as *vespera* is used for “evening.” *Cena*, supper, is named from the fellowship of those eating. For the Greeks call what is common *koinon*. Hence *coenaculum* is named from the common fellowship of those eating, and *coenobium* from the common life of those living together.

From Pentecost throughout the whole summer—if the monks have no agricultural labor, or if excessive heat does not interfere—let them fast on Wednesday and Friday until the ninth hour. Hence Isidore says:

> The second, alternate-day fast, begun on another day after Pentecost, extends until the autumnal equinox, namely, for three days in each week because of the summer heat of the sun.

Fructuosus says:

> From Easter until Pentecost the meal is to be taken at the sixth hour. From Pentecost until the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, alternate-day fasts are to be maintained.

On the remaining days, let them eat dinner at the sixth hour. This sixth-hour dinner, if they have work in the fields or if the heat of summer is excessive, is to be continued; and this should be left to the abbot’s care. *Prandium*, dinner, is so called from the preparation of refreshment. When he says that the sixth-hour dinner is to be continued, he means that it is to be carried out constantly and daily. Because of the fatigue of labor and the heat, fasts are continually to be broken during the summer season. To continue means to do daily, to repeat, or to do without interruption.

Let him so moderate and arrange everything that souls may be saved and whatever the brothers do may be done without justified murmuring. Every day the shepherd’s skill and care must tend toward this: that the souls of his sheep may be saved and that they may be fattened on holy virtues and eternal pastures. Let the sheep also do what they do without justified murmuring.

Justified murmuring is that which monks do not willingly or without cause, but overcome and compelled. The murmuring of one person rises because of another’s wrongdoing. The justified murmuring of monks commonly arises from the unjust oppression of superiors, as blessed Gregory says: “For the earth cries out against its possessor when the Church justly murmurs against its shepherd.”

From the Ides of September until the beginning of Lent, let the brothers always take their meal at the ninth hour. A question arises: how can he say here that they are to fast every day from the Ides of September, when in Chapter 48 he will say: “From Easter until the Kalends of October, after rising from the table at the sixth hour, let them rest”? This is resolved as follows: if they have work in the fields or a grape harvest in the vineyards, where they are occupied by the work itself, let them eat at the sixth hour until the Kalends of October; but if they have no such work, let the general fast begin from the Ides of September.

During Lent, however, until Easter, let them take their meal in the evening. Hence Isidore again says:

> The first is the daily fast of Lent, during which a greater observance of abstinence remains among monks, when they abstain not only from dinners but also from wine and oil.

The monks take their meal in the evening, following the example of the Lord himself, of whom it is read not that he dined but that he supped, when Scripture says: “When evening came, Jesus reclined with the twelve Apostles, and while they were supping he said …” (Matt. 26). For this reason fasts were appointed to be broken at the ninth hour on all days, so that something more extended might be added to the forty days—that is, until evening.

Evening itself should be observed in such a way that those being refreshed do not need the light of a lamp, but finish everything while it is still daylight. At all times, whether at supper or at another meal, the hour should likewise be regulated so that everything takes place in daylight. Everything should therefore be finished, completed, and carried out in the light of day, so that there is no need for lamplight and everything may accordingly be performed and regulated at the appropriate hours. Thus, rising more quickly and eagerly during the nights, they may fulfill what the prophet urges, saying: “In the nights lift up your hands toward the holy place, and bless the Lord” (Ps. 133).

When it says “whether at supper,” supper is understood as the meal that takes place after dinner, when the brothers eat twice. “The hour of refreshment,” however, is understood here as the time when, after the fast has been completed, they eat only once in the evening.

## CHAPTER XLII. That no one should speak after Compline

At all times monks should devote themselves to silence, but especially during the hours of night. Elsewhere too we read that the rule of silence is to be observed at all times, as the sequence of Holy Scripture declares through the prophet: “The service of justice is silence” (Isa. 32). And also: “Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Ps. 140).

Therefore, as soon as Compline has been completed, let silence immediately enter among the brothers, and let them lie down in their beds in such a way that no one speaks to another. We ought to keep silent after Compline so that, appropriately, at the beginning of the night office we may say: “O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise” (Ps. 50). That is, let us ask God during the night office to open our lips, which his protection had closed at Compline.

Therefore at all times, whether it is a day of fasting or a day of dinner—if it is a day on which dinner is taken—as soon as they have risen from the meal, let everyone sit together in one place, and let one person read the *Collations* or the *Lives of the Fathers*, or certainly something that edifies the hearers.

But let him not read the Heptateuch or the Books of Kings, because, for weak understandings, it will not be useful at that hour to hear this Scripture. Let them be read at other hours. When it says “or certainly something that edifies the hearers,” this is understood to refer to the homilies of the Fathers, in which the edification of the hearers has been fully written. Or it may refer to expositions of catholic books composed by orthodox men, in which holy teaching sufficiently overflows for holy monks.

When he says “but not the Heptateuch or the Books of Kings,” attention must be paid carefully to what follows: “for weak understandings,” he says, “it will not be useful at that hour to hear this Scripture.” For sincere, sound, and keen understandings, the Heptateuch, the Books of Kings, or any history of the divine Scriptures is forbidden at no time, because they can recognize figures and meanings in them and receive an example of salvation by reading them.

For those who cannot draw spiritual understanding from them, he rightly prohibits the Heptateuch or the Books of Kings from being read at that hour. Each person should then, built up by the divine word, proceed both to the office of Compline and to his own place, edified. At other hours, however, either before everyone in the church at the proper time or individually in the school of reading, they should read these books according to the discipline of reading.

If it is a day of fasting, once Vespers has been said, let them immediately proceed after a short interval to the reading of the *Collations*, as we have said. After four or five leaves have been read, or as much as the hour permits, and everyone has come together, anyone who happens to have been occupied with the task assigned to him should come during this interval of reading.

A *collatio* means confession, conversation, or discussion, where, while some confer about the divine Scriptures, others offer suitable answers to questions, and matters that had long lain hidden become clear to those conferring. When it says “if anyone happens to be occupied with what was assigned,” the duty of obedience entrusted to him is understood; “he should come” is understood when everyone comes together. A commission means something entrusted or commended. Hence the text continues:

Therefore, when all have been placed together, let them complete Compline. Here he makes no exception for the abbot, the provost, or the deans, who sometimes, while others are chanting in the church, devote this hour to drinking, storytelling, or counsel. He commands everyone without exception to come together at this hour of the *Collation* and to chant Compline together.

When they leave Compline, no one should have permission to speak anything to anyone again. If anyone is found to transgress this rule of silence, he should be subject to a more severe punishment, except if the need of guests arises or the abbot happens to order someone to do something. Even this, however, should be done with the greatest gravity, moderation, and propriety.

Elsewhere too we read:

> From the hour of Compline, when prayer is offered for going to sleep, no one at all should presume to speak, unless a great need of the monastery requires it. Anyone whom the abbot, or indeed the provost who bears responsibility for the others, has appointed to speak should make every effort to do so.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On those who come late to the Work of God or to table

As soon as the signal for the hour of the divine office has been heard, let them leave behind whatever may be in their hands and run with the greatest haste. Yet let them do so with gravity, lest frivolity find fuel. Therefore, let nothing be preferred to the Work of God.

Hence a certain master of monks says:

> Whenever the signal for the divine work sounds, whether at the daytime or nighttime hours, one must rise immediately with the greatest haste, as though the king’s herald were sounding. Every task that was in one’s hands must be set aside, so that nothing may be preferred to the Work of God. With the mind intent upon the herald’s sound and leaning upon the Work of God, let the monk hasten with all gravity and gentleness to intone the glory of his majesty and to return thanks for his mercy.

Hence Cassian says:

> When the sound of the signal has been heard for these prayers, a monk ought to leap up with such speed that—not to mention other craftsmen—even the one engaged in the work of writing Scripture should not dare to complete the letter he has begun at the very moment when the striking sound reaches his ears.

Another master likewise says:

> When the signal in the oratory has been struck, let everyone who hears it, before running, make the sign of the cross on his forehead, responding, “Thanks be to God.” Then let those who are working throw down their task, and let craftsmen abandon their tools; let scribes leave their letter unfinished. Let every hand of the brothers abandon what it was doing. Let the foot hasten immediately, with gravity, to the oratory, and the mind to God, so that they may come at once to the first prayer. And let the gathering of the brothers entering the oratory boil over like a swarm of bees rushing to honey, so that the place of the holy oratory, which had been silent, may immediately be filled with the cries of the priests.

If anyone comes to the nocturnal vigils after the “Glory” of the ninety-fourth psalm—which for this reason we wish to be prolonged and said slowly—let him not stand in his proper place in the choir, but stand last of all, or in the place that the abbot has established separately for such negligent persons, so that he may be seen by the abbot or by everyone, until, when the Work of God has been completed, he repents through public satisfaction.

We have judged that they should stand at the end or separately so that, being seen by everyone, they may be corrected by the very shame of it. Hence Cassian says:

> At the nocturnal prayers, an allowance for delay is granted until the second psalm. Nevertheless, before that psalm has ended and the brothers fall down for prayer, let the latecomer hurry to enter and join the congregation. If he has delayed longer, even briefly, when the Vigils are finished he should not fail, submitting himself with true humility, to seek pardon for his negligence, as we said above: he should be ordered to stand in the last place assigned to such negligent persons, wait there in fear of shame, and, after the course has been completed, make satisfaction before the departing assembly of the brothers by an extended request for pardon.

For if they remain outside the oratory, there may perhaps be someone who returns to his bed and falls asleep, or at least sits outside or devotes himself to stories, and an opportunity may be given to the Evil One. But let him enter inside, so that he may neither lose everything nor fail to amend what remains.

Elsewhere too we read:

> They should not be separated entirely outside, lest, overcome by sleep, they fall asleep, or an opportunity be given to the evil enemy to approach in some way. Once inside, he does not lose everything he had begun, and he is broken by shame and fear while he is seen by everyone. When the others go outside after completing the office, let the one who has been left in the church because of his tardiness chant twelve psalms in addition to the order of the course. But if he has missed his entire course, especially during the nighttime hours, when he has no other work to perform, let him be punished with an additional penalty.

At the daytime hours, whoever comes to the Work of God after the verse and the “Glory” of the first psalm—which is said after the verse [alternative reading: “does not arrive”]—should, according to the law mentioned above, stand at the end. He should not presume to join the choir of those chanting until he has made satisfaction, unless perhaps the abbot has granted permission. Even then, however, the guilty person must make satisfaction for this.

Hence Saint Fructuosus says:

> At the daytime prayers, whoever has not arrived for the first psalm should not dare to enter the oratory with the others, but should be assigned a penance.

Cassian says:

> If anyone has not arrived before the psalm that has been begun is finished, he should not dare thereafter to enter the oratory among the chanting brothers, but should stand outside at the door until the psalms are finished and the congregation is released. Then, with his penance prostrated upon the ground, he should seek pardon before everyone from the abbot for his negligence or tardiness. If he refuses to make satisfaction, he will in no way have fellowship with the brothers in prayer.

When it says “yet in such a way that the guilty person makes satisfaction for this,” it means that he is to be received into the choir by the abbot’s permission in such a way that, after completing the course, he must still make satisfaction for the negligence he committed until he receives pardon from the abbot and full and peaceful remission follows.

[Col. 0881B]

As for table, whoever does not arrive before the verse—which all are to say together and pray, and after which all together are to approach the table—should, because of his negligence or fault, be corrected for this up to the second time. If he does not amend again, he should not be permitted to share in the common table. Separated from the fellowship of everyone, he should eat alone, with his portion of wine removed, until he makes satisfaction and amends.

The same punishment should be suffered by one who is not present for the verse that is said after the meal. Hence a certain master of monks says:

> Those who are not present for the antiphon or the first verse of the table should eat and drink apart, without the signal, and without having given or received the blessing, and without anyone’s speech.

And rightly should someone who did not speak with God before the meal be refreshed without human speech. Whoever is not present for the later verse of the table should receive the same punishment as the one who did not speak with God before the meal.

These corrections or excommunications, however, are established only for those who are late by their own will and negligence and are occupied by no necessity. Those occupied for the benefit of the monastery should rightly be remembered by those present in the oratory.

Hence Isidore says:

> Whoever comes late to the table should either do penance or return to his work or bed in fasting.

Basil says:

> If he could have attended but did not take care to do so, let him confess the fault of his negligence and remain without food until the hour on the following day when they assemble for food.

No one may presume to take any food or drink before the appointed hour or afterward. Hence Fructuosus says:

“Let none of the monks presume to break his fast, nor, before they eat together in common with the others, or after they have eaten, dare to taste or touch anything belonging to eating or drinking, nor presume secretly to store up or possess anything privately.”

Hence Cassian says:

“In every way, care must be taken that before or after the hour when all the brothers eat together, no one presume to eat anything, however or however little, outside the table; so that even apples lying beneath the trees in their season may not merely be tasted but even touched, apart from what is eaten in common, without sacrilege.”

But if something is offered to someone by a superior and he refuses to accept it, then, at the hour when he wishes for what he previously refused, he is to receive neither what he first refused nor anything else at all, until he has made suitable amends. This is a hyperbaton: understood in a different arrangement, it is as follows: If something is offered to someone by a superior and he refuses to accept it, then, at the hour when he wishes—understand, “to accept it”—let him either receive what he previously refused or nothing else at all.

Hence blessed Basil says:

“For what is said here about food may likewise be observed in the same manner concerning every matter that pertains to the uses of the body. Therefore such a person, who refuses to accept what is offered, deserves that, even if he asks, he should not receive it until the one who presides has tested him; and when he sees that the fault of his mind has been cured, then he will also provide whatever is necessary for the uses of the body.”

## CHAPTER XLIV. Concerning those who are excommunicated, and how they are to make satisfaction

Whoever is excommunicated from the oratory and from the table for a more serious fault shall, at the hour when the Work of God is celebrated in the oratory, lie prostrate before the doors of the oratory, saying nothing. With his head placed on the ground and lying prostrate, he shall throw himself at the feet of all who come out of the oratory. He shall do this until the abbot judges that sufficient satisfaction has been made. What the more serious faults are has already been stated above.

Now we must speak about the fitting satisfaction of the guilty. As Isidore says, their only meal shall consist of bread and water in the evening; their clothing shall be a shorn garment, or perhaps a hair shirt; their bed shall be bare ground, or perhaps a mat—that is, a reed mat—upon the ground.

Hence a certain master of monks says:

“But if a brother has committed a grave fault, he shall be excommunicated from both, that is, from the oratory and from the table. He shall not attain his superior’s forgiveness until, lying prostrate before the threshold of the oratory and, with a tearful voice, during the intervals when the hours of psalmody cease, he has made satisfaction to God and to all by promising amendment.”

When he comes at the abbot’s command, he shall throw himself at the abbot’s feet, then at the feet of all the brothers, so that they may pray for him. Then, if the abbot commands it, he shall be received into the choir or into whatever rank the abbot determines. Yet he shall not presume to impose a psalm, a reading, or anything else in the oratory unless the abbot again orders him to do so.

At every hour, while the Work of God is being completed, he shall throw himself upon the ground where he is standing, and shall thus make satisfaction until the abbot orders him to cease from this satisfaction.

Hence Isidore says:

“This is the satisfaction of offenders: when the period of penance has been completed, the one who has been summoned shall come; he shall lie prostrate on the ground; at the abbot’s command he shall rise from the ground; when he has risen, he shall ask forgiveness from all for his negligence; and he shall obtain pardon after the measure of this corrective satisfaction.”

Those who are excommunicated from the table alone for lesser faults shall make satisfaction in the oratory. They shall always do this until the abbot’s command, until he blesses and says, “It is enough.” When he says “blesses,” this is understood as: “May the Lord forgive you.” When he says “It is enough,” the implied meaning is: “Satisfaction has been made for this fault.”

## CHAPTER XLV. Concerning those who make mistakes in the oratory

If someone makes a mistake while reciting a psalm, responsory, antiphon, or reading, and is not humbled there before everyone with satisfaction, he shall be subjected to a greater punishment, since he refused to correct through humility what he had done wrong through negligence.

Children, however, shall be beaten for such a fault. When it says that they are subjected to a greater punishment, the implied meaning is: “as though he had been humbled there before everyone.” When it says that children are to be beaten for such a fault, the implied meaning is: “unless they have been humbled there before everyone.”

This concerns those who make mistakes rarely but, though often corrected, are not amended—even if they have been humbled there—so that they may be beaten, corrected, and no longer so often make mistakes.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Concerning those who offend in any other matters

If someone, while engaged in any work—in the kitchen, cellar, workshop, bakehouse, garden, or any craft—or while laboring in any place, commits some offense, breaks or loses something, or exceeds the bounds in any other way, and does not immediately come before the abbot or the congregation, voluntarily make satisfaction, and disclose his offense, but it becomes known through someone else, he shall be subjected to a stricter correction.

Hence Cassian says:

“If someone has broken or lost something, he shall not otherwise wipe away his negligence unless he has long entreated God, prostrate upon the ground before all the brothers, until he is released by the abbot’s prayer.”

The negligences mentioned above are to be weighed according to their proper measure, and offenders are to be corrected according to their age—that is, whether they are young, elderly, or adult.

If he gives the abbot or the superior a pure confession, and it becomes clear that what happened by accident was not done by his will, it is enough for him to amend what he did wrong with a satisfaction accompanied by pardon. But if it becomes known not through his own confession but through another’s disclosure, he shall undergo penance according as the magnitude of the fault requires.

If the cause of the sin is hidden in the soul, he shall disclose it only to the abbot or to spiritual elders who know how to heal their own and not expose or make public the wounds of others.

We exhort, moreover, that if a brother has committed one of the greater faults, one that pertains to the soul’s greater condemnation, he should reveal it more privately, through a pure confession, to his abbot, lest, while he is ashamed to uncover the fault of his mind at this time, he conceal inwardly, together with the guilt of the fault, the face of the devil.

## CHAPTER XLVII. Concerning announcing the hour of the Work of God

It shall be the abbot’s concern, by day and by night, to announce the hour of the Work of God, either announcing it himself or entrusting this care to a suitably diligent brother, so that everything may be completed at the proper hours.

Hence a certain Father says:

“He to whom this has been entrusted—that is, one found suitable for this work, who is attentive and tireless in mind—must arrange the hours according to the abbot’s provision, so that the Work of God is not delayed. He must not presume to awaken the brothers for vigils at whatever hour he pleases, but must invite the whole congregation to the service of prayer in such a way that he is found negligent in neither respect: neither by being overcome by sleep and passing the appointed hour of the night, nor by anticipating it in haste. But if, for whatever reason, the proper order has been departed from, so that the hours are not kept according to their order, they shall be condemned by an added penalty.”

After the abbot, let them appoint psalms and antiphons in their proper order, assigning them to those who are suitable. No one shall presume to sing or read unless he can perform the service itself in such a way that the hearers are edified. Let him do this with humility, seriousness, and fear, and let him do so at the abbot’s command.

When it says, “After the abbot, let them appoint them in their proper order,” it is not speaking of the order in which they entered, but of those whom the abbot has ordered and who can perform this work well. Concerning them it also said above: “Let the brothers not read or sing in order, but those who edify the hearers.” They, too, must act cautiously and humbly, just as they act in an orderly manner. Hence what follows: “Let no one presume to sing or read unless he can,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Concerning daily manual labor

Idleness is the enemy of the soul. A monk who is idle in body can never be idle in mind with respect to filthy thoughts. For through idleness lusts and desires for harmful thoughts grow, as Solomon says: “Every idler is occupied with desires, and idleness devises many evils.”

Therefore, brothers, we exhort you not to love idleness, but, through the sincere agreement of unity, let each one labor according to his strength. Let him cast away from himself this vice, if he has been such until now, and promptly present himself for every work, because it is written: “Do not hate laborious works, nor agriculture, created by the Most High” (Ecclesiasticus VII).

If the apostles performed bodily work by which they sustained bodily life, how much more should monks, who ought not only to provide the necessities of their own life with their hands, but also to relieve the needs of others through their labors?

Those who possess bodily strength and sound health, if they are idle in work, are known to sin twice over: not only do they fail to labor, but they also corrupt others and invite them to imitate themselves. For each person turns to God so that, serving him, he may be devoted to labor—not so that, given over to idleness, inertia, and laziness, he may feed himself.

Those who wish to devote themselves to reading in such a way that they do not work are themselves rebellious, because they do not do what they read there. For it is written there: “Let those who work eat their own bread” (Proverbs XXVIII).

Hence it is said through the prophet concerning an idle soul: “Enemies saw her and mocked her sabbaths” (Lamentations I). Enemies mock when they see her sabbaths, since evil spirits draw the very leisure of idleness toward unlawful thoughts.

Therefore the brothers should be occupied at fixed times in manual labor and at fixed hours in sacred reading. We therefore believe that the two periods should be arranged in this manner: from Easter until the Kalends of October, they should go out in the morning and labor at whatever is necessary from the first hour until nearly the fourth hour. From the fourth hour until approximately the sixth hour, they should devote themselves to reading.

“Let them act” means “let them hurry” or “let them work sufficiently”; this is the meaning of “let them act.”

Hence Isidore says:

“A monk ought to work at his appointed times and devote himself to prayer and reading at their appointed times. A monk must have suitable hours assigned to each service. The portions of time are assigned to their respective works in the following way. In summer, one ought to work from morning until the third hour; from the third until the sixth one ought to devote oneself to reading; then one ought to rest until the ninth. After the ninth, one ought to work again until the evening time.”

After the sixth hour, when they rise from the table, let them rest on their beds in complete silence. If someone wishes to read, let him read to himself in such a way that he does not disturb another. Let None be celebrated earlier, at the middle of the eighth hour, and then let them work again at whatever must be done until Vespers.

But if the need of the place or poverty requires them to occupy themselves personally with gathering crops, let them not be saddened, because they are truly monks if they live by the labor of their hands, as did our fathers and the apostles. For it is written: “Because you shall eat the labors of your hands, you are blessed, and it shall be well with you” (Psalm CXXVII).

Therefore, as blessed Ferriolus says, we decree that a monk who, without fixed solemnities or evident illness, lets a day pass without work shall be excluded from the meal, in accordance with the Apostle’s command: “Those who do not labor shall not eat” (II Thessalonians III).

Nevertheless, let everything be done with moderation, for the sake of the fainthearted. “Fainthearted” means one having a small, little, or diminished spirit, or indeed one who is despairing.

Hence blessed Pachomius says:

“The brothers must not be compelled to do more work; rather, moderate labor should encourage all to work. Let there be peace and harmony among them, and let them willingly submit to their superiors, sitting, walking, and standing in their proper order, and competing with one another in humility.”

From the Kalends of October until the beginning of Lent, let them devote themselves to reading until the full second hour. At the second hour let Terce be celebrated, and until None let all labor at their assigned work.

When the first signal of the ninth hour has been given, let each one withdraw from his work and be ready when the second signal sounds. After the meal, let them devote themselves to their reading or to psalms.

Let remembrance of the Work of God be maintained: while their hands are occupied outwardly in work at the proper temporal opportunity, inwardly let the mind be sweetened by meditation with the tongue on psalms and remembrance of the Scriptures. If anyone who violates this rule takes pleasure in chatter, let him be punished with the penalty of silence.

During the days of Lent, let them devote themselves to their reading from morning until the full third hour, and until the full tenth hour let them work at whatever is assigned to them.

Monks who are working ought to meditate and sing psalms, so that the song of the word of God may console the labor itself with delight. Above all, they must labor bodily during Lent, with the mind’s intention fixed upon God. The hands must be engaged in daily work in such a way that the mind is not turned away from God.

During these days of Lent, let everyone receive individual books from the library, which they shall read through in their entirety and in order. These books are to be received at the beginning of Lent. “From the library” means from the room where the books are stored. For what is called *bibliotheca* in Greek is called in Latin “a repository of books.”

Above all, one or two elders should be appointed to go around the monastery during the hours when the brothers are free for reading, and to see whether perhaps a brother is found to be *acediosus*, occupied with idleness or chatter and not attentive to reading. Such a person is not only useless to himself but also distracts others.

If, God forbid, such a person is found, he shall be corrected once and a second time. If he does not amend, he shall undergo regular correction in such a way that the others are afraid.

*Acediosus* means tedious, anxious, of a vain mind, or light-minded: one who, moved by weariness of mind or lifted up by lightness of spirit, neither permits himself to read nor allows others to devote themselves to reading. He is found useless to himself through wandering about and opposed to those who are reading.

He loves idleness and chatter, and therefore draws both himself and others away from sacred reading—that is, he separates or disturbs them. He must be corrected in such a way that the others, seeing his very severe correction, will no longer dare to commit such a disturbance, and that no brother will dare to join another brother in conversation at unsuitable hours.

Hence the implied statement follows:

“Nor shall brother join brother at unsuitable hours.” Those are unsuitable hours for idle chatter which are suitable for sacred reading. When it says, “Nor shall brother join brother at unsuitable hours,” it does not prohibit useful or holy fellowship among holy people; rather, it forbids harmful fellowship, full of harmful chatter, among idle and *acediosi* people.

On Sunday let everyone devote himself to reading, except those assigned to various offices. Hence the ancient Fathers said:

“On the Lord’s Day let them do nothing else except devote themselves to God, lest on some pretext they wish to excuse themselves or others. Nevertheless, I charge you, brothers, that no work be found on that holy day, but that the day be spent only in hymns, psalms, and spiritual songs.”

If someone is so negligent and lazy that he is unwilling or unable to meditate or read, let work be assigned to him so that he is not idle.

“Lazy” means full of laziness or negligence. The word *desidiosus* derives from *desidere*, “to sit very much” and to love idleness.

Solomon says concerning such a person: “The lazy man hides his hand under his armpit and does not bring it to his mouth.” Here he speaks of two persons. One is the person who, although able to read or meditate, refuses to do either through laziness of heart, preferring to devote himself to idleness or vain chatter.

The other is the person who, although willing, is unable through ignorance either to read or to meditate. Therefore, lest they be idle, work in which they may labor must be assigned to both.

Such work or craft should be assigned to sick or delicate brothers that they are neither idle nor crushed by excessive labor. Their weakness must be considered by the abbot.

“Delicate” means nourished on delicacies and brought up on various banquets. Therefore, being unaccustomed to more strenuous labors, such a person, because of bodily tenderness or weakness, must be tolerated with the sick in a pious manner and treated more humanely and mercifully.

Those who have the strength to labor must not murmur against them. Rather, both these delicate persons and the sick should be cared for by the healthy and, as has been said, treated more humanely and mercifully. Their weakness—that is, their fragility or inability—must be considered by the abbot as by a pious father as well as a ruler.

## CHAPTER XLIX. Concerning the observance of Lent

Although the monk’s life ought to observe the discipline of Lent at all times, “although” here stands for “even though.” For unquestionably, since the world has been crucified to the monk and he to the world, he ought to chastise his body, bring it into servitude, and at all times present himself as a servant of God, exercising himself in various necessities, labors, vigils, fasts, and other virtues.

Yet because this virtue belongs to few—namely, to those of whom it is written, “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew XX)—we advise that during these days they guard their life with complete purity.

“Complete purity” means complete sincerity and simplicity of heart: doing nothing for vainglory or human praise, but doing with a simple heart and pure mind what follows:

“Let us all alike wash away during these holy days all the negligences of other times.”

For concerning this season of Lent it is written: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now are the days of salvation.” During these days, let each of us, insofar as his strength permits, mortify the flesh, afflict its desires, drive shameful lusts from his heart, and in this way repent during these holy days for the negligences of other times.

Hence what follows:

“That is done worthily if we abstain from all vices.” “We abstain” means “we refrain from” or “restrain ourselves from” all vices.

“With prayers and tears.” For it is written: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew V); and, “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Psalm CXXV).

“Let us devote ourselves to reading, compunction of heart, and abstinence.”

Hence Isidore says:

“All progress proceeds from reading and meditation. For reading of the holy Scriptures confers a double gift: either because it trains the understanding of the mind, or because it leads a person, drawn away from the vanities of the world, to the love of God.”

Compunction of heart is humility of mind with tears, arising from remembrance of sin and fear of judgment. Perfect compunction in those who have been converted is that affection which drives away from itself every affection for carnal desires and fixes its intention, with the whole effort of the mind, upon contemplation of God.

For the person abstains well from food who also abstains from acts of wickedness and from the ambitions of the world.

Therefore, during these days let us add something to the customary measure of our service. “The customary measure” means the accustomed or usual fast of our abstinence, to which something additional must still be added during the days of Lent.

Hence it adds:

“Let us offer special prayers and abstinence from food and drink, so that each person, beyond the measure imposed upon him, may offer God something from his own will with the joy of the Holy Spirit.”

The monk ought to offer his vow to the Lord God with the joy of the Holy Spirit, hoping to receive from him the kingdom of heaven. For whoever serves or gives something to the Lord with cheerfulness and joy will receive a hundredfold from him and, in addition, possess eternal life.

Let him offer it with joy and do what follows:

“That is, let him subtract from his body some food, drink, sleep, talkativeness, and buffoonery, and with the joy of spiritual desire let him await holy Easter.”

Rightly should those rejoice with Christ at Easter concerning the Lord’s resurrection who, through abstinence for his sake, consented to have their bodies crucified. For those who in the present life have withdrawn something from the flesh’s desires or resources deserve to be richly nourished forever with the divine delights of the soul.

Because they were willing to be troubled for a little while, in this brief time, for the Lord’s sake, they will justly deserve to rejoice with him in the future.

Nevertheless, let each person tell his abbot precisely what he is offering, and let it be done with the abbot’s prayer and will. For what is done without the permission of the spiritual father will be counted as presumption and vainglory, not as a reward. Therefore everything must be done with the abbot’s consent.

Hence a certain master of monks says:

“Let the abbot say to all the brothers: ‘Whoever wishes to labor for his soul and to abstain from something, we grant him free choice. Whoever does not wish to do so shall receive what the rule establishes under this heading and shall be content with the measure of Lent.’

“Those of the brothers who wish to abstain from something shall humble themselves at the abbot’s knees, giving thanks for the permission granted to undertake a good act. After this humility, let them also tell the abbot with their own mouths what each wishes to abstain from.”

## CHAPTER L. Concerning brothers who labor far from the oratory or are on a journey

Brothers who are entirely distant while engaged in work and cannot arrive at the proper hour at the oratory, if the abbot considers that this is indeed the case, shall perform the Work of God there where they are working, bending their knees with godly fear.

Likewise, those who have been sent on a journey must not allow the appointed hours to pass them by. As they are able, let them perform the service for themselves and not neglect to render the measure of their service.

Hence blessed Pachomius says:

“Whether he is on a ship, in the monastery, in the field, on a journey, or engaged in any service, let him not omit the times for prayer and psalmody.”

Hence Basil also says:

“Each person must observe his own rule in his work, like a member in the body. He will suffer loss if he neglects to fulfill what has been assigned to him, and he will be in greater danger through negligence of the common welfare of the brothers.”

Therefore he ought to complete with mind and devotion what is written: “Singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord” (Ephesians V).

If he cannot be bodily present with the others at the place of prayer, wherever he may be found, let him complete what belongs to devotion.

Nevertheless, care must be taken lest someone who is able to complete at the proper time what must be completed and to arrive instead fabricate excuses because he wishes to talk, as though he were occupied with the work of his service. Whoever does this both provides a stumbling block for the others and incurs the guilt of negligence himself.

Hence another master of monks says:

“When spiritual brothers travel without a layman, let them turn aside briefly from the road, joined together, and bend their knees while singing. After the prayer, let them return to the road, immediately remaining silent from every extraneous word out of reverence for the Work of God; and, walking in this manner, having asked for a blessing, let them begin the appointed psalm.”

## CHAPTER LI. Concerning brothers who do not travel far

Brothers who set out for any message and hope to return to the monastery that same day shall not presume to eat outside, even if anyone invites them, unless perhaps their own abbot orders them to do so. If they act otherwise, they shall be excommunicated.

Hence the ancient Fathers said:

“Let no one eat or drink outside the monastery. The discipline of the rule does not permit this: they must not even take cheap fruit, nor presume to drink water itself before the lawful meal.”

But if someone, having left for any place without the knowledge of the abbot or superior, joins himself to gluttony or drunkenness; or if, having been sent to a nearby place, he does not immediately return to his cell after the necessity has been discharged because of his frivolity or gluttony; or if he is detained in such an offense—as the canons teach—let him either be separated from communion for thirty days or be corrected by being beaten with rods.

## CHAPTER LII. Concerning the monastery’s oratory

Let the oratory be what it is called, and let nothing else be done or stored there.

When the Work of God has been completed, let everyone leave in silence, and let reverence be shown to God, so that a brother who perhaps wishes to pray privately may not be hindered by another’s misconduct.

But if someone wishes to pray more privately, let him simply enter and pray, not in a loud voice but with tears and concentration of heart. Therefore, anyone who does not perform such an action shall not be permitted to remain in the oratory after the Work of God has been completed, as has been said, lest another suffer hindrance.

Hence blessed Augustine says:

“In the oratory no one should do anything except what it was made for, from which it also received its name. Or if perhaps some wish to pray outside the appointed hours, when they have leisure, let those who think that something must be done there not be an impediment to them.”

Again, elsewhere:

“In the oratory, apart from the worship of God through prayer and psalmody, absolutely nothing should be done, so that the works continually performed there may correspond to its name. Thus, if someone enters to supplicate the Lord outside the appointed hours, another’s occupation should not delay his vow.”

## CHAPTER LIII. Concerning receiving guests

All arriving guests are to be received as Christ, because he himself will say: “I was a guest, and you received me” (Matthew XXV).

Hence the Apostle also exhorts us among other things, saying: “Pursuing hospitality” (Romans XII). By saying that hospitality is to be pursued, he shows not merely that we should receive a guest who comes to us, but also that we should seek them, be attentive, pursue them, and search everywhere for guests, lest they perhaps sit in the streets or lie outside without shelter.

Recall Lot, and you will find that the guests did not seek him, but that he himself sought guests; and this was to pursue hospitality.

Hence blessed Macarius also says:

“Pursue hospitality in every way, and do not turn away your eyes or send the poor away empty, lest the Lord perhaps come to you in the guest or in the poor person, see you hesitating, and despise you. Rather, show yourself cheerful toward everyone and act faithfully.”

Therefore, when guests arrive, they are to be received eagerly, knowing that for this they will obtain the final recompense, when at the judgment the Lord will say to those who are on his right: “I was a guest, and you gathered me in; for what you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matthew XXV).

And suitable honor is to be shown to all. “Suitable” means fitting, appropriate, or worthy—what is done when each person is given what is fitting and in the manner that is fitting.

For although one charity embraces everyone inwardly, outwardly it is fitting to minister differently to the poor and differently to the powerful. An equal seat is not to be prepared for everyone, nor is an equal provision of food suitable for all. Rather, with charitable discretion, a suitable place, suitable food, a suitable bed, and suitable honor must be provided for everyone, so that, received appropriately by us, they may return to their own homes without complaint, as friends.

Especially to members of the household of faith and to travelers. “Member of the household” means a familiar friend or companion. We should understand such people in two ways: either all Christians generally, who share with us one faith and one baptism; or, specifically, monks, who with us offer to God a special worship of God and the service of religion.

“Traveler” means one situated in the territory of a distant homeland.

Therefore, as soon as a guest has been announced, the superior or the brothers should go out to meet him with every service of charity. Since two kinds of persons usually come to the monastery, he reasonably commands that they be met in two corresponding ways: a superior should meet superiors, and a brother should meet brothers.

If a king, bishop, or someone powerful at the highest level arrives, the abbot should go out to meet him. If someone of another rank arrives, another person should go out to meet him.

First, let them pray together, and thus join themselves in peace. “In peace” means “with the kiss of peace.” They ought to be peaceful, and the sons of peace ought to join one another in a holy kiss.

Hence what follows:

“The kiss of peace must not be offered before prayer has been said, because of demonic deceptions.” For if the devil, though dark, can transform himself into an angel of light, he can certainly also transform himself into the person of a guest. This is recorded as having already happened both in the *Dialogues* and in the *Lives of the Fathers*. Such an illusion of a phantom cannot stand or cause harm if ready prayer proceeds from the heart of a holy monk.

In the greeting itself, let every humility be shown. “Every humility” means complete, full, and perfect humility—not feigned, but flowing from a pure heart, true and sincere.

How it is to be shown, listen to what follows:

“To all guests who arrive or depart, Christ, who is received in them, shall be adored with the head bowed or with the whole body prostrate upon the ground.”

Here, as above, he introduces two kinds of arriving persons: one of ordinary rank, before whom the brother merely bows his head; another of the highest rank, before whom he adores with his whole body prostrate upon the ground. Yet in both cases the Lord Jesus Christ, who is received, is adored.
