After they have been received, let the guests be led to prayer. Then let the superior, or whomever he commands, sit with them. Let the divine law be read before the guest, so that he may be edified; after this, let every human kindness be shown to him.

“Every human kindness” means every compassionate affection and the full and perfect service of love that ought to be shown to guests in the provision of food, drink, and everything suitable for them.

Let the superior break his fast for the sake of the guest, unless perhaps it is an especially solemn fast day that cannot be violated. The brothers, however, shall continue the customary fasts.

The fast days that cannot be violated are understood to be the days of holy Easter, Lent, the Litanies, and the four Ember seasons of the year, or when a vigil of a feast day is to be held—when not only canons and clerics but also Catholic laypeople fast.

The brothers shall continue the customary fasts, lest the solemnity of the fast be removed from the whole monastery for the sake of one guest. To show charity toward the guest, he commands only that the superior break the fast; and especially for the honor of the guest himself, he commands that the senior of the monastery break it. But this is not to be done for every guest, only for foreign brothers or for those distinguished persons who visit the monastery late.

The abbot shall give water to the guests’ hands. The abbot and the entire congregation shall wash the feet of all guests.

Hence Fructuosus says:

“Services of charity, with the greatest reverence and attentiveness, are to be provided to guests or traveling brothers. In the evening their feet are to be washed; if they are exhausted from the journey, they are to be anointed with oil. Beds, a lamp, and soft coverings are to be provided, and, when they depart, provisions for the journey are to be placed at their disposal according to the measure of the monastery.”

After their feet have been washed, they say this verse: “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple” (Psalm XLVII).

As though it said: “In this guest we have received a visitation of your mercy in the midst of your temple, in the midst of your monastery’s temple.”

Alternatively: “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple”—that is, in the midst of our heart, which the Apostle says is entirely a temple. We have received the arrival of this guest with the love of charity.

The reception of the poor and of travelers is to be offered with every care and attentiveness, because Christ is received especially in them.

Hence Pachomius says:

“When some people come to the door of the monastery, if they are clerics or monks, let them be received with greater honor. Their feet shall be washed, according to the command of the Gospel, and they shall be led to the place of the guesthouse. Everything suitable for the use of monks shall be provided.”

Hence Isidore says:

“Although the good of hospitality ought to be extended graciously to everyone, a more abundant honor of hospitality should nevertheless be shown to monks and clerics. Let lodgings be provided for them, let their feet be washed, and let suitable expenses be supplied for the sake of this same kindness.”

For the terror of the rich itself demands honor for them. Since suitable honor must be shown to everyone, service must nevertheless also be prepared for the rich—not merely through fear of their terror, but according to the measure required by discretion. For according to the Apostle, we must render to everyone what is due: “fear to whom fear is due, honor to whom honor is due.”

The abbot’s kitchen and that of the guests shall be separate, so that guests arriving at uncertain hours—for guests are never lacking at a monastery—may not disturb the brothers. Two brothers shall enter this kitchen for a year, and they shall carry out that service well. They shall be provided with assistance as they need it, so that they may serve without murmuring. Again, whenever they have less work, they shall leave and engage in whatever work they are ordered to do. This consideration shall apply not only to them but to all the monastery’s services: whenever assistance is needed, it shall be supplied; and whenever they are free, they shall obey the one giving orders.

For many judge that, just as there was a kitchen separate from that of the brothers and situated in another place, so the abbot’s table was not then set in the common refectory with the other tables, but was separated in another chamber, which the frequent arrival of guests would often find prepared with food. But now, by the great council of bishops, abbots, and the other Franks, a salutary decision has been reached: for his own protection and that of the brothers, the abbot shall have a table in the common refectory, where, when guests are present, he may eat with them, but when they are absent, he may dine before the brothers with whomever he wishes.

A brother shall likewise be assigned to the guest house, one whose soul is possessed by the fear of God. There shall be beds adequately made up there, and the house of God shall be wisely administered by wise men. The beds are called *strati* (“spread out”) from *sternere*, “to spread.” *Strati* is related to *scoriati*. For *scoria* is what we call a mat or reed mat. The ancient monks used to sleep only on such things and made their little beds only with them. Anyone whose mind is possessed by fear of the Lord must undoubtedly already be counted among the wise. For it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; good understanding belongs to all who practice it” (Ecclesiasticus 2). It is therefore necessary that the house of the Lord—that is, the house built in the monastery for the Lord’s poor, or established for the fulfillment of his command—be wisely administered by such wise men. Hence a certain master of monks also says: “The guest chamber shall be established apart from the monastery, with beds made up, where visiting brothers, especially those who are unknown, may sleep and place their baggage.”

A brother to whom this duty has not been assigned shall under no circumstances associate or converse with guests. If he encounters or sees one, he shall greet him humbly, as has been said, ask his blessing, and pass on, saying that he is not permitted to converse with a guest. “He shall not associate with guests” means that he shall not join them in making conversation. But if he encounters them or sees them standing near him, he shall ask their blessing and pass on. If a guest asks him something, he shall answer, saying, “I am not permitted to speak with a guest.” Hence blessed Macarius also says: “No one except the brother entrusted with care of the guest house shall answer those who arrive; nor shall any brother be permitted to converse except the one in charge, or those whom he himself has ordered to do so.”

## CHAPTER LIV. That a monk must not receive letters or *eulogiae* without the abbot’s command

Under no circumstances may a monk receive or give letters, *eulogiae*—that is, blessed gifts—or any little presents, whether from his parents, from anyone else, or from one another, without the command of his abbot. If anything has even been sent to him by his parents, he must not presume to accept it unless it has first been reported to the abbot. If the abbot orders it to be received, it shall be within the abbot’s power to whom he orders it to be given. The brother to whom it had perhaps been sent must not be saddened, lest an occasion be given to the devil. Whoever presumes to act otherwise shall be subject to regular discipline.

Hence blessed Augustine says: “If anyone should advance so far in evil that he secretly accepts letters or any little gifts from someone, and confesses this voluntarily, he shall be spared, and prayer shall be offered for him. But if he is discovered and convicted, he shall be corrected more severely, according to the judgment of the superior.” Blessed Basil likewise says: “No monk shall accept any gift or letters, nor presume to give anything to anyone without the abbot’s permission.” Elsewhere also it is written: “Whoever presumes to receive letters or little gifts from anyone, if he does not immediately make public both who gave them and what he received, shall be subjected to the strictest discipline. Whatever has been sent shall be assigned to strangers and unknown persons, or certainly consumed by fire.”

Certainly, if anyone has contributed something for his own children or for persons connected with him by any relationship, once it has been brought into common use, it shall be given to whoever needs it. If the abbot orders that what was sent to someone be given to him, he shall receive it with thanksgiving, like the other gifts of the faithful.

When he says, “Let him not be saddened, lest an occasion be given to the devil,” this is understood to mean either through sadness, envy, or murmuring. Through the sadness which he keeps in his heart, an occasion is given to the devil to harm the monk, because, according to the Apostle, there is a sadness which, through the devil’s interference, becomes an occasion of harm in the soul. If the recipient is envied, an occasion is likewise given to the devil to harm the monk through envy, for it is written: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world. Those who belong to his party imitate him.” Or if he should murmur because what was sent to him is not given to him, then through murmuring an occasion is given to the devil to harm the monk. For those who murmured in the desert perished through serpents. Every monk who does one of these things because what was sent to him is not given to him shall be subject to regular discipline, lest, remaining undisciplined, he perish eternally because of these vices.

## CHAPTER LV. On the clothing and footwear of the brothers

Clothing shall be given to the brothers according to the character of the places where they live and according to the temperature of the air, because more is needed in cold regions and less in hot ones. This consideration shall therefore belong to the abbot. When he says that clothing is to be given according to the character of the places, it seems to me that he is speaking of a place requiring hard work, and not of one requiring so much labor. There are monasteries already well established and situated in pleasant places, where less work is done and less clothing and footwear are needed. When he says “or according to the temperature of the air,” he explains this himself by adding: “because more is needed in cold regions and less in hot ones.” Considering this most prudently, he said:

“Now let the prudent abbot carefully consider the temperature of the air and the places in which the monks live: whether they are hot, cold, or temperate; rough, hard, or agreeable. According to his ability, let him faithfully provide his monks with what is necessary, so that they may serve the Lord without necessity and live peacefully without justified murmuring.”

Nevertheless, we believe that in temperate places it is sufficient for each monk to have a hooded garment and a tunic: a woolly hooded garment in winter, a clean or old one in summer, and a scapular for work. “Temperate places” means places neither very cold nor very hot. He calls a *cuculla* what we now call a *cappa*, a cloak. *Cuculla* is formed as a diminutive from *casula*, and *casulla* from *casa*; *cuculla* is likewise a diminutive of *casulla*. What he calls a *scapulare* for work we now call a *cuculla*.

For the feet: foot-cloths and leggings. By *pediles* he means what we now call socks or foot-coverings. By *caligae* he means what we call *subtalares* or socks. *Caligae* are so called from the calluses of the feet, or because they are tied; hence they are also called *calcearii*. Of *pediles* Isidore says: “Foot-coverings are to be used in the monastery as long as the violence of winter requires, or while the brothers are traveling on foot or setting out for the city.” Fructuosus likewise says: “In winter those who wish may put on foot-coverings,” that is, from the Kalends of November to the Kalends of May. During the remaining summer months they are to be protected only with the comfort of leggings.

The monks must not quarrel about the color or thickness of any of these things, but accept whatever can be found in the province where they live, or whatever can be bought more cheaply. Hence Ferreolus says: “Let him also avoid in these things white or excessively red coloring, by which the appearance of the body is often commended to those who see it, to the wearer’s destruction.” That is, he must not strive to possess such things, lest they bear witness to his vanity, and lest, while wishing to adorn his body with clothing, he fail to care for the adornment of his soul.

Isidore says: “A monk ought to be equipped, not luxurious. Just as a monk’s dress should not be conspicuous, so it should not be excessively shabby. An expensive garment draws the mind toward wantonness; one that is too cheap either produces distress of heart or contracts the disease of vainglory.” Basil says: “If we ought to strive to be the least of all and the last of all, it is certain that we must also count ourselves last of all in clothing.” Cassian says:

“A monk’s clothing ought to be such that, covering the body, it merely removes the shame of nakedness and blunts the assault of cold, not such as nourishes an occasion for vanity. It should be so cheap that, through no novelty of color or design, he is considered distinguished among the other spiritual brothers; and it should be so free from the carefulness of excessive concern that it is not disfigured either by stains gathered through neglect or by filth. Finally, the garment itself should be so separated from the adornment of this world that it is common in the dress of all God’s servants. For whatever among God’s servants is not worn by all, but is assumed by one or a few, is either superfluous or proud, and must therefore be judged harmful, since it displays not the appearance of virtue but of vanity.”

The abbot shall provide garments of suitable size, so that they are neither too short for those who use them nor excessively long, but measured. If garments are too short, they will be ridiculous; if too long, they will be damaging. For just as a short garment produces ridicule, an excessively long one produces waste of cloth. Therefore, to prevent these things, everything shall be made to measure.

When receiving new garments, they shall always return the old ones immediately, to be stored in the wardrobe for the poor. Hence blessed Fructuosus says: “Whatever among the monks’ clothing, footwear, or bedding has become old, when they receive new things, shall all be distributed by the abbot to the poor.” Aurelianus likewise says: “If anything remains from the brothers’ use—whether gold, clothing, or provisions—the holy abbot shall have it distributed by the steward, or by any trustworthy person, to the poor, strangers, or captives. When they receive new clothing, they shall return the old to the abbot, to be distributed to beginners or the poor.”

[Col. 0896A]

It is sufficient for a monk to have two tunics and two hooded garments, for the nights and for washing these things. Whatever is beyond this is superfluous and must be removed. They shall also return their foot-coverings and whatever has become old when they receive something new.

Hence Isidore says: “Let monks be content with three tunics, two cloaks, and one hooded garment each, presuming to have nothing else in their clothing beyond these.” Saint Fructuosus likewise says: “The monks’ clothing must not be abundant or superfluous. Two woolly hooded garments, one simple little cloak, three tunics, and two *staminea* must suffice for every necessary complaint.” Ferreolus says: “A monk must not seek superfluous clothing, since the Lord says to his disciples: ‘Nor have two tunics.’”

We must understand the “two tunics” not numerically, if they seem necessary because of winter, but as counting as excessive if they are kept beyond actual use. Whatever is beyond this will therefore be considered another’s property. For whatever the avaricious possessor locks away, he uses the chest more than the master. To avoid this, the blessed apostle rises as our greatest witness, saying: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these. Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and a snare of the devil, and into many foolish and harmful desires which plunge people into destruction and perdition” (1 Timothy 6).

Those who are sent on a journey shall receive trousers from the wardrobe and, when they return, shall return them there washed. Their hooded garments and tunics shall be somewhat better than those they ordinarily have; they shall receive them from the wardrobe when they set out on a journey and return them there washed when they come back.

The use of trousers may be permitted to anyone, especially those engaged in the ministry of the altar. But if someone does not wish to make a habit of this, he must not be reproved, since even now it is established that many monasteries, including those in these regions, do not have this practice. As for the statement that the hooded garments and tunics used on a journey should be somewhat better than those they ordinarily have, this is to be done in regions where they are accustomed to use very cheap clothing. Where the clothing is better, it is not to be changed for journeys.

*Trousers* are so called because they cover the thighs; we also call them *feminalia* and *braccae*. They are called *braccae* because they are short. For *brachin* in Greek means “short.”

The bedding shall be sufficient: a mat, a *sagum*, a *lena*, and a pillow. *Sagum* is a Gallic word. It is called a square *sagum* because among them it was originally square or fourfold. We now call it, by diminution from *sagum*, a *sagellum*. A *lena* is a type of woolly garment which we call a *copa* [variant: *toxa*]; others call it a *galnapa*. By *capitale* he means what we call a feather pillow. Isidore also speaks of this provision:

“A monk may not possess elegant or varied furnishings. His bedding shall be a mat and a covering, two woolly skins, a *galnapa*, a towel, and two small pillows at his head.”

These beds, nevertheless, must frequently be searched by the abbot, lest private property be found in them. If anything is found belonging to someone which he did not receive from the abbot, he shall be subject to the gravest discipline. To eradicate this vice of private possession from the roots, the abbot shall provide everything necessary: a hooded garment, tunic, foot-coverings, leggings, trousers, knife, writing stylus, needle, small towel, and writing tablets, so that every excuse of necessity may be removed.

Hence blessed Fructuosus also says: “The abbot or superior shall turn over and search the bed of each monk twice a week, to see that no one has anything superfluous or hidden there.” Awls, needles, and various threads for sewing and repairing clothing are to be supplied to them by the abbot; and whenever necessity demands it, they shall have the opportunity to wash and mend their clothing. Saint Pachomius also says:

“No one shall possess anything beyond what is prescribed by the common rule of the monastery: neither tunic, cloak, skin, coin, nor pillow at the head, except those things distributed by the Father of the monastery through the superiors.”

The abbot must always consider the statement in the Acts of the Apostles: “Distribution was made to each according to his need.” Thus the abbot must consider the weakness of those in need, not the evil will of those who envy them. In all his judgments he must think of God’s recompense. Hence Isidore says:

“Clothing is not to be distributed equally to everyone, but with discretion, according to what each person’s age and rank require. We read that the apostles acted in this way, as it is written: ‘Everything was held in common among them, and distribution was made to each according to his need’ (Acts 4). Each brother’s sufficiency or need must be examined, so that those who have may be content, and those who do not have may receive.”

## CHAPTER LVI. On the abbot’s table

The abbot’s table shall always be with guests and pilgrims. Whenever there are fewer guests, however, it shall be within his power to invite whichever of the brothers he wishes. He shall always arrange for one or two of the elders to remain with the brothers, for the sake of discipline. Hence the ancient fathers said: “A visiting brother may not eat with the brothers except with the Father who presides, so that he may be edified.” When there are no guests, the abbot may eat with whichever brothers he wishes. Nevertheless, he shall leave the elders with the brothers for their protection.

[Col. 0897D]

## CHAPTER LVII. On the craftsmen of the monastery

If there are craftsmen in the monastery, they shall practice their crafts with all humility and reverence, provided that the abbot has ordered it. If one of them becomes proud because of his skill, on the grounds that he appears to contribute something to the monastery, such a man shall be removed from that craft and shall not return to it unless, after he has been humbled, the abbot again orders him to do so.

Hence Cassian says: “If anyone contributes more than others to the monastery from his own work and sweat, he must not become puffed up at all, nor flatter himself because of the great gain acquired through his work, nor presume to claim anything more or more luxurious for himself than the accustomed frugality of daily food. Rather, considering himself a stranger to such things, he must carry through to the end the virtue of the nakedness he has embraced.”

When he says, “Such a man shall be removed from that craft,” this means that he shall be suspended from the work of the craft which had been entrusted to him; he shall no longer practice it until he has been humbled again. For “to raise up” and “to suspend” are understood here as the same thing.

If anything made by the craftsmen is to be sold, those through whose hands the transaction is conducted must take care not to commit any fraud. Let them remember Ananias and Sapphira, lest they—or all who commit fraud in the monastery’s possessions—suffer in their souls the death which those two endured in the body (Acts 5). The death which monks suffer in their souls by committing fraud is worse and harsher than the bodily death suffered by Ananias and Sapphira. Bodily death is common to all and temporary; the death of the souls of the wicked is punitive. The former separates the body from the soul, while the latter separates the soul from the Creator. The former sends the body into the grave; the latter sends the soul into hell.

In the prices themselves, however, let the evil of avarice not creep in. Rather, let goods always be sold somewhat more cheaply than they are sold by secular people, so that God may be glorified in all things. Hence a certain master of monks says:

“When each craft has produced some profit beyond what is needed for the monastery’s use or for sending *eulogiae*, after the quality of the price has been examined, let it always be sold for a lower price than could be obtained from secular people, so that in this respect spiritual people may be recognized as distinct and separated from secular practices. They do not seek profit above justice for the sake of commerce, which is hostile to the soul; rather, even in accordance with justice itself, they agree to accept a lower price, so that they may not be thought to practice their crafts for the sake of greed and avarice.”

Avarice is not a small evil but a great one. It is a fire burning in the heart of the avaricious person, unquenchably aflame and continually consuming. Hence it is written in the book of blessed Job: “Fire will consume the tents of those who gladly accept gifts” (Job 15). Explaining this, blessed Gregory says: “Fire consumes the tents when the heat of avarice devastates the thoughts of the mind.” Solomon likewise says: “The one who pursues avarice troubles his own house” (Proverbs 15), and, “The avaricious person will not be satisfied with money” (Ecclesiastes 5). From avarice many other vices spring up, as it is written: “The root of all evils is avarice” (1 Timothy 6). For this vice generates not only very many hidden evils but also many manifest ones.

## CHAPTER LVIII. On the discipline for receiving brothers

When someone newly comes for conversion, admission must not be granted to him easily; rather, as the Apostle says, “Test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (1 John 4). Hence the ancient fathers also said:

“If someone, inflamed by the ardor of faith and renouncing the world, chooses a monastery of strict discipline to seek refuge in it, permission to enter must not immediately be granted because of his novelty. Rather, it must first be investigated carefully whether he has come voluntarily or has been compelled by some necessity.”

But in accordance with the Apostle’s words, “Test the spirits to see whether they are from God,” he must be carefully tested, lest he be one of those of whom the Lord says: “They will come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves; you will recognize them by their fruits” (Matthew 7). The testing distinguishes whether the devil’s temptation or Christ’s call to the monastery has brought him there.

Therefore, if the newcomer perseveres in knocking, and after four or five days he appears to bear patiently the insults and difficulty of entry inflicted upon him, and to persist in his request, admission shall be granted and he shall remain for a few days in the guest chamber.

By the insults inflicted, he means those which he suffers in the guest chamber from the porter for the sake of testing, as blessed Fructuosus says concerning such a person:

“He shall carry bedding for guests or pilgrims, heat water for their feet, and perform every service humbly. Carrying a bundle of wood daily on his back, he shall give it to the weekly servers. Thus, subjected to every hardship and useful labor, his resolve having been completed, proved in conduct and refined by labors, and having received a blessing in the church, he shall be given to the fellowship of the brothers.”

The text continues:

Afterward he shall be in the novices’ chamber, where he shall meditate, eat, and sleep. By “the novices’ chamber” he means not the chamber of guests but of those who knock at the door. There the newcomer shall meditate, either with those whom he finds there or with the master assigned to him, on canticles, psalms, hymns, or the precepts of the Rule which he is to be taught and observe. Therefore one who renounces the world must by no means begin with delay [variant: lukewarmness], lest through that very delay [variant: lukewarmness] he fall back into love of the world.

An elder shall be assigned to him who is suitable for winning souls. He shall attend to him with the greatest care and be concerned whether he truly seeks God, whether he is diligent for the work of God, for obedience, and for insults.

“Diligent for the work of God” means for those things which properly belong to God: prayer, divine reading, nocturnal vigils and the daily offices, fasting, and every divine service. “For obedience” means because obedience is better than sacrifice. “For insults” means that, if he has come for the name of Christ, he may bear them patiently.

Blessed Fructuosus says of this: “A convert from the world, as the decrees of the Fathers teach, must not be received unless he has first offered proof of himself in work and hardship, in insults and abuse.” Blessed Basil likewise says:

“Before the novice is joined to the body of the brotherhood, he ought to be assigned certain difficult tasks, even tasks that seem to involve insults. It must be observed whether he fulfills these willingly and confidently, lest he bear their shame heavily, and whether he is found diligent and ready in labor.”

All the hard and difficult things by which one goes to God shall be announced to him. By “hard things” he means rigid, strong, or laborious things, so that he may say with the Psalmist: “Because of the words of your lips I have kept to difficult ways.” By “difficult” he means strict, forceful, or narrow and confined, concerning which the Lord says: “Narrow and confined is the way that leads to life.” He should listen to the one who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.”

Hence the ancient fathers also said: “When such men wish to be freed from the hiding places of the world and approach the monastery, they shall be kept for a week before the gates, and hard and laborious things shall always be proposed to them. If they persevere in knocking, entry shall not be denied them; rather, the Father who presides shall permit such men to enter and shall show them how they can keep the life of the brothers and the Rule.”

If he promises perseverance in his stability, after the passage of two months this Rule shall be read to him in order, and he shall be told: “Behold the law under which you wish to serve as a soldier. If you can observe it, enter; if you cannot, depart freely.”

“If you can observe it, enter” means: if you can observe the precepts of this Rule, enter to serve as a soldier. But if you cannot, depart freely before you submit your neck to the yoke of the Rule and become subject to its service. It should be noted that he does not say, “Behold the law under which you may rest, or live quietly in leisure,” but “under which you wish to serve as a soldier,” so that you may understand that human life upon earth is a military service, and that his days are like the days of a hired laborer. Therefore, for the sake of eternal reward, he must endure everything for the Lord who wishes to enter his service, and, like gold, be tested by the file, hammers, and the fire of the furnace, so that he may reach the Lord’s diadem and crown.

If he still remains, he shall then be led into the aforesaid novices’ chamber and tested again in every kind of patience. Hence Isidore says:

“For it is not fitting that anyone should be received inside who, having left the world, turns with pious and salutary humility to the service of Christ, unless, while still outside, his humility or patience has first been proven. For this reason, during the period of testing we serve under the abbot’s command and gladly bear the hard and difficult things ordered by the abbot, so that after the pilgrimage of this life we may deserve to reign with the Lord.”

When it says, “Then he shall be led into the aforesaid novices’ chamber,” although it had already said, “Let him be in the novices’ chamber,” this does not mean that he left that chamber, went to the place of instruction—or to whatever place the abbot had selected—to hear the precept of the Rule, and then returned to the novices’ chamber. Hence Saint Aurelius says: “By God’s command we first established this as something to be observed: if anyone comes for conversion, the Rule shall be read to him in the guest hall.”

After the passage of six months, the Rule shall be read to him so that he may know for what purpose he is entering. Hence Ferreolus says: “After this, by order of the abbot, the Rule of the monastery shall be read to him, so that thereafter, if he is about to depart, he may overlook nothing, and, if he is to remain, he may find nothing unfamiliar.” One of the elders shall therefore be assigned to instruct him in regular discipline, so that from then on he may recognize everything he ought to do and the persons whom he ought to serve.

If he still remains, after four months this same Rule shall again be read to him. Thus the novice’s year is completed from the time when he came knocking at the monastery. During this year, while he remains in the novices’ chamber, the Rule has been read to him three times in order. Not only blessed Benedict but also the other Fathers commanded that this period be observed for the novice. They said:

“No one shall be permitted to change his habit until the year has been completed. But if a penitent should have such great compunction that he demands this through continual supplication, it must not be denied him. Nevertheless, what is granted to one who asks faithfully must not thereby be regarded as generally permitted.”

Hence blessed Fructuosus says:

“After being entrusted for one year to a spiritual elder, he shall not immediately be mixed with the congregation, but shall first be instructed in every exercise of good works. If any convert, distinguished by good and pure conduct, has been approved by the judgment of the abbot or of other spiritual brothers, then, according to the merit and purity of his conscience, he may be a cleric and be joined to the fellowship of the brothers, according to what the abbot or the best of the brothers determines should be done.”

If, after deliberation with himself, he promises that he will observe everything and keep everything commanded to him, he shall then be received into the congregation, knowing that the law of the Rule has established that from that day he may neither leave the monastery nor shake his neck free from beneath the yoke of the Rule—a yoke which, after such prolonged deliberation, he was permitted either to refuse or to accept.

The word *habita* (“having been held”) is derived from *habere*, “to have.” *Deliberatio* means meditation or consideration. Thus, after deliberation has been held, the reconsideration has already been concluded. Concerning this statement, a certain master of monks says:

“When the Rule has been completed in the reading to the novice, the abbot shall first answer him as follows, lest he perhaps be unable to keep the provisions of the Rule. When he says that he can obey everything, and the new brother responds that he will keep everything stated by the abbot and is ready in deed for everything; and if he professes that he will fulfill all things, then he shall be received into the congregation of monks. Once received, he must neither presume nor be permitted to leave the monastery until his death, because of the prophetic saying: ‘One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life’ (Psalm 26).”

The one who is to be received shall promise his stability in the oratory before everyone, as well as the conversion of his conduct and obedience before God and his saints, so that, if he ever acts otherwise, he may know that he will be condemned by the one whom he mocks. He shall promise and say as follows:

“I, so-and-so, in this monastery of that saint, promise my stability, the conversion of my conduct, and obedience according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, before God and his saints.”

When he has bound himself by this promise, he shall be subjected to the rules written above, intending eventually to please the Lord through diligence in good works. If he ever acts otherwise—that is, if he willingly departs from the regular life—he must know that he will be condemned by God, whom he mocks.

Concerning this promise he shall make a written petition in the name of the saints whose relics are there and of the present abbot. The novice shall formulate the petition in the following manner:

“Carefully considering the beginning of my monastic service, I recognize that at first entry into the monastery was not easily granted to my request, but that, after I had knocked for a long time, a place in the guest house was scarcely assigned to me through mercy. Having stayed there for a few days, I proceeded to the novices’ house, where the hard and difficult things were first carefully announced to me by an elder, and the promise of my stability was simply awaited [variant: fulfilled with supplication].

That elder, threatening me, impressed these terrifying words upon my ears: ‘Know for certain that if, contrary to your promise of regular observance, you turn back and look behind you, you will not be fit for the kingdom of heaven. Moreover, know that you will be cast out from those precincts clothed in the same garments in which the monastery’s enclosure received you. And because the world had ruined you when stripped of your old rags and likewise stripped of vices, it is fitting that it should receive back its servant clothed in both kinds, to be kept forever as a disgrace to all.’

“But strengthened by David’s example, I cried out to the Lord, saying: ‘Because of the words of your lips I have kept to difficult ways’ (Psalm 16), knowing with complete certainty that if I share in Christ’s passion, I shall also share in his resurrection. Strengthened by these and similar divine oracles, I declared that I would steadfastly endure everything for the sake of eternal life.

“When the Father saw our steadfastness, he ordered the Rule to be read to us three times during the year in due order, and likewise to be handed over to us, with the warning of the one who admonished and the instruction of the one who learned: ‘Behold the law under which you wish to serve as a soldier. If you can observe it, enter; if you cannot, depart freely.’

“Seeing, therefore, that this most orderly and prolonged period had been granted to me, I set aside the opportunity for doubt and, tearfully begging, earnestly ask that you deem me worthy now to be joined to your body. Having now wisely undertaken deliberation concerning my salvation, I promise that, with the Lord’s help, I will observe in all things the provisions of the Rule, willingly keep the commands of my abbot, and, with the Lord’s favor, obey all the orders of the elder brothers.

“For the sake of eternal freedom, I further promise that from now on I will faithfully subject myself to the laws of this Rule, so that from this day I may no longer leave the monastery or shake my neck free from beneath the yoke of the Rule—a yoke which, under the yearly period of choice, I was permitted either to reject or to accept. Rather, as I have said, putting away every excuse, I promise the stability of the monastery and the conversion of my conduct. For the service of my profession, the reward of eternal life, and fear of Gehenna, I humbly submit myself to serve in holy obedience before God and his angels.

“And so that this petition of my promise may be firmly kept by you, I hand over this written petition, made in the name of the saints whose relics are contained here and of the present abbot, to be kept forever; and, confirmed by my own hand, I place it upon the altar, to be observed perpetually in this monastery.”

Hence the text continues:

The novice shall write this petition in his own hand. If he does not know letters, someone whom he has asked shall write it for him; the novice shall make his mark and place it with his own hand upon the altar. Elsewhere also we read:

“If the novice enters with his possessions, then the written deed or donation of his possessions made to God or to the monastery shall be placed upon the altar by the hand of the donor himself. The brother shall say: ‘Behold, Lord, together with my soul and my poverty, whatever you have given me I return and offer back to you. I wish my possessions to be there where my heart and soul shall be, though under the authority of the monastery and of the abbot whom, Lord, you have appointed over me in your place, when you say: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me”’” (Luke 10).

Once he has placed it, the novice himself shall immediately begin this verse:

“Receive me, O Lord, according to your word, and I shall live; and do not let me be put to shame in my hope” (Psalm 118).

The entire congregation shall respond to this verse three times, adding, “Glory be to the Father.” Then the novice brother shall prostrate himself at the feet of each person, so that they may pray [Col. 0903B] for him; and from that day onward he shall be reckoned as a member of the congregation.

It is the voice of one who repents and turns back to God, saying: “Receive me, O Lord, according to your word, and I shall live,” and so forth. For one who has withdrawn far from God by sinning, and who, as though dead to the knowledge of God, has lain hidden for a long time in the tomb of sin, is humbled again through repentance and, so that he may live eternally after being received, tearfully entreats the Lord. Therefore, having prostrated himself at the feet of all the brothers, he ought continually to ask them to pray for him, even while [the text reads *deceptus*, “deceived”] in the congregation.

Hence a certain master of monks says: “After these words have been spoken, the novice brother himself shall say this responsory: ‘Receive me, O Lord, according to your word, and I shall live,’ and so forth.” After this responsory the abbot says this verse: “Confirm, O God, what you have accomplished in us” (Psalm 67). [Col. 0903C] After this verse has been said, and peace has immediately been given to him by everyone, the abbot shall complete the rite.

From this it is understood that, after the “Glory” mentioned above has been said by all, everyone together with that novice ought again, in silence as is customary, to say the Lord’s Prayer; and when the abbot says, “And lead us not into temptation,” they should all respond in the customary manner, “But deliver us from evil.” Then the abbot, praying over the novice, shall say this prayer:

“Receive, we beseech you, O Lord, this servant of yours, fleeing to you from the storm of this world and the snares of the devil, so that, received by you and saved from the present age, he may rejoice that in the future he has been happily rewarded by you. Through …”

Then, after the kiss has been given to everyone, he too shall be reckoned as a member of the congregation.

If he possesses any property, he shall either distribute it beforehand to the poor or, after making a formal donation, transfer it to the monastery, reserving nothing for himself from the whole of it; for he knows that from that day onward he will not even have control over his own body. When it says “after making a formal donation,” this means religiously, in the presence of witnesses and the entire congregation of the monastery.

Hence elsewhere the Fathers of the monks have said: “If a novice wishes to bring any property into his cell, it shall be placed on the table in the presence of all the brothers.” Hence a certain master of monks also says: “Together with his soul, let him offer everything to God and to the monastery’s oratory by a donation, with religious witnesses subscribing—bishop, priest, and deacon, or the clergy of that territory—and in the instrument itself let him stipulate that, if he should ever wish to depart from the monastery, he shall leave the monastery without his possessions and without God’s forgiveness of his sins.” [Col. 0904A]

Immediately, therefore, in the oratory he shall be stripped of his own garments in which he is clothed and dressed in the garments of the monastery. Here, as it seems to me, if he is wearing secular clothing, he should first be tonsured, and then clothed in the monastery’s garments.

Hence a certain ancient master of monks says: “When, therefore, he has completed an entire year in the monastery blamelessly with the other brothers, only then, without any hesitation, shall he be tonsured, or shall the garments of the holy calling be exchanged for him.” Cassian likewise says: “When someone has been received into a monastery, he must be so faithfully stripped of all his former possessions that he is not permitted any longer even to keep the garment in which he came dressed from the world; but, brought forward into the midst, he shall be stripped of his own garments and [Col. 0904B] clothed by the abbot’s hands in the monastery’s garments.”

When the novice is tonsured, before he is tonsured the priest shall say this prayer:

“Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that just as this servant of yours loses the hair of his head here, so he may at the same time lose the vices of his heart and body, so that, renewed alike in body and mind, he may be able happily to reign with you forever. Through …”

Those garments, however, from which he was stripped shall be put away in the wardrobe and kept, so that, if at some time, persuaded by the devil, he should consent to leave the monastery—which God forbid—he may then be stripped of the monastery’s garments and cast out.

Hence Cassian says: “The garments that he took off shall be handed over to the superior, who shall keep them until the progress of his way of life has been made clearly known through various temptations and trials. If, however, any murmuring or disobedience is detected in him, he shall be stripped of the monastery’s garments with which he had been clothed, dressed again in his former garments kept by the superior, and expelled outside, because it is not lawful for him to depart with the monastery’s garments that he received.”

Hence a certain master of monks says: “The secular garments that he removed when he changed clothes shall be carefully put away and preserved, both in the case of laymen and also of one who has been firmly converted, lest—something that must not happen among the converted—when he wishes to return again to his former vomit and chooses once more to retrace the paths of the world, and cannot be restrained by any bonds of Scripture or admonition, he should give back to Christ what belongs to him: that is, stripped of the holy garments or sacred habit, and resembling the world in the garments in which he came, he should return to the world at the devil’s prompting, and the habit won from Christ should not be polluted in the world by the fugitive.” [Col. 0904D]

Nevertheless, he shall not receive the petition that the abbot took from above the altar; rather, it shall be kept in the monastery. He orders that the petition be preserved so that through it, even against the man’s will, the abbot may, if he wishes, bring him back into the monastery and keep him there in submission. Or, if he should perhaps claim that he is not a monk, overcome by that petition he shall be reduced to the service of monastic life.

## CHAPTER LIX. On the sons of nobles or poor people who are offered

If someone of noble birth offers his son to God in a monastery, and the boy is still underage, his parents shall make the petition mentioned above. With the offering, they shall wrap the petition itself and the boy’s hand in the altar cloth, and thus offer him.

Hence Basil says: “Infants ought nevertheless to be received, with the will and consent of their parents—indeed, offered by the parents themselves—in the testimony of many, so that every occasion for the slander of wicked people may be excluded. Once they have been received, if they should transgress their purpose, they ought no longer to be seen as those who have offended against the Lord, since, with him as witness, they have violated the covenant of their confession. But if a person sins against another person,” he says, “they will pray for him to the Lord; but if he sins against God, who will pray for him?”

Hence Isidore says: “Whoever has been entrusted to a monastery by his own parents must know that he is to remain there perpetually. For Hannah piously offered to God the boy Samuel, whom she had borne and weaned; and he remained in the ministry of the temple to which his mother had assigned him, and served where he had been placed.”

From this it is understood that by “parents” he means no others than the father or mother who begot him, because Hannah offered Samuel, whom she herself had borne, to serve in the temple of the Lord, and no one else did so.

Regarding his possessions, they shall either make a promise in the present petition, under oath. “Under oath” means with an oath. Everyone swears by means of his superior. Therefore he says “under oath,” because he is under the oath by which he swears and under the one by whom he swears. [Col. 0905C]

For they shall never, either personally, through a substituted person, or in any manner whatsoever, give him anything or provide him with any opportunity to possess anything. A “substituted person” is one who has been placed or appointed in another’s stead. A substitute is one placed in another’s position, as though “subtracted” [the text explains the term through a wordplay]. Hence we also call a consul “suffect” one who is substituted for another.

Or, if they do not wish to do this and wish to offer something to the monastery as alms for their own reward, they shall make a donation to the monastery from the possessions they wish to give, reserving usufruct for themselves, if they so wish. By “usufruct” he means what we call the right of usufruct: that is, they shall donate those possessions to the monastery by a testamentary instrument, reserving the usufruct for themselves, and from those possessions they shall pay themselves the annual census imposed upon them.

[Col. 0905D]

“And thus let everything be closed off.” That is, let every opportunity be closed, obstructed, and denied by which the boy might thereafter be endangered. For it is unlawful that one who is attempting to escape the snare of this world should reserve something by which the devil’s assault could entangle him.

“So that no suspicion may remain for the boy by which, deceived, he could perish”—which God forbid—“as we have learned by experience.” For he had seen young men leave the monastery on such an occasion and abandon God’s service for earthly possessions and love the world; therefore he says, “as we have learned by experience.” If this happened rarely then, we now know that it happens very frequently.

Concerning this chapter a certain master of monks says: “When the son of some noble wishes to flee into a monastery for the service of God, he shall not be received beforehand unless, as we said above, he has promised to fulfill every obedience. Then the parents should also be summoned, so that it may be learned what their intention regarding him is. If the parents are more consenting to his wishes, the abbot shall summon them to the monastery and ask them about the vow of the son who is turning to God, so that he may be seen to be devoted or offered by those who begot him.

“When, therefore, the parents have responded that they gladly wish to fulfill what he desires, the abbot shall say to them: ‘Thus, considering the matter, O parents, we rightly advise you before God concerning your son: if you wish to offer your son worthily to God, first strip him of the world. For if something remains with you to be preserved for him in the world, he will at some time experience the tickling of diabolical desire, just as a dog delights to return to its vomit; and, having put his hand to the plow and looking back, he will no longer be fit for the kingdom of heaven. At some point, leaving the monastery, secure in his portion and in what you have preserved for him, he will desire to return to your secular household; wishing to be co-heir with his brothers, he will begin to return as husband and master of his possessions, and, restored to his former pleasures and displays, he will desire nothing but marriage.

“‘Therefore, as we said above, if you wish to offer him worthily to God, let his portion be divided into three equal parts. One part, distributed by the abbot’s hands, shall be given to the poor or needy; another part he shall leave to you or to his brothers as a gift, as he proceeds to the company of the saints [the word in the supplied text, *exagilario*, is uncertain]; and the third part, useful as provisions for his journey, he shall carry with him to benefit the needs of the monastery of the saints.

“‘But if both alternatives seem burdensome to you—so that you neither listen to God by giving alms to the poor and redeeming your son’s soul, nor accept our counsel by dividing his portion and removing his secular property—then give your son to God stripped and alone. Promise him under oath by the holy Gospels that thereafter he shall have nothing from your patrimonial property, so that, now firmly persevering in the Lord, he may know that he has nothing to hope for from the world, seeing himself alienated from you and from it, and desire only heavenly things.

“‘The essential point is that he possess nothing from the world from which, whether you live or die, he might now hope to receive anything from your possessions; for one to whom the world has once been crucified ought not again to take delight in it.’”

It follows:

“Likewise, let the poorer people act in the same way. Those who possess nothing at all shall simply make a petition and offer their son with the offering before witnesses.”

When this handing over of sons—whether noble or lowborn, rich or poor—is carried out, it should be declared in this form:

“Although it has been established by law and held from ancient times that parents should hand over their children to the Lord in the temple of the Lord, together with offerings, so that they may happily serve the Lord, without doubt this example is beneficially provided for us to follow concerning our own children. For it is just that we render to our Creator the fruit that is due from us.

“Therefore I hand over this son of ours, named so-and-so, together with the offering in his hand and the petition, all wrapped in the altar cloth, before witnesses, to the name of the saints whose relics are contained here and of the present abbot, to remain according to the rule. Thus, from this day onward, it shall no longer be permitted for him to shake his neck free from the yoke of the rule; rather, let him know that he must faithfully observe the statutes of that same rule and serve the Lord with a thankful heart together with the others.

“And so that this handing over of ours may remain unshaken, I promise under oath before the Lord and his angels that never by myself, never through a substituted person, nor in any manner through the resources of my possessions will I ever give him opportunities to leave the monastery. And so that this petition may remain firm, I have confirmed it with my own hand and delivered it to be strengthened by witnesses.” [Col. 0907B]

## CHAPTER LX. On priests who wish to live in the monastery

If someone from the order of priests asks to be received into the monastery, his request should certainly not be granted quickly. He says that it should not be granted quickly so that his steadfastness may be tested by inquiry and his perseverance in knocking may be recognized, because it is written: “Seek and you will find; knock and it will be opened to you” (Matthew 7; Luke 11). Or, alternatively, it is so that it may be tested whether he comes inspired by the Holy Spirit or moved and tempted by some other spirit.

Nevertheless, if he persists completely in this request, he must know that he will observe the entire discipline of the rule. By “the discipline of the rule” he means the regular teaching in all things and the precepts of holy instruction. For “discipline” derives its name from learning. Whatever is learned holily in a regular school is properly called discipline. Regular instruction consists in observing the precepts of that same rule, in corrections, reprimands, and various judgments. “The one who perseveres in these to the end will be saved.”

Nothing shall be relaxed for him, so that what is written may apply: “Friend, why have you come?” (Matthew 26). Judas had come to betray the Lord and, as an excuse, offered him a false kiss. The Lord said to him: “Friend, why have you come?” This means: “Do what you have come to do; you have come to betray me, not to kiss me. Stop giving a false kiss and hasten to betray your teacher and Lord.” [Col. 0907D]

This is how one must speak to priests and to all who live under the rule, who do not take care to obey its precepts in everything: “Friend, why have you come? Do what you have come to do. You have come to obey, not to command; to work, not to be idle; to exercise yourself in works, not to devote yourself to chatter; to humble yourself, not to be proud. Therefore, friend, why have you come? You have come to observe the precepts of the rule. Insofar as you are able, with the Lord’s help, observe them, so that by observing them you may be justified and by despising them you may not perish.”

Nevertheless, he may be permitted to stand after the abbot, to give blessings, or to conduct Masses, provided that the abbot orders him to do so. Otherwise, he must presume to do none of these things, knowing that he is subject to regular discipline, and he should instead provide everyone with examples of humility.

A priest who, having been well disciplined in the world because of his love of God, the uprightness of his conduct, and the moderation of his regular life, comes to the monastery to serve the Lord there in quiet, to grow more and more in virtues, and to live in the monastery as a father of monks, displaying an example of holiness and surpassing the others in holy virtues—such a man may rightly be permitted to stand after the abbot, to give blessings, and to conduct Masses. Even this he must do not presumptuously, but when ordered and directed by the abbot.

But one who, weighed down by the burden of sin, has been removed from priestly honor in the sight of God and seeks the monastery’s enclosure so that, subdued by penance, he may live there always humbled—such a person should not seek a position of this kind; rather, he ought humbly to be content with the place of his own order.

If, perhaps, he has been appointed in the monastery because of ordination or for some other reason, he should observe the place he occupied when he entered the monastery, not the place granted him out of reverence for the priesthood. By “because of ordination” he means either because he was ordained a priest or because he received from the abbot the ministry of ordination—that is, authority to ordain something—in the monastery. “Or for some other reason” implies that he may have been elevated in the monastery; he should observe that earlier place, and so forth.

Concerning this chapter a certain master of monks also says: “If priests choose to live in monasteries for the love of God, for discipline, or for the moderation of a holy life, let them be called ‘fathers of the monastery’ in name alone, and let nothing else be permitted them in the monasteries except to gather, complete, and sign the prayers. Let them neither presume nor be permitted anything else, unless they claim some authority of ordination, governance, or administration; but the abbot, who has been appointed over the entire flock, should judge or defend every form of permission or ordering of the monastery’s governance together with the rule.

“For this reason we establish that they be called ‘fathers of the monastery’ by the name of honor alone: because of the consecration or ordination of the priesthood. For if those priests choose to use the monastery’s food, clothing, or footwear, they should also choose to work daily in common according to the apostolic precept, mindful of the Holy Spirit, who showed in the apostles an example concerning himself and said: ‘We did not eat our bread without payment’ (2 Thessalonians 3). Again he says: ‘We worked with our hands so that we might not burden any of you’ (1 Corinthians 4). And he himself likewise says: ‘Whoever does not work, let him not eat’ (2 Thessalonians 3).

“Therefore, if they refuse for a very long time to seek their sustenance by the labor of their hands while remaining idle, after being admonished by the abbot with the testimony of many religious men, let them return to the churches. But if—which God forbid—they wish to leave not peacefully but rather amid scandal, let them be seized, stripped of the monastery’s possessions, and expelled through the closed gate, because they themselves ought to do what they preach to others.”

If any of the clergy wishes to join the monastery with the same desire, he shall be placed in a middling position. He too, however, must promise to observe the rule or to remain permanently.

Here he orders that those clerics be placed in a middling position who, not weighed down by the burden of sin but out of love of God and desire for regular life, wish to join the brothers in the monastery. As for the others, as has already been said above concerning priests, each one should humbly be content with the place of his own order.

## CHAPTER LXI. On foreign monks and how they are to be received

If a foreign monk comes from distant provinces and wishes to live in the monastery as a guest, and is content with the custom of the place that he finds, and does not disturb the monastery through his own excess but is simply content with what he finds, he shall be received for as long as he wishes.

“Content” refers to food, drink, clothing, labors, and the monastery’s customs in other matters. If, however, in all these things he does not disturb the monastery through his own excess—that is, by making excessive demands or criticisms—he shall be received for as long as he wishes.

Hence Basil says: “It is fitting that entry be granted him because the outcomes of things are uncertain. For sometimes it may happen that, over time, he advances, delights in the holiness of the life, and remains in what he has begun, as we know has often happened. Nevertheless, he must be treated with greater caution and care, so that whether he truly remains or advances, or whether the freedom of our institutions is being tested, it may be found sound and pure. In this way we shall please God, and he will advance if he is truthful; or, if he is pretending, he will be ashamed.”

[Col. 0909C]

Nevertheless, if he reasonably and humbly criticizes or points out anything in the spirit of charity, the abbot should handle it prudently, lest perhaps the Lord has directed him there for this very reason. When he says, “If he criticizes anything with the humility of charity,” he means matters concerning the service of God, observance of the rule, and keeping the Lord’s commands. If, concerning all these matters, the guest offers some correction in charity or orders it to be corrected, he should gladly be heard, and whatever needs correction should be corrected promptly, because, with the Lord at work, one person is frequently corrected through another.

If afterward he wishes to confirm his stability, such a desire should not be rejected, especially because his life could have been known during the time of his hospitality. How he is to confirm his stability—whether only in his heart, or in heart and word together—is not stated explicitly here. But, as may be understood, just as the novice promises his stability before God and his saints, so that if he ever acts otherwise he may know that he will be condemned by the one whom he mocks, so this man too, although he does not make a promise because he already has one, should nevertheless confirm his stability in heart and word together before God, his saints, and suitable witnesses, lest he deserve condemnation for his great and unlawful wandering.

But if he is found to be excessive or vicious during the period of hospitality, he should not only not be joined to the body of the monastery; he should also be courteously told to depart, lest others too be corrupted by his misery.

“Excessive” refers, as was said above, to food, drink, or the other observances of the rule. “Vicious” means one accustomed to vice and frequently falling into the stain of vice. For one who loves vice, frequently practices it, and has been made wretched by it is appropriately called vicious. Hence what follows here: “Lest others be corrupted by his misery.” A life that is vicious and soiled by sins is called miserable. It is called misery because it makes those who love it miserable, as it is written: “Sins have made us miserable” (Proverbs 14). [Col. 0910A]

But if he is not such a person as deserves to be expelled, then not only should he be received into the congregation if he asks to be admitted; he should even be persuaded to remain, so that others may be instructed by his example, and because in every place one serves the same Lord and serves as a soldier under one king.

The wicked must be expelled and driven away, lest others be corrupted by their companionship; the good, however, must be received, retained, and drawn in, so that others may be improved by their companionship. The former are to be expelled so that their vices may be avoided; the latter are to be retained so that others may imitate their holy and honorable life.

The persuasion used with a good guest whom one wishes to retain shall be this: one should say to him, “Stay, brother, immovable with us in this monastery, so that others may be instructed by your good example. There is no need to seek elsewhere the one who is always known everywhere. We serve the same Lord in this place, and we serve as soldiers under the same king. There is one Lord in every place, whom his servants serve daily, and one King of kings, under whom his soldiers always serve everywhere. Therefore you have no need to seek another place where you may serve the Lord better, because here, by laboring well and serving the Lord, you can obtain the kingdom of heaven.” [Col. 0910C]

If the abbot recognizes that he is such a man, he may also place him somewhat higher.

When he says, “If he recognizes him to be such,” he means one who deserves to be placed in a higher position. A holy and proven life ought to be exalted in the monastery, not a noble person. God’s servant is to be honored not according to the nobility of his parents or the splendor of his clothing, but according to the merit of his life.

The abbot may establish not only a monk but also one of the aforementioned ranks of priests or clerics in a higher position than that in which they entered, if he recognizes that their life is of such quality. They are not to be exalted because they are ordained priests or clerics, but because they have been proven by the merit of their life and found holier than the others in their conduct. Thus it is not the abbot’s presumption but the holiness of their actions that exalts them.

Let the abbot beware of ever receiving a monk from another well-known monastery to live there without the consent of his abbot or letters of recommendation, because it is written: “What you do not want done to you, do not do to another.”

Hence the ancient Fathers said: “It is not permitted to receive brothers from another monastery without the will of the one who presides over them as father; not only should one not receive them, one ought not even see them,” since the Apostle says: “The one who has made his first faith void is worse than an unbeliever.” But if he asks the father who presides over him to enter another monastery, let him be commended by that father to the one who presides where he desires to be, and then let him be received.

That monk must know that however many brothers he finds in the other monastery, he has that many superiors. Nor should attention be paid to what he was before, but what he has begun to become should be tested. Once received, if he appears to possess anything, whether possessions or books, he shall no longer be permitted to own them, so that he may be perfect—he who could not become an elder elsewhere.

Hence blessed Ferreolus says: “We do not wish, and we forbid and prohibit, that a monk or cleric of another place or monastery be received for any reason, taking such precautions out of zeal for charity lest something new be introduced when the stain of scandal arises. For Scripture says: ‘Whatever you do not want done to you, do not do to another’” (Matthew 7).

[Col. 0911B]

## CHAPTER LXII. On the priests of the monastery

If an abbot asks that a presbyter or deacon be ordained for him, he shall choose from his own monks one who is worthy to exercise the priesthood. The abbot ought to know the confession of all his monks, and then, choosing from among them the one whom he finds worthy, he shall order him to be ordained deacon or presbyter, selecting in them the merit of regular life and understanding of wisdom.

Once ordained, he must beware of arrogance or pride. He must presume nothing except what the abbot commands him, knowing that he is all the more subject to regular discipline. Let him not forget, on account of the priesthood, obedience to the rule and discipline; rather, let him advance more and more in the Lord.

For it is written: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Ecclesiasticus 3). The monk must therefore beware of the boastfulness of arrogance and of pride, the mother of all vices. Just as pride is the origin of all crimes, so it is the ruin of every virtue. Pride is worse than every vice for this reason: it is assumed by persons of the highest rank and by rulers, and it arises from works of justice and virtues. Thus pride is rightly the beginning of every sin, because unless disobedience precedes it, the guilt of transgression does not follow.

He shall always observe the position in which he entered the monastery, except for the ministry of the altar. That is, always maintaining humility, let him keep his place in all things according to the rule, and so let him approach for the kiss of peace, for communion, for beginning the psalm, for standing in the choir, and in every place whatsoever, except for the ministry of the altar—that is, unless he is serving at the altar. When assisting at the altar, he stands first, offers the sacrifice, and prays first for everyone, even if he is found to be last in rank. Therefore, in that place, neither position nor rank is to be maintained.

And if the choice of the congregation and the abbot’s will should wish to promote him because of the merit of his life—“to be promoted” means to be honored or exalted, and to be raised from a lower position to a higher one—it is right that one who, relying on the love of God, agrees to humble himself more than others should be exalted among men.

For the monk who surpasses the others in prudence and moderation, chastity, faith, humility, charity, [Col. 0912A] obedience, and every sincere purity ought to be honored above the others.

Nevertheless, he must know that he is to observe the rule established for him by the deans or superiors. If he presumes otherwise, he shall be judged not as a priest but as a rebel. If he has observed well the rule established for him, he will be honored both with the dignity and with the name of priest. But if he does not observe it, he will be called neither priest nor even monk, but rebellion, because he has subsequently, in pride and defiance, invalidated the covenant that he had earlier promised voluntarily and peacefully. “Rebellion” is the name given to one who, after peace has been made, renews the war.

If, after frequent admonition, he does not correct himself, even the bishop shall be brought in as a witness. If he still does not amend, he shall be expelled from the monastery once his faults have become clear, provided that his defiance is such that he refuses to submit to or obey the rule. For if he proves so perverse that he will not amend either out of love for Christ or out of reverence for the bishop, he shall be expelled from the monastery once his faults have become clear and the matter has been made known to all the neighbors.

## CHAPTER LXIII. On the order of the congregation

Let them preserve their ranks in the monastery in such a way that the time of their conversion and the merit of their life are taken into account, as the abbot has established.

Hence blessed Fructuosus says: “The one who was first converted in the monastery shall walk first, sit first, receive the eulogy first, communicate first in the church, speak first when the brothers are questioned about some matter, say the psalm first, stand first in the choir, serve the weekly office first, and extend his hand to the table first.

“Nor is age alone to be sought among the brothers; rather, what is to be considered is conversion and the purpose of labor and devotion. Therefore this discernment must be awaited from the elder, so that he may honor each one according to how fervent he sees him to be in the love and worship of God. It is not the nobility of lineage, the wealth that anyone possessed in the world, or advanced age that is to be sought, but uprightness of life and the merits of the most ardent faith that must be weighed. For the one who is closer to God must also be judged superior.”

Let the abbot not disturb the flock entrusted to him. How the abbot disturbs the flock entrusted to him is explained by what follows:

“Nor, as though exercising unrestricted power, let him arrange anything unjustly.” Thus, by arranging something unjustly, the abbot disturbs the flock entrusted to him. For this reason he makes that person worse and heaps upon himself an increase of condemnation for his unjust arrangement. Hence what follows:

“But let him always consider that he will have to render an account to God for all his judgments and actions.” Other people will have to render an account to the Lord in judgment only for their own actions; abbots, however, and all who preside over others, will have to render an account to the Lord not only for their own evil actions but also for their unjust judgments when they come with him to the supreme judgment.

The abbot must greatly fear, for he must render an account to the Lord equally for his thoughts, actions, and judgments. He must carefully consider what the Lord says: “With the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged” (Matthew 7); and, “With the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Luke 6). He must also tremble with terror at what is written: “The strictest judgment will be made against those who rule; the powerful will suffer powerful torments” (Wisdom 6). [Col. 0913A]

Therefore, according to the ranks that he has established or that the brothers themselves possess, they shall approach for the kiss of peace, for communion, for beginning the psalm, and for standing in the choir. In every place whatsoever, age shall not determine rank or prejudice anyone, because Samuel and Daniel, though boys, judged priests.

Hence Isidore says: “Whoever first enters the monastery sits first, walks first, says the psalm first, extends his hand to the table first, communicates first in the church; age is not sought among them, but profession.”

When it says, “Samuel and Daniel, though boys, judged priests” (1 Kings 7; Daniel 13), this is understood of Eli and of those who wished to oppress Susanna. Samuel judged the priests when he saw the sons of Eli sinning, judged them transgressors in his heart, and condemned them. He likewise reproved and judged Eli because he did not restrain them with strict correction or hold them back from iniquity.

Daniel judged the priests when he reproved those men, full of wicked thoughts, who wished to condemn Susanna through false testimony, condemned them, and declared that they deserved to be slain by the angelic sword.

[Col. 0913C]

Therefore, except for those whom, as we said, the abbot has preferred by higher judgment or degraded for definite reasons, all the rest shall be ranked according to the time of their conversion. For example, one who came to the monastery at the second hour of the day must know that he is junior to the one who came at the first hour of the day, whatever his age or rank may be.

Elsewhere it is written: “The abbot must take care that, in order, just as they were converted in the monastery, so they may be established in their rank, except when the abundance of a religious way of life has deserved that someone be promoted further, or when serious fault has required that someone be moved backward.”

But discipline must be maintained in every respect for the boys by everyone. The more the abbot sees that a younger age is fragile in wrongdoing, the more he ought to increase his diligence in guarding it.

[Col. 0913D]

Therefore, the juniors shall honor their seniors. Here the honor of possessions is not demanded; reverence in words and conduct is sought.

The seniors shall love their juniors. The Lord Jesus Christ, who is the firstborn among many brothers, loved his younger apostles, giving them an example and saying: “I give you this commandment: that you love one another, just as I have loved you” (John 13).

In the very use of names, no one shall be permitted to address another by his bare name. Rather, seniors shall call their juniors “Brothers,” while juniors shall call their seniors “Nonnos” [“fathers” or “elders”], which signifies paternal reverence.

Just as paternal reverence was then displayed among them by calling the seniors “nonnos,” so now among us it is required that, because of that same paternal reverence, our seniors be called “Lords” [*domni*]. Whether our seniors are called “nonnos” or “domni,” and whether the juniors are called “brothers,” everything is entirely fitting. The essential point is that none of the brothers should ever be called by his name alone.

Since the abbot is believed to act in Christ’s place, let him be called “Lord” and “Abbot,” not by his own assumption of the title, but out of honor for and love of Christ. He himself, however, should reflect and conduct himself so that he may be worthy of such honor. It should be noted that he did not say: “Because the abbot presides over all, surpasses all, and is above all, therefore let him be called ‘Lord’ and ‘Abbot’”; rather, he says: “Because he is believed to act in Christ’s place, let him be called ‘Lord’ and ‘Abbot.’” Therefore the abbot who does not rightly act in Christ’s place among the brothers receives and assumes this name unworthily. Hence it follows: “Not by his own assumption, [Col. 0914B] but out of honor for and love of Christ.” For he ought to live—without reproach—in conduct, speech, judgments, life, and in every command of the Lord, truthfully saying to the Lord: “I have not departed from your judgments”; and thus, out of honor for and love of Christ, he should bear this name. First he ought rightly to act in Christ’s place, and only then to receive that sacred name of his, lest, if perhaps he should wish to assume it unworthily or rashly, he take upon himself condemnation rather than justification. When he says: “He himself should reflect and conduct himself so as to be worthy of such honor,” this is understood to concern his salvation: he should fear being condemned under such a name if he has lived wrongly, but if he has lived rightly, he should rejoice at being justified under such a name.

Whenever brothers meet one another, the younger should ask the elder for a blessing. When a senior passes by, the junior should rise and give him his seat. Nor should the junior presume to sit down unless his elder instructs him to do so, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “Outdoing one another in showing honor” (Rom. XIII). Hence another Father of the monks also says: “Whenever brothers meet one another on the road or in any place, they should, with all humility, bow to one another and ask for a blessing. If one of them is the elder, the younger should first ask for a blessing; only then should the elder proceed.
