If, while the brothers are seated, another arrives, those who are younger in rank should rise and offer the elder a place. The juniors should in no way, through pride, contradict their seniors; rather, with all humility, whether questioned or corrected, they should answer. If a junior sees an elder falling into any offense, he should direct him to confess to the abbot or superior, not by reproaching him, but rather by grieving for him. The elder should act similarly toward the junior.”

Children, little boys, or adolescents should, in the oratory and at the tables, take their appointed places with discipline. “Take their places” means “receive them”; and with discipline, propriety, and chaste fear they should keep their appointed places. Wherever they may be, once placed in order, they should walk, stand, and sit accordingly. Hence it follows:

“Outside, however, or wherever they may be, they should be kept under custody and discipline until they reach an age of understanding.” As has already been written: “The more the abbot sees that an age is vulnerable to sinning, the greater custody he should assign to it for its salvation.”

[Col. 0915A]

## CHAPTER LXIV. On Appointing an Abbot

In appointing an abbot, this principle should always be observed: that the man whom the entire united congregation, according to the fear of God, or even a small part of the congregation, chosen with sounder judgment, has elected should be appointed. The one to be appointed should be chosen for the merit of his life and the teaching of his wisdom, even if he is last in the order of the congregation. Hence blessed Fructuosus says:

“The abbot should always be chosen from the monastery’s own monks: a holy, discerning, serious, chaste, beloved, humble, gentle, and learned man, who, tested by long experience and instruction, has been well trained in all the qualities mentioned above; who excels in abstinence and shines in teaching; who despises elaborate feasts and the custom of a more luxurious table; who rejects excessive drinking of wine; who provides for all the brothers in common as their own most loving father; whom neither sudden and immoderate anger casts down, nor pride exalts, nor sorrow and faintheartedness break, nor lust corrupt; who displays discernment in patience and gentleness together with anger; who so attends to the needy and poor that, in the compassion of Christ, he recognizes himself as a servant and not merely as a superior; and whose speech and life should be so harmonious that what he teaches in words he confirms by diligent works. Advancing with the two-edged sword, whatever he instructs others by word, he himself should continually practice with zeal, so that neither action destroys speech, nor inappropriate speech, conversely, weakens good action.”

[Col. 0915C]

But if the entire congregation should, through its own vices—which God forbid—unanimously choose a person who consents to those vices, and if those very vices should become known to the bishop in whose diocese that place lies, or to abbots or neighboring Christians, let them prevent the wicked consensus from prevailing and appoint a worthy steward over God’s household. Let them know that they will receive a good reward for this if they act chastely and out of zeal for God, just as, conversely, they will incur sin if they neglect it. For this reason he commands that the bishop, abbots, or even neighboring Christians prevent a vicious man from becoming abbot, because no one remained in the congregation who ought to prevent it. It is as though he said: “Even if all those within consent to have a vicious abbot, let the Catholic men outside resist firmly and not agree with them, lest a vice wickedly nourished by all take root in the monastery; and once it has taken root, lest its inhabitants come to be hated by all their neighbors. Rather, let the vice, rejected by all, perish and, trampled underfoot, vanish, so that virtues may grow among the monks and vices perish. Then, seeing their good works, their neighbors may glorify God, who granted them both the will to act well and a worthy shepherd and steward.”

The abbot who has been appointed should always consider what a burden he has undertaken and to whom he will have to render an account of his stewardship. For he who receives monks to govern receives not a small but a great burden to bear: from it come the sweat of labor and the increase of honor’s pleasure. He has begun to govern the souls of the brothers, concerning whom he will be compelled to render an account of his stewardship to the Lord. “Stewardship” means his administration or governance. Properly speaking, a steward is the governor of an estate; hence he receives his name. Sometimes, however, he is called a steward not from governing an estate, but from administering an entire household.

He should know that it is more necessary for him to benefit than to preside. For by benefiting, the abbot profits both himself and others. If he produces gain and brings progress to others, he acquires the Lord’s favor for himself and pours the teaching of salvation into others. He educates others in righteousness and acquires eternal rewards for himself. By presiding, however, while he lives, he always imposes labor upon himself and fear upon others; he generates excessive care for himself and the punishment of labor for others; he incurs great anxiety for himself and frequently inflicts unjust injuries upon others. If those who preside have carried out all these duties well, with discretion and for God’s sake, imposing the punishments of fear upon those who wish to sin so that they may not sin, and restraining sinners with severe discipline and righteous judgment, they will obtain at least a small measure of grace from God. But if they neglect to do these things and wish only to exalt themselves because they are superiors, they will not only remain empty of the reward of recompense, but will also lament in hell the punishments of their arrogance. Therefore he says: “He should know that it is more necessary for him to benefit than to preside.” For presiding sometimes gains a small good for him, but sometimes a great evil; whereas benefiting always gains for him good, always an eternal reward.

He must therefore be learned in divine law, so that he knows and has from which to bring forth things new and old. It is as though he said: “Let the abbot be learned in divine law, which consists of the New and Old Testaments, and from it let him know and understand how to bring forth to the brothers testimonies both new and old.” When he says “and have,” this means that a treasure of wisdom and knowledge should be stored in his breast, from which, whenever necessary, he may bring forth testimonies new and old. Or certainly, let the abbot himself be learned, intelligent, experienced, wise, and such a vessel filled with wisdom that, whenever he wishes, he has at hand a new and an old testimony to bring forth.

Let him be chaste, sober, merciful, always exalting mercy above judgment, so that he himself may obtain mercy. For it is written: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V). Conversely: “Judgment without mercy awaits the one who has not shown mercy.” He therefore exalts mercy above judgment who, after carrying out judgment, does not punish the wicked with strictness, but mercifully spares him and frees him from the condemnation he deserves. Hence it is also written elsewhere: “Mercy triumphs over judgment” (James II), that is, mercy is placed above judgment, because where a work of mercy is found, even if there is something in the judgment that ought perhaps to be punished, the fire of sin is extinguished as though by mercy.

Let him hate vices and love the brothers. In one and the same person we can both love our brotherhood and hate vices if they are present. For it is one thing that he is a brother, another that he is a vicious man. Let us therefore love our brotherhood in him and hate his viciousness. Let us attack the vice in him, and, once he has been corrected, love our neighbor as ourselves. Hence blessed Gregory also says: “Yes, truly, we ought to show our neighbors such a discrimination of hatred that in them we love what they are and hate what obstructs us on God’s path.”

In correction itself let him act prudently: that is, let him act cautiously, moderately, and with great restraint. “And do nothing to excess.” This saying has been expressed by poets, by our teachers, and by many Catholic and learned men in many appropriate places, and it can be understood of both good and evil actions. Of the good, there is the saying: “Do not be excessively righteous,” and similar statements. As for evil, it is not our place to give an example, since the Lord entirely forbids both excess and deficiency. Let us now hear the following words to understand why blessed Benedict places this saying here.

“Lest, while he wishes too eagerly to scrape away the rust, the vessel be broken.” Here he uses “rust” for the contagion of sin and “vessel” for the frailty of the soul. It is as though he said: “Cleanse the monk’s soul from the contagion of sin in such a way that, once broken, you do not plunge it into despair. Do not lose through an excessively harsh condemnation the one whom you could win through moderate judgment.” The monk’s vessel, when it is being made sound improperly, is broken more quickly when his mind, harshly rebuked for his fault, is either deeply disturbed by despair of pardon or continually considers falling away through flight or departure from the monastery. To prevent this, the abbot should always provide carefully, wisely, and cautiously; and he should always attend diligently to what follows. For it follows:

“Let him always be suspicious of his own frailty.” When the abbot attentively regards his own frailty with suspicion and patiently, discreetly, and cautiously considers the frailty of others, he judges rightly. Hence the Apostle Paul also says: “Brothers, if a person is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. VI). It is as though he said: “Since you too are human and can be tempted in some way and need help, you ought therefore to support the one who is tempted.” Those who have been placed under the condition of weakness rightly support the weak. It follows:

“Let him remember that a bruised reed is not to be broken” (Isa. XLII). That is, he should not drive a monk broken by the stains of sins and shattered by various vices into the pit of despair or into the lapse of flight, as has been said. The one who gives a sinner an occasion not for salvation but for destruction undoubtedly breaks the bruised reed. Hence blessed Jerome also says: “Whoever does not extend a hand to the sinner and does not bear the burden of his brother breaks the bruised reed.”

“In saying this, we do not mean that he should permit vices to be nourished.” Since above he imposed moderation upon just correction, here he warns against the nourishment that would allow vices to grow. Lest, while the sinner’s discipline is moderated, the tinder of vices grow and flourish. Hence he plainly continues:

“But let him cut them away prudently and with charity, according to what he sees to be expedient for each person, as we have already said.” Whatever is done in the service of charity undoubtedly contributes to the progress of salvation. The same provision for salvation is suitable for one person in one way and for another in a different way. Therefore, acting as a physician, the abbot should strive to heal one person in one manner and another according to the quantity or quality of the offense. And in all these holy and discerning actions:

“Let him strive to be loved more than feared.” That is, let him exercise among his subjects the work of love more than that of fear; let him soothe them more through paternal affection than frighten them through the punishment of his tyranny. Hence it follows:

“Let him not be turbulent or anxious.” A turbulent person is one disturbed by the agitation of anger, sorrowful, troublesome, or fierce. An anxious person is one filled with acedia or anxiety.

“Let him not be excessive or obstinate.” An excessive person is one who is lavish or prodigal, or an excessive and wasteful dispenser of the monastery’s goods. An obstinate person is one who is insuperable, hardened, persistent, and obdurate.

“Let him not be jealous or excessively suspicious, because he will never rest.” A jealous person is one filled with zealous concern and burdened by suspicion; he suspects that even things that do not happen are happening in his absence, and fears that things no one commits are being committed in secret. Therefore his spirit never rests.

“In his commands let him be provident and considerate, whether the matter is spiritual or worldly. Let him distinguish and moderate the tasks he assigns.” Works according to God are these: vigils, fasts, abstinence, [Col. 0918C] and similar practices. Worldly works, however, are those performed only for the body and not for the soul: plowing, digging, reaping, and all similar bodily tasks. Yet moderation governed by discretion must be maintained in all these spiritual and bodily works, lest the hearts and bodies of those laboring excessively alike fail, leaving only harmful grumbling behind.

“Considering the discretion of holy Jacob, who said: ‘If I make my flocks labor more in walking, they will all die in one day’” (Gen. XXXIII). In this passage Jacob represents rulers, and his sheep their subjects. Following his example, whether they are occupied in spiritual activity or bodily work, the action and capacity of their labor should be moderated so that neither the strength of their souls collapses nor the vigor of their bodies grows weary. Their entire labor should be so regulated that they eagerly desire to exercise themselves still more in their tasks than their superiors wish to assign them. Hence it follows:

“Taking these and other testimonies concerning discretion, the mother of virtues, let him so moderate everything that there may be something the strong desire and the weak do not flee.” The work of monks must therefore be moderated with discretion, which is the mother of all virtues, so that there may be—namely, such a work—as the strong desire to perform or complete, while the weak do not flee from the work itself or from its burden.

“And above all, let him preserve the present Rule in everything.” Above all and before everything else, blessed Benedict commands the abbot to observe the Rule, so that he who is first in name may be first in action, and may complete by his deeds what he proclaims by his office. Let him first carry on his own shoulders or necks what he commands the brothers to carry, and learn by experience whether the burdens he imposes upon the brothers are light or heavy. Let him judge first, in regard to his own primacy at table, the virtue of frugality, and learn by experience the abstinence he proclaims with his tongue, lest perhaps his subjects say in silent thought: “How beautifully he preaches abstinence to us with a full belly!” The preaching of abstinence is acceptable when it is sung by fasting mouths. In all these matters the abbot should know that this applies to him, and he himself should first enter the narrow path of the Rule by which he admonishes others to enter.

“So that, having served well, he may hear from the Lord what the good servant who distributed wheat to his fellow servants at the proper time heard: ‘Amen, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions’” (Luke XII). For the good minister—that is, the good abbot—will hear from the good Lord, the recompensor of all good things, what that servant deserved to hear who faithfully distributed wheat to his fellow servants. He heard: “Amen, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions.” This desirable and beloved voice will also be heard by the good abbot who has faithfully ministered wheat—that is, the word of preaching—to his fellow servants, that is, to his brothers, and has himself fulfilled it in his deeds. When he says: “He will set him over all his possessions,” this is understood to mean all the heavenly joys of the kingdom—not that these alone will possess the Lord there, but that they will enjoy eternal possession more abundantly than the other saints. “Those who are learned will shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like the stars forever and ever.” The Apostle also says: “Let the presbyters who preside well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching” (1 Tim. V).

## CHAPTER LXV. On the Superior of the Monastery

It often happens that serious scandals arise in monasteries through the appointment of a superior. For we have heard that this has often already happened; now, however, we must remedy it. We must choose under the abbot such a person as will undertake the care of the monastery and the office of superior, faithfully fulfill and guard the duties entrusted to him, and do nothing rashly through pride, lest he be one of those whom the following words reveal:

“Since there are some who, inflated by the evil spirit of pride, regard themselves as second abbots, assume tyranny for themselves, nourish scandals, and create dissensions in the congregation.” Tyranny is an improper honor acquired through pride of heart. A superior assumes it proudly when he demands that the improper honor of an abbot be accorded to him; thus he nourishes scandals among the brothers and prepares dissensions in the monastery.

[Col. 0920A]

“And especially in those places where the superior is appointed by the same priest or by the same abbots who appoint the abbot.” Their custom at that time was that, whenever an abbot was appointed, the superior was also appointed by the same bishop and by the other abbots standing present. But because the vice of pride arose from this, today among us he is no longer appointed by another; rather, obedience to the office of superior is imposed upon him by his own abbot, so that whenever it seems appropriate to the abbot, he may be removed from the ministry of superior, lest a source of pride arise in him. Hence it follows:

“How absurd this is can easily be understood, because from the very beginning of his appointment he is given an occasion for pride, when his thoughts suggest to him that he has been stripped of the authority of his abbot, because he was appointed by those by whom the abbot also was appointed.” To prevent these evils, a superior should be chosen or appointed who is shown to edify others by the example of his life, not one who destroys by living badly; who offers a model of humility, not one who displays the defiance of his pride. For it is written below:

“Hence envies are stirred up.” That is, between the superior and the abbot, when one does not wish to regard the other as superior. There is no virtue, and scarcely any ministry, that does not have the evil of envy opposing it.

“Quarrels, detractions, rivalries, dissensions, and disorders.” Quarrels and detractions arise, along with all the other things mentioned, between the superior and the abbot, especially through their followers. Dissensions arise because what one agrees should be done with his own people, the other disagrees should be done with his. Disorders arise because what one arranges by issuing orders, the other overturns by issuing contrary orders. Hence what follows occurs:

“And while the abbot and the superior hold contrary opinions, it is inevitable that, under this dissension, their souls should be endangered. Those who are under them, while flattering the opposing parties, go to destruction. The evil of this danger falls upon the heads of those who made themselves the authors of such disorder. Woe to me, miserable man, that those who ought to have saved themselves lose both others and themselves, and the rest, by living badly. Those who ought to have led others to the kingdom of heaven go themselves—and plunge their followers—with themselves into the pit of destruction and the abyss of hell.”

When he says: “The evil of this danger falls upon the heads of those who made themselves the authors of such disorder,” he seems to be speaking of those who appointed the superior just as they appointed the abbot. They ought to have entrusted the governance of one monastery not to two but to one; and, so that dangerous scandals would not arise between two, they ought to have committed the care of their congregation to the abbot alone. Hence it follows:

“Therefore we judge it expedient, for the preservation of peace and charity, that the governance of his monastery depend upon the abbot’s authority.” He himself ought personally to provide for all the needs of his monks, both bodily and spiritual; to offer the assistance required by present necessity; to lift the hearts of his subjects toward the praise of the Creator by admonishing them; and to correct those whom he finds blameworthy through sluggishness or laziness, according to their fault or age, either by rebuke or by flogging.

“And if it can be done, let every useful function of the monastery be organized through deans, as we arranged earlier, according to what the abbot has ordered, so that, when responsibility is entrusted to several, one may not become proud.” For at present we need the abbot, the superior, the deans, and the priest together and continually, so that each may labor humbly in the office entrusted to him and in the appropriate order. No regular occasion for pride is given to them; rather, a burden is imposed upon them, under which they must proceed groaning and oppressed.

“But if either the place requires it or the congregation requests it, and the abbot judges it expedient with reason and humility, let the abbot himself appoint as superior whomever he chooses, with the counsel of brothers who fear God.” [Col. 0921B] Nevertheless, let this superior perform with reverence whatever his abbot has entrusted to him, doing nothing against the abbot’s will or arrangement. For the more he is set over the others, the more carefully he ought to observe the precepts of the Rule. Blessed Benedict diligently commands this superior, just as the abbot, to observe the Rule in everything. If, through pride, negligence, or laziness, he omits any of the things contained in the Rule, he will be subject to all the condemnations that the Rule contains. Hence the following appropriately comes next:

“If this superior is found to be vicious, deceived by prideful exaltation, or proven to be a despiser of the holy Rule, let him be admonished in words up to four times. If he does not amend, let regular disciplinary correction be applied to him. If he is not corrected even then, let him be deposed from the office of superior, and another who is worthy be substituted in his place. If afterward he is not quiet and obedient in the congregation, let him also be expelled from the monastery.”

Thus far it has been set out what the superior ought not to be; from this point onward, what he ought to be must be demonstrated from the sayings of the Fathers. The superior of a monastery should be appointed not for the length of his years but for his conduct. Many are raised up by the extent of their years, but the disgrace of a sluggish life restrains them and reduces them to the immaturity of childhood. The superior should therefore be serious in conduct, skillful in speech, strong in understanding, vigilant in consideration, energetic in progress, compassionate in correction, moderate in discipline, chaste in action, sober in conduct, equitable in administration, adorned with humility, patient, gentle, not turbulent, not angry, not stained by the vice of pride or arrogance, not prodigal, not talkative, but armed with every act of religious devotion. He should know how to assist the sick in their conduct and rouse the sluggishness of the lukewarm. The abbot should be able to rest his confidence in him, so that he deviates in nothing from the abbot’s commands; rather, being subject in everything and held to the orders of his senior, he should neither oppose the abbot’s will nor do or arrange anything to be done contrary to it. Instead, he should do everything by asking him, according to what is written: “Ask your father, and he will show it to you; your elders, and they will tell you” (Deut. XXXII). He must always ask, so that subject souls may differ in nothing from the counsel of their elders and the sheep may deviate in nothing without the will of their shepherd. The superior himself should do nothing except what the Father commands, especially in a new matter; whatever proceeds from established custom, he should preserve according to the monastery’s rules. Let him act so that he neither causes weariness to the abbot nor burdens the brothers through his lack of moderation. The senior of the monastery who is placed over the brothers should observe these things, referring everything to the abbot, or especially whatever he has not been able to resolve himself.

Let the abbot nevertheless consider that he will render an account to God for all his judgments, lest the flame of envy or jealousy burn his soul. There should be no taint of envy even among laymen; how much less among religious men and the superiors of a monastery. The abbot should love the superior, and the superior the abbot, as a brother ought to love a brother. The abbot should remember, if any flame of envy or jealousy touches him, lest he share in the wicked envy of Cain, who through jealous resentment killed his righteous brother Abel; and through jealous resentment Esau became an enemy to his brother Jacob; and through jealous resentment Joseph was sold by his brothers. Although jealous resentment is designated by the name of a single vice, it produces many branches through different vices. For the taint of envy burns up every shoot of the virtues. It devours every good thing with its pestilential heat, consumes understanding, burns the breast, afflicts the mind, and ravages the human heart like a plague. Against this vice, the weapons of peace and charity must be prepared in the souls of the abbot, all holy rulers, and their subjects.

## CHAPTER LXVI. [Col. 0922C] On the Porter of the Monastery

At the gate of the monastery let a wise old man be placed, one who knows how to receive a message and give a reply, whose maturity does not permit him to wander about. It should be noted that he did not say: “Let an old man in age be placed at the gate,” but said: “Let a wise old man be placed.” This makes clear that what is sought in the porter is not bodily age but the old age of wisdom and understanding. Hence it is also said through a certain wise man: “Venerable old age is not that of long duration, nor is it reckoned by the number of years. The gray hairs of a person are understanding, and the age of old age is an unblemished life” (Wis. IV). Hence it is said to Moses: “Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders of the people” (Num. XI). What else is required in these men than old age of heart? For when it says, “whom you know to be elders of the people,” it is plainly shown that old age of mind, not of body, is to be chosen.

The porter should have a cell beside the gate, so that those who come may always find him present and receive a reply from him. Hence other ancient Fathers of the monks also said: “Let the porter take care to receive everyone who comes within the gates, giving them a courteous reply with humility and reverence, announcing to the abbot or the seniors who has come and what he has requested. If anything is sent or entrusted to any of the brothers, let nothing reach him before it has first been reported to the abbot or the seniors.”

“And as soon as someone knocks or a poor person cries out, let him answer, ‘Thanks be to God,’ or give a blessing.” Here blessed Benedict elegantly presents two kinds of visitors. One is the powerful person, who, if he finds the monastery gate closed, knocks on it with his hand or a staff. The other is the poor person, who does not knock but merely cries humbly at the gate. For these he composed sufficiently appropriate replies for the porter: when he hears the voice of the poor person, he should give thanks to God; when he encounters the powerful person, he should humbly ask him for a blessing.

“And with all gentleness, in the fear of God, let him give a reply promptly and with the fervor of charity.” Hence another teacher of the monks says: “The porters of the monastery should be such men that, through the maturity of old age, they edify everyone’s reward; men to whom the world is silent, who no longer desire anything from present displays, but cling to the Creator with the whole affection of their hearts, each saying: ‘But it is good for me to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God.’ Let them always show such an example to those who arrive that, outside, the name of the Lord may be glorified by strangers, according to what the Lord says: ‘Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven’ (Matt. V). And inside, together with their companions, let them prepare the profits of reward while they undertake the care of all on behalf of everyone outside. Let them be so upright in conduct, with humility as the teacher of virtues, that they display every charm of patience through friendly conversation. Let them care above all for the poor, pilgrims, and guests, because Christ is received in them, as he himself says: ‘Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me’ (Matt. XXV). Let him presume to give anything outside, minister to anyone, or receive anything from outside only with the abbot’s permission. From the evening signal until the completion of the second hour, let the outer doors of the gates in no way be opened, nor let any entrance from outside be made available; but if necessity arises, let all business be conducted through the window.”

“If the porter needs assistance, let him take a younger brother.” Hence another Father says: “A cell should be established for two brothers inside the gates of the monastery. They should close the monastery after those who leave, open it for those who enter, and announce arrivals to the abbot. Let them guard the vessels and other utensils they carry for the use of guests as though they were consecrated to God, lest through their neglect they fail to receive a reward from the one whose property they do not preserve but allow to be plundered.”

If it can be done, the monastery should be constructed in such a way that everything necessary—that is, water, a mill, a garden, a bakery, and various crafts—may be carried on within the monastery, so that the monks have no need to wander outside, since this is wholly unprofitable for their souls. Hence another Father of the monks says: “Everything necessary ought to be inside the monastery gates: ovens, machines, a cooling place, gardens, and everything necessary, so that the brothers need not frequently go outside. When all these things have been established inside, the monastery gate should always be closed, and on the outside it should have an iron knocker, so that when it is struck by someone arriving, those inside may be informed of the arrival. The baking work, however, will belong to laymen. They should clean the wheat themselves and, as is customary, grind it themselves. The monks should prepare only the dough and make their own bread with their own hands.”

“We wish this Rule to be read frequently in the congregation, lest any of the brothers excuse himself through ignorance.” Hence blessed Augustine also says: “So that you may be able to look at yourselves in this little book as in a mirror, lest through forgetfulness you neglect anything, let it be read to you once a week. When any of you find yourselves doing what is written, give thanks to the Lord, the giver of all good things. But when any of you sees that something is lacking in himself, let him grieve over the past, beware of the future, and pray that his debt may be forgiven and that he may not be led into temptation.” Hence Bishop Aurelius also says: “Lest through forgetfulness you neglect anything, read it once every twenty days, that is, on the Kalends.” We, however, read our Rule not only once on the Kalends or once a week, but also daily at the conference, so that we may be able to know its precepts and understand them thoroughly, and, understanding them or retaining them in memory as far as possible, may, with Christ’s help, be able to fulfill them in our works.

## CHAPTER LXVII. On Brothers Sent on a Journey

Brothers who are to be sent on a journey should commend themselves to the prayers of all the brothers and of the abbot. With these brothers who are to be sent on a journey prostrate before the altar and asking for prayer from all, the priest should say the following verses, beginning them himself and having the others respond:

“Save your servants, my God, who hope in you.”

“Make my steps firm in your paths, so that my footsteps may not slip.”

“Your word is a lamp for my feet, O Lord, and a light for my paths.”

“God has commanded his angels concerning you, that they guard you in all your ways.”

When these things have been completed, the priest should say this collect of prayer:

“May the good angel of the Lord accompany you, so that, when the course of obedience has been completed, you may return to us again with joy, through the Lord, etc.”

But no brother should be sent on a journey alone. The teaching of the Fathers instructs us, saying: “Two or three brothers should go out together to seek what is necessary—men who are trusted, not those who pursue talkativeness or gluttony.”

“And at the final adoration of the Work of God, a commemoration of all the absent should always be made.” At this point, before the fiftieth psalm is begun, the priest should say: “Let us pray for our absent brothers.” When the brothers respond: “Save your servants, my God, who hope in you,” the priest should continue and say: “Send them help, O Lord, from the sanctuary.” The brothers should respond: “And from Zion protect them.” The priest should then say: “O Lord, hear my prayer.” The brothers should respond: “And let my cry come to you.” Then the fiftieth psalm should follow, sung by all.

Returning brothers from a journey must, on the very day they return, lie prostrate on the floor of the oratory during all the canonical hours while the Work of God is being completed, and ask prayers from all on account of their transgressions, lest perhaps on the road some sight or hearing of an evil thing, or idle conversation, may have slipped in. He says “on account of transgressions,” that is, on account of a lapse into wrongdoing. But for which transgressions he speaks, he himself explains, saying: “Lest perhaps on the road some sight or hearing of an evil thing, or idle conversation, may have slipped in.” Understand what evil thing he means from the prophet’s words. For he says:

> He who shakes his hands free from every gift,  
> and stops his ears lest he hear of bloodshed,  
> and closes his eyes lest he see evil—  
> he shall dwell on high (Isa. XXXIII).

When those returning from a journey have prostrated themselves on the floor of the oratory and asked for prayer, the priest shall say this collect over them:

> We ask you, almighty God, that you may graciously forgive these servants of yours, whom you have caused to return safely to us from their journey, for whatever they committed there through the hindrance of human frailty; through the Lord, etc.

Hence Isidore also says: “When brothers depart outside, or return, let them receive a blessing after all have been gathered together in the church.”

Nor should anyone presume to report to others whatever he has seen or heard outside the monastery, for this is a very great cause of destruction. If anyone should presume to do so, let him be subject to regular punishment. Hence blessed Pachomius says: “When brothers have returned from outside the monastery, they must not dare to narrate to others at all whatever they have done or heard outside.” Hence another Father also says: “Let them in no way relate to their fellow brothers the stories they have heard or understood from secular persons or from anyone else.” If they transgress any of these things that we have mentioned, let them be corrected by regular penance. But if such matters are disclosed through humble satisfaction, let the brother’s fault be judged according to the humility seen in the one confessing. If, however, he incurs the crime of obstinacy, the measure of his penance shall be increased.

Likewise, anyone who presumes to leave the monastery precincts, or to go anywhere, or to do anything, however small, without the abbot’s command, is subject to the same rule. Hence blessed Pachomius says: “No one shall have permission to go out into the field, to walk about in the monastery, or to proceed outside the monastery wall, unless he has asked the superior of the house and that superior has granted it.” Hence Cassian also says:

> The junior must be so thoroughly imbued with obedience to the rule that, without his elder’s permission, he must not presume by his own authority not only to leave his cell, but even to attend to natural necessity. Nor may he undertake, without the knowledge and direction of his elder, even those things that are useful—that is, cleaning his cell, carrying water, or doing anything else that may be necessary.

While the brothers are engaged in meditation, no one may involve himself in other affairs, nor may he consider himself free to leave the school. Whoever breaks out into such presumption shall, as he deserves, be subjected to excommunication. If someone sent for the monastery’s necessities refuses to go, or murmurs while walking, or wishes to leave with some delay, then, if the abbot so decides, he shall no longer be sent; he shall immediately receive the punishment of excommunication, and shall know that he has acquired pride and resisted the divine command.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. If impossible tasks are imposed upon a brother

If some heavy or impossible task is perhaps imposed upon a brother, let him indeed accept the command of the one giving it with complete gentleness and obedience. But if he sees that the burden greatly exceeds the measure of his strength, let him patiently and appropriately explain the reasons for his inability to the one placed over him.

He says “with complete gentleness,” that is, with complete moderation and mildness. For gentle is the person who inflicts injury upon no one; the word *mansuetus* (“gentle”) is explained as though from *manu assuetus*, “accustomed to the hand.” Such must a monk be, not insolent or proud. Hence it follows:

> Without behaving proudly, resisting, or contradicting.

By behaving proudly, he resists his teacher when, by despising his words and commands, he contradicts him. By resisting, he contends when he openly refuses to do what he is ordered to fulfill. By contradicting, he opposes when he loudly protests that he will not do what he is ordered to do. A monk is forbidden to act in this way, as the text continues:

> But if, after he has made his suggestion, the prior persists in his command, let the junior know that this is expedient for him, and, trusting through charity in God’s assistance, let him obey.

Hence Basil says:

> Freely obey everything that is enjoined upon you for the sake of religion, even if it exceeds your strength. Do not despise it, but faithfully explain the reason for your inability to the one who gives the command, so that through his moderation what is burdensome for you may be lightened and you may be free from the fault of contradiction. For whoever loves God faithfully and purely, and is certain of the Lord’s reward, does not consider what is commanded sufficient for him, but always seeks an increase in his work, desires more than is enjoined, and wishes what he does to appear beyond his strength.

Hence Cassian says:

> True obedience is this: although something difficult is commanded, one nevertheless strives to complete it without examining the matter and without any hesitation. Murmuring nothing about its impossibility, he receives in full faith and devotion whatever has been said as commanded not by a human being but by God. Obedience must thus be preferred to all virtues, so that everything may be placed after it and the monk may be content to undergo every loss, provided that he does not appear to violate it in any respect.

## CHAPTER LXIX. That one monk must not presume to defend another in the monastery

Every precaution must be taken lest, on any occasion, one monk presume to defend or, as it were, protect another in the monastery. To protect means to support, to bring aid, or to serve as a safeguard. Hence Basil also says in terrifying words:

> Whoever agrees with sinners and defends another who is at fault shall be accursed before the Lord and before human beings, and shall be corrected with the severest rebuke.

Hence blessed Pope Gregory also says:

> Sinners defend another sinner in the very matter in which they are conscious of guilt themselves. For each person fears for himself when he sees another being corrected. Therefore they rise up unanimously against the words of those who correct them.

Hence Solomon says: “A congregation of sinners is a bundle of tow” (Ecclus. XXI). It follows:

> Even if they are joined by any degree of kinship.

Nor should monks presume to do this in any manner, because from it a very serious occasion of scandals can arise. If anyone transgresses these provisions, let him be restrained more severely. Hence another Father says:

> If anyone consents to another’s error and advises him to humble himself more slowly, let him know that he must be judged guilty in the same way as the other.

Hence blessed Columbanus says:

> We permit no one in any way to defend a neighbor or kinsman in the monastery. Why should someone defend another who no longer lives for himself but for Christ, whom he imitates and with whom he remains crucified? Therefore, if he has lost his own wills in order to fulfill Christ’s will in himself, why should he defend the offenses of others? Let his love be impartial toward a kinsman and toward every other brother who is not joined to him by blood, and let him not strive to protect anyone placed under the discipline’s authority, lest he leave the vice of defending others among them. For one who fears the Lord, if he sees his brother going astray, ought to show him what is holy and point out the right path, so that, walking in the fear of God, he may fulfill Solomon’s saying:

> Rescue those who are being led to death,  
> and do not cease to deliver those being led to destruction.

## CHAPTER LXX. That no one should presume to strike or excommunicate anyone indiscriminately

“Indiscriminately” means disorderly, without examination, and without rational measure.

To avoid every occasion of presumption in the monastery, we order and establish that no one may excommunicate or strike any of his brothers unless authority has been given to him by the abbot. A brother should not extend his hands to strike another according to an admonition or the anger of his heart; rather, he ought to correct him humbly and admonish him out of zeal for charity. Hence blessed Aurelius says:

> If a brother dares to lay hands upon a brother, let him receive legitimate discipline.

Those who sin, however, shall be rebuked before everyone, so that the others may have fear. It is written in Leviticus:

> You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but openly rebuke him, lest you bear sin on his account (Lev. XIX).

Hence blessed Augustine says:

> The Apostle is not contrary to the Lord when he says, “Rebuke those who sin before everyone, so that the others may have fear,” while the Lord says, “Reprove him between yourself and him alone”; both things must be done. The remedy must correspond to the diversity of the infirmity of those whom we have undertaken not to destroy but to correct and heal: one must be healed in one way, another in another.

For children up to the fifteenth year of age, diligent discipline and supervision shall be provided by everyone. But this too must be done with complete measure and reason. Hence a certain master of monks says:

> We command that little children up to the fifteenth year not be excommunicated, but be beaten for their faults. After fifteen years, however, it is fitting that they no longer be beaten but excommunicated, because they now understand how they ought to repent and amend.

A person of more mature age who presumes to become inflamed in any degree without the abbot’s command, or who becomes inflamed against the children without discretion, shall be subject to regular discipline. Hence Ferreolus says:

> A monk inflamed against a monk—which is most disgraceful—must not presume to lay hands upon him, except those to whom it belongs either to know or to exercise judgment concerning the manner of correction, lest, when one sins, the others’ audacity to presume should increase.

It follows:

> For it is written: “What you do not want done to you, do not do to another” (Tob. IV; Matt. VII).

No one wishes to be harmed by anyone; therefore he too ought not to harm anyone, but rather brotherly charity ought to grow between them. And toward those whom someone rebukes, he ought to preserve such an affection as a father has for a son or a physician for a sick person.

## CHAPTER LXXI. That the brothers should be obedient to one another

The good of obedience must be shown to the abbot by everyone, but the brothers must also obey one another in such a way that they know they will go to God by this path of obedience. Hence other Fathers have said:

> The virtue of obedience is to be sought and practiced according to each person’s strength, and at the first word of an elder all the brothers who hear must rise. Whoever does not rise shall ask forgiveness, repent as much as the elder judges, and fulfill what was commanded.

> After the command of the abbot or of the superiors appointed by him has been given.

“After it has been given” means after it has been placed first, commanded beforehand, ordered, or prescribed.

We do not permit private commands to be placed above it. By “private” he means individual, personal, and the commands of particular persons. The private commands of individuals must be set aside on account of the commands of the abbot or superiors; nothing is to be done over and against their command. It follows:

> From now on, let all juniors obey their priors with complete charity and concern. If anyone is found to be contentious, let him be corrected. Although it may seem difficult, obedience must be rendered even unto death, according to the example of the Lord, who obeyed the Father unto death. Everyone ought to serve his brother as he serves his own abbot or father, as the Apostle says: “Serve one another in the fear of Christ” (Gal. V).

If a brother is corrected for any very small reason by the abbot or by any of his priors, in whatever manner; or if he lightly perceives the spirit of any prior to be angry or disturbed against him, even to a small degree, he must immediately, without delay, lie prostrate on the ground at that person’s feet, making satisfaction, until that disturbance is healed by a blessing. Hence blessed Basil says:

> We ought to obey the one who urges us to the work of the command with the same disposition with which a hungry child obeys the words of one commanding him to be fed, or with which every human being receives from another whatever pertains to life—indeed, even more so, since the future life is much more precious than the present, as the Lord also said: “My commandments are eternal life” (John XII).

If anyone scorns to do this, let him be subject either to corporal punishment; or, if he is obstinate, let him be expelled from the monastery. Elsewhere it is written:

> At the first questioning by an elder—whether an *aeconomus* [the reading is uncertain] or any brother—forgiveness must be sought, and he must lie prostrate on the ground until the elder has completed the questioning. If the elder repeats the questioning, he too must repeat his request for forgiveness. If anyone is found slow to ask forgiveness, or has uttered words contrary to religious discipline, or has spoken in excuse of his fault, he must be sent to prison and do penance according to the elder’s judgment until he is corrected. If he is found obstinate, he must be separated from the brothers.

## CHAPTER LXXII. On the good zeal that monks ought to possess

Just as there is an evil zeal of bitterness, which separates one from God and leads to hell, so there is a good zeal, which separates one from vices and leads to God and eternal life. The evil zeal of bitterness, which separates one from God and leads to hell, undoubtedly proceeds from envy and hatred of a brother. Concerning this zeal blessed Cyprian says:

> To be jealous of and envy another’s good is not a small evil but a great and serious one.

Solomon also says: “Jealousy and anger shorten one’s days” (Eccles. XXX). Without doubt, that which separates human beings from God and subjects them to the devil is not a small evil but a great one. It separates from the Father and leads to the deceiver; it separates from life and leads to death; it separates from glory and leads to punishment.

Struck by this zeal of envy, Cain killed his brother Abel. Struck by this zeal, the sons of Jacob sold their brother Joseph. Struck by this zeal, the Pharisees and scribes handed the Lord over to death through Judas’s treacherous kiss.

Therefore God’s servant ought not to possess this zeal of bitterness, but rather the zeal that separates from the devil and leads to Christ; that separates from death and leads to life; that separates from vices and leads to virtues; that separates from torment and leads to the kingdom of heaven. This zeal is born from love of the virtues, not from hatred of a brother; from the fountain of charity, not from the fuel of hatred. This zeal grants salvation to the soul, preserves faith, and loves every form of uprightness.

The Lord exercised this zeal when he drove from the temple those who were selling and buying, after scourging them. Phinehas also, through zeal for righteousness, deserved to receive the office and honor of the priesthood.

Let monks therefore exercise this zeal with the most fervent love—that is, let them anticipate one another in honor. Hence the Apostle says:

> Loving one another with brotherly charity, anticipating one another in honor, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord (Rom. XII).

We are then fervent in spirit if we are cold toward the world. Since the Lord does not love those who are cold and is nauseated by the lukewarm, he wishes us, who live under the law in the spirit, to have nothing slack and nothing lukewarm in ourselves, but to carry out everything with fervor of spirit and the warmth of charity and faith. Hence it appropriately follows:

> Let them bear one another’s weaknesses, whether of body or of character, with the greatest patience.

He truly fulfills this who truly possesses charity, of which it is written: “Charity is patient” (1 Cor. XIII). Hence the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. VI), that is, charity.

> Let them eagerly offer obedience to one another.

For it is written: “Obedience is better than sacrifice.” And the Apostle says: “Obeying one another in the bond of peace” (Eph. IV).

> Let no one pursue what he judges useful to himself, but rather what is more useful to another.

Hence the Apostle says: “Charity does not seek what is its own” (1 Cor. XIII); that is, it does not think only about what is useful to itself, but about what it may provide by serving others beneficially.

> Let them offer brotherly charity with chaste love.

Charity is not divided, nor does it envy anyone, as it is written: “Charity is not jealous; it does not act wrongly” (1 Cor. XIII), that is, perversely, because it does everything in due order, utterly excludes every vice, and willingly embraces another’s happiness as its own. Hence the text itself continues:

> Let them fear God and love their abbot with sincere and humble charity.

For it is written: “He who fears God neglects nothing” (Eccles. VII). Whoever truly fears God therefore loves his abbot with sincere and humble charity. Sincere and humble charity is what the Lord commands us to have when he says: “This is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you” (John XIII). We ought to love one another for this purpose: that we may possess the Lord and remain in God. This is the love by which God becomes all in all, and by which we ought to love one another.

Let them prefer absolutely nothing to Christ, who may bring us all together to eternal life. Amen.

Why we ought to prefer nothing to Christ, let us listen with attentive ears to what follows. He says: “Who may bring you to eternal life.” For no one else can bring us to eternal life; no one except him alone can bring us to the eternal kingdom. According to the Psalmist, he says: “He is the Lord our God, and we are his people and the sheep of his pasture” (Ps. XCIX). Although he is almighty, he gave no other price, but handed himself over to death alone for us. In his mercy he adopted us as sons and promised us the kingdoms of heaven as coheirs. Therefore we ought to prefer nothing to him, since he is our God, nor should we equate anything in the created order with the Creator of all things.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. That not every observance of righteousness is established in this Rule

We have written this Rule so that, by observing it in monasteries, we may show ourselves to possess at least some decency of conduct or the beginning of a religious life. We ought to observe the institutions of this Rule all the more easily because we see that it contains a lighter form of religious life. For one who neglects to observe these small matters cannot ascend by the straight path to greater things capable of shaping his life perfectly. For it follows:

> For one who strives toward perfection, there are the teachings of the holy Fathers, whose observance leads a person to the height of perfection.

The life, teaching, and action of Elijah and of the other prophets of that time are nothing other than an example and norm for the monks of this time. In the New Testament, the pattern of John and of all the apostles is likewise the pattern for all monks who live rightly. Hence it follows:

> What page, or what discourse of divine authority in the Old and New Testaments, is not the straightest norm of human life? Or what book of the holy catholic Fathers does not resound with this purpose: that we may reach our Creator by the straight course? The Conferences of the Fathers, their institutions and their lives, and also the Rule of our holy Father Basil—what else are they but examples and instruments of virtue for monks who live well and obey?

Hence blessed Isidore says:

> There are many precepts and institutions of monks, found scattered through the writings of the holy Fathers; some have also handed them down to posterity composed in a more elevated or obscure manner. Therefore, whoever strives to pursue that entire ancient discipline of yours may proceed as far as he wishes and walk at an even pace along that difficult and narrow boundary. But whoever is unable to fulfill so many commands of the elders should set his foot within the discipline of this boundary and should not seek to turn beyond it, lest, while striving too rashly after lower things, he lose both the life and the name of a monk. Therefore, just as those earlier precepts bring the perfect to the summit, so these will bring others to the goal. Let the perfect preserve those precepts; let those converted after sin follow these.

Therefore, servants of God, soldiers of Christ, despisers of the world, we wish you to preserve these things in such a way that you maintain in every respect the greater precepts of the Fathers. The fullness of holy religious life and the perfect teaching of the spiritual life are recited to us daily in the rules of those holy Fathers, whose proven life, by God’s gift, has also been granted authority to teach.

For us, however, who are sluggish, living badly, and negligent, there is the shame of confusion. When we hear that the lives of the holy elders were endowed with such great virtues, we are truly covered with the blush and shame of confusion, because we are scarcely able to attain their perfection. Yet the words that follow give us the boldness of confidence:

> Therefore, whoever hastens toward the heavenly homeland, complete, with Christ’s help, this little Rule of beginning that has been written down; and then, under God’s protection, you will finally reach the greater heights of teaching and virtue mentioned above. Amen.

For the one who does these things, life will be eternal.

In the manner of a father, blessed Benedict exhorts us: if we wish to ascend to the heavenly homeland, let us first hasten to complete this little Rule of beginning, and so, with Christ’s help, let us strive to advance toward the teaching of the greater Fathers and hasten to climb the sublime heights of virtue. We ought gladly to obey him and gladly hear his precepts, because blessed is the one who can rightly fulfill this Rule; blessed is the one who, while still placed in the present life, is able to ascend to the heights of virtue.

But happier than all these is the one whose life after the present life will be eternal; blessed is the one who will always be able to reign with the saints, live with the angels, rejoice with both, and live happily forever with the Lord himself. May he happily lead us to that life who in the present mercifully reigns and governs, Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, lives and remains forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0931]

# THE ROYAL WAY OF ABBOT SMARAGDUS

*(From D’Achery’s* Spicilegium, *vol. I, p. 238.)*

[Col. 0931]

## D’Achery to the Most Cultivated Reader

The author of this work entitled *The Royal Way* is not Smaragdus, priest and monk of Aniane in Septimania and in the diocese of Maguelonne, who flourished in learning and holiness in the time of the Emperor Louis the Pious; nor is he the same Smaragdus, abbot of the monastery of Lüneburg in Saxony, since that monastery was founded by Hermann, duke of Saxony, around the year 972. Rather, he is Smaragdus, abbot of Saint Michael—commonly Saint-Mihiel—in the diocese of Verdun. This opinion is approved by the very learned Lucas Holstenius, who recently illuminated the literary world in Rome like a brilliant star.

He says:

> “In the manuscript codex of the most serene queen [of Sweden], from which this copy was accurately transcribed, the first folio is missing. It contained the author’s preface to Louis the Pious, under whom, as I believe, the epitaph published by the Sammarthan brothers tells us that he died. The reason for attributing this work to Smaragdus is the letter of the Emperor Charles to Pope Leo III appended to it at the end, which the same Smaragdus is said to have published. From this it appears that this Smaragdus is the author of the account of the conference held at Rome in the sacristy of the Vatican basilica between the envoys of Charlemagne and Pope Leo, which Jacques Sirmond published in volume II of the *Councils of Gaul*, p. 256, since the testimonies mentioned at the beginning of the account are contained in Charles’s letter.

> “Moreover, it is clear from the style and manner of treatment that the book called *The Diadem of Monks* is the offspring of this Smaragdus; others plainly and mistakenly make its author Smaragdus, abbot of Saint Michael in Saxony. For the book of the most serene queen was written before the time of the Saxon emperors who built the monastery of Lüneburg. Nor can it be doubted that both works are by one and the same author, since much is read as copied word for word from one into the other, as can be seen in *The Diadem of Monks*, which is prefaced by the same sequence of chapters and, as I have said, by the same words, although adapted in different ways to the two kinds of life. Compare only chapters 6, 7, 8, and 9, and the matter will be evident at a glance.”

Indeed, Smaragdus himself rather clearly implies at the beginning of his account that he not only collected what took place at Rome concerning the Creed of the Faith between Pope Leo and the envoys of Charlemagne, but was also present at it, where he says:

> “After these things had been said, I learned that certain matters had preceded more by conversation than by disputation; the sequence of their meanings or words does not sufficiently return to my memory, except insofar as it came from that point, etc. As far as I am able to recall, this was the course of the meanings and the summary conclusion of the latest definitions,” etc.

For those legates—Jesse, bishop of Amiens, and Adalard, abbot of Corbie—had brought Smaragdus with them to Rome, since he was exceptionally versed in ecclesiastical matters, so that his learning might serve them as assistance.

Furthermore, it will be clear to the reader that when Smaragdus dedicated his work to the king, he was already advanced in age. Although in this work he does not praise any holy Fathers by name, he nevertheless continually scatters, as it were, flowers gathered from their teachings, as every learned person will be able to judge. Finally, how much Louis—who acquired the surname “the Pious”—profited from Smaragdus’s admonitions is revealed by Louis’s excellent character and distinguished deeds, both in governing himself and in governing the empire.

[Col. 0933]

## Dedicatory Letter

[Col. 0933B]

Almighty God, O most illustrious king, when he willed and where he willed, nobly brought you forth from a royal and noble lineage, and mercifully led you to the bath of regeneration. He anointed your head with the oil of sacred chrism and graciously adopted you as a son. He appointed you king of the people of the earth and commanded you to become heir of his own Son in heaven. Enriched with these sacred gifts, you rightly bear royal diadems.

First, because you descend from a king’s loins and a royal lineage, it fittingly belongs to you to govern many kingdoms well and wisely. Second, both the anointing of sacred chrism and the confession of faith, confirmed by deed and action, establish that you are a king. Third, the King of kings mercifully adopted you as a son while you were still a little child, so that you might happily possess an eternal kingdom with Christ.

These bright and illustrious signs proclaim you a king from infancy and confirm you as king. It remains for you carefully to preserve and defend by deeds and conduct the royal gifts that you have received from the Lord. For we shall remain only a short time in this life in which we live, since we travel by the way of all flesh and hasten daily with swift course toward the promised homeland.

It remains, therefore, that we diligently inquire only about that road which desires to lead us safely from robbers and cleansed of vices to the homeland we long for. The Prophet exhorts us concerning this when he says:

> Stand upon the roads, and look, and ask about the ancient paths, which is the good way; and walk in it, and you will find refreshment for your souls (Jer. I, 16).

This road, then, which may lead us safely to eternal rest, must be sought by us carefully and discerningly. Once it has been found with the Lord showing it to us, we must walk along it cautiously and wisely, turning neither to the right nor to the left. Let that saying of the prophet come to mind, which proclaims:

> There is a way that seems right to human beings, but its end plunges down to hell (Prov. XIV, 12).

But lest any one of us, wandering into this by ignorance, fall into a wrong path, the prophet Isaiah piously admonishes us:

> Your eyes shall see your teacher, and your ears shall hear the word of one admonishing behind you: “This is the way; walk in it,” so that you do not turn aside either to the right or to the left (Isa. XXX, 20).

When the Israelite people were passing through foreign kingdoms and pressing toward the promised homeland, they sent messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites, saying:

> I beg you to let me pass through your land. We shall not turn aside to the right or to the left, but shall walk along the royal road until we have crossed your borders (Num. XXI, 21).

Therefore, most noble king, if you wish happily to press toward the heavenly homeland of promise, you must diligently seek the royal road. Since you are a king on earth and are hastening toward the kingdoms of heaven, you must run along the royal road. It is well worn and anciently rubbed smooth by the footsteps of holy kings.

Along it Joshua, hastening with the firmest step, crushed the necks of many kings, laid low the armies of the wicked, overturned the walls of Jericho, and divided the promised land among the Israelite people by the measured line.

Along it David, walking without deviation, spared his persecutor Saul, killed Goliath with a stone’s blow, freed God’s people from the reproach of the Philistines, and made his kingdom secure forever.

Along it, when Hezekiah walked firmly, the Lord mercifully visited him, recalled him from his bed of death, and added fifteen years to his life.

Still walking along it, Solomon was filled with wisdom like a river with water; but when he departed from it, he brought an unforgivable stain upon his glory.

Walking along it fearlessly, the righteous king Uzziah crushed the high places, removed various abominations from God’s people, and received many justifications from the Lord.

[Col. 0934D]

Behold, most noble king, you clearly see how kings walk to God by the royal road, and how kings also, together with the other saints, happily fly toward the kingdoms of heaven. For the royal road is the one called holy by the prophet (Isa. XXXV, 9). The same prophet says that the unclean shall not pass along it; nor will the lion—that is, the devil, who prowls about roaring and seeking whom he may devour—be found there; nor will the evil beast, namely the demon, climb upon it. Rather, it is a straight road, and those whom the Lord has redeemed and set free shall walk along it.

We know and rejoice that, with the Lord’s help, you walk along it daily, and, believing faithfully that you will come to eternal glory, we do not doubt that you will reach it. The only thing required is that you complete the good work you have begun and bring it to the end of perseverance, because it is not the one who begins but the one who perseveres who will be saved.

Now, with the Lord showing mercy to you, O king, I shall begin to describe the royal road, along which, if you walk, you will have no stumbling block, but at the end you will receive from the Lord, with joy, a perfect and eternal kingdom. On this road we appropriately place the step of love first.

[Col. 0935A]

# THE BOOK BEGINS

## CHAPTER ONE. On love of God and neighbor

Therefore, most gentle king, love the Lord as he commanded: with all your heart, all your soul, and all your strength (Deut. XI, 5). Love him because he loved first. For John, who reclined at the supper upon the fountain of love, says in his Epistle:

> Brothers, let us love one another, because he loved us first (1 John IV, 19).

Human frailty could not love the Lord unless he first loved our nature. Everything we are able to do belongs to him. Through him giving life, we live; through him strengthening us, we move. For no human being possesses anything that he has not received; and if even willing what is good is not established in human freedom, how much less its accomplishment?

He loved you before you existed, and therefore he created you so that you might exist. Giving him praise, holy Scripture cries out:

> You love all things that exist, and hate nothing that you have made; for you would not have made anything if you had hated it (Wis. XI, 25).

The Lord loved you, O most gentle king; he created you, gave you life, nourished and guarded you, led you to the bath of regeneration, renewed and governed you, and brought you to the age of understanding. While you were still a little child, he exalted you splendidly to a royal throne. God mercifully did all these things for you through love.

Open, therefore, O king, the eyes of your heart, and recognize to what extent you were loved by Jesus Christ our Lord before you existed, so that you may not doubt that his blood was poured out for you. Lift your heart toward love of your Creator; love the Lord your God not moderately or partially, but, as was said above, with all your heart, all your soul, and all your strength, so that you prefer no one’s love to the love of your Lord.

Understand this by his own teaching. For he says:

> Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me (Matt. X, 37).

Indeed, if we love God with our whole heart, we must not prefer the love of parents or children to his love.

But if you love God, O most devout king, with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, you must love your neighbor as yourself: “For on these two commandments the whole law and the prophets depend” (Matt. XXII, 40). Therefore, whoever does not love God and his neighbor does not fulfill the law and the prophets. And true and perfect love consists in this: that God be loved and one’s neighbor also be loved. For it is written: “He who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see? And we have this commandment from God: that he who loves God should love his brother also” (1 John IV, 20).

The very author of love, the Lord Jesus Christ, impressing the commandment of love upon our minds, says: “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John XIII, 34–35). For that disciple who drank the streams of charity from the Lord’s breast, breathing forth the love of God and neighbor, also said: “Beloved, let us love one another, because charity is from God, and everyone who loves his brother is born of God and knows God. But whoever does not love his brother does not have charity and does not know God. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his charity is perfected in us” (1 John IV, 7).

Peter too, chief of the apostles, gently exhorting us to love one another, says: “Therefore be prudent, sober, and watchful in prayers; but above all, have continual mutual charity among yourselves, because charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. IV, 8). It must be noted that he did not say: “Have temporal charity, which is sometimes with you and sometimes departs from you”; but he says “continual,” so that it may remain with you continually and never depart from your hearts. Blessed is the virtue of love and charity, which covers a multitude of sins in this way and erases them from the hearts of the faithful, so that they may never perish forever.  
[Col. 0936A–C]

Some people commonly ask who the neighbor is whom God commands us to love with such genuine affection. We, however, call every faithful Christian our neighbor, who is named not only our neighbor in reason but also our brother in faith: for we have one God and the same Father, and by his grace we have been reborn. Therefore, every Christian in general is called the neighbor of a Christian. Setting out the individual classes of such persons, the Apostle commands that they be loved: “Husbands, love your wives, and do not be bitter toward them” (Eph. V, 25). The same Apostle exhorts parents that their children be loved, saying: “Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger” (Eph. VI, 4). The same Apostle admonishes that servants be loved, saying: “Masters, provide your servants with what is just and fair, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven” (Col. IV, 1). Elsewhere Scripture also says of them: “If you have a servant, let him be as your own soul; treat him as a brother” (Ecclus. XXXIII, 31).

The Apostle commands that friend and enemy alike be loved, when he admonishes us to love the friend in God and the enemy for God’s sake. For the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. V, 44). Behold, it is plainly evident whom the Lord commands us to love as our neighbor: namely, wives and children, servants, friends, and enemies. Under these names every Christian is recognized as being called a neighbor, and everyone is commanded by the Lord to be loved. Blessed, therefore, is the virtue of love and charity, which embraces everyone, loves everyone, and, as though all were one neighbor, stores the love of all in the secret chambers of the mind.

Truly blessed is it: it nourishes the virtues and destroys sins; suppresses anger, locks away hatreds, drives out greed, restrains quarrels, and likewise puts all vices to flight; it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things; amid insults it is secure, amid hatreds beneficent, firm in truth; it is not torn away by wicked assailants, not stolen by thieves, not carried off by plunderers, not destroyed by a flood, not consumed by fire, not divided by heresy. It stands undivided, remains unconquerable, endures beyond explanation, perseveres unshaken, rejoices incorrupt; it is the bond of all virtues, the glue of souls, the harmony of minds, the fellowship of the elect, and the rejoicing of angels. So that it may not be broken by adversities, it strengthens the mind courageously; so that it may not be overcome by anger, it restrains it rationally. Truly, as I see it, this is a royal virtue, which breaks the bread of joy for all in the palace, offers the wine of gladness to all, grants sweet kisses to all, and, loving everyone, embraces them with outstretched arms.

Hold fast, therefore, O most illustrious king, this bright, blessed, and royal virtue. Let it be with you, remain with you, rise with you, proceed with you, rejoice with you, and feast with you; for it is fitting that so royal a virtue should continually be present at a king’s banquet.  
[Col. 0936D–0937B]

## CHAPTER II. On Observing the Lord’s Commandments

Since, with the Lord’s help, we have begun to write about the royal road, it is necessary that we place upon it the steps of our conduct firmly, diligently, and orderly, so that the one who runs along it may find there not a harmful obstacle but a profitable and eternal joy. Let us see what command the very author of love grants us to preserve after the practice of love. For he says: “If you love me, keep my commandments; and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may remain with you forever” (John XIV, 20).

Consider, therefore, O most merciful and gentle king, how greatly our Lord Jesus Christ loves us: with a promise, he requires our love for him from us, and says that the Holy Spirit will remain with us forever if, after loving him, we keep his commandments. For, as we have already said above, we believe that all good things come to us from him; from him we first receive both the will to do good and the ability to perform it. We are loved so that we may love; we are cherished so that we may cherish; we are known so that we may know; we are helped so that we may act and, by acting, grow rich in virtues.

Therefore, if the love of God and of your neighbor delights you, it follows that you should do what he has commanded, because you love him insofar as you do it. For no one can sincerely love God who does not faithfully fulfill his commandments. Understand this from the Lord’s own teaching. He says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him. And he who does not love me does not keep my words” (ibid., 24).

The apostle John, filled with love for the Lord, also says in his Epistle: “By this we know that we have known him, if we keep his commandments. He who says that he knows him and does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him. But whoever keeps his word, truly in him the charity of God is perfected” (1 John II, 3). The Book of Job, likewise consecrated by the Lord’s own voice, bears witness to this, speaking especially of kings: “He does not withdraw his eyes from the just, and he establishes kings forever upon the throne, and they are exalted. He also opens their ear to correction and speaks so that they may turn back from iniquity. If they hear and obey, they will complete their days in good and their years in glory; but if they do not hear, they will pass away by the sword and perish in folly” (Job XXXVI, 7, 10 ff.).

Job himself, giving good and upright testimony about himself, says: “My foot has followed his steps; I have kept his way and have not turned aside from it. I have not departed from the commands of his lips, and I have hidden the words of his mouth in my bosom” (Job XXIII, 11–12). We always wish to hear such testimony about you, O good king, and frequently to see such conduct.  
[Col. 0937C–0938B]

The Lord himself, admonishing the Israelite people concerning his love and the observance of his commandments, says: “And now, Israel, hear the precepts and judgments that I teach you, so that by doing them you may live in them. Observe and beware lest you ever forget the Lord your God. And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, except that you fear your God, walk in his ways, love him, serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and keep the commandments of the Lord and his ordinances, which I command you today, so that it may be well with you?

“But if you listen to the voice of the Lord your God, so as to do and keep all his commandments that I command you today, the Lord your God will make you higher than all the nations that dwell upon the earth. All these blessings will come upon you and overtake you, if only you listen to his commandments. Blessed shall you be in the city, and blessed in the field. Blessed shall be the fruit of your womb, the fruit of your land, and the fruit of your cattle; the herds of your oxen and the flocks of your sheep. The Lord will send a blessing upon your storehouses and upon all the works of your hands. The Lord will cause your enemies who rise against you to fall before your face” (Deut. IV, 1; VIII, 11; X, 12; XXVIII, 1 ff.).  
[Col. 0938C–D]

The Lord, adding still more concerning Israel, says: “If you walk in my precepts, keep my commandments, and do them, I will give you rains in their seasons, and the earth will yield its produce, and the trees will be filled with fruit. The threshing of the harvest will overtake the vintage, and the vintage will overtake the sowing; you will eat your bread to satiety, and you will dwell in your land without fear. I will give peace within your borders; you will sleep, and there will be no one to terrify you. I will remove the evil beasts, and the sword will not pass through your territories.
