You will pursue your enemies, and they will fall before you. Five of you will pursue a hundred foreigners, and a hundred of you ten thousand; your enemies will fall by the sword before your face.

“But if you do not listen to me and do not do all my commandments; if you despise my laws and reject my judgments, so that you do not do what I have established and make my covenant void, I too will do this to you. I will visit you swiftly with poverty and a burning fever that will consume your eyes and waste away your souls. You will sow your seed in vain, for it will be devoured by your enemies. I will set my face against you, and you will fall before your enemies; you will be subjected to those who hate you, and you will flee when no one pursues you” (Lev. XXVI).

Through Isaiah also the Lord cries out to Israel and says: “If only you had attended to my commandments! Your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea; your offspring would have been like sand, and the descendants of your womb like its grains. It would not have perished, and its name would not have been destroyed” (Isa. XLVIII, 18–19).  
[Col. 0938D–0939B]

It is therefore good for you, O king, to love the Lord your God and, because of your great love for him, to guard his commandments attentively and diligently. For his commandments are holy and just, and exceedingly beneficial to those who observe them. Therefore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit will come to you and make their joyful dwelling with you in a dwelling that is truly their own; and you will be blessed forever by being visited by such a guest. Therefore your days will be completed in blessings, and your years in glory. Therefore your peace will happily multiply, and your joy will be filled forever like a river.

## CHAPTER III. On Fear

Behold, with God’s help we have now reached the third step of the royal road, on which we must set the straight step of our conduct. But because we are unable to act by ourselves, let us diligently question the prophet of that same Lord whose road we are traveling.

The gracious and humble David, filled with the Holy Spirit, is present with us, and he shows where, after observing God’s commandments and rendering blessed service, we must set the foot of our conduct. He says: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Ps. II, 11). The Apostle likewise admonishes us, saying: “Work out your salvation with fear” (Phil. II, 12).

Behold how the royal road lies open; behold how clear it is; behold how it offers itself freely to those who come toward it. It spreads itself smooth for travelers and presents itself bright to those who tread it. For what could be clearer? What brighter? What could be more fitting than that the one who loves the Lord should observe his commandments and act according to them—and that the one who acts should act not vainly or boastfully, but with fear of God, not attributing empty and fruitless praise to himself for his good work, but continually returning worthy thanks to the Lord, who both fills him with the fruit of good works and grants him happy assistance in doing them? For it is written: “Those who fear the Lord have hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and protector” (Ps. CXIII, 11).  
[Col. 0939C–D]

Fear God, therefore, O most gentle king, so that he may continually provide you with protection and happy assistance, and so that your voice, joined with the voice of Mary, Moses, and Aaron, may cry out to the King of kings and say: “The Lord is my helper and protector, and he has become my salvation” (Exod. XV, 2).

Let your voice also, joined with the voice of King David and filled with the jubilation of exultation, cry aloud and say: “The Lord is my strength, my firmament, my refuge, and my deliverer; my God, my helper, and I will hope in him. My protector, and the horn of my salvation, and my upholder. Praising, I will call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies” (Ps. XIX, 3–4).  
[Col. 0940A]

Fear God, therefore, O king, so that he may grant you perpetual strength of soul and body, provide firmness of mind and eternal assistance, make the horn of your kingdom exalted, and strengthen the arm of your power with vigor. In praise of fear Solomon says: “The fear of the Lord adds days” (Prov. X, 27).

Fear God, therefore, O king—but with that fear which remains forever and ever; with that chaste fear which will add to the days of this present time eternal days, everlasting days, immortal days, enduring days; indeed, one day without evening and without end, a day filled with joyful happiness, filled with unfailing light, supported by an angelic company—a day which night does not interrupt, darkness does not obscure, cloud does not cover, summer heat does not make unbearable, and winter cold does not render sluggish. It is a day that will be one for you with the saints, shared with the angels, eternal with both; a day that will grant you joyful fellowship with the angels, make you a companion of the patriarchs, count you among the prophets, and make you a companion of the apostles in their exultation.  
[Col. 0940B]

Solomon himself says in praise of good fear: “The fear of the Lord is the fountain of life” (ibid., XIV, 27). Therefore, if you wish, O king, to live happily forever, you must hasten gladly to the fountain of life. For it is the fountain of life that, continually providing the cup, will take away eternal thirst and, with glory, bestow the crown of immortality.

Solomon himself again says: “The fear of the Lord gives life” (ibid., XIX, 27). You see, therefore, O king, that in the fear of the Lord the fullness of life is found; you see that the fear of the Lord provides us with immortal and eternal life. For the present life is not supported by a fullness of days, but the future one is. In the midst of our days we are taken away, and while we are still thinking that we are living, we are snatched from this life. Thus the just king Hezekiah says: “I said in the midst of my days: I shall go to the gates of hell,” and so forth. “My life has been cut off like that of a weaver; while I was still beginning, he cut me off; from morning until evening you will finish me” (Isa. XXXVIII, 10–12).

That the fullness of wisdom, the fullness of fruits, the fullness of offspring, and the treasure of salvation are found in the fear of God is all comprehended in one statement by the Book of Ecclesiasticus, which says: “The fullness of wisdom is to fear God; and its fullness, from its fruits, will fill his whole house through generations, and its storehouses with its treasures. The crown of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, filling him with peace and the fruit of salvation; and he saw and counted it, and both are gifts of God” (Ecclus. XI, 20).  
[Col. 0940C–D]

The same book again salutarily admonishes you to fear the Lord, saying: “Keep his fear, and grow old in it. You who fear the Lord, await his mercy, and do not turn away from him, lest you fall. You who fear the Lord, believe him, and your reward will not be made void. You who fear the Lord, hope in him, and mercy will come to you for your delight. You who fear the Lord, love him, and your hearts will be enlightened” (Ecclus. II, 6).

Solomon himself again says: “The fear of God is not to despise the just poor man, nor to honor the sinful rich man. For however great and powerful a judge he may be in honor, he is not greater than the one who fears God. How great is the one who finds wisdom and knowledge! Yet he is not above the one who fears God. The fear of God has placed itself above all things. Blessed is the person to whom it has been granted to possess the fear of God. The fear of the Lord is like a paradise of blessing, and it has covered him above all glory” (Ecclus. X, 25; XXV, 23; XL, 28).  
[Col. 0941A–B]

You see, therefore, O king, that this too is a royal virtue: in it is confidence of strength; in it the fullness of life is found; in it the fullness of fruits is nourished; in it the lineage of offspring grows; through it the fruit of salvation and peace flourishes; through it a saving treasure is stored; through it the hearts of the righteous are enlightened; through it their reward increases in many ways. Truly it is true: “Blessed is the one to whom it has been granted to possess the fear of God” (Ecclus. XXV, 15).

Hear still further, and attend carefully, O king, to what the Lord promises through the prophet Malachi to those who fear him. “For you who fear my name,” he says, “the sun of righteousness shall rise, and healing shall be in its wings; and you shall go out and leap like calves from the herd; and you shall trample the wicked, when they have become ashes, beneath the soles of your feet” (Malach. IV, 2).

You too, therefore, must fear the name of the Lord, so that Christ, the sun of righteousness, may rise for you; so that he may drive away the darkness of your mind, remove ignorance from your heart, pour in the light of understanding, direct the rays of wisdom toward you, extend to you the memory of discernment, lay the necks of your enemies beneath your feet to be trampled, and, while you rule, defend the kingdoms of the faithful from the plots of their enemies.

## CHAPTER IV. On Wisdom

We ought to give abundant thanks to God, who commands us to proceed toward the heavenly kingdoms by the royal road, so that, walking along straight paths, we may happily deserve to reach our heavenly homeland. Let us therefore turn neither to the right nor to the left; with a firm and solid step we must advance along the royal road appointed for us, and to chaste and holy fear we must join heavenly and holy wisdom, so that, united by both virtues, we may deserve to attain immortal life.

For Scripture says: “The fear of the Lord is the crown of wisdom” (Ecclus. I, 22). And: “The beginning of wisdom is to fear God” (ibid., 16). And: “The fullness of wisdom and the root of wisdom,” as Scripture says, “is the fear of the Lord” (ibid., 20, 25). If, therefore, the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, its fullness, its crown, and its root, it clearly appears that one depends upon the other and that one follows the other. And for this reason they must be placed close together, not separately. Accordingly, we appropriately place wisdom after fear, because, as it is written, wisdom does not enter a malevolent soul but into one that fears God (Wis. I, 4).  
[Col. 0941C–D]

Fear God, therefore, O most illustrious king, and prepare your soul to receive wisdom, so that, as a king with wisdom, you may wisely travel the royal road. For the Book of Wisdom, crying out especially and frequently to kings, says: “Therefore, O kings, these are my words, so that you may learn wisdom and not fall away; for those who keep what is just will be justified justly. She is glorious, and wisdom never withers; she is easily seen by those who love her and is found by those who seek her” (Wis. VI, 10, 13).

You hear, therefore, O most illustrious king, that this heavenly voice is addressed especially to kings, among whom, by the generosity of divine grace, you are one; and the divine oracle frequently cries out to kings that they should act wisely. Hence we earnestly beseech your most illustrious excellence to learn divine and glorious wisdom diligently, seek it attentively and constantly, and investigate it not lukewarmly or slowly, but keenly and watchfully; desire it above gold and silver.

For thus it is written of her: “The desire for wisdom leads to everlasting kingdoms. If you delight in thrones and scepters, O kings of the peoples, love wisdom, so that you may reign forever with her. Love the light of wisdom, all you who rule over peoples” (Wis. VI, 21).  
[Col. 0942A–B]

We therefore ask you, most holy king, to attend carefully to what Solomon says about himself and what he says in praise of wisdom. For he says:

“I too am a mortal man, like everyone else, and descended from that earthly one who was formed first; in my mother’s womb I was fashioned as flesh. For ten months I was formed from blood, from the seed of a man, through the pleasure of sleep that accompanies it. When I was born, I received the common air, and I fell upon the earth, made in the same way, and I uttered my first cry, weeping, like everyone else. I was nourished in swaddling clothes and with great care. No king had any other beginning of birth. There is therefore one entrance into life for all, and a similar exit.

“For this reason I prayed, and understanding was given to me; I called, and the spirit of wisdom came into me. I preferred her to kingdoms and thrones, and I considered riches nothing in comparison with her. I did not compare any precious stone with her, for all gold is but a little sand in comparison with her, and silver will be regarded as clay before her. All good things came to me together with her, and innumerable riches through her hands; I rejoiced in all things, because this wisdom went before me,” and so forth.

“For she is more precious than the sun and is found before all the arrangement of the stars; compared with light, she takes first place, for night succeeds it, but wickedness does not overcome wisdom. She reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly. I loved her and sought her from my youth; I asked to take her as my bride, and I became a lover of her beauty. She glorifies her noble birth, having fellowship with God; indeed, the Lord of all loved her.

“For she teaches sobriety and prudence, justice and virtue, than which nothing is more useful for human beings in life. Because of her I shall possess immortality, and I shall leave eternal remembrance to those who are to come after me. I shall govern peoples, and nations shall be subject to me. Terrible kings will fear me when they hear of me; among the multitude I shall be found good, and in war courageous” (Wis. VII, 1–29; VIII, 1–7, 13).  
[Col. 0942C–0943A]

Consider and understand, O most noble and illustrious king, that wisdom is a royal virtue. It proceeds unfathomably from the exceedingly rich treasure of the King of kings, and it is not given to the negligent, the proud, the envious, or the malevolent, but granted to the gentle, the humble, and those who fear God.

Truly, without any doubt, wisdom is a royal virtue, to which prophetic speech cries out especially that kings should learn wisdom. Wisdom is a royal virtue because it justifies kings who act well; it shines upon them with the unquenchable light of knowledge; it illuminates the eyes of the heart; brightens the senses of the mind; provides subtle understanding; grants bodily health; bestows honor upon morals; multiplies infinite treasures; strengthens the power of the kingdom; and makes one a participant in God’s friendship, filling him with the spirit of wisdom and understanding, counsel and strength, knowledge and piety, and fear of the Lord.

It grants kings justice and prudence, strength and temperance; supplies virtue and sobriety; makes them stable in the kingdom, reliable in speech, gracious in eloquence, cheerful in giving, humane in mercy, gentle in answering, keen in discernment, mild in prosperity, secure in adversity, sharp in understanding, tranquil in action, bright in countenance, and strong in war.

Wisdom grants kings the ability to arrange wisely the kingdoms subject to them, and gently makes peoples already possessed by them serve them. It also makes them bravely defeat threatening foreign peoples, subject savage nations, and trample fierce kings; and, so to speak, the entire ordering of the kingdom consists in wisdom.

For wisdom is a great treasure: whoever finds it will find life, and whoever possesses it will have the crown of immortality. It is the Lord’s hidden treasure, not revealed to everyone. Thus the most renowned man Job bears witness concerning wisdom, saying:

“But where is wisdom found, and what is the place of understanding? A human being does not know its price, nor is it found in the land of those who live softly. The abyss says: ‘It is not in me’; and the sea says: ‘It is not with me.’ Gold of Ophir cannot be given for it, nor can silver be weighed in exchange for it. Gold and glass cannot equal it, nor can vessels of gold be exchanged for it. High and exalted things will not be remembered in comparison with it. Yet wisdom is drawn from hidden places,” and so forth.

“Where, then, does wisdom come from, and what is the place of understanding? It is hidden from the eyes of all the living, and it is also concealed from the birds of heaven. Destruction and death say: ‘With our ears we have heard its fame.’ God understands its way, and he himself knows its place,” and so forth. “And he said to humanity: ‘Behold, the fear of the Lord—that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding’” (Job XXVIII, 12–13, and following).  
[Col. 0943B–0944A]

As you see, O most illustrious king, a great and unfathomable reputation for wisdom resounds here. It is without doubt a royal virtue, with which pure gold or gold of Ophir cannot be compared, nor the finest silver equaled, nor translucent glass matched. In comparison with it, sardonyx becomes worthless, sapphire is counted as nothing, and topaz is despised. Golden vessels are not proudly displayed, the purest dyes are not weighed, and no precious or varied gems are considered of value. Truly, as you see, wisdom is a royal virtue and is especially to be loved by kings.

Love her, therefore, O most illustrious king, so that you may be loved by her. For her voice sounds thus in Proverbs: “I love those who love me,” she says, “and those who watch for me early will find me” (Prov. VIII, 17).

Prepare your royal breast through good works in such a way that she may always delight in dwelling in your counsel. Let her teach you through inward thoughts whatever you ought to accomplish in your actions. Counsel is hers, and she makes it known to whom she wishes; prudence is hers, and she extends it to whom she wishes; strength is hers, and she grants it to whom she wishes; the kingdom is hers, and she entrusts it to whom she wishes and in whatever measure she wishes.

For her voice cries out through Solomon in Proverbs in this manner: “I, wisdom, dwell in counsel, and I am present with learned thoughts. Mine is counsel and equity; mine is prudence; mine is strength. Through me kings reign, and lawmakers decree what is just. Through me princes rule, and the powerful determine justice. I love those who love me, and those who watch for me early will find me. With me are riches and glory, abundant wealth and justice. For my fruit is better than gold and precious stone, and my produce better than chosen silver. I walk in the ways of justice, in the midst of the paths of judgment, so that I may enrich those who love me and fill their treasures” (Prov. VIII, 12, 14).  
[Col. 0944B–C]

Therefore, O king, so that Christ may fill your earthly treasures and grant you eternal ones, cry out from the depths of your heart, cry out with the full concentration of your mind, and, with Solomon, do not cease pouring forth prayers to the Lord. Pray continually, pray frequently, pray earnestly, pray without ceasing to God, and say:

“God of my fathers and Lord of mercy, who made all things by your word, and by your wisdom established humanity to rule the creature made by you, to govern the world with equity and justice, and to judge judgment with an upright heart: Give me Wisdom, the attendant at your thrones, and do not reject me from among your children, for I am your servant and the son of your handmaid, a weak man and of short life, and inferior in understanding of judgment and laws. Send her from your holy heavens, and from the throne of your majesty, so that she may be with me and labor with me, that I may know what is acceptable to you. For she knows and understands all things, and she will lead me soberly in my works, guard me by her power, and my works will be acceptable. I shall govern your people justly, and I shall be worthy of my father’s thrones” (Wis. IX, 1).  
[Col. 0944D]

Truly, O king, blessed is the virtue of wisdom; whoever finds it is made blessed by it. Wisdom prepares life for her children, supplies justice to those who love her, and grants prudence to those who cherish her. Whoever holds fast to her will inherit eternal life, for God loves the one who loves wisdom. In temptation she walks with him; at the outset she chooses him, strengthens him, leads him along a straight path, uncovers her secrets to him, and stores up knowledge and understanding of prudence for him.  
[Col. 0945A]

## CHAPTER V. On Prudence

After the illumination of wisdom and the treasures of knowledge, the person who desires to run happily along the royal road ought, by the Lord’s gift, to be filled with prudence. For prudence is a royal virtue and was greatly loved by earlier kings. Thus it is written of King David: “He went out to everything that Saul sent him to do, and he acted prudently” (1 Kings XVIII, 5).

Prudence is so called as though from *providentia*, “foresight.” The king ought to foresee from afar what he must do, so that after acting he will not regret having acted. For everything he does, both toward God and toward human beings, he ought to do prudently and with foresight. He must do everything justly, everything rightly, everything wisely and prudently, lest the king’s actions or counsels, like those of other people, incur the tongue of reproach.

For one who governs many things by the Lord’s gift must arrange everything prudently with deep counsel. Thus the very prudent Solomon says in Proverbs: “He who is wise governs many things with prudence.” He also says: “By wisdom a house is built, and by prudence it is strengthened” (Prov. XXIV, 3).

For prudence is a great virtue, especially in a king’s breast: it prudently rules and governs every kingdom. Prudence is the adornment of all virtues, the glory of speech and the beauty of discourse, as it is written: “The teaching of the prudent is a golden ornament, and like a bracelet on the right arm” (Ecclus. XXI, 24).

Prudence is the guardian of the mouth, the governance of action, the temperance of the heart, the moderation of the tongue, and the balance and weighing of all words and matters. Thus it is written: “The words of the prudent are weighed in the balance” (ibid., V, 28).

Again it is written: “Refine your gold and silver, make little doors for your words, and straight bridles for your mouth” (Prov. XXVIII, 29). Again it is written: “Open your mouth for the mute, and for the causes of all the children who pass by; open your mouth, decide what is just, and judge the needy and the poor” (Prov. XXXI, 8).

For everyone will be filled with good things from the fruit of his mouth, and he will be repaid according to the works of his hands (Prov. XII, 14). Malachi too, speaking in the person of the Lord, says: “I broke my covenant with him, the covenant of life and peace; I gave him fear, and he feared me, and he trembled before my name. The law of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found upon his lips. He walked with me in peace and equity, and turned many away from iniquity” (Malach. II, 5).

Paul says to the Colossians: “Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (Col. IV, 6).  
[Col. 0945B–D]

Love, therefore, O king, this most illustrious and royal virtue, which may order the governance of your kingdom for you and grant you discernment in action; which may direct the steps of your conduct and arrange the movements of your thought; which may build for you a royal house fruitful in offspring and strengthen it once built; which may supply you with an abundance of the adornments of virtue and of possessions; which may exalt the horn of your kingdom and grant strength to your arm; which may provide your mouth with the law of truth and multiply in your heart the understanding of wisdom; which may subject to you the necks of many peoples and make you beloved by all; which may place a golden ornament upon your speech and bestow a silver gift upon your lips; which may provide your works with continual protection and fitting glory.  
[Col. 0946A]

## CHAPTER VI. On Simplicity

[Col. 0946B]

Great indeed is the virtue of prudence; but it is necessary that it be tempered by the virtue of simplicity. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10:16). Walk, therefore, most noble king, from virtue to virtue, and, continually advancing toward what is better, do not turn aside from the royal path; but firmly set your step from prudence into simplicity. For simplicity is the royal way, beloved from ancient times by holy kings. Indeed, the Lord gives this laudable testimony concerning Job, a laudable man, saying to the devil: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth, a simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil?” (Job 1:8).

[Col. 0946C]

Concerning Moses also Scripture recalls, saying: “He was the gentlest of all the people who dwelt on the earth” (Num. 12:3). In particular, the Book of Wisdom cries out and says to kings and the ministers of kings: “Love justice, you who judge the earth; think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart, for he is found by those who do not tempt him” (Wis. 1:1). In general, Solomon likewise says in Proverbs concerning all the saints: “The simplicity of the upright shall guide them” (Prov. 11:3); “He who walks simply shall be saved” (Prov. 28:18). Paul, moreover, says: “I want you to be wise in what is good and simple in what is evil” (Rom. 16:19). Prudence must continually sharpen the hearts of the elect toward what is good, and simplicity must temper the sharpness of prudence, lest either prudence exceed the measure of uprightness,

[Col. 0946D]

or simplicity grow sluggish through the deceit of ignorance.

For simplicity is the royal way, which guides the steps of kings in simplicity, so that, advancing by royal paths, they may happily reach the heavenly kingdoms. Run, therefore, king, firmly along the paths of simplicity, so that you may more quickly reach everlasting life, promptly receive the rewards of immortality, and be clothed in the robe of peace and glory.

## CHAPTER VII. On Patience

Pass again, king, from virtue to virtue, and move happily from simplicity into patience. Possess patience if you wish to possess your soul gently. Thus God, the author of our salvation and peace, says in the Gospel: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19). Solomon also says: “The instruction of a man is known through patience, and it is his glory to pass over an offense” (Prov. 19:11). Paul likewise says: “Put on, therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of mercy, kindness, humility, modesty, and patience, bearing with one another and forgiving one another if anyone has a complaint against another; just as the Lord forgave you, so also should you” (Col. 3:12 ff.).

For that this virtue is also a virtue of rulers, Solomon testifies in Proverbs, saying: “Patience softens a ruler, and a gentle tongue breaks hardness” (Prov. 25:15). The Apostle, moreover, cries out to those same rulers, saying: “Correct the restless, console the fainthearted, support the weak, be patient toward all” (1 Thess. 5:14).

[Col. 0947B]

The Apostle James says: “Patience has its perfect work, so that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing” (Jas. 1:4). Therefore, the virtue that softens rulers, teaches them to correct the restless, and brings the work of kings to perfection is without doubt a royal virtue. Walk in it, therefore, most gentle king, and love it, because, running along it, you will encounter no stumbling block, but in the future you will find full and eternal joy.

For patience is a great virtue: it does not injure the one who injures it, but loves him; it forgives injuries to the one who inflicts them, rather than returning them; it does not harm the one whom it could harm, but spares him. Patience is what commends us to God and guards and preserves us from every evil. It is what tempers anger; it is what restrains the tongue; it is what governs the mind; it is what preserves peace; it is what carries out discipline moderately; it breaks the impulse of lust; it suppresses the violence of fury; it extinguishes the fire of quarrels; it restrains the power of the rich; it refreshes the poverty of the poor; it makes people humble in prosperity and strong in adversity, gentle toward injuries and insults; it conquers temptations and endures persecutions.

[Col. 0947C]

It is what firmly fortifies the foundations of our faith; it is what nobly advances the growth of our hope; it guides us so that we may hold fast to the way of Christ; it confirms us so that we may persevere as children of God.

Love this virtue, therefore, king; cherish it; hasten to embrace it with joy and with all your strength. For truly it is the royal way, and those who advance along it are brought happily to the eternal kingdom. Take care not to turn aside to the right or to the left. Know that, just as patience is the good belonging to the Lord, so impatience is the devil’s evil. And just as the one in whom Christ dwells and remains is found to be patient, so the impatient person always proves to be one whose mind is possessed by the devil’s wickedness. But you, king, hold to the royal way and do not turn aside from it; by this happy and blessed virtue, place your foot successfully upon the way called justice.

[Col. 0947D]

## CHAPTER VIII. On Justice

That it is a royal duty to practice justice and judgment, Jeremiah testifies, where the Lord commanded, saying: “Go down to the house of the king of Judah, and there speak this word, and say: Hear the word of the Lord, king of Judah, who sit upon the throne of David—you, your servants, and your people who enter through these gates. Thus says the Lord: Practice judgment and justice, and rescue the one oppressed by force from the hand of the slanderer; do not grieve the stranger, the orphan, or the widow, nor oppress them unjustly; and do not shed innocent blood in this place. For if you truly do this word, kings sitting upon the throne of David will enter through the gates of this house, riding in chariots and on horses, they and their servants and their people. But if you will not hear these words, I swear by myself, says the Lord, that this house shall become a desolation” (Jer. 22:1–5).

[Col. 0948A]

Love justice, therefore, king, if you wish to enjoy perpetual life and to be honored by it forever. For it is written: “If you pursue justice, you will attain it, and you will put it on like a robe of honor; you will dwell with it, and it will protect you forever, and on the day of recognition you will find strength” (Ezek. 8:5).

Since you are a king on earth, therefore, love judgment and justice, so that you may be a son of the King in heaven. Imitate by your deeds the one whom you proclaim as Father in your words. Love justice and practice it, because your heavenly Father loves and practices it. For he says through Jeremiah: “I am the Lord who practices mercy, judgment, and justice on the earth; for these things please me, says the Lord” (Jer. 9:24). With all your strength you ought to imitate him, with whom you hope to live forever.

[Col. 0948B]

Thus the Lord says through the prophet Ezekiel: “If a man is righteous and practices judgment and justice; if he has not eaten upon the mountains, nor lifted his eyes toward the idols of the house of Israel; if he has not violated his neighbor’s wife, nor approached a menstruating woman; if he has not grieved anyone; if he has returned the pledge to the debtor; if he has clothed the naked; if he has given his bread to the hungry; if he has taken nothing by force; if he has not lent at interest, nor received more; if he has turned his face away from iniquity; if he has rendered true judgment between one man and another; if he has walked in my commandments and kept my judgments, so as to practice truth—he is righteous; he shall surely live, says the Lord” (Ezek. 18:5–9).

Love, therefore, king, justice and judgment, which is the royal way, trodden from ancient times by earlier kings. Through it good desire will be given to the just; through it the just will be delivered from distress; through it their seed will be established forever; through it their house will receive abundant strength. By holding to it, the memory of the just will endure with praises; by following it, the saints will be loved by God; by guarding it, they will be exalted by him; by observing it, they will be honored by him; by trusting in it, they will be without fear, like a lion.

[Col. 0948C]

Those who labor in it will obtain eternal blessing; those who practice it will receive an everlasting reward, as it is written: “God’s gift remains with the just, and his blessing hastens toward his reward” (Ecclus. 1:7). This is the royal way, along which, king, advancing, you will quickly reach the everlasting kingdoms.

But temper justice, and carefully beware the left-hand path of cruelty. For tempered justice holds to the royal way; but if it is not carefully tempered, it quickly slips into cruelty.

[Col. 0948D]

## CHAPTER IX. On Judgment

But so that this may not happen to you, Scripture admonishes you for your salvation, saying: “In judging, be merciful to orphans as a father, and be as a husband to their mother; then you will be like an obedient son of the Most High, and he will have mercy on you more than a mother” (Ecclus. 4:10).

Job also says: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame; I was a father to the poor, and I investigated most diligently the case I did not know. I crushed the jaws of the wicked and snatched the prey from his teeth. I once wept over the one who was afflicted, and my soul had compassion on the poor” (Job 29:15).

For King Solomon also approves that this is a royal virtue, saying: “The king who judges the poor with truth—his throne shall be established forever” (Prov. 29:14). If you wish, therefore, O king, that your throne be established by the Lord, do not cease to justify the poor and the orphan; do not cease to assist the widow and the oppressed; do not cease to defend the stranger and the desolate. Assist the wretched, raise up the fallen, strengthen the broken, comfort and reinforce the weary; do not cease to support the beggar with wealth; do not cease to free the oppressed from the hand of the sinner.

Hear what the Lord cries out through David to kings and judges of kings, saying: “Judge the needy and the orphan; justify the humble and the poor. Rescue the poor, and deliver the needy from the hand of the sinner” (Ps. 81:3).

[Col. 0949A]

Agreeing with this sentence, the Book of Ecclesiasticus says: “Deliver the one who suffers injury from the hand of the proud” (Ecclus. 4:9). Isaiah likewise proclaims, saying: “Seek judgment, assist the oppressed, judge the orphan, defend the widow; and come and accuse me, says the Lord. If your sins are like scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; and if they are red like crimson, they shall become white like wool. If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isa. 1:17–19).

See, therefore, and attend carefully, O king, to what happens to the defenders of the poor. God declares himself their debtor and repayer; he promises sinners the whiteness of snow and pledges the purity of white wool; finally, he grants them to eat the good things of the land—namely, of that land of which it is written: “The saints shall possess double in their land” (Isa. 61:7), and concerning which the Psalmist says: “I believe that I shall see the good things in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13).

[Col. 0949B]

You see that the good things of the eternal land are granted to those kings who here are defenders of the poor. The fruits of the eternal land are granted as food to those who here know how piously to defend the poor—namely, the finest fruits of the angels, eternal fruits, everlasting fruits, sweetest and most beloved fruits, full of abundance and richness, full of gladness and joy, full of happiness and glory.

O how blessed is the life of righteous kings! Here it shines, supported by temporal goods, and forever rests immortally with the angels. Here it is nourished by earthly delights; there it is clothed with the splendor of glory. Here it is surrounded by throngs of peoples; there it is accompanied by angelic choirs. Here it delights in the multitude of human beings; there it rejoices with the choir of angels. Here the army of earthly rule obeys it; there it exults in the army of the Redeemer. Here, clothed in a royal robe, it shines; there it gleams with the glory of immortality. Here it bears the diadems of a king; there it resounds with the joy of exultation. Here it is called the son of an earthly king; there it is confirmed as the son of the heavenly King. Here it fittingly receives a great inheritance of an earthly kingdom; there it happily receives a blessed portion of the heavenly kingdom.

[Col. 0950A]

Do not cease to labor with all your strength, most illustrious king, so that this may happen to you. No one will be happier than you if, with the Lord’s help, these things happen to you; no one will surpass you in glory if these things are happily bestowed upon you by the Lord.

[Col. 0950B]

## CHAPTER X. On Mercy

For whoever, with the Lord’s help, desires piously to defend the poor and widows, strangers and orphans, ought, if able, mercifully to wipe away their want with his goods and frequently to support their beggary with alms. As it is written: “My son, do not defraud the poor of alms, and do not turn your eyes away from the poor. Do not despise the hungry soul, and do not provoke the poor in his need. Do not afflict the heart of the needy, and do not delay giving to one in distress. Do not reject the request of the afflicted, and do not turn your face away from the needy; do not turn your eyes away from the poor. Incline your ear to the poor without sadness, repay your debt, and answer him peacefully and gently”

[Col. 0950C]

(Ecclus. 4:1 ff.). “For the sake of the commandment, take up the poor, and because of his need do not send him away empty. Enclose almsgiving in the heart of the poor, and it will plead for you against every evil. It will cleanse you beyond the shield of the mighty and the lance against your enemy” (Ecclus. 29:12, 15, 18).

Solomon also indicates in Proverbs that this virtue is royal, for he says: “Mercy and truth preserve the king, and his throne is strengthened by clemency” (Prov. 20:28). David likewise speaks both of himself and of all who mercifully give alms: “Blessed is the man who understands concerning the needy and the poor; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him” (Ps. 40:1).

Job also, simple and upright and fearing God, giving true testimony concerning himself, says confidently: “If I denied the poor what they wanted, and caused the eyes of the widow to wait; if I ate my morsel alone, and the orphan did not eat of it—for from my infancy compassion grew up with me, and it came forth with me from my mother’s womb; if I despised the one who was perishing because he had no clothing, and the poor man without covering; if his sides did not bless me, and he was not warmed by the fleeces of my sheep; if I raised my hand against an orphan, even when I saw myself superior in the gate—may my shoulder fall from its joint, and may my arm be broken with its bones” (Job 31:16–22).

[Col. 0950D]

For the one who hopes to treasure up riches in heaven through these things ought not to distribute alms sluggishly, slowly, or fearfully. We ought to give alms to the poor with great cheerfulness of mind, since what is cheerfully distributed to the poor is undoubtedly given to the Lord himself. For the Lord himself will say at the judgment to those who will be at his right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; naked, and you clothed me; sick, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me” (Matt. 25:34–36).

When they ask and wish to know when they had done these things, the Lord will answer them: “When you did it for one of the least of these my brothers, you did it for me” (ibid., v. 40).

[Col. 0951A]

Therefore, king, if you wish to receive the kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world, you ought frequently to extend alms to the poor for Christ’s sake. You will experience him as your rewarder forever if, for his sake, you cheerfully extend bread to the poor; from him you will obtain eternal mercy if, for his sake, you extend a full hand to the poor.

For the one who is not himself merciful cannot merit God’s mercy; nor will the one who has not shown humanity toward the poor man’s plea obtain anything from divine compassion through prayers. Thus the Spirit of truth says through Solomon: “He who closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be heard” (Prov. 21:14).

The angel Raphael also encourages us to give alms willingly and generously, saying: “Prayer with fasting is good, and almsgiving is better than storing up treasures of gold, because almsgiving delivers from death; it is what purifies sins and makes one find mercy and eternal life”

[Col. 0951B]

(Tob. 12:8). The angel reveals and affirms that through alms our petitions become effective, through alms life is redeemed from dangers, and through alms souls are delivered from death.

How good it will be for you, O most noble king, how sweet and pleasant, when your creator, redeemer, and governor himself, before all the angels and archangels, patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, with the entire army of the world—that is, of heaven and earth—gathered together, mercifully places you at his right hand and addresses you with the others in these words: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

[Col. 0951C]

Therefore, most gentle and illustrious king, prepare service for the Lord your God with complete faith, devoted mind, and continual action. Give Christ clothing on earth, so that you may receive heavenly clothing from him; give him food and drink, so that with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob you may deserve to reach the eternal banquet.

What eternal joy and what great and supreme glory will be yours when the Lord begins to repay you with heavenly things for earthly things, everlasting things for temporal things, great things for small things, lasting things for perishable things, enduring things for painted or deceptive things, the most firm things for fragile things, and what will remain for what passes away!

[Col. 0951D]

Therefore, king, make a portion of your revenues for your Lord; make Christ a sharer in your earthly possessions, so that he may also make you a co-heir of the heavenly kingdoms. For he granted you everything you possess, and in the poor he asks you for alms, which he will afterward return to you a hundredfold. He wishes to make you exalted in eternal honor, and in the poor he asks from you a small honor.

## CHAPTER XI. How the Lord Is to Be Honored by Deeds

The Lord is shown to be honored by works of mercy, as it is written: “He who slanders the needy reproaches his Maker, but he who has mercy on the poor honors him” (Prov. 14:31). Solomon likewise says: “My son, honor God, and you will prosper.”

Jesus son of Sirach says: “Honor God with all your soul, and honor the priests, and cleanse yourself with your arms. Give them their portion, as it was commanded you, of the firstfruits and of purification; and cleanse yourself from your negligence with a little. Give the offering of your arms, and offer the sacrifice of sanctification to the Lord, and the firstfruits of holy things; extend your hand to the poor, so that your propitiation and blessing may be completed” (Ecclus. 7:33, 36).

[Col. 0952A]

That this virtue is without doubt also a royal virtue, the Lord cries out to King David, and through him urges other kings to honor him, saying: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me; and there is the way by which I shall show him the salvation of God” (Ps. 49:23). King David himself says concerning himself: “I will confess to you, Lord my God, with my whole heart, and I will glorify your name forever, because it is good” (Ps. 85:12).

It is worthy and just that kings honor God for all human beings, because they are honored by him on behalf of all human beings. Honor God, O kings, because he first honored you. For his voice cries out through Solomon and says: “I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel, and I am present among the learned in thought. Counsel is mine and equity; prudence is mine; strength is mine. Through me kings reign, and lawgivers decree what is just. Through me princes rule, and the mighty decree justice. I love those who love me, and those who watch for me early shall find me. With me are riches and glory” (Prov. 8:12, 14, 18).

[Col. 0952B]

Honor, therefore, king, the Lord your God with all your strength. He has already bestowed so much praise upon you and has promised you so much honor still to come. Here he has already granted you the instruction of kingship, together with prudence and strength; there he has promised you the immortality of eternal life.

[Col. 0952C]

Here he has raised you, an earthly man, into kingship; there he has promised you heavenly rule. Here he has granted you temporal joy; there he has promised eternal joy. Here he has given you a broad inheritance of a kingdom; there he has promised you the most extensive possession of paradise. Here he supplies abundance in riches; there he prepares what you will later receive. Here he has already clothed you in royal purple; there he will further clothe you in the robe of immortality. Here he has already placed royal diadems upon your head; there he will still place the crown of eternity. Here he has granted flourishing kingdoms; there he will give great and indescribable joys. Here he has bestowed manifold gifts; there he has promised bright and everlasting kingdoms. Here he has granted you to pass your days without sadness; there he will grant you to live with a life everlasting and without end.

[Col. 0952D]

Here he has given you strength in the armies; there he will give you blessed fellowship with the angels. Here he has bestowed earthly and manifold riches; there he has promised heavenly riches, shared with all the saints—namely, those eternal riches of which the Apostle says: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9).

## CHAPTER XII. On Tithes and Firstfruits

Honor, therefore, most illustrious king, the Lord your God by your conduct and deeds; honor the Lord your God in your lifetime with tithes, firstfruits, and all offerings, as it is written: “My son, if you have anything, do good with it, and offer offerings worthy of God; remember that death does not delay” (Ecclus. 14:11).

[Col. 0953A]

For the Lord also, commanding the children of Israel in the law, said: “When you have completed the tithe of all your crops, in the third year of tithes you shall give it to the Levite, the stranger, the orphan, and the widow, so that they may eat within your gates and be filled. And you shall speak in the sight of the Lord your God: ‘I have taken from my house what was sanctified, and I have given it to the Levite, the stranger, the orphan, and the widow, as you commanded me. I have not passed over your commandments, nor have I forgotten your order. I have not eaten of it in my mourning, nor separated anything in any uncleanness, nor spent anything of it on a funeral’” (Deut. 26:12–14).

Again the Lord says through the prophet Malachi: “Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, so that there may be food in my house, and test me in this, says the Lord. If I will not open for you the floodgates of heaven and pour out a blessing upon you in abundance, and if I will not rebuke for your sake the devourer, so that he does not corrupt the fruits of your land, and so that the vine in the field is not barren, says the Lord of hosts. And all nations shall call you blessed, for you shall be a desirable land, says the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 3:10–11).

[Col. 0953B]

See, therefore, and understand wisely, most illustrious king, the good and excellent giver, who, although he has given you countless royal riches, commanded you to bring only tithes and firstfruits into the storehouse. While you are still placed on earth, honor him with tithes and firstfruits; but he, when he has placed you in heaven, will enrich you with angelic riches.

Consider, king, how sweet your fellowship with righteous kings will be, how pleasant the company of patriarchs, how sweet the companionship of prophets, how illustrious the kinship of apostles, how joyful the dignity of martyrs, how excellent the glory of virgins, how delightful and honorable the equality of angels, and how blessed the inexhaustible life that remains throughout the ages of ages. You will receive this great and indescribable treasure in the future if now you honor your God with tithes and firstfruits.

[Col. 0953C]

## CHAPTER XIII. How Treasure Is to Be Stored in Heaven

And so that the treasure of our possessions may be stored in heaven, the Lord admonishes us in the Gospel, saying: “Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys” (Matt. 6:20). Again in the Gospel he says to the rich man: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you possess, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21).

[Col. 0953D]

Place your treasure in heaven, therefore, most illustrious king, where you need not fear an enemy or attacker, where you need not fear a hidden thief or robber, whom no public plunderer or marauder can seize. For your homeland is paradise; in your homeland, which you will later receive, you ought to store up many treasures.

A great multitude of beloved ones awaits you there; a numerous throng of parents, brothers, and sisters longs to see you there, secure already in their own immortality but still anxious for your salvation. The choir of patriarchs awaits you there; the company of prophets desires you; the band of apostles and all the saints longs to behold you.

O what great joy it is to reach the fellowship of all these saints and to come into the happy embrace of them all! What supreme and perpetual happiness it is there to behold the glorious choirs of the apostles; there to take part in the sacred number of the rejoicing prophets; there to stand among the shining throng of virgins, martyrs, confessors, and all the saints triumphing for the Lord!

[Col. 0954A]

Therefore, so that you may deserve to reach the blessed fellowship of these, king, deposit good treasures from your possessions daily in heaven, and do not store up evil ones. For there are evil treasures as well as good ones, as it is written: “The good man brings forth good from the treasure of his heart. And the evil man brings forth evil from an evil treasure” (Luke 6:45).

For the one whom pride inflates, anger inflames, rapacity disturbs, cruelty spurs on, ambition delights, and lust precipitates—what else does he do but store up for himself treasures of iniquity? Concerning such people the Apostle Paul says: “God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is improper, being filled with all iniquity, wickedness, fornication, avarice, depravity, full of envy, murder, contention, deceit, malignity; whisperers, detractors, hateful to God, insulting, proud, arrogant, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, foolish, disorderly, without affection, without fidelity, without mercy” (Rom. 1:28–31).

[Col. 0954B]

Concerning them he also adds: “According to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s just judgment” (Rom. 2:5).

## CHAPTER XIV. What Kind and How Great a Treasure a Man Stores Up for Himself in Life, Such and So Great Will He Find after Death

Whatever kind and however great a treasure each person, while still alive, stores up in heaven, such and so great will he find after death. Thus Paul says to the Galatians: “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a man sows, that he will also reap. For he who sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh; but he who sows in the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit. Let us not grow weary in doing good, for in due season we shall reap without failing. Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to all, especially to those who are of the household of faith” (Gal. 6:7–10).

[Col. 0954C]

Solomon likewise says: “He who sows iniquity will reap evils. He who is inclined toward mercy will be blessed” (Prov. 22:7–8). Be inclined toward mercy, king, so that you may deserve to receive grace from God. Sow in the present age by giving to the poor what you yourself may reap in the future with manifold interest. Send your bread into the bellies of the hungry, so that you may find it multiplied in the eternal homeland. Thus Solomon says: “Cast your bread upon passing waters, for after many days you will find it” (Ecclus. 11:1).

What, then, is it to cast bread upon passing waters, unless it is to give alms to the poor and needy who are passing from this age? And what is “after many days you will find it,” unless it means that in the future age of recompense you will receive from it a generous reward?

[Col. 0955A]

## CHAPTER XV. On Not Trusting in Riches

And since the Lord has mercifully granted you royal and abundant riches in the present age, you ought to act diligently so that you may find many of them stored up in the future homeland. For no riches are truly to be called riches except those that have been happily stored in the heavenly treasury.

Hear, therefore, king, the Apostle, and do not trust in the perishable riches of this present age, but in those by which, when distributed to the poor, you will have built a heavenly treasure. For the Apostle Paul says: “Command the rich of this age not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment; to do good, to become rich in good works, to give readily, to share, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may attain the true life” (1 Tim. 6:17–19).

[Col. 0955B]

For the work of mercy and justice supports a person after death, not riches. Thus Solomon says: “Riches will not profit on the day of vengeance, but justice will deliver from death. For he who trusts in his riches will fall, but the just will flourish like a green leaf” (Ecclus. 5:10; Prov. 10:2 and 11:28).

David likewise says: “Do not hope in iniquity, and do not desire plunder. If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61:11). He sets his heart upon riches who believes that happiness consists uniquely in them. Such a person sets his heart upon them in this way: he does not wish to distribute his possessions to the poor, but rather to pursue them. He does not wish to spend his gold, but to trample upon it; he does not wish to give his patrimony generously to the needy, but to preserve it, gathered together, for his heirs.

[Col. 0955C]

And therefore they find nothing after death, because in life they give nothing to the poor. Concerning them the Psalmist aptly says: “They have slept their sleep, and all the men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75:6).

To this end Solomon brought forward a considered judgment concerning his riches, saying: “I magnified my works; I built houses for myself and planted vineyards; I made gardens and orchards and planted them with trees of every kind; I built for myself pools of water, to irrigate a forest of trees producing shoots. I acquired male and female servants and had a large household, as well as herds of cattle and great flocks of sheep, beyond all who were before me in Jerusalem. And I saw in all these things vanity and affliction of spirit, and that nothing endures under the sun” (Eccl. 2 ff.).

[Col. 0955D]

The Psalmist does not condemn the possession of abundant riches, but forbids the heart to be set upon them. The just accumulation of riches will not harm you if generous distribution is present. From them the gift of mercy is extended to the needy; from them the nakedness of the poor is covered; from them the want of strangers is supplied; from them the misery of orphans is wiped away; from them consolations are given to widows; from them the hunger of the starving is driven away; from them the thirst of the thirsty is dispelled; from them the needs of the sick are supplied; through them those who receive are freed from misery, and their faithful steward will be enriched in the future.

[Col. 0956A]

## CHAPTER XVI. On Not Boasting in Riches, but in Humility

Therefore, the riches stored in the heavenly treasury remain forever; but those held in the perishable age pass away and perish. One must not boast in perishing riches, any more than one must trust in them; rather, one should rejoice and boast in good and great virtues.

That the rich ought not to boast in riches but in humility, James testifies, saying: “Let the humble brother glory in his exaltation, but the rich in his humility” (Jas. 1:9). Do not boast, therefore, king, in riches, but in humility. Be humble; be founded in humility. Although you are exalted, great, and supreme, hold fast to humility.

[Col. 0956B]

Thus it is written: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before the Lord, for great is the power of God alone, and he is honored by the humble” (Ecclus. 3:20). You see, therefore, king, that if you hold fast to humility, you will have grace, you will also have glory, and, moreover, you will find rest for your soul.

Thus your Lord, your redeemer and teacher, your creator and governor, teaches you whom you ought to follow and shows you what you ought to learn, saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart; and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:29). The same Lord cries out through the prophet and says: “But upon whom shall I look, except upon the poor and contrite in spirit, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2).

If, then, you wish God to look favorably upon you, to exalt, glorify, and raise you up, humble yourself in his sight. Thus the apostle James says: “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you” (James 4:10). Along this royal road of humility, the mighty king David, clothed in purple and crowned with the priestly fillet, ran steadfastly and cried out:

“Lord, my heart is not exalted, nor are my eyes lifted up; neither have I walked in great matters, nor in things too wonderful for me. If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul” (Psalm 130:1–2).

Great indeed is the virtue of humility, and wondrous is its role as mother and nurse of all the virtues. Yet this virtue is not acquired by anyone through human will; rather, it is mercifully bestowed by the Lord upon whom he wills. For this reason it rises among the outstanding virtues as especially honored, because divine majesty graciously assumed it.

That this virtue is also royal is shown by the deeds of the ancient kings. In humbling the proud Saul, the Lord says: “When you were little in your own eyes, you were made head of the tribes of Israel; and the Lord anointed you king over Israel” (1 Samuel 15:17). The implied sense is: “When you considered yourself great in your own eyes, you became little and despised in my eyes.”

When David was reproached by Michal, Saul’s daughter, because he had humbled himself, he said: “I will play, and I will become even more contemptible than I have been, and I will be humble in my own eyes” (2 Samuel 6:22).

You see, then, king, that one of these men was cast down from the royal throne through pride, while the other was raised to royal glory through humility. Thus the saying was fulfilled in them:

“Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew 23:12).

When one of them had been elevated in his own eyes, he was justly humbled in the eyes of the Lord; when the other had been humbly despised in his own eyes, he was fittingly exalted in the eyes of God. Humble yourself, therefore, king, in your own eyes, so that you may be exalted in the eyes of the Lord; for the more humble you are in your own estimation, the more glorious you will be in the sight of the Most High.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Peace

No one exalts himself more before God than the one who humbles himself before himself for God’s sake. For this reason the humble person is exalted by the Lord, so that he may be called a son of God and an heir of Christ. So greatly must he pursue peace: the son of peace ought to seek peace and pursue it.

The Apostle accordingly admonishes us, saying: “Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Hebrews 12:14). The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9).

Among his divine commandments and saving teachings, when he was already near his passion, the Savior commended this precept and commandment to us for observance. He said: “I give you my peace” (John 14:27). As he ascended into heaven, the Lord left this to us as an inheritance, and through his most faithful king and prophet David he commanded us to follow it:

“Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it” (Psalm 33:15).

If we wish to follow this with sincere hearts, we shall be heirs of Christ; but if we desire to be heirs of Christ, we must live in the peace of Christ. If we are sons of God, we must be peacemakers. The sons of God ought to be peaceful and humble, gentle in mind, simple in heart, pure in speech, innocent in spirit, harmonious in affection, and faithfully and unanimously united with one another.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Zeal for Righteousness

Proceed along the royal way, king; do not turn away from it either to the right or to the left. Hold to the way of humility and peace in such a manner that you do not depart from zeal for righteousness. Hold, I say, king, to humility and peace; cry out to God with David and say:

“Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Psalm 68).

The Lord truly fulfilled this saying in his actions when he drove from the Temple those who were buying and selling, after scourging them. Phinehas, son of Eleazar, also deserved to receive from the Lord a covenant of everlasting priesthood because of his zeal for righteousness. The Lord said to Moses:

“Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, turned away my wrath from the Israelites, because he was moved by zeal for me against them, so that I would not destroy the Israelites in my zeal. Therefore say to him: Behold, I give him the covenant of my peace, and it shall be for him and for his descendants after him a covenant of an everlasting priesthood, because he was zealous for his God” (Numbers 25:11).

Therefore, most gentle king, let zeal for the Lord’s house reasonably consume you, for in that house of God—which is the Church—you too are a member of Christ. The members ought to follow the head.

If you see anything perverse in the Church of Christ, strive to correct it and do not cease to amend it. If you see anyone in the house of God, which is the Church, running toward sexual excess or drunkenness, prohibit, forbid, and restrain him—if zeal for God’s house consumes you. If you see someone swollen with pride, savage in anger, intoxicated with violence, envious of his brother through spite, inflamed by lust, devoted to plunder through greed, or violent through cruelty, restrain them all, threaten them all, and curb them all with the utmost severity.

Do whatever you can in accordance with the person you represent, the royal office you bear, the name of Christian that you possess, and the role of Christ that you fulfill. Do not cease striving to gain Christ, since you were gained by Christ, and fulfill in yourself the words: “Zeal for the house has consumed me.”

This zeal grants salvation, preserves faith, guards chastity, loves righteousness, and protects the Church of God with glorious vitality.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Clemency

Remember that you must exercise zeal for righteousness in such a way that you do not abandon the duty of humility and clemency. Hear what is written: “Clemency prepares life, and the pursuit of evils, death” (Proverbs 11:19).

This virtue is not to be undervalued, but sought with the greatest zeal and held firmly, since it prepares immortal and eternal life for us. You must arrange everything not with a turbulent spirit, but with clemency.

Though you may shine with gold and purple, you must not cast aside the clemency of humility; though you may gleam in royal splendor, do not depart from the clemency of humility; though you may be surrounded by a multitude of peoples, nevertheless hold fast to devoted clemency. For it is a royal virtue and the guardian of good kings. By preserving it, their descendants will be protected and their throne made firm. Thus it is written:

“Mercy and truth guard the king, and his throne is strengthened by clemency” (Proverbs 20:18).

It is clemency that makes peoples serve the king joyfully; it is clemency that makes the king’s face shine with the greatest delight, as Solomon says: “In the brightness of the king’s face there is life, and his clemency is like the latter rain” (Proverbs 16:15).

It is clemency that supplies everyone in the royal palace with pleasure and joy; it is clemency that multiplies generous gifts for all the king’s children; it is clemency that gladdens children, young people, and the aged; it is clemency that makes joyful offspring run through every corner of the palace; it is clemency that offers kisses to some and embraces to many.

Therefore, most clement king, I wish the virtue of clemency always to shine upon your face as well, so that it may provide joy for all and love for all.

## CHAPTER XX. On Counsel

So that you may do all these things with counsel, divine Scripture admonishes you through Solomon, saying: “The prudent person does everything with counsel” (Proverbs 13:16). Jesus, son of Sirach, also says: “My son, do nothing without counsel” (Ecclesiasticus 32:24).

And so that you may always live wisely, with discipline and counsel, Solomon again admonishes you, saying: “Hear counsel and receive instruction, so that you may be wise in your latter days” (Proverbs 19:20). “Those who do everything with counsel are governed by wisdom” (Proverbs 13:10). “Plans are scattered where there is no counsel, but where there are many counselors, they are confirmed” (Proverbs 15:22).

He says again: “The heart delights in ointment and various fragrances, and the soul is sweetened by the good counsels of a friend” (Proverbs 27:9). “War is undertaken with deliberation, and there is safety where there are many counsels” (Proverbs 24:6).

Counsel is indeed a great matter, exceedingly necessary for kings, not to be undervalued but placed above gold and silver. Divine Scripture itself confirms this, saying: “Gold and silver are the setting of the feet, but a pleasing counsel stands above both” (Ecclesiasticus 40:25).

You see, then, king, how royal a virtue counsel is, how Scripture proclaims it to be above gold and silver, and how it cries out that counsel flows abundantly like a fountain. All who travel the royal roads have therefore loved this virtue of counsel.

Strengthened by the virtue of counsel, Noah steadfastly built the ark over a hundred years and guided it through the Flood. Strengthened by the virtue of counsel, Abraham fearlessly departed from his kindred and prudently dwelt among foreign peoples. Firmly believing through the virtue of counsel, Isaac received from the Lord the blessing of all nations for himself.

Hearing his mother’s counsel, Jacob inherited his father’s blessing, received his brother’s birthright, and grew abundantly into the twelve tribes through his sons. Through this virtue of counsel, Moses, the last, governed six hundred thousand people through the wilderness. Through this virtue of counsel, his brother Aaron faithfully carried out the sacred ministry and priestly office by governing it.

Through this virtue of counsel, Phinehas, son of Eleazar the priest, filled with zeal for the Lord, pierced Zimri and the Midianite prostitute with a sword, and restrained the Lord’s raging anger, which was already hanging over the people. For this reason he left the blessing of perpetual priesthood to his descendants.

Receiving this virtue of counsel from Moses, his teacher, Joshua killed the kings of thirty nations and destroyed their kingdoms, overturned the walls of Jericho, brought God’s people into the promised land, and divided it among them by a rational plan, stretching out a measuring cord.

Through this virtue of counsel, Samuel governed God’s people by judging them justly. Through this virtue of counsel, David killed Goliath, played with lions, and prudently and bravely governed the kingdom he had received. Through this virtue of counsel, Solomon ruled the nations in peace and built a lofty temple for the Lord in Jerusalem.

Through this virtue of counsel, Elijah consumed two groups of fifty with heavenly fire, withheld rain from heaven at the proper time, and again, with the Lord’s assistance, restored it at the proper time. Through this virtue of counsel, the martyrs handed themselves over to temporal death so that they might receive eternal life from the Lord. Through this virtue of counsel, virgins and confessors persevered in the Lord’s service to the end.

Therefore you too, king, do everything you do with counsel, because it is written:

“And in all these things, pray to the Most High that he may direct your way in truth. Before all your works, let a truthful word precede you, and before every action, a firm plan” (Ecclesiasticus 37:19–20).

For if the great Lord wills, he will fill you with the spirit of understanding; he himself will send you utterances of wisdom like rains, open your mouth in prayer for what is good, and your memory will not be erased forever (Ecclesiasticus 39:8 and following).

## CHAPTER XXI. That Everyone Must Beware of Pride

Thus far, with God’s help, we have set out in order what you ought to do, king. Let us now beneficially explain what you ought thereafter to avoid. For a person who carefully avoids evil is no less virtuous than one who beneficially gathers good.

It is therefore necessary, most illustrious king, that in all your actions you carefully guard the royal way, and, walking safely along it, firmly place your steps in your conduct. Holding the right-hand paths happily, beware of the left with caution and care.

The right-hand way is the virtue of humility, which nourishes the other virtues and leads those who live well to eternal life. The left-hand way is the vice of pride, which nourishes the other vices and leads those who consent to it evilly into eternal punishment.

Pride is the first and greatest vice. As it is written in Ecclesiasticus:

“Pride is hateful before God and human beings. Pride is the beginning of every sin. Whoever holds fast to it will be filled with curses, and it will overthrow him in the end. Therefore the Lord dishonored the assemblies of the wicked and destroyed them utterly. God destroyed the seats of proud leaders and made the meek sit in their place. God dried up the roots of proud nations and planted the humble from among those nations. The Lord overturned the lands of the nations and destroyed them to their foundations; he dried them up, dispersed them, and caused their memory to cease from the earth. God destroyed the memory of the proud and preserved the memory of the humble” (Ecclesiasticus 10:7 and following).

The Lord also, giving through Ezekiel a comparison between humble and proud people by means of trees, says:

“All the trees of the region shall know that I am the Lord: I have humbled the lofty tree and exalted the lowly tree; I have dried up the green tree and caused the dry tree to flourish. I, the Lord, have spoken and acted” (Ezekiel 17:24).

The Lord also says in the Gospel:

“Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew 23:12).

The Lord himself, threatening the proud through Jeremiah, says:

“Behold, I am against you, proud one, says the Lord God of hosts, for your day has come, the time of your visitation. The proud one will fall and collapse, and there will be no one to raise him up. I will kindle a fire in his cities, and it will devour everything around him” (Jeremiah 50:31).

Pride is a great evil. It cast the devil down from heaven and expelled humanity from paradise. Every day it also presses the wretched down from the state of righteousness into the depths, and after death plunges them into hell.

Pride first elevates a person in thought and afterward raises the elevated person up in action. First it makes him swollen in the secrecy of his heart, and afterward makes him fall headlong in public. The proud fall outwardly from the place where the wretched were first elevated inwardly.

A person who, through pride, despises his creator lies justly subjected to sin. You therefore, most prudent king, fear and beware of the evil of pride above all. Turn away from the servile left-hand way and run swiftly along the right-hand way, which is royal.

Love and hold fast to humility, and carefully heed what the Lord proclaims to you through Scripture. He says:

“They have appointed you ruler; do not exalt yourself. Be among them as one of them. Take care of them, and thus sit securely, with all your care completed, so that you may rejoice because of them and receive the crown as an ornament of grace” (Ecclesiasticus 32:1–3).

## CHAPTER XXII. On Zeal and Envy

To be jealous of and envy another’s good is not a small matter, but a great and serious sin. At the beginning of the world the devil was struck by the jealousy of envy and perished first, and so he destroyed others as well.

When he saw humanity made in the image of God, he burst into jealous envy and deceived the wretched human being by persuasion. In his misery he also lost the angelic blessedness that he had possessed. From that time, as it is written, “through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wisdom 2:24).

Those who belong to his side imitate him. The wicked Cain imitated him and, through jealous envy, killed his righteous brother Abel. Through jealous envy Esau became an enemy to his brother Jacob. Through jealous envy Joseph was sold by his brothers. Through jealous envy Saul became David’s enemy and persecutor. And not to prolong the account by reviewing each case individually, the Jewish people perished through jealous envy, preferring to envy Christ rather than believe in him.

Although the jealousy of envy is considered under the name of a single vice, it produces many branches through various beginnings. It is the root of all evils and the fountain of vices. Hatred rises from it; hostility proceeds from it. Jealousy inflames greed and excites ambition.

Through the wicked jealousy of envy, fear of God is cast aside, the teaching of Christ is neglected, the day of judgment is not anticipated, pride is inflated, savagery is embittered, faithlessness transgresses, impatience is shaken, discord rages, and anger burns. No one who has become subject to another’s power can any longer restrain or govern himself.

From this every bond of peace is broken; from this brotherly charity is violated; from this truth is corrupted and unity divided; from this people rush into heresies and schisms while priests are slandered and bishops envied. Through jealousy a person becomes proud; through jealousy the mind is perversely changed.

Food is not pleasant to such people, nor is drink enjoyable. They continually sigh over another’s prosperity and groan. Hence the threatening face, the grim expression, the pallor of the countenance, trembling lips, the gnashing of teeth. What more need I say? From the jealousy of envy arises the fountain of all vices.

Therefore, most gentle and noble king, love everyone, embrace all with paternal and royal affection, and carefully avoid this exceedingly great and destructive evil of hatred. The apostle James says:

“Where jealousy and contention exist, there is instability and every evil practice” (James 3:16).

You see, then, how deadly is the resentment of envy. It burns up every seed of virtue; it devours every good thing with pestilential heat; it consumes understanding; it burns the breast; it afflicts the mind and, like a kind of plague, feeds upon the human heart.

Therefore, king, let goodness of spirit, filled with generosity, confront the jealousy of envy in you. Let brotherly charity and the weapons of love be prepared against envy. Love peace with everyone; preserve peace with all. Embrace everyone in gentleness and charity. Strive to be loved sweetly by all people on earth, so that you may deserve to rejoice happily with the angels in heaven.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Not Returning Evil for Evil

Love your neighbor as yourself, with a pure spirit and sincere mind, so that even if he has sinned against you, you may forgive him and not return evil for evil, as it is written:

“Do not say, ‘I will repay evil’; wait for the Lord, and he will deliver you” (Proverbs 20:22).

Therefore you too must forgive from your whole heart the person who sins against you, and wait for God, so that you may be freed from your own sin. Do not seek revenge against the person who has wronged you. For it is written:

“Whoever wishes to take vengeance will find vengeance from the Lord, and the Lord will keep a strict account of his sins. Forgive your neighbor who harms you, and then your sins will be forgiven when you pray” (Ecclesiasticus 28:1).

But since you are a king and the son of the supreme King, imitate your good Father, God, and forgive your neighbor’s sins, so that yours too may be forgiven by the Lord.

Do for your neighbor what you wish your God to do for you. Do not seek revenge upon your neighbor, lest, when the Lord takes vengeance, your offenses be demanded of you. “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21).

What you do not want God to do to you, do not do as a human being to another human being. It is found written in both Testaments: “What you do not want done to you, do not do to another.”

If, then, someone takes care not to do to another what he in no way wishes to suffer from another, he certainly takes care not to despise his neighbor when lifted up by pride; he takes care not to provoke his brother to anger when moved by ambition; he takes care not to tear him apart with the bite of envy.
