When anyone considers doing to another what he wants done to himself by another, he undoubtedly considers that he should repay the wicked with good and the good with better; show gentleness to the insolent; to demonstrate the grace of kindness to the humble; to show those who have gone astray the way of righteousness; to call the divided back to peace; to provide what is necessary for the needy; to lift up the afflicted with a word of consolation; and faithfully to supply his neighbors with everything he is able to provide.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Restraining Anger

Since a person is accustomed, through anger, to take revenge upon another, the Apostle therefore forbids us to sin through anger, saying:

“Be angry and do not sin. Do not let the sun go down upon your anger. Do not give place to the devil” (Ephesians 4:26).

You see, then, most gentle king, that the person who seeks revenge upon his brother through anger makes room for the devil in his own heart and, insofar as it depends on him, causes the Sun, who is Christ, to set.

For Christ is rightly understood through the sun, and the devil through darkness. The sun and darkness cannot dwell together in the same small human breast. When light dwells there, darkness is driven away; when darkness remains, light is excluded.

Nor can sweetness dwell with bitterness, brightness with gloom, conflict with peace, or storm with tranquility. Therefore, most gentle king, with the Lord’s help lay aside anger, and do not return vengeance through anger.

Attend carefully to what the saying of Paul, who admonishes us, declares. He says:

“But now put away from yourselves all anger, indignation, and malice” (Colossians 3:8).

James also says: “The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (James 1:20). Solomon says: “Jealousy and anger shorten one’s days, and anxious thought brings old age before its time” (Ecclesiasticus 30:26).

Our Lord himself, the adornment and glory of his whole Church, preacher and teacher, example and model, creator, governor, and ruler, completely removing us from anger against a brother, says:

“Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5:22).

Kings must therefore be especially careful not to carry their anger into action. For the anger of a king is not equal to that of an ordinary person. Concerning the anger of a king it is written: “Like the roaring of a lion is the anger of a king” (Proverbs 19:12). And again: “The anger of a king is a messenger of death” (Proverbs 16:14).

Therefore, the more powerful the anger of a king is in inflicting vengeance, the more it must be restrained and cautious in the most faithful kings.

But you, most gentle king, if you wish to run along this Royal Way that we are writing about and happily ascend to the heavenly and royal homeland, be gentle and most mild. If anger bursts forth, restrain it; if it overtakes the mind, calm it; if it rises up in the spirit, suppress it. If the fury of anger strikes the mind, let brotherly love suppress it; let brotherly sweetness temper anger; let brotherly charity temper hostility; let brotherly affection mitigate indignation.

Anger is a great vice. Through anger wisdom is lost, justice abandoned, the fellowship of love dissolved, the harmony of peace broken, and the law of truth forfeited. When agitated by the goads of anger, the body trembles, the tongue stammers, the face burns, the beating heart quivers, and the troubled eyes grow dim.

Therefore, king, so that these things may not happen to you, bridle your anger and arrange everything with patience. Your word is full of authority, and no one can resist it. Arrange, therefore, what must be arranged with peace, and govern what must be governed with tranquility, so that you may rule your kingdom well and justly and rejoice forever as possessor of your soul.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Not Yielding to Flatterers

Flatterers are accustomed to incite powerful people to consent to returning evil for good. In doing so they prepare eternal fire for themselves and bring ruinous harm upon those people.

Remember to avoid such people carefully, most discerning king, and examine with the greatest sharpness and caution who they are. In no way and under no agreement should you deign to consent to such people, lest, while flattering and praising you, they turn you away from the royal way and make you place your steps in your conduct upon a crooked path.

It is written concerning such flatterers: “An iniquitous person flatters his friend and leads him along a bad way” (Proverbs 16:29). Again, concerning rulers who consent to flatterers, it is written: “A ruler who willingly listens to a lying word has all wicked ministers” (Proverbs 29:12).

Again, concerning flatterers: “A deceitful tongue does not love truth, and a slippery mouth works ruin” (Proverbs 26:28). Again, concerning those who consent to them: “The wicked obeys an iniquitous tongue, and the deceitful obeys lying lips” (Proverbs 17:4).

Therefore, most illustrious king, beware the slippery and deadly ruin of flatterers, and do not let their unsound deceits deceive you under the appearance of friendship. Hear what is written about them:

“The hypocrite deceives his friend with his mouth” (Proverbs 11:9).

Again it is written about them: “Those who call you blessed are themselves deceiving you; they confuse the path of your feet” (Isaiah 3:12).

The Holy Spirit therefore admonishes you through divine Scripture concerning what you ought to do among such people, saying:

“As silver is tested in the smelting furnace and gold in the furnace, so a person is tested by the mouth of one who praises” (Proverbs 27:21).

Behold what a just and upright ruler is found among the tongues of those who praise and flatter: brighter than silver and more splendid than gold. These things will nevertheless happen to him if he agrees with divine Scripture, where it says:

“The desire of kings is for just lips; the one who speaks rightly will be guided” (Proverbs 16:15).

Pay careful attention, king, and see whether, in the sight of the supreme King, the person who speaks rightly is guided. In your sight also, the person who speaks not flattering but truthful words ought to be guided.

Therefore reject from your ears persuasive and deceptive speeches; reject the flattering tongue of flatterers. They sound good, but deceive badly; they sing sweetly, but stain wickedly; they promise pleasant things, but destroy the soul.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Avoiding Greed

Therefore, king, do not turn from the straight and royal path either because of flatterers or because of gifts, nor deign to bend your royal step toward the evil of greed.

A divinely inspired saying is found that especially condemns the greed of kings. Solomon says in Proverbs:

“A just king raises up the land; a greedy person destroys it” (Proverbs 29:4).

Again he says: “The one who pursues greed troubles his household, but the one who hates gifts will live” (Proverbs 15:27).

In the Gospel the Lord says to his disciples: “Beware of all greed, because a person’s life does not consist in the abundance of the things he possesses” (Luke 12:15).

Agreeing with this saying, Ecclesiastes says: “The greedy person will not be satisfied with money, and whoever loves riches will gain no fruit from them” (Ecclesiastes 5:9).

The prophet Habakkuk also says: “Woe to the one who gathers evil greed within his house, so that he may set his nest on high and suppose that he can escape from the hand of evil” (Habakkuk 2:19).

The apostle Paul proclaims, saying: “Every fornicator, or impure person, or greedy person—which is idolatry—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God” (Ephesians 5:3).

Therefore, most generous king, love mercy and flee greed, so that you may deserve to have an eternal inheritance with Christ. Be generous to everyone and munificent toward all, so that through you the land of your kingdom may not be wickedly destroyed but happily raised up.

Do not trouble your household like a greedy person; rather, build it as a generous one. Greed is a great and immense evil. It is a fire burning inextinguishably and consuming without ceasing.

Concerning greed it is written in the book of blessed Job: “Fire will devour the tents of those who willingly accept gifts” (Job 15:34).

Just as the body dwells in a material building, so the mind dwells in the counsel of thought. The fire devours tents when the heat of greed devastates the mind’s thoughts.

Greed knows no measure, understands no restraint, postpones the end of possessing, and, although it devours everything, knows absolutely no satiety. It is always hungry and begging; it is needy and filled with poverty. Although it gnaws everything with savage teeth, it still horribly admits and cries that it is hungry.

Although it is one vice in name, many other vices spring up and emerge from it, as it is written: “Greed is the root of all evils” (1 Timothy 6:10).

It produces not only many hidden evils but also many public ones. From it counterfeiters are found with wrinkled brows in the assembly; from it assassins appear in the midst of the city; from it poisoners arise in public; from it crime is openly committed; from it wickedness operates publicly.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That No House Should Be Built from the Property of Others

But you, king, as the son of the most pure King, cleanse your royal hands by shaking off every harmful gift, because it is written:

“The one who shakes his hands free of every gift, who stops his ears so as not to hear of bloodshed, and closes his eyes so as not to see evil—this person will dwell in the heights” (Isaiah 34:15).

Therefore, so that you may deserve to sit happily upon a throne in the heights, do not enlarge or build a house for yourself from the gifts of the poor. For it is written:

“The one who builds his house with the expenditure of another is like one who gathers his stones in winter” (Ecclesiasticus 21:9).

Jeremiah also says:

“Woe to the one who builds his house in injustice and his upper rooms without judgment; who oppresses his neighbor for no reason and does not repay him his wages. He says: ‘I will build myself a spacious house and broad upper rooms’; who opens windows for himself, makes cedar ceilings, and paints them with vermilion” (Jeremiah 22:13).

Isaiah cries out and says to such people:

“Woe to you who join house to house and connect field to field, all the way to the boundary of the place. Will you dwell alone in the midst of the earth? These things are in my ears, says the Lord of hosts” (Isaiah 5:8).

Solomon also prohibits this very thing, saying:

“Do not encroach upon the boundaries of the little ones, and do not enter the field of orphans” (Proverbs 23:10).

The almighty Lord has granted you, king, broad and flourishing kingdoms full of riches, and has divided among you the many estates of your parents. He has given you very extensive revenues from the treasury and honored you with the gifts of many powerful people, from which you can construct royal palaces.

Beware lest a royal house be built for you from the tears of the poor and the resources of the wretched.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That Judges Should Demand No Rewards for Administering Justice

Therefore command your judges, king, that they demand no worldly reward for justice. Command them not to seek temporal profits for a just judgment but eternal ones; not to demand a perishable payment but one that endures; to examine the case, not the person, whether the party is poor or rich; and in all things to preserve truth, not the gifts of ambition.

The person who seeks present gifts does not hope for future glory. Whoever greedily accepts gifts here in exchange for justice will receive no eternal rewards afterward.

Against the perversity of delinquent judges it is said through Moses: “You shall execute what is just and only what is just” (Deuteronomy 16:20).

The one who exercises justice for God’s sake, not for greed, therefore executes justice justly. Everyone who judges rightly carries a balance in his hand; in its two pans he bears justice and mercy. Through justice he pronounces the sentence for sin, and through mercy he moderates the punishment for sin, so that with a just balance he corrects some things according to equity and pardons others through compassion.

## CHAPTER XXIX. That a Deceitful Balance Must Not Be Found in Your Kingdom

Therefore forbid, most just and upright king, that a deceitful balance exist in your kingdom. Hear what the Lord prohibits to the people of Israel:

“You shall not have different weights in your bag, a larger and a smaller one; nor shall there be in your house a larger and a smaller measure. You shall have a just and true weight, and your measure shall be equal and true, so that you may live for a long time upon the land that the Lord your God gives you. For the Lord your God abominates the person who does these things” (Deuteronomy 25:13).

Solomon also says: “A weight and a weight are an abomination to the Lord; a deceitful balance is not good” (Proverbs 20:23). Again he says: “A deceitful balance is an abomination to the Lord, but an equal weight is his will” (Proverbs 11:21).

Indeed, it is a great perversity to abandon the Lord’s judgments for earthly advantage. For it is a hidden deceit and a diabolical work to alter fraudulently, for earthly profit, a just and legally established measure, or to change divinely instituted weights for the deception of a brother.

We hold as something handed down by the Lord and faithfully confirmed by him that “the whole law and the prophets depend upon love of God and neighbor” (Matthew 22:40).

Therefore, whoever deceives an innocent person with a deceitful balance, or with a smaller measure or weight used deceitfully, loves neither the neighbor whom he fraudulently supplants nor God, whose laws and commandments he tramples while despising them.

He is thereby convicted of driving the laws and prophets far from himself through disobedience, since through disobedience he does not keep the Lord’s commandments.

## CHAPTER XXX. That Captivity Must Be Prevented

Therefore prohibit, most clement king, that captivity occur in your kingdom. Be the most faithful son of that Father to whom you cry daily with the other brothers: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matthew 6:9).

Whatever he loves in his love, love likewise; whatever he forbids when he hears it, forbid likewise. Faithfully imitate him with whom you hope to reign forever.

For when giving Moses his command, he says:

“If a person is found soliciting one of his brothers, the Israelites, and has received payment after selling him, he shall be put to death, and you shall remove the evil from your midst” (Deuteronomy 14:17).

Through the prophet Amos he also cries out and says:

“For three crimes of Gaza, and for four, I will not turn away from it, because they carried away an entire captivity in order to shut them up in Edom” (Amos 1:6).

Again in the same place:

“For three crimes of Tyre, and for four, I will not turn away from it, because they shut up an entire captivity in Edom and did not remember the covenant of brothers” (Amos 1:9).

Again he says:

“For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I will not turn away from it, because he sold the righteous for silver and the poor for a pair of sandals” (Amos 2:6).

So that slaves may be treated justly and rightly, and so that they may be set free, Isaiah cries out and says:

“This is rather the fast that I have chosen: loosen the bonds of wickedness, undo the oppressive bundles, release those who have been broken, as free persons, and break every burden” (Isa. 58:6).

Ecclesiasticus likewise says:

“Do not injure a slave who is working faithfully, nor a hired servant who gives his life. Let a sensible slave be beloved by you as your own soul; do not defraud him of his freedom, nor abandon him when he is in need” (Ecclus. 7:22–23).

Again, the same book says:

“If you have a faithful slave, let him be to you as your own soul; treat him as a brother” (ibid. 33:51).

The Lord also gave this command through Jeremiah to the people of Israel concerning slaves. For he says:

“Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I made a covenant with your fathers on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery, saying: When seven years have been completed, each person shall release his Hebrew brother who has been sold to him and has served you for six years; and you shall send him away from you as a free man. But your fathers did not listen to me, nor did they incline their ear. And you have now turned and done what is right in my eyes, proclaiming liberty, each person to his neighbor. And you entered into a covenant in my presence, in the house over which my name has been invoked. Then you turned back and profaned my name: each of you brought back his male slave and each his female slave, whom you had released to be free and their own masters; and you subjected them, so that they should be your male and female slaves. Therefore thus says the Lord: You have not listened to me, proclaiming liberty, each person to his brother and each to his neighbor. Behold, I proclaim liberty to you, says the Lord—liberty to the sword, to pestilence, and to famine—and I shall make you a terror to all the kingdoms of the earth” (Jer. 34:13).

Truly, a human being ought to obey God and obey his commandments insofar as he has been given the ability to do so. Among the other saving commandments and righteous works, because of God’s immense love, each person ought to release his slaves, considering that nature did not subject them to him, but fault: for we were created equal in status, but by fault some have been subjected to others. Let us also consider that if you forgive, you will be forgiven. For you too, lord, are oppressed by the yoke of status. Therefore, most just and pious king, honor your God for all things, because, as it is written, “He has honored you above all”—whether in the slaves subjected to you or in the riches granted to you—by making the former free and giving alms from the latter; do not cease obeying his commandments.

Be a father to the poor, a nourisher of orphans, a lover of the fatherless, a defender of widows, a provider for foreigners, and, according to the ministry of the rule, a defender and governor of everyone. By Christ’s gift and the abundance of his grace, be full of wisdom; be endowed with prudence; be enriched with simplicity; be firmly grounded in patience, yet raised up by zeal for rectitude. Be gentle and peaceful toward all, yet inflamed by zeal for rectitude. In seeking justice, be a diligent investigator; in judging, a most cautious executor, yet in such a way that mercy is always placed before judgment. Remember that the person who has mercifully forgiven his brother will receive mercy from the Lord.

If you diligently carry out and fulfill these things, the Lord will strengthen your kingdom, exalt your throne, and confirm your arm, because the Lord confirms the arm of whomever he wills and grants his sword, with his aid, for the achievement of victory. Thus he says through the prophet Ezekiel:

“And I shall strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and I shall give my sword into his hand; and I shall break the arms of Pharaoh, and they shall groan with the groaning of the slain before his face. And I shall strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, but the arms of Pharaoh shall fall; and they shall know that I am the Lord, when I give my sword into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he stretches it out over the land of Egypt” (Ezek. 30:24).

For the Lord weakens and breaks the arm of whomever he wills. He also says this to Ezekiel:

“Son of man, I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt; and behold, it has not been wrapped so that health might be restored to it, so that it might be bound with cloths and bandaged with linen, so that, after receiving strength, it might be able to hold a sword. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against Pharaoh king of Egypt, and I shall crush his strong arm, though it is already broken; I shall make the arm fall from his hand. And I shall scatter Egypt among the nations, and I shall scatter them through the lands” (ibid. 30:21).

And it is written in the Psalm:

“You have turned away the help of his sword, and you have not aided him in battle” (Ps. VIII, 44).

That the Lord also knows victory before it occurs, he himself says through Ezekiel:

“You therefore, son of man, thus says the Lord God: Say to every winged creature and to all birds and to every beast of the field: Assemble, hasten, gather from every side to my sacrifice, which I sacrifice for you, a great sacrifice upon the mountains of Israel, that you may eat flesh and drink blood. You shall eat the flesh of the mighty and drink the blood of the leaders of the earth: of rams and lambs, goats and bulls, and of all fattened and well-fed animals. You shall eat fat until you are satisfied and drink blood until you are drunk, from the sacrifice that I shall sacrifice for you; and you shall be filled at my table with horse and mighty horseman and with all men of war, says the Lord God” (Ezek. 39).

## Chapter XXXI. On Seeking the Lord’s Protection

You therefore, illustrious king, so that the Lord may grant you strength in your arm and victory in battle, always seek his aid and flee for refuge to his protection. For it is written:

“The name of the Lord is a most powerful tower; the righteous runs to it and is exalted” (Prov. 18:10).

Therefore salvation does not consist in the multitude of a people or in abundant armor, but in calling upon the name of the Lord. Heavenly protection is a stable and unshaken defense. Since kings ought diligently to seek it, King David should be imitated with affection; humbly entreating the Lord, he says:

“Hear, O God, my prayer; attend to my supplication. From the ends of the earth I cried out to you; when my heart was anxious, you raised me up upon a rock. You led me, because you became my hope, a tower of strength in the presence of the enemy” (Ps. 60:1).

The rock and the tower here signify Christ. For the person who does not doubt that he is founded upon Christ’s faith rightly declares himself raised up upon this rock. And the person who, trusting in his aid, arms himself with virtues is defended in this tower. This tower is full of virtues, not swords; it fights by the word, not by battle; it does not defend locally, but with universally unconquerable strength it protects and guards its chosen ones.

## Chapter XXXII. On Prayer

One must also observe that King David reached this heavenly protection by praying. Beginning in this way, he said:

“Hear, O God, my prayer when I entreat you; deliver my soul from fear of the enemy. You have protected me from the assembly of the malicious, from the multitude of those who work iniquity,” and so forth (Ps. 63:1).

You too, therefore, most faithful king, so that, supported by the Lord’s aid, you may defend your kingdom, continually seek his protection by praying. In the Psalms you have innumerable examples of prayer from that same King David.

We shall also set down here a very few examples from Solomon. He says:

“The Lord is far from the impious, but he will hear the prayers of the righteous” (Prov. 15:29).

“The one who keeps the law multiplies prayer” (Ecclus. 35:1).

Again, the same book says:

“Prayer in humility will penetrate beyond the clouds” (ibid., v. 21).

The Lord says in the Gospel:

“Whatever you ask for in prayer, believing, you will receive” (Matt. 21:22).

“Therefore keep watch at every time, praying that you may be worthy to escape all these things that are to come and to stand before the Son of Man” (Luke 21:36).

Paul also says:

“Be devoted to prayer, praying at every time, keeping watch in the spirit with all perseverance” (Rom. 12:12; Eph. 6:18).

James, moreover, says:

“Pray for one another, so that you may be saved; for the continual prayer of a righteous person has great power” (Jas. 5:16).

And we too always pray with the Apostle for you, that God may deem you worthy of his calling and fulfill every good purpose and work of faith with power, so that the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified in you and you in him, according to the grace of our God and Lord Jesus Christ.

But we are confident in the Lord concerning you, that you both do and will do the things that we command. May the Lord direct your hearts in the love of God and in the patience of Christ (Eph. 3:4). Amen.

The book of Smaragdus the abbot, called *The Royal Way*, ends here.

## Acts of the Roman Conference

Or, [Note: [Col. 0971B] “The account that was held,” etc. It appears in Baronius under the year 809, no. 54 through no. 63 inclusive, and runs as follows: “After the testimonies had been read by the aforesaid envoys,” etc., as above. After this Pope Leo, guardian of antiquity, rising as the champion of what had been presumed without the consent and authorization of the Apostolic See, not only made clear by discussion and commands, in words, what he wished to be done; he also thought that an indelible monument should be erected, by which posterity would learn that nothing ought to be added to the sacred Creed. Accordingly, in the basilica of Saint Peter—not of Paul, as someone has asserted—he arranged for two silver tablets to be affixed at the confession of Saint Peter himself. On one of them the Creed was to be read written in Latin, while on the other it was inscribed in Greek without any addition of those four syllables, *Filioque*, but he wished it to remain whole in its original purity. Anastasius mentions these tablets in his account of Leo, when, speaking of the gifts presented to the basilica of Saint Peter, he says the following after first mentioning certain ornaments offered to that church: ‘Here,’ he says, ‘for love and protection of the orthodox faith, he had two silver shields made, written both with the Creed, one indeed in Greek letters and the other in Latin, seated on the right and left above the entrance to the body, weighing ninety-four pounds and six ounces of silver.’ Thus far his account. At what time, and on what occasion, those words, *Filioque*, were likewise received into the Creed in the Roman Church by the authority of the Roman pontiff, we shall discuss in its proper place, since another occasion requires it; and likewise when the same Creed began to be sung in that church, a treatment in its proper place will be appropriate. Walafrid Strabo, a writer of this period, reports in *On Ecclesiastical Affairs*, chapter 22, that this practice of singing the Creed had become common in Gaul and Germany from the time of the condemnation of the Felician heresy; and that for the same reason the Constantinopolitan rather than the Nicene Creed was sung in church, namely because the Constantinopolitan seemed more suitable to musical melodies. But why not rather [sing] this one, since it is fuller, inasmuch as it expresses more explicitly the divinity of the Holy Spirit? — Sev. Bin.] the account that was held concerning the Creed of faith in the sacristy of the holy Apostle Peter, between Lord Leo, most holy and co-evangelical pope of the city of Rome, and the bishops Bernarius and Jesse, together with Abbot Adalard, envoys of Lord Charles the emperor, in the second indiction, written by Smaragdus, abbot of Saint Michael.

(From Labbe, *Councils*, vol. VII.)

After the testimonies had been read in order by the aforesaid envoys [Note: [Col. 0972C] The testimonies of the holy Fathers mentioned at the beginning of this account, according to Holstenius, are appended in the Vatican manuscript itself to the conference. In the manuscript of the most serene Queen of the Swedes there is also a letter of the Emperor Charles to Leo III concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son, sent through the aforementioned envoys—Bernarius, Jesse, and Adalard—which Abbot Smaragdus also published and which has recently been brought to light after the Roman synods collected by Holstenius. — Labbe.], and after they had been heard most carefully by the apostolic lord, he said:

“I think thus; I hold thus, together with these authorities and with the authorities of Sacred Scripture. If anyone should wish to think or teach otherwise concerning this matter, I oppose him; and unless he is converted and wishes to hold to this understanding, I utterly reject the person who thinks otherwise.”

After these words, I know that certain matters had previously been discussed more by conversation than by disputation. The sequence of their meanings, or words—except insofar as it concerned this matter—does not sufficiently come to mind. When the conference had progressed to the point that it was now to be a more definite disputation rather than a conversation as above, and although the words may not have been exactly the same, as far as I can recall this was the course of their meanings and the overall conclusion of the final definitions:

**Envoys:** Since, as you say, this must be believed with the utmost certainty, held immutably through believing, and defended most steadfastly wherever necessary through holding it, should not those who do not know it be taught, while those who know it should be confirmed so that we may hold it more attentively?

**Pope:** That is so.

**Envoys:** If that is so, if someone does not know this or does not believe it in this way, can he be saved?

**Pope:** Whoever is capable of attaining this understanding with finer insight, yet refuses either to know it or, knowing it, to believe it in this way, cannot be saved. There are many matters; among them is this one: the higher mysteries and more subtle sacraments of the sacred faith, to the investigation of which many are able to attain, while many others, impeded either by the length of their years or by the quality of their understanding, cannot. Therefore, as we said, the person who can and refuses cannot be saved.

**Envoys:** If, then, this is so—or rather, because it is so—that it is not permissible not to believe, and that it is permissible to teach without remaining silent, why is it not permissible to sing, or to teach by singing?

**Pope:** It is permissible, I say; it is permissible to sing while teaching and to teach while singing. But in prohibited matters it is not permissible to insert anything unlawfully, whether by writing or by singing.

**Envoys:** Since, then, it is known to both sides that you consider or declare it unlawful for that Creed to be inserted by singing or writing because those who composed the same Creed did not insert it, as they did the other articles, and because the subsequent principal councils—the Fourth, namely Chalcedon, and also the Fifth and Sixth Councils of Constantinople—forbade anyone to compose a new Creed beyond the Creed, under any necessity or devotion to save human beings, and forbade inserting anything into the old Creed by removing, adding, or changing anything, there is no need to dwell on that matter any longer. But this is what I ask, and this is what I beg you to state: since it is good to believe this, would it likewise have been good today to sing it as well as to believe it if it had been inserted by them?

**Pope:** Certainly it would have been good, and very good, since it is so great a sacrament of the faith that whoever is capable of attaining it may not fail to believe it.

**Envoys:** Would those authors not have acted well at that time if, by adding only four syllables, they had made so necessary a sacrament of the faith clear to all future ages?

**Pope:** Just as I do not dare to say that they would not have acted well if they had done so—for undoubtedly, just as they knowingly omitted the other things that they omitted, enlightened not so much by human as by divine wisdom, so too I do not dare to say that they understood this less fully than we do, or failed to consider why they left it out, or why, once it had been left out, they forbade it to be inserted thereafter, just as they forbade the other additions. You and your companions must see what you think about yourselves. For I do not say that I place myself above them; rather, may it be far from me to presume to equate myself with them.

**Envoys:** May it also be far from us, Father, with our God protecting us, to think or say any of these things, whether inflated by pride or driven by desire for human praise in divine matters—as though we presumed not merely to place ourselves above them but even to equate ourselves with them. We ask and labor only in consideration of the circumstances of our own time and of the weakness of our brothers, out of charity, so that, because the end of the world is approaching, a time which, as has been foretold, will also be perilous, we may be able above all to benefit our brothers in these matters. We strive to make the faithful firm in the Lord in the sacrament of faith; and therefore, because we have found that the aforesaid Creed is sung by some, and because we understand that this accords with the faith of the Church, and have thereby come to know that even now many learned people—and, without end, those who are to be instructed until the end of the age—will be taught about so great a mystery if it is held in this way, though they would by no means be instructed unless it were sung, it seemed better to us to instruct so many by singing than to leave the unlearned without instruction by remaining silent. If your Paternity knew how many thousands today know this because it is sung, who would never have known it unless it were sung, perhaps you would agree with us and, with your consent as well, acquiesce in its being sung.

**Pope:** For the present I agree. Nevertheless, I ask you to answer me: all the mystical sacraments of this faith that are not contained in the Creed, without which no one who is capable of attaining this understanding can be a Catholic—should these also be inserted into the Creeds and, for the sake of shortening things for those of lesser understanding, added according to each person’s preference?

**Envoys:** By no means, because not all things are equally necessary.

**Pope:** Even if not all, certainly very many things similar to these are necessary, and unless they are believed by those capable of understanding them, people cannot be Catholics.

**Envoys:** Can you give us something—not something more sublime, but at least something similar—that is lacking from this Creed?

**Pope:** Indeed I can, and I can give many such things.

**Envoys:** Give one first, and, if necessary, add another.

**Pope:** Since what is being done is being done in friendly contention, and what is being sought is being sought for the salvation of both parties—and would that whenever anything of this kind is sought in greater or lesser ecclesiastical or Catholic interests, it were sought in every respect peacefully and without perverse intention!—let us be given an opportunity for consideration, lest we speak rashly about such venerable mysteries; and we shall give whatever the Lord grants concerning them.

After a suitable interval of a night had been granted, the Pope said:

“Is it more salutary to believe, and dangerous not to believe, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as from the Father, than to believe that the Son, God Wisdom, was begotten from God Wisdom, and God Truth from God Truth, and yet that both are essentially one God, one Wisdom, and one Truth—even though it is clear that this was not inserted into the same Creed by the holy Fathers? If these two points, as befits wise men, suffice in such a familiar disputation to bring you to agree with us and recognize that so many earlier Catholic Fathers, who either did not insert this matter under discussion into the Creeds or, as stated above, forbade it to be inserted in the same way as the other articles, did not omit it through present ignorance or future negligent foresight, and forbade what had been omitted to be inserted, then we gladly refrain from piling up testimonies. You should know, however, that not only according to the essence of divinity but also according to the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, with God as our author and on the authority of those same Fathers, we can offer arguments and points of such force that they are able not only to satisfy the wise but also to overwhelm the foolish.”

**Envoys:** It is not necessary, I say, to labor over whether we do not know what we know; for whatever the others know concerning this matter, we know by God’s authority, or, if we do not know it, we are able to know it.

**Pope:** “This is what amazes us,” he said: that although you can rest without labor that produces progress, you labor in order not to rest.

**Envoys:** We do not labor in order not to rest, but lest, through sluggishness, we lose the reward of pious labor. Without abandoning more diligent inquiry and avoiding obstinate contention, we still consider the gain acquired through this in the hearts of those who seek to be greater than the harm done to those who added it, as though they were obstinate despisers of the constitutions of the Fathers. For it is one thing arrogantly to trample upon and despise good things, and another to make good things better through benevolence.

**Pope:** Although in certain cases it is good for this to be done, it does not therefore follow that it ought to be done everywhere. Many testimonies could be added to prove that this is so, but the matter is abundantly clear in itself: how much better it is for each person to strive to make any good thing useful precisely as it is; or, if he attempts to make that very good thing better, first to beware and carefully consider that, by presuming beyond what he ought, he may corrupt what was salutary in itself and make it harmful. Unless someone should wish to assert, concerning the present matter or similar articles—which it is permissible to teach and learn without danger to oneself—that the lawful order of teaching ought to be abandoned, and that one should leave things in a state in which thereafter neither teacher nor learner could be innocent, but both would justly be judged guilty of transgression. This perhaps touches you, if you do not disdain to hear it, and not without reason: here, what until now anyone wise in the Church of God could know and could teach without thought of wrongdoing, from now on not merely will the foolish be unable to learn, but even the wise person himself will be unable to sing it without transgression, or to teach anyone by singing it as you wish. And while you choose to benefit many by a path other than the one you ought to follow, you leave no one in this particular matter whom you would not harm if he followed you. For as to what you have taught above, the person who does such a thing devoutly in search of its fruit should not be judged or regarded in the same way as the person who presumes to do it through a stubborn command. This defense—or, if it may be called so, evasion—does not apply here and does not address the point, because the Fathers neither distinguished nor decreed that the benevolent person might presume to do this but the malevolent person might not; they simply decreed that no one should.

**Envoys:** Was it not you who gave permission for that same Creed to be sung in the church? Did the practice of singing it originate from us here? For the same custom of singing came from there to here, not from us to there. How, then, have we sung it until today?

**Pope:** I gave permission for it to be sung, but not for anything to be added, removed, or changed by singing. And, to speak more explicitly because you compel me: as long as it was sufficient for you to sing and celebrate the sacred mysteries in such matters according to the practice of the holy Roman Church, there was no need for us either to labor over these matters or to give others an occasion for laboring over them. As for your claim that you sing in this way because you heard that others in those regions, earlier than you, sang it, what has that to do with us? We do not sing it; we read it, and by reading we teach, yet neither by reading nor by teaching do we presume to add anything by inserting it into the same Creed. Whatever we recognize as lacking from the aforesaid Creeds that is nevertheless in accord with the faith, we do not, as has often been said, presume to insert; rather, we take care to provide it in the places and at the times appropriate to it.

**Envoys:** Therefore, as I see it, your Paternity decrees that the matter under discussion must first be removed from the often-mentioned Creed, and only then may it lawfully and freely be learned and taught by anyone, whether by singing or by transmitting it.

**Pope:** Without a doubt, this is decreed on our part; and we also strongly urge that it be accepted on your part.

**Envoys:** Although, as you yourself said above, what is being sought is being sought for the salvation of both parties, once the things you wish have been removed, it is good for the same Creed to be sung.

**Pope:** It is certainly good. Yet we say this not by commanding, but by permitting it as before, because we do not fail to recognize that, just as then, so now too, if it is done sincerely, it can be useful to those in need.

**Envoys:** Since, as you say—and you speak truly—it is good to sing that same Creed, if a sentence full of correct faith is removed from the middle, will that same sentence be condemned by everyone as though it were contrary to the faith? What advice, then, will you give so that this may not pass into some disaster?

**Pope:** If I had been asked before it began to be sung in this way, I would certainly have replied that it should not be inserted. But now—and I say this not as an assertion but as a matter considered together with you, insofar as it occurs to my mind—it seems to me that both things can be done in this way: gradually, at the palace, since it is not sung in our holy church, the custom of singing the same Creed should be allowed to lapse. In this way it may come about that, since it was not the authority of anyone issuing a command but rather the novelty of hearing it that caused it to be sung, if you abandon it, everyone will abandon it. Thus, insofar as possible, both things may perhaps be done without impropriety: what is now rightly believed by those who previously did not know it may continue to be believed, while the unlawful custom of singing it may be removed without injury to anyone’s faith.

# Appendix to the Works of Smaragdus

## Charters of Louis the Pious and his son Lothar for the Monastery of Saint Michael

(From Baluze, *Miscellanea*, book IV.)

### I. Charter of Louis the Pious for the Monastery of Saint Michael in the County of Verdun

In the name of the Lord God, our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

Let the practical concern of our faithful—namely, our counts and vassals, or anyone who appears to hold benefices from the estate of the monastery of Saint Michael, where the venerable man Smaragdus presides as abbot—know that, just as our lord and father commanded, so we too command that you not neglect to give to the same monastery every year, from those same benefices, the ninths and tenths of everything in full.

Therefore, by this letter we command all of you who hold benefices from the property of the aforesaid monastery through our generosity or that of our counts or vassals not to neglect to give every year, as stated above, the ninths and tenths to the aforesaid venerable Smaragdus and his successors, or to the envoys of the same monastery, without any opposition or negligence. Let no one delay in bringing assistance, according to his means, for restoring the houses of that Church.

And let no one who holds a benefice from the property of the aforesaid monastery presume to act against this command of ours; rather, let him observe it in all things just as it has been commanded by us, or in whatever way he wishes to possess the grace of God and our favor, or the benefice itself. And so that you may believe this more certainly, we have commanded it to be sealed below with our ring.

Given on the third day before the Ides of July, in the third year of the reign of Lord Louis, most serene Augustus [Note: [Col. 0975D] This is unusual.], in the ninth indiction. Done happily at the palace of Theodonis Villa, in the name of God. Amen.

### II. Charter of Louis the Pious and his son Lothar concerning the freedom to elect an abbot

In the name of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothar, emperors Augustus, by divine ordination and providence.

If, for the love of God, we generously grant appropriate benefits to places devoted to divine worship and to those serving him in those places, we do not doubt that a reward of eternal recompense will be repaid to us by the Lord. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, both present and future, and also to their successors, that we have granted not only to the old monastery called Castellio but rather to the new one, which, with the Lord’s help, was built from its foundations in our time and is called Marsupium. It is situated in the county of Verdun, on the river Meuse or the stream Marsupium, and was constructed in honor of the holy archangel Michael, where at the present time, by God’s favor, Abbot Smaragdus presides, together with the monks dwelling there through the ages.

Whenever the aforesaid abbot or his successors depart from this life by divine calling, so long as those monks are able to find among themselves someone capable of governing that community according to the rule of Saint Benedict, they shall, by this authority and consent of ours, have permission to elect abbots. Thus may it please those servants of God who serve there continually to implore the Lord’s mercy for us, for our wife and offspring, and for the stability of our entire empire, granted and preserved for us by God.

And so that this authority of our confirmation may retain inviolable and unshaken firmness throughout future times, we have subscribed it below with our own hands and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

### III. Charter of Louis the Pious concerning a certain exchange made by Abbot Smaragdus

In the name of the Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine ordination and providence, emperor Augustus.

If we confirm by our edicts those things that the faithful of our empire have exchanged among themselves for their own needs, we exercise imperial custom, and we wish that the same arrangement afterward remain established by the firmest legal right. Therefore, let the diligence of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable man Hildoin, abbot, made known to our serenity that the religious Abbot Smaragdus, from the monastery of Saint Michael, which is built in the county of Verdun on the river Marsupium, where it flows into the river Meuse, together with certain men named Adalhard, Rodald, and Aldarnus, had recently made an exchange among themselves of certain properties for their common advantage and benefit.

The aforesaid Abbot Smaragdus therefore gave from the estate of his monastery to the aforesaid men, for their own possession in the county of Bar, in the district or villa called Lauziacus, one mansus with its boundaries and adjoining lands. In return, as compensation for this property, the aforementioned men gave to the abbot, for the use of the aforesaid monastery, from their own property in the county of Verdun, in the district or villa called Godinovilla, one meadow.

He declared that he had the two exchanges, written in identical form and strengthened by the hands of good men, in his possession. But for their complete security he asked our highness to confirm those exchanges anew and more fully by a command of our gentleness. We did not wish to deny his request; rather, know that we have confirmed and granted everything to them in all respects, just as we do for each of our faithful who make a just request.

Therefore, commanding, we order that whatever one party has justly and reasonably transferred to the other party, it shall henceforth hold and possess by the firmest legal right under this authority of ours; and whatever it wishes to do with it, let it enjoy complete freedom of action.

### IV. Charter of Louis the Pious concerning the liberty and immunity of the aforesaid Monastery of Saint Michael

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

If, for the love of God, we generously grant appropriate benefits to places devoted to divine worship and to those serving him in those places, we do not doubt that a reward of eternal recompense will be repaid to us by the Lord. Therefore, let the prudence of all our faithful, both present and future, know that the venerable Abbot Smaragdus from the monastery of Castellio, which is called Marsupium and is built in honor of the holy archangel Michael, the holy ever-virgin Mary, and Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, brought to us the immunity charter of our lord and father, Charles of blessed memory, most pious Augustus.

In it we found inserted that he himself and his predecessors, namely the earlier kings of the Franks, had always held the aforesaid monastery under the fullest protection and guardianship of immunity, on account of divine love and reverence for that holy place. Nevertheless, for the sake of security, the aforesaid Abbot Smaragdus asked us to add the grace and authority of our firmness to the paternal authority, for the love of God and reverence for the aforementioned saints. We gladly agreed to his request, granted everything accordingly, and confirmed it by this charter of our authority.

Therefore, commanding, we order that no judge, nor anyone exercising judicial power, dare in our time or in the times to come enter the churches, places, fields, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery—which it lawfully and legally possesses at the present time, or which divine piety may thereafter wish to increase as belonging to that holy place—for the purpose of hearing cases, exacting fines, taking sureties, unjustly coercing the people of that monastery, whether free persons or slaves dwelling upon the land of the monastery, or demanding any redhibitions or unlawful pretexts. Nor may anyone presume at all to exact the things mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid abbot and his successors be permitted to possess the property of the monastery in peace under the protection of our immunity. Whatever the fiscus might have expected from it, we grant entirely to the aforesaid monastery for eternal recompense, so that it may contribute to the support of the poor and the stipends of the monks serving God there throughout all future time and for its increase. Thus may it please the servants of God who serve there continually to pray to the Lord for us, for our wife and offspring, and for the stability of our entire empire, granted and preserved for us by God.

And so that this authority of our immunity may be held more firmly and preserved more carefully, we have subscribed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of June, by Christ’s favor, in the third year of the reign of our lord Louis, most serene emperor, in the ninth indiction. Executed at the royal palace of Aachen, in God’s name.

[Col. 0979B]

### V. Charter of Louis the Pious concerning the freedom of carts and pack animals

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divinely ordained providence emperor Augustus.

Let it be known to all bishops, abbots, counts, vicars, and centenarii, as well as to collectors of tolls, officials, and agents, [Col. 0979C] that we have granted to the monks residing in the monastery that is [Col. 0980A] situated in the place called Castellionis, named Mansurpium, which was built in honor of Saint Michael the archangel, Saint Mary ever-virgin, and Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, where also the venerable man Smaragdus serves as abbot, that no one should presume to demand or exact any toll or other exaction from the carts and pack animals carrying necessities for that monastery or for the congregation serving God there.

Likewise, no one should presume to exact any tribute from the *patellae* (pans or vessels) that are at Marsallus and in the Lower Vicus, on anything that is brought for their use and necessity; rather, they shall possess this as granted and bestowed by our alms.

Therefore we order and command that no one whatsoever dare accept from the carts or pack animals of the aforesaid monks, carrying their necessities, any toll wherever the treasury might have been able to exact one—neither toll, nor *tranaticum* [a transport charge], nor *portaticum* [a portage charge], nor *pulveraticum* [a road or dust charge], nor any levy imposed upon meeting or passage, nor any tax, nor any requisition. Rather, by this authority of ours, let it be lawful for their people, with their carts and pack animals and the things they carry, to go and return freely and securely wherever they are traveling, without anyone’s unlawful opposition. And if they remain for any length of time in any place, or buy or sell anything, let absolutely nothing be demanded from them, as has been said.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of September, in the third year of the reign of Louis, most pious Augustus, in the tenth indiction. Executed at the royal palace of Aachen, prosperously, in God’s name. [Col. 0980C] Amen.

[Col. 0979]

## Letter of Charlemagne to Pope Leo concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, edited by Abbot Smaragdus

(See volume 98 of this *Patrologia*, col. 923, among the letters of Charlemagne.)

## In the year of the Lord 818

# Magnus, Archbishop of Sens

[Col. 0979]

## Historical Notice concerning Magnus

(From *Gallia Christiana*.)

[Col. 0979D]

Magnus, archbishop of Sens, was consecrated by Leo III in the year 801, while he was residing at Rome in the retinue of Charlemagne. Returning to Sens, he turned aside to the monastery of Saint Peter; on the following day he was carried by the people and clergy as far as the principal church of Saint Stephen, with hymns and songs. This custom is still observed at Sens to the present day.

Sent by Emperor Charlemagne together with Count Godefrid, he served as a royal commissioner to Orléans, Troyes, Langres, Besançon, and Autun in the year 802. There survive letters in formal style [Col. 0980D] from Ebroin, archbishop of Bourges, to Magnus, archbishop of Sens, written concerning the priest Dadobert in the year 810.

Pressed by letters from Charlemagne, he induced Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, to write a book on the order of baptism; Theodulf dedicated it to Magnus, and Magnus dedicated it to Charlemagne in the year 812. Magnus also dedicated to him the notes which he had collected, being highly skilled in legal knowledge. In turn, Emperor Charlemagne donated to Magnus, for the benefit of the basilica of Saint Stephen, villas, estates, various ornaments, and exceedingly precious relics of the saints. [Col. 0981A]

Charlemagne’s son Louis the Pious sent Magnus, in the year 817, a copy of the rule for canons, prepared by decision of the synod of Aachen, commanding that it be observed in his province.

At the further command of Magnus, the *Life of Saint Severinus*, abbot of Agaunum, written by his disciple Faustus, [Col. 0982A] was corrected by an anonymous editor.

Magnus died in the year 818 and was buried in the church he had built in honor of the Savior, in the vineyards, for the burial of the canons. In the course of the twelfth century this church was granted to the Augustinian canons regular.

[Col. 0981]

# Magnus of Sens: Booklet on the Mystery of Baptism, Published at the Command of Charlemagne

(Marten., *Ancient Ecclesiastical Rites*.)

[Col. 0981B]

Most glorious emperor, we, your servants—namely Magnus and my other colleagues, although unworthy bishops belonging to the diocese of Sens—have presumed to make known to your greatness that we humbly and most willingly received your command. To the extent that our weakness permitted, we have diligently sought and investigated, concerning the mystery of baptism, as it is contained in your letter, how we ought to understand and observe your instruction.

If we have dared to do this, we offer praises to your immeasurable clemency, because you have deigned to awaken us from the sleep of foolishness and ignorance, just as you are always and everywhere solicitous. Indeed, through this we and many others ought to be, and are, more learned and better, thanks to almighty God and to you.

Nevertheless, we ask your clemency that your kindness forgive us because we have not been able to report everything to you as we ought; rather, we shall follow in due order what the Fathers left to us through their examples and what we have understood in part according to our own weakness. [Col. 0981C]

Baptism is translated from Greek into Latin as *tinctio*, “dipping” or “immersion,” because in it a person is changed for the better by the Spirit of grace. For this reason the infant is immersed three times in the sacred font, so that the threefold immersion might mystically signify Christ’s three-day burial; and the raising from the water is an image of Christ rising from the tomb.

Therefore the mystery of baptism can in no way be completed except under invocation of the Holy Trinity, because it is right that the person who was created in the image of the Holy Trinity should be restored to that same [Col. 0981D] image.

A catechumen is interpreted as one who hears or is instructed, so that, before approaching the sacred font, he may hear and learn the mystical sacraments of the Christian religion, and then learn the faith of the Holy Trinity, the Creed, and the other things taught by Christian law.

*Scrutiny* means inquiry, because through it an investigation is made of how the Catholic faith is retained in their hearts. Alternatively, *scrutiny* derives from examining, because the catechumens are then to be examined to see whether they firmly hold the correct faith of the Creed recently handed down to them.

*Symbol*—in Greek, *symbolon*—is interpreted in Latin as “indication,” “sign,” or “collation.” It is an indication because through it the integrity of the faith is indicated; a sign because, when it is rightly retained and understood, the faithful are distinguished from unbelievers; and a collation because in it the apostles gathered together the whole integrity of the faith.

Thus those who are to be baptized profess that they believe in God the Father almighty, in his Son Jesus Christ, in the Holy Spirit, and in the rest of the Creed. Although infants cannot profess this of themselves, the Catholic faith confesses it through the hearts and mouths of those who hold them: namely, that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one in essence, one in power, and one in eternity; one invisible God, without beginning and without end.

Thus the Trinity must neither be divided in substance nor completely confused personally, while the distinct property of each person is preserved: the Father unbegotten; the Son begotten and born from the Virgin Mary, crucified, dead, risen, ascended into heaven, and seated at the right hand of the Father; and from there he will come in the same flesh to judge the living and the dead.

The Holy Spirit is neither begotten nor unbegotten, but proceeds from the Father and the Son. They also confess one Catholic Church and the communion of all the saints—that is, the assembly of all the faithful in Christ—and they believe in the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, life after death, and reigning with Christ forever and ever. Amen. [Col. 0982B–C]

*Abrenunciation* means rejection or detestation, because before baptism each person, on account of original sins, is a slave of sin. Therefore he renounces the devil, who is the prince of sin, and all his works and all his pomps—that is, his vices—in order to reject his condemnation. This renunciation is rightly followed by confession of the Holy Trinity, so that where sin abounded, grace may abound still more.

Those who are to be baptized are breathed upon by the priest of God, so that the prince of sinners may be driven out from them, an entrance may be prepared for Christ the Lord, and through that breathing they may deserve to receive the Holy Spirit.

*Exorcism*—in Greek, and in Latin *conjuratio*, “conjuration,” or a word of rebuke—is directed against the devil. Therefore each person coming to baptism is exorcized, so that he may become a temple of the living God. By nature he had become a temple of the devil; but when the devil withdraws, Christ enters through the priest’s exorcism, and the person becomes a dwelling place of God. [Col. 0982D–0983A]

They receive salt in the sacrament of baptism so that, by tasting it, they may receive the seasoning of wisdom, may not lose the savor of Christ, and may not become tasteless and foolish. What they naturally possessed as tasteless, they should through Christ’s grace have thoroughly seasoned with salt.

Their ears and nostrils are touched with spittle, and *effeta* is said—that is, “Be opened.” The nostrils are touched so that, as long as life accompanies them, the breath of life and the sense of smell remain in their nostrils, they may continually persevere in Christ’s service. Their ears are likewise touched so that they may always listen to and attentively hear the saving teaching of the Christian religion and faith, and reject all the ridiculous suggestions of the devil.

[Col. 0983B]

The breast is anointed with holy oil so that, by the sign of the Christian cross, an entrance may be shut to the devil and an entrance prepared for Christ the Lord.

The shoulders are marked so that, consecrated on every side as a temple of God, they may be fortified against every obstacle from Satan. This is also marked again in the anointing of the breast and shoulders, so that the person may receive strength and perseverance in good works.

After the bath of sacred regeneration, the baptized are clothed in white garments, to signify the mystical mystery of the rising Church, or on account of the joy of new regeneration, the purity of life, and the beauty of angelic splendor.

Then the head is anointed with sacred chrism, which in Latin is called *unctio*, “anointing,” so that, having been consecrated for the kingship and priesthood [Col. 0983C] of the Church, they may receive the grace of Christ’s name and become members of him who redeemed them and is their head.

Afterward they are covered with a mystical veil, so that they may understand that they bear the diadem of royal and priestly dignity and possess the adornment of royal dignity and the covering of the priestly head. Thus they may be protected against vices by a priestly veil, spiritually adorned with the jewels of virtues, and anointed with the unction of the most holy chrism, so that they may deserve to become a dwelling place of the Holy Trinity.

When all the sacraments of baptism have been completed, finally, through the laying on of hands by the chief priest, they receive the Spirit of sevenfold grace, so that they may be strengthened in the true faith through the Holy Spirit. The laying on of hands is therefore performed so that the Holy Spirit may be summoned and invited through the blessing.

Finally, it must be understood that, just as the other sacraments of baptism are visibly performed by priests and invisibly consecrated by the Lord, so the grace of the Holy Spirit is given to the faithful through the laying on of bishops’ hands and confirmed by the Lord. [Col. 0984A]

Lastly, they receive communion in the body and blood of the Lord so that they may become members of him who suffered and rose for them; and through visible bread and wine the soul may be nourished with invisible food, just as the Lord himself says: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink; and whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.” The Church observes this custom of receiving the Eucharist, handed down by the Lord, so that when someone is reborn through water and the Holy Spirit, he may be nourished by the Lord’s body and drink his blood; and, having been given into Christ’s body, he may remain in Christ and Christ in him. [Col. 0984B]

Thus ends the Sequerianus codex; but the Saint-Albinus manuscript of Angers adds the following:

For from a little child newly born to a decrepit old man, just as there is no one who does not die to sin in baptism, infants die only to original sin, while adults die also to all the sins they have added by living wrongly, as well as to the sin they brought with them at birth.

[Col. 0984C]

The sacrament of baptism is what the baptized person possesses, while the sacrament of administering baptism is what the person who is ordained possesses. Just as a baptized person does not lose the sacrament of baptism if he withdraws from unity—for no sacrament is to be wronged—so, if he departs from the wicked, both depart; if he remains among the wicked, both remain.

Therefore, just as baptism is accepted when it was not possible for the person who departed from unity to lose it, so baptism must be accepted when it was given by one who did not lose the sacrament of giving it when he departed.

[Col. 0983C]

# In the year of the Lord 818

# Saint Leo III, Roman Pontiff

[Col. 0993]

## Historical Notice concerning Saint Leo

(Mansi, *Ample Collection of Councils*, vol. XIII.)

[Col. 0993A]

Leo

[Note: [Col. 0993A] Leo. In the year of our Redeemer 795, on January 26, the very day on which Hadrian died, Leo III, the successor of that name, was elected. From his youth he had been well trained in ecclesiastical discipline and adorned with every virtue, and God had raised him to the pontifical see so that he might suffer and accomplish great things. At the beginning of his pontificate he is said to have suffered a burning of the flesh from a kiss that a woman had pressed upon his hand; it is added that he cut off the kissed hand himself and decreed that thereafter only the pontiff’s feet, not his hands, should be kissed. Both stories, however, are an old woman’s tale, more than merely fabulous. For it is established that even before that time it had been customary to kiss the pontiff’s feet, not his hands.

To honor Charles the Great as the most powerful defender of the Roman Church—not, as the innovators slanderously claim, in order to surrender possession of the city—Leo, following the example of his predecessors, sent him through a legation as an episcopal gift and present the golden keys of the confession of Saint Peter and the banner of the city of Rome, just as the patriarch of Jerusalem sent him keys together with a banner of the holy places as a blessing. On this occasion King Charles sent Engilbert, [Col. 0995D] abbot of the monastery of Saint Richarius, to return to the pontiff the most splendid gifts which that king had acquired from the treasure seized from the Huns (Annals of the Franks). The pontiff converted the treasures he received into ornaments for the churches and distributed them among the clergy, and he completed everything that Anastasius records before that persecution, apart from the other works he reported four years later, when Leo had returned from Germany.

Constantine V, after forcing his lawful wife into a monastery, married another woman named Theodora and crowned her empress. When Tarasius of Constantinople did not excommunicate the adulterer, Tarasius himself was judged unworthy of the company of the pious; those who, together with Theodore the Studite, rebuked the adulterous emperor were sent into exile. As Constantine continued thus to add crime to crime, he deservedly lost his eyes, imperial power, and life by order of his mother, whom he had stripped of the empire—an act prompted by zeal for justice, not for the kingdom. After Irene had held the recovered empire alone for five years, she was deprived of power and sent into exile by Nicephorus, a most impious man, supporter of all heretics, and most wicked despiser of the Roman Church and all clerics, in the year of the Lord 802; there she died the following year. (Theophanes, Annals, under Nicephorus.)

Leo restored Adolphus, king of the Northumbrians, to his kingdom after he had been expelled from it, through a legate of the Apostolic See (Annals of the Franks).

After the death of the emperor Charles, whom Einhard reports to have died piously and devoutly at Aachen in the year of Christ 814 after being seized by a fever, wicked men again rose up against the pontiff at the beginning of Louis’s reign and laid grave plots against his life. When the pontiff learned of this and ordered that the offenders be prosecuted according to law, a great sedition was stirred up at Rome. After numerous massacres, plunderings, and fires, so many and such great evils followed that the emperor Louis had to send Bernard, who had succeeded his brother Pippin in the kingdom of Italy, into the city. The Frankish annals relate in greater detail how these events occurred.

By the authority of this pontiff, at the request of King Alfonso, surnamed the Chaste, and through the intercession of Charles the Great, the episcopal see of the Church of Iria was transferred to Compostela. When the revered body of the apostle Saint James was discovered there and made especially illustrious by miracles, everyone judged it worthy and fitting, out of reverence for the apostolic dignity, that the place should be distinguished by the honor of an episcopal see. Thus all who have described the affairs of Spain report. Concerning Pope Leo, Walafrid Strabo writes in Book 21 of On Ecclesiastical Affairs that it had come to the knowledge of the faithful that he had often celebrated the solemn rites of Mass seven or nine times in a single day—perhaps so that by this means he might implore greater assistance from God, for he was daily afflicted by great and very grievous troubles. S. BIN.]

the third, a Roman by nationality, son of Azuppius, occupied the see for twenty years, five months, and seventeen days. From childhood he had been nourished and educated in the wardrobe of the patriarchate, and spiritually instructed in all ecclesiastical discipline. Skilled both in the Psalter and in the sacred divine Scriptures, he was made subdeacon and promoted to the dignity of the priesthood. He was a chaste man, eloquent in speech, and steadfast in spirit.

Whenever he found an outstanding monk or a servant of God, he did not cease to devote himself entirely with him to divine conversation and prayer. He was exceedingly cheerful in giving alms and also a most assiduous visitor of the sick, preaching to them according to Scripture [the Scriptures], so that they might redeem their souls [so that, through care for the poor, they might redeem their souls] by almsgiving.

Many who assented to his preaching secretly distributed to the poor, day and night, whatever he commended for Christ’s sake [whatever they possessed]. He frequently offered the fruit of souls to God for their salvation [they offering it]; and while he thus shone especially in the wardrobe, and the wardrobe-supervisor loved his most diligent care, he was loved most warmly by everyone.

[Col. 0995B] Therefore, by divine inspiration, in one accord and with one will, he was elected by all the priests and dignitaries, by all the clergy, by the nobles, and by the entire Roman people, through God’s providence, on the feast [birthday-feast] of blessed Stephen, the first martyr. On the following day, the feast [birthday-feast] of Saint John the apostle and evangelist, he was ordained pontiff in the Apostolic See, to the praise and glory of almighty God.

He was a defender of ecclesiastical property, a most powerful conqueror of adversaries, exceedingly gentle, and a distinguished and benevolent lover of that Church; slow to anger and quick to show mercy. He returned evil to no one for evil and inflicted no vengeance according to merit; rather, pious and merciful, from the time of his ordination he strove to render justice to all. He greatly increased the *rogam* [it appears to mean *rogam*, that is, an allowance] for his clergy, especially in the priesthood.

In the basilica of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, his own nourisher, he made a golden thurible before the entrance of the altar, weighing seventeen pounds. In the confession of the same apostle he also made *rugae* of the purest gold, with various gems, weighing forty-nine pounds. Likewise, three large silver crowns weighing 307 pounds. He also made white silk curtains with rose-colored decoration, bearing in the middle a cross of *chrysoclavus* [gold-and-purple embroidery] and one *periclysis* of *fundatus* [gold textile].

After repairing and roofing the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle—that is, the greater nave, and another nave above the altar, together with the four-sided portico and the fountain, as well as the silver doors—he also completely restored anew the tower with its chambers, from the bottom to the top, everything in every part. In particular, he placed on the gable beneath the great arch an image of the Savior, painted with the other figures in marvelous beauty, for the adornment of the aforesaid church. In the same manner he made and installed similar images in the basilica of blessed Paul the apostle and in the basilica of the Savior, in the manner of those images [that is, similar images].

[Col. 0996B] He also restored anew the roof and fabric of the title-church of blessed Anastasia, which through negligence had decayed from ancient times and was almost collapsing.

Likewise, he carefully renewed the title-church of Saint Sabina. In that church the same outstanding prelate made five silver crowns weighing fourteen pounds; two baskets weighing three and a half pounds; and nine engraved [interwoven] bowls weighing eleven pounds.

He also made in the basilica of the Blessed Mother of God, called *ad Praesepe*, a ciborium of the purest silver weighing 611 pounds. He likewise made silver *rugae* at the entrance to the presbytery weighing eighty pounds, and a large white silk curtain bearing a *periclysis* and a cross of *fundatus*.

Indeed, on the most sacred high altar he made a vestment of *chrysoclavus* bearing scenes of the Nativity and of Saint Simeon, and in the middle a *cheritismon* [greeting]. He also made in the chamber of the same church and in the four-sided portico three silver crowns weighing there 145 pounds [55 pounds] and nine ounces.

Meanwhile, in the basilica of blessed Lawrence, Christ’s martyr, situated outside the walls, he made three silver images of the Savior, blessed Peter the apostle, and Saint Lawrence, weighing altogether fifty-four and a half pounds. On the sacred altar he placed a silk *chrysoclave* vestment bearing scenes of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection.

He also renewed the roof and fabric of the churches of the blessed martyrs Felix and Adauctus near Saint Paul the Apostle, as well as the basilica of Saint Menas, the title-church of blessed Vitalis, Christ’s martyr, and the cemetery of blessed Sixtus and Cornelius on the Appian Way. He likewise renewed the cemetery of Saint Zoticus on the Lavican Way.

He similarly restored the church of the Holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, our Lady, situated at Fonticana, which had decayed through long neglect.

The same prelate made in the basilica of the teacher of the world, blessed Paul the apostle, [Col. 0997B] a confession and *rugae* of refined gold, set with precious gems in the likeness of those of blessed Peter the apostle, weighing 156 pounds. Above the same sacred altar he placed a golden image of the Savior and the twelve apostles, weighing seventy-five pounds. He also newly constructed the chamber of that basilica in the manner of the chamber of blessed Peter the apostle, and, especially, three silver crowns weighing together 220 pounds.

He made fifteen large silk curtains, stamped with designs, bearing a *periclysis* and a cross of *bathinus* or *fundatus*. Forty-three large miscellaneous curtains, covered with fourfold cloth, hung on the arches. Twenty small stamped curtains, adorned with fourfold cloth, hung on the smaller arches. Likewise, ten small *stauracin* curtains hung on the arches, and another ten, three of which had a *periclysis* of *chrysoclavus*. Four curtains were of equal Alexandrian thread. One *alithinus* curtain, woven in a circular pattern, had a *periclysis*, wheels with latticework, and in the middle a cross [Col. 0997C] with gems; and four matching wheels of Tyrian thread.

In the basilica of blessed Andrew, near blessed Peter the apostle, he made silver *rugae* weighing eighty pounds. He also made in the basilica of the Savior, called the Constantinian basilica, a chamber of marvelous size.

This beneficent prelate made on the high altar of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, a *chrysoclave* vestment adorned with precious gems, bearing scenes of the Savior granting blessed Peter the apostle the power of binding and loosing, and scenes representing the Passion of the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul. It shone with marvelous grandeur on the feast of the apostles.

He also made a vestment in the title-church of Eudoxia, over the altar, of Tyrian material, bearing large griffins, two *chrysoclave* wheels with a cross, and a *periclysis* of purple and *chrysoclavus*.

This distinguished prelate made in the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle a silver *pharus* before the presbytery, with thirty silver bowls, and an octagonal basket in the middle weighing sixty-three pounds. In the silver *canthari*, both around the altar and in the presbytery, he placed silver *cerostata* weighing there 212 pounds.

On the altar of blessed Petronilla he placed one *stauracin* vestment bearing a *periclysis* of purple, or *chrysoclavus*. He also made in the basilica of the Savior, which is also called the Constantinian, a vestment bearing a scene of the Crucified One and of the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, with a *periclysis* of *chrysoclavus*.

He also made in the basilica of blessed Clement one *stauracin* vestment bearing a *periclysis* of *chrysoclavus*. He also made on the silver arches of the church of God’s apostle very beautiful *stauracin* curtains.

This eminent pontiff, in the title-church of blessed Susanna, where he had been ordained priest, found the building briefly destroyed and its walls already decayed through long neglect. Because of his great love, he enlarged the structure, dug down anew, and laid the firmest foundations. After excavating the site, he built above those foundations a lofty church of extraordinary splendor, with a very large apse, marvelous mosaic vaults, and a decorated chamber or presbytery; he adorned the pavement with beautiful marbles. On the right and left he also built its porticoes with marble columns.

He established a baptistery there and offered gifts: three golden bowls of *fundatus*, weighing four and a half pounds; two golden crosses with gems, weighing one pound; silver rods weighing three pounds [Col. 0998B] and seven ounces; one silver lamp weighing five pounds; and three silver images weighing thirty-five pounds.
