He made the confession of the same altar of the purest silver, weighing 103 pounds and two ounces. He made eight silver columns, two *gammadia*, and two arches with five silver crosses, together with fifteen bowls weighing altogether 150 pounds. He made a *diacopton* cross weighing fourteen pounds. He made a basket of Cafutian cedar weighing twelve and a half pounds.

He made one large silver crown with thirty-two dolphins, weighing thirty-two pounds. He also made one silver basket weighing eighteen pounds, and another silver basket weighing eighteen pounds. He made gilded silver straining vessels weighing four pounds and three ounces. He made silver bowls with gilded griffins weighing two pounds. He made two silver crowns with eighteen dolphins, weighing nineteen pounds.

Indeed, the same eminent prelate made in that church one *chrysoclave* vestment with a *periclysis* of *chrysoclavus*, and another purple vestment bearing in the middle a cross of *chrysoclavus*. He made four *chrysoclave* panels ornamented with gems, and four *chrysoclave gammadia* on the same vestment, with a *periclysis* of *chrysoclavus*.

He also made in the Lateran patriarchate a great dining hall, more splendid than all the other dining halls and decorated in keeping with the greatness of his name. He laid the firmest foundations, adorned it around with marble slabs, and paved it with patterned marble. He decorated the chamber with various columns, both porphyry and white, carved and furnished with vessels and lilies, together with the doorposts. He adorned the apse and two other apses with mosaics, painting various scenes over the marble inlay and likewise decorating the surrounding area.

In the basilica of blessed Prisca the same prelate made one gilded *fundatus* chalice and three crowns, one of which bore ten dolphins and the other two nine each, as well as eight bowls weighing altogether twenty-nine pounds. He made a white silk vestment adorned around the edge with Byzantine purple and bearing on the front a cross of *chrysoclavus*.

This venerable and most holy prelate, while he lived according to ecclesiastical order in the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church and maintained the rite of orthodox faith, constructing and tastefully adorning extensive buildings everywhere, both in various churches and in the patriarchate,—

[Note: [Col. 0997D] One day, when Pope Leo was proceeding, as usual, in the litany called by everyone the Greater Litany, Anastasius, after recounting the pontiff’s munificence toward the holy buildings, adds here how the nephews of Pope Hadrian, serving in the first ranks of the Roman clergy and wasting away with envy, persecuted Leo because of his election. While he was engaged in the sacred procession, they gouged out his eyes and cut out his tongue; he then miraculously recovered his sight and speech, reached King Charles, and returned to Rome protected by his guardianship and patronage.

These events are also recorded in the Frankish Annals and by Ado in his Chronicle, where he says that sacrilegious hands were laid upon the pontiff on April 25, 799. Add that, when Leo was fleeing from Rome to Germany to reach King Charles, he passed through Cologne and came to the place where the venerable body of the man of God Severinus rests. There, contrary to the custom he had observed on the road, he entered the church to pray. His companions, astonished, asked the reason. According to Surius, under October 23, he replied: “This is the house of the protector of this place; therefore I did not dare to pass it without greeting him.” Hence, he says, the custom arose among the inhabitants that once each week they should come to the tomb of Saint Severinus and ask with humble devotion to be supported by his patronage throughout the entire week.

In the translation of Saint Liborius, under July 23 in Surius, it is written that Leo consecrated an altar at Paderborn and placed in it relics of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, which he had brought with him from Rome. These events certainly occurred on Pope Leo’s first arrival in Germany.

He came to Germany a second time in the year of the Lord 804. Concerning this visit of the pontiff, the Frankish Annals say: “In the middle of November it was reported to Charles that Pope Leo wished to celebrate the Nativity of the Lord with him, wherever this might be possible. Charles immediately ordered his son Charles to receive him honorably at Saint Maurice. He himself set out to meet him at the city of Rheims, and there received him, and so forth.”

A fuller account of what Leo did in Germany, which altars he consecrated at Cologne, and by what miracles he enrolled Saint Swibert among the canon of the saints, is found in a letter of Ludger in Surius, under March 1.

In the Life of Charles it is recorded that Leo prayed for his persecutors, interceded for them, and obtained that they should not be punished in their bodies but merely sent into exile, although they had been condemned to death as guilty of the crime of lèse-majesté. S. BIN.]

when one day [Col. 0999A] he proceeded, as usual, in the Litanies which everyone calls the Greater Litanies, where the people were supposed to meet him in a sacred procession, celebrate the Litanies and the solemn rites of Mass with the priests according to annual custom, and pour out prayers to almighty God for the salvation of the Christian people; and when, according to the ancient tradition, the litany had been proclaimed by a notary of the holy Roman Church in the church of Saint George, martyr of Christ, on his feast, all the men and women, with devout minds and in a great company, hurried to the church of blessed Lawrence, martyr of Christ, called that of Lucina, where the aforementioned gathering was taking place.

When the venerable pontiff had gone out from the patriarchate, the wicked and so-called Paschal, the *primicerius*, came to meet him without a chasuble and hypocritically asked his pardon, saying, “I am ill, and therefore I have come without a chasuble.” Then the most holy prelate forgave him.

Likewise Campulus, the treasurer, sharing their deceit, proceeded with him in pontifical service. They spoke sweet words to him which they did not have in their hearts—malignant, wicked, and perverse men, false Christians, utter pagans, sons of the devil. Satanically gathering together, filled with evil intentions, they secretly stood armed along the route before the monastery of Saints Stephen and Sylvester, which Pope Paul had founded. Suddenly leaping out from their place of ambush, they rushed together to slaughter him impiously—as it is unspeakable even to say—Paschal standing at his head and Campulus at his feet, according to their wicked plot.

When this had happened, all the people around him, unarmed and prepared for God’s service, terrified by the weapons, turned and fled. But the ambushers and perpetrators of evil, like Jews, with no regard for divine or human honor and in beastlike fashion, seized him and threw him to the ground. Stripping him by tearing away his clothes without any mercy, they cruelly attempted to gouge out his eyes and blind him completely.

For his tongue was cut out, and, as they themselves then believed, they left him blind and mute in the middle of the street. But the wicked Paschal and Campulus, like true pagans and impious men, dragged him to the church of that monastery, before the confession, and in front of the venerable altar again cruelly tore out his eyes and tongue. Beating him with various blows and clubs, they mangled him and left him half alive, rolling in blood, before the altar. Afterwards they left him under guard in the monastery.

Terrified that he might be stolen from them by Christian men, they then devised a wicked plan. As the abbot of the monastery of Saint Erasmus [Gerasimus] himself testified, the wicked Paschal, who was then *primicerius*, Campulus the treasurer, and Maurus of Nepi secretly summoned him to them during the night and sent him to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Sylvester with several wicked accomplices and fellow criminals.

[Col. 0999D] Thus during the night they took him away [Col. 1000A] [drew him off] and brought him to the monastery of Saint Erasmus, where they shut him in strict and narrow confinement. But almighty God, who had foreseen their malice and patiently endured it for a long time, wonderfully destroyed their wicked efforts.

For it happened, with God’s cooperation and blessed Peter the apostle’s assistance, that when the aforesaid pope was being sent by those executioners into custody at the monastery of Saint Erasmus, the Lord consenting and blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, interceding, he recovered his sight and his tongue was restored to him for speech.

To show that almighty God had bestowed upon his servant his accustomed mercy and a great miracle, faithful Christian men—namely, Albinus the chamberlain with other God-fearing believers—secretly took him from the monastery and brought him to the basilica of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, where his most sacred body rests.

All who heard and saw the wonders of God, who had rescued the innocent and just pontiff from the hands of his enemies, glorified the Lord God, saying: “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who alone works great wonders and has not abandoned those who hope in him” (Psalm 71). In him he fulfilled his mercy, so that the glory of God might be revealed and his wonders manifested, just as he had promised to those who hope in him, as the Psalmist says: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life; from whom shall I tremble?” (Psalm 26). And again: “Your word, Lord, is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths” (Psalm 118).

And truly, by rescuing him from darkness, the Lord restored his light and his tongue for speaking; he restored strength to all his limbs and, wonderfully guiding him in all his works, strengthened him.

As much joy as the Christian and faithful people experienced, so much grief and sorrow afflicted those men. Not knowing what to do and thinking themselves to be in danger, they sought to kill themselves. When they could think of nothing else to do, they plundered and destroyed the house of Albinus, the faithful servant of blessed Peter the apostle and of the same pontiff.

As the pontiff entered the aula of blessed Peter the apostle, the glorious duke Winichis of Spoleto, with his army, immediately met him there. When he saw the supreme pontiff seeing and speaking, he received him with reverence and led him to Spoleto, glorifying and praising God, who had glorified him through such great wonders.

When this became known throughout the various cities, the faithful Romans hastened to him. Together with certain bishops from those cities, Roman priests and clerics, and the leading men of the cities, he proceeded to the most excellent lord Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans.

When that most Christian, orthodox, distinguished, and most merciful king heard, he immediately sent Archbishop and chaplain Hildivald and Count Ascharius to meet him. Afterwards he again sent his own excellent son, King Pippin, with other counts to meet him [Col. 1000D] [Col. 1001A], and went out himself until the great king met him. He received him reverently and honorably, with hymns and spiritual songs, as the vicar of blessed Peter the apostle. They embraced one another and kissed one another with tears.

When the pontiff began the *Gloria in excelsis Deo* and all the clergy joined in receiving it, a prayer was offered over the entire people. Then the most kindly lord, King Charles the Great, seeing the aforesaid pontiff, gave thanks to God, who had worked such great wonders upon his servant through the intercession of the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, and had brought the aforementioned wicked men to nothing.

After the serene king had kept him for some time in great honor, the aforesaid wicked men and sons of the devil, hearing of this, and after the dreadful and wicked burnings they had carried out against the possessions and property of blessed Peter the apostle, plotted—God opposing them—to bring false accusations [contrary and false accusations] against the most holy pontiff and to send them afterward to the aforesaid king, although they could in no way prove them. They made such accusations because they wished to humiliate the holy Church through their ambushes and wickedness—things too shameful to name.

But while the aforesaid pontiff was living with great and appropriate honor before the most merciful and mighty king, archbishops, bishops, and other priests came from every direction, together with the counsel [son] of that most pious great king, and all the distinguished Franks. With God going before them, they honorably sent him back [sent him as he was returning] to Rome, to his Apostolic See, with the greatest honor, as was fitting [dismissed him]. Through every city they escorted him to Rome as though they were receiving the apostle himself.

Then the Romans, receiving their shepherd with overwhelming joy, all together, on the vigil of blessed Andrew the apostle—the leading clergy with all the clerics, the nobles and senate, the entire military, the whole Roman people, the nuns, deaconesses, and most noble matrons, together with [Col. 1001C] all the women, and all the foreign guilds, namely those of the Franks, Frisians, Saxons, and Lombards—joined together and received him at the Milvian Bridge with standards, banners, and spiritual songs. They led him into the church of blessed Peter the apostle, where he celebrated the solemn rites of Mass. All together they faithfully shared in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

On the following day, celebrating the feast of blessed Andrew the apostle according to the ancient custom, he entered Rome with great joy and gladness and entered the Lateran patriarchate.

[Col. 1002A]

After several days, the most faithful envoys who had come with him for pontifical service—namely the most reverend archbishops Hildivald and Arno; the most reverend and holy bishops Cunibert, Bernhard [Berahard], Hatto, and Tesse [Iesse]; as well as Flaccus, the elected bishop; and also the glorious counts Helmgoth, Rothegarius, and Germanus—sat in the dining hall of that lord Pope Leo. For a week and more they investigated the most wicked criminals, asking what malice they had harbored against their own pontiff. Neither Paschal nor Campulus, nor their followers, had anything to say against him.

Then the envoys of the great king seized them and sent them into Francia.

[Note: [Col. 1001C] After he had been received shortly afterward with great honor, the honor with which the pontiff welcomed Charles when he came to Rome is explicitly described by the Frankish Annals in these words:

“On the day before Charles came to Rome, Pope Leo met him at Nomentum and received him there with great reverence. After the evening meal at which they refreshed themselves together, Charles remained there while the pontiff proceeded to the city. On the following day, after sending out to meet him the banners of the city of Rome and arranging in suitable places companies of foreigners and citizens who would sing praises to the approaching king, Leo himself, with the clergy and bishops, received him as he dismounted from his horse and ascended the steps. After offering a prayer, he led him into the basilica of blessed Peter while everyone sang. This took place on November 24.” S. BIN.]

After a short time, when the great king himself had arrived at the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle and had been received with great honor, [Note: [Col. 1001D] Charles the Great acted. In these words he describes the proceedings of the synod held concerning the case of Leo, on the eighth day after Charles had come to Rome. ID.] he ordered archbishops, bishops, abbots, and all the nobility of the Franks and Romans to assemble in that same church.

The great king and the most blessed pontiff sat together and had the most holy archbishops and abbots seated, while the remaining priests and nobles of the Franks and Romans stood, so that they might reject [examine] the crimes that had been alleged against the gracious pontiff.

All the archbishops, bishops, and abbots, hearing them unanimously, said: “We do not dare to judge the Apostolic See, which is the head of all the Churches of God. For by it and by its vicar we are all judged; but it is judged by no one, as has been the ancient custom. Rather, as the supreme pontiff himself shall determine, so will we obey canonically.”

The venerable prelate replied: “I follow in the footsteps of my predecessors, the pontiffs, and I am prepared to purge myself of such false accusations, which have been wickedly raised against me.”

On the following day, when all the archbishops, bishops, and abbots were present in the same church of blessed Peter the apostle, together with all the Franks who were in the service of the same great king and all the Romans in that church, the aforesaid venerable pontiff embraced the holy four Gospels of Christ in the presence of everyone, ascended the ambo, and said in a clear voice under oath:

“Concerning these false crimes which the Romans who wickedly persecuted me have laid against me, I have no knowledge, nor do I acknowledge that I have committed such things.”

When this had been done, all the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and clergy, after the Litany had been performed, gave praise to God, to the Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, our Lady, to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to all the saints of God.

[Note: [Col. 1001D] Afterwards, when the feast of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ arrived in the aforesaid basilica, he here relates by what form and rites he crowned as emperor Charles, who had deserved exceptionally well of the Roman Church, and transferred the entire empire from the Greeks to the kingdom of the Franks and to his successors.

The same history is narrated in nearly the same words by Einhard, Charles’s secretary, an eyewitness and observer of the events, in his Life of Charles; by Paul the Deacon; by Theophanes in the Frankish Annals (Binius is mistaken); by the Annals composed under Louis; by Aimoinus; by Ado of Vienne in his Chronicle; by Regino; and by all Greek and Latin writers alike. No one except a stubborn and shameless heretic could deny a history so famous and attested by so many writers.

That all these events occurred with the greatest justice, with immense benefit to the whole Church, and moreover by God’s providence, will, and counsel, has been clearly, learnedly, and solidly demonstrated against the heretics and innovators of our time by the two most distinguished ornaments of the apostolic college, Bellarmine and Baronius. The latter, in volume 9 of his Annals under the year 800, says that Bellarmine succeeded so happily in what he attempted concerning the transfer of the empire against Illyricus that neither we nor others need labor greatly over it, but rather ought to rejoice and give thanks to that most powerful defender of the truth, because by his immense labor he has spared us from having to thrust a sickle into so dense and immeasurable a forest of lies. ID.]

After this, when the feast of the Nativity of our Lord [Col. 1003A] Jesus Christ arrived, everyone again assembled in the aforesaid basilica of blessed Peter the apostle. Then the venerable and beneficent pontiff with his own hands crowned him [Charles the Great] with the most precious crown.

At that time all the faithful Romans, seeing the great protection and affection he had shown toward the holy Roman Church and its vicar, unanimously cried out in a loud voice, by God’s will and through the intercession of blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven:

“To Charles, most pious Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor: life and victory!”

Before the sacred confession of blessed Peter the Apostle, after invoking many saints, this was said three times, and by all he was constituted emperor of the Romans. Immediately the most holy bishop and pontiff anointed Charles and his most excellent son, the king, with holy oil on that very day of the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ. After Mass had been celebrated [Note: After the celebration of the Masses. The offerings that Anastasius describes here were presented by Charles to the Roman basilicas in the year of Our Lord 800—or, if one begins counting from the Nativity of the Lord, in the year 801. SEV. BIN.], the most serene lord emperor himself offered a silver table with its feet, weighing [lacuna].

[Col. 1003B]

Moreover, in the confession of that same apostle of God, together with his most excellent son the king and his daughters, he offered various vessels of the purest gold for the service of that table, weighing [lacuna]. He also offered a golden crown with large gems, hanging above the altar, weighing fifty-five pounds; a larger golden paten with various gems, weighing thirty pounds; a larger chalice with gems and two handles, weighing fifty-eight pounds; likewise, a larger cast chalice with a siphon, weighing thirty-seven pounds; and yet another larger cast chalice, weighing thirty-six pounds.

He also offered upon the most sacred altar of blessed Peter the Apostle, and indeed in the basilica of blessed Paul the Apostle, a smaller silver table with its feet, weighing fifty-five pounds, together with various silver vessels of extraordinary size belonging to the use of that table.

[Col. 1003C]

Likewise, in the basilica of the Savior of Our Lord Jesus Christ, which is called Constantinian, he offered a cross with hyacinth-colored gems, which the life-giving pontiff ordered to be carried before him in the litany at the request of that most pious emperor. He also offered an altar with silver columns and a ciborium.

He likewise offered a Gospel book of the purest gold adorned with gems, weighing [lacuna]. And in the basilica of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, at the Crèche, he offered larger silver vessels, weighing [lacuna].

Afterward, when those most wicked evildoers—namely Paschalis, together with Campulus and their followers—had been brought into the presence of the most pious lord emperor, while the most noble Franks and Romans stood around them and all reproached them for their evil counsels and deeds, Campulus rebuked Paschalis, saying: “At an evil hour I saw your face, since you sent me into this danger.” The others likewise, each condemning the other, revealed their own offenses. When the most pious emperor recognized them as so cruel and wicked, he sent them into exile in the regions of Francia.

The aforementioned most holy pontiff caused a wonderfully beautiful apse to be made beside the church of blessed Peter the Apostle, in the greater dining hall, decorated with mosaic; and two apses, on the right and left, gleaming with marble and painting. He also laid out the pavement with marble designs, and, together with other spacious buildings, constructed them attractively both at the ascent of the staircase and behind the dining hall.

Likewise, in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle he made a gold-embroidered textile adorned with precious gems, bearing a representation of the Lord’s Resurrection. He also made, between the silver arches, white silk curtains and beautiful curtains of *stauracium*.

After his return, and because of his great affection, he made for that same foster-father of his a wholly new presbytery of marble, of great beauty, sculpted and attractively erected. Above the high altar he also made four curtains of *holosericum alythinum*, with rods and gold-embroidered roses.

On that same altar he made a Tyrian textile bearing scenes of the crucified Lord. In the church of the teacher of the world, blessed Paul the Apostle, he made four curtains of *holosericum alythinum*, and an *alha* textile above the altar, embroidered with gold and bearing a representation of the holy Resurrection. He also made another gold-embroidered textile bearing scenes of the Nativity of the Lord and of the Holy Innocents. He further made another Tyrian textile bearing scenes of the healing of the blind man and the Resurrection.

The same most holy bishop made in the basilica of the Blessed Mary at the Crèche a white, gold-embroidered textile bearing a representation of the holy Resurrection. He also made another textile with gold-embroidered roundels bearing scenes of the Annunciation and of the holy Joachim and Anne.

In the church of blessed Lawrence outside the walls, the same bishop made a white rose-colored textile with gold embroidery. He also made another white textile of *stauracium*, embroidered with gold and pearls, to be placed over his holy body.

In the titular church of Callistus he made a gold-embroidered textile of Byzantine purple, bearing a representation of the Lord’s Nativity and of Saint Simeon. Likewise, in the church of Saint Pancratius he made a Tyrian textile bearing a representation of the Lord’s Ascension. In Saint Mary at the Martyrs he made a Tyrian textile as above; in the titular church of Saint Sabina, likewise; in the deaconry of Saint Boniface, likewise; and in the deaconry of Saint Mary called *Cosmidin*, likewise.

[Col. 1004C]

In the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian he made a textile of Byzantine purple, with a border of gold embroidery and pearls. Likewise, in the church of Saint Valentine he made a gold-embroidered textile, and another extraordinarily beautiful textile of *fundatus*. In the deaconry of Saints Nereus and Achilleus he made a textile of *stauracium*. In the deaconry of the Holy Mother of God, called *Dominica*, he made a textile of *stauracium*.

That life-giving pontiff himself made in the venerable monastery of Saint Sabas a silver *butron* with its basket, weighing twelve pounds, and a textile of *stauracium* with gold embroidery and pearls. In the monastery of Saint Erasmus he made a textile of *stauracium* with a cross and *gammadia*, together with its *paratrapeta*, and with a border of gold embroidery.

In the titular church of Pammachius he made two textiles: one of *stauracium* with a border of gold embroidery, and another of *imizinum*.

The often-mentioned most holy bishop newly repaired the church of blessed Andrew the Apostle, situated at the thirtieth milestone on the Appian Way at *Scilice*, together with its baptistery and portico. In that church he established a presbytery, where he also offered gifts both in silver and in textiles and books.

[Note: In the ninth indiction, when punishment for our sins was impending, an earthquake suddenly occurred on the day before the Kalends of May, and the church of Saint Paul, etc. The Frankish annals likewise describe these events in the Life of Charlemagne, under the year 801, in these words: “The emperor Charlemagne departed from Rome on the seventh day before the Kalends of May and came to Spoleto. While he was there, on the day before the Kalends of May, in the second hour of the night, a very great earthquake occurred, and all Italy was violently shaken. In that earthquake the roof of the basilica of Saint Paul the Apostle at Rome fell for the most part, together with its beams, and in some places cities and mountains collapsed, etc.” Anastasius recounts at length what ornaments and expenditures he contributed after the earthquake for restoring, enlarging, and embellishing the aforesaid basilica of Saint Paul and several others. What he records as having been offered to the churches by the pontiff before the earthquake, however, was offered by him after he had returned from Germany. ID.]

In the ninth indiction [Year 801], when punishment for our sins was impending, an earthquake suddenly occurred on the day before the Kalends of May, and the church of blessed Paul the Apostle, shaken by that earthquake, collapsed in all its structures.

When the great and illustrious pontiff saw this, he fell into profound distress and began to lament both the silver and the other objects that had been cast down and broken there. But with the Lord’s approval, and with the blessed prince of the apostles protecting him, the aforementioned pontiff, applying all his strength to the task and restoring it with great and exceptional vigor as it had existed in ancient times, brought it into a better condition. He adorned it with marble in finer form, covered with marble both the presbytery and the entire church, and renewed its portico.

At the same time, in the canopy above the altar he newly restored all the roofwork and offered there three golden images: namely, those of the Savior, Our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the blessed princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul. He also placed above the doorposts at the entrance a gilded silver image of the Savior, weighing sixty pounds.

He newly restored all the silverwork there that had been shattered, and adorned the windows of that church with bronze of extraordinary beauty.

[Col. 1005B]

In the basilica of the Savior, called Constantinian, the aforementioned pontiff placed two textiles above the altar: one with gold embroidery and gems, bearing a representation of the Savior entering the holy city; the other gold-embroidered and adorned with precious gems, bearing a representation of the Lord’s Resurrection.

Around the altar he placed four red silk curtains and four white ones with gold embroidery. He also placed three curtains before the images, with a border, and thirty-seven additional white silk curtains.

On the altar of blessed Venantius he made a textile of *fundatus*, with two curtains. In the oratories of Saints John the Baptist and John the Evangelist he made textiles of *stauracium*, with gold embroidery, and two curtains.

The same aforementioned pontiff made above the altar of blessed Peter the Apostle a textile with a vine of the purest gold, adorned with the most precious gems and pearls. In its center it bore the face of the Savior, and of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and of the twelve apostles. He used twenty-five pounds of gold for it.

He also made another gold-embroidered textile bearing a representation of the Greater Litany. He further made another textile with three gold-embroidered panels, displaying the account of the Lord’s Passion and reading: “This is my body, which will be given for you,” and so forth. Likewise, he made a larger curtain of *fundatus*.

He also made, between the silver arches, Easter curtains with borders of *stauracium*: five with gold embroidery, ninety-three in number; and in the arches forty-eight larger white curtains.

He made fifteen *gabathae* of the purest gold, hanging in the canopy before the altar and adorned with gems, weighing sixty-five and a half pounds. He also made before the confession a panel of the purest gold, weighing twenty-nine pounds.

He placed above the larger doors two gilded silver images, weighing ninety pounds. He also made two silver *canthara* in the presbytery, weighing fifty pounds, and adorned the windows of that church with Cyprian metal. He also decorated other windows with glass of various colors.

In the basilica of the teacher of the world, blessed Paul the Apostle, he made a gold-embroidered textile bearing in the center the Savior, and on the right and left the blessed Peter and Paul preaching to the nations, with a border of gold embroidery and precious gems.

Above the altar of blessed Andrew he made a gold-embroidered textile with pearls, and he adorned the presbytery with marble. On the altar of blessed Petronilla he made a white silk textile with panels of gold embroidery and a cross, and there he adorned the presbytery with carved marble.

He made six silver columns and two *regulares* of the purest silver, weighing together eighty pounds. Over the body of blessed Gregory, confessor and pontiff, he made a white silk textile with panels of gold embroidery and a cross.

Likewise, in the basilica of the Holy Mother of God at the Crèche he made an Alexandrian curtain with a border of *stauracium*, another white curtain with a border of *stauracium*, and another white curtain with a border of Byzantine purple, hanging above the altar. Before the Crèche he placed white curtains with borders of Byzantine purple.

He also made twelve curtains inside the larger doors and before the sacristy, and inside the Crèche he made a textile of *alithinum* with gold embroidery.

In the basilica of blessed Lawrence the martyr outside the walls he made a Tyrian curtain with a border of *stauracium*. In the basilica of blessed Pancratius the martyr he made a ciborium of the purest silver, weighing 367 pounds.

In the titular church of Callistus, in honor of the holy Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, he made a silver ciborium weighing 504½ pounds.

In the titular church of Eudoxia he made a white textile with a border of gold embroidery. In the titular church of Saint Cecilia he made a textile of *stauracium*. In the titular church of Saint Eusebius he made a textile of *fundatus*. In the titular church of Saint Vitalis he made a textile of *stauracium* with a cross of gold embroidery.

[Col. 1006B]

In the titular church of Saint Pudentiana he made a textile as above. In the titular church of Saint Anastasia he made a textile of *fundatus*. In the titular church of Saint Praxedes he made a textile of *stauracium* with a border of Byzantine purple. In the basilica of blessed Lawrence at *Formoso* he made a textile of *quadrapulum*.

In the monastery of Saint Anastasius he made a textile of gold embroidery, depicting the Passion of that martyr, and a silver *pharus* with an octagonal basket, weighing twenty-five pounds.

In the monastery of Saint Sylvester he made two textiles: one Byzantine textile with gold embroidery in the greater basilica, and another of *fundatus* in the oratory.

In the monastery of Saint Lucy at *Renatis* he made a textile of *fundatus* with gold embroidery. At Saint Angelo in *Fabiano* he made a textile of *fundatus*. In the deaconry of Saint Lucy at the Seven Ways he made a textile of *fundatus*.

In the deaconry of Saints Sergius and Bacchus he made a textile of *stauracium*. In the deaconry of Saint Lucy at *Orfea* he made a textile of *stauracium*, and in the deaconry of Saint Eustachius he made a textile of *fundatus*.

That venerable and life-giving pontiff, protected by God, made in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle, his foster-father, a crucifix of the purest silver in the middle of the basilica, weighing seventy-two pounds.

Likewise, in the Lateran patriarchate he made a dining hall of extraordinary size, adorned with a mosaic apse, and ten other apses, on the right and left, painted with various scenes, containing apostles preaching to the nations and adjoining the Constantinian basilica. In that place he also set couches and, in the middle, a porphyry basin pouring forth water. He also paved its floor with various marbles.

In the titular church of Saint Quiriacus he made a textile of *stauracium* with a border of Byzantine purple, with gold embroidery around the edge and, in the center, a cross of pearls.

In the cemetery of Saint Sixtus on the Appian Way he made a textile of *stauracium*, with a cross of gold embroidery in the center. In the titular church of Callistus, above the altar behind the apse, he made a textile of *stauracium*, with a cross of gold embroidery in the center; and there likewise he made six curtains of *stauracium*.

In the titular church of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs he made a textile of *stauracium*, bearing in the center a cross of gold embroidery. In the titular church of Saint Marcellus he made a textile of *stauracium*.

At the same time, in the church of the holy martyr Sabina he made a textile of *fundatus*, with a border of Byzantine purple and, in the center, a cross of gold embroidery. In the basilica of Saint Lawrence at *Formoso* he likewise made a textile of *fundatus*.

The church of blessed Paul the Apostle called *Conventus*, situated in the territory of Orvieto within the boundaries of Suana, Clusium—or Tuscia—and Castrum, had already rotted away from excessive age, and beasts used it as a refuge; moreover, its relics had been removed. The same most holy bishop and pontiff ordered it to be cleansed, newly restored all its roofs and porticoes, placed a textile of *stauracium* on its altar, and ordered the relics to be reinterred.

Likewise, in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle situated at Albano, which was already on the point of collapsing from excessive age, he newly restored all its roofs.

The same life-giving pontiff made in the basilica of blessed Hippolytus the martyr in the city of Portus two textiles of *stauracium*: one over his body and another on the high altar. In the titular church of the holy martyr Sabina he made four curtains of *stauracium* with borders of Byzantine purple.

In the oratory of the Holy Mother of God situated in the hospice at *Firmis* he made a most beautiful textile of *stauracium*.

That pontiff, protected by God and illustrious, established that litanies should be celebrated during the three days before the Lord’s Ascension—namely, on Monday, when the pontiff, with all the clergy and the entire people, would go out from the church of the Mother of God at the Crèche, with hymns and spiritual songs, proceeding to the church of the Savior called Constantinian; on Tuesday, when they would go out from the church of the holy martyr Sabina and proceed to blessed Paul the Apostle; and on Wednesday, when they would go out from the church of Jerusalem and proceed to the church of blessed Lawrence the martyr outside the walls.

He also made in the titular church of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs a textile of *stauracium*, bearing in the center a cross of gold embroidery.

The same most holy bishop made in the basilica of blessed Agapitus the martyr in the city of Praeneste a textile of *stauracium* with a border of *fundatus*, and in the center a cross of gold embroidery.

In the church of blessed Clement, situated at Velletri, the same most holy bishop made a textile of *stauracium*. Likewise, in the titular church of blessed Chrysogonus he made a textile of *stauracium* with a border of Byzantine purple.

In the titular church of blessed Lawrence at Lucina he made a textile of *stauracium* with a border of Byzantine purple. In the titular church of blessed Mark he made a textile of *stauracium* with a border. In the titular church of blessed Lawrence in Damasus he made a textile likewise.

In the titular church of blessed Sixtus he made a textile of *stauracium* with a border of Byzantine purple; and likewise in the deaconry of blessed Hadrian, in the church of blessed Martina, and in the ancient deaconry he made textiles of *stauracium* with borders.

Likewise, in the deaconry of the blessed archangel he made three textiles: one of *stauracium* with a border of Byzantine purple, and two others of Tyrian fabric with borders of Byzantine purple; and two further Tyrian textiles with borders of *fundatus*, bearing scenes of elephants. In the deaconry of Saint Theodore he made a textile of *stauracium* with a border.

In the deaconry of blessed George he made a textile of *fundatus* with a scene of elephants, or various scenes, with a border of *fundatus*. In the deaconry at *Gyro* he made a textile of *stauracium* with a border of Byzantine purple. Likewise, in the deaconry on the Via Lata he made two Tyrian textiles with borders of Byzantine purple.

In the deaconry of Saint Agatha he made a textile of *stauracium* with a border of Byzantine purple. In the basilica of the blessed archangel situated at *Septimum* he made a textile of *stauracium* with a border of Byzantine purple.

In the monastery of Saint Agapitus situated at the Chains, he made a textile of *stauracium*.

[Col. 1007D]

The same most merciful bishop made in the church of blessed Agnes the martyr, where her body rests, a textile of *fundatus* with a border of Byzantine purple. In the church of blessed Apollinaris he made a textile of *stauracium* with a border of Byzantine purple.

The same most merciful bishop also made in the titular church of Saints Martin and Sylvester two textiles of *stauracium*: one with a border of *fundatus*, and the other of Byzantine purple.

In the deaconry of Saint Vitus he made a textile of *stauracium* with a border of *fundatus*. In the church of blessed Eugenia, where her holy body rests, he made a textile of *stauracium* with a border of Byzantine purple.

In the church of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill he made two textiles of *stauracium*: one on the high altar and the other over the bodies of the holy martyrs Primus and Felicianus.

At the same time, in the basilica of blessed Euphemia he made a textile of *stauracium*, and in the basilica of the blessed archangel situated in the Street of the Patricians he made a textile of *stauracium*.

He also made above the tomb of blessed Sebastian the martyr on the Appian Way at the Catacombs two larger textiles: one of *stauracium* and the other of *fundatus*. There, above the tombs of the apostles Peter and Paul, he made two textiles of *stauracium* and *fundatus*, or Byzantine purple.

The same most holy bishop made in the basilica of blessed Lawrence the martyr, situated below the city of Tibur, a textile of *stauracium*. In the oratory of Saint Stephen at Saint Peter, which is called the Greater, he made a textile of *stauracium*.

In the basilica of blessed Hyacinthus situated in the Sabine territory, where his body also rests, he made a most beautiful textile of *stauracium*.

The same pontiff, protected by God and illustrious, made above the altar of blessed Peter the Apostle, his patron, a textile of gold embroidery of extraordinary size, bearing a representation of the Lord’s Nativity and adorned with the most precious gems and pearls.

In the aforesaid church he made curtains of *stauracium* and *fundatus*, hanging between the larger columns on the right and left, sixty-five in number.

[Col. 1008B]

He also made three other larger white silk curtains hanging before the doors at the entrance. There too his Blessedness made a crucifix of the purest silver, of extraordinary size and decoration, standing beside the high altar and weighing fifty-two pounds. Above it he made six *gabathae* with a cross of the purest silver, hanging before the larger arch on the right and left and weighing together twelve and a half pounds.

The illustrious pontiff also made there curtains of *stauracium*, hanging on silver arches around the altar and in the presbytery, ninety-six in number. Of these, two had crosses of gold embroidery with roundels in the center, and another eight had borders of gold embroidery.

He also made in the aforesaid church arches with their columns of the purest silver, in the middle of the presbytery, weighing together 251½ pounds.

The same life-giving pontiff made there a repoussé, chased cross of the purest gold, hanging in the canopy before the altar with twelve candles, weighing thirteen pounds.

[Col. 1008C]

The aforesaid venerable pontiff also made in the basilica of the teacher of the world, blessed Paul the Apostle, larger cast chalices of the purest silver, from the gifts of that apostle, hanging from the larger arch, eleven in number; and others hanging between the larger columns on the right and left, forty in number, weighing together 267 pounds.

This same life-giving bishop, filled with divine inspiration, made in the basilica of blessed Paul the Apostle a ciborium with its columns above the altar, of extraordinary size and beauty, of the purest silver, weighing 2,015 pounds.

He also made a repoussé, chased cross of the purest gold, hanging in the canopy before the altar and weighing thirteen pounds; and a red curtain hanging before the altar, bearing in the center a cross of gold embroidery and a border of gold embroidery.

[Col. 1008D]

Likewise, in the basilica of the Holy Mother of God at the Crèche he made five *gabathae* of the purest gold, weighing eight and a half pounds, and a cross of the purest gold weighing ten pounds. He also made a larger crown of the purest silver weighing thirty-six pounds.

There too he made forty-two white silk curtains hanging between the larger columns on the right and left, eleven of them rose-colored. Around the altar he also made other rose-colored white silk curtains, hanging from the ciborium’s arch, four in number; one of these had gold embroidery and pearls. He also made another larger white curtain hanging before the larger doors at the entrance.

He newly repaired all the roofs of the church of blessed Aurea situated at Ostia.

The church of blessed Marcellus situated in the Fourteenth Region, which had been burned by fire, the same life-giving bishop wholly restored anew.

In the basilica of the Savior called Constantinian he made four white silk curtains around the altar, one of which had in the center a panel with a cross of gold embroidery.

[Col. 1009A]

In that same basilica of the Savior, Our Lord Jesus Christ, he renewed the magnificently decorated high altar of the purest silver, weighing sixty-nine pounds.

In the basilica of the Holy Mother of God at the Crèche he made a gold-embroidered textile adorned with pearls, bearing a representation of the Lord’s Nativity.

He also made two silver arches in the presbytery with four columns, and five other arches, weighing 133 pounds.

The same distinguished bishop made in the basilica of the Holy Mother of God at the Crèche a red *alithinum* textile, bearing in the center a gold-embroidered panel with a scene of Our Lord Jesus Christ and Saint Simeon when he was presented in the Temple, and with a border of gold embroidery around it.

He also made another gold-embroidered textile bearing a representation of the Dormition of the Holy Mother of God, decorated with precious gems and pearls, with a border of gold embroidery and a gold-embroidered border around it.

[Col. 1009B]

In the deaconry of that Mother of God, our Lady, called *Dominica*, he made a red *alithinum* textile bearing in the center a gold-embroidered panel with a representation of that same Mother of God, adorned with pearls, and with a border of gold embroidery.

In the deaconry of that Mother of God, called *Antiqua*, he made above the high altar a ciborium of the purest silver, weighing 212 pounds.

The aforementioned venerable and illustrious pontiff made in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle, his foster-father, a repoussé *gabatha* of the purest gold adorned with precious gems. It hangs before the image of that apostle at the entrance of the vestibule and weighs seven and a half pounds.

He overlaid with very bright gold the front of the sacred altar of that prince of the apostles from bottom to top, together with the lamps below and above; likewise, within the confession, the standing Savior, with the blessed apostles Peter and Paul on his right and left, likewise wearing crowns of precious gems; and the pavement of that confession, weighing 453 pounds and six ounces.

He further made above that sacred altar a gold-embroidered textile bearing a representation of the Lord’s Ascension and Pentecost, with a border of gold embroidery.

Likewise, in the place mentioned above, he made an image of that prince of the apostles at the Gate of the Men, of the purest gold and precious gems, of extraordinary size and beauty, weighing nineteen pounds and three ounces.

Most especially, the same most blessed pontiff made there cast screens at the entrance of the presbytery—that is, on the right and left—as well as at the entrance of the vestibule, of the purest silver, weighing together 1,573 pounds.

He also made turned or revolving columns [*volatiles*; perhaps *tornatiles* or *versatiles*] at the entrance to the nave, on the right and left, on the side of the men and of the women, eight in each group, weighing together 190 pounds; and eight silver arches, weighing together 143 pounds.

The same most blessed pontiff made in the basilica of blessed Andrew, mentioned above, a *regnum* of the purest gold adorned with precious gems, weighing two pounds and five ounces.

Likewise, above the altar of blessed Petronilla, mentioned above, he made a golden *regnum* with the most precious gems, weighing two pounds and three ounces.

In the same manner, above the altar of the Holy Mother of God mentioned above, which is called *Mediana*, he made a textile of *fundatus* with a border of gold embroidery, bearing a representation of the Lord’s Annunciation.

The same most blessed pontiff made in the basilica of the teacher of the world, blessed Paul the Apostle, forty-seven silver baskets, weighing together 247 pounds.

In the monastery of Saint Agatha the martyr above the Subura he made a red *alithinum* textile bearing in the center a gold-embroidered panel with a border of gold embroidery.

In the monastery of Saint Pancratius situated behind the basilica of the Savior, called Constantinian, he made a textile of *fundatus*.

He made for blessed Peter the Apostle, his patron, a golden Gospel book ornamented around with green, hyacinth-colored, and white gems, of extraordinary size, weighing seventeen pounds and four ounces.

He made a particularly fine golden chalice adorned with various precious stones, weighing twenty-eight pounds. Likewise, he made a golden paten weighing twenty-eight pounds and nine ounces.

In the basilica of that apostle he made four gilded cherubim of the purest silver, standing above the capitals of the silver columns with the ciborium and weighing ninety-three pounds.

The same distinguished bishop also made there a golden image of the Savior, standing on the beam above the entrance to the vestibule, weighing seventy-nine pounds.

In the basilica of the teacher of the world, blessed Paul the Apostle, he made two angels of the purest gilded silver, standing beside the image of the Savior at the entrance to the vestibule, weighing 100½ pounds.

He also made a porphyry *polycandelum* hanging in the canopy before the confession on golden chains, which weigh one pound.

Most especially, at the entrance to the basilica mentioned above, above the larger doors, he made five silver images, weighing there 229 pounds.

There too he made two pairs of gilded *aquamanus antipempta*, weighing together fourteen pounds.

The same prescient bishop made there larger, movable, repoussé, cast *cerostatae* of the purest silver, weighing together eighty-six pounds and eight ounces.

He also made two larger, cast, double-branched, repoussé lamps, weighing there fifty-seven pounds, and his Blessedness ordained that they should burn every night before the altar of that apostle.

[Col. 1010C]

Inspired by divine grace, he covered the larger beam beneath the principal arch with the purest silver, weighing 1,352 pounds.

This illustrious pontiff also made there, on the high altar, a gold-embroidered textile of extraordinary size and beauty, bearing representations of the Savior, Our Lord Jesus Christ, his holy Mother, and the twelve apostles, with a border of gold embroidery, adorned everywhere with pearls, and decorated on both sides with Byzantine purple and gold embroidery. The distinguished bishop ordered that it be placed there on the feasts of the apostles.

There he also made above the principal cross a *panoclysta* of very bright gold, adorned with precious gems, weighing forty-two pounds and two ounces.

He also made four pairs of *cerostatae*, covered with gilded silver, weighing together seventy-seven pounds.

[Col. 1010D]

The venerable and illustrious pontiff made above the altar of blessed Petronilla a ciborium with porphyry columns, of the purest silver and of extraordinary size, weighing 348 pounds. He also made a silver image standing beneath the arch of that ciborium, weighing 10½ pounds.

The same pontiff, protected by God and illustrious, made in the basilica of the teacher of the world, blessed Paul the Apostle, above the high altar, a gold-embroidered textile bearing a representation of the Lord’s Resurrection, adorned with pearls and with a border of gold embroidery.

Likewise, he made two images of the apostles, adorned with pearls, of gilded silver, weighing eighty-six pounds.

This most merciful pontiff made in the basilica of the Holy Mother of God at the Crèche, above the altar, a gold-embroidered textile bearing a representation of the Lord’s Resurrection, of extraordinary size and beauty, with a border of gold embroidery and adorned everywhere with pearls.

[Col. 1011A]

In the titular church of the Holy Mother of God called Callistus, he made a *regnum* of the purest gold, hanging above the high altar and adorned with precious gems, weighing one pound.

In the deaconry of that Mother of God, called *Dominica*, he made a *regnum* of pure gold, hanging above the high altar and adorned with precious gems, weighing two pounds.

This most blessed bishop, filled with divine inspiration, made in the basilica of the Mother of God at the Crèche, at the entrance to the Crèche, silver doors of the purest silver, weighing together 127 pounds. Above those doors he placed a small *fundatus* curtain with a border of gold embroidery.

He also made three Tyrian curtains above the larger doors at the entrance to the basilica, with borders of *fundatus*.

The same distinguished bishop made in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle eighteen larger chalices of the purest silver, resting upon silver beams and weighing together 182 pounds.

[Col. 1011B]

There too he made larger, cast *cerostatae* of the purest silver, standing before the confession and weighing 198 pounds.

He covered the beam of the purest silver that is above the golden image at the entrance to the vestibule; it weighs 126½ pounds.

He also made there two cast lamps of the purest silver, weighing together twenty-seven pounds.

He ordained that on Sundays and on holy solemnities they should stand on either side beside the lectern, and that, when the sacred readings were being read, they should shine with the splendor of their light.

Here he made for the blessed apostle Andrew a ciborium of the purest silver over the high altar, weighing 305 pounds. This eminent pontiff, divinely inspired, observed that the baptistery mentioned above was already close to collapse because of its excessive age, and that the space was too narrow for the people who came for baptism. Therefore, beginning from the foundations, he rebuilt the baptistery in a circular form with generous breadth and restored it to a better condition. He established the sacred font in the middle, with a more spacious area, adorned it all around with porphyry columns, and placed a column in the middle of the font. On the column he set a lamb of the purest silver pouring forth water, weighing 18 pounds and 10 ounces. He also built the high altar beneath the apse, and covered its front and confessio—that is, its *rugae*—for the adornment of the sacred altar with the finest silver, weighing altogether 48 pounds. He also placed upon it a covering of *stauracium* and made an over-covering there of the purest silver. Above this over-covering he placed an arch and *gammadiae* of silver, weighing altogether 80 pounds. He also set up three images there, weighing 37 pounds and 10 ounces. He adorned the baptistery all around with various paintings.

The oratory of the Holy Cross mentioned above, which was already on the verge of collapse because of its excessive age, this eminent shepherd rebuilt from the foundations, together with its apse, as a new structure, and brought it to completion. He adorned the apse, decorated with mosaic and various paintings, with marbles of wondrous brilliance. There he also offered a ciborium over the altar with its columns, and covered the front of the altar with the purest silver, weighing 121 pounds and 2 ounces. A *regnum spanoclystum* of the purest gold, with a cross in the middle, hung above the altar; the pieces together weighed 1 pound and 11 ounces. He also supplied four other silver columns and, above them, an over-covering of the purest silver; these weighed 64 pounds and 3 ounces. Three silver arches weighed 43 pounds and 8 ounces. Three gilded silver images weighed 30 pounds. Twelve openwork silver baskets (*canistri interrasiles*) weighed altogether 78 pounds; twenty-one openwork silver bowls (*gabathae interrasiles*) and one cross weighed altogether 50 pounds. One altar covering of *fundatum* work, another of *blatthin* with *chrysoclavus*, and yet another white covering rose-colored and decorated with *chrysoclavus*. A small *chrysoclavus* curtain, ornamented with a crucifix and pearls. Seven *stauracium* curtains, four *fundatum* curtains, and six small Tyrian curtains hanging from the over-covering before the images. Twelve white silk curtains, decorated all around with *fundatum* work. One large white, rose-colored curtain, decorated above with *quadrapulum*, and another red curtain with *bubalus*, hanging before the great doors. Four small *stauracium* curtains hanging from the over-covering before the images, as well as eleven miscellaneous silk curtains. At the fountains mentioned above he made three Tyrian curtains hanging from the over-covering before the images, and twenty-one other silk curtains.

Here he made for the blessed apostle Peter, his patron, a distinguished gold cup, *spanoclystum* (or *epanoclistum*), adorned with various precious stones and weighing 30 pounds. In the same way he made a gold paten, likewise *spanoclysta*, similarly adorned with precious stones and weighing 25 pounds. Over the ciborium of the high altar he made for the blessed apostle Peter four large *canthara* of the purest silver, containing gilded silver candles in the middle and weighing altogether 140 pounds. The aforementioned eminent pontiff made there an apostolic censer of the purest gold, weighing 2 pounds and 5 ounces. He made a covering for the high altar, decorated with *chrysoclavus* and various designs, which he ordered to be placed there four times a year, at the twelve readings. He made there four large crowns of the purest silver, weighing altogether 154½ pounds. He also made there a lectern of the purest silver, of remarkable size, weighing 143 pounds. He also made silver *cerostata* standing beside the lectern, weighing altogether 49 pounds. Upon these *cerostata* he made two cast, two-wicked lamps of pure silver, weighing 27 pounds. He decreed that they should stand on either side beside the lectern on Sundays and holy feast days, and that, when the sacred lessons were read, they should shine with the splendor of their light. He made fourteen *pharocanthara* in the presbytery of the finest silver, weighing altogether 433 pounds. He also made eight columns and four arches of silver, weighing there 173 pounds.

He also made sixty-four cast silver cups, hanging between the large columns on the right and left sides of the basilica; together they weighed 461 pounds.

The same prescient bishop also covered the high altar of the blessed apostle Andrew with gilded pure silver, magnificently adorned, weighing altogether 135 pounds. Twelve silver *canthara* weighed altogether 52 pounds. Twelve silver baskets weighed 78 pounds.

He also covered the altar of the blessed Petronilla with gilded pure silver, adorned with various designs, weighing altogether 162 pounds and 8 ounces. He likewise covered the altar of the blessed Gregory, confessor and pontiff, entirely with gilded silver, weighing 127 pounds.

In the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, mentioned above, he made a large Alexandrian silk curtain (*cordina*), having *fundatum* work attached in the middle and decorated all around with *fundatum* work. He also made two apostolic censers of the purest gold. One of them he placed inside, above his body; it weighed 2 pounds. The other, weighing 2 pounds and 8 ounces, preceded the processions.

This beneficent bishop made two apostolic censers of the purest gold in the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul. He also covered the front of the altar of Holy Mary, Mother of God, at the Crib, with finely worked gilded silver, weighing 86 pounds. There he made two crowns of pure silver weighing 54 pounds. He made large Alexandrian silk curtains decorated all around with *fundatum* work.

This eminent pontiff, through the generosity of almighty God and of blessed Peter, the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, offered crowns and baskets of the purest silver throughout the holy churches of this blessed Rome, for the forgiveness of his sins, as follows:

In the church of our Lord and Savior, called Constantiniana, he made crowns of the purest silver weighing 23 pounds.

In the basilica of Holy Mary, Mother of God, at the Crib, he made a crown of pure silver weighing 13 pounds. In the basilica of Holy Mary, Mother of God, at the title of Callistus, he made a silver crown weighing 13 pounds and 3 ounces.

In the diaconia of that Mother of God, called Antiqua, he likewise made a silver crown weighing 13 pounds. In the church of Holy Mary, Mother of God, at the Martyrs, he made a silver crown weighing 12 pounds and 3 ounces. In the diaconia of that Mother of God, called Cosmedin, he likewise made a silver crown weighing 12 pounds. He also made, in the diaconia of Holy Mary, Mother of God, called Dominica, a silver crown weighing 9 pounds. In the diaconia of Holy Mary, Mother of God, situated on the Via Lata, he made a silver crown weighing 9 pounds. In the diaconia of Saint Mary in Cyro he made a crown weighing 8 pounds. Indeed, in the diaconia of the blessed Mother of God situated outside the gate of the blessed apostle Peter, he made a silver crown weighing 5 pounds and 3 ounces. In the diaconia of that Mother of God situated at Hadrian’s, he likewise made a silver crown weighing 5 pounds.

In the oratory of Holy Mary, Mother of God, situated in the xenodochium of Firmus, he made a silver basket weighing 2 pounds and 7 ounces.

In the church of the blessed apostle Peter he made a basket of the purest silver weighing 22 pounds. In the church of the blessed apostle Paul he likewise made a basket of the purest silver weighing 22 pounds, 4 ounces, and 8 [ounces?].

In the church of the blessed apostle Andrew, called Eudoxia’s, he likewise made a silver crown weighing 9 pounds. In the church of the blessed John the Baptist, situated beside the Lateran patriarchate, he made a silver crown weighing 5 pounds. In the church of the blessed John the Evangelist, situated in the same place, he made a silver crown weighing 5 pounds. In the church of Saint Stephen, situated on the Caelian Hill, he likewise made a silver crown weighing 7 pounds and 11 ounces. In the basilica of the apostles, situated on the Via Lata, he made a silver crown weighing 13 pounds. In the mausoleum of the blessed Petronilla, situated at the church of the blessed apostle Peter, he made a silver crown weighing 20 pounds. In the church of Jerusalem, situated at the Sessorian, he made a silver crown weighing 5 pounds. In the church of the blessed Lawrence, situated outside the walls, he likewise made a silver crown weighing 13 pounds. In the church of the blessed martyr Apollinaris he made a crown weighing 5 pounds and 4 ounces. In the basilica of the blessed martyr Pancratius, situated outside the walls, he likewise made a silver crown weighing 8 pounds. In the church of the blessed martyr Valentine, situated outside the walls, where his body rests, he made a silver crown weighing 6 pounds. In the title of the blessed martyr and pontiff Clement he made a silver crown weighing 15 pounds.

In the title of the blessed Aquila and Prisca he made a silver crown weighing 6 pounds. In the title of Saint Balbina he likewise made one.

In the church of the holy martyr and pontiff Sixtus he likewise made a crown. In the title of the holy martyr Lawrence, called Lucina’s, he likewise made one weighing 4 pounds and 10 ounces. In the title of the holy martyr Lawrence, called Damasi, he made a silver crown weighing 5 pounds. In the church of that martyr situated at Formosus’s, he made a silver basket weighing 2 pounds and 7 ounces. In the title of Pammachius he made a silver crown weighing 10 pounds. In the title of Aemiliana he likewise made a silver crown weighing 4 pounds.

In the title of Saint Eusebius he made a silver crown weighing 6 pounds. In the title of Praxedis he made a crown weighing 5 pounds. In the title of Pudens he made a silver crown weighing 9 pounds. In the title of the blessed martyr Vitalis he made a silver crown weighing 9 pounds and 3 ounces. In the title of the holy martyr Susanna he likewise made a crown weighing 10 pounds. In the title of Saint Cyriacus he made a silver crown weighing 5 pounds.

In the title of the blessed martyr Marcellus he made a silver crown weighing 10 pounds. In the title of the blessed martyr Mark he likewise made one. In the title of the blessed Anastasia he made a crown weighing 7 pounds and 9 ounces. In the title of Cecilia he likewise made a silver crown weighing altogether 10 pounds and 1 ounce. In the title of the blessed martyr Chrysogonus he made a silver crown weighing 5 pounds.

In the diaconia of Saints Nereus and Achilleus he made a silver crown weighing 6 pounds and 5 ounces. In the diaconia of Saint Lucia, situated at the Seven Ways, he made a silver crown weighing 6 pounds and 7 ounces. In the diaconia of Saint Boniface he likewise made a crown weighing 7 pounds. In the diaconia of Saint George he made a silver crown weighing 5 pounds. In the diaconia of Saint Theodore he likewise made a crown weighing 6 pounds and 8 ounces. In the diaconia of Saints Sergius and Bacchus he made a silver crown weighing 6 pounds. In the diaconia of Saints Cosmas and Damian he made a silver crown weighing 5 pounds and 8 ounces. In the diaconia of Saint Adrian the martyr he made a silver crown weighing 6 pounds. In the diaconia of the Holy Archangel he likewise made a silver crown weighing 6 pounds. In the diaconia of Saint Eustachius he likewise made one weighing 6 pounds and 5 ounces. In the diaconia of Saint Lucia, situated at Orfea, he likewise made a silver crown weighing 6 pounds and 2 ounces.

Likewise, in the diaconia of the blessed martyr Vitus, situated at the Macellum, he made a silver crown weighing 6 pounds. In the diaconia of Saint Agatha he likewise made a silver crown weighing 5 pounds. In the diaconia of Saint Sylvester, situated beside the blessed apostle Peter, he made a silver crown weighing 4 pounds. In the diaconia of Saint Martin, situated beside the blessed apostle Peter, he likewise made a silver crown weighing 5 pounds and 3 ounces. In the title of Saints Sylvester and Martin, situated beside Orfea, he made a silver crown weighing 6 pounds and 2 ounces.

[Col. 1015A]

This God-protected and eminent pontiff made in the monastery of Saint Sabas a silver crown weighing 8 pounds and 10 ounces. In the monastery of the blessed martyr Anastasius he likewise made a silver crown weighing 8 pounds, 4½ ounces. In the monastery of Saint Andrew, situated on the Clivus Scauri, he likewise made a crown of pure silver weighing 5 pounds. In the monastery of the blessed martyr Agatha, situated above the Subura, he likewise made one. In the monastery of Saint Erasmus, situated on the Caelian Hill, he made a silver crown weighing 4 pounds and 2 ounces. In the same way he made, in the monastery of Saint Sylvester, a silver crown weighing 6 pounds and 3 ounces. In the monastery of the blessed martyr Lawrence, called Pallacini, he made a silver basket weighing 2 pounds and 7 ounces. In the monastery of Saint Pancratius, situated beside the basilica of the Savior, he made a silver crown weighing 5½ pounds. In the monastery of Saints Andrew and Bartholomew, called that of Honorius, he made a silver basket weighing 3 pounds. In the monastery of Saint Stephen, situated beside the Lateran, he made a silver basket weighing 2 pounds. Likewise, in the monastery of that first martyr Stephen, situated at the church of the blessed apostle Peter, he made a silver basket weighing 3½ pounds. This beneficent bishop made, in the monastery of Saints John and Paul, situated beside the blessed apostle Peter, a silver basket weighing 3 pounds. In the same way he made, in the monastery of Saint Martin, situated as above, a basket weighing 4 pounds and 2 ounces. In the monastery of Saint Stephen mentioned above, called Catagalla Patricia, he likewise made a silver basket weighing 2½ pounds. Likewise, in the monastery of Saint Caesarius, situated at the church of the blessed apostle Paul, he made a silver basket weighing 3 pounds. In the monastery of Saint Stephen mentioned above, he made a basket weighing 2 pounds. In the monastery of Saints Cosmas and Damian, situated beside the Crib, he made a silver basket weighing 2 pounds and 2 ounces. In the monastery of Saint Andrew, called Massa Juliana, he made a silver basket weighing 2 pounds. In the monastery of Saint Adrian, situated beside the Crib, he likewise made a basket weighing 2 pounds. In the monastery of Saint Cassian, situated beside the blessed martyr Lawrence outside the walls, he made a silver basket weighing [an unstated number of] pounds.

In the monastery of Saint Stephen, situated as above, he made a silver basket weighing 2½ pounds. In the monastery of Saint Victor, situated at Saint Pancratius, he made a silver basket weighing 2 pounds and 7 ounces. In the monastery of Saint Chrysogonus he likewise made a basket weighing 3 pounds.

This beneficent bishop made, in the monastery of Saint Mary called Ambrosius’s, a silver basket weighing 2 pounds. In the same way he made one in the monastery of Saint Mary called Julia’s, as above. In the monastery of Saint Andrew, situated beside the basilica of the apostles, he likewise made one.

Likewise, in the oratory of Saint Stephen, situated at Dulcitius’s, he made a silver basket weighing 2 pounds and 5 ounces. In the oratory of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, situated at Callinicus’s, he likewise made a basket. In the monastery of Saint Agapitus, situated beside the title of Eudoxia, he likewise made a silver basket, [the text reads *et semis*, “and a half,” but the weight is not otherwise stated]. In the oratory of Saint Agnes, situated in the monastery called Duo Furna, he made a silver basket weighing 2 pounds and 8 ounces. In the oratory of Saint Vitus, situated in the monastery called “of Sardas,” he made a silver basket weighing 3 pounds. In the monastery of Saint Bibiana he likewise made a silver basket weighing 2 pounds and 9 ounces. In the oratory of Saint Lucia, situated in the monastery of Renatus, he made a silver basket weighing 2 pounds.

In the oratory of Saint Mary, situated in the monastery of Michael, he likewise made a silver basket weighing 2 pounds and 2 ounces. In the monastery of Saint Sergius he likewise made a basket weighing 3 pounds. This beneficent bishop also made, in the oratory of Saint Agatha situated in the monastery at Africanus’s, a silver basket weighing 3 pounds. In the monastery of Saints Euphemia and the Archangel, situated beside the title of Pudens, he likewise made a silver basket weighing 5 pounds. In the monastery of Saint Isidore he likewise made a basket. In the oratory of Saint Agatha, situated in the monastery of the Temple, he likewise made a basket. In the oratory of Saint Caesarius, situated in the monastery of Corsus, he likewise made a basket weighing 2 pounds and 3 ounces. In the monastery of Saint Semitrius he likewise made a silver basket. In the oratory of Saint Mary, situated in the monastery of Aqua Salvia, he likewise made one. In the monastery of Saint Donatus, situated beside the title of Saint Prisca, he made a silver basket weighing 2 pounds and 5 ounces. In the monastery of Saint John, situated on the Aventine, he likewise made a silver basket weighing 2 pounds. In the oratory of Saint Mary, situated in the monastery of Lutara, he made silver baskets weighing 2½ pounds. In the monastery of Jerusalem, situated at the church of the blessed apostle Peter, he made a silver basket weighing 2 pounds. In the monastery of Saint Agnes, situated outside the Nomentan Gate, he made silver baskets weighing 5 pounds. In the monastery of Saint Eugenia, situated outside the Latin Gate, he likewise made a silver basket weighing 5 pounds; and in the oratory of Saint Gregory, situated in the Campus Martius, he made silver baskets weighing 3 pounds. This beneficent bishop made in the title of the blessed Sabina a silver crown weighing 8 pounds. In the diaconia of Saints Sylvester and Martin, situated beside Orfea, he likewise made a silver crown weighing 6 pounds and 2 ounces. In the oratory of Saint Lucia, situated in the xenodochium, he likewise made a silver basket weighing 2 pounds and 4 ounces. In the oratory of Saint Abbacyrus [“Abba Cyrus” or “Cyrus”], situated in the xenodochium, he made a silver basket weighing 2 pounds. In the oratory of Saints Cosmas and Damian, situated in the xenodochium called Tucium, he likewise made a silver basket weighing 2 pounds and 1 ounce. In the oratory of Saint Peregrinus, situated in the Lord’s hospital at the Naumachia, he made silver baskets weighing 5 pounds and 1 ounce.

The aforesaid pontiff made, in the basilica of our Lord Jesus Christ, called Constantiniana, two *chrysoclava* coverings over the high altar: one bearing the scene of the Lord’s resurrection, and the other bearing the scene of the life-giving and venerable cross of the Lord. Eight *canthara* of the finest silver weighed altogether 27 pounds and 6 ounces. He covered the *rugae* before the entrance to the altar with the purest silver, weighing 48 pounds and 8 ounces. Silver crowns weighed 12 pounds. At the fountains mentioned above he made ten white silk curtains, decorated all around with *fundatum* and *quadruplum* work.

He entirely and completely restored the roof of that church, together with its four-sided portico and the area at the fountains. He also enclosed and adorned the windows of the apse with glass of various colors. He repaired the other windows of the basilica with bronze metal, and in the body of the basilica he made two curtains: one larger, white, of *fundatum* work, and another smaller, white and rose-colored.

The same bishop made in the basilica of Holy Mary, Mother of God, called at the Crib, two rose-colored silver *canthara* with *periclysis* of *fundatum* work, weighing there 23 pounds; and two columns weighing 21 pounds and 5 ounces. A cross with a bowl of pure silver weighed 5 pounds altogether. In the diaconia of that Mother of God, called Antiqua, he made four genuine *tetravila*, decorated all around with *quadruplum*. In the oratory of Saint Andrew mentioned above he made two silk curtains, decorated as above.

In the title of that Mother of God, called Callistus’s, he made a white, rose-colored silk covering, having in the middle a panel of *chrysoclavus* with the scene of the Presentation of our Lord Jesus Christ and of Saint Simeon, with a *periclysis* of Tyrian cloth. Four red genuine *tetravila*, bearing crosses with *gammadiae* and having a Tyrian *periclysis* around them. One large Tyrian curtain, hanging before the image, with a *periclysis* of *blatthin*. Three small red genuine curtains with a cross-pattern in the middle, hanging before the silver images, with a *periclysis* of *blatthin*. One large silk curtain in the body of the basilica. He also made gilded silver images, one of them with gems, and one silver arch with its *gammadiae*. Above the *cerostata* he made one lamp. Two censers weighed altogether 95 pounds and 7 ounces.

The same prescient bishop made for the blessed apostle Peter a gold cup adorned with various precious stones, which preceded the processions, weighing 13 pounds. In the basilica of that apostle he made a *chrysoclavus* curtain hanging above the entrance to the vestibule. He also made another larger curtain with *chrysoclavus*, hanging from a silver beam before the image of the Savior above the entrance to the vestibule. A large crown of the purest silver weighed 53 pounds and 8 ounces. A silver lamp hanging beneath that crown weighed 23 pounds. Four other silver crowns weighed 57 pounds. Eight baskets weighed altogether 40 pounds.

[Note: [Col. 1017D] For love and protection of the orthodox faith, he made two silver shields inscribed with both Creeds. When the Gauls and Spaniards had added the word *Filioque* to the Creed without authorization, and had publicly sung the Nicene Creed with that addition during the solemn celebration of Mass, it seemed to Pope Leo to be in the Church’s interest that, on these two public silver tablets preserved in a public place, both Creeds should be inscribed together, in Greek and Latin, without any addition of the word *Filioque*, so that thereafter nothing could be added to the sacred Creed. He attached these two silver tablets in the basilica of Saint Peter, not, as the Master of the Sentences writes in Book I, distinction 11, in the church of Saint Paul. When and on what occasion the Roman Church received that word *Filioque* into the Creed by authority of the Roman pontiff, for another reason requiring it, we have already explained elsewhere. SEV. BIN.]

For love and protection of the orthodox faith, he made there two silver shields inscribed with both Creeds: one in Greek letters and the other in Latin letters. They hung on the right and left above the entrance to the body of the church and weighed there 94 pounds and 6 ounces. There in the body of the basilica he made one large silk curtain of *fundatum* work, decorated all around with *fundatum*. One large white, rose-colored silk curtain, hanging from the large beam above the golden images, was decorated all around with *fundatum*. Above the fountains he made nine white silk curtains, decorated all around with *fundatum*.

[Col. 1017D]

Here, in the place mentioned above, he covered the altar of the most blessed Leo, confessor and pontiff, with the finest gilded silver, weighing altogether 109 pounds. He likewise covered the altar of the blessed Gregory, confessor and pontiff, with the finest gilded silver, weighing everywhere 127 pounds.

This God-appointed and eminent pontiff covered and adorned the altar of the blessed apostle Paul with the purest silver; it weighed 155 pounds. He also covered its confessio and the front of the altar with the purest gold, weighing there 121 pounds and 8 ounces. Above the entrance to the body of the church he made a silver shield on which he had the Creed of the orthodox faith inscribed; it weighed 32 pounds. There he made three large crowns of the purest silver, weighing altogether 93 pounds. In the basilica he made a most beautiful large silk curtain of *quadruplum* and *fundatum* work.

The aforesaid venerable and eminent pontiff made in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, his patron, over the high altar, a ciborium with its four columns, of gilded pure silver, magnificently decorated with various scenes and of remarkable size; it weighed 2,704 pounds and 3 ounces. The ciborium that he removed from there he placed over the high altar in the basilica of the Blessed Mother of God, called at the Crib. He made a silver cross and placed it there, weighing 12 pounds and 3 ounces. He also made there four red genuine *terravela*, one of them with *chrysoclavus*.
