In the mausoleum of the blessed Petronilla, situated at the church of the blessed apostle Peter, he made three large and eight smaller white curtains, decorated all around with *fundatum*.

The same eminent pontiff made, before the confessio of the prince of the apostles, angels of the purest silver on the right and left, weighing there 146 pounds. He also made two other angels of gilded pure silver, standing on the large beam above the entrance to the vestibule, on the right and left beside the golden image of the Savior; they weighed altogether 63 pounds. He made four other smaller angels of gilded pure silver, in the same place, on the right and left; they weighed altogether 68 pounds. He also made six small gilded silver columns in the entrance to the vestibule, painted with various scenes; they weighed altogether 147 pounds. He made a large cross of gilded pure silver, standing beside the high altar, weighing 22 pounds. He also made a large arch of gilded finest silver above the entrance to the vestibule, weighing 131½ pounds.

In the confessio of the blessed Leo, confessor and pontiff, he made, in the place mentioned above, a Gospel book of gilded finest silver, above the entrance to the vestibule, weighing 48½ pounds. He made there one small column of pure silver weighing 17 pounds. This God-protected and eminent pontiff made in the diaconia of the Holy Archangel a paten and a cup of the purest silver, weighing together 10 pounds.

Protected by divine inspiration, he made in the basilica of the Savior, called Constantiniana, a ciborium with its four columns, of the purest silver, painted with various scenes and adorned with grilles and its small columns, of remarkable size and beauty; all together they weighed 1,227 pounds. He also entirely restored anew the roof of the basilica of Holy Mary, ever-Virgin, our Lady, called at the Crib. The chambers beside the church of the blessed apostle Peter, prince of the apostles, had decayed through excessive age and were almost collapsing. This distinguished bishop, laying the strongest foundations, rebuilt them from the ground up and restored them to a better condition. He also made, beside the large column mentioned above, an upper bathhouse built in a circular form and magnificently adorned. He newly restored the steps at the entrance to that basilica, both above the portico and in the atrium. Beside these steps, on the right side of the atrium, he built from the foundations a house of remarkable size and beauty, in which he also placed couches. Beside that house he built, for the support of Christ’s poor and of pilgrims, a bathhouse magnificently adorned from its foundations.

This eminent bishop, divinely inspired, newly built from the foundations a hospice for the blessed apostle Peter at the place called Naumachia. There he adorned various buildings and built anew a church in honor of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. In it he also placed the bodies of the holy martyrs of the Church of Christ, which he had brought there, and built everything necessary for the aforesaid hospice.

[Col. 1019B]

He also offered urban and rural estates there for the sustenance of Christ’s poor, as well as of visitors and pilgrims who come from distant regions, for the exaltation of the holy Church of God and the salvation of the Roman people.

In particular, the monastery of Saint Stephen, Christ’s first martyr, called Catagalla [Greek: κατὰ Γάλλαν, “at Galla’s”] Patricia, had already decayed from excessive age and had partly collapsed. This prescient pontiff, undertaking the work, laid firm foundations from the ground up together with the oratory and restored it to a better condition. He also rebuilt anew the steps by which one enters the church of the blessed apostle Peter from the church of the holy apostle Andrew, since they had been worn away by age.

In the same way he almost entirely rebuilt from the foundations the monastery of the blessed Martin, confessor and pontiff, situated in the place mentioned above, which had been greatly damaged by age. He newly restored the roof of the basilica of the holy apostle Andrew, called Catabarbara [Greek: κατὰ Βαρβάραν, “at Barbara’s”] Patricia, which had been consumed by age for a very long time. Likewise, he rebuilt anew the roof of the blessed martyr Lucia, situated at Orfea. He also restored to a better condition the roof of the blessed martyr Balbina, which was already almost collapsing. In the same way he magnificently restored the roof of the basilica of the blessed martyrs Cosmas and Damian, situated on the Sacred Way. Likewise, he restored to a better condition the roof of the basilica of the holy martyr Martina, situated at the Three Fates.

Furthermore, he newly restored the roof of the titulus of the blessed martyr Lawrence, which is called *of Damasus*. This most holy and illustrious pontiff also newly and magnificently repaired, with the most prudent care, the roof of the basilica of the blessed martyr Valentine, situated on the Via Flaminia, which was already on the point of collapse from excessive age. He newly repaired everything, inside and out, in the roofed colonnade of the basilica of the apostles on the Via Lata; indeed, he also newly repaired the roof of the basilica of the blessed martyr Agatha, situated above the Subura, which had already decayed from excessive age. This most holy prelate built in the Lateran patriarchate, from the foundations, an oratory in honor of the blessed archangel, constructing it with extraordinarily solid and distinguished workmanship. He adorned it everywhere with mosaic, or with various paintings, and with the most beautiful marble stones of different colors. He also presented there all kinds of sacred treasures, both gold and silver, as well as various curtains.

He newly restored from the foundations the *macrona* of that Lateran patriarchate, which extends from the Campus and beyond the images of the apostles and which was on the point of collapse from excessive age; he restored its roof and also its pavement from the bottom to the top, and laid it out more splendidly with extremely strong marble. He also newly made the ceiling of that *macrona* and magnificently decorated it with paintings of various scenes.

This venerable and illustrious pontiff, protected by God, made around the altar of the blessed apostle Peter, his spiritual nourisher, red *tetravela* of genuine scarlet silk (*holoserica alythina*) having panels or roundels of gold-and-purple embroidery (*chrysoclavo*) depicted with various scenes, together with stars of gold-and-purple embroidery. In the middle there were also crosses of gold-and-purple embroidery, adorned with pearls and decorated with extraordinary size and beauty; these are hung there for the adornment of the sanctuary on feast days.

In the same manner as above, he made other white rose-colored silk *tetravela* for Easter, having panels and roundels of gold-and-purple embroidery, as well as crosses with gold-and-purple embroidery, made with pearls and bordered with a gold-and-purple embroidered *periclysis*. He also made four other small curtains in the same place, one for each ciborium-column, bearing tigers in gold-and-purple embroidery and decorated around the edge with *blatthin* [purple cloth]. He likewise placed four other small curtains of the same design in the basilica of the teacher of the world, the blessed apostle Paul, on the ciborium-columns.

The aforesaid venerable pontiff newly and more splendidly restored all the roofs of the basilica of the blessed martyr Agapitus, situated in the city of Praeneste, as well as the roofs of another basilica situated beside it, which were already on the point of collapse from excessive age. In the same manner he newly repaired the roofs of the basilica of the blessed first martyr Stephen, situated on the Via Latina at the third milestone, which had already been worn out by the passage of many years and were close to ruin. He also newly restored the roofs of the basilica of the blessed martyr Basilides, situated on the Merulana.

This venerable and illustrious pontiff, protected by God, made in the basilica of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, which is called Constantiniana, from his own silver for that basilica five crowns with their dolphins, thirty-five baskets, and eight *gabathae* [shallow basins], weighing altogether 276 pounds.

In the basilica of the Holy Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary, our Lady, which is called “at the Manger,” he made a curtain of cloth woven with gold thread (*fundatum*), decorated around the edge with *blatthin*, hanging in the portico above a magnificently decorated seat. He made forty miscellaneous curtains, some of *fundatum*, others of *stauracium*, and decorated around the edge with *quadrapulum* and *blatthin*. In the same place, before the entrance to the manger, he made a lamp (*pharus*) in the form of a net, of the purest silver, with five baskets, weighing altogether thirty-seven and a half pounds.

The same most holy prelate, filled with the illumination of the Holy Spirit, made for the blessed apostle Peter, his spiritual nourisher, a distinguished tetragonal gold chalice, *spanoclystum*, adorned with various precious stones and weighing thirty-two pounds. He also made a gold *spanoclysta* paten of extraordinary size, weighing twenty-five pounds and nine ounces.

In the basilica mentioned above he made a lamp in the form of a net, with a basket and crosses of the purest silver, hanging beneath the principal golden lamp. He also made another larger lamp in the form of a net, with twenty baskets, hanging beneath a large silver beam for the adornment of the holy church. It weighed there 2,104 pounds and seven ounces.

This pontiff made in the basilica of the teacher of the world, the blessed apostle Paul, a crucifix of the purest silver, of extraordinary size and magnificently decorated, weighing fifty-two pounds. He also made there white rose-colored silk *tetravela*, one of which had in the middle a cross of gold-and-purple embroidery and *gammadiae* of gold-and-purple embroidery. He also made nine white silk curtains, rose-colored, decorated around the edge with Tyrian purple. There he made eight *gabathae* of hammered (*fundatae*) pure silver, hanging from the bronze lamp in the middle of the basilica; they weighed there fourteen pounds.

He adorned the entrance of the body of the basilica with white marble, with wonderful beauty, and placed bronze doors there. Above the marble columns standing around the altar of that teacher of the world, where wooden beams had formerly been placed and had also decayed from excessive age, this holy bishop had lilies set upon those columns; above the lilies he placed *platoniae* of marble or metal, and adorned the work with paintings of extraordinary size. In the same place he made five larger Alexandrian curtains, hanging above the greater doors at the entrance of the basilica and magnificently decorated.

This most holy and illustrious pontiff made in the basilica of the Holy Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary, our Lady, at the Manger, magnificently decorated white rose-colored silk *tetravela*. In the same place, inside the manger, he made a white rose-colored silk covering, decorated around the edge with gold-and-purple embroidery and having in the middle a cross with roundels of gold-and-purple embroidery, together with four white rose-colored silk curtains decorated around the edge with Tyrian purple.

In the deaconry of that Mother of God, which is called *Dominica*, he made a white rose-colored silk covering having in the middle a panel of Tyrian purple with a scene of the Crucifixion. He also made wheels of gold-and-purple embroidery, decorated around the edge with *quadrapulum*. In the same place he made a *fundatum* curtain decorated around the edge with *blatthin*.

In the deaconry of that Mother of God, which is called *Cosmedin*, he made a white silk covering with a panel of gold-and-purple embroidery bearing a scene of the Lord’s resurrection, and around it a band of gold-and-purple embroidery. At Saint Mary “at the Martyrs” he made a white rose-colored silk covering with a panel of Tyrian purple bearing a scene of the Crucifixion, and a wheel of gold-and-purple embroidery decorated around the edge with Tyrian purple. He also made, for placement outside the gate of the blessed apostle Peter in the deaconry of the aforementioned Mother of God, a covering of Tyrian purple, magnificently decorated.

This venerable and illustrious pontiff made in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, his spiritual nourisher, twenty-two hammered baskets of the purest silver, both in the four-sided colonnade and within the body of the basilica, weighing altogether 125 pounds. He made forty-eight hammered, *signochristae* *gabathae*, hanging in the four-sided colonnade and in the bronze lamp in the middle of the basilica, weighing altogether 101 and a half pounds. He made three silver lamps, standing upon silver beams, weighing ninety-three pounds. He made two silver arches, weighing forty-one pounds and eight ounces.

He made larger curtains of *blatthin*, hanging from the silver beams on the right and left sides of the presbytery. He also made thirty curtains around the seat, decorated around the edge with *quadrapulum*.

He made forty-seven small curtains of *fundatum*, decorated around the edge with Byzantine *blatthin* and lined with Neapolitan *blatthin*. Also, within the body of the basilica, he made a larger Alexandrian curtain of extraordinary size and beauty, decorated around the edge with Tyrian purple.

He made twenty-five small white rose-colored silk curtains, decorated around the edge with *blaubin*, one of which was decorated with *stauracium*. Above the altar of the blessed Andrew, in the place mentioned above, he made a white rose-colored silk covering with a panel of gold-and-purple embroidery bearing a scene of the Lord’s resurrection, and around it a band of gold-and-purple embroidery.

He also made above the altar of the blessed Petronilla a white rose-colored silk covering with a panel of gold-and-purple embroidery bearing a scene of the Lord’s resurrection, and around it a band of gold-and-purple embroidery. In the same manner, in the oratory of the holy Mother of God mentioned above, in the middle, he made a white rose-colored silk covering having in the middle a cross of gold-and-purple embroidery and decorated around the edge with Tyrian purple.

In the oratory of that Mother of God mentioned above, which is called “of Lord Pope Paul,” he made a white silk covering decorated around the edge with *mizilo*. In the monastery of Saint Martin mentioned above, he made a white rose-colored silk covering having in the middle a cross of gold-and-purple embroidery with a border of Tyrian purple.

He made in the basilica of the apostles on the Via Lata, above the principal altar, a white rose-colored silk covering having in the middle a panel of *stauracium* with a scene of the Lord’s resurrection, and around it a covering of gold-and-purple embroidery. He also made roundels of gold-and-purple embroidery with a border of Tyrian purple. He made small red *tetravela*, decorated around the edge with *fundatum*, one of them with gold-and-purple embroidery. He made two small red Alexandrian curtains, decorated around the edge with *stauracium*. Within the body of the basilica mentioned above, he made a larger *fundatum* curtain, magnificently decorated and adorned around the edge with Tyrian purple, with crosses of Tyrian purple in the middle.

This distinguished prelate made in the titulus of the holy martyr Sabina, above the principal altar, a white rose-colored silk covering having in the middle a panel of *stauracium* with a scene of the Lord’s resurrection, and around it a band of gold-and-purple embroidery.

In the same manner, in the titulus of the holy martyr Susanna, above the principal altar, he made a white rose-colored silk covering having in the middle a panel of gold-and-purple embroidery with a scene of the Lord’s resurrection, and around it a band of gold-and-purple embroidery.

He made in the basilica of the blessed first martyr Stephen on Caelian Hill a white rose-colored silk covering having in the middle a panel of *stauracium* with a scene of the Lord’s resurrection, and a cross of gold-and-purple embroidery.

Also, in the deaconry of the blessed martyr George, above the principal altar, he made a white rose-colored silk covering having in the middle a panel of *stauracium* with a scene of the Crucifixion, decorated with Tyrian purple, and roses of gold-and-purple embroidery.

This venerable and illustrious pontiff, protected by God, made in the basilica of the holy Mother of God, which is called “at the Manger,” out of excessive love for that Lady of ours, a lamp of the purest silver with a lamp and its *cereaptum* [*ceraptum*, lamp-support], weighing altogether forty and a half pounds.

His Beatitude also decreed that it should stand beside the lectern on Sundays and holy solemnities, and shine with the splendor of its light for the reading of the sacred lessons.

In the church of the blessed apostle Peter he likewise made a lamp of the purest gilded silver, magnificently decorated, with a lamp and its *cereaptum*, weighing altogether ninety and a half pounds. Indeed, in the same place, for the blessed apostle Peter, beneath the image of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ crucified, he made a crown of the purest silver beneath that image of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ made in the form of the Crucified One, and placed it there, for love of our Lord Jesus Christ, for the splendor of the lamps, weighing … pounds.

The basilica of the blessed Apollinaris, bishop and martyr, which was founded near the city of Ravenna, had beams that, through the passage of years and the great age of earlier times, had decayed excessively and were then almost on the point of collapse. That same venerable father, inspired by God, sent there and, through his most diligent and provident care, newly and firmly restored all the roofs of that church together with its four-sided colonnades, bringing it back to a better condition.

Above the altar of that sacred basilica, for the honor of almighty God and of the blessed apostle Peter, from whose gifts and donations he made a rose-colored silk covering having in the middle a cross of gold-and-purple embroidery with roundels, and silk wheels bearing scenes of the Annunciation, or the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, as well as the Passion, Resurrection, Ascension into heaven, and Pentecost, decorated around the edge in the same manner as the covering, with gold-and-purple embroidery. He also made there a basket of the purest silver with its chains, weighing fifteen pounds.

The Alban episcopal residence, together with the church founded in the name of the blessed Pancratius, was burned through some negligence or carelessness, by diabolical contrivances, after the morning praises, and was consumed by fire from the foundations to the highest roof. But the most merciful and diligent pontiff, with God’s help and through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, laid a firm foundation and wonderfully restored the aforesaid church anew; together with its repaired roofs, and with God’s assistance, he brought it into a better condition.

As a true lover of God and worshiper of the holy churches of God, he made above the principal altar of the aforesaid church two coverings, one of which had larger wheels bearing griffins and was decorated around the edge with *fundatum*. He also made four silk *tetravela* of genuine scarlet (*alýthina*), decorated around the same altar with the finest Tyrian purple.

He also made in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, in the place mentioned above, a rose-colored covering bearing a scene of our Lord Jesus Christ when he extended his hands and seized the blessed apostle Peter from the waves of the sea.

The same most blessed and illustrious pontiff made in the basilica of Saint Cyriacus a white silk covering having around it a border (*periclysis*) of *fundatum*, and in the middle a scene of the Resurrection; around the altar he made white *tetravela* having borders of Tyrian purple.

In the titulus of Saint Vitalis he made a white silk covering having a border of *fundatum*, and in the middle a scene of the Resurrection. In the deaconry of the holy Archangel he placed a white silk covering having a border of Tyrian purple, and in the middle a scene of the Ascension. Likewise, above the altar of Saint Abbacyrus he offered a similar covering.

Furthermore, in the deaconry of the holy martyr Agatha, this most holy pontiff made a white silk covering having Tyrian purple [the text appears incomplete here], and in the middle a scene of the Resurrection.

In the titulus of Pammachius, above the altar of Saints John and Paul, he made a white silk covering decorated around the edge with *fundatum*, bearing scenes of the Crucifixion, Ascension, and Pentecost. Likewise, in the church of the blessed martyr and pontiff Clement, he made a white covering with gold-and-purple embroidery, bearing scenes of the Resurrection, or Ascension, and also Pentecost.

Moreover, in the church of Saint Cyriacus situated on the Ostian Way, he made five curtains of *quadrapulum*, bearing a scene of the Savior calling his disciples from the boat. Above the holy altar of that martyr he placed a covering of *fundatum*.

This pontiff, protected by God and illustrious, made in the basilica of the Holy Mother of God, ever-Virgin Mary, our Lady, at the Manger, silver crowns with twelve dolphins, weighing 102 pounds and nine ounces. He also made seven silver *phara canthara* with their dolphins, weighing eighty-five and a half pounds.

The same most blessed prelate made in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, his spiritual nourisher, before the presbytery, a revolving lamp of the purest silver with crowns and crosses, weighing there thirty-five pounds and six ounces.

He also renewed below, where the most sacred body of that prince of the apostles rests, a golden image bearing the face of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and of the holy Mother of God, our Lady Mary, and of the blessed apostles Peter, Paul, and Andrew, as well as of the blessed martyr Petronilla. He added there twenty-one pounds and three ounces of refined gold.

Indeed, in the same place, before Saint Andrew, he clad the altar of the blessed Martin, confessor of Christ, with gilded pure silver, from the former gift of Abbot Fridigisus [alternative reading: “from the earth formerly … of Abbot Fridigisus”], weighing altogether seventeen and a half pounds.

He also made in the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul, teacher of the nations, five silver *phara canthara* with their dolphins, weighing sixty-seven pounds and four ounces.

This venerable and illustrious pontiff, inspired by God, seeing that the church of the blessed martyrs Nereus and Achilleus was already failing from excessive age and being filled with overflowing water, built beside that church, anew and from the foundations, on higher ground, a church of extraordinary size and beauty.

In it he also offered these gifts: six silver baskets weighing altogether fifteen pounds; a ciborium of the purest silver weighing 215 pounds; a gilded chalice and paten of the purest silver weighing twelve pounds and ten ounces; a crown above the altar of the purest gold, adorned with various precious stones, weighing two pounds and six ounces; and two coverings, one of them white silk bearing scenes of the Lord’s Nativity, Resurrection, Ascension, and Pentecost, decorated around the edge with gold-and-purple embroidery, and the other of Tyrian purple.

In the basilica of the Blessed Mother of God at the Manger he likewise made a crown of the purest *spanoclyst* gold, adorned around the edge with various precious stones and gold-and-purple embroidery, weighing four pounds and seven ounces.

He made twenty-four silver *communicales* for the several districts, to precede the processions at the stations, carried by acolytes; they weighed altogether … pounds. In the same manner, in the basilica of the blessed apostle, his protector, he made a crown of the purest gold, adorned with various precious stones, weighing seven pounds.

He also made in the deaconry of Saints Nereus and Achilleus miscellaneous silk curtains, number … .

He newly restored the roofs of the blessed martyr Agapitus, situated beside the basilica of the blessed martyr Lawrence outside the wall, because they had already decayed from excessive age. Indeed, in the titulus of the blessed Prudentiana he made a white silk covering decorated around the edge with Tyrian purple.

After this most blessed pontiff had ruled the Roman and apostolic see most gloriously for twenty years, five months, and sixteen days, [Note: [Col. 1023C] “He was taken from this light,” etc. In the year of the Lord 816, and the third year of Emperor Louis. SEV. BIN.] he was taken from this light and departed to eternal rest. He held three ordinations in the month of March: thirty priests, eleven deacons, and 126 bishops in various places. He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter on the day before the Ides of June, in the ninth indiction, and the episcopate was vacant for ten days.

[Col. 1023]

# Letters of Saint Leo III

[Col. 1023D]

## Letter I. King Cenwulf of the Mercians to Pope Leo III

Concerning the abolition of the archbishopric of Lichfield and the restoration of the dignity of the Church of Canterbury, which Pope Adrian I and King Offa had divided.

To the most blessed and truly most beloved lord Leo, Roman pontiff of the holy and apostolic see, Cenwulf, by the grace of God king of the Mercians, together with the bishops, dukes, and every person of rank under our authority: greetings of most sincere love in Christ.

[Col. 1024D]

We always give thanks to almighty God, who, having acquired the Church with his precious blood, amid the various storms of this world, continually accustoms himself to draw her toward the harbor of salvation by new leaders, taking the former ones to life, and to pour new light upon her, so that she may not be darkened by any error of shadows but may walk with unhindered step along the way of truth.

Therefore the whole Church throughout the world rightly rejoices, because, when the true rewarder of all good things had led the most glorious shepherd of his flock, Adrian, above the heavens, to be rewarded eternally, he nevertheless in his loving providence raised up a prize for his sheep—he who knows how to bring the Lord’s flock to the sheepfolds, not to a lower life.

We also, whom the extremity of the world holds, rightly glory in this above others: that his exalted position is our salvation, and his prosperity our perpetual joy, because from the place whence the apostolic dignity comes to you, the truth of the faith has become known to us.

Therefore I consider it fitting humbly to incline the ear of our obedience to your holy commands, and to fulfill with all our strength whatever appears rightly to us to be followed according to your piety; but whatever is found contrary to reason is to be avoided promptly and meanwhile cut away from us altogether.

But now I, Cenwulf, by the grace of God king, humbly beseech your Excellency that, without offending your spirit, I may be permitted to address you concerning our advancement, as we desire, so that in the tranquil peace of your compassion you may receive me into your embrace, and that him whom no capacity of merit raises up may the abundant richness of your blessing enrich for governing his people.

May the Almighty, through your intercession, raise up with me the nation whom your apostolic authority instructed in the beginnings of the faith, against the attacks of foreigners, and may he deign to enlarge by himself the kingdom that God himself has given us.

This blessing all who ruled the Mercians before me with the scepter deserved to obtain from your predecessors. I, in my humility, ask for it, and from you, most holy father, desire to obtain it, so that first of all, by the lot of adoption, you may receive me as your son, just as I love you as a father and always embrace you with all the strength of my obedience.

For amid such great persons holy faith ought to be preserved and inviolate charity guarded, since paternal piety and the happiness of children in God are to be believed to exist together, according to the words of Hezekiah: “The father shall make known your truth to his children, O Lord.”

In these words I implore you, beloved father, not to refuse to make the Lord’s truth known through your sacred words to your son, although unworthy, so that through your sound instruction, with God’s help, I may deserve to reach the purpose of a better life.

Moreover, most sweet father, together with all our bishops and every person of rank among us, I beg you kindly to answer us concerning the many matters of inquiry on which we have thought it proper to seek your greatest subtlety, lest the tradition of the holy Fathers, and the rule handed down by them to us, be in some way corrupted among us as though it were unknown. May your direct word come to us in love and gentleness, so that by God’s mercy it may produce in us a fruitful result.

The first matter is this: our pontiffs and all our most learned men say among us that, contrary to the canons and the apostolic statutes established for us by our most blessed father Gregory, as you know, the authority of the metropolitan of Canterbury is divided between two dioceses. Yet, by the command of that same father, twelve bishops ought to be subject to his jurisdiction, as is read in our churches in the letter that he sent to his brother and fellow bishop Augustine, concerning the two metropolitan bishops of London and York—a letter that we do not doubt is also kept among you.

But that first pontifical dignity, which had then been established for London under the honor and adornment of the pallium, was on that account offered and granted to Canterbury.

For when Augustine of blessed memory, who, at the command of the blessed Gregory, ministered the word of God to the English people and most gloriously presided over the churches of Saxony [Note: What is now England was formerly called transmarine Saxony.], died in that same city, and his body had been buried in the church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, which his successor Saint Lawrence consecrated, it seemed to all the wise men of our nation that metropolitan honor should be held in that city where rests the body of the man who implanted the truth of the faith in these regions.

Yet King Offa first attempted to divert this honor, as you know, because of the hostility he had incurred with the venerable Lambert and the people of Canterbury, and to divide it between two dioceses; and your most pious fellow bishop and predecessor Adrian, at the request of the aforesaid king, began to do what no one had previously presumed to do, and raised the prelate of the Mercians to the dignity of the pallium.

Nevertheless, we blame neither of them, whom Christ, as we believe, triumphs with eternal victory.

Still, we humbly beseech your Excellency, to whom the keys of wisdom have rightly been entrusted by God, to inquire into this matter with your wise men and afterward deign to write back to us what seems right to you for us to observe, lest the seamless tunic of Christ suffer the schism of some disagreement among us. Rather, through your sound teaching, may it be directed, as we desire, toward the unity of true peace.

With great humility and love we have written these things to you, most blessed pope, earnestly beseeching your clemency to answer kindly and justly the matters that we have necessarily set forth.

You should also graciously examine the letter that Archbishop Atheraldus wrote to you before all our provincial bishops, at greater length, concerning his own affairs and the needs of all Britain; and whatever the rule of faith demands concerning the matters written in it, remember to disclose to us on the page of truth.

Therefore, last year we also sent my embassy, and that of the bishops, through Abbot Wada. But he received that embassy and conducted it sluggishly—indeed, foolishly.

Now, however, beloved father, I send you through my ministers Brine the priest, Fildas, and Ceolberth a small gift as a token of love: 120 mancuses with this letter. I ask you to receive it kindly and to deign to grant us your blessing.

May almighty God preserve you unharmed for a long time, to the praise of his holy Church.

## Letter II. Pope Leo III to King Cenwulf of the Mercians

He answers the preceding letter and willingly grants everything requested.

To the most excellent son, Cenwulf, king of the province of the Mercians, Saxony: Pope Leo.

[Col. 1027A]

Our most reverend and holy brother Atheraldus, archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, came to the most holy thresholds of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, faithfully fulfilling the vows of prayer and presenting to our apostolic see the cause of his priesthood. He brought us the words of your royal Excellence, contained in two letters directed by you.

Finding in them your great humility and upright faith, we give thanks to almighty God, who has adorned and distinguished your most prudent Excellence in all things: toward the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, by having you share love with us and humbly consent in all things to the apostolic censures.

Furthermore, in one of those letters we found that, if you had been near us, you would gladly have laid down your life for us in return for the grace of our apostolic office, and that you greatly rejoice in the Lord at our prosperity; and when the letters of our most sweet admonition reach the ears of your unanimity, you confess that you receive them with all sweetness and spiritual joy of heart, as sons receive a father’s gift.

You also acknowledged that you had ordered a modest blessing from your means to be offered to us—120 mancuses—which we received with great love for the salvation of your soul.

The aforesaid archbishop and his companions were honorably and kindly received by us, and we gladly arranged for him to be assisted in his needs.

Meanwhile, trusting your most prudent Excellence, since it was stated in your own royal letters that no Christian dares to oppose our apostolic sanctions, we strive with all our efforts to issue and proclaim whatever is useful to your kingdom. Thus, when our aforesaid brother Archbishop Atheraldus, or the entire synod, expounds to your royal Excellence, to all the leaders of your nation, and to the whole people of God the canonical judgment proclaimed by the evangelical and apostolic teaching and by the holy Fathers, as well as by our holy pontifical predecessors, you must in no way resist any part of their orthodox teaching.

Our Lord and Redeemer says in the Gospel: “Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward” (Matthew 10).

How much more, then, should this be done for that same lord archbishop, whom you have praised to us so highly—as indeed he deserves: a most renowned and learned man, whom you know to be prudent, adorned with good morals, and worthy before God and human beings.

Behold, therefore, dearest, most beloved, and most excellent son, good king, in these assertions of yours we praise almighty God, who has shown you such a bishop—one who, as a true shepherd, can prescribe worthy repentance in words according to the teaching of the holy Scriptures, rescue from the lower hell the souls of those subject to his priestly authority, lead them away from unquenchable fire, bring them into the harbor of salvation, and offer on their behalf a worthy and spotless sacrifice in the presence of the divine majesty of almighty God.

And because the aforesaid archbishop pleased us exceedingly in all his holiness and conduct of life, and because we trust him greatly, we have, by the authority of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose vicariate we exercise, though unworthy, granted him such a prelacy that, if any of his subjects—whether kings and princes or the whole people—transgresses the Lord’s commandments, he may excommunicate that person until he repents; and if he remains impenitent, “let him be to you as a heathen and a publican” (Matthew 18).

Concerning Atheraldus, now made archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, the eminence of your bishops asked us to render him justice concerning those dioceses of his—both episcopal and monastic—from which, as you learned, he was unlawfully stripped, and which were taken away from his venerable see, which he had formerly held.

After examining everything in detail, we found in our sacred archives that Saint Gregory, our predecessor, had given the entire diocese, numbering twelve, to the blessed Augustine, his archbishop and fellow servant, and had confirmed his right to consecrate bishops.

Therefore, having discovered the truth, we have restored to him in full, by our apostolic authority, the ordinations and confirmations as they had existed in ancient times, and we have delivered to his Church a privilege of confirmation to be observed according to the judgment of the sacred canons.

## Letter III. To Charlemagne

Concerning the privilege of the chapel at Eresburg.

Leo, servant of the servants of God, to Charles the Great [king of the Franks], Roman emperor.

Rejoicing in every way at your pious request, we do not delay to grant what you command.

Therefore, since you conquered this mountain of Eresburg together with all Saxony and offered it to God, and consecrated it through us to the blessed Peter, [Note: There are also letters of Pope Gregory VII, quoted in their proper place, concerning Saxony offered by Charlemagne to Saint Peter. In the same year the patriarch of Jerusalem sent Charlemagne, through his monk, the keys of the most holy sepulchre of our Redeemer; when he dismissed him, Charles attached to him Zacharias the priest, to convey gifts to those holy places (*Annales Francorum*). The piety and power of so great a most Christian king had become known even in the East, so that all looked to this one man as the sole glory and ornament of the Christian religion in those most calamitous times, when they groaned beneath the Saracens’ yoke. Moreover, for the restoration of the churches of Jerusalem, Charles ordered a collection in the manner of his forefathers. A heading on this matter in his *Capitularies* reads: “Concerning alms to be sent to Jerusalem, for restoring the churches of God, at the coming Nativity of the Lord.”] we decree that it be free from human authority and subject only to the jurisdiction of the brothers gathered there for the service of Christ.

To ensure that they suffer no hindrance in this matter, and that no confidence of rebellion be prepared for the invaders of your kingdom, by the authority of Saint Peter we prohibit under anathema that anyone should ever dare to place military defenses on that mountain, or plunder the estates that you have granted, or the tithes around the mountain within the two Saxon *rastae* that you assigned there.

For those who preserve these provisions, let there be peace from God the Father; for those who violate them, excommunication and eternal separation from the company of the blessed.

Given at Eresburg through the hands of the librarian and chancellor of the Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, in the year of our Lord …, the fourth year of Leo III, indiction 7 [or 8], on the day of the dedication of the chapel at Eresburg.

## LETTER XIV. TO RICULPH, BISHOP OF MAINZ. He gives thanks for gifts sent by him and in return sends relics of Saint Caesarius, which Riculph had requested.

[Note: The most reverend and in his writings, disputations, and labors on behalf of the Catholic Church by far the most illustrious man, Lord Johannes Pistorius, a theologian, jurist, and most celebrated physician, most distinguished counselor of His Sacred Imperial Majesty, a patron whom I must venerate with perpetual respect, sent me from the extensive and most noble Viennese library of that same Sacred Imperial Majesty an ancient manuscript codex. In it, among other ancient monuments, I found and transcribed this letter of Pope Leo III, addressed to Riculph, archbishop of the Church of Mainz, and incorporated it into this new edition of our letters, decretals, and councils.

The same codex contained the manuscript of the First Council of Mainz, held under Pope Leo III in the year of the Lord 813 by the authority of Riculph, archbishop of Mainz. Since, however, it differed little at the beginning from what exists in the edition of Surius, while at the end it was mutilated, I noted in the margin no, or at least very few, variant readings.

From the same man, who is most devoted to the Christian commonwealth and the Church, an original manuscript exemplar of the Council of Constance was sent to me from Constance, not without great expense, labor, and inconvenience on his part. What fruit and usefulness this will have for the whole Church we shall indicate below. Other materials discovered and communicated to this edition through the study and industry of this and other most learned men I shall mention at the appropriate places with the greatest gratitude—not, indeed, with any other intention than that you may understand, most dear reader, that nothing has been inserted or added to this work which was not received from men of the greatest learning and proven reliability.

Severinus Binius.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy Riculph, bishop.

[Col. 1030B]

When the venerable Bishop Bernharius, together with the religious abbot Adalhard, envoys of our son, the most serene Emperor Charles, had arrived at the threshold of the blessed chief apostles, and had announced to us everything prosperous and salutary concerning the aforesaid son of ours, his most exalted offspring, and all his faithful, we offered immense thanks to almighty God.

Meanwhile the aforesaid Bishop Bernharius presented us with a most beautiful gift and a letter from Your Holiness. When we read the letter again, we returned thanks to your reverend fatherliness, because you do not fail to remember us in your prayers that are pleasing to God. As for the many gifts with which you continually enrich us for love of the blessed apostle Peter, we believe in almighty God that you will receive a worthy recompense from him, both here and in the future, from that keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom. As you requested, we have sent Your Holiness, through the same venerable Bishop Bernharius, relics of Saint Caesarius.

## LETTER XV, OR THE STATEMENT OF THE ORTHODOX FAITH OF POPE LEO

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the Eastern Churches.

We send you this statement of the orthodox faith, so that both you and the whole world may hold the true and inviolate faith according to the holy Roman Catholic and Apostolic Church.

We believe in the holy Trinity—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—one almighty God, of one substance, one essence, and one power, creator of all creatures, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things: the Father from himself, not from another; the Son begotten from the Father, true God from true God, true light from true light—not, however, two lights, but one light; the Holy Spirit proceeding equally from the Father and the Son, consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Son.

The Father is wholly God in himself; the Son is wholly God, begotten from the Father; the Holy Spirit is wholly God, proceeding from the Father and the Son. Yet we do not say that there are three Gods, but one almighty, eternal, invisible, immutable God, who is wholly present everywhere, not divided into parts, but wholly in all things—not locally, but personally; who, without changing himself, created mutable things and governs what he has created; who always remains what he is, to whom nothing accidental can occur, because nothing can be added to or taken away from the simple nature of divinity, because he always is what he is, to whom the first is always present, for whom the eternal is eternal, and for whom being, living, and understanding are the same.

These three are one God. These three are the same God and Lord: a true and eternal Trinity in persons, and a true and eternal unity in substance, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one substance. This holy Trinity is no more in the three persons named together than in any one person named once, since each person is fully substance in himself. Yet there are not three substances, but one God, one substance, one essence, one eternity, one greatness, and one goodness: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The Father is not something different in nature from the Son or the Holy Spirit, nor are the Son and the Holy Spirit different in nature from the Father, for they have one nature. But the Father is one person, the Son another person, and the Holy Spirit another person. In the Father there is eternity; in the Son, equality; in the Holy Spirit, the bond of eternity and equality. All three are one in substance, essence, omnipotence, and divinity.

For just as the same holy Trinity is inseparable in substance, so it is inseparable in its works, although the works of God are specially attributed to certain persons: to the Father, for example, the voice that sounded from heaven over Christ when he was baptized; to the person of the Son, the assumption of humanity; and to the person of the Holy Spirit, the dove in whose form the same Holy Spirit descended upon the same Son baptized according to his humanity. Nevertheless, without any doubt, the whole holy Trinity effected both that voice and that dove in Christ’s humanity, for its works are inseparable.

We believe that the same Son of God, the Word, was eternally born from the Father, consubstantial with the Father in all things, and was born in time from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. He has two births: one eternal, from the Father, and the other temporal, from his mother. This Son of God was conceived through the conception of his flesh and born through the birth of his flesh. We confess that true God was conceived and true God was born—the same true God and true man, one Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, perfect from the beginning and in two natures, impassible and passible in the singularity of one person, mortal and immortal.

He was crucified in our weakness, yet always lives in his own power. He died by the death of his flesh and was buried; then, after descending to the dead, condemning and despoiling the prince of all wickedness, he returned and rose on the third day. With a triumph of glory, in the sight of his disciples, he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father—that is, in the majesty of divinity. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.

The wicked will see him judging in the form in which he was crucified, not in the humiliation in which he was unjustly judged, but in the glory in which he will justly judge the world. The vision of his majesty is the eternal blessedness of all the saints.

Whoever does not believe rightly according to this faith is condemned by the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church, founded by Jesus Christ our Lord himself, to whom be glory forever. Amen.

## LETTER XVI. TO ATHELARD, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY. He sends the pallium and recognizes him as primate of all England.

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Athelard, archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, forever.

It is especially fitting to episcopal discretion that the bishops of the Churches should, in accordance with their irreproachable faith, be granted a hearing, and that what they desire us to carry out through blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, and through us—provided it does not conflict with canonical decrees—should be brought to effect. Thus, when they obtain what they desire, they may become more ardent in their love of religion.

We have therefore judged it necessary to exhort and entreat your fraternal fatherliness concerning the dioceses of England entrusted to you—that is, concerning the bishops and monasteries, both of monks and of clerics and of women. As your Church has held them from ancient times, as we have learned from a search of our sacred archive, so we confirm that they are to be held by you and your successors.

The holy and distinguished preacher, Pope Gregory, ordered all the Churches of the English and confirmed them canonically as forever subject to the blessed Augustine, archbishop and his legate, through the sacred use of the pallium. Therefore we write to you by the authority of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, to whom power was given by the Lord God, who said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16).

Indeed, according to the judgment established by the holy canons, although unworthy, we who exercise the place of that same blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, grant to you, Athelard, and to your successors, that all the Churches of the English, as they have existed from ancient times, shall forever lawfully and irrevocably remain in your metropolitan see, in recognition of their subjection.

If anyone—which we do not desire—should attempt to act against the authority of this our definition or of this apostolic privilege, we decree by apostolic authority that, if he is an archbishop or bishop, he shall be deposed from the episcopal order; likewise, if he is a presbyter, deacon, or any other minister of sacred ministry, he shall be removed from his order. If he is one of the laity, whether king, prince, or any person great or small, he shall know that he is excluded from participation in holy communion.

By the authority of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, whose ministry we discharge, we grant this charter of privilege to you, Athelard, and to your successors, to hold forever. For its confirmation we have affixed our subscription with our own hands and ordered it to be sealed in our name. We also ordered it to be written by Sergius, our archivist, in the month of January.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, through the hand of Eustachius, first secretary of the holy Apostolic See, while our lord Charles, most pious emperor, consul, Augustus, crowned by God, great and peace-making emperor, was reigning, in the second year after his consulship, in the tenth indiction.

## LETTER XVIII. OF ALL THE BISHOPS AND PRIESTS OF THE WHOLE OF BRITAIN TO LEO. Concerning the succession of the archbishops of Canterbury.

All the bishops and priests of the entire island of Britain send greetings in Christ to the venerable Pope Leo.

We wish Your Fatherliness to know, as we read in the histories of the English written by Bede, our historiographer and praiseworthy teacher, that our predecessors did not have to undertake so great a labor—namely, to travel all the way to Rome for the sake of the pallium—as later became customary.

That aforesaid teacher wrote that the blessed Pope Gregory sent Augustine the preacher to the English people, not yet ordained a bishop, but as a monk, together with other fellow workers of the same religious order. After the conversion of that people, Augustine himself was ordained archbishop by Aetherius, archbishop of Arles, in accordance with the instructions he had received from the holy father Gregory.

While still alive, Augustine ordained Laurence as his successor, following the example of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, who is said to have consecrated Clement as his assistant and successor. After Laurence, Mellitus received the see of the Church of Canterbury; after Mellitus, Justus. Both of them received exhortatory letters from Boniface, pontiff of the Roman and Apostolic See, by whose authority they were permitted to ordain bishops. The form of that authority is as follows:

> “To Justus, my most beloved brother, Boniface sends greetings. We have sent the pallium to Your Fraternity through the bearer of this letter, prompted by our zeal for kindness; and we also grant you authority to celebrate ordinations of bishops whenever necessity requires and the mercy of the Lord goes before you, so that the Gospel of Christ may be extended through the preaching of many among all peoples who have not yet been converted, and so forth.”

This Justus had previously been ordained bishop by Augustine, as had Mellitus. Justus himself also ordained Paulinus bishop. Pope Honorius sent the pallium to Paulinus after learning that the people of Northumbria, together with their king, had been converted to the faith of Christ through Paulinus’s preaching.

After the death of the aforesaid Justus, Paulinus ordained Honorius archbishop of the Church of Canterbury. The aforesaid Pope Honorius also sent him the pallium and a letter containing these words:

> “To my most beloved brother Honorius, Honorius sends greetings. In accordance with your request and that of our sons the kings, by this present decree we grant you, in the place of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, the authority that, whenever divine grace commands one of you to be summoned to itself, the one who survives shall ordain another bishop in the place of the deceased.
>
> “For this reason we have sent one pallium to each of you, so that you may celebrate that ordination, and by the authority of our decree may perform an ordination pleasing to God. We have been compelled to grant you this because of the great distances of land and sea that lie between you and us, so that no loss may in any way come upon your Churches under cover of any pretext, but rather that you may more fully extend the devotion of the people entrusted to you. May God preserve you unharmed, most beloved brother.”

Albinus, or Alcuin, the greatest of scribes, also wrote to Offa, king of the English, saying that an archbishop should always be ordained by an archbishop and that the pallium ought to be sent to him by the apostolic lord. But the dissensions of kings disrupted this ordination, so that what ought to have been done could not be done, although the holy canons had most firmly decreed that ecclesiastical statutes should never be violated on account of royal dissensions.

At that time the holy and apostolic men fulfilled that praiseworthy command of our Savior: “You have received freely; give freely” (Matthew 10:8). At that time the simoniacal heresy languished without strength, because the gift of God was not bought with money but was given freely, just as he himself had commanded.

Yet those who sell the grace of God must fear what the apostle Peter said to Simon: “May your money be with you unto perdition; you have neither part nor lot in this matter” (Acts 8).

## NOTICE concerning the following epitome of a letter of Pope Leo III

[Our very ancient manuscript codex from Lucca, containing a collection of canons reduced to epitome, likewise presents the following letter of Leo, or synopsis of a letter. We understand from the person to whom it is said to have been sent that it belongs to this Leo. For it was addressed to Alcuin, who lived contemporaneously with no pontiff named Leo except the third.]

[Col. 1035A]

From a letter of Leo to Alcuin: TRIPLE IMMERSION IS TO BE PERFORMED IN BAPTISM. Letter of Charlemagne to Offa, king of Mercia.

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, sends greetings in Christ of present prosperity and eternal blessedness to the venerable man and dearest brother Offa, king of the Mercians.

Among royal dignities and the more exalted persons of the world, the rights of friendship joined in peaceful unanimity and the harmony of holy charity are accustomed to be preserved from the inmost affection of the heart, and this is of great benefit. If we are commanded by the Lord’s precept to dissolve the knots of enmity, how much more ought we to take care to bind together the bonds of charity?

Therefore, dearest brother, mindful of the ancient pact between us, we have taken care to send this letter to Your Reverence, so that the treaty founded upon the root of faith might flourish in the fruit of charity. Having reread the letters of Your Fraternity, which your envoys have brought to us at various times, we have endeavored to answer each of your authoritative requests appropriately.

First, we give thanks to almighty God for the sincerity of the Catholic faith, which we have found commendably written in your pages. We recognize that you are not only very courageous protectors of your earthly country, but also most devoted defenders of the holy faith.

As for pilgrims who desire, for the love of God and the salvation of their souls, to visit the thresholds of the blessed apostles, let them go peacefully and without any disturbance on their journey, carrying with them what they need, just as we formerly permitted. But we have found that certain people fraudulently mix themselves among them for the sake of trade, pursuing profit rather than serving religion. If such persons are found among them, let them pay the tolls established in the appropriate places; the others are to go free in peace.

You also wrote to us about merchants. By our command, we wish them to have lawful protection and patronage in our kingdom, according to the ancient custom of trade. If they suffer unjust oppression anywhere, let them appeal to us or to our judges, and we shall order full justice to be done. Likewise, if any of our people suffer injustice under your authority, let them appeal to the judgment of your equity, so that no disturbance may arise anywhere between our peoples.

Concerning the presbyter Odhberht, who, returning from Rome, came—so he usually says—out of love for God, wishing to live as a pilgrim rather than to accuse you, let Your Affection know that we sent him to Rome with the other exiles who had fled beneath the wings of our protection through fear of death. There, in the presence of the apostolic lord and of your archbishop N., to whom, as your letters informed us, they had bound themselves by oath, their case may be heard and judged. Thus, where the intervention of pity did not help, the decision of equity may help.

What could be safer for us than that the judgment of apostolic authority should decide a case in which the opinions of certain persons disagree?

I have sent you the black stones which Your Reverence requested. Let an envoy come to inspect what sort your mind desires; wherever they are found, we shall gladly order them to be given and assistance to be provided for transporting them.

But just as you informed us of your desire concerning the length of the stones, so our people request from you, concerning the length of the cloaks, that you order them to be made such as used to come to us in ancient times.

Let Your Affection also know that we have sent some blessing from our dalmatics or pallia to the individual episcopal sees of your kingdom, and to Aethelred, as an alms for the lord Adrian, our apostolic father and your friend. We ask that you carefully order prayers to be offered for his soul. We have no doubt that his blessed soul is at rest; nevertheless, we wish to show our faith and affection toward a friend most dear to us.

The blessed Augustine also commands that intercessions of ecclesiastical piety ought to be made for all, asserting that interceding for a good person benefits the one who does so.

We have also sent something from the treasury of human goods which the Lord Jesus has granted us in his free kindness through the metropolitan cities. To Your Affection, for the joy and thanksgiving of almighty God, we have endeavored to send one belt, one Hunic sword, and two silk cloaks, so that divine mercy may everywhere be proclaimed among the Christian people and the name of our Lord Jesus Christ glorified forever.

We beg you to have continual intercessions made for us and our faithful—indeed, for the whole Christian people—so that the most gentle goodness of the heavenly King may deign to protect, exalt, and enlarge the kingdom of holy Church.

May almighty God deign to preserve Your Dignity’s excellence unharmed, in long prosperity, for the protection of his holy Church, most desired brother.

Often a wolf pursuing a lamb has been held back by a voice;

Often a ewe, fleeing the greedy wolf, has looked back.

Often dogs and hares have lain beneath one shadow,

And a neighboring blue *cervula* stood upon a rock [the source prints bracketed *Cervnla*, apparently “little doe”];

And the chattering crow sat peacefully with Pallas’s bird,

And the dove was joined to the hawk.

I laughed at the deceiver who pretended to love;

The bird-catcher had fallen into his own snares.

Love enters minds; by practice, practice is learned;

Whoever can pretend to be sane will be sane.

# LETTER OF NICEPHORUS OF CONSTANTINOPLE TO LEO, SUPREME PONTIFF, translated by Theodore Peltanus, theologian of the Society of Jesus

[Note: Ignatius, disciple of Nicephorus, gives a most accurate summary of this letter in his Life of Nicephorus, under 13 March, chapter 4. Harduin.]

## SUMMARY

Because of the devil’s snares, the frequent falls of human life, the dog-like bites of the malicious, the gravity of the office, and many other matters of this kind, he teaches that it is difficult to discharge the episcopal office with dignity and public usefulness. He consequently adds that he ought not to have been appointed to that function, since he can scarcely order his own life rightly. He explains what manner of life he followed before becoming bishop and by what method and circumstance he came to the patriarchate of Constantinople.

He implores the assistance of the Roman pontiff, his faith, and his prayers before God. He praises the faith of the Romans commended by the Apostle and praises it himself; nevertheless, he adds that the grace of faith belongs not only to ancient Rome but also to the new Rome, indeed to all peoples and nations, because the apostolic word had spread throughout the whole world.

He then appends his confession of faith and declares at length and elegantly that he is alien from all the errors and heresies that have ever arisen, whether at Constantinople or anywhere else, against Christ and his Church. He embraces in every respect the Roman Church, which is the mother of the others, together with its faith, all the councils celebrated by its authority, and everything else in any way pertaining to the unity of faith. For this reason the letter deserved to be placed among those that concern the union of the Churches.

Finally, he excuses himself for having written to the Roman pontiff and given an account of his faith later than was proper. It is clear that the Leo to whom this letter was written was the second or third of that name, because he says that the Second Council of Nicaea was celebrated in his own time, although it is known to have been held under the pontificate of Adrian I. Adrian was succeeded by Leo III.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.] [Col. 1037A]

[Note: We compared the Greek text with the manuscript codex of the excellent library of the Seguier family, and in many places expanded and illustrated it.]

To the most holy and most blessed brother and fellow minister in all things, Lord Leo, pope of ancient Rome, Nicephorus, by the mercy of God bishop of Constantinople, greetings.

Truly great, admirable, and worthy of every word of praise is whoever is that faithful and prudent servant such as is described in those sacred and evangelical parables. Appointed by the Lord over his household, administering the word entrusted to him with judgment, spending neither wastefully nor extravagantly but according to necessity for those entrusted to him, making good use of what he has received, promptly giving his fellow servants their measure of grain, and supplying and distributing to each what is appropriate in due proportion, he thereby draws upon himself all the favor and goodwill of his master and carries away from him the promised reward.

Moreover, in all the matters over which his master appointed him steward, he proves himself capable of the office. For he is thoroughly competent and excellent, combining and displaying faith with the greatest prudence. In one respect he shows goodwill and gratitude toward his master and refuses nothing of what has been entrusted to him; in another, with proper reasoning, sobriety of mind, attention, and integrity, he conveys to those who deserve it what has been expended for the common benefit.

For these things he is deemed worthy of the master’s protection and hears the words: “Well done, good and faithful servant; you were faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your lord.” Such are the rewards and works of that servant.

[Col. 1040A]

But I have been assigned not among those capable of administering and directing such things, but among those who need to be administered and led. I am exceedingly small, the least of all, utterly lacking such good fortune and favorable destiny; and therefore, because of my weak and sluggish nature and my deficiency in the necessary remembrance of divine things—or, rather, in what is more necessary to say, because I have not set my own affairs in order and have not risen above what is low and earthbound—I would never have chosen to undertake the guardianship and care of souls.

Those who have not advanced in the improvement of their own concerns will scarcely be capable of arranging those of others well.

[Note: Baronius, under the year 811, preserves an old translation of this same letter, which the Reverend Father Fronto Ducaeus of the Society of Jesus sent him after transcribing it from a manuscript at Verdun. Ducaeus was also the first to place the Greek text printed by Hieronymus Commelinus alongside Peltanus’s translation.]

For, judging and considering myself unworthy of that gift and grace, I ought rather to be counted unworthy of that blessedness and deserving of misery and lamentation, lest I become like that wicked and evil servant of the opposite lot and disposition, who, through great laziness and lack of self-control, postpones his master’s coming, becomes harsh and unbearable toward his fellow servants, and associates with drunkards. When the master comes unexpectedly, he will divide him in two and number him among the hypocrites.

Nor should I become like the one who received a talent, placed it under the earth, and hid it, and who was therefore bitterly reproached—not only deprived of the interest and increase that should have been gained, but also stripped of the principal and sent into the outer darkness.

Would that I might not be caught in such things, set before many as an example, and become a shaking of the head to those who see me, once convicted and condemned by him who knows all things and examines our affairs; and would that I might not be punished sufficiently by the scourges of unholy actions, so that those found liable for similar things might be corrected by what happened to me and accept amendment.

[Col. 1040D]

Since, then, by God’s permission and forbearance I was brought beneath his yoke, and I have not willingly undertaken this service and ministry—for I came here under compulsion, as almost everyone here knows, in circumstances such as were previously mine and to which they have led—I must explain how this came about.

One person chooses one occupation or craft, another something else, whether small or great, as each is moved by free choice and selects for himself what he will do. Since human opinions are manifold, their deliberations diverse, their characters different, and their manner of life varied in every way, the choices of life are likewise divided and dispersed in many forms and advance toward infinite variety and multitude.

Some, among the artisans, have chosen to take up that pitiable and wandering life; others are seen to practice the laborious work of agriculture. Some choose from commerce its love of gain and wealth, or from seafaring its love of travel and danger; others devote themselves to various crafts. To avoid naming each individually, I pass over them.

Others, few indeed and select, have embraced the ascetic and philosophical way of life. They have purified both souls and bodies, and by this means have been deemed worthy to draw near to God and hasten toward the heavenly and blessed inheritance. Others, adorned with learning in the liberal sciences and arts and honored for good character, have cultivated their souls as works of the Muses, according as whatever seemed pleasant and dear to each person was suited to the inclination of his nature.

This is how matters stood for me in the present life.

When, therefore, I reached manhood, having passed beyond the first stage of youth, and was already spending time around the imperial courts, I encountered a certain military service—not idle or relaxed, but one carried out through hands and pens. For I happened to be among the imperial secretaries, whom the Latin language customarily calls *a secretis*.

For some time I was yoked to this service and bound by human affairs. Coming to recognize the instability of the things of this life, I began to turn over unceasing thoughts and reflections. I considered that whoever is occupied with these matters would find it difficult and almost impossible to touch higher things, and that, especially for one who has attained a better hope, failure would be unlikely.

I judged some things to belong to those who play and others to those who are serious. I declared that I would bid farewell to the former and embrace the latter with all my strength. I examined myself to see whether it would be better for me to be found distinguished in these things than to appear afterward beautified by those others.

The best of the prophets taught me that I should make myself a lawgiver; another wise man proclaimed that all things here are vanity of vanities and asked what profit a person has from all his toil under the sun. Another announced that the form of this world is passing away. Struck by these and by the commands of other sacred Scriptures, and remembering what I learned sung by one renowned among the outsiders for wisdom—“It is better to live as a private person than to possess the greatest power while intending to accomplish nothing worthy”—I cut short the present stage as a fading glory.

I immediately turned toward examining myself.

Therefore, when God in some fashion came to my aid, I despised the office, withdrew far from the imperial court and the disturbances of the city, and settled in some remote and elevated place, rugged and difficult to approach. A few miles from the Propontis, separated from the imperial city, I endeavored to make my dwelling there, intending, if possible, to take up the solitary life.

I was also urged on by a great desire for the desert and quiet, hoping that nowhere else but there would I meet the end of my life. But since it is not possible for everything to turn out according to everyone’s intention, and since necessity governs certain matters and God brings the outcome of undertakings to whatever end he wishes, the same thing happened to me.

My plans failed. I do not know by what judgments the God who permitted and overlooked these matters knows it, but I was torn away from my beloved solitude and brought back to the imperial city. This occurred, as God is witness, by the vote and judgment of those who at that time occupied seats in the imperial palace—the common sacred body of the Church and the senate—who together decided the matter as unavoidable and irretractable. For the ruler of the imperial city had already died, as a human being undergoes the human condition; and those very men, although he had often postponed the matter and acted arrogantly, advanced me to this priestly throne, an act arising more from tyranny than from persuasion.

[Col. 1044B]

Since, therefore, unwillingly, I have come beneath this yoke and have assumed these cares, not worthily or as befits the grace bestowed, I fear first the varied and intricate contrivances of the sophist of evil and the uprising of wicked and invisible spirits. I fear that they may find me naked and unarmed, stripped of the achievements of virtue.

They have not yet seen me trained in spiritual and divine exercises, or practiced and tested in combat against them. They may seek, by the arrows of sin, to wound and tear apart the chosen troop of the Church and to dissolve its orderly array, laughing at the fall of one who commands without judgment and without knowledge.

Then, seeing the intrusive and enviable nature of authority, I fear the deceitful and malicious character of those who are jealous and carefully watch everything we do, whether it is good or otherwise. They do not see the beams lying in their own eyes, nor are they willing to cleanse the mote from their eyes, but they investigate the splinters of others. For trifles utterly small and worthless, and for matters deserving no consideration, they wickedly arm their tongues against those who are eminent and attack them bitterly and most unjustly from both sides.

But having undertaken this contest, what helper and assistant shall I use except God, who permits these things? From him I ask that, with a compassionate and favorable eye, he look upon my modesty, strengthen my right hand, and guide me both toward his will and toward the safe governance of those entrusted to me.

He is also delayed by these difficult and distressing matters, either bringing us back for the sake of our improvement from our wickedness, or exposing to us the evil and perverse character of those others, so that no hidden bitterness, deceitfully lurking in the soul, may remain concealed, but that what is hidden may come into the open and become manifest.

[Col. 1045B]

If, as Solomon says, a brother helped by a brother is like a fortified city and a kingdom made secure, then I ask for the assistance of many other prayers; above all, however, I shall use the holy prayers and intercessions before God of your most desired and sacred fraternity in the Spirit. These bring us the greatest benefit and assistance, as prayers that draw near to God and are offered toward the heavenly and intellectual altar, when you approach and hear him purely, both in silence and in cries, as Moses and Samuel and others like them are heard to have done in the Spirit.

For this reason, help me in my weakness and raise your holy hands on high. We are persuaded that power proceeds from boldness, when we draw mercy down upon ourselves from above and make God favorable toward us, so that he may strengthen and invigorate what is weak and feeble.

Clothed in the breastplate of faith and wearing the helmet, may we stand bravely against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this age, and against the spiritual forces of wickedness, with whom our struggle has been established. May the vigor of our souls be preserved firm and unshaken. May we deal successfully and wisely with those who obey and those who resist; may we adopt them as children of the Church, equip them as rational sheep of Christ’s chosen flock, and prepare them to dwell in the divine fold of the Church. May they become invulnerable to the wolves that mercilessly tear them apart, sealed with the signs of concord and harmony, remaining secure and unwounded, so that they may be subject to Christ, the head of us all and chief shepherd, and submit their necks willingly to him.

May we be purified and made radiant, and become children of perfect light, so that we may be able to impart radiance and purification to others. May speech be given to us in the opening of our mouths, so that we may fill our hearers with the Spirit and proclaim without weariness and with the greatest vigor the power of the mysteries among us—by the grace of him who makes the tongue of the stammerer clear, makes lame feet stand upright, and holds and strengthens them to run well toward the preparation of the Gospel.

May we multiply the talent entrusted to us and in due time return to the master what is owed, together with its interest. May we labor in the good vineyard and bring back the excellence of our work, bearing generously the heavy and most burdensome part of our labors and bravely enduring the heat of the day, so that we may not be counted with those who came at the eleventh hour in the distribution of the reward.

May the faculty of vision in our minds be illumined, and may we gaze through the Spirit’s telescope, so as to become hearers of prophetic voices and eager servants of divine commands. Having received this gift, may we cleanse and wash away everything that clouds the eye of the soul and casts a shadow over the intellect within us.

May we guard ourselves on every side and preserve ourselves from the missiles of our opponents, remaining unharmed. May we foresee the sword when it comes as a divine scourge upon sinners, so that, if God grants it, when the divine messenger announces the assault and propitiates God, both he and those to whom he preaches may escape wrath. If not, may I at least save my own soul, like that righteous Lot, who secured the salvation of his own soul from the conflagration.

Here, then, let this account of your prayer and spiritual cooperation come to an end.

It is now time to behold the great trumpet of truth, the loud-voiced herald of the Gospel, the unforgettable Paul, who was greatly summoned by the ancient faithful Romans, leaping, as it were, in the Spirit, exulting and taking pride in the earnestness and warmth of their faith, bearing witness to it, and proclaiming that it resounded and was announced to all the ends of the world. Writing to them, he appears to say:

> “I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.”

Since the pure and uncorrupted faith of the Gospel among us, than which no other exists, is neither confined within Roman boundaries nor limited by the ends of the world, but has spread and overflowed so far beyond them, I am moved by prophetic and apostolic voices to say:

> “Throughout all the earth the sound of the divine proclamation has gone out, and to the ends of the inhabited world the words of those who proclaim it.”

If we must speak of it in even loftier terms, this faith is also proclaimed in heaven among the highest intellectual powers.
