For if there is one Church in heaven and on earth, and if we hear of the Church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, and of the Jerusalem above, the city of those justified by faith—whose architect and maker is God, who reconciled heavenly things with earthly things and broke down the dividing wall, and who, through ineffable condescension, took upon his shoulders what was lost and united it with those who are saved and remain—then rightly and justly we possess this unity and uninterrupted concord, when creation is united with faith in understanding and harmony. For God is known not only in Judea.

Those who have received the new name of Romans, built upon one and the same foundation of faith—namely, the wise workmanship of the apostles and prophets, with Christ our Savior and God, the cornerstone—do not in any respect fall short in faith of those who came before them.

For in the Church of God there is no precedence by rank, just as there is neither Jew nor Greek, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free; rather, all are one in Christ. Therefore let the divine Paul boast and exult greatly among us, magnifying himself as he joins the new to the old and compares them as one in doctrines and proclamations.

Following his teachings and admonitions, and strengthened by the confession of our faith in which we stand and boast, we openly proclaim our convictions concerning this faith, so glorious and blameless to us, with which we worship God and which we insist we must breathe continually—or, according to the editor’s suggested reading, “in which we hold the air”—and with which we assert that we shall depart from this life, strengthened and guarded by grace from above. We have no other way to proceed, advance, order the present life well, or attain the good things reserved for the worthy in the life to come.

I confess and believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker, master, and Lord of all; and in his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, the true God, the pre-eternal Word, begotten from him without beginning and ineffably, beyond the grasp and understanding of every intellectual and sensible creature; and in the Spirit of truth, the giver of life and all-holy.

I believe in one Trinity, consubstantial, above substance, invisible, incomprehensible, inseparable, immutable, simple, undivided, uncompounded, without extension, eternal, incorporeal, without quality or quantity, equal in honor, equal in glory, and equal in divinity; intangible, not subject to touch, without form, infinitely good, ever-shining light, triple light, light above light, always existing in the same manner and according to the same order.

It possesses an overseeing and perfecting power over all things, shining intellectually and indivisibly upon all rational and intellectual beings through the providential outpouring of divine light, in proportion to the receptivity of those who are illumined. It preserves them in being and well-being as substantial realities, not as mere names. It is glorified and worshiped with one divinity, authority, and kingship by every visible and invisible creature.

[Col. 1052A]

Of the three contemplated in the Trinity, the Father is without beginning and exists without cause; he is from no one, for he possesses being in himself.

The Son is not without beginning in the sense of being without a source, for he is from the Father; the Father is the beginning of the Son as his cause. But if one understands “beginning” as temporal beginning, then he too is without beginning, for he is the maker of time and is not subject to time. Begotten, yet shining eternally and without separation with the Father, he is the radiance of glory and the impress of the Father’s hypostasis.

The Holy Spirit has his existence from the Father, not by being begotten but by proceeding. He is contemplated eternally with the Father and the Son. He is not without beginning because of his procession from the Father—for the Father is also his beginning in the sense of cause—but he is without beginning in time.

There is therefore one God, the Father, from whom are all things; one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things; and one Holy Spirit, in whom are all things.

From the three perfect persons comes the one, supremely perfect and first-perfect divinity. They differ from one another in distinguishing and personal properties, but each, when mentally distinguished from the others—though they are naturally inseparable because of the unity of essence—is confessed and believed by us to possess in fullest measure every property of divinity.

The three, joined to one another, are worshiped by us as one God: triadically according to hypostasis, but monadically according to essence. What we honor is monarchy, not polyarchy, because of the disorderly and factional confusion of Greek stupidity.

This monarchy is not the limitation to a single person, which would reflect the imperfection and elementary condition of Jewish poverty and infancy, but the monarchy displayed by equality of nature, harmony of will, identity of movement, and the united inclination of those who proceed from the Father toward the One—something impossible in created nature.

Thus speaks the great Gregory among theologians, and no part of the joined and connatural divinity contemplated in the Trinity is divided.

Let the wicked belief and madness of the serpent-like Arius be removed and cut away from us. The same Trinity is indivisible, neither divided nor alienated in glory and eternity. The divine hypostases do not change into one another or merge into one another; rather, the eternity of each is preserved unaltered and unmixed in each. Far away, then, let the deceptive confusion of the vain-minded Sabellius be driven and banished.

I venerate and worship the mystery determined before all ages and revealed in the last times for the salvation of our entire race, accomplished through the great condescension and ineffable dispensation of Christ, the one true God of our holy and life-giving Trinity, so that from the source of our being, through his ineffable goodness, we might also receive our well-being as a gift.

I confess and believe that the one Son and Word of God, belonging to the life-giving and blessed Trinity, worshiped and glorified eternally together with the Father and the Holy Spirit as consubstantial and co-enthroned, moved by boundless love for humanity toward pity for his own creature, through the Father’s good pleasure and compassion and through the grace and cooperation of the all-holy Spirit, descended from heaven and lived among human beings.

He did so in order that he might restore by grace us who had long been condemned by sin, fallen from the paradise of delight, and subjected to corruption, and make us participants in the divine nature.

Having dwelt in the womb of the Virgin, who was truly and properly the Mother of God and whose soul and body had first been purified by the Spirit, he took from her our whole nature into himself. Just as at the beginning he had fashioned human beings as living creatures, so he came forth as God incarnate, remaining what he had been—God.

He preserved as a virgin, even after childbirth, her who had given birth in a manner beyond nature and beyond utterance, so that her natural virginity was in no way changed. This manifested truly that, in the course of his birth, he remained unaltered and unchanged.

[Col. 1053C]

He who is connatural with the Father and consubstantial with us in all things, except sin, took hold of the seed of Abraham and shared in flesh and blood as we do. He assumed flesh animated by a rational and intellectual soul, which had not previously existed independently of the supreme union. Rather, one rational, living flesh is believed in the connaturality according to Christ.

He did not dwell among us merely by grace as in a tent, but the whole of him was joined to the whole of human nature. He accomplished the union without confusion, without division, and beyond nature, so that the essences of divinity and humanity that came together might remain in their natural properties and in no way pass into one another.

[Note: More correctly, “according to the appellations … to exist in one another by reason of the natural conjunction,” so that the sentence means: “Let us piously understand them, according to their appellations, as existing in one another by reason of the natural conjunction.” Harduinus.]

Even if, according to the wording concerning the natural conjunction, we piously understand them as entering into one another according to their expressions, because of the joining of the names, we nevertheless believe that they are distinguished only in conception and not in reality, because of the supernatural union of the things that came together.

We believe that the singular and unified character of the hypostasis remains undivided and unbroken.

Let the imaginary confusion and commingling of the deceiver Eutyches [Eutyches] and Dioscorus be overthrown. Accordingly, we confess the same one to be created and uncreated, pre-eternal and beyond time, heavenly and earthly, circumscribed and uncircumscribed, passible and impassible, without mother and without father: the one according to his ineffable, beginningless, and pre-eternal generation from the Father; the other according to the hidden and incomprehensible union effected for our sake.

We proclaim his two births, incomprehensible and beyond reason. For the only-begotten Son, who existed in the form of God and was in the bosom of the Father—that is, who had shone forth from the Father before the ages in the Father’s essence—emptied himself at the consummation of the ages and assumed the form of a servant, that is, our essence.

[Col. 1056B]

The union in Christ according to hypostasis brings together the things from which the Savior consists, one with another: the invisible with the visible, the passible with the impassible, and so forth—not one person with another, God forbid.

We confess the same one to be perfect, true God, and perfect man. We assign the differences to the natures while recognizing one and the same person even after the incarnation. We do not divide him into two sons because of the difference between the natures that came together in the hypostatic union.

Thus the mad Nestorius is expelled from the divine court, while Christ completes all the works of his divine-human activity. As God, the same one performed divine things, working through them the divine signs and miracles; as man, the same one willingly received sufferings and insults.

Therefore, in accordance with and necessarily following the two natures, I confess two natural operations also, equal in number to the natures, since they signify and constitute the very essences, or natures, according to the pious and God-befitting traditions of our God-wise Fathers.

Likewise I profess two wills, or natural volitions, of the one and same Lord and God Jesus Christ. I know him to be endowed with will according to each of the natures in which and from which he exists and is conceived; just as he acts, so he wills. He came willingly to the saving passion.

I believe that he was crucified not in the essence in which he shines together with the Father—for although it is said, by the principle of interchange, that the Lord of glory was crucified—but in the earthly nature that he assumed from us, according to which he took our clay-like formation and became a curse for us.

He did this to make us participants in the blessing that is with him, and according to the flesh he endured the death of criminals, so that in his flesh he might condemn sin, the sting of death, and abolish him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil.

His body was handed over to burial but preserved incorruptible, without the ineffable and inexpressible union being divided in any way, even though his rational and intellectual soul was separated from it during the three-day interval. With that soul he himself also descended into Hades and, as the chief and divine Peter said, went and proclaimed the resurrection to the spirits in prison, granting them freedom and release.

He became for us the firstfruits of incorruption, in which he rose as the firstborn from the dead. For he rose as God, trampling down death, opening the way of resurrection for all flesh, and restoring us who had fallen through the fall of sin.

After the resurrection he appeared to the women, announced joy to them, and dispelled the grief that had entered our race through the female sex. He was also seen by his inspired disciples, confirming to them the mystery of his resurrection and showing through the eating of food and the touch of the wise Thomas upon his divine side who he was, the same person he had been before the resurrection.

He was taken up into heaven and sat at the right hand of God the Father with the humanity he had assumed. With that humanity he will again come in divine glory and with authority over all creation. He will sit as judge, rendering to each according to what he has done. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ.

After this I also believe in the resurrection of the flesh, when the transformation of the world takes place, so that our mortal nature may put on immortality and our corruptible nature incorruption.

I confess one baptism for the remission of sins, performed into the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit according to the evangelical and divine tradition.

These venerable doctrines and mysteries of our orthodox and holy worship, in accordance with the lofty and pure theology handed down to us by the divine initiators of the mysteries, the saving dispensation of God’s Word toward us, and all proclamations comparable to these, I preserve and embrace with complete acceptance and faith.

I also accept and request the intercessions and supplications before God, first and especially those of our all-pure, all-blameless, and ever-virgin Lady, the Mother of God; then those of the divine and heavenly powers, the holy and most celebrated apostles, the blessed prophets, the glorious and victorious martyrs, the God-bearing Fathers, and all the saints who from eternity have pleased the Lord.

They live forever in him, for “the souls of the righteous are in the hand of the Lord.” Through them I receive the greatest salvation of soul and body.

I worship and embrace their venerable relics, since they are a remedy for sufferings of soul and body. I therefore praise their honorable and God-filled way of life and their unforgettable struggles and contests; I honor their tombs and crown them with the highest honors, because they poured out their blood for the glory of God, the Savior of us all, and despised this temporary life for love of him, becoming imitators of his life-giving and saving passion.

At the same time, I venerate the holy image of Christ, Savior of all, and the sacred images of his all-pure Mother and Mother of God, and I assign to them the worship of honor.

In addition, I gladly accept and honor the seven holy and ecumenical councils, together with the divine, supernatural, and saving doctrines defined and proclaimed in them by our holy and God-bearing Fathers, whom the Holy Spirit appointed at the proper times to shepherd and govern his Church.

First, I accept the council of the 318 most celebrated Fathers who assembled at Nicaea against the impious and frenzied Arius. Having expelled him from the Church, it proclaimed to us through the holy and divine creed the true and perfectly straight faith. It dogmatically taught in an orthodox manner that the divine Word and Son of God is not a creature but consubstantial with the Father and coeternal with him, true God and creator of all.

[Col. 1060C]

Next, I accept the council of the 150 divinely inspired Fathers assembled in this imperial city. It overthrew the impious fighter against the Spirit, Macedonius, expanded the meaning of the holy creed, clarified it by the words concerning the Holy Spirit, and affirmed that the Spirit is true God, consubstantial with the Father and the Son, and not a creature. It also expelled Apollinarius of Laodicea, truly foolish and senseless, from the Church.

After it came the holy council of the 200 sacred teachers first assembled at Ephesus against the vain-minded Nestorius and his blasphemies. Having deposed him, it wisely defined one hypostasis of Christ our God according to the union and two natures without confusion and without division. It declared the same person God and man and confessed holy Mary to be truly and properly the Mother of God.

After this came the 630 divine and God-bearing Fathers assembled at Chalcedon. They condemned the impious Eutyches and Dioscorus and their dark and obscured confusion. Having anathematized them, the council piously proclaimed the same Christ and our God perfect God and perfect man, in two natures and one hypostasis, without confusion and without division.

I also accept the holy Fifth Council, again assembled in that God-guarded city, consisting of the 165 holy Fathers. It cut out the impious doctrines of Theodore, Nestorius, Origen, Didymus, Evagrius, and those of like belief—doctrines previously hidden from many but then bitterly sprouting and budding forth. For through the fables they invented, they followed Jewish and Greek opinion rather than Christian doctrine.

Next I accept the Sixth Ecumenical Council, also assembled in this imperial city, consisting of 170 holy men. It proclaimed the properties, natural operations, and wills of Christ’s natures. It anathematized Theodore, bishop of Pharan; Honorius; Cyrus; Sergius; Pyrrhus; Paul; and Peter, who had entered the priesthood in the Church by God’s permission; as well as Macarius, called the president of Antioch, and Stephen, his disciple; and also Polychronius, the old man childish in mind. These men taught one will and one operation in our Savior Christ and God.

After and in addition to this, I accept the Seventh Holy Council, assembled for the second time at Nicaea in our own age and consisting of 150 Fathers. It sealed all the preceding holy councils and received the veneration of the sacred and holy images, handed down to the Church from the beginning, decreeing that they should be venerated in a manner comparable to the form of the life-giving cross.

We expelled from the Church those who spoke empty words against these images in contempt and destruction of them and accused Christians of venerating them as gods—namely, Theodosius, Basil, and Sisinnius, who by God’s forbearance occupied priestly thrones.

I accept these aforementioned holy ecumenical councils, and I embrace the doctrines and labors of all the distinguished and blessed Fathers as unimpeachable teaching and the foundation of salvation. I accept those whom the Catholic Church receives and reject those whom it rejects.

I reject and utterly repudiate those from Simon Magus onward who have fallen completely away from piety down to the present day, who are mixed up in the opinions of evil and destructive doctrines, who have rejected the tradition of the saints, and who have dared to mix the bitter seed of weeds with the field of orthodoxy. I anathematize them and all who follow them, spurn them as a plague upon the Church of Christ, and subject them to the anathema.

We have therefore declared our mind in these matters to your most blessed and God-taught fraternity, following the ecclesiastical institution established from above as a living herald and using our writing as a means of bringing about the bonds of love in Christ and of mutual harmony and concord.

May your fraternity, most desired in the Lord, reply to us first with prayers before the Lord, and then with appropriate words and actions that support and instruct us, so that by your laws and teachings we may stand firm, unceasing and uncorrupted in this faith. May we preserve without alteration all its mysteries handed down from above, remaining within the boundaries of the ecclesiastical fold, gathering all the rational sheep of the sacred flock by the divine trumpet, by the clear resonance of apostolic and spiritual teaching, and by God-inspired sounds.

May we keep them unharmed from the beasts that plot against them, marked with the anointing and name of Christ, the chief shepherd.

[Col. 1064B]

Complete by your own efforts what is lacking on our part, as brothers who love one another and are affectionate, so that your abundance may serve our deficiency. Whatever is lacking in us in words and deeds, strengthen and increase through the priestly and reverent dignity of your life. Do not be sparing with the gift given to you; for it brings no diminution to those who give abundantly, but in due season returns fruits of honor in multiplied measure to those who freely bestow it.

Support us, who are weaker, with the God-given power you possess, strengthen our feet for the path of the Gospel, and do not cease to offer counsel that is beneficial and directed toward salvation.

Thus, just as in confession we possess unity and undifferentiated agreement, so, joined and bound together in the bond of love, may we preserve among ourselves the unbroken gift of peace in the ministry entrusted to us. That ministry preserves the Church undivided and harmonious, so that the intelligible city of the great King, fortified and guarded, may remain unconquered and unassailable against every assault and device of invisible enemies and of those who run about it seeking to devour one of those enrolled and marked in the Spirit.

Against them we bring forward not carnal weapons but spiritual weapons: the shield of faith and the sword of the word, which is the word of God. With the sling of the Spirit we drive far away and chase off their savage boldness, overthrowing the engines and devices of sin.

May we be deemed worthy of divine protection and assistance, and may he make our commonwealth tranquil and peaceful, so that at the restoration of all things, at the last trumpet, we may be found worthy to meet without condemnation the author of our life when he comes in the glory of the Father with his holy angels; may we enter the bridal chamber with the wise virgins and enjoy the angelic banquet, becoming heirs of the good things reserved for the worthy in Christ, the true God, through the intercession of his undefiled and blameless mother and of all the saints. Amen.

If we have met these matters so late in the course of time, let no one wonder or accuse our judgment. Rather, let your God-loving fraternity know that the hard and relentless will of authority prevailed, and was able to prevent us from making use of what had been decided. It was not that priestly custom had been neglected and fallen away, nor that through laziness we had become indifferent to what was necessary and proper for ecclesiastical men.

Let your holy soul also understand—if it intends to blame me for the delay—that it too has experience of how difficult it is to resist powers that impose their own wills and strive to fulfill every desire.

For the one who obstructed us seemed to put forward a respectable pretext for what had been done on account of the anointing, and to proclaim and complain that you had torn yourselves away from the Church.

Accordingly, since you yourselves have suffered in these matters what was forced upon you, you can be indulgent toward those who unwillingly encounter similar things.

For this reason, I think there will be no need for further arguments in defense of the delay; they may appropriately be set down here, and what is now being done and completed bears witness to them.

The key has been broken, the gate has been opened, the stones of stumbling have been removed from the road, every smooth and level way has been prepared, the distressing obstacles have departed, the scandals have been removed, the hindrances from that side have been dissolved, and a free light has shone upon the Church.

Therefore the works of love and of the prevailing priestly custom have found room to be accomplished and brought to completion.

But there are some who have not cared about divine things. For the sake of their own glory, they have been eager to see what sort of judgment they will meet from the divine tribunals. Since they are devoted to the present open glory and magnificence, they have set their affairs against one another.

We, however, placing our concern upon the glory of God, the honor and concord of the Church, and the preservation of the sacred institutions, hold to what belongs to us. For our most recently revealed pious and mighty emperor, a true child of the Church, distinguished by God-pleasing character and good works, we send fervent prayers and supplications to God, who crowned him and reigns with him—or, according to the variant, counsels him.

We pray that God may grant him a peaceful life and preserve his imperial rule for the longest possible time, adorning him with victories over barbarians, guiding the Christian commonwealth successfully, forming him in zeal for orthodoxy and observance of the divine commandments, and granting him, through the continuance of his authority, the favor of prosperous children.

[Col. 1068A]

[Note: Here the Seguier manuscript ends, its final folio having been cut off.]

To Michael, the most holy metropolitan of Philadelphia [variant: “fellow-brother”], the Christ-loving city, we have entrusted these present synodical letters for our beloved and desired fraternity.

We are persuaded, from his earlier request and conversation, that he will be looked upon and received by you with goodwill. We also ask, for the sake of our modesty, that the reception, honor, and rest you grant him may be especially genuine and familiar.

For he possesses a very warm and genuine affection toward you, displays zeal and readiness in the affairs of the Church, and excels in word, life, and virtue. If God grants him success and moves you, he is to bring back to us tokens of love and concord—namely, copies of your honored letters, written by your own hand—for our greater spiritual joy and for the strengthening of our friendly disposition in the Lord.

We greet most warmly all the fraternity that is with you in Christ.

Be strong in the Lord, and pray earnestly for us, most holy and most blessed brother. Possessing as mediator and fellow worker before God, our common protector and helper, the great and chief apostle, do not hesitate to offer him prayers on behalf of us, his unworthy servants.

As a token of the love in the Lord that mediates between us, we have sent to Your Fraternal Beatitude a golden *enkolpion* (breast ornament). One face is enclosed with crystal; the other is decorated in encaustic; inside it is another *enkolpion* containing portions of the precious wood.

We have also sent a white *sticharion* and an unstitched brown *phenolion*, together with an *epitrachelion* and an *encheirion*, embroidered with gold.

Receive these, with God granting success and preservation, as a modest offering [the following recipient/object is textually uncertain]; for the sake of remembrance, we have ordered these items, skillfully wrapped in linen, to be marked with a lead seal.

[Col. 1038A]

## Textual variants in the supplied Greek text

The following bracketed readings belong to the Greek recension printed after the Latin translation. They are retained here with their precise local sense rather than being silently absorbed into the English prose.

- **Opening salutation and the faithful servant ([Col. 1037B]):** after *πιστός* (“faithful”), the bracketed addition **καὶ φρόνιμος** adds “and prudent.”
- **The author’s natural weakness ([Col. 1040A]):** printed **νωθεστέρῳ** means “more sluggish”; bracketed **νοθεστέρῳ** means “more spurious” or “less genuine.” In the same sentence, bracketed **ᾖς περ εἰπεῖν οἰκεινότερον** gives “which, to speak more properly, would be more fitting,” in place of the printed wording about what is more necessary to say.
- **Each person’s natural bent ([Col. 1041B]):** printed **ἐπιβόλῳ** denotes the inclination or aptitude of nature; bracketed **ἐπιβουλῷ** would instead denote nature’s hostile or plotting design.
- **Reflection on transitory affairs ([Col. 1041C]):** the printed **βοῦς** is “ox”; bracketed **νοῦν** is “mind,” yielding the intelligible reading “I unfolded my mind and stirred my thoughts.”
- **Prompted by sacred Scriptures ([Col. 1041D]):** printed **κατακουτιζόμενος** is corrupt; bracketed **κατακοντιζόμενος** means “being pierced as by darts,” here by the similar admonitions of Scripture.
- **Withdrawal near the Propontis ([Col. 1044A]):** printed **διειργόμην** means “I was separated” from the imperial city; bracketed **διειργεμένην** changes the construction to a feminine participle, “separated,” agreeing with an implied place or region.
- **Return to the palace ([Col. 1044B]):** bracketed **πάλιν** adds “again”: he was led back again to the imperial court.
- **The flock’s defense ([Col. 1045C]):** printed **φυλαχθῆναι** is “to be preserved”; bracketed **διαφυλαχθῆναι** intensifies it, “to be thoroughly preserved.” Printed **λογικῆς** makes the phrase “sheep of the rational, chosen flock”; bracketed **λογικά** instead directly calls them “rational sheep” of Christ’s chosen flock.
- **Remaining unharmed ([Col. 1045D]):** bracketed **διαμένοντας** reads “remaining” unassailable and unwounded, replacing the printed **ἐπάρχοντας**, “being/presiding.”
- **The stammering tongue ([Col. 1048A]):** printed **γλῶσσαν μογγίλαλον** means “a stammering tongue”; bracketed **μογιλάλων** gives “the tongue of stammerers.”
- **Paul’s thanksgiving ([Col. 1048C]):** bracketed **διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ὑπὲρ πάντων ὑμῶν** supplies “through Jesus Christ for all of you” in “I thank my God … because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.”
- **Creation’s concord in faith (before [Col. 1049B]):** printed **συνοῖσεν** gives the sense that creation “brought together” concord and unanimity with faith; bracketed **σύνεισιν** reads “comes together” or “understands.”
- **Equality in the Church ([Col. 1049B]):** bracketed **οὐ Σκύθης** adds “nor Scythian” to “neither Jew nor Greek, barbarian, slave, nor free.”
- **Perseverance in the faith ([Col. 1049C]):** Harduin proposes the extended reading **ᾗ τὸν ἀέρα, ἀκλινῶς ἔχομεν· ᾗ καὶ συναπέρχεσθαι τῆς ἐνθένδε ζωῆς κατισχυριζόμεθα, τῇ ἄνωθεν χάριτι δυναμούμενοι καὶ φρουρούμενοι, ὡς οὐκ ἔστιν ἄλλην ὁδεῦσαι ἢ ἐπιβῆναι ἢ τὰ τῆς παρούσης ζωῆς εὖ θέσθαι**: “in which we hold our course unwaveringly; with which we are confident of departing from this present life, strengthened and guarded by grace from above, since there is no other way to travel or ascend, to order the present life well,” before the text continues, “or to attain the good things laid up for the worthy in the age to come.”


  **Exact unterminated Harduin conjecture as supplied:** `Hard. forte, ᾗ τὸν ἀέρα, ἀκλινῶς ἔχομεν· ῇ καὶ συναπέρχεσθαι τῆς ἐνθένδε ζωῆς κατισχυριζόμεθα, τῇ ἄνωθεν χάριτι δυναμούμενοι καὶ φρουρούμενοι, ὡς οὐκ ἔστιν ἄλλην ὁδεῦσαι ἢ ἐπιβῆναι ἢ τὰ τῆς παρούσης ζωῆς εὖ θέσθαι [Col. 1049C] ἢ τῶν ἐντῇ μελλούσῃ ἀποκειμένων τοῖς ἀξίοις ἀγαθῶν ἐπιτεύξασθαι .`
- **The divine light ([Col. 1049D]):** printed **προνοίᾳ** is the “providence” of the divine light; bracketed **προχύσει** is its “outpouring.” Bracketed **καὶ εὖ εἶναι** adds “and well-being” to preservation in being.
- **The Son as radiance ([Col. 1052A]):** bracketed **ἁπαύγασμα** is an orthographic form of printed **ἀπαύγασμα**, “radiance,” without a distinct English meaning.
- **Divine monarchy ([Col. 1052C]):** printed **ἡ ἑνὸς προσώπου περιγραφή** is “the circumscription of one person”; bracketed **ἦν ἐν προσώπων περιγραφῇ** reads “was in a circumscription of persons,” changing both syntax and number.
- **Eutyches and Dioscorus ([Col. 1056A]):** bracketed **Εὐτυχέος** is the genitive “of Eutyches,” in place of the printed form **Εὐτυχίου**; the referent is unchanged.
- **The crucified Lord of glory ([Col. 1056D]):** printed **λέγεται** means “is said”; bracketed **γέγραπται** means “is written.” Printed **γερᾷ** describes the assumed nature as “aged/old”; bracketed **γεηρᾷ** gives the expected “earthly nature.”
- **Proof of the Resurrection ([Col. 1057B]):** bracketed **ὡς** adds “that/how” before “who he was even before the Resurrection,” as shown by eating and Thomas’s touch.
- **Supplying what is lacking ([Col. 1064B]):** printed **ἐποικοδομήσητε καὶ ἐπαυξήσητε** addresses the recipients, “that you may build up and increase”; bracketed **ἐποικοδομήσηται καὶ ἐπαυξήσηται** is singular passive, “that it may be built up and increased.” Printed **ὑμῖν** is “to you”; bracketed **ἡμῖν** is “to us.”
- **Need for an explanation ([Col. 1065B]):** printed **ἀλογίας** means “irrationality” or “lack of reason”; bracketed **ἀπολογίας** means “defense” or “explanation.” Printed **ἀναπέπται** is a defective form in “the gate has been opened”; bracketed **ἀναπέπταται** supplies the regular “has been thrown open.”
- **Prayer for the emperor ([Col. 1065D]):** printed **συμβασιλεύοντα** calls God the one “reigning together with him”; bracketed **συμβουλεύοντα** calls God the one “counseling him.”
- **Michael’s title ([Col. 1068A]):** printed **Φιλαδέλφου** identifies him as metropolitan of Philadelphia; bracketed **συναδέλφου** reads “fellow-brother.” The accompanying note records that the Seguier manuscript ends here because its final folio was cut off.

Two earlier bracketed Latin readings are also retained: **bonitas**, “goodness,” in the prayer that the heavenly King protect and enlarge the Church; and **Cervnla**, apparently *cervula*, “little doe,” in the poem’s line about the blue animal standing upon a rock.

**Exact source spellings retained:** **ᾖς περ εἰπεῖν οἰκεινότερον·** (“which, to speak more properly, would be more fitting”); **λογικὰ** (“rational,” directly modifying the sheep); and **συμβουλευοντα** (“counseling him,” printed without an accent in the supplied text).

Source/review notes: The complete supplied letter and doctrinal argument are retained, including their citations and boundary fragments.

To Pope Leo of ancient Rome, brother and fellow minister in every respect, most holy and most blessed: Nicephorus, by the mercy of God bishop of Constantinople, sends greetings in the Lord.

Truly great, and worthy of every praise and admiration, is anyone who is such a faithful and prudent servant as the one described in the sacred parables of the Gospel. For, appointed by the Lord over his household, he distributes to the flock entrusted to him the word—not needlessly, wastefully, or imprudently, but with judgment and according to the need and benefit of those in want—and at the proper time dispenses to his fellow servants their measure of wheat, finally distributing to each what is necessary, suitably and in due proportion. Thus he earns no ordinary grace and goodwill with his master [Col. 1038B] and surely attains the prize of the promised blessedness. Indeed, making progress in all the matters of which he has been appointed steward, diligently striving to attain what has been promised, and everywhere applying faith together with prudence and skill, as well as the care and concern that are owed, he admirably demonstrates his goodwill and grateful disposition toward his master.

Therefore, since he loses none of those entrusted to his faith, but by appropriate prudence, sobriety of understanding, diligence, and sincerity vigorously advances the salvation and freedom of each, supplying the necessary means for attaining them, it comes about that, favored by the Lord and graciously visited by his arrival, he hears that joyful Gospel saying [Col. 1038C]: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:23). Such, then, are the works and rewards of that faithful servant.

[Col. 1039A]

But I am not one who can properly regulate and administer these things; rather, I am one who plainly needs the direction and guidance of others. For I am exceedingly insignificant, truly the lowest of all, utterly unworthy of so splendid a lot and so great an office. Accordingly, the Church—which the Apostle defines as the house of God—ought by no means to have been entrusted to a man so weak and feeble by nature, and still for the most part deprived of the benefit of divine purification (not to mention anything more serious). Nor, since I have not yet sufficiently learned to govern and rightly order myself, and have not yet adequately despised those base and earthly things, ought I in any way to have undertaken the care and governance of souls, when even those endowed with greater gifts of mind and body [Col. 1039B] can scarcely reach the end of this administration.

But after I had once been raised to this office—which I always judged myself unworthy of and still judge myself unworthy of—would that, if I do not entirely deserve that title of blessedness, I may at least not fall into such calamities and miseries that, drawn away from rectitude by a perverse and obstinate disposition, I experience the contrary lot: the ruin and fate of that evil servant. For, indulging greatly in laziness and excess, he neglected the arrival of his master, showed himself harsh and intolerable toward his fellow servants, and kept company and fellowship with drunkards. Then, at his master’s sudden arrival, he was cut asunder and, as we read, received the same portion as the hypocrites in the sulphurous [Col. 1039C] lake.

Or may I at least not become like the man who, after burying the talent he had received and hiding it underground, was harshly and severely accused; not only was the interest—and that multiplied—demanded of him, but he was also stripped of the principal itself and cast into the outer darkness (Matt. 25). May I not be found among their number, nor be set forth as an example for the mockery and shaking of the head of all who look on; nor, rebuked and condemned by him who knows and searches all our deeds, be compelled one day to pay the deserved penalties for my wicked actions, so that those who might perhaps be about to fall into similar crimes, warned by my example and punishment, may restrain themselves from wrongdoing and amend their lives.

Since, therefore, with God’s permission and connivance I have taken up this yoke [Col. 1039D], and have accepted the present ministry and service unwillingly and almost by force, I shall briefly explain what my occupation and manner of life were in former years, as is known to almost everyone.

People have different interests and occupations, greater or lesser according to each person’s inclination, and everyone chooses for himself, at his own discretion, what he hopes will be profitable. For just as human opinions are varied, and their counsels diverse, so too their customs and manners differ; accordingly, their choices and ways of life are separated from one another in various fashions, and in a certain sense reach a kind of infinity [Col. 1042A].

Some have resolved to endure the practice of a mechanical life, however base, wretched, and uncertain; others you may see devoted to the labors and hardships of agriculture; some are led by the pursuit of commerce, profit, and the accumulation of wealth. Nor are there lacking those who, driven by a desire to visit foreign places, expose themselves to the dangers of navigation. And, not to linger over the enumeration of individuals, some pursue other laborious arts. A few more select people, embracing that solitary and philosophical way of life, exercise and purify both soul and body, and in this manner succeed in drawing near to God and attaining that heavenly and blessed life.

You will also find some devoted to the cultivation of eloquence and the logical sciences and disciplines, who, refined by honorable conduct, make their minds workshops of the Muses [Col. 1042B]. In short, each person embraces one kind of life or another according as it is pleasing and congenial to him and as the inclination of his nature leads him.

My own manner of life, however, was as follows. As soon as I assumed the manly toga, I was immediately drawn into the courts of princes and obtained an office that was neither base nor idle, but active and honorable, since it was carried out for the most part through the industry of hands and pens. I was appointed imperial notary, whom the Latins call *a secretis*.

For some time bound to this service and entangled in worldly affairs, I began seriously to consider with myself the instability of the present life. After frequent and varied waves of thought, I came to see that it was difficult, almost impossible, for those occupied with such worldly affairs ever to reach higher and more divine things [Col. 1042C]. And when I reflected that these matters were nevertheless frivolous and perishable, whereas those other things were serious and eternal, I resolved and firmly determined within myself to bid farewell to the former at the earliest opportunity and thereafter devote myself to the latter with hand and foot.

It occurred to me that it would be better if I excelled even moderately in those higher matters and were approved in them than if I were regarded as most elegant and splendid in those lowest matters; and it would be far more advantageous if I possessed myself and were, in a certain sense, a law unto myself than if I attended to the affairs of others. Thus, considering these things again and again, and bearing in mind that everything is subject to vanity, according to the word of the most excellent prophet, and that nothing remains for a human being from all the labor with which he labors under the sun (Prov. 8:1), and that the form of this world passes away, according to the teaching of the wise man [Col. 1042D] (1 Cor. 7:31), according to the judgment of the Chosen Vessel, and carefully weighing many other Scriptures that speak in the same sense, I silently revolved in my mind the saying of a certain most celebrated philosopher: “It is better,” he said, “to live as a private person than to possess the greatest power, if one is going to accomplish nothing extraordinary.” I came to regard all glory that flatters the present as a mere tale.

I therefore immediately turned my attention to consideration of myself and promised myself the sure help of God [Col. 1043A]. I renounced every honor and every authority, withdrew from the imperial court and civil disturbances, and took possession of a certain retreat and rugged, almost inaccessible rock, situated many stadia from the imperial city in the region around the Propontis. There I firmly resolved to spend my life, to attempt the solitary way of living—which I had long before desired with extraordinary longing—and to breathe my last breath nowhere except in that place.

But since it is impossible for everything to turn out for everyone according to his heart’s desire—for in many things a kind of fated necessity rules, and human efforts often achieve an outcome not as a person wishes but as God wills—it happened that I too was frustrated in the hope of my purpose and plan [Col. 1043B]. For from that pleasant and friendly solitude I was, by some judgment—God, who permitted it, or perhaps ordained it, knows why—dragged back to the imperial palace. Certainly, by the will of those who at that time occupied the thrones of the empire, and by the vote of the entire clergy and senate, who were contriving an inexcusable and unavoidable act—for the bishop of the imperial city had died and had paid the debt owed by human beings—I was unwillingly and with much protest, God is my witness, advanced to this episcopal see. By tyranny rather than by deliberation or any persuasion whatsoever, I was placed in charge of governing others.

Since, therefore, although unwilling, I was compelled to submit my neck to the yoke and to undertake the care of souls neither worthily nor in a manner sufficiently consistent with charity [Col. 1043C], I fear greatly the various and exceedingly intricate devices and snares of the author of all evil, the assaults of malignant and invisible spirits, and their innate savagery. I fear that they may suddenly attack me while I am unthinking and deprived of every adornment and defense of virtue—for they know that I have not yet been adequately trained in spiritual and divine exercises, nor are they unaware that I have hitherto been entirely inexperienced in the art of fighting against them—and that they may wound me with the darts of sins.

In this way they could scatter the ecclesiastical flock, throw into confusion the well-ordered battle line, and finally mock more insolently the ruin of one who directs the battle ignorantly and incompetently. Moreover, since I see that every rule is generally exposed to the weapons of envy and slander, I regard the schemes and depravity of the envious with considerable suspicion, for they are accustomed to observe our affairs with the greatest curiosity, whether they are going well or badly [Col. 1043D].

While they do not notice the beams in their own eyes and do not try to remove the inflammation from their own sight, they carefully search out the specks in the eyes of others. On account of matters exceedingly slight, base, and almost worthless, they wickedly and venomously exercise their tongues against those in authority, hurling bitter and criminal attacks from both sides.

Yet, having undertaken this contest with enemies of such great power, whose help and protection could I more suitably implore than that of the one who permitted these things—that is, God? I therefore continually invoke his strength and assistance, and repeatedly entreat him to look upon my lowliness with a benevolent and merciful eye, to support me with his right hand, and always to direct me according to his will and toward the salutary governance of my subjects.

If, in the present difficulties and troubles, he makes his aid less manifest, this happens because of our wickedness, so that by this means he may draw us toward the amendment of our lives. Or it happens for this reason: that he may make known openly the malignity and perversity of those against us, lest the poisonousness of the deceitful, cleverly hidden in their hearts, remain unknown, but that whatever lies concealed and hidden in their minds may be brought entirely into the light.

Since, then, “a brother helped by a brother is like a fortified city and a palace secured with bars,” as Solomon testifies somewhere (Prov. 18) [Col. 1046A], I ask for a great deal of prayer, just as I also need a great deal of protection. But above all I presently desire and most earnestly long for the holy prayers and intercessions with God of your holy and, in spirit, most beloved fraternity.

For since your prayers, no less than those of Moses and Samuel—or of anyone else who has ever been like them—because of their purity approach God most closely and are carried straight to that heavenly and spiritual altar, we do not doubt that they will bring us the greatest help and benefit. Bring help, therefore, to my weakness, and raise your holy hands on high [Col. 1046C].

For we trust that the effectiveness of your confidence will not fail, but that God’s mercy and goodness, summoned by it, will suddenly come to our aid and strengthen and reinforce our weakness and frailty. Thus, clothed in the breastplate of faith and covered with the helmet of hope (Eph. 6; 1 Thess. 5), we may fearlessly resist the authorities, the rulers, and the powers of the darkness of this age, as well as the spirit of wickedness, against whom we are engaged in perpetual struggle; and may retain a firm and unshaken steadfastness of mind.

Moreover, may we skillfully and suitably win for Christ those who have hitherto rebelled and resisted, and restore them as adopted children to the holy Church of God. May we make them sheep of Christ’s rational and chosen flock, and lead them into the sacred folds of the Church [Col. 1046D], lest they be seized by wolves accustomed to tear them savagely apart. Thus may all of us, finally armed with the tokens of agreement and concord, no longer be torn apart by any ambushes or bites, but be subjected to Christ, the head of us all, and submit our necks to him with humility and obedience.

Pray, I beg you, and entreat with insistence that he himself may deign to enlighten and cleanse us, so that, made sons of perfect light, we may also be able to enlighten and cleanse others. May he likewise supply a word in the opening of our mouth, so that we may fill our hearers with the Spirit and proclaim the power of our mysteries vigorously and with great earnestness, always supported by his grace (Eph. 6)—the one who makes the tongues of the stammering eloquent, and confirms and strengthens the feet of the lame so that they may run eagerly to preach the Gospel [Col. 1047A].

May he also multiply the talent entrusted to us, so that at the proper time we may be able to return what is owed to the master of the household, not without interest. May he grant us not only to labor in that fertile vineyard, but also, bearing the weight and hardship of our work with equanimity and enduring the heat of the day, to receive the reward of our labor, and to equal in receiving our payment those who entered at the eleventh hour without an agreement (Matt. 20).

Finally, may he enlighten the eye of our mind, so that, illuminated by spiritual light, and with whatever disturbed the soul’s vision and darkened our understanding removed and washed away, we may draw more clearly from the meaning of the prophetic utterances [Col. 1047B], perform the ministries of the divine commandments more eagerly, guard and protect ourselves more diligently lest we be struck by the darts of our adversaries, and more cautiously foresee the sword of divine wrath hanging over sinners.

Then, if it is possible, having recognized the danger and appeased the divine power, may both we ourselves and the rest over whom we have been appointed leaders escape the coming wrath. But if we cannot attain both things, may I at least save my own soul, following the example of that righteous man Lot, who strove to rescue his soul from the conflagration (Gen. 19:22). Let your prayers, then, and the efforts of your spiritual protection be directed toward this.

But since circumstances have provided the occasion, I wish at this point to hear that great and resounding trumpet, that most eloquent herald of the Gospel, the Apostle Paul. Exulting greatly in spirit over the fervor of the ancient Romans and their steadfastness in faith and religion, and boasting, with a kind of holy glorying, in the Epistle he writes to them that their piety and faith are proclaimed and celebrated throughout the whole world, he publicly bears witness among other things in these words [Col. 1047C]: “I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world” (Rom. 1:8).

But is that pure and sincere faith of our Gospel, outside which there is no other, confined within the boundaries of the Romans alone? Certainly not. It is circumscribed by no boundaries of any particular place, but spreads so widely and is propagated after being spread, that the prophetic and apostolic voices, bursting forth, do not hesitate to affirm that the sound of divine preaching has gone out into all the earth and that the words of the heavenly heralds have resounded to the ends of the world [Col. 1047D] (Rom. 2; Ps. 10).

Indeed, to say something still greater, it is not excluded even from heaven itself or from the highest intellectual powers (Rom. 8). For although that higher Church of the firstborn justified in heaven—the city of those justified by faith, the heavenly Jerusalem—has God as the founder and architect of the city; and although he reconciles earthly things with heavenly things, tears down the dividing wall, and saves the lost sheep, carried upon his shoulders, through an astonishing descent and an ineffable condescension, joining it to those who had remained, and is called by other names of this kind, it is nevertheless not one Church and another Church, but one and the same Church of heaven and earth [Col. 1050A]. Therefore it is not without reason that everywhere we possess one undivided Church through the fellowship of faith. For God is known not only in Judea, but in every place to which the mind or understanding can reach.

Accordingly, we too, who have received the name of New Rome, being built upon one and the same foundation of faith—namely, the apostles and prophets, those supremely wise architects, with Christ meanwhile laid down as the cornerstone and foundation, Christ who is God and the Savior of us all—do not believe that, so far as the integrity of faith is concerned, we are inferior in any way to the ancient Romans.

For in the holy Churches of God there is no distinction of earlier and later, just as there is none between Jews and Greeks, slaves and free, barbarians and Scythians; rather, we are all one in Christ (Col. 3) [Col. 1050B]. Therefore let the divine Paul also glory in us and think magnificently of us; and, joining the new to the ancient, doctrine to doctrine, and preaching to preaching, let him rejoice equally over both.

For we have attained his teaching and instruction as they did, and in that teaching we remain rooted and established in the confession of our faith. In it we also stand and glory, and with open and unveiled face we proclaim the opinion we hold concerning a religion so glorious and blameless. In it we serve God, and, strengthened and firmly established by heavenly grace, we earnestly desire to persevere in it unceasingly for as long as we breathe and to depart from this life. For there is no other way by which we may rightly and holily order the present life and surely attain the good things stored up for the worthy in the age to come [Col. 1050C].

Accordingly, I confess that I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of all things, master and lord of all; and in his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, true God, the eternal Word, begotten from the Father from eternity in an ineffable and incomprehensible manner—indeed, in a manner that no spiritual or sensible creature can attain—and in the life-giving and most holy Spirit.

I believe in the *homoousian* Trinity, supersubstantial, invisible, incomprehensible, indivisible, unchangeable, eternal, undivided, simple, free from every part, every composition, every body, every quantity and quality [Col. 1050D]; possessing the same honor, the same glory, and the same divinity; subject to neither touch nor contact; without any figure; infinitely good; a light that knows no decline; threefold in light, supremely radiant, always disposed in an equal and identical manner; a power that beholds all things and brings all things to completion.

By the ray of the divine light, he spiritually and inseparably illumines all things endowed with reason and understanding, and preserves all things that are illumined and exist suitably, according to the nature of each, both in being and in well-being. He is known in things that subsist, not merely in bare names. He is glorified with one divinity, equal power, and an equal majesty of reign [Col. 1051A], and is worshiped and adored by all visible and invisible creatures.

Of the three *hypostases* that we contemplate in the Trinity, the Father is one: without a beginning, having no cause of his existence. For he is not from another, but has being from himself and in himself. The Son is another: he is not without a principle, for he is from the Father; the Father is the principle and origin of the Son. But if one considers the beginning of time, the Son is without a beginning just as the Father is, for he is the creator of the ages and is not subject to time. By an inseparable and eternal generation he shines forth from the Father, as the splendor of his glory and the imprint of the paternal substance.

The Holy Spirit is yet another. He has his substance from the Father, not by a new event but by procession, and shares the same eternity with the Father and the Son [Col. 1051B]. He is eternal, though not without a principle, since he proceeds from the Father; for the Father is his principle with respect to origin, and also his source. But with respect to time, he too is without a beginning.

There is therefore one God, the Father, from whom are all things; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things; and one Holy Spirit, in whom are all things. From these three perfect persons there is constituted one most perfect, indeed in itself absolutely complete, Godhead.

The *hypostases* are distinguished from one another by distinctive and personal properties. For each of the persons, even if it cannot be separated from another because of the unity of essence, is nevertheless distinguished from the other by its personal property and by the conception of the mind [Col. 1051C]. Each is known and believed to be perfect God, that is, adorned with all the properties of divinity; yet all are one in divinity.

Again, although the three are joined together, nevertheless one God is adored. Here, then, there is trinity according to substance and unity according to essence. Thus, in opposition to the insane and disorderly rebellion of pagan madness and confusion, we worship not a plurality of rulers but a monarchy.

This monarchy is not defined by the limitation of one person—for that would introduce the imperfection and crudity of Jewish narrowness—but is declared by the equality of nature, the concord of will, the identity of movement, and the identical inclination of each toward one purpose. Yet, according to that supreme theologian Gregory, this cannot occur in a nature subject to generation [Col. 1051D]. For the unity and kinship of the Godhead contemplated in the Trinity is in no way pulled apart or divided into parts, as happens in created things when individual subjects are multiplied.

Far from us, then, be the insane and frenzied opinion and fury of Arius. The Trinity is wholly undivided in glory and eternity, and in no respect alienated from itself. Yet the divine persons do not, for this reason, permeate one another—that is, they are not transformed into one another. Each remains unchangeable, unconfused, and eternal. Let the deceptive confusion of the insane and foolish Sabellius be banished and driven far away.

I also venerate and adore the mystery of the incarnation [Col. 1054A], predestined before all the ages but revealed in the last times for the salvation of the entire human race. It was accomplished through the great and wondrous descent of one person of the holy and life-giving Trinity—namely, Christ, our true God—and through his ineffable dispensation, so that from the source from which we had received existence through his inexplicable goodness, we might also receive well-being.

Therefore I confess and believe that there is one subject of the supremely rich and blessed Trinity: namely, the Son and Word of God, who together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit is worshiped and glorified throughout all eternity, being coessential and coequal with them. Moved by infinite goodness and mercy toward his own creature, with the Father’s will and compassion added, and with the grace and cooperation of the Holy Spirit, he descended from heaven and lived among human beings [Col. 1054B], in order that he might save us by grace—us who had long before been condemned because of sin, expelled from the delights of paradise, and subjected to corruption—and make us participants in the divine nature.

Dwelling in the womb of the Virgin who was truly and properly *Theotokos*, “Mother of God,” and adapting a soul and flesh to himself through the Holy Spirit, he assumed our entire nature, just as he had fashioned the human being in the beginning, and came forth as God incarnate.

He also preserved as a virgin after childbirth the Virgin who had given birth in a supernatural and ineffable manner; her virginity remained in no respect changed or damaged according to nature, signifying through the process of the second birth that no alteration or change whatsoever had come upon her nature [Col. 1054C].

He who is of the same nature as the Father became in every respect coessential with us, sin alone excluded. For, having assumed the seed of Abraham, he became a participant in flesh and blood just as one of us, and assumed flesh vivified by an intelligent soul. The flesh did not in any way preexist that supreme union; rather, flesh, a soul endowed with reason, and union with the Word all came to be simultaneously.

Nor did he dwell in our nature according to grace alone. Rather, wholly joined to the whole of human nature, he effected a union that was unconfused, indivisible, and supernatural. For the divine and human natures, coming together, remain and continue unchanged in their natural properties, and in no respect are they transformed into one another [Col. 1054D].

Nevertheless, because of that natural joining and union, we consider it pious to allow the communication and mutual interchange of names. For, on account of the physical and wondrous union of the natures that come together, we establish here a certain distinction of one and the same thing—not in reality, but only in conception.

Moreover, because the singularity and indivisible, uninterrupted unity of the person always remains and endures together with the distinction of the natures—for we banish far from here the monstrous fraud and confusion or mixture of the impostor Eutyches and Dioscorus—it follows that we confess one and the same person to be created and uncreated, eternal and temporal, heavenly and earthly, circumscribed and uncircumscribed, passible and impassible, without mother and without father [Col. 1055A].

The one set of predicates applies because of his ineffable, eternal birth from the Father, preceding every age; the other because of his mysterious and incomprehensible union with our nature. For we acknowledge his two births, which surpass every sense and every understanding. The only-begotten Son, who was in the form of God and in the bosom—that is, in the essence—of the Father, and who from eternity shone forth from him, emptied himself at the end of the ages and assumed the form of a servant—that is, our substance [Col. 1055B].

The union in Christ according to *hypostasis* joins one thing to another: the visible to the invisible, the passible to the impassible, and the other elements of which the Savior is constituted. Yet it does not constitute one person and another; far be that from us. For we confess one and the same perfect God and likewise perfect human being.

Although we attribute a difference of natures to Christ, we nevertheless recognize him as one and the same even after the incarnation. And, so that foolish Nestorius may be driven away from the divine enclosures, because of the diversity of the natures coming together in the hypostatic union, we do not introduce two sons or a duality of sons. Rather, we attribute all Christ’s actions—which were indeed *theandric*, that is, simultaneously those of God and of a human being—to one person [Col. 1055C].

As God, he performed divine works, namely signs and miracles; as the same human being, he voluntarily underwent sufferings and endured insults and humiliations. Accordingly, in agreement with the two natures—or rather, necessarily, in accordance with the pious and divine traditions of our divine fathers—I glorify in him two natural operations, which are in a certain sense the indicators and constitutive principles of the natures and substances themselves.

In the same way I venerate two natural wills of one and the same God and our Lord Jesus Christ. According to each nature, from which and in which he exists and is understood, we attribute to him the faculty of willing. For just as he acts and voluntarily exposes himself to saving suffering, so also he wills.

Again, I believe that he himself was crucified—not in the nature in which he shines and reigns with the Father, although, because of the *communicatio idiomatum*, “the Lord of glory” is said to have been crucified—but in the nature that is earthly, according to which he assumed our earthly mass and became a curse because of our sins, so that he might make us participants in his blessing [Col. 1055D].

He patiently endured the death of the flesh inflicted by the wicked, so that in his flesh he might condemn the sting of death, that is, sin, and destroy him who held the power of death, that is, the devil.

I believe that, after his body had been committed to burial, he preserved it incorrupt, in no way separated from that mysterious and incomprehensible union, even though during that three-day interval it had been deprived of its soul [Col. 1058A]. With that soul he also descended into hell and preached resurrection and granted freedom and redemption to the spirits who were in the flesh, as the divine chief of the apostles, Peter, explains.

To us also, as the firstborn of the dead, he became through the resurrection a beginning of incorruption. For he rose as God, trampling death underfoot and opening a way for all flesh to resurrection, raising together with himself, in a certain sense, us who had fallen into death through the fall of sin.

I believe that after his resurrection he appeared to the women and, abolishing the grief that had come to us through a woman, announced joy and gladness to them.

I believe that he showed himself alive to his divine disciples, confirmed the mystery of his resurrection, and demonstrated that he was the very same person he had been before the resurrection by eating and by displaying his sacred side, which the wise Thomas touched [Col. 1058B].

Finally, I believe that he was taken up into the heavens, sat down at the right hand of God the Father, and will one day come again, with the body he assumed, not without glory and divine majesty. He will sit as judge and render to each according to the account of his life. For we must all be revealed before the tribunal of Christ.

I believe that after this world has been renewed and, in a certain sense, transformed into another element, there will also be a resurrection of the flesh, so that this mortal of ours may put on immortality and the corruptible may put on incorruption (Rom. 14).

I also confess one baptism for the remission of sins, which is performed according to evangelical and apostolic tradition in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

These venerable dogmas and divine mysteries of our orthodox and sacred worship, which the divine and sacred teachers have handed down to us according to sublime and most pure theology, as well as the saving dispensation of the divine Word toward us and all other doctrines and proclamations resembling and agreeing with these, I embrace and preserve with complete acceptance and faith [Col. 1058C].

I also kiss and seek the patronage and intercessions of the saints with God: first and above all, those of the most holy and immaculate ever-virgin, our Lady, the Mother of God; then those of the divine and heavenly powers; the holy and most celebrated apostles; the blessed prophets; the most glorious and unconquered martyrs; the divine Fathers; and finally all the saints who from the beginning of the world have pleased the Lord and live in him and through him without any end whatsoever—for “the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God” (Wis. 3:1)—so that through them I may obtain the greatest salvation of soul and body [Col. 1058D].

I likewise adore and kiss their venerable relics, since they bring certain salvation and healing for the diseases of souls and bodies. I also accept and praise their venerable and divine manner of life, and their most celebrated struggles and contests [Col. 1059A]. I honor and venerate their sacred tombs and graves. Finally, I judge them worthy to be adorned with the highest honors and exalted with the greatest praises, because for the glory of God, the Savior of us all, they poured out their blood and courageously despised this fleeting present life because of their love for God, imitating his life-giving and saving sufferings.

Likewise, I embrace and accept not only the venerable icons of Christ, the Savior of us all, and the venerable images of the most holy Mother of God, but also the sacred representations of all the saints, and I show them the veneration that their honor rightly requires.

Moreover, I reverently and salutarily venerate and embrace the seven holy and ecumenical synods, together with all the supernatural and saving dogmas and decrees enacted and defined in them by our holy and divine Fathers [Col. 1059B], whom the Holy Spirit once appointed to govern and shepherd his Church.

First of all, I accept the sacred synod of the 318 most celebrated Fathers who once assembled at the city of Nicaea against the impious and furious Arius. This synod both expelled the author of impiety from the Church and set forth for us the true and orthodox faith through that sacred divine Creed. It orthodoxly defined that God the Word and Son of God is not a creature, as Arius maintained, but *homoousios* with the Father—“of one substance”—and truly God and Creator of all things.

[Col. 1059C]

Next I accept the synod of the 150 holy and most divine Fathers, which was convened after Nicaea in this imperial city and deprived the most impious Macedonius, the opponent of the Holy Spirit, of his office. It showed that the Holy Spirit is not something created, but true God, in every respect *homoousios* with the Father and the Son; it explained the sacred Creed more fully in its words concerning the Holy Spirit, and it also expelled from the Church Apollinarius, a truly foolish and deranged man.

After this I accept the sacred synod of the 200 holy Fathers and teachers, which assembled at Ephesus against the mad Nestorius and his blasphemous utterances, removed him from his rank and office, and defined that Christ and our God is one person, while his two natures are united with one another without confusion or division.

[Col. 1059D]

It declared that he is one and the same God and man together, and finally pronounced that the holy virgin Mary is truly and properly *Theotokos*, “God-bearer.”

Fourth, I embrace the sacred synod of the 630 divine and God-inspired Fathers convened at Chalcedon. It condemned the most impious Eutyches and Dioscorus, together with their obscure and dark confusion. After striking them down with an anathema, it devoutly proclaimed that one and the same Christ, our God and Lord, is both perfect man and again perfect God, existing in two natures but in one person, without confusion or division.

Then, in turn, I accept the fifth sacred synod of the 165 holy Fathers,

[Col. 1062A]

which was again convened in this divine city dedicated to God and which justly cut away the impious doctrines of Theodore, Nestorius, Origen, Didymus, Evagrius, and the other heretics who followed the doctrines mentioned above. These doctrines had formerly been hidden from many, but at that time were once again producing bitter branches and shoots. For what those men professed in their deranged minds and fables was more consistent with the imagination of Jews and pagans than with the faith of Christians.

After this I also venerate the sixth holy and ecumenical synod of the 170 holy men, again assembled in this imperial city. On the basis of Christ’s two natures, it distinguished and proclaimed his properties, natural operations, and wills. It subjected to anathema Theodore, bishop of Pharan; Honorius;

[Col. 1062B]

Cyrus; Sergius; Pyrrhus; Paul; Peter—who, by God’s permission, had insinuated themselves through corruption and fraud into the priesthood of the Church; Macarius, bishop of Antioch; Stephen, the disciple of Macarius; and Polychronius, an immature and deranged old man. For these men taught that only one will and one operation should be attributed to Christ our Savior.

Finally, I receive the seventh sacred synod of the 150 holy Fathers, celebrated again in our own age in the city of Nicaea. It confirmed and, so to speak, sealed all the preceding sacred synods and their doctrines and decrees. It also received and defined the veneration and worship of the sacred and venerable images, which had been handed down to the Churches from the beginning, declaring that they are to be venerated no less than the image of the life-giving Cross.

[Col. 1062C]

Accordingly, we expel from the Churches those who, to the insult and destruction of these images, assail Christians with futile chatter, as though Christians had until now regarded and venerated them in place of gods. Such are Theodosius, Basil, and Sisinnius, who by God’s permission presided over episcopal sees.

I therefore accept these aforementioned sacred and ecumenical synods, and embrace from my heart the doctrines and writings of all the elect and blessed Fathers, since they contain teaching free from every reproach and the foundation of salvation. Finally, all whom the Catholic Church receives, I too receive; and all whom she rejects, I likewise reject.

I also curse and detest in every way those who, taking their name from Simon Magus and stripped entirely of piety, have persisted down to the present day in weakening the tradition of the saints through opinions of depraved and destructive doctrines, and in mixing the poisonous seed of weeds into the field of the orthodox faith. All these, I say, and all their followers I curse, reject as plagues of the Churches of Christ, and anathematize.

[Col. 1062D]

Therefore, following the ordinance of the Churches which has prevailed from the beginning, we have thought it right, by means of these our letters—as though by a living herald, and using them as pledges of charity, mutual concord, and friendship in Christ between us—to greet you and make our judgment known in this manner to you, most blessed and instructed of God.

[Col. 1063A]

May your most greatly desired brotherhood in the Lord, reciprocating toward us with prayers poured out to the Lord, with timely words, and also by your actions, strengthen and instruct us, so that, supported by your laws and your teaching, we may remain steadfast, simple, and free from every defect in this faith; may retain unshaken all the mysteries which from the beginning have been handed down in it or concerning it; and may finally gather our entire rational flock—marked with the name and anointing of the supreme Shepherd and established within the enclosures of the ecclesiastical fold—into one assembly through the clear sounding of that divine and apostolic spiritual trumpet of doctrine and through divinely inspired voices, preserving it unharmed from the bites of lurking beasts.

[Col. 1063B]

If anything has been omitted by us, complete it yourselves with friendly and fatherly affection, so that your abundance may supply our poverty. Whatever, I say, is lacking to us either in words or in deeds, add and build upon it with the authority worthy of a venerable priest. For the charisma communicated to you will suffer no diminution by this means; indeed, generous sharing brings no reduction of goods, but in due time returns multiplied and glorious fruits.

Therefore, support us, as though we were the weaker, by your divine strength; make our feet fit to run along the path of the Gospel; and do not neglect to suggest anything whatever that may appear salutary or useful. Thus, just as we preserve unity and concord in faith and confession, so may we also be joined and bound together by the bond of charity, and continually preserve among ourselves the indivisible gift of peace, which reconciles the concord and unity of the Churches, while remaining faithful to the ministry entrusted to us.

[Col. 1063C]

In this way the city of the great King, fortified and surrounded on every side, may remain inaccessible to all the deceits and assaults of invisible enemies, who continually prowl around, eagerly waiting to devour someone marked out within it and sealed by the Spirit. Against these invisible enemies we set not carnal but spiritual weapons: namely, the shield of faith and the sword of the word, which is the word of God. Thus, demolishing and pursuing the fortifications and engines of sin with the sling of the Spirit, may we drive away and break their cruel audacity.

[Col. 1063D]

Then, having obtained divine protection and assistance in this way, may the conduct of our life remain quiet and peaceful; and at the resurrection, when the final trumpet sounds, may we be judged worthy, without condemnation for our life, to go forth with the holy angels to meet the one who is coming in the glory of the Father, and, together with the wise virgins, to enter the bridegroom’s chamber, forever enjoying the spiritual and angelic banquet and becoming heirs of those blessings which are stored up in Christ, the true God—not for the unworthy—through the intercession of his immaculate and blameless mother and of all the saints. Amen.

No one should therefore be surprised that we have come to you somewhat late by what we have set forth thus far, nor should anyone on that account bring our reputation under accusation. Rather, your brotherhood, beloved of God, should be firmly persuaded that priestly custom has by no means grown obsolete here, nor have we neglected through contempt or sloth anything that is fitting for ecclesiastical men. The harsh and implacable decision of an overwhelming authority prevented us from using our decrees.

[Col. 1066A]

May your blessed soul therefore forgive us if I have incurred any blame through my delay, and consider that it is by no means easy to oppose powerful men who are carried away by their own will and strive to accomplish whatever they have resolved in their minds.

For, thinking that they had found a highly plausible reason by which they might then prevent us, already initiated into the priesthood, from exercising our office, they angrily charged us—and spread the report everywhere—that you were alienated from the Church of Constantinople and had rashly torn yourselves away from it. Since, therefore, this violence or injury also affected you, you will kindly pardon those who, against their will, were constrained by the same necessity.

But since we have now written to your holiness about the present condition of the Church and of this place, and have firmly resolved to write in due time about what will happen here, I think that no longer is there need for a more extended defense. For the barrier that was obstructing us has now been broken through; the door is open; the stumbling stones have been removed from the middle of the road; the way is broad, level, free of obstacles, and made smooth for travel; sad things have disappeared far from our eyes; scandals and seditions have fallen silent;

[Col. 1066C]

all obstacles have finally been removed, and the former lights of the Church have been restored. Consequently, whatever belongs properly to charity and priestly custom, having regained its place, can henceforth be carried out and observed without difficulty.

Meanwhile, however, there are still some who make light of divine things, who undertake anything for the sake of their own reputation, and who give no thought to the divine judgment that hangs over them.
