But just as it is customary and pleasing for them to gaze greedily upon present glory and splendor, and for that reason to conspire among themselves, so it is entirely appropriate that we should devote ourselves in every way to the glory of God, ecclesiastical decorum, concord, and observance of the sacred canons; that we should apply ourselves day and night to our duties; and that we should offer continual prayers and supplications for our most pious and most powerful emperor, already proclaimed as such, a sincere and genuine son of the Church, and nobly adorned by conduct pleasing to God and by an honorable way of life.

[Col. 1066D]

We should pray to God, who crowns him and administers the kingdom together with him, that he grant him a peaceful life and an empire of the greatest possible duration; adorn him with victories over barbarians; grant him the happy governance of the Christian order; stir him to zeal for the orthodox faith; and finally perfect him in the observance of the divine commandments, so that he may leave to his children, together with the enduring power and greatness of the kingdom, an honor and glory that are far from ordinary.

[Col. 1067A]

Furthermore, we have entrusted these synodical letters of ours to Michael, most holy and beloved of Christ, metropolitan of the city of Philadelphia, to be delivered to your beloved and desired brotherhood. Although, judging from the speech and conversation we have had with him, we have no doubt that you will receive him with every kindness and look upon him with joyful eyes, nevertheless, for the sake of our own smallness, we ask that he be received and refreshed by you as a genuine brother, familiarly and honorably.

For he is a man who embraces your affection with sincere and ardent feeling, displays great zeal and readiness in ecclesiastical matters, and appears to excel greatly in speech, integrity of life, and virtue. With God directing him and moving your hearts, for our greater spiritual joy and for the more perfect affection of our love in the Lord, he will bring back to us, in response to these presents, the tokens of your love and concord—that is, your venerable letters.

We salute most warmly in Christ the entire brotherhood that is with you. Farewell in the Lord. Pray for us, most holy and most blessed brother, having obtained as mediator and fellow-worker with God our common patron and helper that great and foremost apostle; do not disdain to offer intercessions for us, unworthy servants of his.

As a sign of the charity which exists between us in the Lord, we have sent to your fraternal blessedness a golden *encolpium*. One side of it is enclosed in crystal, the other fashioned by casting.

[Col. 1067C]

Within it is another *encolpium*, into which pieces of precious wood have been carved and inserted. Along with these we have sent a white *sticharium*, a chestnut-colored woven *phenolium*, and also an *epitrachelion* and an *enchirion*, variegated and ornamented with gold. We have elegantly wrapped these objects in a linen cloth and had them sealed with lead, so that, as a memorial, they may be transferred under God’s guidance and humbly offered to that merciful apostolate.

[Col. 1067C]

## The Privileges of Saint Leo

[Col. 1067D]

[Col. 1067]

### I. Pope Leo III grants a privilege to the Benedictine monastery of nuns at Horreum near Trier  
*(About the year 792.)*

[Mansi, *Collection of the Councils*]

I, Leo, vicar of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles—indeed unequal to his merits, but exercising in his place, by virtue of his dignity, the Roman episcopate—have received with the greatest reverence and honor the monastery of Horreum, restored for the service of divine worship by Modowald, archbishop of Trier, with the assistance of blessed Modesta, his niece, from the royal granaries from which it also received its name, after the departure of the blessed virgin Irmina, who first undertook to advance this place.

Thus, when the mother of this congregation has passed from this life, no outsider may in any way be substituted for her; rather, one of the sisters themselves shall be appointed, with the leading men of the Church of Trier giving their considered support, the sisters possessing the right of election, and the bishop himself devoutly consenting.

May this privilege, supported by such authority, remain stable and fixed forever in the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, of our holy predecessor Peter, and of all God’s elect. If any prelate deprives those dwelling here of so great a privilege, let him be condemned by eternal judgment. So be it, so be it. Amen, amen.

[Col. 1069A]

[Col. 1069]

### II. Bull of Leo III, Supreme Pontiff, by which he confirms the transfer of the episcopal see of Regensburg from the monastery of Saint Emmeram to the church of Saint Stephen and proclaims its complete exemption  
*(Year 795.)*

[Mansi, same work]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, almighty God, Leo the pope.

We wish it to be known to all the faithful of the Christian religion, both present and future, how the most Christian emperor, the august Charles, desiring, with God’s inspiration, to make Christ the possessor of his inheritance, transferred into our immunity and that of our successors, for the sake of protection, a certain monastery near the walls of the city of Tyburnia—which was built by Tiberius Caesar Augustus and is now commonly called Regensburg—which was constructed in honor of Saint Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, of the prince of the apostles Peter, and of Saint George the martyr. There the illustrious martyr and bishop of Poitiers, Emmeram, rests bodily.

[Col. 1069B]

And we, immediately and freely assenting in piety to his petition for the love of Christ, decreed that this should be done and ordered a formal document of our authority to be written concerning it. The third bishop of that city, Adalwin by name, in accordance with our decree and authority, in the presence of the most pious emperor Charles, transferred the episcopal chair by due process at a synodal council, with the judgment of the bishops, clergy, and also the noble laymen of that place. By canonical authority he established it in the city at the church of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, and thereafter assigned it to his own ownership and authority and to those of his successors.

In exchange, the aforementioned most Christian emperor granted to that place where the episcopal see now is, on its southern side, forty decempedal measuring-rods; on the other side, one hundred; in length, two hundred and seven; also the church of Saint Peter and the church of Saint Paul beside the walls of the aforementioned city; Wimintingen; Egilolfesheim; and the church near Nappurch called Bersana.

[Col. 1069C]

He also confirmed that the monastery of God’s precious martyr Emmeram should remain forever under the power of emperors or kings, and confirmed that the rector and abbot of the same monastery should pay seven gold pieces each year to Rome at the altar of Saint Peter.

This transfer and confirmation took place in the year 798 from the Incarnation of the Lord, by our authority. If any emperor or king should grant this same holy church to anyone, let him be anathema.

The congregation of the monastery, however, shall have free power to appoint an abbot, according to the decree of Saint Benedict, without contradiction from anyone. We have received the aforementioned monastery, together with its monks and everything already granted to it or to be granted in the future, into our immunity and that of our successors. May it prosper. Amen.

[Col. 1070A]

[Col. 1070]

### III. Privilege of Pope Leo for the monastery of Saint Benedict at Conversano  
*(Year 815.)*

[Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, vol. VII, p. 702]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and wishes perfection in the regular life to Eustasius, beloved son of God, elected abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict at Conversano, which without intermediary belongs to the Holy See.

The administration of the Apostolic See, which we serve, although unworthily, and the care and solicitude for all the Churches that occupy us require that we attend with special affection to the provision of those Churches which are known to belong to the Roman Church.

Recently, through Dorotheus, subdeacon and monk, you humbly petitioned us that this monastery—in which forty monks once served God—was found, because of the impiety of the Saracens who had poured into Italy and the schism of the Greek princes, after the death of your predecessor, our beloved son Theophylactus, abbot of the aforesaid monastery, so completely deprived of support that among the monks who had survived there after the devastation of this region there was neither a larger nor a sounder party for choosing a successor.

[Col. 1070B]

Finally, on the advice of Caufridus, our beloved son in Christ and abbot of the sacred monastery of Saint Benedict at Bari, since access to the City was then unsafe, certain monks of his monastery and part of the monks of the priory of Saint [lacuna], called Portus Asperus, at Monopoli—whom we regard as gathered from your community in the charisma of the Paraclete Spirit—elected you, our beloved son Eustasius, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May.

Therefore you informed us and this holy see, humbly asking that we deign, by apostolic kindness, to confirm the same election.

We, kindly assenting to your prayers, confirm and establish by apostolic authority you, the aforementioned Eustasius, canonically elected abbot of the aforesaid monastery situated at Conversano, together with all the honors, revenues, and jurisdictions of that monastery, and with the privileges hitherto granted to your predecessors by this holy see.

[Col. 1070C]

We admonish you that, while presiding over it, you should surpass your subjects and the others in vigilance, teaching, and integrity of conduct; admonish and correct them in charity; and edify them by your example.

For you should know that, while religious men preside in this holy service, it is fitting that they display not the power of their order or the dignity of their pastoral office, but equality of condition; nor should you parade yourself before men as their ruler. Remember that our ancient Fathers were not so much kings of men as shepherds of sheep.

Those who are placed in positions of governance and appear first in undertaking ecclesiastical duties are the brightest mirrors of the Church, so that their subjects, rejoicing in their example, may undertake the ministries assigned to them and render obedience with delight.

Dorotheus also added, in the name of your monastery and the whole community, that, after the expulsion of the Lombards, substantial disputes arose—not without this holy see and our [lacuna]—because the more powerful men of the region and soldiers had invaded the property of the Churches and committed a crime,

[Col. 1070D]

and because what had remained after the harshness of the Saracens and the impiety of the Greeks was seized by the shameful greed and unjust hostility of fellow countrymen, the path of law and piety having been abandoned. For the so-called right of war is rejected by the Christian Church as profane.

Therefore, strive by your diligence to draw these possessions peacefully back to their ancient ownership, and see that they are restored to this sacred monastery, while the sanction of our most pious beloved son, the prince and king of the Franks, remains in force throughout every part of Italy, so that counts, judges, the *strategos*, and the *catapan* may restore the property of the Churches to the Churches without the forms of a judicial process.

Since hostile weapons have now fallen silent, we command that monks should not enter into secular quarrels, nor raise legal questions without consultation, nor, after the manner of military audacity, fall into arrogance because of their liberty.

[Col. 1071A]

It seems absurd that among the religious of Saint Benedict ecclesiastical liberty should be distorted into reckless license, lest the ministries of monks appear to wicked men to be despised. Whatever, therefore, must be sought or answered for your aforesaid monastery, do not forget to do this through an advocate.

If the property of the Churches is found to have been impiously devastated by the Greek princes in the East, or in certain territories of Italy belonging to the Greek empire, through the arrival of the Saracens, we rejoice in the Lord that all these things may soon be restored.

If anyone, after the aforementioned sanction of the most pious king of the Franks, thinks that he has a complaint against this monastery of Conversano, and is unwilling to settle or bring his lawsuit before you as abbot or before the monks, we wish and decree that the complaint be brought before us or our legates, so that [lacuna] judgment, without respect of persons, may preserve justice for each person, with God as author.

[Col. 1071B]

Moreover, we confirm and grant by apostolic authority all the liberties and immunities of the aforesaid monastery, as well as the liberties of the bishops and the exemptions from secular authority granted to that sacred monastery and its entire community by the beloved emperors and other faithful persons mentioned above. The aforesaid Dorotheus reported to us that most of the documents recording these privileges had been burned by the mad fury of the enemies and rebels of the Holy Roman Church.

We command that the text of the present document be entered in the registers by our beloved brother in Christ, the librarian. We strengthen all these provisions, and the confirmation itself, by the protection of this present writing.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our confirmation and constitution, then, after being warned a second and third time, unless he provides appropriate satisfaction for his affairs, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor; let him recognize that by the judgment of God he has made himself guilty of the iniquity committed; and let him be excluded from the most holy body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen. Amen. Amen.

Given at Rome, in the monastery of Saint Anastasius, by the hand of John, librarian and cardinal of our Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Kalends of December, in the year of the Lord 815, indiction 9, in the twentieth year of the pontificate of our lord Leo III, pope, by divine providence.

Nicholas, priest, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, titular of Santa Croce in Jerusalem.

Eustachius, titular priest of Santa Prassede, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church [lacuna].

Theophylactus, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.

[Col. 1072C]

Stephen, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, titular of Saint Mark.

Boniface, cardinal, titular of Saint [lacuna]

John, librarian of the Holy Roman Church.

## In the Year of the Lord 818

## Stephen IV, Roman Pontiff

[Col. 1071C]

## Historical Notice on Stephen IV

[Mansi, *Collection of the Councils*, vol. XIV]

[Col. 1071D]

### Stephen

[Note: [Col. 1071D]

Stephen. In the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 816, on the twenty-second day of June, the Roman clergy, by unanimous agreement, substituted Stephen IV, thoroughly versed in the sacred canons and disciplines, in place of Leo III.

When, for the purpose of obtaining peace and unity, he had departed in the second month after his election for Gaul to visit the emperor Louis—as Aimoinus relates—an otherwise unknown but nevertheless truthful author, whom many customarily call Ademar, writes in chapters 38 and 39 of his *Life of Louis* that the following events took place, in addition to those which Anastasius records above:

“Now the emperor, having learned in advance of the arrival of the pope Stephen, ordered his nephew Bernard to accompany him. He also sent other envoys to meet him as he approached and escort him with due honor. He himself decided to await his arrival at Rheims. He ordered Hildebold, archchaplain of the sacred palace, Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, John of Arles, and a large number of other ecclesiastical ministers to go out to meet him, dressed in priestly vestments.

[Col. 1073B]

“Finally, when the pope was a mile from the monastery of the holy confessor Remigius, the emperor received him with the greatest honor, as the vicar of blessed Peter. He met him as he dismounted from his horse and personally supported him as he entered the church, while the various orders of the Church sang, in such great exultation, ‘We praise you, O God,’ and the rest. When this hymn had ended, the Roman clergy proclaimed the praises due to the emperor, and the apostolic lord concluded them with a prayer. When these things had been completed, the emperor withdrew into the inner rooms of the house; the pope explained the reasons for his arrival, and, after they had shared together the blessing of bread and wine, the emperor returned to the city, while the apostolic lord remained there.”

These details concerning the pope’s visit to the emperor are found in the *Life of Louis*. Theganus, chorepiscopus of Trier, says the following in chapters 16, 17, and 18 of his little book *On the Deeds of Louis*, to which Walahfrid Strabo prefixed a preface.

[[Col. 1073D] Flodoard should also be consulted, book II of the *History of Rheims*, chapter 19.]

Concerning Louis III’s adoration of the pope’s feet, the crown of the empire placed upon Louis and upon his wife Irmingard, and the miracles that most clearly illuminated the death of the pope after his return to Rome, he says:

“Immediately after Stephen assumed the pontificate, he ordered all the Roman people to promise fidelity to Louis with an oath, so that in this way the agitated populace might be restrained. He then sent his legates to the aforementioned prince and informed him that he would gladly see him at whatever place he might choose.

“When Louis heard this, he was filled with great rejoicing and began to celebrate. At once he ordered his envoys to go to meet the holy pontiff, offer the greatest greetings, and prepare the necessary services. After the envoys, Lord Louis himself went to meet the aforementioned pontiff, encountering him in the great field of the people of Rheims.

[Col. 1073D]

“Each dismounted from his horse. The prince prostrated his entire body on the ground three times before the feet of so great a pontiff; then, rising the third time, he greeted the pontiff with these words: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; the Lord is God, and he has shone upon us.’ The pontiff replied: ‘Blessed be the Lord our God, who has granted our eyes, according to King David, to see.’

“They embraced and kissed one another and proceeded peacefully to the church. After they had prayed for a long time, the pontiff rose and, with his clergy, proclaimed royal praises for him in a loud voice.

“Afterward the pontiff honored him with great and numerous honors, as well as Queen Irmingard and all his nobles and ministers. On the following Sunday, in the church, before the solemn celebration of Mass, in the presence of the clergy and all the people, he consecrated him and anointed him as emperor, and placed upon his head a golden crown of wondrous beauty, adorned with the most precious gems, which he had brought with him.

[Col. 1074B]

“He called Irmingard queen Augusta and placed a golden crown upon her head. As long as the most blessed pope remained there, they spoke daily about the welfare of the holy Church of God.

“After this, the emperor honored him with great and countless gifts, three times as many and more than he had received from him, as he always used to do, giving more than he received. He dismissed him to return to Rome with his legates, whom he ordered to provide him with honorable service everywhere along his journey.

“After he reached Rome, within a few days it became clear through certain miracles wrought by God’s manifestation that he was truly a living worshiper of God.”

The decree concerning the election of the Roman pontiff which exists under the name of Stephen IV, in Distinction 33, canon 28, *Quia sancta*, does not appear to belong to Pope Stephen. This is so, first, because, as has been shown above, schismatic impostors frequently sought to deceive the Church in this matter; and also because the emperor Louis, in the constitution issued by him at the beginning of the pontificate of Pope Paschal concerning the donation made to the Roman Church, wished the election and coronation of the Roman pontiff to be free, and wished him to be subject to no other requirement or obligation than to inform the imperial majesty of his election and consecration, as Paschal, Stephen’s successor, is seen to have done in this matter.

Gratian reproduces Louis’s constitution in Distinction 63, canon 30—“I, Louis”—but in an incomplete and mutilated form. **SEV. BIN.]**

A Roman by birth, son of Marinus,

[Note: [Col. 1072D] He held the see for seven years and seven months. That Stephen survived his return from Gaul by only three months is attested, after the authority of Theganus cited above, by Aimoinus in these words: “Stephen, less than two months after his consecration, hastened to come to the emperor by the most rapid journeys”; and below, concerning the time of his return, he adds: “In the third month after he had come to Rome had not yet elapsed when, around the eighth day before the Kalends of February, he died.”

It is therefore necessary to conclude that a copyist’s error caused the figure of seven months, as it appears here in Anastasius, to be replaced elsewhere by merely seven years, and in some authors by seven years and seven months. See Baronius, year 817, no. 1. ID.]

He held the see for seven years and seven months [seven months, day 3]. [Col. 1072D]

From his earliest years he was brought up and educated in the Lateran patriarchate under the late Pope Hadrian. Born of noble ancestry and an illustrious family, while still a child he devoted himself diligently to learning the knowledge of sacred discipline.

When the aforementioned Pope Hadrian of holy memory died, Pope Leo succeeded him. Seeing that the aforementioned Stephen possessed good conduct and humility, Leo promoted him to the order of subdeacon.

[Col. 1073A]

When he saw him devoting himself more and more to spiritual studies, with the Lord’s consent he raised him to the rank of deacon. From that time, excelling in spiritual studies in many ways, Stephen displayed the greatest care both in skillfully and clearly proclaiming divine and evangelical words to the people and in carrying out ecclesiastical tradition.

Thus the grace of the Holy Spirit shone in his heart, so that in everything he was proved effective and capable. Accordingly, before the aforementioned Pope Leo departed this life, it came to pass that, since the Roman people loved him with the warmest affection, that outstanding and most holy man Stephen was immediately elected to the sacred height of the pontificate.

[Col. 1073B]

With one affection and equal love, they led him to the church of the blessed apostle Peter; and, by the ordering of God’s providence, he was consecrated pope of the world.

When this most holy man had been established in the pontificate, he undertook a journey to Francia, to the most pious and serene lord Louis, emperor, for the sake of confirming the peace and unity of the holy Church of God.

[Col. 1074A]

When he reached Francia, he was received by the aforementioned most pious prince and by the people of the Franks with such honor and exaltation that it can scarcely be expressed in words. The Lord deigned to grant him such favor that he obtained in every respect everything he is known to have asked of the emperor.

Indeed, because of his love for the pope, that most pious prince, in the regions of Francia, beyond all the gifts he bestowed upon him, granted a royal estate from his own treasury to the blessed apostle Peter for perpetual use by a written decree.

[Col. 1074B]

That sacred bishop, taking as his example our Redeemer, who for us deigned to descend from heaven and rescue us from the captivity of the devil, brought back with him, out of piety toward the Church, all the exiles who were being held there in captivity because of the crimes and injustices they had committed against the holy Roman Church and against Pope Leo.

In the church of the blessed apostle Peter at the Chains, he made a thurible of silver, gilded on top, weighing [lacuna] pounds.

He likewise made *gabathae* of silver weighing [lacuna] pounds.

[Col. 1075A]

He likewise made silk curtains with a *periclysis*, of *fundatum* fabric, numbering [lacuna].

Indeed, in the same church he made a garment of gold-embroidered silk (*chrysoclave*) with gems, bearing a representation of the history of the blessed apostle Peter.

He also made *fundatum* curtains, numbering [lacuna].

And in the monastery mentioned above he made a gold chalice adorned with gems, weighing [lacuna] pounds.

And a silver paten, gilded on top, weighing [lacuna] pounds.

He also made a gold cross adorned with gems, weighing [lacuna] pounds.

The aforementioned venerable and illustrious pontiff also made at Saint Theodore in the Sabellum a gold cross adorned with gems, and a silver chalice, weighing [lacuna] pounds.
.

But the aforesaid venerable and illustrious [Col. 1076A] pontiff made in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter *Ad Vincula* a paten and chalice of silver gilded on the exterior, weighing … pounds. Likewise, in the place mentioned above, he made a silver crown with its pendants, weighing … pounds. Moreover, in the oratory of Saint Barbara the martyr in Subura, he made a *fundatum* vestment. Likewise, in the basilica of blessed Helena, he made a *fundatum* vestment. Having been taken from this light by divine summons, he departed to eternal rest. He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter. He held one ordination in the month of December: nine priests, four deacons, and five bishops for various places; and the episcopal see was vacant for two days.

## In the Year of Our Lord 824

## Paschal I, Roman Pontiff

[Col. 1075C]

## Historical Notice on Paschal I

[Mansi, *Collectio Conciliorum amplissima*, vol. XIII]

[Col. 1075B]

[Note: [Col. 1075B] Paschal. In the year 817, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, Paschal—renowned for the miraculous extinguishing of a fire—was unwillingly taken from the monastery and raised to the pontificate with the remarkable agreement of the entire people and clergy. Immediately he informed Louis of his reluctant election. Shortly afterward he sent a second embassy to Louis and requested, as Thegan says in *The Deeds of Louis*, that the dispute concerning the boundaries of Dalmatia between the Romans and the Slavs be settled; but what he obtained through that embassy is not known.

The Iconoclasts persecuted the Orthodox with the greatest severity. Those whose martyr’s glory they envied they afflicted with the harshest punishments and sufferings of imprisonment and exile. Theodorus Studites, that most distinguished confessor, recalled in letters addressed to Paschal, and in two embassies sent to him, with what injustice they had persecuted the Orthodox confessor; at the same time he implored aid and defense against them. Paschal received these letters and envoys kindly and returned to Theodorus and the other Easterners letters full of consolation. He added the embassy described above by Anastasius.

Theodorus, the false patriarch of Constantinople, had sent *apocrisiarii*—papal envoys or representatives—to steal ecclesiastical communion by this covert means. But when the pontiff learned of their arrival, he did not even wish them to be considered worthy of entering the city. Baronius derives this account from Michael and Theodorus Studites, under the year 817.

After the death of the empress Irmingard, of the most noble Bavarian family, the emperor Louis married Judith, daughter of Count Welf, and honored her with the title of Augusta. (*Annals of the Franks.*)

After Leo the Armenian was killed in the East, Michael Balbus succeeded him. Having recalled all the Orthodox exiles by an edict, he abolished the seven-year persecution and restored the much-desired peace of the Church. For this reason Theodorus, released from exile, wrote to the emperor and, in error, praised him highly as a professor of the Orthodox faith.

When the emperor Michael ordered the Catholics to meet with the heretical Iconoclasts and to deliberate together concerning the doctrines of the faith, the Catholics met privately and unanimously replied that it was unlawful and contrary to the ecclesiastical canons for Catholics to meet with heretics. They therefore earnestly requested—and obtained—that they not be ordered to do anything contrary to the canons.

During this pontificate Lothair came to Rome and was crowned emperor. When this had been done, a revolt arose at Rome, and two prominent men of the Roman Church were killed. Because Paschal was suspected by Lothair on account of their deaths, he cleared himself lawfully by oath of his opponents’ calumny. (*Author of the Life of Louis, in the Frankish annals.*) SEV. BINN.]

Paschal, a Roman by nationality, son of Bonosus, sat for seven years, five months, and [three] sixteen [17] days. From the earliest period of his life he had been dedicated to divine worship and, in the patriarchium of the most holy Church, had been instructed in the study of divine and saving Scripture, especially educated both in the Psalter and in the sacred books of the New and Old Testament. Elegant and perfect in every goodness, he was first made subdeacon and afterward honorably ordained deacon and priest.

He was a holy, chaste, devout, innocent, magnanimous man, devoted in speech and full of modesty; with excessive cheerfulness and joy he appropriately distributed among the poor in alms everything he possessed. Accordingly, he devoted himself more frequently, day and night, to divine conversation with religious and holy monks, and he flourished humbly and honorably in prayers, vigils, and daily [Col. 1076B] fasts.

When his predecessor, the lord Pope Leo, thrice blessed, saw him so watchful in such pursuits and so devoted to religion, he entrusted to him the governance of the monastery of the blessed Stephen, the first martyr, beside the basilica of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. For it is written: “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place or under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light” (Matthew 5).

He prudently and usefully corrected the profits of this temporal life by directing them toward the eternal, and religiously adorned his subjects with an example of good living and correction grounded in piety. He also provided the grace of hospitality for pilgrims and the lame who, out of love for the blessed apostle Peter, came from distant regions to his threshold. He usefully supplied what was necessary and cheerfully distributed in secret whatever they needed.

[Col. 1077A] He increased daily in the work of God until his predecessor, the lord Pope Stephen, departed from this light to eternal blessedness. When, therefore, his reputation for so many examples of good works had spread especially far and wide, and almighty God had granted that he should arrange the governance of the Church under his pious direction, he was raised to the apostolic see by all the priests, nobles, the entire clergy, the leading men, and the whole Roman people, in harmonious agreement and with one and the same will, through divine counsel, for the praise and glory of almighty God.

For he was a most fitting observer of the precepts and institutions of the fathers and pontiffs, of the canons, and also of the sanctions of the laws; from the time of his ordination he was a most noble promulgator of every norm of justice, slow to anger and quick to show mercy. He returned no evil for evil and assigned no punishment according to anyone’s offense; rather, he was always merciful, loving and governing all the citizens and the Roman people entrusted by God with pious affection.

Indeed, with the greatest zeal and care, according to his customary religious devotion, he cultivated, restored, and most devotedly adorned all the churches of God in every respect.

This most blessed bishop searched for and found many bodies of saints. He honorably reburied them with the greatest care within the city, to the honor and glory of God. He also greatly increased the stipends (*roga*) allotted to all his clergy in the presbytery and stored every treasure in the heavenly treasury, especially on behalf of captives and exiles. He not only redeemed men and women from overseas regions with gold and silver, but also searched for them along distant roads, finding them everywhere—in the regions of Spain and in each individual locality—and, like a good and true shepherd, brought them back to their own places.

He made for the sacred altar of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, a vestment of extraordinary size, exceedingly beautiful and richly adorned, woven of gold and jewels, representing the history of how that same apostle was freed from his chains by an angel.

In the same venerable basilica, before the entrance leading to the body, at the place called Ferrata, he established an altar and honorably placed in it the revered body of the blessed Sixtus, martyr and pontiff. Above it he also suitably constructed an arch adorned with mosaic.

Likewise, in that most sacred church of the blessed apostle Peter, near the entrance leading to Saint Petronilla, he built an oratory of the greatest size and beauty and adorned it splendidly. He decorated its columns and vaulted ceiling with mosaic and beautiful metals. In it he honorably and memorially reburied the bodies of the most blessed martyrs Processus and Martinianus, to the honor and glory of almighty God.

In its apse he set a very beautiful gilded silver image, with various scenes arranged among marble inlays [*concrustationes*]. [Col. 1077D] It weighed sixty-two and a half pounds, together with silver lilies weighing seventeen pounds and two ounces. He also provided seven bowls (*gabatae*) of the purest silver, weighing altogether thirteen and a half pounds and two ounces.

He made three gilded silver images in the same venerable place: one of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and two of the other blessed martyrs, Processus and Martinianus, weighing altogether thirty-six pounds. He also offered another image of the purest gold for the adornment of the aforesaid oratory, weighing thirteen pounds and three ounces.

Likewise, he provided eight baskets of the purest silver, weighing altogether forty-three pounds. He also placed there a silver basin for the sponge used during the nocturnal services, weighing seven pounds and nine ounces. Indeed, he fittingly adorned the same venerable place with keys fashioned in the form of a cross, decorated with the purest gold and marvelous gems; they weighed … pounds.

There also he established a *regularis*, which he overlaid with silver plates and which weighed twenty pounds. Above it he placed two silver arches and four *gammadiae*, weighing altogether sixty pounds. He also surrounded the altar’s *propitiatorium* with silver plates and most nobly enclosed its sacred confession inside and out with its *regulae*, which together weighed … pounds.

Above the altar of those same most blessed martyrs he placed two vestments: one of *fundatum*, with a cross of *chrysoclavus*, and the other of *quadruplum*, magnificently adorned. He likewise decorated seven larger curtains of *fundatum*, bordered with a sewn *periclysi* of *blatta*.

[Note: [Col. 1077D] Nor should this be passed over in silence. He describes the fire miraculously extinguished by Pope Paschal. If this account is true, it is probable that Paschal did not even incur any suspicion of the crime and murder attributed to him, although the author of the Life of Louis describes the contrary in explicit terms. SEV. BIN.]

Nor do we think that this should be passed over in silence: at that same time, through the devil’s cunning and the negligence of certain people of the English nation, their entire settlement—which in their language is called a *burgus*—was consumed by a spreading blaze, so completely that not even traces of the former habitation could be found in that place. The fire’s raging force destroyed nearly the whole portico leading to the basilica of the prince of the apostles.

When the thrice-blessed pontiff perceived this, as it were, in the silence of the night, he suddenly ran barefoot and on foot, out of love for the church of the blessed apostle Peter and because of the pilgrims’ terrible devastation. Such mercy of almighty God attended his arrival that He did not permit the fire’s force to advance beyond the place where that angelic pontiff first stood.

By his supplication of God’s clemency, and through the struggle of the faithful multitude who were present, the line of fire was extinguished by God’s mercy. Thus it happened that he remained standing in that place throughout the whole night until dawn.

Afterward, when the thrice-blessed shepherd considered the poverty of those pilgrims, which had arisen through the snares of diabolical deception, he bestowed upon their needs such gifts and benefits as he was always accustomed to give. He supplied abundantly gold and silver, clothing for their bodies, all other necessary provisions, and even a plentiful supply of timber, so that they might usefully restore their dwellings as they had previously stood in that place. He also restored the portico destroyed by that disaster, rebuilding it more suitably, better, and with the greatest strength.

This distinguished and venerable pontiff made in the church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and his patron, forty-six *chrysoclavus* curtains for the presbytery arches, bearing scenes of the apostles’ miracles which the Lord deigned to perform through them.

The church of the most blessed martyr of Christ, Praxedes, which had once been built in ancient times but was now so weakened by excessive age that it threatened to collapse from its foundations, was likewise taken in hand by that venerable pontiff. Foreseeing its ruin and devoting himself to the church, he was often watchful there; he transferred it to another place not far away and raised it to a better condition than it had formerly possessed.

[Note: [Col. 1078D] “He adorned the apse of the same church with mosaic work,” and so forth. The apse itself, beautiful and intact with sacred images executed in mosaic, still exists. See Baronius, year 818, no. 15. ID.]

He adorned the apse of the same church with mosaic work in various suitable colors. Likewise, he completed and embellished the triumphal arch with the same metals in a marvelous manner.

This most blessed and illustrious pontiff, concerned by pious care that many bodies of saints which had long lain in cemeteries should not remain neglected, searched for them, gathered those he found, and transported them with profound reverence into the church of the aforesaid holy martyr of Christ, Praxedes, which he had marvelously renovated and rebuilt. All the Roman people accompanied the procession, while bishops, priests, deacons, and clerics sang praise to God.

These things were carried out through the innermost vigilance of that most holy and angelic bishop, so that the prayers of the saints whose bodies had been reburied there—unceasingly pleasing God above the stars—might aid him before almighty God.

In the same place he built a monastery from its foundations and dedicated it under the name of Saint Praxedes the virgin. He gathered into it a Greek congregation and introduced it there, so that day and night it might diligently offer to almighty God and to his saints resting there the praises of Greek psalmody and melody.

Indeed, by granting it numerous estates and urban and rural properties, he enriched the venerable monastery abundantly and beyond measure. Moreover, in the same church he made an oratory of the blessed Zeno, martyr of Christ, where he placed his most sacred body and richly adorned the oratory with mosaic.

In the same church he made a silver ciborium weighing eight hundred and ten pounds. He also magnificently adorned the *propitiatorium* of the sacred altar with silver plates. Finally, he beautifully fashioned and decorated its confession, enclosing it inside and out with its *rugulae*; together they weighed three hundred pounds.

Above the altar of the same venerable place he made a *regnum spanoclystum* of yellow gold, adorned with various stones, weighing five and a half pounds and two ounces. On that sacred altar he made a *chrysoclavus* vestment of extraordinary size and beauty, decorated with various scenes.

Likewise, in the place mentioned above, he offered another *chrysoclavus* vestment made of gold and jewels, bearing a scene of virgins, magnificently arranged and adorned with burning torches. Finally, for the sacred body of the same virgin he offered an image made of patterned silver plates, [Col. 1079C] weighing ninety-nine pounds.

This most kind bishop made in the aforesaid monastery an oratory of the blessed Agnes, virgin of Christ, adorned with extraordinary beauty.

Finally, the church of the holy Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, our lady, called *Dominica*, which had been built long ago and was already close to ruin, the aforesaid pontiff carefully rebuilt from its foundations, making it larger and better than it had been before. He also marvelously adorned its apse with mosaic.

There he offered many gifts, namely, a silver ciborium weighing three hundred and thirty-two pounds. He elegantly adorned the *propitiatorium* of the sacred altar with silver plates. He also wonderfully completed and decorated its confession, with its *rugulae*, inside and out; it weighed one hundred and fifteen pounds and three ounces.

Likewise, in the place mentioned above, he made a bowl (*gabata*) of the purest gold, weighing two pounds and eight ounces. He also made a silver arch and two columns with two *gammadiae*, weighing … pounds.

Indeed, on the sacred altar he made a *chrysoclavus* vestment bearing, with extraordinary beauty, a scene of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ. Again, in the place mentioned above, he made a most beautiful *staurace* vestment with a *periclysi* of *blatta*.

He also made another Byzantine *blatta* vestment bearing a panel of *chrysoclavus* with the face of the holy Mother of God, and standing angels in attendance, with a *periclysi* of *staurace*. Likewise, he made another *staurace* vestment bearing peacocks, with a *blatta* cross in the middle. Furthermore, he made two *quadrapulum* vestments bearing in the middle a *blatta* cross.

Likewise, in the place mentioned above, he made a vestment woven of gold with a *periclysi* of *blatta*. He made one red silk cover. [Col. 1080A] He also made four red silk curtains around the altar, with *gammadiae* and crosses of *quadrapulum*.

This venerable bishop offered at the beam before the altar vestibule three Tyrian curtains and five of *quadrapulum*. In the larger arches of the same church he made twenty *quadrapulum* curtains; in the presbytery arches, four small *staurace* curtains; and likewise, at the entrance to the presbytery, two Tyrian curtains.

This most kind pontiff made at the entrance of the aforesaid church very large curtains of *quadrapulum*, most beautifully adorned with a *periclysi* of *fundatum*.

For this servant of Christ, the almighty Lord, and the aforesaid pontiff, continually foresaw and diligently cared for the churches of God with the greatest concern. One day, when he had come for the sake of prayer to the church of the holy virgin of God and martyr of Christ, [Note: [Col. 1079D] the church of Cecilia. Here he describes how the body of Saint Cecilia was found, covered with golden garments still soaked with blood, after Cecilia herself had revealed the place. The Vatican Codex, from which Baronius recounts the story in the year 821, nos. 2 and 3, contains much else that is lacking in Anastasius at this point.] Cecilia, the walls of that church were already so shaken by extreme age that they were about to collapse from their foundations. Seeing that they had decayed through the long passage of time and, almost broken by ruin, had remained for many years in a dilapidated state, he set himself to the work and began to build a new church on the same site in magnificent fashion, striving to complete it much better than it had been.

Nor do we think that the following should be omitted. One day, as he was going to the church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in order to celebrate the vigils before that same blessed apostle Peter according to custom and, before his confession, to sit and sing the morning praises at daybreak on Sunday, he was suddenly overcome by sleep. He saw a young girl standing beside him, with a virginal appearance and clothed in angelic garments, speaking these words:

“We give you many thanks, because you have abandoned the contest concerning me, after lending your ears to widely circulated reports based on deceptive accounts” [that is, because you abandoned lending credence to uncertain rumors long spread about me]. “For you were so devoted to me that we could speak to one another with our own mouths.”

The aforesaid pontiff listened carefully and earnestly began to ask who she was who spoke such words to him and by what name she was called. She replied:

“If you seek my name, I am called Cecilia, the servant of Christ.”

Then the supreme bishop said to her:

“How can I believe this, since it was formerly reported that the body of that venerable martyr of Christ, Cecilia, had been secretly carried away by the men of Aistulf, king of the Lombards, after he had taken Rome by force?”

When the venerable pontiff had made this known to her, the servant of almighty God said:

“It is entirely true that the Lombards eagerly sought me in order to find me. But, through the help of my Lord Jesus Christ and the aid of my lady, the holy Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, they could neither find me nor carry me away from here as they wished.

“Therefore, just as you have begun to seek how you may find me, do not cease applying yourself with continual labor. For it has pleased the Lord God, for whose love and honor I suffered, that you should find me and place me in the church that you have newly built.”

Having said this, she disappeared from the eyes of the one who was watching.

Then, after the morning praises had been completed, the venerable pontiff, on the evidence [reading: indication] of so certain and undeniable a revelation, began to search with increased effort here and there for the place where her most sacred body lay buried.

By God’s gift, while he was diligently searching, he found it in the cemetery of Praetextatus, outside the Appian Gate. It was clothed in golden garments, together with the body of her venerable spouse Valerianus, and also the linens full of the martyr’s blood, when, struck by the impious executioner, she was consecrated as a martyr of Christ the Lord who reigns forever.

Those linens, which had wiped away the blood of the holy martyr, were found wrapped around the feet of that body, full of sacred blood from the executioner’s triple blow. He handled and gathered all these things with his own hands and, with great honor, placed the body of the virgin inside the walls of this Roman city, in the church dedicated in the name of that holy martyr, to the praise and glory of almighty God.

He placed it beneath the sacred altar together with her most beloved spouse Valerianus, and with the martyrs Tiburtius and Maximus, as well as the pontiffs Urbanus and Lucius.

For the honor and assistance of these saints he built, beside her church, a monastery in honor of the virgins and martyrs Agatha and Cecilia, at the place called *Colles Jacentes*. In it he established a congregation of monks serving God, who were to sing day and night in the aforesaid title of Saint Cecilia, offering daily praises to almighty God.

For the support of the monastery, the preparation of its lights, its usefulness and the stipends of the monks, and also out of the love and affection that he appeared to bear toward his predecessor, the lord Pope Leo III of blessed memory, he took the hospice of Saint Peregrinus, situated beside the blessed apostle Peter at the place called Naumachia. His predecessor had built it, but through the negligence and abandonment of its superiors it seemed to be wasting away in poverty.

Therefore, with pious assistance, he provided for the aforesaid hospice, together with its estates, farmsteads, holdings, tenant farmers, houses, households, and all the things that had been justly and reasonably donated to it by his predecessor according to the provisions of the laws. Whatever he himself had added through pious devotion for the enlargement of the aforesaid monastery—whether fields, vineyards, houses, rural dependents, or other property—he confirmed by a document of his authority for the congregation of monks named above in that monastery.

This most holy bishop, out of love for the venerable saints, had the apse of the church adorned with mosaic work and made a ciborium of extraordinary size in silver, weighing five hundred and a half pounds [Col. 1081C] and eight ounces.

Finally, he beautifully completed and decorated the *propitiatorium* of the sacred altar and the confession, inside and out with its *rugulae*, using silver plates; together they weighed sixty-four pounds and five ounces.

For the sacred body of the same virgin he offered an image made of silver plates, weighing ninety-five pounds. He also made before the altar vestibule a *regularis* covered with silver plates, together with two columns. There he placed one arch and two *gammadiae*, weighing altogether one hundred and a half pounds.

There he himself offered three gilded silver images, weighing altogether forty-eight and a half pounds. The aforesaid bishop also made twenty-six larger silver chalices for the arches of the same church, weighing altogether one hundred and nine and a half pounds.

Likewise, in the place mentioned above, he offered two silver baskets weighing two pounds and eight ounces. He made a bowl (*gabata*) of the purest gold weighing three pounds.

The aforesaid [Col. 1081D] pontiff made two silver baskets called *Enafoti*, weighing ten pounds; three silver bowls (*gabatae*), weighing five pounds; and a gilded silver censer weighing one pound.

This most kind bishop offered on the sacred altar a Byzantine *blatta* vestment bearing in the middle a panel of *chrysoclavus* with the scene of how the angel crowned blessed Cecilia, Valerianus, and Tiburtius, and adorned with a *periclysi* of *chrysoclavus* of extraordinary beauty.

Likewise, there he made a vestment of *fundatum alythinum*, bordered around with a *periclysi* of *oloverus*.

Out of love for the same virgin he made another *fundatum porphyreticum* vestment, bearing in the middle a cross beautifully decorated in woven gold. Moreover, on the aforesaid altar he offered a white, patterned vestment with small roses, bearing in the middle a *blatta* cross with *psilli*, and most beautifully adorned with a Byzantine *blatta* *periclysi*. He also offered in the aforementioned *Itarium* a *quadrapulum* vestment.

[Col. 1082A]

The venerable pontiff made four *alythinum* curtains hanging around the altar, bearing crosses and *gammadiae* of *fundatum* and *quadrapulum*. In the small chest where he placed the venerable head of the same virgin, he made a small Tyrian vestment with a *blatta* *periclysi*.

In the place mentioned above he offered a green *fundatum* vestment, and also another *staurace* vestment with an *oloverus* *periclysi*, as well as a *blatta* vestment with a *fundatum* *periclysi*. He also made, for the chest containing the body of the aforesaid virgin, a *quadrapulum* vestment with a *periclysi*.

Furthermore, he made another *staurace* vestment with an *oloverus* *periclysi*. In the aforesaid church he made twenty-five Tyrian curtains with a Byzantine *blatta* *periclysi*. Likewise, four green curtains with an *oloverus* *periclysi*. In the place mentioned above he offered three *alythinum* curtains with a *blatta* *periclysi*. He likewise offered two small *fundatum* curtains with a *blatta* *periclysi*, and two Tyrian curtains with a *fundatum* *periclysi*.

This venerable and illustrious pontiff made twelve *fundatum* curtains through the arches of the aforesaid church and fourteen of *quadrapulum*. He also made twelve small curtains in the presbytery arch, with Byzantine *blatta* *periclysi*. This venerable bishop, protected by God, made at the entrance of the same church a large curtain of *quadrapulum* and *staurace*, most beautifully adorned.

That same pontiff, who was often concerned with vigilant care for the monasteries built throughout the surrounding region, inquiring into what each possessed, found that the monastery of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, situated beyond the aqueduct of the Lateran patriarchium, was completely desolate in its possessions. The congregation of female servants of God living there was so impoverished that it could offer no praises to almighty God and his saints.

Moved to pity by his investigation, the venerable shepherd made arrangements so that the servants of God might live properly and religiously. He gathered monks there and established a community, enriching the monastery with many resources. He greatly and sufficiently increased its lands, tenant families, holdings, vineyards, houses, and urban and rural properties, so that the congregation residing there, freed from every necessity, might sing night and day, with harmonious music, praises and hymns to God alone and to his saints in the venerable church of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ situated beside the Lateran.

Moreover, in the oratory of the most blessed martyrs Processus and Martinianus, situated within the church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—which he himself had also built—he offered an image of the purest gold bearing the face of the holy Mother of God, weighing ten pounds and four ounces.

There he also made a Byzantine *blatta* vestment bearing two panels of *chrysoclavus* with the faces of the blessed Peter and the holy martyrs Processus and Martinianus, and beautifully decorated with a *chrysoclavus* *periclysi*.

There too he offered a *holoserica* vestment bearing in the middle a panel of *chrysoclavus* with the scene of the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, and most beautifully embellished with a Byzantine *blatta* *periclysi*.

Moreover, for those same saints he offered nine *holoserica* curtains with *quadrapulum* and Byzantine *blatta* *periclysi*. In the place mentioned above he made six small Tyrian curtains with a *fundatum* *periclysi*. He also made a gilded silver censer of remarkable workmanship, weighing one pound.

In the oratory of the most blessed martyrs Sixtus and Fabianus, the aforesaid pontiff made three silver bowls (*gabatae*), weighing five pounds and six ounces. Before the image of the same oratory he made a curtain of *chrysoclavus*, magnificently decorated.

Above their venerable altar he made an *alythinum* vestment bearing in the middle a Byzantine *blatta* cross and likewise a *blatta* *periclysi*. In the same oratory the aforesaid pontiff offered a *holoserica* vestment bearing in the middle two crosses of *chrysoclavus* and a *staurace* *periclysi* adorned with various pearls.

There he also made another *fundatum* vestment bearing in the middle a *blatta* cross. He likewise made, for the adornment of the aforesaid oratory, four *alythinum* curtains with a Byzantine *blatta* *periclysi*. He also made four *holoserica* curtains with *quadrapulum* and *oloverus* *periclysi*.

This most kind bishop made in the church of the blessed martyrs Cosmas and Damian on the Sacred Way a Tyrian vestment bearing in the middle a panel of *chrysoclavus* with the face of our Lord Jesus Christ and those of the blessed martyrs Cosmas and Damian with three other brothers, together with a cross of woven gold and a most beautifully arranged and decorated *oloverus* *periclysi*.

Finally, above their holy altar he offered a Tyrian cover, magnificently decorated. Indeed, before the vestibule of that altar he made three Tyrian curtains with a Byzantine *blatta* *periclysi*.

The venerable pontiff also made in the monastery of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, situated in the territory of Reate, a *chrysoclavus* vestment with the scene of how our Lord Jesus Christ shines in heaven with the archangels and apostles, beautifully adorned with various pearls.

Likewise, in the aforesaid monastery, for the adornment of the sacred altar, he offered another *fundatum* vestment bearing Byzantine *blatta* crosses and magnificently decorated with a *chrysoclavus* *periclysi*. In the same manner, in the church of the blessed martyr Menas, he made a *quadrapulum* vestment with a Byzantine *blatta* *periclysi*.

This most holy and angelic bishop offered in the church of the blessed apostle Peter at Centumcellae a gilded silver chalice and paten, weighing four pounds and three ounces.

Moreover, in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, his protector, he made a Gospel book with *blatta* [binding or ornamentation] of silver, weighing eight pounds and eight ounces.

The most kind bishop also made in the monastery of the protomartyr blessed Stephen at Saint Peter four white *holoserica* vestments, bearing in the middle a cross of woven gold with various pearls and magnificently decorated with a *blatta* *periclysi*.

Likewise, in the place mentioned above, the aforesaid pontiff offered a *fundatum* vestment bearing in the middle a cross woven of gold and a *chrysoclavus* *periclysi*. Finally, the aforesaid bishop made in the same monastery a *fundatum* vestment bearing in the middle a panel of *chrysoclavus* with the face of the holy Mother of God and those of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and a *blatta* *periclysi*.

There he himself offered two *staurace* vestments bearing in the middle *chrysoclavus* crosses and a *blatta* *periclysi*. He also made, for the adornment of that oratory, a large *quadrapulum* curtain bearing in the middle three crosses woven of gold and a *blatta* *periclysi*.

In the deaconry of the blessed Archangel he offered a Byzantine *blatta* vestment bearing in the middle a *chrysoclavus* cross and most beautifully arranged and decorated with a *chrysoclavus* *periclysi*.

Moreover, in the church of the blessed martyr Cecilia [Col. 1083D] he made a silver basin, where he also placed the precious head of the same virgin; it weighed eight and a half pounds.

Likewise, in the church of the blessed martyr Quiriacus at the Baths, the aforesaid bishop offered eight *fundatum* curtains.

This pontiff, supported by God, made in the oratory of the holy Archangel—which his predecessor, the lord Pope Leo, had formerly established and built—a white *holoserica* vestment bearing in the middle a panel of *chrysoclavus* with the scene of the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, and magnificently decorated with a *chrysoclavus* *periclysi*.

Likewise, there he offered another *fundatum* vestment with a Byzantine *blatta* *periclysi*. The aforesaid pontiff also made in the same oratory another *quadrapulum* vestment, sewn around and beautifully arranged and decorated with the scene of the Mother of God.

Furthermore, that same supreme pontiff, orthodox and moved by divine inspiration, observed that the church of our Lady, the holy and undefiled virgin Mary, at the Praesepe, had once been constructed in such a manner that, after the pontiff’s seat, women standing for the solemn celebrations of the Mass seemed to stand close beside the pontiff. Thus, if the pontiff wished to converse about anything with those assisting him, the very close presence of the women made it impossible for him to do so without their intervention. He therefore considered how a spacious area might be made there, so that the seat could be moved from its position. Applying himself diligently to the work, he began unceasingly to raise the seat, which had been placed lower down, so that he might pour out prayers to the Lord more familiarly, insofar as he could modestly avoid the company of the people.

Finally, he constructed the seat, which had formerly been most beautifully decorated with splendid marbles, and constructed approaches on every side by which one might ascend to it. Raising the pavement of the altar, he paved it with the most precious marbles. He also erected there, before the sacred altar’s confession, six columns of purple color; above them he placed a beam of white marble, joining them on the right and left with purple marble and adorning them with carvings, thereby decorating them quite suitably.

He repaired the presbytery of that church, which had previously existed, making it better with various marbles. He magnificently decorated the propitiatory of the sacred altar, or confession, inside and outside, together with its small grilles, in the purest gold; it weighed 174 pounds and 6 ounces. Likewise, he beautifully fitted out and gilded the altar of that basilica with silver plates bearing various scenes; they weighed 385 pounds.

That most benevolent and distinguished prelate also offered there six vessels of the purest gold with various gems, weighing 20 pounds and 6 ounces. He decreed that lamps should always burn day and night before the most holy altar.

Supported by divine inspiration, he offered in the aforesaid basilica eight silver arches with sixteen columns, weighing together 218 pounds and 8 ounces. He also made, before the altar’s vestibule, larger silver grilles weighing 78 pounds. He likewise offered there six silver *canthara*, weighing together 60½ pounds.

In the same manner, through the larger arches of the aforementioned church, he made forty-two large hanging silver chalices, all of which together weighed 281 pounds. The venerable prelate, out of love for that same virgin, our Lady, also offered there four silver crowns, weighing 62½ pounds and 3 ounces. Likewise, in the place mentioned above, he offered two silver baskets, weighing 13 pounds [the source reads *peasantia*, apparently for *pensantia*, “weighing”].

He also made there a gilded silver image with the face of blessed Mary, Mother of God, weighing 17 pounds and 3 ounces. The servant of Christ, the almighty Lord, offered on the sacred altar of the aforesaid basilica two vestments of *chrysoclave*, bearing the story of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, and adorned with a *periclysis* decorated magnificently with various gems and pearls.

He also offered there another vestment of *chrysoclave*, bearing the story of how our Lord Jesus Christ was baptized by John in the Jordan, with a *periclysis* of *chrysoclave* magnificently ornamented. Likewise, in the place mentioned above, he fitted out a vestment of *chrysoclave*, bearing the story of the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, with a *periclysis* of *chrysoclave*, adorned with various pearls.

The most blessed and venerable aforementioned pontiff, moved by divine love, made there, on the already mentioned altar, a vestment likewise of *chrysoclave*, bearing the story of how blessed Mary, Mother of God, was assumed bodily, with a *periclysis* of *chrysoclave*, furnished and decorated with various pearls. For that most benevolent prelate made there another vestment of *chrysoclave*, bearing the story of the ascension of Christ our Lord, properly decorated. Likewise, in the place mentioned above, out of love for that same virgin, he constructed another vestment of *chrysoclave*, bearing the story of how the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles, adorned with various pearls and decorations. Indeed, in the same place he equipped another vestment with *chrysoclave*, modestly fitted out and decorated with the story of the palms.

The aforementioned pontiff also fitted out another vestment of *oloverum* with a *periclysis* of *fundatus*. Likewise, for ordinary days he offered two *fundatus* vestments, beautifully adorned with a *periclysis* of *quadrapulum*. Moved by divine inspiration, that most holy prelate himself made, beneath the larger arches of the aforementioned basilica, fourteen curtains of *fundatus*, fourteen of *quadrapulum*, and likewise fourteen of *imizilo*.

The servant of our Lord Jesus Christ, out of love for that same Lady, made beneath the presbytery arches of the aforesaid church twenty-six curtains of *chrysoclave*, bearing the story of our Lord Jesus Christ and the Nativity or Assumption of that undefiled virgin. Likewise, beneath those arches he offered twenty-four curtains of *quadrapulum*, sewn around with various scenes. Indeed, the servant of Christ the almighty offered above, in view of the apse, an Alexandrian cloth magnificently decorated.

He also offered on the larger beam of that basilica a large *fundatus* curtain, having seven beams of *chrysoclave* and a *periclysis* of Byzantine purple (*blatta Byzantea*). He also made, for the adornment of that basilica, six *quadrapulum* curtains on that beam, and four *imizilo* curtains. The pontiff himself also made, beside the altar’s vestibule, twelve *quadrapulum* curtains in the apse. In the same place, six purple curtains. The venerable prelate also made, at the entrance of the aforementioned basilica, a large Alexandrian curtain, elegantly decorated with various scenes. Likewise, for ordinary days, he offered there another Alexandrian curtain, magnificently ornamented.

[Col. 1085C] The most benevolent and distinguished pontiff offered in the aforementioned basilica six white silk curtains on the larger beam, with a *periclysis* of *fundatus*. He also installed there, magnificently, four other white curtains of Byzantine purple (*blatta Byzantea*). Likewise, in the apse of that basilica he placed six white curtains with a *periclysis* of *fundatus*.

And because there that thrice-blessed shepherd bestowed such care and vigilance as he often expended upon the condition of God’s holy churches, he also magnificently fitted out and decorated, on both sides, the altar of the Praesepe of the aforesaid basilica, or its venerable confession, with the purest gold and various scenes; it weighed 134 pounds and 4 ounces. Likewise, he made there a gilded silver work with various scenes, weighing 254 pounds and 4 ounces [the syntax and placement of the weights are defective in the source].

He also offered there three vessels of the purest gold with various gems, weighing 8 pounds and 10 ounces. Moreover, he placed there curtains of *alythinum* with a *periclysis* of Byzantine purple.

This holy prelate, out of the excessive love of his heart, made in the church of blessed Cecilia a *chrysoclave* vestment bearing the story of the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, magnificently painted and ornamented.

That venerable and distinguished pontiff, protected by God, made the propitiatory of the sacred altar of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, where his most holy body rests, a *spanoclistum* of yellow gold, painted with various scenes and magnificently decorated. It weighed 200 pounds. Likewise, in the aforesaid church, out of love for that apostle of God, his patron, he offered forty-six *chrysoclave* curtains beneath the presbytery arches, bearing the story of the passion and resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Similarly, in the church of the blessed martyrs Cosmas and Damian on the Sacred Way, he made a silk vestment, most beautifully fitted out and decorated. For that most benevolent prelate made in the basilica of the blessed Mary, ever-virgin Mother of God, our Lady, at the Praesepe, two gold vessels decorated with various gems, weighing 6 pounds. Likewise, there he offered an apostolic vessel of the purest gold weighing 5 pounds. Again, in the place mentioned above, he made eight silver *phara canthara*, weighing together 82 pounds. Out of love for that same Lady, he offered in the aforesaid basilica four columns and one arch, weighing together 60 pounds.

The often-mentioned pontiff made on the venerable altar of that church a white vestment having in its center a cross of *chrysoclave*, sewn around with various gems and adorned with beauty; he also attached there another vestment of Byzantine purple, similarly decorated with a *chrysoclave* cross and most honorably adorned with various stones. He also made, for the adornment of the aforesaid church, *chrysoclave* curtains beneath the presbytery arches, bearing the story of the passion and resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 1086C]

He also offered on the larger beam of the oft-mentioned church six other curtains with a *periclysis* of *quadrapulum*. Likewise, on the beams of that basilica he made seven *fundatus* curtains. He also offered silk curtains around the altar of the aforesaid church, bearing a *periclysis* of *quadrapulum*, four in number. The venerable prelate also made in the church of the blessed Mother of God, known as the Dominica, silver grilles weighing 66 pounds.

He also made in the church of the blessed Mary, Mother of God, our Lady, situated at Savina in the episcopal residence, a *fundatus* vestment with a *periclysis* of Byzantine purple.

Finally, he died, called by God. He was buried in the church of blessed Peter the apostle. He held two ordinations, one in December and the other in March. [He ordained] priests . . . . . ., six deacons, and bishops in various places . . . . . . His episcopate was vacant for four days in January, in the first indiction.

[Col. 1085]

# LETTERS OF POPE PASCHAL I

(Mansi, same work.)

## FIRST LETTER: On the Discovery of the Relics of Saint Cecilia

When the summit of the supreme apostolic dignity is recognized as shining forth with divine brilliance in this world, and when one strives to display the contest with greater zeal in celebrating God’s praises [*we endeavor*], the pastoral care of the same apostolic office imposed upon us the duty of proclaiming abundantly and confirming by apostolic judgment those matters recognized as pertaining to the stability of pious places.

And since it is fitting for our apostolic governance that we should gather, with the greatest vigilance, within the enclosure of this nourishing city the various bodies of the saints that had long lain neglected, honorably and for the honor of almighty God—and among them the body of blessed Cecilia the martyr—we ought to have sought them with complete vigilance. Since rumor had long spread among certain people that the body of that blessed Cecilia had secretly been carried away by Aistulf, king of the Lombards, we believed that the matter had consequently been set aside under the veil of near-oblivion.

Nevertheless, with the Lord’s merciful favor, one day, while we were seated before the confession of blessed Peter the apostle, observing the harmony of those singing psalms as Sunday’s morning light was appearing, and while sleep was somewhat weighing upon the frailty of our body, a most beautiful girl appeared before us, lovely in both her virginal appearance and her clothing. Looking at us, she said:

“We give you many thanks because you have abandoned, without cause, the contest that you had undertaken and that had been spread abroad through deceptive reports [*contest*], for you have approached me so closely that we might converse familiarly by our own mouths.”

When we had carefully questioned her, asking, “Who are you, and what is your name? What are you attempting by warning [or presumptuously undertaking] such things?” she replied: “If you ask my name, I am called Cecilia, the servant of Christ.”

I then said to her: “How can we believe this, when it was reported long ago that the body of that most sacred martyr had been carried away from here by the Lombards?”

She answered: “It is true that they greatly desired and sought me, but the grace of my Lady, Mary, ever-virgin Mother of God, was present, so that they could neither find me nor carry me farther from here, as they wished. But continue as you have begun, and work unceasingly as you are working, because it has pleased almighty God to reveal me to you. Strive to bury my body, together with the other holy bodies that are beside me, within the walls of the city.”

Having said this, she departed.

Then, in order to make this revelation known, setting aside every difficulty, we immediately and without hesitation resolved to seek the body of that venerable virgin. With God’s consent and his customary assistance, we hurried to the cemetery of Saint Sixtus, or Praetextatus, situated outside the Appian Gate—as is clearly recounted in her most sacred passion—and found her among her fellow bishops, in golden garments, with her venerable bridegroom.

There we also found the linens with which the most sacred blood had been wiped from the wounds inflicted when the executioner had cruelly struck her three times [*had attacked her with three blows*]. They had been rolled together at the feet of the most blessed virgin and were full of blood. Touching and handling all these things with our own hands, we honorably brought them, together with the venerable body, within the walls of this Roman city.

Out of love for her whom we had so desired, we restored from new foundations the title which Saint Pope Gregory I, the distinguished teacher, had dedicated with pious devotion and which had fallen into disrepair. With God’s merciful favor, we dedicated and placed beneath the sacred altar of the blessed apostle Andrew and Gregory the confessor the body of that same virgin with her most beloved bridegroom, as well as the martyrs Tiburtius and Maximus, and also Urban and Lucius, both pontiffs.

There, after the monastery of the blessed apostle Andrew and Gregory the confessor had been restored for the praise of the Creator, and likewise in honor of the holy virgins and martyrs Agatha and Cecilia, within the church at the place called the Hill of the Lying-down [*Collis Jacentis*].

[Note: [Col. 1087D] Of Protus and Hyacinthus: a place near the title-church, where the bodies of the aforesaid martyrs were located.]

For the congregation of monks serving God there, we unanimously made provision for the daily praises, for assistance, and for the continual provision of lamps, as well as for the usefulness and support of the monks, to be rendered day and night to the Lord our God with due devotion, and so forth.

## SECOND LETTER: To Bernard, Archbishop of Vienne

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend and holy brother Bernard, archbishop of the holy Church of Vienne.

Because we have learned that Your Holiness has undertaken the governance of the Church of Vienne, we rejoice greatly in the Lord our God on that account. Therefore, in the apostolic capacity, we admonish you prudently and attentively to devote your zeal to guarding God’s flock.

You requested from the apostolic see, as was fitting, the use of the pallium. There is no doubt that it possesses authority both for the honor of priestly office and for displaying unanimity with the blessed apostle Peter, throughout the entire flock of the Lord’s sheep entrusted to him. We have therefore willingly granted it to you and to your Church of Vienne, as founded by those same apostles, according to the custom of our predecessors, in order to display the charity of that apostolic see toward you and your Church. We kindly designate that you are to use it according to the custom of the Church.

We necessarily admonish your Fraternity to carry out the work of the Church entrusted to you, with God’s favor, in such a way that, by the zeal with which you have obtained and are adorned with this dignity, you may strive still more to adorn it through integrity of conduct, liveliness of concern, and preservation of the faith.

We also wish all the privileges formerly granted to your Church by our predecessors to remain unchanged for you and your successors.

Written by the hand of Theophylact, notary and archivist, in the month of December, in the tenth indiction. Farewell.

Given by the hand of George, librarian of the holy apostolic see, on the Nones of December, while our most pious lord Augustus, Louis, crowned by God, the great and peaceful emperor, was reigning, in the fourth year of his empire and the third of his patriciate.

[Col. 1088D]

## THIRD LETTER: To Louis the Emperor

The honor of the saints in this world principally consists in venerating continually, by divine favor, whatever places have been consecrated to their names. But this cannot be fully accomplished unless it is done by the appointed caretakers in those places, since men are not venerated for the sake of places, but places for the sake of good people.

Therefore, whoever swears locally to any saint has unquestionably sworn to the honor of those who have specifically been appointed there to perform divine worship. Nor do such people seem, as far as they are able, to have neglected the protection of those things properly acquired, since the caretakers of the places, their honor, and their religion are contained in these matters.

For this reason, every person who makes a vow ought carefully to strive that the caretakers of that sacred place where his vow is made may, insofar as it depends on him, rest there peacefully and without disturbance. Nor should the things lawfully belonging there perish or be removed to their detriment.

Therefore, reverend and most beloved son in Christ, Louis, remember the holy vows that you promised a short time ago before the holy relics, as well as your clergy and faithful, in honor of Saint Peter. For this reason, defend as your own the estates situated under your authority. Also preserve our legate Leo the exorcist, who resides there, unharmed from injury, so that—God forbid—you may not incur among men the reputation of perjury, but may obtain before the Lord the sanctity of your deeds.

[Note: [Col. 1089D] Labbe published this letter from Ughelli, but so mutilated and full of errors that at times scarcely any coherent sense can be extracted from it. The Palatine scholars, who published the Italian historians collected by Muratori, present a more faithful version from the autograph, expressed on tree bark—or, as we would more appropriately judge, on Egyptian papyrus—and preserved in the Ambrosian Library of Milan. Its beginning is likewise read, in exactly the same words, in the *Liber Diurnus* of the Roman pontiffs, edited by Garnerius, chapter 7, no. 9. Garnerius remarks that from it several errors that entered this bull of Paschal could be corrected. Since no one has yet undertaken that task, that task awaits us: we shall give the bull from the Milanese autograph.]

## FOURTH LETTER: To Petronacius, Archbishop of Ravenna

### On the Confirmation of the Privileges of the Church of Ravenna

Paschal, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his reverend and most holy brother Petronacius, archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna, and through you to that Church in perpetuity.
