Since a pious will toward desires and the intention of praiseworthy devotion ought always to be assisted by apostolic efforts, vigilant care must be applied so that matters lawfully conducted and appropriate to the equity of the person concerned cannot be disturbed by any resistance, but may remain permanently by irrefragable right before God. For this reason, by promulgated apostolic decrees, whatever is proper and required by the law of reason must be confirmed as possessions.

(Thus far the *Liber Diurnus*.)

Therefore, since Your Fraternal Holiness sent us, through Sergius, the religious deacon of your holy Church of Ravenna, the privilege of our predecessor, the former pope Hadrian, in which he confirmed the privileges of the former emperor Leo—drawn up by Epiphanius, formerly the religious notary, archivist, and *apocrisarius* of the holy Church of Ravenna, who had been sent by Damian, archbishop of venerable memory—in order that the earlier formulas confirmed by that emperor Leo might be sacred, including those privileges which the divine-memory Justinian and the other most pious emperors had granted to your holy Church, together with other pious provisions, and so that its boundaries might be granted and promulgated without sacrilege or violent seizure: Your Holiness also requested that this same document receive firmness through our apostolic letters.

Therefore, assenting, we decree more fully and confirm all privileges issued for your holy Church of Ravenna, whether by our predecessors—namely, the pontiffs Hadrian and Leo, of holy memory, or their predecessors—or by emperors, or through gifts of kings, or through donations, sales, or testaments made by Christian people. We order and confirm that all such grants to your holy Church, both generally and specifically, shall possess the firmness of permanent confirmation.

No place or right subject to the authority of your holy Church may be judged, supported by any device, or dared by any power whatsoever, under a civil or military pretext, to be usurped, removed, violated, or subjected to a new construction. If anyone attempts to restore or rebuild a ruined or fallen church, he shall not have permission to do so before the customary blessing has first been given and the holy and venerable cross has been set up there by Your Paternal Holiness.

Nor shall clerics beloved of God who come from the jurisdiction or city of another bishopric and reside there presume to perform priestly ministry in the churches subject to you without your command. Rather, Your Holiness shall hear and define the boundaries and activities of all the most religious clerics who come from elsewhere, and shall bring them to effect according to the tenor of the divine laws and the most sacred rules.

The foundations of your monastery of the holy first martyr Stephen, so called and lying beside the palace, together with all the religious monks belonging to it, all venerable sanctuaries and monasteries, and the other venerable places existing within the diocese, shall be subject to Your Holiness’s jurisdiction and power, and through you to your holy Church. All their sacred privileges shall be preserved intact in these matters.

No one shall impose any disturbance, forced service, burden, or levy upon any part of your holy Church. Nor shall anyone remove for military service the tenant farmers, sharecroppers, or slaves subject to your holy Church. If they have been enrolled for military service, we shall help release them and discharge them from service, so that they may return to your venerable jurisdiction.

If anyone rashly attempts to violate such provisions, he shall not only derive no advantage from those matters which we have piously decreed, which you have justly requested from us, and which are contained in the present apostolic document, but shall also, for such atrocious boldness, be made to suffer the loss of all his possessions and shall in no way escape the danger of punishment of his soul. All this is sufficiently established by the mere presentation of this apostolic writing.

If anyone acts against this apostolic command of ours, he shall pay five pounds of refined gold; moreover, he shall be bound by the bonds of anathema and subjected to perpetual condemnation.

We ordered this decree of confirmation, made by us, to be written by Timothy, notary and archivist of our see, in the month of July, in the twelfth indiction. + Farewell. +

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of July by the hand of Sergius, librarian of the holy apostolic see, while our perpetual lord Augustus, Louis, crowned by God, the great and peaceful emperor, was reigning in the sixth year, and also while Hlothar, the new emperor, his son, was reigning in the year . . ., in the twelfth indiction.

[Note: [Col. 1091C] Gratian, *Causa* 1, question 3, chapter 7, “If anyone should object,” and the other collectors of decretals cite a certain canonical fragment inscribed with the name of Paschal. The Roman correctors of the same work assert that it was excerpted from a letter of Pope Paschal, and that the letter exists whole or almost whole in the Vatican Library, in a manuscript collection of decrees issued by Roman pontiffs. From this they also infer that it belongs to Paschal I, since in that collection it follows the letters of Hadrian II in due order; whereas the decrees of Paschal II are placed immediately after Urban II, as the succession of the pontiffs requires.

I myself found this same letter in an appendix by an anonymous author to a manuscript of Burchard, preserved by the cathedral library of the Church of Saint Martin of Lucca. I undertake to publish it here all the more willingly because I believe it has not yet been published and because it is more complete than the version of the Roman correctors. It is inscribed as having been given to the archbishop of Milan; from the silence of the Roman copy, I understand that this inscription is lacking there.

From the same manuscript I also infer that it belongs only to Paschal I, since its title reads, “Letter of Pope Paschasius,” and writers of that period customarily designated Paschal I in this way. The manuscript is from the beginning of the twelfth century. This is demonstrated by the example of Ivo of Chartres, who, in his letter 20 to Reudo, or Eudo, the seneschal of Normandy, published by Juretus, designates Paschal I by the same appellation.

Finally, Pope Urban II, who preceded Paschal II, cites testimony from this very letter—which Paschal, clearly Paschal I, acknowledges in his letter to Lucius among Labbe’s letters, no. 17—namely, the same passage that appears in chapter 7, “If anyone should object,” question 3.

[Col. 1092D]

After writing this, I came upon this same letter quoted by Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg, in his *Commentary on Psalm XXV*, p. 519 of Pez’s edition. At the end, however, it differs considerably from our version. For Gerhoh’s epilogue to the letter agrees with the canon of the Council of Toledo that I found in the same manuscript in which I discovered this letter of Paschal; indeed, it is written immediately after it.

If it is permissible to draw an inference from this, I think that Paschal’s letter was read at some Council of Toledo whose acts have perished, and that the Fathers immediately composed a canon on its basis. This was the reason why, in Gerhoh’s manuscript, one was appended to the other. Whatever the case may be, I present the letter from my manuscript, marking in parentheses the variants found in Gerhoh.]

## FIFTH LETTER: To the Archbishop of Milan [Gerhoh: “To the Milanese”]

Whoever, when able, does not defend a brother from death incurs the guilt of fraternal [or eternal] death. We too, who have heard of the supreme danger threatening Your Excellency, incur the penalty of the gravest guilt if we remain silent. For the Lord solemnly testifies through the Prophet [*the Lord prophesying*] that the person who, by remaining silent, conceals the wickedness of the impious truly sheds blood.

We have heard—and we are greatly astonished—that the sacred orders among you are being sold for money, although anyone who attempts or accepts such a thing is entirely shown to be a heretic. The Holy Spirit thunders through Gregory: “Whoever is ordained for money is promoted in order to become a heretic.”

[Note: [Col. 1092D] Gregory, *Letters*, book IV, letter 56.]

And to show that the cause of this little letter of ours was not presumption [*presumption*], but fear, that same blessed author continues:

“Whoever, according to the office entrusted to him, does not burn vehemently against the heresy of simony and of the neophytes should not doubt that he will share the portion of him who first committed this sacrilegious offense.”

[Col. 1091C] Since these words express heretical, simoniacal, and neophyte heresy, they make it entirely clear that this crime is also deserving of eternal death. Augustine declares this through a divine oracle, saying:

“Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in any way, that every heretic or schismatic, even if he gives many alms or sheds his blood for Christ, must be handed over with the devil and his angels to the fire of eternal punishment, unless before the end of this Catholic life he has been incorporated into and restored to the Church.”

[Note: [Col. 1092D] Augustine, *On Faith*, chapter 39.]

This is why the Lord drove the buyers and sellers from the Temple; the earth swallowed Dathan and Abiram when they sought office; and Peter condemned Simon when he attempted to do so. Peter also condemned all simonists with ecclesiastical weapons by perpetual anathema [the source has *Petrus* repeated or omitted uncertainly].

It is exceedingly shameful that the Church, now established in the fullness of its strength, should succumb to so savage an enemy, when at the beginning of its infancy it had triumphed over him with such power.

[Note: [Col. 1092D] Canon 5, “If anyone should object,” question 3.]

But if anyone should object that not consecrations are being sold, but the things that result from consecration, he seems indeed to say something, but in fact understands nothing at all.

[Col. 1092B] For since the bodily Church, or a bishop, an abbot, or anything of that kind, can accomplish nothing without bodily and external possessions, just as the soul does not live temporally without the body—

[Note: [Col. 1092D] See Urban II’s letter 17 to Lucius.]

whoever sells one of the two things without which the other cannot be possessed does not leave the other unsold. Yet sacred canon utterly destroys this objection, since it prohibits the procurator or defender of a Church or of a rule from being appointed for money, and likewise cuts down, with the sword of anathema, those who intervene in so great a crime.

What more is there to say? If the anathematized and excommunicated—who, as genuine heretics, simonists, and neophytes, have been separated from the number of the faithful [and from the Church]—are such, who does not see that the Masses and prayers of such priests or clerics provoke the Lord to anger against the people, whom we had believed could be appeased by such acts?

For it is written: “Everything that is not from faith is sin” (Romans 14:23). And, again, the place of true sacrifice does not exist outside the Catholic Church. Hence it is also said: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second correction” (Titus 3:10).

[Col. 1093A] How, then, do we avoid such bishops, abbots, or other clerics if we hear their Masses, when, if we even pray together with them, we incur excommunication?

To believe that such men are at least priests is wholly erroneous, since Peter says to Simon: “May your money be with you unto perdition, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money” (Acts 8:20).

When it says, “you thought,” it is clear that he is condemned not for having done the thing, but because he believed that he could do it.

[Note: [Col. 1093B] Thus far Gerhoh. In his text the following is appended: “And we likewise prohibit under anathema that same thing concerning the heresy of simony, as the holy synod decreed: let no one sell any consecration of churches, archpresbyterate, commendations of altars, or transfers of churches. Whoever leases, sells, or buys one, let him be anathema. Amen.” And all answered three times: “So be it, so be it.” Thus the letter to the same person concludes.]

Yet to suppose is less than to believe. Since, therefore, to be any kind of heretic is a certain and indubitable condemnation, what benefit is there in having driven Arians, Sabellians, Photinians, and impious Manichaeans from almost the entire world, if the heresy of simony and of the neophytes—which, as blessed Gregory says, “first arose in the holy Church through diabolical fraud”—pollutes the Church’s chastity with a most foul contamination, as though it were the first and greatest corruption?

Therefore, for the sake of the Lord and in the Lord, we ask and beseech Your Excellency and all Christ’s faithful: if you desire to have a share in Christ, strive with all your strength so that this savage plague, which by raging everywhere among all peoples has already condemned them to eternal death, may be utterly destroyed by your authority and example. Otherwise—God forbid—you may continue to sin against the Spirit, and that sin may not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come.

## Editor’s Note on This Letter

At first I thought that I had once been the first to publish this letter. Then I found it almost complete in Gerhoh. Finally, when I had already submitted it to the press, I found it complete in Ivo, *Decretals*, part II, chapter 84, where he cites it under the prefixed title: “From the Decrees of Pope Paschal.”

## In the Year of the Lord 820

# REMIGIUS, BISHOP OF CHUR

[Col. 1093]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON REMIGIUS

[Hartzheim, *German Councils*, vol. II.]

[Col. 1093]

Remigius, also called Remedius, bishop of Chur in Rhaetia, lived between 813 and 830 and was, according to Stumpf, *History of German Switzerland*, book X, p. 584, the nineteenth bishop of that Church. According to Bucelinus, however, he is listed as the twenty-third bishop, in the first part of *Sacred Germany*.

The forty-nine chapters that follow are excerpted from Isidore’s forged letters attributed to the ancient Roman pontiffs. They were probably written under Charlemagne, indeed at his command, as Goldastus writes; on this point I have considerable doubt. For the Isidorian collection was by no means known to Charlemagne, just as the Dionysian collection was given to him by Pope Hadrian. He frequently inserts authorities from Sacred Scripture; otherwise, he compiled his chapters from those forged letters.

[Col. 1093]

# CANONS OF REMIGIUS FOR HIS DIOCESE

(Hartzheim, same work.)

[Col. 1093C]

## I. On Permission Concerning the Body of the Lord

(From Clement’s letter to James, bishop of Jerusalem.)

Certainly, such a quantity of whole burnt offerings should be offered on the altar as ought to suffice for the people; but if any remains, it must not be kept until the following day, but must be consumed with fear and trembling through the diligence of the clergy. Those, however, who consume the remaining portion of the Lord’s body left in the sacristy must not immediately assemble to partake of ordinary food, nor suppose that they may mix with the holy portion food which, digested through the intestines, is discharged into the privy. Therefore, if it is distributed in the morning on the Lord’s Day, the ministers who have consumed it must fast until the sixth hour; and if they have received it at the third or fourth hour, until evening. Thus the sacraments are to be safeguarded by a secret and everlasting sanctification.

## II. On the Sacred Vessels

(From the same letter.)

With regard to the sacred vessels, this is how one must act. If the altar cloth, the cathedra, the candlestick, or the veil has been worn out by age, let it be consigned to the fire; for it is not permitted that anything which has been in the sacristy be treated improperly, but everything must be given over to the fire. Their ashes too must be brought into the baptistery, where there is no passage, or else thrown into a wall or into the hollows of pavements, so that they may not be defiled by the feet of those entering.

The altar cloths and veils which have been soiled in the service of the sanctuary must be washed within the sacristy by deacons together with humble ministers. They must not carry the veils of the Lord’s table outside the sacristy, lest perchance some dust from the Lord’s body should fall improperly when the linen is carried outdoors, and this should become a sin for the person performing the task. Therefore we command the ministers to guard them carefully within the sacristy. The altar cloths are to be washed in one basin, and the veils in another.

## III. In What Place Mass Is to Be Celebrated

(From the letter sent by Clement to all bishops, priests, and deacons.)

You must therefore recognize the Lord’s will here—that is, while you are placed in the present life—where there is a place both for action and for sacrifice. For it is not permitted to sacrifice or celebrate Mass in other places, except in those where the proper bishop has ordered it, or which have been consecrated by a regularly ordained bishop who holds a city. Otherwise these things are neither to be done nor properly celebrated.

## IV. On Obedience to Be Rendered to Bishops

(From the same letter of Blessed Pope Clement.)

You who exercise the Lord’s priesthood and have been placed upon the watchtower ought to know more, so that you may be able fully to teach the peoples subject to you and, with the Lord’s assent, provide them guidance toward the kingdom of heaven. Hence Truth itself says: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the others in parables,” and so forth.

For it is your task, since you exercise the Lord’s embassy, to teach the peoples; their task is to obey you as God. If all priests, deacons, subdeacons, and the remaining clergy do not obey us bishops; if all rulers, both of higher and lower rank, and the remaining peoples, tribes, and tongues do not obey; they shall be not only disgraced but also exiled from the kingdom of God and from the fellowship of the faithful, and shall be excluded from the thresholds of God’s holy Church.

For it is your task to instruct them, while theirs is to obey you as God, whose embassy you exercise, as the Lord says: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me, and whoever receives you receives me”; and, “Whoever receives me receives him who sent me” (Luke 10:16; 9:48).

## V. Nothing Is to Be Done Without the Bishop’s Permission

(From the same letter, among other matters.)

Therefore all the faithful, and above all priests, deacons, and the remaining clergy, must take care that they do nothing without the permission of their own bishop. No priest is to celebrate Mass in his parish without the bishop’s command; no one is to baptize or do anything without his permission.

Likewise, the remaining people, both great and small, must do whatever is to be done with his permission. They must not depart from their parish without his leave, nor presume to remain there when they arrive. Their souls have been entrusted to him; therefore they must do everything on his counsel, and nothing without consulting him.

## VI. That It Is Necessary for Everyone to Receive Baptism

(From the letter of Blessed Pope Clement, written to Julius and Julian and their other colleagues.)

Whether a person is just or unjust, baptism is altogether necessary. For the just person, it is necessary that perfection may be fulfilled in him and that he may be regenerated for God; for the unjust, that remission may be granted for the sins he has committed.

## VII. That Those Baptized Must Be Confirmed by the Bishop

(Also from the same letter.)

Everyone must therefore hasten, without delay, to be reborn for God and thereafter to be confirmed by the bishop—that is, to receive the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit—for the end of each person’s life is uncertain.

When a person has been regenerated through water and subsequently confirmed by the bishop, as has been stated, with the sevenfold grace of the Spirit—for otherwise he can in no way be a perfect Christian—he must not, without necessity, remain without a place among the perfect through negligence or choice. Rather, he must possess what we received from Peter and what the other holy apostles taught at the Lord’s command. Finally, through good works he must show in himself the likeness of the Father who begot him.

After this he must recognize how to honor God. His honor consists in living as God wills. He wills each person to live in such a way that he knows neither murder nor adultery; that he avoids hatred and greed; rejects and abhors anger, pride, and boastfulness; and keeps envy and all things similar to these entirely alien from himself.

## VIII. What Baptism with Water Contributes to the Worship of God

(Also from the same letter.)

First, because what has pleased God is fulfilled; second, because the frailty of the former birth—which came to you through a human being—is cut away when it is regenerated from the waters and renewed for God. Only then will you be able to attain salvation; otherwise it is impossible.

For the true prophet testified to you together with the sacrament, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless someone is born again from water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:3).

## IX. That Sacrifice Is Not to Be Offered Everywhere or by One Person Alone

(From the letter of Pope Anacletus, written to all bishops and all the remaining faithful.)

Those who sacrifice perfectly to God ought not to be harassed, but supported, consoled, and venerated by everyone. When they sacrifice to the Lord, however, they must not do so alone, but must bring witnesses with them, so that they may be shown to sacrifice perfectly to God in places consecrated to the Lord.

For the authority of divine law says: “See that you do not offer your holocausts in every place that you see, but in the place that the Lord your God has chosen” (Deuteronomy 12:13).

A bishop sacrificing to God must have witnesses with him, as prescribed, and more than another priest. Just as he holds a higher rank of honor, so he requires a greater increase of testimony.

On the more solemn days he must have with him either seven, five, or three deacons—who are called his eyes—and subdeacons and the remaining ministers. Clothed in sacred vestments, they must stand before and behind him, while priests stand opposite, to his right and left, with contrite hearts and humbled, bowed faces. They are to guard him against malicious people and give their consent to the sacrifice.

## X. Church Property Is Not to Be Taken

(From the same letter of Pope Anacletus.)

Therefore whoever seizes, takes away, or defrauds Christ’s money and the Church’s property is a murderer, and shall be reckoned a murderer before the judge’s sight. Whoever seizes his neighbor’s money commits iniquity; whoever takes away the Church’s money or property commits sacrilege.

## XI. On the Ordination of Bishops

(From the letter of Pope Anacletus written to all the bishops of Italy.)

The ordinations of bishops are to be celebrated by all those who are in the same province, by apostolic authority. Coming together, they must conduct a careful examination, and celebrate a fast with all prayers. On the Lord’s Day, at the third hour, they are to pray and lay hands upon them with the holy Gospels which they are going to preach, and, following the example of the prophets and kings and the practice of the apostles and Moses, anoint their heads with sacred oil. For all sanctification rests in the Holy Spirit, whose invisible power has been proclaimed through the holy chrism. In this manner they are to celebrate the solemn ordination.

If all cannot possibly assemble together, they must nevertheless give their assent through their prayers, so that in spirit they may not be absent from the ordination itself.

Moreover, the blessed James, the first archbishop of the Jerusalemites, who was called James the Just and was named the Lord’s brother according to the flesh, was ordained by the apostles Peter, James, and John. They thereby gave a model to their successors, so that no one should ever be ordained by fewer than three bishops, with all the others giving their assent, and so that the ordination should be celebrated by common agreement.

## XII. On the Accusation of Priests

(From the same letter.)

The accusation of those about whom you wished to consult us must be made only by suitable and highly approved men, who are free both from suspicion and from crimes. For the Lord did not wish those who handle his sacred body to be defamed by base, rejected, or unsuitable persons, nor did he permit them to be calumniated. Rather, he himself drove sinful priests from the temple with his own scourge.

It is therefore clear that high priests—that is, bishops—are to be judged by God, not torn apart by human beings or by men of corrupt life, but rather supported by all the faithful.

## XIII. On Complaints against Priests

(From the same letter.)

If anyone becomes hostile toward priests or their churches, or has some grievance against them, let him first return to them in a spirit of charity, so that, admonished in friendly conversation, they may remedy what ought to be remedied and amend through charity what they recognize as requiring just correction.

But if some presume to tear them apart, accuse them, or harass them before doing this, let them be excommunicated and not absolved until they have performed penance through worthy satisfaction, since the injury done to them concerns Christ, whose embassy they exercise.

## XIV. On the Twofold Order of Priests

(From the letter of Anacletus written to all bishops and the remaining priests of Christ.)

The order of priests is twofold, brothers, and as the Lord established it, no one ought to disturb it. You know that the apostles were chosen and appointed by the Lord and afterward dispersed through various provinces to preach.

When the harvest began to grow, he saw that there were few laborers and commanded that seventy disciples be chosen to assist them. Bishops hold the place of the apostles, and priests that of the seventy disciples.

Bishops, however, are not to be established in castles or small cities. Priests are to be ordained and appointed by bishops throughout castles, small cities, and villages, one in each of their respective titles. No more than these two orders of priests have been conferred upon us, nor did the apostles teach any others.

## XV. On Those Who Despise Their Superiors

(From the same letter.)

It is necessary that rulers be feared by their subjects and corrected by them, so that those who do not fear divine judgments may at least fear human punishment and dread sinning.

Those who corrupt the life and morals of teachers are worse than those who seize the possessions and estates of others. The former take away things that are outside us, even though they are ours; but our detractors and corrupters of our morals, and those who arm themselves against us, deceive us in our very selves. Therefore they are rightly disgraced and deservedly expelled from the Church.

## XVI. On Those Who Expose the Faults of Teachers

(From the same letter.)

The damage done to morals differs greatly from the damage done to temporal possessions, since the latter are outside us, whereas the former are within us.

Those who expose the faults of their teachers or superiors are condemned by the sentence concerning Ham, the son of Noah—just as Ham did not cover his father’s nakedness but displayed it for ridicule.

## XVII. On Tolerating the Pastor’s Reprehensible Morals

(From the same letter.)

If a teacher or pastor of the Church deviates from the faith, he is to be corrected by the faithful. But for reprehensible morals he is to be tolerated rather than harshly disciplined, because the rulers of the Church are to be judged by the Lord, as the Prophet says: “God has stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he distinguishes among the gods” (Psalm 81).

Therefore every faithful person, if he sees or learns that his people are swelling up against their pastor or that the clergy are engaged in slander, must strive with all his strength to root out this vice and correct it prudently. If they prove incorrigible, he must not presume to associate with them in any affairs before they have been reconciled with their teacher.

For priests and all the remaining faithful alike ought to exercise the greatest care concerning those who are perishing, so that through their rebuke they may either be corrected from their sins or, if they prove incorrigible, separated from the Church.

## XVIII. That a Bishop Must Not Leave His Church Without a Regular Transfer, Nor Be Removed from It

(From the letter of Pope Evaristus, written to all the brethren throughout Egypt joined to the Lord.)

Priests exercise Christ’s embassy in the Church. Just as the Church, his bride, is joined to him, so bishops are joined to their respective churches, each according to his portion.

Just as a husband must not neglect his wife but must love, chastely guard, and prudently govern her, so a bishop must treat his Church. And just as a wife who is under her husband’s authority must obey, love, and cherish her husband, so the Church must obey, love, and cherish her bishop in all things, as her own soul, because the former is done carnally, while the latter is done spiritually.

Just as a husband must not commit adultery against his wife, so a bishop must not commit adultery against his Church—that is, he must not abandon the one to whom he was consecrated, except through unavoidable necessity or an apostolic or regular transfer, and join himself to another.

And just as a wife is not permitted to leave her husband and, while he is alive, marry another and commit adultery against him—even if her husband has committed fornication—but, according to the Apostle, must either be reconciled to her husband or remain unmarried, so a Church is not permitted to abandon or separate from her bishop in order to receive another while he is alive. She must either retain him or remain unmarried; that is, she must not receive another bishop while her own is alive and thereby incur the crime of fornication or adultery.

For if she has committed adultery—that is, if she has joined herself to another bishop, or brought another bishop over herself, or caused or desired him to be installed—she must either be reconciled to her own bishop through the severest penance or remain unmarried.

## XIX. A Bishop Must Not Be Defamed or Expelled, Nor Another Installed in His Place

(From the same letter.)

We have heard that some bishops among you have been defamed and torn apart, driven from their cities—for bishops cannot be established elsewhere except in cities of some importance—and that others have been installed in their places while they were still alive.

Therefore we write to you so that you may know that this is not permitted, but that the proper bishops must be recalled and restored in complete integrity.

Those, however, who hold their brides in adulterous disgrace—whom we understand, according to the foregoing statement, to be their wives—are to be expelled as adulterers, made infamous, and barred from ecclesiastical honors.

If they have any complaint against them, it is to be investigated after these matters have been carried out and settled by the authority of this holy see.

## XX. Judgment Must Not Be Rendered Rashly

(From the same letter.)

Almighty God, in order to restrain us from delivering a precipitate judgment, although all things are naked and open before his eyes, nevertheless did not wish to judge the evils of Sodom merely on hearsay, before he had clearly ascertained what was being said.

Hence he himself says: “I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know.”

Almighty God, from whom nothing is hidden and to whom all things are manifest even before they occur, deigned to investigate this and many other matters—which, to avoid length, we have not inserted here—for no other reason than to give us an example, so that we might not be precipitate in examining and judging affairs, and so that we might not presume to believe anyone’s evil before proving it.

By his example we are warned never to be hasty in pronouncing judgment, or to judge rashly and carelessly matters that have not been investigated, however they may appear, as the voice of Truth says: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged; for with the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged,” and so forth.

Heard reports of evil should move no one, and no one should ever believe statements made indiscriminately without certain proof. Instead, he must first investigate carefully what he has heard, lest anyone act precipitately.

## XXI. On Documents Extorted by Force

(From the letter of Pope Alexander, written to all the orthodox throughout various regions.)

Among other things he says:

“Likewise, if documents of this kind have in any way been extorted from such persons through fear, fraud, or force, as though they might thereby free themselves—by whatever device they were written or authenticated by them—we decree that they shall cause them no prejudice or harm. Nor, with the Lord and the holy apostles and their successors as our authority, do we ever permit them to suffer any infamy, calumny, or deprivation of their own property on this account. In such matters, however, a confession must be made not under compulsion but voluntarily.”

## XXII. On a Complaint against a Bishop or Church Authority

(From the same letter.)

If anyone believes that he has a just complaint against a bishop or church authorities, he must not first approach primates or other judges before he has personally approached those whom he considers to have injured him—not once but very often—in a friendly manner, so that he may receive from them either his justice or an explanation.

If he acts otherwise, let him be deprived of communion by them and by the others, as a despiser of the apostles and the other Fathers.

## XXIII. Nothing but Bread and Wine Mixed with Water Is to Be Offered on the Altar

(From the same letter of Alexander, successor of Pope Evaristus.)

For, as we have received from the Fathers and reason itself teaches, neither wine alone nor water alone is to be offered in the Lord’s chalice, but both mixed together, because both are said to have flowed from his side during his Passion.

Truth itself instructs us to offer the chalice and bread in the sacrament when it says: “Jesus took bread, blessed it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat; this is my body.’” Likewise, after he had supped, he took the chalice and gave it to his disciples, saying: “Take and drink from it, all of you, for this is the chalice of my blood, which will be poured out for you for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:26; 1 Corinthians 11:24).

Crimes and sins are wiped away through these sacrifices offered to the Lord. Therefore his Passion, by which we were redeemed, must be commemorated in them, repeatedly recited, and these offerings must be presented to the Lord.

By such sacrifices the Lord will be pleased and appeased, and will forgive great sins. Nothing in the sacrifices can be greater than the body and blood of Christ, and no offering is superior to this; rather, it surpasses all others.

It must be offered to the Lord with a pure conscience, completed with a pure mind, and venerated by everyone. Just as it is superior to the rest, so it must be cultivated and venerated above the rest.

## XXIV. On Sprinkling Holy Water

(From the same letter.)

We bless water sprinkled with salt for the people, so that all who are sprinkled with it may be sanctified; and we command all priests to do the same.

For if the dung of a heifer, sprinkled upon the people, sanctified and cleansed them, much more will water sprinkled with salt and consecrated by divine prayers sanctify and cleanse the people.

And if the barrenness of water was healed through the sprinkling performed by the prophet Elisha (2 Kings 2:20), how much more will holy water, consecrated by divine prayers, remove the barrenness of human things, sanctify and cleanse the polluted, multiply other blessings, turn aside the devil’s snares, and defend a person from the wiles of the cunning spirits?

## XXV. Communion Must Not Be Given to Those Who Disturb Priests

(From the letter mentioned above, written to all bishops established throughout various regions.)

Whoever obstructs your embassy turns aside the advancement not of one person but of many. Just as he harms many, so he must be rebuked by many and deprived of the fellowship of the good.

Because he obstructs God’s cause and disturbs the state of the Church, he must therefore be kept away from its thresholds. Everyone must beware of such a person, and he must not be received into the communion of the faithful until he has made satisfaction.

For this was established long ago: “Let the one who disturbs the state of the Church be kept away from its thresholds; let the one who turns aside the good of the faithful not communicate with the faithful.”

## XXVI. Those Who Do Not Assist Priests Are Called Schismatics

(From the letter mentioned above.)

Whoever belongs to your fellowship but withdraws from your assistance will be shown to be more a schismatic than a priest.

“Behold,” says the Prophet, “how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell together” (Psalm 132:1). Those who withdraw from their brothers’ support do not dwell together; and what is worse, they prepare ambushes or set traps for their brothers.

A little later:

“We, therefore, who wish both to be called and to be the Lord’s disciples, ought to bear Christ’s cross and suffer with our brothers, not prepare ambushes or pits of any kind for them, because the one who digs a pit for his brothers deserves like treatment.

“Do not err, brothers, for God is not mocked. For this reason the Lord entrusted his Church to you: so that you might labor for everyone and not neglect to provide assistance to all who are oppressed.

“Hence the Lord also speaks through the Prophet, saying: ‘Judge judgment in the morning, and rescue those oppressed by force from the hand of the slanderer, lest my indignation go forth like fire, burn up, and have no one to extinguish it’” (Jeremiah 21:12).

You, therefore, who have been placed by the Lord upon the highest watchtower, must take note of and suppress those who stir up seditions and scandals against their brothers, lest you perish together with them.

## XXVII. Sacred Vessels Must Not Be Handled by Anyone Except Those Consecrated to the Lord

(From the letter of Pope Sixtus, successor of Pope Alexander, written to all bishops.)

Let your wisdom know, dearest brothers, that in this holy apostolic see it has been established by us, the other bishops, and the remaining priests of the Lord that sacred vessels are not to be handled by anyone except those consecrated and devoted to the Lord.

For it is utterly unworthy that the Lord’s sacred vessels, whatever they may be, should serve human uses or be handled by anyone except men serving and devoted to the Lord. Otherwise, because of such presumptions, the angry Lord might inflict a plague upon his people, and those who have not even sinned might suffer or perish, since the just very often perishes on account of the wicked.

Take care, brothers, that you do not henceforth permit such things to be done in your churches, lest the flock redeemed by the precious blood of Christ—God forbid—fall headlong into destruction.

## XXVIII. On the Seven-Week Fast to Be Observed by Clerics before Easter

(From the letter of Pope Telesphorus written to all bishops.)

We trust that your holy faith, founded upon the teaching of the apostles, holds this doctrine and expounds it to all peoples—those who in no way dissent from the decrees of the apostles and their successors, through whom it is right that the others should be instructed.

Therefore know that it has been established by us and all the bishops assembled at this apostolic see that, for seven full weeks before holy Easter, all clerics called to the Lord’s lot must fast from meat.

For just as the life of clerics ought to be distinct from the conduct of laypeople, so there ought also to be distinction in fasting. Just as laypeople and secular persons do not wish to admit them into their accusations, so the life and conduct of clerics must always be distinct and separate from those of secular laypeople in every respect.

And just as clerics are more devoted to divine worship and are called familiar with the Lord Savior, so they must be distinguished in morals, conduct, and holiness.

Therefore, during these seven weeks, let all clerics fast from meat and delicacies, and strive day and night to cling to the Lord through hymns, vigils, and prayers.

## XXIX. On the Time of Mass, and That the Angelic Hymn Is to Be Said Only at the Appropriate Time

(From the same letter.)

On the holy night of the birth of the Lord Savior, let them celebrate Masses and solemnly chant the Angelic Hymn in them, because on that same night it was announced by an angel to the shepherds, as Truth itself testifies, saying:

“Shepherds were in that region, keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock. And behold, an angel of the Lord stood beside them, and they were afraid with great fear. The angel said to them: ‘Do not be afraid, for behold, I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people. For today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David. And this will be a sign for you: you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and placed in a manger.’

“And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will’” (Luke 2:8ff.).

At other times, however, celebrations of Mass are not at all to be held before the third hour of the day, because it is written that at that same hour the Lord was crucified and the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles.

Bishops, however, are to recite the same Angelic Hymn at the appropriate time and place in the solemn celebrations of Mass.

## XXX. That No One Absent Is to Be Accused, and Who May Not Accuse

(From the same letter.)

We also exclude accusers and accusations that the laws of the world do not admit. We decree that no credence is to be given to an accuser who, in the absence of his adversary, has brought forward a case before a just examination of both parties.

Nor are unsuitable persons to be admitted as accusers. We consider all who arm themselves against the Fathers infamous. For all Fathers are to be venerated, not rejected or ambushed.

Those who associate with enemies, or who are regarded as suspect, are likewise not to be admitted, because their hostility tears apart even the innocent.

Our Fathers established this strongest of walls, and we establish it with them against your persecutors. By this remedy may their machinations be driven away, and may you deserve to serve your Savior as holier and more secure persons.

## XXXI. On Metropolitans: No One May Hear Cases Except at the Instance of the Provincial Bishops

(From the letter of Pope Hyginus, written to all who flourish in apostolic faith and doctrine.)

Moreover, brothers, without prejudice to the privilege of the Roman Church in all matters, no metropolitan may hear anyone’s cases except at the instance of all the other bishops of his province. Otherwise proceedings conducted without being examined in the presence of all of them will be void, and if he does so, he must be restrained by his brothers.

## XXXII. On the Day on Which Easter Is to Be Celebrated

(From the letter of Pope Pius, written to all who remain in apostolic faith and doctrine.)

Moreover, we wish you to know that the Lord’s Easter is to be celebrated annually on the Lord’s Day.

At that time Hermes, a teacher of faith and the Scriptures, shone among us. Although we celebrated that Easter on the aforesaid day, some nevertheless doubted about it. To strengthen their souls, an angel of the Lord appeared to Hermes in the form of a Shepherd and commanded him that everyone should celebrate Easter on the Lord’s Day at its proper time.

Therefore, by apostolic authority, we instruct you also that everyone must observe the same, because we too observe it. You must not in any way disagree with the head.

## XXXIII. That No One May Take Church Estates and Apply Them to His Own Uses

(From the letter mentioned above, written to the Italian brethren.)

It has been brought before the apostolic see that there are contentions and rivalries among you, and that some apply to human uses estates dedicated to divine uses, withdrawing them from the Lord God to whom they were given so that they may serve their own purposes.

Therefore the insult of that usurpation must be removed by everyone, lest estates assigned to the mysteries of heaven be harassed by certain intruders.

If anyone presumes to do this, let him be considered a sacrilegious person and judged as such. We have also heard that the clerics and priests of the Lord who do this are persecuted and defamed, so that their persecutors, adding evil to evil, become worse, without understanding that the Church of God consists in the priests and grows into the temple of God.

Just as the person who devastates God’s Church and strips or invades its estates and gifts becomes sacrilegious, so the person who persecutes its priests is guilty of sacrilege and is judged sacrilegious.

## XXXIV. That Fornication Is Not a Graver Sin Than Sacrilege

(From the same letter.)

Fornication is therefore not a graver sin than sacrilege. Just as the sin committed against God is greater than that committed against a human being, so it is more serious to commit sacrilege than to fornicate.

## XXXV. That No Archbishop Is to Be Called a Primate Except One Who Holds a Principal City

(From the letter of Pope Anicius [possibly Anicetus], written to all the churches established throughout the provinces of Gaul.)

No archbishop is to be called a primate except one who holds a principal city whose bishops the apostles and their successors regularly established as patriarchs or primates.

An exception may be made if some people should thereafter be converted to the faith and, because of the multitude of bishops, it becomes necessary to establish primates among them.

The others who have obtained other metropolitan sees are not called primates but metropolitans.

## XXXVI. On the Ordinations of Bishops

(From the same letter mentioned above.)

Concerning the ordinations of bishops, about which you wished to consult us, we have found that certain decrees were already made long ago in the spirit of our predecessor Anacletus.

For we know that the blessed James, who was called the Just and was also named the Lord’s brother according to the flesh, was ordained bishop of Jerusalem by the apostles Peter, James, and John.

If so great a man was ordained by no fewer than three apostles, it is plainly evident that, by the Lord’s institution, they handed down the rule that a bishop should be ordained by no fewer than three bishops.

As the number of bishops increases, however, more should be added unless necessity intervenes. That is, if an archbishop dies and another bishop is to be ordained, all the bishops of the same province must assemble at the metropolitan see, so that he may be chosen and ordained by all.

The man who is to preside over all of them ought himself to be chosen and ordained by all of them. The remaining provincial bishops, if necessity requires, may, with the consent of the others, be consecrated by three bishops at the command of the archbishop.

It is better, however, if he himself, together with all of them, chooses the one who is worthy and all together consecrate the pontiff.

Although this has been granted under the pressure of necessity, the rule prescribed and stated concerning the consecration of an archbishop—that all his suffragans are to ordain him—may in no way be changed. For the one who presides over them must be appointed by all the bishops over whom he presides.

If anyone presumes to act otherwise, it is beyond doubt that the act has no force, because his ordination, conducted in that manner, will be invalid.

## XXXVII. That Women Consecrated to God and Nuns Must Not Touch Sacred Vessels or Consecrated Cloths, or Carry Incense around the Altars

(From the letter of Pope Soter, written to the bishops established throughout the provinces of Italy.)

It has been brought before the apostolic see that women consecrated to God, or nuns, touch sacred vessels and consecrated cloths among you and carry incense around the altars. No one of sound judgment can doubt that all these practices are full of blame and reproach.

Therefore, by the authority of this holy see, we decree that you cut out all these practices completely as soon as possible. So that this plague may not spread more widely, we command that it be removed throughout all the provinces with the utmost persistence.

## XXXVIII. That Baptism Is to Be Celebrated by Catholics at Easter

(From the letter of Pope Victor written to Bishop Theophilus.)

Our predecessors have already established that the feast of holy Easter must be celebrated on the Lord’s Day, and we command you solemnly to celebrate it on that same day, because it is not fitting for the members to disagree with the head or to undertake contrary practices.

From the fifteenth day of the moon of the first month until the twenty-first day of that same month, this feast is likewise to be celebrated.

At the same time baptism is to be celebrated by Catholics. Nevertheless, if necessity arises or the danger of death threatens, gentiles coming to the faith are to be baptized wherever and whenever the need occurs—whether in a river, in the sea, or in springs—provided only that the confession of Christian belief has been clearly expressed.

They must also pay the greatest attention to what they have promised in baptism, so that they may be found faithful rather than unbelieving.

## XXXIX. That the Cases of Bishops Must Not Be Decided Without Consulting the Roman Pontiff

(From the same letter.)

[Col. 1106D]

The matters which you are to judge have been brought before the apostolic see, and it is not lawful for you to determine them apart from [perhaps: because of] our authority—namely, the cases of bishops. Hence it is clear that, from the time of the apostles onward, it was established and approved that a bishop accused or judged by bishops of his own province in any matter may freely appeal and have recourse to the pontiff of the apostolic see. He is to arrange for the case to be reconsidered either personally or through his vicars; and while the pontiff is conducting a second judgment of his case, no one else is to be placed or ordained in his stead. For although the bishops of the province may investigate the case of the accused pontiff, they are not permitted to determine it without consulting the Roman pontiff.

### XL. How many witnesses there should be for bishops, and that no one is to be judged in his absence

*(From a letter of Pope Zephyrinus written to all those established throughout Sicily.)*

When patriarchs or primates examine an accused bishop, they are not to pronounce a final sentence before, supported by apostolic authority, either the accused himself confesses his guilt or he is convicted by innocent and regularly examined witnesses. These witnesses must not be fewer in number than those disciples whom the Lord ordered to be chosen as assistance to the apostles—that is, seventy-two.

We also remove from episcopal accusation or testimony slanderers, who are to be uprooted by divine authority, and the authors of enmities. Let no one of the highest rank or of lesser rank be attacked or destroyed by accusations; let no certain sentence be pronounced in a doubtful matter; and let no judgment be upheld unless it has been conducted according to proper order.

No one is to be judged in his absence, because both divine and human laws prohibit this. The accuser, moreover, must be entirely free from suspicion, because the Lord wished his pillars to stand firm, not to be shaken by just anyone. No one is to be bound by a sentence not pronounced by his own judge, since the laws of the world likewise command that this be done.

For any accused bishop may, if necessary, choose twelve judges by whom his case is to be judged justly. He is not to be heard or excommunicated before those judges themselves have been chosen, and before he has been regularly summoned—first by an assembly of his own bishops—his case is to be heard justly and discerned reasonably by them. The conclusion of his case, however, is to be brought before the apostolic see, so that it may be settled there; nor is it to be concluded beforehand, as was formerly established by the apostles or their successors, before it has been supported by the authority of that see.

[Col. 1107C]

### XLI. That no bishop stripped of his property is to be summoned to judgment before he has been restored to his own possessions

*(From the same letter, written to the brothers serving the Lord throughout Egypt.)*

For it has been reported to the apostolic see through our representatives that certain of our brothers—namely, bishops—are driven from their churches and proper seats, that their furnishings are taken from them, and that they are then summoned to judgment naked and stripped of everything. This is wholly unreasonable, since the statutes of the apostles and their successors, as well as the commands of emperors and the provisions of the laws, make provision for precisely this matter, and the authority of the apostolic see forbids it.

Therefore it was commanded in the ancient statutes that bishops who had been expelled and stripped of their possessions should recover their own churches, that all their property should first be restored to them, and that only then, if anyone wished to accuse them justly, the judges should determine that the accusers were to do so at equal risk. The bishops were to be men of sound judgment and were to assemble in the church, where the witnesses of each party who appeared to have been oppressed would be present. They were not to be required to answer before all that belonged to them and to their churches had been completely restored to them according to law.

### XLII. On ordinations

*(From the same letter.)*

Conduct the ordinations of presbyters and Levites at the proper time and solemnly, with many people standing present; and appoint to this work men who are worthy and learned, so that through their fellowship and assistance you may rejoice greatly.

### XLIII. On conspiracy against bishops

*(From a letter of Pope Callistus written to all the bishops of the cities of Gaul.)*

We have heard that the crimes of conspiracies are flourishing in your regions, and that the people are conspiring against their bishops. The cunning of this crime is abominable not only among Christians but also among pagans, and it is forbidden by the law of outsiders. Therefore the laws condemn those guilty of this crime—not only ecclesiastical laws but also the laws of the world—and they condemn not only those who conspire but also those who consent to them.

Our predecessors, together with a very large number of bishops—whoever among them are established or exist in the priestly order or among the clergy—commanded that the conspirators fall from the honor they held; they ordered the rest to be deprived of communion and expelled from the Church. This applied not only to those who acted but also to those who consented to them.

### XLIV. Excommunicated persons are not to be admitted to communion

*(From the same letter.)*

No one is to receive those who have been excommunicated by priests before a just examination of both parties. No one is to join them in prayer, food, drink, or a kiss, nor even greet them. For whoever knowingly communicates with excommunicated persons in these or other prohibited matters is, according to the teaching of the apostles, himself to be subjected to a similar excommunication. Therefore both clergy and laity must abstain from those with whom they do not wish to suffer the same fate.

### XLV. Boundaries not to be transgressed

*(From the same letter.)*

No one is to usurp another’s boundaries, nor presume to judge or excommunicate another’s parishioner, because such a judgment or excommunication will neither be valid nor possess any force. No one is bound or condemned by the sentence of any judge except his own. Hence the Lord also says: “You shall not move the ancient boundary markers” (Prov. 22:28).

No primate or metropolitan is to presume to excommunicate or judge the church or parish of a diocesan bishop, or anyone belonging to his parish, or to undertake anything without that bishop’s counsel or judgment. Rather, he must observe what was established by the apostles, the Fathers, and our predecessors and confirmed by us: if any metropolitan bishop, except in matters belonging solely to his own parish, attempts to act in anything outside it without the counsel and consent of all the bishops of his province, he shall be subject to the danger of losing his rank, and what he has done shall be regarded as invalid and void.

But whatever it may be necessary to do or arrange concerning the cases of provincial bishops, their churches, clergy, and secular persons is to be done with the agreement of all the provincial bishops—not with any display of domination, but through the most humble and harmonious administration.

### XLVI. On the fall of a priest

*(From the same letter.)*

But if anyone should fall in any way, let us bear with him and correct him with fraternal affection, as the blessed Apostle says: “If anyone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual must instruct such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. 6:1). “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2).

Moreover, holy David repented of deadly crimes, yet remained in honor. The blessed Peter also shed the bitterest tears when he repented of having denied the Lord, yet he remained an apostle. And through the prophet the Lord promises sinners, saying: “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, I will remember none of all his iniquities” (Ezek. 18:22).

Those who think that priests, after a fall, cannot minister to the Lord if they have performed worthy penance, and cannot enjoy their honors if thereafter they have led a good life and guarded their priesthood worthily, are mistaken. Indeed, those who think this not only err, but also seem to scatter and drive away the keys entrusted to the Church, concerning which it is said: “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 18:18). Otherwise this saying is either not the Lord’s or is not true.

We, however, firmly believe that both the Lord’s priests and the other faithful can, after worthy satisfaction, be restored to their honors. The Lord testifies through the prophet: “Will one who sleeps not add [the effort] to rise, and will one who is turned away not return?” (Ps. 40:9). And elsewhere: “I do not desire,” says the Lord, “the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. 33:11).

The prophet David, doing penance, said: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a princely spirit” (Ps. 51:14). After his penance he himself both taught others and offered sacrifice to God, giving an example to the teachers of the holy Church that, if they have fallen and have performed worthy penance before God, they can do both.

For he taught when he said: “I will teach the wicked your ways, and the impious will turn back to you” (Ps. 51:15). And he offered sacrifice to God when he said: “A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 51:19). Seeing that his own crimes had been cleansed through penance, the Prophet did not hesitate, by preaching and offering to the Lord, to heal the sins of others.

Again, after a little:

For David says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Ps. 32:1). Thus a person is cleansed from sin and rises from his fall by the grace of God, remaining in his former office according to the authorities cited above. Let him beware lest he sin again, and let the evangelical sentence remain in him which says: “Go, and do not sin again” (John 8:11).

Hence the Apostle says: “Therefore, let sin not reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires; nor offer your members as weapons of wickedness to sin, but offer yourselves as those living from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness to God.”

### XLVII. On the possessions of the churches

*(From a letter of Pope Urban written concerning common life and the offerings of the faithful.)*

“The multitude of believers were of one heart and one soul, and none of them said that any of the things he possessed was his own; rather, everything was common among them. With great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord, and great grace was upon them all. For no one among them was needy: all who possessed fields or houses sold them, brought the prices of what they sold, and laid them at the apostles’ feet. They were distributed to each according to his need.

“Joseph, who was surnamed Barnabas by the apostles—which is interpreted ‘son of consolation’—a Levite, a Cypriot by birth, having a field, sold it, brought the price, and laid it at the apostles’ feet,” and so forth (Acts 4:32–33).

When the high priests, the others, the Levites, and the remaining faithful saw that greater benefit could be provided if they handed over to the churches over which bishops presided the inheritances and fields they were selling—for from their revenues more abundant and more excellent provisions could be supplied to the faithful living a common life, both in the present and in the future, than could be supplied from the price of the properties—they began to hand over to the mother churches the estates and fields that they customarily sold, and to live from their revenues.

These possessions belonged, and still belong, to the jurisdiction of the individual parishes of the bishops, who hold the place of the apostles; and they must always belong to them in future times. Through them the bishops and their faithful stewards must provide everything necessary to all who wish to live a common life, as best they can, so that no needy person may be found among them.

These possessions are called the offerings of the faithful, because they are offered to the Lord. Therefore they must not be diverted to uses other than ecclesiastical purposes and the needs of the Christian brothers mentioned above and of the needy, because they are the vows of the faithful and have been handed over to the Lord for the fulfillment of that work.

But if anyone, God forbid, acts otherwise, let him receive the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira and become guilty of sacrilege, as were those who defrauded the prices of the aforementioned possessions.

### XLVIII. Dedicated estates are not to be invaded

*(From the same letter.)*

Everyone must attend to this faithfully, guard it carefully, and drive away the insult of such usurpation, so that estates dedicated to the uses of heavenly mysteries are not harassed by intruders. If anyone does this, then, after the severity of the appropriate punishment that must lawfully be inflicted upon sacrilegious persons, let him be condemned to perpetual disgrace and handed over to the prison of hell, or undergo exile by perpetual deportation, since, according to the Apostle, such a person must be handed over to Satan “so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord” (1 Cor. 5:5).

### XLIX. On the bishop’s seat

*(From the same letter.)*

The fact that elevated seats are found established in the churches of bishops and prepared upon a throne teaches, by its material form, that observation and the power of judging, loosing, and binding have been given to them by the Lord. Hence the Savior says in the Gospel: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven.”

[Note: [Col. 1111A] The remainder is missing, as are the chapters of Bishop Noting which he added to Remedius, according to Goldast’s testimony.]

# [APPENDIX]

[Col. 1111A]

## SOME NOTES ON THE COLLECTIONS OF SMARAGDUS THE ABBOT ON THE EPISTLES AND GOSPELS READ THROUGHOUT THE COURSE OF THE YEAR

[Col. 1111B]

Every attentive reader will easily understand that Smaragdus the abbot’s continuous commentary on the individual Gospel and Epistle readings, now finally reprinted after three centuries and a further five lustra of years, from what is said to be the first edition, has much to commend it.

It displays, above all, the common character of nearly all ecclesiastical writers who flourished from approximately the eighth century onward: a truly pious, humble, and learned disposition, by which, relying less upon themselves, they diligently reworked the writings of the ancient Fathers, extracted their opinions and sayings word for word, and inserted them into their own books or sermons.

Smaragdus himself testifies that he “undertook to gather this one book from many, and from the treatises and published sermons of the great Fathers, as from great rivers and the gulfs of the sea, became at once a channel and an abridger.”

He is especially and distinctively noteworthy because he wished twenty authors—both distinguished and exceedingly rare—to shine before him. From him we learn that he drew from Hilary, Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, Cyprian, Cyril, Gregory, Fulgentius, Chrysostom, Cassiodorus, Eucherius, Isidore, and Bede, all famous on everyone’s lips; then from Tichonius and Primasius, less well known or largely lost; “and to be read with caution,” from Pelagius and Origen; and finally from Victor and Figulus or Frigulus, a man of uncertain name about whom, until now, there has been profound silence among all whom I have known.

Moreover, I would readily suppose that Smaragdus was led to reconstruct this Chain by the same zeal by which at that time Paul Warnefrid, Alcuin, Hrabanus Maurus, and Haymo of Halberstadt eagerly competed and, as it were, conspired with one another. When the liturgy of the Roman Church had recently been introduced throughout Gaul, and when Charles—rightly and deservedly called the Great—was its principal sponsor, he himself, as he testifies in his letter to Paul the Deacon, had encouraged every highly learned man to bring forth and publish to the people homilies of the ancient Fathers by which the individual readings might be illuminated.

They willingly complied with the wishes of so great a prince and served the needs of the Christian people by making public various collections of nearly the same subject. Our own author, however, followed the common and well-trodden path by a route of his own. While others attached complete homilies to each individual reading, he wove a continuous commentary from various sermons or books by different authors.

Finally, another reason has arisen for lingering briefly over Smaragdus’s Commentary: although even in the largest libraries both the single printed edition of this Commentary and a handwritten copy are extremely rare, we found a manuscript of remarkable and sufficiently good quality, now preserved in the Bolognese library. We had once rapidly examined it; then the distinguished and diligent V. D. Haigneré reviewed it for our purposes with great kindness. Since only a few spare hours—and those not entirely free—were granted both to him and to me amid the haste of printing, there was scarcely an opportunity to insert the notes, hastily scraped together here and there, in their proper places.

That manuscript, now Bolognese, was formerly kept in the library of the celebrated abbey of Saint-Bertin at Saint-Omer. I have no doubt that it is the very manuscript of which we read on pages 208–209 of the recently published Chartulary of that abbey:

“Lord John had books of no small value written, whose titles, to commend his diligence, I have not been unwilling briefly to append . . . . . . THE BOOK OF HOMILIES OF THE WHOLE ANNUAL CYCLE, divided into two volumes . . . arranged in full, he left to his successors.”

Our manuscript is indeed divided into two volumes and is written in an eleventh-century script, from the time when John, abbot from 1083 to 1095, presided over the Saint-Bertinian community. The first volume bears the number XXV, the second number XLIII; formerly in the library of Saint-Bertin they carried the numbers 83 and 84. The first also bears this recent title, placed on its spine: *Exposition of the Epistles and Gospels*; the second: *Jerome on Scripture*.

The manuscript is written throughout by the same hand. It is fairly complete, with a few leaves cut out, torn, or [Col. 1113A] damaged here and there by damp and age. There is no title written in the old hand in the first volume of the manuscript. Only in a sixteenth-century hand one reads the following, part of which has been cut away:

“AN EXPOSITION OF SOME EPISTLES AND GOSPELS . . . . . FROM THE VIGIL OF THE LORD’S NATIVITY UNTIL AFTER EASTER.”

[Col. 1113A]

## PREFACES

It should first be noted that in the prefaces there are variant readings and certain additions:

| Printed edition | Manuscript |
|---|---|
| *mavelle* | *malle* |
| — John Chrysostom | — John |
| — Figulus | — Frigulus |
| — *Ut si quis nativa* (“So that if anyone [has] native …”) | — *Ut si quis nociva* (“So that if anyone [has] harmful …”) |
| — *non desinet* (“he will not cease”) | — *non desinat* (“let him not cease”) |
| — *Cujus confortatu sedulo* (“By whose diligent strengthening”) | — *Cujus confortatus edulio* (“Strengthened by whose nourishment”) |

What follows in the printed editions belongs to the *Book of the Comes*—concerning which see the works of Saint Jerome, vol. XI, p. 487, and from that point correct the note of the old editor—but is absent from the Bolognese manuscript.

The verses of Smaragdus are also missing. In their place two other prologues have been inserted there: the first from Cassiodorus on the Psalms; the second excerpted from Jerome on the Epistle to the Romans. Title: “THE PREFACE BEGINS.”

“Why,” it is asked, “did the Apostle wish, after the Gospels, to send these Epistles to the individual churches? Clearly, so that he might fortify the beginnings of the newborn Church when new circumstances arose, cut away present and emerging vices, and exclude future disputes.

“Paul wrote ten Epistles to the universal churches, to show that the New Testament does not differ from the Old. For he arranged his Epistles according to the number of the Decalogue, so that, by as many Epistles as Moses had freed the people from Pharaoh through commandments and signs, he might here teach those acquired from slavery to the devil and idolatry.

“For he sent only four to disciples. In the case of the Romans, the Apostle did not first lay the foundation of faith, as he did among the others, for they had already believed through the preaching of other disciples. They needed only to be strengthened by Paul, as he himself says: ‘For I long to see you, so that I may impart some spiritual gift to you for your strengthening.’”

[Note: [Col. 1113D] Hrabanus Maurus has the same passage, vol. V, p. 170.]

[Col. 1113C]

## THE COLLECTIONS BEGIN

### ON THE VIGIL OF THE LORD’S NATIVITY

Reading from the Epistle of blessed Paul to the Romans.

“‘Epistle,’ in Greek, is called in Latin *supermissa* (‘sent over’). For Greek *epi* means Latin *super* (‘over’), and *stola*, ‘sent.’ Thus there is *epigramma*, that is, ‘over the letter’; *epitaphium*, ‘over the tomb’; and *episcopus*, ‘overseer.’ In the same way epistles are called *supermissae* (‘sent over’), because they are found added over and above the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospels.”

“Romans are interpreted as ‘sublime’ or ‘thundering,’ because of their power and strength.

“Paul.

“Our first question seems to arise concerning Paul’s very name: why is the one who is called Saul in the Acts of the Apostles now called Paul? In the divine Scriptures we find certain names changed, as Abram into Abraham, Jacob into Israel, Simon into Peter. Some, however, used two names: Solomon, who was also called Jedidiah; Zedekiah, who was also called Jehoiachin; Uzziah, who was also called Azariah. Matthew is likewise Levi; and the one whom Matthew writes as Lebbaeus, Mark writes as Thaddaeus.

“According to this custom, therefore, it seems to us that Paul also used two names. As long as he ministered to his own people, he was called Saul, which also seemed more naturally to be the vernacular name of his homeland. He was called Paul, however, when he wrote instructions for Greeks and Gentiles. For the very words of Scripture, ‘Saul, who is also Paul’ (Acts 13), clearly show that the name Paul was not first imposed upon him at that moment, but indicate that it had been his former name.”

[Note: [Col. 1113D] In the printed editions this is attributed to Origen, and rightly so; the printed text, which begins “We have already spoken about Paul” [Col. 1114D], plainly requires our passage. Compare vol. IV, p. 461.]

Then come the materials which, below, where we discuss Victor of Capua, we give first place, whereas in the printed editions they are placed before Origen’s *saying* (ῥῆσις).

It would have been worthwhile, in comparing the manuscript with the work of subsequent editors, first to verify three matters relating to the annual cycle itself, or to the order of the entire book; then to identify distinctly the passages belonging to each author; and especially to examine what is drawn from the rarest authors, Frigulus, Victor, and Pelagius. There is scarcely time for us to identify these three matters individually.

[Col. 1114B]

## I. ON THE ANNUAL CYCLE

### On the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity

A double reading is given: one from the Apostle, Romans 1; the other from Isaiah 62, which seems to reflect the old Gallican rite. Then, without any distinction, there follow the readings now found in the Roman Missal for the first and third Masses, at night and during the day, except that in place of the Epistle to Titus 2, Isaiah 9 is read again. Nothing is found for the Mass at dawn.

We shall pass over the other variants that can be noted in relation to the customary order, which anyone can readily detect, since our concern now is only with the disagreement between our manuscript and the printed text.

At the Octave of the Lord. First Sunday after the Theophany. In Septuagesima. In Sexagesima. In Quinquagesima. First Sunday of the first month. Sunday in the Thirtieth. Sunday in the Twentieth. Monday after the Twentieth. Sunday of indulgence at the Lateran [printed edition: on Palm Sunday]. [Col. 1114D] Easter Monday at Saint Peter’s. Sunday in the Octave [thus in what follows] of Easter, and so forth.

The first volume of our manuscript ends with the Greater Litany; the second begins with the Ascension, under this heading in the first hand:

“Here begins the text of the second book, on the Ascension of the Lord.”

Then:

Sunday after the Ascension of the Lord. Sunday at Pentecost. After the seventh Sunday [in the printed edition, after the sixth]. On the vigil of Saint John the Baptist. On the feast of Saint John. [Col. 1115A] On the vigil of Saint Peter. Eighth Sunday after Pentecost.

On the feast of the holy archangel, after the Gospel of the first week before the Lord’s Nativity has been expounded, the manuscript has, as does the printed edition:

“Thus far, with Christ’s help, the expositions of all the Sundays and of many festivals, proceeding in order through the suitable readings, have successfully completed the year. From this point we have set down the expositions of the readings for the feasts of the holy martyrs, virgins, and confessors. On the feast of the apostles—”

[Col. 1115A]

## II. ON THE PASSAGES OF VARIOUS AUTHORS

It would be of the greatest value to examine carefully and at leisure all the authors cited in that Commentary and to identify every passage individually. Since we earnestly ask that others undertake this more freely, it will be enough for us to point out the way and place signs as guides for the journey, by which the hidden names of the individual authors may be recognized, and to describe in a word or two the beginnings of the passages as they appear in the Bolognese manuscript.
