## III. ON SOME LESS FAMILIAR AUTHORS CITED IN SMARAGDUS’S COLLECTION

Anyone who pays attention will discover that none of the authors whom Smaragdus attached to his Chain is to be neglected. In collections of this kind from the ninth century, manuscripts certainly very ancient are represented, manuscripts not copied carelessly but, as many reliable testimonies elsewhere establish, diligently sought out, carefully collated, accurately corrected, and—by order of Charlemagne and under the instruction, through both words and his famous example, of Alcuin, who acted as Cassiodorus’s successor in Gaul—faithfully reproduced.

The notes that would have to be added in passing would grow immensely if we undertook to compare the four manuscripts of Smaragdus—namely, the three Ulrich manuscripts and the one Bolognese manuscript—with the various editions of the individual Fathers.

The twenty authors whom our author named in the preface and then distinguished by their respective sigla, as shown above, would not be the only ones to come under examination. Other authors, excerpted here and there either in strict or in flowing speech, would also require the same care. Among these—though I may perhaps not name them all—are an old chronographer, perhaps African; the author of the *Concordance*, whom I would gladly identify as Smaragdus; one called Juvencus, a name exceedingly rare there and otherwise wholly unknown; Canorius, p. 72; Sedulius, pp. 140 and 188; Arator, incorrectly printed in the edition as *orator*, p. 355 and again p. 390; Josephus, p. 389; Neoteric, a Greek interpreter, p. 451; and an anonymous poet, p. 546, etc.

We have scarcely one task left to attempt: namely, to touch briefly, from the printed text and the Bolognese manuscript, upon the principal rarer authors cited by Smaragdus.

## § I. FRIGULUS
Whom Ulrichius made out to be Figulus—whether from his own manuscripts or through carelessness is unclear—the Bologna codex clearly and distinctly identifies as Frigulus; no one, so far as I know, before or after Smaragdus has mentioned him even in the slightest record. Nor was he known only to our author; rather, in the printed text itself, with the sigla omitted or altered, he has disappeared so completely that he seems once more to have been submerged beneath the waters, and now to be recoverable only from the manuscripts. If you should perhaps fish him out with the aid of the sigla, you will encounter no small difficulty in recognizing him, for two reasons: first, because his name, on account of the nearly similar initial letters, was readily confused with the name of PRIMASIUS; and second, because whenever the Bologna codex regularly reads *Figulus*, the printed text—perhaps with the support of the Ulrichian manuscripts—writes *Fulgentius*. Yet, apart from the fact that Primasius is so polished and Fulgentius so distinguished that there should scarcely be any danger of confusing either of them with the more recent, uncouth, rough, excerptive author Frigulus—if I am not mistaken—there are other considerations. On the one hand, only a few writings of Primasius survive, and these differ entirely from ours; on the other, Fulgentius’ works are wholly concerned with dogmatic matters and become exegetical only *ἐν παράδῳ*, “in passing.” This Frigulus, however, is much occupied with elucidating the wording of particular passages; he readily investigates etymologies and pursues various origins of things, scraping together material from every direction. He closely resembles the Irish or Gallic compilers who, around the time of Charlemagne, were accustomed to plunder the ancients. Be that as it may, I thought it worthwhile to select, by way of example, a few passages and reproduce them according to the authority of the Bologna codex—passages sufficient to ensure that the character and period of that author will not remain entirely obscure.

**FRI.**

**I. “Now the generation of Christ was as follows.”** Why did he say not “of Jesus Christ,” but only “of Christ”—that is, why did he place not both names but only one? As this is handed down by the elders, he reserved it for the history that follows immediately, when the angel says: “And you shall call his name Jesus,” and so forth. Since the evangelist foresaw that he would soon write how he was called, he ought not to anticipate and forestall it. “Generation” may mean Christ himself, generated in the flesh, so that “the generation of Christ” is equivalent to saying “the generation which is Christ”; or, as some read it, the order of the words may be: “Now Christ’s generation was as follows”—that is, “this genealogy pertains in this way to Christ.”

**FRI.**

**II. “Behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph, saying: Arise and take the Child and his Mother.”**

He does not say “your Child,” nor “the woman’s,” but by a special privilege the name of the Child alone is used.

**FRI.**

**III. “Now in the evening of the sabbath, which dawns toward the first day of the sabbath, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb.”**

[Col. 1120A]

[Note: [Col. 1119D] The manuscripts of Ulrichius add: “from Augustine,” who is explicitly cited below; but Frigulus drew his material from various authors.]

“Now in the evening of the sabbath.” The fact that different times of the women’s visit are described in the Gospels is not a sign of falsehood but an indication of their diligent visitation. “Which dawns toward the first day of the sabbath.” By “the first part of the night,” which is evening, he wished to signify the whole night; at the end of that night the women came. Why, then, does he call the night “evening”? Because in the evening it was permitted to bring spices, once the sabbath had passed. It is as though he said: “They came during the night that follows the sabbath,” at which time they were free to come; or, “in the evening of the sabbath,” not as the day was becoming evening, but as the night was becoming evening—that is, they came at the end of the night. From the beginning of the world, day preceded night up to the passion of Christ. From the passion of Christ onward, night precedes day.

Or it should be read in this way: “in the evening of the sabbath”—that is, at dawn, which shines at the beginning of the night, remaining throughout the night and growing bright in the morning. Perhaps, therefore, these women remained there from the beginning of the night until morning. But Mark says: “And very early,” and so forth. It appears, however, that the Lord rose at the hour of morning, since, according to Augustine, he is described as having been in the tomb for forty hours: four hours remaining of the day on which he was crucified, twelve hours of the sabbath night, twelve hours of the sabbath day, and twelve hours of the night of the Lord’s Day. Thus he lay in the tomb for forty hours; and for this reason he manifested himself frequently to his apostles for forty days after the resurrection.

With regard to the word “evening,” many hold different opinions. For in the Greek Gospel it is written:

> ὀψὲ δὲ σαββάτων τῇ ἐπιφωσκούσῃ εἰς μίαν σαββάτων

that is: “In the evening of the sabbath, which dawns toward the first of the sabbaths.” Here *ὀψὲ* appears, which is a feminine noun, and *τῇ*, which is a feminine pronoun. Hence some maintain that *vesper* (“evening”) is a common noun, belonging to both masculine and feminine gender, whose ablative is *vespere* [some maintain that one should say *vespera*, not *vesperae*, making it feminine]. Others read the passage more subtly in this way: “Mary came on the first day of the sabbath, which dawns in the evening of the sabbath.” Others understand it as though *sabbatum* means “rest”: “in the evening of rest, which dawns toward the first day,” and so forth. “The first”: Sunday is called the first day, because it was worthy to see the Lord rise, and through Christ the world be born and restored.

**IV. “Then the devil took him into the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him: If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.”** The devil’s voice always wants everyone to fall downward.

He means Jerusalem by “the holy city.” The pinnacle of the temple, therefore, was the seat of the teachers, a platform in the middle of the temple; and thus it is evident that the devil lies in wait even in holy places. But a question arises: how are the temptations said to have taken place in the desert, when this one is attested to have occurred both in the holy city and above the pinnacle of the temple? Some say that the other temptations took place in the wilderness and this one in Jerusalem; others say that this one too took place in the wilderness, but was shown only in the mind.

**FI.**

**V. “Gehenna” is a compound name formed from GE and HENNA.** *Ge* means “valley”; *gehenna*, however, means “gratuitous valley.” For it was the Valley of the Sons of Edom, near Jerusalem, in which many corpses of the dead lay; hence the name *gehenna* is appropriately applied to hell.

**FRI.**

**VI. “In which a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water.”**

That is, four men—Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth—and their four wives: Puerfara, Parfia, Catafluia, and Fluia.

**FI.**

**VII. “But I say to you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.”**

“In all his glory”—that is, in every variety of clothing and luxury, or in the greatness of his kingdom. “Like one of these”: “lilies” is understood.

[Col. 1121A]

**VIII. “Now as Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee.”**

This sea is called by many names because of the surrounding lands: the Sea of Galilee, Lake Chinnereth, the Lake of Gennesaret, the Sea of Tiberias, the Salt Lake, and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 1121D] In the printed edition, “from Eucherius” is prefixed.]

**IX. “He saw two brothers, Simon who is called Peter,”** and so forth. Why are they called fishermen? So that no one might think that the word of God spread more widely through the eloquence of preachers. It is not the sons of kings, nor the scribes, who are first recorded as having been called, but fishermen.

“Fishermen”—[Note: [Col. 1121D] Ibid., from Jerome.]—and uneducated men are sent to preach, so that the faith of believers might not be thought to arise from eloquence or learning, rather than from the power of God.

“Two by two”—[Note: [Col. 1121D] Our codex again identifies Frigulus in the margin; Ulrichius replaced him with “from Fulgentius.”]—they are called and sent two by two, appropriately. For Scripture says: “Woe to one alone, because when he falls he has no one to lift him up.” There is, indeed, a twofold teaching: love of God and love of neighbor. Filled with this, they preach the good Testament—that is, the Law and the Gospel.

**X. “And proceeding from there,”** and so forth.

At first, a person casts the nets of his desire into the sea of this age, in order to catch, like fish, dead works. But when Christ comes mercifully, he changes the former instruments through compunction of heart, so that, casting once more the net of good desire into the sea of the age, he may bring fish of good virtues in the ship of the flesh to the harbor of life, leaving behind the devil as a fugitive—for this is how *Zebedaeus* is interpreted.

The names of the four apostles signify two peoples. Simon means “obedient,” while Peter means “recognizing”; he signifies the Jewish people, who first obeyed the Lord’s commands and recognized their Creator. James, whose name means “supplanter,” signifies the same. Andrew means “manly”; he signifies the people of the nations, who act manfully in the faith of Christ. The same is signified by John, whose name means “the grace of the Lord,” for the nations have been saved by the grace of God.

These four names are also contained in the conduct of every individual: Simon, by obeying God; Peter, by recognizing his own sin; Andrew, by manfully enduring labors; Jacob, by supplanting the vices of the flesh; John, by receiving the grace of God. Or these four names should be understood as referring to the four principal virtues. A person is obedient when he possesses prudence in recognizing his sins. He is manly when he has acquired temperance for enduring toil. He is a supplanter when he has received fortitude for overcoming vices. He is the grace of God when he has found true justice in fulfilling the commandments.

**XI. “The Magi”**—[Note: [Col. 1121D] A little farther below our codex inserted the name Frigulus, where others do so. Since the preceding material seems to require this, I think the entire passage we present was collected by Frigulus from Victor, Jerome, Juvencus, and Gregory.]—who went to worship the Lord, are thought by some to have been descendants of Balaam, learned in astronomical science. They say that the star was not one of the recognized constellations, since it did not move in the same celestial order as the others. It was borne along by its own motion to point out the place where the Lord had been born.

Others say that they were grandsons of Balaam, sons of Beor, because they followed his sect.

Others say that they were Persians, as Canorius says in verse:

[Col. 1121D]

> Then he orders the Persians also to hasten their swift advance.

[Note: [Col. 1122D] Compare Juvencus, *Historia Evangelica*. The same verse appears somewhat differently in the printed edition, and the variation in reading is certainly noteworthy:
>
> “Then Herod orders the Persians to continue their journey.”]

Jerome says: The Chaldeans affirmed that the stars were gods; hence the name of their god indicates the true God. They are therefore thought to have been Chaldeans, since it says: “We saw his star in the east”—that is, being situated in the east, or from the east toward the west, we saw the star arise.

Having laid the foundations of the historical account, let us contemplate its spiritual meaning. Bethlehem, which means “house of bread,” signifies the Church, or the human heart, in which Christ—who said, “I am the living bread”—is born. Herod, whose name means “leathern” or “skin of glory,” signifies the devil reigning in the world.

The three Magi signify the human race together with physics, ethics, and logic. Physics means natural philosophy; ethics means moral philosophy, for the Greeks call customs *ἔθεα*; logic means rational philosophy, for “reason” is called *λόγος* in Greek. The Magi, who question the priests, signify the Church of the nations; the priests signify the Law or the Synagogue.

[Note: [Col. 1122D] The printed editions prefix Gregory as the author of this passage.]

One must ask why, when the Redeemer was born, an angel appeared to the shepherds, whereas a star—not an angel—led the Magi to worship him. Clearly, since the Jews used reason, a rational creature, namely an angel, ought to preach to them. Because the Gentiles did not know how to use reason, they were led to know the Lord not by a voice but by signs. Prophecy was given to the Jews as believers, signs to the Gentiles as unbelievers.

## § II. SAINT VICTOR OF CAPUA

The name of Saint Victor, bishop of Capua, lies almost as unknown in literary history as that of Frigulus, although he is much more deserving of being remembered with a better reputation. I hope that the materials we are soon to publish in the first volume of the *Spicilegium Solesmense* will contribute substantially to restoring him to new light. They include:

1. Quite extensive fragments from his *Scholia on the Pentateuch*, extracted from the now-lost writings of the very ancient authors Saint Polycarp, Origen, Severus of Gabalas, Diodore of Tarsus, and others;

2. A notable fragment from his book *Reticulum*, or *On Noah’s Ark*;

3. A clear confirmation of the authority of fragments excerpted by Victor of Capua from the same Saint Polycarp’s *Book of Responses*, printed above in volume LXVIII of the *Patrologia*;

4. Finally, a Latin translation of the *Evangelical Harmonies* of Ammonius of Alexandria, inserted in the same work, p. 251.

5. If to these one adds what is found in various ninth-century collections—those of Smaragdus, Hrabanus, and others—the works of Saint Victor of Capua can easily grow into a volume of substantial size.

Therefore, in order that fuller knowledge might be had of that distinguished and learned author, we thought it appropriate to append what Ughellius reports about him in *Italia Sacra*:

> “Saint Victor, after Saint Germanus had been taken from human affairs, was elevated to the episcopal throne in the year of salvation 541, at the beginning of February. He sat in the episcopal office most holily for thirteen years and thirty-eight days. He died in the year 554, at the beginning of April, on the second day. He is commemorated in the Roman Martyrology on 17 October; Bede calls him a most holy and learned man in *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 49. For he refuted the Paschal cycle of Victorius, or Victorinus of Aquitaine, as Bede himself testifies. His cycle was received and approved at the Fourth Synod of Orléans, canons 1 and 2. Victor’s preface to the *Harmony of the Gospels* of Ammonius of Alexandria is extant. Ado also mentions him in his *Chronicles* under the year of salvation 527; Marianus Scotus under the year 560; Trithemius writes that he lived in the year 580; and Sigebert, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 20, testifies that he wrote at the command of Pope Honorius.

> “All of these are thought to be in error because of an ancient epitaph which the Monk says still existed in the house of Quintus Johannes Hieronymus of Capua, near the seat called Antimario. A stone pavement there bore the following epitaph, engraved within a carved crown:

> **VICTOR, BISHOP. HE SAT THIRTEEN YEARS AND THIRTY-EIGHT DAYS. HE WAS DEPOSITED ON THE THIRD DAY BEFORE THE NONES OF APRIL, IN THE THIRTEENTH YEAR AFTER THE CONSULSHIP OF BASILIUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, IN THE SECOND INDICTION.**

> “The thirteenth year after the consulship of Basilius is certainly the year of Christ 554, coinciding with the second indiction. Therefore, since he died at the beginning of April after sitting for thirteen years and thirty-eight days, he had already been raised to the chair in February of the year 541. Hence those who extend Victor’s dates to the years 560 and 580 are convicted of error. Those who place him in the year 527 should be understood as indicating that from that time Victor’s name, as that of a most holy and learned man, began to be celebrated, although he was not yet bishop.

> “But someone may say: the epitaph and the Roman Martyrology do not agree. In the one, his deposition is recorded on the fourth day before the Nones of April; in the other, his feast is commemorated on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November. This presents the slightest difficulty, since such differences commonly occur in the Martyrology, and not without reason. In establishing the feasts of the saints, people customarily consider not only death and deposition, but also discovery, translation, reinterment, the commemoration of some suffering endured or miracle performed, as well as conversion, ordination, canonization (Baronius, volume IX, year 804, no. 11), and other matters of that kind. Therefore there could not fail to be some legitimate reason why the feast of Saint Victor was established on 17 October, although he was deposited on 2 April.

> “The same Monk further adds concerning Victor’s epitaph: ‘I shall not omit that the epitaph of Saint Victor counts years and days exceeding thirty, which is not in keeping with ancient custom. In ancient epitaphs, years, months, and days are distinctly recorded when the days exceed two months; but if there is only one month, it is permitted either to count thirty days while leaving the month unmentioned, or to record the remaining days in the final month.’ He cites two inscriptions from Capaccio; we have observed many others in the *Book of Epigrams of the City*, including one that stood in the house of the very learned Pomponius Laetus:

> **TO THE DEPARTED SPIRITS. THE PARENTS MADE THIS FOR SECUNDUS, THEIR DESERVING SON. HE LIVED ONE YEAR AND FORTY-SEVEN DAYS.**

> “Moreover, Vincentius Verax writes in the *History of the Monastery of Montevergine* that the sacred relics of Victor were found, together with those of other saints, beneath the high altar of the church of that monastery in the year 1480, on 27 July; there they are honored annually, although the Capuan Breviary contains no commemoration of Victor.”

In publishing Smaragdus’ chain, Ulrichius treated Victor no less unjustly than Frigulus. After initially designating him by a distinct name, he thereafter and consistently wrote, absurdly, *ex Vulg.* in place of Victor. Whether this indicates the common version of Sacred Scripture, or the ordinary or common gloss, is entirely unknown. Therefore, just as we have acted in the case of Frigulus, we shall here give selected passages of Victor, in order to begin rather than conclude his defense.

**I. Victor, bishop of Capua, says:** Paul. “He who had previously been called Saul the persecutor, after hearing a voice from heaven, ceased from his purpose of persecution and was thereafter called Paul, *ἀπὸ τῆς παύλης*”—that is, “from cessation.”

[Note: [Col. 1123D] Compare Pertz, *Scriptores*, VI, pp. 24, 141, 315.]

**VI.**

**II.** [Note: [Col. 1123D] In the printed editions, incorrectly: “Vulg.”] Why is Jacob not rather named as the son, while David is said to be the son, with many ancestors left out in between, unless it was to declare the royal origin from which Christ’s birth was foretold to come?

**VIC.**

**III.** By a divine gift, having first received the power of adoption, they afterward attained the status of being worthy to be sons of God.

**UI.**

**IV. “He is not puffed up.”** This mode of expression must be carefully considered. For charity itself cannot, in its own nature, either be jealous or be puffed up; rather, every person who becomes a participant in that same charity is not puffed up and is not jealous, being truly enriched by the gift of charity. The Apostle uses the same mode of expression elsewhere when he says: “He who knew no sin, for our sake he made sin” (2 Cor. 5:21), “so that we might become the righteousness of God in him.” We are not made righteousness by believing, but become participants in righteousness—that is, we are found righteous through faith in Christ. By “sin” he means a sacrifice for sin, as Isaiah says: “They shall eat the sins of my people”—that is, things offered as a sacrifice for sin.

**VI.**

**V. “The tempter seeks to recognize what he did not deserve to know.”** His venerable birth was then scarcely known to a few, to whom he himself nevertheless deigned to reveal it. But the prince of this age [remained ignorant of] these three mysteries: virginity, childbirth, and the passion.

[Note: [Col. 1124D] The codex has *principi*; immediately afterward *deest*, “is missing”: “remained hidden.”]

**VI.** The veil of the temple is torn, so that what had been honorably hidden might become common and worthless because of such a crime; and, as Josephus reports, voices of the heavenly powers wishing to depart from the temple are said to have been heard. At the resurrection of the Lord, however, the faithful see no signs of terror but every indication of joy. Angels gleaming in white garments; people run joyfully to the tomb, where they would find not a dead man but recognize that death had been conquered; the women are addressed in a peaceful voice. What more shall I say? All the mysteries of eternal salvation are revealed.

It should also be noted that the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour—that is, when the sun was about to withdraw from the center of the world—when he also said to the thief: “Today you will be with me in paradise.” For it is written concerning Adam when he sinned that he heard the voice of the Lord God after midday (Gen. 3:8).

**VII.** Love (*dilectio*) retains a greater degree than affection (*amor*). Therefore, when the Lord said, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” Peter did not dare to confess that he possessed the measure of *dilectio*, but humbly professed that he loved (*amare*) him. For the higher love is preferred to affection. Finally, when the Lord questioned Peter a third time, because he did not say, as in the previous two instances, “Do you love me?” but “Do you have affection for me?”, Peter was saddened. Why did he not say in the third question, “Do you love me?” but “Do you have affection for me?” It was as though he was no longer being asked about the higher order of *dilectio*, but about the lower grace of *amor*.

**UI.**

**VIII. “And he gave him the name,”** and so forth. How did he receive this so that he might be worshiped—the giver of all heavenly gifts, whom we know, through divine testimonies, to have been worshiped not only by patriarchs and prophets but also by angels and powers, cherubim [and seraphim]?

[Note: [Col. 1125D] The words in brackets are absent from the codex.]

Or how is he said to have been exalted, when he is said rather to have been humbled through the flesh he assumed? Yet if you consider that the Word became flesh, you will not be surprised that he is reported as exalted or as having received a name worthy of proclamation. In him human nature is understood to have been exalted. You, O man, through his assumption of flesh, obtained the dignity of the name. For these things are said of him from the moment when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

**VIC.**

**IX.** John’s account is not contrary when he reports that Mary Magdalene came to the tomb at dawn, while Matthew says that in the evening of the sabbath Mary Magdalene came with the other Mary to the Lord’s tomb. For Matthew uses “evening” to mean lateness and delay, as though he said: “At the late hour of the night.” We say that something happens late whenever many hours have passed beyond the appointed time; and because a large part of the night had already elapsed when the Lord rose, Matthew calls it “evening”—that is, late or delayed. John signifies the same by saying “at dawn,” although it was still dark; thus the hour may be understood as near the morning.

“Because of fear of him the guards were terrified and became like dead men; and the angel answering said to the women: Do not fear them” [Note: [Col. 1125D] The codex has “you”]. The guards, terrified with fear and stunned like the dead, lie there; yet the angel consoles not them but the women: “Do not fear them.” Let them, he says, be afraid. Let terror remain in those in whom unbelief remains. But you, because you seek Jesus who was crucified, hear that he has risen and fulfilled his promises. Come and see where the Lord was laid. If you do not believe my words, believe the empty tomb; then go quickly and announce to his disciples that he has risen and will go before you into Galilee—that is, into the rolling ground of the Gentiles, where error was formerly slippery and they could not place their feet with a firm and steady step.

“They went out quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, running to announce it to his disciples.”

A twofold emotion held the minds of the women: fear and joy—the one arising from the greatness of the miracle, the other from the desire for the risen Lord. Yet each emotion quickened their feminine steps. They went to the apostles so that through them the seed of faith might be scattered (sic).

**VI.**

**X.** He says: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth.” Here there is the tetragrammaton, which the Hebrews teach to designate the ineffable name of God; yet elsewhere in Scripture we read: “They will call upon me, and I will not answer them.” The statement now placed here without qualification—“Whoever calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved”—must be understood as referring to a sincere invocation: one expressed with humility of heart, in which God is invoked with confession of the true doctrine.

More is added below under the same sigla, which you may see above, cols. 505 and 506, A and B. It would be tedious to copy it out again, and I would not dare to ascribe it to Victor with sufficient confidence.

**UI.**

**XI.** To loosen a sandal is to uncover the limbs covered by it. Who could most clearly explain the naked word—that is, the word of divine discourse—by contemplation, unless perhaps by explaining it through certain images? This is what he says: “I am not worthy”—that is, “I am not sufficient to reveal fully all the mysteries of Christ after removing the veil of words.”

## § III. PELAGIUS

We have now come to a name more famous than the preceding ones and to a case as complicated as any that has ever arisen—a truly difficult question requiring examination. For both in the preface and throughout the work, whether in the printed editions or in our codex, it is expressly asserted that Pelagius is brought forward there together with his writings, which must indeed be read cautiously but are genuine. Almost nothing of him survives, however, apart from a few passages inserted into Augustinian refutations and a certain *Breviarium* on the fourteen Epistles of the Apostle.

That abbreviated Commentary, diligently purged and cut down in many places by Cassiodorus, departed so far from Pelagius that for many centuries of the Christian era it lay hidden under the false name of Jerome. The opinion did become established that the work of the British heresiarch remained for a long time in Gaul; indeed, in the seventeenth century, if some are to be believed, it was said to have been concealed in the library of the monastery of Corbie and to have perished after being secretly stolen through the fraud of certain persons.

I do not know anyone who spoke more confidently than the abbot of Saint-Michel, who said that he had possessed the work, extracted passages from it, and transferred them to his own use. It is therefore especially important, if other manuscripts should appear, to compare them with the printed text above and with the sigla of the Saint-Bertin codex just described, so that it may safely be determined what can rightly be ascribed to him.

To bring these notes to an end, I intend to review a few passages once more in such a way that anyone may see at a glance which readings in the printed Pelagian text agree with ours—those distinguished, as they say, in italic type—and which disagree with it, marked by Roman letters. The latter generally display a much fuller and richer text, which someone may suspect to be the original, not yet reviewed and abbreviated by Cassiodorus. We have thought it absolutely necessary to declare, however, that throughout this entire chain Pelagius and Primasius are so indiscriminately interwoven in the same passages, with one substituted for, named as, and confused with the other, that until further manuscripts bring light into such darkness, we must despair of safely separating the passages belonging to each.

**PELG.**

**1. “But in everything let us present ourselves.”** He who summons the desire to virtue himself mercifully supplies us with virtue; and if we desire it, we are assisted by the one who commands that it be cultivated.

**“As ministers of God.”** Ministers of God ought to minister to God in everything [Note: [Col. 1126D] The printed edition has “imitate”], and by their works be recognized as worshipers of the true God. Just as he allows himself to be blasphemed by evil people and, in the present life, does not withhold his benefits even from the ungrateful, so we must not be overcome by evil but overcome evil with good.

**“In great patience.”** Not in little or moderate patience, but in great patience.

**“In tribulations.”** Every injury is called a tribulation.

**“In necessities.”** That is, let us endure everything that is necessary in the manner in which it must be endured.

**“In distresses.”** Distress is every form of want.

**“In blows, in prisons.”** This urges us to endure, if necessary for Christ, what he too endured when the people and the magistrates gathered against him and, after inflicting many blows with rods, sent him into prison.

**“In seditions, in labors, in watchings.”** Here he describes not insignificant elements of patience. In exercises of labor, there must be no less watchfulness of the mind than of the body.

**“In chastity, in knowledge.”** Just as bodily chastity is necessary for us, so is chastity of mind. That is true chastity which is polluted neither in mind nor in deed, and which, because of the merit of purity, also grants us knowledge. It should be noted that knowledge is a species of virtue [Note: [Col. 1127D] The printed edition has “virtues”], provided that a person is instructed by it and not puffed up.

**“In long-suffering.”** That is, in prolonged endurance. Long-suffering is the courage of the mind in enduring adversities.

**“In gentleness.”** Gentleness exists when we generate bitterness in no one through our words and fulfill the statement of the same Apostle: “Let all bitterness, and anger, and blasphemy be taken away from you, with all malice.” And let us say that testimony of Wisdom: “His jaws are sweetness, and [he is] the object of every desire.”

**“In the Holy Spirit.”** That is, possessing these things, let us make ourselves worthy of his dwelling through sincerity of heart [Note: [Col. 1127D] The printed edition has: “while preparing ourselves as a dwelling worthy of him.”]

**“In unfeigned charity.”** Charity is unfeigned when we do for others everything that we want done for ourselves. As the Apostle John says: “Let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth.” Charity is also unfeigned when we correct offenses and faults in our brothers with a kindly disposition.

**2. “Through glory and dishonor.”** That is, through the glory of virtues and the dishonor of scourges, contempt, and prisons [Note: [Col. 1127D] The printed edition has “prison”].

**“Through evil report and good report.”** Let us receive all these things equally with patience [Note: [Col. 1127D] The printed edition has “let us endure”]. Let neither those who praise us exalt us nor those who slander us cast us down. For it is sometimes necessary that both groups lie [Note: [Col. 1127D] The printed edition has “both sides”]. But, returning to our conscience [Note: [Col. 1128D] The printed edition has “looking back”], we ought not to believe others about our good qualities more than we believe ourselves [Note: [Col. 1128D] The printed edition has “to place greater confidence in others”].

**“As deceivers and truthful.”** Why “deceivers”? Because they teach a person to despise what he possesses and hope for what he does not possess; to pass by what is set before the eyes with turned-away and closed senses; and to pursue what is removed from sight with insatiable desires. By saying “deceivers and truthful,” he explained evil report and good report, because some called them deceivers, while others called them not only truthful but, on account of their virtuous works, gods. It is therefore no wonder that the apostles were called deceivers, since concerning the Lord himself some said, “He is good,” while others said, “No, but he deceives the crowd” (John 7).

**“As unknown and known.”** Unknown to the faithless and ungrateful; known to the faithful and righteous.

**“As dying, and behold, we live.”** This means reaching the point of despair concerning life [Note: [Col. 1128D] The printed edition has “to death”], as when Paul was thought to have died after being stoned, yet rose and taught at Lystra (Acts 13).

**“As chastised and not killed.”** As we read: “The Lord has chastised me severely, but he has not handed me over to death” (Ps. 117). We speak of chastising both with words and with blows, as Pilate says concerning the Lord: “Having chastised him, I will release him”—that is, having scourged him with blows.

**“As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing.”** Sorrowful in the severity of their appearance, but rejoicing in heart even amid tribulations [Note: [Col. 1128D] The printed edition has “tribulation”], in expectation of recompense. For it is written: “Your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John 16).

**The holy Lord’s Day at Easter.**

**3. “Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump.”** That is, let nothing remain in you of the corruption of the former nature; but be sincere, with the brightness of grace and the radiance of righteousness.

**“As you are unleavened.”** That is, made unleavened through baptism, which Christ granted us through his passion, being sacrificed not now in the form of a lamb but in the reality of his body. Therefore leave nothing of your former way of life in yourselves that could corrupt the sincerity of your nature.

**“For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.”** It is as though he said: Christ is not sacrificed for us symbolically as the lamb was for the Jews, but in reality he is slain for us every day, and we celebrate Passover every day if we have no leaven of malice and wickedness. The Jews ate unleavened bread for seven days; and because the world was made in seven days, which continually turns in its ordered course [Note: [Col. 1128D] The Bologna codex has *revolvuntur*; the printed edition incorrectly has *revolvit*. Primasius also has the passage, although his editor left it unresolved, saying: “The passage suffers from an incurable defect.” Here you now have a clear reading from our manuscripts], we simply celebrate Passover if during these days we conduct ourselves purely and sincerely. For what else is leaven than the corruption of nature, which, having first departed from its natural sweetness, has been corrupted by adulterous sourness?

**“Therefore let us feast.”** That is, let us who continually abstain from the leaven of malice and wickedness celebrate the solemnities of salvation through acts of salvation, and let us be filled inwardly with the unleavened bread of simplicity and truth.

**I Corinthians, chapter XII.**

**4. “Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says,”** and so forth. Whoever anathematizes—that is, whoever rejects the Lord Jesus with a certain detestation—does not have the Holy Spirit. Whoever believes in the Lord Jesus has the Holy Spirit. Since we read, “Whoever does not have the Son does not have the Father,” we can recognize from this testimony that whoever does not believe in Christ must not be thought to have the Holy Spirit either, as we read in Romans: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his” (Rom. 8). How, then, does the Lord not know the workers of iniquity, even if they have performed miracles, and how is God denied through evil works?

And no one can say, “Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit. That is, someone who does not believe fully in the Holy Spirit confesses the Lord Jesus without cause, or confesses him in words without cause while denying him by his deeds. He teaches the Corinthians that unless they said “Lord Jesus” in the Holy Spirit—that is, while living in good works—it could not otherwise benefit them.

“There are divisions of graces,” etc. That is, not only the gift of tongues but also various kinds of charisms are distributed by the Lord. Here he wishes to show that the graces of the Holy Spirit are divided, not the Spirit himself.

[Col. 1129A]

“And there are divisions of ministries,” etc. In what follows he recalls that ecclesiastical ministries are [distributed], ordered by the Holy Spirit—that is, by God’s arrangement—saying: “Some indeed he placed in the Church, first apostles, then prophets,” etc. For by saying, “but the same Spirit,” and “but the same God,” he shows that he is speaking entirely about the divinity of the Holy Spirit.

“And there are divisions of operations.” That is, the different powers by which various works were performed. In other words, it is the same Spirit who works all these things in everyone—that is, in the faithful and believers.

“To each is given the manifestation,” etc. The manifestation of the Spirit means that it may be made manifest that a person has received the Holy Spirit for the benefit and salvation of many. For they are enriched with the gifts of grace not only for their own sake but for the sake of the faithful; or for the benefit of unbelievers, so that they may believe, and of believers, so that they may be strengthened. Or “the manifestation of the Spirit” means that, through spiritual teaching, he makes each person’s conscience manifest [Col. 1129B], as he says below: through prophetic correction, the hidden things of his heart are made manifest. Or it means that, enlightened by the Spirit, the human mind recognizes things through spiritual discernment.

“To one, indeed, through the Holy Spirit, is given a word of wisdom.” That is, so that he may be able to discuss and teach wisely, suitably, and rationally what he has received through the inspiration of grace.

“To another, a word of knowledge.” Knowledge consists in opening up mysteries, or in knowing and recounting past events, or in proclaiming what is to come at the judgment.

Thus, from this point onward, the same author—apparently Pelagius—continues to the end of the Epistle, as it appears in the printed editions, with a few variants.

## I Corinthians, chapter XVI

### 5. “For I make known to you the Gospel,” etc.

Here, setting aside the order of preaching, he turned to the teaching of the resurrection, since some of the Corinthians were doubting the resurrection.

“Which you received.” That is, which you have received; and he says this so that they would not appear not to have believed it.

“In which also you stand.” That is, persevering in good works; through whose teaching you stand [firm] for heavenly things [Note: [Col. 1129D] Edition: “you have been raised up.”].

“Through which also you are saved.” That is, through whose teaching you hope for the salvation both of souls and from various illnesses [Note: [Col. 1129D] Same place: “you are saved.”] of bodies, because without faith in the resurrection the hope of salvation utterly perishes.

“By what reasoning I preached to you.” [As if he said:] The whole rationale of our preaching is this: that you should believe in the resurrection, which is the reward [Note: [Col. 1129D] Same place: “the first thing.”] of all who have believed in Christ [Note: [Col. 1130D] Same place: “serve Christ.”]. Otherwise, all the labor of fasts and of all the tribulations that you endure for Christ in this life is futile.

“If you hold fast, unless you believed in vain.” That is, unless you have forgotten, or certainly unless you do not hope for the reward of your faith or labor in rising again, you believe in vain.

[Col. 1129D]

“For I delivered to you first of all.” That is, from the beginning, when I preached to you, I delivered the mystery of the resurrection, which is established as the first thing belonging to our faith.

“What I also received.” He said that he received it either from the Law, or from the elders [Note: [Col. 1130D] Same place: “from those who came before,”], or from the Lord himself through revelation.

“That Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures.” So that the blessed Apostle might confirm with greater authority what he was preaching—that this was Christ, the Savior of the world—he says: “The one whom Moses and the prophets announced.” Therefore he recalls that he was foretold according to the Scriptures, so that the following might apply: “Like a sheep he is led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he is silent”; and this: “He was handed over because of our iniquities, and by his bruising we have been healed” [Col. 1130A] (Isa. LIII), along with many other things concerning his passion that you will find in the divine Scriptures.

“And that he was buried.” So that the saying of Isaiah might apply: “And he will give the ungodly in exchange for his burial and the rich in exchange for his death.” Likewise, he himself says: “His burial has been taken away from the midst.”

“And that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures.” You have it in Hosea: “He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight” (Hos. VI).

“And that he was seen by Cephas.” That is, by Peter; for Cephas is a Syriac name. He appeared to Peter, as it is written in the Gospel, that he appeared to Simon.

“And afterward by the eleven.” When he entered to them with the doors shut. This is to be understood because not all the appearances are written in the Gospel, but only those sufficient for the faith of the hearers.

“Then he was seen by more than five hundred brethren at once, of whom,” etc. So that greater faith might be placed in the matter, he introduced a multitude of witnesses, many of whom are said to be living and could, if questioned, tell what they had seen; but many others are said already to be sleeping in death.

“Then he was seen by James.” He appeared separately to James the son of Alphaeus. For they report that James himself, the son of Alphaeus, testified at the Lord’s Supper, saying that he would not eat bread until he saw Christ rising from the dead.

“Then by all the apostles.” Many here wish all seventy apostles to be understood—the ones whom the Lord sent out two by two to preach.

“Last of all,” etc. He appeared to him on the road, when light surrounded him; or he says this concerning the temple, so that they would not think he was recounting things heard rather than seen. He calls himself “as one untimely born” because he was dead to the Synagogue and born for the Church, as one untimely born whose life had been despaired of unless he had been forcibly drawn in by the Lord’s grace [Col. 1130C]. He was drawn in by preaching, not by chains. And, though he had been an object of astonishment for the unprecedented nature of his vices, he was perfect in instruction in the Law. Or he was called “untimely born” because the mother, the Synagogue, had borne him badly conceived and imperfect.

“For I am the least of the apostles.” He says this about himself out of humility; otherwise, he was the least in time, not in labor. For elsewhere he says: “I labored more than all of them.”

“Because I am not worthy to be called an apostle,” etc. Explaining why he was not worthy, he says: “Because I persecuted the Church of God.” By his example he teaches us that, even if we make progress in the present, it is better to mourn the past; for it is better to remember sins that have been forgiven than to forget those committed. For it is written: “My son, you have sinned; do not add again to it, but pray concerning your former sins” (Ecclus. XXI).

“But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain.” The grace by which we were redeemed did not seek labor, effort, or merit from me. But daily grace after baptism expects daily service of labor.

## II Corinthians, chapter IX

[Col. 1130D]

“He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly.” That is, whoever gives little to the needy will receive little reward; each person will receive eternal rewards according to works of mercy.

“And he who sows with blessings will also reap from blessings.” As the devotion has been, so will the recompense be. Whoever, with a grateful heart and adequately, supplies either alms from temporal goods or words of preaching to one in need will receive rewards from the Lord adequately and abundantly. For the miser will have no reward for what he gives unwillingly; a blessing becomes eternal for the giver, while almsgiving becomes present for the recipient.

[Col. 1131A]

“Each one as he has determined in his heart, not from sadness or compulsion.” That is, as much as he has decided or chosen to give to the poor—not under constraint but voluntarily. Tobias said to his son: “If you have much, give much; if little, share little with those in need” (Tob. IV).

“For God loves a cheerful giver.” Solomon says: “In every gift, make your face cheerful” (Ecclus. XXXV). Indeed, in the language of the divine Scriptures, the Lord wishes his giver to be cheerful.

“God is able to make every grace abound toward you.” So that those who give alms will not fear want, he sets God’s power before them in the work of mercy. By “every grace” he means either an abundance of grain and an increase of crops and fruits, or an abundance of understanding and insight into wisdom.

“So that, always having sufficiency in all things.” As if he said: The Lord will give you every sufficiency, both spiritual and bodily, so that you may fulfill every good work—with a free mind, whether devotion in mercy or instruction in teaching [Col. 1131B].

“He dispersed; he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever and ever.” That is, he divided and gave to many—not to one but to many—because the prayer of many is greater than that of one. From temporal goods, if they are distributed well, eternal righteousness is acquired.

“He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for eating,” etc. We understand this as spoken of the seed of the word in the holy Gospel, where the Lord, explaining the parable of the seed to his disciples, says: “The seed is the word of God.” As if the Apostle were saying to preachers: God, who gave them the office of teaching, does not withhold food for the body; or: he who grants you the ability to distribute will by no means allow you to hunger.

“And he has multiplied your seed.” That is, he will increase your possessions, or your words: “Give, and it will be given to you,” says the Lord. For whoever, on God’s behalf, gives either the nourishment of the word of preaching or of mercy will receive it multiplied, both here and in the future.

“And he will increase the growth of the fruits of your righteousness.” By “the growth of the fruits of righteousness” he means either material resources or the teaching of words; for Solomon says that the wise person will be satisfied with the fruit of his lips.

## II Corinthians, chapter III

### 7. “We have such confidence through Christ toward God.”

As if he said: That confidence is unconquerable which comes not from us but from Christ, by which grace commends us to God through your faith more than any human letter could do.

“Not that we are sufficient to think anything from ourselves.” That is, we accomplish nothing through our own wisdom or power in the matter of your salvation. For he wishes to show that, in saving the nations, he neither thinks nor does anything through his own judgment or ability, since a few humble, uneducated, and almost rustic men could never have saved the whole world without God’s grace.

He prefaced this because he was about to say that he had undertaken a ministry so much greater than Moses’ as the New Testament is greater than the Law, which, by mysteries shadowing Christ, kept him hidden within itself. He does not say this to claim anything for himself, but so that through his teaching, which is in Christ, he might more easily recall them from the false apostles.

“Who made us competent ministers of the New Testament.” That is, competent to fulfill the apostolic office.

“Not of the letter but of the spirit.” That is, not of the carnal Law but of spiritual precepts.

I was annotating this at Paris, on the Kalends of September, in the year of salvation 1851. Brother J.-B. Pitra, Benedictine monk, from the Abbey of Solesmes.
